Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Composed by Guǒ Xiàng, styled Zǐxuán, from Hénán
As for Zhuāngzǐ,
he may be said to understand the fundamental,
thus he never concealed his unrestrained words,
for his speech, though not conforming, stood alone in response.
When one responds without conformity,
even if correct, it is of no use;
when words do not align with affairs,
even if lofty, they cannot be practiced;
compared to those who remain tranquil and unmoving,
acting only when compelled by necessity,
there is indeed a difference.
This may be said to understand the mind of non-action.
When the mind is free from deliberate action,
it responds according to what it encounters,
its responses fitting the moment,
and words are spoken with utmost caution.
Thus, embodying transformation itself,
it flows through all ages and merges with all things—
how could it ever engage in solitary debates or wander in discussions beyond the mundane world?
This is why, though unorthodox, it stands as the foremost among the Hundred Schools of Thought.
Although Zhuāngzǐ had not fully embodied it,
his words reached the ultimate.
He penetrated the system of heaven and earth,
ordered the nature of all things,
comprehended the changes of life and death,
and illuminated the Way of inner sagehood and outer kingship.
Above, he knew that the Creator has no substance;
below, he understood that things create themselves.
His words are vast and expansive,
his meaning profound and mysterious.
The ultimate of ultimate Ways,
fusing subtlety with elegance;
serenely dismissing attachments,
yet free without arrogance.
Thus it is said, not knowing where righteousness should go,
one acts wildly and recklessly yet treads the great path;
holding food in mouth, one rejoices in tranquility,
with full belly, wandering in primal chaos (1).
Ultimate benevolence reaches the point of no kinship (2),
filial piety and compassion end in universal forgetfulness,
ritual and music return to innate ability,
loyalty and trust emanate from heavenly radiance.
Using this radiance, their simplicity forms naturally,
thus the spiritual vessel transforms alone in the dark and silent realm, with sources and streams deep and long (3).
Thus, where its long waves surge,
and its lofty winds fan,
it flows in harmony with the nature of things,
and suits the people's desires.
It broadens what is narrow,
and loosens what is bound.
Even before the work of cleansing is applied,
the grounds for arrogance and boastfulness dissipate.
Therefore, reading his book,
one transcends and feels as if already aligned,
passing through Kūnlún,
traversing the great void,
and wandering in the halls of the indistinct and elusive.
Even those who are greedy
or restless and hasty individuals,
if they briefly grasp its lingering fragrance,
savor its overflowing streams,
and catch a glimpse or echo of its essence,
will feel expansive enough to forget their forms and embrace a sense of self-contentment,
how much more those who delve into its profound sentiments and relish its enduring years!
Thus, they become ethereal, pure, and far-reaching,
departing from the dust and returning to the profound ultimate.
【Collation】(1) The character "芒" in the Song edition by Imperial Remonstrator Zhào is written as "茫".
(2) The character "仁" has been amended based on the Ancient Yi Series' reprinted Song edition.
(3) "源流深長" in Imperial Remonstrator Zhào's edition is written as "源深流長".
Composed by Táng Dynasty's Master Chéng Xuányīng of Xīhuá.
Zhuāngzǐ is one who
expounds the profound roots of the Way and its Virtue,
narrates the subtle tenets of profound mystery,
elucidates the tranquility of non-action,
illuminates the obscure nature of spontaneous transformation,
bridges the nine schools of thought,
encompasses the hundred philosophers,
truly representing the ultimate teaching within the realm,
and indeed embodying the subtle words beyond the phenomenal world.
His surname is Zhuāng,
given name Zhōu,
courtesy name Zǐxiū,
born in Méng County, Suīyáng, in the state of Sòng,
studied under Master Chángsāng,
and received the title of Immortal Nánhuá.
At the dawn of the Warring States period,
amid the decline of the late Zhōu dynasty,
he lamented the meagerness of mortal fortunes,
grieved over the decay of virtue and the Way,
and thus, stirred with fervent resolve,
composed this discourse.
His words are grand and extensive,
their meaning profound and far-reaching,
beyond the hearing of lesser minds,
how could shallow understanding ever fathom them!
The term "zǐ" (子) mentioned here,
is an honorable title for virtuous individuals,
as the ancients referred to their teachers as "zǐ".
It is also said that "zǐ" denotes a book title,
not only serving as the collective name for three chapters,
but also as a common designation for the Hundred Schools of Thought.
As for the term "nèi piān" (内篇),
"nèi" (inner) is named in contrast to "wài" (outer),
and "piān" (chapter) refers to the compilation of bamboo slips.
In ancient times, bamboo was treated and used as slips,
strung together with leather cords;
assembling these slips formed a "piān",
much like joining papers to form a scroll today.
Hence, Yuán Kǎi stated:
"Major events were recorded on bound bamboo tablets,
while minor matters were written on single slips or boards."
The "nèi" chapters discuss fundamental principles,
while the "wài" chapters narrate events and deeds.
Though events may be evident,
they cannot be understood without principles;
though principles may be profound,
they cannot be manifested without events;
to first elucidate the subtle principles,
the "nèi piān" are thus designated at the beginning.
Since the "nèi piān" contain profound principles,
separate chapter titles were often established beyond the text itself,
and Guō Xiàng accordingly annotated them directly under the titles,
as seen with chapters like "Xiāo Yáo" (Free and Easy Wandering) and "Qí Wù" (The Adjustment of Controversies).
Starting from the "wài piān" onward,
the titles are taken from the first two characters of each chapter,
such as "Pián Mǔ" (Webbed Toes) and "Mǎ Tí" (Horses' Hooves).
Regarding the term "Free and Easy Wandering,"
interpretations have varied throughout the ages.
Now, broadly outlining the main points,
I shall briefly offer three explanations.
These three are as follows:
First,
Gù Tóngbó states:
"Xiao means
to dissolve;
yao means
distance.
Dissolving all burdens of deliberate action,
one perceives from afar the principle of non-action.
To wander thus,
is therefore called 'free and unfettered'."
Second,
Zhī Dàolín said:
"Things are treated as things but not enslaved by things,
thus leisurely, nothing awaits me;
mysterious perception is unhurried yet swift,
hence distantly, there is nothing it cannot accomplish.
Roaming the world in this manner,
thus it is called 'Carefree Wandering'."
Third,
Mù Yèyún:
"The term 'free and unfettered'
refers to the name of one who indulges in madness and attains self-contentment.
With supreme virtue filling the inside,
there is no moment without comfort;
forgetting oneself to respond to things,
there is nowhere one cannot reach!
Wandering the world in this manner,
thus it is called 'free and unfettered wandering'."
The Inner Chapters elucidate the fundamental principles,
the Outer Chapters narrate the events and deeds,
and the Miscellaneous Chapters mix explanations of principles and affairs.
Although the Inner Chapters clarify the fundamental principles,
they do not lack accounts of events;
although the Outer Chapters focus on events and deeds,
they contain profound principles;
however, the division into chapters for teaching purposes
is based primarily on their predominant content.
Therefore, those who establish the beginning of Xiaoyao (Free and Easy Wandering)
refer to masters who have attained the Dao,
with wisdom and virtue bright and keen,
all their actions are fitting,
encountering things with carefree ease,
hence they name things with "Xiaoyao."
The sage who needs no reliance,
reflects opportunities like a mirror,
having understood the dual wisdom of expedience and reality,
thus can greatly harmonize with all realms,
so "Qí Wù" (The Sorting Which Evens Things Out) follows it.
Once pointing out that horses (and hooves) are one with heaven and earth,
blending all things into unity,
the mind becomes tranquil and serene,
enabling the preservation and nurturing of life,
thus "Yǎngshēng Zhǔ" (The Master of Nurturing Life) follows it.
Having forgotten both good and evil,
where realm and wisdom are both sublime,
following changes and accepting transformations,
one can navigate human society,
so "Rénjiān Shì" (The Human World) follows it.
With inner virtue perfected,
one can thus appear disjointed in virtue,
externally engaging with things,
then rising and falling along with them,
inner and outer in deep accord,
thus "Dé Chōng Fú" (The Sign of Virtue Complete) follows it.
Like still water reflecting clearly,
engaging with things without intent,
forgetting virtue and form,
reaching the ultimate in harmonizing outer and inner,
able to shape and perfect all beings,
so "Dà Zōngshī" (The Great and Venerable Teacher) follows it.
The true sages of old,
knowing heaven and knowing humanity,
shared achievements with the creator,
being both tranquil and responsive,
then guiding and driving all beings,
thus "Yìng Dìwáng" (Responding to Emperors and Kings) follows it.
From "Pián Mǔ" (Webbed Toes) onward,
all take the first two characters of the chapter as the title,
with no additional meaning,
and now they are not further sequenced in chapters.
Since ancient times, eminent scholars,
recluses of the Jin and Han dynasties,
have all engaged in studying it,
providing exegetical commentaries;
though their annotations leave no room for criticism,
all containing elegant expressions,
they were capable of probing its hidden meanings.
I, Xuán Yīng, despite my mediocrity and ignorance,
have studied it from a young age,
devoting myself to meticulous research and deep reflection for thirty years.
Following the thirty chapters annotated by Zǐ Xuán,
I have ventured to compile detailed explanations,
totaling thirty volumes.
Although the language and sentiments may be crude and unpolished,
they still reflect the intended direction of my thoughts and endeavors;
I dare not presume to leave this for posterity,
but merely record it to aid my own memory.
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'tí' is erroneously redundant in the Song edition as well,
and is deleted based on the meaning in the chapter "Discussion on Making All Things Equal":
"Heaven and earth are one attribute; the ten thousand things are one horse."
When Master Guō Qìngfàn completed his Collected Annotations on the Zhuāngzǐ,
he presented it to me, Xiānqiān, to read.
That year coincided with the turmoil of the Eastern Barbarians,
and I rose with a sigh, saying:
Did Zhuāngzǐ have no alternative in his heart?
He encountered an age blocked and obstructed,
with no means to save it,
his spirit wandered in the vast emptiness,
verified the boundlessness of the small and the great,
and probed the beginning and end of heaven and earth.
Struck with awe, he thus produced these words.
Zōu Yǎn said:
"What the Confucians call the Central Kingdom
occupies merely one part out of eighty-one in the world.
Beyond the Red County and Divine Province there exist nine other continents,
encircled by minor seas,
with the great ocean surrounding them."
Huì Shī said:
"I know the center of the world lies
north of Yān
and south of Yuè."
Zhuāngzǐ praised them,
also speaking of Shū and Hù boring holes in Hùndùn causing its death,
their theories seeming to foresee the future and deduce its ultimate end,
how extraordinary these remarkable men were!
Zǐgòng made a well-sweep for drawing water,
and the old man of Hànyīn laughed at him.
Today's mechanical devices and contrivances
exceed the well-sweep by ten thousandfold.
If Zhuāngzǐ were to see them,
what would he do?
The clans of Mán and Chù fought over territory on a snail's horn,
leaving tens of thousands of corpses,
and the pursuit of the defeated lasted ten days.
How many of today's Mán and Chù clans exist,
and what would Zhuāngzǐ do about them?
Thus, with Huángdì as sovereign, there still existed Chīyóu;
with Yáo as sovereign, there still were Cóngzhī, Zōng, Kuài, and Xū Áo.
Huángdì and Yáo were not fond of stirring up affairs,
yet they desired to empty their states,
punish their people,
making it evident that they could not govern through emptiness and stillness.
This is certain.
As for that Zhuāngzǐ,
he sought their methods but failed to find them,
and so intended to stand alone in the vast wilderness,
hoping to preserve his body intact and enjoy his life—
how could he possibly extend his reach to the entire world!
Moreover, its texts have once been prominently known in later ages.
During the Jin Dynasty, it evolved into the School of Mysterious Learning,
yet it offered no solution to the turmoil of the Hú and Jié tribes;
in the Tang Dynasty, it was revered as the True Classic,
but it provided no remedy for the calamities of the Ān Lushān and Shǐ Sīmíng rebellions.
It merely served to admonish the extravagance of rulers
and to temper the greed and desires of the common folk in decadent times,
perhaps offering a modest measure of assistance.
And its text is exceptionally marvelous,
Guō Jūn cherishes and admires it ceaselessly,
hence the creation of this compilation with annotations,
supplementing it with literary insights,
enriching it with broad knowledge.
If Zhuāngzǐ were to see it,
would he not say, "This is still but my dregs"?
Even so,
without tracks, how can one trace the footsteps?
Without dregs, how can one observe the ancient beauty!
Guō Jūn, with this book, serves as the heir to the written word,
and shall gather all under heaven as descendants who chant along the Luo River!
In the twentieth year of the Guangxù reign, cyclical year Jiǎwǔ, twelfth month of winter,
Chángshā, your foolish younger brother Wáng Xiānqián respectfully composes.
【Text Explanation】〔"Inner Chapters" (supplemented according to the Tongzhitang edition of Jingdian Shiwen)
〕The term "inner" is established
in contrast to "outer".
Shuowen explains:
"chapter"
means written text.
The character is composed with bamboo radical;
the version with grass radical is merely a plant name,
which is incorrect.
@【Commentary】Although things may differ in size,
when placed in the field of self-fulfillment,
then each thing follows its nature,
each affair matches its capability,
each (［The character "each" appears as "name" in Zhao's advisory edition from Song dynasty.)
fulfills its proper role,
their freedom is one and the same,
how can there be any competition between them!
◎Qìng Fān's case: Liú Yìqìng's Shishuo Xinyu, "Literature" category states:
The "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of Zhuangzi
has always been difficult to understand;
though various renowned scholars have delved into it,
none could surpass the interpretations of Guō Xiàng.
Zhī Dàolín, while at Báimǎ Temple,
conversed with Grand Master Féng,
and the discussion turned to "Free and Easy Wandering".
Zhī remarkably proposed new ideas beyond those two scholars,
establishing different meanings outside what other worthies had said,
all of which were insights the various renowned scholars had failed to grasp,
and later his interpretation came to be adopted.
Liú Xiàobiāo's annotation states:
Xiàng Zǐqī and Guō Zǐxuán's meaning of "Free and Easy Wandering" says:
"When the great peng soars to ninety thousand li,
and the small quail flits from elm to sandalwood,
though their sizes differ,
each follows its nature,
if each fulfills its proper role,
their freedom is one and the same.
However, among the myriad things,
all depend on certain conditions,
only when they obtain what they depend on,
can they then wander freely.
Only the sage can merge with things and follow great changes,
thereby being able to wander constantly without dependencies.
Not only does he achieve freedom himself!
He also enables dependent things not to lose what they depend on,
and by not losing, they become one with great freedom."
Zhī's discourse on "Free and Easy Wandering" says:
"Free and Easy Wandering
illuminates the mind of the ultimate person.
Zhuangzi established words about the great way,
and conveyed his meaning through the peng and quail.
The peng, because its path of life is vast,
thus loses comfort in physical exertion;
the quail, being content with proximity, laughs at distant journeys,
harboring self-satisfaction within its heart.
The ultimate person rides the correctness of heaven and ascends with joy,
wandering boundlessly in carefree freedom.
Mastering things without being mastered by things,
then distantly, nothing constrains me;
mysteriously responsive without acting,
reaching speed without haste,
then freely, there is nowhere不适.
This is what constitutes Free and Easy Wandering.
If having desires and being satisfied with what one has,
content with what satisfies,
joyfully as if in natural innocence,
it is like the hungry being once full,
or the thirsty once quenched,
how could they forget the sacrificial offerings for coarse food,
or abandon wine cups for fine liquor!
If not utterly sufficient,
how could that be Free and Easy Wandering!"
This is what Xiàng and Guō's commentary did not fully express.
@【Text Explanation】［逍］Pronounced xiāo,
also written as 消.
［遙］Pronounced as usual.
Also written as 摇.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The characters 逍遥 are not收录 in Shuowen,
the correct form is 消摇.
The Lǐ Tángōng says "消摇于门",
the Hànshū, biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, says "消摇乎襄羊",
Jīngshān quotes Tài Xuán Xī Shǒu "虽欲消摇",
"天不之兹",
Hàn Kāimǔ Stone Quē says "则文耀以消摇",
Wénxuǎn, Sòng Yù's Jiǔbiàn, says "聊消摇以相羊",
Hòu Hàn, biography of Dōngpíng Xiàn King Cāng, says "消摇相羊",
in all these cases the characters are written with water radical for 消,
and hand radical for 摇.
Táng interpreter Zhànrán's Zhǐguān Fǔxíng Chuán Hóngjué quotes Wáng Màoyè saying:
"消摇"
means the idea of harmony, ease, and comfort.
When the ultimate principle is internally sufficient,
one is always at ease;
settling the mind and responding to things,
there is nowhere one does not penetrate.
Wandering the world in this manner,
hence it is called 消摇.
Also said:
Principle has no hidden depths,
消散ly fitting,
form has no great or small,
摇然ly penetrating,
therefore it is called 消摇.
His explanation of 消摇's meaning
is superior to that of other scholars.
［遊］Pronounced as usual.
Also written as 游.
"Free and Easy Wandering"
is the chapter title,
its meaning derives from being leisurely, unconstrained,
joyful and self-fulfilled.
◎Qìng Fān's case: My father, the Assistant Minister, said:
In the "Under Heaven" chapter, Zhuangzi himself says his way and art are substantial and cannot be stopped,
roaming above with the creator.
The first chapter being called "Free and Easy Wandering"
is Zhuangzi using his boundless words to express himself.
The commentary saying although sizes differ,
freedom is the same,
seems to miss Zhuangzi's intent.
◎Also case: Wénxuǎn, Pān Ānrén's Qiūxìng Fù annotation quotes Sīmǎ Biāo saying:
"Speaking of free and easy non-action enables wandering in the great way."
The explanatory text is missing.
［夫小大］Initial sound marker.
［之场］Zhí pronounced cháng.
［事称］Chēng pronounced chèng.
［各当］Dāng pronounced dàng.
［其分］Fēn pronounced fèn.
(In the Northern Sea there is a fish,
its name is Kūn.
The size of the Kūn,
no one knows how many thousand lǐ it spans.)
【Commentary】Míng,
means the sea,
taking its vast and boundless expanse,
hence (wéi) [wèi] = wéi and wèi were often used interchangeably in ancient times,
now distinguished by meaning.
Not repeated hereafter.
= zhī míng.
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shí Zhōu Jì states:
The Míng Sea has towering waves a hundred zhàng high even without wind.
Within the immense sea,
there exists this giant fish,
to illustrate that the nature of things is spontaneous,
thus it is highlighted at the beginning of the chapter.
Xuán Zhōng Jì states:
In the east, there is a giant fish,
travelers spend one day passing its head,
seven days passing its tail;
when it gives birth for three days,
the blue sea turns red because of it.
Hence, it is known that great beings are born in great places,
not solely in the Northern Sea.
@【Glossary】《Běi Míng》also written as míng in some versions,
pronounced mì jīng fǎn,
meaning the Northern Sea.
Jī Kāng said:
it takes its vast and boundless expanse.
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì stated:
profound and limitless,
thus called míng.
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shí Zhōu Jì states:
water that is black is called the Míng Sea,
with towering waves a hundred zhàng high without wind.
◎Qìng Fān's case: Huì Lín's Yīqièjīng Yīnyì vol. 31, Dàshèng Rù Léngqié Jīng vol. 2, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Míng,
refers to the North and South Poles.
Far from the sun and moon,
hence named míng.
Glossary omitted.
《Kūn》Xú pronounces as kūn,
Lǐ gives hóu wēn fǎn.
Name of a large fish.
Cuī Zhuàn said:
Kūn should be jīng (whale),
Jiǎnwén agreed.
◎Qìng Fān's case: Fāng Yǐzhì said:
Kūn originally meant small fish or fry,
Zhuāngzǐ used it to mean a giant fish.
His explanation is correct.
Ěryǎ Shì Yú:
Kūn,
fish roe.
All fish offspring are called kūn,
Lǔyǔ "yú jìn kūn ér",
Wéi Zhāo's note:
Kūn,
fish roe.
Zhāng Héng's (Dōng) [Xī] = corrected according to Wénxuǎn.
= Jīng Fù "jiū kūn ér",
Xuē Zōng's note:
Kūn,
fish roe.
Shuōwén does not have the character kūn.
Duàn Yùcái said:
Unborn fish eggs are called kūn.
Kūn is the same as the character for egg (luǎn),
Xǔ Shèn wrote it as ●,
ancient pronunciation read like guān,
also read like kūn.
Lǐ Nèi Zé "rú yú luǎn jiàng",
Zhèng read luǎn as kūn.
All that are not yet hatched are called eggs,
those already hatched are called offspring.
Kūn means fish eggs,
thus Shūzhòng included it with the character ●.
Zhuāngzǐ referred to an extremely large fish as Kūn,
this is a parable of the equality of things,
what is called unrestrained and free to suit oneself.
Glossary quotes Lǐ Yí saying Kūn,
is the name of a large fish,
Cuī Zhuàn and Jiǎnwén both said Kūn should be jīng (whale),
all are mistaken.
《qí jǐ》pronounced jū qǐ fǎn.
Same below.
(It transforms into a bird,
named Péng.)
【Note】The reality of Péng and Kūn,
I have not examined in detail.
The main idea of Zhuāngzǐ,
lies in wandering freely and unrestrained,
acting through non-action and attaining self-contentment,
thus he explores the extremes of small and large to illuminate the suitability of inherent nature.
For the broad-minded scholar,
it is appropriate to grasp the convergence and overlook the寄托,
not necessary to elaborate on every detail with forced explanations.
As long as it does not harm the grand intent,
all can be briefly passed over.
@【Commentary】The four seasons race like the wind,
the three lights roll up like lightning,
hence carrying mountains and leaving the old behind,
lifting boat-like valleys to rush towards the new.
Thus, transforming a fish into a bird,
aims to clarify the great principle of transformation.
@【Textual Analysis】"Péng" is pronounced as bù dēng fǎn.
Xú gives the sound as péng.
Guō gives it as fǔ dēng fǎn.
Cuī pronounces it as fèng,
saying:
Péng is the ancient character for fèng (phoenix),
not the fènghuáng that comes in auspicious times.
Shuōwén explains:
péng and Péng,
are both ancient forms of the character fèng.
The character péng resembles the shape of a bird.
When the phoenix flies,
flocks of birds follow in tens of thousands,
hence péng is used to mean faction or clique.
Zìlín states:
Péng,
means a clique,
anciently used as the character for phoenix.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
"yǐ péng" was originally written as "yǐ Péng",
now, considering the context, it is corrected.
◎Qìng Fān's case: Guǎngchuān Shūbá Bǎohé Zhōng Míng, Tōngyǎ 45 both quote Sīmǎ as saying:
Péng is the phoenix.
This is missing in the Textual Analysis.
"Fū Zhuāng" is pronounced as fú.
All sentence beginnings are the same.
"Xìng fèn" is pronounced as fú wèn fǎn.
The following are all the same.
"Dá guān" is pronounced as gǔ luàn fǎn.
"Yí yào" is pronounced as yī yáo fǎn.
(The back of the Peng bird,
no one knows how many thousand miles it spans;
when it rouses itself to fly,
its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky.)
【Commentary】The fish is discussed in terms of its size,
to show that its head and tail are difficult to comprehend;
the bird is described by its back,
also indicating that its length is unfathomable.
Hence, the text below states that none have known its full extent.
It beats its angry wings,
vigorously shaking its feathered plumage,
intending to soar on the wind,
and about to strike the water.
Then it cuts through the clouds and mists,
bearing the blue sky on its back,
soaring and gliding,
reaching and brushing against the heavens,
casting its shadow and spreading shade,
as if the clouds at the edge of the sky were descending in procession.
@【Explanation】"Clouds hanging from the sky": Sīmǎ Biāo says:
Like clouds suspended at the sky's edge.
Cuī states:
"Hanging,"
meaning the border,
its size is like one side of the sky's clouds.
(This bird,
when the ocean moves, will migrate to the Southern Darkness.
The Southern Darkness
is the Lake of Heaven.)
【Annotation】Only the vast sea can carry its body,
only ninety thousand li can support its wings.
Is this due to some peculiar preference?
It is simply that a great entity must be born in a great place,
and a great place must naturally give rise to such a great entity.
This principle is inherent in nature,
with no fear of loss,
so why should one trouble their mind about it?
@【Commentary】Yùn means "to move."
Shì indicates reference,
pointing to this roc bird.
Its form is massive and heavy;
if it does not move within the ocean,
it cannot elevate itself.
All this is inevitable,
not a matter of preference.
Moreover, as the form transforms,
the essence follows suit.
In the past, it was a fish,
swimming in the Northern Sea;
now it becomes a bird,
soaring to the Southern Darkness.
Although rising and sinking differ in nature,
the freedom remains the same.
Similarly, life and death, gathering and parting,
are met with acceptance;
through countless changes,
the self remains intact.
The transformation from fish to bird,
moving from north to south,
symbolizes the bird as a creature of the skies
and the south as the direction of enlightenment;
the fish represents a submerged being,
and the north the realm of darkness.
This illustrates turning toward light and away from darkness,
abandoning stagnation for progress,
using the north-south and fish-bird imagery to show the path of the Way.
The great oceans and vast rivers,
originating from creation,
are not made by humans,
hence called the Lake of Heaven.

Yùn means "to migrate."

Yùn means "to travel."

The movement of heaven is like a wheel hub,
meaning heaven travels ceaselessly.
This "yùn" should also be interpreted as traveling.
Zhuangzi says the roc travels unceasingly over the sea,
then migrates to the Lake of Heaven to rest.

Xǐ means "to shift."
Duàn's note:
Moving intermittently but ultimately stopping,
then shifting its place.)
The following text quoting Qíxié's words about resting in June can corroborate this.

and the explanations by Sīmǎ and Xiàng Xiù cited in the textual analysis,
are all incorrect.

(Qí Xié is one who records anomalies.
The words of Xié say:
"When the Péng bird migrates to the Southern Ocean,
it strikes the water for three thousand lǐ,
then spirals upward on the whirlwind for ninety thousand lǐ.")
【Commentary】With wings so large, it is difficult to lift off;
thus it must spiral on the whirlwind before it can ascend.
Only after ninety thousand lǐ is it fully self-supporting.
Having such wings,
how could it possibly leap up abruptly
and descend after just a few fathoms?
All this is unavoidable,
not done by choice.
@【Subcommentary】The surname is Qí,
the given name Xié—this is a person's name.
It is also said to be a book title,
meaning there was a book of jests in the state of Qí.
"Zhì" means to record.
"Jī" means to strike.
"Tuán" means to struggle;
"fúyáo" means a whirlwind.
The book authored by Qí Xié
largely records strange and anomalous events.
Zhuāngzǐ quotes it as evidence
to show that his own account is not unfounded.
Since the great Péng is bound for the Southern Sea,
it cannot take off abruptly;
therefore, it lifts and strikes both wings,
stirring the water for three thousand lǐ,
staggering forward,
before it can leave the water.
Then it twists and turns,
heaving with anger and circling about,
supported by the wind and air,
swaying as it rises.
Its journey spans ninety thousand lǐ,
taking half a year in time;
only when composed and fully resolved
does it speak of resting.
It merely goes as far as sufficient—
how could it be acting out of personal sentiment?

@【Commentary】The Ěryǎ states:
Outside the city walls is the suburbs,
beyond the suburbs is the pasturelands,
and beyond the pasturelands is the wild.
This speaks of the time of spring,
when the yang energy stirs,
and from afar, the marshes and lakes
appear like galloping horses,
hence they are called "wild horses."
Stirred-up soil is called "dust,"
and the finer particles are called "grime."
Between heaven and earth,
the exhalations of living things blow upon one another to lift the Roc.
The myriad beings are diverse and jumbled,
all things are varied and uneven,
their forms and natures differ,
and what they depend on varies appropriately.
Thus, the Roc beats its sky-shading wings,
riding on the wind to roam freely;
the cicada spreads its swiftly rising wings,
darting among elms and sandalwoods in contentment.
These all act according to their nature,
endowed by the creator,
without intent toward distance or nearness,
how could they harbor thoughts of pride or conceit!
Those who embody this principle—
why speak to them of boasting or striving!

Is the azure of the sky
its true color?
Or is it because it is so far away and has no limits?
When it looks down from above,
it is
just like

@【Comment】Now observing the azure of the sky,
we ultimately do not know whether it is the true color of the sky,
or if the sky is so distant that it has no limits.
When the Péng looks down from above at the earth,
it is just like a person looking up from the
earth at the sky.
Then it stops and heads south,
meaning the Péng does not know the distance of the journey,
but its vigor is sufficient to sustain itself and go forth.
@【Subcommentary】Looking up at the vault of heaven,
it is extremely remote;
the blue sky is high and far,
beyond all calculation;
the vast and hazy azure—
how could it be the true color of the sky!
Yet the Péng dwells in the mid-heavens,
while humans reside on the earth below;
when the Péng looks down,
it is no different from humans looking up.
Since humans cannot discern the true color of the sky,
how could the Péng know the distance of the earth!
Relying on its own strength to suffice,
it proceeds to the Southern Sea;
the Péng's planning and estimation
end here.

(If the accumulation of water is not deep,
then it lacks the strength to bear large boats.
Pour a cup of water into a depression in the hall,
and a mustard seed can serve as a boat;
but place a cup there and it will stick,
for the water is shallow and the boat is large【一】.)
【Note】This all clarifies why the Péng soars high:
it is because its wings are large.
For small entities, the resources needed are not large,
while for large entities, what is used cannot be small.
Thus, principles have their utmost distinctions,
things have their fixed limits,
each sufficient to match their circumstances,
their success is one and the same.
If one loses the essence of forgetting life
and strives for existence beyond what is most appropriate,
tasks not undertaken according to one's strength,
actions not in accordance with one's nature,
then even wings that span the sky cannot be without limit,
and sudden flights cannot be without hardship.
@【Commentary】"Qiě" is borrowed,
a tentative and brief expression.
"Fú" initiates,
at the beginning of speech.
"Jī" means to gather.
"Hòu" means deep.
"Bēi" is a small vessel.
"Ào" is a muddy depression,
referring to sunken areas in the hall or courtyard.
"Jiè" is grass.
"Jiāo" means to stick.
This is the start of an analogy.
If one overturns a cup of water in a muddy depression in the hall,
using a grass blade as a boat,
it will float without hindrance;
but if using the cup as a boat instead,
it is certainly impossible.
Why?
Because the water is shallow and the boat large,
causing it to stick to the ground and not move.
Thus, a large boat requires deep water,
while a small mustard seed does not need a vast flow.
If each fits its size appropriately,
then all things can be free and unbound.

(When the accumulation of wind is not thick,
it lacks the strength to bear large wings.
Therefore, at ninety thousand li,
the wind lies beneath them.)
【Explanation】This is a combined analogy.
If water is not deep and abundant,
it cannot float a large boat;
if the wind is not lofty and strong,
large wings have no means to soar to the heavens.
Thus,
small birds in half a morning
dart up to the elm and sandalwood trees;
while the great roc at ninety thousand li
has the swirling wind billowing beneath it.
(Only then does it ride the wind;
bearing the blue sky on its back with nothing to obstruct it,
only then does it set its course southward.
【Comment】The reason it now sets its course southward
is not due to a fondness for heights or admiration for distant places,
but because without accumulated wind, obstruction and blockage would prevent its passage.
This is the carefree wandering of the great Péng.

it could thus ascend;
with layered accumulation of wind blowing,
only then could it fly.

riding the wind's spine below,
once soaring to the heavens,
it journeys for six months before resting.
Nets cannot reach it,
arrows cannot harm it,
the calamities of breaking and blocking
— how could they befall it!
Truly, by matching conditions appropriately,
it naturally attains its place,
wandering carefree to the southern sea —
is this not fitting indeed!

their bellies still full;
those going a hundred li away

those going a thousand li away

then even the great Peng cannot consider itself nobler than the small bird,
nor does the small bird envy the Celestial Pond,
and thus their glory and contentment are abundant.

their freedom and ease are one.

relying on wind and water to soar high,
thus mock its large form and toilsome labor,
and delight in their own small substance and ease.
Moreover, leaping no more than a few ren high,
they dart among elm and sandalwood to perch;
when tired, without reaching the distant woods,
they land to rest and rise again,
free and content in their nature,
finding joy within.
Why must one spend six months,
traverse ninety thousand li,
endure the toil of journeying,
heading south for what purpose?
Those who laugh at the great from a small perspective,
boasting and striving yet ceasing to be free,
such a thing has never existed.

Small knowledge cannot comprehend great knowledge,
the short-lived cannot comprehend the long-lived.
How do we know this is so?
The morning mushroom knows nothing of the lunar cycle,
the summer cicada knows nothing of spring and autumn—
these are examples of short lifespans.
In the south of Chǔ there is the Mínglíng tree,
for which five hundred years count as one spring,
and five hundred years as one autumn;
in high antiquity there was the great Dàchūn tree,
for which eight thousand years counted as one spring,
and eight thousand years as one autumn.
Yet Péng Zǔ is nowadays uniquely famous for his longevity—
when common people compare themselves to him,
is it not pitiable!
【一】【注】All things have their own nature,
and each nature has its limit.
All are as their years and knowledge,
how could this be reached by straining and admiring!
From here down to Lièzǐ,
it successively lists the greatness and smallness of years and knowledge,
each trusting in its own aspect,
none being sufficient to surpass the others.
Then it unifies them with the person who has no dependence,
discarding that and forgetting self,
obscuring these various differences,
different aspects attain the same gain and I have no merit or fame.
Therefore, to unify small and great,
is to have no small and no great;
if there is indeed small and great,
then although the great péng and the quail,
the official and the rider of the wind,
are equally burdened things.
To equalize death and life,
is to have no death and no life;
if there is indeed death and life,
then although the great chūn and the cicada,
Péngzǔ and the morning mushroom,
are equal in being short-lived.
Thus, to wander in having no small and no great,
is to be boundless;
to be obscure in neither dying nor being born,
is to be limitless.
If one is carefree but tied to having a direction,
then although released to wander, there will be limits,
not yet able to have no dependence.

【Four】【Commentary】When the disparity in years and wisdom is as vast as this,
compared to what the multitude grieves over,
it can indeed be sorrowful.
Yet the multitude never grieves over this,
because each nature has its limits.
If one understands these limits,
then even a hair's breadth cannot be outstripped,
so what in the world is there to grieve about?
Things never desire the small from the perspective of the great,
yet the small inevitably envy the great.
Therefore, the distinctions between small and great each have their fixed roles,
beyond the reach of envy or desire.
Then the burden of envy and desire can be eliminated.
For grief arises from burdens,
and when burdens cease, grief departs.
If grief departs and one's life and nature are not at peace,
such a thing has never existed.
【五】【疏】Péng Zǔ,
surnamed Jiǎn,
named Kēng,
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū.
He excelled at nurturing his nature,
could harmonize the cauldron,
presented pheasant soup to Yáo,
and Yáo enfeoffed him at Péngchéng.
His Way could be taken as ancestral,
hence he was called Péng Zǔ.
Passing through the Xià and Shāng dynasties to the Zhōu,
his age reached eight hundred years.
"Tè" means unique.
It signifies singularity.
Because of his long life and longevity,
his reputation alone was known in the world.
Yet people of the world compare themselves to Péng Zǔ,
which is deeply lamentable;
those who do not grieve
do so because Péng Zǔ possessed a nature of remote longevity,
not of the same vital class as themselves,
placing it beyond words,
not daring to sigh in sorrow.
Thus, we know that life has its limits;
how could it be that only Péng Zǔ is unattainable by even a hair's breadth?
Thereupon, we equalize the great tree and the fungus,
blend Péng's longevity with early death,
each resting in their own lot, and life's nature finds peace.

@【疏】Tāng was a descendant of Emperor Kù,
and a descendant of Xiè,
with the surname Zǐ,
given name Lǚ,
and courtesy name Tiānyǐ.
His mother, Fú Dū,
saw a white vapor piercing through the moon,
and conceived Tāng through divine influence.
He had a broad lower face and a pointed upper face,
and was nine feet tall.
He served as a feudal lord under the Xià dynasty,
possessing sage-like virtue,
and the feudal lords rallied to him.
Encountering the tyranny of Jié,
he was imprisoned at Xiàtái.
Later, he was freed,
and formed an alliance with the feudal lords at Jǐngbó,
met Jié at the ruins of Kūnwú,
and fought a great battle in the wilderness of Míngtiáo,
after which Jié fled to Náncháo.
After Tāng defeated Jié,
he offered the empire to Wù Guāng,
but Wù Guāng declined.
Tāng then ascended the throne,
establishing his capital at Bó,
which was later renamed Shāng,
making him the founding ruler of the Yīn dynasty.

a worthy man during Tāng's time,
also said to be a scholar under Tāng.

Tāng regarded him as a teacher,
so Tāng inquired of Jí,
seeking the ultimate Way,
stating that the natures of things differ,
each having its inherent disposition,
and by following them directly,
one should act accordingly.
Yīn Tāng sought further understanding,
delving into profound mysteries,
and Zhuāngzǐ approved of his inquiry,
hence deeming it correct.

reaching its zenith by fulfilling itself completely.
Previously mentioned, the two creatures have different wings,
hence their destinations vary;
one soars to the celestial pond,
the other spends its life among elms and sandalwoods,
each simply satisfying its form adequately,
unaware of the reasons behind it.
Now speaking of the distinction between small and large,
each possesses its innate essence,
which is beyond the reach of forced admiration,
and each rests content in its natural disposition,
without lamenting their differences,
hence it is reiterated.
@【Exegesis】"Qiě,"
means "about to,"

"Chì,"

"Yàn,"

"Áoxiáng,"
means frolicking or playing.
The yàn sparrow, a small bird,
roams freely in the marsh,
leaping and bounding with ease,
finding contentment within the brushwood and weeds,
thus it scoffs at the distant journey of ninety thousand li,
and delights in flying just a few rèn high.
This illustrates the inherent differences between small and large natures,
discussing how each finds sufficiency without duality.

The same below.

a small marsh.

[the character],

【Collation】(1) Tàishān,
the Zhào Jiànyì edition reads as "dàshān",
the Shìdétáng edition reads as "Tàishān".
(2) The character "yóu" is amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Thus, those whose knowledge qualifies them for a post,
whose conduct suits one locality,
whose virtue pleases one ruler,
and whose ability gains trust in one state,
regard themselves in just such a manner.
Yet Sòng Róngzǐ would laugh at them.
Moreover, if the whole world praised him, he would not be encouraged;
if the whole world condemned him, he would not be discouraged.
He fixed the distinction between inner and outer,
and discerned the boundary between honor and disgrace.
That was all.
Nevertheless, there was still something he had not established.
Now, Lièzǐ rode on the wind and traveled about,
cool and skillful,
returning only after fifteen days.
In his pursuit of happiness,
he did not strive anxiously.
Though he avoided walking,
he still had something to depend on.
But if one rides the true course of heaven and earth,
and masters the changes of the six vital energies,
to wander in the infinite,
what would he have to depend on?
Therefore, it is said:
"The perfect person has no self;
the spiritual person has no merit;
the sage has no fame."
【One】【Annotation】It is like a bird finding contentment in its own corner.
@【Explanation】Hence, this follows from previous discourse,
while "fú" serves as a transitional phrase for what follows.
"State" refers to the domain of the five noble ranks,
and "district" denotes twelve thousand five hundred households.
Some possess wisdom and strategic acumen,
qualifying them to hold an official post;
some have established reputations and renown,
enabling them to unite their local communities;
some embody profound virtue and broad learning,
making them fit to rule as sovereigns,
govern states effectively,
and bring peace and nurture to the common people.
These three types,
endowed with differing innate capacities,
exhibit varying levels of excellence and deficiency,
yet in their respective sufficiencies,
they are inherently equal.
Each, recognizing their own abilities,
is like a bird finding contentment in its own corner.
@【Glossary】"Zhì xiào" [知效] is read with "zhì" meaning wisdom.
The following "hù" is pronounced with a falling tone.
"Xíng" [行] is read with a low falling tone.
"Bǐ" [比] is pronounced pízhì,
while Xú reads it as fúzhì.
Lǐ notes:
It means to unite.
"Ér zhēng" [而徵] is read with its standard pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means trustworthiness.
Cuī and Zhī state:
It means to accomplish.
◎Qìng Fān's analysis: Regarding "ér zhēng yī guó" [而徵一國],
the Glossary and Guō's annotation lack explanation,
and Chéng's interpretation reads "ér" as a transitional word,
which is incorrect.
The character "ér" should be read as "néng" (ability),
as "néng" and "ér" were phonetically close and interchangeable in ancient usage.
"Official," "district," "ruler," and "state" form parallel pairs,
just as "wisdom," "benevolence," "virtue," and "ability" do,
making it clear that "ér" is not a transitional word.
In Huáinánzǐ's "Yuándào" chapter, "ér yǐ shǎo zhèng duō,"
Gāo's annotation states:
"Ér,"
means "néng."
Annotations in Lǚshì Chūnqiū's "Qù Sī" and "Bù Qū" chapters all say:
"Ér,"
means "néng."
In Mòzǐ's "Shàngtóng" chapter:
"Thus, the ancient sage kings, with their ability, carefully established uniformity to appoint righteous leaders."
Also:
"Why is the world governed?"
"Only because they used their ability to enforce uniformity in principles in governance."
In the "Fēi Mìng" chapter:
"They did not use their ability to correct the desires of their ears and eyes."
In Chǔcí's "Jiǔ Zhāng":
"Who in the world could know it?"
In the Qí Cè:
"Who among you can join me in going to the feudal lords?"
In all these, "ér" is used interchangeably with "néng."
In Yáo Diǎn, "róu yuǎn néng ěr,"
the Hàn Dūyóu Bān inscription writes it as "ér ěr."
In Gāo Yáo Mó's "néng zhé ér huì,"
the Wèi Wèi Héng Fāng inscription writes it as "néng zhé néng huì,"
and the Shǐjì's Xià Běn Jì writes it as "néng zhì néng huì."
The Lǐ Yùn Zhèngyì states:
"Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn writes 'néng' as 'ér' throughout."
These are examples of this usage.
【二】【注】Not yet equalized,
hence there is laughter.
@【疏】"Zǐ" is an honorific for one with virtue,
whose surname is Róng,
a person of the state of Sòng.
"Yóurán" means
"like this."
Although Master Róng could forget existence,
he had not yet dispelled non-existence,
hence the laughter.
Those who serve as officials
cling to ranks and emoluments,
while those of empty tranquility
still harbor mockery;
seeing this is why they are not equalized.
Previously, using the small to laugh at the great
showed that the great do not boast;
now using the great to laugh at the small
shows the small do not aspire;
yet those whose nature and destiny are not at peace
have not yet heard of the principle.
@【釋文】"Sòng Róngzǐ": Sīmǎ and Lǐ say:
A person of the state of Sòng.
Cuī says:
A worthy person.
"Yóurán xiào zhī": Cuī and Lǐ say:
"Yóu"
means the appearance of laughter.
The case implies considering it as laughter.
【三】【注】Truly self-content.
means all.
"Quàn,"
means to encourage and urge.
"Jǔ,"
means resentment and dejection.
Róngzǐ followed his nature and embraced the Way,
aloof and transcending the mundane,
even if the whole world praised and lauded him,
it would not increase his encouragement,
and if all under heaven criticized and disparaged him,
it would not add to his dejection,
truly self-content.
@【釋文】《譽之》 pronounced as "yú."
《加沮》 pronounced as "cí lǚ" in reverse,
means to defeat.
【Four】【Annotation】Regard the self as internal and things as external.
@【Commentary】Róngzǐ knew that internally it is not the self,
and externally it is not things either,
dismissing both internal and external,
forgetting both things and the self,
thus the distinction between internal and external is settled without error.
【Five】【Annotation】Glorifying oneself and humiliating others.
@【Exegesis】Forgetting encouragement and discouragement in praise and blame,
blending hardship and success with glory and disgrace,
thus able to reflect clarity in the mind and wisdom,
discerning the realm of things with profound insight,
no longer internalizing self and externalizing objects,
glorifying oneself and humiliating others.
@【Textual Notes】"Zhi jìng" is pronounced with jǐng as in jū lǐng fǎn.

【Six】【Comment】Cannot surpass this again.
@【Explanation】This,
refers to this.
Cease,

Róng Zǐ's wisdom and virtue are fully contained herein.

【七】【注】Content with oneself,
thus at ease in the world.

acting directly according to principle,
never employing cunning to seek,

Dwelling beyond worldly affairs,
he was therefore not one who acted anxiously.

Same below.

【Eight】【Comment】Only capable of considering oneself correct,
yet unable to be without any limitations.

means to establish.
Róngzǐ abandoned the existence to prove non-existence,

shù,

【Nine】【Annotation】Língrán,
describes a state of lightness and subtlety.
@【Exegesis】His surname was Liè,
given name Yùkòu,
a native of Zhèng.
He was a contemporary of Duke Xū of Zhèng,
studied under Húqiūzǐ Lín,
and authored eight volumes of texts.
He attained the Way of the Wind Immortal,
riding the wind to travel,
ethereally and lightly ascending,
hence praised for his excellence.
@【Interpretive Text】The "Lièzǐ" by Lǐ Yún states:
a man of Zhèng,
named Yùkòu,

traveling by riding the wind,

《Líng》pronounced as líng.

Lièzǐ,

The interpretive text is missing.
【一０】【Note】If there is something to wait for,
then even riding the wind to travel,
cannot encompass everything in a single moment.
@【Explanation】Xún,
means ten days.
Having attained the state of a wind immortal,
roaming across the world,
every fifteen days, one returns home,
yet unable to ride on everything without exception,
thus it is impossible to encompass all in one moment.
【一一】【注】It is by nature that he rides the wind,
not by earnestly seeking it.
@【疏】致 means
to obtain.
That Liè Yùkòu attained the blessing of riding the wind
was due to his indifference to heat and cold,
his open-mindedness and acceptance of fate,
unrelated to deliberate choices or rejections,
or fervent pursuit.
To clarify the essence of cultivating the Dào,
the key lies in forgetting the mind;
if one employs intellectual calculations,
they drift far from it.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
"Not earnestly striving,"
is akin to what the Lǐjì describes as "in all under heaven, only one person."
Attaining blessings
refers to fully realizing natural harmony.
Riding the wind and traveling
still awaits the movement of natural instinct.
Guō Xiàng stated,
"It is by nature that he rides the wind,
not by earnestly seeking it,"
which is mistaken.
【一二】【注】Without wind, one cannot travel;
this necessarily entails dependence.
Only that which rides upon everything is free from dependence.
@【疏】Riding the wind to ascend lightly,
though spared from walking,
without wind, one does not advance,
thus still requiring reliance.
From officials below to Sòng Róng and Liè Yùkòu,
varying in wisdom and virtue, superior or inferior,
since they have not yet fully forgotten distinctions,
all fall into the category of dependence.
Only by following the nature of all things,
wandering the path of transformation,
and achieving the ability to ride upon anything,
can one fully realize the sublime essence of carefree wandering.
【13】【Commentary】Heaven and Earth are
the collective name for all things.
Heaven and Earth take all things as their substance,
and all things must take spontaneity as their norm.
Spontaneity is
that which acts not yet occurs naturally.
Thus, the great Péng bird's ability to soar high,
the quail's ability to stay low,
the great chūn tree's ability to live long,
the morning mushroom's ability to live briefly—
all these are what spontaneity can achieve,
not what deliberate action can achieve.
Acting not yet occurring naturally,
this is why it is considered the norm.
Therefore, one who rides the norm of Heaven and Earth
is thereby following the nature of all things;
one who masters the transformations of the six qì
is thereby roaming the path of change;
proceeding in this manner,
how could any journey have an end!
Whatever is encountered is ridden,
so what more would one depend on!
This is the carefree wandering of the person of utmost virtue, who mysteriously unites self and other.
If there is dependence,
then even Lièzǐ's lightness and subtlety
still could not travel without wind.
Thus, one must obtain what one depends on,
and only then can one wander carefree.
How much more so for the great Péng bird!
Only one who merges with things and follows the great transformations
can be constantly free without dependence.
How could this be limited to merely freeing oneself!
Moreover, they also accommodate those who have dependence,
enabling them not to lose what they depend on.
If what is depended on is not lost,
then they become one with the great freedom.
Thus, between having dependence and having no dependence,
I cannot claim they are equal;
but as for each resting in its own nature,
the heavenly mechanism operating spontaneously,
receiving without conscious knowledge—
here I cannot distinguish them as different.
If even having no dependence is not enough to distinguish one from having dependence,
how much less so the size or minuteness among those who have dependence!
@【Subcommentary】Heaven and Earth are
the collective name for all things.
All things are
different designations for spontaneity.
The six qì:
Lǐ Yí says:
dawn's morning clouds,
noon's bright sun,
sunset's flying spring,
midnight's hàngxiè,
plus Heaven's and Earth's two qì make the six qì.
Also, Dù Yù says:
The six qì are
yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Also, Zhī Dàolín says:
The six qì are
Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons.
"Biàn" means
change.
"Wū hū" means
"on what" or "upon what."
It means the sage who has no dependence,
with an empty mind embodying the Dào,
thus can ride the correct principle of the two modalities (Heaven and Earth),
follow the spontaneity of all things,
master the six qì to wander carefree,
and blend with all beings to transform.
If there is nothing that is not followed,
then what journey would not be free!
Illuminated and penetrating to the infinite,
upon what would one still depend!
@【Textual Explanations】"The six qì": Sīmǎ [Zhēng] says:
Yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Lǐ [Yí] says:
Dawn is morning clouds,
midday is bright sun,
sunset is flying spring,
midnight is hàngxiè,
Heaven's mysterious (black) and Earth's yellow [qì] make the six qì.
Wáng Yì, annotating the Chǔ Cí, says:
The Língyáng Zǐ Míng Jīng states:
In spring, eat morning clouds;
morning clouds are
the yellow qì when the sun is about to rise.
In autumn, eat setting darkness;
setting darkness is
the red-yellow qì after the sun has set.
In winter, eat hàngxiè;
hàngxiè is
the qì of the north at midnight.
In summer, eat bright sun;
bright sun is
the qì of the south at midday.
Together with Heaven's mysterious and Earth's yellow qì,
these are the six qì.
Hàng,
pronunciation hù dǎng fǎn.
Xiè,
pronunciation xià jiè fǎn.
Zhī [Dàolín] says:
The qì of Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons.
◎Qìng Fán's case: The Textual Explanations cites various masters' interpretations of the six qì,
each differing.
Sīmǎ takes yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, (míng) [light] as the six qì;
this theory is the most ancient.
Lǐ [Yí] takes dawn, midday, sunset, midnight plus Heaven's mysterious and Earth's yellow as the six qì;
this seems rather forced.
Wáng Yì and Zhī Dàolín take Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons as the six qì.
Now, the qì of Heaven and Earth,
its greatness is beyond compare,
the four seasons all receive the qì of Heaven and Earth to be their qì;
it seems improper to list the four seasons alongside Heaven and Earth to make six.
Wáng Yìnglín says:
The six qì are
lesser yīn sovereign fire,
greater yīn damp earth,
lesser yáng minister fire,
yángmíng dry metal,
greater yáng cold water,
and juéyīn wind wood,
with fire uniquely having two.
Heaven takes six as its node,
so qì takes six periods to complete one cycle.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn recounts Yī Hé's words:
Heaven has six qì,
(the note says:
Yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, (míng) [light].
) which descend to produce the five flavors.
This matches the numbers five and six in the Sù Wèn.
(Quán Zǔwàng says:
Heaven five Earth (five) [six] (four),
appears in the Great Yì (Yìjīng);
Heaven six Earth five,
appears in the Guóyǔ.
[Thus, (five) the Hàn Shū states,
five and six are the central union of Heaven and Earth.
However, the Zuǒ Zhuàn's theory
also differs from the Sù Wèn.
) Shěn Kuò's Bǐ Tán:
The six qì:
medical experts match them with the six spirits.
The so-called Qīnglóng (Azure Dragon)
is the qì of the east, juéyīn;
other symbolic correspondences are all like this.
Only the north has two:
called Xuánwǔ (Dark Warrior),
the qì of greater yáng cold water;
and Téngshé (Flying Snake),
the qì of lesser yáng minister fire.
In humans, this corresponds to the kidneys;
the kidneys are two:
left is greater yáng cold water,
right is lesser yáng minister fire—
this is the intersection of Kǎn and Lí.
The central (tàiyáng) [tàiyīn] earth corresponds to Gōuchén (Hook Array),
matching the spleen.
Theories on the six qì
are numerous and contentious, tangled and confused,
with no consensus reached.
In my humble opinion, there are two theories worth noting:
First,
the six qì in the Hóng Fàn are rain, sunshine, heat, cold, wind, and timeliness.
Rain
corresponds to wood;
sunshine,
to metal;
heat,
to fire;
cold,
to water;
wind,
to earth;
these are the five qì.
When the five qì are timely,
they represent the harmonious qì of the five phases;
combining them makes the six qì.
Qì can be harmonious or discordant;
discordance leads to change,
and change should be mastered;
hence it is said, "master the changes of the six qì."
Second,
the six qì are the six emotions.
The Hàn Shū, Yì Fèng zhuàn, quotes Fèng's teacher on the six emotions:
The emotion of the north
is fondness (hào);
fondness manifests as greed and wolfishness;
Shēn and Zǐ govern it.
The emotion of the east
is anger;
anger manifests as hidden (è) [thievery] (zei);
Hài and Mǎo govern it.
The emotion of the south
is hatred (è);
hatred manifests as integrity and steadfastness;
Yín and Wǔ govern it.
The emotion of the west
is joy;
joy manifests as magnanimity and generosity;
Sì and Yǒu govern it.
The emotion of above
is pleasure;
pleasure manifests as treachery and deceit;
Chén and Wèi govern it.
The emotion of below
is sorrow;
sorrow manifests as fairness and justice;
Xū and Chǒu govern it.
These two theories seem worthy of reference for verification.

It means change.

"biàn" should be read as "biàn" (change).

"Biàn"
means change.
The Yì Jīng, Kūn wén yán: "(yóu) [yóu] biàn zhī bù zǎo biàn yě" (because change was not discerned early),
Xún [Shuàng]'s version has "biàn" (change).
"Biàn" and "biàn" were used interchangeably in ancient times.
Cuī's interpretation as "hé" (harmony)
is mistaken.
"Wū hū": Pronunciation wū.
The annotation is the same.
【一四】【Note】Without self,
thus comply with things,
complying with things leads to perfection (eight).
@【Explanation Text】《Without self》pronounced as jǐ.
The note is the same.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
In current editions, 'wú' is written as '无',
and the following are the same.
《And rule》pronounced as yú kuàng fǎn.
Some editions also read as 'perfection'.
【一五】【Note】Things have never ceased to arise from spontaneity,
yet they inevitably delight in relying on acupuncture and stones,
thus when the principle is fulfilled, the traces vanish.
Now, by following along without assisting,
and becoming one with the ultimate principle,
there is therefore no achievement.
@【Interpretation of Text】"於針" is read as zhèn (鸠) [or rather, 鸩] (jiǔ) fan,
or some read it as zhēn (林) fan.
【一六】【Comment】The term "sage" is
merely a name for one who has attained the nature of things,
yet it is insufficient to describe the means by which this attainment is realized.
@【Explanation】"Ultimate" refers to the essence,
"divine" refers to the function,
and "sage" refers to the designation.
Thus, in terms of essence, we speak of the ultimate;
in terms of function, we speak of the divine;
in terms of designation, we speak of the sage.
In reality, they are one and the same.
Reaching the spiritual pinnacle,
it is therefore called the ultimate;
unfathomable as yīn and yáng,
it is therefore called divine;
rectifying the names of all things,
it is therefore called sagehood.
In one person,
these three aspects exist,
and to illustrate the distinct functions and names,
the distinction among three persons is made.
These three persons
are precisely the ones mentioned earlier who ride the correctness of heaven and earth and master the transformations of the six breaths.
To conclude the unattached virtue of such a person,
and to illuminate their essence and function,
the phrase "therefore it is said" is used.
◎Qìng Fán's case: The "Wén Xuǎn" annotation to Rèn Yǎnshēng's "Letter to the Grand Marshal's Office" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
The divine person is without merit,
meaning they cultivate the natural way,
and do not establish merit.
The sage is without fame,
meaning they do not establish a name.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "境" as "竟",
matching the explanatory text.
The Zhào Jiànyì edition uses "境".
(2) The Tang manuscript lacks the character "而".
(3) The character "独" has been added following Wáng Shūmín's suggestion.
(4) The character "六" has been emended based on the Kùn Xué Jì Wén.

Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu
saying:
"When the sun and moon have risen, if the torch fire does not cease,
would it not be difficult
for it to shine?
When the seasonal rain falls, if one still irrigates,
would it not be toilsome
for the moisturizing?
With you, Master, in position, the empire would be well governed,
yet I still preside over it.
I see myself as inadequate.
I beg to hand over the empire to you."
【First】【Text】Yáo was the son of
Emperor Kù,
surnamed Yīqí,
styled Fàngxūn,
with his mother Qìngdū
(Kù) conceiving him after encountering a red dragon.
He was ten feet tall,
with a narrow upper body and full lower body,
eyebrows of eight colors,
feet treading the Wing Star,
and possessed sagely virtue.
At age fifteen,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Táng.
At twenty-one,
he succeeded his elder brother to the imperial throne,
established his capital at Píngyáng,
and was called Táotáng.
He reigned for seventy-two years
before abdicating to Shùn.
He died at the age of one hundred twenty-eight,
was buried in Yángchéng,
and posthumously honored as Yáo.
According to the rules of posthumous naming,
"assisting goodness and transmitting sainthood is called Yáo,"
meaning he had the merit of passing the throne to Shùn.
Xǔ Yóu was a hermit,
surnamed Xǔ,
named Yóu,
styled Zhòngwǔ,
from Yángchéng in Yǐngchuān.
He lived in seclusion on Jī Mountain,
studied under Nièquē,
ate from the mountains,
and drank from the rivers.
Yáo, knowing his worth,
offered him the imperial throne.
Upon hearing this,
Xǔ Yóu went to the river to wash his ears.
Cháofù, watering his calf,
led it away to avoid him,
saying:
"You have defiled my water."
After his death,
Yáo built a tomb for him,
posthumously honoring him as the Duke of Jī,
who was actually Yáo's teacher.

there is no need for the moisture of irrigation.

stepped back to promote others,

highly praising Zhòngwǔ.

Xǔ Yóu said:
"You govern the world,
and the world is already well-governed.
If I were to take your place,
would I be doing it for fame?
Fame
is but the guest of reality.
Should I become a mere guest?
The wren nesting in the deep forest
occupies no more than a single branch;
the field mouse drinking from the river
takes no more than a bellyful.
Go back and rest, my lord,
I have no use for governing the world!
Even if the cook fails to prepare the sacrifice,
the priest does not step over the wine vessels and stand in his place."
【一】【注】He who can bring order to the world
is one who does not govern the world.
Thus, Yáo governed by not governing,
not by governing it through active rule.
Now that Xǔ Yóu has already achieved perfect clarity and order,
there is nothing to replace him with.
Yet the actual governance came from Yáo,
hence the saying about his governance,
so we should look beyond the words to grasp their implications.
However, some argue:
"He who governs through active rule
is Yáo;
he who does not govern, yet enables Yáo to govern,
is Xǔ Yóu."
This is far from the truth.
For governance arises from non-governance,
action emerges from non-action,
and this is fully embodied in Yáo—
how could it rely on Xǔ Yóu?
If one claims that only by sitting silently in the mountains and forests can it be called non-action,
this is why the discussions of Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozi are rejected by those in power.
Those in power inevitably dwell in the realm of action and do not turn back,
and this is the reason for it.
@【疏】"Governance"
means order.
"Already"
means fully.
It is said that Yáo governed the world,
long achieving peace and prosperity,
with all lands near and far
completely tranquil and orderly.
Why trouble to yield to me,
excessively refusing with elaborate words?
Yet reading Zhuāngzǐ's text seems to贬低Yáo and elevate Xǔ Yóu,
while examining Guō Xiàng's commentary appears to贬低Xǔ Yóu and favor Yáo—
why is this?
It aims to clarify that Fàngxūn (Yáo) was a great sage,
and Zhòngwǔ (Xǔ Yóu) a great worthy,
but the paths of worthiness and sageliness
are far apart.
Thus, Yáo, bearing the screen in Fényáng, lost the world,
while Xǔ Yóu, not changing his customs, stood alone on the high mountain:
comprehensive illumination versus partial immersion,
can be clearly discerned.
Therefore, Zhuāngzǐ drew on the traces of abdication,
hence the discourse on the torch fire;
while Mr. Guō discerned the mind of non-dependence,
further articulating the theory of non-governance.
This can be said to probe the subtle and seek the hidden,
fully understanding the text and aligning with its meaning,
so we should seek its intended implications,
without any slight doubt.
@【釋文】"Able to make" is pronounced lì chéng fǎn,
similarly below.
【二】【Note】Those who act according to their own will confront things,
while those who follow things are in harmony with them and do not confront them.
Thus, Yáo had no opposition in the world,
while Xǔ Yóu became a peer to Jì and Qì.
How can we say this is so?
Those who merge with things
are thus inseparable from the multitude of things.
Therefore, with a mindless and mysterious responsiveness,
they follow only what they sense,
drifting like an unmoored boat,
with east and west not of their own making.
Thus, there is no action they do not share with the common people,
and no place they go where they are not the ruler of the world.
To be a ruler in this way
is like the sky being naturally high—
this is truly the virtue of a ruler.
If one stands alone aloft atop a high mountain,
it is not that such a person has a sentiment for self-preservation,
but rather upholding a biased preference for one family.
How can one monopolize this!
This is merely one thing among the vulgar,
and being an outer minister to Yáo.
If an outer minister were to replace the inner ruler,
this would have the name of being a ruler but not the substance of fulfilling the role of a ruler.
@【Commentary】Xǔ Yóu reclined proudly on Mount Jī,
roaming freely by the Yǐng River,
detesting the stench of glory and profit,
and loathing the filth of fame.
Yet Yáo earnestly extended his invitation,
still hoping he would replace himself.
If Xǔ Yóu were to ascend the throne,
he would assume the title of a ruler of ten thousand chariots.
However, reality gives rise to names,
and names arise from reality.
Reality is the inner, the host;
names are the outer, the guest.
To abandon the host and take the guest,
to lose the inner and seek the outer,
is not what recluses value.
Therefore, it is said, "I will be the guest."

【First】【Commentary】Jiān Wú and Lián Shū
were both ancient men who embraced the Way.
Jiē Yú,
whose surname was Lù,
given name Tōng,
courtesy name Jiē Yú,
was a worthy recluse of the state of Chǔ,
a contemporary of Confucius.
He feigned madness and did not take office,
often making farming his occupation.
The king of Chǔ, knowing his worth,
offered him a hundred yì of gold
and two teams of four horses each,
but he did not accept.
Thereupon, the husband carried on his back and the wife bore on her head,
and they roamed the mountains and seas,
with none knowing their final whereabouts.
Jiān Wú heard that Jiē Yú's words were exaggerated and lacked a standard,
so he asked Lián Shū,
inquiring about their meaning and intent.
And as for saying "I heard from Jiē Yú,"
it means he heard Jiē Yú's words.
Master Zhuāng entrusted these three worthies to illustrate Yáo's singular sagehood,
and the account of what was heard is fully detailed in the following text.

【一】【注】These are all metaphorical expressions.

how could they know that the utmost of the utmost remains undiminished!
Now, speaking of the person of kingly virtue and placing him on this mountain,
is to clarify that the world has no means to recognize him,

) Táng Yīn Jìngshùn's Lièzǐ Shìwén quotes Shānhǎi Jīng saying:
Gūyè State is in the sea,
surrounded by mountains to the southwest.
From the state south, traveling by water one hundred lǐ,
is called Gūyè Mountain.
Further southwest three hundred eighty lǐ,
is called Gūyè Mountain.
Guō says it is where the river water passes by the sea.
Meaning looking afar at the various Gūyè Mountains arrayed between the sea and river.
Differs from the current version of Shānhǎi Jīng.
Suíshū Dìlǐ Zhì,
Línfén has Gūyè Mountain,
this is the Gūyè from Dōngshān Jīng.
Zhuāngzǐ's so-called Gūyè Mountain,
north of the Fén River is this one.
According to Qín Shì Ēnfù's Lièzǐ Bǔzhù says:
Línfén Gūyè,
is now Jiǔkǒng Mountain west of Píngyáng Prefecture.
There are no so-called northern and southern Gūyè around it.
Evidenced by Yīn Shì's Shìwén,
then the two entries for Northern Gūyè and Southern Gūyè in Dōngshān Jīng,
should be under "surrounded by mountains to the southwest" in Hǎinèi Běi Jīng.
For there must be various Gūyè arrayed around,
and then it can be named Liè Gūyè.
Moreover, Yīn based his Shānhǎi Jīng on the Táng period version,
presumably the ancient version was originally so,
unknown when it was omitted in transcription,
inserted after the Gūyè Mountain entry in Dōngshān Jīng,
thus forming the current version.
Fortunately, there is Lièzǐ Shìwén,
which can correct Shānhǎi Jīng's error.
And Zhuāngzǐ mentions Gūyè twice,
one in the North Sea,
one in Línfén,
also avoiding mixing them into one.
(Bì Shì Yuán's annotation on Shānhǎi Jīng quotes Zhuāngzǐ,
mistakenly mixes them as one.
) Although the text is all metaphorical,
and the locations of the mountain names,
are all indeed verifiable,
it is still worthwhile to discuss and verify them.

【二】【注】Both consume the five grains, yet only one becomes a divine person,
indicating that the divine person is not created by the five grains,
but uniquely endowed with the wondrous breath of nature.
@【疏】The five grains are:
millet, broomcorn millet, hemp, beans, and wheat.
It is said that sacred and divine individuals,
descending to be born and responding to things,
embody the essence of purity and refinement,
endowed with the finest energy of yīn and yáng.
Although they follow things to sustain themselves,
they are not formed by the five grains;
relying on wind and dew for clarity and emptiness,
how could the four seasons alter them!
@【釋文】《吸》Pronounced as xī, with the initial "x" and the entering tone.
【Three】【Treatises】Wisdom illuminates with spiritual penetration,
being unattuned yet conforming to all things,
hence it is said to ride the clouds and ether.
Without haste yet swift,
manifesting and transforming without constancy,
hence it is said to harness the flying dragon.
Dwelling upon the myriad things yet the spirit transcends beyond the six directions,
hence it is said to wander beyond the four seas.
【Four】【Commentary】One who embodies the spirit, dwells in numinousness, and exhausts principles to reach the utmost subtlety,
though silently abiding in a quiet hall,
mysteriously unites with what lies beyond the four seas.
Thus, riding the two primal forces and mastering the six energies,
they harmonize with the multitude and guide the myriad things.
If there is nothing that does not comply,
then floating clouds become their chariot;
if there is no form that is not borne,
then flying dragons become their steed.
Forsaking the self, they attain spontaneity;
though tranquil, they require no reliance.
Sitting in forgetfulness, walking in forgetfulness,
acting through forgetfulness,
thus their movement is like dragging dry wood,
their stillness like gathered dead ashes.
Hence, it is said their spirit is concentrated.
When their spirit is concentrated,
then what is not concentrated attains spontaneity on its own.
The world all levels what they see and judges by it—
how could they ever believe in this!
@【Exegesis】Concentrated
means stillness.
Blights and plagues
refer to diseases.
The ripening of the five grains
signifies a fruitful year.
The sage’s form is like dry wood,
their mind like dead ashes,
their essence and traces unified in the moment,
movement and stillness both wondrous,
concentrated illumination silently penetrates,
an empty bosom benefits all things.
Thereby, the four seasons follow in order,
the five grains flourish abundantly,
humans are free from calamities,
and creatures avoid untimely deaths.
The sage’s presence in the world
possesses such efficacy;
Jiānwú, not comprehending these profound words,
deemed them mad and did not believe.

Lián Shū said:
"Indeed.
The blind cannot be shown the beauty of patterns and colors,
the deaf cannot be made to hear the sounds of bells and drums.
Is it only physical forms that have deafness and blindness?
Knowledge also has them.
These words of his,
refer precisely to you.
Such a person,
with such virtue,
embraces all things to bring order to the age, seeking unity—
who would toil and trouble to make the world his business!
Such a person,
nothing can harm him;
even if a great flood reached the sky, he would not drown,
even in a great drought when metals and stones melt and earth mountains scorch, he would not feel the heat.
From his dust and chaff,
he could still mold and cast a Yáo or a Shùn—
who would be willing to take things as his business!
A man of Sòng traded ceremonial caps to the Yuè people,
but the Yuè people cut their hair short and tattooed their bodies,
so they had no use for them.
When Yáo governed the people under heaven
and brought order to the politics within the seas,
he went to see the four masters on the distant Gūyé Mountain,
north of the Fén River,
and in a trance, forgot his empire."
【一】【注】They do not know the ultimate wonder of the most profound words,
and instead consider them mad and do not believe,
this is the deafness and blindness of understanding.
@【疏】The blind,
refers to eyes without any slit,
dark and obscure like a drum's skin.
The deaf,
are those with ear ailments.
The blind,
are those with damaged visual faculties.
Now, seeing with the eyes and hearing with the ears,
are the common conditions of beings,
but if one is both blind and deaf,
they cannot be shown sounds or appearances.
Similarly, the most profound words and wondrous truths,
only those with liberated understanding can know.
Foolish and deluded individuals,
never awaken in their entire lives,
truly due to the blindness and obscurity of intellectual hindrances,
unable to illuminate and perceive,
how could this be limited to physical form alone!
Thus, upon hearing the words of Jiē Yú,
they deemed them mad and did not believe.
From here onward,
is Lián Shū's reply to Jiān Wú's words.

【三】【注】The mind of the sage
reaches the ultimate convergence of the two polarities (yin and yang),
and exhausts the subtle principles of all things.
Thus, it can embody transformation and respond to change,
with no direction in which it is not applicable,
encompassing all things,
with nothing that is not so.
The world, because of its disorder, seeks me,
but I have no fixed mind.
If I truly have no fixed mind,
then why would I not respond to the world?
However, those who embody the profound and reach the ultimate subtlety,
the means by which they interconnect with the nature of all things,
and mold the transformations of the world,
thereby achieving the renown of Yáo and Shùn,
constantly do so by acting through non-action.
Who would laboriously strain their spirit and vex their thoughts,
treating affairs as affairs,
and only then be capable?

Therefore, Lǎozǐ says, "Act through non-action,"

【Four】【Annotation】If one is at peace with the harm they've received,
then harm cannot truly harm them;
when harm cannot harm them,
then external things also do not harm them.
【Five】【Commentary】There is no going without being at ease,
thus wherever one is, it is all suitable.
Life and death do not change the self,
how much less between drowning and heat!
Therefore, the ultimate person is not entangled in calamities and difficulties,
not because they avoid them,
but because they follow reason directly forward and naturally meet with good fortune.

being suited to water and fire,
then one does not drown nor burn.
Suppose there were disasters like the yang nine melting metal,
or catastrophes like the hundred six flooding heaven,
chaotic as they may be from their side,
what are they to me!
Thus, Guō Xiàng's commentary says,
life and death do not change the self,
how much less between drowning and heat!

【Six】【Commentary】Yáo and Shùn are merely
names from worldly affairs;
those who create names
are not the names themselves.
Thus, what are Yáo and Shùn?
How could they be limited to just the names Yáo and Shùn?
They must possess the substance of divine sages.
What people now call Yáo and Shùn
are merely labels for their dust and chaff.
@【Exegesis】Scattered matter is called dust,
greasy residue is called grime,
unripe grain is called chaff,
grain husks are called bran—
all are worthless things.
Melting metal is called casting,
molding clay is called pottery.
According to posthumous naming conventions,
"assisting goodness and transmitting sageliness" is called Yáo,
"benevolent sageliness and abundant brilliance" is called Shùn.
Now Yáo, being supremely sagely,
transcended form and name with exquisite subtlety,
concealed his traces to blend with the dust of the world,
and beings cherished his virtue,
hence established names and posthumous titles to manifest his sagely essence.
Yet names are crude conventions,
no different from chaff and bran;
posthumous titles are worldly matters,
how do they differ from dust and grime?
Subsequently, through flattery and deceitful fabrication,
people forged that dust and grime into Yáo,
and molded this chaff and bran into Shùn.
How could they understand that the subtle essence defies verbal description!
Thus, who would willingly engage with such superficial matters?

【Seven】【Commentary】This begins the analogy.
Zī (资),
means goods.
The Yuè state bordered closely on rivers and lakes,
cut their hair short and tattooed their bodies,
to avoid the harm of flood dragons.
Zhāngfǔ,
is the name of a cap.
Thus Confucius, born in Lǔ,
wore a gown with large sleeves;
grew up in Sòng,
and wore the Zhāngfǔ cap.
And Sòng was actually the descendant of Wēizǐ,
while Yuè was the lineage of Tàibó,
the two states traded back and forth,
thus using the Zhāngfǔ cap as a commodity.
Moreover, the Zhāngfǔ cap originally served as a head ornament,
requiring coiled hair to support the cap,
but the Yuè people cut their hair short and tattooed their bodies,
making the commodity utterly useless.
Similarly, glory and splendor are originally attachments,
wealth and honor give rise to arrogance.
Yáo, having embodied the Way and thoroughly forgotten worldly concerns,
thus could have no use for the world.
Therefore, Guǒ's annotation states,
that Yáo had no use for governing the world,
is just like the Yuè people having no use for the Zhāngfǔ cap.
