【Eight】【Commentary】Yáo's having no use for governing the world
is just like the Yuè people having no use for ceremonial caps.
Yet one who renounces the world
is precisely whom the world reveres.
Although the world reveres Yáo,
he never possessed the world,
so he profoundly forgot it,
and often let his mind wander in the realm of absolute obscurity.
Though situated above all things, he was always free and unfettered.
The term "Four Masters" is metaphorical,
used to illustrate that Yáo was not confined to his identity as Yáo.
In reality, Yáo embodied obscurity,
while his traces were those of Yáo.
Viewing obscurity from his traces,
the inner and outer realms differ,
which is not surprising.
The world only sees Yáo as Yáo;
how could they recognize his obscurity?
Thus, seeking the Four Masters overseas while confining Yáo to what is visible,
and claiming that those who flow with things
lose their freedom and ease,
fails to understand that the path to the farthest reach follows what is near,
and the highest convergence lies in what is lowly.
If one arrogantly considers solitary loftiness as the ultimate and remains untainted by worldly burdens,
such a person is a recluse of the mountains and valleys,
not one who is free from dependence.
How can they be worthy of discussing the ultimate and roaming in the boundless?
@【Exegesis】Governance
refers to orderly management;
administration
refers to moral influence.
This is a combined metaphor.
The Fén River originates from Tàiyuán,
flowing west into the Yellow River.
The north side of a river is called "yáng,"
so today's Píngyáng County in Jìnzhōu,
located north of the Fén River,
was the ancient capital of Yáo.
"Profound" denotes silence and vastness,
a term for depth and distance.
"Forgetting" means to let go,
implying liberation and detachment.
As for the "Four Masters,"
they represent the four virtues:
first, the root;
second, the traces;
third, neither root nor traces;
fourth, beyond both root and traces.
It means Yáo reflected inward to the source of his mind,
perceiving the realm of Dào clearly,
transcending these four propositions,
hence it is said he went to see the Four Masters.
The sage has no fixed mind,
responding to stimuli as they arise,
thus capable of orderly governing all states,
and harmonizing the nine regions.
Though he concentrated his spirit on the Four Masters,
sitting upright at Fényáng;
while ruling over myriad affairs,
he profoundly forgot the world.
This illustrates that root and traces are one,
substance and function are identical,
illuminating both emptiness and form,
activity and stillness simultaneous.
Thus, Gūyè is no different from Fényáng,
and the mountain forests are no distinct from the imperial court!
The world judges by what they see;
how could they believe this?
Mǎ Biāo identified the Four Masters as Nièquē,
showing he failed to grasp the profound principle;
Liú Zhāng associated the Fén River with the Shè Mountain,
further confusing the immediate facts.
The interpretation here
differs slightly from these.
Thus, Guō Xiàng's commentary states,
"The Four Masters are metaphorical,
to clarify that Yáo was not confined to his identity as Yáo."
The world only sees Yáo's traces;
how could they recognize his obscurity?

It is because Yáo never possessed the world in his heart;
his heart was that of the divine being of Gūyè,
his body also like that of the divine being of Gūyè.
Though he ruled from the court,
he was as free as if roaming beyond the seas.
Thus, that distant mountain
was no different from being near the capital.
(The Four Masters are not actual persons;
to substantiate them by name is forced.
) The commentaries and exegesis elucidate
with utmost subtlety.
I previously argued in one discussion
that the mountain names should not be conflated,
but fearing it might miss Zhuāngzǐ's profound meaning,
I address it again here.
Fén River:
Sīmǎ and Cuī's versions both write "Pén River,"
as in ancient pronunciation, "Fén" was read like "Pén,"
not referring to a different river.
See Qián Dàxīn's Yǎng Xīn Lù for explanation.
"Profound": Xú reads as wūliǎo fǎn.
Guō reads as wǔpián fǎn.
Lǐ notes:
"Profound"
means as if lost in thought.
◎Lú Wénchāo remarks:
Guō must have considered it
thus giving this pronunciation.
"Forgot": reads as xīlàng fǎn,
same in the commentary.
"Absolute obscurity": reads as wángdīng fǎn.
"Realm": reads as jìng.
Also written as "boundary."
◎Lú Wénchāo remarks:

【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the ancient Tibetan edition from Fangying Temple on Tiantāi Shān, where "blind" is written as "gǔ" (瞽).
(2) The character "suǒ" (所) has been amended based on the Sòng edition.
(3) The character "míng" (冥) has been amended based on the commentary text.
(4) The character "tián" (窴) has been amended according to the Bàojīngtáng original edition.
It seems the original engraved edition also contains errors.
Shuōwén:
"Tián" (窴),
means "to block,"
derived from the radical "xué" (穴),
with "zhēn" (真) as its phonetic component.
Xú Xuàn gives the pronunciation as "dài nián qiē."
This is the modern character "tián" (填).
"Wǔ pián" and "dài nián" share the same rhyme but belong to different rhyme groups,
so it is likely not the correct character.
Using "tián rán" to describe "losing the world"
is also incongruous in expression.
It is suspected that Guǒ's edition used "míng" (冥),
and the Shìwén omitted the two characters "zuò míng" (作冥) after Guǒ.
The character "míng" (冥) was historically interchangeable with "mián" (瞑) and "mián" (眠).
In the chapter "Liè Yùkòu," the phrase "gān míng hū wú hé yǒu zhī xiāng" (甘冥乎无何有之乡)
is explained in Shìwén as:
"Another version writes it as 'mián' (瞑),
pronounced as 'mián' (眠)."
Yú Yuè suggested that the Huáinánzǐ chapter "Chù Zhēn"’s phrase "gān mián hū hùn xián zhī yù" (甘瞑乎溷澖之域) originates from this,
where "gān mián" means "gān mián" (甘眠).
Shuōwén:
"Mián" (瞑),
means "to close the eyes,"
derived from the radical "mù" (目) and "míng" (冥),
with "míng" (冥) also serving as the phonetic.
Xú Xuàn stated:
"Nowadays, it is commonly distinguished as 'mián' (眠),
which is incorrect."
The pronunciation is "wǔ yán qiē."
In the Hànshū, Yáng Xióng’s biography uses "mù míng xuàn ér wú jiàn" (目冥眴而无见),
where "míng xuàn" is equivalent to "mián xuàn" (瞑眩) in Mèngzǐ’s "Téng Wéngōng,"
both being binomes with the same rhyme.
It is also written as "xuàn mián" (眩眠) or "xuàn mǐn" (眩湣),
such as in the Shǐjì, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú’s biography: "shì xuàn mián ér wú jiàn xī" (视眩眠而无见兮) and "hóng yǎo miǎo ér xuàn mǐn xī" (红杳渺而眩湣兮).
These characters share similar meanings and pronunciations.
Lù’s "míng" is pronounced "wǔ pián qiē,"
while Xú’s "mián" is "wǔ yán qiē,"
and the Hànshū’s Yán commentary gives "míng" as "mò jiàn fǎn,"
Sūn Shì’s Mèngzǐ Yīnyì gives "mián" as "mò diàn qiē,"
the Shǐjì Suǒyǐn cites Sū Lín’s "mǐn" pronounced as "mǐn,"
all belonging to the same rhyme group,
(In ancient times, there was no light labial sound,
"wǔ" and "mò" had the same initial.)
The only difference is in the tone (level or oblique).
"Míng" (冥) and "yǎo" (窅) also share interconnected meanings,
hence they are often used together.
In the chapter "Xiāo Yáo Yóu," the phrase "běi míng yǒu yú" (北冥有鱼)
is explained in Shìwén citing Jiǎn Wén:
"yǎo míng wú jí" (窅冥无极),
hence it is called "míng," which is correct.
The two characters are also similar in form,
so the current edition uses "yǎo" (窅),
while Guǒ's edition uses "míng" (冥).
Guǒ's commentary here uses "míng" four times in succession,
all elaborating on the concept of "míng rán,"
serving as solid evidence.
The "yǎo" in the preceding phrase "gù yǎo rán sàng zhī" (故窅然丧之)
is suspected to have originally been "míng" (冥) as well,
later altered by copyists based on the current edition's main text.
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
"The King of Wèi gave me seeds of a great gourd[一],
I planted them and they grew to bear fruit weighing five shí,
when used to hold water or soup,
its firmness couldn't support its own weight[二].
Splitting it to make ladles,
then the gourd was too large and shallow to hold anything.
It wasn't that it wasn't impressively big,
but I smashed it because it was useless[三]."
【One】【Commentary】His surname is Huì,
given name Shī,
a native of the state of Sòng,
who served as the chancellor of the state of Liáng.
"Wèi" means to speak.
It refers to discourse.
"Yí" means to give.
It denotes presenting.
"Hù" is a type of gourd.
It belongs to the category of páo.
The King of Wèi is King Huì of Liáng.
In the past, he resided in Ānyì,
and his state was named Wèi.
Later, pressured by the powerful state of Qín,
he moved to Dàliáng,
and subsequently changed the state's name to Liáng,
arrogating the title of king.
The reason Huìzǐ used this analogy of the large gourd
was to satirize Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
which, although their rhetoric and themes were grand and expansive,
were not pertinent to practical affairs.
Hence, he expressed these words to provoke further discussion.
@【Explanatory Text】"Huìzǐ" Sīmǎ comments:
His surname is Huì,
given name Shī,
served as the chancellor of Liáng.
"The King of Wèi" Sīmǎ states:
It is King Huì of Liáng.
According to records, Wèi moved from Hédōng to Dàliáng,
hence it was called Wèi,
or sometimes referred to as Liáng.
"Yí" is pronounced yí by Xú,
Guō gives the pronunciation as yǔ zhì fǎn,
meaning to give.
"Dà hù" is pronounced hù by Xú.
"Zhī zhǒng" is pronounced zhāng yǒng fǎn.
【二】【疏】"Shù" refers to
planting and cultivation.
"Shí" means
seeds.
Huì Shī, having obtained the gourd seeds,
cultivated them to maturity,
and the resulting fruit was very large,
capable of holding five shí.
Yet when he tried to use this gourd to hold water or liquid,
it was hollow and fragile, not sturdy,
so it could not support its own weight when lifted.
@【释文】《而实五石》Sīmǎ comments:
Its interior capacity is five shí.
《以盛》Pronounced as "chéng".
【Three】【Annotations】To split,
means to divide and separate.
Gourd ladle,
is a scoop.
"Hùluò,"
means flat and shallow.
"Xiāorán,"
signifies empty and large.
"Pǒu,"
means to break open.
When used to hold water,
it is too hollow and fragile to bear its own weight;
when split to make a ladle,
it is too flat and shallow to contain much.
Everyone deemed it useless,
so it was broken and discarded.
This criticizes Zhuāngzǐ's words,
as they fail to address the urgent needs of the time,
much like this gourd,
and should thus be discarded.
@【Explanatory Text】"Pǒu zhī" is pronounced pǔ kǒu fǎn.
"Wéi piáo" is pronounced pí yáo fǎn.
Xú reads it as fú yáo fǎn.
"Zé hù" is pronounced hù guō fǎn,
Sīmǎ pronounces it as hù.
The same applies below.
"Luò" Jiǎnwén states:
"Hùluò,"
is like vast and empty.
Sīmǎ says:
"Hù,"
means to spread out;
"luò,"
means to fall away.
It describes its shape as flat and shallow,
so when filled with water, it falls apart and cannot hold it.
"Xiāorán" is also written as 枵.
Xú reads it as xǔ xiāo fǎn.
Lǐ says:
"Xiāorán,"
describes an empty and large appearance.
Cuī writes it as ●,
Jiǎnwén agrees.
"Wú wèi" is pronounced yú wèi fǎn.
"Pǒu zhī" Xú reads as fāng gòu fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to smash.
◎Qìng Fān's case: In the Wénxuǎn, Xiè Língyùn's poem "Departing from the Capital Upon First Arriving at the Commandery" notes citing Sīmǎ:
"Hù,"
means to spread out;
"luò,"

"Xiāorán,"

"Pǒu,"

◎Yú Yuè says:

"Xiāo" and ●,

In the Wénxuǎn, Lǐ Shàn's note on Xiè Língyùn's poem "First Departing from the Capital" cites this text as "xiāo,"
which should be followed.

Emptiness implies largeness,

Zhuāngzǐ said:
"You are certainly clumsy in utilizing great things.
There was a man of Sòng who excelled at making an anti-chapping salve,
and for generations his family made a living by bleaching silk in water.
A visitor heard about this,
and offered to buy the recipe for a hundred pieces of gold.
The man gathered his clan to discuss it, saying:
'For generations we have been bleaching silk,
earning no more than a few pieces of gold;
now we can sell this technique for a hundred pieces of gold in one morning.
Let us give it to him.'
The visitor obtained it,
and used it to persuade the King of Wú.
When Yuè created trouble,
the King of Wú put him in command of the army.
In winter, they fought a naval battle against the Yuè people,
and thoroughly defeated them,
for which he was granted a fief with partitioned land.
The ability to prevent chapped hands was the same in both cases;
it was one and the same skill.
Yet one used it to gain a fief,
while the other couldn't avoid bleaching silk—
this was due to the difference in how it was applied.
Now you have a gourd that can hold five shí,
why not consider making it into a large buoy to float upon the rivers and lakes,
instead of worrying that it's too big and has nothing to hold?
Then your mind must still be hampered by brambles!"
【一】【Note】This medicine can prevent hands from chapping,
hence they often wash silk floss in water.
@【Subcommentary】Píng means
floating;
pì means
rinsing.
Kuàng means
silk floss.
Shìshì means
generations.
People of Sòng in deep winter wade into water,
rinsing silk floss to make qiānlí,
their fingers develop sores,
chapped like a tortoise's back.
Thus, generation after generation inherits,
passing down this medicine within families,
to keep their hands from chapping,
enabling them to always rinse silk floss in water,
preserving this livelihood,
never failing or abandoning it.
Another interpretation says:
Pì means
to separate;
kuàng means
raw silk,
referring to the act of separating raw silk in water.
@【Textual Explanations】"Guīshǒu" is pronounced with "guī" as kuìbēi fǎn.
Xú gives jǔlún fǎn.
Lǐ gives jūwēi fǎn.
Xiàng says:
It means chapped.
Sīmǎ says:
The cracks resemble the pattern on a tortoise shell.
Another says:
Like a tortoise's constricted shrinkage.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
The Textual Explanations cites Sīmǎ saying the cracks resemble a tortoise's pattern,
and another saying like a tortoise's shrinkage,
both interpretations are unsatisfactory.
Xiàng said it means chapped,
Guō's note also says it can prevent hands from chapping,
thus, "guī" should be read as "jū".
For "guī" has the sound of "qiū",
as in the Later Hàn Shū·Xīyù Zhuàn where "Qiūcí" is read for "Guīcí",
that's the case.
In ancient times, the sound of "qiū" was the same as "qū",
hence it can also be read as "jū".
"Jū" means
cramped or constricted,
"bù guī (two)" means
not cramped.
The tortoise pattern theory is incorrect,
while the shrinkage theory is right,
but there's no need to explain it in terms of resembling a tortoise.
◎ Lǐ Zhēn comments:
"Guīshǒu",
Textual Explanations says Xú pronounces it as jǔlún fǎn,

Note that "guī" and "jūn" are alliterative.
In volume 11 of the Zhòngjīng Yīnyì:
"Jūn",

Chapped and cracked hands and feet are called "jūn",

Below, it cites this text from Zhuāngzǐ and Guō's note as evidence.
Thus, Xuán Yìng considers "guī" and "jūn" interchangeable in sound and meaning.

"Jūn",

In the Hàn Shū·Zhào Cōngguó Zhuàn,
the general and soldiers were cold,

Wén Yǐng explained:
"Jūn" means
chapped and cracked;
"zhú" means
cold sore.

frozen skin, chapped and frostbitten.
"Bù guīshǒu" means

"Jūn",

"Píng" is pronounced by Xú as fújīng fǎn.
"Pì" is pǔlì fǎn.
Xú gives fūlì fǎn.
Guō and Lǐ give kèlì fǎn,
"pì",

【二】【疏】A piece of gold measuring one cubic inch and weighing one catty is considered one unit of gold.
A traveler from another country,
happened to hear of it,
and requested to purchase a technique for treating hand sores,
thus spending the price of a hundred units of gold.
@【Explanation】"A Hundred Units of Gold" Lǐ Yún states:
A piece of gold one cubic inch in size and weighing one catty is one unit of gold.
A hundred units of gold
means a hundred catties.
【Three】【Explanations】Yù,
means to sell.
The valuation was already high,
so the clan gathered to discuss.
For generations practicing washing silk floss,
the profits were quite meager,
but one morning selling the skill,
the wealth obtained was immense.
With different mouths speaking in unison,
all said, "We agree to give it."
@【Interpretation】"Shù jīn" is pronounced with "shù" as sè zhǔ fǎn.
"Yù" is pronounced yù.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to sell.
"Jì" may also be written as "jì" in some versions,
pronounced as jié bǐ fǎn.
【Fourth】【Memorial】Wú and Yuè are neighboring states,
their lands connected by rivers and seas,
where armed conflicts arise,
inevitably employing warships.
In the harsh winter,
soldiers' hands often chap and crack.
Yet the visitor, endowed with heroic talent,
and born with profound wisdom,
having obtained the remedy,
then persuaded the King of Wú.
When the Yuè army threatened to invade Wú,
the King of Wú appointed him as commander.
Relying on this renowned medicine,
the soldiers' hands remained unchapped.
As soon as the banners were raised,
the Yuè forces fell into disarray.
Achieving this great victory,
they returned triumphantly with offerings of victory,
their merits prominently recognized,
and were enfeoffed with lands and titles.
@【Commentary】"To persuade" is read with the initial sharp tone,
and also as in its regular pronunciation.
"To invade" is read with the initial rising tone.
"The General" reads Zǐ Jiàng in reverse.
"Great Defeat" reads Bì Mài in reverse.
【Five】【Dispersion】means uncertainty.
It is not fixed.
Medicinal formulas have no inherent skill or clumsiness, yet their users apply them differently.
Thus, a traveler obtained it and was enfeoffed as a marquis,
while a person from Sòng used it for washing silk.
This illustrates the difference in the skill or clumsiness of their application.
【Six】【Annotation】The calabash gourd,
is not something that grows straight and unimpeded.
This chapter speaks of how each thing has its proper use;
if one finds its proper application,
then wherever it goes, it can be carefree and unbound.
@【Explanation】"Lǜ" means
to tie or net it.
"Zūn" refers to
lacquering it like a wine jar,
binding it with ropes,
using it to cross rivers and lakes,
what southern people call a "waist boat."
"Péng" is
the name of a grass,
twisted and not straight.
"Fū" is
an exclamation, a sigh.
It says that a large gourd floating on rivers and lakes
can serve as a boat to save from drowning;
likewise, the ultimate teaching flourishing in the world
can rescue and ferry the deluded masses.
However, Huì Shēng, having a "péng heart,"
was unable to directly comprehend the profound principles,
thus wrongly raised the analogy of smashing it,
criticizing Zhuāngzǐ's writings.
This misuse,
is deeply lamentable.
@【Textual Notes】"Bù lǜ yǐ wéi dà zūn" in some versions also written as "zūn".
Sīmǎ explains:
Zūn is like a wine vessel,
tied to the body,
floated on rivers and lakes,
allowing one to cross by oneself.
"Lǜ"
means to knot or attach.
This is the so-called waist boat.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:

Péng,

Shuōwén:
缚,

縳,

Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
"I have a large tree,
people call it the shù.
Its main trunk is gnarled and unfit for the carpenter's line,
its small branches are curled and unfit for the compass and square.
Planted by the roadside,
craftsmen would not give it a glance.
Now your words,
grand but useless,
are what everyone alike rejects."
【一】【疏】The ailanthus tree,
belonging to the same category as lacquer trees,
emits a very foul odor when smelled,
making it a despised type of wood.
The names in the world,
are generally all illusory and false,
and when people smell it together,
they do not know its true nature,
hence it is said that people call it "chū."
@【释文】"Chū" is pronounced as chì yú fǎn,
a name for a tree.
【二】【疏】Gnarled and swollen,
refers to the burls and knots.
Twisted and bent,
not straight or upright.
Compasses make circles and squares make angles.
Tú,
means the way.
Trees like the chū and lì,
useless timber,
with roots and trunks gnarled and swollen,
branches and stems contorted and curled,
untouched by the marking line,
unsuitable for squares or circles,
stand by the roadside,
yet craftsmen do not even glance at them.
@【Explanatory Text】《Yǒng zhǒng》pronounced as zhāng yǒng fǎn.
Lǐ says:
yǒng zhǒng,
is like pán yǐng.
《Bù zhòng》pronounced as dīng zhòng fǎn.
Same below.
《Juǎn qū》also written as quán,
same meaning.
Pronounced as quán,
Xú reads as jì ruǎn fǎn.
Lǐ reads as qiū yuán fǎn.
【Three】【Analyses】The tree, being gnarled and unfit for timber,
is overlooked by the craftsman;
likewise, words that are impractical and absurdly useless
are shunned by the masses.
This is a fitting analogy.
@【Explanation】"Tóng qù" is read as in its usual pronunciation.
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as qiānglǚ in reverse.
◎Qìng Fān's case: Grand yet useless,
meaning far-fetched and irrelevant to practical matters.
In the "Wén Wáng Shì Zǐ" chapter of the Book of Rites, it is said to extend to oneself to improve one's ruler,
with Zhèng's annotation stating:
"yú" is read as "yū",
meaning broad,
or grand.
Thus, "grand" and "far-fetched" share the same meaning.
In the Dàodé Jīng of Lǎo Zǐ,
it is said that all under heaven deem the Dào grand, yet it seems unlike anything,
which also conveys the meaning of this "grand" character.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Have you alone not seen the wildcat and the weasel?
They crouch low and lie in wait,
awaiting the careless prey;
leaping east and west,
not avoiding heights and depths;
they get caught in traps,
and die in nets.
Now take the yak,
its size is like a cloud hanging from the sky.
It can be considered large,
yet it cannot catch mice.
Now you have a large tree,
worried about its uselessness,
why not plant it in the land of nothingness,
the wilderness of vast emptiness,
wandering aimlessly by its side,
carefree and at ease, sleeping beneath it.
It won't die by the axe,
nothing will harm it.
Being of no use,
how could it suffer hardship?"
【First Commentary】The wildcat,
is a type of feral cat.
"Tiàoliáng"
means running and leaping about.
"Pì"
refers to laws or mechanisms,
indicating devices like traps.
"Wǎnggǔ"
are nets and snares.
Have you not seen how the wildcat catches mice?
It crouches low,
lying in wait for the careless mouse;
leaping east and west,
not avoiding high or low ground;
yet it falls into the trap's mechanism,
dying within the nets,
all because it is deluded by small gains,
failing to consider the greater consequences.
Similarly, some kneel and bow,
clinging to the traces of sages,
falsifying their emotions and distorting their nature,
to seek temporal advantages.
Though they may achieve their desires initially,
they will inevitably face peril and ruin later.
Figures like Shāng Yāng, Sū Qín, and Zhāng Yí
exemplify this.
How is this different from the wildcat dying in nets while catching mice?

【二】【疏】The lí niú,
also known as the máo niú,
originates from the southwestern barbarians.
Its form is exceedingly large;
when viewed from afar in the mountains,
it resembles clouds on the horizon.
In the marshes and wetlands,
it roams freely, nurturing its nature,
yet when leaping and pouncing on mice,
it is no match for the wildcat.
This is akin to Zhuāngzǐ's words:
not mingling with the common customs,
it can be used to govern the state and cultivate the self,
enduring both in length and duration.
@【Interpretation of Text】"Lí niú": Guō reads it as Lǚ zhī fǎn.
Xú and Lǐ pronounce it as lái.
Also pronounced as lí.
Sīmǎ says:
It is the máo niú.
【Three】【Explanations】There is nothing,
as if there were nothing at all.
Mò,
means without.
It refers to a vast and uninhabited place,
regardless of what things,
all are nonexistent,
hence it is called the land of nothingness.
@【Interpretation of the Text】"The land of nothingness and the wilderness of vastness" refers to a place of utter stillness and non-action.
Jiǎnwén states:
Mò,
means great.
【Four】【Shū】Wandering aimlessly,
is the term for acting freely;
carefree and unfettered,
is the expression for self-contentment;
these are different words with the same meaning,
interchangeable in text.
The useless tree,
with its lush branches and leaves,
sways and casts shade,
blocking the sun and attracting the wind,
so travelers passing by,
linger and rest,
pacing back and forth, gazing around,
sleeping beneath it.
This is akin to Zhuāngzǐ's teachings,
of non-action and emptiness,
which allow one to be carefree and follow one's nature,
providing shelter for all living beings.

Cuī's version writes it as fāng yáng,

Guǎngyǎ states:
Páng yáng,

【Five】【Comment】For all things great and small,
if they lose their proper measure,
then the principles of benefit and harm become equal;
if they are used in their appropriate place,
then all things can roam freely.
@【Explanation】Gnarled and unfit for timber,
twisted and of no practical use,
craftsmen pay it no heed,
and no axe is laid upon it.
Thus, the disaster of premature death
has no way to befall it,
allowing it to live out its natural lifespan,
fulfilling its inherent vitality.
The usefulness of the useless—
how could it ever suffer hardship!
This is like Zhuāngzǐ's words:
to diverge from the mundane and unite with the Dào,
one can preserve and nurture oneself,
and maintain one's innate genuineness.
Since one does not meet premature demise on worldly paths,
how could one willingly endure hardship in the course of life!
【Collation】(1) The quoted text in Que Wu originally had "困苦" as "窮困".

【一】【注】To deem oneself right and others wrong,
to praise oneself and dislike others,
is a tendency found in all things.
Since this is so,
therefore, although right and wrong differ, others and oneself are equal.
【Explanation】"Discussion on Making All Things Equal": "Lì" is read with a falling tone.
"Lǐ" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
"And detest": "Wù" is read with a departing tone.
Nánguō Zǐqí leaned on his armrest and sat,
looking up to the sky and exhaling slowly,
appearing detached as if having lost his counterpart.
Yánchéng Zǐyóu stood waiting in front of him,
and said:
"What is this about?
Can the body truly be made like a withered tree,
and the mind truly be made like dead ashes?
The one leaning on the armrest now
is not the one who leaned on the armrest before."
【一】【Note】To unite Heaven and humanity,
to equalize self and other,
so externally there is none with whom to share joy,
yet silently dissolve into one body,
as if having lost one's counterpart.
【Commentary】He was the younger brother of King Zhāo of Chǔ,
the Minister of War under King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
and his courtesy name was Zǐqí.
The ancients were simple and sincere,
often taking their place of residence as their designation.
As he lived in the southern outer city,
he was thus called Nánguō,
similar to cases like Shìnán Yìliáo or Dōngguō Shùnzǐ.
This man embraced the Way and upheld virtue,
with an open mind that forgot worldly concerns,
so Zhuāngzǐ admired his purity and elevated character and placed him at the beginning of the discussion.
"Lèaning"
means to rely on.
"Sighing"
means to lament.
"Tàrán"
describes a state of release.
"Match"
means a pair,
referring to the body and spirit as a pair,
and things and the self as a dual match.
Zǐqí leaned on his armrest, sitting in oblivion,
concentrating his spirit in distant thoughts,
looked up to the sky and sighed,
wonderfully awakening to the natural way,
departing from form and discarding intellect,
his body slackened as if falling away,
both body and mind set aside,
things and the self both forgotten,
thus appearing as if he had lost his matching counterpart.

【二】【注】Dead ashes and withered trees,
are taken for their lack of emotion.
Those who follow nature and forget right and wrong,
in their bodies solely rely on innate genuineness,
so what else is there!
Thus, stillness is like standing as a dried-up tree,
movement is like waving a withered branch,
sitting is like dead ashes,
walking is like drifting dust.
The demeanor in action and stillness,
I cannot unify;
as for being unintentional yet naturally attained,
I cannot duplicate.

so that his form became no different from a withered tree,
and his mind indistinguishable from dead ashes.
There must be a wondrous method,
he asked to be shown the way.

now encountering the reclining desk,
it truly differs from times past.
He marveled at its serene detachment and absence of emotion,
hence expressing the intent of astonishment and doubt.

Zǐqí said:
"Yǎn,
isn't it excellent
that you ask this!
Now I have lost myself,
do you know this?
You have heard the pipes of men but haven't heard the pipes of earth;
you have heard the pipes of earth but haven't heard the pipes of heaven!"
【一】【Note】I have lost myself,
I have forgotten myself;
I have forgotten myself,
so what thing in the world is worth recognizing!
Therefore, completely forget the external and internal,
then transcendently attain both.
【Commentary】"Er",
means "you".
"Sàng",
means "to forget".
Approving of his question,
thus saying "isn't it indeed excellent".
Whereas Zǐqí had forgotten both realm and wisdom,
and severed both things and self,
Zǐyóu did not comprehend,
and thus was startled and doubtful,
therefore (Zǐqí) demonstrated the ability of leaning on the table,
"Do you somewhat know it or not?"
【二】【注】Lài,
refers to the xiāo.
Now, xiāo pipes vary in length,
with differing notes in the gōng and shāng scales,
hence producing myriad distinct sounds—short, long, high, and low.
Although the sounds are myriad and distinct,
the principle they embody is one and the same,
so then, superiority or inferiority has no place among them.
Comparing this to natural phenomena,
different sounds are all alike in this regard,
and each arises from its own source,
thus the lài of heaven and earth becomes apparent.
【Commentary】（Regarding the term "lài" (籁），
it refers to a panpipe，
measuring one foot two inches in length，
with sixteen pipes，
resembling a phoenix's wings，
created by Shùn.
The varying lengths of the panpipes，
each receiving air adequately，
serve as a metaphor for natural phenomena，
all endowed by nature，
hence these two sages are cited to elucidate the meaning of the three types of lài.

Although I have heard its name,

so I ask about the three types of lài,

Zǐqí said:
"When the great earth exhales its breath,
it is called wind.
It only does not blow,
but when it does, then all the hollows roar angrily.
And do you alone not hear its whistling?
In the towering mountains and forests,
the hollows and cavities of huge trees a hundred spans around,
are like noses,
like mouths,
like ears,
like square sockets,
like circles,
like mortars,
like depressions,
like pools;
[sounding like] rushing water,
whizzing arrows,
scolding,
inhaling,
shouting,
wailing,
moaning in the depths,
gnashing of teeth.
The front ones sing 'yú' and the following ones sing 'yóng'.
A gentle breeze brings a small harmony;
a whirlwind brings a great harmony.
When the fierce wind passes, then all the hollows become empty.
And do you alone not see the swaying,
the trembling?"
【一】【注】The Great Mass is
nothingness.
As for the exhalation of breath,
how could it be a thing?
The breath simply puffs out spontaneously from the mass.
In the birth of things,
all emerge spontaneously from the mass.
Thus, the substance of the mass is vast,
hence it is named the Great Mass.
【Commentary】"The Great Mass" is the name for the Creator,
and also a designation for Nature.
It means that the principle of Nature
universally generates all things,
without knowing the reason why it is so, yet it is so.
Within the Great Mass,
it exhales and emits breath,
and this breath is still called wind.
【Translated Text】"Dà kuài" is read with the pronunciation kǔ guài fǎn.

It describes the appearance of the great simplicity,
some scholars interpret it as "dà huái",
Bān Gù agrees.
The Huáinánzǐ writes it as "dà mèi".
Some interpreters consider it as non-existence,
some as primordial energy,
some as the undifferentiated whole,
some as heaven,
which are all erroneous.

【五】【Note】This briefly illustrates the similarities among the various openings.
【Commentary】The apertures and cavities,
are holes in trees.
The brackets,
are the wooden pieces at the top of pillars,
which are what we now call dougong (cap blocks).
The enclosures,
are pens for confining animals.
Since the tree is a hundred arm-spans around,
the holes are also exceptionally numerous,
so some resemble human mouths and noses,
some resemble animal pens,
some resemble human ear canals,
some resemble the brackets of buildings,
some are sunken and twisted with swollen protrusions,
some are low-lying and uneven.
Their forms and shapes are endless,
but these eight types are briefly described here.
It is just like the myriad things in the world,
which vary in kind and category,
some ugly, some beautiful,
all endowed by the forces of creation.

【Six】【Annotation】This briefly enumerates the distinct sounds of the many orifices.
【Explanation】"Jī" refers to
the sound of water rushing turbulently.
"Xiāo" is
the sound like that from the hole in an arrowhead.
"Chì" is
the sound of scolding.
"Xī" is
the sound like breathing.
"Jiào" is
the sound like shouting.
"Háo" is

"Yǎo" means
deep,

acting according to their innate tendencies,
none fail to achieve balance.

【Seven】【Annotation】The tones of gōng and shāng, though ever-changing in myriad ways,
in their harmonies and magnitudes,
all correspond to what they have received and each fits its proper measure.
【Commentary】Líng,
is a gentle breeze.
Piāo,
is a strong wind.
Yúyóng,
both refer to the sound of trees swaying and following one another in the wind.
Thus, the línglíng clear breeze,
produces a harmonious sound that is soft;
the swift and violent piāo wind,
produces a harmonious sound that is loud;
each corresponds to what it receives,
with neither superior nor inferior,
illustrating that all things are endowed with natural energy.
【Translated Text】"Chàng yú" is read as it is.
"Chàng yóng" is pronounced with the fifth tone and the initial consonant gōng.
Xú also has a pronunciation as yú.
Another reading is with the fifth tone and the initial consonant dǒu.
Lǐ says:
Yú yóng,
refers to the harmony of sounds.
"Líng fēng" is pronounced as líng.
Lǐ says:
Líng líng,
means a gentle breeze.
"Xiǎo hé" is pronounced with the initial h and the fourth tone.
The same applies to the following and annotations.
"Piāo fēng" is pronounced with the initial bí and the tone yáo,
or alternatively with the initial fú and the tone yáo.
Lǐ pronounces it with the initial fū and the tone yáo.
Sīmǎ says:
It means a swift wind.
The Ěryǎ states:
A whirlwind is called piāo.
"Bù chēng" is pronounced with the initial ch and the fourth tone.
"Qí fēn" is pronounced with the initial f and the fourth tone.
The same applies to the following without explicit notation.
【Eight】【Comment】Jì,
means to cease.
When fierce winds arise, all cavities become full;
when they cease, all cavities become empty.
Though fullness and emptiness differ,
in each achieving their state, they are the same.
【Commentary】Lì means
great,
fierce.
Jì means
to cease.
It says that when the great wind ceases, all the cavities become empty;
when it moves, all the cavities become full.
Though emptiness and fullness differ,
each attains its state equally.
Moreover, the waxing and waning of the four seasons,
the generation and destruction by the two principles (heaven and earth),
are without intent in their nurturing,
how could they purposefully engage in slaughter!
【Explanation】"Lì Fēng": Sīmǎ explains:
Great wind.
Xiàng and Guō explain:
Fierce wind.
"Jì": pronounced zǐ xì fǎn.
Xiàng explains:
It means to stop.
◎Qìng Fán's commentary notes: When the fierce wind ceases,
"jì" means to stop.
In the poem "Zǎi Chí" from the Yōng Fēng,
Máo's commentary states:
"Jì",
means to stop.
When the wind stops, then all sounds become silent,
hence it is said that all apertures become empty.
【Nine】【Annotation】Tiáotiáo (diāodiāo) [dāodāo],
describes the appearance of swaying.
It means that since the sounds of things differ,
the movements of their forms also vary.
Although the movements are not the same,
they achieve uniformity,
so how could Tiáotiáo alone be right and (diāodiāo) [dāodāo] alone be wrong!
【Commentary】"而" (ér),
means "you".
"调调 (diāodiāo) [刀刀]" (diāodiāo),
describes the appearance of swaying.
It speaks of how the forms of things differ,
and their movements also vary.
Although there are distinctions in their swaying,
ultimately, there is no difference of right or wrong.
Moreover, fullness and emptiness, gathering and scattering,
life and death, adversity and success,
are the natural principles of things,
inevitably so.
How could there be judgments of right or wrong, good or bad within them!
【Translated Text】"Tiáotiáo" is pronounced as tiáo.
"Dāodāo" is given by Xú as the reverse of dūyáo.
Xiàng states:
Tiáotiáo and dāodāo,
both describe a swaying appearance.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In old versions, both were written as diāo,
which is vulgar;
now they are changed to follow the standard form.
"Dòngyáo" is read as the characters' usual sounds,
also with the alternate pronunciation yángzhào.
【Collation Notes】(1) The variant text cites Li's edition: 翏 is written as 飂,
pronounced as lìqiè.
(2) The character 刀 is amended according to the Shidetáng edition and Lu's collation,
with corresponding changes in the following annotations and commentary.
(3) Likely missing two characters, "作喑," after "一."
In the chapter "Wandering in the North," it states: "The living are the yǐnyì of things,"
with the pronunciation note: yǐn sounds like yīn,
citing Lǐ and Guō's explanation:
"yǐnyì"
describes the appearance of gathered breath.
"喑气" also refers to gathered breath.
(4) The character 许 is amended based on the original version of the pronunciation notes.
(5) In the original Bàojīngtáng edition, 唯 is written as 脽,
which is incorrect.
This edition uses 唯,
also not accurate.
The character should be 虽.
(6) 由 and 犹 were used interchangeably in ancient times,
now distinguished by meaning,
and will not be repeated hereafter.
(7) The character 乌 is amended according to the original version of the pronunciation notes.
(8) The character 众 is amended based on the Shidetáng edition and the preceding annotation.
The Zhào Jiànyì edition also uses 异.
(9) The character 也 is added following the contextual pattern of the surrounding sentences.
Zǐyóu said:
"Earthly pipes are the myriad apertures;
human pipes are the arranged bamboo flutes.
I venture to ask about the heavenly pipes."
One]
【一】【疏】The sounds of the earth are from holes and cavities,
the sounds of humans are like those of flutes and pipes,
all can be seen with the eyes,
thus they can be understood.
Only the sounds of heaven are profound and mysterious,
difficult to grasp all at once,
I dare to present my humble thoughts,
and dimly seek resolution for my doubts.
【Explanatory Text】"Bǐ Zhú" is pronounced with the characters "pí zhì" as the phonetic components.
Another pronunciation is "bì lǐ" as the phonetic components.
Lǐ's pronunciation uses "fú bì" as the phonetic components.
The annotations follow the same.
Zǐqí said:
"The ten thousand things are blown upon differently,
yet each makes itself as it is,
each takes from itself,
so who is it that stirs them?"
【一】【注】This is the piping of Heaven.
Now the piping of Heaven,
is it some separate substance?
It is but the various apertures and bamboo tubes,
interacting with all that has life,
converging to form a single Heaven.
Non-being, being non-existent,
cannot produce being;
being, before it is produced,
cannot in turn produce anything.
Then by whom are things produced?
They spontaneously generate themselves.
They generate themselves,
but not by any 'self'.
Since I cannot produce things,
and things cannot produce me,
then I am spontaneous.
Being so of itself,
it is called natural.
It is natural,
not made,
hence we speak of 'Heaven'.
〔Speaking of 'Heaven'〕(一) is to clarify its spontaneity,
how could it refer to the blue sky!
Yet some say the piping of Heaven驱使万物服从自己.
But Heaven cannot even possess itself,
how much less possess things!
Thus Heaven is
the collective name for all things,
with nothing specifically designated as Heaven,
who then could主宰驱使万物?
Therefore things generate themselves without any external source,
this is the Way of Heaven.
【Commentary】Heaven is the collective name for all things,
a distinct appellation for the spontaneous,
how could it merely refer to the azure sky!
Therefore, what is called the piping of Heaven—
could it be some separate entity?
It is simply the blending of various apertures and bamboo tubes, connecting with living beings, that's all.
To seek what it is that generates life—
indeed, there is no such thing.
Thus, externally it does not depend on anything,
internally it does not draw from the self,
it arises abruptly,
transforming independently.
Hence, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
"That which is so of itself is called natural."
Therefore, to speak of it as natural
is to clarify its spontaneity.
And it is said that the myriad sounds differ.
Now, the wind is but one substance,
while the apertures are infinitely varied;
though they differ in size,
each corresponds to what it receives,
all following their own awareness—
how could they rely on anything else!
This is the piping of Heaven.
Thus we know that spring's growth and summer's maturation,
the eyes seeing and the ears hearing,
drawing examples from one's own body in proximity,
or attributing them to external things afar—
none know their cause,
all fail to discern their reason.
Let them be of themselves,
each fulfilling their own role adequately,
acting in accordance with their nature,
not guided by mind or intellect—
this is what is meant by "nurturing and maturing,"
and this encapsulates the essence of the piping of Heaven.
【Explanation Text】"Qǐ fù": read with the sound "fú yòu".
"Mò shì": read with the sound "dīng lì".
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the annotations of Wénxuǎn Xiè (Xuānchéng) [Língyùn]'s poem "On the Ninth Day Following Duke Sòng at Xìmǎtái Seeing Off Minister Kǒng", it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
chuī wàn,
means the weather breathes warmth,
nourishing all things,
with forms and energies differing.
yǐ,
means to stop,
allowing each to attain its nature and then cease.
The annotations in Xiè Língyùn's poem "Recalling the Mountains on the Road" and Jiāng Wéntōng's miscellaneous style poems quote the same.
The explanatory text is missing.
【二】【Note】All things attain this state naturally;
who is it that angrily compels them to be so?
This further elucidates the piping of Heaven.
【Commentary】"Self-attainment"
means achieving by oneself.
It speaks of how the openings of wind differ,
and their forms and sounds vary,
yet when each attains its own fulfillment,
there is no beginning that isn't equal.
But when agitation stirs to create sound,
who is it that makes it so!
It aims to clarify that all beings are entangled in complexity,
and all phenomena are uneven,
yet within their own allotments, they attain by themselves,
never lacking sufficiency.
Some fly, some run,
who causes them to be so?
Thus we know that whether drumming or agitating,
none can discern their ruler.
This is to further elucidate the meaning of the piping of nature.
【Explanation】"This heavy" is read with the retroflex initial and the rising tone.
【Collation】(1) These four characters have been supplemented based on the Shidetang edition.
(2) The two characters "Líng Yùn" have been emended according to the original text of the Wénxuǎn.
Great knowledge is broad and unhurried,
small knowledge is cramped and busy.
Great speech is clear and bright,
small speech is chattering and contentious.
In sleep, their souls interact,
upon waking, their forms open up.
Engaging with the world, they form connections,
daily their hearts contend.
Some are hesitant,
some are secretive,
some are meticulous.
Minor fears make them apprehensive,
major fears leave them disoriented.
Their outbursts are like arrows from a crossbow,
as they take charge of judging right and wrong.
Their retentions are like sworn oaths,
as they guard their victories.
Their decline is like autumn and winter,
signifying their daily dissipation.
Once they sink into their actions,
they cannot be made to return.
Their repression is like being sealed,
showing their aged and desiccated state.
Hearts near death
cannot be restored to vitality.
Joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness,
worry, lament, change, and stubbornness,
frivolity, recklessness, openness, and posturing—
music emerges from emptiness,
mushrooms form from steam.
Day and night alternate before us,
yet none know where they sprout.
Enough, enough!
Enough, enough!
Morning and evening we encounter this,
is this how life arises?
【一】【注】This likely reflects differences in understanding.
【Commentary】"Xiánxián" means
broad and ample.
"Jiànjiàn" means
to distinguish and differentiate.
Those who possess great wisdom and broad-mindedness,
follow their nature with emptiness and tranquility,
neither affirming nor denying anything;
whereas people with petty knowledge and narrow views,
have constricted and hurried spirits,
making choices and rejections.
[Making choices and rejections] (note 2),
hence they create divisions and distinctions;
having neither affirmations nor denials,
thus they remain leisurely and ample.
【Translated Text】"Great wisdom" is pronounced as zhì.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
"Xiánxián": Lǐ Yún said:
It means having no outward appearance or countenance.
Jiǎn Wén stated:
It describes a broad and extensive manner.
"Jiànjiàn": pronounced as gǔ xián fǎn,
meaning to make distinctions or separations.
◎Yú Yuè remarked:

"Petty wisdom is observant and discerning"

The explanatory text says it means to make distinctions,

【二】【注】This is likely a difference in dialect.
【Commentary】"Yǎnyǎn" means
fierce and intense.
"Zhānzhān" refers to
excessive and wasteful words.
When elucidating grand principles with profound discourse,
it is like a raging fire sweeping across the wilderness,
cleansing and leaving nothing behind.
The trivial arguments of Confucians and Mohists,
mired in contentious debates,
merely result in verbose excess,
offering no benefit to the methods of teaching.
【Interpretation】"Yányán": pronounced yú lián and yú fán with two readings,
also read as tán.
Lǐ's version writes it as dàn,
pronounced tú làn.
Lǐ Yí states:
It means agreeing with right and wrong.
Jiǎn Wén states:
A magnificent appearance.
"Zhānzhān": pronounced zhān.
Lǐ Yí states:
A trivial argumentative appearance.
Cuī's edition writes it as yán.
【Three】【Annotation】This likely refers to the difference between waking and dreaming.
【Commentary】Vulgar individuals,
with minds restless and agitated,
cling obsessively to past circumstances,
unable to find even a moment's stillness.
Thus, in their dreams,
their souls recklessly engage with illusions;
when they awaken,
their physical forms become exposed and susceptible to contamination.
【Interpretation】"Hún jiāo" Sīmǎ explains:
The spirit is interwoven and confused.
"Qí jué" is pronounced in ancient times as gǔ xiào fǎn.
"Xíng kāi" Sīmǎ explains:
The eyes open and the mind awakens.
【Four】【Annotation】This is likely an anomaly in the interaction.
【Commentary】Gòu means
to combine.
Jiào means
deep,
which refers to digging pits in the ground to store grain.
Mì means
hidden.
Engaging with worldly affairs,
combining the senses and their objects,
when deluded thoughts become heavy,
one feels the days are insufficient,
thus cherishing every moment,
the mind struggles with time.
The mind pursues external conditions,
with countless variations in emotions and dispositions,
to summarize briefly,
there are these three distinctions.
【Explanatory Text】"Engaging with others forms connections": Simǎ comments:
In human interactions,
one builds bonds of affection.
"The relaxed ones": (wèi) [mò] dàn fǎn.
Jiǎng Wén states:
It means a broad-minded heart.
"The deep ones": gǔ xiào fǎn.
Simǎ comments:
It means profound.
Lǐ comments:
It means a cave.
According to the case, storing grain in an underground pit is called a窖 (jiào).
Jiǎng Wén states:
It means a deep heart.
【五】【Note】This is likely an anomaly caused by fear and panic.
【Commentary】Zhuì zhuì means
apprehension and fear.
Màn màn means
dejection and dismay.
When circumstances are adverse or favorable,
the mind is constantly anxious and calculating,
worrying that things will not succeed,
with fear and dread intermingling in the heart.
Thus, with minor fears, one trembles and is filled with apprehension,
while with major fears, one becomes lax and falls into dejection.
【Transcription】"Small fear" is pronounced with a curved, brave tone.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
"Anxious" is pronounced as zhī ruì.
Lǐ Yún says:
A cautious appearance.
The Ěr Yǎ states:
It means fear.
"Calmly" Lǐ Yún says:
An appearance of equating life and death.
"Palpitate" is pronounced qí jì.
【Six】【Explanation】Jī,
is the trigger of a crossbow.
Guā,
is the nock of an arrow.
Sī,
means to control.
It is said that the mind's emergence to pursue objects
is as swift as an arrow's nock;
employing emotions to fend off harm
is as fierce as a crossbow's trigger.
It solely governs the judgment of right and wrong,
with no other implications.
【Translated Text】"Jī Guā" (ancient pronunciation: gǔ huó fǎn).
Jī refers to
the trigger of a crossbow.
Guā means
the notch of an arrow.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: In the Wén Xuǎn, Bào Míngyuǎn's "Kǔ Rè Xíng" commentary quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Speaking of life and death, right and wrong,
evaluating good and bad through mutual comparison,
then the arrival of disaster and ruin
is like the release of a crossbow's trigger.
The explanatory text is missing.
