) The Shì Míng explains:
A crossbow,
(implying force or anger) the part that hooks the string is called the tooth (yá),
outside the tooth is the housing (guō),
below it is the hanging blade (xuán dāo),
collectively named as
the mechanism (jī), meaning it is as ingenious as a machine.
(The meanings of jī guā and shū jī are different.
Shū is the door pivot,
jī is the door threshold.
Guǎng Yǎ states:
It is a ●.
● is the same as kǔn.
Shuō Wén explains:
Kǔn,
is the door threshold.
Wáng Yǐnzhī said:
Shū is the door pivot,
used for smooth rotation.
Jī is the door threshold,
used to stop the door.
Therefore, when shū and jī are mentioned together,
it refers to the regulated opening and closing.
In classical texts, jī and guā are both mentioned in the context of the crossbow's trigger.
【Seven】【Annotation】This likely pertains to the differences in movement and stillness.
【Explanation】"Zǔ" means
"to invoke curses."
"Méng" means
"to swear an oath."
It speaks of directing intentions toward right and wrong,
akin to invoking curses;
the mind grasps its objects,
no different from swearing oaths.
Firmly holding fast and resolutely,
the intent lies in overcoming external things.
【Transcription】"Zǔ" is read as cè jù fǎn.
"Méng" is pronounced as míng,
Xú reads it as wǔ gēng fǎn,
Guō reads it as wǔ bìng fǎn.
【八】【Note】Its decline and diminishment wane daily to such an extent.
【Commentary】When the bleak autumn withers and falls,
the harsh winter enforces its stern silence,
the scenes of nature shift and change,
swiftly as if passing by in a blink.
How could the foolish and deluded
ever become aware of it!
They only contend over vain rights and wrongs,
unaware of the daily renewal and decay,
the aging of humans,
whose condition follows this pattern alike.
【Translated Text】"Its severity" is pronounced with the initial 'sh' and the rhyme 'e' in the fourth tone,
while Xú reads it as 'sh' and the rhyme 'i' in the fourth tone.
The same applies to the annotations.
【九】【注】Thus, there were those who drowned and thus perished.
【Commentary】Being mired in worldly circumstances,
this has persisted for a long time,
the actions undertaken
betray the Way and deviate from truth.
Wishing to restore one's original nature and return to the source,
there is no means to attain it.
【Transcription】"其溺" is pronounced as nǔ dí fǎn,
while Guō's reading is nǔ jiǎo fǎn.
【一０】【Note】Those who are submerged in desires,
growing older and more deeply mired,
are indeed like this.
【Commentary】"Yàn" means
to sink and drown.
Those in the stream of delusion,
sink and drown in desires,
their confused passions firm and solid,
resembling being bound by ropes.
Not only do they indulge wantonly in their prime years,
but they even grow more deeply mired as they age.
【Explanation】"Its suppression": pronounced yā yè fǎn,
Xú reads yú yǎn fǎn,
also yú gǎn fǎn.
"Like sealed": Xú reads gǔ xián fǎn.
"Old channel": also written as overflow,
same meaning.
Pronounced yì,
Guō reads xǔ jú fǎn,
also jǐ zhì fǎn.
【一一】【Note】They benefit from avoiding calamities and taking misfortunes lightly,
secretly forming alliances to fulfill their ambitions,
there are those who act in this way.
【Commentary】Mò means
"without."
Yáng means
"life."
A heart that is addicted and stagnant
approaches the realm of death,
and if one wishes to return it to the path of life,
there is no way to achieve it.
【Explanation】"Near death" means close to it.
"Returning to life" refers to yang,
which signifies life.
◎Jià Shìfù said:
The day is spent with the heart in combat,
endlessly changing without exhaustion.
Those who govern right and wrong possess a mechanism of myriad responses,
while those who cling to victory hold a single, fixed view.
Some, long weary, think of turning back and wither like autumn's command;
others, deeply deluded and unawakened, drown in their actions.
There are also those who deeply conceal their mechanisms,
no longer retaining the vitality of the living.
The mutual entanglement of human hearts
each observes the mechanisms hidden within,
to probe and seize them.
【一二】【Note】This is likely a case of differing temperaments.
【Commentary】Ordinary individuals, in their foolish confusion,
become deeply attached to aversion and craving:
Craving brings joy and delight,
while aversion leads to sorrow and anger.
However, sorrow and joy are more profound,
whereas happiness and anger are relatively superficial.
Thus, happiness arises from inner contentment,
and joy manifests in dancing and clapping.
Anger is immediate resentment and hatred,
while sorrow involves full-bodied wailing and lamentation.
Worry entails brooding over the future,
and sighing expresses regret for the past.
Change means altering former ways,
and dejection implies submission without resistance.
Frivolity denotes restlessness and impatience,
and indulgence refers to extravagance and dissipation.
Temptation opens the door to desires,
and seductiveness embodies coquettishness and allure.
The minds and consciousnesses of sentient beings
transform and shift endlessly.
To summarize briefly,
there are these twelve aspects.
By examining them carefully,
the nature of human emotions becomes evident.
【Text】"Āi Lè" - the pronunciation of "Lè" is luò.
"Zhí" is read with the initial "zh" and the final "í".
Sīmǎ explains:
It means a motionless appearance.
"Yáo" - Guō pronounces it as yáo,
while Xú and Lǐ give it as chì diào.
"Yì" is pronounced as yì.
"Tài" is read with the initial "ch" and the final "ài",
and Lǐ also provides another reading as nú zǎi.
【13】【Comment】This likely refers to an anomaly in the transformation of events.
From this point upward,
it briefly illustrates the boundless nature of the heavenly flute;
from this point downward,
it clarifies the naturalness of boundlessness.
Each thing is inherently natural,
unaware of why it is so, yet it is so,
so although their forms differ ever more,
their being-so is ever more the same.
【Commentary】The xiao and guan flutes, being hollow within,
can thus produce elegant music;
the steaming moisture of humid heat,
can thus give rise to morning mushrooms.
This is like the two primal forces and the myriad things—
illusory and unreal,
born from non-being into existence,
just as with mushrooms and music.
Since fleeting illusions are thus,
how can joy and anger be applied!
【Transcription】"Zhēng" is pronounced as zhī yīng fǎn.
"Chéng jūn" is pronounced as qí yǔn fǎn.
Xiàng states:
It means to tie.
"Yǐshàng" is pronounced as shí zhǎng fǎn.
【一四】【Note】Day and night alternate,
replacing the old with the new.
All things between heaven and earth,
change and renew daily,
moving forward with time.
What causes them to sprout?
It is simply so of itself.
【Commentary】The sun governs the day and the moon the night,
their cycles revolving in succession,
alternately taking turns,
each preceding and following the other.
Delving into their origins and sequences,
none can truly grasp their true form.
【Explanation】"Méng" is pronounced as wǔ gēng fǎn.
【一五】【Note】It speaks of its spontaneous generation.
【Commentary】Cease,
means to stop.
Delving into day and night,
the before and after are hard to know;
stirring the mind to speculate,
is not as good as coming to rest.
Again, probing deeply into dawn and dusk,
examining darkness and light repeatedly,
still one cannot fathom their origins,
and fundamentally does not grasp their beginnings and ends.
Wishing to clarify that all phenomena in the world
are illusory and not real,
seeking the nature of birth and death,
one finds their very essence is quiescent.
Therefore, the Lǎojīng says,
"Meeting it, you do not see its head;
following it, you do not see its back."
The principle is thus.
【Transcription】"Dàn Mù" is also written as Mò,
with the same pronunciation.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang edition, where "xù" is written as "yì".
(2) Supplemented following the pattern of the sentence below.
(3) "Nù yě" amended according to the Shì Míng.
The following three characters "zé guā" are deleted in accordance with the Shì Míng.
(4) In the Shìdétáng edition, "qí" is written as "zì".
Without that, there is no me;
without me, there is nothing to grasp.
This is also close to the truth,
yet we do not know what causes it.
If there is a true ruler,
we simply cannot find its trace.
It acts and is trustworthy,
yet we do not see its form.
It has reality but no form.
The hundred bones,
nine apertures,
and six organs are all present within,
complete and existing.
With which of them am I to identify?
Do you delight in them all equally?
Or do you have a favorite?
Are they all servants and concubines?
Are these servants and concubines incapable of governing each other?
Do they take turns being ruler and subject?
Or is there a true lord among them?
Whether we seek and find its reality or not,
it neither adds to nor detracts from its genuineness.
Once we receive this completed form,
we do not forget it but await its end.
Clashing and grinding with things,
our journey ends like a gallop,
with nothing able to stop it—
is this not sorrowful?
Toiling all one's life without seeing success,
weary and exhausted without knowing the return—
is this not pitiable?
If people say one is not dead,
what good is it?
As the body transforms,
the mind follows it into the same state—
is this not the greatest sorrow?
Is human life truly so bewildered?
Or am I alone in this bewilderment,
while others are not bewildered?
If one follows their formed mind and takes it as their teacher,
who alone is without a teacher?
Why must it be those who understand change and have self-attained minds?
Even fools have them.
To have right and wrong before the mind is formed
is like setting off for Yuè today and arriving yesterday.
This is to take non-existence as existence.
Taking non-existence as existence—
even a divine Yǔ
could not understand it,
so what can I alone do about it?
【一】【注】That,
is nature.
Nature gives birth to me,
and I am naturally born.
Therefore, nature
is my own nature—
how could it be far away!
【Commentary】"Bǐ" refers to
nature itself.
"Qǔ" means
to receive or be endowed.
If it were not for nature,
who could give birth to me?
If there were no self,
who would receive from nature?
Thus, I am nature,
and nature is me.
The principle is not distant,
hence it is said that this is also near.
【二】【Note】All things are as they are,
each existing naturally,
not acting upon one another by force.
Therefore, by letting them be, harmony naturally follows.
【Commentary】It is said that I receive from nature,
its principles are already complete.
Feet walk and hands grasp,
ears listen and eyes see,
their functions are ready for use,
each has its own role.
Nurturing and maturing them,
they do not act by mutual command,
there is no need for deliberate effort,
simply let them be as they are.
【Transcription】"Xiāng wèi" read as yǔ wěi fǎn.
The following does not mean the same.
【Three】【Commentary】All things and all emotions,
their inclinations and aversions differ,
as if there were a single true ruler causing them to be so.
One sets out to search for the traces of this true ruler,
yet ultimately cannot find them,
thus it becomes clear that all things are spontaneous,
with nothing making them so.
【Commentary】Although the limbs differ in form,
their functions vary accordingly,
as if possessing an inherent nature,
yet ultimately lacking a governing master.
Where do the traces of their origins
come into being?
【Explanatory Text】"而特" Cuī (崔) states:
Tè (特),
is a particle.
"其眹" Lǐ (李) reads chú rěn fǎn (除忍反).
It means an omen.
"趣舍" is read qī yù fǎn (七喻反).
The character may also be written as 取 (qǔ).
The lower part is read shě (捨),
or sometimes shè (赦).
All instances below follow this pattern.
Qǐ suǒ "suǒ bǎi fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Now, as for the traveler,
they trust that their journey can be undertaken.
【Commentary】Trusting in oneself and acting accordingly,
following what satisfies the heart,
the natural mechanism unfolds on its own,
moving in accordance with one's nature,
self-sufficient and self-fulfilled,
how could there be any need to rely on external things!
【Five】【Annotation】The form by which it can be implemented is not seen.
【Commentary】All things act according to their own nature,
without manifesting any visible signs of trustworthy conduct.
【Six】【Annotation】When the emotion corresponds to the object,
its form does not appear distinctly.
【Commentary】There is the intelligence capable of action,
but lacks the physical form that trusts itself.
【Transcription】"Qíng dàng": Dīng làng fǎn,
all below are the same.
"Bié jiàn": Xián biàn fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】Entrust it to nature,
and all will be preserved without exception.
【Commentary】The hundred articulations refer to
the hundred bone joints.
The nine orifices
mean the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, mouth, and the two lower excretory openings.
The six depots
are the six bowels,
namely the large intestine, small intestine, bladder, and triple burner.
The term "depot"
refers to the five depots,
which are the liver, heart, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.
The word "gāi"
means complete.
It is said that the skeletal structure is on the outside,
the depots and bowels are inside,
and the orifices connect the interior and exterior.
These three aspects together form the whole body,
hence it is said to exist.
【Explanation】"百骸" is pronounced with 戶皆反.
"六藏" is pronounced with 才浪反.
According to tradition, the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys
are called the five zàng.
The large intestine, small intestine, bladder, and sānjiāo
are called the six fǔ.
The body separately has nine zàng qì,
corresponding to heaven, earth, and human.
Heaven is used to assess the qì of the head and corners,
human to assess the qì of the ears and eyes,
earth to assess the qì of the mouth and teeth.
Each of the three sections has its heaven, earth, and human,
three times three makes nine,
with five shén zàng,
and four xíng zàng,
hence nine.
Now here it mentions six zàng,
but the source is not seen.
◎ Lǐ Zhēn said:
The explanation states,
this mentions six zàng,
but the source is not seen.
Chéng's commentary then forced an interpretation, taking six as the six fǔ,
and zàng as the five zàng,
leading to inconsistency with the earlier explanation of the hundred officials and nine orifices,
making the interpretations not uniform.
According to the Nàn Jīng, chapter 39,
the five zàng can also be considered as six zàng,
meaning the kidney has two zàng.
The left one is the kidney,
the right one is the mìngmén.
The mìngmén
is said to be the dwelling place of the essence and spirit.
Its qì connects with the kidney,
hence it is said there are six zàng.
"賅" is pronounced with 徐古來反.
Sīmǎ explains it as complete.
The Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ agrees; Jiǎn Wén says:
It means comprehensive.
【八】【Note】It is simply that (two) exist.
【九】【注】If all explanations are spoken,
then there is partiality.
With partiality, one cannot be all-encompassing and preserve;
hence, without speaking, it naturally exists,
without acting, it naturally arises.
【Commentary】It is said that the six sense faculties and nine orifices
all belong to one body;
how could there be closeness or distance,
or private attachment and preference?
If there is deliberate attachment and preference,
then there is partiality.
To be partial toward one's own body
is unreasonable and unacceptable.
Everything is left to its natural placement,
each having its own inherent governance.
Since this is so for the body,
it is likewise for external things.
【Explanatory Text】"All said" is pronounced as yuè,
the same applies to the annotations.
Nowadays, many editions directly use the character yuè.
The same approach is followed in subsequent instances.
【一０】【Note】If everyone treats things as their own,
then ambitions exceed their proper bounds,
superiors and inferiors encroach upon each other,
and none will serve as ministers or subjects.
With the talents of ministers and subjects,
yet not content with the duties of ministers and subjects,
then error arises.
Hence, it is known that the relationship between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
like hands and feet, outer and inner,
is the natural order of heaven's principle,
how could it be something contrived by the perfected ones!
【Commentary】"Chén qiè" refers to the lowly status of men and women.
Moreover, within a single human body,
there also exists a distinction between ruler and subject.
For instance, when perceiving beauty, the eyes act as the ruler while the ears serve as subjects;
when walking, the feet act as the ruler while the hands serve as subjects.
This arises from natural principles—
how could it be something artificially created by humans!
It is not a matter of intentional closeness or distance
that establishes the roles of ruler and subject.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states:
"Those esteemed by the times become rulers,
while those whose talents don't meet the world's needs become subjects."
This principle applies equally
to governing a state and cultivating one's person—
there is no difference between internal and external.
【一一】【Note】Servants and concubines each have their own proper roles,
which is not insufficient for mutual governance.
Mutual governance means,
like hands and feet, ears and eyes,
the four limbs and all parts of the body,
each has its own duties and they function by mutually controlling one another.
【Commentary】Servants and attendants in their employment,
each have their designated duties,
just as hands grasp and feet walk,
each fulfilling their own roles adequately.
Would the hand, being insufficient, make the foot do the walking?
It is that the natural mechanism operates spontaneously,
unintentionally cooperating yet achieving order.
Using these hands and feet as an example,
all matters can be understood.
【Translated Text】"Ér gēng" is pronounced as gēng.
【一二】【注】Those who are deemed worthy by the times become rulers,
while those whose talents do not meet the demands of the age become ministers.
Just as heaven is naturally lofty,
earth is naturally humble,
the head naturally stays above,
and the feet naturally remain below,
how could there be any exchange?
Though not deliberately arranged, it is inherently fitting.
【Commentary】The head naturally resides above,
the feet naturally remain below;
the eyes can perceive colors,
the ears can hear sounds.
Yet their usage and neglect occur at different times,
hence there are distinctions of nobility and baseness.
How could this be due to deliberate intentions about high and low positions,
or alternating roles as ruler and subject?
It is simply that when appointments are made without conscious design, they naturally fall into their proper places.
【Explanation】"其遞" is pronounced as dì.
Xú further gives the pronunciation as dì.
"不應" means the response in a dialogue.
"無錯" is pronounced with the initial consonant as qī and the final as sù.
The same applies below.
【一三】【Comment】If things are left to their natural course,
then there is no falseness.
【Commentary】Simply set aside concerns and forget them,
there is no need for deliberate effort or intention,
this is the True Lord's wondrous path,
which resides within it.
Another explanation:
the True Lord refers to the true master mentioned earlier.
It means that the mind of grasping and rejecting,
colors like green and yellow,
originally lack self-nature,
they are formed through conditional combination,
neither self nor other,
neither non-existent nor existent,
hence hypothetical questions are posed,
to clarify that there is no true lord.
【14】 【Comment】 All who attain their true nature,
employing it for their own actions,
even if they are lowly servants,
still disregard praise or blame and find peace in their duties.
Thus, whether understood or not,
they remain self-composed.
But if paths of undeserved fortune are opened,
allowing the lower to encroach upon the higher,
things lose their authenticity,
and people forget their roots,
then in the realm of praise and blame,
every move becomes fraught with error.
【Subcommentary】When mind and circumstances interact,
desires and defilements arise therefrom.
Thus, obtaining what accords with one's feelings
is called benefit;
if one fails to obtain it,
it is called harm.
These words mean ordinary emotions are deluded and attached,
having gains and losses that disturb the heart;
when observed through the wisdom of the Dao,
there is neither harm nor benefit to one's true nature.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
When self and others are contrasted, right and wrong emerge,
and these mental distinctions of right and wrong
enter first and become the master.
Approving or disapproving,
following others to be driven,
all are like servants and concubines,
while the hundred bones, nine orifices, and six viscera are all subjugated to follow.
Now, this subjugation and following to be driven by others
and the mind's own mastery—
are they truly distinguishable,
or truly indistinguishable?
If the mind's mastery holds right and wrong,
what concern is it of others!
Seeking to obtain human sentiment to approve or disapprove
cannot bring benefit,
nor can failing to obtain it bring harm.
Yet once a form of right and wrong is constructed,
the mind is driven to follow it,
clinging unyieldingly throughout life—
this is what is called a "formed mind."
A formed mind
is why servants and concubines submit to being driven.
【Explanatory Text】"Suī fù" is read with the retroflex initial and the falling-rising tone.
The same applies below.
"Huǐ yù" is pronounced with the level tone.
"Wù sàng" is read with the voiceless initial and the falling tone.
【15】【Comment】It means each nature has its own allotment,
so the wise hold on to their wisdom to await their end,
while the foolish cling to their foolishness until death.
How could there be anyone capable of altering their nature midway!
【Commentary】All beings receive their physical forms and inherent nature,
each with their own limits and measures.
It is impossible to transform the foolish into the wise,
how could one change the ugly into the beautiful!
Thus, once physical form and nature are established,
they never vanish midway.
One should simply abide within their allotted portion,
and await the fulfillment of their natural lifespan.
【1.6】【Comment】The myriad beings in their multitude,
with adversity and compliance intermingling,
each trust in their biased views and indulge in their actions,
unable to reflect upon themselves.
This is what the multitude of people lament,
and indeed it is lamentable.
Yet the multitude have never considered this as lamentable,
for such is their inherent nature.
Since each thing follows its own nature,
then what thing is truly worthy of lamentation?
【Commentary】Conflict,
is opposition.
Compliance,
is accord.
The multitude of beings in their endless activities,
fervently chase after external conditions.
Since conditions can be either opposing or accordant,
the mind then clings to what is right or wrong.
Actions carried out over a full year,
pass swiftly as if in a gallop;
only aware of coveting conditions,
never once ceasing.
Reflecting upon the nature of things,
it is profoundly lamentable.
【17】【Comment】The desires of all beings are boundless,
and few are those who know contentment.
Thus, having attained this, they do not stop,
but chase after that instead.
All toil exhaustively their entire lives,
never satisfying their ambitions,
only ceasing upon death.
Therefore, the moment of their accomplishment is never to be seen.
【Commentary】All beings are driven by competition,
few know contentment.
Thus, gaining this without rest,
they chase after that.
Therefore, they toil exhaustively their whole lives,
perish in greed and cruelty,
clutching at shadows and chasing the wind—
when will their efforts ever bear fruit?
【Explanation】"Zhě xiān" is pronounced as "xī qiǎn fǎn".
【一八】【Note】All things are driven by their preferences to the point of exhausting their bodies,
until they become weary and drained.
They do not understand the purpose or the ultimate meaning behind these preferences they hold!
【Commentary】Wěirán describes
an exhausted and fatigued appearance.
Yet, with deep affection for what one loves,
the mind and spirit are toiled,
and once both body and soul are worn out,
one becomes wěirán and distressed.
Simply due to blind faith,
one becomes fond of such greedy competition,
and if we question their intentions,
they do not even know where they are headed.
Such extreme foolishness and ignorance
is deeply lamentable and pitiable.
【Explanation】"苶然" is pronounced as nǎijié fǎn,
while Xú and Lǐ pronounce it as nǎixié fǎn.
Cuī reads it as niǎn,
explaining:
a look of forgetfulness.
Jiǎnyuén states:
the appearance of exhaustion and illness.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
苶,
in the current annotated edition, is written as 薾 (five).
The Shuōwén cites the line from the Shījīng "bǐ ěr wéi hé,"
but the pronunciation and meaning differ from this.
◎ Qìng Fān's note:
苶,
Sīmǎ writes as 薾.
The Wénxuǎn annotation to Xiè Língyùn's "Guò Shǐníng Shù" poem quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
薾,
means an extreme appearance.
The explanation text is missing.
"所好" is pronounced as hūhào fǎn.
The same applies below.
【One Nine】【Annotation】It means that its reality is the same as death.
【Commentary】Xī,
means "why".
To be so deeply mired and stagnant,
trapped without ceasing,
damages one's conduct and endeavors,
and offers no benefit to the spirit and vitality,
it can be said that even on the days one is alive, it is as if one were in the years of death.
【二０】【Note】It speaks of one's mind and form both galloping away,
exhausted yet not turning back,
compared to what ordinary people grieve over,
this is truly the greatest of sorrows.
However, ordinary people have never considered this a cause for grief,
thus what they commonly mourn
is not worthy of sorrow.
【Commentary】So it is,
meaning it is like this.
Thoughts and moments continuously shift,
each new instant flows and fades away.
As one transforms and ages,
the mind and consciousness follow, becoming dull and obscure.
Both form and spirit change together,
hence it is said to be so with it.
Among the sorrows of the world,
none is more severe than this.
【二一】【Comment】All the matters above,
occur without knowing the reason why they are so,
hence they are called obscure.
Now, those who do not know all unknowingly come to know by themselves,
and living beings all unknowingly come to live by themselves without knowing the reason for their existence.
Although the myriad things differ,
when it comes to living without conscious knowledge,
there is none that is not the same in this regard.
Therefore, under heaven, nothing is not obscure.
【Subcommentary】Máng means
darkness and obscurity.
It speaks of how all people during their lives
are thus benighted and deluded,
the entire world is confused—
how could there be a single person who is not deluded!
But Zhuāngzǐ, as one who embodies the Dào and is a true person,
with wisdom that is clear and penetrating,
stoops to identify with the dusty common world,
hence says, "and only I am in darkness."
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation slightly deviates,
and now I do not follow it.
【Transcription】"Máng hū" mò gāng fǎn,
yòu yīn wáng.
Máng,
máng mèi yě.
Jiǎn wén yún:
máng,
tóng yě.
【二二】【注】The mind that is sufficient to govern the functions of the entire body
is called the established mind.
If people take their own established minds as their teachers,
then each person has their own teacher.
Since each person has their own teacher,
they entrust themselves to it and find it naturally fitting.
【Commentary】Those who confine their emotions and cling obstinately,
holding onto the biased views of a single school,
are said to have a preconceived mind.
Following and adhering to such a narrow-minded heart,
taking it as a standard to emulate,
if everyone in the world does this,
then who alone would be without a teacher?
【二三】【Note】To replace the unformed with the formed
is not a matter of knowledge,
but rather an innate understanding of the heart.
Thus, even the foolish follow their own formed minds,
unwilling to employ what they perceive as shortcomings and discard what they deem strengths.
【Commentary】Among the foolish and deluded types,
they stubbornly cling to their own views of right and wrong,
never considering that others' reasoning might be superior,
nor acknowledging their own shortcomings.
They only seek to criticize others' flaws
and claim superiority for themselves.
Such individuals
can be found everywhere,
and it is invariably the ignorant and unwise
who first fall into this category.
【Explanatory Text】"Yǔ yǒu" is pronounced as yù.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
According to Shuōwén,
"dài"
means to alternate.
What is considered right today,
may be deemed wrong tomorrow,
yet once fixed in the mind,
right and wrong emerge alternately without end,
hence it is said to understand alternation.
If the mind considers it right,
then it takes what is called right and affirms it;
if the mind considers it wrong,
then it takes what is called wrong and denies it;
hence it is said the mind makes its own choices.
"Ér shě" is pronounced as shě,
and the character is also written as 捨.
The same applies below.
【二四】【Note】If one arrives in Yuè today,
how could they have arrived yesterday?
If it has not yet formed in the heart,
how can right and wrong arise?
Those who understand right and wrong
are something the multitude cannot do without,
thus the perfect person accommodates both.
【Commentary】The road to Wú and Yuè is distant,
requiring the accumulation of weeks to reach;
if one sets out on the journey today,
how could they have arrived yesterday?
This aims to clarify that right and wrong, self and other,
arise from deluded thoughts.
If it is said that the mind has not yet arisen,
from where would right and wrong emerge?
Thus, differentiation comes first, and then right and wrong;
one must first embark on the journey before reaching Yuè.
【Explanation】"Xī zhì" Cuī says:
Xī,
means evening.
Xiàng says:
Xī zhě,
refers to yesterday.
◎Jiā Shìfù says:
Right and wrong,
are formed through the interaction between others and oneself.
Yet one's mind must first have a standard of right and wrong,
and thereafter deem something right and affirm it,
or deem something wrong and negate it.
The human mind responds infinitely to myriad things,
thus right and wrong also become infinite.
Right and wrong arise from the human mind,
which is why opinions about things are never uniform.
【二五】【Note】Principle has no right or wrong,
yet the deluded believe it exists,
this is treating non-existence as existence.
Once a deluded mind is formed,
even a sage cannot resolve it,
thus leave it to its own course and refrain from forcing understanding.
【Commentary】Xià Yǔ,
styled Wénmìng,
was the son of Gǔn,
and the father of Qǐ.
According to the rules of posthumous naming:
"Flowing springs and unimpeded streams are called Yǔ,"
and it is also said:
"Receiving the throne and achieving success is called Yǔ."
Principles inherently lack right and wrong, yet the confused create them,
this is using non-existence as existence.
Deluded attachments have long persisted,
the confused mind has become entrenched,
even if there were a divine sage like the great Yǔ,
he could not make them understand and awaken.
Zhuāngzǐ deeply cherished compassionate salvation,
yet what could he alone do?
Therefore, he left them to their own devices,
not forcing them to know.
【Explanation】"Bù qiǎng" pronounced with the third tone for its character.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it reads as "if there is action, there is existence."
(2) Zhào's edition originally writes "mù" for itself.
(3) (4) The characters "bǐ" and "cǐ" have been emended based on the Sòng edition and the Shìdétáng edition.
(5) The Shìdétáng edition writes "ěr."
(6) The character "jiē" has been supplemented according to the Dàozàng Jiāo Hóng edition.
Words are not like the wind blowing;
those who speak have something to say,
but what they say is not fixed.
Do they really say something?
Or have they never said anything?
They think it differs from the chirping of fledglings,
but is there really a distinction,
or is there no distinction?
How is the Way obscured that there comes to be true and false?
How is speech obscured that there comes to be right and wrong?
Where does the Way not exist?
Where does speech not apply?
The Way is obscured by petty achievements;
speech is obscured by flowery rhetoric.
Hence we have the rights and wrongs of the Rú and Mò schools,
each affirming what the other denies and denying what the other affirms.
To affirm what they deny and deny what they affirm,
nothing is better than clarity.
【一】【Note】Each has its own explanation,
thus differing from a uniform blowing.
【Commentary】Just as names and words are to the wind's blowing,
both are methods of sound,
and the speaker must engage in explanation and debate,
hence it is said there is speech.
【Explanation】"Chuī yě" is read as the character's usual pronunciation,
also read as chì ruì fǎn.
Cuī states:
Chuī,
is akin to a lái.
【二】【Note】What I consider right, others consider wrong;
what they affirm,
I in turn deny;
hence nothing is settled.
The lack of settlement
arises from the partiality in our respective viewpoints.
【Commentary】Although such statements exist,
they differ from the wind blowing,
yet all claim themselves to be right,
and unanimously declare others wrong.
Since both sides are emotionally biased,
the matter remains undecided.
【Three】【Commentary】Believes there are words, does it?
Yet it is not sufficient to establish anything.
【Four】【Comment】Do you think there are no words?
Then, according to oneself, there already are words.
【Commentary】"Guǒ" means
determination.
What one considers right,
another deems wrong;
what one considers wrong,
another regards as right.
Since right and wrong are not fixed,
what can words ultimately convey!
Hence, it is insufficient to claim there are definitive statements.
However, with biased views on both sides,
each clinging to their own right and wrong,
based on what they themselves say,
it cannot be considered that there are no statements at all.
【Five】【Annotation】Words and the chirping of fledglings
achieve the same end;
whether there is distinction or not,
truly cannot be determined.
The sentiments under heaven need not be the same, yet what is spoken cannot differ;
hence right and wrong become tangled and numerous,
with none knowing where to establish certainty.
【Commentary】"Biàn" means
to distinguish.
When a fledgling bird is about to emerge from the egg and chirps,
it is called the sound of a gòu.
It is said that it is still encased in the shell, hence called gòu.
Now, when people are one-sided and stubborn,
unable to determine right from wrong,
how is that different from the chirping of a gòu bird—
having sound but no distinction!
Therefore, to claim that one's speech differs from the gòu's chirp
is likely insufficient to be considered a true distinction.
【Transcription】"Kòu" is read as kǔdòu fǎn,
Lǐ pronounces it as gòu.
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to a bird chick that is about to hatch.
【Six】【Explanation】How can it be,
meaning where is it?
The ultimate Way is empty and penetrating,
neither true nor false,
so where does it hide that truth and falsehood arise from it?
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
The following instances are the same.
"Zhēn wěi" in one version is written as zhēn guǐ.
Cuī's version has it as zhēn rán.
【Seven】【Annotation】Where is the Dao not present!
Why do words become obscured and have truth and falsehood,
And the names of right and wrong arise in such confusion?
【Commentary】The ultimate teaching and the ultimate words,
neither negating negation nor affirming affirmation,
where could there be concealment or obscurity?
How could there be that which is right and that which is wrong?
【Text】"Dào yān" yú qián fǎn.
【Eight】【Commentaries】all preserved.
【Commentary】To exist means
to be present.
It molds and shapes living beings,
circulates without ceasing,
with its way reaching everywhere—
where is it not present!
Therefore, it is in both the artificial and the genuine, yet it is neither purely genuine nor purely artificial.
【Nine】【Annotations】All are acceptable.
【Commentary】The profound truth of the Way,
adapts to the nature of things, giving life or bringing death.
How could it be said to be concealed in any circumstance?
Thus, it can affirm what is right and deny what is wrong,
yet it is not about negating what is already negated or affirming what is already affirmed.
【10】【Commentary】Minor accomplishments refer to
virtues such as humanity and righteousness among the five virtues;
those who achieve some success in minor paths
are called having minor accomplishments.
When the world is shallow and times are decadent,
only humanity and righteousness are practiced,
unable to follow the great Way.
Thus, it is said that the Way is obscured by minor accomplishments,
yet the Way itself cannot be obscured.
Therefore, Lǎojūn stated,
"When the great Way is abandoned,
humanity and righteousness arise."
【一一】【Note】The minor achievements and fleeting glories,
though they conceal themselves within the Dao,
cannot truly hide the Dao.
Thus, truth and falsehood, right and wrong,
manifest through these glories but find their end in genuine appropriateness,
appearing in minor accomplishments yet vanishing in the greater whole.
【Commentary】"Flourishing rhetoric" refers to
superficial and argumentative expressions,
flowery and ornate words.
It is precisely because one is mired in flowery debate
that the ultimate truth becomes obscured and hidden.
Therefore, Laozi's classic states,
"Truthful words are not beautiful;
beautiful words are not truthful."
【Explanation】"Dàng" is pronounced with the tone of dīng làng.
The meaning can be inferred from context later,
and will not be repeated.
Appears in "Xiàn biàn fǎn."
【一二】【Commentary】In the past, there was a man from Zhèng named Huǎn,
who studied in the land of the Qiú family.
After three years, his skills were perfected, and he transformed into a Ru.
The Ru trace their origins to Yáo and Shùn,
take Wén and Wǔ as exemplars,
practice the way of benevolence and righteousness,
and distinguish the positions of noble and humble,
hence they are called Ru.
Huǎn's younger brother was named Dí.
Huǎn transformed his brother,
who then became a Mò.
The Mò,
follow the way of Yǔ.
They esteem the worthy and revere rituals,
practice frugality and universal love,
and would wear down their bodies from head to heel to save the common people,
this is called Mò.
However, the two, Huǎn and Dí,
though close as brothers,
each adhered to one teaching,
and constantly disputed each other's right and wrong.
Huǎn resented his brother,
and, overwhelmed with emotion, died.
Yet, the distinctions between self and other, right and wrong,
have existed for a long time.
The intensity of their contention
originated from these two worthies,
thus pointing to these two worthies as the leaders who disrupted the community.
This shows that when the Way is lost and words are obscured,
then the distinctions of right and wrong are strictly enforced.
【13】【Comment】The Confucians and Mohists each condemned the other's views,
yet the world was dominated by Confucianism and Mohism.
Thus, the hundred schools of thought arose simultaneously,
each clinging to their own perspectives,
without ever transcending their own frameworks.
【Commentary】Under heaven, none do not consider themselves to be in the right,
and regard others as wrong;
likewise, they too deem you wrong,
while holding themselves to be right.
Thus, each uses their own right to affirm the other's wrong,
and each uses their own wrong to negate the other's right.
【Transcription】"Gēngxiāng" is pronounced as gēng.
【一四】【Note】That which has right and wrong
is what Confucianism and Mohism affirm;
that which has neither right nor wrong
is what Confucianism and Mohism deny.
Now, to affirm what Confucianism and Mohism deny
and to deny what Confucianism and Mohism affirm
is precisely to clarify the absence of right and wrong.
To clarify the absence of right and wrong,
nothing is better than using Confucianism and Mohism to mutually illuminate through refutation.
Through mutual illumination by refutation,
what is affirmed is shown not to be right, and what is denied is shown not to be wrong.
If what is denied is not wrong, then there is no wrong;
【Commentary】The world considers others to be wrong
and uses oneself as the standard of right.
Now, to overturn wrong into right,
and right into wrong,
there is no better way than to employ their perspectives and ours,
comparing them back and forth to clarify.
Through this mutual comparison,
what is deemed wrong, if not truly wrong, then there is no wrong;
what is deemed right, if not truly right, then there is no right.
With no right, there is no wrong,
hence it is known that right and wrong are both illusory.
◎ Jià Shìfù said:
Guō Xiàng stated,
having right and wrong is what the Confucians and Mohists affirm,
while having no right and no wrong is what the Confucians and Mohists deny.
Now, to affirm what the Confucians and Mohists deny and deny what they affirm,
there is no better way than to use the Confucian and Mohist views to compare and clarify each other,
so that what is affirmed is not truly right and what is denied is not truly wrong.
Observing now the texts of Mòzǐ and Mèngzǐ's refutations of Yáng and Mò,
Confucians and Mohists mutually judge each other as right or wrong,
each relying on their own views to seek victory:
what Mohists affirm as right,
Confucians condemn as wrong.
This is how right and wrong come into being,
and how the distinctions between self and other arise.
Self and other have opposing forms,
and with right and wrong standing in opposition,
the right and wrong they hold are not true right and wrong,
but exist due to the persistence of self-other views.
There is no better way than to use clarity,
which means returning to what is clear from both self and other,
mutually drawing upon them for verification.
Guō's annotation is mistaken.
【Text Explanation】"反覆" is read as fǎn fú.
The same applies below.
【Collation Note】(1) The character '裘' has been amended according to the "Yú Fǔ" chapter.
All things are that (the other),
all things are this (the self).
Viewed from that (the other) they are not seen;
from one's own knowledge (of self) they are known.
Hence it is said: 'That (the other) comes from this (the self),
and this (the self) is conditioned by that (the other).'
This is the theory of the mutual production of this and that.
Nevertheless,
when there is birth, there is death;
when there is death, there is birth;
when there is approval, there is disapproval;
when there is disapproval, there is approval;
because of right, there is wrong;
because of wrong, there is right.
Therefore the sage does not proceed along these lines,
but illuminates the matter with Nature (Tiān),
and also follows this (principle).
This (the self) is also that (the other),
that (the other) is also this (the self).
That (the other) has a system of right and wrong,
and this (the self) also has a system of right and wrong.
Is there really a distinction between that and this?
Or is there really no distinction between that and this?
When that (the other) and this (the self) lose their opposition,
it is called the pivot of the Dào.
When the pivot is fitted into the center,
it responds infinitely.
The right is an infinite affirmation,
the wrong is also an infinite negation.
Therefore I say: there is nothing like using the light (of reason).
To use a finger to show that a finger is not a finger is not as good as using a non-finger to show that a finger is not a finger;
to use a horse to show that a horse is not a horse is not as good as using a non-horse to show that a horse is not a horse.
Heaven and Earth are one finger;
the myriad things are one horse.
【一】【注】All things affirm themselves,
hence there is nothing that is not right;
all things negate others,
hence there is nothing that is not wrong.
If nothing is not wrong,
then there is nothing right in the world;
if nothing is not right,
then there is nothing wrong in the world.
With neither wrong nor right,
thus is the profound unity achieved.
【Commentary】It is said,
All things affirm themselves,
hence there is nothing that is not right;
all things negate others,
hence there is nothing that is not wrong.
If nothing is not wrong,
then there is nothing right in the world;
if nothing is not right,
then there is nothing wrong in the world.
With neither wrong nor right,
mysterious unity is thus achieved.
This commentary exhausts the principle,
requiring no further explanation.
【二】【疏】Since they themselves are what they are,
this means they do not see themselves,
but knowing themselves to be right,
they then understand it;
as for things that are biased,
the pattern is always like this.
If one can truly see others and see oneself,
then there is neither right nor wrong.
【Three】【Commentary】When things are partial,
they all fail to see what others see,
and only know their own knowledge.
Knowing their own knowledge,
they then consider themselves right.
Considering themselves right,
they then regard others as wrong.
Therefore, it is said that "that" arises from "this,"
and "this" also depends on "that"—
"that" and "this" give rise to each other through mutual dependence.
【Commentary】That exists in relation to this,
right depends on wrong,
this is the fundamental principle of textual discourse.
Now, saying "that arises from this"
uses concise language and subtle reasoning,
to present the opposing position;
intending to demonstrate that by presenting that, this becomes clear,
by presenting right, wrong becomes evident.
Yet "that" and "this," "right" and "wrong,"
come into being through mutual dependence,
and when scrutinized and analyzed,
are found to be fundamentally empty in their essence.
【Four】【Comment】The transformation of life and death
is like the progression of the four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
Thus, although the states of life and death differ,
in each finding peace in their respective circumstances,
they are one and the same.
Now, the living consider themselves alive as life,
while the dead consider what the living call life as death;
then there is no life.
The living consider death as death,
while the dead consider death as life;
then there is no death.
With no life and no death,
there is nothing definite or indefinite,
hence the debates between Confucians and Mohists
are something I cannot agree with;
as for each being immersed in their own lot,
that is something I cannot differ from.
【Subcommentary】"Fāng" means
"about to."
It speaks of this and that, right and wrong,
no different from the discourse on life and death.
Now, the alternation of life and death,
is like the succession of cold and heat.
The living regard life as life,
while the dying perceive life as death.
Similarly, those who are right consider this as right,
and those who are wrong take this as wrong.
Thus, it is known that because of right, there is wrong;
because of wrong, there is right.
If right arises from wrong,
then there is no absolute right;
if wrong arises from right,
then there is no absolute wrong.
Therefore, there is neither absolute right nor absolute wrong,
neither absolute life nor absolute death,
neither absolute affirmation nor absolute denial—
so why debate over this and that?
【五】【注】Those who possess a broad and open mind,
base themselves on the world's rights and wrongs yet hold no rights or wrongs of their own.
Therefore, not following the path of rights and wrongs, yet having rights and wrongs without the worry of being improper,
is simply because they illuminate what is natural and are not deprived of it.
【Commentary】Heaven is
nature itself.
The sage attains enlightenment,
not using this to affirm right and wrong,
but directly abiding in emptiness and stillness,
illuminating with the wisdom of nature.
Only through this right and wrong does one attain neither wrong nor right,
ultimately not rejecting existence to separately realize non-existence.
【Six】【Annotation】I too am being acted upon by them.
【七】【Note】He too considers himself to be in the right.
【Commentary】I consider myself to be right,
yet am considered wrong by others;
I regard others as wrong,
while they also consider themselves to be right.
【Eight】【Annotation】This one also considers itself right and the other wrong,
just as the other considers itself right and this one wrong.
Both this and the other have within their own natures one aspect that is right and one that is wrong.
【Commentary】This side considers itself correct,
and that side also considers itself correct;
this side deems that side wrong,
and that side also deems this side wrong;
thus each possesses one correctness,
and each possesses one wrongness.
【Nine】【Annotation】Now if we wish to call that "that,"
yet that in turn considers itself "this";
if we wish to call this "this,"
yet this in turn is regarded as "that" by that;
therefore, the distinctions of "that" and "this," "being" and "non-being,"
have not yet reached a definitive conclusion.
【Commentary】Regarding the notions of self and other, right and wrong,
they stand in mutual dependence,
and upon repeated examination,
their entire substance proves illusory.
To deem oneself correct
is to affirm existence;
to be defined by the other as "other"
is to negate existence.
Existence and non-existence, self and other—
cannot be definitively determined.
【Transcription】"Bǐ Fù" fú yòu fǎn.
Same below.
【一０】【Note】"Pair" means
counterpart.
"That" and "this" are relative to each other,
yet the sage follows both.
Thus, one without a fixed mind merges with things,
and never stands in opposition to the world.
〔The pivot is
the essential point〕(1).
This resides at the pivotal point and converges with the profound ultimate,
to respond to that which is without fixed direction.
【Subcommentary】"ǒu" means
"duì" (corresponding).
"shū" means
"yào" (essential).
To embody that both sides are empty,
and both affirmation and negation are illusory,
concentrating the spirit to perceive alone without opposition in the world—
this can be said to grasp the profound ultimate,
and attain the essential pivot of the Way.
Previously, it provisionally questioned existence and non-existence,
with dependencies and refutations unsettled;
here, it further clarifies self and other,
inherently empty in their very substance.
The former is shallow, the latter deep—
hence the sequence.
【Explanation】"Dào Shū" is pronounced as "chǐ zhū" in reverse.
Shū,
means essential.
"Yǐ Yìng" refers to the response in dialogue.
The previous annotation is the same.
Later, one can infer the meaning,
and no further pronunciation will be repeated.
【一一】【Note】Disputes and contradictions
cycle endlessly without bound,
hence termed as a ring.
At the center of the ring,
lies emptiness;
now, by viewing disputes as a ring and attaining its center,
one finds neither right nor wrong.
With neither right nor wrong,
one can thus respond to all disputes.
As disputes are infinite,
so too are the responses limitless.
【Subcommentary】The state of transcending relativity and undergoing spontaneous transformation
constitutes the fundamental origin of the Dao,
and is the essential principle for learning;
hence it is called the pivot.
The ring
metaphorically has two apertures;
the center
represents the single path of true emptiness.
The center of the ring is empty,
illustrating the absence of right and wrong.
Since right and wrong are infinite,
responses to them must also be infinite.
◎ Jià Shìfù remarked:
When both right and wrong transform, the Dao persists within,
hence it is called the pivot of the Dao.
Grasping the pivot of the Dao to wander within the center of the ring—
the center
is emptiness.
Right and wrong revolve and recur,
chasing each other endlessly,
as if in a cyclical loop.
Wandering in this emptiness,
one is not enslaved by right and wrong,
and only then can respond to the infinite.
◎ Qìng Fān's case note: Táng Dynasty Buddhist scholar Zhànrán, in his "Zhǐguān Fǔxíng Chuán Hóng Jué," cites an ancient commentary on Zhuāngzǐ stating:
Because the inner emptiness of the circular ring embodies boundlessness,
it is called the center of the ring.
【一二】【Note】All under heaven consider themselves right and others wrong,
hence what is right and what is wrong
coexist endlessly without resolution.
Only those who navigate emptiness and attain the center,
open-minded and free from attachments,
can ride upon this and wander freely.
【Commentary】All things inherently affirm themselves,
thus affirmation is an endless cycle;
all things inherently negate others,
thus negation is also an endless cycle.
Only by forgetting both self and other,
discarding both affirmation and negation,
and attaining the Way at the center of the circle,
can one greatly harmonize with all living beings,
and ride upon it to wander freely.
【一三】【疏】指，
is the finger.
马，
is a gaming tally.
喻，
means to compare.
This speaks of how people hold fast to their own views of right and wrong,
with differing sentiments between others and oneself,
so they use their own finger to compare with another's finger,
thereby making the other's finger not a finger;
then again, using another's finger to compare with your finger,
your finger, in relation to the other's finger, again becomes not a finger.
Since the meaning of 'finger' is thus,
the same applies to 'horse'.
The reason for singling out 'finger' among all things
is to clarify that by looking close at one's own body,
nothing is more essential than the finger,
and by projecting afar onto objects,
nothing precedes the horse in determining victory or defeat,
hence these two examples are used to illustrate right and wrong.
【一四】【Comment】To consider oneself right and others wrong
is the constant condition of self and others.
Thus, using my finger to illustrate another's finger,
then that other's finger, in relation to my finger, uniquely becomes a "non-finger."
This is using a finger to illustrate that a finger is not a finger.
If, in turn, we use that other's finger to illustrate my finger,
then my finger, in relation to that other's finger, again becomes a "non-finger."
This is also using a non-finger to illustrate that a finger is not a finger.
To clarify that there is no right and no wrong,
nothing is better than reciprocally illustrating them.
By reciprocally illustrating,
then others and I,
since both adhere to our own correctness,
are also equal in mutual denial.
Being equal in mutual denial,
then under heaven there is no right;
adhering to one's own correctness,
then under heaven there is no wrong.
How can we understand that it is so?
If right were truly right,
then under heaven there could not be those who deem it wrong.
If wrong were truly wrong,
then under heaven also could not be those who deem it right.
Now, right and wrong have no master,
they are chaotically confused,
showing that these trivial matters are each believed through biased views yet converge in uniformity.
Looking up to observe and down to examine,
there is none that is not so.
Therefore, the ultimate person knows that heaven and earth are one finger,
the myriad things are one horse,
hence vastly serene and peaceful,
and heaven, earth, and the myriad things each assume their proper roles,
content in their self-attainment,
with no right and no wrong.
【Commentary】Though the world is vast,
it can be obscured by a single finger;
though the myriad things are numerous,
they can be fully comprehended through a single horse.
How do we know this is so?
Now, if we use the opposites of self and other, right and wrong, to mutually illustrate,
then what is considered right is not right,
and what is considered wrong is not wrong.
Thus, we know that the two realms and the myriad things
have neither right nor wrong.
【Explanatory Text】"Heaven and earth are one finger, the ten thousand things are one horse." Cuī's commentary states:
A finger is
one part among the hundred parts of the body;
a horse is
one entity among the ten thousand things.
"Hàorán" is pronounced with hù lǎo fǎnqiè.
【Collation Notes】(1) The three characters "pivotal importance" have been supplemented based on Jiāo Hóng's edition.
(2)(3) The characters "yǐ" and "fù" have been emended according to the Song edition.
(4) The three characters "then the world" have been supplemented based on Jiāo Hóng's edition.
What is acceptable is acceptable,
what is unacceptable is unacceptable.
The Way is formed by walking it,
things are called so because they are deemed so.
Why are they so?
They are so because they are deemed so.
Why are they not so?
They are not so because they are deemed not so.
Things inherently have what makes them so,
things inherently have what makes them acceptable.
There is nothing that is not so,
nothing that is not acceptable.
Thus, for this reason, we cite the small stalk and the large pillar,
the leper and the beauty Xī Shī,
the extravagant, the cunning, the strange, and the monstrous—
the Way connects them as one.
Their division is
their completion;
their completion is
their destruction.
In all things, there is neither completion nor destruction—
they return to being connected as one.
Only the enlightened know how to connect them as one,
and for this reason, they do not rely on distinctions but lodge in the ordinary.
The ordinary is
the useful;
the useful is
the connected;
the connected is
the attained;
when one attains this, one is close to the Way.
It is simply following what is so.
Following it without knowing why it is so—
this is called the Way.
To labor one's spirit and intelligence to achieve oneness without knowing its inherent unity—
this is called "three in the morning."
What is meant by "three in the morning"?
A monkey keeper distributing chestnuts said,
"I will give you
'three in the morning and four in the evening.'"
All the monkeys were angry.
He then said,
"Then, four in the morning and three in the evening."
All the monkeys were pleased.
The name and the substance were not diminished, yet joy and anger were employed—
this too is simply following what is so.
Thus, the sage harmonizes with right and wrong and rests in the balance of nature,
this is called walking both paths.
【一】【注】What is acceptable to oneself,
is called acceptable.
【二】【注】What is not permissible for oneself,
is called impermissible.
【Commentary】The principle itself is without right or wrong,
yet things have compliance and opposition.
Therefore, what aligns with one's intentions is deemed acceptable,
while what contradicts one's feelings is deemed unacceptable.
Since both compliance and opposition are empty,
it is known that acceptability and unacceptability are both illusory.
【Three】【Annotations】There is nothing that is not accomplished.
【Commentary】The Great Way is vast and expansive,
nurturing all living beings,
permeating all things,
and achieving everything without exception.
Thus, what can be accomplished is accomplished through what is possible,
yet it does not cling to the possible;
what cannot be accomplished is due to the impossible,
yet it also does not fixate on the impossible.
【Four】【Annotations】There is nothing that is not so.
【Subcommentary】The sentiments of creatures are topsy-turvy,
failing to comprehend compliance and opposition,
vainly scheming over right and wrong,
recklessly affirming and denying.
【Five】【Expositions】When both mind and realm are empty,
and both things and self are illusory,
upon what then is there a "so"?
Why cling to it as "so"?
Upon what is there a "not so" that makes it "not so"?
【Six】【Annotation】Each affirms what it affirms,
each approves what it approves.
【Commentary】Sentient beings are attached and obstinate,
encountering any circumstance they become deluded,
they stubbornly assert that something is so,
they stubbornly assert that something is acceptable,
how could they know that what is acceptable is actually unacceptable,
and what is so is actually not so!
【Seven】【Dissertations】The multitude of beings, and so forth,
each cling to their own views,
all affirming what they affirm,
approving what they approve.
【Explanatory Text】"Nothing is not so, nothing is not permissible." Cui Ben's version adds further: Permissible in what is permissible,
yet impermissible in what is impermissible;
impermissible in what is impermissible,
yet permissible in what is permissible.
【八】【注】The stem lies horizontally while the pillar stands vertically,
Lì is deemed ugly and Xīshī beautiful.
What is meant by equalizing
must not necessarily be equalizing forms and appearances,
nor unifying standards and measures!
Therefore, by citing vertical and horizontal, beauty and ugliness,
the vast, deceitful, strange, and bizarre,
each being as it is,
each acceptable in its own right,
though principles may vary in myriad ways, their natures are equally realized.
Hence it is said, the Way connects them as one.
【Subcommentary】For this reason,
eight matters are briefly cited to refute it.
Tíng,
refers to the roof beam.
Yíng,
refers to the house pillar.
Lì,
means a diseased and ugly person.
Xīshī,
was King of Wú's beautiful consort.
Huī,
is a term for broadness and greatness.
Guǐ,
is a designation for strange transformations.
Jué,
refers to a deceitful and cunning heart.
Guài,
means monstrous and aberrant things.
Now, whether aligned vertically or horizontally, beautiful or ugly,
things appear in myriad differences;
with broadness, cunning, strangeness, and aberration,
worldly sentiments use them to create inversions.
Hence, there are rights and wrongs, what is permissible and what is not,
confusingly clinging to their distinctions.
Now, viewing it through the mysterious Dào,
originally there is no duality,
thus, though the forms of beauty and ugliness are myriad and diverse,
the innate nature of self-attainment is singular,
therefore it is said: the Dào connects all as one.
【Explanation Text】"故為" is read as yú wěi fǎn.
The following occurrences of "為" are all the same.
"莛" is read by Xú as tíng,
and by Lǐ as tǐng.
Sīmǎ says:
It means a roof beam.
"楹" is read as yíng.
Sīmǎ says:
It means a house pillar.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Sīmǎ interprets "莛" as a roof beam
and "楹" as a house pillar,
hence Guǒ's remark that "莛" is horizontal and "楹" is vertical.
According to the Shuōwén dictionary:
means stem.
The interpretation as a roof beam
is not its original meaning.
In the Hànshū's biography of Dōngfāng Shuò, it says "striking a bell with a 'tíng'",
and in the Wénxuǎn's "Response to a Guest's Challenge", "tíng" is written as "筳".
Lǐ's annotation quotes the Shuōyuàn:
"If you set up the world's most resonant bell
and strike it with a 'tíng',
how could it produce any sound?"
"筳" and "莛" are interchangeable.
Thus, in ancient texts, "莛"
refers to something small.
"莛" and "楹" are contrasted in terms of size,
while "厲" and "Xī Shī" are contrasted in terms of ugliness and beauty.
The traditional interpretation is incorrect.
"厲" is read as is,
meaning ugly.
Lǐ reads it as lài.
Sīmǎ says:
It refers to a disfiguring disease.
"Xī Shī": Sīmǎ says:
It refers to Xià Jī.
According to records, she was the beauty presented by Gōu Jiàn to the King of Wú.
"恢": Xú reads as kǔ huí fǎn,
meaning large.
Guǒ reads it as kǔ huī fǎn.
The Jiǎnwén edition writes it as "弔".

Note that "弔" is read as dí.
The following character "" is the same as "詭".
"弔詭" appears later in the text.
