and Xú reads it as jiǔ bǐ fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means perverse.
"憰怪" is read as jué.
Lǐ says:
means contrary.
means strange.
◎ Jiā Shìfù comments:
What is acceptable or unacceptable,
what is right or wrong,
the enlightened set aside and do not use,
yet they embed utility within non-utility,
thus unifying them into one.
"楹縱" is also written as "從" in some editions,
with the same meaning.
Read as jiāng róng fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Things may be seen as scattered from one perspective, yet as complete from another.
【Commentary】Things may scatter here,
and gather there,
to illustrate that gathering and scattering are impermanent,
and cannot be rigidly fixed.
This further raises points for discussion regarding the principle of non-duality.
【Interpretation】"Its division" is read as the character's original pronunciation.
【一０】【Note】What I regard as completion, others might call destruction.
【Commentary】What may be considered completion in one context,
could be seen as destruction in another.
When it comes to the utilization of things,
such differences exist,
such as plucking feathers to make a felt blanket,
or cutting down trees to build a house, and so on.
【一一】【注】For completion and destruction arise
from seeing oneself and not seeing others.
Thus, without completion and destruction,
there is neither right nor wrong.
【Commentary】Affirmation and negation, right and wrong,
arise from partiality and fixation.
Since affirmation and negation are not fixed,
and right and wrong have no absolute basis,
therefore, there is no real affirmation or negation—
they are interconnected and unified.
【Translated Text】"Fù Tōng" fú yòu fǎn.
【一二】【疏】寓，
means to lodge.
庸，
means to use.
Only those who have attained the Way,
concentrating their spirit in profound reflection,
can thus discard those two biases,
and unify them into one.
For this reason,
they achieve success without dwelling on it,
using yet forgetting the use,
thereby lodging the use among all talents.
【一三】【Note】The enlightened are not confined to any single perspective,
thus they spontaneously forget themselves,
and entrust appropriateness to self-directed action.
Those who act self-directedly
invariably achieve clarity and self-fulfillment.
【Commentary】One who achieves the highest merit yet attributes it to all things,
governs millions yet entrusts tasks to diverse talents—
is this not the sage alone!
Thus, responding without conscious intent,
his spiritual awareness flows unimpeded,
truly embodying the Way in obscurity,
as if obtaining the Mysterious Pearl in the Red Waters.
【14】【Comment】Jǐ,
means to exhaust.
The ultimate principle is fully realized in self-attainment.
【Commentary】Jǐ means
to exhaust.
As for attainment,
internally it does not rely on the self,
externally it does not rely on things,
without thought and without action,
transcending learning and transcending dependence,
spontaneously attained,
indeed without any cause,
corresponding with principle,
thus it can exhaust the subtle.
【Interpretation】"Jǐ yǐ" pronounced as jī,
meaning exhausted.
Same below.
Xú Jùyī's annotation.
【一五】【Note】The enlightened follow what exists without creating anew.
【Commentary】The enlightened person who has attained the Way,
neither acts nor has a mind of their own,
thus they can follow right and wrong without being attached to right or wrong,
and conform to self and others without distinguishing between self and others.
They simply follow along accordingly,
how could they impose their own emotions!
【一六】【Comment】The enlightened person's following of what is so,
how could they know to follow it because it is good and thus follow it?
They do not know the reason for following, yet follow naturally;
therefore, it is called the Dào.
【Commentary】"Afterwards" is a term
that connects what precedes with what follows.
The ultimate person has no fixed mind,
responding only when stimulated,
like a bright mirror,
or an empty valley,
following the course of all things,
influencing living beings,
unaware of the reason for being so,
unaware of the reason for responding,
how could there be any personal preference for praise or blame, or attachment to gain and loss!
Adapting methods according to individuals,
this can be called the way of nature.
【Interpretation】"Called the Dào" is the punctuation by Xiàng and Guō.
Cuī reads it as "called the Dào and toil,"
saying:
Following spontaneity is the function of the Dào.
【一七】【Comment】The mysterious Dao and wondrous unity,
are constantly deep and tranquil,
not achieved as non-dual only after mental deliberation and strategizing.
Yet foolish people exhaust their spirits, stumbling through debates and arguments in pursuit of unity—
their approach is no different from that which is not unified,
and thus cannot be relied upon.
They do not understand the ultimate principle,
which is inherently undifferentiated and unified.
How could one need to consciously apply the mind
to then call it non-dual!
【一八】【Comment】This begins the analogy.
◎Jiāshìfù said:
It is called "morning three",
clearly taking "morning three" as its meaning.
As the chestnuts were distributed in the morning,
thus they were pleased to get four,
and angry to get three,
all because what they saw was only a corner of the immediate present,
hence it is called being conditioned.
The comment stating that unifying all things into one and considering them as one is no different from the confusion of the multitude of monkeys, interpreting "conditioned" in this phrase,
is greatly mistaken.
【一九】【Note】As for the one who is enlightened regarding unity,
how could they labor their spirit?
If one exhausts their divine intelligence in striving for unity,
it is not reliable,
and there is no difference from those who are not unified.
It is also like the confusion of the multitude of monkeys,
who, based on their preferences, consider themselves correct.
【Commentary】This explains the analogy.
Jū,
is a macaque.
Fù,
means to bestow.
Xù,
is an acorn,
resembling a chestnut but smaller.
Lièzǐ said:
In Sòng there was an old man who raised macaques,
and he was adept at understanding their intentions.
He teased the macaques, saying:
"I will give you acorns,
three in the morning and four in the evening,
is that enough?"
All the macaques rose up in anger.
He then said:
"I will give you four in the morning and three in the evening,
is that enough?"
All the macaques prostrated themselves in delight.
Three in the morning and four in the evening,
or four in the morning and three in the evening,
in terms of the total number seven,
they are exactly the same.
The name is not diminished,
nor is the substance reduced,
yet one brings joy and the other anger,
demonstrating foolish confusion in their use.
This is also like following one's own preferences,
and considering oneself correct.
It is similarly like toiling the mind and thoughts,
debating and embellishing words,
mixing all things into one and taking that as unity—
how is this any different from the confusion of the macaques!
【Text Explanation】"Jū Gōng" pronounced with seven and xú tones,
also read as zī and lǜ tones.
Sīmǎ explains:
Jū Gōng,
is an official in charge of monkeys.
Cuī states:
a keeper of monkeys.
Lǐ notes:
an old monkey.
According to the "Guǎngyǎ":
jū,
means macaque.
"Assigned Xù" pronounced as xù,
Xú reads it as shí and rǔ tones,
Lǐ pronounces it as yǔ.
Sīmǎ explains:
it refers to acorns.
"Three in the Morning, Four in the Evening" Sīmǎ explains:
three shēng in the morning,
four shēng in the evening.
"What They Like" pronounced as hū and bào tones.
The following text follows the same pronunciation.
【二０】【Note】Not favoring any one side,
thus entrusting it to self-balancing and then ceasing.
【Commentary】Heavenly Equilibrium refers to
the principle of natural and impartial balance.
The sage who comprehends the Way
maintains an open mind without attachment,
thus able to harmonize affirmations where none exist,
and align with negations where none are present.
This is how they quell intellect in the realm of equilibrium
and rest the mind in the state of natural spontaneity.
【Explanatory Text】"Tiān Jūn" is also written as "均" in some versions.
Cuī Zǐyún states:
"Jūn"
refers to a potter's wheel.
【二一】【Note】Entrusting the right and wrong of the world.
【Commentary】Without departing from right and wrong, one attains the absence of right and wrong,
hence it is called "twofold practice."
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "gè".
(2) The character "lài" has been emended based on the annotation below.
The people of old,
their knowledge had reached the ultimate point.
What was that ultimate point?
Some believed that there had never been anything—
that was the ultimate point,
the fullest extent,
beyond which nothing could be added.
Next were those who believed there were things,
but there had never been boundaries set.
Next were those who believed there were boundaries,
but there had never been judgments of right and wrong.
When judgments of right and wrong appeared,
it was because the Dào was impaired.
The impairment of the Dào
led to the formation of preferences.
Is there really such a thing as formation and impairment?
Or is there really no such thing as formation and impairment?
Where there is formation and impairment,
there is the playing of the lute by Zhāo Wén;
where there is no formation and impairment,
there is the not playing of the lute by Zhāo Wén.
Zhāo Wén's playing of the lute,
Shī Kuàng's rhythm-keeping with his staff,
and Huìzǐ's leaning against his desk—
the knowledge of these three masters was nearly perfect,
and they all carried it to the end of their lives.
But it was their fondness for it
that made them differ from others,
and their fondness for it
led them to wish to make it clear to others.
They sought to clarify what was not meant to be clarified,
and so they ended in the obscurity of discussions about hardness and whiteness.
And their sons, too, ended with the strings of their fathers' harps,
accomplishing nothing all their lives.
If such cases can be called accomplishment,
then even I have accomplished something.
But if such cases cannot be called accomplishment,
then neither things nor I have accomplished anything.
Therefore, the dazzling of doubts and uncertainties
is what the sage aims to avoid.
Thus, he does not use such knowledge but finds his lodging in the ordinary.
This is what is called using clarity.
【One】【Explanation】arrives,
the name for reaching the ultimate.
The pure ancient sages,
applied wisdom in subtle mystery,
though they again blended their light and mingled with the ordinary,
yet their wisdom was without knowledge,
their actions did not contradict tranquility,
constantly true and wondrous in essence.
The meaning of what is attained,
is detailed in the following text.
【Èr Shū】By posing hypothetical questions,
where does one reach the ultimate?
【Three】【Comment】This means forgetting heaven and earth,
abandoning all things,
externally not perceiving the universe,
internally not aware of one's own body,
thus able to be open and unburdened,
moving along with all things,
and responding to everything without exception.
【Commentary】"未始"
means "never yet."
All phenomena in the world,
are entirely non-existent;
only matter and the self,
both internally and externally, are equally empty.
The four propositions are all negated,
leaving a vast and tranquil void.
The principle is exhausted here,
with nothing further to add.
In response to the previous question,
the intent is to clarify the ultimate truth.
【Four】【Annotation】Although not entirely forgotten,
one can still forget their distinctions.
【Commentary】The great sage at the initial stage of learning,
bordering on the realm of the saint,
although perceives the distinction between emptiness and existence,
has never clung to them rigidly.
【五】【Note】Although one may not yet be able to forget the distinction between self and other,
one can still forget the right and wrong between them.
【Commentary】The desires of the senses are hard to eliminate,
as attachments to material things already exist;
distinguishing delusions is easier to dispel,
for views of right and wrong are still forgotten.
【Six】【Annotation】Having no right or wrong is what makes one complete.
【Commentary】To affirm what is not and deny what is,
reflects the shallow sentiments of the vulgar;
to neither affirm nor deny anything,
embodies the profound insight of the enlightened.
Thus, it is understood that when distinctions between self and others are emphasized, the ultimate Way remains hidden;
when debates over right and wrong cease, the subtle truth is fully preserved.
【Seven】【Annotation】When the Dao is deficient, then emotions become biased and attachments form,
unable to forget attachments and relinquish selfishness,
thus failing to mysteriously unite self and other (two).
【Commentary】The way of emptiness and mystery,
having already been impaired,
the feelings of attachment and desire
thus become prominent.
【八】【Note】Being and non-being,
this one cannot know,
and so it reaches the ultimate.
【Commentary】"Guo" means
determination.
The Way neither increases nor decreases,
while things may be deficient or complete.
Therefore, when things achieve completion,
it is said that the Way is diminished,
yet the Way is actually without deficiency.
Hence, a hypothetical argument is set forth to clarify its meaning.
Since existence and non-existence are not determined,
deficiency and completion are, in principle, not factual records.
【九】【注】The sounds cannot be exhaustively enumerated.
Thus, when playing wind or string instruments,
even with intricate finger techniques,
many sounds are inevitably omitted.
Yet those who hold the yuè flute or pluck the strings
aim to manifest sounds through them;
in manifesting sounds, some are lost,
while by not manifesting them, the sounds remain whole.
Therefore, one who seeks perfection but incurs loss—
this is like Zhāowén playing the qin;
one who does not seek perfection and thus incurs no loss—
this is like Zhāowén not playing the qin.
【Commentary】His surname was Zhāo,
and his given name was Wén,
an ancient master of playing the qin.
When Zhāo played the qin,
although it was said to be skillful,
striking the shāng note would cause the jué note to be lost,
and plucking the gōng note would miss the zhǐ note.
It would be better to set it aside and not play,
so that the five notes remain complete.
This is like having completion and deficiency,
where holding onto emotions leads to deviation from the Way;
having neither completion nor deficiency,
forgetting intellect is what allows one to unite with truth.
【Translated Text】"Kě shèng" pronounced as shēng.
"Cāo xián" with the initial consonant qī and the final dāo,
"Zhí yuè" with the initial consonant yáng and the final zhuó.
"Zhāo Wén" according to Sīmǎ:
an ancient master of the qín.
【一０】【Note】Jǐ means
to exhaust.
Those three masters,
all wished to argue and clarify what they themselves did not truly understand,
hence their knowledge was exhausted and thoughts drained,
bodies wearied and spirits fatigued,
some leaning on their staffs dozing off,
others reclining against parasol trees closing their eyes.
【Commentary】Shī Kuàng,
styled Zǐyě,
was the court musician of Duke Píng of Jìn,
profoundly knowledgeable in musical tones and rhythms.
Zhī means
a pillar.
Cè refers to
a drumstick,
also said to be a rhythm-beating stick.
Wú is
a zither;
but this is not considered so today.
Since Zhāo Wén was already capable of playing the zither,
how could two others share the same skill?
Moreover, checking the classics and records,
there is no text stating that Huìzǐ was skilled in the zither.
The mention of leaning on the wú
merely means using a wú table to lean on while discussing,
similar to reclining on an armrest.
Jǐ means
to exhaust.
Zhāo Wén excelled at playing the zither,
Shī Kuàng had a marvelous understanding of music,
and Huì Shī delighted in discussing names and principles.
Yet the natures of these three men,
endowed by heaven,
each displayed their abilities to the world.
The world failed to comprehend,
and they themselves grew weary and lax,
leading them to prop up their sticks and doze,
or again, lean on tables and close their eyes.
The abilities of these three
were all exhausted in this manner.
【Explanation】"Zhi Ce": Simǎ comments:
Zhi means
to prop up.
Ce refers to
a cane.
Cuī comments:
raising the cane to beat time.
"Jù Wú": Wú is pronounced as wú.
Simǎ comments:
Wú means
a zither.
Cuī comments:
it refers to string instruments like the qín and sè.
"Zhī Zhī": Zhī is pronounced as zhì.
"Ér Míng": Míng is pronounced with the fanqie spelling "wáng qiān fǎn".
【一一】【Note】Relying on its prosperity,
thus it can last long;
otherwise, it would have been exhausted early.
【Commentary】Those like Huì Shī,
all being in the prime of youth and robust,
were thus able to wield their physical and intellectual capacities.
But by the time of their declining years,
their vigor and acuity diminished,
they were bound to face prolonged hardship.
【Explanation Text】"Thus recorded in later years" Cui remarked:
It was written down to the present day.
【一二】【Note】It speaks of these three individuals,
who exclusively cherish what they themselves understand,
believing themselves to be distinct from the masses.
【Commentary】The three masters each indulged in their own preferences,
becoming deeply engrossed and delighting in them,
just as they were about to boast of their abilities,
considering themselves uniquely different from others.
【13】【Comment】It clearly shows everyone,
intending to make them share my preferences.
【Commentary】The reason why one exhausts one's body and spirit in ceaseless devotion to it is,
to make one's own doctrines and methods clear to all people.
【一四】【Note】This is like playing the reed organ to a cow.
They ultimately do not understand,
so one's own doctrines and methods end up remaining obscure.
【Commentary】"Bi" refers to
the multitude of people.
"Suǒ míng" means
the Way and its techniques.
"Bái"
refers to Gōngsūn Lóng's defense of the White Horse Discourse.
His surname was Gōngsūn,
his given name was Lóng,
and he was from the state of Zhào.
During the time of the Six States,
his disciples such as Kǒng Chuān
firmly upheld this discourse,
spreading it across the world,
silencing the mouths of the multitude,
but not convincing their hearts.
It speaks of how things possess different natures,
and what they favor varies individually.
Thus, it is understood that the ways of the three masters differ,
and are not comprehended by the multitude.
To forcefully display what is not understood
ultimately results in mutual obscurity.
How is this any different from stubbornly holding to the White Horse Discourse to dazzle and confuse the world?
Although the eloquence flows expansively,
in the end, there is speech but no reason!
【Explanatory Text】"On Hardness and Whiteness" Simǎ comments:
It refers to the debate on hard stone and white horse.
Also states:
Gōngsūn Lóng had a method for tempering swords,
called hardness and whiteness.
Cuǐ's opinion is the same.
Further states:
Some say,
proposing the theory of spear and shield as hardness,
debating the name of white horse as whiteness.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
"Fá" means shield,
also written as ●,
also written as 瞂,
the pronunciations are all the same.
"Gǔ huáng" is pronounced as huáng.
【15】【Note】Zhāowén's son continued the legacy of his father's literary endeavors,
yet ultimately achieved no completion.
【Commentary】Lún means
thread or continuation.
It is said that Zhāowén's son also bore his father's legacy,
carried on his endeavors,
exhausted his allotted years,
yet ultimately achieved nothing.
How much more so for others—
how could they dare to be negligent?
【Translated Text】"Zhi Lun" is pronounced as lún.
Cuī states:
It refers to the strings of a qín or sè.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
In the explanatory text, "lún" is pronounced as lún,
and Cuī says it means the strings of a qín or sè.
However, considering the context of "wén zhī xián zhōng,"
this meaning does not fit well.
Guō's annotation says,
Zhāo Wén's son thus continued the legacy of Wén,
which interprets "lún" as "xù" (legacy or thread).
Now, examining it based on the text's meaning,
the preceding passage states, "They tried to clarify what was not meant to be clarified,"
hence ended in the obscurity of 'hard and white'.
"Zhī mèi" (the obscurity) and "zhī lún" (the lún)
must correspond in parallel structure.
In the "Xì Cí Zhuàn" of the Zhōu Yì,
it says, "Therefore, it can encompass and understand the ways of heaven and earth,"
Jīng Fáng annotates:
"Lún,"
means to know.
In the "Shuō Shān Piān" of Huái Nán Zǐ,
"Using the small to understand the large,"
"using the near to discuss the far,"
Gāo Yòu annotates:
"Lùn,"
means to know.
The ancient characters "lún" and "lùn" are interchangeable.
In Huái Nán Zǐ, it is used in contrast with "míng" (to clarify),
so "lún" also means to clarify.
"Yǐ wén zhī lún zhōng,"
means to end with what Wén knew,
that is, to end with Wén's clarity.
For they tried to clarify what was not meant to be clarified,
hence ended in the obscurity of 'hard and white';
and Zhāo Wén's son ended with Wén's clarity,
which still amounts to clarifying what was not meant to be clarified,
therefore, the text below says, "thus, throughout life, they achieved nothing."
Guō's annotation does not fully grasp its intended meaning.
【16】【Comment】Although these three sought understanding from others,
those others ultimately failed to comprehend,
hence they achieved nothing throughout their lives.
If these three could be considered successful,
then even my lack of success could be deemed an achievement.
【Commentary】I am
one of the common people.
If the three masters differ from the common people,
and thereby consider themselves accomplished,
then since the common people differ from the three masters,
they too may be called accomplished.
【17】【Comment】All things understand themselves but not others.
If others are not understood,
one claims they are incomplete.
Then all things would mutually regard each other as incomplete.
Thus, the sage does not display this to glorify that,
nor does he abandon himself to chase after external matters.
Instead, he follows and entrusts them,
allowing each to darkly fulfill their own capacities.
Hence, he indirectly completes all without omission.
Now, these three men wish to make their own preferences clear to others—
is that not deluded!
【Commentary】If the three masters and the multitude of beings interact yet cannot be said to achieve completion?
Thus it is known that the multitude of people and the three masters,
both sides ultimately have no achievement.
【一八】【Note】The sage is without self.
Thus, the dazzling of confusing doubts,
is planned and confined;
the vast, bizarre, and strange,
is connected and unified;
causing all differences to rest securely in their own peace,
and the multitude not to lose what they affirm,
then the self is not used by things,
yet the utility of all things is employed.
If all things are self-utilizing,
then who is right and who is wrong?
Therefore, even in wild and unrestrained changes,
and crooked, peculiar anomalies,
bend and follow them,
entrusting them to self-use,
then though their uses are myriad and varied,
they become clearly self-evident.
【Commentary】The sage is one who,
aligns his virtue with heaven and earth,
matches his brilliance with the sun and moon.
Thus, he can conceal his traces like an ordinary person,
hide his light while interacting with others,
never dazzling the multitude,
nor confusing the common people,
nor boasting of himself to lead others,
but each confined within their own limits,
forgetting personal concerns and harmonizing with all things,
thereby entrusting utility to the talents of the many.
With such a mindset,
this can truly be called sagely wisdom and genuine knowledge.
【Interpretation】"Huá yí": ancient pronunciation as gǔ mò fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means chaotic.
"Qū qí": pronunciation as qiú wù fǎn.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Jiangnan Gu Zang edition as reading: "Although I have not achieved completion, it can be said to have been achieved."
(2) In Zhao Jianyi's edition, "I" is written as "this."
(3) The character "zhàng" (杖) has been emended based on the Shi Wen.
(4) The character "míng" (冥) has been emended based on the Song edition and the Shi De Tang edition.
Now suppose someone speaks here,
I do not know whether it is of the same category as this?
Or whether it is not of the same category as this?
Whether it is the same category or not,
when grouped together as a category,
then there is no difference from that.
Even so,
let me try to speak of it.
There is a beginning,
there is what has not yet begun to have a beginning,
there is what has not yet begun to have that which has not yet begun to have a beginning.
There is being,
there is non-being,
there is what has not yet begun to have non-being,
there is what has not yet begun to have that which has not yet begun to have non-being.
Suddenly there is non-being,
but I do not know which of being and non-being is really being and which is non-being.
Now I have already spoken,
but I do not know whether what I have called speaking is really speaking,
or whether it is really not speaking?
Under heaven, nothing is greater than the tip of an autumn hair,
yet Mount Tài is small;
no one lives longer than a child who dies young,
yet Péng Zǔ died young.
Heaven and earth were born with me,
and the ten thousand things and I are one.
Since they are already one,
how can there be speech?
Since I have already called them one,
One and speech make two,
two and one make three.
Proceeding from this onward,
even the most skillful calculator cannot keep up,
let alone an ordinary person!
Therefore, from non-being to being we reach three,
how much more from being to being!
Do not proceed this way,
but rely on this instead.
【一】【注】Now if we say there is no right and wrong,
then how can we know whether this statement is similar or dissimilar to those claiming existence?
If we wish to call them similar,
then I take "non-being" as correct,
while others take "non-being" as incorrect—
this makes them dissimilar.
Yet although their judgments differ,
they still cannot avoid having judgments,
thus making them similar to the others.
Hence it is said: "Similar and dissimilar ultimately become mutually similar,"
making them no different from the others.
Therefore, to achieve ultimate dissimilarity,
nothing surpasses having no mind—
first dismissing both right and wrong,
then dismissing the very act of dismissal.
Dismissing repeatedly until there is nothing left to dismiss,
then when neither dismissal nor non-dismissal remains, right and wrong naturally vanish.
【Commentary】"Category" refers to
groups of things that are similar in kind.
However, living beings are foolish and deluded,
clinging to "right" and clinging to "wrong."
Now, this discourse aims to reverse such worldly sentiments,
shatter these deluded attachments,
so it provisionally speaks of neither right nor wrong,
thereby using it as the true Way.
Hence, it further states "mutually forming categories,"
which then dismisses even the notion of neither right nor wrong.
Afterward, dismissing it again and again,
one finally reaches the profound mystery.
【二】【Note】The ultimate truth is beyond words,
yet words are used to convey its kind,
hence I tentatively entrust it to these words.
【Commentary】Cháng,
means to attempt.
Although the ultimate principle is beyond words,
without words, the principle cannot be explained.
Therefore, we attempt to use words
to approximate its meaning.
【Three】【Comment】Where there is a beginning, there is an end.
【Commentary】This hypothetical question is raised
to clarify that the ultimate Way has neither beginning nor end,
thereby dispelling notions of both commencement and cessation.
【Four】【Annotation】 This means there is no beginning or end, and life and death are one.
【Commentary】"Wèishǐ" means
"has not yet."
This is another hypothetical question,
asking whether there has never been a beginning or end.
This dispels the notion of having no beginning or end.
【Five】【Annotation】To unify them,
is not as good as not unifying them and yet they align naturally;
this, in turn, is to forget about the unification itself.
【Commentary】This again poses a hypothetical question,
suggesting there might be something that has never had a beginning.
This then dismisses the notions of having no beginning and no end.
【六】【Note】Where there is existence, there is the presence of beauty and ugliness, right and wrong.
【Commentary】All phenomena in the universe,
are entirely illusory.
Therefore, by pointing out this existence,
it clarifies that through existence one realizes emptiness.
This phrase dispels attachment to existence.
【Seven】【Annotation】Having 'having' and 'not having' yet not knowing 'not having not having',
then right and wrong, likes and dislikes are still not detached from the heart.
【Comment】A hypothetical question arises about the existence of non-existence.
Now it is clarified that not only does existence imply non-existence,
but also non-existence implies non-non-existence.
This statement dispels the notion of non-existence.
【Transcription】"Hǎo wù" are both read as they are normally.
"Wèi lí" is pronounced with the initial "l" and the rhyme "zhì" in the opposite tone.
【八】【Note】One knows there is no non-being,
yet still cannot be without knowing.
【Comment】A hypothetical question arises: has there ever been a case where existence and non-existence do not coexist?
This sentence negates the negative.
【九】【疏】A hypothetical question arises: there is what has never been, what has never had existence or non-existence.
This phrase negates neither non-existence nor existence.
Progressing from shallow to profound,
moving from the coarse into the subtle,
it begins with existence,
and ends with non-non-existence.
Thus it is clear that
it transcends the hundred negations,
and surpasses the four propositions.
The previous discussion of beginning and end
clarifies the aspect of time;
now speaking of existence and non-existence,
this distinguishes the nature of dharmas;
only time and dharmas
are both empty and tranquil.
【一０】【Note】This is entirely forgetting one's knowledge,
and then suddenly beginning to comprehend nothingness.
Comprehending nothingness,
then heaven and earth, all things,
self and others, right and wrong,
become suddenly clear and truly so.
【Commentary】Previously, we entered the root of neither existence nor non-existence through the traces of existence and non-existence;
now, we emerge from the substance of neither existence nor non-existence into the function of existence and non-existence.
The term "suddenly" is used
to clarify that substance and function are simultaneous;
in an instant,
it is certainly not distant.
For the mysterious Way is profound and obscure,
the true essence subtle and elusive.
Thus, when suddenly functioning,
it manifests existence and non-existence while being neither;
when functioning as substance,
existence and non-existence are neither existence nor non-existence.
Therefore, existence and non-existence are indeterminate,
substance and function are not constant.
Who can definitively determine non-existence?
Who can definitively determine existence?
This again uses the function of existence and non-existence to illuminate the substance that is neither existence nor non-existence.
【Transcription】"俄而" is pronounced slowly as "é".
"確斯" is pronounced with "què" in the fourth tone and "sī" in the first tone.
斯,
also written as 澌,
pronounced as "sì",
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as "sī lì".
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
斯 means to exhaust,
which shares the same meaning with 澌 and 賜.
【One】【Annotation】To claim there is no right or wrong,
is itself a claim.
【Explanation】"即復" is pronounced as fú yòu fǎn.
【一二】【Note】Again, not knowing whether to call it existence or non-existence,
thus one becomes utterly clear without the slightest trace in the chest.
【Commentary】"Wei" means
"to speak".
Master Zhuāng again does not speak.
The principle emerges through teachings that involve speech,
such as the previously mentioned "I beg to attempt speaking" category.
Since these words are employed to explicate the principle,
it is unknown whether these words are definitively speech,
or definitively non-speech.
To clarify that the principle is neither silent nor spoken,
the teaching is also neither absent nor present.
Fearing that learners might stagnate in textual literalism,
therefore these words are presented.
【Explanation】"Xiān jiè" is pronounced as gǔ mài fǎn,
also pronounced as jiè.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, jiè is written as jiè.
【13】【Comment】If we compare things by their physical forms,
then Mount Tài is larger than an autumn hair.
But if each thing abides by its inherent nature,
and all things reach their ultimate state in obscurity,
then a large form is not considered excessive,
nor is a small form considered insufficient.
If each is fully satisfied in its nature,
then the autumn hair is not uniquely small for its smallness, and Mount Tài is not uniquely large for its largeness.
If we consider nature's fulfillment as greatness,
then nothing under heaven is more fulfilled than an autumn hair;
if what is fulfilled in nature is not considered great,
then even Mount Tài could be called small.
Hence it is said: "Nothing under heaven is larger than the tip of an autumn hair, and Mount Tài is small."
If Mount Tài is small,
then there is nothing large under heaven;
if the autumn hair is large,
then there is nothing small under heaven.
Without small or large,
without longevity or brevity of life,
thus the ephemeral cicada does not envy the great chūn tree but is content in its own joy,
and the quail does not prize the celestial lake but finds its glory and wishes fulfilled.
If satisfied with what is natural and at peace with their innate destiny,
then even Heaven and Earth are not considered long-lived yet coexist with me,
and the myriad things are not considered different yet share the same attainment with me.
So, how could the existence of Heaven and Earth not be simultaneous?
And how could the attainments of the myriad things not be unified?
【Commentary】In autumn, animals grow fine fur,
the tips of which are extremely minute,
hence the term "the tip of an autumn hair."
A person who dies while still in swaddling clothes
is called an infant who dies young.
"Tài"
means great.
Now, in the birth of things,
their forms and vital energies differ,
some being small, some large,
some dying young, some long-lived.
Yet, if we speak in terms of their inherent nature,
none are not self-sufficient.
Therefore, taking inherent sufficiency as greatness,
nothing in the world is greater than the tip of a hair;
taking lack of excess as smallness,
nothing in the world is smaller than Mount Tài.
If Mount Tài is considered small,
then nothing in the world is large;
if the tip of a hair is considered large,
then nothing in the world is small.
Since small and large are thus,
so too are early death and longevity.
Hence, though the two realms (heaven and earth) are vast,
the sufficiency of their inherent natures is equal;
though the myriad things are numerous,
the principle of self-fulfillment is one.
Previously, it was clarified that there is neither end nor beginning,
neither being nor non-being;
here it is clarified that there is neither small nor large,
neither early death nor longevity.
【Translated Text】"Autumn Hair" as per the character.
According to the character, it should be written as "háo."
Sīmǎ explains:
Rabbit hair becomes fine in autumn.
Wáng Yì annotates the Chǔ Cí, saying:
It refers to sharp fur.
It is noted that fur becomes soft and fine by autumn,
hence it is used to metaphorize smallness.
"Dàshān" is pronounced as tài.
"Shāngzǐ" refers to one who dies young.
Some say:
Those under nineteen years of age are considered shāng.
【一四】【Note】All things and all forms,
find contentment in their own being,
thus attaining oneness.
Since they are already one,
there is nothing for principle to articulate.
【一五】【Note】Names and designations arise from lack of clarity.
Things may fail to manifest their own unity and thus chase after others through this,
hence the designation "one" is used to rectify them.
Once it is called "one",
there is already speech about it.
【Commentary】The profound Way is dark and quiescent,
its principle transcends form and sound,
yet to guide those lost on the path,
designations thus arise.
Therefore, although the One is a mysterious unity,
it still pertains to the realm of names and teachings.
Since it is called the One,
how can it be said to be without words!
【一六】【Note】To use words to speak of the One,
yet the One is not the words,
then the One and the words become two.
The One is already one,
and the words make it two;
with one and two,
how can it not be called three!
To use one word to speak of the One,
still results in three,
let alone tracing its branches,
where all things have different names,
even with good counting,
none can record them all.
Thus, those who unify are no different from others,
while those who forget the One are silent and naturally unified.
【Commentary】The principle of wondrous unity,
being beyond verbal expression,
thus shows that attempting to describe unity with words renders unity no longer word-bound.
Moreover, unity being established as one,
and speech further articulated;
with one and speech coexisting,
two designations arise.
Then, juxtaposing the later two designations
against the earlier wondrous unity,
with one and two present,
how can it not be called three!
Proceeding from three onward,
even if there were experts skilled in calculation and calendrics,
they could not reckon the ensuing numbers,
let alone ordinary people!
【Explanation】"Shū Chēng" is pronounced with the initial "chǐ" and the final "zhèng" in the falling tone.
"Shàn Shǔ" is pronounced with the initial "sè" and the final "zhǔ" in the falling tone.
【One Seven】【Annotation】The One,
is without words,
yet with words it reaches three.
How much more when tracing its countless derivatives,
could they ever be exhausted!
【Commentary】"Zì" means
"from."
"Shì" means
"to go."
The ultimate principle is without words,
and once words arise, names are established.
Therefore, proceeding from wordlessness to having words,
as soon as words are spoken, they reach the point of three.
How much more so when moving from having words to having words,
with branches and streams dividing into tributaries,
could they ever be exhausted?
This clarifies that all myriad phenomena
originally have no names,
but from nothingness, existence is born,
and thus it comes to this.
【一八】【Note】Each rests in what they are capable of,
which is the utmost correctness.
【Commentary】All phenomena are empty and illusory,
how could names and words alone be otherwise!
Thus we know that non-being is not non-being,
being is not being.
The names and categories of being and non-being
are fundamentally tranquil in their very essence.
Since one does not proceed from non-being to reach being,
how could one then proceed from being to reach being?
Therefore, one places no intention in comings and goings,
but simply follows the nature of things.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "qiǎn" is written as "yí",
and the same applies to the following instances.
(2) In Zhào's edition, "jì" is written as "cháng".
(3) The three characters "gǒu gè zú" are supplemented based on Zhào's edition and the Shìdétáng edition.
(4) The characters "ruò" and "fēi" are emended according to Zhào's edition and the Shìdétáng edition.
(5) The character "mìng" in Zhào's edition is written as "fēn",
while in the Shìdétáng edition, it is "mìng".
(6) The character "yǔ" is supplemented based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(7) In Zhào's edition, "wàng" is written as "wáng".
The Way has never known boundaries,
and words have never been constant.
It is for the sake of this that distinctions are made.
Let me speak of these distinctions:
there are left and
right;
there are relationships and
duties;
there are divisions and
distinctions;
there are rivalries and
contentions.
These are called the eight virtues.
As for what lies beyond the six directions,
the sage acknowledges its existence but does not discuss it.
As for what lies within the six directions,
the sage discusses it but does not pass judgment.
Regarding the historical records of the former kings in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the sage passes judgment but does not argue.
Thus, in making divisions,
there is what is not divided;
in making distinctions,
there is what is not distinguished.
It may be asked:
Why is this?
The sage embraces all things,
while the common people argue over them to show off to one another.
Hence it is said: those who argue fail to see the whole picture.
The Great Way is not declared;
the great argument uses no words;
the great benevolence is not benevolent;
the great integrity does not demean;
the great courage is not aggressive.
The Way that is displayed is not the Way;
words that argue fall short;
benevolence that is constant does not accomplish its end;
integrity that is too pure is not trusted;
courage that is aggressive does not succeed.
If these five are practiced, they will nearly lead to the right direction.
Therefore, knowing to stop at what one does not know
is the ultimate.
Who knows the argument that needs no words,
the Way that is not declared?
If there is one who can know this,
they may be called the Reservoir of Heaven.
Pour into it, and it is never filled;
draw from it, and it never runs dry,
yet one does not know where it comes from.
This is called the Hidden Light.
【一】【注】It is imperceptibly present everywhere.
【Commentary】The Way is omnipresent,
yet where it exists, it is as nothing;
vast and boundless,
how could it have any borders?
【Explanation Text】"The Way has never had boundaries" Cuī said,
it is the seventh chapter of the Qí Wù,
this connects to the previous chapter,
yet Bān Gù stated it is in the outer chapters.
【二】【注】Each speaks from their own perspective,
thus right and wrong are not fixed.
【Commentary】The principle is empty and all-pervading,
having no boundaries or limits.
Therefore, teachings adapt to the objects,
and likewise lack fixed constancy.
【Three】【Commentary】The Way has no boundaries,
thus all things can freely establish their own domains.
【Comment】Zhěn,
means boundary lines.
The principle has no limits or domains,
teachings adapt according to the changes in things,
for this reason,
the divisions of zhěn are not the same.
【Explanation Text】"For 'wéi shì'", read as yú wěi fǎn.
"With 'yǒu zhěn'", Xú reads as zhī rěn fǎn,
Guō and Lǐ pronounce it as zhēn.
It refers to the boundaries and field paths.
【Four】【Expositions】（Zhěn）hypothetically poses the question's intent,
to initiate the subsequent text.
【Five】【Annotations】Each has its own convenience.
【Commentary】Left is
yang,
right is
yin.
Although the principle is tranquil and quiescent,
teachings must adapt to circumstances.
Realms differ,
ascent and descent vary,
hence there are east and west, left and right,
spring and autumn, life and death.
【Explanatory Text】"There is left, there is right" Cui's edition writes as 宥 (yòu),
meaning 'in宽容 (yòu)'.
◎Lú Wénchāo (Lú Wénchāo) says:
The old version had Cui's edition writing as 有 (yǒu),
which is erroneous.
Considering the following statement 'in 宥 (yòu) also',
then it should clearly be written as 宥 (yòu).
Now corrected.
"Different conveniences" read with the fanqie 婢面 (bì miàn).
【Six】【Annotation】Every thing has its principle,
every affair has its proper way.
【Commentary】Lún means
order.
Yì means
appropriateness.
When myriad things are entangled and complex,
there is order present within them;
when all affairs are varied and uneven,
each follows what is suitable and convenient.
【Explanation Text】"Yǒu lún yǒu yì" - the Cuī version writes it as "yǒu lùn yǒu yì".
◎Yú Yuè says:
The explanatory text states,
the Cuī version writes it as "yǒu lùn yǒu yì",
which should be followed.
The text below says,
outside the six directions,
the sage preserves without discussing;
within the six directions,
the sage discusses without debating.
It also says,
thus, in division,
there is non-division;
in argumentation,
there is non-argumentation.
What is referred to as division and argumentation there,
corresponds to having division and having argumentation here;
then what is referred to as discussion and debate there,
corresponds to having discussion and having debate here.
【Seven】【Annotation】Groups are divided and categories are differentiated.
【Commentary】To distinguish means
to differentiate.
Although the flying and running creatures are numerous,
each has its own group classification;
the natures of things are immensely diverse,
and they naturally follow categorical distinctions.
【Explanatory Text】"Yǒu fēn" is read as it is pronounced.
The annotations are the same.
"Lèi bié" is pronounced with a rising tone on the second character.
The following instances are all the same.
【Eight】【Annotation】To pursue together is called 'contending',
to debate face-to-face is called 'striving'.
【Commentary】Creatures by nature are dim-witted and stubborn,
adhering obstinately to distinctions between self and other.
Consequently, they vie for victory and defeat,
debating right and wrong face to face.
【Explanation】"Zhēng" means the contention in a fight.
The annotation is the same.
【Nine】【Annotation】Briefly analyzed and distinguished,
there are these eight virtues.
【Subcommentary】Virtue is the name for
function and effect.
The functions and effects of all living beings
transform and change endlessly;
to outline and present them,
there are these eight types.
This then explains the earlier meaning of having boundaries.
【一０】【Note】As for what lies beyond the six directions,
it refers to that which is outside the inherent nature of all things.
Regarding the external aspects of things' nature,
although principles may exist there,
they are not within the inherent nature.
Thus, they have never moved the sage,
and therefore the sage has never discussed them.
If they were to be discussed,
it would be pulling all things to learn what they cannot.
Hence, by not discussing what is external,
the eight boundaries are equally attained through self-fulfillment.
【Commentary】The term "six directions" refers to
heaven, earth, and the four cardinal directions.
Beyond the six directions lies
the realm outside the inherent nature of all living beings,
the domain of the profoundly mysterious ultimate Way.
The profound principle is formless and elusive,
transcending the limitations of the four propositions;
the subtle truth is imperceptible and silent,
surpassing what is beyond the six directions.
Since it cannot be articulated even by divine speech,
it is therefore acknowledged but not debated.
【一一】【Note】Arrange their natures and bring them to peace.
【Commentary】Within the six directions,
it refers to the inherent nature endowed to all living beings.
Such choices and rejections,
all arise from deluded emotions.
Tracing back to their origin,
they are equally illusory.
The sage, responding to their opportunities and inspirations,
sets forth and responds to them.
Since it is said to rely on emptiness,
there is also nothing to discuss in detail.
Therefore, the text below states,
I too am speaking recklessly.
【一二】【Note】Follow the established path and solidify it to the utmost appropriate extreme,
without clinging to one's own correctness to criticize others.
【Commentary】The Spring and Autumn Annals represent
an era.
The classics are
canonical decrees.
The former kings refer to
the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
To record means
to document.
Thus, by tracing back to Xuānyú and Xū,
emulating Yáo and Shùn,
chronicling the times,
and forming them into canons and counsels,
they set a path for all living beings,
transmitting through human generations.
Yet, when sages deliberate,
they benefit their own time,
never rigidly clinging to debates of right and wrong,
nor stagnating in outdated traces.
【13】【Comment】Things differentiate themselves by their own nature,
and matters distinguish themselves on their own.
Those who seek to differentiate them according to their own views
fail to see that others distinguish themselves independently.
【Commentary】The principle itself is without distinctions,
yet things have right and wrong.
Therefore, within that which has no boundaries or domains,
to give rise to views that involve divisions and debates—
such are the scholars of narrow perspectives,
people stuck in partiality.
How could they possibly dissect the subtleties
or differentiate among matters and objects?
【Transcription】"故分" is read as it is pronounced.

【一四】【Commentary】Posing hypothetical questions to challenge doubts,
gives rise to the meaning and purpose.
【一五】【Comment】Holding non-argumentation in one's heart,
the sage has no such heart.
【Commentary】The sage who comprehends the principles,
with a mind attuned to the Way in obscurity,
is thus capable of embracing both self and others,
encompassing right and wrong,
like withered wood and cold ashes,
without any distinction whatsoever.
【1.6】【Comment】He did not see the other party's self-defense,
so he argued what he knew to show it.
【Explanation】The multitude of people,
which is another term for sentient beings.
Ordinary and deluded,
they have not yet understood the illusory and false,
hence they argue about what they know,
showing their perception through material things.
Not only do they fail to see the inherent distinctions of others, but they also do not recognize their own wondrous path,
thus it is said that there is something they do not see.
【一七】【Note】Refers to self-designation,
without any specific appellation.
【Commentary】The Great Way is vast and empty,
transcending form and name,
neither visible nor audible,
thus it cannot be described.
This means that those who embody the Way
likewise dissolve their voices.
【Transcription】"Bù chēng": chǐ zhèng fǎn,

【一八】【Note】Already distinct in itself.
【Commentary】Having profoundly comprehended the true essence,
there is nothing that can be described.
Thus, even when discoursing exhaustively on all things,
the words spoken are as if nothing has been said.
【One-Nine】【Comment】Exists of itself without affection.
【Commentary】Nurturing all beings,
loving without intention,
is like the springtime,
not an act of benevolence.
【二０】【Comment】The perfectly contented one,
neither welcomes nor rejects things as part of the self,
thus leaving no room for pride or humility.
【Commentary】Those who profoundly comprehend,
perceive through emptiness and existence,
knowing all realms are illusory,
with nothing worthy of greed,
where both self and objects are void,
what is there to yield or concede?
【Transcription】"Not modest" Guo's reading is with a deceitful tone.
Xu's pronunciation is humble.
【二一】【Comment】There is no direction that is not smooth,
thus there is no peril that cannot be ventured into.
【Commentary】"Zhi" means
to oppose.
Internally harboring compassion,
externally extending oneself to interact with others,
thus able to humbly conform to worldly customs,
graciously rescuing all living beings,
emptying oneself to respond to opportunities,
ultimately without any opposition.
【Interpretation】"Bù zhì": Xú reads it as "zhī chǐ fǎn",
also pronounced as "qí",
Lǐ reads it as "zhī yí fǎn".
It means to harm.
Lǐ says:
It means vigorous.
【二二】【Note】Using this to elucidate that,
both this and that are lost.
【Commentary】To proclaim one's own achievements and fame,
flaunting them before others,
this is but wanton artifice,
not the true Way.
【Explanation】"Dào Zhào" is pronounced as zhào.
【Two or three】【Note】Unable to reach their own portion.
【Commentary】Unable to remain in profound silence,
one becomes entangled in mere words and terminology,
employing flowery language and superficial arguments,
failing to grasp the profound truth.
【二四】【Note】Things do not have constant affection,
and constant affection inevitably fails to be all-encompassing.
【Commentary】Unable to forget affection and abandon knowledge,
mysteriously uniting others and self,
yet constantly harboring kindness,
always embracing familial feelings,
wishing to demonstrate achievements,
but finding no opportunity to manifest them.
【二五】【注】Distinctly honest and pure,
is merely one who covets fame,
not truly incorruptible.
【Commentary】Brilliantly different from the common customs,
outstanding and unmatched by the crowd,
his intention lay in fame and reputation,
not in genuine integrity.
【二六】【Note】The courage of defiance and rebellion,
is detested by all under heaven,
leaving no ground to set foot on.
【Commentary】To abandon compassion and yet be brave,
is to act against the nature of things,
causing the multitude to detest it,
and inevitably leading to no successful outcome.
【二七】【注】These five things,
all injure what is proper through forced action,
failing to rest in their innate nature,
yet seeking endlessly from without.
What lies outside cannot be sought yet they seek it,
comparable to using a circle to learn squareness,
or a fish admiring birds.
Though they may aspire to be like the luán and fèng phoenixes,
or emulate the sun and moon in their regularity,
the closer they approach those ideals,
the farther they stray from reality,
and the more they acquire through learning, the more they lose of their nature.
Therefore, by equalizing all things, the burden of partial preferences is removed.
【Commentary】Round,
means circular.
Nearly,

Therefore, in ancient times, Yáo asked Shùn, saying:
"I wish to attack Zōng, Kuài, and Xū Áo,
yet even when facing south on the throne, I feel unsettled.
What is the reason for this?"
Shùn replied:
"Those three rulers,
still exist among the brushwood and mugwort.
If you feel unsettled,
why is that?
In ancient times, ten suns rose together,
and all things were illuminated by them—
how much more so by virtue that surpasses the sun!"
【一】【Note】Because the way of peaceful governance had not yet been widely practiced,

Zōng, Kuài, and Xū Áo
were the names of three small vassal states during Yáo's time.
"Facing south"

Shùn
was the sixth-generation descendant of Zhuānxū.
His father was Gǔsǒu,
his mother was Wòdēng,
who conceived Shùn after sensing a great rainbow.
Shùn was born at Yáoxū,
hence he took the surname Yáo.
He resided by the Guī River,
and was also called Guīshì.
He had double pupils in his eyes,
hence his courtesy name was Chónghuá.
Renowned for benevolence and filial piety in his locality,
Yáo heard of his virtue,
married him to his two daughters,
and enfeoffed him at Yú.
At age thirty,
he oversaw all administrative affairs,
and at thirty-three,
he received Yáo's abdication.
After ascending the throne,
he established his capital at Púbǎn.
He reigned for forty years,
then yielded the throne to Yǔ.
After his demise,
he was buried in the wilderness of Cāngwú.
As the three states had defaulted on their tributes,
it was necessary to hold them accountable,
but with plans unsettled,
he attended court displeased.
To elucidate the principle of equalizing things,
the dialogue was thus attributed to the two sages.

As the Huáinánzǐ states,
in the time of Yáo, ten suns once rose together,
scorching the grains and crops,
withering the plants and trees,
while monstrous boars and giant serpents
all became plagues to the people.
Thereupon, Yáo sent Yì to shoot down the ten suns from above,
and thus nine of them fell;
below, he slew the giant serpents,
thereby eliminating the people's plagues.
Now, when ten suns ascend to the heavens,
illuminating all six directions,
even a place hidden under an overturned basin
may still remain unlit.
Yet, where sagely virtue reaches,
no darkness goes unillumined.
Wielding these two wisdoms,
surpassing those three lights,
and then wishing to stir up arms
to compel others to follow oneself—
in the way of governing with tranquility and trust,
can this truly be called broad and penetrating?
