the current version mistakenly writes xiáo as sǎn.
In Huáinánzǐ's Yuán Dào Piān,
"not mixing with things,"
"the epitome of purity,"
and in Jīng Shén Piān,
"not mixing with things, and the world naturally submits,"
the current versions both mistakenly write it as sǎn.
(Gāo's annotation says:
sǎn,
means mixed appearance.
Examining the usage of sǎn in various texts,
it does not carry the meaning of disorderly,
hence sǎn should all be xiáo.
) "Zhī jìng" pronounced as jìng.
Most current versions write it as jìng.
The same applies below.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào counsel version lacks the character 'gù'.
(2) The Zhào version omits the two characters 'lüè jǔ' and the character 'yǐ' in 'zhī'.
(3) The character 'dòng' has been amended according to the original text of the correct meaning.
(4) The character 'hòu' has been supplemented based on the original text of the Shǐjì.
Niè Quē said:
"If you do not know benefit and harm,
then would the perfect person inherently not know benefit and harm?"
【One】【Annotation】Unable to fully grasp the nature of not knowing,
thus still harboring doubt that the ultimate person ought to know.
This is a dilemma yet unresolved.
【Commentary】Niè Quē said,
not yet realizing that neither side understands the other,
he further raised doubts about gains and losses.
He asked:
"You are a perfect man,
you ought to know gains and losses.
If you truly do not distinguish them,
you are as lost and benighted as one wandering at night."
He posed this challenge again,
hoping to elicit a later response.
【Text】"Wèi jiě" is pronounced as xiè.
Wáng Ní said:
"The perfect person is divine!
When great marshes burn, they cannot make him hot;
when the Yellow River and Han River freeze, they cannot make him cold;
when violent thunder splits mountains and fierce winds shake seas, they cannot startle him.
Being such a one,
he rides upon the clouds and mists,
mounts the sun and moon,
and wanders beyond the four seas.
Death and life cause no change in him,
how much less the concepts of benefit and harm!"
【一】【Note】Without intention, yet nothing is not in accord.
【Commentary】The Ultimate is the substance of sublime perfection;
the Divine is the function of the unfathomable.
The sage empties himself,
responding to things without fixed methods,
knowing yet not knowing,
discerning yet not discerning.
How could one use words, thoughts, or conjectures to comprehend the Perfect Person!
【二】【注】When one's spirit is whole and form complete, and the body merges with all things,
even when encountering the most extreme changes, it never ceases to be oneself.
Therefore, there is a vast emptiness without the slightest sting of resentment in the chest.
【Commentary】Hù means
frozen.
Though plains and marshes burn and blaze,
and rivers and the Milky Way freeze solid,
with thunderbolts bursting forth to shatter mountains,
and raging winds surging wildly to shake the seas,
the ultimate person, with spirit concentrated and no signs emerging,
embodies unity with all things.
Since water and fire bring no disaster to them,
how could wind and thunder startle or alarm them?
【Explanation】"沍" is pronounced as hù with a falling tone.
Xú further gives the pronunciation as hè with a falling tone.
Lǐ pronounces it as hè with a high-level tone.
Xiàng says:
It means frozen.
Cuī says:
沍,
is akin to dried up.
◎Jiāshìfù remarks:
Even if a great flood reaches the heavens, one is not drowned;
in a severe drought when metal and stone melt and mountains scorch, one does not feel the heat.
By not letting external matters become one's concern,
and preserving the creation and transformation of heaven and earth within one's own heart,
then the external environment cannot burden one.
This is how Zhuāngzǐ aspires for himself,
hence he frequently touches upon it.
"蠆" is pronounced as chài with a falling tone,
also pronounced as zhì.
"介" is pronounced as guài with a falling tone,
also pronounced as jiè.
【Three】【Comment】Entrusting things and moving on,
it is not I who act.
【Commentary】If so,
it is still like this.
Empty and indifferent without intent,
comparable to clouds and mist,
it shelters all beings,
and acts in accordance with things.
【Four】【Annotation】There is day and night, but no death and life.
【Commentary】The alternation of darkness and light,
allows for the distinction between day and night;
abiding in harmony and accepting the times,
there is no difference between life and death.
Yet, to control and guide all creatures,
and to transport all living beings,
thus arises the concept of riding and harnessing.
【五】【注】Only by being without knowledge and letting the world act on its own,
can one gallop through all things without exhaustion.
【Commentary】Movement and stillness are simultaneous,
the mysterious response is instantaneous,
sitting upright within the cosmos,
yet the mind wanders beyond the four seas.
【Six】【Comment】Being one with transformation as the essence,
thus death and life are as if one.
【Seven】【Annotation】Considering the triviality of gains and losses in the face of life and death,
it becomes even less worthy of concern.
【Commentary】Gains and losses are but the fluctuations of life's journey.
Since life and death are as natural as day and night,
and one rides the transformations to roam freely,
how much less should gains and losses compared to life and death
ever be worth troubling one's mind about!
【Collation Note】(1) The character "piāo" was added based on the version by Junior Censor Zhào.
(2) The character "chài" was amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Què Zǐ asked Cháng Wú Zǐ, saying:
"I have heard from the Master that
the sage does not engage in worldly affairs,
does not pursue profit,
does not avoid harm,
does not delight in seeking,
does not follow the path;
speaking without speaking,
not speaking yet speaking,
he roams beyond the dust and grime.
The Master considered these wild and rash words,
but I regard them as the way of sublime truth.
What do you, my good sir, think of this?
【一】【Note】Matters come of themselves and principles respond accordingly,
it is not a case of following and serving them.
【Commentary】"Wù" (务),
means "shì" (事, affair).
"Zhū" (诸),
means "yú" (于, regarding).
Jū Què (瞿鹊) was a disciple of Cháng Wú (长梧),
hence he addressed his teacher as "fūzǐ" (夫子, master).
The sage who embodies the Dào (道),
forgets personal concerns and merges with things,
although involved in affairs, does not consider them as tasks.
Blending into the dusty world,
serenely without intention,
how could they direct their mind and harbor emotions,
following after matters and objects!
Since Jū Què (瞿鹊) wished to seek improvement,
he thus recounted what he had heard in the past.
【Transcription】"Qú Què" is pronounced with the initial "其" and the final "俱" in reverse.
"Cháng Wúzǐ" Lǐ says:
He lived beneath the tall Chinese parasol tree,
hence he was named after it.
Cuī says:
His name was Qiū.
Jiǎn Wén says,
Cháng Wú was a feudal lord.
"The Master" Xiàng says:
He was the teacher of Qú Què.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
Qú Quèzǐ must have been a descendant of the seventy disciples,
and when he referred to hearing it from the Master,
it meant he heard it from Confucius.
Later, Cháng Wúzǐ says,
"This is what even Huángdì found bewildering to listen to,
so how could I, Qiū, be sufficient to know it?"
Qiū is Confucius's personal name,
and because Qú Quèzǐ was recounting Confucius's words,
Cháng Wúzǐ thus said, "How could I, Qiū, be sufficient to know it?"
However, readers who do not grasp the meaning
mistakenly think that "Qiū" refers to Cháng Wúzǐ referring to himself by name,
hence the transcription states,
Cháng Wúzǐ,
Cuī says his name was Qiū.
This is greatly incorrect.
Later it is said,
"Both you and I, Qiū, are in a dream,"
and "I say your dream is also a dream."
The term "I"
is Cháng Wúzǐ referring to himself.
Since it says both "Qiū and you are in a dream,"
and "I am also in a dream,"
then how could Qiū be taken as Cháng Wúzǐ's name?
【二】【注】Advancing straightforwardly with abandon,
making no evasions or concessions.
【Commentary】To transgress means
to evade.
One who embodies the critical juncture of fate between hardship and success,
and comprehends that gains and losses have their due times,
therefore reasons straightforwardly and advances directly,
without evading or pursuing anything.
【Three】【Commentary】Seeking it brings no joy,
taking it directly incurs no anger.
【Commentary】Subtle enlightenment follows what is contrary.
Therefore, when things are sought, there is no joy in obtaining them.
【Four】【Annotation】It is uniquely the ultimate.
【Commentary】The sage's wisdom is concentrated and profound,
illuminating all things without emotional attachment,
neither welcoming nor sending away,
neither arising nor ceasing,
and thus never allows a clinging mind to act within the void-penetrating ultimate Way.
【Five】【Annotation】All those who have designations,
are not what I call them,
they each designate themselves,
hence there is no situation where they have designations and I have none.
【Commentary】"Wei" (to speak),
refers to verbal teaching.
The sage who embodies the Dao,
being empty, tranquil, and utterly quiescent,
descends from the origin to manifest in traces,
responds to stimuli and thereby communicates.
Thus, he can embody principle and teach,
having no words yet possessing words;
teach while embodying principle,
possessing words yet having no words.
【Transcription】"Chēngwèi" is pronounced as chǐ zhèng fǎn.
The following are to be read in the same manner.
【Six】【Annotation】All that is not of true nature,
is but dust and grime.
【Commentary】Harmonizing the light and blending with the dust,
dwelling in defilement yet remaining undefiled,
thus, even amid the clamor of worldly affairs,
the mind roams freely beyond the realm of dust and grime.
【Interpretation】"Ér yóu" in the Cuī version is written as "ér shī".
【Seven】【Negligence】 is rash and careless,
still hasty and rough.
Xi,
means what;
Ruo,
means like;
how.
What is called not following the Dao and so on,
is to exhaust principles and fully develop one's nature.
Qū Què intended to practice the subtle Way,
while Cháng Wú used hasty and rough words.
Not knowing how its principles are,
and what to consider as correct.
【Translated Text】"Mèng" is read as it is.
Xú gives the pronunciation as wǔdǎng fǎn,
and alternatively as wǔzàng fǎn.
"Làng" is read as it is,
Xú gives the pronunciation as lìdàng fǎn.
Xiàng says:
Mènglàng,
pronounced as mànlán,
refers to having no direction or decision.
Lǐ says:
It is like a rough outline.
Cuī says:
It describes something not refined or essential.
◎Qìng Fān's note: The commentary on Wénxuǎn, Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Wūdū Fù" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Mènglàng,
is vulgar or rustic speech.
This is missing in the explanatory text.
Also noted:
Mènglàng,
is similar to mòluò,
meaning not detailed or meticulous.
(See Liú Kuí's commentary on Wénxuǎn, Zuǒ Sī's "Wūdū Fù".
) Mòluò is also written as móluè.
In the Mòzǐ's "Xiǎo Qǔ Piān",
it says móluè wànwù zhī rán.
Móluè means
a comprehensive term.
Mòluò, móluè, and mènglàng
are all phonetic variations of the same sound.
"Zhī xíng" is read as it is,
and also pronounced as xià mèng fǎn.
Chángwú Zǐ said:
"This is what even Huángdì found perplexing,
so how could I, Qiū, be sufficient to know it!
Moreover, you are also calculating too early,
seeing an egg and seeking the rooster that crows at dawn,
seeing a pellet and seeking a roasted owl."
【一】【疏】"Tīngyíng" refers to
a state of being perplexed and unclear.
Now, the ultimate Way is profound and mysterious,
not something that can be fully grasped through words and names.
Even though the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
who were indeed sages,
attempted to explain and debate the highest principles,
they could not exhaust its subtleties.
In the end, they were left perplexed,
doubtful and unclear.
What kind of person am I,
that I could possibly comprehend it fully?
There was originally a version that used the character "Huáng,"
which then refers to Xuānyuán.
【Interpretive Text】"Huángdì" is also written as Huángdì in another version.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Huáng and Huáng are interchangeable.
The current version reads Huángdì.
"Tīng" is pronounced with the fanqie initials chì and dìng.
"Yíng" sounds like the yíng in polishing gems.
It is also written as yíng in some versions,
with the fanqie initials yú and jiǒng.
Xiàng and Sīmǎ explain:
tīng yíng
means being perplexed.
Lǐ explains:
it describes a lack of brightness in appearance.
Cuī states:
it refers to something small and unclear, not fully apparent.
In Xiàng and Cuī's version, it is written as ● róng.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
according to the supplement to the character dictionary:
the character ● is found in Buddhist texts.
Suíhán states:
● is the same as huī.
【二】【注】All things have their inherent nature,
and principles reach their ultimate state.
Following this path directly,
one mysteriously aligns with it spontaneously,
beyond what words can convey.
Thus, those who speak of it do so recklessly,
and those who hear it are left bewildered.
Even the Yellow Emperor,
could not make all things free from concerns,
and ultimately, listeners remain perplexed.
Therefore, the sage entrusts what is appropriate beyond the dust of the world,
and mysteriously harmonizes beyond the realm of sight and sound,
illuminating through nature without opposing calculations,
letting things be as they are without forcing explanations.
Now, Quèzǐ, upon hearing such rash words, immediately considers them the practice of sublime Dao,
which is no different from seeing an egg and demanding it crow at dawn,
or seeing a pellet and seeking the roasted meat of an owl.
Those who cannot rest content with the times and follow the flow, yet probe into changes and seek transformations,
worrying about death while alive,
clinging to "this" to debate "that,"
are all followers of opposing calculations.
【Commentary】The xiāo is the péng bird,
the one that Jiǎ Yì composed a rhapsody about.
It is as large as a hen,
resembling a spotted dove,
with a bluish-green color.
Its meat is very delicious,
suitable for making soup and roasting,
and it is found south of the Yangtze River.
However, while the egg has the potential to become a chicken,
at the egg stage, it cannot yet herald the dawn;
while the pellet has the function of obtaining an xiāo,
at the pellet stage, it is not yet fit for roasting.
This is akin to how teaching can expound profound principles,
but the teaching itself is not the principle.
Now, Qū Què has only just heard the discourse
and considers it the sublime Way,
which is to reckon its utility too early.
【Text Explanation】"And you" is read as "rǔ".
The same applies below.
"Also great" is read as "tài",
while Xú and Lǐ pronounce it with the initial "chì" and the final "zuǒ".
The same applies to the annotations.
"Timely night": Cuī explains,
"Timely night"
means keeping watch at night,
referring to the rooster.
"Seeing the bullet" is read with the initial "tán".
"Owl" is read as "yú xiāo".
Sīmǎ explains:
A small turtledove,
suitable for roasting.
The "Máoshī Cǎomù Shū" states:
It is as large as a spotted dove,
green in color,
and its meat is very delicious.
"Although again" is read with the initial "fú".
The same applies to all instances below.
The annotations in the following chapter also follow this standard.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "Huáng" was amended according to the Shidetang edition.
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "fū".
I have spoken to you recklessly,
and you have listened to me recklessly.
Why not lean against the sun and moon,
and embrace the universe?
Blend everything into harmony,
set aside confusion and obscurity,
and honor all things equally as if they were servants.
The common people toil diligently,
while the sage remains simple and ignorant,
blending ten thousand years into a single pure unity.
All things are like this,
and in this way, they mutually encompass one another.
【一】【注】To speak of it would be reckless,
so I venture to speak of it recklessly.
【Explanation】"Chang wei": read as "yú wěi" in reverse.
【二】【注】If one were to truly heed baseless talk,
it would also be premature planning.
So, let's also heed it recklessly,
why?
【Commentary】Yǔ,
means "I".
Xī,
means "what".
The ultimate truth is beyond words,
to speak of it is rash.
I shall try to recklessly explain it to you,
and you may recklessly listen—how about that?
Also, it is said,
"xī" is the pronunciation of "hé" (what).
【Three】【Commentaries】Taking life and death as day and night,
is an analogy akin to the sun and moon;
regarding all things as one entity,
is a metaphor for embracing the universe.
【Commentary】Páng (旁),
means to depend on.
Xié (挾),
means to harbor or conceal.
Heaven, earth, and the four directions are called space (yǔ),
the passage from ancient to modern times is called time (zhòu).
The sage who aligns with the principle,
forgets both things and self,
and thereby encompasses all existence,
uniting life and death in obscurity.
Hence, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
taking life and death as day and night,
is the metaphor of páng rì yuè (beside the sun and moon);
regarding all things as one entity,
is the metaphor of xié yǔ zhòu (embracing space and time).
【Translated Text】"Beside the sun and moon" is read as bó zàng fǎn,
Xú reads it as fú zàng fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to rely on.
Cuī's version writes it as bàng.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
The official school edition changes bàng to páng,
which may not be correct.
◎Jiā Shìfù states:
Guō Xiàng uses "nǚ yǐ wàng tīng zhī xī" as a break,
but upon careful consideration of the text's meaning,
"xī páng rì yuè xié yǔ zhòu" forms its own clause,
meaning by what means can one transcend beyond heaven and earth.
Qìng Fān's case: páng should be a loan character for fàng.
Fàng,
means to rely on.
In the Analects, "Lǐ Rén" chapter, "fàng yú lì ér xíng,"
both Zhèng and Kǒng annotate:
fàng,
means to rely on.
In the Mozi "Fǎ Yí" chapter, "fàng yī yǐ cóng shì,"
fàng also means to rely on.
It is also interchangeable with fāng.
In the Book of Songs, "wéi jiū fāng zhī,"
means the magpie has a nest and the turtledove relies on it.
(See Wáng's Jīngyì Shùwén.
) It is also interchangeable with páng.
Páng rì yuè,
means to rely on the sun and moon.
The interpretation by Sīmǎ as relying on should be considered correct.
Cuī's version writing it as bàng is incorrect.
"Hold" is read as hù dié fǎn.
Cuī's version writes it as fú.
"Universe" is read as zhì jiù fǎn.
Shīzǐ says:
Heaven, earth, and the four directions are called yǔ,
past, present, and future are called zhòu.
Shuōwén explains:
The utmost reach covered by boats and carriages is called zhòu.
【四】【注】Because there exists what is deemed lowly,
thus the distinction between noble and humble arises,
leading to confusion and disorder,
with none able to rectify it,
as each considers themselves correct in their own perspective.
Therefore, the way of spontaneous harmony,
is best achieved by setting it aside without words,
entrusting it to natural occurrence.
Vast and tranquil,
it means without the boundaries of waves.
【Commentary】●，
is the appearance of non-differentiation。
To set aside，
is to let be。
Confusion，
is disorder。
Obscurity，
is darkness。
Servant，
refers to the likes of menials and attendants，
generally a derogatory term。
Now, the emotions of things are inverted，
falsely clinging to honor and lowliness。
The sage, wishing to dispel this delusion，
embraces the way of harmoniously uniting them as one ●，
by nothing other than confounding and muddling，
following along and letting things be，
treating servants as equals in honor，
thus unifying the noble and the humble。
【Explanatory Text】The "●" is sometimes written as ●.
Guō reads it as mǐn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as wǔ zhěn fǎn,
Lǐ as wǔ fěn fǎn.
It describes the appearance of having no waves or boundaries.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to merge.
Xiàng reads it as chún,
and says:
It is like the two lips coming together.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
In current annotated editions, "wave" is written as "cover" (note five),
which seems to be an error.
"Slippery" is given by Xú as gǔ méi fǎn,
meaning chaotic.
Xiàng's version writes it as gǔ,
with the same pronunciation.
Cuī gives it as hù bā fǎn,
and says:
It refers to the mouth of a arrow-straightening tool (originally written as 'wood', corrected to 'mouth' in note six).
"Confused" is read by Xú as hūn.
Xiàng says:
Gǔ hūn,
means undecided.
Cuī's version writes it as ,
with the pronunciation wǔ jīn fǎn,
and says:
It means a rope.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
It was previously written as hūn.
The Song edition uses the radical 'clan',
and in the annotations, both hūn and hūn use the radical 'clan',
now follow this.
【Five】【Annotation】Galloping through the realm of right and wrong.
【Six】【Annotation】The appearance of proceeding directly with unfeigned ignorance.
【Commentary】Yì yì (restless toil) refers to
the appearance of constant agitation.
Yú chūn (foolish simplicity) means
the demeanor of being without knowledge.
Ordinary people
chase after external things,
toiling without rest;
those who embody the Dào,
forget knowledge and abandon illumination,
remaining simple and seemingly foolish.
【Translated Text】"Chūn" is read by Xú as tú bēn fǎn.
Guō reads it as zhì běn fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means chaotic and indistinct.
Cuī [says]:
It describes a thick appearance.
Some say:
It means to bind.
Lǐ reads it as chǒu lún fǎn.
【七】【注】Purity means
being unadulterated.
When one examines the myriad ages and their transformations,
ordinary people deem it chaotic,
thus they toil anxiously, wearying their bodies and unsettling their minds, striving to abandon that and embrace this.
Only the great sage holds no attachments;
thus, he moves forward simply and directly, uniting with the changes.
Uniting with the changes, he constantly wanders in solitude.
Therefore, even when blending myriad years,
with thousands of differences and countless variations,
the Way is formed through practice,
so past and present are one formation;
things are deemed so because they are called so,
thus all things are one in their suchness.
There is nothing that is not so,
no time that does not achieve completion;
this can be called purity.
【Commentary】The sage,
aligns his virtue with the dual forces of nature,
shares his essence with all things,
thus able to adapt to changes and transformations,
harmonizing with the world.
Though eras pass through ancient and modern times,
and ages traverse peace and peril,
mingling amidst the dust of worldly affairs,
with countless differences and variations,
he remains serene and composed,
unburdened by concerns,
embracing unity with purity,
and eternally abiding in the sublime ultimate.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
The masses are restless and toiling,
comparing today,
and comparing tomorrow.
What seems right today,
appears wrong tomorrow;
what seems unequivocally wrong today,
may not seem so tomorrow.
The sage, in his apparent simplicity,
does not rely on such judgments but dwells in the ordinary,
encompassing all ages to reach the fullest extent.
Unity means
a seamless whole without distinctions of this and that;
perfection means
a harmonious state without discrepancies of right and wrong;
purity means
a tranquil mind without debates over truth and falsehood.
The sage, through this, responds to the changes of all things and harbors them boundlessly within,
thus embodying the principle of encompassing all ages while remaining unified and pure.
【Transcription】"Chù xīn" is read as chì lǜ fǎn.
"Cān róu" is read as rú jiù fǎn.
【八】【Note】There is nothing that is not so.
【Nine】【Comment】Accumulation,
means storing up.
If one stores this up over ten thousand years,
then ten thousand years become as one;
if one affirms this across all things,
then all things are entirely affirmed.
Thus, one does not know the positions of life and death,
nor the outcomes of victory and defeat between self and others.
【Commentary】Accumulation means
to amass.
Human emotions and attachments
have persisted for a long time.
Hence, when broadly discussing all things,
none fail to affirm themselves and negate others;
when vertically examining past and present,
all invariably deem themselves right and others wrong.
Despite the multitude of all things,
and the vastness of past and present,
the accumulation of right and wrong
never ceases.
The sage conforms to the world’s rise and fall,
active yet ever tranquil,
blending with myriad ages while remaining purely and steadfastly unified.
【Explanatory Text】"Xiāng Yùn" is also written as "縕".
Xú gives the pronunciation as yú fèn fǎn,
Guō gives it as yú běn fǎn,
Lǐ gives it as yú wèn fǎn.
It means accumulation.
【Collation】(1) Zhū Guìyào's edition has the character 若 following 奚.
(2) Zhào Jiànyì's edition writes ●,
same below.

stating:
芚,
pronounced with the initial 治 and final 本,
describes the appearance of ignorant straightforwardness.
(4) The character 為 was amended according to the reprinted Sòng edition.
(5) The Shìdétáng edition writes 被,

How do I know that loving life is not a delusion?
How do I know that hating death is not like an orphan who has strayed and does not know the way home?
Lì Zhī Jī,
was the daughter of the border guard of Ài.
When the state of Jìn first captured her,
she wept till her tears drenched the collar of her robe.
But when she came to the king's palace,
shared his luxurious bed,
and feasted on fine meats,
she regretted her earlier tears.
How do I know that the dead do not regret their former longing for life?
【一】【注】Life and death are one and the same,
yet people speak only of life,
wishing to oppose the course of transformation,
hence it is unknown whether this is not delusion.
【Commentary】The forging of all things,
has never been unequal;
the transformations of life and death,
follow the same principle.
Yet to favor life and detest death alone,
is nothing but delusion!
【Transcription】"予惡" pronounced as wū.
The following occurrences of "惡" are all the same.
"說" pronounced as yuè.
The annotation is the same.
"相背" pronounced as pèi.
【二】【注】When young, one loses one's original dwelling,
called "weak and lost."
Those who are weak and lost
then become content with wherever they are and do not know to return to their homeland.
How can we know that life is not like being weak and lost,
how can we know that death is not like returning home, yet we detest it?
【Commentary】"Weak" refers to a tender age,
"loss" means to be bereft of.
It describes a youth encountering turmoil,
losing their homeland,
then settling in another land without knowing to return,
which is called being lost in youth.
Emerging from non-existence into existence,
is called life;
returning from existence to non-existence,
is called death.
Thus, clinging to life and detesting death,
is it not akin to being lost in youth without knowing to return!
【Text】"Wù sǐ" is read as wù lù fǎn.
Same for the annotation.
"Ruò sàng" is read as ruò sàng fǎn.
Same for the annotation.
"Shǎo ér" is read as shǎo zhào fǎn.
"Yān zhī" is read as yān qián fǎn.
Same below.
【Three】【Annotations】Within a single lifetime,
emotions change like this.
At such moments,
one cannot understand the other,
let alone the transformation of life and death—
how could we ever truly know each other!
【Commentary】Long ago, Duke Mù of Qín and Duke Xiàn of Jìn jointly attacked the state of Lìróng,
obtaining one beautiful woman
and two jade rings.
Qín took the rings while Jìn took the woman,
who was the daughter of the border guard of the Ài territory in the Lìróng state.
Sad,
indeed.
Initially leaving Lìróng,
parting from her relatives,
she harbored a longing for her homeland,
thus her tears soaked her lapels.
Later, upon arriving in the state of Jìn,
she received profound favor and affection,
sharing the same square bed with Duke Xiàn in peaceful repose,
with abundant feasts filling the kitchens.
Once her affections had shifted,
she regretted her earlier weeping.
Within a single lifetime,
emotions can change so drastically.
How much more so with the difference between life and death—
how can we truly understand it?
Zhuāngzǐ uses allegorical language,
hence he refers to Duke Xiàn as a king.
As for "arriving at the king's place," Cuī Zǐ states:
During the Warring States period, the feudal lords usurped the title of king,
hence they referred to Duke Xiàn as the king.
"Kuāng" is also written as 匡 in some versions.
Xú Mǎng pronounces it with the initial "qǐ" and the rhyme "kuáng."
"Chuáng" is pronounced by Xú Mǎng as "chuáng."
Sīmǎ Biāo explains:
Kuāng chuáng
means a comfortable bed.
Cuī Zǐ states:
Kuāng
signifies square.
Another explanation says:
It is a proper bed.
【四】【注】Qí,
means to seek.
【Commentary】Qí.
It means to seek.
Lì Jī arrived in Jìn.
She regretted her earlier weeping,
How can we know that the dead do not in turn regret their initial intention to seek life when they were alive!
【Transcription】"Qí" is pronounced like "pray,"
meaning to seek.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào's advisory version, it is unknown that there originally were the two characters "suǒwèi" below.
(2) Zhào's version lacks the character "zhī".
One who drinks wine in a dream,
weeps at dawn;
one who weeps in a dream,
goes hunting at dawn.
While in the dream,
he does not know it is a dream.
In the midst of the dream, he even interprets his dreams;
only upon waking does he realize it was a dream.
Moreover, only after a great awakening can one know that this is a great dream.
Yet the foolish believe themselves to be awake,
confidently thinking they know.
"Are you a lord?
A herdsman?"
How stubborn!
Qiū and you,
are both in a dream;
I who say you are dreaming,
am also in a dream.
Such words,
are called paradoxical.
If after ten thousand generations one encounters a great sage
who understands their meaning,
it would be as if meeting them in a single day.
【一】【注】This is a transformation in the affairs of waking and sleeping.
If the affairs change,
the emotions also differ,
then the desires in life and death cannot be the same.
Thus, when alive, one delights in life,
and when dying, one delights in death.
Although life and death are different,
each fulfilling their own wishes is the same principle.
So what attachment is there then!
【Commentary】The transformation between life and death
is like the difference between waking and dreaming.
Since the nature of waking and dreaming is distinct,
the essence of life and death must also differ.
Yet in the world, there are cases where waking brings misfortune while dreams bring fortune—
so why should it be impossible for death to hold joy and life to hold sorrow?
Thus we know that between wakefulness and sleep,
there is nothing truly binding.
【Transcription】"Lè Shēng" is pronounced as luò.
The same applies below.
【二】【注】From this perspective,
at the moment of death,
one does not even realize they are dying but instead follows their own aspirations with contentment.
【Commentary】At the moment one is about to dream,
one does not know that the dream is a dream;
similarly, on the day one is about to face death,
one does not know that death is death.
Each follows their own inclinations,
so what is there to cling to!
【Three】【Comment】Dreaming is but again within a dream divining one's dream,
which is no different from being awake.
【Four】【Note】When encountering situations,
there is nothing insufficient,
why worry about death while still alive!
【Commentary】When a person is in the midst of a dream,
they believe it to be real,
and likewise interpret the dream's omens,
pondering the good or ill fortune.
Only after awakening
do they realize it was a dream.
Therefore, while alive, one should delight in life,
and when death comes, one should be at peace with it.
Why should one worry about death while still living!
【Transcription】"Jiao'er" is pronounced as jiào.
The same applies to the following and annotations.
【Five】【Annotation】The greatly awakened one is a sage.
The greatly awakened one is one who knows that all those who harbor worries and anxieties in their hearts have not yet awakened.
【Commentary】The multitudes of people in turmoil,
the teeming masses of beings,
rush about in the realm of purposeful action,
lost in the depths of a great dream.
Only the sage who embodies the Dào
awakens clearly and alone,
knowing that all who harbor worries in their hearts have not yet awakened.
【Six】【Annotation】The foolish, in their grand dreams, believe themselves to be awake,
thus secretly regarding what they favor as sovereigns and what they despise as servants,
joyfully trusting in the biased views of a single school,
which can be called obstinate and narrow-minded.
【Commentary】The delusions of human emotions,
are as benighted as one wandering at night,
dazed as if in a dream,
yet they consider themselves awake,
and whisperingly debate what they think they know.
What their emotions favor is elevated to the status of a ruler,
what their emotions despise is treated like a herdsman or stable hand,
to hold such sentiments as one's emotional disposition,
can indeed be called obstinate ignorance.
(Note: "Mù" refers to herding cattle,
"Yǔ" refers to tending horses.)
【Explanatory Text】"Qiè qiè" Sīmǎ comments:
It means scrutinizing closely.
"Mù hū" Cuī's version writes it as qí hū,
stating:
dì qí,
describes a posture of straining like a sheep.
"Suǒ hào" is pronounced with the fanqie hū and bào.
The annotation is the same.
"Suǒ wù" is pronounced with the fanqie wū and lù.
【Seven】【Annotation】Unable to forget words yet attain spiritual understanding,
thus it is not the great awakening.
【Commentary】Qiū is the name of Chángwú.
Even one who illuminates and comprehends the true origin
is still said to be dreaming;
how much more so for the foolish masses,
who are utterly confused—could they possibly be awakened!
【Transcription】"Shén jiě" is pronounced as "xiè".
Xú gives the pronunciation as "hù jiě fǎn".
【八】【注】This is like interpreting a dream within a dream itself.
To consider oneself in a dream
is still to be unawakened,
let alone those who smugly believe themselves to be fully awake!
【Commentary】When deluded emotions lack awareness,
discussing dreams remains within the dream itself;
verbal explanations are not the truth,
exquisite arguments still dwell within language.
Therefore, interpreting dreams within a dream
reveals why all dreams are ultimately empty;
examining words through words
exposes why language is inherently illusory.
This passage employs the metaphor of interpreting dreams within a dream,
concluding with seemingly reckless discourse.
【九】【注】Extraordinary discussions,
are not understood by ordinary people,
thus they are called uniquely profound and peculiar,
yet their profound comprehension remains unrecognized.
【Commentary】That the entire world is but a dream,
this is indeed profound discourse.
Such extraordinary statements,
pay no heed to convention,
uniquely lofty and peculiar,
startle and differ from worldly sentiments.
Unless one is of pure understanding,
how could one grasp such profound depths!
【Translated Text】"Diao" is read as its usual pronunciation,
also pronounced like "di,"
meaning to arrive.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The character "you" was missing in the old version,
now added.
"Gui" is pronounced with the fanqie "jiu wei,"
meaning different.
【一０】【Note】It is extremely rare to be able to shed all attachments and mysteriously unite life and death.
【Commentary】Moreover, it takes ten thousand years in the world to encounter a great sage once,
who understands that the three realms are entirely empty,
the four forms of life are non-existent,
and all dialogues between self and others
occur within a dream.
Such an enlightened person
is indeed rare to meet;
discussing whether the wait is long or short,
it is as if meeting them occurs between dawn and dusk.
Thirty years constitute one generation.
【Explanation】"其解" is pronounced like "crab" (xiè),
and Xú gives the pronunciation as hù jiě fǎn.
"蛻然" is pronounced like "towel" (shuì),
and also has the pronunciation shǐ ruì fǎn.
Suppose you and I argue.
If you beat me,
and I don't beat you,
are you indeed right,
and I indeed wrong?
If I beat you,
and you don't beat me,
am I indeed right,
and you indeed wrong?
Is one of us right,
and the other wrong?
Or are both of us right,
or both wrong?
You and I cannot know each other's minds,
and others are inherently shrouded in obscurity.
Whom shall I have arbitrate it?
Have one who agrees with you arbitrate it?
Since they already agree with you,
how can they arbitrate it!
Have one who agrees with me arbitrate it?
Since they already agree with me,
how can they arbitrate it!
Have one who disagrees with both you and me arbitrate it?
Since they already disagree with both you and me,
how can they arbitrate it!
Have one who agrees with both you and me arbitrate it?
Since they already agree with both you and me,
how can they arbitrate it!
Then you and I and others all cannot know each other's minds,
so whom shall we wait for?
【First】【Argument】"Ruò",
"ér",
all refer to you.
Are you not superior to me?
This is a rhetorical question.
Now, right and wrong, self and other,
are entirely unreal in their essence.
Those who are confused,
arbitrarily judge what is good and bad.
Suppose I and you engage in a debate:
you win and I do not,
does your victory necessarily mean you are right,
and my loss necessarily mean I am wrong?
Certainly not.
【二】【Note】Ruò,
ér,
all mean "you".
【Commentary】Suppose I surpass you,
and you fall short of me,
does that necessarily mean I am right,
and you are definitely wrong?
Each holds to their biased views,
which are insufficient to rely upon.
【Three】【Doubtful Statements】"Huò,"
means uncertainty.
Between you and me,
whether something is right or wrong,
when we each speak our minds,
the outcome remains undecided.
Thus, if it's right, it may not be absolutely right;
if it's wrong, it may not be entirely wrong either.
【Four】【Negations】If all are affirmed, then there is nothing wrong;
if all are denied, then there is nothing right.
Thus, right and wrong, self and other,
arise from deluded emotions.
【五】【注】Not knowing, then one infers;
not seeing, then one debates;
yet debating is not enough to have self-confidence,
because it confronts things.
Arguing and confronting all day leads to darkness and obscurity,
ultimately unable to correct it,
thus one should leave it to self-correction.
【Commentary】Two parties, you and I,
each hold biased views,
both claiming to be right,
thus unable to understand each other.
To truly understand,
one must recognize that
what is wrong in oneself
may be right in the other.
Suppose there is another person
appointed to judge right and wrong—
this person would still have partialities,
not free from judgments,
each clinging to false perceptions,
collectively leading to confusion.
The mind inevitably harbors favoritism,
hence these views remain murky and unclear.
With three parties each holding firm,
who can arbitrate fairly?
"Murky" here means lacking clarity.
【Explanation】"Dàn'àn": Greed and darkness reversed.
Lǐ says:
Dàn'àn,
an unclear appearance.
【Six】【Comment】Since I have brought you to see the same thing,
Then I am no different from you.
Being no different from you,
How can I achieve correct concentration!
This further explains the first line.
【Explanation】"È néng" is pronounced as "wū".
The same applies to all instances below.
【Seven】【Annotation】To agree with it for the same reason,
is not enough to be believed.
【Commentary】The annotation states,
it is only because they are the same that it is thus,
which is not sufficient to be believed.
This further explains the second line.
【Eight】【Comment】They oppose each other because of their differences,
which is also insufficient to rely upon.
【Subcommentary】Since it distinguishes between self and other,
it consequently gives rise to distinctions of right and wrong.
Once distinctions of right and wrong arise,
how can they be considered reliable?
This further explains the third line.
【九】【注】If what is deemed right is truly right,
then no one in the world can dispute it;
if what is deemed wrong is indeed wrong,
then there is also no basis for anyone to affirm it.
Yet now, people affirm what they agree with and deny what they differ on,
and with both agreement and disagreement present, right and wrong lose their anchor.
Therefore, notions of right and wrong
arise from a fondness for debate and find rest in the balance of nature,
entrusted to dual paths and settled through self-correction.
【Commentary】When both sides bend to accommodate each other,
right and wrong are compromised on both ends,
without distinguishing between self and other,
how can one possibly rectify it?
This explains the fourth line.
【一０】【Note】Each is correct in itself.
Relying on others is insufficient to correct oneself,
thus nothing in the world can mutually correct all.
Therefore, entrust it to self-correction, and perfection is achieved.
【Commentary】You, I, and others,
are all people who inherently suffer from obscurity and ignorance.
Altogether there are three individuals,
each holding a different viewpoint,
all claiming that they are correct,
hence none understand one another.
Since these three cannot reach a conclusion,
what need is there for yet another person!
If we were to await another person,
how would that differ from the previous situation!
To rely on that person,
means that there is no need to rely on anyone.
What is meant by harmonizing them with the Heavenly Equality?
It is said:
To regard "is" as "is not,"
and "so" as "not so."
If "is" is truly "is,"
then the difference between "is" and "is not" requires no argument;
if "so" is truly "so,"
then the difference between "so" and "not so" requires no argument.
The transformations of sounds depend on each other,
yet they are as if they do not depend on each other.
Harmonize them with the Heavenly Equality,
follow them through with boundless extension,
thereby exhausting one's years.
Forget the years and forget righteousness,
soar in the boundless,
and thus dwell in the boundless."
【一】【注】Tiānní refers to,
the natural distinctions.
【Commentary】Heaven is
natural spontaneity.
Ní means
differentiation.
When subjective attachments to self and others,
and judgments of right and wrong lack foundation,
even multiple perspectives and arguments
cannot rectify them.
Therefore, hypothetical propositions are established,
presented through questions and answers,
harmonized with the natural differentiation,
guiding toward neither right nor wrong.
The meaning of tiānní
is elaborated in the following text.
【Text】"Hé zhī" is read as the character's standard pronunciation,
Cuī gives the fanqie reading as hú wò fǎn.
"Tiān ní" Lǐ reads with the sound yá,
Xú reads with the sound yì,
Guō reads with the sound wǔ dǐ fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means division.
Cuī says:
Sometimes written as 'ní',
the sound is the same,
meaning boundary.
Bān Gù said:
"Tiān yán."
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In old editions, 'yá' was mistakenly written as 'Cuī',
now corrected according to the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter.
'Ní' has a sound close to 'yán',
hence Jì Ní is also written as Jì Yán.
【二】【Note】Right and wrong, affirmation and denial,
when self and other are mutually opposed,
hence there is no argument.
With no argument,
they are harmonized by the Heavenly Equality,
simply resting in their natural allotment,
without relying on the other to correct them.
【Commentary】"Argument" means
"distinction".
Matters of right and wrong, affirmation and denial,
arise from deluded thoughts.
When examined through reason,
they are entirely illusory.
What is deemed right is not truly right;
what is affirmed is not truly affirmed.
How do we know this is so?
If right were definitively right,
it would inherently differ from wrong;
if affirmation were definitively affirmation,
it would inherently differ from denial.
Yet now, what one calls right,
another calls wrong;
what another affirms,
this one denies.
Thus we know that right/wrong and affirmation/denial
share the same fundamental principle,
while people arbitrarily oppose each other
and create false distinctions.
Therefore, there is no true argument to be made.
【Three】【Comment】The debate of right and wrong is like transformed sounds.
These transformed sounds depend on each other,
yet both are insufficient to correct one another,
hence it is as if they do not depend on each other.
【Commentary】The distinctions between right and wrong, self and other,
are formed through mutual dependence.
When examined through reasoning,
this dependence itself is unreal.
Hence, in the shifting expressions of discourse,
such dependent concepts arise;
since these concepts are not genuine,
the dependence becomes an illusory dependency.
Dependency is thus non-dependency,
revealing the nature of non-reliance.
◎ Jiāshìfù remarked:
Adapting to the changes of things
is called transformative discourse.
What is deemed right or wrong,
affirmed or denied,
lies with people.
Whether relying on others to validate right and affirmation or
being self-validating and spontaneous without such reliance,
neither should affect the inner mind—
this is what is meant by harmonizing through the Heavenly Equality.
【Four】【Annotation】Harmonize it with the natural distinctions,
let it follow the transformations of the infinite,
proceed along this path,
and the realm of right and wrong will naturally vanish,
while the essence of life and destiny will naturally be fully realized.
【Commentary】"Mànyǎn" means
transformation and change.
"Yīn" means
to follow.
"Qióng" means
to exhaust.
By harmonizing with the natural distinctions,
there is thus no right or wrong;
by following the limitless transformations,
one can thus remain unobstructed and unattached.
Then, by abiding in accordance and accepting the times,
one fulfills the lifespan decreed by heaven's mandate.
【Explanatory Text】"Màn" is pronounced by Xú as wàn,
Guō gives the pronunciation wǔ bàn fǎn.
"Yǎn" is pronounced by Xú as yǐ zhàn fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
Mànyǎn
means without limit.
【五】【注】Forgetting the years thus mysteriously unites life and death,
forgetting righteousness thus fully penetrates right and wrong.
Right, wrong, life, and death are swept away into oneness,
this is the ultimate principle.
The ultimate principle flows boundlessly into infinity,
therefore, those who entrust themselves to it cannot have limitations.
【Commentary】"Zhèn" means
"unhindered flow."
"Jìng" means
"exhaustion."
"Yù" means
"lodging."
As for years,
they are what life is endowed with;
since they are the same in life and death,
that is why one forgets years.
Righteousness
is determined by right and wrong;
since it is unified with right and wrong,
that is why one forgets righteousness.
This then dismisses the previously known meaning of the endlessness of right and wrong.
Subsequently, life, death, right, and wrong are swept away into oneness,
hence one can penetrate and flow with subtle principles,
illuminating the boundless thoroughly.
Lodging words in the boundless,
yet there is no boundlessness to flow through,
this again dismisses even the limitless.
【Explanation】"Zhèn" is read as its common pronunciation.
Cuī (a commentator) says:
It means to stop.
Also pronounced with the "zhī rěn" fanqie spelling.
"Wú jìng" is read as its common pronunciation,
meaning ultimate.
Cuī writes it as "jìng" (border).
【Collation】（一）The citation from the Jiangnan Guzang version in Que Wu is correct; below, "wu bian" is also written as "qi wu bian le,"
and below, "ran ye" also has "wu bian" written as "yi wu bian le."
The penumbra asked the shadow, saying:
"A moment ago you were moving,
and now you've stopped;
a moment ago you were sitting,
and now you've risen;
how is it that you have no fixed manner of your own?"
【一】【注】Wǎngliǎng,
is the faint shadow outside the shadow.
【Commentary】Wǎngliǎng,
is the faint shadow outside the shadow.
Nǎng,
means past,
(specifically) direction.
means solitary.
Zhuāngzǐ used allegories to elucidate profound principles,
thus employing the shadow and the penumbra,
to clarify the concept of independent transformation.
And the penumbra asked the shadow:
"You were walking just now and now you stop,
you were sitting before and now you rise.
If so, your walking, stopping, sitting, and rising,
are controlled by the form,
merely wishing to follow and chase after others,
entirely lacking the will and integrity of independence,
why is that?"
【Interpretation】"Wǎngliǎng" Guǒ's commentary states:
A subtle shadow outside the main shadow.
Xiàng's commentary states:
The shadow of a shadow.
Cuī's version writes it as wǎnglàng,
stating:
The appearance of existence and non-existence.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: Wǎngliǎng,
Sīmǎ writes as wǎnglàng.
The commentary on Bān Gù's "Fù of Silent Understanding" in the Wénxuǎn quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Wǎnglàng,
refers to the layered shadows outside the main shadow.
The explanatory text quotes Cuī's version as writing wǎnglàng,
stating the appearance of existence and non-existence,
which differs in meaning from Sīmǎ's interpretation.
"Jǐng" is pronounced with a drawn-out tone,
or as the character's usual reading.
Some versions write it as yǐng,
which is colloquial.
"Nǎng" is pronounced by Xú as nǎidàng.
Lǐ's commentary states:
It means in the past.
"Wútè" is written in some versions as chí.
Cuī's commentary states:
Tè,
is a particle.
Xiàng's commentary states:
Wútè means
having no fixed pattern in movement and rest.
"Cāo yǔ" is pronounced as yú.
Jǐng said:
"Am I dependent on something to be so?
Is what I depend on also dependent on something else to be so?
Am I dependent on the snake's scales or the cicada's wings?
How can I know why it is so!
How can I know why it is not so!
【One】【Annotation】It speaks of the natural mechanism of heaven operating spontaneously,
sitting or rising without dependence.
One who attains uniqueness without dependence—
who can fathom the reason for it,
and how could one demand an explanation for its cause?
【Commentary】The forms and substances of all things
are all endowed by nature.
Though events may seem to have causes,
the principle lies in non-dependence.
Even forms and shadows, though not distant,
still possess natural spontaneity.
Hence it is said: all things, diverse as they are, are nothing but solitary transformations.
【Two】【Annotation】If we demand what it relies on and trace its origins,
then the tracing and demanding will be endless,
ultimately arriving at relying on nothing,
and thus the principle of independent transformation becomes clear.
【Commentary】What the shadow relies upon,
is precisely the form.
If we suppose the shadow relies on the form,
and the form relies on the Creator,
then may I ask, what does the Creator in turn rely upon?
This would lead to an endless chain of reliance,
ultimately ending in non-reliance.
【Three】【Comment】If one waits for the snake's shed skin or the cicada's wings,
then there is no basis for independent action,
which is not difficult to understand.
The reason it is not understood now
is precisely because one does not rely on such categories but transforms independently.
【Commentary】In the past, various commentators and Guǒ Shēng in their annotations
all said that "snake's fu" refers to the undulating scales on its belly.
And "cicada's wings" are the cicada's wings.
They stated that the snake relies on its fu to move,
the cicada relies on its wings to fly,
and the shadow depends on the form to exist,
but this is probably not so.
If it were about relying on wings to fly
or depending on feet to run,
then flying birds and running beasts
are endless in variety;
why bother singling out the snake's fu
and specifically using it as an analogy?
Now, the current interpretation is that fu
refers to the snake shedding its skin,
and cicada's wings
mean the cicada's shell.
This signifies that when the snake sheds its old skin
or the cicada emerges with a new shell,
it happens without knowing why,
without discerning how it occurs,
transforming independently and being born,
thus demonstrating no reliance.
And these two creatures, the snake and cicada,
by shedding their skin and shell,
are noted as unique among things,
which is why they are cited.
Therefore, the Outer Chapters say,
"Do I rely on the snake's fu or the cicada's shell?"
From this, we understand that the meaning of form and shadow
is no different from that of fu and shell.
【Explanation】"Shé Fù" is pronounced as fù,
and Xú also gives the pronunciation as fū.
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to the uneven scales on a snake's belly that allow it to move.
"Jǔ",
is pronounced as shì nǚ fǎn,
"yǔ",
is pronounced as yú nǚ fǎn.
"Tiáo" is given by Xú as the pronunciation tiáo.
【四】【注】Some in the world say that the penumbra depends on the shadow,
the shadow depends on the form,
and the form depends on a creator.
I ask:
As for this creator,
does it exist or not?
If it does not exist,
then how could it create things?
If it exists,
then it is insufficient to give form to the multitude of beings.
Therefore, only by understanding that the multitude of forms are things in themselves can one begin to speak of creation.
Thus, when entering the realm of existing things,
even the penumbra,
there is none that does not transform independently in the profound darkness.
Hence, there is no sovereign creator,
and things each create themselves.
Things each create themselves without depending on anything,
this is the principle of heaven and earth.
Thus, self and other condition each other,
form and shadow arise together,
though mysteriously united,
it is not a relationship of dependence.
Understanding this principle,
one will cause all things to return to their roots within themselves without relying on the external,
with no gratitude toward the outside and no arrogance within,
thus they spontaneously come into life without knowing why they live,
equally attain without knowing why they attain.
Now, the penumbra's connection to the shadow,
still means they arise together rather than depend on each other,
thus though all things gather and collectively form heaven,
each distinctly appears independently.
Therefore, the penumbra is not controlled by the shadow,
nor is the shadow directed by the form,
nor is the form transformed by non-being.
Then transformation or non-transformation,
affirmation or negation,
following others or acting from oneself—
all occur spontaneously,
how can I know the reason why!
Thus, by letting things be without interference,
root and branch, inner and outer,
all smoothly attain their place,
merging without trace.
If instead one blames proximate causes and forgets their spontaneity,
esteeming things externally,
losing mastery internally,
then preferences and desires arise.
Even if one seeks to equalize them,
the preferences already exist in one's heart—
how can there be any leveling!
【Commentary】Whether one waits or does not wait,
whether it is so or not so,
the innate mechanism unfolds of its own accord,
with no one knowing its master.
How could it be a matter of applying intention to deliberate inquiry or pondering through conscious thought!
【Text】"Sāng" is pronounced with the tone "xī làng fǎn".
【Collation】（一）The character '卒' has been emended based on the Song edition and the Shìdétáng edition.
（二）In the Shìdétáng edition, '物' is written as '化'.
Once, Zhuāng Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
a butterfly fluttering about joyfully,
feeling perfectly content with himself!
He did not know he was Zhuāng Zhōu.
Suddenly he awoke,
and there he was, unmistakably Zhuāng Zhōu.
He did not know whether Zhuāng Zhōu had dreamed he was a butterfly,
or a butterfly was now dreaming it was Zhuāng Zhōu.
Between Zhuāng Zhōu and the butterfly,
there must certainly be a distinction.
This is called the transformation of things.
【One】【Annotation】Indulging in self-satisfaction,
proceeding with joy and delight.
【Commentary】Xǔxǔ describes
a joyful and carefree appearance.
Yù means
to understand clearly.
The alternation of birth and cessation,
the succession of cold and heat,
are indeed the constants of heaven and earth,
the principle of all things.
Yet Zhuāngzǐ illuminates with the bright mirror to shine light,
roams freely with the highest goodness,
thus able to entrust the awareness of dreaming to life and death,
and place self and others in the transformation of things.
Therefore, dreaming of being a butterfly,
xǔxǔ and satisfying his heart;
awakening as Zhuāng Zhōu,
qúqú and fulfilling his aspiration.
【Translated Text】"Húdié" Xú reads as tú with a xié tone.
Sīmǎ and Cuī say:
It means jiádié (butterfly).
"Xǔ" Xú reads as kuàng with a yǔ tone,
meaning a joyful appearance.
Cuī's version writes it as piān.
"Zì yù" Lǐ says:
Yù,
means pleasure.
"Zhì yǔ" reads yǔ as yú.
The same applies below.
Cuī says:
Yǔ,
means an exclamation (like "ah" or "oh").
【二】【注】When he dreams of being a butterfly and does not know he is Zhuāng Zhōu,
it is no different from a violent death.
Yet wherever he is, there is nothing that does not suit his will;
thus, those who cling to life while alive
must inevitably cling to death when dying.
From this perspective,
it is clear that those who mourn death while alive are mistaken.
【Commentary】Just as one becomes a butterfly,
clear and distinct in awareness,
delighting in the moment and content in spirit,
exceedingly joyful and at ease,
one only speaks of being a butterfly,
and does not recognize Zhuāng Zhōu.
The dead do not know the living,
and the principle is the same.
【Three】【Annotations】From Zhōu's perspective,
thus it is called awakening,
but it may not necessarily not be a dream.
【Commentary】Jùjù,
describes the appearance of being startled and moved.
In a moment's time,
the dream ends and one awakens,
startled and bewildered, reflecting and realizing,
only then is it Zhuāng Zhōu.
Therefore, the note says,
from Zhuāng Zhōu's perspective,
it is thus called awakening,
but it is not necessarily not a dream.
【Explanation】"然覺" is pronounced in ancient Chinese as "gǔ xiào fǎn".
"蘧蘧" is pronounced by Xú as "qú",
alternatively as "qí lǜ fǎn".
Lǐ's commentary states:
It describes a physical appearance.
Cuī's version writes it as "據據",
citing the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter which says "據然覺".
【Four】【Annotation】Today's ignorance of the butterfly
is no different from the dream's ignorance of Zhōu;
yet each satisfies the aspiration of its moment,
thus there is no way to prove that the butterfly is not dreaming of being Zhōu.
There are those in the world who doze off and dream of passing a hundred years,
then there is no way to prove that today's hundred years are not the dream of a doze.
【Commentary】In the past, dreaming of being a butterfly,
brought great joy and fulfillment;
now, becoming Zhuāng Zhōu,
also speaks of contentment with one's will.
Thus, since awakening and dreaming have no fixed reality,
how can one distinguish between the truth and illusion of Zhuāng Zhōu and the butterfly?
【五】【Note】The distinction between waking and dreaming,
is no different from the discrimination between life and death.
Now, the reason one can understand and find contentment,
lies in the fixed nature of their division,
not in the absence of division.
【Commentary】In both waking and dreaming states,
there are butterflies and there is Zhuāngzǐ.
One speaks of illusory emptiness,
yet it is not without boundaries and distinctions.
【Six】【Commentary】Time does not pause even for a moment,
and the present does not persist in existence,
so yesterday's dream
has transformed by today.
The change between life and death,
how could it be any different from this?
Why trouble one's mind over it!
When focused on one thing, we are unaware of another—
such is the case of dreaming of being a butterfly.
Taking examples from people,
within a single lifetime,
the present does not know what comes after—
such is the case of Lì Jī.
Yet foolish people smugly believe they know the joy of life
and the sorrow of death,
unaware of what is called the transformation of things.
【Commentary】For renewal follows renewal in transformation and change,
each thing in flux gives way to the next,
akin to the exhausted finger (pointing),
or to this crossing of arms.
Thus, Zhōu's butterfly awakening from a dream,
in the briefest moment,
the later knows not the former,
the present knows not the past.
So why fret over death while alive,
vainly stirring up sorrow and grief!
Hence we understand that life and death, coming and going,
are but the natural transformations of things.
【Explanation】"Kě Lè" is pronounced with the falling-rising tone for "kě" and the falling tone for "lè".
【一】【Note】Life is sustained through nurturing,
thus the art of nurturing life represents the ultimate principle.
However, if nurturing exceeds its proper bounds,
and instead harms life through excessive care,
that is not the true master of nurturing life.
【Transcription】This is the foundation of nurturing life.
My life has a limit【一】,
but knowledge has no limit【二】.
To pursue the limitless with the limited
is perilous;
【三】and when one persists in seeking knowledge despite this,
it is perilous indeed【四】.
In doing good, avoid fame;
in doing wrong, avoid punishment【五】.
Follow the middle path as your constant principle【六】,
and you will be able to protect your body,
preserve your life,
care for your parents【七】,
and live out your natural lifespan【八】.
【一】【Note】The allotted nature each has its limit.
【Commentary】Limit,
means allotment.
Life is the vessel that receives form,
endowed by nature,
whether foolish or wise, long-lived or short-lived,
each has their allotted limit.
And knowing when to stop and guarding one's allotment,
not straying beyond it,
is the subtle art of nurturing life.
Yet among the common people,
there is none who does not refer to themselves as "I,"
thus all who call themselves "I"
possess a finite existence.
【Explanatory Text】"Yǒuyá" originally also written as 崖,
pronounced as yú jiā fǎn.
【二】【注】When lifting heavy or carrying light objects, one's spirit and energy remain composed as usual,
this is due to the limitations of physical strength.
However, those who value reputation and strive for victory,
even if they exhaust their utmost strength,
still cannot satisfy their desires,
which shows that knowledge knows no bounds.
Hence, the concept of knowledge
arises from misjudgment and vanishes in the obscure ultimate.
The obscure ultimate means
adhering to one's inherent capacity without adding even a hair's weight of excess.
Therefore, even bearing a weight of ten thousand jun,
if it matches one's ability,
one suddenly feels unaware of the weight on the body;
even responding to myriad affairs,
one remains undisturbed, unconscious of tasks being upon oneself.
This is the essence of nurturing life.
【Commentary】The forms and natures of things
each have their limits,
yet the intellect that discriminates among them
pursues objects without bounds.
This leads to the mind being distressed and the body wearied,
without ever satisfying its desires,
unable to abide by its allotted portion—
such is not the master of nurturing life.
【Explanatory Text】"而知" is pronounced as "zhì".
The same applies to the annotations below.
"好勝" is pronounced as "hào shèng".
The following is pronounced as "shēng zhèng".
"雖復" is pronounced as "suī fù".
The same applies throughout below.
"絕膂" is pronounced as "jué lǚ".
"以慊" is pronounced as "yǐ qiǎn",
meaning sufficient.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In ancient times, it shared the same sound as the "qiàn" in "慊恨" (resentment),
and neither uses the pronunciation "qiè" as the correct interpretation for "sufficient".
【Three】【Comment】Using a finite nature to seek limitless knowledge,
how can one avoid exhaustion?
【Commentary】Life has its limits,
while knowledge is boundless.
Thus, using a finite life to pursue infinite knowledge
inevitably exhausts the body and spirit, leading to peril.
【Explanatory Text】"Dài yǐ" Xiàng explains:
It means exhausted and distressed.
【Four】【Comment】Already trapped by knowledge yet not knowing when to stop,
and again using knowledge to rescue oneself,
this is nurturing while harming it,
truly a great peril.
【Commentary】Boundless knowledge
has been applied before;
deliberate learning
attempts to remedy it afterward—
hoping to avoid peril,
how could that be possible!
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
Toiling restlessly in pursuit of knowledge,
reaching for the limitless,
ultimately ends in peril.
Such restless knowledge stored in the mind
is sufficient to burden one's nature and harm the heart.
Becoming oblivious and transforming with things,
serene and spiritually focused,
prevents such knowledge from arising in the heart,
preserving one's nature continuously,
erasing knowledge to preserve life whole.
Hence it is said: persisting in the pursuit of knowledge leads only to peril.
【五】【注】Forgetting good and evil and abiding in the center,
allowing all things to act on their own,
silently uniting with the ultimate appropriateness,
thus punishments and names stay distant from oneself, and the complete principle resides within.
【Commentary】Those engaged in mundane learning,
though numerous in followers,
in essence,
nothing takes precedence over good and evil.
Thus, doing good always approaches fame and praise,
while doing evil invariably borders on punishment and execution.
From this, it is clear that worldly wisdom and mundane learning
are insufficient to rescue prior knowledge,
and instead exhaust the mind and spirit,
only increasing peril.
【Explanation Text】"Wú jìn" means the nearness of being close by.
The same applies below.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotation in Jī Shūyè's "Poem of Hidden Resentment" from the Wénxuǎn quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Do not cultivate fame.
Wear coarse cloth and embrace jade,
defile and debase one's body,
so as not to be crude in form.
The explanation text is missing.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Chuánshān stated,
things like sounds and colors that cannot be named as good,
are evil.
"Mèn rán" is pronounced with the fanqie "wáng běn fǎn,"
and also sounds like "mén."
"Yuǎn jǐ" is pronounced with the fanqie "yú wàn fǎn."
【Six】【Annotation】Follow the middle path to make it the constant practice.
【Commentary】Yuán means
to follow,
dū means
the center.
Jīng means
constancy.
When both good and evil are forgotten,
and punishments and names are simultaneously dismissed,
one can then follow the Way of the One Center,
abide in the virtue of true constancy,
remain empty and impartial while responding to things,
and move along with the world.
The subtlety of nurturing life
lies precisely in this.
【Explanatory Text】"Following the Central as the Constant Path" Lǐ Yí explains:
Following,
means to comply.
Central,
means the middle.
Path,
means the constant.
Guǒ and Cuī share the same view.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wèi," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Following,
means to comply.
Central,
means the middle.
To comply and abide by the Way in the center, making it constant.
The explanatory text is missing.
◎Lǐ Zhēn states:
In the "Discussion on Bone Cavities" from Sù Wèn,
the Governor Vessel,
originates below the lower abdomen in the center of the bone.
In the "Root and Conduit" chapter of Líng Shū,
the seventh consecutive vessel,
the vessel at the center of the neck,
is the Governor Vessel.
In the human body, only the spine is centered,
and the Governor Vessel runs alongside the spine and ascends,
hence it is interpreted as the center, with the Governor being one of the extraordinary vessels.
Zhuāngzǐ precisely uses the vessel as a metaphor,
hence the subsequent phrases about preserving the body and maintaining life.
Jiā Shìfù states:
Chuánshān says,
among the eight extraordinary vessels,
the Conception and Governor Vessels govern the breath of respiration.
The central vessel in the front of the body is called the Conception Vessel,
and the central vessel in the back of the body is called the Governor Vessel.
The Governor,
resides in stillness and does not lean to either side,
having the position of a vessel but without physical form.
Following the Central means,
with a subtle and refined energy,
to move along emptiness,
stopping where it cannot proceed,
and thus movement naturally complies,
to appropriately attain its center.
【Seven】【Annotation】Nurturing parents to bring them comfort.
【Transcription】"To nourish" is pronounced as yǎng, with the initial consonant like that of yáng and the final like that of shàng, in a reverse spelling method.
The same applies to the annotation.
【Eight】【Annotation】If one attains the mean and silently measures,
then there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Nurturing life does not seek excess,
but rather aims to preserve principle and fulfill one's years.
【Commentary】Only by skillfully abandoning the two extremes and abiding in the singular mean,
can one preserve one's physical form,
and maintain the wholeness of one's life principle.
Externally, one can thus fulfill filial duties to parents,
greatly conforming to human relationships;
internally, one can nurture and protect one's vital spirit,
exhausting one's heavenly endowed nature.
【Collation】(1) Based on Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "qí".
(2) The character "mài" has been amended according to the original text of the Sùwèn.
Cook Dīng was dissecting an ox for Lord Wénhuì.
Where his hand touched,
where his shoulder leaned,
where his foot stepped,
where his knee pressed,
there was a whirring sound,
and the knife swooshed—
each movement in perfect rhythm.
It matched the dance of Sānglín,
and harmonized with the music of Jīngshǒu.
【一】【疏】Páo Dīng,
refers to the person in charge of kitchen duties,
which is today's provision of meals.
It is also said:
Dīng,
is a name.
Wén Huì Jūn,
is King Huì of Liáng.
To dissect,
means to slaughter and cut it.
To press down,
is to stab with the lower horn.
It is said that Páo Dīng was skilled at butchering oxen,
seeing the patterns within,
so he used his hands to touch and feel,
leaned on it with his shoulder,
stepped on it with his foot,
and pierced it with his knee,
thus causing the skin and flesh to separate,
with a crisp sound responding,
advancing to apply the ceremonial knife,
and with a loud sound, it was greatly dissected.
This is probably using Páo Dīng as a metaphor to illustrate the art of nurturing life.
【Explanatory Text】"Páo Dīng" is written as 胞 in Cuī's edition,
which is the same.
Pronounced as bái jiāo fǎn.
A cook,
Dīng is his name.
Guǎnzǐ records a butcher named Tú Niú Tǎn who could dismember nine oxen in one morning,
with a knife sharp enough to shave hair.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In the Lǐjì, Jì Tǒng mentions huī bāo,
also identical to páo.
"Wèi" is pronounced yú wèi fǎn.
"Wén Huì Jūn" according to Cuī Sīmǎ:
that is Liáng Huì Wáng.
"Suǒ yǐ" Xú gives the pronunciation as yú qǐ fǎn,
Xiàng gives yǎn bǐ fǎn,
Xú also gives yú zhù fǎn,
Lǐ pronounces it as yāo.
"Suǒ yǐ" Xú gives jū bǐ fǎn,
Xiàng gives yú bǐ fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means to stab.
"Huā rán" Xiàng gives hū jué fǎn,
Xú gives xǔ jué fǎn,
Cuī pronounces it as huà,
also gǔ jué fǎn,
Lǐ also gives hū lì fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
The sound of skin and bone separating.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
Previously, jué was all written with bèi,
which is incorrect.
Now it is corrected to be written with jú.
The following are all the same.
"Xiǎng rán" is pronounced xǔ zhàng fǎn,
Guō gives xǔ liàng fǎn.
Some versions may omit the character rán.
"Zòu" is read as the character itself.
Cuī says:
It means to hear.
"Huō" is pronounced hū huò fǎn,
Xú gives xǔ bì fǎn,
Tā gives tā yì fǎn,
also pronounced as mài.
Cuī says:
The sound is close to huò,
and it is louder than huā.
【Two】【Annotation】It speaks of how he applied skill with convenience,
being adept at understanding everything,
thoroughly grasping the principles to the utmost,
fitting well with the nature of the ox,
and harmonizing with musical rhythm.
【Commentary】Sānglín
is the name of the music of Yīn Tāng.
Jīngshǒu,
a movement of the Xiánchí music,
was the music of Yáo.
Páodīng's spirit and expression were composed,
perfectly understanding the nature of the ox;
then the sounds of his cutting and carving
harmoniously matched the musical notes,
thus resonating with Sānglín
and aligning with the rhythm of Jīngshǒu.
【Explanation Text】"Zhōng Yīn": Dǐng Zhòng fǎn.
The following are all the same.
"Sāng Lín": Sīmǎ says:
Tāng's music name.
Cuī says:
Sòng's dance music name.
According to the case, it is as recorded in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, where the dance master marked it with a feathered banner.
"Jīng Shǒu": Xiàng Sīmǎ says:
A movement of the Xián Chí music.
Cuī says:
The name of a musical movement.
Some say:
The name of a musical performance.
"Yīn Biàn": Bì Miàn fǎn.
"Xián Jiě": pronounced as Xiè.
Wén Huì Jūn said:
"Ah,
excellent!
How can skill reach such a level?"
【一】【疏】Ah,
a sigh of admiration.
Lord Huì, having seen the cook Ding skillfully apply his technique with ease,
the rhythm of his blade's movement,
distantly harmonized with musical movements,
thus praised his artistry as having reached such a level.
【Transcription】"Xī" is pronounced as xī by Xú.
Lǐ says:
It is an exclamatory sound.
"Jì" is pronounced with the initial j and the rhyme qǐ.
The same applies below.
The cook put down his knife and replied:
"What I love is the Way,
which goes beyond mere skill.
When I first began to dissect oxen,
all I could see was the whole ox.
After three years,
I no longer saw the ox as a whole.
Nowadays,
I meet it with my spirit rather than looking with my eyes.
My sensory knowledge ceases while my spiritual desire moves forward.
Following the natural grain,
I slice through the major seams,
guide the knife through the large cavities,
according to its inherent structure.
I never touch veins, tendons, or ligatures,
let alone the big bones!
A good cook changes his knife once a year—
because he cuts.
An average cook changes his knife once a month—
because he hacks.
Now my knife has been in use for nineteen years,
dissecting thousands of oxen,
yet its edge is as sharp as if newly ground.
For the joints have gaps,
and the knife's edge has no thickness;
inserting what has no thickness into gaps,
there is certainly plenty of room for the blade to move about.
That is why after nineteen years my knife's edge is as sharp as if newly ground.
Nevertheless,
whenever I come to a complicated part,
and see it difficult to handle,
I become cautious and alert,
my vision focuses,
my movements slow down.
I move the knife very slightly,
until with a gentle flop the ox is dismembered,
like a clod of earth crumbling to the ground.
Then I stand holding the knife,
look all around,
linger with satisfaction,
wipe the knife clean, and put it away."
【一】【注】It is simply that the principle is directly conveyed through the skill,
what is valued is not the skill itself.
【Commentary】He set aside the sacrificial knife,
responding to the way of nurturing life,
thus relying on his skill,
to present it to the ruler.
Another explanation:
"advancing"
means surpassing.
What he valued was the way of nurturing life,
which surpassed the technique of butchering oxen.
【Transcription】"Suǒ hào" is read with the fourth tone for "hào."
The annotation is the same.
【二】【注】Unable to perceive the principle in its quietude (三).
【Commentary】When first learning butchering,
one has not yet understood the underlying principles,
and sees only the ox.
Similarly, when first cultivating life,
one has not yet illuminated the true realm,
thus encountering obstacles at every turn.
【Three】【Annotation】Only perceive its principle as idle.
【Commentary】Having wielded the knife for so long,
one suddenly perceives the principles within the gaps,
so that upon merely glimpsing an ox,
one already knows it is hollowed out.
This is akin to having long practiced the Way,
where wisdom's illumination gradually brightens,
and all perceived worldly realms
are nothing but illusion.
【Four】【Annotation】Darkness harmonizes with principle.
【Commentary】Encounter means
to meet.
Having passed through nineteen years,
it aligns with the wondrous numbers of yīn and yáng,
guiding the spirit to comprehend principles—
how could it rely on the eyes to perceive it!
It is just like those who cultivate the Way:
marvelously uniting with the ultimate,
they extend the mind’s intelligence to illuminate emptiness—
how could they use their eyes to grasp the dust!
【Interpretation】"Spiritual Encounter" Xiàng explains:
Unconsciously uniting with principle,
is called spiritual encounter.
【Five】【Annotation】When the offices of surveillance and oversight are abolished,
one follows their heart and complies with principle.
【Commentary】Officials refer to those in charge of administration;
it means, for example, the eyes govern colors and the ears manage sounds.
Once the spirit connects,
there is no need to rely on sight,
hence the governing functions of the eyes and other senses
all come to a halt,
allowing one to follow the heart's desires
and act in accordance with reason.
Those who are skilled in nurturing life
embody the same principle.
【Explanation Text】"The senses know where to stop" is read with the character's usual pronunciation.
Cuī Zǐ states:
"Official knowledge,"
means having something under one's charge.
Xiàng Xù reads it as "wisdom."

Bǐ,
refers to the multitude.
The sage embraces emptiness,
responding as things evoke,
pitying the millions,
compassionate for all living beings,
not awaiting earnest requests,
he expounds the teachings for them.
Therefore, upon his death,
the masses gathered,
wailing in grief,
as if for a mother or child.
This is because ordinary emotions cling stubbornly,
mistakenly perceiving life and death,
moved by the sage's grace,
leading to this mourning.
Judging by this,
thus it is known they are not disciples of Lǎojūn.

【Four】【Annotation】What is endowed by natural disposition,
each has its inherent lot,
which cannot be evaded,
nor can it be increased.
【Comment】This means,
to reprimand the mourner.
"Bèi" (倍)

It refers to fleeing from one's natural disposition,
and adding worldly sentiments,
mistakenly perceiving death as lamentable,
thus forgetting the inherent endowment one has received.

【Five】【Annotation】Being excessively moved by external matters,
not stopping at what is appropriate,
is to evade the natural way.
One will then gallop through the realms of sorrow and joy,
and even if the punishment of Chǔ has not yet been inflicted, the nature and emotions are already distressed—
is this not a form of punishment indeed!
【Commentary】Those who evade the principles of heaven
and go against worldly emotions,
with sorrow and joy burdening their hearts,
find their minds and spirits in distress and suffering.
It is akin to being beaten with rods and canes,
how could it not be a form of punishment and execution!
The enlightened ones of ancient times
held such views.
【Transcription】"Dà" is pronounced as tài.

【Six】【Annotation】It arises spontaneously at the time.
【Seven】【Annotation】It is justifiable that he should die.
【Commentary】The term "Fūzǐ" refers to
Lǎojūn.
Qín Shī sighed at how Lǎojūn, as a great sage,
profoundly understood the fundamental origin.
Thus, his coming into life
was in accordance with the times to descend and be born;
his serene passing
likewise followed the natural order to return to authenticity.
【八】【注】For sorrow and joy arise from loss and gain.
Now, those who are profoundly connected and adaptable to change,
are at peace at all times,
and settled in every circumstance.
Unconsciously becoming one with the Creator,
then everywhere is none other than oneself.
How could there be any gain or loss,
or any distinction between death and life?
Therefore, by accepting what is received,
sorrow and joy have no place to intrude in between.
【Commentary】When one is content with life,
one does not grow weary of living;
when one accepts death with equanimity,
one does not dread dying.
Through all the myriad transformations,
there has never been anything that is not oneself;
wherever one finds oneself, one is at ease,
thus sorrow and joy do not disturb the heart.
