freed from bondage and the true essence of life is attained.
This is the key to nurturing life.
【Commentary】The term "Dì" (帝) refers to
Heaven.
That which is bound by life and death is called the "tether,"
thus, being free from life and death is the release from the tether.
When life and death cannot bind one,
and sorrow and joy cannot enter,
the ancient sages called this the natural liberation.
Moreover, Lǎojūn, the great sage,
merged life and death into one,
so how could he evade the punishment of Heaven
or chase after sorrow and joy?

【一】【注】Qióng,
means to exhaust;

is like the previous firewood.
The previous firewood points to it,
pointing exhausts the principle of the former firewood,
thus the fire passes on and does not extinguish;
the heart-mind receives nourishment within,
so life continues without interruption;
it clarifies that nurturing life is the reason why life exists.
【Commentary】Qióng means
to exhaust.
Xīn refers to
firewood.
Wéi means
to move forward.
It is said that when a person lights a fire,
pushing it forward with their hands,
those who understand the principle of fully igniting the fire
will see that even if the front firewood is exhausted,
the rear firewood continues it,
with the front and rear succeeding one another,
thus the fire does not go out.
This is also like those who are skilled in nurturing life:
they follow change and accept transformation,
moving along with all things,
hence the old self renews into the new self,
without any attachment or longing,
never ceasing to be oneself,
thus continuing without interruption.

【二】【注】Time does not come again,
and the present does not pause for a moment.
Therefore, in human life,
each breath is a gain in itself.
The past breath is not the present one,
so by taking in nourishment, life continues;
the former flame is not the later one,
so with fresh firewood, the fire is passed on.
As the fire is transmitted and life endures,
it is because nourishment attains its utmost efficacy.
How could the world know that when it ends, it is reborn anew!
【Commentary】Those who are deluded and forgetful
are enslaved by their attachments and stubbornness.
How could they know that renewal never ceases,
thoughts and moments flow incessantly,
the self of yesterday
has already ended by today,
and the self of today
will be reborn again hereafter?

Yán Huí went to see Zhòngní,
and asked to take his leave【一】.
【First】【Commentary】His surname was Yán,
given name Huí,
courtesy name Zǐyuān,
a man of Lǔ;
among Confucius's three thousand disciples,
he was the one who excelled across all four categories of virtue and entered the inner chamber as a direct disciple.
Zhòngní,
whose surname was Kǒng,
given name Qiū,
courtesy name Zhòngní,
was also a man of Lǔ,
a descendant of the Yīn dynasty's founder Tāng,
born in the declining era of the Zhōu dynasty,
possessing sagely virtue,
and was Yán Huí's teacher.
The origins and deeds of these figures
are fully recorded in Confucian historical texts,
but since the purpose here is to interpret Zhuāngzǐ,
with an emphasis on metaphysical abstraction,
they will not be recounted in exhaustive detail.
However, the affairs of the human world
are truly entangled and difficult,
interacting with others for their benefit
is inherently challenging,
so Yán and Kǒng are invoked here to illustrate methods of transformative guidance,
and these sages are employed to elucidate the art of mental fasting.
Thus, Kǒng the sage and Yán the worthy.
【Explanation】Yán Huí was a disciple of Confucius,
with the surname Yán,
given name Huí,
courtesy name Zǐyuān,
and a native of the state of Lǔ.
Said:
"Where are you going?"
【一】【疏】Xī,
means "what".
〔Zhī〕,
means "to go to".
This is questioning Yán Huí about where he intends to go.
He said:
"I am going to Wèi."
【一】【疏】Wèi,
was the capital of King Zhòu of Yīn,
and also the fief of Kāng Shū,
which is now Wèi Prefecture in Jí Commandery.
This is where Yán answered Kǒng's question about where he wished to go.
He said:
"Why do this?"
【One】【Memorial】Intending to go to Wèiguó,
what should be said?
The heavy responsibility placed on Yán Shēng's luggage is implied.
He said:
"I, Huí, have heard of the ruler of Wèi,
who is in the prime of his years,
and acts autocratically;
he recklessly employs the resources of his state,
yet fails to see his own faults;
he lightly sends his people to their deaths,
so that the dead fill the marshes like reeds,
and the people have nowhere to turn.
I once heard our Master say:
'Leave well-governed states,
go to troubled ones;
at a doctor's door are many sick.'
I wish to apply what I have heard to devise a principle,
hoping that the state may thereby be cured!
【一】【注】He does not share the same desires as the people.
【Commentary】The ruler of Wèi,
namely Kuǎikuì, the son of Duke Líng,
was dissolute and deluded,
indulging his passions without principle.
In his youth, he was robust and fearsomely fierce,
acting alone in cruelty and defying the will of others.
Yánzǐ recounted what he had heard in reply to Confucius.
【Explanatory Text】"The ruler of Wèi" Sīmǎ comments:
It refers to Duke Zhuāng of Wèi, Kuǎikuì.
According to the Zuǒzhuàn,
Duke Zhuāng of Wèi only entered the state in the winter of the fifteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
by which time Yán Huí had already died,
so it could not be Duke Zhuāng;
it must be the exiled Duke Zhé.
"His conduct" is read with the falling-rising tone for the character.
"Alone" Cuī notes:
It means acting on one's own authority.
Xiàng comments:
It means being different from others.
Guō states:
Not sharing the same desires as others.
【二】【注】The ruler of men,
in his actions must ride upon the people,
with one burst of anger can cause corpses to lie strewn and blood to flow,
with one moment of joy can have carriages and official caps block the roads.
Therefore, the way a ruler of men employs the state
must not be taken lightly.
【Commentary】The people are the foundation of the state;
when the foundation is firm, the state is tranquil.
If one fails to cherish and value the common populace,
but instead seeks to belittle and disregard their utility,
to hope for no collapse or overthrow,
how could that be possible!
【Three】【Comment】None dared to remonstrate.
【Commentary】His strength was sufficient to ward off remonstrance,
his eloquence enough to gloss over faults,
thus the common people were filled with fear and swallowed their voices,
and though he had errors, none dared to admonish him.
【Four】【Annotation】To lightly employ it in situations of mortal peril.
【Commentary】Without halting movement or stillness,
remaining composed and self-assured,
yet lightly employing the nation's people,
casting them into perilous grounds.
【Five】【Note】The entire state is driven to a fatal situation,

Speaking of how many they are,
it is measured by the state as a whole,
if one tries to count them,
it is difficult to ascertain in haste.
Indulging oneself alone,
without pity for the common people,
viewing the nation's citizens,
as mere grass blades and straws in marshes and swamps.

one may not yet have reached the essence of others' dispositions,
and though renowned for not contending,
one may not yet have touched the hearts of people.
Yet to forcefully impose words of benevolence and righteousness as standards before a tyrant

which is called bringing calamity upon them.
Those who bring calamity upon others

Moreover, if he truly delighted in the worthy and despised the unworthy,

has never understood the resolve of Yán Huí,

【二】【注】When presenting a luminous pearl at night to someone,
few would not press their hand to their sword,
for they do not understand its nature.
Now, Huí's virtue, trustworthiness, and reputation for non-contention,
are things they have not comprehended.
If one forcibly measures them against standards of benevolence and righteousness,
they will say that Huí seeks to belittle others to elevate himself.
Therefore, the ultimate person does not labor their will to govern the world,
but responds to things with an open mind,
so that sincerity and trust shine through heaven and earth,
and non-contention flows through all things.
Only then do all things return to their embrace,
and heaven and earth do not oppose them.
Thus, when virtuous words are uttered, the world echoes in response;
when illustrious conduct is revealed, all within the six directions unite in answer.
Only then can one endure the cold and heat,
traverse order and chaos,
without clashing against the scales that go against the grain.
【Commentary】The words of the plumb line and ink marker,
refer to the five virtues of sagely wisdom.
Huí's moral character,
the ruler of Wèi had not comprehended,
yet he forcefully employed the methods of benevolence and righteousness before a violent man;
the recounted fine words of the ancient kings
were bound to incur the ruler of Wèi's loathing,
hence it was not permissible.
【Text】"Er qiang" is read with the two characters' respective pronunciations.

【Three】【Comment】If one does not believe and accept it,
then they may think it competes with their own reputation and instead harm them.
【Commentary】Mìng means name.
The Marquis of Wèi did not understand your intentions,
thinking that you were plotting harm against him.
Having encountered suspicion and doubt,
you were bound to face retaliation in return.

【Four】【Annotation】If one can delight in the virtuous and detest the foolish,
hear of righteousness and submit to it,
then they are an enlightened ruler.
If they are an enlightened ruler,
then it is not that they lack virtuous ministers,
and your going there would not be particularly remarkable;
but if they are not so,
going will certainly bring harm.
Therefore, to go with intention,
no venture would be suitable;
to respond without intention,
the response will come naturally,
then no venture would be unsuitable.
【Commentary】Danger means
proximity.
Alas,
an exclamation of sorrow.
If you go to Wèi,
you will inevitably approach peril and ruin,
harmed by violent individuals,
deeply lamentable indeed.
Moreover, if the Marquis of Wèi were truly able to delight in and cherish the virtuous,
and despise the unworthy,
then his court would naturally be filled with noble men,
having dismissed and banished petty individuals.
With loyal ministers already present,
what need would there be for you!
If you go there,
how would you differ from those men!
Since there is no difference,
your departure would be of no benefit.

【Five】【Annotation】You must remain silent and speak not,
for should you speak, the lords and princes will surely exploit their authority as rulers to outmaneuver you with their sharp arguments,
using them to reject remonstrance and conceal their faults.

to speak.
Wánggōng refers to
the Marquis of Wèi.
If you go to Wèi,
you should only remain silent and not speak.
If you offer admonitions or advice,
you will inevitably face execution or humiliation.
Moreover, the Marquis of Wèi relies on the power of a thousand chariots,
wields the authority of the five ranks,
covers up his faults and rejects remonstrance,
engaging in sharp debates.
Since you are already terrified,
how could you have the opportunity to correct and support him!

【Commentary】Yíng means

Although Marquis Wèi was dissolute and tyrannical,
he was exceptionally eloquent and intelligent,
and with the authority of a ruler,
he oppressed loyal and admonishing officials.
Therefore, Yán Huí felt fear in his heart,
and his eyes became dazzled and confused.

【Seven】【Annotation】Cannot again distinguish oneself from them.
【Commentary】Even if one has the intention to remonstrate,
one dares not show overt disagreement;
with a compliant expression and demeanor,
one harmonizes with others peacefully.
【八】【Note】Barely able to save oneself from trouble.
【Commentary】The Marquis of Wèi, being of high rank and prestige,
possessed an awe-inspiring dignity.
Yán Shēng feared that disaster might befall him,
and thus was filled with countless worries and fears.
Therefore, he busied himself with words to protect himself,
scarcely having any leisure for composure.
【Nine】【Explanations】Form,
is manifestation.
Since one fears calamities,
thus one submits and complies superficially,
bowing, kneeling, bending, and clasping hands—
thus the traces of form are manifested.
【Interpretation】"Róng jiāng xíng zhī" refers to kneeling and bowing.
【一０】【Note】This is to temporarily set aside oneself in order to follow others.
【Commentary】It is not merely that the external form follows compliance,
but also that the inner heart is in harmony and agreement,
yet failing to advance in goodness and instead furthering that person's faults.
【一一】【Note】Failing to rescue in time,
only serves to enhance their prestige further.
【Commentary】Using,
means to employ.
Employing fire to extinguish fire,
only intensifies the fierce blaze;
employing water to control water,
only swells the waves even more.
Thus, Yánzǐ's actions,
merely served to complete the tyranny of Duke Wèi,
failing to correct or advise,
can be said to have aggravated the situation.
【一二】【Note】Adhering to the old ways as usual,
unwilling to change.
【13】【Comment】To remonstrate without having gained trust,
even earnest words become harmful.
【Commentary】Your loyal and sincere words,
if not trusted and adopted in the near term,
then even if offered with genuine intent to advise,
will inevitably lead to punishment and execution before a tyrannical ruler.
【Collation Notes】(1) The "quē wù" cites the Jiangnan Guzang edition, where "shù" is written as "xuàn".

Moreover, in ancient times, Jié executed Guān Lóngpáng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
These were men who cultivated their own virtue to care for the people below them,
and with their humble position opposed their rulers above.
Thus, their lords, because of their cultivation, pushed them to their doom.
This is the peril of those who seek fame.
In the past, Yáo attacked Cóngzhī and Xū'áo,
and Yǔ attacked Yǒuhù.
Their states were reduced to ruins and specters,
their bodies suffered punishment and execution,
yet their use of military force did not cease,
nor did their pursuit of gain ever end.
These are all examples of seeking fame and profit—
have you not heard of them?
Fame and profit
are what even the sage cannot overcome;
how much less can someone like you!
【一】【注】Lóng Péng and Bǐ Gàn,
though in lowly positions, bore the worries of those above,
were not those whose duty it was.
【Commentary】According to the principles of posthumous naming,
one who plunders the people and kills many is called Jié,
one who destroys righteousness and harms the good is called Zhòu.
His surname was Guān,
his given name Lóngpéng,
a worthy minister of Xià Jié,
who was beheaded despite his utmost loyalty.
Bǐgān,
a paternal uncle of Yīn Zhòu,
had his heart cut out for his faithful remonstrance.
Yǔfǔ means to cherish and nurture.
Fú signifies opposition and perversity.
These two individuals,
both were excellent aides of ancient times,
cultivated their own character,
upheld loyalty and integrity,
from their positions as subordinates,
worried about the people under their sovereign's rule.
Though the ministers were virtuous and the rulers without virtue,
by opposing their sovereigns,
they both suffered execution and humiliation.
Citing the past to prove the present,
it serves as a sufficient mirror for reflection.
Thus, we know that Yán Huí's attempt to transform Wèi
was not feasible in principle.
【Explanation】Guān Lóngpáng: A worthy minister of Xià Jié.
Wángzǐ Bǐgàn: The paternal uncle of Yīn Zhòu.

【二】【Note】This is to prevent the subject from gaining a reputation for surpassing the ruler.

to fall,
to entrap,
to poison.
Jié of the Xià and Zhòu of the Yīn,
rulers without virtue,
did not assess their own capabilities,
yet still coveted fame and praise.
Thus, they took advantage of the refinement and efforts of worthy ministers,
only to unleash their venom and entrap them.
Their intent was to compete for reputation and chase after profit,
which ultimately led them to this outcome.

【Three】【Commentary】A tyrant does not merely seek to indulge his desires,
but also seeks fame,
yet what he seeks is not by the right path.
【Commentary】The two rulers Yáo and Yǔ,
have already been explained previously.
Cóngzhī,
Xū'áo,
and Yǒuhù,
are all names of states.
As for Yǒuhù,
it is present-day Hù County in Yōngzhōu.
A dwelling without people is called "empty";
a ghost without descendants is called "wraith."
This means that the rulers of these three states,
were all without virtue,
fond of raising armies
to attack other states.
Not only did they greedily seek material gains,
but they also schemed to pursue empty fame,
consequently causing their territories to become desolate mounds,
their people to be wiped out,
themselves to suffer execution,
and their ancestral temples to collapse and perish.
Their greed for fame and pursuit of profit
reached such an extreme;
this is known to all, past and present,
how is it that you alone have not heard of it?
【Translated Text】"Cóng zhī" is pronounced as cái gōng fǎn.

These are all evidence.
【四】【注】A ruler who cherishes fame and covets desires,
even if again a Yáo or Yǔ,
cannot be overcome and transformed,
so we join the multitude to attack him,
yet you wish to go empty-handed,
and transform him with the Way?
【Commentary】As for the mediocre and tyrannical rulers,
greedy for profit and seeking fame,
even if faced with sage sovereigns like Yáo and Yǔ,
they cannot be won over by virtue.
Thus, armies are still raised
to punish crimes and eliminate evil.
How much more so for a commoner like Yánzǐ,
attempting to transform others empty-handed?
The impossibility of such an outcome
is undoubtedly clear.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition does not have the character "之".
Although this is so,
you must have a reason for it,
so try telling me about it!
【一】【疏】Cháng,
means to try.
Your transformative teachings,
although not yet widely spread,
since you wish to request to go forth,
surely there is a reason for it.
Try to state your intentions,
and tell me about them.
【Text】"Yǔ wǒ" is pronounced with "yú" as in "yú jù" and "wǒ" as in the third tone.

It was previously recorded as "yú yù" in the third tone,
which is incorrect.

Yán Huí said:
"If I am upright and humble,
diligent and single-minded,
would that suffice?"
【一】【注】Align its form and empty its mind.
【Commentary】Rectify one's posture,
to exhaust the reverence of a subject;
empty and broaden the mind,
to pour out the sincerity of remonstrance.
Having received the noble command,
I dare to relate the reasons.
【二】【Note】It means being modest and not duplicitous.
【Explanation】Exert oneself in both body and mind,
serve the state with utmost sincerity,
be loyal and cautious in words and deeds,
so that there is no room for error.
【Three】【Memorials】As with the previous two methods,
can they be implemented?
He said:
"Ugh!
How can it be done!
With yang energy filling him and arrogance evident,
his countenance unstable,
what ordinary people would not oppose,
he suppresses others' genuine feelings,
seeking to indulge his own mind.
Called daily cultivation of virtue, it does not achieve even that,
let alone great virtue!
He will remain stubborn and unyielding,
outwardly compliant but inwardly unreflecting—
how could this possibly do!"
【一】【Note】It is not yet permissible to speak.
【Commentary】To detest evil,
is like asking "where,"
meaning where can it be acceptable,
indicates it is not yet acceptable.
【Explanation】"È è" are both pronounced as wū,
similarly hereinafter.
【Two】【Annotation】It speaks of the ruler of Wèi's nature of excessive yang filling within and greatly manifesting without,
being the utmost in strength and dominance.
【Commentary】Yáng,
means firm and fierce.
Chōng,
means full.
Kǒng,
means extreme.
This says that the ruler of Wèi, with a nature of firmness and fierceness, fills his inner heart,
being extremely violent and forceful,
and displays it outwardly in his actions.
【Three】【Annotation】Unpredictable in joy and anger.
【Commentary】When things go as one wishes, there is joy;
when they go against one's will, there is anger;
the spirit, expression, and complexion
have never been constant.
【Four】【Annotation】None dared to oppose it.
【Commentary】Being of a violent and cruel nature,
his might and ferocity were extraordinary,
so how could remonstrating scholars and virtuous men
possibly oppose or contradict him!
【五】【注】For the utterly obstinate and unyielding,
when others use joyful matters to move them,
they trample upon and then suppress these gestures,
in order to seek self-indulgent freedom and thereby fulfill their extravagant desires.
【Commentary】Àn means
to suppress.
Róngyǔ means
indulgence or letting loose.
When people offer admonitions and move with virtuous deeds,
the ruler instead suppresses and frustrates them due to their loyal advice,
seeking pleasure and indulgence,
thus fulfilling his intentions of wanton dissipation.
【Text】"Cuò zhī" is pronounced as zǐ wò fǎn.
"Cóngróng" is pronounced as qī róng fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Words are few yet many,
without the victory of retreat and descent.
【Commentary】The Marquis of Wèi's lack of virtue,
has been long-standing.
Even if gradually nurtured by daily moral influence,
it still could not be achieved,
let alone the grand model of sage-like wisdom,
how could one hope for that!
【Seven】【Annotation】Thus, one holds to their original intent.
【Commentary】A ruler who conceals his faults and remains in the dark,
unable to accept remonstrance with an open mind,
stubbornly clinging to his own views,
who would be willing to change from evil to good?
【Eight】【Comment】Outwardly agreeable yet inwardly unyielding,
that is, previously upright and empty yet striving for unity,
meaning this is not enough to transform them.
【Commentary】Externally adopting a posture of kneeling with hands clasped,
to display utmost obsequiousness,
while inwardly being submissive and compliant,
not daring to criticize or disparage.
With such an approach to request action,
what benefit would the action bring?
The way to transform Wèi,
how could it possibly be achieved!
This shows that the previously proposed empty and superficial strategy is not suitable for implementation.
【Transcription】"Bù zī" Xiàng and Xú pronounce as zǐ.
Cuī says:
It means to slander.
【校】（一）趙諫議本快作使。
"Then I am inwardly upright and outwardly accommodating,
forming my views and drawing comparisons from the past.
Being inwardly upright means
being a companion to Heaven.
As a companion to Heaven,
one knows that the Son of Heaven and oneself are both sons of Heaven.
So why should one expect others to approve of one's words,
or fear that they might disapprove of them?
If so,
people call one a child,
and this is what is meant by being a companion to Heaven.
Being outwardly accommodating means
being a companion to people.
Bowing, kneeling, and bending in salute
are the rituals of a minister.
Since everyone does them,
how dare I not do so?
By doing what others do,
others will find no fault with me,
and this is what is meant by being a companion to people.
Forming views and drawing comparisons from the past means
being a companion to antiquity.
Although the words may be instructive,
they are actually reproaches.
They existed in ancient times,
not originating from me.
If so,
although straightforward, they cause no harm,
and this is what is meant by being a companion to antiquity.
Would this be acceptable then?"
【一】【注】Yán Huí further elaborated on these three points.
【Commentary】Having previously presented two matters,
which were already criticized,
now three points are established,
hoping they will be appropriate.
This marks the heading,
below which its meaning is explained,
as Yán Shēng recounted himself to briefly convey to Xuānní.
【Explanation】"而上" is pronounced as "shí zhǎng fǎn".
The same applies below.
【二】【Note】All things are without inherent nobility or baseness,
for the attainment of life is one and the same.
Thus, whether good or not good,
it is left to the impartial judgment of all,
with not a single demand made upon others.
【Commentary】This section explains the meaning.
Qí,
means to seek.
It says that my inner self is simple and sincere,
joining with the natural principles as companions.
Thus, I know that both the emperor and I
are endowed with what is natural,
so we can forget the distinction between noble and humble in the roles of ruler and subject,
disregarding good and evil in matters of honor and disgrace.
Why then would one still boast of reputation to avoid evil
or seek goodness from others?
With such an open mind,
one may come close to aligning with reason.
【Interpretation】"Qí hū" is pronounced as qí.
【Three】【Annotations】Rely on the natural principles,
extend one's own nature to trust in destiny,
like an infant going straightforwardly.
【Commentary】Ran,
means "like this."
Tongzi,
refers to an infant.
If as previously explained,
reasoning straightforwardly,
one's conduct resembles that of an infant,
hence people call them a child.
To conclude the earlier meaning,
this is therefore called being a companion to Heaven.
【Four】【Dissertations】As for outwardly displaying compliance,
adapting to worldly ways,
it is to align with the human relationships as one's kind.
Raising hands and kneeling with feet,
bowing deeply and bending the body,
lowering and lifting in prostration,
these are the rites of a subject.
Yet harmonizing with the dust and grime,
accepting the rise and fall of things,
if all others practice this,
should I alone refrain from doing so?
Thus, by doing what others do,
one incurs no resentment or hostility from them.
【Transcription】"擎" - Xú reads it as jīng.
"跽" - Xú reads it as jǐ.
The Shuōwén dictionary says:
It means kneeling for a long time.
"曲拳" - pronounced quán.
"無疵" - pronounced cī.
【Five】【Annotation】The external form is adaptable and compliant,
following what is appropriate for human affairs.
【Subcommentary】This concludes the preceding three points.
【Six】【Annotation】Accomplished in the present and compared with the ancient.
【Commentary】The matter of loyal remonstration,
is accomplished in the present,
the righteousness between ruler and subject,
is compared to that of antiquity,
hence it is likened to ancient loyal ministers such as Bǐ Gān,
this is its meaning.
【Seven】【Annotation】Though it is a common teaching,
it truly carries a tone of veiled criticism.
【Commentary】Zhé,
means to reprimand.
The words presented,
although they appear as teachings,
when considering their intended meaning,
truly carry a heart of subtle criticism and reproach.

◎ Yú Yuè says:
The preceding text states,
"Do not listen with your ears but listen with your mind;
do not listen with your mind but listen with your vital breath."
In this text, "listening stops at the ears"
should instead read "the ears stop at listening,"
as the transmission and copying have mistakenly inverted it,
which elaborates on the meaning of "do not listen with your ears."
It means that the function of the ears is merely to stop at listening,
hence one should not listen with the ears.
"The mind stops at matching,"
which elaborates on the meaning of "do not listen with the mind."
It means that the function of the mind is merely to stop at matching,
hence one should not listen with the mind.
"Matching" means to harmonize,
that is, to unite with things.
If one unites with things,
then it is not what is meant by "being empty and awaiting things."
"The vital breath is empty and awaits things,"
which elaborates on the word "vital breath,"
clarifying that one ought to listen with the vital breath.
Guō Xiàng's annotation speaks of discarding the ears and eyes and abandoning the mind and intentions,
mistakenly reading the two words "matching" and "vital breath" together.
Not only does this lose the meaning,
but it also results in an ungrammatical sentence.

"Mén" and "dú" are parallel terms,
but "dú" and "mén" are not of the same category.
Shuōwén states:

means thick.
Grasses that harm people,

"Dú" is actually a loan character for "dǎo."
Xǔ explains under "dǎo":
it means to protect,

and is read like "dú."
This aligns with the annotation's meaning of self-security.
Zhāng Xíngfú's "Shuōwén Fāyí" says:
"Dǎo" refers to
piling earth to form a platform for transmitting signals,
which is what "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" calls "building high towers on the royal road,"
placing drums on them,
so the sound can be heard from far and near.
"Dǎo" should be a corruption of "dǎo."
"Dǎo" is a place of defense,
hence its meaning is borrowed for protection.
The character "dú" in the Yìjīng, Zhuāngzǐ, and Lǎozǐ,
precisely carries this meaning,
(in Lǎozǐ's "settle it, thicken it,"
and in the Zhōuyì's "with this, secure the world and the people follow it,"
the character "dú" is used as a loan in both cases.
) This is why "Guǎngyǎ" includes the interpretation of "dú" as security.
Note: "Dǎo" is the original character for "dú,"
making it directly comparable to "mén,"
hence the parallel use of "mén" and "dú."

【八】【注】It states that things have no inherent nobility or baseness,
for there is none that does not communicate with itself through the mind's knowledge, the ears, and the eyes.
Thus, what the world calls knowing,
is it really knowing because one desires to know?
What is called seeing,
is it seeing because one aims to see?
If knowing and seeing could be attained by desiring and acting,
then desiring to be virtuous could make one virtuous,
and aiming to be sage could make one sage, could it not?
Surely, it cannot.
Yet the world does not understand that knowing is self-knowing,
and thus seeks to know by forcing knowledge;
it does not see that seeing is self-seeing,
and thus tries to see by forcing sight;
not realizing that life is self-generating,
it further attempts to generate life by acting upon it.
Hence, upon seeing the eye, one seeks the clarity of Lì Zhū,
and upon seeing the ear, demands the acuity of Shī Kuàng,
causing the spirit and mind to race within,
while the ears and eyes are exhausted and lost without,
resulting in discomfort in one's being and failure to merge with things.
Without such merging,
how can one harmonize with the changes of the human world,
and respond to the rhythms of successive generations?
This has never been possible.

few are accomplished satisfactorily without following the Dào.
If a matter is not accomplished,
there is bound to be the calamity of human retribution;
if it is accomplished,
there is bound to be the affliction of yīn-yáng imbalance.
To have no affliction whether the matter succeeds or fails—
only one with virtue can achieve this.'
I eat plain food without seeking delicacies,
and my cook has no desire for cooling drinks.
Yet now I receive the command in the morning and drink ice by evening—
is this due to the internal heat within me!
I have not yet encountered the actual situation of the mission,
but already suffer the affliction of yīn-yáng imbalance;
if the mission fails,
there will surely be the calamity of human retribution.
Facing these dual dilemmas,
as a minister, I feel inadequate to bear them.
Please, do you have any advice to offer me?"
【一】【注】They valued his mission,
wishing to seek something.
【Commentary】Yǐn Chéngzǐ, the great-great-grandson of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
was named Zhūliáng,
styled Zǐgāo,
who received the fief of Yè for his sustenance,
presumptuously adopted the title of Duke.
The title of king,
in the Spring and Autumn period, was actually held by the ruler of Chǔ as a viscount,
yet he presumptuously claimed the title of king.
Qí,
was the descendant of Tàigōng of the Jiāng surname.
Their ancestor was one of the Four Peaks under Yǔ,
who was enfeoffed at Lǚ,
hence Tàigōng was called Lǚ Wàng.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Tàigōng at Yíngqiū,
which became the state of Qí.
The two states of Qí and Chǔ,
established friendly relations and exchanged visits,
with envoys bearing jades and silks,
continuously without interruption,
sometimes seeking aid in emergencies and difficulties,
other times requesting troops to demand accountability for offenses,
the matters were of no light significance,
and the responsibilities entrusted were weighty,
therefore Zhūliáng was concerned,
and sought advice from Zhòngní.
《Yègōng》 Pronounced as shè.
《Zǐgāo》 A senior official of Chǔ,
served as the county magistrate of Yè,
presumptuously titled himself 'gōng',
with the surname Shěn,
given name Zhūliáng,
courtesy name Zǐgāo.
《Jiāng shǐ》 Pronounced as suǒ lì fǎn.
Same for the annotations and the following 'dài shǐ'.
【二】【注】They fear that merely replying with respect in vain,
yet are unwilling to urgently respond to their request.
【Commentary】The Marquis of Qí, Jì Ěr, in his comings and goings,
lacked sincerity in heart,
yet when it came to receiving the envoy of Chǔ,
he was exceedingly earnest and attentive.
The matters he requested
were not granted approval.
The command he bore was weighty,
hence he harbored this concern beforehand.
【Three】【Memorials】The humble will of a common man,
cannot be swayed,
how much less so the five ranks of nobility,
how could they be swayed!
Judging by this,
it is indeed a cause for deep anxiety.
【Explanation】"慄之" is pronounced as lì.
Lǐ Yí says:
It means to fear.
【Four】【Annotation】There is no matter, great or small,
that seldom fails to achieve joy through words.
This is what Zhòngní once told Liáng.
【Commentary】The term "Zǐ" refers to
Zhòngní.
"Guǎ" means few.
As for managing affairs and their sequences,
they are indeed multifaceted.
Although their scale may vary,
none does not find joy and satisfaction in achieving completion.
Therefore, Zhū Liáng cited what was previously received,
to initiate the subsequent mechanism.
【Translated Text】"Cháng Yǔ" is read as yú jù fǎn.
The same applies below.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, cháng is written as cháng.
【Five】【Annotation】Those who take success as joy,
will become angry when they do not succeed.
This is what the King of Chǔ could not avoid.
【Commentary】If emotions are discordant and obstructive,
affairs will not reach fulfillment,
thus arises the principle of human relationships,
and the concern for penal punishment.
【Six】【Annotation】Although the person's troubles have departed,
the conflict of joy and fear rages within the chest,
indeed forming icy knots in the five viscera.
【Commentary】Joy brings forth the expansion of yang,
while sorrow leads to the contraction of yīn.
When matters are successfully accomplished,
and the inner feelings are genuinely satisfied,
the worries of the past transform into the joys of the present.
Joy and fear intermingle in a single heart,
yīn and yang clash fiercely within the five viscera,
causing cold and stagnation to accumulate and congeal—
how could this not be a cause for distress?
Hence, the following text states.
【Explanation】"藏矣" pronounced as cáng yǐ, with the pronunciation guide "才浪反" indicating the reading.
【七】【Note】Success and failure, if left to fate without causing worry in the heart,
only the virtuous can achieve this!
【Commentary】How can one settle gains and losses in the spiritual abode,
entrust success and failure to the path ahead,
and not burden the heart with worry or joy—
is it not only the one with abundant virtue who can do so!
【八】【Annotation】Facing the fire yet not thinking of cooling off,
clearly indicates the frugality and simplicity of the provisions.
【Commentary】Zāng means
good.
Qīng means
cool.
Bearing the weighty command,
the heart is filled with fear and trepidation,
thus using coarse food,
with no time for fine meals.
Since the provisions are frugal and meager,
the cook does not wish for coolness,
the fire is not lit much,
so there is no heat to avoid.
【Transcription】"Zhi" is found in all various editions.
The Jianwen version writes it as "rè".
"Cū" is pronounced as "cū",
also read as "cáigǔ" in reverse.
"Ér bù zāng" is read as "láng" in reverse,
meaning good.
A full stop.
Another pronunciation is "cáiláng" in reverse,
with the sentence extending to the character "cuàn".
"Cuàn" is pronounced as "qīluàn" in reverse.
"Wú yù qīng" is read as "qīxìng" in reverse,
the character should properly follow "".
Following ""
is a borrowed usage.
"Qìng",
means cool.
"Zhī rén" refers to those who cook with fire for food without seeking coolness,
indicating that the fire is small and the food should be frugal and plain.
"Suǒ zhuàn" is read as "shìliàn" in reverse.
【Nine】【Annotation】The reason for eating frugal fare yet feeling inner heat and drinking ice is,
truly out of concern for the difficulty of affairs,
not for the sake of fine food.
【Commentary】Zhū Liáng received the edict at dawn,
and by evening was drinking ice,
which fully illustrates his terror, worry, and sorrow,
with his inner heart burning fiercely.
His inquiry into the Way is driven by heartfelt urgency,
expressing and illuminating this state of mind.
【Explanatory Text】"Inner Heat and" pronounced as yú.
The following "cautious and" is the same.
Xiàng comments:
Those who eat rich foods will inevitably have inner heat.
【一０】【Note】When a task is not yet accomplished, one only fears it may not succeed.
If it indeed fails to succeed,
then fear knots within and punishment ensnares from without.
【Commentary】When the outcome of a situation remains uncertain,
and success or failure is unknown,
yet one harbors worry or joy in their heart,
this is the affliction of yīn and yáng.
If matters go awry,
and inevitably fail to achieve their aim,
then the duty of a minister comes into play,
and the net of punishment will ensnare them.
With these two afflictions,
where can one escape blame?
【釋文】《則恐懼》qiū yǒng fǎn.
【一一】【疏】I am unworthy to serve as a minister,
undeservedly filling the role of a lowly envoy,
holding a high position but lacking virtue,
insufficient to bear such responsibility.
You, being a sage,
with compassion that benefits all beings,
surely have a purpose for this—
I earnestly await your instruction!
【Transcription】"以任" is read as ér lín fǎn,
another reading is ér zhèn fǎn.
【Collation】（1）The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, which has this line as: "Rarely is there one who does not follow the Way to achieve joy."
Zhòngní said:
"There are two great bonds in the world:
one is
fate;
the other is
righteousness.
A child's love for their parents
is fate,
and cannot be dispelled from the heart;
a minister's service to their ruler,
is righteousness,
for there is no place without a ruler,
and nowhere to escape between heaven and earth.
These are called the great bonds.
Therefore, those who serve their parents
find peace in it regardless of the circumstances—
this is the pinnacle of filial piety;
those who serve their ruler
find peace in it regardless of the tasks—
this is the height of loyalty;
those who attend to their own hearts
do not let sorrow or joy easily affect them,
knowing what cannot be helped and accepting it as fate—
this is the pinnacle of virtue.
As ministers and children,
we are inherently bound by unavoidable duties.
Attend to the reality of affairs and forget yourself—
how would there be leisure to delight in life and dread death!
You, my master, may proceed now!"
【一】【疏】Discipline,
is the Dharma.
Within the universe,
there are extremely many teachings and laws,
but to discuss them concisely,
none surpass two matters.
The meaning and purpose of these two matters
are fully listed below.
【二】【注】It naturally solidifies and binds,
making it impossible to undo.
【Commentary】The filial son serves his parents,
exhausting himself in love and respect.
This nature of his,
originates from what is innate,
followed from the heart spontaneously,
and thus cannot be undone.
【Three】【Comment】When a thousand people gather,
without one person to lead them,
they will either fall into chaos or disperse.
Therefore, having many virtuous individuals does not justify having many rulers,
and lacking virtuous individuals does not justify having no ruler.
This is the way of Heaven and humanity,
the appropriate course that must be followed.
【Commentary】The relationship between ruler and subject, superior and inferior,
is inherently fixed by principle.
Thus, a loyal minister serves his ruler,
even unto death to fulfill his integrity.
This arises from a mutual commitment to duty and righteousness,
not merely from innate nature.
Although the world is vast,
there is no land without a ruler.
If one bears guilt and blame,
where then can one flee to evade fault?
Therefore, upon receiving the command, one sets out immediately,
with no need for hesitation or deliberation.
【Four】【Annotation】If the ruler could flee and the parents could be spared,
then it would not be enough to serve as a warning.
【Commentary】This concludes the meaning of the great precepts concerning sovereign and parents discussed earlier.
【Five】【Memorial】A filial son in caring for his parents,
must focus on compliance and suitability,
when entering officialdom to seek emolument,
should not choose between high or low positions,
but be content with whatever comes his way,
only then can he be called truly filial.
【Six】【Memorial】Rites serve to honor the sovereign and attend to affairs,
with utmost dedication to loyalty and integrity,
handling matters regardless of difficulty or ease,
accepting them as destiny,
how can one pick and choose based on advantages or disadvantages,
and only then carry them out!
Those capable of acting thus
embody the highest virtue of loyal ministers.
【七】【注】To recognize what cannot be changed as fate and accept it with peace,
then there is neither sorrow nor joy,
how could there be any forced application of effort!
Therefore, silently regard what one encounters as fate without imposing one's will upon it,
blend seamlessly with what is most appropriate and hold no grief or joy within,
even when serving ordinary people,
one will still find ease in every situation,
let alone when it comes to rulers and parents!
【Commentary】Those who cultivate the Way and find tranquility in their minds and wisdom
perceive no distinction between adversity and favor,
understanding gain and loss as one.
Thus, they can navigate the realm where sorrow and joy first arise
without acting rashly or impulsively,
knowing that hardship and success are inevitable.
How could human emotions control this!
Therefore, they settle their hearts and comply with fate,
not contradicting the natural order.
Unless one possesses the profound virtue of the ultimate sage,
who could be like this!
【Text】"Āi Lè" - the pronunciation of "Lè" is as in "luò".
The same applies to the annotations below.
"Shī hū" - read as the character's usual pronunciation.
Cuī reads it with a fanqie of "yǐ chì",
stating:
it means "to shift".
◎Qìng Fān's note: "Shī" should be read as "yí",
"bù yì shī"
is akin to saying "not shifting or changing".
In the outer chapters of "Yànzǐ Chūnqiū", "jūn chén yì shī",
in "Xúnzǐ·Rú Xiào Piān", "āi xū zhī xiāng shī yì zhī",
and in "Hànshū·Wèi Wǎn Zhuàn", "rén zhī suǒ shī yì",
in all these cases, "shī" is read as "yí".
Stated directly, it is "yì shī",
while inverted, it becomes "shī yì".
(Based on Wáng's "Reading Notes".
【八】【Note】Events inevitably reach their conclusion,
principles are inherently ever-flowing,
thus entrusting them leads to successful outcomes,
yet if one's personal survival is not ensured after success,
such a thing has never occurred,
so why trouble one's mind over one's own person!
【Commentary】When ministers and sons serve their sovereign and father,
they must dedicate their lives and exhaust their sincerity,
acting immediately upon encountering matters,
without room for selection or hesitation,
forgetting themselves to manage affairs diligently,
which is indeed appropriate.
If unavoidable circumstances arise,
they should accept and carry out their duties.
【Nine】【Annotation】Principle knows no obstruction,
thus one should follow encountered situations and advance directly.
If one's belief in the Way is not steadfast and personal likes and dislikes linger in the heart,
unable to proceed together with utmost appropriateness while scheming for life and worrying about death,
I have yet to see anyone capable of accomplishing their affairs in this manner.
【Commentary】Since he is designated as an envoy,
there is no room for personal likes or dislikes,
for he is carrying out his sovereign's command.
His sole duty is to proceed to Qí,
so how could he have the leisure to contemplate life or death!
【Explanation】"而惡" is pronounced as wù with the falling tone,
and the same applies to all instances below.
I beg to reiterate what I have heard:
In general, when dealing with nearby states, one must win their trust through good faith,
and with distant states, one must convey loyalty through words,
which inevitably need to be transmitted by someone.
To relay messages that please or anger both sides
is one of the most difficult tasks in the world.
For words that please both sides are bound to be full of excessive praise,
and words that anger both sides are bound to be full of excessive condemnation.
All forms of exaggeration are falsehoods,
and falsehoods undermine trust,
leading to misfortune for the messenger.
Therefore, as the adage goes:
'Convey the true sentiments,
not the exaggerated words,
and you will nearly preserve yourself whole.'
【一】【注】Recently having the opportunity to meet,
thus through their sincerity, they verify closeness and mutually submit in admiration.
【Transcription】"復以" reads as fú yòu fǎn.
The same applies to the annotation below.
【二】【注】To convey meaning through words from afar.
【Commentary】When interacting with those nearby,
one should use sincerity to foster harmony;
when separated by great distance,
one should use words to express loyalty.
This is Confucius drawing from his own experience to advise Zhū Liáng.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhuàn yì" is read with the pronunciation of "zhàng zhuān" in reverse.
The same applies to the following text and annotations.
【Three】【Commentary】Regarding words of joy and anger,
if they exceed the truth,
the one who transmits them should ensure that neither side loses balance,
thus it is not an easy task.
【Commentary】Words convey meaning,
sometimes through messengers,
when mutual understanding is reached,
emotions like joy and anger arise abruptly.
To serve as such an envoy,
is no easy task in human affairs.
【Explanatory Text】"Two angers" is read as written.
The same applies to the annotations.
Another version also uses "resentment."
The same applies below.
"Not easy" is pronounced with a rising tone for "easy."
The same applies to the following text and annotations.
【Four】【Annotation】Excess,
means going beyond.
Words of joy and anger often exceed their appropriateness.
【Commentary】Excess,
means going too far.
When two individuals,
exchange feelings of joy and anger,
if they follow their emotions,
then words of praise or criticism are bound to be excessive.
【Five】【Annotation】It seems these are not the words of that person,
as if the transmitter fabricated them.
【Commentary】"Lèi" means
"similar to."
Exaggerated statements,
being not entirely truthful,
cause listeners to doubt,
as if making them fabricate falsehoods.
【Six】【Annotation】He was perplexed and doubtful about it.
【Commentary】Mò,
is an expression of a doubtful appearance.
Since it seems like the transmitter might have fabricated it,
thus arises a heart of disbelief,
leading to a state of doubt and skepticism.
【Seven】【Annotation】To transmit words beyond what was heard
seems like absurd fabrication (1).
If the recipient harbors doubts,
then the transmitter of the words is arbitrarily held accountable for the severity of the fault.
【Commentary】The recipient harbors doubts,
his heart filled with disbelief,
yet he passes the message to the envoy,
and calamity thus befalls him.
【八】【注】Even if one hears a momentary lapse of speech, do not spread it;
one must consider the person's usual disposition and seek their sincere intent,
then one is close to being complete.
【Commentary】When navigating human affairs,
the task of an envoy is truly difficult.
One must investigate common sentiments and ensure that both host and guest reach a compromise,
without conveying momentary emotions of joy or anger,
leading to words that are difficult to interpret.
If one can act in this manner,
they may nearly achieve self-preservation.
The Master quotes the maxims of ancient sages
to establish a path for future generations.
【Explanation】"而要" is read as yāo with the second tone.
"则近" means near, with jìn as in proximity.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition reads as "wàngdàn".
Those who compete with skill and strength,
begin with openness,
but often end with deceit;
when it reaches its extreme, there is much cunning artifice.
Those who drink according to ritual,
begin with order,
but often end with chaos;
when it reaches its extreme, there is much wanton pleasure.
All affairs are like this.
They begin with sincerity,
but often end with meanness;
their commencement is simple,
but their conclusion is inevitably grand.
【一】【注】I have always enjoyed theatrical performances.
【Explanation】"Gòng hǎo" is pronounced with the sound "hū bào fǎn".
【二】【Note】When the desire to prevail over emotions reaches its peak,
it covertly arises to harm others (two).
【Commentary】Yáng,
signifies joy.
Yīn,
signifies anger.
When people compete in strength through play,
it is not without cunning and skill.
At the beginning, it is jest and banter,
with emotions rooted in delight;
but as it reaches the end,
resentment and anger arise in the heart,
driven by the desire to win,
subtly resembling mutual harm.
In the world, joy and anger,
the transformation of emotions follows this pattern.
This example uses a contest of strength to illustrate it.
◎ Jiāshìfù said:
All that is manifest and visible is called yáng,
while what is hidden and latent is called yīn.
Those who compete in cunning often employ covert schemes,
exhausting the use of their minds to seek victory over one another.
【Three】【Notes】No longer following principles.
【Commentary】When anger reaches its peak,
and the desire to prevail is extreme,
then emotions often become deceitful and unpredictable,
with all sorts of cunning and trickery emerging.
【Explanatory Text】"Dà zhì" is pronounced as tài,
originally also written as tài.
Xú gives the pronunciation as chì zuǒ fǎn.
The same applies below.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
Nowadays, the book writes it as tài.
"Qí qiǎo" is read as per its usual pronunciation,
also given as kǔ xiào fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】There is distinction between noble and humble,
and precedence in ceremonial toasts.
【Explanation】"Hū zhì": "zhì" is read with the pronunciation of "zhí lì" in reverse.
"Yǒu bié": "bié" is read with the pronunciation of "bǐ liè" in reverse.
【Five】【Annotation】Indulging in excessive drinking and lewdness.
【Commentary】"Zhi" means
to manage.
In the interactions between host and guest, with toasting and reciprocity,
there is a natural order and propriety.
After becoming disheveled and donning caps askew,
there is no longer any distinction between noble and humble.
Initially, order prevails over chaos,
and all things follow this principle.
This uses drinking as an analogy.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhàn" is read as zhí lín fǎn,
also as dá nán fǎn.
"Miǎn" is read as miàn shàn fǎn.
"Yínyì" is read as yǐ zhī fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Indulging in debauchery and excess,
reaching every extreme without exception.
【Commentary】After the feasting and rewards were bestowed,
wanton indulgence became extreme,
with ceaseless singing and dancing,
no longer adhering to ritual propriety,
employing numerous strange and extraordinary means,
how boundless was their joy and revelry.
【Seven】【Annotation】Troubles arise from simplicity,
matters originate from subtleties,
this is an inevitable trend.
【Commentary】Common emotions and ordinary affairs,
are likewise so.
Without exception, they begin with sincerity and trustworthiness,
but end in vulgarity and wickedness;
initially arising simple and small,
later inevitably becoming vast and great.
Thus, complexity is born from simplicity,
and events arise from subtlety.
This is the combined metaphor.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
"Liàng" (sincere) and "bǐ" (vulgar),
are not antithetical in the text.
The passage above states,
(Starting) begins with yang and often ends with yin,
begins with order and often ends with chaos,
where yin and yang, order and chaos, are all antithetical,
yet "liàng" and "bǐ" are not antithetical.
"Liàng" is suspected to be a miswriting of the character "zhū."
"Zhū" is read as "dū."
In the "Shì Dì" chapter of the Ěr Yǎ,
Sòng has Mèng Zhū, while the Shǐ Jì's "Běn Jì of Xià" writes it as Míng Dū,
which is an example of this.
Beginning with "dū" and often ending with "bǐ,"
"dū" and "bǐ" are precisely antithetical.
Because the character is interchangeably written as "zhū,"
and further miswritten as "liàng,"
the original meaning was thus lost.
The "Quán Yán Piān" of Huái Nán Zǐ states,
"Therefore, what begins with 'dū' often becomes greater than 'bǐ,'"
which is based on Zhuāng Zǐ,
and can be used for correction.
In that text, the character "dà" (great) is a miswriting of "zú" (end),
as explained in Wáng Shì Niàn Sūn's "Reading Notes."
【Collation】(1) The character 'tài' has been amended according to the Shidetang edition and the Lu collation.
(2) The Shidetang edition lacks the two characters 'zhě yě'.
(3) The phrase 'cè biàn' has been amended based on Liú Wéndiǎn's revised and corrected edition.
(4) In the Shidetang edition, 'huāng' is written as 'liú'.
【One】【Comment】Words are like
wind and waves;
thus, when acted upon, the substance is lost.
【Subcommentary】Water forms waves when stirred by wind,
analogizing how the mind experiences joy or anger through words.
Thus, one who acts on joy or anger based on such wind-and-wave-like words
loses grasp of the true principle.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: "Bō" should be read as "bō" (to sow/spread).
Zhèng's commentary on the "Yǔ Gòng" states:
"Bō"
means to scatter.
"Bō" (wave) and "bō" (sow/spread)
are interchangeable in ancient characters,
indicating that wind, when it spreads, easily stirs motion.
"Fēng bō" (wind spreading) is set in parallel with "shí sàng" (loss of truth),
so it cannot be interpreted as "waves."
(In the "Wài Wù" chapter, Sīmǎ's note on "bō chén" refers to "ministers of turmoil,"
where "bō dàng" means "to sow disorder."
) In the 23rd year of Duke Xī in the "Zuǒ Zhuàn," "bō jí Jìn Guó,"
"bō" should also be read as "bō,"
meaning it spread and reached the state of Jìn.
(Based on Wáng Yǐnzhī's "Jīngyì Shùwén."
) In the "Yǔ Gòng," "Xíng Bō jì zhū,"
the versions of Mǎ, Zhèng, and Wáng all write "Xíng Bō,"
the "Suǒyǐn" explains it as the meaning of overflowing and spreading.
These are all evidences for this interpretation.
【Explanatory Text】"Shí sàng" read as xī làng fǎn.
Same for the annotations below.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
"Shí sàng"
means something like gain and loss.
"Shí" refers to
possessing and preserving it;
"sàng" means
neglecting and forgetting it.
To gain and lose alternately
is a great peril in action,
hence it is called dangerous.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation,
stating that acting leads to the loss of substance,
and that avoiding disturbances and not acting prevents the loss of substance,
is likely mistaken.
【二】【注】Thus, leaving behind the winds and waves without acting,
then the substance is not lost.
When matters attain their true essence,
then danger can be pacified and turmoil can be settled.
【Commentary】The wind stirs the water's surface,
making it easily agitated,
just as losing the essence of truth
leads to peril without difficulty.
【Three】【Commentary】The emergence of anger and resentment
arises from no other cause
but often stems from clever words that exaggerate the truth,
and biased language that misses the mark.
【Commentary】The display of anger and resentment,
arises from no other cause
but often stems from frivolous deceit, cunning words, one-sided arguments, and flattering speech.
【Explanatory Text】"Piān cí" is pronounced as piān.
The Cuī version writes it as piǎn,
pronounced as biàn.
【Four】【Annotation】It is like a wild beast,
driven into a desperate situation,
its cries urgent and emotions exhausted,
then harmonious sounds cease and breath becomes unregulated,
suddenly bursting into violent rage,
both giving rise to flaws and confronting each other.
【Commentary】When a wild beast is in dire straits,
driven into a desperate situation,
with its life on the verge of death,
it cries out without choosing its tone,
its breath stifled and pent-up,
a fierce rage arises in its heart,
suddenly erupting in violent fury,
as it attacks and bites humans.
This serves as the starting analogy.
【Explanation】"Breath" is read as the character itself.
Xiàng's version writes it as ● device,
saying:
the Mǎ family reads it as rest.
Device,
means breath.
Cuī's version writes it as ●●,
saying:
panting ● is not harmonious.
Also written with the character bì.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the explanatory text, breath is written in one version as device.
Breath and device were anciently used interchangeably,
breath being the standard character,
device the borrowed one.
In the "Wén Wáng Guān Rén" chapter of the Dà Dài Lǐ Jì, "his breath is broad and gentle,"
the Zhōu Shū writes breath as device,
which is evidence of this.
"Fluttering" Xú reads as fú fú fǎn.
Guō reads as fū mò fǎn.
Lǐ pronounces it as fú.
Cuī pronounces it as bó.
"Heart fierce" is read as the character itself,
Lǐ pronounces it as lài.
"Trampling it" zǐ liù fǎn.
● Pronounced as "yí" with a selling tone,
also pronounced as "yì".
Another version is written as "疣",
pronounced as "yóu".
"疵" is pronounced as "cī" with a scholar's selling tone,
also as "qí" with a uniform plan tone.
If the above is written as "疣",
then this is pronounced as "cái" with a talent's knowing tone.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
It is likely read the same as "yá zì".
【Five】【Annotation】When one is broad-minded enough to accommodate all things,
all things will inevitably gravitate towards him.
If one is excessively critical and meticulous,
then a mindset of pettiness arises without one even realizing it.
Therefore, the great person magnanimously allows all things to flourish in their own natural realm,
not forcing others beyond their capabilities,
not draining others of their joy,
thus fostering complete and harmonious relationships throughout the world.
【Commentary】When criticism is overly harsh and exacting,
and pressure is applied too severely,
then ill intentions will abruptly arise in response.
Emotions and circumstances interact with each other,
as is the natural way of things.
Thus it is known that agitation leads to the loss of rulership,
while leniency wins the support of the masses.
【Explanation】"Kè hé" is pronounced as xìng gé fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】If one is not self-aware,
how can one know where fortune and misfortune converge!
【Commentary】Being impatient and contrary to others,
inevitably leads to rejection,
repeatedly provoking each other,
without understanding the reason.
Moreover, if at the time one responds with incompetence,
then who could foresee the eventual disaster?
【Explanation】"Suǒ qí" is read as the character,
and also pronounced with the initial consonant of "cái" and the final of "jì".
◎Qìng Fān's case: the commentary in Wénxuǎn, Bào Míngyuǎn's "Imitating Ancient Poems", quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Who knows the ultimate end of calamity (five).
【Seven】【Annotation】It transmits that reality.
【Commentary】Upon receiving the sovereign's command,
it should be transmitted truthfully,
and one must not alter it based on momentary emotions of joy or anger.
【八】【Annotation】Let it accomplish itself.
【Commentary】Directly stating the ruler's command,
entrusting the matters to their circumstances,
without the need for persuasion or encouragement,
forcefully ensuring their accomplishment.
【Nine】【Annotation】Benefiting is not for those who bear reality.
【Commentary】Content with the Mandate of Heaven,
following one's nature and indulging emotions,
there is no need to add superfluous words,
exceeding the original measure.
【一０】【Note】This matter is perilous.
Therefore, he altered his sovereign's command,
forcibly urging the completion (of the matter),
which, in terms of the actual situation,
placed the great undertaking in grave peril.
【一一】【Note】The perfection of beauty depends on its timely transformation,
akin to planting,
which cannot be achieved in a single day.
【Commentary】What the heart finds beautiful,
is accomplished through spontaneous intent,
not driven by encouragement or reward,
hence it can endure.
◎ Jiàshìfù remarked:
Beauty lies in persisting in its path until transformation is achieved,
a single day's accomplishment
is not to be relied upon,
while ugliness, once formed, becomes too late to change.
The distinction between beauty and ugliness is subtle,
and thus the difficulty or ease manifests.
Therefore, to pursue beauty and avoid ugliness
is human nature,
yet circumstances often do not align,
leading some to act contrarily and grow accustomed and content with it.
The intended meaning seems somewhat disconnected.
【一二】【Note】If one urges and forces the completion of what they dislike,
then regret and failure will soon follow.
【Commentary】What the heart detests,
if forced and persuaded to accomplish,
will not last long,
and soon there will be regret and change.
【Textual Explanation】"Suǒ wù" is pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
"Quàn jiào" is pronounced as qí zhàng fǎn.
The following "jiào" is the same.
【13】【Commentary】When residing in the human world and engaging in society,
carrying out orders as an envoy,
the wise teachings of ancient sages
should be deeply heeded with caution and vigilance.
【一四】【Note】Entrusting an object to convey one's intent.
【Commentary】The one who transforms in solitude,
blends traces among human realms,
riding on material things to roam freely,
operating with an empty mind to accord with the world—
how could there be any peril in this!
【一五】【Note】He who accepts the inevitability of principle,
achieves the full accord of the Mean,
and this is the highest form of interacting with all things.
【Commentary】What is termed "inevitability"
is the certainty of principle.
Entrusting oneself to inevitable matters,
nurturing a balanced and harmonious heart—
this indeed represents the ultimate attainment of truth,
the most profound way to respond to all things!
【16】【Comment】One should accept the actual outcome reported by Qí,
why contrive intentions on their behalf in the meantime!
【Commentary】Follow one's own destiny,
act according to reason,
why must one preemptively harbor anxieties,
to orchestrate outcomes (thus).
【Transcription】The first "wèi" is read as in its basic meaning,
the second is pronounced with the fanqie spelling yú wèi fǎn.
【一七】【Note】Simply fulfilling one's duty is easiest,
but acting based on personal likes and dislikes,
thus makes it difficult.
【Commentary】Directly expressing genuine emotions,
entrusting to the decree of Heaven,
is very simple and uncomplicated,
how could there be any difficulty!
What is considered difficult here,
is said to be not difficult.
【Collation Notes】(1) The character 'fū' has been moved down according to the Shidetang edition.
(2) In the Shidetang edition, 'dà' is written as 'tài'.
(3) The character 'yě' has been added based on the Shidetang edition.
(4) The character 'pò' has been amended to 'pò' following the explanatory text below, as the original conveyed excessive urgency.
(5) Originally misplaced below the explanatory text,
it has now been corrected.
(6) The character 'chéng' has been revised according to Liú Wéndiǎn's amended and corrected edition.
Yán Hé was about to become the tutor of the crown prince of Wèi Línggōng,
and he asked Qú Bóyù:
"Suppose there is a person here,
whose nature is innately cruel.
If I act without principles in dealing with him,
it will endanger our state;
if I adhere to principles in dealing with him,
it will endanger my own life.
His intelligence is just sufficient to recognize others' faults,
but he does not understand the reasons behind these faults.
In such a situation,
what should I do?"
【One】【Narrative】Surname Yán,
given name Hé,
a virtuous man from Lǔ.
The crown prince,
is Kuǎikuì.
Yán Hé traveled from Lǔ to Wèi,
intending to become the tutor to the crown prince.
【Text Explanation】"Yán Hé" is read as Hú là in reverse pronunciation.
Xiàng and Cuī's version writes it as 廅.
A virtuous recluse of Lǔ.
◎ Lú Wénchāo said:
The current version writes 廅 as 盍.
"Duke Líng of Wèi" in the Zuǒ Zhuàn says his name was Yuán.
"Great Son" is pronounced as tài.
Sīmǎ explained:
It refers to Kuǎikuì.
【Èr】【Shū】's surname is Qú,
his given name is Yuàn,
his courtesy name is Bóyù,
a virtuous senior official of Wèi.
Kuǎikuì possessed a naturally vicious character,
indulging in slaughter to satisfy his desires.
Since he was a person of Wèi,
it is said there was someone here.
He was to become the tutor of the crown prince,
thus he sought guidance from a wise man.
【Translated Text】"Qú" is read with the pronunciation of its location.
"Bó Yù" is the name of Yuàn,
a senior official of Wèi.
"Tiān shā" is read as written,
meaning like nature killing things.
Xú gives the pronunciation as listed.
【Three】【Commentary】The nature of petty individuals is such that,
when guided by rules and regulations, they resent being constrained;
yet if allowed to act without restraint, they bring chaos to the state.
【Commentary】"Fǎng" means
"model" or "standard."
Endowed with a violent and stubborn nature,
they do not practice benevolence and righteousness.
Imposing methods upon them,
they resent being regulated,
which endangers their own safety;
indulging them without restraint,
they become dissipated and reckless,
leading to the downfall of the state.
【Explanatory Text】"Wú Fāng" Lǐ Yún said:
Fāng means
Dào (the Way).
【Four】【Annotation】Not realizing that the people's faults stem from oneself,
thus blaming the people for their offenses without self-correction.
【Commentary】When one's own governance lacks virtue,
and there is no repentance or reform,
yet the common people are blamed for crimes,
the punishments and killings become excessively severe.
Only seeing the suffering of the black-haired masses,
one fails to realize that the fault lies with oneself.
Since it is known that like the wind bending the grass,
it is understood that the responsibility rests with the ruler.
【Explanation】"Its knowledge" is pronounced as wisdom.
【Fifth】【Memorial】Indeed,
it remains so.
What can be done about it?
I inquired of the Way from Qú Yuàn,
hence I present the reasons herein.
Qú Bóyù said:
"An excellent question indeed!
Be cautious,
be prudent,
and rectify your own person!
In outward form, nothing surpasses conformity;
in inner mind, nothing surpasses harmony.
Although this is so,
both of these approaches have their perils.
Conformity should not lead to immersion;
harmony should not lead to expression.
If outward conformity leads to immersion,
it will result in collapse and ruin,
in downfall and stumbling.
If inner harmony leads to expression,
it will result in reputation and fame,
in strangeness and calamity.
If he acts like an infant,
then join him in acting like an infant;
if he acts without boundaries,
then join him in acting without boundaries;
if he acts without limits,
then join him in acting without limits.
By penetrating to this,
you enter into a state without flaw.
【一】【注】Repeated interactions and gatherings,
are all means to cultivate one's character.
【Commentary】Admonition means
encouragement.
One cannot lead by example oneself.
Guard and caution the crown prince,
do not lightly offend or provoke,
tread the path of righteousness oneself,
and adapt to circumstances appropriately.
The earlier part praises his ability to inquire,
while the later part shows him the method.
【Transliteration】"Zhèng nǚ" is pronounced as rǔ.
The same applies below.
"Fǎn fù" is pronounced as fāng fú fǎn.
【Two】【Annotation】Forms do not conflict with each other,
harmonizing yet remaining distinct.
【Commentary】The body complies and approaches,
without violating the rites between ruler and subject.
The mind is harmonious and compliant,
blending in outwardly while accomplishing tasks effectively.
【Three】【Memorials】The first two articles,
briefly outline the methods.
Since they are not yet fully perfected,
there still remain their associated troubles and burdens.
【Four】【Annotation】Conformity means the form follows smoothly,
integration means then becoming one with it.
【Commentary】Guō's annotation says,
"Conforming is adapting in form,
while entering means thoroughly aligning with it."
【五】【Note】Those who harmonize use righteousness to aid,
those who stand out naturally show off their achievements (two).
【Commentary】The mind is harmonious and compliant,
Skillfully guiding and receiving others,
Attributing achievements to the crown prince,
Not displaying one's own abilities,
This is the way of not stepping forward.
【Six】【Annotation】If one simply agrees with them,
then it would be like failing to support something on the verge of collapse,
and perishing together with them.
Therefore, one should model oneself after heaven and earth,
but without insisting on minor differences.
【Commentary】Diān means
to overturn.
Miè means
to perish.
Bēng means
to collapse.
Jué means
to be defeated.
If one follows and joins them,
entering into that evil together,
then it is like not supporting what is toppling and endangered,
thus leading to overturning and perishing,
collapsing and being defeated,
perishing together with them.
【Explanatory Text】"For '蹶'" Xu reads as qí yuè fǎn.
Guo pronounces it as jué.
Li reads it as jǔ wèi fǎn.
"'摸格'" is pronounced mò hú fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In the current edition, '摸' is written with the wood radical as '模'.
【七】【注】When one displays harmony oneself,
and even bears the sound of enduring disgrace;
to aid the reputation of others,
they will resent being surpassed,
and recklessly spawn calamities.
Therefore, one should remain obscure as if in darkness,
mysteriously blending with light and dust,
so that afterward, none can draw close,
none can estrange,
none can benefit,
and none can harm.
【Commentary】When things transform abnormally, they become portents.
A calamity,
is a disaster.
Although one may blend with the light and merge with the dust,
if one conspicuously displays one's own wisdom,
failing to conceal one's brilliance and obscure one's traces,
then one gains a reputation for aiding others.
Kuǎi Kuì resented his superiority over himself,
accusing him of recklessly creating ominous signs,
and thus harmed him over the matter.
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Harmony,
begins with the mutual complementation of the five flavors,
where sweetness and pungency are used together,
blending seamlessly without distinct form.
If one brings them to the surface and displays them,
then it is no longer harmony.
Timing one's joy and anger,
adapting to their urgency or leisure,
to regulate and subdue their mechanisms,
without engaging in resistance or opposition.
Where there is resistance or opposition, there is inevitably coming and going;
harmony does not desire to emerge,
for it entails no resistance.
【Transcription】"Niè" is pronounced as yàn liè fǎn.
"Jiāng wù" is pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
"Mèn rán" is pronounced as mén.
【八】【Note】Do not establish sharp edges to go against its scales.
【Commentary】"Tǐng" means
field border.
"Qí" means
raised plot.
"Yǔ" means
to share.
"Rù" means
to converge.
In navigating the world and interacting with things,
the way is truly difficult.
One cannot simply conform and agree with everyone,
nor can one constantly generate conflict and opposition.
Sometimes, like an infant's simplicity and ignorance,
one may even be without knowledge;
sometimes, like a field without ridges,
completely lacking boundaries;
indulging in extravagant desires and greed,
allowing fierce slaughter.
Only then guide them with virtue,
and regulate them with rites.
Those who understand this principle
will then grasp the way of being unburdened.
【Interpretation】"Infant" Lǐ Yí says:
It metaphorically signifies having no intentions.
Cuī says:
It metaphorically signifies wandering proudly.
No boundaries: "boundaries" is pronounced with the initial "t" and the final "ing" with a rising tone.
"Fields": pronounced with the initial "h" and the final "ui" with a level tone.
Lǐ Yí says:
Boundaries and fields,
refer to the ridges between fields.
Having no ridges means
having no dignified demeanor.
Cuī Shū says:
It metaphorically means adhering to principles.
"Without limits": Sīmǎ Biāo says:
It means disregarding the law.
"Without flaw": pronounced with the initial "s" and the final "i" with a rising tone.
It means a fault or defect.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character 也 (yě).
(2) The characters 以 (yǐ) and 也 (yě) have been deleted based on the Zhào Jiànyì edition and the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The character 模 (mó) has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the collation by Lú.
Do you not know the praying mantis?
It angrily raises its arms to block a chariot's path,
unaware that it is incapable of the task,
yet this is due to its admirable ability【一】.
Take this as a warning,
be cautious!
If you repeatedly flaunt your talents and offend others,
you will be close to peril【二】.
【一】【注】The mantis's angry arm,
is not without valor;
yet when it stands against the wheel rut,
it is simply no match.
Now, if one knows something is beyond their capability but still insists on forcing themselves to take on the task,
it is just like the mantis's angry arm.
【Commentary】The mantis,
is an insect with axe-like limbs.
When the mantis angrily raises its arms to block the path of a grand carriage's wheels,
although it again relies on its own admirable abilities,
it certainly cannot overcome the weight of its responsibility.
This metaphorically illustrates how Yán Hé intended to use his own talents to confront the heir apparent's power,
how is it any different from the mantis angrily raising its arms against the carriage wheels!
【Explanation Text】"Bù shèng" is pronounced as "shēng".
◎Qìng Fān's case: The Imperial Readings volume 946 quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
It is not that they lack fine talent,
but rather they are simply not up to the task.
The explanatory text is missing.
【二】【注】Accumulate your talents,
cultivate your virtues,
yet to offend this person,
is a path of peril.
【Commentary】Accumulation,
means storing up.
And,
means you.
Peril,
means danger.
Since you have been appointed as the crown prince's tutor,
you ought to be cautious and prudent.
Now, however, you hoard your talents and abilities,
boasting of your own excellence,
and challenging the authority and power,
which will inevitably lead to peril and ruin.
Do you not know the keeper of tigers?
He does not dare to offer them living creatures,
for fear of arousing their fury in killing them;
he does not dare to offer them whole animals,
for fear of arousing their fury in tearing them apart;
he gauges the times of their hunger and fullness,
and comprehends the nature of their fierce temper.
Tigers are a different species from man, yet they fawn upon those who feed them,
because the keeper follows their nature;
and so they kill,
because he goes against it.
【一】【注】Fear that he might become enraged because he harbors a murderous intent.
【Commentary】Do you know the method of raising tigers in the world?
Creatures like pigs and sheep
should not be fed alive to fierce beasts,
for fear that they may become enraged due to the killing.
◎Jià Shìfù said:
It is close,
meaning that its angry glare at the mantis
is nearly there.
This is one who does not assess their own capability.
When a tiger is angry,
it can still be tamed;
when a horse is excellent,
yet made to break the bit, destroy the headgear, and shatter the chest in fury—
there is no other reason
than not to provoke it.
For a mantis to provoke a chariot's track,
what benefit does it seek to do so?
【Transcription】"For it" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
The same applies below.
【二】【注】If one were to make the tiger bite and divide it by itself,
then it would become enraged due to the exertion of force.
【Commentary】You should know that even if one throws a dead object to an animal,
it is still necessary to first divide and decide,
if letting the tiger tear it apart by itself,
there is a fear that it might become enraged due to the effort.
【Explanation】"Fēn zhī" is read as it is.
【Three】【Annotation】Understand the reason for their anger and comply with it.
【Commentary】Knowing the times of hunger and fullness,
understanding the measures of joy and anger,
being versed in the principles of things,
how could there still be danger and ruin!
【Four】【Annotation】Following reason, even different species can generate affection;
defying moral principles, even the closest kin may turn weapons against each other.
【Commentary】When following their nature brings contentment,
even tigers and wolves can be tamed and familiarized;
when opposing it leads to harm,
even the closest kin may turn weapons against each other.
The ways to please oneself are the same,
and the methods for dealing with things show no distinction.
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
To channel their angry hearts,
naturally has its function.
What is called compliance
does not mean striving to indulge their desires,
nor does it mean allowing them to kill without guiding them to express anger,
or letting them act recklessly without giving vent to their fury.
If only one avoids provoking their anger,
their hearts often find a way to express themselves naturally,
then it is compliance.
Those who love horses
may use a basket to hold their dung
and a large shell to catch their urine.
But if a gadfly should alight on them
and they slap it at the wrong time,
the horse will break the bit, injure its head, and bruise its chest.
The intention reaches its utmost, yet the love is lost.
Should one not be cautious?"
【一】【注】Urine and feces are of the lowest filth,
yet they are contained in a precious vessel—
this is the ultimate expression of love for the horse.
【Comment】Shèn refers to
a large clam.
The act of treasuring horse dung
lies in the intention to value it highly.
Dung and urine are of the lowest worth,
yet containing them in a large shèn
shows an emotional fixation,
leading to such an extreme.
【Explanation】"Shèng shǐ" is pronounced as chéng.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
"Shǐ" might be written as "shǐ",
and they are the same.
"Yǐ shèn": Xú reads it as shì zhěn fǎn,
a type of clam.
"Niào" is pronounced as niào diào fǎn.
【二】【注】In a bustling throng, all are mounted on horses.
【Explanatory Text】"" is pronounced as wén.
Some versions write it as ●,
which is the same.
"虻" is pronounced as méng gēng fǎn.
僕緣》普木反，
徐敷木反。
向云：
僕僕然，
虻緣馬稠穊之貌。
崔音如字，
云：
僕御。
◎Wáng Niànsūn says：
In my opinion, both Xiàng's and Cuī's explanations are incorrect.
僕 means 附，
referring to gadflies clinging to and infesting the horse's body.
僕 and 附，
are similar in sound and identical in meaning.
In the "Jì Zuì" chapter of the Dàyǎ, it says "jǐng mìng yǒu pú,"
Máo's commentary states：
僕，
means 附.
Zhèng's annotation says：
"The great mandate of Heaven again attaches to you."
The Wénxuǎn's commentary on the "Zǐxū Fù" quotes the Guǎngyǎ as saying：
僕，

(Note: The current Guǎngyǎ does not contain this phrase.
