The "Qún Zhù" is directly abbreviated and reversed.
【Three】【Comment】Although it saves them from the disaster,
it catches the horses by surprise.
【Explanation】"而拊" Li reads as fǔ,
also read as fù,
one reading as fù.
Cui's version writes it as fǔ,
pronounced as fù.
【Four】【Annotation】Taking them by surprise,
thus startling them into coming here.
【Commentary】Pú (僕) means
gathering.
Fǔ (拊) means
patting.
Xián (銜) means
bridle.
Suddenly, there were gadflies,
swarming around the horse.
The owner, out of affection and care,
abruptly patted the horse,
intending to eliminate the pests.
Without a fixed timing,
startling the horse unexpectedly,
it suddenly became frightened and alarmed.
As a result, the horse broke free from its bridle,
tore apart the reins,
and the person was trampled by its hooves,
suffering a crushed head and shattered chest.
【Five】【Note】When the intention reaches the point of eliminating harm,
acting rashly to address it,
leading to destruction and shattering,
one loses the very reason for cherishing it.
Therefore, in dealing with worldly affairs,
at the juncture of adversity and favor,
one must not be incautious.
【Commentary】Loss,
means to forfeit.
Where the intention reaches,
lies in loving the horse.
Once it is damaged,
one immediately loses what was loved.
In human interactions involving objects,
the principle is the same.
When opportunities and responses are mismatched,
calamity is encountered.
The analogy of patting the horse
should be deeply heeded with caution.
◎ Jiāshìfù said:
People interacting with one another form the world,
and from this arise beauty and ugliness,
compliance and opposition are distinguished,
accord and discord take shape.
Thus, great troubles are born from this,
claiming that others are not worthy to associate with,
yet how can one know that oneself is not worthy to associate with others!
To conduct oneself by being of no use,
this is the way to attain it.
Virtue is corrupted by fame,
knowledge emerges from contention,
this is the central theme of this chapter.
The five sections at the end of the chapter
advise discarding fame and contention,
only then can one move freely in the human world.
【Transcription】"Shuàirán" is read as shū lǜ fǎn.
Some versions have it as "cù",
read as qī hū fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The character '至' has been emended according to the main text and Guō Xiàng's annotations.
Carpenter Shí went to Qí,
arriving at Qūyuán,
where he saw the Guardian Lì Tree.
It was large enough to shelter several thousand oxen,
and measured a hundred arm-spans around,
its height towering over the mountain at eighty feet before branching out,
with over ten places where it could be used to build boats.
Onlookers crowded like a marketplace,
yet Carpenter Bó did not even glance at it,
and continued on without stopping.
A branch
is suited for it.
Qūyuán,
is a place name.
Its path is winding and twisting,
much like the Huányuán path to the west of Sōngshān,
which is of the same kind.
Lì,
is the name of a tree.
Shè,
is the earth deity.
Sacrificing to a mound of earth is called shè.
Shè,
means to spit forth,
signifying its ability to produce all things,
hence it is called shè.
Jiàng is a general term for craftsmen,
while Shí is the personal name of a skilled one.
This man traveled from Lǔ to Qí,
passing through a winding path,
where he saw this extraordinary tree,
gnarled and useless as timber.
He wished to illustrate that in navigating human society,
one must use uselessness as a form of usefulness.
【Transcription】"Qūyuán" is pronounced as yuán.
Sīmǎ explains:
Qūyuán,
means a winding path.
Cuī states:
It is the name of a road.
"Lì" is pronounced with the initial l and the final ì.
Lǐ notes:
It is a type of tree,
another explanation:
it is a cluster.
◎ Lú Wénchāo remarks:
The character for cluster,
in many editions is written as cǎi,
which is erroneous.
Now it is corrected according to the Song edition.
means to bind or restrain.
The tree at the Lì shrine,
exceptionally taller than ordinary trees,
with branches and leaves providing shade,
could shelter several thousand cattle.
When measured with a rope,
its circumference was roughly a hundred feet.
The Jiāngnán edition of the text often mentions its size in shading cattle,
but lacks the phrase "several thousand,"
which suggests this edition is mistaken.
Moreover, the tree in Shāngqiū,
already capable of accommodating a thousand chariots,
how could the tree at Qūyuán
only shade a single ox?
Judging by this standard,
the version stating "several thousand" is correct.
【Explanatory Text】"Bì Niú": Must be read with the sound 'shì' as the fanqie spelling.
Lǐ Yí says:
The ox stands by its side, yet it is not seen.
"Xié": Xiàng and Xú give the fanqie spelling as 'hù jié',
Xú also provides 'hǔ jié'.
It means to bind or restrain.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the "Wénxuǎn", the annotation to Jiǎ Yí's "Essay on Faults of Qín" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Xié,
means to encircle.
This explanation is missing in the explanatory text.
"Bǎi Wéi": Lǐ Yí says:
A diameter of one foot is called a wéi,
so it would be about ten zhàng.
【Three】【Explanations】Seven chi is called a rèn.
This tree stands straight and towering over seventy chǐ,
only then does it grow upright branches,
blocking the sun and brushing against the clouds.
Those suitable for making ships
are as large as several dozen trees combined nearby.
Such is its appearance.
【Translated Text】"Ten rèn": The Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ states:
Four chǐ are called a rèn.
Another view holds that seven chǐ are called a rèn.
Cuī's version writes "a thousand rèn."
Some say:
Eight chǐ are called a rèn.
"Páng shí shù": the pronunciation is as given in the gloss.
Cuī says:
Páng,
means side branches.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Páng should be read as fāng,
as the ancient characters were interchangeable.
In the "Gāo Yáo Mó" chapter of the Shàng Shū, "fāng shī xiàng xíng wéi míng,"
the Xīn Xù, "Jié Shì" chapter writes fāng as páng,
in the "Fǔ Xíng" chapter, "fāng gào wú gū yú shàng,"
the Lùn Héng, "Biàn Dòng" chapter writes fāng as páng,
all of which serve as evidence.
In the "Zài Yòu" chapter, "chū rù wú páng,"
means "coming and going without direction,"
this is proof within this text that páng is used as a loan character for fāng.
In the "Zhēng Yuè" poem of the Shī Jīng, "mín jīn fāng dài,"
Zhèng's annotation states:
Fāng,
means "moreover" or "about to."
"Those that can be used to make boats number about ten,"
means that those suitable for boat-making are approximately ten in number.
The explanatory text quotes Cuī as saying,
páng,
refers to side branches,
likely because he did not realize páng was a loan character for fāng,
thus mistaking a function word for a word with concrete meaning.
【Four】【Explanations】Cease,
means to stop.
The tree was unusually large,
and many people came to see it.
Only Carpenter Shí knew it was useless timber,
walking along the path straight past it,
without ever stopping to look.
【Translated Text】"The Observer."
Pronounced as in ancient "Huàn" with a reverse tone,
also read as "guān."
"Master Craftsman Bó,"
where Craftsman Shí is his courtesy name.
The Cuī version also records it as Shí.

◎Qìng Fān's case notes: In the annotations of Hé Píngshū's "Ode to the Hall of Blessings," Wáng Zǐyuān's "Ode to the Cave Flute," Jī Shūyè's "Ode to the Lute," Sīmǎ Shàotǒng's "Poem Dedicated to Shān Tāo," and Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Commands" from the Wénxuǎn,
all cite Sīmǎ as saying:
Craftsman Shí,
courtesy name Bó.
The original text's explanation is missing.
"Unceasing" is pronounced with a reverse tone of "Dīng liè."
【Collation Note】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the two characters for "several thousand,"
which is consistent with the Commentary,
but the Quēwù cites that the editions of Lǐshì from Jiāngnán and Zhāng Jūnfáng include them.
The disciple, having tired of looking at it,
ran to catch up with Carpenter Shí,
and said:
"Ever since I took up the ax to follow you, Master,
I have never seen timber as beautiful as this.
Yet you, Sir, would not even glance at it,
and walked on without stopping.
Why is that?"
【一】【疏】The disciples marveled at the flourishing grandeur of the Lì Shè,
and stopped to gaze upon it.
Having carried their satchels to follow their teacher,
they had never seen timber as remarkably large as this.
[Remarkable] The craftsman paid it no heed,
so they hurried to catch up,
and thus inquired about it.
【Transcription】"Yàn" is read as yàn with the fourth tone,
also as yān with the first tone.
He said:
"Enough,
speak no more of it!
It is a useless tree.
If you make a boat from it, it will sink;
if you make a coffin from it, it will quickly rot;
if you make vessels from it, they will quickly break;
if you use it for doors, it will exude sap;
if you use it for pillars, they will be worm-eaten.
This is a timber of no quality,
of no use whatsoever,
and that is how it has been able to live so long."
【一】【疏】Finished,
cease.
Artisan Shí understood that the large tree's lack of utility,
was not what the common world could use,
and disliked his disciple's excessive words,
so he reprimanded him to stop and not speak further.
【二】【疏】The oak tree has a heavy trunk,
used for boats it sinks;
near soil it often decays,
made into coffins it quickly breaks.
The sparse and scattered tree,
lives out its natural lifespan,
also being a useless timber,
thus attains leisure and freedom.
【Explanatory Text】"Scattered wood": pronounced as xī dǎn fǎn,
Xú's version reads xī dàn fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Then quickly": pronounced according to the character.
Xiàng and Cuī's version writes it as shuò.
Xiàng's version reads suǒ lù fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Rotten": pronounced fú fǔ fǎn.
【Three】【Weaknesses】Among human tools and implements,
what is valued lies in their sturdiness.
Since the oak is brittle and weak,
its early destruction is beyond doubt!
【Four】【Explanation】Mán,
refers to the exudation of resin.
Dù,
are insects inside wood.
When used as doors or windows, they ooze resin and exude sap,
when used as beams or pillars, they become worm-eaten and unstable.
【Translated Text】"Liquid" is pronounced as yì.
"Mán" is pronounced with the initial consonant of "m" and the final of "án".
Xiàng and Lǐ read it with the initial "m" and the final "ān".
Guō reads it with the initial "w" and the final "àn".
Sīmǎ says:
Liquid,
refers to bodily fluids.
Mán,
describes the oozing of grease continuously.
Cuī says:
It refers to the secretion of black fluid.
◎Lǐ Zhēn states:
In the "Guǎngyùn" rhyme book, volume 20, rhyme Yuán:
Mán,
means the heart of the pine tree,
and also a name for a type of wood.
The "Shuōwén" dictionary says:
Mán,
is the heartwood of the pine tree.
Duàn comments:
Suspects there might be omissions or errors,
it should mean the heart of the pine tree,
or alternatively, a name for a type of wood.
Lù's reference is to an ancient version of the "Shuōwén".
Considering that the heart of the pine tree contains resin,
the terms liquid and mán precisely derive from this meaning.
It describes the grease exuding like the heart of the pine tree.
This showcases the exquisite use of language in the "Zhuāngzǐ".
Both the subcommentary and the explanatory text have unclear meanings.
Also, the "Guǎngyùn" explains ● as pine resin,
Duàn suggests that this is an error where mán is mistaken for pine resin.
I suspect that ● might be a variant form of mán.
"Moth" is pronounced with the initial "d" and the final "ù".
【Five】【Annotation】Not counted among the usable types,
hence called scattered wood.
【Commentary】Loose and brittle,
thus the useless tree,
when put to use, proves incompetent,
which is why it avoids an early demise.
Carpenter Shí returned home,
where the Oak Tree appeared to him in a dream, saying:
"How do you intend to compare me?
Do you mean to compare me to useful trees?
Take the hawthorn, pear, orange, and pomelo,
all fruit-bearing trees;
when their fruits ripen, they are stripped,
and being stripped is a humiliation;
their large branches are broken,
and their small ones are torn away.
This is because their abilities make their lives bitter,
so they do not live out their natural lifespans but die midway,
bringing destruction upon themselves from the mundane world.
All things are like this.
Moreover, I have long sought to be of no use,
nearly died because of it,
and only now have I achieved it,
making it my greatest usefulness.
Had I been useful,
how could I have grown to such greatness?
Besides, you and I are both mere things—
why must you judge me as a thing?
And you, a scattered man nearing death,
how can you understand a scattered tree!"
【一】【注】All usable wood is considered fine-grained wood.
【Commentary】"Wūhū" means "at what" or "how."
"Ruò" means "you."
"Yǔ" means "I" or "me."
Usable wood is considered patterned or valuable wood.
Carpenter Shí returned to sleep,
and the oak tree at the altar appeared in his dream,
asking Carpenter Shí:
"What are you comparing me to?
Are you likening me to worthless, scattered wood?
Or are you comparing me to useful, patterned wood?"
【Explanation】"Appearing in a dream": Hú Jiàn's annotation.
"You will": read as "rǔ".
"How can": read as "wū".
Same for the following instances.
【二】【疏】When on a tree, it's called a fruit,
like pears and crabapples;
when on the ground, it's called a gourd,
such as melons and calabashes.
How could you compare me to these kinds?
【Transcription】"Zhā" is read as zè jiā fǎn.
"Jú" is read as jūn bì fǎn.
"Yòu" is read as yóu jiù fǎn.
Xú reads it as yǐ jiù fǎn.
"Guǒ luǒ" is read by Xú as lì guǒ fǎn.
【Three】【Annotation】All things are harmed by their own utility.
【Commentary】As for fruits and melons,
their flavors are edible;
once their seeds and fruits ripen,
they immediately face being plucked and fallen.
Thus, the large branches break and suffer damage,
while the small branches sprout and spread.
Is this not because their delightful tastes make them desirable,
thereby causing bitterness in their lives?
Words of slander and humiliation
refer precisely to this.
Moreover, to be born in spring and fall in autumn
is to fulfill one's natural lifespan;
being struck down midway,
is called an untimely death.
Yet sentient beings with consciousness and insentient things,
ordinary people and objects in the world,
all have their lives cut short due to their usefulness,
hence this concluding statement: there is none that is not so.
Pǒu,
means to strike.
【Textual Explanation】"Xiè": Xú reads as sīliè fǎn.
Cuī states:
"xiè"
is the same as "xiè".
◎Yú Yuè says:
The meaning of the character "xiè",
does not apply here,
so it is likely incorrect.
"Xiè" should be read as "yè".
In the "Fēi Xiàng" chapter of the Xúnzǐ, "jiē rén zé yòng yè",
Yáng's commentary:
"yè",
means to pull or lead.
"Xiǎo zhī yè",
refers to being pulled or led.
In the "Qī Yuè" poem of the Shījīng,
"qǔ bǐ fǔ qiāng",
"yǐ fá yuǎn yáng",
is what is referred to here as "dà zhī zhé".
It also says,
"yī bǐ nǚ sāng",
which is what is referred to here as "xiǎo zhī yè".
Zhèng's annotation states:
"nǚ sāng",
means young branches.
Young branches are the same as small branches.
"Yī" is a borrowed character for "jǐ".
In the Shuōwén Jiězì, hand radical:
"jǐ",
means to pull to one side,
which is the same meaning as "yè".
"Kǔ qí": read as the character's usual pronunciation.
Cuī's version writes it as "kū".
"Pǒu": pǔ kǒu fǎn.
Xú reads as fāng gòu fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】There are those who look askance at me,
only the present Master Shí understands it.
【Explanation】"幾死": pronounced as qí,
also pronounced as jī.
The same applies below.
"數有": pronounced as shuò.
"": pronounced as pì.
"睨": pronounced as nì.
【五】【Note】Accumulating what seems useless becomes the great utility for aiding life.
【Commentary】Being useless and unrefined,
one is certain to preserve one's life intact.
The oak at the altar sought this,
its origin is long-standing indeed.
Yet the mediocre and clumsy craftsman,
suspecting it to be fine-grained timber,
frequently looked back and forth,
intending to cut it down,
fearing the axe's premature blow,
it neared the brink of death.
Now encountering the master craftsman,
who recognized my lack of utility,
I have just managed to preserve my life,
making me of great use.
Jī,
means near.
【Six】【Comment】If it is useful,
it will inevitably be exploited over time.
【Commentary】If I were a fine timber with useful material,
I would inevitably suffer from being cut down,
perishing early under the axe,
how could I then grow so tall and live such a long life!
【Seven】【Remonstrance】You and I,
are both creations of the universe,
how can we truly understand each other or other things!
Why then,
this is but a rhetorical question.
【Eight】【Note】To jest at the master carpenter Shí.
【Commentary】Carpenter Shí considered being useless as a state of carefreeness,
while the oak tree at the altar believed that having talent led to being deemed useless.
Therefore, it referred to Shí as a carefree person.
Flaunting one's abilities in the mundane world
brings one close to an untimely death;
I, through being idle and useless,
thus preserve my life intact.
You are a carefree person nearing death—
how could you understand that I am a useless tree?
It entrusted these words in a dream
to mock Carpenter Shí.
【Transcription】"And nearly died of it" is a full stop,
Xiàng's reading is the same.
Another reading connects it with the following "scattered man" to form a sentence,
Cuī's reading is the same.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "久" has been emended based on the Shidetáng edition.
Artisan Shí awoke and analyzed his dream.
His disciple said:
"If it hastily seeks uselessness,
then why make it into the village altar?"
【一】【疏】Diagnosis,
means divination.
After Master Shí woke up,
he pondered over his dream during sleep,
divining and interpreting it,
and explained it to his disciples.
【Translated Text】"Jué" is read as gǔ xiào fǎn.
"Ér zhěn" according to Xú is read as zhí xìn fǎn.
Sīmǎ Xiàng states:
Zhěn,
means divining dreams.
◎Wáng Niànsūn says:
Xiàng Xiù and Sīmǎ Biāo both state that
zhěn,
refers to divining dreams.
However, the following text all discusses the matter of Carpenter Shí and his disciples regarding the lìshè tree,
with no mention of dream divination.
Zhěn should be read as zhěn (畛).
The Ěryǎ states:
Zhěn (畛),
means to inform.
Guō's commentary cites the Qūlǐ saying,
"Zhěn (畛) to the ghosts and spirits."
Zhěn (畛) and zhěn (診),
are interchangeable in ancient script.
This means that Carpenter Shí, upon waking, told his dream to his disciples,
not that he was divining dreams.
【二】【注】Still dissatisfied with considering the establishment of a community as a source of honor,
they do not hasten to embrace uselessness for its own sake.
【Commentary】The allegory of the oak tree's essence,
lies in taking uselessness as a means to preserve its life in its entirety.
So why would it serve as a village shrine to glorify itself?
The disciples did not comprehend this,
hence they raised this question.
He said:
"Hush!
Do not speak!
He is merely lodging there temporarily,
thinking that those who do not understand him would reproach him.
If it were not for being a shrine tree,
would it not have been cut down?
Moreover, what he preserves is different from the masses,
yet you judge him by conventional righteousness,
is that not far off the mark!"
【一】【注】The shrine has naturally existed here all along,
it is not that this tree sought to become the shrine.
【Commentary】Ruò,
means "you".
Bǐ,
refers to the shrine.
You should just be cautious and discreet,
do not speak lightly.
The spirit of that shrine,
has come to reside there on its own,
it is not because this tree (the oak) [lè] serves as the shrine.
【二】【注】This means that this tree, because the earth god was considered not to know it, was thus insulted and harmed;
how could it be considered an honor!
【Commentary】Gòu,
means disgrace.
Considering this earth deity to be unaware that I regard the useless as useful,
valuing the preservation of life,
yet it presumptuously comes to entrust itself,
deeply incurs reproach and criticism,
instead becomes a source of shame,
how could this be considered an honor!
【Explanatory Text】"Gòu" Lǐ Yún says:
Pronounced as hū dòu.
Xú pronounces it as gòu.
"Lì" is read as is.
Sīmǎ explains:
Gòu,
means humiliation.
Lì,
means ailment.
【Three】【Notes】(Wood)〔Root〕(Two) They consider themselves as using uselessness for usefulness,
then even if they do not become the altar,
they ultimately do not come near the harm of being cut down.
【Commentary】Originally, being sparse and useless,
it thus preserved its path to life.
Had it not been the sacred tree,
would it have escaped the harm of being cut down?
【Explanation】"且幾" pronounced as jī,
or sometimes as qí.
"翦乎" pronounced with zǐ qiǎn fǎn.

In the "Wei Zheng" chapter of the Analects, the text says "filial piety is only filial piety",
both Huáng Kǎn's version and the Han stone classics write it as "于".
In the "Shěn Yìng" chapter of Lü's Annals, it says "then the former kings were sagely",
Gāo's annotation:
means "乎".
These are all examples.
"不近" means "not close to" as in proximity.
Same meaning below.
【Four】【Annotation】They regard having no guarantee as a guarantee,
while the multitude regards having a guarantee as a guarantee.
【Commentary】The sparse and scattered tree,
by being useless preserves its life,
while the patterned wood types,
due to their talent and ability break and die young,
this is why they are considered different from it.
【Five】【Comment】Benefiting people and nurturing things,
prohibiting the populace from wrongdoing,
is the meaning of the community altar.
As for the useless,
they remain tranquil and inactive, yet all talents naturally find their use;
those who are used each find their proper order without interference from them,
this is how the three useless ones preserve their lives entirely.
You use the community altar to praise them,
is that not far-fetched indeed!
【Commentary】The useless tree, being unfit for timber,
is endowed by the Creator;
relying on its uselessness,
it thereby preserves its life.
Yet when the village spirit is entrusted to it,
it becomes an object of reproach and scorn.
Further, to praise it with the meaning of the village altar
strays even farther from the truth.
【Explanation】"Yì yù" is pronounced as yú.
The annotation is the same.

In current editions, the character yù is written as yù.
"Cháng wù" is pronounced with the initial dīng and the rhyme liǎng.
"Bó rán" is pronounced with the initial bù and the rhyme gè.

(2) The character '本' has been amended based on the commentary text and the Shidetang edition.

Nánbó Zǐqí was wandering on Shāng Hill,
when he saw a huge tree of extraordinary appearance.
A thousand chariots, each drawn by four horses,
could be sheltered under its shade.
Zǐqí said,
"What kind of tree is this?
It must be of extraordinary timber!"
He looked up at its smaller branches,
but they were twisted and could not be used as beams or rafters.
He looked down at its massive trunk,
but it was split and cracked and could not be used for coffins.
He licked one of its leaves,
and his mouth became sore and injured;
he sniffed it,
and it made him wildly intoxicated,
for three days without ceasing.
【一】【Note】The shade cast by its branches,
can conceal and shelter a thousand chariots (this is so) (three).
【Commentary】Bó means
elder.
His Way is most revered,
worthy to be the elder of things,
hence he is called Bó,
referring to Nánguō Zǐqí.
Shāngqiū,
a place name,
located in the region of Liáng and Sòng.
A team of four horses is called a shèng.
Lài means
shade.
Zǐqí, within the state of Sòng,
passed through the area of Shāngqiū,
encountered a great tree,
extraordinary beyond the ordinary,
the tree trunk thick and tall,
its branches and leaves lush,
casting shadows and spreading shade,
providing extensive coverage,
connecting chariots in a row,
could shelter four thousand horses.
【Translated Text】"Nán Bó" Lǐ Yún says,
that is, Nán Guō.
Bó,
means elder.

harmed by heat.
"Jiāng Bì" the original also writes as bì.

also as bēi wèi.
Cuī's version writes as bǐ,
saying:
means to shelter.
"Suǒ Lài" sounds like lài.
Cuī's version writes as lài.
Xiàng says:
means shade,

Lǐ agrees.

【二】【疏】Zǐ Qí, having seen this tree,
could not recognize its name,
suspecting it possessed extraordinary capabilities,
which led to its immense size.
【Three】【Explanations】The axle's explanation is,
like the rotation of a carriage axle,

Encircling the body forms the inner coffin,
the inner coffin,

Encircling the inner coffin forms the outer coffin.
For beams and ridgepoles must be straight,

inner and outer coffins rely on sturdiness,

if one sniffs it with the nose,

Chéng,

Zǐqí said:
"This indeed is a useless tree,
that it has managed to grow to such great size.
Alas, the spiritual man
uses this worthlessness!
【一】【疏】Throughout its form, it is deemed useless,
which can be said to be the great talent for preserving life;
the multitude considers it of no use,
yet it is precisely the marvelous function of aiding all things;
thus, it can avoid being cut down by the axe and provide shade for a thousand chariots.
【二】【注】The king is untalented in the affairs of the hundred officials,
thus the hundred officials manage their duties,
with the clear-sighted ones serving as his vision,
the sharp-eared ones as his hearing,
the wise ones as his strategists,
and the brave ones as his defenders.
What, then, does he do?
He remains in profound stillness alone.
When all talents fulfill their roles appropriately,
then the untalented becomes the very foundation upon which talents rely.
Hence, the world gladly supports him without weariness,
and he rides upon all things without causing harm.
【Commentary】The ultimate person is divine,
thus the yin and yang are unfathomable;
blending traces among humans,
harmonizing light so it does not dazzle.
Hence, they can deepen roots and secure foundations,
achieving long life and enduring vision,
serving as boats and vessels for all things,
providing shade and shelter for the common people.
Like that oak shrine,
compared to this extraordinary tree,
thus we marvel at the utility of the divine person—
being useless,
is indeed great usefulness.
【Explanatory Text】"Wéi zhī" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
The following occurrences of "wéi zhī" are all the same.
【校】（一）赵谏议本乘作臣。
In the state of Sòng, there was a place called Jīngshì,
suitable for catalpas, cypresses, and mulberries.
Those that grew thick enough to be grasped with both hands
were cut down by those seeking stakes for monkeys;
those three or four arm-spans around
were felled by those seeking lofty beams for grand buildings;
those seven or eight arm-spans around
were chopped down by noble or wealthy families seeking coffin planks.
Thus, they never lived out their natural lifespans
but met premature destruction under axes and hatchets—
such is the calamity of being useful timber.
Similarly, in sacrificial rites, a white-faced ox, a snub-nosed pig,
or a person with hemorrhoids cannot be offered to the river.
These are all things that shamans and priests know well,
considering them inauspicious.
Yet, it is precisely these that the spiritual person deems most auspicious.
【一】【疏】Jīngshì,
is a place name.
In the state of Sòng, there is the land of Jīngshì,
where three types of trees—catalpa, cypress, and mulberry—thrive,
all of them straight and upright,
suitable for use as timber.
This briefly illustrates how trees with valuable timber are often cut down prematurely,
contrasting with the previous mention of useless trees that survive intact due to their lack of utility.
【Translated Text】"Jīngshì" Sīmǎ comments:
It is a place name.

Jūhóu (狙猴),

Yì (杙),

Trees of gǒng and bǎ size,
their timber is not large,
suitable only for cutting into gān and jué,
to strike and fend off míhóu (獮猴).

【Commentary】Because it is useful,

【Six】【Annotation】The shamans and invocators perform exorcisms,
discarding these three things,
must meticulously select pure and complete offerings,
only then dare to use them.
【Commentary】Sǎng means
forehead.
Kàng means
high.
Zhì refers to
a disease of downward leakage.
When shamans and invocators display dogs for sacrificial rites,
or select cattle and pigs for exorcism rituals,
they must choose pure-colored animals meticulously,
picking the finest ones,
to demonstrate sincere reverence as if the deities were present,
hoping to mystically connect with spirits and gods.
Yet now there are pigs with high snouts and broken foreheads,
calves with white foreheads that are not pure red,
and people afflicted with the foul disease of hemorrhoids,
all three being unclean,
thus they cannot go to the sacred river to perform sacrifices.
In ancient times, people were drowned in rivers to sacrifice to the River Earl,
until Xīmén Bào, as magistrate of Yè,
put an end to it,
and this is an example of such practices.

【Seven】【Annotation】The shamans and invokers here also understand that those who are useless are preserved.
【Eight】【Commentary】Those who preserve their lives wholly,
are considered by the world as auspicious.
Shamans and priests deem the unfit as inauspicious and do not employ them,
yet it is precisely through this inauspiciousness that they preserve their lives wholly,
which is indeed the greatest auspiciousness.
The spiritual person,
is one without a fixed mind and follows along with things.
Therefore, what the world calls the greatest auspiciousness,
the spiritual person does not oppose.
【Commentary】Female practitioners are called wū,
male practitioners are called xí.
Zhù refers to those
who hold tablets and read sacrificial texts.
Xiáng means
auspiciousness or goodness.
When wū, xí, and zhù shǐ perform exorcism rituals,
they recognize these three types [of sacrificial animals] as unworthy for offerings,
thus discard and refrain from using them,
considering them inauspicious objects.
However, sagely individuals,
whose wisdom equals the transformative power of nature,
understand that being unskilled and useless
actually enables preservation of life.
Thus, the notions of white-foreheaded and upturned-nosed [animals being inauspicious],
or that hemorrhoids signify misfortune,
are merely the narrow views of petty ritualists—
how could they represent the profound wisdom of great minds!
Therefore, incompleteness in talent
is precisely what divine persons regard as auspicious and greatly beneficial.

There was a hunchback named Zhílí Shū.
His chin was hidden down by his navel.
His shoulders were higher than the top of his head.
His topknot pointed at the sky.
His five organs were squeezed together upward,
and his two thighs pressed against his ribs.
By sewing and washing,
he could make enough to feed himself.
By sifting rice and cleaning it,
he could make enough to feed ten people.
When the authorities called for soldiers,
the hunchback walked among them with his sleeves rolled up.
When the authorities called for laborers,
the hunchback was excused from service because of his chronic illness.
When the authorities gave grain to the sick,
he received three measures and ten bundles of firewood.
If a man whose body is deformed
is still able to nourish himself
and live out his natural lifespan,
how much more can a man whose virtue is deformed!

【八】【注】The divine person is of no use to things,
yet each thing attains its own utility.
He attributes achievements and fame to the multitude of talents,
merges with things profoundly without leaving a trace,
thus avoiding the harms of the human world.
He abides in the constant beauty of reality,
this is one who fragments his virtue.
【Commentary】To fragment one's form
is to still forget form;
to fragment one's virtue,
is to still forget virtue.
Moreover, those who are fragmented and afflicted by disabilities
merely forget their form;
since they are not sages,
they are unable to forget virtue.
Those who forget virtue
have wisdom that encompasses all things yet return their wisdom to simplicity,
possess brightness equal to the three lights yet revert their brightness to obscurity.
Thus, they can achieve success without claiming it,
act without relying on it,
attribute merit and fame to the multitude of talents,
merge with all things without leaving traces—
these are the ones who forget virtue.
Those who forget form are sufficient to nourish their lives and live out their years,
avoiding the harms of the human world;
how much more so for those who forget virtue!
The superiority and inferiority, the depth and shallowness,
indeed cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Thus, it is known that those who fragment their virtue—
are they not only the sages!

Confucius went to Chǔ,
and the madman of Chǔ, Jiēyú, passed by his gate, saying:
"O phoenix, phoenix,
how has virtue declined!
The future cannot be awaited,
the past cannot be pursued.
When the world has the Way,
the sage succeeds;
when the world lacks the Way,
the sage survives.
In these present times,
we barely escape punishment.
Happiness is lighter than a feather,
yet none know how to bear it;
calamity is heavier than the earth,
yet none know how to avoid it.
Enough, enough,
this approaching others with virtue!
Perilous, perilous,
this marking the ground to hasten!
Brambles, brambles,
do not harm my path!
My path twists and turns,
do not injure my feet!"
【One】【Annotation】One should go forward in accordance with the times,
fully embodying the appropriateness of convergence and communication.
The rise and fall of the world,
are too insignificant to be perceived,
hence it is said, "What does it matter?"
【Commentary】"何如"
means the same as "如何".
means "to go to".
At that time, Confucius was traveling from Lǔ to Chǔ,
and lodged at a guesthouse.
In Chǔ, there was a worthy man,
with the surname Lù,
given name Tōng,
courtesy name Jiēyú,
who knew that Confucius was traveling on official invitations,
and sang a song to mock and criticize him.
"Oh, phoenix, oh phoenix,"
thus lamenting the sage,
comparing him to a bird that appears as an auspicious omen,
that appears when the Way prevails,
and should hide when the Way is lost.
How can you, possessing such sagely virtue,
go to a state in decline and chaos!
【二】【注】One should adapt to what is appropriate at the moment.
【Commentary】In the age to come,
there may be sovereigns who embrace the Way and are worthy of accepting offers of appointment,
but the timing of fate moves as swiftly as a galloping horse,
so one cannot afford to wait.
As for the times that have passed,
rulers like Yáo and Shùn,
their transformations have long since faded,
and they cannot be sought again.
One should align with what is fitting for the present moment,
without the trouble of looking ahead and behind.
【Three】【Annotations】Entrust it to spontaneity,
and principles naturally form and emerge.
Formation and emergence are not of my doing;
how could they change their course for order or chaos!
Those who govern seek completion on their own,
thus they leave behind achievements without failure;
those in chaos (two) seek survival on their own,
thus they forget life yet do not perish.
【Commentary】In the case of a ruler who follows the Way,
in an era of prosperity and enlightenment,
the sage expands the Way and implements teachings,
achieving success throughout the world.
When encountering a benighted sovereign,
or in a time belonging to a decadent age,
it is fitting to preserve one's life and avoid harm,
concealing one's brilliance and obscuring one's traces.
【Explanation】"Qǐ wèi": read as yú wèi fǎn.
"Zhì luàn": read as zhí lì fǎn.
Same below.
【Four】【Annotation】Without looking ahead or behind,
yet fully engaging with the opportunities of the present,
silently merging with the era and the world,
then the subtle harmony can be complete,
and punishment and fame can be avoided.
【Commentary】"Fāng"
means "should."
Now in this time of chaos and turmoil,
which coincides with the declining era of the Zhōu dynasty,
acting cautiously and speaking humbly
can barely spare one from punishment and execution.
Yet to insist on following in the footsteps [of the ancients] and respond to summons for office,
is that not reckless!
These are the words of Jiē Yǔ,
mocking and criticizing Confucius.
【Transcription】"Jǐn" is pronounced as jìn.
【五】【注】Feet are capable of walking, so let them roam free;
hands are capable of grasping, so let them take hold as they will;
listen to what the ears hear,
see what the eyes behold,
halt at what one does not know,
cease at what one cannot do,
employ what is naturally usable,
act for one's own sake,
indulge one's inner nature without the slightest concern for what lies beyond,
this is the utmost ease of non-action.
That one practices non-action yet fails to preserve one's life and nature wholly—
such a thing has never occurred;
that one's life and nature are whole yet not blessed with good fortune—
such a principle has never been heard of.
Therefore, good fortune
is precisely what was earlier referred to as wholeness,
not something borrowed from external things;
how could it bear the weight of a goose feather placed upon it!
To act in accordance with one's nature,
without overstepping bounds in action,
is the utmost ease in the world;
to lift what lifts itself,
to carry what carries itself,
is the utmost lightness in the world.
Yet, knowing with limitless knowledge harms one's nature,
the heart, with desires and aversions, unsettles one's authenticity;
thus, one abandons this utmost ease of non-action to practice that utmost difficulty of action,
discards the utmost lightness of self-lifting to take up the utmost heaviness of carrying others,
this is the constant affliction of the world.
【Explanation】"Zhi Yi" uses the fanqie method with "yi" as the initial and "chi" as the final.
The same applies below.
"Zhi Yi" is pronounced with the fourth tone.
"Yu Wu" uses "wu" as the initial and "lu" as the final.
【Six】【Annotation】When one acts according to their inner nature,
even carrying a weight of ten thousand jun does not feel heavy;
when external things are imposed upon them,
even a weight no more than a zīzhū becomes unbearable.
There are those who cannot bear it.
To act from within
is a blessing,
hence blessings feel extremely light;
to act from without
is a calamity,
hence calamities feel extremely heavy.
When calamities are at their heaviest and one does not know to avoid them,
this is the great delusion of the world.
【Commentary】The capacities of sight, hearing, knowledge, and ability
seem to have their limits.
Restraining oneself within these limits
allows for the preservation of one's life;
seeking what lies beyond these limits
inevitably leads to premature demise.
Preserving life is thus considered a blessing,
while premature demise is regarded as a calamity.
Yet the blessing within one's limits
is lighter than a goose feather,
and those driven by greed and contention
fail to realize it is borne within themselves;
the calamity beyond one's limits
is heavier than the solid earth,
yet those obstinately deluded
do not know to avoid it and let it depart from their persons.
This is the constant affliction of the common customs,
hence the examples of Confucius and Lù Jì are invoked to illuminate their burden.
【Translated Text】"Knowing to Avoid" the old version writes it as "set,"
saying:
to place.
"Cannot Overcome" pronounced as "shēng."
【七】【注】To draw a line on the ground and make people follow it,
its traces cannot be concealed;
to impose oneself upon things while having one's own ego,
one fails to merge with things.
Therefore, the great person does not use self-illumination to shine upon others but allows them to illuminate themselves;
does not impose virtue upon people but entrusts them to attain their own virtue,
thus able to permeate all things and mysteriously unite self and others,
seamlessly becoming one with the world, bringing harmony and blessings both internally and externally.
【Commentary】"Ji" means
to stop.
"Dai" means
danger.
Zhòngní was born at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
during an era of moral decay,
upholding the ways of the sages,
traveled through states responding to summons,
frequently faced rejection and expulsion,
repeatedly suffered slander and criticism.
Therefore, he repeatedly said "enough,"
meaning it would be better to stop and not proceed.
If one employs the five virtues to govern the common people,
abandoning oneself to imitate others,
it will inevitably lead to endangering oneself,
just like drawing tracks on the ground,
making others chase after them,
merely wasting skillful effort,
with no way to cover them up.
Leading others by one's own example,
the principle is the same.
【Explanation】"Huà dì" is pronounced as huò.
【八】【注】Míyáng,
is akin to losing one's yang.
Losing yang and embracing solitude,
without being swayed by external influences,
then my integrity remains whole.
If everyone in the world preserves their own integrity,
then all who refer to themselves would undoubtedly be whole as well.
【Commentary】Lost means
to perish.
Yang means
brightness,
movement.
Lù Tòng advised Confucius,
urging him to conceal his traces and hide his light,
advocating the non-action of solitary freedom,
forgetting and discarding the wisdom of responding to things,
thus remaining within one's proper bounds,
without harming our way of whole and complete living.
【Interpretation】"Mì Yáng" Simǎ says:
Mì Yáng,
is latent yang,
meaning feigned madness.
【Nine】【Annotation】It fulfills its course,
and that is sufficient in itself.
【Commentary】Xì means
emptiness.
Qū means
compliance.
To empty one's mind,
and follow the nature of things,
then whoever calls upon me will find satisfaction.
【Transcription】"郤曲": 去逆反。
The character dictionary writes it as ●.
The Guangya says,
means crooked.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
I note that now both the Shuowen and Guangya write it as .
◎ Qìng Fān's case: 郤,
the transcription quotes the character dictionary as writing it as ,
which is correct.
The Shuowen says:
means to walk crookedly,
from the radical ,
with the phonetic component 只.
The Guangya says:
means crooked.
The Jiyun writes it as ,
and says:
It refers to the crookedness of objects.
Another interpretation is to receive crookedly.
The Yupian gives the pronunciation as qiū jǐ fǎn.
The Shuowen also says:
(reads like yǐn.
) means to hide,
depicting the shape of something crooked and concealed.
The character originally was written as ● from the component ●,
but now it is written as .
【Collation】(1) The variant text quotes Zhāng Jūnfáng's version, where "wú xíng" is written as "què qǔ".
(2) Those who govern and those who bring chaos,
The Shìdétáng edition lacks both instances of the character "zhě".
(3) The character "dé" has been amended according to Zhào Jiànyì's edition.
The mountain trees are plundered by themselves,
the torch-fat is consumed by its own fire.
therefore it is cut down;
lacquer is useful,
therefore the trees are tapped.
All men know the usefulness of being useful,
but no one knows the usefulness of being useless.
【一】【疏】To plunder,
is to fell.
The trees in the mountains,
such as catalpa and zi,
because they possess useful timber,
are indiscriminately plundered and felled.
Fat can provide bright illumination,
serving to fill lamps and torches;
because it is useful,
it is thus boiled and burned.
Is it only fat and trees?
It is the same with people.
【Explanation】"The mountain trees are plundered by themselves; the fat fire is fried by itself." Zǐrán's rebuttal.
Sīmǎ's commentary says:
The tree grows the axe handle,
yet it ends up felling itself;
the fat fuels the fire,
yet it ends up consuming itself.
Cuī's commentary says:
Because the mountain has trees,
therefore the fire burns them.
【二】【疏】Cinnamon's heart is pungent and fragrant,
hence it faces felling;
lacquer is used for making vessels,
thus it is tapped;
both possess useful qualities,
yet perish under the axe.
【Three】【Commentary】When useful, one accomplishes tasks with others;
when useless, one preserves one's own life.
To sacrifice one's flesh and skin for the world
is something the world recognizes.
But to enable the common people to maintain their self-preservation while both they and oneself find contentment—
this is a subtlety that lies within oneself, unnoticed and unawares.
【Commentary】Catalpa, cypress, orange, and pomelo,
as well as torch grease, cinnamon, and lacquer,
these are considered useful.
The tree at Qūyuán,
the tree at Shāngqiū,
the ox with a white forehead,
and the pig with an upturned snout,
these are deemed useless.
Yet people in the world all flaunt their own talents and abilities, pursuing the utility of usefulness,
unaware that embracing a fragmented virtue constitutes the utility of uselessness.
Thus, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
being useful means achieving merit with others,
while being useless ensures the preservation of one's own life.
【Explanation】"Mèn rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant of "wáng" and the final of "běn" in reverse.
【一】【注】When virtue fills the interior,
it responds to things externally.
The external and internal mysteriously unite,
truly as if following a decree while leaving behind the physical form.
【Explanation】Cuī Zǐ states:
This is the evidence of discarding physical form and abandoning knowledge,
to fill it with virtue.
【Collation Note】(1) This item should be revised according to Zhào Jiànyì's version.
In the state of Lǔ there was a amputee named Wáng Tái,
and the number of his followers was equal to that of Zhòngní.
Cháng Jì asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Wáng Tái
is an amputee,
yet his followers split the state of Lǔ evenly with you, Master.
He neither instructs when standing,
nor discusses when sitting;
yet people go to him empty
and return full.
Can there truly be teaching without words,
and mental fulfillment without form?
What manner of man is this?"
【One】【Account】His surname was Wáng,
his name was Tái,
and he was a man of Lǔ.
Having one foot amputated was called being maimed.
Although his form was crippled and maimed,
his heart was truly empty and forgetful,
thus he is honored as the embodiment of virtue and placed at the beginning of the chapter.
【Translated Text】"The Lame One" is pronounced as wǔ hū fǎn,
also pronounced as jiè.
Lǐ Yún said:
Having one's foot cut off is called wù.
According to this, the seal script characters for wù and jiè are similar in appearance.
"Wáng Tái" is pronounced as tái,
and Xú also pronounces it as dǎi.
It is a person's name.
【Two】【Annotation】How many disciples were there to match:
Confucius.
【Commentary】"Ruò" means
"like" or "as if."
Those who follow Wáng Tái in his travels and receive instruction from him,
have disciples nearly as numerous as those of Zhòngní.
【Explanatory Text】"Follow it" is read as the character's usual pronunciation,
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as cái yòng fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Similar to" ruò,
means "like,"
referring to how many disciples are like the master.
【Three】【Disciples】Surname Cháng,
given name Jì,
was a virtuous man of Lǔ.
Wáng Tái traveled about,
outwardly forgetting his physical form,
inwardly filled with virtuous substance,
thus those who followed him as wandering scholars
numbered a full three thousand,
sharing half of Lǔ's disciples with Confucius's followers.
Cháng Jì had not yet grasped his essence,
and therefore harbored doubts.
【Explanatory Text】"Cháng Jì": Some say:
he was a disciple of Confucius.
【Four】【Annotations】Each attains their own sufficiency.
【Commentary】Though the disciples were many,
none gave lectures or explanations,
standing they did not teach,
sitting they held no discussions.
When seeking knowledge, they went with empty minds,
and upon grasping the truth, returned with fulfilled hearts.
Another interpretation:
lacking learning and virtue,
one also goes in vain.
【Explanatory Text】"Standing without teaching, sitting without discussing," Sīmǎ comments:
Standing without imparting knowledge,
sitting without engaging in debate.
【五】【注】It is strange that despite his maimed form, his mind was perfectly content.
When the mind is whole,
it leaves the physical form behind,
forgets the five internal organs,
and suddenly journeys alone,
yet nothing under heaven can separate from it.
【Commentary】He taught his disciples,
yet never engaged in verbal debates.
Austere and unyielding as he was,
beyond any physical description,
the profound Way and ultimate virtue
were fully realized within his heart.
It is because he inherently possessed these qualities
that the multitude followed him.
【Transcription】"Wǔ Zàng" is read as cái làng fǎn.
The same applies hereafter.
【Six】【Commentary】Cháng Jì was puzzled by how someone so maimed and incomplete could gather such an immense following.
Wishing to highlight the beauty of virtue fulfilled,
he thus posed this question.
Zhòngní said:
"The Master,
being a sage,
I, Qiū, have merely lagged behind and not yet gone to him.
I shall take him as my teacher,
let alone those who are not as good as I am!
Why limit it to the state of Lǔ!
I shall lead all under heaven to follow him."
【一】【疏】Confucius addressed Wáng Tái as Fūzǐ,
responding to Cháng Jì saying:
"Wáng Tái is a sage who embodies the Way,
it is you who fail to recognize the person,
hence your doubts arise.
I, Qiū, am merely uneven and lagging behind,
not yet able to serve him in the past.
I shall honor him as a master and mentor,
consulting and inquiring about the Way,
let alone those of later learning,
who are not as advanced as I am!
To seek improvement and hold it close to the heart,
is indeed appropriate."
【Explanation】"Qiū was merely behind and had not yet gone." Lǐ's commentary says:
He was naturally behind the crowd,
and had not yet managed to go to the teacher.
◎Qìng Fán's case note: "Zhí" here means "tè" (merely/only).

In the "Loyalty and Integrity" chapter of "Mr. Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals," it says "tè Wángzǐ Qìngjì wèi zhī chì ér bù shā ěr" (merely because Prince Qìngjì was prepared for it and did not kill him),
Gāo's annotation:
"Tè,"
is equivalent to "zhí."
In the "Bǎi Zhōu" poem of the Yōng style, "shí wéi wǒ tè" (it is truly for me alone),
the Hán (text) [Poetry] writes "tè" as "zhí."
In the "Biography of Shūsūn Tōng" from "Records of the Grand Historian," it says "wú zhí xì ěr" (I was merely joking),
while the "Book of Hàn" writes "zhí" as "tè."
【二】【Note】When the spirit is whole and the mind is complete,
then the body merges with all things.
One who merges with all things
cannot be distanced by the entire world,
how much less by just a single state!
【Commentary】Xī means
"why".
"Why merely borrow the single state of Lǔ!
Qiū intends to guide and lead all within the four seas,
to receive and uphold the great virtue,
yet still fear not having fully exhausted the Way."
【Interpretation】"Néng yuǎn" is read as yú wàn fǎn.
Cháng Jì said:
"He is a man who has lost his foot,
yet he is revered as a teacher by the king,
so he must be far superior to ordinary people.
If that is the case,
how does he employ his mind differently?"
【一】【疏】King,
means flourishing.
Yong,
means ordinary.
Xiansheng,
refers to Confucius.
That Wang Tái,
is a person who is maimed and crippled,
yet his disciples and followers,
outnumber those of Confucius.
Because of this, it is strange and astonishing,
he responds differently from the common flow,
and is certainly far removed from ordinary people.
【Explanatory Text】"而王" is read as yú kuàng fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
means to surpass.
Cuī Yún:
refers to a ruler or leader.
"其與庸亦遠矣" means to be far different from the ordinary.
Cuī Yún:
yōng,
refers to a common person.
Even the two worthies Shūguǎng and Shūshòu were like this,
and still it was so.
Wáng Tái's abundant virtue is such that,
all things are drawn to him.
I wonder by what wisdom and effort,
what unique method does he employ?
Cháng Jì is not mistaken
to raise this doubt.
Zhòngní said:
"Death and life are indeed matters of great importance,
yet they cannot cause him to change along with them.
Even if heaven and earth were to overturn and collapse,
he still would not perish with them.
Being thoroughly aware of the flawless and not shifting with external things,
he commands the transformations of things and guards his ancestral foundation."
【一】【注】Although people change daily,
the transformation of life and death
is the greatest of all changes.
【二】【注】He remains one with transformation,
thus life and death do not alter him.
【Commentary】Though mountains shift and boats submerge in stealthy retreats,
and firewood points to the ceaseless flow of change,
even if all phenomena in the world follow this principle,
life and death remain the most significant.
However, Wáng Tái's mind merges with the creator,
moving along with the transformations;
his traces blend into the human world,
journeying together with life and death,
thus he remains unaltered by what seeks to change.
【Three】【Comment】This is to follow it.
【Commentary】Lost,
means to lose.
Even if the round sky were to overturn,
and the square earth were to collapse,
since one is oblivious to safety and danger,
therefore, it has never caused the loss of the self.
【Explanation】"Though heaven and earth cover" pronounced as fāng fú fǎn.
"Fall" also written as duì,
pronounced zhí lèi fǎn.
Lǐ Yún said:
Even heaven and earth cannot change oneself,
how much less life and death!
【Four】【Annotation】Clarifying the inherent appropriateness of human nature and destiny.
◎Qìng Fān's case: "wú jiǎ" should be an error for "wú xiá",
meaning to examine oneself and find no flaws,
thus allowing things to change naturally without being enslaved by them.
The Huáinánzǐ's Spiritual Chapter correctly writes "examine having no flaws".
Both "xiá" and "jiǎ" share the phonetic component "jiǎ",
leading to their easy confusion.
(Shǐ Jì) The Hereditary House of Zhèng records someone enticing and seizing the great officer Fǔ Jiǎ of Zhèng,
while the Zuǒ Zhuàn writes it as Fù Xiá.
The Lǐ Jì's Tán Gōng chapter mentions Jiān Jiǎ,
whereas the Hàn Shū's Table of Ancient and Modern Persons writes it as Gōng Jiān Xiá,
which serves as evidence for this.
【Five】【Annotation】Let things transform of their own accord.
【Commentary】The spiritual mind is serene and composed,
embodying the true essence in a wondrous way.
Since it aligns with the Dao,
it remains unchanged and unaffected by external things.
【Six】【Comment】To take transformation as destiny,
and be without conflict.
【Transcription】"Guài wǔ": wǔ gù fǎn.
Originally also written as 遻.
Same below.
【Seven】【Annotation】Not departing from the ultimate standard of what is right.
【Commentary】One who is attuned to the ordained fate,
detached from external matters,
embracing only fate and material existence,
moves in harmony with transformation,
acting without contradicting stillness,
thus abides eternally in its fundamental origin.
【Explanation】"Bù lí" is read with the fourth tone on "lì" and the second tone on "zhì".
【Collation Note】(1) The Quēwù cites the Jiangnan ancient Tibetan edition, which has the character "者" following "宗".
Cháng Jì said:
"What does that mean?"
【One】【Memorial】Profoundly difficult to comprehend,
I further request a resolution to my doubts.
Zhòngní said:
"From the perspective of their differences,
the liver and gall are as distant as Chǔ and Yuè;
from the perspective of their similarities,
all things are one.
One who is like this
does not even know what is suitable for the ears and eyes,
but lets the mind wander in the harmony of virtue;
regarding things as unified and not seeing what is lost,
viewing the loss of a foot as like shedding a clod of earth."
【一】【注】When the natures of calmness and bitterness differ greatly,
then the feelings of beauty and ugliness are in opposition.
【Commentary】All things flourish and multiply,
yet all return to emptiness and stillness.
Those who are deluded and confused
falsely cling to right and wrong,
and within the profound Dao of mystery,
arbitrarily create distinctions.
How is this different from the liver and gallbladder, which
originally belong to the same body,
yet like Chǔ and Yuè, distant and far apart,
separated by thousands of miles?
But within a single body,
they create a separation of thousands of miles.
Those who hold divergent views
are all like this.
【Transliteration】"Gāndǎn" Dīng Lǎn fǎn.
"Měi'è" Wū Lù fǎn.
Xià jiē tóng.
"Qíng bèi" is pronounced as "pèi".
【二】【注】Though the objects of admiration differ,
they share the quality of being admired.
When each admires what they admire,
then all things share a single beauty;
when each affirms what they affirm,
then the world shares a single truth.
If we emphasize differences based on distinctions,
then nothing in the world is without difference.
Yet one with vast and boundless perspective
governs heaven and earth,
embraces all things,
and knows distinctions are not worth distinguishing.
Thus, by emphasizing commonalities based on shared traits,
then nothing in the world fails to be alike;
further knowing commonality is not worth possessing,
one thus embraces non-being based on what is absent,
so right and wrong, beauty and ugliness,
all dissolve into non-existence.
To affirm oneself and negate others,
to admire oneself and despise others—
from those of average wisdom downward,
even to insects,
none fail to be this way.
Yet this only understands the self without understanding others.
As for those who mysteriously penetrate and seamlessly unite,
they illuminate the world through the world itself.
The world never says "I am wrong,"
thus revealing the absence of wrong in the world;
it never says "others are right,"
thus revealing the absence of right in the world.
Without right or wrong,
blended into oneness,
they can thus ride change and embrace transformation,
confronting things without fear.
【Commentary】As for those who are profoundly perceptive,
they possess a vast and comprehensive view,
seeing the two realms and all things
as one finger or one horse;
thus, they can let go of personal concerns and entrust themselves to things,
greatly harmonizing with all living beings.
However, those who focus on similarities see their sameness,
while those who focus on differences see their distinctions.
When it comes to the ultimate discourse on the realm of all wonders,
it is neither different nor the same.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhōng zhì" is pronounced with the tone for wisdom.
"Bù shè" is pronounced with the retroflex initial and the entering tone.
【Three】【Comment】What is appropriate arises from what is not appropriate.
When there is neither beauty nor ugliness,
then there is nothing inappropriate.
When there is nothing inappropriate,
thus one forgets (two) its appropriateness.
【Commentary】What suits the ears and eyes
is suited to sounds and colors.
Moreover, ordinary emotions make distinctions,
becoming engrossed and fixated on sounds and colors,
hence there is what is suitable and unsuitable,
what is acceptable and unacceptable.
Yet Wáng Tái blends all things into one,
darkly unifying life and death—
how could he harbor views of beauty and ugliness among the senses and their objects!
【Four】【Annotation】When all forgetting is fitting,
therefore there is nothing not entrusted.
If everything is entrusted yet not attained,
such a thing has never existed;
if nothing is unattained yet not harmonious,
such a case has never been heard of either.
Thus, by releasing the mind within the realm of the Dàodé,
one becomes expansively without inappropriateness,
and openly without discomfort.
【Commentary】Thereafter, he merged with all things into one,
unaware of what is suitable for the eyes and ears,
thus able to wander in the realm of the Way and its Virtue,
roaming freely in the domain of the ultimate Way.
【五】【注】By embodying the ultimate subtlety of numerical principles in the mind,
one can thus be in harmony with all things without distinction.
Being in harmony with all things without distinction,
then life, death, and transformation—
wherever they occur, they are none other than myself.
Therefore, life is my moment of existence,
death is my compliance;
existence is my gathering,
compliance is my dispersal.
Though gathering and dispersal differ,
I recognize both as myself.
Thus, life is indeed me,
yet there has never been a gain;
death is also me,
yet there has never been a loss.
The transformation of life and death,
regarded as one and the same,
once this oneness is perceived,
then one is detached and unbound,
mysteriously unifying self and other,
viewing life and death as waking and sleeping,
the physical form as a temporary lodging,
departing from life like shedding worn sandals,
losing a foot like discarding soil.
I see nothing that can entangle or disturb such a mind.
【Commentary】Looking at things,
is like observing objects.
Wáng Tái unified life and death,
equalizing self and others.
Life is my time,
not seeing it as a gain;
death is my compliance,
not seeing it as a loss;
viewing all things,
blending them into one.
Thus, even with a severed foot,
he regarded it as discarded earth.
【Explanatory Text】"Suǒ sàng" is pronounced with the initial "息" and the final "浪" in the fanqie method.
The same applies to the occurrences below and in the annotations.
"Shuō rán" is pronounced with the initial "始" and the final "銳" in the fanqie method,
and also can be read as "yuè".
"Tuō jù" is pronounced with the initial "九" and the final "具" in the fanqie method.
The character is also written as "屣",
pronounced with the initial "所" and the final "買" in the fanqie method.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, the book writes it as "屣".
"Duàn zú" is pronounced with the initial "丁" and the final "管" in the fanqie method.
【Collation】(1) The character "附" has been added based on Liú Wěndiǎn's revised edition.
(2) The Shìdétáng edition has "亡".
The same applies below.
(3) The Shìdétáng edition has "擴".
(4) The Shìdétáng edition has "說",
while the Zhào Jiànyì edition has "悅".
Cháng Jì said:
"He cultivates himself through his wisdom,
and attains his mind through his mind.
Having attained the constant mind,
why should things gather around him?"
【一】【注】It is suspected that Wáng Tái failed to forget knowledge and thus preserve himself.
【Commentary】That refers to
Wáng Tái.
It is said that Wáng Tái cultivated goodness and improved himself,
yet still employed his mind and knowledge.
This expresses doubt that he had not yet achieved forgetting knowledge and relying solely on his inner self.
【Interpretation】"For oneself" pronounced as wèi jǐ fǎn.
【二】【注】It is regrettable that one cannot let go of the mind and attain self-realization.
【Commentary】It is suspected that Wáng Tái did not forget to let go and follow nature,
yet still used the mind to attain the mind.
Now, one who attains the mind
has no thoughts or deliberations,
forgets knowledge and perception,
like dead ashes or a withered tree,
placid and without emotion.
Placing it within the square inch [of the heart],
it arises beyond the realm of sight and sound,
aligning with the covering and supporting of the two primal forces,
following the three luminaries to shine and illuminate.
Mingling with dust and filth yet not disturbing its spirit,
treading through hardship and obstruction yet not opposing its considerations,
not attaining is attainment,
and attainment lies in non-attainment—
this is true attainment.
If one attains it through the methods of intellectual knowledge,
it is not genuine attainment.
【Three】【Commentary】Those who attain their constant mind,
proceed with equanimity.
Fearing that they may not proceed with equanimity when encountering things,
they thus constantly make things come to them.
【Commentary】"Zuì" means
to gather.
If one can empty the mind and forget, achieving plainness and blandness,
thereby obtaining the true constant heart,
one should naturally harmonize one's light and conceal one's brilliance,
not differing from the common.
How could one stand out alone from all things,
causing the masses to turn to them!
【Interpretation Text】"Zuì zhī" is read as "cú huì fǎn",
and according to Xú, it is "cǎi huì fǎn".
The same applies to the annotations below.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to gather.
◎ Jiā Shìfù comments:
Wisdom manifests externally,
while the mind resides internally;
using one's wisdom to attain the mind
is to follow the external to preserve the internal.
The mind is
the ceaseless true mechanism,
the constant mind is
the fundamental essence without falsehood;
using one's mind to attain the constant mind
is to verify the Dao through the substance.
Shuōwén explains:
Zuì,
means to confront and take,
as if to say nothing can confront it.
Guō Xiàng's punctuation is incorrect.
◎ Qìng Fān's case in Shuōwén:
means to accumulate,
derived from ● (mò dí qiē.
) and qǔ,
with qǔ also indicating the sound.
Xú Kǎi states:
In ancient times,  was used for the gathering of things.
People often see "zuì",
but rarely see "",
hence in texts and transmissions, the character "" is all written as "zuì".
Zhòngní said:
"People do not mirror themselves in flowing water but in still water【一】,
for only what is still can still the stillness of others【二】.
Receiving life from the earth,
it is only the pine and cypress that remain verdant in both winter and summer【三】;
receiving life from heaven,
it is only Shùn who alone is upright【四】,
fortunate to rectify his own life,
thereby rectifying the lives of others【五】.
As for preserving the evidence of one's beginning,
the substance of fearlessness:
a single brave warrior,
may valiantly charge into the nine armies.
One who seeks fame and can demand much of himself,
can still be like this—
【六】how much more one who governs heaven and earth【七】,
stores the myriad things【七】,
merely lodges the six bodily parts【八】,
reflects through ears and eyes【九】,
unifies all that is known by understanding,
and whose heart-mind has never died【一０】!
Such a person will choose a day to ascend afar,
and people will follow him【一一】.
How could he be willing to take things as his concern【一二】?"
【一】【注】Still water's ability to reflect clearly,
is not because it seeks stillness for the sake of reflection.
Thus, when Wáng Tái gathered a crowd,
the crowd naturally came to him—
how could it be that he drew others to make them follow him!
【Commentary】A mirror is for
reflecting.
Still water retains the ability to mirror
because it is clear and calm;
Wáng Tái gathers a crowd
because he is tranquil and serene.
Still water has no intention of reflecting objects;
objects reflect themselves in it.
How could Wáng Tái have any intention of attracting others?
Yet the multitude naturally comes to gather around him.
【Explanation】"Jian" is pronounced as gǔ zàn fǎn.
"Flowing Water" in Cui's version is written as "Mei Water",
stating:
"Mei" might be written as "flowing".
◎Qìng Fān's note: Flowing water contrasts with still water in the text.
Cui's version uses "Mei",
which is incorrect.
In clerical script, "flowing" is sometimes written as (涿)〔●〕 (seen in the Stele of Chancellor Shǐ Chén's Offering at the Confucian Temple).
Its shape resembles "Mei",
hence Cuì mistakenly took it for "Mei".
In Huáinánzǐ's "Discourse on Mountains" chapter, it says, "No one mirrors themselves in the rain of 'Mei'",
with Gāo's annotation:
"Rain of 'Mei'",
or written as "flowing puddles".
This further confirms that "Mei" is a miswriting of "flowing".
【二】【注】If one acts upon it,
then one cannot reside in the stillness of all things.
【Commentary】"Wéi" (only),
means solitary.
"Wéi zhǐ" (only stopping) refers to water being originally calm and clear,
"néng zhǐ" (able to stop) means retaining and reflecting people,
"zhòng zhǐ" (all stopping) signifies things coming to be mirrored.
It is like Wáng Tái forgetting worldly concerns and embracing emptiness and tranquility,
thus capable of accommodating and guiding all living beings,
due to this ability,
which is why he becomes the gathering point for the masses.
【三】【注】The pine and cypress uniquely receive the concentrated qi of nature,
thus they can stand out as the most distinguished among all trees,
not because they strive for it and thereby attain it.
【Commentary】All plants and trees
rely on the rich earth for sustenance.
As for those endowed with a firm and robust nature,
remaining unwithered even in the depths of winter,
such as pine and cypress trees that through all four seasons of the year
consistently preserve their verdant entirety,
this is due to the inherent endowment they receive,
not a matter of deliberate intent.
Wáng Tái gathered followers,
and the principle is the same in his case.
【Four】【Annotation】It is said that those who uniquely receive the pure energy of nature are extremely rare.
Among the lower beings, only the pine and cypress possess it;
among the higher beings, only the sages do.
Therefore, all that is not upright comes seeking uprightness.
If all things were inherently complete and green,
then there would be no value in the pine and cypress;
if each person were self-upright,
then there would be no admiration for the great sages nor a rush to follow them.
【Subcommentary】Humans embody the three powers (heaven, earth, and humanity),
receiving their mandate from the azure sky.
With round heads and square feet,
their kind is exceedingly numerous.
As for those who stand out with upright and genuine qi,
only Yú Shùn is unique.
How could it be due to deliberate effort?
It is simply a natural disposition.
Wáng Tái's alignment with the Dào
carries the same meaning.
Guō Xiàng's annotation states that the lower heads are only the pines and cypresses, and the upper heads are only the sages—
but human heads are on top,
and if removed from the top, they die;
tree heads are at the bottom,
and if removed from the bottom, they die.
Therefore, humans are called the upper heads,
and trees are called the lower heads.
Thus, the upper heads feed on the side heads,
and the side heads feed on the lower heads.
The lower heads
are the plants and trees;
the side heads,
the insects and beasts.
【五】【Note】It is fortunate that it can correct itself,
not that it is corrected by means of correction.
【Commentary】Receiving the vital energy from the profound heavens,
one is able to rectify the way of life;
it is not through deliberate intent,
but by fortunately following nature.
Since one can correct oneself,
one can also correct others.
Correcting oneself and others,
benefiting both self and others,
perfecting inner and outer conduct—
this is what is called a great sage.
Yú Shùn was such,
and Wáng Tái likewise.
However, Shùn yielded the throne to others,
hence he is held as the exemplar.
【Six】【Annotation】Not that he could abandon reputation and yet be without non-action.
【Commentary】Zhēng means
accomplishment,
trustworthiness.
The Son of Heaven has six armies,
feudal lords have three armies,
hence nine armies in total.
Suppose there is a person,
endowed with a courageous and martial spirit,
who preserves the heart of a good beginning,
faithfully fulfills the integrity of a commendable end,
harboring an unafraid resolve within,
displaying a valiant and fierce demeanor outwardly.
Then, charging straight into the nine armies,
in pursuit of fame and position,
they can still subdue their heart to seek renown,
forgetting death and life.
How much more so for Wáng Tái!
The manifestation of embodying the Dào
is detailed in the following text.
【Explanation Text】"The Sign of Preserving the Beginning" Lǐ Yún says:
Sign,
means accomplishment,
one can preserve and accomplish from beginning to end.
"Nine Armies" Cuī (original) [Lǐ] (six) says:
The Son of Heaven has six armies,
feudal lords have three armies,
together making nine armies.
Jiǎn Wén says:
Military texts speak of attacking the nine heavens,
seizing the nine earths,
hence they are called the nine armies.
"Zì Yào" is read with the first tone yáo.
【Seven】【Comment】Silently, there is nothing that is not embodied.
【Commentary】To govern the two modes of existence is called being the official of heaven and earth;
to encompass the universe is called being the storehouse of all things.
When a brave warrior enters the army,
seeking only fame and position,
he can still disregard his own life,
forgetting life and death.
How much more so for one who serves as the official of the two modes
and blends all things into one,
viewing death as life—
is this not fitting indeed!
【Eight】【Annotation】What is called a traveler's lodge.
【Commentary】"Yù" means
"to lodge."
"Liù hái" refers to
the head and four limbs of the body.
Wáng Tái understood that the physical body is not the true reality,
comprehending that all things are genuine.
Therefore, he could blend the defilements of dust within the mundane world,
lodging his spirit within the physical form.
It was merely a temporary encounter,
how could it be bound to it!
【Transcription】"The Six Body Parts" Cuī said:
hands, feet, head, and torso.
【Nine】【Annotation】People use their eyes and ears,
and also use their eyes and ears,
but they do not solely depend on them.
【Commentary】Resemblance,
means likeness.
Blending the light and mingling with the dust,
it seems to employ the ears and eyes,
but it is not a necessity.
【一０】【Note】When knowledge moves in step with transformation,
there is no place it does not merge with,
this is the oneness of knowledge.
When the mind follows life and death in their course,
there is no moment that is not life,
this is the mind that has never died.
【Commentary】The act of knowing is
wisdom.
What is known is
the object.
The wisdom that can know illuminates the object that is known,
the object and wisdom merge indistinguishably,
there is no distinction between the knower and the known,
thus knowing and not knowing
become one and interconnected.
Although one follows the patterns of things and transforms with them,
the mind has never witnessed death,
how could there be any obstruction between them!
【一一】【Note】It is because they do not miss opportunities that they are considered selective,
yet this person has no need for selection,
for they act in accordance with the natural course and move at the right time.
Thus, those who rely on borrowed means
are esteemed for this reason.
【Commentary】That Wáng Tái,
did he really select an auspicious day to ascend to the mysterious Way?
Surely it was not so,
but rather, he directly established emptiness and tranquility, forgetting all concerns, and thus comprehended it.
The ultimate person has no deliberate mind,
like still water that retains a reflection,
and the vain and artificial people of the world
follow him because of this.
【Translated Text】"Bǐ qiě" is read according to its standard pronunciation.
Xú reads it as zǐ yú fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Jiǎ rén" is read as gǔ yǎ fǎn,
meaning to borrow.
Xú pronounces it as xiá,
reading it connected to the previous sentence,
with the character "rén" linking downward.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: "Dēng jiǎ" is equivalent to "dēng gé."
"Jiǎ" and "gé" were used interchangeably in ancient times.
In the Book of Songs, "zòu gé" is sometimes written as "zòu jiǎ,"
which serves as evidence.
The Erya states:
"Gé,"
"zhì,"
"dēng,"
all mean to ascend.
The use of both "dēng" and "gé"
reflects the ancient practice of using compound expressions.
In the Chu Ci's "Lí Sāo," the line "zhì shēng huáng zhī hè xī xī"
also uses "zhì" to mean ascent.
【一二】【Note】Because of their tranquility and indifference, they are preserved.
【Commentary】Only that Wáng Tái,
profoundly genuine and united with the Dao,
had illusory things naturally come to him,
yet how could he ever have taken them as his own concern!
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition, which has the character "正" (correct) below "也" (ye).
Yu Yue considers the character "在" (zai) below to be a miswriting of "正".
(2) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition, where this sentence reads as "尧舜独也正" (Yáo and Shùn alone are correct),
with the five characters "在万物之首" (at the head of all things) following "正".
(3) In the Tang manuscript, "官" (official) is written as "宫" (palace).
(4) The Shidetang edition lacks the character "耶" (ye).
(5) In Zhao Jianyi's edition, "鍾" (Zhōng) is written as "種" (zhǒng).
(6) The character "李" (Lǐ) is emended according to the Shidetang edition.
Shēntú Jiā
was a man who had lost a foot,
and studied under Bóhūn Wúrén together with Zhèng Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn said to Shēntú Jiā:
"When I go out first, you stay behind;
when you go out first, I stay behind."
The next day,
they again shared the same hall and sat on the same mat.
Zǐchǎn said to Shēntú Jiā:
"When I go out first, you stay behind;
when you go out first, I stay behind.
Now I am about to go out;
can you stay behind,
or can you not?
Moreover, when you see the prime minister, you don't avoid him;
do you consider yourself equal to the prime minister?"
【One】【Commentary】His surname is Shēntú,
his given name is Jiā,
a virtuous man of Zhèng,
who had lost one foot.
His surname is Gōngsūn,
his given name is Qiáo,
his courtesy name is Zǐchǎn,
a virtuous senior official of Zhèng.
Bó Hūn Wúrén,
is the esteemed title of the teacher.
Bó,
means elder.
Hūn,
means obscure.
His virtue placed him above worldly matters,
concealing his brilliance as if in obscurity,
thoroughly forgetting both self and others,
hence he was called Bó Hūn Wúrén.
Zǐchǎn and Shēntú,
both studied the profound Way,
although their paths in life were vastly different,
they shared Bó Hūn as their teacher,
thus these three figures are used here to illustrate the meaning of virtue's fulfillment.
【Explanatory Text】"Shēntú Jiā" Lǐ Yún states:
Shēntú,
is the surname;
Jiā,
is the given name.
"Wú Rén" in the Miscellaneous Chapters is written as Mào Rén.
【二】【注】Ashamed to walk alongside one who has been punished by foot amputation.
【Commentary】Zǐchǎn held power on the main road,
enjoying glory and wealth;
Shēntú, born with a mutilated form and missing a foot,
had no dignified appearance.
Although Zǐchǎn had studied under Bóhūn,
he had not yet achieved forgetfulness and detachment,
still clinging to favor and disgrace,
feeling ashamed to see a deformed body.
Therefore, he preemptively restrained himself,
insisting that Shēntú must not stand beside him.
【Transcription】"The Amputee" is pronounced yuè,
also read as wǔ guā fǎn.
【Three】【Comment】Directly questioning him,
intending to ensure he does not rival oneself.
【Commentary】Zǐchǎn retained concerns for honor and disgrace,
while Shēntú forgot distinctions between nobility and baseness.
Although previous discussions had occurred,
neither paid heed to the other's views,
hence they dwelled under the same roof
and sat together upon the same mat.
Gōngsūn, observing this situation,
therefore posed a direct question to them.
【Four】【Annotation】He often prided himself on being in power,
so it was directly stated that he was the minister in charge of Qí's government,
which was considered sufficient to illustrate his arrogance (1).
【Commentary】"Defiance" means
avoidance.
For the paths of advancement and seclusion differ,
and the conduct of the noble and the humble is distinct.
I hold the reins of court governance,
thus being noble and great;
you, however, are lowly and physically impaired,
and should show me exceptional respect.
Failing to defer humbly,
you instead seek to equate yourself with me.
【Collation】（一）In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, there is the character "yě" after "xùn".
Shēntú Jiā said:
"At our master's gate,
is there truly one who holds governance acting like this?
Do you, sir, delight in your governance and thus look down upon others?
I have heard it said:
'When a mirror is clear, dust and grime do not settle on it;
if they settle, it is not clear.
Long association with a worthy person leaves one without fault.'
Now, the one from whom you take your greatness,
is our master,
yet you still speak in such a manner,
is that not a fault?"
【一】【Note】This passage discusses virtue,
not the calculation of status.
【Commentary】Sir,
Bó Hūn,
who entered the gate of the Way,
profoundly understood the myriad mysteries,
blended honor and disgrace into one,
and equalized life and death.
Are you so certain that governing the state makes you self-important,
that it must be like this?
【Explanation】"之處" is pronounced as chānglǜ fǎn.
【二】【注】He laughs at him for being proud of his position in office,
and wanting to be ahead of all things.
