【Commentary】You still delight in the love of glory and splendor,
boast of your political achievements,
push others behind,
and desire to be ahead of all things.
With such views as these,
how can it be called learning the Way?
【Explanation】"而說" is pronounced as "yuè".
The same applies to the annotations.
【Three】【Comment】To serve an enlightened teacher yet still not rid oneself of a mean and stingy heart,
this is truly a fault.
【Commentary】A mirror,
is a looking glass.
When a mirror is clear, dust and grime do not settle on it;
if they settle, it is not bright and reflective.
Similarly, if one long dwells with the virtuous, one will be without faults;
if one has faults, it is not due to the wise and sagely.
What you now adopt,
that which can be esteemed and great,
is the Dào of the Master.
Yet the Dào of the Master
involves withdrawing oneself, emptying and forgetting.
You, however, are self-praising,
deeply contradicting the profound meaning,
and speaking in such a manner—
is this not a fault indeed!
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"You have already reached such a state,
yet still contend with Yáo for virtue.
Considering your own character, is it not enough to make you reflect upon yourself?"
【一】【注】If it is a physical disability.
【Two】【Comment】This means one does not reflect on oneself,
yet wishes to look down upon those in positions of authority,
and stand alongside the virtuous.
Considering your virtue,
it is indeed insufficient to make up for the flaw of physical impairment.
【Commentary】"Fǎn" means
"to return" or "to restore."
It is said that Shēntú, despite being physically impaired to such an extent and unaware of it himself,
still wishes to compare himself with me and walk side by side,
which can be described as contending with Yáo for goodness.
Although you possess virtue,
how is it worth mentioning!
Using virtue to compensate for physical impairment
is still not enough to restore wholeness.
【Interpretation】"Zhēng shàn" is read as it is written.
【Collation】(1) The Que Wen cites editions by Wén, Chéng, Lǐ, and Zhāng that do not have □.
Shēntú Jiā said:
"Many are those who justify their faults and claim they do not deserve punishment,
few are those who refrain from justifying their faults and admit they do not deserve to survive.
To know what cannot be helped and to accept it calmly as fate—
only the virtuous can do this.
We wander within the archer Yì's range.
The center of his target
is where arrows are meant to strike;
yet to avoid being hit—
that is fate.
Many are those who, with their whole feet, laugh at my lack of them,
and I would flare up in anger;
but upon coming to our master's place,
my anger would dissipate and I'd return to myself.
Is it not that our master cleanses me with goodness?
I have studied under our master for nineteen years,
yet he has never been aware that I am a man without a foot.
Now you and I wander in the realm of the inner spirit,
yet you seek me in the realm of the external form—
is that not a mistake?"
【一】【Note】Many confess their own faults and misdeeds,
thinking themselves among the many who should not perish.
【二】【Note】Silently aware of his faults,
he himself believed that those deserving death were few.
【Commentary】Those who show off their own merits,
shift blame onto others,
claim they have no faults,
and believe they should not perish—
such people
are very numerous in the world.
Those who do not display their flaws,
take the blame upon themselves,
admit their own mistakes,
and feel they do not deserve to live—
such people
are rare in the world.
Zhèng Zǐchǎn, with his extravagance and self-aggrandizement,
is also an example of this in terms of righteousness.
【Three】【Explanations】Ruò,
means to comply.
The innate qualities and physical form,
are endowed by the mandate of heaven.
Although one may possess knowledge and schemes,
there is nothing one can do about it.
Only by accepting and complying with it,
can all that is achieved be fitting.
Unless one possesses great virtue,
who can be like this!
【Transcription】"Zhi Bu Ke" is read according to the character's usual pronunciation,
and also pronounced as "zhì".
【Four】【Comment】Yì,
was an expert archer in ancient times.
The range covered by his bow and arrows constituted the zone of danger.
When benefit and harm clash,
then all under heaven become like Yì.
Those who do not forget themselves and their knowledge to flow along with things
are all wandering within Yì's zone of danger.
Even when Zhāng Yì went out
or Dān Bào stayed in seclusion,
they still could not avoid being struck,
so whether one is hit or not,
depends solely on fate.
Yet people in their insignificance each have their encounters,
unaware that (four) fate operates of itself.
Thus those who escape the harm of arrows
consider themselves skillful,
rejoicing in their own superiority,
but when they cannot avoid it,
they regret their error with wounded will and shamed spirit -
these are ones who fail to understand the true nature of fate.
My coming to life,
is not something I brought about myself,
thus throughout this single lifetime,
within these hundred years,
whether sitting up or rising, walking or stopping,
moving or still, pursuing or abandoning,
emotions, nature, knowledge, and abilities,
all that I possess,
all that I lack,
all that I do,
all that I encounter,
none are truly mine -
principle simply operates of itself.
Yet to forcibly generate joy and sorrow amidst this
is again to go against nature and be lost (five).
【Commentary】Yì,
was an expert archer during the time of Yáo.
The reach of his arrows,
was called the "archery range."
It is said that Yì was so skilled at archery,
that no arrow he shot was in vain,
and within the archery range,
all was inevitably devastated,
regardless of birds or beasts,
few managed to escape.
If by chance something escaped,
it was due to the will of Heaven,
whether one escaped or not,
was not determined by skill or clumsiness,
without discarding form and forgetting wisdom,
all roamed within Yì's archery range.
Thus it is known that Shēntú, with his amputated foot,
was suddenly struck by one of Yì's arrows;
Zǐchǎn, with his body intact,
by chance escaped within the range;
since it was not a matter of human effort,
it is not worth boasting about.
【Interpretation】"Yì" is pronounced as yì,
with an alternative reading by Xú as hú xì fǎn.
He was a skilled archer,
existing during the Xià dynasty of Táng.
Another account says:
he was the ruler of Yǒuqióng who usurped the Xià.
"Gòu" is pronounced as gòu,
meaning to draw a bow.
◎ Jiā Shìfù commented:
According to the Yùpiān dictionary:
gòu,
refers to drawing a bow or crossbow.
In the Hànshū biography of Zhōu Yàfū,
it says "gòu gōngnǔ dài mǎn."
To wander within Yì's range of arrows,
is to encounter danger everywhere.
Yet, there is a vast area where one might be hit,
but if one positions oneself not to be hit,
then the upper string and lower grip,
along with the arrow nock in between,
may instead cause injury due to a rebound.
In the act of wandering alike,
being hit or not,
is a matter of chance occurrence,
and accepting what cannot be controlled is fate.
This speaks to the innocence of the footless, not being their fault.
"Zhōng" is read as in its usual pronunciation.
"Yāng" is pronounced as yú liáng fǎn,
formerly as yú cāng fǎn.
Guō's note says:
The area reached by bow and arrows is the gòu zhōng.
"Zhòng dì" is pronounced as dīng zhòng fǎn.
The following "not hit," note "hit area," and "hit or not" share the same reading.
"Shàn Bào" is pronounced as shàn.
【五】【注】All of them, unaware of destiny, thus had this laughter (six).
【Six】【Annotation】To see his ignorance of fate and become angry,
this in turn is also ignorance of fate.
【Commentary】"Fèi rán" means
a heart of violent cruelty.
When people do not understand the Mandate of Heaven,
they wrongly judge what is deficient and complete,
considering their own form as good,
and scoff at others who are maimed or incomplete.
Such individuals
are numerous in their kind.
Resenting their ignorance,
they flare up in sudden rage,
directing anger at others—
this, in turn, shows they do not know the Mandate of Heaven either.
【Explanation】"Fú rán" is read as fú fú fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】Seeing the sage's understanding of fate and detachment from form,
thus abandoning the anger of the past and returning to normalcy.
【Commentary】Going to Bó Hūn's place,
receiving the teaching without words,
then abandoning the previous anger and returning to the constant nature.
【VIII】【Commentary】Is it because the gentleman has cleansed me with virtuous teachings?
Or is it that I have been able to reflect upon myself?
This is to forget oneself and cast off burdens (VII).
【Commentary】Having just entered the master's school,
I entered the empty chamber,
abandoned anger and resentment,
and reflected repeatedly on ordinary matters.
Do I not realize that the master cleanses my heart with virtuous water?
Or is it that my innate nature is capable of self-reflection?
Advancing and retreating, I search and reproach myself,
unable to fathom the reason.
This, in turn, makes me forget the mind of learning,
and lose its burdens.
【九】【Annotation】It is because one forgets the physical form.
【Commentary】Bó Hūn and I roamed in the Way and its Virtue,
thus we could exhaust the subtle essentials of yīn and yáng,
and reach the utmost refinement of the supreme principles.
Since we had already discarded wisdom and forgotten form,
how could we perceive my physical mutilation!
【Explanatory Text】"Zhi Wu Jie" is also written as "Zhi Wu Wu,"
both versions are acceptable (9).
【一０】【Note】The physical form is external,
while one's virtue lies within.
Now, you are engaging with me through virtue,
not through physical interaction.
Yet you seek my external appearance—
is that not a mistake?
【Commentary】Guǒ's annotation states:
The physical form is external,
while one's virtue is internal.
Now, you are engaging with me through virtue,
not interacting with my physical form.
Yet you seek my external appearance (instead of inner goodness),
is that not mistaken?
The meaning of this annotation requires no further elaboration.
【Transcription】"Zǐ suǒ" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "sè" and the rhyme as in "bǎi".
The same applies to the annotations.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "zhòng" (眾).
(2) The Quēwù quotes the Zhāng Jūnfáng edition with "wú zhī zì wù yé" (吾之自寤邪) five characters after "xié" (邪).
(3) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "yǐ" (矣).
(4) The Zhào Jiànyì edition has the character "wǒ" (我) after "zhī" (知).
(5) The Zhào edition lacks the character "yě" (也).
(6) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "yǐ" (矣).
(7) The Shìdétáng edition writes "qiǎn" (遣) for "yí" (遺),
and lacks the character "yǐ" (矣).
(8) The character "néng" (能) is added based on the commentary text.
(9) In current editions, "shū" (書) is written as "wù" (兀).
(10) The character "hǎo" (好) is emended based on the commentary text.
Zǐchǎn looked startled, changed his expression, and altered his countenance, saying:
"You need not speak of it!"
【一】【注】Once enlightened, one grows weary of their excessive words.
【Commentary】"Cùrán"
describes an expression of shock and shame.
Zǐchǎn had not yet managed to let go of attachments and desires,
often being preoccupied with external matters.
Once criticized and blamed,
he then felt startled and fearful,
changing his arrogant and boastful demeanor,
altering his repulsive expression.
He realized that understanding had arrived,
without needing to speak of it.
【Translated Text】"Cù" is pronounced as zí lù fǎn.
"Nǎi chēng" is read according to its usual pronunciation,
meaning to lift or raise.
Also pronounced as chǐ zhèng fǎn.
In the state of Lǔ, there was a man named Shūshān Wúzhǐ who had lost his toes.
He walked on his heels to see Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said,
"You were not cautious,
and previously brought such misfortune upon yourself.
Even though you come now,
what good will it do?"
【一】【Note】Zhǒng means
frequent.
【Commentary】Shūshān,
is his style name.
Zhǒng,
means frequent.
This maimed and crippled man,
residing in the State of Lǔ,
although having suffered the punishment of foot amputation,
still possessed a heart for learning,
thus he came frequently,
seeking teachers and inquiring about the Way.
Since he lacked toes,
he was therefore named after this condition.
【Translated Text】"Shūshān Wúzhǐ" pronounced as zhǐ.
Lǐ Yún said,
Shūshān,
(is his) [style name] (note one),
lacked toes on his feet.
◎Lú Wénchāo commented:
The style name is suspected to be the clan name.
"Zhǒng" is pronounced as zhū yǒng fǎn.
Xiàng Guō explained:
It means frequent.
Cuī stated:
Having no toes,
hence he walked on his heels.
"Jiàn" is pronounced as xián biàn fǎn.
【Two】【Neglects】In cultivating your character,
you failed to be cautious and prudent,
violating the legal statutes,
having previously encountered official punishment,
enduring hardships and difficulties,
leaving your body damaged to such an extent.
Now you come seeking improvement,
what could possibly be achieved!
【Transcription】"Zǐ bù jǐn qián" ends the sentence.
Another reading takes "jǐn" as the end of the sentence.
【Collation Notes】(1) Every character has been revised according to the Shidetang edition and Lu's collation.
Wúzhǐ said:
"It is precisely because I did not understand my duties and lightly used my body,
that I thus lost my foot.
Now that I have come,
there still remains that which is more honorable than feet,
and I am thus striving to preserve it whole.
Heaven covers all things without exception,
earth bears all things without exception—
I regarded you, Master, as heaven and earth;
how could I have known you would still be like this!"
【一】【注】When a person is born,
the principle of life naturally arises.
Simply let it be without interference and allow it to grow on its own—
this is how one values their body and understands what truly matters.
If one forgets this natural growth,
and instead becomes overly cautious and anxious about it,
this is to recklessly misuse the body and fail to grasp what is essential.
Hence, the five internal organs conflict within, and the hands and feet suffer injury without.
【二】【注】Losing one foot is not enough to impair his virtue,
showing that the physical body is but a temporary lodging.
【Three】【Annotations】Remove their arrogance and caution,
let them live naturally,
this is the way to preserve integrity.
【Commentary】Wúzhǐ associated with others in a respectful and cautious manner,
valuing virtue above physical form,
solely striving to borrow fame and reputation,
unaware of the importance of preserving the way of life.
Consequently, he violated the statutes and regulations,
suffering such mutilation.
Although his body was impaired,
his virtue remained intact,
hence he frequently sought to pursue and discuss,
striving to preserve the way and virtue.
Comparing virtue to physical form,
it is said that what is honored is the preservation of the feet.
Preservation here means
existence.
【Transcription】"Qù qí" Qiāng Lǚ fǎn.
【四】【注】Heaven does not act to cover,
thus it can eternally cover;
Earth does not act to carry,
thus it can eternally carry.
If Heaven and Earth were to act to cover and carry,
then there would be times when they rest;
if a boat could sink and act to float people,
then there would be times when it submerges.
Therefore, when things act with intention, they are not sufficient to complete their existence.
【Explanation】"Not doing" is read as "bù wéi" with a fanqie spelling of "yú wěi fǎn".
The following instances of "not doing" and "doing" are all the same.
【五】【注】Blaming him for not being cautious,
and not reaching to Heaven and Earth.
【Commentary】Heaven and Earth nurture all things,
sheltering and supporting without partiality,
and the sage's virtue aligns with both celestial and terrestrial principles,
thus certainly extending universally without abandonment.
How could one know that the Master would not even forsake the physically impaired?
Could a heart devoted to skillful salvation
truly be like this?
Confucius said:
"I, Qiū, am indeed uncultured.
Why do you not enter, Master?
I beg to hear what you have to impart!"
【One】【Memorial】What Confucius presented
was merely the traces of sages;
The Toeless One sought learning
to preserve his whole life.
Answering shallow questions with profound insights
only results in vulgar simplicity.
Wúzhǐ left.
Confucius said:
"Disciples, strive diligently!
That Wúzhǐ,
is a man who has lost his feet,
yet still seeks learning to make amends for the wrongdoings of his past actions,
how much more should those of complete virtue do so!"
【一】【注】Having heard what was heard, they departed,
fully preserving their non-action.
【Commentary】The Master,
had no toes.
"Hú"
means "why."
Zhòngní, feeling his own vulgarity and inadequacy,
was genuinely much ashamed,
so he bent down to the toeless one,
inviting him into the inner chamber,
to speak of the ways of the mundane world he had heard.
After staying long in a makeshift hut,
and reiterating like a straw dog used in rituals,
the toeless one disliked hearing it,
hence he silently departed.
【二】【注】One who embodies perfect virtue lives as if forgetting life itself.
【Commentary】Exhortation,
means to encourage.
Even one who has lost toes and is physically impaired,
still values the preservation of life,
mending their deficiencies and flaws,
repenting their past actions.
How much more so for the virtuous and noble,
who are complete in both form and virtue,
living yet forgetting life itself,
are those whose virtue fills them from within.
Disciples and the like,
should be encouraged in this manner.
【Transcription】"Qiánxíng" is read with the lower tone in Mèng.
Wúzhǐ said to Lǎodān:
"Is Kǒngqiū not yet
a perfected person?
Why does he so diligently take you as his teacher?
He still seeks to be known for strange and extraordinary names,
not knowing that the perfected person considers these to be his own shackles?"
【一】【注】It is strange that he is again studying under Lǎo Dān.
【Commentary】"Bīnbīn"
signifies a respectful and diligent demeanor.
Those who possess profound virtue,
exhaust principles and reach the ultimate subtleties,
forget words and abandon learning,
following their nature, they know innately.
Yet Confucius clung to written characters,
solely practicing the traces of the sages,
with respectful diligence,
inquired about rites from Lǎojūn.
Judging by your standards,
it is thus known that he was not as accomplished as the ultimate person;
what manner of learner are you?
【Translated Text】"Yǔ lǎo" is pronounced with "yǔ" as in "yú jù" and the reverse.
"Bīn bīn": Sīmǎ explains:
A respectful appearance.
Zhāng states:
It is like esteeming the worthy.
Cuī says:
There is a sense of closeness and distance.
Jiǎn Wén remarks:
An appearance of being fond of fame.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
The meaning of "bīn bīn",
as cited in the explanatory text,
all interpret it literally,
failing to grasp the ancient explanation.
"Bīn bīn"
is akin to "pín pín" (frequently).
In the Hànshū, the biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú mentions "rén pín bìng lǘ",
Yán's annotation says:
The character "pín" is sometimes written as "bīn",
which is an example of this.
In the Shījīng, the "Sāng róu" chapter states "guó bù sī pín",
while the Shuōwén Jiězì, under the radical "mù", writes it as "guó bù sī pín".
In the Shūjīng, the "Yǔ gòng" chapter says "hǎi bīn guǎng chì",
and the Hànshū, Treatise on Geography, records it as "hǎi pín guǎng xì".
These all serve as evidence that the sounds "bīn" and "pín" are interchangeable.
The Guǎngyǎ, under explanations:
"Pín pín",
means frequent or comparative.
In Yángzǐ Fǎyán, the "Xué xíng" chapter,
"pín pín zhī dǎng",
is even more so than ● this.
All can explain the meaning of this "bīn bīn".
【二】【Note】Those without a core purpose
follow others in learning just for the sake of learning.
However, the learners of ancient times studied for self-cultivation,
while today's learners study for the sake of others,
and the drawback has escalated to the point of doing what others do.
Those who learn from others to attain self-realization
follow their inherent nature;
those who abandon themselves to imitate others and chase external things
seek extraordinary fame.
Such extraordinary fame,
in fact, arises from the ordinary (二).
Therefore, learning is not meant to create illusions and oddities,
yet illusions and oddities inevitably stem from learning;
rituals are not intended for flowery embellishment,
yet flowery embellishment inevitably arises from rituals.
This is an inevitable principle,
which even the utmost sages cannot avoid,
hence they regard it as their own shackles (三).
【Commentary】Qí means
to seek.
Chùguǐ means
something strange and deceitful.
On the hands, it is called zhì;
on the feet, it is called gù,
which are today's shackles and fetters.
That Zhòngní,
walking in the footsteps of the sages,
studied strange and deceitful, bizarre and unusual matters,
only seeking empty and illusory, fantastical and transformative reputations.
He did not know that those who embody the Way beyond the mundane world, the ultimate persons,
use such teachings and reputations as their own shackles and chains.
【Transliteration】"Qiě Qí" pronounced as Qí.
"Chù" is pronounced with the initial "ch" and the final "ù".
"Guǐ" is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "uǐ".
Lǐ Yún says:
Chùguǐ
means strange and unusual.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
Shū and guǐ do not align in meaning,
shūguǐ should be read as diàoguǐ.
In the chapter "Discussion on Making All Things Equal," it is called diàoguǐ,
which is the same as here.
The use of shū instead of diào
is due to the interchangeability of ancient characters,
as seen in the sixteenth year of Duke Āi in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, where "Hàotiān bù diào"
is quoted by Zhèng Zhòng in the Zhōu Guān Dà Zhù zhí as "Mǐntiān bù shū,"
providing evidence for this.
◎Qìng Fān's case notes: Chùguǐ is also written as chùguǐ.
(See the essay "Shāng Lè" in the Lǚ Lǎn.
) Chù
is similar to chù.
Xuē Zǒng annotates in the "Xī Jīng Fù" saying:
Guǐ,
means different.
Gāo Yòu annotates in the "Běn Jīng" chapter of Huái Nán Zǐ saying:
Guǐwén,
refers to strange and unusual patterns.
"Huàn" is pronounced with the initial "h" and the final "uàn".
Also written as ●.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In old versions, ● is written as ●.
According to Shuō Wén, it is written as ●,
derived from the reverse of "yǔ".
"Zhì" is pronounced with the initial "zh" and the final "ì",
Guō Zhēn gives it as one pronunciation.
It refers to wood on the feet.
"Gù" is pronounced with the initial "g" and the final "ù",
meaning wood on the hands.
"Wéi jǐ" is pronounced as wéi jǐ.
The following "wéi rén" is the same.
"Shě jǐ" is pronounced as shě jǐ.
【Collation Notes】(1) The "Que Wu" cites Zhang Jūnfáng's version, where "qí" is written as □.
(2) The Shìdétáng edition includes the character "yě".
(3) The Shìdétáng edition omits the character "yě".
(4) The character "zuò" is supplemented based on the "Zhūzǐ Píngyì".
Lǎodān said:
"Why not directly enable them to regard life and death as a single thread,
and consider the permissible and impermissible as one continuous principle,
to release their shackles?
Would that be acceptable?"
【One】【Annotation】Desiring to merge with the direct principle through obscurity,
hoping it leaves no trace.
【Commentary】On the day Wúzhǐ previously met Zhòngní for discussion,
why did he not make Kǒngqiū forget benevolence and righteousness,
blend life and death into one,
and equalize right and wrong?
Once the systematic coherence is harmonized,
it becomes the celestial liberation,
is this not akin to removing his shackles,
and releasing him from fetters and manacles!
【Explanation】"Yīguàn" is pronounced with the ancient reading of "luàn".
Wúzhǐ said:
"Heaven punishes him,
how can it be released!"
【一】【注】Now, Confucius was not without profound understanding.
He considered the principles of spontaneity,
that when walking, a shadow follows,
and when speaking, an echo accompanies.
To accord with things is to establish reputation and traces,
yet one who accords with things does not do so for the sake of reputation.
Not acting for reputation is the ultimate attainment,
but one ultimately cannot escape reputation.
So who can unravel this dilemma?
Thus, reputation is but shadow and echo,
and shadow and echo are the shackles of form and sound.
Understanding this principle,
one can then discard reputation and traces;
discarding reputation and traces,
one can then cease striving for them;
ceasing to strive for them,
one can then preserve one's innate nature and life.
【Commentary】Zhòngní established the statutes of Wén and Wǔ,
traced back to Yáo and Shùn,
edited the Shī and Shū,
codified the rites and music,
was impoverished in Chén and Cài,
besieged in Shāng and Zhōu,
adhered to benevolence and righteousness,
yet suffered such humiliation and disgrace.
It is like how a shadow follows when one walks,
and an echo responds when one speaks—
a natural tendency,
an inevitable outcome.
Thus, once old traces are revived,
flaws and conflicts arise.
To wish to avoid hardship and ruin,
how could it be possible?
Therefore, the natural punishment and execution
are inescapable.
【Interpretation】"Xiǎng suí" is pronounced as xǔ zhàng fǎn.
It is also written as xiàng.
The same applies below.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní:
"In Wèi there is an ugly man,
named Āitáituō.
When men associate with him,
they long for him and cannot leave.
When women see him,
they plead with their parents saying, 'I would rather be this gentleman's concubine than another man's wife'—
and there have been more than ten such cases, with no end in sight.
No one has ever heard him initiate anything,
he always just harmonizes with others.
He holds no ruler's position to save people from death,
nor accumulates wealth to fill people's bellies.
Moreover, his ugliness shocks the world,
he harmonizes but doesn't initiate,
his knowledge doesn't extend beyond the four directions,
yet both males and females gather before him.
This must mean he has something extraordinary about him.
I summoned him to observe,
and indeed he was shockingly ugly.
After staying with me
for less than a month,
I began to appreciate his character;
before a full year had passed,
I came to trust him.
When the state lacked a prime minister,
I offered him the governance of the state.
He responded only after seeming indifferent,
vaguely as if declining.
I felt ashamed,
yet eventually entrusted the state to him.
Not long after,
he left me and departed.
I grieved as if having suffered a loss,
as if there were no one to share joy with in this state.
What kind of man is this?
【一】【Note】È,
means ugly.
【Commentary】"È" means
ugly.
It speaks of a man from the state of Wèi,
whose appearance was repulsive,
yet his inner virtue was abundant,
and all things were drawn to him.
Thus, "Āi Tái" refers to this ugly countenance,
and hence it was used as his name.
【Explanation】"Wù rén" means wù,
ugly in appearance.
"Āi Tái" is pronounced as tái,
and according to Xú, also pronounced as dài.
"Tā" is read as "tuó hé fǎn".
Lǐ Yún said:
Āi Tái,
refers to an ugly appearance;
Tā,
is his name.
【二】【疏】A wife is one who is
equal,
meaning her status is equal to her husband's.
A concubine is one who
connects,
appropriately able to serve the gentleman.
Āitái, with his talents complete and virtues fulfilled,
became the refuge for all beings,
greatly harmonizing with the multitude of lives,
making them forget their ugliness.
Thus, he caused men to dwell with him,
clinging in admiration, unable to part;
women, admiring his talents and virtues,
vied to become his concubines.
The number reached over ten and did not stop,
showing how many were drawn to his righteousness;
not becoming anyone's wife,
it highlighted how his Way could move all beings.
【Three】【Strategies】Erase traces and conceal origins,
modestly position oneself behind others,
merely respond and harmonize as needed,
never induce or lead the initiative.
【Transcription】"Cháng Hé" is read as hù wò fǎn.
The same applies below.
【Four】【Annotation】Things do not proceed through power and influence.
【Commentary】A sovereign ruler,
must be capable of pardoning faults and forgiving offenses,
showing compassion for the dead and protecting the living.
Tái Tā, impoverished and a commoner,
held no position facing south (as a ruler),
devoid of power and influence,
yet could aid others.
This illustrates that his care for people did not stem from authority or force.
【五】【Note】It is clear that he did not go there seeking food.
【Commentary】The purpose of storing grain in granaries
and attracting scholars and masses to gather
is fundamentally to fill their stomachs.
Yet Táitā, having no accumulated provisions,
how could he draw people to him?
This clarifies that their admiration for righteousness was not driven by the prospect of food.
◎Lǐ Zhēn remarks:
The character "wàng" in "wàng rén",
should be read like the "wàng" in the Yìjīng's phrase "yuè jī wàng".
According to Shuōwén Jiězì:
"wàng"
means the moon is full.
It is a different character from "wàng".
A full belly signifies satiety,
just as a full moon is called "wàng",
hence the analogy is drawn.
This employs the same literary technique as the phrase "fù yóu guǒ rán" in the "Xiāoyáo Yóu" chapter.
Using "wàng" as a substitute for "wàng"
fails to capture its subtlety.
【Six】【Annotation】Míng does not go because of the beauty of form.
【Commentary】Tái Tuó's appearance and form,
were exceptionally crude and ugly.
Speaking of his repulsiveness,
it could startle the whole world.
This clarifies that his ability to gather a crowd,
did not stem from physical attractiveness.
【Explanation】"Wù hài" is read as Hú Kǎi's pronunciation.
Cuī's version writes it as "hài".
【Seven】【Annotation】Not summoned, yet they come.
【Commentary】Like the echo in a deep valley,
direct and without intent,
it neither uses words to summon nor engage,
nor does it arise from being the first to initiate things.
【八】【Note】Not to tax one's mind beyond what is proper.
【Explanation】Domain means
division.
Forgetting the mind and dismissing wisdom,
following nature and embracing authenticity,
one has never toiled in thought or exercised concern,
beyond the boundaries of the four directions.
【Text】"Yì Sī" is read as xī sì fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Those with perfect talent do no harm to things,
therefore, entering among beasts, they do not disrupt the herd,
entering among birds, they do not disturb their flight,
and thus become the forest and marsh of all things.
【Commentary】Male and female are categories of birds and beasts.
Those who possess complete talent
flow with the same current as all things.
Humans harbor no intention to harm creatures,
and creatures hold no fear of humans in their thoughts.
Therefore, birds and beasts gather in flocks before them.
【Translated Text】"Male and Female Mating in Front" Lǐ Yún says:
It belongs to the category of birds and beasts.
"Disorderly Movement" is pronounced with a rough tone, as in "háng".
【一０】【Commentary】First, he lacks power and influence,
second, he lacks wealth and official salary,
third, he lacks handsome appearance,
fourth, he lacks eloquence in speech,
fifth, he lacks knowledge and cunning.
Now, when people gather around someone,
it is surely not without reason.
Yet today, Tái Tuó is relied upon by the masses,
not because of the aforementioned five attributes.
From this, it is evident
that he is indeed different from ordinary people.
【一一】【Note】It has been less than a month, yet I already sense he has far-reaching prospects.
【Commentary】Having heard of his peculiarity,
I thus summoned him for an audience.
His appearance was indeed repulsive,
truly enough to startle the world.
Sharing his company
for no more than twenty days,
observing his conduct,
and discerning his inclinations,
I found his spirit serene and detached,
seemingly profound and far-reaching.
【一二】【Note】Entrusted him with the governance of the state.
【Commentary】As the days and months have passed over a long time,
the tempering and refinement have deepened even more.
Therefore, having lived together for a year,
their feelings have grown mutual trust and reliance.
However, the state lacks a capable minister,
and the governance has not yet flourished.
It is hoped that a worthy person might be persuaded to serve,
to transmit and uphold the state's administration.
【Transcription】"期年" is pronounced as jī.
" 传国" is read with the pronunciation zhùan.
【一三】【Note】Glory and disgrace are not enough to startle his spirit.
【Commentary】Responding only after being withdrawn,
it is the demeanor of being unaware,
also an appearance of emptiness and tranquility.
Since there is no attachment to profit and rank,
how could there be any intention for glory and splendor?
Therefore, like those worldly people,
one responds to them with a withdrawn manner.
【Explanation】"Mèn rán" is pronounced as mén.
Lǐ Yún says:
It means an unconscious appearance.
Cuī (wǔ) says:
It refers to a short moment.
"Hòu yìng" means the response in a reply.
【一四】【注】When others speak, I also speak.
【Commentary】"Fàn ruò" means,
an appearance of being aimless and unconstrained.
Although not startled by favor or disgrace,
it also aligns with the world through humility and deference,
hence, like an ordinary person, when offered a position, one declines it as well.
【Translated Text】"Fan" is pronounced as fú jiàn fǎn,
meaning not tied.
【1.5】【Commentary】"Ashamed" means
feeling shamed.
"Finally" means
in the end.
"How long" refers to
a brief moment.
"Distressed" means
being worried.
"Guǎrén" is a humble self-reference by a ruler of the fifth rank.
Having met the virtuous man,
his demeanor was broadly detached and empty,
making my heart feel ashamed and embarrassed,
yet I cherished him with earnest affection,
ultimately wishing to entrust him with state affairs,
humbly requesting him to serve as a minister and advisor.
In just a brief moment,
he fled and departed,
causing the loss of a wise chancellor.
Truly, I harbor distress and worry,
my emotions so bewildered,
as if something were left behind and lost.
Although I rule the state of Lǔ,
I find no joy in it.
Joy comes with his arrival and sorrow with his departure,
so deeply moved am I—
what person, what method,
could lead to such a state as this?
【Explanatory Text】"Chǒu hū" Lǐ Yún:
Chǒu,
means ashamed.
Cuī Yún:
means embarrassed.
"Wú jǐ" read with the pronunciation jǐ.
"Yǔ lè" read with the pronunciation lè.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "ten several" is written as "several ten."
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, there is a character "ér" above "guǎ."
(3) The character "ér" is deleted according to Zhào's edition and the commentary text.
(4) The character "zhī" is added based on the main text.
(5) After "Cuī," it is suspected that the two characters "zuò xián" are missing.
Zhòngní said:
"I, Qiū, once traveled to the state of Chǔ,
and came upon piglets suckling from their dead mother.
After a short while, they started in alarm and all abandoned her, running away.
It was because she no longer saw them as herself,
and no longer resembled her kind.
What they loved in their mother
was not her physical form,
but what animated that form.
When soldiers die in battle,
they are buried without the ceremonial fans;
for someone whose feet have been amputated,
there is no point in cherishing their shoes—
in both cases, they have lost their foundation.
The consorts of the Son of Heaven
do not trim their nails
nor pierce their ears;
a man who has taken a wife remains at his post outside
and is not sent on further missions.
If preserving the physical form is enough to warrant such treatment,
how much more so for one who has preserved their integrity in virtue!
Now, Āitáituó, without speaking, gains trust;
without achieving merit, he draws closeness;
he makes people offer him their state,
only fearing that he might not accept—
this must be one whose talent is whole and whose virtue leaves no trace."
【一】【注】To drink milk.
【Interpretation】"Once served as an envoy to Chǔ" - shǐ,
pronounced with the fǎnqiè spelling suǒ lì.
Some versions also write it as "traveled,"
and another version simply states "once in Chǔ."
"Zǐ" in some editions is written as tún,
pronounced with the fǎnqiè spelling tú mén.
"Shí yú" is read as yǐn,
with the fǎnqiè spelling yì jǐn.
The same applies to the annotations.
In older versions, it was read according to the regular character pronunciation,
and Jiǎnwén's edition is the same.
【二】【Note】The living are categorized by talent and virtue,
but upon death, talent and virtue depart,
so the living flee due to loss of category.
Thus, one who embodies virtue deeply,
(is) (two) compared to an infant,
goes everywhere as such an infant,
and nothing in the world harms them,
this is because they have gained their category and thus illuminate themselves.
If emotions truly align with the category,
then even if forms differ, things will harbor no harmful intent;
if the emotional category is lost,
(even) then (even) (three) forms alike as mother and child are insufficient to secure their resolve.
【Commentary】Duke Āi expressed his inner thoughts to inquire of Confucius,
and Confucius used piglets as a metaphor
to respond to Duke Āi:
"I once led my disciples,
traveling through the land of Chǔ,
and happened to see piglets suckling from their dead mother.
In the blink of an eye,
after a short while,
they abandoned their dead mother
and all scattered and fled.
They no longer recognized their own kind,
hence they acted this way."
Therefore, Guǒ's annotation states,
the living identify their kind by talent and virtue,
but death causes talent and virtue to depart,
so the living lose recognition of their kind and flee.
This illustrates that Duke Āi, lacking talent and virtue from the start,
was not of the same kind as them,
hence they abandoned him and left.
Táituó, with his complete talent and virtue,
comparable to an infant,
naturally deserved
the affection and closeness of all beings.
【释文】"眴若" also appears as 瞬 in some versions,
pronounced as shùn.
Sīmǎ comments:
a startled appearance.
Cuī states:
the eyes moving.
Referring to the dead mother's eyes moving.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
"眴若"
is akin to "眴然".
In the chapter "Xú Wúguǐ," when the monkeys saw him,
they fearfully abandoned and fled.
Here it says "眴若",
there it says "恂然",
the wording differs but the meaning is the same.
Both "眴" and "恂" are borrowed characters for "●".
In Shuōwén, the xī radical section:
means an expression of alarm.
Derived from xī,
with xún as the phonetic component.
"眴" and "恂" also have xún as their phonetic,
hence they can be used interchangeably.
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
a startled appearance,
which captures the meaning.
"眴若皆弃之而走" means
all the young ones were startled and ran away.
Initially, they did not realize it was their dead mother,
so they approached to eat;
shortly after, they sensed her death,
hence all were startled and fled.
The term "眴若"
refers to the young ones,
not the mother.
The explanatory text also cites Cuī as saying,
the eyes moving,
meaning the dead mother's eyes moved.
But then the mother would not be dead,
which contradicts the following meaning.
The text below says "did not see themselves in her" and
"could not regard her as their kind",
with Guō's annotation stating,
the living are categorized by talent and virtue,
and death strips away talent and virtue,
so the living flee due to the loss of that category.
If following Cuī's explanation,
the dead mother's eyes still moved,
meaning her talent and virtue had not departed,
why would they flee over the loss of category?
【Three】【Comment】That which gives form to one's nature is
talent and virtue.
【Commentary】Guǒ's annotation states,
that which gives form to the body is talent and virtue.
And talent and virtue
are the essence and spirit.
The piglet loves its mother,
loving her essence and spirit;
people admire Táituó,
admiring his talent and virtue.
【Four】【Note】The feather canopy is,
what military valor relies upon.
For those who die in battle, there is no military valor,
so where would the feather canopy be applied!
【Translated Text】"Shà zī" is read as suǒ jiǎ fǎn,
meaning a fan,
created by King Wǔ.
Sòng Jūn states:
It is a martial decoration.
Lǐ Yún says:
zī,
means to send off.
Cuī's version writes it as shà xiān,
pronounced as kǎn,
referring to the tombs of ancestors.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
Originally, there was no character "yún" after Lǐ,
but it is deemed necessary,
so it is now added.
【Five】【Annotation】The reason for cherishing shoes is
for the sake of the feet.
【Transcription】"Wéi zú" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】The ceremonial fan and shoes take the martial prowess of the feet as their foundation.
【Commentary】The shà is
a martial ornament,
created by King Wǔ,
or some say made by the Duke of Zhōu.
Its shape resembles a square fan,
adorning both sides of the chariot.
When the army marches to battle,
if one falls in combat and dies,
on the day of their burial,
the shà is not used as a provision.
From this, it is known that the shà is provided for martial purposes,
just as shoes are used by the feet,
and the body is directed by the spirit;
without feet, shoes have no use,
without martial purpose, the shà has nothing to provide for,
without the spirit, the body has nothing to receive.
Thus, the shà and shoes are fundamentally based on feet and martial function,
while appearance and form originate from talent and virtue;
if these two lack their foundation,
they are both rendered useless.
【Seven】【Annotation】To preserve one's physical form intact.
【八】【注】Fearing to harm his physical form.
【Commentary】When emperors and kings select consorts for their palaces,
they choose women for the inner court,
piercing ears and trimming nails,
fearing to harm their forms.
When commoners take wives,
they cease external affairs,
avoiding labor and exertion,
concerned about impairing their beauty.
This is to cite analogies repeatedly to illustrate the ideal of a complete talent.
【Explanatory Text】"Bù dé fù shǐ" — fú yòu fǎn.
Same note at the end of the chapter.
Cuī Běn writes it as "bù dé fù shǐ (yǐ)〔rù〕" (five),
saying:
No longer entering for duty.
◎ Jiā Shìfù says:
Not trimming nails,
not piercing ears,
means that without embellishment, the true nature is revealed.
Stopping externally and not reusing,
means not engaging in other matters so that the spirit becomes focused.
Guō Xiàng believed it was for fear of injuring one's form,
which is mistaken.
【Nine】【Annotation】The selection of consorts and the joy of new matrimony,
are fundamentally intended for physical attraction.
Therefore, the completeness of form,
even (six) serves to convey the affection of the supreme,
and uphold the virtue of chaste women.
【Explanation】"Form and Beauty" reads as hū bào in reverse.
【一０】【Note】When virtue is complete, all things love him;
this is fitting.
【Commentary】Ěr,
means "so" or "thus".
When the physical form is fully intact,
it can still summon true beings,
move chaste maidens,
how much more so when virtue is complete!
This is an analogy.
Therefore, Guǒ's annotation states,
"When virtue is complete, all things love it,
and rightly so!"
【一一】【Commentary】Affection is demonstrated through achievements,
trust is manifested by words.
Now, Tàituó, without having spoken, has already been entrusted with confidence;
originally without merit, he is bestowed with genuine closeness.
Thus, the Marquis of Lǔ, with an open heart, entrusted him with the governance of the court,
humbling himself and yielding,
fearing only that he might not accept.
Such a person
must possess complete wisdom and ability, yet attribute achievements to others;
therefore, his virtue remains unseen.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character 'ér'.
(2) The character 'zhě' is deleted according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) 'Zé' and 'suī' are transposed according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(4) The character 'bǐ' is added based on the commentary text.
(5) The character 'rù' is emended according to the original Shìwén.
(6) In the Zhào edition, 'yóu' is written as 'wú'.
Duke Āi asked:
"What is meant by 'perfection of talent'?"
【First】【Memorial】Although previously raised,
the meaning was not yet clear,
hence this doubt is expressed,
hoping for a later response.
Zhòngní said:
"Life and death, survival and demise,
poverty and prosperity, wealth and destitution,
wisdom and incompetence, slander and praise,
hunger and thirst, cold and heat—
these are the transformations of affairs,
the workings of fate.
Day and night alternate before us,
yet knowledge cannot trace back to their origins.
Therefore, they should not disturb one's harmony,
nor enter the spiritual storehouse.
Maintain harmony and ease,
flowing freely without losing joy;
let day and night blend seamlessly
while engaging with all things in a springlike manner—
this is what we call 'perfection of natural capacity'."
【一】【注】Its principle is inherently proper,
and cannot be escaped.
Therefore, human life
is not a mistaken existence;
all that comes with life
is not without reason.
Though heaven and earth are vast,
and all things numerous,
what I encounter happens to be just this,
so even heaven, earth, divine spirits,
the state's sages and worthies,
with utmost strength and wisdom, cannot alter it.
Thus, all that is not encountered
cannot be encountered,
and what is encountered
cannot be avoided;
all that is not done
cannot be done,
and what is done
cannot be left undone;
hence, accepting it brings natural harmony.
【Commentary】Although the two realms are vast,
and the myriad things are numerous,
what one encounters in life
happens precisely at this moment.
Thus, the preceding eight pairs
all pertain to the transformations of things and events,
the flow of Heaven's decree,
which lingers without halting,
and pushes forward without departing,
arranging and entrusting to transformation.
What one encounters is thus fitting.
Unless one is a person of abundant virtue,
who could be so!
This is the meaning of Zhòngní's response to Duke Āi regarding the preservation of innate nature.
【Explanation】"Praise and Blame" is pronounced as yú.
【二】【注】Destiny's course and events' transformation,
ceaselessly move through day and night,
cannot be pushed away when coming,
nor detained when departing.
Thus, those of complete talent
follow whatever they encounter and accept it.
【Translated Text】"Bù shě" is pronounced as shě.
【Three】【Commentary】The beginning is not what knowledge can plan,
and the past is not where emotions can linger.
Therefore, to understand that fate must proceed,
and affairs must change—
how could one plan the start from the end,
or cling to the old while in the new?
Even with the utmost wisdom, one cannot plan it.
As for the passing of what has gone,
what can I do about it!
【Commentary】Destiny's course and events' transformations,
their speed is like galloping;
succession and change flow on,
ceasing not day or night.
One preceding, another following,
revolving in cycles back and forth,
even with utmost wisdom,
none can fathom or measure it.
How then could one cling to the new or yearn for the old,
or plan for the end at the beginning?
Surely, it is not so.
Only by following change and accepting transformation,
can one roam freely wherever one goes.
【Four】【Annotation】If one truly understands that life and death are inherently proper,
then even in the face of life and death, poverty or success,
amidst countless changes and transformations,
one remains calm and composed, with harmony and principle residing within.
【Commentary】Slippery means
disorder.
Although events change and fate shifts,
one follows form and embraces transformation,
remaining calm and composed as always,
without disrupting the path of central harmony.
【Transcription】"Yǐ gǔ" is pronounced as in gǔ (bone).
"Dàn rán" is pronounced with the initial as in "tán" (a variant reading).
【Five】【Annotation】The spiritual residence is,
the abode of essence and spirit.
One who is supremely content,
does not let worries and troubles affect their spirit,
as if they pass by the outer skin and fade away.
【Commentary】The term "spiritual mansion" refers to
the dwelling place of the essence and spirit,
which is what is called the heart.
It endures the cold and heat of the seasons,
Involving the governance and chaos,
with a thousand changes and myriad transformations,
moving along with all things,
never holding onto intentions,
how could one still be concerned about them!
【Six】【Comment】If one can ensure that their harmonious nature does not become disrupted,
and their spiritual abode remains tranquil and at ease,
then even when facing the most extreme changes,
they will not lose their innate serenity.
【Commentary】Duì means
universal joy.
It embodies the understanding of adversity and prosperity,
penetrates life and death,
thereby making all encounters harmonious and joyful,
the heart content and at ease.
Whether traversing smooth or perilous paths,
one remains serenely self-possessed,
never losing this state of comfort and delight.
【Explanation】"於兌" is read as tuó wài fǎn.
Lǐ Yí says:
It means pleased.
"閒豫" is pronounced as xián.
【Seven】【Annotation】To vanish into the ordinary and accept it as one's constant duty.
【Commentary】Xi means
interval.
The flow and turning of Dàituó,
ceaseless day and night,
with thoughts interconnected,
also without interruption.
【Explanation】"Wú Xì": Qù nì fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
Jiàn yě.
【八】【Note】That on which all living beings rely.
【Explanation】Compassionate radiance nurtures all living beings,
grace moistens both animals and plants,
bestowing benevolence and kindness upon all things,
akin to the vitality of spring.
【Nine】【Annotation】Conform to the four seasons and transform together.
【Commentary】This refers to
pointing out previous matters.
A person of complete talent,
assists all beings,
nurtures the myriad things,
responds and acts in accordance with the times,
with a mind of no-mind,
illuminates by meeting the opportune moment.
【Interpretation】"This is to connect and give rise to timeliness within the heart." Sīmǎ's commentary says:
Connecting with the ultimate Way, harmony and vital energy reside in the heart.
Lǐ's commentary says:
Connecting with all things to bestow life,
following the four seasons and acting in unison.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
In current editions, "hū" is written as "yú".
【一０】【Comment】Summarizing what was previously discussed,
this is the meaning of having complete talent.
【Collation Notes】(1) In the Dunhuáng manuscript, "郤" is written as "陈".
(2) The character "凡" is supplemented based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The character "斯" is emended according to Liú Wéndiǎn's revised and corrected edition.
"What is meant by virtue that does not manifest itself?"
【一】【疏】Having already grasped the essence of talent,
one has yet to comprehend the meaning of virtue that does not take form.
By further questioning each other,
we may hope to hear the later teachings.
He said:
"Levelness is the ultimate state of still water.
It can serve as a standard,
for it preserves its nature internally while remaining undisturbed externally.
Virtue is the cultivation of harmonious perfection.
When virtue leaves no trace,
all things cannot but adhere to it."
【一】【Note】Under heaven, nothing is more level
than still water.
【Commentary】"Tíng" means
to stop.
And under heaven, what is evenly level
is nothing greater than still water.
Therefore, the preceding text says, "One does not mirror oneself in flowing water but must mirror oneself in still water."
This is raised as an analogy,
to illuminate the meaning that virtue does not manifest outwardly.
【二】【注】Being impartial to the point of equanimity,
thus the world finds its standard in it.
【Three】【Annotations】Internally preserving one's clarity,
externally free from deceit and falsehood,
with profound insight and thorough illumination,
impartial and selfless towards all things,
thus one can maintain complete fairness and implement the law.
【Commentary】The nature of water is clear and pure,
reflecting objects like a mirror.
No matter how skilled the master craftsman is,
without water, he cannot level things.
Thus, what can maintain its clarity without rippling
can guide the craftsman's path,
allowing a thorough discernment of beauty and ugliness.
Hence, the following text states that when water is level, it serves as a standard,
and the master craftsman takes it as a rule.
Moreover, the ultimate person, immersed in truth and united with the Way,
harmonizes light and benefits all things,
setting an example for all living beings.
Active yet ever tranquil,
thus it is said that they preserve it within and do not stir without.
【Translated Text】"Qíng wéi" is read as yú wěi fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān examines that qíng wéi means qíng wěi.
In ancient times, the characters wéi and wěi were used interchangeably.
In the Shǐjì, Xiǎo Sīmǎ's edition of the Wǔdì Jì writes "píng zhì nán wéi,"
while the Hànshū, in the biography of Wáng Mǎng, writes "nán wěi."
The Lǐ Yuè Lìng writes "wéi yín qiǎo,"
with Zhèng's commentary stating:
"In the current Yuè Lìng, it is written as wéi zuò zhà wěi."
In the Zuǒzhuàn, Dìng Gōng's twelfth year, it says "zǐ wěi bù zhī,"
with the Shìwén noting:
"wěi,"
in one version is written as wéi.
In the Xúnzǐ's Xìng È piān,
it states that what can be learned and mastered,
and accomplished through practice in humans is called wěi.
Here, wěi means wéi.
All these serve as evidence.
【Four】【Annotation】When affairs are able to be accomplished,
and things are able to be harmonized,
this is called virtue.
【Commentary】To accomplish all affairs,
and harmonize with all things—
who but one of great virtue could achieve this!
One must first cultivate oneself and establish conduct,
before one can accomplish affairs and harmonize with things.
Only when things are harmonized without losing oneself
can it be called virtue.
【Five】【Annotation】There is nothing that is not accomplished,
nothing that is not harmonized,
this is the virtue that does not manifest itself.
Therefore, the world delights in promoting it and does not tire of it.
【Commentary】One whose brightness rivals the sun and moon yet attributes illumination to darkness,
whose achievements equal creation yet credits accomplishments to all things—
this is the virtue that shows no form.
Therefore, one who embodies virtue profoundly,
likened to a newborn child,
is joyfully upheld by all under heaven without aversion,
for such a person never becomes estranged from all beings.
【Interpretation】"Néng Lí" is read with the initial consonant "l" and the tone "zhì" in reverse.
【Collation】(1) The character "利" has been amended according to the commentary text below the line "名實不入" in the chapter "Yìng Dì Wáng".
The same applies hereafter.
(2) This character has been amended based on the annotation text.
Duke Āi another day told Mǐn Zǐ:
"At first, I thought that by facing south and ruling the world,
holding the principles of the people and worrying about their deaths,
I had considered myself to be most enlightened.
Now that I have heard the words of the ultimate person,
I fear I lack the substance of it,
lightly using my own person and risking the loss of my state.
Between me and Kǒng Qiū,
it is not a relationship of ruler and minister,
but merely one of virtuous friends."
【One】【Comment】Those who hear of the virtue-filled influence,
even if they are like Duke Āi,
still wish to leave behind their physical form,
forgetting nobility and baseness.
【Commentary】His surname was Mǐn,
given name Sǔn,
courtesy name Zǐqiān,
a disciple of Xuānní (Confucius),
counted among the four categories of disciples,
renowned for his filial virtue,
a native of the state of Lǔ.
"Another day" refers to a different occasion.
"Facing south"
signifies the position of a ruler.
Initially unenlightened,
he took pride in the ruler of Lǔ,
upholding laws and order,
worrying for the multitude of people,
nurturing and educating them,
fearing they might die young.
He considered such governance methods
to be the most excellent and enlightened.
Now, hearing the words of Confucius,
who expounded on the meaning of talent and virtue,
the Marquis of Lǔ gained understanding
and realized his previous errors.
The notion of ultimate enlightenment and concern over death
became illusory;
the grand idea of maintaining order while facing south as ruler
held no true substance.
Thereupon, he let go of his physical form,
discarded his intelligence,
abandoned distinctions of nobility and humility,
forgot about ranks and titles,
viewed the state of Lǔ as insignificant as a snail's horn,
regarded his own existence as fleeting as a shadow through a crack,
befriended Confucius to cultivate virtue and morality fully,
and respected the Minister of Justice to differentiate the roles of ruler and subject.
Thus, it is understood that the teachings of Zhuāng and Lǎo
possess a pure and far-reaching influence,
and the beauty of virtue fulfilled
reaches such a state as this.
【Explanation】"Mǐnzǐ" refers to Mǐnzǐ Qiān, a disciple of Confucius.
Yīnqí Zhīlí Wúshèn persuaded Duke Líng of Wèi,
and Duke Líng was pleased with him;
yet when he looked at a whole person,
their neck seemed too long and slender.
Wèng Àng...
Yǎng Jùquǎn persuaded Duke Huán of Qí,
and Duke Huán was pleased with him;
but when he looked at whole men,
their necks seemed too scrawny.
Thus when a virtue excels, its physical form may be overlooked;
when men do not overlook what should be overlooked but overlook what should not be overlooked,
this is called true oversight.
Therefore the sage roams freely,
with knowledge as a curse,
agreements as glue,
virtue as a connection,
and skill as commerce.
The sage does not scheme,
so what use has he for knowledge?
He does not carve,
so what use has he for glue?
He has no loss,
so what use has he for virtue?
He does not trade,
so what use has he for commerce?
These four things
are nourished by Heaven.
Being nourished by Heaven
means being fed by Heaven.
Since one is fed by Heaven,
what use has one for man!
He has the form of man
but not the sentiments of man.
Having the form of man,
he associates with men;
not having the sentiments of man,
right and wrong cannot affect him.
How petty and small
is that by which he belongs to man!
How vast and great
is his unique perfection of Heaven!
【一】【Note】When partiality leans one way (1),
then the ugly becomes even more appealing and the beautiful becomes even uglier.
【Commentary】"Yīn" means
crooked,
referring to walking with a bent back and on tiptoes.
"Shèn" refers to
lips,
meaning the limbs are cracked and split,
hunched over and disabled,
and additionally lacking lips.
"Pén" is
a basin.
"Dòu" means
neck.
"Jiān jiān" describes
a slender and small appearance.
Yet, though crippled and disabled,
they walk on tiptoes;
with goiters and tumors
as large as basins and jars.
These two individuals,
embodying the utmost wretchedness in the world,
were both able to forget their physical forms and establish virtue,
embodying the Way and discussing profound mysteries.
Consequently, they made the rulers of Qí and Wèi
admire their character and cherish them,
praising their great virtue,
unaware of their deformities,
and upon glancing at the necks of whole men,
found them instead small and slender by comparison.
【Transcription】"Yīn" is pronounced as yīn,
Guo gives the pronunciation as wū nián fǎn.
"Qǐ" is pronounced as qǐ,
Guo gives the pronunciation as qí nì fǎn.
"Zhī lí wú shèn" - Xú gives the pronunciation as shì zhěn fǎn,
also pronounced as chún.
Simǎ says:
Yīn,
means bent;
Qǐ,
means standing on tiptoes.
Yīn qǐ zhī lí,
refers to feet often bent,
walking with an improper posture, curled and shrunken.
Wú shèn,
is a name.
Cuī says:
Yīn qǐ,
means a hunchback.
Zhī lí,
means a stooped person.
Shèn,
is the same as chún (lip).
Jiǎn Wén says:
Qǐ,
means walking.
Shèn,
means buttocks.
◎Qìng Fān's note: Huì Lín's Yīqièjīng Yīnyì, volume one hundred, in the upper part of Zhào Lùn, quotes Simǎ as saying:
Qǐ,
means to look.
This is missing in the transcription.
"Shuō wèi" - pronounced as shǐ ruì fǎn,
also as the regular pronunciation.
The same applies to the following "shuō Qí Huán".
"Shuì zhī" - pronounced as yuè.
The same applies to the following "shuì zhī".
"Dòu" - pronounced as dòu,
means neck.
"Jiān jiān" - pronounced as hú yàn fǎn,
also as hú ēn fǎn.
Lǐ says:
a frail and small appearance.
Cuī says:
like xuán xuán (profound).
Jiǎn Wén says:
an upright appearance.
◎Lǐ Zhēn says:
Examining the Kǎogōng·Zǐrén chapter, "wén shù mù qiān dòu",
the note says:
Qiān,
means a long-necked appearance,
which aligns with the meaning of jiān jiān.
It is known that jiān is an abbreviated loan character,
the original character should be qiān.
This can also be used to supplement the transcription with an additional meaning based on Zhèng's note.
"Wèng" - pronounced as wū sòng fǎn,
Guo gives the pronunciation as yú chǒng fǎn.
"Àng" - pronounced as wū zàng fǎn,
Guo gives the pronunciation as yú liǎng fǎn.
Lǐ says:
wèng àng,
means the appearance of a large goiter.
Cuī agrees.
"Dà yǐng" - pronounced as yī lǐng fǎn.
Shuōwén says:
means a tumor.
【二】【注】If one's virtue excels in accommodating things,
then things forget their ugliness;
if it excels in opposing things,
then things forget their goodness.
【Commentary】The one with the large goiter was deformed and disjointed,
yet his virtue and character were profound and enduring,
so much so that the Marquis of Qí and the rulers of Wèi
overlooked his physical ugliness.
【Three】【Commentary】When alive, they are cherished;
when dead, they are discarded.
Thus, virtue is
what the world does not forget;
form is
what principle does not preserve.
Therefore, those who forget form
are not truly forgetting;
those who remember form but forget virtue
are indeed truly forgetful.
【Commentary】Sincerity means
reality.
What is forgotten is
the form;
what is not forgotten is
virtue;
it is easy to forget the form but difficult to forget virtue.
Therefore, the form is referred to as what is forgotten,
and virtue as what is not forgotten.
Forgetting the form but not forgetting virtue—
this is the true forgetting.
This is the meaning of virtue not taking form.
【Four】【Annotation】Wandering in the realm of self-contentment,
when released, there is nowhere it does not reach—
this is the perfection of talent and virtue.
【Commentary】Both self and others are dismissed,
both form and virtue are forgotten,
thus one roams freely in the realm of transformation,
wandering in the domain of utmost emptiness.
【Five】【Note】These four naturally generate each other,
their principle is already inherent.
【Commentary】The ultimate person's path traverses the three pure realms and spiritually journeys through the six directions,
thus accumulating wisdom to rescue from calamities and misfortunes,
practicing restraint to rein in a scattered mind,
cultivating virtue to connect with all living beings,
and employing skillful means to benefit the multitude.
These four matters,
all sentient beings possess them,
yet the great sage compassionately saves,
mingling with the dust and conforming to all things.
【Explanation Text】"而知" is pronounced with the meaning of wisdom,
the same applies below.
"為孽" is pronounced with the initial "yú" and the final "liè".
Sīmǎ explains:
Wisdom gives rise to strange phenomena.
"約為膠" Sīmǎ explains:
After constraints, there is something like glue and lacquer.
Cuī explains:
Oaths and pledges are what create firm bonds.
"德為接" Sīmǎ explains:
Spreading virtue to interact with things.
"工為商" Sīmǎ explains:
With craftsmanship, commerce and trade arise.
【Six】【Annotation】Nature is already complete,
thus the sage has no use for his own self.
【Commentary】Evil,
what is it?
The ultimate person does not bring calamity through schemes and plans,
so what use is wisdom?
They do not disrupt by carving and chiseling,
so what need is there for adhesives?
The root does not lose the Way,
what purpose does employing virtue serve?
Not valuing hard-to-obtain goods,
there is no toil for merchants.
It is solely for harmonizing the light and benefiting things,
that therefore these exist.
【Explanation】"How is it used" is pronounced as wū,
the same below.
"Not carved" is read as zhúo.
"No loss" is read as sàng.
【Seven】【Annotation】It speaks of what is naturally endowed.
【Commentary】Yù,
means to eat.
To eat,
means to receive.
Heaven,
is nature.
Through these four matters previously mentioned,
the common people possess them,
receiving them from nature,
each following their own nature,
the sage complies with them,
thus having no need for personal intervention.
【Explanation】"Tiān Yù" is pronounced as yù,
meaning to nourish.
"Tiān Sì" is pronounced as sì,
and can also be read according to its original character.
【八】【注】Since one is endowed with this by nature,
its principle is already complete.
Thus, even if one ponders deeply to avoid calamity,
or takes clear precautions to evade misfortune,
nothing happens without reason;
all are convergences of heaven and earth,
guided by the ultimate principle.
If it must be thought of,
it is not my own thinking;
if it must not be thought of,
it is not my own not thinking.
Some think and avoid it,
some think yet cannot avoid it,
some do not think and avoid it,
some do not think and still cannot avoid it.
In all these cases, it is not up to me,
so why strive for it?
Simply let things take their course and they will arrive naturally.
【Commentary】Endowed by nature,
each has their allotted portion.
Why must one go beyond this to add the excesses of human sentiment!
To defy heaven and indulge human will,
is indeed the path to regret.
【Transcription】"Shòu shí" is read as the character's standard pronunciation,
also pronounced as sì.
"Chén sī" is read with the fanqie spelling xī sì fǎn,
and also as the character's standard pronunciation.
"Miǎn nàn" is read with the fanqie spelling nǎi dàn fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Observing its form and appearance, it resembles a human.
【一０】【Note】It is as if breaking off the branch of a withered tree.
【Commentary】The sage shares the dust of the world,
bearing the appearance of living within it;
embodying the Way, empty and forgetful,
free from the emotional concerns of right and wrong.
【Transcription】"Jue ruo" is read with the pronunciation of "qi wu" in reverse.
【Dried wood】is read with the pronunciation of "ku lao" in reverse.
【One-One】【Comment】Things cluster by kind and group by division,
the natural way of the Dao.
【Explanation】Blending the light and mingling with the traces,
gathering together in the mundane world.
This explains having a human form.
【Interpretation】"Qún fēn" is read as the character itself.
【One Two】【Comment】Devoid of emotion,
hence entrusted to the things.
【Commentary】Like that divine truth,
it utterly lacks conscious awareness;
having already forgotten self and others,
how could there be right and wrong!
This explains the absence of human emotions.
【1.3】【Comment】Its form and appearance resemble those of a human.
【Commentary】Belonging means
being connected.
Traces of the deceitful and clamorous customs,
the form is tied to the crowd of people,
not different from other beings,
hence it is called insignificant.
This concludes that there is merely the form of a human.
【Translated Text】"Miǎo" is pronounced as wáng xiǎo fǎn.
Jiǎnyún stated:
It means lowly.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes: In Huìlín's "Sound and Meaning of the Entire Canon" volume 98, and the "Extensive Propagation of Enlightenment Collection" sound scroll 15, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Miǎo,
means to look high.
The explanatory text is missing.
【14】【Comment】Being without emotions,
thus one is vast and capable of undertaking everything.
To be capable of undertaking everything
is what those with emotions cannot achieve.
Therefore, being without emotions uniquely accomplishes the way of Heaven.
【Commentary】Áo,
describes a lofty and grand appearance.
The vast and lofty teaching,
causes all realms to be forgotten,
wisdom and virtue are profound and deep,
with concentrated illumination that is broad and far-reaching.
Therefore, it praises the great man,
who alone achieves the ultimate of naturalness.
This concludes the sentiment of having no human attachments.
【Interpretation】"Ao hu" is pronounced with the fanqie of "wu" and "gao,"
and Xu Xuan gives the fanqie of "wu" and "bao."
Jianwen says:
It means to wander freely.
Now it is taken to mean roaming or wandering.
"Du cheng qi tian" is read as the characters are.
Cui Zhuan's version writes the character "tian" as "da,"
and says:
Being similar to humans
is what makes it small;
aligning emotions with heaven
is what makes it great.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "xìng".
(2) The character "wàng" is emended according to the main text.
(3) In Zhào's edition, "dú" is written as "jí".
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
"Are people inherently without emotions?"
【First】【Explanation】The previous text states,
having the form of a human,
but without human emotions.
Huì Shī cited this statement to raise a question.
Does what Zhuāngzǐ refers to as a person
necessarily have no emotional concerns?
However, the two sages Zhuāngzǐ and Huì Shī,
both wandered their minds beyond the mundane world,
hence they often drew upon this as a basis for discussion.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Yes."
【One】【Explanation】Indeed,
it is so.
Acknowledging what was asked,
therefore the reply is "indeed."
Huìzǐ said:
"If a person is without emotions,
how can they be called a person【一】?"
【一】【疏】Without emotions and intellect,
how can one be called human?
This is Huì Shī's pressing inquiry,
posed to Zhuāngzǐ.
【一】【注】Human life comes into being,
not through the agency of emotions;
what life inherently knows,
how could it be known through emotions?
Thus, one may have the desire to become a Lí Kuàng yet fail,
yet Lí Kuàng, through emotionlessness, attained acuity and wisdom;
one may have the desire to become a sage or worthy yet fail,
yet sages and worthies, through emotionlessness, became sages and worthies.
How could it be that only sages and worthies are distant and Lí Kuàng is hard to admire?
Even the most foolish, deaf, blind, or those like crowing roosters and barking dogs,
though they may have the desire to act,
ultimately cannot achieve it either.
Regardless of distance or proximity,
even if only a fraction away from oneself,
in the realm of Yán Huí and Confucius,
one ultimately attains nothing.
Therefore, observing all things in the world,
and turning back to examine one's own body,
eyes and ears cannot exchange roles to accomplish tasks,
hands and feet cannot substitute functions to achieve work.
Thus, when an infant is first born,
it does not use its eyes to seek milk,
nor its ears to face light,
nor its feet to grasp objects,
nor its hands to walk.
How could it be that the hundred bones have no fixed duties,
the body and appearance no inherent masters,
and are solely governed by emotions to control them!
【Commentary】What is meant by "evil"?
The Way that is empty and penetrating
gives it its appearance;
the principle of spontaneity
discards its physical form.
Since it possesses both shape and appearance,
how can it not be called human?
Moreover, form and appearance
are essentially not different.
The Way and spontaneity
are interchangeable in their expression.
To make this meaning clear,
it is therefore stated repeatedly.
【Explanation】"How can" is pronounced as wū.
The following "how can" is the same.
"Bark" is pronounced as fú fèi fǎn.
"One part" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
"Sufficient to grasp" is pronounced as qī cāo fǎn.
Huìzǐ said:
"Since we call it a person,
how can it be without emotions【一】?"
【一】【注】They have yet to understand that physical appearance is not the true essence.
【Commentary】Since it is named a human being,
it inherently possesses emotions and considerations.
If devoid of emotions and consciousness,
how could it be called a human?
This shows that Huì Shī did not understand that physical appearance is not equivalent to emotions.
【Interpretation】"Unresolved" is pronounced with the sound of "crab."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This is not what I mean by emotions.
By being without emotions,
I mean that one does not let likes and dislikes internally harm one's body,
but always follows nature and does not artificially enhance life."
【一】【Note】If we take right and wrong as emotions,
then those who have no right and wrong, no likes and dislikes,
even if they possess physical form,
are merely human in appearance—
where then would emotions find their place?
【Commentary】The emotions I speak of refer to
judgments of right and wrong, preferences and aversions, likes and dislikes, etc.
If there were neither right nor wrong,
even with physical form and appearance,
one would merely be a human in body,
where then would emotions find their place!
【二】【注】To act appropriately and proceed straightforwardly,
is not driven by personal emotions.
【Subcommentary】What Zhuangzi refers to as being without emotions
does not mean having a heart like wood or stone.
It merely states that one should not use likes and dislikes to dwell on matters beyond one's inner nature,
thereby achieving one's true nature and inwardly ordering one's being.
Why is this?
To harbor the wisdom of empty illumination
is the emotion of being without emotions.
【Three】【Annotation】It stops at what is appropriate.
【Commentary】Following the principle of natural spontaneity,
one takes this as the norm;
halting at the limits of one's inherent endowment,
unaware of the bounds of life.
Huìzǐ said:
"If one does not enhance life,
how can one have this body?"
【One】【Annotation】It is not yet clear that life arises of itself,
the principle is self-sufficient.
【Commentary】If one does not rely on the way of life for sustenance,
how could this body exist?
It is not yet understood that life arises of itself,
and principle is self-sufficient.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The Way gives you features,
Heaven gives you form,
do not injure yourself internally with preferences and aversions.
Now you externalize your spirit,
exhaust your essence,
leaning against a tree to chant,
reclining on a withered parasol tree to doze.
Heaven selected your form,
yet you clamor about 'hard and white'!"
【一】【注】The principle of life is already fully present within one's physical form,
simply abide by it and the body will be preserved.
【Commentary】The Way and its manifestations,
the principles of life are already complete;
one should merely let them be,
without exerting deliberate effort.
【二】【注】Feelings of liking and disliking,
are not means to enhance life,
but only serve to harm the body,
because life has its inherent limits.
【Commentary】This is to further respond to the questions that follow.
【Translated Text】《Do Not Let Likes and Dislikes》"Hào" is pronounced with a rising tone.
Below, "wù" is pronounced with a falling tone.
The annotation is the same.
《Only Sufficient》"zhī" is pronounced as "zhī".
【Three】【Commentary】If the spirit does not rest within the bounds of its inherent nature,
it becomes externalized;
if the essence does not cease at the limit of its self-generation,
it becomes wearied.
Thus, when walking, one leans against a tree and sighs;
when sitting, one reclines against a parasol tree and dozes off—
this speaks of how those with emotions bring trouble upon themselves.
【Commentary】The withered parasol tree,
refers to a side table for leaning on.
Huìzǐ had not yet abandoned the trap and snare (i.e., the means to an end),
being deeply engrossed in internal fame and reasoning,
neglecting external spiritual awareness,
toiling and exhausting his essence and spirit.
Thus, when walking, he would lean against a tree and chant,
and when sitting, he would recline on the table and discourse.
As a result, his body was weary and his mind exhausted,
leading him to doze off from fatigue and lethargy.
【Explanatory Text】"倚樹" is read with the pronunciation yǐ shù.
"據槁" is read with the pronunciation kǔ lǎo.
"梧" is pronounced as wú.
"而瞑" is pronounced as mián.
Cuī states:
Leaning on the qín and sleeping.
"而睡" is read with the pronunciation chuí bì.
【Four】【Commentary】It says that all that you do,
exhausting the spirit and straining the essence,
leaning against a tree or resting on a parasol tree,
both chanting and dozing,
this is what the world calls emotion.
Yet it speaks of being chosen by heaven,
clarifying that what is called emotion is not born of emotion itself,
let alone anything else!
Therefore, even the myriad things and countless forms,
their actions and choices,
all come from within non-emotion,
so why employ emotion in between them!
【Commentary】"Xuǎn" means
to bestow.
"Míng" means
to speak of.
The Way of Nature
has bestowed upon you your form;
whether your life is short or long, your appearance beautiful or ugly,
its principle is already determined.
There is no need to labor your intentions
to seek extra life beyond your lot.
Yet you, endowed with innate intelligence,
analyze and distinguish names and principles,
cling to your own virtues,
and flaunt them before the crowd.
How is this any different from Gōngsūn Lóng's "White Horse Discourse,"
which claims a white horse is not a horse,
stubbornly upholding this argument,
and priding himself on it?
Truly, there are such words but not the reality;
they may silence the mouths of the crowd,
but they cannot subdue the hearts of the crowd.
Now, your extravagant boasting beyond what is proper
is precisely of this kind.
【Transcription】"Tiān Xuǎn" pronounced as xuān zhuǎn fǎn,
formerly read as sī huǎn fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The sentiment in the Zhào Jiànyì edition reads as this.
(2) The names have been altered according to Liú Wéndiǎn's interpretation.
【一】【注】Although heaven and earth are vast,
and the myriad things are abundant,
what they revere and take as their teacher is the absence of intention.
【Explanation】"The Great Ancestral Teacher" Cuī said:
Discard the form and forget life,
one should greatly honor this method.
To know what Heaven does,
and to know what man does,
is the ultimate knowledge.
To know what Heaven does is to live in accordance with nature;
to know what man does is to use the knowledge of what one knows
to nurture the knowledge of what one does not know,
to live out one's natural lifespan without dying prematurely midway—
this is the perfection of knowledge.
【一】【注】One who understands the actions of Heaven and humanity
recognizes that all are natural;
thus, internally, one lets go of the self and externally merges with things,
becoming mystically united with the multitude,
and by entrusting to this way, there is nothing that cannot be achieved.
【Commentary】Heaven refers to
what is natural.
The ultimate means
the name for reaching the pinnacle.
What Heaven accomplishes
refers to the dimming and brightening of the three luminaries,
the giving of life and execution of death in the four seasons,
the unfurling and rolling up of wind and clouds,
and the cold and warmth of thunder and rain.
What humans accomplish
refers to grasping with hands and walking with feet,
seeing with eyes and hearing with ears,
knowing in the mind what is skillful and clumsy,
and all that is carried out in action.
To know that what Heaven accomplishes
is entirely spontaneous,
unrelated to deliberate cultivation or creation,
how could it stem from knowledge or effort!
Therefore, by inwardly releasing oneself from the body,
and outwardly merging with all things,
one attains a vast and comprehensive perspective,
mysteriously uniting with the multitude,
exhausting principle and fulfilling nature,
thus it is called the ultimate.
【二】【注】Heaven refers to
what is natural.
Those who strive to act cannot truly act,
whereas acting occurs through spontaneous action;
those who strive to know cannot truly know,
whereas knowing arises through self-awareness.
It is self-awareness,
meaning not deliberate knowing,
and since it is not deliberate knowing, true knowledge emerges from non-deliberate knowing;
it is spontaneous action,
meaning not forced action,
and since it is not forced action, true action arises from non-action.
Action arises from non-action,
