thus non-action is taken as the foundation;
knowledge emerges from non-deliberate knowing,
thus non-deliberate knowing is regarded as the essence.
Therefore, the authentic person discards deliberate knowing yet attains knowledge,
refrains from forced action yet accomplishes deeds,
lives in accordance with nature,
attains understanding through sitting in oblivion,
hence the notion of knowledge is transcended and the name of action is relinquished.
【Commentary】Clouds move and rain falls,
rivers originate from mountains and valleys,
these are not matters of human effort,
but are naturally born of heaven.
What can be known and what is known
are all spontaneous.
This explains the earlier statement about knowing the actions of heaven.
【Explanatory Text】"Heaven-born" Xiàng and Cuī's version reads as "lost and born."
"Know as" is pronounced with the initial "ch" and the rhyme "èng" in fǎnqiè.
【Three】【Commentary】In human life,
though the body measures but seven feet, it must possess the five constant virtues;
hence, even this small frame
is sustained by the entire cosmos.
Thus, all that exists in heaven and earth,
everything that is,
cannot be absent for even a day.
If a single thing is missing,
then the living have no means to survive;
if a single principle is not fulfilled,
then one's natural lifespan cannot be completed.
Yet, of what the body possesses,
some are known, some unknown;
of the principles that exist,
some are acted upon, some not.
Therefore, what is known through knowledge is few, while what the body possesses is many;
what is done through action is little, while the principles that exist are vast.
Those in authority cannot fully grasp them and demand completeness.
What people know need not be the same, yet what they do dare not differ;
for difference gives rise to artifice,
and once artifice arises, genuineness is never preserved.
This has never been the case.
Some delight in knowledge tirelessly, exhausting their entire bodies,
yet their focus is on but one branch while the whole root withers—
this is using what they know to harm what they do not know.
As for the height of knowledge,
it understands that human actions have their limits,
thus it accepts without forcing;
it understands that human knowledge has its bounds,
thus it employs without excess.
Therefore, knowledge does not trap itself in boundlessness;
then within the whole being,
the known and the unknown
silently converge and are preserved intact—
this is using what one knows to nurture what one does not know.
【Commentary】What humans do,
refers to how the four limbs and hundred body parts each have their functions.
What the knowing faculty knows,
means the eye knows colors,
thus taking colors as what is known.
What the knowing faculty does not know,
means the eye can know colors,
but cannot know sounds,
thus taking sounds as what is not known.
Then the eye sees for the hands and feet,
the feet walk for the ears and nose,
although there is no intentional mutual assistance,
the function of aiding one another is accomplished.
Therefore, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue,
four limbs and hundred body parts,
alternately serve one another,
each having its designated role.
The clarity and obscurity of the mind,
also have their limits,
using what falls within its capacity,
it ultimately does not force knowledge.
This is using what one's knowing faculty knows to nurture what one's knowing faculty does not know,
thus enabling one to live out their natural lifespan,
without untimely premature death.
One who can act in this way,
may be called a person of supreme and excellent knowledge.
【Transliteration】"Bù sàng" read as xī làng fǎn,
all below are the same.
"Huò hào" read as hū bào fǎn.
Same below.
"Bù qiáng" read as qí liǎng fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, the character is written as 彊.
Even so,
there is a concern.
For knowledge depends on something to be considered correct,
but that on which it depends is particularly unstable.
How can we know that what I call heavenly is not actually human?
Or that what I call human is not actually heavenly?
【一】【注】Although aware of prosperity,
it is not as good as forgetting awareness and entrusting to Heaven, so there are no worries.
【Commentary】Although wisdom is magnificent and splendid,
it still carries worries and burdens;
it is not as good as forgetting wisdom and embracing solitude.
【二】【Note】The wise are not yet able to be without what can or cannot be,
so they must inevitably have dependencies.
As for those who follow nature in their being,
they respond to things appropriately.
【三】【注】When there is dependence, there is no constancy.
【Commentary】Knowledge must confront objects;
without objects, it is not applicable.
Since objects are uncertain and subject to birth and cessation,
knowledge too is impermanent, dependent and subject to loss.
Only when both objects and knowledge are forgotten,
and both the perceiver and the perceived are extinguished,
can one reach a state of having no fixed "must" or "must not,"
and only then will there be no afflictions.
【Four】【Commentary】My life has its limits,
which is Heaven's doing;
the mind desires to extend it,
which is human effort.
However, this is merely what humans call it,
for all things are none other than [Heaven's doing] (1).
Heaven's doing
refers to what is natural;
if all humans are natural,
then order and chaos, success and failure,
encountering opportunities or not,
are not due to human actions,
but all are natural.
【Commentary】Drawing analogies from one's own body in the near,
and entrusting them to external objects in the far,
the ability to know and apply them
is all inherently natural.
This reveals that between Heaven and humanity,
the principle ultimately converges into oneness.
Thus, to speak of Heaven is to speak of humanity,
and to speak of humanity is to speak of Heaven.
How could the ordinary masses
comprehend this profound meaning!
The term "I" mentioned here
is Zhuāngzǐ's self-reference.
This represents the merging of humanity and Heaven,
and the unification of things and the self.
【Transcription】"Yōng jù" Xú qí shù fǎn.
"Zé zhì" zhí lì fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The two characters "tiān yě" have been supplemented according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Only after there is a True Person can there be true knowledge.
What is meant by a True Person?
The True Person of old
did not oppose the few,
did not boast of achievements,
and did not scheme over matters.
Being such a one,
when making a mistake, they felt no regret,
and when right, they took no pride in it.
Being such a one,
they did not tremble when climbing high,
did not get wet when entering water,
and did not feel heat when stepping into fire.
This is how knowledge can ascend to the level of the Way.
【一】【注】Only when there is a True Person,
can all the knowledge under heaven attain its authenticity and remain unconfused.
【Commentary】The sage,
truly capable of merging with the truth and uniting with the Way,
forgets self and discards worldly attachments.
Embracing this sagely virtue,
only then can one possess this genuine knowledge,
thus unifying with the true person and being free from worries and burdens.
The state of the true person,
is detailed in the following text.
【Èr Shū】posed hypothetical questions,
to better reveal their intent.
【Three】【Comment】When few are not opposed,
then those who wish are many.
【Commentary】Guǎ means
few.
Drawing from the past to govern the present,
honoring the fundamental while suppressing the peripheral,
maintaining an open mind to accept all things,
greatly accommodating the masses of living beings,
even if they are few,
never opposing or contradicting them.
【Four】【Annotation】Do not rely on one's achievements to place oneself ahead of all things.
【Commentary】Acting without claiming possession,
nurturing without dominating,
how could this mean arrogantly clinging to achievements
and striving to be ahead of all things?
【Five】【Annotation】Charging ahead with unwavering resolve, the multitude of scholars naturally unite,
not through schemes and strategies that bring them together.
【Commentary】Being humble, tranquil, and free from desires,
the troops and masses naturally rally to him,
not because of deliberate scheming or strategies to win them over.
【Transcription】"Bù mó" is read with the character "mó" pronounced as "mò".
【Six】【Annotation】Simply to preserve oneself entirely and be without fault,
not because gains and losses weigh on the mind.
【Subcommentary】The opportune moment has passed,
yet there is never a heart of regret or remorse;
by chance, the mandate falls appropriately,
yet one does not regard it as a personal achievement to be proud of.
◎Yú Yuè says:
"Passed" here means
having committed some fault in matters.
"Appropriate" means
acting in a way that is fitting.
In the sentiments of ordinary people,
when they commit a fault in matters, they feel regret,
and when they act fittingly, they consider it a personal gain.
The true person is not like this.
Hence it is said: "They pass without regret,
are appropriate without self-satisfaction."
The main text clearly speaks of "passing,"
yet Guǒ's annotation claims it is entirely appropriate and without fault,
which is a misinterpretation.
【七】【注】It is said that the ascent of knowledge to the Dao
is as distant as this.
The principle is inherently complete in itself,
not out of fear of death.
Thus, the true person walks on land not to avoid getting wet,
stays away from fire not to escape the heat,
and commits no faults not by deliberate correctness but by natural appropriateness.
Therefore, though they do not regard heat as heat, they never approach fire;
though they do not regard wetness as wetness, they never tread on water;
though they do not regard death as death, they never lose their life.
So, as for life,
is it life because it is made to be so?
And as for completion,
is it completion because it is achieved to be so?
Thus, one who entrusts all and finds nothing unattained
is the true person.
How could they harbor any deliberate intentions toward what they encounter?
【Commentary】Lì means
fear.
Rú means
wetness.
Dēng means
to ascend.
Jiǎ means
to arrive.
The true person understands that life and death are not two,
embodies that safety and danger are one,
thus able to enter water and fire,
without ever harboring concern,
ascend heights and tread peril,
how could they again be startled or afraid.
Those with genuine knowledge
possess such capability,
ascending to the mysterious Way,
thus achieving such a state.
【Explanation】"Not trembling" is pronounced as lì.
"Not moistened" is pronounced as ér zhū fǎn.
"Ascending to the beyond" is pronounced as gèng bǎi fǎn,
meaning to arrive.
"Distant fire" is pronounced as yú wàn fǎn.
"Having measure" is pronounced as gǔ ài fǎn.
The ancient true person,
sleeps without dreaming【一】,
awakens without worries【二】,
eats without savoring flavors【三】,
and breathes deeply.
The true person breathes from the heels【四】,
while ordinary people breathe from the throat.
Those who are submissive,
their speech is choked as if obstructed【五】.
Those with deep desires and cravings,
have shallow natural instincts【六】.
【一】【注】Devoid of intentional thought.
【二】【注】One should be content with whatever situation one encounters.
【Commentary】Dreams are
the illusions of emotions and desires.
However, the true person has no emotional concerns,
and transcends thoughts,
so even when asleep,
they remain tranquil and dreamless.
Upon awakening to enlightenment,
they are ever at ease and free from worries.
【Transcription】"其覺" is read as gǔ xiào fǎn.
【Three】【Comment】It is only right to eat.
【Commentary】Blending into human society,
sharing the dust and eating,
not indulging in flavors,
thus unaware of their excellence.
【Four】【Annotation】It originates from the very foundation.
【Commentary】The heel,
is the root of the foot.
The true person's mind and nature are gentle and unhurried,
their wisdom and insight are concentrated and tranquil,
even down to their breath,
which is also slow and deliberate.
It comes from the heel,
illustrating their depth and stillness.
【Explanatory Text】"Deep and profound" Lǐ Yún states:
The appearance of inner breathing.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarks:
Preserving breath in a place without breath,
then containing it deeply,
tranquil and silent,
without exiting or entering,
without going or coming,
where pent-up anger cannot knot,
and desires cannot impose,
the hundred bones, nine orifices, and six viscera,
none are involved in its circulation,
and retreating to entrust it to the heels,
thereby nurturing breath in the profound, subtle, vast, and thick, dwelling in the boundless.
"With the heels" Zhǎng Yǒng fǎn.
Wáng Mùyè says:
Raising breath from the heels,
permeating the body deeply.
【Five】【Annotation】The vital energy is not flowing smoothly.
【Commentary】The throat,
is the gullet.
Gagging,
is choking.
Ordinary people,
with their minds racing and striving,
their speech and panting,
only emerge from the throat.
Their emotions are agitated, their breath hurried,
unable to be deep and calm,
bending and rising intermittently,
their qi is not harmonized,
so within the throat, it constantly feels like gagging and choking.
【Explanation Text】"With the throat" Xiàng states:
Panting and palpitating breaths,
use the throat as the regulator,
speaking of the effects caused by desires racing uncontrollably.
"Its throat" pronounced as yì.
Guō pronounces it as è,
è being the throat.
"Like choking" pronounced as huò wā in reverse,
Xú gives it as hú guà in reverse,
also pronounced as guà.
Cuī once pronounced it as yú jiā in reverse,
meaning blocked,
referring to the breath in the throat being obstructed and not flowing freely.
Jiǎn Wén says:
Wā,
means to vomit.
【Six】【Annotation】Deeply rooted and tranquil to the utmost,
then return to oneness without desires.
【Commentary】Those who are deeply addicted to worldly pleasures and have strong desires and passions
are so because their innate intelligence and spiritual faculties are shallow and dull.
If one's wisdom and insight were profound and far-reaching,
how could they be like this!
【Interpretation】"其耆" is pronounced as shì zhì fǎn.
The true person of ancient times,
knew neither delight in life
nor aversion to death;
living, felt no elation,
dying, offered no resistance.
Unconsciously they went,
unconsciously they came—that was all.
They did not forget where they began,
did not seek out where they would end.
They received life and welcomed it,
they forgot life and returned to it.
This is what it means not to use the mind to repel the Way,
not to use humanity to assist Heaven.
Such is the true person.
【一】【注】He who embodies transformation as his substance.
【Commentary】When qi gathers, life begins,
and this life is my moment of existence;
when qi scatters, death comes,
and this death is my compliance with nature.
Having embraced the mysteries of transformation,
one thus does not harbor joy or aversion in the heart.
【Explanation】"Shuō shēng" is pronounced as yuè.
"È sǐ" is pronounced with the initial wū and the falling tone.
【二】【注】Serenely accepting it and letting it be.
【Commentary】When the time comes for birth,
there is originally no emotion of joy;
when the time arrives for death,
how could there be any intention to resist or avoid it!
【Interpretation】"Bù xīn" is pronounced as xīn,
also pronounced as qí.
"Bù jù" is also written as jù,
pronounced as jù.
Lǐ Yún said:
When pleased, one engages in life's affairs,
when resisting, one detests death.
【Three】【Commentary】Entrust it to the ultimate principle,
thus coming and going without difficulty.
【Commentary】Xiāorán means
an unbound appearance.
To transform alone freely,
roaming at will according to principle,
even though death departs and life comes,
there has never been any attachment to it.
【Transcription】"Xiāorán" is pronounced as xiāo.
It is also written as shū.
Xú pronounces it as shū,
Guǒ gives the fanqie reading as yǔ jiǔ,
Lǐ pronounces it as yōu.
Xiàng says:
Xiāorán
means being natural and without intention, yet things come about by themselves.
Guǒ and Cuī say:
It describes the appearance of moving about without difficulty.
Sīmǎ says:
Shū,
means a swift appearance.
Lǐ agrees.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Previously, "jiǔ" was mistakenly written as "dōng",
now it is corrected according to the Song edition.
【Four】【Annotation】Throughout all transformations from beginning to end,
they have forgotten everything,
how could they merely forget their own existence,
and still go on to explore the meaning of death!
【Commentary】Beginning,
is birth.
Ending,
is death.
Both birth and death are dismissed,
with no lingering attachments whatsoever.
How could one merely forget life and one-sidedly seek death?
Beginning and ending are equally balanced,
so whatever is encountered is thus fitting.
【Transcription】"Yóu Fù" fú yòu fǎn.
Below, fēi fù tóng.
【Five】【Comment】No matter what one receives,
encountering it brings nothing but suitability.
【Commentary】It expresses joy in the encounter.
【Six】【Annotation】Returning does not arise from consciousness,
but is the ultimate attainment.
【Commentary】It refers to before birth.
【Seven】【Annotation】Humans are born tranquil,
which is the nature of Heaven;
stirred by external things,
it becomes the desires of human nature.
The stimuli from things are endless,
and if humans chase desires without restraint,
then the Heavenly principle is extinguished.
The Zhēnrén knows that using the mind goes against the Dào,
and interfering with Heaven harms life,
hence they refrain from such actions.
【Commentary】This is called:
it refers to the preceding text,
summarizing its essence.
Juān,
means to discard.
It means that the wisdom and benevolence mentioned above forget life,
which can be said to not use a mind of grasping and rejecting,
discarding the path of emptiness and penetration;
nor using human emotions to discriminate,
adding to the portion of naturalness.
One who can be like this
is named a true person.
【Explanatory Text】"Juān": Xú reads it as quán fǎn.
Guǒ writes it as yī,
pronounced yī rù fǎn.
Cuī says:
Some write it as jí,
which is used for sailing boats.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Yī was mistakenly written as jí in old versions.
Checking below, it says some write it as jí,
so here it should be yī.
◎Yú Yuè says:
The character juān is incorrect.
The explanatory text states:
Guǒ writes it as yī,
Cuī says some write it as jí,
which is used for sailing boats,
making the meaning even more incomprehensible.
It is suspected that these are all miswritten forms of the character bèi.
Bèi is the same as the character bèi (to turn the back),
hence Guǒ's annotation says,
"The true person knows that using the mind means turning away from the Way,
and assisting Heaven harms life."
This shows that the version Guǒ referred to indeed wrote it as bèi.
"Zé bèi": pronounced pèi.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "shòu" is written as "ài".
(2) "Bù yǐ xīn juān dào" should be "bù yǐ xīn sǔn dào".
"Sǔn":
The current edition is damaged and mistakenly written as "juān".
The Suoyin commentary in the "Biography of Jiǎ Yì" from the Records of the Grand Historian quotes this text correctly as "sǔn".
Such a person,
their mind is focused,
their countenance is serene,
their forehead is broad and lofty;
they are chilly like autumn,
warm like spring,
their joy and anger connect with the four seasons,
and they harmonize with all things without anyone knowing their limit.
【一】【注】To dwell in contentment is what is meant by aspiration.
【Subcommentary】If, as previously mentioned, one does not abandon the mind of the Way and so forth,
it is because the mind harbors the strength of will that enables such attainment.
Hence, the Classic of Laozi states,
"Those who force their way have will."
◎Jiāshìfù comments:
Guō Xiàng's annotation says,
"Residing securely constitutes will,"
which should be interpreted as stabilizing one's mind and will.
The Shuōwén dictionary explains:
"Will"
is where the mind directs itself.
The Shāngshū records,
"Like an archer having a target,"
to which Kǒng's subcommentary states:
"Just as an archer has a target,
what the will focuses on
is the desire to hit the center."
Buddhist texts speak of the suchness of nature and characteristics,
eternally abiding and unchanging,
which corresponds to what is referred to here as stabilizing the mind and will.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: The Shuōwén does not include the seal script for "zhì" (will),
so the citation must originate from works like the Zìlín or other character dictionaries.
【Transcription】"Its heart's aspiration" should be "its heart forgets",
"aspiration" is a graphic error for the character "forget".
【二】【注】Though active, it does not harm tranquility.
【Explanatory Text】"Róng●" is also written as jì.
The Cuī version has it as ●.
Lú Wénchāo says:
In old editions, it was mistakenly written as jiā,
now corrected,
as discussed earlier.
This book uses jì.
【Three】【Annotation】Kuí,
the appearance of great simplicity.
【Commentary】Sǎng means
forehead.
Kuí describes
a great simplicity in appearance.
When a true person descends into the world,
their aura stands out as extraordinary,
not only are their wisdom illuminating and insight clear,
their willpower vast and universal,
but also their majestic demeanor is composed and elegant,
their countenance dignified and solemn.
The sun-like forehead and moon-like curves
belong to this category.
【Explanation】"其顙" is pronounced as xì dǎng fǎn.
Cuī states:
It means a flaw.
"頯" is pronounced by Xú as qù guǐ fǎn,
by Guō as kǔ duì fǎn,
by Lǐ as yīn chóu,
alternatively as yīn kuí,
meaning authority.
Wáng states:
It signifies simplicity without adornment.
Xiàng's version uses ●,
stating:
● rán,
describing the appearance of great simplicity.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
means large.
Pronounced as wǔ zuì fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Killing creatures is not for the sake of intimidation.
【Explanation】"Qī rán" is pronounced as "qī xī fǎn".
【Five】【Annotation】Living beings are not for the sake of benevolence.
【Interpretation】"煖然" is pronounced as xuān,
with the alternative reading of huǎn according to Xú.
【Six】【Annotation】One who embodies the Way and aligns with transformation,
shares the warmth and severity with the cold and heat,
yet has never held any intention.
However, possessing the appearance of warmth and severity,
and the rhythm of life and death,
thus attributes its name to joy and anger.
【Commentary】The sage has no personal intentions,
responding only when stimulated,
wielding authority and kindness as situations demand,
tempering severity and leniency in accord with opportunities.
Like the frost descending in austere autumn,
it harbors no innate desire to wither and destroy;
akin to the growth and nurturing in vibrant spring,
how could it deliberately intend benevolence and favor!
Thus, the true person acts like thunder rolling and winds stirring,
trees flourishing and blossoms blooming,
their sheltering and upholding align with the dual forces of heaven and earth,
their joy and anger resonate with the rhythms of the four seasons.
【Seven】【Annotation】Having no mind towards things,
thus not depriving them of their proper nature;
there is nothing that is not proper,
hence no one knows its limit.
【Commentary】When a true person responds to the world,
they answer the call according to the moment,
engaging with all beings,
there must be appropriate means.
With an open heart and compassionate love,
they always excel at saving others,
their capacity equal to the vast emptiness,
thus none can know their limits.
Thus when a sage employs arms,
he may destroy a state without losing the hearts of the people;
his bounty and favours extend to all generations,
but it is not because he loves them.
Therefore, one who delights in communicating with things is not a sage;
one who shows affection is not benevolent;
one who observes the timeliness of Heaven is not a worthy;
one who cannot harmonize benefit and harm is not a gentleman;
one who acts for reputation and loses his own nature is not a scholar;
and one who loses his own life and is not true to himself is not a fit person to employ others.
Such persons as Hú Bùxié, Wù Guāng, Bó Yí, Shū Qí, Jīzǐ, Xū Yú, Jǐ Tuō, and Shēntú Dí
all performed the tasks of others,
found satisfaction in what brought satisfaction to others,
but not satisfaction in what would have brought satisfaction to themselves.
【One】【Memorial】Yáo attacked Cóngzhī,
Yǔ attacked Yǒuhù,
Chéng Tāng overthrew the Xià,
Zhōu Wǔ campaigned against the Yīn,
all of which aligned with the timing of Heaven above,
and conformed to human affairs below.
Therefore, they raised arms,
to console the people and punish the guilty,
and although they extinguished states,
they did not lose the support of the common people.
【Explanation】"A state perishes yet does not lose the people's hearts." Cuī Zǐ explains:
It means perishing an enemy state and winning over its people's hearts.
【二】【注】By perishing what the people's hearts desire to perish,
thus one does not lose the people's hearts.
The sun ascends to the sky by day,
illuminating all six directions,
not out of love for people that it shines upon them.
Therefore, when a sage is in the world,
warm as if the spring sun naturally brings harmony,
so those who receive its moisture do not give thanks;
chill as if the autumn frost naturally descends,
thus those who wither and fall do not harbor resentment.
【Commentary】Benefiting all beings and nourishing them,
this is akin to the spring sun,
not merely for a fleeting moment,
but extending across ten thousand generations.
Yet, treating the common people as straw dogs,
thus there is no sentiment of partial affection.
【Three】【Commentary】The sage has no joy,
it is simply that nothing obstructs and all things naturally flow through.
【Commentary】When a mirror is suspended high on a platform,
it reflects objects as they come before it,
neither welcoming nor sending them off—
how could it possess any personal inclination?
The great sage responds to circumstances,
and the principle is the same.
Harmonizing without initiating,
does not mean delighting in communication.
Thus, it is understood that imposing one's will upon things
is not the way of the sage.
【Four】【Annotation】The utmost benevolence holds no partiality,
it abides by principle and endures of its own.
【Commentary】The utmost benevolence has no partiality,
for having partiality is not the utmost benevolence.
【Five】【Annotation】Those who are timely with Heaven
are not as virtuous as those who forget timeliness and naturally unite with it.
【Commentary】Observing the waxing and waning of celestial phenomena,
awaiting the opportune moments of heavenly timing,
these are but minor wisdoms,
hardly the qualities of a great sage!
【Six】【Annotation】If one cannot unify the path of right and wrong and instead pursues benefit while avoiding harm,
then it damages virtue and burdens one's proper conduct.
【Commentary】If one fails to comprehend the unity of adversity and prosperity,
balance gains and losses,
yet chooses emotions of glory and disgrace,
and clings stubbornly to right and wrong,
then one cannot even achieve self-understanding,
how could one possibly guide others as a noble person!
【Seven】【Comment】A skilled scholar,
leaves behind fame and is self-content,
thus his name matches his reality and blessings respond to his person.
【Commentary】Those who feign their actions to seek fame,
lose their inherent nature,
these are but the common folk,
not the followers of the Dào.
【Transcription】"Xíngmíng": read as "hà Mèng fǎn".
"Fúyìng": the "yìng" as in response.
【八】【Note】Having lost one's own nature and forcing it to follow external things,
one becomes greatly enslaved;
how could one possibly enslave others!
【Commentary】Forcing one's actions and losing authenticity,
seeking fame and forgetting oneself,
this is to be driven by others—
how could one ever drive others!
【Nine】【Annotation】These are all cases of abandoning oneself to emulate others,
sacrificing for them to the detriment of oneself.
【Commentary】His surname was Hú,
courtesy name Bùxié,
a virtuous man of antiquity.
It is also said
he was a virtuous man during Yáo's era,
who declined Yáo's offer to abdicate the throne,
and drowned himself by leaping into a river.
Wùguāng,
a figure from Huángdì's time,
was seven feet tall.
Another account states:
he lived during the Xià dynasty,
consumed elixirs to nurture his nature,
enjoyed playing the qín,
declined Tāng's offer of the empire,
and sank into the Lú River with a stone tied to himself.
Bóyí and Shūqí,
the two sons of the lord of Gūzhú in Liáoxī,
descendants of Shénnóng,
bore the surname Jiāng.
After their father's death,
the brothers yielded the throne to each other,
neither willing to inherit the position.
Hearing of the virtuous rule of the Western Earl,
they went to observe.
They encountered the death of King Wén,
and King Wǔ's campaign against Zhòu.
Yí and Qí grasped the reins of his horse to admonish him,
but King Wǔ did not heed them.
They then retreated to Shǒuyáng Mountain in Hédōng,
refusing to eat its grain,
and eventually starved to death.
Jīzǐ,
a virtuous minister of the Yīn tyrant Zhòu,
remonstrated with him to no avail,
and was enslaved and punished.
Xūyú
was the name of Jīzǐ.
Another interpretation:
he was the son of the Chǔ official Wǔ Shē,
named Yún,
courtesy name Zǐxū,
a minister to King Fūchāi of Wú.
His loyal admonitions were ignored,
and he gouged out his eyes before dying,
his body sunk in the river.
Jì Tuō,
surnamed Jì,
named Tuō,
was a recluse during Tāng's time;
hearing that Tāng had offered the throne to Wùguāng,
he feared it might extend to him,
so he led his disciples to drown themselves in the Kuǎn River.
Shēntú Dí heard of this,
and consequently threw himself into a river.
These several individuals
all feigned emotions and falsified conduct,
upheld lofty ambitions to establish their names,
agitated beyond their proper bounds,
and thus came to such ends.
Starving themselves or drowning themselves,
they shortened their lives and met premature deaths,
yet their fine reputations and good fame
were recorded in historical texts.
This shows they were driven by others—
how could they have been the ones directing others!
Pleasing the ears and eyes of the masses,
how could they have found contentment for their own natures and dispositions!
【Explanatory Text】"Hú Bùxié" Simǎ comments:
An ancient worthy man.
"Wù Guāng" Huángfǔ Mì states:
A person from the time of Huángdì,
with ears seven inches long.
"Bóyí Shūqí" were the two sons of the lord of Gūzhú.
"Jīzǐ Xūyú" Simǎ says:
Xūyú
is the name of Jīzǐ,
as seen in the Shīzǐ.
Cuī concurs.
It is also said:
Shīzǐ states:
Jīzǐ Xūyú
lacquered his body to appear leprous,
let down his hair and feigned madness.
Another account says:
Shīzǐ states:
It refers to Bǐgān,
with Xūyú being his name.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The correct meanings in the books Wēizǐ, the Zuǒ Zhuàn fifteenth year of Xī, and the Analects eighteen,
all quote Simǎ as saying:
Jīzǐ,
was named Xūyú.
This differs from the explanatory text.
"Jì Tuō" is pronounced tú hé fǎn.
"Shēntú Dí" was a person from the Yīn era,
who carried a stone and drowned himself in the river.
Cuī's version writes it as Sītú Dí.
"Jiē shě" is pronounced shě.
The same applies below.
【Collation Note】(1) The Shìdétáng edition omits the character 'méng'.
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, 'xiào' is written as 'xùn'.
The ancient true person,
in demeanor, was principled yet not partisan,
appearing deficient yet not submissive;
aloof like a solitary vessel, yet not rigid,
expansive in emptiness, yet not ostentatious;
serenely joyful as if pleased!
Resolute as if compelled by necessity!
Accumulated vitality brightens my countenance,
and harmonious virtue brings me to rest;
majestic, as if embodying the world!
Vast and boundless, beyond restraint;
composed, as if fond of seclusion,
unconcerned, forgetting speech.
Taking punishment as the foundation,
ritual as the wings,
knowledge as timeliness,
and virtue as the path.
Taking punishment as the foundation
means leniency even in severity;
taking ritual as the wings
enables navigation through the world;
taking knowledge as timeliness
responds to necessity in affairs;
taking virtue as the path
is like saying one ascends the hill with those who have feet—
yet people truly consider this diligent practice.
Thus, whether they favor it or not, they are one;
whether they dislike it or not, they are one.
In their oneness, they are one;
in their non-oneness, they are one.
Their oneness aligns with Heaven as companion,
their non-oneness aligns with humanity as companion.
Heaven and humanity do not overcome each other—
this is what is called the true person.
【一】【注】He aligns with all things appropriately, yet does not form cliques.
【Commentary】"Zhuàng" means
traces.
"Yì" means
appropriateness.
When traces descend in the same era,
following what is suitable to each thing,
and one empties oneself to be impartial and even,
there is truly no bias or faction.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
Guǒ's annotation explains "yì" as appropriateness,
"péng" as faction,
interpreting based on the surface meaning,
is particularly mistaken.
This speaks of its appearance,
how can it speak of its virtue?
"Yì" should be read as "é",
both "é" and "yì" derive their sound from "wǒ",
hence they can be used interchangeably.
In the "Tiāndào" chapter, "zhuàng yì rán",
"yì rán" means "é rán".
"Péng" should be read as "bēng".
In the Yì, the "Fù" hexagram's image statement says "péng lái wú jiù",
the Hànshū "Wǔxíng Zhì" quotes it as "bēng lái wú jiù",
which is correct.
"Its appearance is lofty and not collapsing" means
its appearance is towering and lofty without collapsing.
In the Guǎngyǎ "Shìgǔ" chapter:
"é" means
high;
in the "Shìxùn" chapter:
"é'é" means
high.
High and large
have similar meanings,
hence in the Wénxuǎn's "Xījīng Fù", "shén shān é'é",
Xuē Zōng commented:
"é'é" means
lofty and large.
In the "Tiāndào" chapter, "yì rán"
can be explained in this way.
Guǒ did not know that "yì" is a borrowed character for "é",
so in this text he explained it as appropriateness,
and in that text he described it as "appearance of self-supporting on tiptoe",
both explanations based on the original characters,
which is mistaken.
【二】【注】Void and empty without remainder,
as if insufficient;
what is placed below it, nothing fails to rise above,
seeming inadequate yet bearing all.
【Commentary】Concealing one's brilliance and embracing humility and emptiness,
it uniquely appears as if one's divine wisdom is insufficient;
acting in accordance with one's nature,
freely and contentedly,
thus there is nothing to inherit or follow from others.
【Interpretation】"Not receiving" as pronounced.
Lǐ Yún:
To welcome.
Also pronounced as zhěng.
"Not ascending" is read with the shí zhǎng pronunciation.
【Three】【Commentary】Often wanders in solitude but does not stubbornly cling.
【Commentary】The gū (觚) signifies
solitude.
Firmness means
rigidity.
Wandering freely,
at ease and self-content,
one roams the realm of solitary transformation without clinging to rigidity.
【Translated Text】"Yǔ hū" is read according to its usual pronunciation,
also pronounced as yù,
similarly stated:
a doubtful appearance.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
"tóng" should be an error for the character "xiàng".
"Qí gū" is pronounced as gū.
Wáng states:
gū,
means standing alone from the crowd.
Cuī states:
gū,
means an edge or corner.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Guō's annotation says,
often wanders in solitude but does not stubbornly hold on,
thus reading "gū" as "gū" (solitary),
yet it does not correspond well with the meaning of not being firm.
The explanatory text quotes Cuī as saying,
gū,
means an edge,
which also does not align with the meaning of not being firm.
It seems both are incorrect.
In the chapter "Yǎngshēng Zhǔ," it says "never encountered the tendons and ligaments,"
let alone the large bone joints,
the explanatory text quotes Cuī:
bones that are not knotted.
It is suspected that this character "gū" is the same as that "gū" (bone joint).
Bones that are knotted,
are the firmest of things;
having bone joints but not being firm,
this is called the true person.
Cuī did not know that "gū" and "gū" (bone joint) are the same character,
hence he gave different explanations before and after.
◎Lǐ Zhēn says:
"Yǔ hū qí gū" pairs with "zhāng hū qí xū" in the text,
the character "gū" is quite inappropriate.
According to the annotations and commentaries,
"gū" is interpreted as solitary.
The explanatory text quotes Wáng:
gū,
means standing independently without leaning.
Both convey the meaning of solitude.
It is known that the versions they referred to must have all used "gū" (solitary),
and "gū" is a loan character.
In the "Ěryǎ Shìdì," it says "gū zhú běi hù,"
the explanatory text states:
another version also uses "gū" (solitary).
This is evidence that "gū" and "gū" (solitary) are interchangeable.
Those who are solitary often have a square and angular nature,
hence the character can also be borrowed as "gū".
The two characters "yǔ hū",
duplicate with "yǔ hū zhǐ wǒ dé yě" below,
it is suspected to be an error here.
The annotation says often wanders in solitude,
seeking the meaning from the character for wandering,
it might originally have been the character "●",
or perhaps the character "".
"Shuōwén" explains:
means to walk peacefully.
means to walk briskly and steadily.
Both meanings align with that of wandering.
【Four】【Annotation】Open-minded and free from concerns,
one thus attains the ultimate truth.
【Commentary】Zhāng,
is an appearance of vastness.
The spiritual abode is broad and unoccupied,
equal in measure to the void,
and with wisdom and virtue being genuine,
thus it is not flashy.
【五】【注】The ultimate person has no joy,
yet is thoroughly harmonious and content,
thus appearing joyful.
【Commentary】Bǐng bǐng,
is an expression of joy.
Following changes and accepting transformations,
whatever is encountered is thus suitable,
truly forgetting joy and anger,
hence it is said to resemble a joyful person.
【Explanation】"Bǐng Bǐng": Xú reads as bǐng,
Guō gives the pronunciation fǔ xìng fǎn.
Xiàng says:
Appearance of joy.
Jiǎnwén says:
Appearance of brightness.
【Six】【Annotation】In movement and stillness, action and rest,
one constantly abides at the ultimate of inevitability.
【Commentary】Cuī,
means to move.
Yǐ,
means to stop.
The true person is concentrated and tranquil,
responding to things without fixed methods,
acting only when compelled,
not because of initiating first, hence,
they respond only when it is unavoidable.
【Translated Text】"Cuī hū" (yú) [qiān] zuì fǎn,
Xú xī zuì fǎn.
Guō qiě léi fǎn.
Xiàng yún:
Appearance of movement.
Jiǎn wén yún:
Appearance of speed.
【Seven】【Annotation】Not to harm oneself because of external things.
【Explanation】Chù,
means to gather.
It also means to advance and benefit.
The mind is like still water,
thus it can gather and nurture all living beings.
Therefore, it responds without emotional attachment,
bestows kindness without depleting itself,
benefiting and enriching me,
yet one's spirit and vitality ultimately remain undiminished.
【Interpretation】"Chù hū" originally also written as ,
pronounced as chì liù fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
an appearance of anger rising in the face.
Wáng explains:
abundant with virtue and fulfillment.
Jiǎnwén explains:
to gather.
【Eight】【Annotation】There is nothing to pursue.
【Commentary】Although one responds to changes according to the world,
engages with beings and adapts to opportunities,
one always remains composed and non-active,
acting from genuine virtue,
which is what is called moving yet ever abiding in stillness.
【九】【注】The ultimate person has no flaws,
yet they walk together with the world,
thus appearing as if flawed.
【Commentary】Lì,
means peril.
The true person remains constant in safety and danger,
oblivious to fortune and misfortune,
blending their light with the world,
which also seems like peril.
For instance, when Confucius was trapped by the people of Kuāng,
or King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
although they encountered peril and hardship,
they did not abandon the practice of non-action.
【Explanation】"Lì" is read as its standard pronunciation.
The Cui version writes it as "guǎng",
stating:
"That which encompasses broadly is 'guǎng'."
◎ Yú Yuè says:
Guō Xiàng's annotation is utterly incomprehensible.
Moreover, according to the intended meaning,
it should say "the world appears like 'lì'",
not conversely say it resembles the world.
Now, in this case, "shì" is a borrowed character for "tài".
In the Xúnzǐ's chapter "Róngrǔ", "jiāo xiè" is the calamity of man,
Liú Shì Táigǒng's supplementary annotation says:
"jiāo xiè" is a variant form of "jiāo tài".
In other chapters of Xúnzǐ, it is sometimes written as "tài",
or as "shì",
or as "tài",
all being the same.
The "xiè" in "lòu xiè",
in ancient times often rhymed with "wài", "dà", "hài", "bài",
also read like "tài".
Also citing Jiǎzǐ's "jiǎn xiè bù kěyǐ dé shì" as evidence.
Thus, using "shì" for "tài",
is like using "xiè" for "tài".
"Fierce and severe" and "arrogant and excessive",
their meanings correspond.
The explanation text says,
"lì",
the Cui version writes as "guǎng",
"broad and great" also corresponds with the meaning of "tài",
for "tài" also means "great".
If read with the original character,
and said to resemble the world,
then it becomes entirely incomprehensible.
◎ Qìng Fān's case: "lì" should correctly follow the Cui version's "guǎng".
Guō Xiàng's annotation explains it as "walking together with the world",
which then carries the meaning of broad and great.
However, having said "without 'lì'",
and then "like 'lì'",
greatly misses the explanatory meaning.
In classics and commentaries, the characters "lì" and "guǎng",
are often confused.
For example, in the Lǐ Jì's "Yuè Lìng", "the Son of Heaven then 'lì shì'",
the Huáinánzǐ's "Shí Zé" chapter writes it as "guǎng shì".
In the Shǐjì's biography of Píngjīn Hóu, "lì xián yǔ lù",
Xú Guǎng says:
"lì" is also written as "guǎng".
In the "Rúlín Zhuàn", "yǐ guǎng xián cái",
the Hànshū writes "guǎng" as "lì".
In the Hànshū's "Dìlǐ Zhì", Qí commandery "guǎng",
the Shuōwén's water radical annotation notes "guǎng" erroneously as "lì".
All these are evidence.
◎ Also, in the case of Yú's statement that "shì" is a borrowed character for "tài",
it is correct.
In ancient times, there was no character "tài",
the character used was "dà".
The characters "dà" and "shì",
in ancient pronunciation and meaning were the same,
hence interchangeable.
In the Lǐ Jì's "Qū Lǐ", "dare not share the same name as the 'shìzǐ'",
the annotation says:
"shì",
or is "dà".
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, the 30th year of Duke Wén, "the great chamber's roof collapsed",
the Gōngyáng version writes it as "shì chamber".
Wèi's Tàishū Yí,
the Gōngyáng writes as Shìshū Yí.
Sòng's Yuè Dàxīn,
the Gōngyáng [writes] as Yuè Shìxīn.
Zhèng's Zǐ Dàshū,
the Lúnyǔ writes as Shìshū.
All these are evidence.
【一０】【注】Lofty and unrestrained, one finds contentment in oneself.
【Commentary】The sage's virtue is vast and great,
lofty and far-reaching in its majesty,
transcending the worldly sphere,
thus it cannot be restrained or controlled.
【Explanation Text】"Proud and aloof" is pronounced with the initial "wǔ" and the rhyme "gāo" in the fanqie method,
while Xú Mǎng uses the initial "wǔ" and the rhyme "dào" for the fanqie.
Sīmǎ comments:
It describes an appearance of lofty aspirations.
Wáng explains:
It signifies being lofty and transcending the vulgar customs.
【One】【Annotation】Vast and profoundly distant,
none can see its gate.
【Commentary】"Lián" means
long.
The sage's virtue is far-reaching and long,
continuous and immeasurable.
The mind knows the path is cut off,
who can see its gate?
In the silent and voiceless state,
it seems as if closed,
not hearing or seeing others.
【Explanatory Text】"Lián hū" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Lǐ Yí says:
"Lián,"
means an appearance of continuous length.
Cuī Màn says:
it means stumbling and difficulty,
pronounced as "niǎn."
"Sì hào" is pronounced with "hào" in the falling tone,
the following instances are all the same.
【一二】【Note】Without knowledge or awareness, the natural mechanism spontaneously activates,
thus appearing tranquil and unperturbed.
【Commentary】Mèn,
is the appearance of having no mind.
Letting go and allowing things to arrange themselves,
acting without effort and maintaining emptiness and tranquility,
one attains the mysterious pearl in the Chìshuǐ,
thus transcending words.
Before this point,
it has sequentially revealed the inner and outer virtues of the true person in benefiting oneself and others.
From here onward,
it clarifies the methods by which the true person benefits all beings and governs.
【Explanation】"Mǎn hū" is pronounced with the initial "wáng" and the final "běn" in reverse.
The character is sometimes written as "miǎn".
Lǐ Yí says:
It describes an appearance of being without equal.
Wáng Sì says:
It means neglect and forgetfulness.
Cuī Shì says:
It means gentle and compliant.
【13】【Comment】Punishment is
the substance of governance,
not something I impose.
【Text】"Zhì zhī" reads as zhí lì fǎn.
【一四】【Comment】Rites are what the world naturally follows on its own,
not something I have established.
【Commentary】Using penal law as governance is
the fundamental substance of governance;
employing rites and music as guidance is
the emblematic adornment of all things.
【一五】【Note】The wise person,
moves with the times,
not initiating by oneself.
【16】【Note】Virtue is something that
follows from others,
not created by me.
【Commentary】Xún means
to follow along.
Using wisdom to illuminate opportunities,
never missing the right moment;
treating others with virtue,
bending to accommodate their circumstances.
The preceding was a brief outline,
what follows from here onward is the explanation.
【Transcription】"Wèi xún" is also written as xiū in some versions,
both are acceptable.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Lù Shì considers both acceptable,
but this is incorrect.
In the following text, "yǔ yǒu zú zhě zhì yú qiū yě,"
it is correct to use xún.
Shuōwén:
xún,
means to follow in order.
If written as xiū, it would have no meaning.
◎Qìng Fān's case notes that writing (xiū) [xún] is correct.
Guǎngyǎ:
xún,
means to follow.
In the commentary on the Shī, Bèi Fēng;
shù,
means to follow.
In clerical script, the characters for xún and xiū are easily confused.
In Yì Xì Cí, "sǔn dé zhī xiū yě,"
the transcription states:
Mǎ reads it as xún.
In Jìnyǔ, "● sǒu xiū shēng,"
the correct meaning in Wáng Zhì is written as xún shēng.
In Shǐjì, the biography of Shāng Jūn, "Tāng Wǔ bù xún gǔ ér wáng,"
Suǒyǐn:
the Shāng Jūn Shū writes it as xiū gǔ.
In Guǎnzǐ, Jiǔ Shǒu piān, "xún míng ér dū shí,"
the current edition is mistakenly written as xiū.
These are all examples.
【一七】【Note】Entrusted with governance, he took his own life,
thus, even in death, he was treated with leniency.
【Commentary】Chuò means
leniency.
The reason for using criminal law as the foundation of governance
is to stop killing by means of killing,
punishing one to deter ten thousand,
thus even though killing is involved, it remains lenient and simple.
Therefore, benevolence is the enemy of the people,
while law is the father of the people.
【Explanation】"Chuò hū" is pronounced as chāng lüè fǎn.
Cuī's version writes it as Nào.
【一八】【Note】Conforming to what the world practices,
thus there is nothing that is not accomplished.
【Commentary】Although rites may represent the attenuation of loyalty and trust,
they serve as the foremost means of governing the world.
Thus, without learning the rites, one has no means to establish oneself;
do not act contrary to the rites,
do not speak contrary to the rites.
If a person is without rites,
why should they not quickly perish?
Therefore, the role of rites in governance
is essential!
They support human relationships,
and are thus widely practiced throughout the world.
【一九】【Note】For high and low receive each other,
it is an irreversible flow;
small and large form groups,
it is an inevitable tendency;
vast and without bias,
it is the storehouse of all knowledge.
To bear the convergence of a hundred streams,
and occupy the pinnacle of guiding people—
what is there to do?
Entrust the knowledge of the era,
commit the inevitable matters,
and leave them to the world, that is all.
【Commentary】Responding to beings according to situational triggers,
applying ultimate wisdom in accordance with the times,
in principle, there are no colors or sounds that can be seen or heard,
yet in practice, there are circumstances of unavoidable necessity.
Therefore, the one who serves as the master teacher,
being open-minded and free from attachments,
entrusts matters to the collective wisdom,
abiding in the inevitable convergence of events,
rides upon it to wander freely.
【二０】【Note】The mound is
that by which the root is established;
speaking in terms of nature,
it is the root of nature.
All things have their own sufficiency,
which lies in their root.
Entrusting all virtues to follow themselves,
thus, with those that have sufficiency, one reaches the root,
and when the root is reached, principle is fully realized.
【Commentary】Qiū (mound) means foundation.
It is the root.
To interact with things through virtue,
is to follow the nature of things.
Each nature has its own portion,
and stopping at that portion brings sufficiency.
By following their inherent nature,
one thus reaches the mound.
◎ Jiā Shìfù said:
Kǒng Ānguó stated,
the records of the nine provinces,
are called the "Nine Mounds,"
and the Zhuāngzǐ·Zé Yáng chapter also speaks of the words of the mound and village,
meaning that wherever one dwells is called a mound.
The ruins of Zhuānxū
are called the "Imperial Mound."
Having feet and being able to walk,
one will ultimately return to their dwelling place.
Those who follow ritual propriety
are as if dwelling in peace,
having feet and inevitably arriving there.
【二一】【Note】All these are formed from that other,
their completion does not lie in oneself,
thus even when managing the utmost of myriad affairs,
one is constantly at leisure and self-content,
suddenly unaware of matters passing through one's person,
unconsciously unknowing of words in one's mouth.
Yet in their great delusion,
people truly say that the perfect person is one who diligently practices.
【Commentary】The ultimate person,
moves like drifting clouds,
stops like the spirit of the valley,
thoroughly forgets the boundaries of perception and wisdom,
responds mysteriously with an empty mind—
how could they harbor intentions to act upon things,
or be emotionally tied to saving others!
Yet ordinary people,
obstinately attached at every turn,
seeing the boat that ferries all beings,
nurturing and sustaining the masses,
truly believe that the sage toils tirelessly.
How could they know that above the Fénshuǐ River,
all is serene and profoundly still?
Hence, the previous text states: "Who would take things as their business?"
【Transcription】"Cháng Xián" is pronounced as xián.
【二二】【Note】Constantly without a mind and thus compliant with others,
therefore likes and dislikes,
what is considered good or bad,
are not different from them.
【Commentary】Having already set aside thoughts of beauty and ugliness,
one also dispels attachments of love and hatred.
Thus, liking and disliking
arise from ordinary emotions,
whereas the sage's wisdom is empty and harmonious,
never failing to be unified.
【Two or three】【Note】When they are one,
they follow Heaven;
when they are not one,
they follow humanity.
The true person unites Heaven and humanity,
equalizes self and others,
and does not use their oneness to differentiate from non-oneness.
【Commentary】The state of oneness is
the wisdom of the sage;
the state of non-oneness is
the sentiment of the ordinary person.
Since the ordinary and the sage are not two,
therefore, all that is non-oneness is unified into oneness.
【二四】【Note】That which has no being yet is one,
is Heaven.
【二五】【Note】That which is them and them, and us and us, is of human making.
【Commentary】To unite Heaven and humanity,
to equalize all phenomena,
and to align with the Mysterious Heaven as one's kind.
To regard others as others and oneself as oneself,
is to group oneself with the common masses.
【二六】【Note】The true person unites heaven and humanity,
harmonizes all outcomes.
All outcomes do not oppose each other,
heaven and humanity do not conquer one another,
thus expansively, there is nothing not unified,
profoundly, there is nothing not present (5),
and mysteriously merging them and us.
【Commentary】Although heaven makes no distinction between self and other,
humans have right and wrong,
yet when examined firmly,
all ultimately return to emptiness and stillness.
If one were to claim that heaven is superior and humanity inferior,
how could that be called equality!
This again merges heaven and humanity into one,
darkly unifying victory and defeat.
One who embodies this essence
may be called a true person.
【Collation】（1）The quoted text in the Que Wu edition, as found in Wén Rúhǎi's, Chéng Xuányīng's, and Zhāng Jūnfáng's versions, reads "xǐ hū" as "xǐ yě".
（2）Additionally, it quotes Wénchéng and Zhāng's versions as having a duplicated character "cuī",
with "yǐ hū" rendered as "yǐ yě".
（3）Also, "shì hū" appears as "shì yě".
（4）In Zhào Jiànyì's version, "qún" is written as "jūn".
（5）The Sòng edition uses "rèn" in place of "zài".
Life and death are
fated,
and their constant alternation like day and night is
ordained by Heaven.
What humans cannot interfere with
are all inherent characteristics of things.
People specifically regard Heaven as their father
and still personally love it—
how much more should they revere what surpasses it!
People specifically consider having a ruler superior to themselves
and still personally die for them—
how much more should they devote themselves to the ultimate truth!
【一】【注】It possesses the constancy of day and night,
which is the way of Heaven.
Therefore, understanding life and death is the ultimate destiny,
not arbitrary or random,
much like night and day—
what is there to be attached to?
【Commentary】The brightness of day and the darkness of night are the constant ways of Heaven;
death and life, coming and going, are the allotted fate of humans.
Heaven cannot be without day and night,
so how can humans be without death and life?
Therefore, by accepting change and following the flow,
what shall I cling to?
【Explanation】"夜旦" is read as written.
Cui's edition writes it as "靼",
pronounced as "dá".
【二】【注】The true person gains the day when in the day,
and gains the night when in the night.
Regarding life and death as day and night,
how could there be anything they do not gain!
That humans have what they do not gain and yet harbor worry and pleasure in their hearts,
is merely due to the sentiments of things,
not in accordance with principle.
【Commentary】Life and death, day and night,
are the constant ways of humans and heaven.
They have never been separate from the self;
what is there to be attached to?
Yet ordinary people,
resisting the transformations of nature,
cannot rest content with the times and abide in harmony,
moving along with change.
Instead, they delight in life and loathe death,
harboring sorrow and joy in their hearts.
This is the stagnant emotion of common beings—
how could it be the penetrating wisdom of the true person!
【Three】【Commentary】Zhuó means
solitary transformation.
The merit of mutual dependence
is never as great as the ultimate state of solitary transformation.
Therefore, what humans depend upon
is Heaven;
what Heaven gives birth to
is solitary transformation.
All people regard Heaven as their father,
hence the alternation of day and night,
the rhythm of cold and heat,
they dare not dislike,
but follow Heaven and accept it peacefully.
How much more so for that which stands alone in solitary transformation,
reaching the realm of profound darkness—
how could one not entrust oneself to it?
Once entrusted to it,
then life and death, change and transformation,
one merely follows what is decreed.
【Commentary】Zhuó refers to
solitary transformation.
Those ordinary people,
endowed with breath from the azure heavens,
uniquely regard Heaven as their father,
cherishing and revering their own bodies,
yet when it comes to day and night, cold and warmth,
they cannot reverse or oppose them.
How much more so for the realm of the profound and obscure ultimate Dao,
the state of solitary transformation and spontaneity,
which gives birth to Heaven and Earth,
opens and divides yin and yang—
one should simply abide in it and let it be,
how could one resist and not comply!
【Translated Text】"其卓" is read with the middle tone and the character 卓 has a fanqie reading of 中學反.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary states that 卓 means to surpass,
to be unparalleled,
to be solitary.
The character is the same as 趠,
as in the Guangya dictionary,
meaning to be preeminent.
It is also written as 逴,
and in the Yupian dictionary:
pronounced chì jiǎo qiē,
meaning to limp.
Limping involves relying on one foot alone,
hence it is called 逴.
Lǐ Shàn's annotation in the "Western Capital Rhapsody":
逴躒,
still means to surpass and be outstanding.
Correcting Errors and Vulgarities:
逴,
refers to leaping over without following the order.
It is also written as 踔.
In the "Biography of King Xian of Héjiān" from the Book of Hàn, it says "踔爾不群" (standing out from the crowd),
and in the "Way of the Ruler" chapter of the Garden of Persuasions, "踔然獨立" (standing alone distinctively).
According to Shuōwén, it should be written as ●.
In the Hé section:
means to stop alone.
Xú Kǎi [said]:
to stop alone,
is to halt outstandingly.
The characters 卓, 趠, 逴, 踔, and ●,
were used interchangeably in ancient times due to their similar sounds.
"敢惡" is read with 惡 having a fanqie of 烏路反.
"之竟" has 竟 pronounced as jìng.
【四】【注】The genuine is that which,
without relying on external things, is so of itself.
That which is natural cannot be avoided;
how could this apply only to the commands of a ruler!
【Commentary】"Surpassing,"
means being superior.
Its true essence is that which previously existed independently.
People alone regard the sovereign as superior to themselves and honorable,
even to the point of sacrificing their lives and dedicating their fates,
not daring to avoid it,
so how much more for the profound Way, which is the ultimate,
the principle of spontaneity?
To wish not to follow and comply,
how could it be possible!
To accept and submit to transformation,
is indeed what is fitting.
When the spring dries up,
the fish are left stranded on the land,
moistening each other with their breath,
and wetting each other with their saliva—
it would be better for them to forget each other in the rivers and lakes.
Rather than praising Yáo and condemning Jié,
it is better to forget both and transform with the Dào.
The great earth bears me with form,
labors me with life,
eases me with old age,
and rests me with death.
Therefore, what makes my life good
is also what makes my death good.
【一】【注】Rather than loving each other in scarcity,
would it not be better to forget each other in plenty!
This is the beginning of the analogy.
The rivers and lakes are vast,
where swimming is free and effortless,
each creature has ample deep water,
with no need to come and go,
forgetting one another,
bonds of affection are severed.
But when the springs dry up in drought,
the sturgeons and weivers suffer hardship,
stranded together on dry land,
gasping with parched gills and fins.
Then they moisten each other with spit,
breathe on each other to provide dampness,
exchanging acts of love and care,
drawing closer in mutual dependence—
compared to the rivers and lakes,
this is far inferior.
Similarly, in the age of the Great Dào,
all beings roamed freely,
hearing the sounds of chickens and dogs,
yet not interacting with one another.
Once the pure customs dissipated,
and shallow trends gradually arose,
teachings emerged from principles,
and the traces of the sages began;
they strained and limped to display benevolence,
stood on tiptoe to enact righteousness,
fathers and sons, brothers,
harbored deceit in their hearts toward each other.
The sages were ashamed of this,
and rightly so.
Thus, it is known that fish, deprived of water, breathe on and moisten each other,
just as people, having lost the Dào, cling to affection and love.
【Transcription】"The spring dries up" is read as hù gè fǎn,
Guō reads it as hù gé fǎn.
The Erya says:
It means exhausted.
"Xū" is pronounced as kuàng yú kuàng fù with two variations.
"Xiāng xiè" is also written as rú,
pronounced as rú,
or alternatively pronounced as rú shù with a reverse tone.
"Mutual Spittle" is pronounced mò.
"Forgetting Each Other" is pronounced wáng.
The same applies below.
【二】【注】Praise and blame both arise from inadequacy.
Thus, one who is utterly content
forgets good and evil,
overlooks life and death,
unites with transformation,
and is boundlessly at ease with all things.
How could they even discern where Yáo or Jié stand?
【Commentary】This combines the metaphors.
Emperor Táng Yáo was a sage ruler,
while Xià Jié was a mediocre sovereign.
Therefore, praising Yáo's goodness and condemning Jié's wickedness,
and tracing back to Yáo and Shùn to inspire future generations,
the rise of benevolence and righteousness
takes this as its foundation.
How could it compare to having neither good nor evil,
forgetting both good and bad;
neither affirming nor denying,
dismissing both right and wrong?
Only then can one transcend life and death,
roaming freely with the changes;
neither going nor coming,
treading the mysterious path and attaining self-realization.
How can this be mentioned in the same breath
as those who cling to the traces of sages?
【Transcription】"Praising Yáo" is pronounced as yú.
The same applies to the annotations.
【Three】【Commentary】Form, birth, old age, and death,
all pertain to me.
Thus, form is the vessel that carries me,
birth is the toil for me,
old age is the repose for me,
death is the rest for me.
Though these four states change,
they have never been anything other than me.
Why should I regret them!
【Commentary】The Great Mass refers to
nature itself.
Form is that which is structured and material,
birth is the beginning of life's emergence,
old age is the time of advanced years,
death is the day when the vital energy disperses.
Yet, carrying a physical form through existence
inevitably involves toil and hardship;
in old age, having become incapable,
there is a temporary respite and leisure;
with death and dissolution, one returns to non-existence,
in principle, it is a return to rest and cessation;
though these four states undergo change, they have never been separate from the self,
so why should I, being at ease, have any regrets?
【Explanatory Text】"Dà kuài" is read with the pronunciation kǔ guài fǎn,
also kǔ duì fǎn,
and Xú reads it as hú zuì fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the Wénxuǎn, Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" annotation quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Dà kuài
means nature itself.
The explanatory text is missing.
"Yì wǒ" is pronounced yì.
【Four】【Annotation】Death and life,
are both fate.
Without goodness, one dies;
with goodness, one lives,
but not solely due to goodness.
So, if we consider my life as good?
Then my death is also good.
【Commentary】Birth, aging, and death are all part of my being.
Therefore, one who regards living well as good
can also consider death as good.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "rú".
To hide a boat in a ravine,
and a mountain in a lake,
may be called secure.
Yet in the middle of the night, a strong man may carry them away,
and the dull-witted know nothing of it.
However fitting it may be to hide the small in the large,
there is still a chance of loss.
But if you hide the world in the world, so there is no place for it to be lost,
this is the great truth of all things.
Merely to have attained human form is a source of joy.
And the human form,
undergoes ten thousand transformations without beginning or end,
could the joy it brings ever be fully calculated?
Therefore, the sage wanders in the realm where nothing can be lost and all is preserved.
To be good in youth and good in old age,
to be good in the beginning and good in the end,
is something people still emulate,
how much more so that which connects all things
and is the foundation of all transformations!
【一】【注】The dialect speaks of the inescapability of life and death's transformations,
thus first presenting the ultimate inescapability,
then illuminating it with the signs of inevitable change,
intending to entrust oneself to transformation without attachment.
【Interpretation】"於壑" is pronounced with the fire radical sound, "huǒ gè fǎn".
【二】【注】The force without force,
is none greater than that of transformation;
thus it lifts heaven and earth to hasten towards the new,
and carries mountains and hills to abandon the old.
Hence, without a moment's pause,
suddenly one has stepped into the new,
so heaven, earth, and all things are in constant motion without cease.
The world is ever renewed,
yet we consider it as the old;
the boat changes daily,
yet we see it as the same;
the mountains alter each day,
yet we view them as before.
Now, in the blink of an eye, it is lost,
all vanishing into the obscure.
Therefore, the self of the past
is no longer the self of today.
I, along with the present, am passing away,
how could I constantly cling to the old (二)!
Yet the world remains unaware of this,
mistakenly believing that what is encountered now can be grasped and held,
is that not deluded indeed!
【Subcommentary】The darkness of midnight
serves as a metaphor for the profound and abstruse nature of truth.
"The one with strength"
refers to the Creator of transformations.
Storing a boat in the ocean's depths
is precisely fitting and appropriate;
concealing a mountain in a marsh
is called finding its proper place.
Yet, the power of the Creator
carries them away swiftly;
changes renew daily,
rushing like flowing water.
Those who are deluded,
their minds foolish and obscure,
truly believe that mountains and boats are secure and firm,
standing motionless and towering.
How could they know that in the darkness, exchanges and shifts occur,
without a moment's rest?
The self of yesterday and the self of today
follow the same principle.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Mountains cannot be concealed in marshes,
nor can they be carried away by any "one with strength,"
making the meaning difficult to comprehend.
"Shān"
should likely be read as "shàn."
In the "Explaining Utensils" chapter of the Ěryǎ,
a net is called "shàn."
In the Máo commentary on the "South There Are Good Fish" poem of the Shījīng, it says:
"Shàn"
refers to a fishing net,
and the Jiān annotation states:
it is what is now called a dragnet.
Storing boats and storing nets
both seem to refer to fishermen's practices,
fearing they might be stolen by others,
hence hiding them.
This is a common occurrence in everyday life,
which is why Zhuāngzǐ uses it as a metaphor.
◎ Jiā Shìfù comments:
Ravines can conceal boats,
and vast marshes can conceal mountains.
However, the operations of the great transformations are endless,
lifting all things in heaven and earth,
shifting day and night,
discarding the old and embracing the new,
without the slightest pause.
Water bears up the boat and holds it steady,
but when the water moves, the boat moves with it;
qì bears the mountain and moves it along,
so when the qì shifts, the mountain shifts too.
"Midnight"
signifies movement within the formless and unmanifest,
unseen by humans.
◎ Qìng Fān's case: In the annotation to Jiǎng Wéntōng's "Miscellaneous Poems" in the Wénxuǎn, Sīmǎ's commentary is quoted:
Boats
belong to the water;
mountains
dwell on land.
Hiding them in ravines and marshes
is not something human intention seeks,
yet it is called secure;
the one with strength may be able to retrieve them.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Explanation】"Nǎi jiē" is read with two variations: qí liè and qí yè.
【Three】【Commentary】Not knowing to become one with transformation,
and thinking to preserve it so it does not change,
then even if it is extremely deep and firm,
each finds its proper place,
there is no way to prevent its daily transformation.
Therefore, those who preserve and possess it
cannot stop its escape;
those who do not preserve but let transformation take its course
cannot be changed by change.
【Commentary】Dùn (遁) means
transformation.
Hiding a boat in a ravine,
concealing a mountain in a marsh—
this is hiding the large;
sheltering a person in a room,
storing objects in a vessel—
this is hiding the small.
Although large and small differ, in both cases the concealment is fitting,
just as thoughts flow in constant flux,
ever renewing and shifting.
Thus, it is understood that the way of transformation
is inescapable everywhere.
【Four】【Comment】When one harbors nothing and accepts everything with equanimity,
then one becomes seamlessly united with all things,
and harmoniously one with the transformations of nature.
Thus, there is no distinction between outer and inner,
no separation between death and life.
Embodying heaven and earth and merging with change,
one finds no place to hide or escape.
This is the profound truth of eternal existence,
not a narrow or trivial notion.
【Commentary】Héng means
constant.
As for storing the world within the world,
how could that be considered storing it?
It is because there is nothing to store.
Thus, one can unify life and death,
merge with transformations,
roam freely within the cosmos,
riding on the creator to wander—
this is storing the world within the world.
Since it changes what cannot be changed,
what room is there for escape?
This is the person who embodies profound stillness,
comprehends the true essence of the great Way,
how could they be like the deluded followers of common customs,
wielding the petty wisdom of the human world?
【Explanation】《Suǒ suǒ》suǒ bǎi fǎn.
【五】【Note】The human form is merely one encounter among the myriad transformations,
not worthy of exclusive delight.
Within the boundless infinite,
all that is encountered is akin to humans;
how can it be that only the human form is delightful while other beings hold no joy?
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the selection of texts, the annotation to Jiǎ Yì's "Rhapsody on the Owl" quotes Sīmǎ's words:
it shall again transform into non-being.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Explanation】"No music" is pronounced as luò.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【Six】【Comment】Originally not human yet transformed into human form,
having transformed into human form,
one loses their original state.
Losing the original state brings joy,
joy from what one encounters.
Transformations are endless,
what is there that one will not encounter!
Finding joy in what one encounters,
how could such joy have an end!
【Commentary】Tè means
"unique."
Fàn means
"to encounter."
When the great furnace of creation
molds and casts all beings,
uniquely encountering a human form
brings joy.
As for human forms,
their appearances are endlessly varied,
and encountering one brings delight—
how boundless is this delight!
Thus, the forms and the joy
are beyond measure.
【Interpretation】"Kě shèng" is pronounced as "shēng".
【七】【注】The sage wanders along the path of transformation,
roams within the ever-renewing flow,
where all things endlessly change,
and he too changes with them endlessly.
Since transformation is boundless,
he too shares in this boundlessness—
who could possibly evade it?
If what seems lost in life is preserved in death,
then when is it not preserved?
【Commentary】That things cannot escape
is natural;
who can flee from the way of nature!
Therefore, the sage wanders his mind along the path of transformation,
indulging freely in the realm of daily renewal,
never beginning without the self,
so how could there be any place it does not exist!
【Eight】【Annotation】This naturally balances within a hundred years,
not excelling in youth and faltering in old age,
failing to embody transformation,
and equalize life and death.
Yet, his tranquility and purity
are still sufficient to guide others.
【Transcription】"Shàn yāo" — Cuī's edition writes it as "jiǎo",
identical.
Pronunciation: gǔ mǎo fǎn.
Another version also writes it as "yāo",
pronunciation: yú biǎo fǎn.
Jiǎng Wén gives the pronunciation as yú qiáo fǎn,
stating:
It means different.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
The current edition writes it as "yāo".
◎ Qìng Fān's note on the character "yāo",
correctly written as "yāo".
"Yāo" and "yāo" were anciently used interchangeably.
In the "Annals of Zhōu" from the Records of the Grand Historian, it mentions the discarded "yāo" child by the young concubine in the rear palace,
Xú Guǎng says:
"Yāo",
some editions write it as "yāo".
Cuī's edition writes it as "jiǎo",
which is incorrect.
"Shàn shǎo" — pronunciation: shī zhào fǎn.
"Pǐ lǎo" — pronunciation: bǐ.
Another edition also writes it as "bǐ".
"Píng cuì" — pronunciation: suī suì fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】This profound unity with all things and embodiment with transformation,
thus makes it revered by the world—
is that not fitting indeed!
【Commentary】To be connected means
to belong.
Human consciousness and nature
differ in brightness and dimness.
There are those who, within a hundred years,
throughout their entire lives,
remain composed and tranquil,
rarely experiencing joy or sorrow.
As for longevity, premature death, aging, or youth,
they harbor no concerns about them.
Although they may not have entirely forgotten life and death,
they also hold no aversion or dislike toward them.
Such individuals are still worthy of being mentors to all things,
with people emulating them.
How much more so for those who unite with all things,
merging indistinguishably with the transformations of existence.
Those who belong to the category of the ultimate person,
must rely on sagely wisdom,
becoming master craftsmen for all things—
is that not fitting indeed!
【Collation Notes】(1) In the Shìdétáng edition, "yāo" is written as "yāo",
the Quēwù cites the Zhāng Jūnfáng edition as reading "shǎo".
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "zāi".
(3) In the Zhào edition, "nǎi" is written as "fāng".
(4) The character "fú" is emended based on the Wénxuǎn.
The Dào,
is sentient and trustworthy,
non-active and formless;
it can be transmitted but not received,
attainable but not visible;
it is self-originating and self-rooted,
existing before heaven and earth,
firmly present since ancient times;
it divinizes spirits and emperors,
gives birth to heaven and earth;
above the Tàijí, yet not considered high,
below the six extremes, yet not considered deep,
born before heaven and earth, yet not considered ancient,
older than the most ancient times, yet not considered aged.
Xīwéi shì obtained it,
and thereby regulated heaven and earth;
Fúxī shì obtained it,
and thereby harmonized with the mother of breath;
the Dipper obtained it,
and has never erred through the ages;
the sun and moon obtained it,
and have never ceased through the ages;
Kānpī obtained it,
and thereby dwelt on Kūnlún;
Féngyí obtained it,
Jiānwú obtained it,
and thereby resided on Tàishān;
Huángdì obtained it,
and thereby ascended to the cloudy heavens;
Zhuānxū obtained it,
and thereby dwelled in the Xuán Palace;
Yǘqiáng obtained it,
and thereby stood at the North Pole;
Xīwángmǔ obtained it,
and thereby sat in Shàoguǎng,
with none knowing her beginning,
nor her end;
Péngzǔ obtained it,
living from the time of Yǒuyú above,
to the five overlords below;
Fùyuè obtained it,
and thereby assisted Wǔdīng,
overseeing the entire realm,
riding the eastern cordon,
mounting the Winnowing Basket and Tail,
to be ranked among the constellations.
【一】【注】There is the emotion of non-emotion,
hence there is non-action;
there is the constancy of non-constancy,
hence there is formlessness.
【Commentary】It shines with clear insight,
possessing feeling.
It responds to opportunities like an echo,
possessing trustworthiness.
It is serene and tranquil,
acting without deliberate action.
Look at it but it cannot be seen,
having no form.
【二】【Note】Throughout the ages, it has been passed down for people to dwell in,
yet none have been able to receive and possess it.
【Transcription】"Kě chuán" is read as zhí zhuān fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
【Three】【Annotations】All were able to accommodate themselves,
yet none could perceive their true form.
【Commentary】Words convey principles,
which can be transmitted.
The essence is beyond measure and quantity,
and cannot be received.
A moment of personal enlightenment,
can be attained.
Detached from form and appearance,
it cannot be seen.
【Four】【Annotation】Clarity does not depend on existence to be nonexistent.
【Commentary】"Zì" means
"from."
"Cún" means
"to exist."
The supremely empty and penetrating Way,
has no beginning and no end.
From ancient times onward,
before heaven and earth came into being,
when the five energies had not yet manifested,
the Great Way already existed.
Therefore, the Lǎojīng says, "There is something formlessly complete,
born before heaven and earth;"
and further states, "Meeting it, one cannot see its head;
following it, one cannot see its back."
【五】【注】It is non-being,
how could it generate the divine?
It does not deify the ghostly emperors, yet the ghostly emperors become divine on their own;
this is the divinity of non-divinity.
It does not produce heaven and earth, yet heaven and earth come into being spontaneously;
this is the generation of non-generation.
Therefore, the outcome of what is called divine is truly insufficient to be considered divine,
and it is in non-divinity that divinity lies.
What merit could there be to claim,
what deeds could there be to rely on!
【Commentary】It means the Great Way can be divine to the spirits of ghosts,
divine to the Heavenly Emperor,
illuminate the three luminaries,
establish and give birth to the two principles,
with the power of ultimate non-being,
possess such functions and effects.
This is being divine without being divine,
giving birth without giving birth,
not making it divine yet it is divine,
not giving birth to it yet it is born.
Therefore, the Lao Jing says, "Heaven attained the One and became clear,"
"Spirits attained the One and became divine."
【Six】【Annotation】This speaks of the Dao's omnipresence.
Thus, in height, it is without height;
in depth, it is without depth;
in duration, it is without duration;
in age, it is without age.
It is present everywhere,
yet wherever it is, it is nothing.
Moreover, that which permeates both above and below without exception
cannot be described as high or low;
that which reaches both inside and outside without fail
cannot be named as surface or interior;
that which moves along with transformation
cannot be spoken of as enduring;
that which is constantly nonexistent from beginning to end
cannot be called old.
【Commentary】Tàijí refers to the five energies,
and Liùjí refers to the six directions.
Moreover, the Dào is above the five energies,
yet it is not considered lofty or distant;
it is below the six directions,
yet it is not considered deep or profound;
it existed before heaven and earth,
yet it is not considered ancient;
it has endured since remote antiquity,
yet it is not considered aged.
This means it is neither lofty nor deep,
neither ancient nor old,
hence the Dào is omnipresent, yet wherever it is, it is as if it were not there.
【Translated Text】"In the Great Ultimate" pronounced as tài.
"Prior to it" one edition reads as prior to it not,
the Cuī edition is the same.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
The current edition reads as one edition reads as prior to it,
without the character "not."
"Before heaven" pronounced as xī jiàn fǎn.
Cháng yú: Dīng zhàng fǎn.
Chēng yě: Chǐ zhèng fǎn.
【七】【疏】Xīwéi Shì,
was the title of an ancient emperor from before the era of written characters.
He attained the Way of spiritual penetration,
thus capable of driving and commanding all beings,
and lifting and guiding the two realms (heaven and earth).
Also, the character used is "qì",
which means "to unite",
to harmonize,
