signifying the ability to blend all things into one,
and to align with the two realms.
【Text】"Xīwéishì" is pronounced Xǔ qǐ fǎn,
Guō Chǔ yī fǎn.
Lǐ reads it as shǐ.
Sīmǎ says:
The name of an ancient emperor.
"Yǐ qiè" is pronounced Xú kǔ jié fǎn,
Guō kǔ xì fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means essential,
to grasp the essence of heaven and earth.
Cuī says:
It means accomplishment.
【Eight】【Explanations】Fúxì,
one of the Three Sovereigns,
was capable of taming oxen and riding horses,
domesticating and raising sacrificial animals,
hence he was called Fúxī.
To inherit,
means to harmonize.
The mother of qì,
is the source of primordial qì,
corresponding to the Dào.
Because he attained the ultimate Dào,
he was able to draw the Eight Trigrams,
expound the six yáo lines,
harmonize yīn and yáng,
and unite with the primordial qì.
【Interpretation】"Fúxì" is pronounced as xì.
The Cuī version writes it as Fúxì Shì.
"To merge with the mother of breath" Sīmǎ explains:
merge,
means to enter.
The mother of breath,
refers to the origin of primordial energy.
Cuī states:
It means to grasp the root of primordial energy.
【Nine】【Explanation】The Weaving Dipper,
is the Northern Dipper,
serves as the guiding framework for all stars,
hence it is called the Weaving Dipper.
Te,
means deviation.
Gu,
means beginning.
Having attained the ultimate Dao,
thus it traverses from start to finish,
sustaining heaven and earth,
with a mind free from any deviation.
【Explanatory Text】"Wéidǒu" Lǐ Yún:
the Northern Dipper,
is what serves as the guiding principle of the world.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
in the current version, "world" is written as "heaven's."
"Zhōnggǔ" Cuī says:
Zhōnggǔ,
means long-lasting.
Zhèng Xuán's annotation on the Rites of Zhōu says:
Zhōnggǔ,
is like saying constant.
"Bùtè" is pronounced tā dé fǎn,
meaning error.
Cuī's version uses "dài" instead.
【一０】【Comment】The sun and moon attest to a single principle,
hence they continuously shine upon all,
never ceasing in their illumination.
【一一】【Commentary】Kūnlún,
is the name of a mountain,
located north of the North Sea.
Kānpī,
is the name of the mountain god of Kūnlún.
To enter,
means to go into.
Kānpī has a human face and the body of a beast,
attained the Way and entered Kūnlún Mountain to become a deity.
【Explanatory Text】"Kān Huài": Xú reads it as fú méi fǎn,
Guō reads it as fú bēi fǎn.
Cuī writes it as Pī.
Sīmǎ says:
Kān Huài,
is the name of a deity,
with a human face and beastly form.
In Huáinán, it is written as Qīn Fù.
"Kūnlún": Kūn,
sometimes written as Mín,
is the same.
Pronounced as kūn.
The lower part is read as lì mén fǎn.
Kūnlún,
is the name of a mountain.
【一二】【疏】His surname is Féng,
named Yí,
a native of Dīshǒu Village, Tóngxiāng, Huàyīn, Hóngnóng.
He ingested eight minerals,
and became a water immortal.
The great river
refers to the Huáng Hé.
The Heavenly Emperor bestowed upon Féng Yí the title of Hé Bó,
hence he roamed and dwelled within the great river of Méngjīn.
【Explanatory Text】"Féng Yí" Sīmǎ comments:
The Qīnglíng Biography states:
Féng Yí,
was a man from Dīshǒu in Tóngxiāng, Huàyīn.
He ingested eight minerals,
attained the status of a water immortal,
and thus became the River Earl.
One account says he drowned while bathing in the river on the Gēngzǐ day of the eighth month;
another says he drowned while crossing the river.
"The Great River" refers to the river.
Cuī's version writes it as the Grand River.
【一三】【Commentary】Jiānwú,
is the name of a deity.
He attained the Dao,
and thus resides at Mount Tài as the god of the great mountain.
【Explanatory Text】"Jiān Wú" Sīmǎ comments:
a mountain spirit,
immortal,
existing until Confucius's time.
Dàshān" is pronounced as tài,
and also as the regular reading.
【一四】【Commentary】Huángdì,
also known as Xuānyuán,
mined copper from Shǒushān Mountain,
and cast a tripod at the foot of Jīngshān Mountain.
When the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended upon it to welcome the emperor.
The emperor then led his ministers and seventy-two members of the rear palace,
riding clouds and dragons by day,
ascended to the heavens,
achieving immortality and departing.
【Explanation】"Huángdì" Cuī states:
He attained the Way and ascended to heaven.
【一五】【Commentary】Zhuānxū,
grandson of the Huángdì,
was the Emperor Gāoyáng,
also called the Mysterious Emperor.
He was capped at the age of twelve,
assisted Shǎohào at fifteen,
and ascended the throne at twenty.
He mined copper from Mount Yǔ to cast a cauldron,
capable of summoning the deities of the four seas,
possessing spiritual marvels.
He passed away at ninety-seven,
attained the Way,
and became the Emperor of the North.
"Xuán" (mysterious)
is the color of the north,
hence he resided in the Mysterious Palace.
【Translated Text】"Zhuān Xū" is pronounced as zhuān.
The following is read as xǔ yù.
"Xuán Gōng" Lǐ's commentary states,
Zhuān Xū,
is Emperor Gāo Yáng.
Xuán Gōng,
refers to the northern palace.
The Monthly Ordinances say:
Its emperor is Zhuān Xū,
its deity is Xuán Míng.
【一六】【Commentary】Yǘ Qiáng,
is the name of a water deity,
also called Yǘ Jīng.
He has a human face and a bird's body,
rides a dragon to travel,
and is a descendant of Zhuān Xū and Xuān Yuán.
Although he attained the Dao,
he did not occupy the imperial throne but became a water deity.
The water element corresponds to the north,
hence his title is the North Pole.
【Explanatory Text】"Yù Qiáng" is pronounced as Yú,
Guō gives the pronunciation as Yǔlóng.
Sīmǎ says:
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
In the islets of the Northern Sea, there is a deity
with a human face and a bird's body,
wearing two green snakes as earrings,
treading on two red snakes,
named Yù Qiáng.
Cuī says:
The Classic of the Great Wilderness states:
The deity of the Northern Sea,
named Yù Qiáng,
has the divine turtle as his messenger.
The Guīcáng states:
In the past, King Mù divined a hexagram with Yù Qiáng.
According to the Classic of Regions Beyond the Seas:
In the north, Yù Qiáng,
with a black body, hands, and feet,
rides on two dragons.
Guō Pú considers him a water deity,
with a human face and a bird's body.
Jiǎnwén says:
He is the deity of the Northern Sea,
also named Yù Jīng,
and is the grandson of Huángdì.
【一七】【Commentary】Shǎoguǎng,
is the name of a mountain in the westernmost region.
Wángmǔ,
the essence of the supreme yin,
has a leopard's tail,
tiger's teeth,
and is skilled at laughing.
During Shùn's time,
Wángmǔ sent an envoy to present a jade ring,
and during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
she offered green peaches.
Her appearance is like that of a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old girl,
very comely,
often sitting on the Shǎoguǎng Mountain in the west,
neither living nor dying,
so no one knows her beginning or end.
【Explanation】"Xīwángmǔ": The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
Her appearance resembles a human,
with a dog's tail,
disheveled hair,
wearing a headdress,
skilled at whistling,
dwelling at the edge of the sea.
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wu of Hàn records:
Xīwángmǔ and Lady Shàngyuán descended to visit the emperor,
possessing beautiful features,
they were divine immortals.
"Shǎoguǎng": Sīmǎ explains:
the name of a cave.
Cuī states:
the name of a mountain.
Some say,
it is the name of a void realm in the west.
【一八】【Commentary】Péng Zǔ,
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū.
He was enfeoffed at Péngchéng,
and his Way could be taken as ancestral,
hence he was called Péng Zǔ.
He excelled in nurturing his nature,
and was one who attained the Way.
As for the Five Hegemons,
Kūnwú was the Hegemon of Xià,
Dàpéng and Shǐwéi were the Hegemons of Yīn,
Qí Huán and Jìn Wén were the Hegemons of Zhōu,
together making the Five Hegemons.
And Péng Zǔ attained the Way,
which is why he lived a long life,
from as early as the time of Yǒuyú,
down to Yīn and Zhōu,
spanning a total of eight hundred years.
【Explanation】"Péng Zǔ" explanation see Free and Easy Wandering chapter.
Cuī says:
Lived seven hundred years.
Some consider him an immortal,
deathless.
"Five Hegemons" read as written.
Also pronounced bà.
Cuǐ and Lǐ say:
Xià dynasty hegemon Kūnwú,
Yīn dynasty Dà Péng and Shǐ Wéi,
Zhōu dynasty Qí Huán and Jìn Wén.
【一九】【Note】The Dào,
has no capability.
This saying about attaining it from the Dào,
is merely to clarify that it is self-attained.
Self-attained indeed,
the Dào cannot cause one to attain it;
if I have not attained it,
I also cannot actively make it attained.
Thus, all who attain it,
externally do not rely on the Dào,
internally do not proceed from themselves,
but emerge spontaneously, self-attained and transforming independently.
Now, the difficulty of life,
lies precisely in this independent transformation and self-attainment.
Once life is attained,
why worry about not attaining life and striving for it?!
Therefore, actively pursuing life is indeed insufficient to preserve life wholly,
because life does not come from one's own striving,
and striving for it harms one's genuine life.
【Commentary】Wǔdīng was the name
of a king of the Yīn dynasty,
known as Gāozōng.
Gāozōng dreamed of obtaining Fù Yuè,
and sent envoys to search for him throughout the land.
At the plank-and-rammed-earth construction site in Fùyán, Héběi County, Shǎnzhōu, they found him.
He became prime minister under Wǔdīng,
and the realm was peacefully prosperous.
Fù Yuè
was an essence of a star.
There is a star called Fù Yuè located above Jī and Wěi,
and Jī and Wěi are among the twenty-eight constellations,
sustaining the eastern direction.
Hence, it is said that he rides the eastern cordon and straddles Jī and Wěi;
and since he is aligned with stars like Jiǎo and Kàng in a row,
it is stated that he is ranked among the constellations.
【Explanation Text】"Fu Yue" is pronounced as yuè.
"Attained it to become chancellor" is pronounced with the xiàng tone.
"Wu Ding possessed the world, rode the eastern cordon, mounted Ji and Wei, and was ranked among the constellations" Sima said:
Fu Yue,
was the chancellor of the Yin dynasty.
Wu Ding,
was King Gaozong of the Yin dynasty.
The eastern cordon,
lies between Ji and Dou,
it is the eastern cordon of the Tianhan Ford.
The Classic of Stars says:
The star Fu Yue is above the tail,
meaning he rode the eastern cordon,
and mounted between Ji and Wei.
Cui said:
When Fu Yue died,
his spirit rode the eastern cordon,
lodged at the dragon's tail,
and thus became one of the constellations.
Now there is the star Fu Yue above the tail.
Cui's version adds below this: "He was born without parents,
after death, he ascended in abstraction, and after three years his form vanished,
this speaks of a spirit that cannot be named,"
totaling twenty-two characters.
"Abruptly" is pronounced with the qì sound.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "wéi".
(2) The character "gǔ" has been emended according to the main text.
(3) In the Shìdétáng edition, "shén" is written as "rén".
(4) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "fū".
Nánbó Zǐkuí asked Nǚyǔ, saying:
"You are advanced in years,
yet your complexion is like that of a child;
how is this?"
【一】【疏】"Kuí" should be an error for the character "Qí",
similar to Nán Guō Zǐ Qí in the chapter "Rénjiān Shì".
Nǚ Yǔ,
was an ancient person who embraced the Dào.
"Rúzǐ",
means like a young child.
Nǚ Yǔ had long heard of the ultimate Dào,
thus able to maintain health and nurture life,
although aged,
still possessed the complexion of a child,
and the appearance of retaining youthful splendor.
Being different from ordinary people,
therefore Zǐ Kuí asked how he achieved this.
【Translated Text】"Nán Bó Zǐ Kuí" Lǐ Yún states:
Kuí should be Qí,
an error due to similar pronunciation.
"Nǚ Yǔ" Xú pronounces as Yǔ,
Lǐ pronounces as Jǔ.
Another version says,
she is a woman.
"Nián Zhǎng" Zhāng reads as zhàng.
◎Lú Wénchāo comments:
The current edition reads as dīng zhàng,
consistent with previous and following instances.
"Rú Zǐ" is also written as Rú,
pronounced as rú yù.
Lǐ Yún explains:
It means a young child.
◎Lú Wénchāo adds:
The current edition uses Rú,
which is the standard form.
He said:
"I have heard the Way."
【一】【注】He who has heard the Dao lets things live naturally,
thus his vital energy and complexion remain complete.
【Commentary】The reply states:
Having heard the Way, one is thus able to preserve life whole;
hence, one reverts to youth and returns to childhood,
with a complexion like that of a young child.
Nánbó Zǐkuí asked:
"Can the Way be learned?"
【One】【Memorial】Observing his countenance and appearance,
which were unlike ordinary people's,
my heart was filled with admiration and longing,
hence I inquired about his methods and arts.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "dào".
Said:
"Alas!
How can it be!
You are not the right person for this.
Now, Bǔ Liáng Yǐ has the talent of a sage but lacks the Way of a sage;
I have the Way of a sage but lack the talent of a sage.
I wished to teach him,
hoping that he might indeed become a sage!
If not,
to impart the Way of a sage to one with the talent of a sage
would be easy indeed.
Yet I still guarded and instructed him,
and after three days, he was able to set aside the world;
having set aside the world,
I guarded him further,
and after seven days, he was able to set aside material things;
having set aside material things,
I guarded him again,
and after nine days, he was able to set aside life;
having set aside life,
he then could achieve the dawn-like clarity;
with dawn-like clarity,
he then could perceive the solitary;
perceiving the solitary,
he then could transcend past and present;
transcending past and present,
he then could enter into the deathless and unbegotten.
What kills life does not die;
what gives life is not born.
As a thing,
it neither sends anything away,
nor welcomes anything;
it neither destroys anything,
nor completes anything.
Its name is 'Yīngníng'.
'Yīngníng' means
being disturbed and yet attaining composure."
【一】【疏】To detest evil is acceptable,
but speaking of it is not.
Nǚ Yǔ kept his mind and spirit inwardly tranquil,
while his appearance and demeanor outwardly shone.
Zǐ Kuí, seeing his countenance,
joyfully requested to learn from him.
[Nǚ Yǔ] disliked what he asked,
so he restrained him, saying he was not the right person.
【Explanation】"Wù è kě" both pronounced as wū.
The following "è" is the same as above.
【二】【疏】Bǔ Liáng,
of the Jī surname,
Yǐ,
was his name.
To be open-minded, focused, and serene is the Way,
while to have wise application and keen intelligence is talent.
It is said that Liáng had the talent for external application but lacked the inwardly focused Way,
and Nǚ Jǔ possessed the serene Way but not the keen intelligence as talent,
each stagnating in one aspect,
not achieving comprehensive excellence.
However, comparing talent with the Way,
talent is inferior and the Way superior.
【Text】"Bǔ Liáng Yǐ" is pronounced as yú qǐ fǎn,
and also as qí qǐ fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
Bǔ Liáng,
is the surname;
Yǐ,
is the given name.
【Three】【Explanations】Shù means to yearn for.
Jī means to be near.
Guǒ means to decide.
When superior scholars hear of the Way,
they still rely on diligent practice;
without diligent practice,
the Way cannot be attained.
Therefore, even with instruction,
one must cultivate learning,
yearning to approach the profound Way,
and resolve to become a sage.
If not so,
teaching is very easy,
but practicing and upholding it
is what makes it difficult.
However, Nǚ Yǔ long heard the ultimate Way,
with a mind concentrated in stillness,
and now, even when wishing to transmit it,
still upholds it personally.
How much more for a beginner,
who cannot afford negligence?
If one merely speaks and hears,
what benefit is there?
Thus, it is not knowing that is difficult,
but practicing it.
【Text】"Yì Yì" is pronounced with the character 易 read as yǐ.
【Four】【Annotation】Outside,
means still left behind.
【Commentary】External means
forgetting.
Being a teacher is not easy,
transmitting the Way is extremely difficult.
When about to teach others,
one thus concentrates the spirit and calms the thoughts,
cultivates and maintains it,
for a total of three days.
Once the mind is empty and tranquil,
all realms become void,
hence, in heaven above and earth below,
nothing truly exists.
【Text】"Cān rì" is pronounced as sān.
【Five】【Annotation】Things are what one needs day and night,
closely tied to oneself and hard to forget.
【Commentary】The myriad realms of the world are distant and remote,
hence they are easily forgotten;
the resources for sustaining life are close and familiar,
thus they are hard to discard.
After maintaining discipline for seven days,
only then can one abandon them.
Therefore, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
material things are what one needs day and night,
being personally essential, they are hard to forget.
【Six】【Annotation】All are lost.
【Commentary】Destroying the body and separating from form,
sitting in oblivion and losing the self,
the operation of the mind having been prolonged,
the abandonment and dismissal gradually deepen.
【Seven】【Annotation】To relinquish life is to not despise death,
not despising death thus one finds peace in whatever one encounters,
open and without obstruction,
acting upon recognizing the opportune moment,
this is the clarity of dawn.
【Commentary】Zhāo,
means dawn.
Chè,
means clarity.
Viewing life and death as one,
forgetting both self and things,
the illumination of wisdom becomes vast and open,
like the morning sun first rising,
hence it is called zhāochè.
【Explanation】"Able to attend morning court" is read as written.
Lǐ reads it with a different pronunciation, giving "chú yáo".
The same applies below.
"Penetrate" is read as written.
Guō Sīmǎ states:
"Morning court",
means dawn.
"Penetrate",
refers to the way of reaching subtlety.
Lǐ states:
One who is capable of profound illumination,
can penetrate far without waiting until morning.
"Not dislike" is read with "wū lù" pronunciation.
The same applies below.
"Open and clear" is read as "huàn huó".
【Eight】【Comment】One should be content with whatever circumstances one encounters,
forgetting the sequence of connections between past and present,
thus perceiving the unique.
【Commentary】The ultimate Dao is congealed and still,
marvelously transcending words and forms,
neither non-existent nor existent,
neither ancient nor modern,
going and coming alone,
utterly independent and absolute.
Beholding this sublime realm,
it is called witnessing the unique.
Thus, the old classic states: solitary and unchanging.
【Nine】【Notes】Go forth together with the solitary.
【Commentary】Entrusting oneself to the ever-renewing work of creation,
following along with all transformations as they occur,
one is not shifted by external circumstances,
hence there is no distinction between past and present.
【一０】【Note】Because there is attachment to life, there is death;
because there is aversion to death, there is life.
Therefore, only when there is neither attachment nor aversion,
can one then be without death and without life.
【Commentary】The meeting of ancient and modern times,
is a convergence.
That there is a distinction between ancient and modern in eras,
and a difference between life and death in laws,
this is but the deluded view of those who hold things upside down.
Since time flows continuously and renews constantly,
there is neither modern nor ancient,
so too the law neither comes nor goes,
and has neither death nor life.
One who comprehends this principle—
could it be none other than the disciple of Nǚ Yǔ!
【一一】【Commentary】To kill,
is to extinguish;
to die,
is also to extinguish.
It is said that this death has never been extinction,
and this life has never been birth.
Once dead and once alive,
one can enter the state of neither death nor life,
thus embodying the Dharma,
which is without birth or extinction.
Since the Dharma neither arises nor ceases,
then how can emotions find joy or aversion in anything!
Accept it, and there will be nothing that does not fit.
【Interpretation】"The killer of life does not die" Lǐ Yí said:
Kill,
means to perish,
one who perishes life does not die.
Cuī said:
Eliminating one's means of livelihood is killing life.
"The giver of life does not live" Lǐ Yí said:
One who boasts of life does not live.
Cuī said:
Constantly managing one's life is giving life.
【一二】【Note】Let it lead itself,
thus there is nothing it does not lead.
【13】【Comment】By allowing things to come of their own accord,
thus there is nothing that does not come.
【Commentary】To "send off" (jiàng) means
to escort.
The Way as an entity,
saves and aids without fixed methods,
although it neither perishes nor is born,
it also is born and perishes,
thus it welcomes endless births,
and escorts immeasurable deaths.
【一四】【Note】Letting things decay on their own,
thus nothing escapes decay.
【一五】【Note】Let it accomplish itself,
thus nothing remains unaccomplished.
【Commentary】Not sending yet sending,
nothing is not destroyed;
not welcoming yet welcoming,
nothing is not generated.
【一六】【Note】One who merges with things,
when things are entangled, they too are entangled,
yet have never been without tranquility.
【Commentary】Yīng means
disturbance and agitation.
Níng means
tranquility and stillness.
The sage, with compassion and benevolence,
aids all living beings through the Way,
whose wondrous essence is beyond naming,
yet is given designations according to phenomena.
Active yet ever tranquil,
though disturbed, remains serene.
【Interpretation】"Yīng": Guō pronounces it as yíng,
Xú gives the fanqie as yú yíng,
Lǐ gives the fanqie as yú yíng.
Cuī states:
It means being entangled or attached to something.
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
Zhào Qí's annotation on Mèngzǐ says:
Yīng
means to press or compel.
When views of self, others, life, and death press within,
and the mechanisms of welcoming, rejecting, success, and destruction press from without,
yet one's heart remains entirely unmoved,
that is called "yīng níng" (tranquility amid entanglement).
Placing oneself in a realm of chaotic, flourishing transformations, where conflicts and collisions abound,
yet the heart remains steadfastly tranquil,
then one is close to achievement,
hence it is said: only after being entangled can one achieve.
【一七】【Note】When all things are entangled and only one is not,
it will be defeated.
Therefore, by entangling and entrusting them,
there is none that cannot be successfully accomplished in its own way (two).
【Commentary】Being able to harmonize one's light and blend with the dust of the world,
active yet ever tranquil,
one can then follow the disturbances of things,
skillfully lending support to their growth and completion.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang edition, which has the character "gù" (故) above "shā" (殺).
(2) The Shidetang edition also uses "yǐ" (矣).
Nánbó Zǐkuí said:
"How did you alone come to hear of it?"
【一】【疏】Zǐ Kuí found Nǚ Yǔ's discourse strange,
as its principles were lofty and profound,
so he asked, "From where alone did you hear of this?"
From this point onward,
there are altogether nine layers,
the first six based on teachings,
the last three grounded in reason,
all being the words by which Nǚ Yǔ instructed Zǐ Kuí.
It is said:
"I heard it from the son of the Deputy Ink,
the son of the Deputy Ink heard it from the grandson of the Luo Recitation,
the grandson of the Luo Recitation heard it from the Clear Vision,
the Clear Vision heard it from the Whispered Assent,
the Whispered Assent heard it from the Diligent Service,
the Diligent Service heard it from the Song of Yu,
the Song of Yu heard it from the Profound Obscurity,
the Profound Obscurity heard it from the Vast Emptiness,
the Vast Emptiness heard it from the Doubtful Beginning."
【First】【Explanation】All,
it means "of".
Deputy,
means deputy or secondary.
Ink,
refers to writing;
writing,
is text.
Principle can give rise to teaching,
hence text is called the deputy or secondary.
Just as fish must be caught with a trap,
principle is also clarified through teaching,
so through writing,
it is understood that initially, comprehension comes from text.
【Explanatory Text】"Fù Mò" Lǐ Yún said:
It can serve as an auxiliary to the profound ink.
Cuī said:
From here onward, these are all names of ancient people,
perhaps allegorically used,
not actual individuals.
【二】【疏】The copied text is called the "secondary ink,"
and reciting from memory is called "repeated chanting."
Initially, understanding is derived from the text,
hence one holds and reads it;
then gradually, one comprehends its principles,
and thus repeatedly chants it.
Moreover, teachings arise from principles,
so they are called the "child;"
and recitation stems from teachings,
hence it is named the "grandchild."
【Explanatory Text】"Luò Sòng" Lǐ Yún said:
Sòng,
means to connect.
It encompasses all without exception.
【Three】【Explanations】Zhān,
means to observe,
and also to reach.
Through diligent reading and thorough memorization,
accumulating effort over time,
one gradually perceives the ultimate principles,
and the spiritual repository becomes clear.
【Translated Text】"Zhānmíng" is pronounced as zhān.
Lǐ Yǐ says:
It means divine clarity and thorough understanding.
【Four】【Explanations】Niè,
means to ascend,
and also refers to whispering privately into the ear.
Once the recitation deepens somewhat,
through teaching, one comprehends the principle,
joy arises in the heart,
privately making a vow,
whispering secretly into the ear.
Having heard of the Way,
one dares not practice it openly,
and this also refers to gradually ascending to sublime and profound sentiments.
【Explanation】"Niè Xǔ": Xú (Yǐ) reads it as shè.
Lǐ (Yí) says:
"Xǔ"
means "to give".
To grasp and preserve it,
is to have nothing to give.
【Five】【Commentaries】Xū means
to await.
Yì means
to employ,
to practice.
Although one may privately feel self-assured,
and wisdom gradually becomes clearer,
it is essential to follow the teachings diligently,
and practice assiduously without negligence.
If one is lazy and does not act,
the Way cannot be attained.
【Explanation】"Xū Yì": Xú pronounces it as xū,
Lǐ pronounces it as rú,
saying:
being weak and cowardly leads to servitude.
Wáng says:
xū,
means to wait.
Yì,
means to nurture and transform.
【六】【疏】Ōu,
means songs and ballads.
Having understood the principle through teaching,
and acting according to the understanding,
thus making the profound virtue manifest and clear,
songs and praises fill the roads.
【Explanation】"於" is pronounced as wū,
and also read according to its regular pronunciation.
"謳" is given by Xú as the pronunciation wūhóu with a rising tone.
Lǐ pronounces it as xiāngyú with a rising tone,
and explains:
"謳" means
to warm or nurture,
resembling the appearance of transformation.
Wáng explains:
"謳" refers to
singing or ballads.
【Seven】【Annotation】Xuánmíng is that by which one designates non-being, yet it is not non-being.
【Commentary】Xuán is a name for what is profound and far-reaching.
Míng is a designation for what is secluded and tranquil.
Since virtuous conduct is inwardly harmonized,
and a fragrant reputation is outwardly manifested,
one gradually ascends to the state of emptiness and ultimate,
thereby reaching the realm of xuánmíng.
【Explanation】"Xuánmíng" Lǐ Yí says:
Forcibly named it xuán,
looking at it appears obscure.
Xiàng Guō says:
Therefore it is named non-being yet not non-being.
【Eight】【Comment】One who ascends through names to reach non-being,
must attain non-being beyond the manifestation of names.
Thus, even the profound and obscure still falls short of the ultimate,
and further pushes reliance onto the realm of boundless emptiness,
which is indeed the mystery within mystery.
【Commentary】Cān,
means three.
Liáo,
means transcendence.
The first transcends being,
the second transcends non-being,
the third transcends both being and non-being,
hence it is called the three transcendences.
The realm of profound darkness,
though subtle, has not reached the ultimate,
therefore only upon achieving the three transcendences,
can one arrive at the doubly profound.
【Transcription】"Cān" is pronounced as qī nán fǎn.
"Liáo" is pronounced by Xú as lì diāo fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
Cān,
means high.
Lofty and vast,
it cannot be named.
【Nine】【Comment】The principle of nature
is such that there are things formed through accumulated practice.
It is by ascending from the near to the distant,
and refining the coarse to the subtle,
that only after seven layers does one reach the concept of non-being,
and after nine layers does one begin to question whether non-being is the origin.
【Commentary】Beginning,
is the root.
The Dao,
transcends these four propositions,
separates from those hundred negations,
where language and the Dao are cut off,
where thought and consciousness are extinguished,
even with triple severance,
one cannot exhaust its subtlety.
And beyond the triple severance,
the fundamental root of the Dao,
is what is called the realm of double mystery,
the gate of all subtleties,
whose meaning is also difficult to grasp and can only be approximately expressed.
Therefore, it is a root that is not rooted,
a root without anything to root in,
tentatively named as the root,
yet there is nothing definite to be rooted in,
hence it is called the tentative beginning.
【Explanatory Text】"Doubting the Beginning" Lǐ Yún said:
Again doubting that there is no such beginning,
then the beginning is not without a name.
Yán cū: Qī hú fǎn.
Qī chóng: Zhí lóng fǎn.
Xià tóng.
Zìsì, Zǐyú, Zǐlí, and Zǐlái, four men in conversation, said:
"Who can take non-being as the head,
life as the spine,
and death as the rump;
who knows that death and life, existence and annihilation, are one body—
with such a one we shall be friends."
【一】The four looked at one another and smiled,
with no discord in their hearts,
and so they became friends with one another【二】.
【First】【Commentary】Zǐsì and the other three men,
it is unclear what source this is based on.
Observing their intentions and deeds,
they were all recluses beyond the mundane world,
their affections as plain as still water,
forming a bond of pure friendship together.
They recounted their mutual understanding in the void and mysterious,
and described their wordless communion in the ultimate Way.
Humanity arises from nothingness,
and nothingness comes first,
hence it is taken as the head;
from nothingness comes existence,
life then follows,
hence life is taken as the spine;
once there is life, there is death,
death comes last,
hence death is taken as the buttocks;
this is indeed natural.
Though the head and buttocks differ,
they are part of one body;
and though life and death are distinct,
they originate from the same source.
One who can grasp this essence
will find everything encountered fitting,
how could there be preferences for survival or demise, joy or aversion in between!
Whoever knows this,
I will befriend them.
【Translated Text】"Zǐ Sì" Cuī states:
Huáinán writes it as Zǐ Yǒng,
who at the age of fifty-four fell ill with a hunchback.
◎Qìng Fán notes: the Cuī version writes it as Zǐ Yǒng,
which is correct.
The current edition of Huáinán's "Jīngshén" chapter writes it as Zǐ Qiú,
differing from the version Cuī saw.
Gù Qiānlǐ said:
Qiú should be Yǒng.
The "Bó Yù" chapter of Bàopǔzǐ states Zǐ Yǒng sighed at the greatness of natural bonds,
with the character correctly written as Yǒng.
Yǒng and Qiú are similar in shape,
and in classical texts, they are often mistaken for each other,
too numerous to list individually.
"Zǐ Yú" is also written as Yǔ,
pronounced yú.
"Zǐ Lí" is pronounced lǐ xī fǎn.
"Wéi Kāo" is pronounced kǔ gāo fǎn.
【二】【疏】They witnessed the Way present,
hence they met and smiled;
sharing alignment with the profound principle,
thus they were in harmony at heart without discord.
Soon, Zǐyú fell ill,
and Zǐsì went to inquire about him.
He said:
"How magnificent is the Creator,
intending to make me into such a contorted form!
Hunched over with a bent back,
with five vertebrae protruding above,
the chin hidden at the navel,
shoulders higher than the head,
and the topknot pointing toward the sky."
The energies of yin and yang were in conflict,
yet his mind was at ease and untroubled.
He hobbled to the well and looked at his reflection,
saying:
"Alas!
The Creator is going to make me into such a contorted form again!"
【One】【Memorial】A friend having fallen ill,
I must go to inquire after him,
acting in accordance with principle,
without straying from the path beyond worldly concerns.
【Èr Shū】great,
meaning grand.
Zàowù,
is akin to the forces of creation.
Jūjū,
describes a contracted, unextended appearance.
Just as a great furnace and master smith,
the Creator shows no partiality,
how could it single out my body to intentionally inflict a constricting ailment!
From this perspective,
it is all a matter of fate.
Zǐyú, understanding the principle,
sighed and uttered these words himself.
【Translated Text】"Wěi zāi" is read as wéi guǐ fǎn.
Xiàng comments:
It means beautiful.
Cuī states:
From here until "looking into the well,"
all are Zǐ Sì's own description of his illness.
"Jū jū" is pronounced as jū by Guō.
Sīmǎ explains:
The body is cramped and contorted.
Wáng says:
It means not stretched out.
【Three】【Annotations】Lì,
means to disrupt and bring chaos.
【Explanation】Hunchbacked with a bent waist,
the backbone is exposed.
Since it is bent forward and not upright,
the internal organs are all positioned upward,
the head lowered so the chin hides at the navel,
the shoulders raised so they stand higher than the crown,
and the throat and neck curved,
largely resembling a superfluous growth.
The two energies of yīn and yáng,
disordered and imbalanced,
thus cause the whole body
to suffer from this severe ailment.
【Translated Text】"Qu Lou" Xu reads as lì zhǔ fǎn.
"Yu Ding" originally also written as Xiang.
Cui's version writes as Gang,
pronounced as xiàng.
◎Lu Wenchao says:
Previously written as Ding,
pronounced as dǐng.
Current version writes as Gang,
pronounced as xiàng.
According to the Song version, Ding is pronounced as xiàng,
suspecting Ding is a miswriting of Gang,
adjusted and corrected after consideration.
"Gou" is read as jù shù fǎn,
Xu reads as gǔ hóu fǎn.
"Zhui" Xu reads as zhī shuì fǎn.
"Zhi Tian" Li says:
Gou Zhui,
refers to the cervical vertebra.
Its shape resembles a zhui (protrusion),
meaning it points upward.
"You Li" pronounced as lì,
Xu also reads as tú xiǎn fǎn.
Guo reads as nú jié fǎn,
says:
chaotic and disordered.
Li agrees.
Cui's version writes as ●,
says:
full.
【Four】【Annotation】They did not consider it a problem.
【Commentary】Life and death are still considered as one entity,
how could illness and suffering still trouble the heart!
Therefore, even though the body is bent and constrained,
the mind and spirit remain leisurely and carefree,
not considering it a matter of concern at all.
【Translated Text】"His mind is at ease" reads the sound as xián.
Cuǐ considers "his mind" to belong to the preceding sentence.
【Five】【Comment】Those who embrace the transformations of nature,
do not sigh for themselves,
but sigh along with all things.
【Commentary】"Bumpy and limping,"
describes a hurried and strained appearance.
It speaks of dragging oneself along with effort,
looking down into a well,
upon seeing one's own reflection,
one is moved to sigh in sorrow.
Considering that the great Dao is natural,
and creation is impartial,
how could it be biased against me,
leaving me alone in such constraint?
To reveal the principles of things,
this lament is thus conveyed.
【Transcription】"Bianxian" is pronounced as step-tian,
the lower part as xi-tian.
Cui's version writes it as Bianxian.
Sima says:
Due to illness, unable to walk,
hence the term bianxian.
"Er jian" is pronounced as gu-zan.
"Yue jie hu" Cui states:
These are the words of Zǐyú.
Zǐ Sì said:
"Do you detest it?"
【One】【Memorial】Our pure friendship,
bonded beyond the mundane world,
seeing your sighs and laments,
thus stirs my surprise and doubt.
【Transcription】"Nǚ" is pronounced as "rǔ".
The same applies below.
Below, it is read with the "wū lù" reverse pronunciation.
He said:
"No,
why should I resent it?
If gradually I were transformed with my left arm into a rooster,
I would thereby seek to herald the dawn;
if gradually I were transformed with my right arm into a crossbow pellet,
I would thereby seek to shoot down an owl for roasting;
if gradually I were transformed with my buttocks into wheels,
and my spirit into a horse,
I would thereby ride upon them,
would I need any other carriage!
Moreover, what we gain
comes at the right time,
and what we lose
follows the natural course;
being content with the timing and abiding by the natural course,
sorrow and joy cannot penetrate one's heart.
This is what the ancients called 'the untieing of bonds,'
but those who cannot free themselves
are entangled by external things.
Besides, things have never prevailed over Heaven for long,
【一】【疏】Lost,
means non-existent.
Existence and non-existence, life and death,
are inherently without intention.
A sigh that is not a sigh,
why despise it as unpleasant!
【Interpretation of the Text】"曰亡" is read according to the standard pronunciation.
A sentence break is made here.
"予何惡" is read with the pronunciation "wù" (falling tone).
This pronunciation applies to the following text and annotations as well.
If read according to the standard pronunciation,
then it should be connected with the character "亡" to form a single sentence.
【二】【Note】Immersion,
means gradual.
When the embodiment of transformation merges with change,
then there is no direction that is not based on cause,
and nothing without cause can come to be.
【Commentary】Suppose the dual energies of yīn and yáng,
gradually transform my left and right arms into a rooster and a pellet,
the pellet then seeks the owl,
the rooster awaits the opportune moment at night.
The buttocks, devoid of consciousness, become wheels,
the spirit, possessing awareness, turns into a horse,
through gradual permeation and transformation,
I ride upon wheels and horse to wander freely.
If one follows and adapts to what is allotted,
then what scenario would not be suitable?
【Interpretation】"浸" is read as zǐ zhèn fǎn.
Xiàng comments:
It means gradual.
"予因以求時夜" in one edition lacks "求".
"為彈" is read as tú dàn fǎn.
"鴞" is read as hù jiāo fǎn.
"炙" is read as zhāng yè fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】When encountering the opportune moment,
the world considers it attainment.
【Four】【Annotation】Time does not pause for a moment,
flowing forward and passing away,
the world calls this loss.
【五】【疏】To obtain is
life,
to lose is
death.
Suddenly gaining
means timely life;
abruptly losing
signifies a natural death.
Thus, being content with the times brings no joy in life,
and abiding by nature holds no aversion to death.
Since there is neither joy nor aversion,
how can worry or pleasure enter in!
【Text】"Āi Yuè" (音洛).
【Six】【Annotation】If one cannot untie oneself,
then all things will entangle together.
Therefore, being able to untie means there is nothing that cannot be untied,
and not being able to untie means there is nothing that can be untied.
【Commentary】Dwelling in compliance, forgetting time,
serene and unattached,
the ultimate sages of ancient times
were called "released from bondage."
As for those who worry about death while alive,
and harbor hatred and aversion in their hearts,
since their inner selves cannot find liberation,
they become bound by external matters.
【Explanation】"County" is pronounced as xuán.
"Solution" is pronounced as xiè,
and the same applies below and in the annotations.
(Same)
Xiang (1) said:
The understanding of the county,
is without any attachment.
【Seven】【Annotation】Heaven cannot be without day and night,
how then can I, without life and death, detest it!
【Commentary】The dark heavens above,
still have the distinction of day and night,
how much more so humans dwelling in the mortal world,
how could they be without the changes of life and death!
Moreover, things cannot overcome heaven,
not only in the present day,
what kind of person am I,
to alone harbor aversion and hatred!
【Collation Note】(1) The character "xiàng" was amended based on the Shìdétáng edition and the original version of the explanatory texts.
Soon, Zǐlái fell ill,
gasping as if nearing death,
his wife and children gathered around him, weeping.
Zǐlí went to check on him,
and said:
"Hush!
Step aside!
Do not disturb the transformation!"
Leaning against the door, he spoke to him:
"How magnificent is the Creator!
What will It make you into next,
where will It take you?
Will It turn you into a rat's liver,
or an insect's leg?"
Three]
【一】【疏】Huán,
means to surround.
Chuǎn chuǎn,
describes rapid breathing.
Zǐyú had just finished speaking,
and in a short moment,
Zǐlái fell ill again,
with breath rushing as if about to die.
As he was nearing the end,
his wife and children gathered around him, weeping.
【Explanatory Text】"Chuǎn chuǎn" is read as chuán zhuǎn fǎn,
also as chǐ ruǎn fǎn.
Cuī's version writes it as zhuì zhuì.
"Huán ér" is read according to its character.
Xú pronounces it as huàn.
Lǐ says:
It means to encircle.
【二】【注】Death and life are like waking and sleeping;
when it is reasonable to sleep,
one does not wish to be disturbed;
similarly, when transforming and dying is fitting,
there should be no cause for grief.
【Commentary】"Chì" is a
scolding sound.
Those who transcend worldly affairs,
unify life and death in obscurity,
yet when a friend approaches death,
they mingle their light to visit and inquire.
Therefore, they scold the relatives,
ordering them to step aside and keep distance,
precisely because they wish to transform,
not wanting to startle or distress them.
【Explanation】"叱避" is pronounced as chāng shī fǎn.
"無怛" is pronounced as dīng dá fǎn.
Cuī Běn's version writes it as "靼",
pronounced as dá.
According to the case, dá
means to startle.
Zhèng Zhòng's annotation in the "Zhōu Lǐ Kǎo Gōng Jì" states "cannot startle or alarm",
which is correct.
【Three】【Explanations】Again,
means to return.
Xī,
means what.
Shì,
means to go.
Leaning by the door observing transformations,
spoke with him.
Sighing at that great creation,
vast and impartial without selfishness,
occasionally becoming human,
suddenly returning to transformation.
Not knowing which path to take beyond the mundane world,
or what thing to transform into.
Perhaps turning your five organs into a rat's liver,
or transforming your four limbs into an insect's arms.
Follow transformation and go,
wherever encountered is fitting.
【Explanation Text】"倚其" pronounced as yǐ qí fǎn.
"鼠肝" Xiàng Zǐ says:
Just discarded into the soil.
Wáng Zǐ says:
Takes the most insignificant and lowly.
"蟲臂" bì,
also written as cháng.
Cuī's version is the same.
Zǐ Lái said:
"For parents towards their children,
whether east, west, south, or north,
they follow commands exclusively.
Yin and yang towards humans,
are no less than parents;
when they draw me near to death and I do not comply,
then I am defiant,
what fault is theirs!
The great earth bears me with form,
toils me with life,
eases me with old age,
rests me with death.
Therefore, what makes my life good,
is also what makes my death good.
Now if a great smith were casting metal,
and the metal leaped up saying 'I must become a Mòyé sword',
the smith would surely consider it inauspicious metal.
Now having once taken human form,
one says 'I am human, I am human',
the creator would surely consider this an inauspicious person.
Now if we take heaven and earth as the great furnace,
and creation as the great smith,
where can we go that would not be acceptable!
Serenely he slept,
and suddenly he awoke.
【一】【注】Since ancient times, there have been those who could defy their parents' commands,
but none have been able to resist the transformations of yīn and yáng or oppose the order of day and night.
【Commentary】From here onward,
these are Zǐ Lái's words in response to Zǐ Lí on his deathbed.
A filial son serving his parents
still hastens to follow their every command.
How much more so with the transformations of yīn and yáng,
who are no less than one's own parents!
Thus, we know that disobeying parental instruction
may sometimes occur in the world;
but resisting yīn and yáng,
such a thing has never existed.
【Interpretation】"不翅" Xú (reads it as) shī zhī fǎn.
【二】【Note】Life and death are like day and night,
not something to be considered distant.
When the time comes to die,
it is not something one can prevent.
Yet, harboring an unwilling heart
only serves to defy the natural order and hasten one's death.
The swiftness of death,
stems from my defiance,
not from the fault of death itself.
That,
refers to death;
in life,
thus death is regarded as the other.
【Commentary】That refers to
the process of creation and transformation.
Within this process of creation and transformation,
I am brought close to death.
If I detest this death and refuse to comply,
then it is I who resist the forces of yīn and yáng,
and oppose the course of change.
Thus, the fault lies with me;
what crime is there on its part?
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation takes death as that.
【Explanatory Text】"Bǐ jìn".
Read as the character's standard pronunciation.
"Zé hàn" also appears in some versions as "捍",

Also pronounced as hàn.

means to resist.
【Three】【Annotation】Principle is always present.
【Commentary】This reiterates the previous text,
to substantiate its meaning.
These words are particularly apt,
hence they are presented again.
The interpretation of the text's intent
does not differ from the earlier purpose.
【四】【注】Human ears, human ears,
one only wishes to be human.
It is like the leaping of metal,
the world all knows the inauspiciousness of metal,
yet cannot let it transform on its own.
As for the way of transformation,
there is nowhere it does not reach,
now once encountering a human form,
how could it be intentionally made?
Life is not intentionally made,
it arises naturally in its time.
To strive and possess it,
is that not delusional!
【Commentary】Xiáng means
good.
Fàn means
to encounter.
Mòyé,
was the name of an excellent sword in ancient times.
In the past, a man from Wú named Gānjiàng forged swords for the King of Wú,
and his wife was named Mòyé,
hence the male sword was called Gānjiàng,
and the female sword Mòyé.
When a great furnace and master smith
melt and cast metal,
they shape it according to the size of the vessel needed,
producing all kinds of objects.
Yet if the metal within the furnace
suddenly leaps and jumps,
earnestly making requests,
wishing to become a fine sword,
the smith would be astonished and sigh,
considering it inauspicious.
Similarly, in the great forge of nature,
which carves myriad forms,
be they birds, beasts, fish, or insects,
it creates all kinds.
If by chance it fashions a human,
who then becomes fond and delighted,
solemnly pleading
to be remade as a human,
within the workings of creation,
this would be regarded as an ominous aberration.
【Interpretation】"I and" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.

【五】【注】Everyone knows that being tied to gold is inauspicious,
so by clarifying that one is no different from gold,
the attachments of emotion can be resolved,
and once resolved, there is nothing that cannot be achieved.
【Commentary】The operation of the two cosmic forces creates and transforms,
using the universe as a furnace,
molding and casting all things,
hammering and forging living beings.
Vast and boundless, it acts without intent,
nurturing and fostering all equally.
Whatever it encounters, it adapts accordingly—
what is there to hate or to delight in?
It arranges and alters all transformations,
with no direction in which it cannot proceed.

Zǐsānghù, Mèngzǐfǎn, and Zǐqínzhāng three men became friends with one another,
saying:
"Who can associate without associating,
act for one another without acting?
Who can ascend to heaven and wander in the mists,
roam the infinite without boundaries;
forget one another in life,
with no ultimate end?"
The three men looked at each other and smiled,
finding no discord in their hearts,
and so they became friends with one another.
【一】【注】One who embodies heaven and earth
and merges with the transformations,
though hands and feet have different duties,
and the five organs serve distinct functions,
never consciously cooperate yet all joints harmonize together—
this is cooperating without conscious cooperation;
never deliberately assist each other yet inner and outer aspects mutually support—
this is assisting without deliberate assistance.
If instead one exhausts their mind to worry over hands and feet,
or mobilizes limbs to tend to the five organs,
then the more earnestly one tends to them, the more internal and external exhaustion ensues.
Therefore, one who regards the world as a single body
harbors no partial affection within it.
【Commentary】These three individuals,
all being recluses beyond the mundane world,
are immersed in the mysteries of transformation,
unified in their view of life and death.
Since their aspirations and conduct align,
they thus form friendships with one another.
Each, adhering to their sincerity,
expresses their sentiments as follows:
Who can, in emptiness and natural spontaneity, become friends with others?
This is precisely befriending without intentional befriending,
acting without deliberate action,
not acting for the sake of acting,
nor befriending for the sake of befriending.
It is like the five organs and six senses,
the four limbs and all parts of the body,
each having its designated functions,
mutually supporting and utilizing one another—
how could there be any conscious intention to interact,
or emotional attachment to closeness or distance?
Although there is no deliberate intention to assist,
the mutual aid is accomplished.
Thus, engaging with others without intentional engagement,
forming friendships through non-action—
the principle is indeed the same.
【Explanation】"Xiāng yǔ" is read as it is.
Cuī says:
It means intimate.
Alternatively, it is sometimes pronounced as yù.
"Xiāng wèi" is read as it is,
or sometimes pronounced with the fanqie spelling yú wèi.
"Ài wèi" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling yú wèi.
【Two】【Annotation】There is nothing it cannot undertake.
【Commentary】"Náo tiǎo,"
means winding and turning.
Ascending to the heavens
signifies purity, loftiness, and effortless elevation;
roaming through the clouds and mist
demonstrates not being confined within them;
thus, one can follow transformations without end,
and become one who moves fluidly with the creator of things.
【Interpretation】"Náo": Xú reads it as shǎo fǎn,
Guō reads it as xǔ yáo fǎn,
"Tiǎo": Xú reads it as tú liǎo fǎn,
Guō and Lǐ read it as tú yáo fǎn.
Also written as "Zhào".
Lǐ says:
náo tiǎo,
means winding and turning,
winding and turning within the profound vastness.
Jiǎn Wén says:
It is the name for cyclical movement.
【Three】【Annotations】Forgetting one's own life,
then there is nothing not forgotten,
thus able to follow changes and embrace transformations,
all without any end or limit.
【Commentary】Reaching the ultimate end,
means death.
Together, we forget life and also forget death,
blending life and death into one,
thus following transformation without end.
【Four】【Annotation】If so, how could they be considered friends?
It conveys the idea that even the closest of kin may lack the intimate affection of familial love.
【Commentary】Having grasped the meaning, they forgot the words,
so they looked at each other and smiled;
their wisdom merged with the realm,
thus they were in perfect harmony at heart.
Sharing the same path beyond the mundane world,
they thus became companions.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition changes it to 'and',
the Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the characters 'fū' and 'zhě'.
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, 'guān' is written as 'guǎn'.
In the Zhào edition, these two sentences read: "Although the hands, feet, and five viscera differ."
After a short while, Zisang Hù passed away,
and had not yet been buried.
Confucius heard of this,
and sent Zigòng to assist with the funeral affairs.
Some were weaving melodies,
others were playing the qin,
harmonizing together as they sang,
saying: "Alas, Sāng Hù!
Alas, Sāng Hù!
You have already returned to your true nature,
while we remain as humans, oh!"
Zigòng hurried forward and asked:
"May I ask, is it in accordance with ritual
to sing before the corpse?"
【一】【疏】"Mò" means "nonexistence".
Three people gazed at each other,
in profound silence without words.
Within a brief moment,
Zǐsānghù died.
Zhòngní, upon hearing this,
sent Zǐgòng to offer condolences,
and instructed him to assist with the funeral arrangements,
welcoming the guests.
To illustrate the distinction between the transcendental and the mundane,
the text thus attributes this to Nǐfù and Qínzhāng.
【Translated Text】"Mò rán" is read as written.
Cuī states:
It means settled.
"Yǒu jiàn" is read as written.
Cuī and Lǐ state:
It means a moment.
The original also uses "wéi jiàn".
◎Qìng Fān's note: Yǒu,
in the explanatory text, is written as wéi.
Wéi jiàn is equivalent to yǒu jiàn.
In ancient times, wéi and yǒu were interchangeable in meaning.
In the Mèngzǐ, Téng Wéngōng chapter,
"Jiāng wéi jūnzǐ yān,"
"Jiāng wéi yěrén yān,"
Zhào Qí's commentary:
Wéi,
means yǒu,
Even small states also have gentlemen and commoners.
Also, "dìzǐ wǔ rán wéi jiàn,"
Commentary:
Wéi jiàn,
means within a short while.
Also, in the Jìnxīn chapter, "wéi jiàn bù yòng,"
Commentary:
Wéi jiàn,
means yǒu jiàn.
Also, in the Liáng Huìwáng chapter, "shàn tuī qí suǒ wéi ér yǐ yǐ,"
The Shuōyuàn, Guìdé chapter quotes Mèngzǐ with wéi written as yǒu.
In the Yān Cè, "gù bù gǎn wéi cí shuō,"
The Xīnxù, Záshì chapter writes wéi as yǒu.
All these serve as evidence.
【Èr Shū】The tune,
is simple.
Some weave reeds into mats,
some play the qin and sing,
harmonizing in joy and delight,
never showing sorrowful expressions.
This is what is called forgetting each other in life,
the ultimate state beyond the mundane world.
【Explanatory Text】"Bianqu": must be read with the fanqie "bi lian fan",
the Zilin gives the fanqie "bu qian fan",
Guō reads it with the fanqie "fu tian fan",
the Shǐjì records the fanqie "fu lian fan".
Lǐ Yún states:
"Qǔ"
means a silkworm tray.
"Xiānghè": read with the fanqie "hu wo fan".
【Three】【Annotations】To cry when others cry,
is the conduct of the mundane world.
To equate life and death,
and forget sorrow and joy,
singing before the corpse,
is the ultimate state of the transcendental realm.
【Commentary】"Jiē lái"
is the sound of singing.
From "Sāng Hù hū" onward,
it is the responsive refrain.
"Yī,"
is the sound of mutual response.
That from non-being emerges being,
is called birth;
from being returns to non-being,
is called death.
You have now returned to emptiness and stillness,
which means returning to the origin and reverting to the true;
yet I still linger in the human world,
a traveler who has not yet returned to his homeland.
Wishing to equalize life and death,
thus I utter this sigh of "yī."
◎Lǐ Zhēn says:
"Jiē lái" is the sound of singing,
yet it is an exclamation.
In the "Shì Míng: Shì Yán Yǔ" chapter:
"Jiē"
means to assist;
when words are insufficient to fully express meaning,
one utters this sound to aid oneself.
"Lái"
means sorrow;
(thus)
They came to share in his sorrow,
hence, by lowering their heads in speech, they beckoned him.
Mèngzǐ Fǎn and Zǐ Qín Zhāng sighed that Sānghù had returned to his true self,
thus they sang this song.
【Textual Explanation】"I still" is written as "alone" in Cuǐ's version.
"People sigh" is pronounced with a reverse of yú yí.
Cuǐ says,
it is a particle.
"Sorrow and joy" is pronounced as luò.
【Four】【Memorial】The rites within the realm
value restraint and decorum.
When a neighbor has a funeral,
even pounding rice ceases.
How much more, when facing the corpse of a friend,
could there be no mourning or weeping,
but instead playing the qin and singing as usual?
Is this in accordance with the rites?
Zǐgòng found this strange,
so he hurried forward to inquire.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "shì" written as "dài".
The Quēwù cites the Zhāng Jūnfáng edition as having "shì".
(2) The character "shǐ" is emended according to the Shìmíng.
The two looked at each other, smiled, and said:
"How could they understand the true meaning of the rites?"
【一】【注】Those who understand the essence of rites
must wander beyond to manage within,
hold to the root to preserve the branches,
and act directly according to genuine feelings.
If, however, one is obsessed with reputation,
constrained by formalities,
then filial piety lacks sincerity,
parental love lacks substance,
and between father and son, brothers,
they harbor hidden feelings and deceive each other.
How can this be the great meaning of rites!
【Commentary】The great rites share the same rhythm with heaven and earth,
unconfined by forms and names,
directly expressing authenticity,
following emotions freely.
How much more so when merging indistinguishably with life and death—
how could sorrow or joy remain in one's heart!
Yet Zǐgòng, a Confucian scholar confined to worldly affairs,
was by nature stubborn and narrow-minded,
valuing only superficial traces,
failing to grasp the wondrous essence.
Such a person—
how could they understand the profundity of rites!
Being ridiculed by those beyond worldly conventions
was indeed fitting.
【Explanation】"How to know" is pronounced as wū,
the following instances are all the same.
"In accordance with feelings" is pronounced as chǐ zhèng fǎn.
Zǐgòng returned,
and reported to Kǒngzǐ,
saying:
"What kind of person is that?
He cultivates no practices,
yet externalizes his physical form,
facing a corpse and singing,
with unchanged complexion,
I cannot describe him.
What kind of person is that?"
【一】【疏】Destiny is
a name.
When Zǐgòng returned from his mission,
he reported to Father Ní, saying:
The sentiments and affairs of those two men are hard to discern.
They cultivate their own virtue and conduct,
without adhering to rituals and propriety,
and forget external forms and bodies,
blending life and death into one,
singing and making music in the face of mourning,
with their spirits and forms unchanged.
Since their way is unfathomable,
it is difficult to name it.
【Explanation】"Wú yǐ mìng zhī" Cuī Lǐ yún:
mìng,
míng yě.
Confucius said:
"They
are those who wander beyond the realm of forms;
while I, Qiū,
wander within the realm of forms.
The beyond and within do not intersect,
yet I sent you to mourn them,
which shows my narrow-mindedness.
They are precisely those who accompany the Creator as companions,
roaming in the single breath of heaven and earth.
They regard life as an attached wart or dangling tumor,
and death as the bursting of a boil or rupturing of an abscess.
Being thus,
how could they know the sequence of life and death!
They borrow from different entities,
entrusting themselves to a unified substance;
they forget their livers and gallbladders,
discard their ears and eyes;
through cycles of beginning and end,
they remain unaware of start or finish;
vaguely drifting beyond the dust and grime,
they wander freely in the enterprise of non-action.
How could they possibly bother with the fussy rituals of worldly customs,
just to put on a show for ordinary people's eyes and ears!"
【一】【注】The principle has its ultimate expression,
where external and internal become mystically united.
There has never been one who reached the ultimate in wandering beyond without being mystically united within,
nor has there been anyone who could be mystically united within without wandering beyond.
Therefore, the sage constantly wanders beyond to mystically unite within,
with no deliberate mind yet conforming to all that exists.
Thus, though he interacts with forms all day long, his spirit and energy remain unchanged;
though he engages with myriad affairs, he remains calm and self-possessed.
Those who see the form but miss the spirit
are commonly burdened by worldly concerns.
Hence, observing him moving alongside all things,
none can say he has abandoned things or departed from humanity;
witnessing him embody transformation and respond to duties,
none can claim he sits in forgetfulness and attains self-fulfillment.
How can one simply say that the sage is not so?
Rather, it insists that the ultimate principle does not include this.
Therefore, Zhuāngzǐ intended to clarify the source revered by the flowing tradition to explain what the world can comprehend.
If he had directly stated that Zhòngní was like this,
some might have used their limited views to reject it.
So, he transcended the sage's inner traces
and entrusted the realm beyond to several figures.
One should forget what is entrusted to seek the main intent of the narrative,
then the way of wandering beyond and mystically uniting within will become clear and evident,
and the book of Zhuāngzǐ
is indeed a discourse that transcends the mundane and encompasses the world.
【Commentary】"Fāng" means
a bounded region.
Those two individuals,
who equated life and death as one,
were not constrained by the traces of teachings,
thus their minds roamed beyond the cosmos.
Whereas Zhòngní and Zǐgòng,
great Confucians who shaped their era,
practiced the righteousness of judgment,
observed the rituals of patterned refinement,
focused their intentions within the realm of sorrow and joy,
and let their minds wander within bounded regions—
this is why they differed.
【Explanation Text】"而淡" is pronounced as "tú zàn" in the reverse tone.
"而離" is pronounced as "lì zhì" in the reverse tone,
the same applies below.
"而應" refers to the response in a dialogue.
The same applies below.
"數子" is pronounced as "suǒ zhǔ" in the reverse tone.
"坦然" is pronounced as "tǔ dàn" in the reverse tone.

◎Qìng Fān's case: In the annotations of Xiè Língyùn's poem "Departing from the Capital upon Arrival at the Commandery" from the "Wén Xuǎn" and the annotations of Xiàhóu Xiàoruò's "Eulogy of Dōngfāng Shuò,"
both quote Sīmǎ as saying:
"Fāng"
means constant,
indicating that one's mind wanders beyond constant teachings.
The explanatory text is missing.
【二】【注】Condolence is
an affair within the mundane world;
applying it to the realm beyond is crude.
【Commentary】The principles of Daoism and Confucianism are separated,
the paths of the inner and outer realms differ,
when comparing their superiority and inferiority,
they do not reach each other.
To use the mundane rituals of the secular world
to mourn a transcendent sage beyond the ordinary realm,
is like displaying straw dogs once more—
an act of extreme vulgarity.
【Transcription】"Shǐ nǚ" is pronounced as rǔ.
The same applies below.
All three annotations are obscured into the obscure,
thus there is no duality.
【Subcommentary】It penetrates the transformations of yin and yang,
and acts as a companion to the Creator in forming humans;
it embodies the undifferentiated unity of all things,
and roams within the single qi of the two modes (heaven and earth).
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī states:
In the chapter "Yìng Dì Wáng" (Responding to the Sovereign),
"I am about to act as a companion to the Creator,"
Guǒ (Xiàng) comments:
"Allow humans to act on their own."
In the chapter "Tiān Yùn" (The Movement of Heaven),
"I do not act as a companion to transformation,"
Guǒ comments:
"Those who act as companions to transformation,"
"allow it to transform on its own."
In my opinion, Guǒ did not understand the meaning of the character "rén."
"Rén"
means "companion" or "counterpart";
"wéi rén"
is akin to "acting as a counterpart."
In the Doctrine of the Mean, "the benevolent person is a 'rén',"
Zhèng (Xuán) annotates:
"Read as the 'rén' in 'xiāng rén ǒu',"
meaning words that mutually regard each other as companions.
In the annotation to the "Fěi Fēng" poem of the Shījīng:
"regarding someone as a companion who can cut and cook,"
"regarding someone as a companion who can assist the Way of Zhōu in governing the people."
In the annotation to the Rites of Recruitment:
"Bowing at each gate,"
"is to show respect by treating each other as companions."
In the annotation to the Rites for the Grand Officer's Feast:
"Bowing at each turn and at the stele is treating each other as companions."
Thus, "rén" and "ǒu" share the same meaning,
hence the phrase "xiāng rén ǒu" existed in the Hàn dynasty.
In the "Yuán Dào" chapter of Huáinánzǐ,
"acting as a companion to the Creator,"
the meaning is the same as here.
(Gāo (Yǒu) annotates:
"wéi" means "to govern,"
which is incorrect.
See also Huáinánzǐ.
) The "Qí Sú" chapter states:
"Above, being a friend to the spirits and gods,"
"below, acting as a companion to the Creator."
This is clear evidence.
◎Qìng Fán's case: In the annotation to Yán Yánnián's "Preface to the Poem on the Third Day of the Third Month" in the Wénxuǎn, Sīmǎ (Biāo) is quoted as saying:
"The Creator is the Dào."

In the annotations to Rèn Yǎnshēng's "Letter to the Grand Marshal's Office," "Edict of Empress Xuāndé," Lù Zuògōng's "Inscription on the Stone Gate," and Shěn Xiūwén's "Stele Inscription for Prince Zhāo of Ānlù of Qí," Sīmǎ is quoted as saying:
"The Creator,"
"refers to the Dào."
This is missing in the Shìwén.
【Four】【Note】Like a wart that hangs by itself,
or a superfluous growth that attaches on its own,
these are temporary accumulations of vital energy,
not something to be pleased about.
【Translated Text】"Xiàn" is pronounced as xuán.
The same applies to the annotation.
"Yóu" is pronounced as yóu.
【五】【Note】Like a wart that falls off on its own,
or an abscess that bursts spontaneously,
this is the natural dissipation of energy,
not something to be regretted.
【Commentary】Those three masters were persons who embodied the Way,
penetrating life and death,
and becoming one with transformation.
Thus, when the qi gathered and they were born,
it was like warts and tumors attaching and hanging—
not something they delighted in;
when the qi dispersed and they died,
it was like boils and abscesses bursting and draining—
not something they regretted.
【Explanation】"Jué": Xú gives the pronunciation as gǔ xué fǎn.
"Huàn": Hú luàn fǎn.

with the pronunciation hú qiú fǎn,
which is likely an arbitrary alteration.
"Kuì": Hú duì fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's case: In the sixteenth volume of Huìlín's "Sound and Meaning of All Sūtras," under the "Great Expansive Three Precepts Sūtra," it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Floating heat causes jū,
and blockage causes yōng.

The same quotations appear in the thirtieth volume of the "Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Who Upholds Humanity," part two, the thirty-seventh volume of the "Cundī Dhāraṇī Sūtra," and the ninety-fifth volume's annotation in the "Sūtra of Correct Refutation."
The explanation text is missing.
【Six】【Annotation】The cycle of life and death,
has never had an end,
going along with it,
then there is no direction that cannot be taken,
thus one does not know where victory or defeat lies.
【Commentary】Prior,
means superior.
Posterior,
means inferior.
Warts, superfluous growths, tumors, and abscesses,
these four are all ailments,
and while the vital energy may gather or disperse,
the illnesses themselves have no superiority or inferiority.
If one uses this to compare life and death,
how can one know where superiority or inferiority lies!
【Seven】【Comment】Jia,
means cause/reliance.
Now life and death, gathering and scattering,
change without fixed pattern,
all are different phenomena.
There is nothing different that is not provisional,
therefore, although the provisional manifestations differ, they together form one unified whole.
【Commentary】Water, fire, metal, and wood,
different substances borrow from one another,
numerous elements lodge and depend,
together forming a single body.
From this, we know that the physical form,
has always been illusory.
【八】【Note】Entrust it to principle and proceed in silent accordance.
【Commentary】Since we know that physical form is illusory,
and there is nothing to cherish or love,
therefore, one can internally forget about the internal organs,
and externally forget about the sensory orifices.
【Nine】【Annotation】Even the five viscera are forgotten,
what thing is worth knowing indeed!
There has never been any knowledge,
thus one can let go and follow the path of transformation,
mysteriously unite with the waves of reversal and return,
and not know the ultimate point of beginning and end (five).
【Commentary】Duān means
a beginning thread.
Ní means
a boundary.
Fǎnfù refers to
coming and going.
Zhōngshǐ refers to
life and death.
Having already forgotten one's physical form and substance,
abandoning the body and discarding acute hearing,
thus one can transcend coming and going, life and death,
and journey together with transformation.
Moreover, transformation is without limit,
hence no one can know its beginning or boundary.
【Explanatory Text】"Fǎn fù" is pronounced as fāng fú fǎn.
"Duān ní" may also be written as 淣,
which is the same.
Pronounced as yá.
Xú pronounces it as yì.
【一０】【Note】What is called the work of non-action
does not mean merely folding hands and remaining silent;
what is called beyond the dust and grime
does not mean hiding away in mountain forests.
【Commentary】Máng rán,
is the appearance of having no knowledge.
Pánghuáng and xiāoyáo,
are both terms for self-attained ease and leisure.
Chéngòu,
refers to tangible things such as form and sound, which are products of deliberate action.
Previously, the physical form was already disregarded,
here, the mind and intellect are also forgotten,
thus allowing freedom beyond the burdens of worldly dust,
and ease in the realm of clarity and openness,
using this non-action to engage in affairs and undertakings.
【Explanation Text】"Máng rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant M and the final ang, in the rising tone.

It describes an appearance of being unbound.

Zhǒng,

is the same as gòu (dirt).

【一一】【Note】What is displayed for the masses to see,
is all but the dust and grime,
not the transcendent, obscure entities beyond the mundane world.
【Commentary】"Kuìkuì" means
being vexed and disordered.
Those several masters,
pure and lofty, empty and tranquil,
arranged themselves to depart from transformation,
following their nature and embracing authenticity.
How could they forcefully engage in ritualized conduct,
constrained by the rites of the mundane world;
displaying dignified manners,
to please the sight and hearing of the masses!
【Translated Text】"Confused" is pronounced as gōng nèi fǎn,
the Shuōwén and Cāngjié Piān both state:
it means chaotic,
"To observe" is pronounced as gǔ luàn fǎn,
meaning to show.
