Zǐgòng said:
"Then, Master, what way do you adhere to?"
【一】【注】Zǐgòng did not hear about nature and the Way of Heaven,
so he saw what it relies on but did not see that by which it relies.
Now, that by which it relies
does not rely on anything,
how could the world ever realize this!
【Commentary】The paths within and beyond the mundane world
differ in depth and shallowness,
so it is unknown which way the Master would follow.
To initiate instruction and inspire understanding,
this doubt is thus posed.
Confucius said:
"Qiū,
I am one of Heaven's punished people.
Nevertheless,
I share this with you."
【一】【Note】Considering the mundane world as shackles,
it clarifies that what is valued lies beyond the mundane.
Those who wander beyond rely on what is within,
and those who detach from others align with customs.
Thus, those who possess the world do not use it for personal gain.
Therefore, by discarding things, one can then enter the community,
and by sitting in forgetfulness, one can then respond to affairs.
The more one discards,
the more one gains.
If one abides in this ultimate state,
then even if one wishes to release it, the principle naturally comes of its own accord,
and this is what neither Heaven nor humanity can pardon.
【Commentary】The traces of the sages and the rites and rituals
are shackles to one's form and nature.
Since Zhòngní adhered to the mundane world,
this follows the principle of spontaneity,
yet he was a man subjected to punishment and execution.
Therefore, the chapter "Virtue Complete and the Seal" states,
"How can the punishment of Heaven be escaped?"
【二】【注】Although bound by the constraints of the world,
it is only to share them with you.
Thus, I have always remained detached on the outside.
【Commentary】Confucius, being a sage,
harmonized his light with all beings,
moved with the waves of the world,
and valued these common rituals.
Although he again descended to dwell within the mundane sphere,
sharing it with you,
his mind wandered beyond the ordinary,
serene and unattached.
Zǐgòng said:
"May I ask about the method?"
【一】【注】Asking about the meaning of wandering beyond yet sharing within.
【Commentary】Fāng means
the Way.
The question asks:
"When traces mingle in the mundane realm,
and the mind wanders beyond the fāng,
how is it that the external and internal mysteriously unite,
and what is this Way like?"
Confucius said:
"Fish are naturally drawn to water,
just as humans are naturally drawn to the Dào.
Those drawn to water
dig ponds and find sustenance;
those drawn to the Dào
find tranquility without striving.
Hence it is said,
fish forget each other in rivers and lakes,
humans forget each other in the arts of the Dào."
【一】【疏】To create,
means to arrive at.
What fish arrive at,
nothing suits their nature more than deep water;
what humans reach for,
nothing brings fulfillment more than the Way and its arts.
Although emotions and intellects are not the same,
this mutual tendency is universal.
This briefly outlines the core meaning,
and the following will provide an explanation.
【Explanation】"相造" is read with the seventh tone,
meaning to visit.
The same applies below.
【二】【Note】Although their achievements differ,
they all proceed from non-action to attain affairs,
from beyond the mundane to share in the inner realm,
then through nurturing sufficiency, life becomes settled.
There is none who does not follow this way.
Yet none are aware of it themselves,
hence accomplishment arises from non-action.
【Commentary】This explains the preceding meaning.
Rivers, lakes, and seas,
are all called the Heavenly Pond.
Fish dwell in the vast waters,
burrowing into the mud and sand,
to sustain and nourish themselves;
similarly, humans abide within the Great Way,
cultivating their nature through purity and emptiness,
roaming freely without worldly concerns,
thus attaining tranquility, stability, and contentment in their inherent nature.
【Translated Text】"Digging a Pond" is also written as "digging the ground" in some versions,
Cuī's version is the same.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
"Dìng" is suspected to be a miswriting of the character "zú".
Dig a pond and thus provide ample support,
do nothing and yet generate sufficiency,
these two sentences follow the same pattern.
"Gěi",
also means sufficient.
"Zú" and "dìng",
are similar in character form and thus easily confused.
In the "Zhòng Kuāng" chapter of the Guǎnzǐ:
"The achievement is fixed by gaining heaven or losing heaven,"
the human affairs are the same.
The current version mistakenly writes "dìng" as "zú",
which precisely corroborates this point mutually.
【Three】【Notes】Each is self-sufficient and forgets the others,
as all under heaven are invariably so.
The perfect person is always content,
hence always forgetful.
【Comment】This concludes the explanation of the preceding meaning.
In deep waters, swimming freely,
each is self-sufficient and forgets the others;
when the Way and its arts fill one within,
partial affections naturally cease;
how could this be spoken of in the same breath as the shallow benevolence and righteousness of gasping for breath on dry land!
Singing before a corpse,
its meaning is likewise thus.
【Transcription】"Xiāng Wàng" is pronounced as wáng.
The same applies below.
Zǐgòng said:
"I venture to ask about the unconventional person."
【一】【注】Where are those who were said to be beyond the mundane and unmatched by worldly conventions,
as previously mentioned?
【Explanation】Jī refers to the name for being unmatched.
Cultivating conduct with non-being,
and being detached from the external form,
they deviate from human relationships,
unmatched by the common customs.
I dare to ask,
what is the way of such a person?
【Translated Text】"Jīrén" is pronounced with the character for "dwelling" and "appropriate" in reverse.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means not paired.
Not paired with others,
refers to being deficient in ritual teachings.
Lǐ gives the reverse pronunciation of "appropriate,"
saying:
It means strange or unusual.
He said:
"An anomalous person
is anomalous among men but equal to Heaven.
Therefore it is said:
He who is a petty man by Heaven's standard
is a gentleman by man's standard;
he who is a gentleman by man's standard
is a petty man by Heaven's standard."
【One】【Comment】One who is united with the inner darkness,
roams in the outer world.
Only by roaming outwardly can one unite with the inner darkness,
entrusting all things to their natural course,
enabling each innate nature to be fulfilled and the way of the sovereign to be accomplished.
This is to be divergent from humanity yet equal to heaven.
【Commentary】From here onward,
it is Confucius's reply to Zǐgòng.
"Móu" means
equal,
identical.
Those who do not cultivate benevolence and righteousness,
do not align with things,
but follow their innate nature,
are in accordance with the principle of naturalness.
【Interpretation】"而侔" is pronounced as móu.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means equal,
and also to follow.
【二】【注】Speaking in terms of nature,
there is no distinction between young and old among humans (1);
speaking in terms of human principles,
those who align with heaven can be called noble individuals.
【Commentary】Those who embrace benevolence and practice righteousness are gentlemen,
while those who violate the Way and betray virtue are petty individuals.
Thus, those who perform strained acts of benevolence,
and employ forced righteousness,
are called gentlemen in human relations,
but are deemed petty individuals by the Way of Heaven.
Therefore, it is known that Zǐfǎn and Qín Zhāng,
not conforming to the vulgar,
were called eccentric individuals,
yet they were truly gentlemen of Heaven.
Repeating these words
reinforces their meaning.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "dà zuò rén".
Yán Huí asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Mèngsūn Cái,
when his mother died,
wept without tears,
felt no grief in his heart,
and observed mourning without sorrow.
Lacking these three expressions,
he is regarded throughout the State of Lǔ as skilled in managing mourning rites.
Can it be that there are those who gain the reputation without possessing the substance?
I find this truly strange."
【一】【疏】His surname was Mèngsūn,
and his given name was Cái,
a virtuous man of Lǔ.
He embodied the singular Way of non-action,
understood the non-duality of life and death,
thus his actions remained within worldly norms,
while his mind roamed beyond material concerns.
During the mourning period for his mother,
he observed all ritual formalities without omission,
his dignified demeanor was composed and elegant,
displaying profound filial appearance;
yet his tears were not torrential,
his heart held no grief,
and his voice expressed no sorrow.
Lacking these three manifestations,
he could not be called a filial son in name,
yet throughout his hometown and state,
all praised him,
saying his conduct during mourning deeply embodied the principles of ritual propriety.
【Explanation】"Mèngsūn Cái" Lǐ Yí says:
Descendant of the Three Huán,
Cái is his name.
Cuī says:
Cái,
sometimes written as Niú.
◎Lǐ Zhēn says:
Taking "excelling in handling mourning" as a sentence break,
the meaning of the text is incomplete,
and it seems awkward in expression.
The three characters "gài Lǔ guó" below should be connected to the preceding part to form a sentence,
and should not be linked with the following "gù yǒu yún yún" to form a sentence.
Here "gài" has the same meaning as in the chapter "Yìng Dì Wáng" where it says "his achievements covered the world,"
meaning that Mèngsūn Cái was renowned for excelling in handling mourning and his fame covered the state of Lǔ.
The "Ěryǎ Shì Yán" says:
Yǎn,
means to cover.
The "Xiǎo Ěryǎ Guǎng Gǔ" says:
Gài,
means to cover.
The "Shì Míng Shì Yán Yǔ" says:
Gài,
means to surpass.
All convey the idea of rising above others,
which is the meaning of the character "gài" here.
【二】【注】The State of Lǔ observed their rituals,
while Yán Huí discerned their hearts.
【Commentary】The word "gài" (蓋) is
a particle used to begin a sentence.
Weeping, wearing mourning garments and hempen bands,
he followed the customary rites of the mundane world;
yet his heart held no grief,
aligning with the transcendent state of detachment.
The people of Lǔ (魯) observed his outward demeanor,
hence he gained a reputation for being skilled at mourning;
but Yánzǐ (顏子) discerned his inner heart,
knowing there was no genuine depth of filial piety.
This is why, upon meeting Mèngsūn Cái (孟孫才),
he immediately felt doubt and astonishment.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character 處.
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, 壹 is written as 一.
Zhòngní said:
"Mèngsūnshì has fully grasped it,
having advanced to understanding.
Only, he could not achieve simplicity,
yet he had already attained some simplicity.
Mèngsūnshì does not know the reason for life,
nor the reason for death;
he does not know what to approach first,
nor what to approach later;
as if transforming into things,
he awaits the transformations he does not know!
Moreover, just when about to transform,
how does one know it is not transformation?
Just when not transforming,
how does one know transformation has already occurred?
I and you specifically,
are we not those who have not yet awakened from the dream?
Furthermore, he has a startling form but no harmed heart,
has a temporary dwelling but no emotional death.
Mèngsūnshì alone is awakened;
when others weep, he weeps too—
this is the reason for his suchness.
One by one.
Moreover, we all speak of "my self" in mutual interaction,
but how can we know that what I call "my self" truly is?
Furthermore, you may dream of being a bird soaring in the sky,
or dream of being a fish diving into the depths.
Do we not know whether the one speaking now,
is the awakened one,
or the dreaming one?
Reaching comfort does not wait for laughter,
offering laughter does not wait for arrangement.
Let things take their course and follow transformation,
then you will enter the vast oneness of heaven.
【一】【注】To exhaust the principles of life and death,
and to respond appropriately to both internal and external circumstances,
one acts in accordance with the movement of Heaven,
which is not matched by mere knowledge.
【Commentary】Advancement means
transcending.
Mèngsūnshì delved into the root of sorrow and joy,
thus he had neither joy nor sorrow;
he exhausted the source of life and death,
thus he forgot both life and death.
Since the essence and its manifestations are unfathomable,
he could harmonize what is internal and external appropriately;
responding to things without a deliberate mind,
how could he be matched by those who rely on knowledge!
【Explanation】"Yìng" as in response and interaction.
【二】【Note】When discerning life and death yet failing to grasp their distinction,
it is like the four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, and summer—merely proceeding in their course.
【Commentary】Life and death are like the four seasons,
comparable to their cycle,
thus Mèng Sūn, in his selection,
could not discern their difference.
【Three】【Annotations】Having simplified yet not attained,
thus there is no unease,
no unease,
hence one does not let the concepts of life and death affect the mind but entrusts them to natural transformation.
【Commentary】Although there is still some selection and discrimination,
ultimately one does not perceive the distinction between life and death,
thus one can remain tranquil amidst transformations without letting sorrow or joy affect the heart.
【Four】【Annotation】Find contentment in whatever one encounters.
【Five】【Annotation】Not contrary to transformation.
【Commentary】"First" means
birth.
"After" means
death.
"As if" means
to follow.
Since one is unified with life and death,
therefore there is neither departure nor approach;
being in harmony with transformation,
thus one follows transformation to become one with all things.
【Six】【Annotation】Life and death revolve endlessly,
becoming one with transformation.
One even forgets the knowledge possessed in the present moment;
how could one needlessly worry about the unknown yet to come?
【Commentary】The transformations of the unknown,
refer to events yet to unfold in the future.
Cease,
means to stop.
The life of the present moment,
is already forgotten and let go of;
how much more so the transformations of the future,
why worry about them in advance!
If one uses the mind to anticipate,
it is better to stop and not act.
【Seven】【Comment】Having transformed and come to life,
how can one know the time before birth!
Not having transformed and dying,
how can one know what comes after death!
Therefore, there is nothing to avoid or pursue,
but to journey together with transformation (two).
【Commentary】Now we are in the very process of transformation as humans,
how can we know about events before transformation in the past!
Being alive and not yet transformed when we die,
how can we know about what happens after death!
We should simply follow reason and move forward,
journeying together with transformation,
without troubling ourselves in life to worry about death,
or pointlessly forming attachments and aversions.
【Textual Explanation】"How to know" is pronounced as wū,
the same below.
"How to know" is pronounced as yú qián fǎn.
All below are the same.
【八】【注】Death and life are like waking and dreaming.
Now in a dream, one believes oneself to be awake;
thus, there is no way to prove that being awake is not a dream.
If there is no way to prove that being awake is not a dream,
then there is also no way to prove that life is not death.
Death and life, waking and dreaming—
their true nature is unknown.
When encountering any state,
one should find contentment in it.
Why worry about one state while being in another!
【Commentary】Dreams occur during the time of deep slumber,
while awakening is the moment of clear understanding.
Even Confucius and Yán Huí,
constrained by the doctrines of reputation and morality,
were lost in the profound dream,
failing to comprehend life and death,
never having awakened even briefly.
【Transcription】"Jué zhě" is pronounced as gǔ xiào fǎn.
This applies to the annotations and all that follow.
【Nine】【Annotation】It is because the three transformations manifest as the startling movements of form,
therefore, one does not let life and death burden or trouble their heart.
【Commentary】That Mèngsūn,
being oblivious to the transformations,
mistakenly perceived life and death as mere physical disturbances,
ultimately harboring neither sorrow nor joy to impair his spirit.
【Explanatory Text】"Hài xíng" is read as written.
Cuī (presumably a commentator) uses "hāi",
saying:
It means having the form of an infant.
【一０】【注】They regard the changes of the physical form as the daily renewal of a temporary dwelling,
and in their true feelings, they do not consider it death.
【Commentary】Dàn,
means daily renewal.
A dwelling,
is the abode of the spirit.
It is the physical form's transformation that constitutes the daily renewal of the dwelling,
while its spiritual nature remains serene and detached,
ultimately free from the burdens of life and death.
【Explanatory Text】"Dàn zhái" are both read as they are normally pronounced.
Wǎng's commentary states,
it changes from morning to evening,
and "zhái" refers to the dwelling of the spirit.
Lǐ's version writes it as "dá huǎng",
with the first character pronounced as "dán mò fǎn",
and the second as "zhì zhà fǎn",
explaining:
it describes a startled and regretful appearance.
Cuī's version writes it as "dá zhái".
"Dá"
means startled.
【一一】【注】The one who is constantly aware,
neither goes nor resists,
thus when others weep, they weep too,
for this is precisely what is appropriate for them (4).
【Commentary】Mèngsūn understood the unity of life and death,
dwelling alone yet awakened,
responding to both internal and external realms,
without contradicting human principles.
When others wept, he wept as well,
naturally following what was appropriate in accordance with things.
【Explanation】"Therefore, it is" — In Cuǐ Zǐzhěn's version, "乃" is written as "惡".
【一二】【Note】Birth and death, transformation and change—
all are myself.
Since all are myself,
what have I to lose?
Never having lost myself,
what have I to grieve about (5)!
Without resistance,
thus when others weep, I weep too;
without grief,
thus I weep but do not sorrow.
【Commentary】In my life and in my death,
both are me,
nothing has ever not been me,
so what have I lost!
If one considers attachment to self as the focus,
then where is it not me!
【一三】【Note】There is nothing that is not us,
thus mysteriously uniting the external and internal,
permeating through ancient and modern times,
renewing daily with transformation,
how could one know where we exist!
【Commentary】Yōng means
constant.
Ordinary people,
with their shallow and narrow understanding,
how could they know that what I call "nowhere is not myself"!
Even if there are countless changes and transformations,
I am always present,
whether the new self or the old self—
what is there to rejoice in or despise!
【Transcription】"Yōng jù" is read as qí shù fǎn.
The same applies to the following chapter.
【一四】【Note】This means being at ease no matter where one goes.
【15】【Comment】When in a dream one believes oneself to be awake,
how can one know that the present is not a dream,
or how can one be sure it is not wakefulness?
The transformation between dreaming and waking
is without fixed boundaries,
thus the change between life and death
is never something to cling to with regret.
【Commentary】Liè means
"to arrive at."
Moreover, being a fish or a bird,
they follow their nature in carefree wandering;
whether facing death or life,
they are naturally self-content.
Since fish and birds have no superiority or inferiority,
how can life and death be a matter of victory or defeat to bind them?
Mèngsūn wonderfully understood this source,
and thus never concerned himself with it.
Furthermore, one does not know whether the current discussion about fish and birds
is a debate in a state of awakening,
or a discourse within a dream?
When one is in a dream,
one believes oneself to be awake;
those who are now awake,
how can they not be in a dream!
Thus, it is known that awakening, dreaming, life, and death
cannot be fixed.
【16】【Comment】When all one's actions are in harmony,
one forgets about harmony itself,
thus not even reaching the point of laughter.
"Pushing aside" refers to
the concept of shifting and transforming.
According to ritual, weeping must convey sorrow,
and offering laughter must convey joy.
If sorrow and joy remain in one's heart,
then one cannot shift and transform along with harmony.
Now, Mèngsūn is constantly in harmony,
so he weeps without sorrow,
progressing together with transformation.
【Commentary】Zào means
"to arrive at."
Xiàn means
"goodness."
Pái means
"to shift and adapt."
When one arrives everywhere and is at ease,
this itself is ease;
how could constant ease require joy and laughter to then be considered happiness!
If one depends on good deeds to move oneself and then feel at ease,
this then is an inability to follow change and accept transformation,
to shift and adapt with all things.
Now, Mèngsūn was constantly at ease,
hence he wept without sorrow.
【Explanatory Text】"Zào shì": qī bào fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
"Xiàn xiào": Xiàng (Xiàng Xiù) says:
Xiàn,
means good.
Wáng (Wáng Sì) says:
means to manifest,
when the mind finds comfort,
it manifests in laughter,
hence called "xiàn xiào."
◎ Jiāshìfù (Guō Sōngnián) says:
"Zào shì" means
to seek comfort through the mind alone,
where both speech and laughter are forgotten.
"Xiàn xiào" means
to take laughter as joy alone,
where all resistance is transformed.
Exerting the utmost force of resistance yet serenely accepting it,
exhausting the function of change yet transcending and departing from it,
thus one wanders beyond all things and becomes one with Heaven.
"Jí pái": pí jiē fǎn.
"Bì lè": yīn luò.
The same below.
【一七】【Note】Being at ease with the shifts and going along with the transformations,
thus one enters into the silent vastness and becomes one with Heaven.
From this point upward,
reaching to Zǐsì,
their ultimate attainment is the same.
The forms of mourning they observed differed,
hence their expressions of song and lament varied.
【Commentary】Being at ease in every situation,
thus peacefully accepting the shifts and changes,
there is never a moment that is not truly oneself,
yet moving along with the transformations.
Only such a person
can enter the wondrous gate of vast emptiness,
the single path of naturalness.
【Transcription】"Liáo" is also written as Liào in some versions,
pronounced with the initial L and the rhyme iāo.
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as liàng jiù.
In Cuī's edition, "Tiān Yī" is written as "Before the enemy arrives, there's no time to laugh,"
"Before offering mustard, there's no time for [gap],"
"Arrangements and the transformations of nature do not reach the subtle,"
"The subtle does not reach the majestic and surging,"
"The majestic and surging does not reach the bamboo divination,"
"Bamboo divination then enters into the profound Tiān Yī."
"The above" is pronounced as shí zhǎng.
【Collation】(1) In Zhū Guìyào's edition, "nǎi" is written as "yíng".
(2) In the Shidetang edition, "wǎng" is written as "shēng".
(3) In the Shidetang edition, "yǐ" is written as "sì".
(4) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, the annotation lacks the initial character "fū"
and the final character "yě".
(5) In the Shidetang edition, "shì wú" is written as "zì wú",
and both instances of "zāi" are written as "yǐ".
Yì'érzǐ went to see Xǔ Yóu.
Xǔ Yóu said:
"What did Yáo impart to you?"
【一】【Note】Zī means
to provide relief.
【Commentary】Yì'ér was
a worthy man of antiquity.
Zī means
to provide assistance.
Yì'ér first paid homage to Emperor Yáo,
and later visited Zhòngwǔ.
The question was asked:
"Emperor Yáo, being a great sage
of exceedingly high virtue,
since you have paid him homage,
what methods of respectful instruction and provision of assistance
did you receive? Pray, relate them."
【Explanation】"Yì'ér Zǐ" Lǐ Yún:
A virtuous scholar.
"Zī Rǔ" zī,
means to provide.
Yì'ér Zǐ said:
"Yáo told me:
'You must personally practice benevolence and righteousness and clearly articulate right and wrong.
【一】【疏】Gōng,
means the body.
Benevolence entails kindness and nurturing all things,
righteousness involves decisive judgment and rectifying wrongs,
affirming what is right means clearly rewarding good deeds,
and rejecting what is wrong means explicitly punishing evil.
These four principles
are esteemed in human relations.
You must personally practice them,
and also clearly articulate them to others.
This is the meaning conveyed in Yáo's teachings.
Xǔ Yóu said:
"So why have you come?
Since Yáo has already branded you with benevolence and righteousness,
and cut off your nose with right and wrong,
how will you roam the path of free and unfettered wandering?"
【One】【Explanation】而，
is you.
奚，
means why.
軹，
is a particle in speech.
Yáo will teach the harm of punishment through actions to you,
the scars are already severe,
why have you come again?
【Explanatory Text】"Wéi zhǐ" is read as "shì" in reverse,
Guō reads it as "rěn" in reverse.
Cuī says:
Zhǐ,
is a particle.
Lǐ says:
It means "correct."
【Two】【Annotation】This means he will bring harm upon himself through penal instruction,
unable to roam again in the realm of self-attainment,
the path of unbound freedom.
【Commentary】Tattooing (qíng),
is carving the forehead.
Cutting off the nose (yì),
is severing the nose.
Reckless and unbridled (zì suī),
means acting without restraint.
Moving and shifting (zhuǎn xǐ),
refers to transformation and change.
The path (tú),
is the Way.
Now, benevolence, righteousness, right and wrong,
damage the true nature,
their harm
is comparable to punishment and execution.
Since you have been tattooed and had your nose cut off by Yáo,
constrained in your innate disposition,
how can you again roam freely and contentedly,
unfettered and unrestrained,
calmly and comfortably following the path of change?
This means you are no longer able to be so.
【Transcription】"Qíng": pronounced as qí jīng fǎn.
"Yì": pronounced as yú qì fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
To destroy the Way and virtue in the name of benevolence and righteousness,
is it not like tattooing (qíng)!
To break the profound unity by distinguishing right and wrong,
is it not like cutting off the nose (yì)!
"Yáo dàng": Wáng Yún says:
Unrestrained and free.
"Zì": pronounced as qī zī fǎn,
or as the common reading.
"Suī": Guō and Lǐ Yún say:
pronounced as xǔ wéi fǎn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as xǔ bí fǎn.
Both Lǐ and Wáng say:
zì suī,
means a self-satisfied appearance.
"Fù yóu": pronounced as fú yòu fǎn.
The same applies below.
Yì'ér Zǐ said:
"Even so,
I wish to wander within its borders."
【一】【注】I dare not seek again to tread the middle path,
but only wish to wander by its hedges.
【Commentary】Although I have suffered this impairment and injury,
my heart of hopeful anticipation remains undiminished.
I dare no longer tread the central path,
but wish to walk along the byways of the way.
【Translated Text】"Its Fan" is pronounced as fǔ fán fǎn,
Lǐ reads it as fán.
Sīmǎ and Xiàng both say:
It means cliff.
Cuī says:
It means boundary.
Xǔ Yóu said:
"Not so.
The blind have no way to share in the beauty of eyebrows, eyes, and complexion,
the sightless have no way to share in the sight of blues, yellows, and the patterns of ceremonial robes."
【一】【疏】A blind person,
has eyes but cannot see things;
a sightless person,
has eyes without any slit, like drum skin.
The pattern shaped like an axe is called fǔ,
two opposing 'jǐ' shapes are called fú.
As for blind and sightless people,
their eyes are already impaired,

It's like Yì encountering Yáo's tattooing and nose-cutting punishment,
where his emotions and intellect were already harmed,
how could he then love and admire profound mysteries,
or observe and appreciate all wonders!

Yì'ér Zǐ said:
"Wú Zhuāng lost her beauty,
Jù Liáng lost his strength,
Huángdì lost his wisdom—
all this happened during the forging and hammering.
How do I know the Creator will not erase my tattoos and restore my severed nose,
enabling me to ride complete and follow you, sir?"
【One】【Annotation】It is said that all things under heaven
are not necessarily self-formed;
according to the principle of nature,
there are also those that require forging and tempering to become vessels.
Therefore, these three individuals
all, upon hearing the Way, forgot their respective pursuits.
These are all metaphorical expressions
meant to dispel the burdens of action and artifice.
【Commentary】Wú Zhuāng,
a beauty of ancient times,
for having heard the Way,
no longer adorned herself,
and naturally forgot her own beauty.
Jù Liáng,
a man of great strength in ancient times,
for having heard the Way and embraced femininity,
thus did not flaunt his strength.
Huángdì,
also known as Xuānyuán,
possessed sagely wisdom,
yet also for having heard the Way,
was able to forget and relinquish his knowledge.
Lú,
means furnace.
Chuí,
means forging.
The three individuals mentioned above,
all because they had heard the Way,
then forgot their original pursuits to align with their true nature,
just like worldly utensils,
which rely on the furnace and forging to become functional.
Now, why not follow the principle of spontaneity,
and let the master instruct me,
to accomplish the Way?
Thus, it is understood that the natural creation of things,
within the furnace and forging process,
implies the meaning of cultivation, learning, and refinement.
【Translated Text】"Wú Zhuāng and Jù Liáng" Simǎ comments:
Both are personal names.
Lǐ comments:
Wú Zhuāng,
means without adornment.
Jù Liáng,
means strong and forceful.
"Lú" is pronounced as lú.
"Chuí" is also written as chuí in another version.
Xú gives the pronunciation as zhī shuì fǎn,
and also zhī fǎn,
another pronunciation is shí fǎn.
Lǐ comments:
Chuí,

bent iron used for blowing air into the fire.
Cuī comments:
Lú is called a wèng (jar).
Chuí should be read as zhuì.
Between the lú and zhuì,
it refers to a small space.
Zhuì is pronounced as zhàng wèi fǎn.
"Duàn" is pronounced as dīng luàn fǎn.
【二】【Note】To follow one's nature and proceed directly
is natural;
to proceed and harm one's nature,
yet to be able to reform after harming it,
is also natural.
How can one know that my natural course should not cease to mend the tattooed face and restore the cut-off nose,
and ride on the achievable path to follow the Master?
Yet to wish to abandon this and not inform,
I fear is not the ultimate intent of the Creator.
【Commentary】"Creation"
is akin to the transformative process of nature.
Although I have been harmed in my innate disposition by concepts of benevolence, righteousness, right and wrong,
how can I know that within the workings of creation,
it does not restore what was cut off and heal the tattooed marks,
allowing me to reform and renew myself,
so that I may ride upon the path that can be perfected,
and follow you, Master, to seek improvement?
Yet you wish to abandon me without instruction,
which I fear goes against the will of creation.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: "Ride upon"
means to carry.
"Perfect"

This is similar in meaning to the line in the poem, "The ceremony is already complete."
Tattooing and cutting off the nose leave the body incomplete;
healing and restoring them
make it whole again.
This means that the Creator has allowed me to meet you, Master;
how can I know it is not so that I may carry a perfected form to follow you?
This interpretation also draws from Xuān's explanation,
which is more profound than Guō's annotation.

Xǔ Yóu said:
"Alas!
It cannot be known.
I shall speak to you of its general outline.
My teacher!
My teacher!
He blends all things without being righteous,
His bounty extends to all ages without being benevolent,
He is older than the highest antiquity without being aged,
He covers and carries heaven and earth, carves and shapes all forms without being skillful.
This is what he wanders in."
【一】【疏】Alas,
it is a sigh of exclamation.
The profound mystery of the ultimate Way,
transcends words and images,
and cannot be fathomed by the mind's reasoning.
Hence, the sigh expresses that it is unknowable.
Since you have earnestly sought further understanding,
it is not fitting to remain silent.
Although it cannot be fully expressed in words,
I shall outline it for you in broad terms.
【Explanation Text】"Yuē yī" Xú pronounces as yī.
Lǐ says:
It is a sighing sound.
Cuī says:
It means chaos.
The original text also writes it as yì,
with the same pronunciation.
Another reading follows the character's usual pronunciation,
meaning to call by the name yì.
"Wǒ wèi" is read with wèi in the falling tone.
The same applies to the annotations.
【二】【注】All these occur naturally,
with no deliberate affection involved in them;
where then can benevolence and righteousness find a place to lodge?
【Commentary】My master is
the ultimate Way.
Yet the ultimate Way cannot be known by the mind;
I shall briefly explain its essence to you:
it is indeed my master.
To shatter,
means to break into pieces.
Just as when the white autumn frost descends,
it shatters and scatters all things—
does it intentionally sever and act out of righteousness?
When the verdant spring's harmonious energy
nurtures and gives birth to all things,
does it intentionally show affection and act out of benevolence?
It is simply so without being made so.
Thus, Xǔ Yóu took the ultimate Way as his master;
since the ultimate Way is as such,
why should you personally adhere to benevolence and righteousness?
This briefly conveys the idea and explains the method to cease branding and restore the nose.
【Transcription】"" is read as zǐ xī fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means "to break into pieces."
◎Lú Wénchāo states:

【Three】【Annotation】Renewing daily.
【Transcription】"Cháng yú" is read as dīng zhàng fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】It is natural,
hence not artful.
【Commentary】Before all phenomena existed,
the Dao was already present.
It possesses complete wisdom and virtue,
hence it is figuratively described as ancient, though in reality it has no age.
Since there is no age,
how can there be oldness?
The intent is to clarify that without being ancient, it is ancient;
without being old, it is old.
Therefore, it is older than the most ancient times yet cannot be considered old.
Although heaven covers and earth supports all things,
they take the Dao as their source.
All forms are carved,
all rely on creation's transformations,
and all receive from nature.
Thus, the concept of craftsmanship vanishes.
Since there is no oldness, no craftsmanship,
no right and no wrong,
what is there for you to articulate clearly?
【Five】【Annotation】He wanders in non-action and learns from having no teacher.
【Commentary】What our master contemplated in his mind,
was merely as stated here.
This then summarizes the meaning of our master's previous teachings as being correct.
Yán Huí said:
"Huí has improved."
【一】【注】It is by diminishing that one benefits.
【Commentary】Yánzǐ received instruction from Master Kǒng,
embraced the teachings and inquired about the Way,
felt his own progress and improvement,
and presented his understanding to his teacher.
Diminishing leads to the benefit of emptiness,
thus regarding diminishment as gain.
Zhòngní said:
"What do you mean?"
【一】【疏】Having already spoken of benefits,
what meaning is intended?
He said:
"Huí has forgotten benevolence and righteousness."
【一】【疏】Forgetting the benevolence of universal love,
abandoning the righteousness of discerning wrongs,
what is spoken of as beneficial,
is this not referring to this!
He said:
"It is acceptable,
but not yet perfect."
【一】【注】Benevolence is the trace of universal love;
righteousness is the merit of accomplishing things.
Loving is not benevolence itself,
yet the trace of benevolence manifests through it;
accomplishing is not righteousness itself,
yet the merit of righteousness becomes apparent.
To hold fast to benevolence and righteousness
is insufficient to understand that love and benefit arise without conscious intent,
hence it is acceptable to forget them.
However, merely forgetting merit and traces
still falls short of profound comprehension.
【Commentary】Having forgotten benevolence and righteousness,
one gradually approaches reason;
yet the liberation of the mind remains shallow,
hence it is still incomplete.
【Explanation】"Gōng xiàn" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
The same applies to the following text.
Another day,
we met again,
and he said:
"Huí has improved."
【One】【Memorial】Another day,
means a different day.
Merely understanding renewal,
time will bring another encounter.
What is said about progress,

【Translated Text】"On another day" — the Cuī version reads as a different day.
The same applies below.
"See again" — read fú yòu fǎn.

He said:

【一】【疏】Rites are the chief cause of desolation and chaos,

He said:

means to destroy and abandon.
黜，

【二】【注】As for sitting in oblivion,
what is there that is not forgotten!
One not only forgets the traces,
but also forgets that which creates the traces.
Inwardly, one becomes unaware of one's own body;
outwardly, one no longer recognizes the existence of heaven and earth.
Only then, in vast emptiness, does one unite with the transformations and become unobstructed in all things.
【Commentary】"Great Penetration"
means the Great Way.
The Way is capable of penetrating and generating all things,
hence it is called the Great Penetration.
Externally, it involves detaching from the physical form,
recognizing everything as illusory,
this explains the "shedding of limbs and body."
Internally, it entails removing conscious thought,
becoming placid and without knowledge,
this explains the "abolishing of intelligence."
Then, like a withered tree and dead ashes,
one merges obscurely with the Great Way,

when transformation occurs, there is no constancy

Ér,

Humbly stepping back to yield,

Zǐyú and Zǐsāng were friends,
and there was continuous rain for ten days.
Zǐyú said:
"Zǐsāng must be in distress!"
He wrapped up some rice and went to feed him.
Arriving at Zǐsāng's door,
he heard something like singing and something like weeping,
as Zǐsāng played the qin and said:
"Was it my father?
Or my mother?
Heaven?
Or man?"
His voice seemed unable to bear the emotion as he hurriedly uttered these verses.
【一】【注】These two individuals assist each other through non-action.
Now, bringing rice to eat together
is simply following the natural principle and acting spontaneously,
not doing so for each other before going.
【Commentary】Rain lasting more than three days is called a prolonged downpour.
Dài,
means nearly.
Zǐsāng was impoverished,
and with this continuous rain,
he was close to starvation and illness.
This matter did not raise doubts in the friendship beyond worldly affairs,
acting according to principle,
even if bringing food,
it was not out of a sense of mutual obligation.
【Explanatory Text】"Lín yǔ" is also written as 淋,

"Guǒ" is pronounced as guǒ.
"Sì" is pronounced as sì.

【Èr Shū】's appointment,

These are the words of song and lament.
Unable to bear this action,
and then suddenly composing poetry in verse.

Zǐyú entered,
and said:
"Your singing of the poems,
why is it like this?"
【一】【Note】It was because he suspected it had feelings,
that he hastened out to distance himself from it.
【Commentary】Unified in life and death,
forgetting sorrow and joy,
[mutually] in non-mutuality,
a friendship beyond the mundane world.
Now you sing poetry,
seemingly harboring resentment,
hence I entered the door in surprise,
asking for the reason behind it.
He said:
"I have pondered over what brought me to such an extreme state but could not find the answer.
Could it be that my parents wished me to be poor?
Heaven covers all without partiality,
earth supports all without bias.
Could it be that heaven and earth deliberately made me poor?
I sought for the cause but found none.
Yet that I have reached such an extreme state
must be due to fate, indeed!"
【一】【注】It speaks of all things being spontaneous,
without any deliberate action.
【Commentary】Parents lovingly nurture,
not wishing their children to suffer hunger or cold;
heaven and earth are impartial,
how could they single me out for poverty!
Reflecting on the governing forces,
all are natural;
seeking the origins,
I find no trace or sign.
That I have reached such dire straits
is all due to the fate bestowed upon me—
so what is there to regret!
【一】【注】One who is without deliberate mind and lets things transform naturally,
should be the ruler.
【Explanation】Cuī Zǐ states:
He practices the teaching without words,
causing all under heaven to consider themselves oxen and horses,
and is fit to be the one who rules as emperor.
Niè Quē asked Wáng Ní,
four questions and four times he did not know.
Niè Quē then leaped up with great joy,
and went to tell Pú Yīzǐ.
【One】【Exposition】Four questions and four unknowns,
referring to the four inquiries in the "Discussion on Making All Things Equal" chapter.
The way of emperors and kings,
is best achieved by forgetting knowledge,
hence this principle is placed at the beginning of the chapter.
Lǎozi said: "Governing the state without cunning is the state's virtue."
【Interpretation】"Niè Quē": "Niè" is pronounced with the fifth tone.
"Quē" is pronounced with a high falling tone.
"Wáng Ní": "Ní" is pronounced with the second tone.
"Four Questions and Four Ignorances" Xiang Xiu commented:
This matter is found in the "Discussion on Making All Things Equal."
Púyīzǐ said:
"And only now do you know it?
Yǒuyúshì falls short of Tàishì.
Yǒuyúshì,
still harbored benevolence to win people over;
he did gain people,
but never emerged from what is not human.
Tàishì,
in sleep, was serene and unhurried,
upon waking, was simple and unadorned;
at one time considering himself a horse,
at another considering himself an ox;
his knowledge was genuine and trustworthy,
his virtue profoundly authentic,
and never entered into what is not human."
【一】【疏】Púyīzǐ,
a virtuous man during Yáo's time,
at the age of eight,
Shùn took him as his teacher,
but he declined the offer to abdicate the throne,
that is, Bèiyīzǐ.
Nièquē grasped the profound essence of unknowing,
and leaped with joy,
hurried to tell Púyīzǐ,
recounting Wángní's deep meaning.
Púyī was a great sage beyond the mundane world,
who comprehended the ultimate way of forgetting words,
the principle of unknowing has long been firm,
and do you now know it?
【Interpretation】"Pú Yī Zǐ": Shī Zǐ states:
Pú Yī was eight years old
when Shùn offered him the empire.
Cuī states:
That is, Bèi Yī,
the teacher of Wáng Ní.
Huái Nán Zǐ states:
Niè Quē inquired about the Way from Bèi Yī.
【二】【注】Both the Yǒuyú shì and the Tài shì,
are merely traces of worldly affairs,
not the means by which these traces are made.
The means by which traces are made
leave no traces themselves,
so how could the world name them?
Since they have never been named,
how could there be any victory or defeat among them?
However, that which leaves no trace
rides upon the myriad changes,
treads through ten thousand ages.
As the world has times of peace and peril,
there are traces that cannot keep pace.
【Commentary】Yǒuyúshì refers to
Shùn.
Tàishì is
Tàihào Fúxī.
In the era of the Three Sovereigns,
the customs were pure and harmonious;
during the time of the Five Emperors,
the social atmosphere became contentious and competitive.
Contentiousness and competition led to the use of cunning to nurture things,
while purity and harmony allowed for following authenticity to govern the world.
The meaning of falling short
can be understood from this.
【Explanation】"Tàishì": Sīmǎ (commentator) says:
an ancient emperor.
Cuī (commentator) says:
an emperor.
Lǐ (commentator) says:
Dàtíngshì;
also says:
an unnamed ruler.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: The Lùshǐ, Qiánjì 7, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
an ancient emperor,
an unnamed designation.
Slightly different from what is quoted in the explanation.
【三】【注】To regard those one favors as the right people,
and those one dislikes as the wrong people,
is to confine oneself solely within the realm of right and wrong.
One who can transcend the domain of the wrong people
is sure to enter a state where there are no wrong people.
Thus, there is neither gain nor loss,
neither approval nor disapproval—
how could this be merely a matter of concealing benevolence to win people over!
【Commentary】Shùn,
harbored benevolence and righteousness within,
sought to win over scholars and commoners,
aiming to gain the hearts of the people.
This was not a state of forgetting all concerns,
but rather naturally uniting the world,
thus not yet stepping out of the realm of right and wrong.
There are also versions that use the character "zāng."
Zāng
means goodness.
Being adept in benevolence and righteousness
refers to one who seeks to win people's hearts.
【Explanation】"Cáng Rén": read as "cái gāng" with a falling tone.
Cuī's commentary states:
It means harboring benevolent intentions to win people over.
The original text also uses "Zāng",
read with a falling tone as "gāng",
meaning good.
Jiǎn Wén's version is the same.
"Yǐ Yào": read as "yī yáo" with a falling tone.
The annotation is the same.

When one's personal views persist,

Emerging from the state of non-human,
one forgets the distinction of non-self.
Entering into the state of non-human,
where the distinctions between self and others are both forgotten,
one does not respond with the mind.
Being a horse or an ox,
it is not only forgetting others,
but also forgetting oneself.
"Suǒ Hào": read as "hū bào" with a falling tone.
"Suǒ Wù": read as "wū lù" with a falling tone.
"Zhī Jìng": pronounced as "jìng".

Yūyū,

does he govern from the outside?

to command it to bear the burden

its meaning is not that of 臬,

One version writing it as 寱

Lǎo Dān said:

His achievements cover the world yet seem not to come from himself,

【One】【Annotation】If there were no enlightened kings in the world,
then none would be able to attain self-realization.
Enabling people to achieve self-realization,
is truly the merit of the enlightened kings.
However, their merit lies in governing through non-action and entrusting the world to its people.
When all under heaven can take responsibility for themselves,
it thus seems as if it were not the achievement of the enlightened kings.
【Commentary】When the sage governs,
his achievements match the transformative power of creation,
his protection is as vast as the profound heavens,
his support encompasses the solid earth,
yet he does not claim credit upon achieving success,
for it is not done by his own doing.
【二】【注】The enlightened kings all comply with the inherent nature of things,
so everyone says, "I am as I am,"

causing them to abandon evil;
lending and borrowing all things,
bestowing upon them blessings and goodness;
yet the mysterious work subtly permeates,
its daily use goes unnoticed,

Then Liezi, considering himself as having not yet begun learning, returned home,
and for three years did not go out.
He cooked for his wife,
fed pigs as if feeding people.
In affairs, he had no personal involvement,
carved and polished, he returned to simplicity,
solidly alone, he stood with his form.
Amidst complexity, he remained sealed off,
and in this oneness, he ended his days.
【One】【Memorial】After Jí Xián fled,
Liè Zǐ then realized his own delusion,
and began to perceive the profundity of Hú Qiū's Way,
while the divine sorcerer's arts were shallow.
Acknowledging his lack of learning,
he begged to retreat and return,
to practice the崇尚 of non-action,
and devote himself to the mysterious endeavor.
【二】【Note】Forgetting distinctions of noble and base.
【Commentary】Without leaving for three years,
he distanced himself from worldly affairs.
He cooked fires for his wife,
forgetting glory and disgrace.
He ate from the same trough as pigs,
treating purity and filth as equal.
【Textual Explanation】"For his" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
"Wife cooks" is read as qī pàn fǎn.
"Feeds pigs" is pronounced as sì.
The same applies below.
【Three】【Annotations】It all depends on what one encounters.
【Explanation】Enlightened to the ultimate principle,
one thus equalizes self and others;
involved in worldly affairs,
there is neither intimacy nor distance.
【Four】【Annotation】Discard the superficial and adopt the substantial.
【Commentary】All endeavors of carving and ornate adornment,
are entirely discarded;
directly embracing authenticity and spontaneity,
one returns to the way of simplicity and plainness.
【Transcription】"Diāozhuó": zhú jiǎo fǎn.
"Qùhuá": qiāng lǚ fǎn.
【五】【Note】External adornments are removed.
【Commentary】Lump-like,
describes the appearance of being without emotion.
Externally eliminating ornamentation,
internally dismissing mind and intellect,
the form of withered wood,
lump-like and without a counterpart.
【Transcription】"Kuài rán" Xú kǔ guài fǎn,
yòu kǔ duì fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Although in motion, the true essence does not disperse.
【Commentary】To guard means
to preserve.
Although one may again traverse the worldly turmoil,
harmonizing one's light while interacting with others,
one preserves the true foundation,
steadfast and unwavering.
【Explanatory Text】"Fen er" is pronounced with the characters "fang" and "yun" as the reverse.
Cui states:
It means a disordered appearance.
"Feng zai" in Cui's version is written as "rong",
stating:
Feng rong,
means scattered and disordered.
◎ Lǐ Zhēn says:
Fen er feng zai,
in the "Yellow Emperor" chapter of the Liezi, it is written as ● ran er feng rong.
According to this, feng rong is correct.
The six sentences are all rhyming verses.
The two lines about feeding pigs,
"ren" and "qin" rhyme.
The two lines about carving,
"pu" and "li" rhyme.
The two lines about fen er,
"rong" and "zhong" rhyme.
The character "zai",
is a transcription error.
The following four are also rhyming verses.
Only Cui's version is not mistaken,
and it is the same as the Liezi.
In the "Book of Documents," "gong wu kun zai",
the "Book of Han" quotes it twice as "gong wu kun wo".
This is an example of "wo" being mistaken for "zai".
It is also one piece of evidence.
【Seven】【Annotation】Let each thing reach its own conclusion.
【Commentary】Movement does not violate stillness,
though bustling and confined it may seem;
Response does not depart from truth,
ever embracing the One from beginning to end.
【Collation】（一）Missing text cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, which has the character 然 following (封)〔纷〕.
Another edition reads (粉)〔纷〕而封戎.
Do not be the repository of fame【一】,
do not be the storehouse of schemes【二】;
do not bear the burden of affairs【三】,
do not be the master of knowledge【四】.
Embody the boundless【五】,
and wander in the trackless【六】;
exhaust what you have received from Heaven【七】,
without seeing it as gain【八】,
which is simply emptiness【九】.
The mind of the perfect person is like a mirror【一０】,
neither sending off nor welcoming (一),
responding without storing【一一】,
thus able to overcome things without harm【一二】.
【一】【注】By following things, each thing naturally corresponds to its name.
【Commentary】The corpse,
signifies the master.
When one has even forgotten and discarded the body,
where then shall the name be placed?
Therefore, there is no longer a master of reputation.
【二】【注】Let each thing make its own plans.
【Commentary】Being empty and tranquil, without a mind,
forgetting concerns and letting things take their course,
thus there is no longer any operation of scheming or deliberation in the spiritual chamber.
【Three】【Annotation】Entrust matters to each and let them take responsibility.
【Commentary】Each follows their inherent nature,
allowing things to act spontaneously,
without further intervention in affairs,
employing their own capabilities.
【Four】【Annotation】Without a deliberate mind, all things naturally govern their own awareness.
【Commentary】Forgetting the mind and eliminating thoughts,
greatly harmonizing with all living beings,
ultimately not employing knowledge,
to dominate over things.
【Transcription】"Zhī Zhǔ" is pronounced as (zhī) [zhì] (note 2).
The annotation is the same.
【Five】【Annotation】Because the world acts on its own,
thus, it gallops through all things without exhaustion.
【Commentary】Having embodied the true source,
one can thus unite with the realm of wisdom through profound accord,
hence it is said that all are boundless.
【Six】【Comment】Entrusting things to their nature,
thus leaves no trace.
【Explanation】Zhèn,
means traces.
Although I roam the world,
aiding the common people,
I conceal my traces and hide my light,
thus leaving no trace.
【Explanation】"Wú zhèn" is pronounced as zhí rěn fǎn.
Cuī said:
It is an omen.
【Seven】【Annotation】When sufficient, then stop.
【Commentary】What is endowed by nature,
differs in every single thing,
each fulfills its own capability,
and thus none is considered insufficient.
【Eight】【Annotation】When one sees gain, one does not know when to stop.
【Commentary】What the eyes see,
though seen, is not truly seen;
what is gained within one's allotted portion,
though gained, is not truly gained.
Since there is no deliberate intention in seeing or gaining,
therefore, though one sees and gains, there is no actual seeing or gaining.
【Nine】【Annotation】Without emptiness, one cannot bear the multitude of realities.
【Commentary】To exhaust what is within one's duty without any sense of attainment,
it is simply a matter of being straightforward and open-minded, forgetting desires and letting go of attachments.
【一０】【注】Observing things without personal bias.
【Commentary】When a mirror is hung high in the hall,
it reflects everything that comes before it.
Similarly, the sage responds with emptiness,
embodying the same principle.
【一一】【Note】Respond when approached,
cease when departed.
【Subcommentary】"Accompanying" means
sending off.
While things come and go, the mirror neither welcomes nor sends off,
immediately reflecting what comes,
never concealing anything.
Similarly, the sage's wisdom is empty and concentrated,
illuminating even the darkest corners,
responding when stimulated by things,
yet not responding with deliberate intent.
Since there is neither welcoming nor sending off,
how could there be any intention to conceal or hide!
【Explanation】"Yìng ér bù cáng": read as written.
Some versions also write it as "zāng",
and it is also read according to the written character.
【一二】【Note】Things come and are mirrored,
the mirroring does not use the mind,
thus even with the vastness of the world,
there is no burden of mental fatigue.
【Commentary】All things undergo birth and decay,
yet the mirror neither conceals nor reveals itself,
thus it can constantly reflect things without being harmed by them.
Similarly, the sage's virtue aligns with the two primal forces (heaven and earth),
his brilliance matches the three luminaries (sun, moon, and stars),
his perception illuminates far and wide,
and his embrace covers all without bias.
His mind operates without strain,
hence he suffers no harm,
and because he surpasses worldly matters,
he remains unharmed.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition reads as 'nì'.
(2) The character 'zhì' was amended based on the original version of the commentary and the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) In the Shìdétáng edition, 'nǎi' is written as 'jí'.
(4) The Zhào Jiànyì edition reads as 'lái zhào'.
The Emperor of the Southern Sea was Shū,
the Emperor of the Northern Sea was Hū,
and the Emperor of the Center was Hùndùn.
Shū and Hū from time to time met each other in the territory of Hùndùn,
and Hùndùn treated them very generously.
Shū and Hū discussed how to repay Hùndùn's kindness,
saying:
"All people have seven openings for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing,
but this one alone has none.
Let us try boring some for him."
They bored one opening each day,
and on the seventh day, Hùndùn died.
The South Sea is a realm of brightness,
thus Shū represents existence.
The North is a domain of obscurity and darkness,
thus Hū represents non-existence.
The center is neither north nor south,
so Hùndùn represents neither non-existence nor existence.
【Text】"Shū" is pronounced as shū.
Lǐ Yí says:
It metaphorizes having form.
"Hū" Lǐ Yí says:
It metaphorizes being formless.
"Hún" is pronounced with the hú běn fǎn.
"Dùn" is pronounced with the tú běn fǎn.
Cuī Shí says:
Húndùn,
has no orifices.
Lǐ Yí says:
The clear and turbid are not yet separated.
This metaphorizes nature.
Jiǎn Wén says:
Shū and Hū take divine speed as their names,
Húndùn takes harmony as its appearance.
Divine speed is likened to action,
Harmony is likened to non-action.
【二】【疏】possess two minds of existence and non-existence,
which converge in the realm of neither existence nor non-existence,
harmonizing the biased attachments of these two extremes into the intention of a single mean,
hence it is said that awaiting this is very excellent.
【Three】【Memorials】The two men, Shū and Hū,
still harbored biased obstinacy,
unable to harmonize and unite,
yet they continued to nurture scholarly ambitions,
presumptuously disliking Hundun's lack of intent,
and claiming that forced interpretations were beneficial.
【Four】【Commentary】Those who act will ruin it.
【Commentary】For by moving the four limbs one becomes mired in worldly conditions,
and by boring the seven apertures one becomes stained with dust,
thus deviating from the utmost purity of primordial chaos,
and following the choices between existence and non-existence;
this is why one does not live out their natural lifespan,
but meets premature death midway.
O, diligent scholars,
strive earnestly and be mindful of this!
Hence, Guō Xiàng's annotation states: "Those who act will ruin it."
【Explanation】"Seven openings" is read with the characters "kǔ jiào" in reverse pronunciation.
The "Shuōwén" states:
They are orifices.
"On the seventh day, Hùndùn died." Cuī notes:
This means going against the natural order,
forcibly opening the ears and eyes.
【一】【Explanatory Text】The chapter is titled after the event it describes.
Webbed toes and extra fingers,
are they inborn?
Yet they are excesses beyond virtue.
Attached warts and hanging tumors,
do they arise from the body?
Yet they are excesses beyond nature.
Those who extensively apply benevolence and righteousness in their usage,
arrange them among the five organs!
But this is not the true way of the Dao and its virtue.
Therefore, webbing between the feet,
connects useless flesh;
branching from the hands,
grows useless fingers;
extensive webbing and branching in the essence of the five organs,
leads to excessive and deviant conduct in the practice of benevolence and righteousness,
and excessive application in the use of intelligence and perception.

joined;
〔"mu" refers to the
foot's〕big

"Zhi zhi" refers to

What arises from nature

"De"

This means Zēng Shǐ inherently possessed these five virtues,

【二】【注】What is long is not considered excessive,
what is short is not considered insufficient.
This shows that both extra digits and superfluous growths arise from one's inherent nature,
not from external additions.
However, whether something is duplicated or not,
its nature (三) is fully sufficient in each case,
yet these particular duplications and appendages
are viewed by the multitude as excessive,
hence they are called extravagances.
But those who are confused sometimes claim they are not part of nature,
and thus wish to cut them off and discard them.
This means the Dào would not be preserved in some aspects,
and dé would not be upheld in others,
leading to talents being discarded among people,
and usefulness being wasted in things.
How could this be the intention of perfect governance!
All things have their small and large aspects,
capabilities have their lesser and greater measures.
What is large becomes duplication,
what is abundant becomes superfluous.
The distinction between duplication and superfluity
exists in all things.
If none of these are accepted,
it would mean completely abandoning the inherent nature of all things.
【Commentary】The superfluous flesh that grows attached,
the small wart that hangs by a thread,
all come into existence only after the form has taken shape.
Therefore, that which arises from the form and exceeds its nature—
for example, Lí Kuǎng, who was endowed with innate intelligence,
which was rooted in his internal organs,
not acquired through artificial learning—
thus does not exceed its nature.
【Explanatory Text】"Attached Wart" is read with the character pronounced as ruì.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It is a wart.
The "Shìmíng" explains:
A piece of flesh grows horizontally,
attached to the body.
Another interpretation says:
It is a knotted tumor.
"Xuán" is pronounced as xuán.
"Yóu" is pronounced as yóu.
"And excessive to nature" Sīmǎ comments:
Nature,
is the fundamental substance of a person.
Webbed toes,
extra fingers,
attached warts,
hanging tumors,
these four things each arise from the form or nature,
but are not the proper state of form and nature,

They are excessive in form,
and superfluous in nature,

Nature,

Webbed toes and extra fingers are present from birth,

These four are used as metaphors for talent, wisdom, moral conduct, and actions.

【Three】【Commentary】Those who merge with all things
do not possess multiplicity.
Hence, those who extensively engage in benevolence and righteousness,
although categorized among the five virtues,
are merely upholding the correctness of one school,
and have not yet achieved a state of being formless with all things while each fulfills its inherent nature and destiny.
Therefore, it is said that this is not the true essence of the Way and its Virtue.
The degree of multiplicity or simplicity
is not inherently limited in the world.
However, the distinction between multiplicity and simplicity
each has its predetermined measure.
Even in the slightest nuance,
one cannot overstep another.
Thus, by each adhering to its own measure,
whether multiplicity or simplicity, all naturally attain their fulfillment.
Yet, the confused, hearing that multiplicity alone cannot rectify simplicity,
consequently wish to abandon multiplicity and embrace simplicity alone.
This is to discard the entire world,
is it not utterly deluded?
【Commentary】Fāng means
the way and technique.
It speaks of the virtue of Zēng and Shǐ,
whose nature abounds in benevolence and righteousness,
arrayed within their inner organs and put into practice.
This is merely the knowledge of one school,
unable to fully merge with the myriad things.
Heaven is capable of merging with things,
thus it should be neither benevolent nor righteous yet respond to benevolence and righteousness,
neither excessive nor deficient yet respond to excess and deficiency,
undergoing a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations,
endlessly with the myriad things,
without any bias or attachment,
hence it is the correctness of the Dào and virtue.
【Transcription】"Five Zàng" is pronounced as cáng with the falling-rising tone,
and the same applies hereafter.
Huángdì Sùwèn states:
the liver, heart, spleen, lungs, and kidneys are the five zàng organs.
【Four】【Annotation】It is simply because one's nature and destiny inevitably make it so,
not because it is useful that it is thus.
【Commentary】The webbed toes,
being of no benefit to walking,
thus even though they are connected,
ultimately become useless flesh;
the extra growth on fingers,
since it does not aid in grasping,
thus even though this flesh is present,
ultimately remains a useless digit.
This aims to clarify that what is endowed by natural innate qualities exists,
not for the sake of aiding utility.
【Five】【Annotation】The inclinations of the five organs,
inherently arise from multiple aspects,
yet the young often recklessly uphold them,
leading to excessive deviations,
thus losing the utmost harmony within the body.
【Subcommentary】Those like Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú,
by nature possess abundant benevolence and righteousness,
and with these innate dispositions,
they are naturally aligned with the internal organs.
Those with meager inherent qualities,
forcibly alter their true feelings to emulate them,
striving to make this their conduct,
seeking to conform to heavenly principle.
Since this is not following their innate nature,
it consequently becomes excessive and deviant.
"Excessive" means
obsessive attachment;
"deviant" means
the appearance of unrighteousness.
【Explanation】"Yín pì" is also written as "pì" in another version,
pronounced pǐ yì fǎn,
while Xú reads it as fū chì fǎn.
This applies to the annotations and the end of the chapter as well.
"Regarding the practice of rén yì" is read with xià mèng fǎn.
Cuī states:
Extra fingers and superfluous growths,
although not part of the nature's correctness,
also emerge from the form,
and cannot be removed.
The emotions of the five organs,
though not the true essence of dào dé,
are also listed within nature,
and cannot be governed.
Now, establishing the teachings of rén yì to govern the emotions of the five organs
is like cutting off extra fingers and superfluous growths;
it harms the principle of naturalness,
and further aggravates the ailment.
"Héng fù" is read fú yòu fǎn.
Except for the annotation at the end of the chapter, all are the same.
"Zhì dàng" is read dīng làng fǎn.
The rest follow this example.
【Six】【Annotation】The use of intelligence and perception,
each has its inherent role;
thus, having multiple methods is not considered excessive,
nor is having few methods considered insufficient.
However, when stirred by desires and emotions,
one often devalues the few and prizes the many.
Seeing what is deemed valuable and forcibly exalting it
leads to exceeding one's natural capacity and distressing one's innate nature.
If one forgets what is prized and preserves their inherent simplicity,
then they will not burden their nature with excess, and all different methods will be complete.
【Commentary】It is said that Lí Kuǎng's innate disposition,
sufficient in acuity and clarity,
is for those deficient by nature,
who feign emotion as a virtue,
to employ this as a method—
is that not indeed fallacious!
