Therefore, those who are excessive in vision
confuse the five colors,
indulge in intricate patterns;
is it not so that the dazzling brilliance of azure and yellow, of embroidered ornaments,
finds its example in Lí Zhū?
Those who are excessive in hearing
confuse the five tones,
indulge in the six pitch standards;
is it not so that the sounds of metal, stone, silk, bamboo, Huáng Zhōng, and Dà Lǚ,
find their example in Shī Kuàng?
Those who branch out in benevolence
pluck up virtue and obstruct nature to gain fame and reputation,
causing the world to clamor and drum in upholding unattainable standards—is this not so?
And thus Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú are examples of this.
Those who are excessive in debate
pile up tiles, knot cords, and string together phrases,
letting their minds wander among arguments on hardness and whiteness, sameness and difference,
wearing themselves out in praising useless words—is this not so?
And Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí are examples of this.
Therefore, all these are paths of excessive appendages and branching growths,
not the ultimate correctness under heaven.
【一】【疏】An axe-shaped pattern is called fǔ.
Two back-to-back jǐ characters are called fú.
The five colors,
are blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
Blue and red together form wén,
red and white together form zhāng.
Huánghuáng,
describes a dazzling appearance.
Is this not Lí Zhū?
It is so.
Yǐ,
is an auxiliary sound.
Lí Zhū,
also named Lí Lóu,
was a man with sharp eyesight during the time of Huángdì,
capable of seeing the finest details from a hundred lǐ away.
【Transcription】"Fǔfú" is pronounced fǔ,
the lower character is pronounced fú.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
White and black are called fǔ,
black and blue are called fú.
"Huánghuáng" is pronounced huáng.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
It means light.
Xiàng and Cuǐ's version writes it as ●.
Xiàng states:
The Mǎ family pronounces it as huáng.
The Máo Poetry commentary states:
Huánghuáng
is equivalent to huánghuáng.
Huáng
is also pronounced huǎng.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The old version wrote "light light,"
now, based on this book, one "light" character is deleted.
"Fēi hū" Xiàng states:
"Fēi hū"
means "it is so."
"Lí Zhū" Sīmǎ states:
A person from the time of Huángdì,
who could see the tip of an autumn hair from a hundred paces away.
Another version says:
He could see a needle's point from a thousand miles.
Mèngzǐ writes it as Lí Lóu.
"Shì yǐ" Xiàng states:
It means "it is so."
【二】【注】Those who have ears and eyes,
have never been troubled by yearning for deafness or blindness,
the trouble often lies in aspiring to be like Lí Kuàng.
Thus, although Lí Kuàng were innately intelligent,
they would become the disruptors of ears and eyes.
【Commentary】The five notes,
refer to gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
The six pitch pipes,
are those such as Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Gūxiǎn, Ruíbīn, Wúyì, and Jiázhōng.
The six pitch pipes are yang,
the six lǚ are yin,
totaling twelve.
Metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, clay, leather, and wood,
these are the eight musical sounds.
Is it not,
meaning to be fixated on these sounds,
is it not indeed Shī Kuàng?
Shī Kuàng,
courtesy name Zǐyě,
music master of Duke Píng of Jìn,
extremely knowledgeable in tones and pitch pipes.
It is said that Lí and Kuàng, these two individuals, were innately perceptive,
yet ordinary and ignorant people rashly develop aspirations and admiration,
thereby losing their inherent nature,
how could they not be troubled!
Thus, the perceptiveness of Lí and Kuàng,
actually becomes the master that confuses the ears and eyes.
【Translated Text】"Five Tones" is also originally written as five notes.
"Master Kuàng" Simǎ comments:
a virtuous senior official of Jìn,
skilled in music theory,
capable of summoning spirits and deities.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
from Nánhé in Jìzhōu,
born without eyes.
【Three】【Commentary】Zēng and Shǐ naturally excel at benevolence,
while those not naturally inclined forcibly admire them.
Admiring them leads to benevolence,
but such benevolence is already artificial.
The world has never admired Jié or Zhí, yet inevitably admires Zēng and Shǐ.
Thus, Zēng and Shǐ's misleading of the world,
causing it to lose its true nature,
is worse than that of Jié or Zhí.
【Commentary】Those who branch out in benevolence,
refer to those who inherently branch into multiple aspects of righteousness,
just like an extra finger growing on a hand.
Promoting the five virtues,
they already deviate into depravity and excess,
thus obstructing their true nature.
Using this to interact with others,
to gather fame and reputation,
they cause the common people to rush about in competition,
like the sound of reed instruments and drums,
which can move things to admiration and aspiration.
However, while Zēng Shěn and Shǐ Yú are naturally adept at benevolence and righteousness,
those who are not adept blindly admire them,
abandoning their own strengths to imitate others' longings,
hence it is said they uphold unattainable standards.
Promoting,
means elevating;
it refers to elevating artificial virtue,
and blocking one's true nature.
Zēng,
refers to the surname Zēng,
given name Shēn,
courtesy name Zǐyú,
a disciple of Zhòngní.
Shǐ,
refers to the surname Shǐ,
given name Qiū,
courtesy name Zǐyú,
a minister of Duke Líng of Wèi.
These two both possessed innate benevolence and filial piety,
hence they are cited as examples.
【Explanation】"Zhuó Dé" is pronounced as zhuó.
Sīmǎ explains,
it means to pull out.
◎Wáng Niànsūn states:
"Sāi" and "zhuó" are not similar in meaning.
"Sāi" should be "qiān",
"zhuó",
"qiān",
both refer to pulling out and taking.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"qiān",
means to take,
(the commentary on "Chǔcí Lísāo" and the "Suǒyǐn" quoting Xǔ Shèn in the "Shǐjì Shūsūntōng Zhuàn",
both agree with the "Guǎngyǎ".
The "Fāngyán" writes it as "qiān",
saying:
to take,
in Nánchǔ it is called "qiān".
The "Shuōwén" writes it as ●,
stating:
to pull out and take.
) to pull out.
(Fán Guāng's commentary on the "Ěryǎ" and Lǐ Qí's commentary on the "Hànshū Jìbù Luánbù Tiánshū Zhuànzàn",
both agree with the "Guǎngyǎ".
) This means that people in the world all pull out their virtue,
pluck their nature,
striving for rén and yì to gain fame and reputation,
not that they block their nature.
The "Huáinánzǐ Chùzhēnpiān" says:
the learning of the vulgar world,
pulls out virtue and plucks nature,
internally distressing the five organs,
externally tiring the ears and eyes,
then begins to attract and stir the finest details of things,
shaking and discarding rén, yì, lǐ, and yuè,
violently displaying wisdom throughout the world,
to summon fame and reputation in the age.
It also says:
now the coming of all things,
pulls out and uproots my nature,
plucks and takes my emotions.
These are all evidence.
In clerical script, the character for hand is sometimes written as ●,
(like the character for "jǔ" written as 举,
the character for "fèng" written as 奉, etc.
) hence the character "qiān" is sometimes written as ●,
its shape resembles "sāi",
and thus it is mistakenly written as "sāi".
"Huáng Gǔ" is pronounced huáng,
referring to the reed of a笙 (shēng).
"Gǔ",
means to move.
"Zēng Shǐ" refers to Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiū.
Zēng Shēn practiced rén,
Shǐ Qiū practiced yì.
"Zhí" is pronounced with a retroflex "sh" sound.
【Four】【Annotation】Those who display their extraordinary arguments
and present their perilous doctrines
have never allowed reflection on the words of Táowù,
but inevitably engage in contentious debates within the sphere of Yáng and Mò,
thus making Yáng and Mò the masters who confound the discourse of the masses.
【Commentary】Regarding Yáng:
his surname was Yáng,
given name Zhū,
courtesy name Zǐjū,
a man of Sòng.
Regarding Mò:
his surname was Mò,
given name Dí,
also a man of Sòng,
who served as a senior official of Sòng;
because he practiced the Way of Mò,
he was thus called Mò.
These two men were both followers of Mò,
endowed with argumentative natures,
both capable of delivering lofty and perilous discourses,
stirring the innate dispositions,
obstinately clinging to right and wrong;
it was as if they concealed and hid their phrases,
making them difficult to understand,
their minds wandered in the realm of learning,
solely fixated on the theory of坚守守白 (holding firm to whiteness),
in the space between right and wrong, similarity and difference,
never departing from the domain of what is not human.
Limping●,
means to hold oneself firm,
also describes the appearance of exerting effort.
Praise,
is to glorify and commend.
Followers of Yáng and Mò,
all prided themselves on their minor learning,
dazzling the masses,
boasting with useless words,
bewildering the multitude.
So then, were Yáng and Mò not indeed masters who confused the crowd?
It is said that they are none other than these Yáng and Mò.
【Text Explanation】"Léi": pronounced as liè bǐ fǎn.
"Wǎ": pronounced as wēi wěi fǎn,
Xiàng's reading is the same,
Cuī reads it as the standard character.
Another interpretation states:
"Wǎ" should be read as "wán".
"Jié shéng" (original) [Lǐ] (two) states:
It refers to trivial arguments and precarious words,
like piling tiles with knotted ropes.
Cuī states:
Gathering useless phrases,
as if piling tiles,
and knotting ropes.
"Cuàn": pronounced as qī luàn fǎn.
The Erya dictionary says:
Concealed.
Another interpretation says hidden.
"Jù": pronounced as jì jù fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
"Cuàn jù".
Refers to heretical theories subtly hidden,
forcing interpretations of texts and sentences.
Another pronunciation is "gōu".
"Bì": the original is also written as "bié".
Xú pronounces it as bì,
Guō pronounces it as fù jié fǎn,
Lǐ pronounces it as bù jì fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
Exhausted.
"Kuǐ": Xú pronounces it as qiū bì fǎn,
Guō pronounces it as xiè.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions write it as ●.
Xiàng pronounces it as qiū shì fǎn,
stating:
Near.
Sīmǎ agrees.
Lǐ pronounces it as què chuí fǎn.
Another interpretation states:
"Bì kuǐ",
describes the appearance of exerting effort beyond one's capacity.
"Yù": pronounced as yú.
◎Jiā Shìfù states:
In the explanatory text,
"bì kuǐ",
describes the appearance of exerting effort beyond one's capacity.
Now, considering "kuǐ yù" is like saying "zhǐ yán".
The Fangyan dictionary states,
half a step is called "kuǐ".
The Sima Fa states,
lifting one foot is called "kuǐ".
"Kuǐ",
is three chi.
"Kuǐ yù" means,
seeking temporary, fleeting fame.
"Bì",
as in the Rites of Zhou's "gōng rén jīn yù bì zhī bì",
refers to being worn out.
Exhausting one's energy and spirit on words that seek near fame but lack practical use,
hence it is called "pián yú biàn".
"Yáng Mò": Cuī and Lǐ state:
Refers to Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí.
"Róng sī": pronounced as xī sì fǎn.
"Táowù": the first part is pronounced as tú dāo fǎn.
The second part is pronounced as wù.
【Five】【Annotation】These several masters all followed their innate nature,
truly having many divergent branches,
each establishing their own school of correctness.
Yet, to impose one standard upon ten thousand,
then the ten thousand will not be correct.
Therefore, the ultimate correctness does not use oneself to correct the world,
but allows the world to each attain its own correctness.
【Commentary】It is said that these individuals all possess innate intelligence and benevolent eloquence,
just like fused toes
or extra digits,
endowed by their inherent nature—
how could these be artificially crafted!
Thus we know that following one's nature often leads to benevolence,
which is indeed the way of having extra or branching appendages.
Yet the foolish and deluded,
abandoning themselves to imitate others,
seek beyond their allotted portion,
persisting without cease.
However, stirring and altering the nature of things,
it is through these few individuals
that one attempts to correct the multitude,
and thus it is not the ultimate Way and proper principle of the world.
【Transcription】"This number" is pronounced with the initial "sh-" and the final "-u," with a rising tone.
In the following text, the pronunciation of this number is the same.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "zhōng" is written as "zhōng".
(2) The character "lǐ" has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original version of the explanatory texts.
That which is truly upright
does not lose the true nature of its life.
Thus, what is naturally joined is not considered "webbed,"
and what is branched is not considered "superfluous";
what is long is not considered excessive,
and what is short is not considered insufficient.
Therefore, though a duck's legs are short,
to lengthen them would cause distress;
though a crane's legs are long,
to shorten them would bring sorrow.
Thus, what is naturally long should not be cut,
and what is naturally short should not be extended—
there is no need to dispel worry.
I wonder, are benevolence and righteousness not part of human nature?
Why then do those benevolent people have so many worries?
【One】【Annotation】When each thing follows its own nature,
that is the ultimate correctness.
Observing from this point onward,
the highest correctness can be seen.
【Commentary】Using the natural correct principle,
to rectify the lives and natures of all living beings,
hence it is called "rectification."
All things attain their own fulfillment,
thus it is said "not losing."
Speaking of nature means it is my own nature,
and what is referred to as life and nature is also my own life and nature,
how could it be distant!
Therefore, the term "correct rectification"
means rectifying through non-rectification,
rectifying yet not rectifying (lacking words) [for it].
From this point upward,
clarifies the faults of forcing one's nature;
from this point downward,
reveals the gains of following one's nature.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
The first "rectify" character is actually an error for "utmost."
The previous text states, "Hence these are all excessive, redundant, and branching paths,"
not the utmost correctness under heaven,
here it says, "That utmost correctness does not lose the essence of life and nature,"
the two passages follow each other.
Now mistakenly written as "correct rectification,"
the meaning becomes unintelligible.
Guō Xiàng forced an interpretation for it,
which is incorrect.
【二】【Note】Using branches to align correctly,
is what is meant by joining to form a pair.
【Three】【Notes】to align with the main branch,
thus the branch is called a fork.
【Commentary】Viewing the branch from the perspective of the union,
one might call the union "joined,"
yet the union is truly not joined;
viewing the branch from the perspective of the union,
one might call the branch "splayed,"
yet the branch is truly not splayed.
【Explanatory Text】"Not acting like a tiptoe" refers to knowing how to return.
The Cui edition writes it as "branch,"
with the same pronunciation.
Alternatively, it can be read as "qú zhī fǎn."
【Four】【Annotation】Using the short to measure the long,
makes the long seem excessive.
【Five】【Annotation】Using the long to measure the short,
is to say the short is insufficient.
【Commentary】The term "long" refers to figures like Zēng Shǐ, Lí Kuàng, Yáng Mò,
who were endowed with innate nature,
embodying benevolence and righteousness,
possessing intelligence and eloquence.
Compared to the common masses,
they are thus called "long."
They act according to their nature,
hence it is not that they have excess.
The term "short" refers to the multitude
who fall short when compared to Zēng Shǐ and the like,
thus called "short."
Yet, they too follow their natural inclinations spontaneously,
so it is not that they are deficient.
【Six】【Annotation】Each has its own correctness,
one cannot use this to correct that and thereby diminish or augment it.
【Commentary】Fú,
are small ducks.
Hè,
are of the same category as cāng.
Jìng,
refers to the legs.
The principle of nature,
nurtures all forms,
although they may differ in length,
each body is fully adequate for its purpose,
all achieving freedom and ease.
Yet, the confused seek to cut the long legs of the crane to lengthen the short legs of the duck to make them equal,
greatly violating the natural order,
going against their inherent nature,
which is the cause of sorrow.
【Transcription】"Fú" is pronounced as fú.
"Jìng" is pronounced as xíng dìng fǎn.
The Explanation of Names says:
It is like a stalk,
straight and long,
resembling the stem of an object.
Another version also writes it as (omitted character).
"Hè" is pronounced as hù gè fǎn.
"Duàn zhī" is pronounced as dīng guǎn fǎn.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【七】【Note】When one knows that their inherent nature is not something to be severed or continued and entrusts themselves to it,
then there is no need to remove worries, and the worries will depart on their own.
【Commentary】All beings receive their nature and form,
each having their inherent limits,
with differences in longevity and intelligence,
fundamentally distinct by nature.
This is like ducks and cranes—
one cannot cut or extend them arbitrarily.
Thus,
each should abide within their own lot;
even without laboring to dispel worries,
worries will naturally fade away.
【Transcription】"Qù yōu" is read with the initial consonant of qǐ and the final of lǚ.
The note: Qù yōu and qù yě are the same.
【八】【注】Benevolence and righteousness are naturally part of human emotions and nature,
and should simply be allowed to follow their course.
【Translated Text】"Intention" is read as its usual pronunciation.
The same applies below.
Also written as "physician".
【Nine】【Annotation】To fear that benevolence and righteousness are not human emotions and to worry about it,
truly can be called excessive worry.
【Commentary】Alas,
it is a sigh of lamentation.
The essence of humaneness and righteousness,
originates from the natural order,
is inherent in following one's nature,
not through imitation.
Those humane individuals,
such as the followers of Zēng and Shǐ,
fail to grasp the true essence,
arbitrarily advocate and encourage,
claiming that the way of humaneness and righteousness can be learned and achieved.
Zhuāngzǐ deeply laments this delusion,
hence he utters this sigh.
To seek beyond one's inherent nature,
is thus called excessive worry.
"Is it not part of human nature?"
refers to what constitutes human disposition.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Quēwù cites the Jiangnan Ancient Treasury edition, stating that "Qí" is written as "Qí".
The current edition uses "Qí",
suspecting that the Shìwén's mention of Cui Ben's version using "Zhī" is an error for the character "Qí",
hence it is said that some read it with the fanqie spelling "qú zhī fǎn".
(2) The characters "zhī" and "wú" are deleted according to Liú Wěndiǎn's revised and corrected edition,
and the character "zhī" is attached below the character "yán".
(3) "Qí fēi" is amended based on the main text.
Moreover, when toes are webbed together,
separating them makes one weep;
when a finger branches abnormally,
biting it off brings cries.
In both cases,
some involve an excess in count,
some a deficiency in count,
yet the distress is the same【一】.
In today's world, benevolent people
strain their eyes with anxiety over the world's troubles【二】;
while those lacking benevolence
rupture the true nature of life in their greed for honor and wealth【三】.
Thus, is it not that righteousness and benevolence are contrary to human nature【四】!
Since the time of the Three Dynasties and below,
why has the world been in such a clamor【五】?
【一】【注】When it is deemed insufficient,
one weeps and cuts it off;
when it is considered excessive,
one cries and gnaws at it.
Acting in such a manner,
even amidst the myriad diversities of all beings,
there is no place to release one's worries.
Only by each abiding in their innate nature,
neither cutting off what is joined nor gnawing at the branches,
can things be flexibly accomplished without harm,
so why worry at all!
Commentary: "Gé" means
to bite off.
"Jué" means
to separate and break apart.
Having more than the proper count
refers to the condition of having six fingers on a branch-like growth.
Having fewer than the proper count
refers to being webbed into four fingers.
Now, these two conditions—webbing and extra digits—
arise naturally,
and should simply be left as they are,
without judgment of excess or deficiency.
Yet, those who are confused cannot let go of their biases,
stubbornly clinging to distinctions of right and wrong,
deeming the extra digits as surplus
and the webbing as insufficient,
arbitrarily seeking to cut the webbing and bite off the extra digits
to achieve the number five.
This harms the natural creation,
hence the weeping and wailing;
thus, whether it's separation or biting off,
the sorrow is the same.
【Explanation】"齕": Lǐ reads it as "hé",
with the pronunciation "hèn fā",
meaning to gnaw or bite with the teeth.
Xú gives the pronunciation "hú wù".
Guō also gives "hú tū".
"啼" is pronounced "tí".
Cuī's version writes it as "諦".
【二】【注】If the manifestations of universal love can be esteemed,
then the vision of the world will be thrown into chaos.
By esteeming these manifestations,
one would only wait until troubles arise to then worry about them,
which is tantamount to plunging people into hardship before rescuing them.
Yet in today's world, this is precisely what is called benevolence.
【Commentary】Hāo means
the confusion of the senses.
Rén is
the trace of universal love.
The present age
is like the end times.
It is said that followers such as Zēng and Shǐ,
practicing this universal love,
cause the confused to abandon themselves and imitate others.
Once the path of blind hope is opened,
the function of the ears and eyes becomes disordered.
When the senses are in disarray, calamities arise.
Then, worrying about the turmoil,
they resort to rén and yì for remedy.
They do not realize that the source of calamities
lies in the traces of the sages.
【Translated Text】"Hāo mù" is pronounced with "hǎo" as the initial and "gāo" as the final.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means chaos.
Lǐ explains:
"Hāo mù,"
refers to an appearance of unrestrained nature.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
In current versions, "kuài" is written as "jué" (note two).
◎ Yú Yuè states:
Both Sīmǎ and Guō's annotation treat "hāo mù" as a single phrase,
interpreting it as confusing the eyes of the world,
but the meaning is quite unsatisfactory.
"Hāo" is actually a borrowed character for "●".
The Yùpiān, section on eyes, states:
pronounced yǔjū qiē,
means clear-sighted or gazing into the distance.
Thus, "●" describes the appearance of looking afar.
When benevolent people worry about the world,
they must gaze far into the distance with this expression,
hence the phrase "● mù" means to gaze with concern for the world's troubles.
"●" and "hāo,"
have similar ancient pronunciations,
allowing them to be used interchangeably.
In the "Líng Tái" poem of the Shījīng, "white birds hè hè,"
the Mèngzǐ, Liáng Huì Wáng chapter writes it as "hè hè,"
and the Wénxuǎn's "Jǐngfú Diàn Fù" writes it as "●●".
Therefore, "hāo" being interchangeable with "●"
is similar to "hè" being interchangeable with "hè" and "●".
The "Wén Yán Zhuàn" of the Zhōu Yì states:
"què hū qí bùkě bá."
The Shuōwén, section on earth, says:
"què,"
means firm and unshakable.
This directly follows the Yì's meaning.
Thus, "què" and "què" are interchangeable,
serving as another example.
"Hāo lìng" is pronounced with "lì" as the initial and "chéng" as the final,
the same applies below.
"Yú nàn" is pronounced with "nǎi" as the initial and "dàn" as the final.
"Hòu zhěng" means to rescue or save, as in "zhěngjiù".
【Three】【Commentary】The reason why wealth and high status can be coveted
is because there are those who exalt them.
If there were no such admirable achievements,
then people would be content with their own lot,
and would accept positions according to their abilities.
How could anyone abandon their own duties to emulate others and covet undue expectations?
【Commentary】Tāo (gluttony)
means greed for wealth.
Those who by nature do not embrace benevolence and righteousness
are called unvirtuous persons.
Their intent lies in coveting profit and emolument,
stealthily seeking nobility and riches.
Thus, they sever their own innate nature,
lose the genuine feelings of their allotted fate,
and falsify their nature with artificial emotions.
They abandon themselves to chase after external things,
largely because the traces of the sages are worthy of esteem,
hence such flaws arise.
From this, it is known that to embrace simplicity and return to purity,
one must renounce benevolence and discard righteousness.
【Translated Text】"Tāo" is pronounced as tǔ dāo fǎn.
Dù Yù's commentary on the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Greed for wealth is called tāo.
【Four】【Exposition】This reiterates the previous main point.
◎Qìng Fān's case: "yì" is read as "yì" (抑).
"Yì" (抑) is sometimes written as "yì" (意),
a function word.
In the Analects, "Xué ér" chapter, "yì yǔ zhī yú" (抑与之与),
the Han Stone Classics writes it as "yì" (意).
In Mozi's "Fēi mìng" chapter, "yì jiāng yǐ wéi lì tiānxià hū",
in Yànzǐ Chūnqiū's miscellaneous chapters, "yì zhě fēi chén zhī zuì hū",
the Hàn Shū's preface states,
"qí yì zhě cóng héng zhī shì fù qǐ yú jīn hū".
"Yì zhě" is the same as "yì zhě",
and both share the same syntactic structure as this sentence.
Sometimes "yì zhě" is used,
sometimes just "yì" alone,
the meaning is also the same.
【五】【注】Benevolence and righteousness naturally stem from human emotions.
Yet since the Three Dynasties,
people have clamored and contended,
abandoning genuine feelings to chase after superficial forms,
as if fearing they cannot keep up.
Is this not excessive worry indeed!
【Commentary】"Zì" means
"from".
"Three Dynasties" refers to
Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
"Xiāoxiāo" describes
a clamorous uproar.
As for benevolence and righteousness,
they originate from innate nature and disposition.
Yet after the Three Dynasties,
people abandoned their true disposition to follow superficial traces,
clamorously competing and chasing after them—
how utterly foolish this is!
Thus, Xià practiced benevolence,
Yīn practiced righteousness,
Zhōu practiced rituals,
all exemplifying this clamorous state.
【Explanatory Text】"Xiāoxiāo" is pronounced as Xǔqiáo fǎn,
and also as Wǔgāo fǎn.
Zìlín states:
It means sound.
Cuī explains:
It describes an appearance of worrying about the world.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition, though, writes it as "jǔ".
(2) The original engraving of the Shìwén writes it as "kuài",
the Shìdétáng edition writes it as "jué".
(3) The Shìdétáng edition writes "qì" as "chéng".
Moreover, those who depend on the hook, line, compass, and square to correct things
are cutting away at their inherent nature【一】;
those who rely on cords, glue, and lacquer to hold things firm
are violating their innate virtue【二】;
bending and contorting through rites and music,
gushing with benevolence and righteousness,
to comfort the hearts of all under heaven—
this is to lose their constant spontaneity【三】.
All under heaven possess a constant spontaneity.
This constant spontaneity means
the curved not needing the hook,
the straight not needing the line,
the round not needing the compass,
the square not needing the square,
joining not needing glue or lacquer,
binding not needing ropes or cords【四】.
Thus, all under heaven grow in natural harmony without knowing how they grow,
and equally attain without knowing how they attain【五】.
Hence, past and present are not twofold,
and cannot be diminished【六】.
Then why should benevolence and righteousness cling incessantly like glue, lacquer, ropes, and cords,
wandering between the Way and its virtue, only to confuse all under heaven【八】!
【一】【疏】The hook makes
curves;
the marking line,
straight lines;
the compass,
circles;
the square,
squares.
Things rely on hooks, lines, compasses, and squares to achieve curves, straight lines, squares, and circles,
but this is not their innate nature;
similarly, when humans depend on teachings and examples to become benevolent and righteous,
it is not their true nature.
For acting genuinely in accordance with one's nature
does not rely on artificial learning.
Therefore, forcing one's nature and fabricating emotions,
abandoning oneself to imitate others in practicing benevolence and righteousness,
is to diminish and damage the innate nature.
【二】【疏】Yuē,
means binding.
Gù,
means firm.
Qīn,
means harm.
Dé,
means true wisdom.
To rely on ropes for binding,
or glue and lacquer for firmness,
this depends on external things,
and is not truly secure;
similarly, imitating Zēng and Shǐ to practice benevolence,
this is artificial and contrived,
not the true nature.
Since it goes against the innate nature,
it therefore harms and injures one's dé.
【Three】【Explanations】Bending,
means to curve.
Breaking,
means to cut off.
Xǔyú,
is like coddling and soothing.
Twisting the straight into curves,
applies the rituals with elaborate formalities;
cutting the long to fit the short,
practices indulgent and unrestrained pleasures;
the benevolence of coddling and partial affection,
the righteousness of Xǔyú that clings to superficial traces.
Using these to falsify the genuine,
to appease the minds of things,
thus causes things to lose their authenticity,
and people to abandon their essence.
Subsequently, discarding the root to chase the trivial,
hence they lose their true, constant, and natural nature.
This summarizes the flaws discussed earlier,
to lead into the merits that follow.
【Explanation Text】"屈" is written as "詘" in Cuí's version.
"折" is pronounced with the fanqie "之熱反",
meaning bending the limbs in rituals and music.
"呴" is pronounced with the fanqie "況於反",
while Lǐ reads it as "況付反".
It is also written as "傴" in some versions,
pronounced with the fanqie "於禹反".
"俞" is read as "yú",
while Lǐ reads it as "yù".
It is also written as "呴" in some versions,
pronounced as "xǔ",
referring to displaying a pleasant expression as the appearance of benevolence and righteousness.
【Four】【Commentaries】All things under heaven
have their own constant nature.
Just as the dodder twists and hemp grows straight,
the head is round and the feet are square;
water freezes in winter and melts in summer,
fish gather in spring and scatter in autumn—
these arise from natural spontaneity,
not by relying on external things.
How could there be any need to apply hooks, lines, compasses, squares, glue, lacquer, ropes, or cords!
Since this is so in form,
it is likewise in nature.
Thus we know that rites, music, humanity, and righteousness
disrupt the constant principles of heaven.
Another explanation:
"Attaching and relying,"
"relying" means
to depend on.
Hence, the *History of the Han* records that
during Emperor Āi's time, those who attached themselves to the Dǒng clan
all rose from common origins to positions of two thousand bushels.
The annotation states:
"Relying" means
to depend on them.
【Translated Text】"纆" is pronounced as mò.
The Guangya says:
It means a rope.
"索" is pronounced as suǒ.
The same applies below.
Five. Commentary: All things have their inherent nature;
if left to their own devices without interference,
they will naturally achieve harmony without even realizing it.
【Commentary】Enticed into life,
creatures receive their vital breath and form.
Some are square, others round;
now curved, now straight.
Nurtured and matured,
each is fulfilled in its nature.
None can discern the reason for this,
nor understand how they came to be.
How could they deliberate with conscious thought
or bind their emotions to gain and loss?
Thus it is known that bending, twisting, coaxing, and soothing
deviate from the natural way.
【Six】【Note】Being one with all things,
thus there is no duality with things and one is always whole.
【Commentary】To perceive beginnings and ends as non-uniform
is the delusion of ordinary sentiment;
to witness past and present as non-dual
is the luminous insight of sagely wisdom.
Thus, through non-generation comes generation,
yet one knows not the means of generation;
through non-acquisition comes acquisition,
yet one knows not the means of acquisition.
Though eras may differ between ancient and modern, the Dharma remains undiminished;
through all transformations and myriad changes,
constancy abides as Oneness.
【Seven】【Annotation】When one attains the Way through commitment,
they embrace simplicity and proceed alone,
continuously borrowing from things,
yet acting without deliberate effort in between.
【Commentary】Xī means
"why."
Liánlián means
"continuous."
The Way and its Virtue,
neither existent nor nonexistent,
neither born nor perishing,
cannot be sought through sage-like wisdom—
how could they be grasped by form and name!
Yet types like Zēng and Shǐ,
whose natures abound in benevolence,
leading others by their own standards,
become stuck in reputation and doctrine.
Their restraints are like binding ropes,
their obstinacy like glue and lacquer—
thought after thought continuing,
endlessly without interruption.
Carrying such conduct,
to roam in the realm of the Way and its Virtue
is like trying to learn squareness from roundness,
or a fish yearning for birds.
Vainly pursuing the name of aspiration,
they ultimately lack the substance of efficacy.
Not forgetting the trap and snare for the fish and hare,
yet losing the already-offered straw dog—
why value this at all!
【Interpretation】"Liánlián" Sīmǎ explains:
It means continuously practicing benevolence and righteousness,
wandering within the realm of the Way and virtue.
【八】【Note】The continuous practice of benevolence and righteousness
is merely sufficient to delude things,
causing them to lose their authenticity.
【Commentary】The teachings of benevolence and righteousness,
the traces of intelligence and acuity,
run counter to the Way of Nature,
and disturb the minds of all under heaven.
【Transcription】"祇足" pronounced as zhī.
"使喪" with a pronunciation of sàng.
The same applies to the following instances where "喪" has already been mentioned.
Minor confusion alters one's direction,
major confusion perverts one's nature.
How do we know this is so?
Ever since Yú Shì summoned benevolence and righteousness to disrupt the world,
all under heaven have rushed about in service of benevolence and righteousness.
Is this not using benevolence and righteousness to alter their nature?
Therefore, I venture to discuss this:
From the Three Dynasties downward,
all under heaven have used external things to alter their nature.
Petty men sacrifice their bodies for gain,
scholars sacrifice their bodies for fame,
great officers sacrifice their bodies for their families,
and sages sacrifice their bodies for the world.
Thus these several types of men,
though their undertakings differ,
and their reputations bear different labels,
in injuring their nature by sacrificing their bodies,
are one and the same.
Zāng and Gǔ,
two men herding sheep together, both lost their sheep.
Asked what Zāng had been doing,
he had been holding a bamboo slip and reading;
asked what Gǔ had been doing,
he had been playing dice and wandering about.
These two men,
though their activities differed,
were equal in losing the sheep.
Bóyí died for fame at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
while Dào Zhí died for gain atop Dōnglíng Mountain.
These two men,
though what they died for differed,
were equal in destroying life and injuring nature.
Why must we approve of Bóyí and disapprove of Dào Zhí?
All under heaven are sacrificing themselves.
If what they sacrifice for is benevolence and righteousness,
then convention calls them noble men;
if what they sacrifice for is goods and wealth,
then convention calls them petty men.
Their sacrifice is the same,
yet there are noble men among them,
and petty men among them;
but in terms of destroying life and impairing nature,
then Dào Zhí is just the same as Bóyí,
so why make distinctions between noble and petty men among them?
【一】【注】Changing east and west directions
does not harm the essence;
yet insisting on benevolence and exalting righteousness,
loses their natural state,
leading them to fatal grounds,
is indeed great delusion.
【Subcommentary】To mistake south for north,
the confusion is still minor;
to cling to traces and lose the truth,
the delusion is far greater.
【Èr Shū】 is so,
thus it is.
This is a hypothetical question to introduce the following text.
【Three】【Commentary】To be unharming to all things
is not for the sake of benevolence,
yet the traces of benevolence manifest;
to make all principles appropriate
is not for the sake of righteousness,
yet the merits of righteousness appear;
thus, being appropriate and unharming
is not the summons of benevolence and righteousness.
However, the world rushes about,
abandoning self to follow others, thereby losing its inherent nature.
Hence, a troubled mind does not arise from ugliness but often lies in beauty;
disturbing the age does not stem from evil but constantly comes from benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, benevolence and righteousness
become the tools that unsettle the world.
【Commentary】The Yú clan refers to
Shùn.
"Zhāo" means
to attract.
"Náo" means
to disturb.
Before the time of Táng Yáo,
people still embraced simplicity and genuineness;
after Yú Shùn,
the pure customs gradually dissipated,
hence, using benevolence, righteousness, and the traces of sages
to comfort the common people,
which eventually led to the masses under heaven
becoming bewildered and rushing about,
losing their true nature and lives,
chasing after the traces of sages.
【Explanation】"To disrupt" is pronounced with a small rising tone,
Guō gives the pronunciation as hū yáo with a rising tone,
and also as xǔ gāo with a rising tone.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means to disturb.
Another pronunciation is nú zhuǎ with a rising tone.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
In the "Discourses of Zhou" from the "Guóyǔ," it says "fond of speaking exhaustively to expose others' faults,"
Wěi's annotation states:
"Expose" means
to raise.
The old pronunciation notes,
"expose" is pronounced as qiáo.
In the "Hànshū," the commentary on the biography of Chén Shèng says "raised the eight provinces and made the peers pay homage,"
Dèng Zhǎn explains:
"Raise" means
to lift.
Sū Lín states:
"Raise" is pronounced as qiáo.
In this text, the character "raise,"
should also be interpreted as to lift and read as qiáo,
meaning to lift up benevolence and righteousness to disrupt the world.
Guō's annotation says,
"Thus, what is appropriate and without harm,"
is not the raising of benevolence and righteousness,
yet the world rushes about,
abandoning oneself to pursue that,
thereby losing its inherent nature,
this is reading it according to its basic meaning.
However, using benevolence and righteousness to attract people,
cannot conversely be said to attract benevolence and righteousness,
from which it can be known that this is incorrect.
"Achievement appears" is pronounced with xián biàn with a falling tone.
【Four】【Annotation】Although the Yú clan had no intention of changing,
the nature of all under heaven had already transformed.
【Commentary】From this perspective,
is it not the use of benevolence, righteousness, and the traces of sages that disrupts the world,
causing all living beings under heaven
to abandon the root in pursuit of the branch and alter their innate nature?
【Explanatory Text】"Xing yu" is pronounced as yú.
This can be understood by grasping the context and nuances,
and the same applies to all subsequent instances.
【Five】【Annotation】From the Three Dynasties and earlier,
there truly existed traces of non-action.
These traces of non-action,
are also what those who engage in action admire.
Admiring them causes one to lose the natural simplicity.
Therefore, even sages have circumstances where they cannot but act,
sometimes exchanging the nature of effortless rule for matters of pacification and governance,
so how much more so for ordinary people!
【Subcommentary】Before the era of the Five Emperors,
the ethos of non-action still prevailed;
after the period of the Three Dynasties,
teachings of purposeful action gradually arose.
As times differed in simplicity and refinement,
and steps varied with the ages,
it led people to abandon their own ways and imitate others,
easily losing their true nature.
To chase after material things without attaining them—
is that not lamentable!
The annotation mentions using laborious toil to replace the nature of effortless rule:
"pányí"
means wounds or hardships.
It refers to figures like Xià Yǔ, who combed his hair in the wind and bathed in the rain,
with hands and feet calloused,
exchanging such toilsome endeavors
for the practice of non-action.
Since those in power acted thus,
the common people followed suit.
【Explanation】"The Three Dynasties" refer to Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
"Yǐshàng" is pronounced with the retroflex initial.
"Pányí" both are read as they are,
meaning wounds or injuries.
According to the characters, it should be written as "bānyí".
【六】【注】When dwelling like quails and eating like nestlings,
moving like birds without pattern,
why cling without sacrifice!
Thus, with the world ever in darkness,
only change is followed,
their traces are the marks of sacrificing for the world;
what is encountered may sometimes involve changes of broken limbs or maimed feet,
these traces are the marks that harm one's nature.
Yet, even when roaming the eight extremes without change in spirit and energy,
with broken limbs but the residing form undisturbed,
then what is there to sacrifice?
There is no sacrifice,
hence, they do not sacrifice what is sacrificed,
and their traces are sacrificed along with the world.
【Commentary】To sacrifice oneself means
to follow,
to manage,
to seek,
to pursue,
referring to what one dedicates their life to follow.
Petty individuals covet profit,
the upright value reputation,
officials sacrifice for a single family,
emperors manage the entire realm,
though what they sacrifice for differs,
the alteration of their nature is the same.
Yet the sage is always in harmony with the world,
though his actions involve sacrifice,
hence there may be afflictions like scars, baldness, or lameness,
but they never burden his spirit.
【Interpretation】"殉" is pronounced as "xùn" with a tone of jùn,
and by Xú, it is pronounced as "xùn" with a tone of lún.
Sīmǎ explains:
it means to strive for.
Cuī states:
to sacrifice one's life and follow is called "xùn".
"鶉" is pronounced as "chún",
and also as "dūn".
"鷇" is pronounced as "kòu" with a tone of dòu.
"禿" is pronounced as "tū" with a tone of mù.
"揮斥" has the first character pronounced as "huī",
and the second as "chì".
【Seven】【Categories】These several individuals,
refer to the four persons from the three previous generations downward.
Their undertakings,
mean that benefits, fame, family, and the world are all different.
Their reputations,
refer to the distinct titles of commoners, scholars, officials, and sages.
It is said that these four individuals,
although their undertakings differ again,
and their reputations carry different titles,
in terms of harming their lives and pursuing material things with their bodies,
there has never been any lack of uniformity.
【Eight】【Commentary】This continues the previous analogy to introduce the following text.
Mèngzǐ states:
Zāng,
refers to a person skilled in learning from others;
Gǔ,
is a young child.
Yángxióng states:
A male marrying a servant woman is called Zāng;
Gǔ,
is a child from a respectable family.
Mù,
means to tend.
Wáng,
means to lose.
This means that these two individuals are each engrossed in their own tasks,
and both have lost their sheep.
【Translated Text】"Zāng" is read as láng with a falling tone.
Cuī states:
A fondness for books is called zāng.
The Dictionary of Local Expressions says:
In the northern regions of Qí,
and the northern outskirts of Yān,
any man who marries a servant woman is called zāng,
and a woman who marries a servant man is called huò.
Zhāng Yī states:
The son of a man married to a servant woman is called zāng,
and the daughter of a woman married to a servant man is called huò.
"Yǔ gǔ" is read according to its standard pronunciation.
The Erya dictionary says:
It means good.
Cuī's version writes it as ●,
and explains:
A young child is called ●.
"Mù yáng" means to herd or tend sheep, as in the word mù for herding.
【Nine】【Explanations】Xī,
means "why".
Cè,
means bamboo slips.
The ancients had no paper,
so they all wrote books on bamboo slips.
Moving along five paths and throwing the jade piece is called bó,
not throwing the jade piece is called sè.
Asking about Zāng and asking about Gǔ,
indeed there is a difference between writing and blocking,
herding sheep and losing sheep,
in reality, there is no further distinction.
《挟》Pronounced as xié.
《筴》This character is also written as 策,
with the initial sound ch- and the final sound -è.
Lǐ Yún said:
It refers to bamboo slips.
In ancient times, they were used for writing books,
each measuring two feet four inches long.
《博塞》Pronounced as sài with the initial sound s- and the final sound -ài.
Sè,
is a category of board games.
The Book of Hàn records:
Wú Qiū Shòuwáng was appointed to an official position for his skill in Géwǔ,
which refers to Bósè.
【一０】【疏】The following combines the analogy.
Bóyí and Shūqí
were both sons of the Lord of Gūzhú.
Gūzhú
was a descendant of the Shénnóng clan,
with the surname Jiāng.
Bóyí,
personal name Yǔn,
courtesy name Gōngxìn;
Shūqí,
personal name Zhì,
courtesy name Gōngyuǎn.
Yí was the elder but born of a concubine,
Qí was the younger but born of the primary wife,
their father often favored Qí,
and repeatedly praised him to Yí.
When their father passed away,
the brothers yielded to each other,
refusing to inherit the previous enfeoffment.
Hearing that King Wén had virtue,
they went to Zhōu.
Encountering King Wǔ attacking Zhòu,
they grasped his horse's reins to admonish him,
but the admonition was not heeded,
so they fled into Shǒuyáng Mountain,
gathering ferns for food,
refusing to eat the grain of Zhōu,
and eventually starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
The mountain is in Hédōng County, Púzhōu.
Thirty lǐ south of Púzhōu city,
one can see the temple and tomb of Yí and Qí,
with forests lush and dense.
Dào Zhí,
the younger cousin of Liǔxià Huì,
personal name Zhí,
had a following of nine thousand men,
often acted as a great robber,
hence he was named by the term "robber."
Dōnglíng,
a mountain name,
also said to be Tài Shān itself,
is within the boundaries of Qízhōu,
fifteen lǐ from Dōngpíng,
where Zhí died on its summit.
【Explanation】"Shǒuyáng" is a mountain name,
located in Púbǎn County, Hédōng.
"Death"
refers to dying of starvation.
"Dōnglíng": Lǐ Yún states:
It refers to Tài Shān.
Another source says:
It is a mausoleum name,
currently called Dōngpínglíng,
belonging to Jǐnán Commandery.

Dōnglíng,
is a mausoleum name,
now belonging to Jǐnán.
The explanation text is missing.
【一一】【Commentary】Bóyí died for fame,
perishing beneath Shǒuyáng;
while Dào Zhí coveted gain,
and fell upon Dōnglíng.
Though what they died for—fame or profit—differed,
in terms of the harm and injury
they were no different from each other.
【一二】【Note】What the world values is life;
now, sacrificing it excessively,
all harm their own lives,
then the right and wrong for which they sacrifice
are not worth further discussion.
【Commentary】From the mundane perspective,
there is beauty and ugliness;
but viewed through the Dao,
what is right and what is wrong?
Thus, Dào Zhí need not be wrong,
and Bó Yí is not uniquely right.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: In Huìlín's Sound and Meaning of the Entire Canon, volume 89, and Biography of Eminent Monks of Liáng, volume 4, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Dào Zhí

The explanatory text is missing.
【13】【Comment】This summarizes the preceding text to establish the meaning that follows.
However, the Way has been lost for a long time,
and it is not appropriate.
Nowadays, the common people all sacrifice themselves,
how could it be only Yí and Zhí!
Following benevolence and righteousness,
they never depart from reputation;
pursuing goods and wealth,
they are bound to chase profit.
Only reputation and profit,
the roots of harming life,
are not the natural principle,
but stem closely from worldly sentiments.
Whether a noble person or a petty one,
cannot be strictly determined by this.
【14】【Comment】The world all considers not maiming as good,
but now all equally maim their lives,
so although what they sacrifice for differs,
it is not worth further consideration.
Why should life be maimed,
why should nature be altered?
All arise from exalting the traces of non-action.
If one knows that traces are formed through non-action,
then one will cease exalting and remove extremes to return to the ultimate state of one's own darkness.
Yáo and Jié would both be equal in self-contentment,
so how could the gentleman and the petty man be distinguished!
【Commentary】Evil,
what is it?
In pursuing fame and gain,
there is a distinction between the noble man and the petty man;
but in harming life and damaging nature,
there is no difference between Dào Zhi and Bó Yí.
This is an inversion by worldly standards,
unrelated to the ultimate truth.
How then can we identify the noble man,
and how distinguish the petty man?
It means there is no distinction.
【Explanation】"You wù" is pronounced as "wū".
"Regarding the distinction between the gentleman and the petty man, how can one choose?" The Cui version does not include the three characters for "the petty man".

(2) The character "jiā" has been added based on the main text.
(3) The character "xù" has been emended according to the Wénxuǎn.
(4) The character "biàn" has been emended following the Shìdétáng edition.
Moreover, those who bind their nature to benevolence and righteousness,
even if they are as accomplished as Zēng Shēn or Shǐ Qiū,
are not what I call good.【一】
Those who bind their nature to the five flavors,
even if they are as skilled as Yú'ér,
are not what I call good.【二】
Those who bind their nature to the five tones,
even if they are as proficient as Shī Kuàng,
are not what I call keen of hearing;
those who bind their nature to the five colors,
even if they are as sharp as Lí Zhū,
are not what I call clear-sighted.【三】
What I call good
does not refer to benevolence and righteousness,
but to being good in one's inherent virtue alone.【四】
What I call good
is not what is referred to as benevolence and righteousness,
but simply following the true nature of one's life.【五】
What I call keen of hearing
does not mean hearing others,
but hearing oneself alone;
what I call clear-sighted
does not mean seeing others,
but seeing oneself alone.【六】
Those who do not see themselves but see others,
do not attain themselves but attain others,
are gaining what others gain without gaining their own gain,
are fitting into what suits others without fitting into what suits themselves.【七】
To fit into what suits others without fitting into what suits oneself,
whether it be Dào Zhí or Bó Yí,
is equally aberrant and perverse.【八】
I feel ashamed in the face of the Dào and its virtue,
therefore, on the one hand, I dare not uphold the conduct of benevolence and righteousness,
and on the other, I dare not engage in aberrant and perverse behavior.【九】
【一】【Note】To connect this to that is called affiliation.
To affiliate with benevolence,
is to sacrifice for benevolence,
hence it is not good.
【Commentary】"Belonging to" means
"being connected to."
"Zāng" means
"good."
"Wú" is
how Zhuāngzǐ refers to himself.
To abandon oneself and imitate others,
gaining material things but losing one's true self,
is the artificial sentiment of the common customs.
Therefore, connecting one's innate nature
to learn the benevolence and righteousness of others,
even if one attains the traces of sages,
like Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú,
goes against one's inherent nature,
and thus is not considered good by the theory of life.
【Explanation Text】"Belonging to it" Guǒ reads it as yù with a rising tone,
meaning to be connected or affiliated.
Xú pronounces it as zhú,
where "belonging"
signifies attachment or adherence.
The same applies throughout the following instances.
【二】【注】Following one's nature leads to the goodness of universal harmony.
【Commentary】Mèngzǐ states:
Yú'ér,
was a man of Qí known for discerning flavors.
Shīzǐ states:
Yú'ér blended ginger and cinnamon,
to prepare meals for his lord.
Now, one who lacks innate talent,
yet imitates things to gain knowledge,
even if they become as skilled as Yú'ér,
it is not due to their inherent excellence.
【Translated Text】"Although as eloquent as Yáng and Mò" – one edition lacks this sentence.
"Yú'ér" is pronounced as yú,
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as shì yú.
Sīmǎ explains:
A person from ancient times skilled in discerning flavors.
Cuī states:
Master Shīzǐ says:
Cook Yú'ér blended flavors with ginger and cinnamon,
preparing meals for the ruler.
Huáinánzǐ mentions:
Yú'ér and Díyá,
tasted the waters of Zī and Shéng and distinguished them.
Another source says:
Yú'ér
lived during the time of the Yellow Emperor.
Díyá refers to Yìyá,
a flavor connoisseur from the era of Duke Huán of Qí.
Another account states:
Yú'ér was also from the state of Qí.
One edition of Huáinánzǐ writes "Shēn'ér" instead,
suggesting that "Shēn" might be a miswriting for "Yú".
【Three】【Commentary】If it is not entrusted to me but rather assigned to others,
then even if they understand it as they do,
I myself have already lost it.
Therefore, each should employ the functions of their own ears and eyes,
and not be tied to Lí Kuàng,
for that is true acuity and clarity.
【Commentary】Lí Zhū and Shī Kuàng,
endowed with innate intelligence,
followed their nature to achieve ability,
which did not come through learning.
Now if one twists their nature with artificial emotions,
abandons oneself to imitate others,
even if they attain understanding,
it is not worthy of being called good.
【Four】【Annotation】Skilled at self-attainment,
forgetting benevolence yet being benevolent.
【Commentary】Dé (virtue)
means dé (attainment).
Those who comprehend the profound Way
do not alter their nature to follow external things,
how could they cling to used straw dogs
or dwell in the transient lodgings of former kings!
Thus, one should understand through self-awareness,
attain through self-realization.
To regard this as excellence
is indeed fitting, is it not?
【Five】【Comment】To deem benevolence and righteousness as good,
one would harm oneself to die for them,
but this, in terms of one's innate nature and life, is ultimately unkind to oneself.
If one is unkind even to oneself,
how can one treat others with kindness!
Therefore, only by following one's innate nature and life,
can one truly extend care to others.
Extending care to others without burdening oneself,
so that both others and oneself share in self-fulfillment,
this can truly be called good.
【Subcommentary】As for Zēng Shēn, Shǐ Yú, Yáng Zhū, and Mò Dí,
these four men practiced benevolence and righteousness,
acting in accordance with their innate nature and following their emotions,
which were endowed by the Mandate of Heaven.
They were like extra toes or fingers—
not acquired through learning.
Yet, those who are confused observe the benevolence and righteousness of Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú,
and claim that emulating them can lead to success;
they hear of the intelligence of Lí Kuàng,
and assert that achieving similar brilliance is inevitable;
how could they understand that these are shaped and nurtured by the Creator!
Thus, Wáng Bì, in his commentary on the Yi Jing, stated,
"If one does not ground emotions in nature,
how can one long sustain their expression?"
This is precisely what is meant here.
【Transcription】"Bù lěi" is read as liè wěi fǎn.
All subsequent instances follow this pattern.
【Six】【Annotation】By severing detachment and abandoning neglect,
and taking it upon oneself to listen and observe,
then the wisdom of all directions is entirely preserved.
【Commentary】Those who yearn for detachment and admire the distant,
gazing at others and hearing of them,
let their minds and spirits race unrestrained,
exhausting and losing their ears and eyes.
This is foolish obscurity—
how can it be called wisdom!
If one listens to what the ears hear,
sees what the eyes see,
preserves one's nature and embraces authenticity,
without being agitated by external things,
then all things become wisdom.
【Seven】【Annotation】This is a case of abandoning oneself to emulate others,
although emulating them may make one seem like them,
one's own self is already lost.
【Commentary】Those who cannot see with the vision of true sight yet strain their eyes to seek the clarity of Lí Zhū's discernment,
who cannot know with the knowledge of true understanding yet exhaust their intellect to emulate Shǐ Yú's righteousness—
this is merely the artificial imitation of others' attainments,
not what is called following one's nature to attain genuine self-realization.
Once this artificial learning manifests outwardly,
mimicking others to please people,
the heart wearies from pretense,
thus failing to find comfort in what truly brings one contentment.
【Explanation】"Shě jǐ" is pronounced as "shě".
【八】【注】If one considers the loss of one's innate nature as depravity and deviation,
then even though the paths of losing it may differ,
the fact of losing it is the same.
【Commentary】"Yín" means
stagnation.
"Pì" means
depravity.
Preserving one's nature and following its course
is the upright path;
pursuing fame and striving for superiority
is deviant and excessive.
Therefore, abandoning oneself to chase after external things,
and opening the path of hoping for undeserved fortune,
whether it be the goodness of Bóyí
or the wickedness of Dào Zhí,
are equally considered depraved and aberrant.
Reiterating the idea of conforming to others' ways
is to build upon the previous text and lead into the following, thereby enhancing the literary momentum.
【九】【注】Ashamed that the Way and Virtue are not practiced,
regretful that the dark cycles leave no trace,
thus I abandon moral conduct,
forget fame and profit,
leisurely let go of burdens,
leaving behind self and forgetting others,
simply like this and nothing more.
【Commentary】The Way of empty penetration,
the virtue of ultimate forgetfulness,
transcends benevolence and righteousness,
devoid of profit and fame.
Zhuāngzǐ wondrously embodied the pivot of the cycle,
roaming his mind beyond the realm of things,
his aspirations and conduct surpassing benevolence and righteousness,
his heart's actions forgetting right and wrong;
embodying the non-being of nature,
he felt ashamed of the inaction of the Way and virtue.
Speaking of high and low,
it reveals the superiority and inferiority of the excesses and deviations of benevolence and righteousness.
Saying "I am ashamed and dare not"
shows humility.
Guǒ Xiàng's note mentions "cóngróng" and "chuī lěi":
"cóngróng"
means leisurely and unrestrained;
"chuī lěi,"
means acting without intention.
"Chuī,"
is the wind;
"lěi,"
is dust;
like the movement of a clear breeze,
lightly lifting fine dust.
【Text】"Kuì hū" Cuī běn zuò ●,
yún:
kuì tóng.
"Zhī xíng" xià mèng fǎn.
Zhù tóng.
"Míng fù" yīn fú.
"Cóng róng" qī róng fǎn.
"Chuī" rú zì,
yòu chāng guì fǎn.
Zì yì zuò chuī.
【一】【Explanation】The title is derived from the key events described.
Horses,
with hooves that can tread on frost and snow,
and coats that can ward off wind and cold,
they graze on grass and drink water,
and leap and gallop with raised hooves—
this is the true nature of horses.
Even if there were ceremonial terraces and grand halls,
they would have no use for them.
When Bólè came along,
he said:
"I am skilled at managing horses."
He branded them,
clipped them,
trimmed their hooves,
and marked them with bridles,
tying them together with halters and tethers,
and confining them in stables and on feeding racks—
and two or three out of ten horses died;
then he starved them,
thirsted them,
drove them,
spurred them,
aligned them,
and ordered them,
with the threat of bit ornaments in front,
and the menace of whips and crops behind,
and more than half of the horses died.
The potter says:
"I am skilled at managing clay—
what is round fits the compass,
and what is square fits the square."
The carpenter says:
"I am skilled at managing wood—
what is curved fits the hook,
and what is straight matches the line."
But is it in the nature of clay and wood
to desire to conform to the compass, square, hook, and line?
Yet generation after generation praises them, saying, "Bólè is skilled at managing horses, and the potter and carpenter are skilled at managing clay and wood"—
this is also the error of those who govern the world.
【一】【注】Both the inferior and superior horses are suited to their own bodies and sufficient.
【Commentary】Hé means
to gnaw;
jiàn means
to tread upon;
yù means
to resist;
qiào means
to lift.
Hooves tread on frost and snow,
hair resists wind and cold,
when hungry, they gnaw grass,
when thirsty, they drink water,
at ease and content with their nature,
they lift their feet and leap about,
seeking sustenance from the Creator;
so how could their true nature ever wish to be tethered, bridled, or stabled for the sake of being fed and cared for!
Moreover, all things vary,
each endowed with its innate disposition;
letting things follow their course and allowing nature to take its own path,
each attains carefree freedom,
without pride or striving,
thus their lives can be preserved.
【Explanatory Text】"Horse": The Explanation of Names says:
It means martial.
Wáng Bì's commentary on the Classic of Changes states:
It is that which moves while being below.
"Hoof" is pronounced tí.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is the nail of a horse's foot.
"Resist" is pronounced yú in the opposite tone.
The Guangya says:
It means to oppose.
Cuī's version uses "avoid."
"Bite" is pronounced hè with a starting sound,
also pronounced hé with an alternate reading.
"Lift" is pronounced qiáo.
"Foot" in Cuī's version is written as "tail."
"And leap" Sīmǎ explains:
Lù means
to jump.
The character dictionary writes it as ●.
● means
the horse is vigorous.
◎Qìng Fán's case analysis: The explanatory text notes Cuī's version as "lifting the tail,"
citing Sīmǎ's explanation,
lù,
means to jump.
The character dictionary writes it as ●,
meaning the horse is vigorous.
Now, considering that "foot" is written as "tail" is correct.
The annotation in the Wen Xuan's "River Rhapsody" by Guō Jǐngchún quotes Zhuangzi exactly as "tail,"
and lù as "lù,"
stating:
Lù,
pronounced as lìu.
The Guangyun:
Lù,
cut with lì zhú,
means lifting and leaping.
Lù, by its character, should be written as ●.
The Shuowen:
means bent shin,
read like kuí.
Thus, lù is a variant form of ●.
Kuí derives from  and lù,
lù derives from foot and lù,
in ancient times, characters with foot and  were often used interchangeably,
as their shapes are similar.
Based on the citation from the Wen Xuan annotation,
it is known that lù is a corruption of lù.
"Nag" is pronounced nú,
meaning a bad horse.
"Steed" is pronounced jì,
meaning a good horse capable of traveling a thousand lǐ.
【二】【Note】The true nature of a horse is,
not to reject the saddle or dislike being ridden,
but simply to have no desire for glory and splendor.
【Commentary】Yì,
means to nurture,
referring to the towers and pavilions where nobles nurture and protect themselves.
It is also said:
Yìtái,
is like the Língtái.
Lù,
means grand,
and proper,
that is, the main hall of the principal chamber.
It is said that the nature of horses
delights in the open fields;
even if there are high towers and grand halls,
they have no use for them.
How much more so for the pure and detached scholars,
the simple and honest people,
who find joy in thatched huts,
and are content with these humble windows,
even if there were vermilion pillars and carved rafters,
what use would they be to me!
【Commentary】"义" is pronounced as xǔ yí fǎn,
or according to its regular reading.
Xú pronounces it as yí,
Cuǐ's version is the same.
One edition writes it as "羲".
"台" Cuǐ says:
Yìtái,
is like a língtái (spiritual terrace).
"路寝" lù,
means correct,
and grand.
Cuǐ says:
Lùqǐn,
is the main chamber.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The Suoyin of the Wei Family in the Records of the Grand Historian quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Yìtái,
is the name of a terrace.
The commentary text is missing.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Yì,
Xú pronounces it as yí,
and it should follow that.
The official Zhou Rites, Sīshī section, Zhèng's note says:
In old texts, yí is written as yì.
This means yì is the ancient character for yí.
Yítái,
is like saying róngtái.
In Huáinánzǐ's "Surveying Obscurities" chapter, róngtái shakes and covers over,
Gāo's note says:
Róngtái,
is a terrace for performing ritual ceremonies.
Yí and róng,
have different names but the same essence,
it is a terrace for performing rituals,
hence it is called yítái.
"而恶" is pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
【Three】【Comment】If one has the intention to govern it,
then it will not be governed.
To govern it is to do good,
and this is not good.
【Commentary】Lièzǐ states:
His surname was Sūn,
given name Yáng,
courtesy name Bólè,
a man skilled in managing horses during the reign of Duke Mù of Qín.
Burning,
refers to searing with hot iron.
Trimming,
means cutting its hair;
carving,
means paring its hooves;
bridling,
means fitting it with a halter.
Hobbling,
means tying its legs together;
fettering,
means binding the front two legs.
Manger,
refers to the feeding trough.
Bedding,
is made by weaving wood into a plank,
placed under the horse's feet,
to remove dampness,
what is called a horse bed.
If one cannot follow the horse's true nature,
and arbitrarily subjects it to burning and trimming,
this already violates natural principles,
and many have died as a result.
Moreover, acting without selfish intent to serve things
is how life is preserved safely;
deliberately trying to control them,
causes natural lifespan to be cut short prematurely.
【Explanation】"Bó Lè" is pronounced with the tone luò,
the same below.
Bó Lè,
surnamed Sūn,
named Yáng,
was skilled at taming horses.
The Shí Shì Star Classic states:
Bó Lè,
is the name of a celestial star,
responsible for overseeing heavenly horses.
Sūn Yáng was skilled at taming,
hence he was named after it.
"Tī zhī" is pronounced with the initials chì lì.
The Zì Lín states:
it means to shave.
Xú gives the pronunciation as shī chì.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions use the character 鬄.
Xiàng pronounces it as hè.
"Luò zhī" is pronounced as luò.
Sīmǎ explains:
burning,
refers to heating iron to brand it;
tī,
refers to trimming its hair;
kè,
refers to paring its hooves;
luò,
refers to bridling its head.
◎ Wáng Niànsūn says:
Sīmǎ Biāo stated,
luò,
means to bridle its head.
It is suggested that luò should be read as luò,
(pronounced luò.
) the character is sometimes written as ●,
commonly used as 雒,
and also commonly as 落.
Luò implies falling off,
removing hair, mane, and hooves is called luò.
The Shuōwén states:
luò,
means to peel off.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
luò,
means to remove.
The Wúzǐ's chapter on training soldiers discusses horse rearing methods:
trimming the hair and mane,
carefully removing the four hooves.
Here, burning, trimming, paring, and branding,
the meaning is somewhat similar.
Sīmǎ interprets luò as bridling,
which is incorrect.
The following text connects it with bridling and hobbling,

◎ Jiā Shìfù says:
Sīmǎ states,
kè,
means paring its hooves;
luò,
means bridling its head.
This interprets luò as luò (bridle).
It is suspected that the first four actions specifically refer to the horse's body,
while the following bridling, hobbling, stabling, and flooring,
begin to address tack and restraints.
Luò should be lào,
referring to what is called branding with a hot needle.
Dù Fǔ's poem,
closely examining the six marks bearing official characters,
six marks,
also referred to as fire brands.
Kè,
means carving the hooves;
luò,
means branding.
Burning and trimming to manage its coat.
Carving and branding to mark its identity.
Interpreting it as bridling is incorrect.
◎ Yú Yuè says:

However, the following text connects it with bridling and hobbling,
which then refers to bridling,
this is likely incorrect.
Luò is suspected to be lào.
The Shuōwén's fire radical newly includes the character lào,
stating:
to burn.
Nowadays, official horses are branded on their skin for identification,
which is exactly this practice.
"Jī" is pronounced as jū yí.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
means a bridle.
"Zhí" is pronounced as dīng yì,
Xú gives the pronunciation as dīng lì,
meaning to hobble.
Lǐ pronounces it as shù.
Some versions use 馵,
which is incorrect.
馵 is pronounced as zhī shù.
Sīmǎ, Xiàng, and Cuī's versions all use 馽.
Xiàng states:

Cuī states:
hobbling the front two feet.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:

by analogy it should be present,
now added.
"Biān zhī" is pronounced as bì rán.
"Zào" is pronounced as cái lǎo,
meaning a stable.
Another explanation:
a trough.
Cuī states:
a horse enclosure.
"Zhàn" is pronounced as (tǔ) [shì] (yī) bǎn.
Xú gives the pronunciation as zài jiǎn,

A wooden platform resembling a latticed bed is called zhàn,

a wooden pen.

shī should be shī,

zhàn,

【四】【注】A skilled charioteer
aims to fully utilize their capability.
Fully utilizing capability lies in allowing them to fulfill their nature,
yet some instead rush and gallop,
seeking to employ them beyond their capacity,
hence many become overburdened and perish.
If one employs the strength of both inferior and fine horses,
according to their distinctions of slowness and speed,
although their hoofprints may reach the edges of the eight wildernesses,
the innate nature of all horses is preserved.
Yet confused individuals, hearing of following horses' nature,
claim it means releasing them without riding;
hearing of the ethos of non-action,
they then say walking is not as good as lying down;
How far they have strayed without return!
This misses Zhuāngzǐ's intent by a great distance.
【Commentary】The bit,
is the mouthpiece,
meaning adorning the cheekpieces with precious materials.
One with leather is called a whip,
without leather is called a switch,
both are rods for horses.
When galloping exceeds limits,
hunger and thirst disrupt the norm,
control them with yoke and harness,
guide them with cheekpieces and reins,
intimidate them with whips and switches,
yet demand abilities beyond their capacity,
thus even inferior horses cannot endure,
and already more than half are exhausted.
When sages and wise men govern things,
the harm is likewise.
【Translated Text】"Zhou" is read as shì jiù fǎn.
"Jue" is read by Xiàng and Xú as qí yuè fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It is a bit.
Cuī says:
It is a bridle bit.
"Shì" is pronounced by Xú as shì.
Sīmǎ says:
It is an arrangement of the bit,
meaning adding decoration to the horse's bridle bit.
◎Qìng Fán's note: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Pān Ānrén's "Xī Zhēng Fù," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Jué,
is the long bit in the mouth of a side horse.
This differs from the interpretation in the text.
◎Also noted: Jué,
sometimes written as jué.

Zōu,

Jué,

or the preparation of bits and bridles,

In the "Xíng Dé Piān" of Yán Tiě Lùn, it says: It is like trying to control a fierce horse without a bit or bridle.
Thus, both the bit and the bridle are used to control the horse.

Cè, initially pronounced as gé.

Zhuā,

【五】【疏】Molding clay is called táo (pottery).
Táo (pottery),
means transformation,
and also means nurturing.
Zhí (clay),
is sticky,
and is also earth.
It means that the potter is skilled at blending water and soil to make earthenware,
employing both square and round shapes,
always conforming to the compass and square.
【Explanation Text】"Táo" is pronounced as dào dāo fǎn,
meaning yáo.
Yáo,
pronounced as yì yì xiāo fǎn.
"Shí" by Xú is pronounced as shí shí lì fǎn.
Cuī says:
It is soil.
Sīmǎ says:
Shí soil can be used to make pottery.
