Sticky soil is called shí.
The Shìmíng says:
Shí,
is zhí.
Zhí is pronounced as zhī zhī shí fǎn.
"Zhòng guī" is pronounced as dīng zhòng fǎn.
The following are all the same.
【Six】【Hook】is for curves,
bending.
The plumb line,
for straightness.
It means that the craftsman is skillful,
adept at working with wood,
so that the curves and straightness of the wood
must align with the hook and plumb line.
【Explanation】"Yìng" as in response to a question.
Subsequent instances without phonetic notation follow this example.
【Seven】【Critiques】The nature of wood and earth,
bestowed by the Creator,
seeks not crookedness or straightness,
nor does it yearn for square or round;
yet potters and craftsmen
recklessly pass judgments.
【八】【注】The world considers those who follow nature without applying artifice as unskilled in governance.
They bend the crooked into straightness,
train nags to become steeds,
and employ rules and compasses to forcibly alter their inherent nature,
persisting until death takes them.
Only then is it called skilled governance.
Is this not a grave error!
【Commentary】This is a general summary of the preceding text to align it with the analogy.
However, worldly sentiments are foolish and deluded,
regarding order as good,
and disorder as falsehood,
yet nothing is more false than this.
【Text】"Rǒu Qū": Rǔ jiǔ fǎn.
"Jiǎo": Jū zhào fǎn.
"Fú": Fáng fú fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The character 'shì' has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original commentary text.
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, 'huò' is written as 'huò'.
I believe those who are skilled at governing the world are not like this.
The people have constant natures,
weaving for clothing,
farming for food—
this is called sharing the same virtue;
unified without forming factions,
it is called the freedom bestowed by heaven.
Thus, in the age of perfect virtue,
their steps were steady,
their gazes unwavering.
At that time,
there were no paths or tunnels through the mountains,
no boats or bridges over the marshes;
all things lived in groups,
neighboring lands connected;
birds and beasts gathered in herds,
plants and trees grew luxuriantly.
Therefore, one could lead birds and beasts by a tether to wander,
and climb up to peer into the nests of magpies.
【一】【注】To govern by not governing,
is the best form of governance.
【Commentary】So,
it is like this.
Zhuāngzǐ says:
I mean that to govern the world well,
it is not as good as the potters and craftsmen of the past.
The methods of good governance
are listed in the text below.
【二】【Note】The virtue of the people,
differs slightly in minor aspects but greatly aligns in major ones.
Thus, what cannot be eliminated from human nature
is food and clothing;
what cannot be abandoned in affairs
is farming and weaving;
these are universal in the world and serve as the foundation.
Those who uphold this way
achieve the pinnacle of non-action.
【Commentary】Those people are the common populace.
It means all living beings possess a true constant nature and do not rely on external things.
Virtue is
attainment.
By following their true constant nature,
each thing is self-sufficient,
hence they share the same virtue.
Guǒ Xiàng states,
"What cannot be discarded from nature are clothing and food;
what cannot be abandoned in affairs are plowing and weaving.
These are shared by all under heaven and serve as the foundation.
Upholding this way,
non-action is achieved to the utmost."
【Explanatory Text】"Qù zhě" is read as Qiāng Lǚ fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】Let it be, and it will naturally become one,
not out of partiality,
hence it is called the liberation of nature.
【Commentary】Dǎng (partiality) means
biased.
Mìng (naming) means
to designate.
Tiān (heaven) refers to
natural spontaneity.
For the Way, being empty and penetrating,
nurtures all living beings,
fostering and rearing them
without bias or partiality.
If one intentionally governs things,
it contradicts that natural spontaneity;
simply letting things be and allowing freedom,
then all things become self-sufficient,
hence it is called "heavenly liberation."
【Explanatory Text】"Tiānfàng" is read as written.
Cuī's edition has it as mù,
stating:
It means to nurture.
【Four】【Annotation】This is the appearance of being self-sufficient within,
having no desires or demands.
【Commentary】"Tiántián" refers to
a contented heart.
"Diāndiān" describes
an upright and lofty appearance.
In the era of supreme purity and harmony,
the time of ultimate primordial virtue,
the mind was already free from right and wrong,
and actions also forgot the distinction between self and others.
Therefore, preserving genuineness and being inwardly fulfilled,
they dwelled in non-action with contentment;
not seeking externally,
they roamed in emptiness and tranquility with lofty uprightness.
【Explanatory Text】"Tiántián": Xú reads it as "tián,"
also pronounced as "tuǎn" in reverse.
Describes a heavy and substantial appearance.
Cuī states:
It means heavy and slow.
Another interpretation:
A calm and unhurried demeanor.
In Huáinán, it is written as "mòmò."
"Diāndiān": Pronounced as "dīng tián" in reverse.
Cuī states:
It means focused and single-minded.
In Huáinán, it is written as "míngmíng."
【Five】【Annotation】Not seeking undeserved gains,
thus being content with one household is sufficient.
【Commentary】A path is a
trail;
a tunnel is a
passageway.
Boats are
vessels.
At that time,
it was the era of supreme virtue.
People knew to abide by their roles,
all things were simple and unadorned,
without contention or seizure,
hence trails and passages could be left unused;
with no coming or going,
boats and bridges were thus abandoned.
【Explanation】"Xī" is pronounced by Xú as xī.
Lǐ says:
It means a path.
"Suì" is pronounced by Xú as suì.
Cuī says:
It means a way.
【Six】【Annotation】In the chaos and vastness, all attain the same gain.
Then, with the entire world, remain indifferent and detached.
How could it be that states differ and families vary!
【Commentary】In the age of primal chaos,
simplicity and harmony prevailed in a state of serene indifference.
Thus, the myriad things without consciousness
were interconnected and shared the same neighborhoods;
while sentient beings with awareness
were bound together and belonged to the same villages and counties.
How could there be differing governance among states or varying customs among households!
【Explanatory Text】"Connecting Their Homelands" Wáng explains:
Since there are no differences between states or distinctions among families,
therefore their homelands are connected.
"Hùn" is pronounced with hú as the initial and běn as the final.
"Máng" is pronounced with mò as the initial and gāng as the final.
"Dàn" is pronounced with tú as the initial and zàn as the final.
"Mò" is pronounced as mò.
【Seven】【Annotation】Satisfy one's nature and stop,
without the desire to conquer and annex,
thus all things are preserved.
【Commentary】When flying birds and running beasts are not harmed,
they form flocks and herds;
when vegetables, grasses, fruit trees, and timber are not cut down,
they achieve luxuriant growth.
【Transcription】《遂長》Dīng zhàng fǎn,
yòu Zhí liáng fǎn.
《無吞》Dūn ēn fǎn,
yòu yīn tiān.
【八】【Note】Being harmless to things,
thus things are tame.
【Commentary】Humans harbor no intention to harm creatures,
and creatures hold no fear of humans in their thoughts.
Thus, mountain birds and wild beasts
can be tethered and roam freely;
the nests of magpies and other birds,
can be climbed to for a peering gaze.
【Transcription】"Pān" is also written as "bān",
pronounced Pǔbān fǎn.
"Yuán" is pronounced as Yuán.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
to pull,
to lead.
"Kuī" is pronounced Qùguī fǎn.
"Wù xùn" is pronounced Sìzūn fǎn,
or sometimes as Chún.
In the age of perfect virtue,
people lived together with birds and beasts,
and mingled with all things as one clan.
How could they know the distinction between gentlemen and petty men?
Being equally without knowledge,
their virtue did not depart from them.
Being equally without desires,
this is called simplicity and purity.
In simplicity and purity, the people's nature was attained.
But when sages appeared,
they strained to practice benevolence,
and struggled to practice righteousness,
and then the world began to be perplexed.
They indulged in music,
and fastidious in rituals,
and then the world began to be divided.
Thus, if the unworked wood were not cut away,
who could make a sacrificial vessel!
If white jade were not broken,
who could make a ceremonial tablet!
If the Dao and virtue were not cast aside,
what use would there be for benevolence and righteousness!
If nature and emotions were not separated,
what need would there be for rituals and music!
If the five colors were not confused,
who would need patterned brilliance!
If the five notes were not disordered,
who would respond to the six pitch-pipes!
Now, to ruin the simple wood in order to make vessels—
this is the crime of the artisan.
To destroy the Dao and virtue in order to practice benevolence and righteousness—
this is the fault of the sages.
【一】【疏】Those who sacrifice themselves to material desires and wickedness are petty persons,
while those who tread the path of integrity and righteousness are noble persons.
Yet if we dwell in nests and caves,
we would be indistinguishable from birds and beasts;
if we merely eat and fill our bellies,
we would blend with all creatures without difference.
How then can we recognize the noble person,
and how can we distinguish the petty person?
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
【二】【注】To know is to deviate from the Way in pursuit of goodness.
【Commentary】Since there is no mind of discrimination,
it aligns with the principle of non-knowing.
Moreover, one does not use perilous virtue to seek conduct,
thus embracing the One without departing from it.
【Transcription】"Bù Lí" is read as lì zhì fǎn.
The same applies to all annotations.
【Three】【Annotation】Desire then departs from nature to adorn itself.
【Commentary】Following the desireless state of the primordial beginning,
all things remain pure and incorrupt;
differing from the superficial extravagance of later ages,
people are all simple and honest.
【Explanation】"Sù pǔ" is pronounced as pǔ bō fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】There is no need for knowledge and desires.
【Commentary】The reason the common people lose their inherent nature
is because they are trapped by desires.
Once they are free from desires and return to simplicity,
their true nature is not lost,
hence it is called attainment.
This single sentence summarizes the excellence of perfect virtue discussed earlier.
【Five】【Annotation】The sage is
the trace of the people attaining their nature,
not that by which the trace is made.
This text says "until the sage,"
which is like saying "until that trace."
【Six】【Annotation】Once the traces of the sage become manifest,
then benevolence and righteousness lose their authenticity, and rites and music drift away from their inherent nature,
merely retaining their outward form and appearance (1).
Where there is a sage, such flaws arise;
what am I to do in such a case!
【Commentary】From here upward,
it elucidates the virtue of pristine simplicity;
from here downward,
it criticizes the flaws of sagely traces.
As for the sages,
they are the ones who practiced sagely traces from the Five Emperors onward.
"Biéxiè"
describes the appearance of exerting force.
"Dìqǐ,"
the demeanor of self-importance and reliance.
"Chánmàn" refers to a heart of indulgence and recklessness,
while "zhāipì" denotes behavior of bending and contorting.
When the way of pristine simplicity fades,
then superficiality and falseness arise.
"Dìqǐ" relies on the righteousness of judging wrongs,
"biéxiè" boasts of partial benevolence,
"chánmàn" values extravagant and licentious pleasures,
"zhāipì" esteems flashy and superficial rituals.
Thereupon, the world becomes divided,
the common people grow perplexed,
disrupting the natural order of heaven,
and it all begins from this.
【Translated Text】"Bié" is pronounced with the initial "b" and the final "ie," in the entering tone.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions write it as "bì,"
with the same pronunciation.
"Sǎ" is also written as "Xuē" in some versions,
pronounced with the initial "x" and the final "ie," in the entering tone.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions write it as "shā,"
with the same pronunciation.
Another pronunciation is with the initial "s" and the final "a," in the entering tone.
"Dì" is pronounced with the initial "zh" and the final "i," in the rising tone,
same as Xiàng's version,
Cuī pronounces it as "tí."
"Qǐ" is pronounced with the initial "q" and the final "i," in the rising tone,
another pronunciation is with the initial "l" and the final "ü," in the rising tone,
Cuī pronounces it as "jì."
Lǐ's commentary says:
"Bié sǎ dì qǐ,"
all describe the appearance of exerting effort to practice benevolence and righteousness.
◎ Qìng Fān's note: Regarding "dì,"
various editions lack explanation.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
"Dì,"
means "wèi."
"Wèi,"
means "dì (wèi)" (two).
([Duàn's note] Old editions erroneously wrote it as "wèi,"
now corrected based on the entry for "dì" and the entry for "●" in the cattle radical section.)
"Chán" is also written as "chán" in some versions,
pronounced with the initial "t" and the final "an," in the departing tone.
Another pronunciation is with the initial "t" and the final "an," in the departing tone.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions write it as "dàn,"
pronounced as "chǎn."
"Màn" is pronounced with the initial "m" and the final "an," in the departing tone.
Xiàng and Cuī's versions write it as "màn,"
with the same pronunciation.
Lǐ's commentary says:
"Chán màn,"
means indulgence and unrestraint.
Cuī's commentary says:
"Dàn màn,"
means excessive and unrestrained.
Another interpretation:
"Chán màn,"
means to pull or drag.
"Tī" is pronounced with the initial "ch" and the final "i," in the entering tone,
another pronunciation is with the initial "sh" and the final "e," in the entering tone.
"Pì" is pronounced with the initial "p" and the final "i," in the entering tone,
Xiàng pronounces it as "bò,"
Xú pronounces it with the initial "f" and the final "i," in the entering tone,
Lǐ pronounces it with the initial "f" and the final "i," in the entering tone.
Some versions write it as "pì,"
with the same pronunciation.
Lǐ's commentary says:
It means correcting and exposing what is evil and deviant to establish ritual propriety.
Another pronunciation is with the initial "f" and the final "i," in the entering tone,
meaning law or rule.
Cuī's commentary says:
"Tī pì,"
means overly detailed or segmented.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
Modern editions write it as "pì."
◎ Jiā Shìfù states:
The explanatory text cites Lǐ as saying,
"correcting and exposing what is evil and deviant to establish ritual propriety,"
Cuī says,
"tī pì,"
means overly detailed.
"Tī pì,"
should be read as "zhāi pǐ."
Wáng Yì's commentary on the Chǔ Cí states:
"Pǐ,"
means to analyze or divide.
"Zhāi" means to pick or select;
"Pǐ" means to separate or divide;
referring to its trivial and fragmented nature.
"Shǐ fēn" is read as it is.
The following "fēn" are all the same.
【Seven】【Explanations】Pure and simple,
is the entirety of wood.
Unbroken,
means it has not been carved.
Shú,
means who.
Xīzūn,
is a wine vessel,
carved with an ox head,
used for offering sacrifices in the ancestral temple.
A Guī is a pointed top with a flat bottom,
and a Zhāng is half a Guī.
This briefly provides metaphors,
to illustrate the governance of contentious rivalry.
【Explanation】"Xī Zūn" pronunciation and meaning.
Zūn,
sometimes written as 樽.
Sīmǎ explains:
painted with the image of a sacrificial ox to adorn the zūn vessel.
Wáng Sù states:
carved into the shape of an ox head.
Zhèng Xuán says:
decorated the zūn with painted phoenix feathers,
making it appear gracefully dancing.
Pronunciation is according to Xiānhé's annotation.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
modern editions write it as 樽,
which is vulgar (third tone).
"Guī Zhāng" pronunciation is zhāng.
Lǐ explains:
both are names of ritual vessels.
Pointed above and square below is called guī,
half a guī is called zhāng.
【Eight】【Exposition】This is a combined analogy.
In the era of the Great Way,
right and wrong were not distinguished;
during the age of ultimate virtue,
love and hatred were not yet discussed.
Without love, human minds naturally subside;
without wrong, the root and traces are thus forgotten.
Therefore, the Classic of Lǎozǐ states: "When the Great Way is abandoned,
benevolence and righteousness arise."
【Nine】【Commentary】Rites are used to regulate conduct,
music is used to harmonize the heart.
If emotions truly do not scatter,
what need is there to harmonize the heart!
If nature truly does not stray,
what effort is needed to regulate conduct!
Thus we know that harmonizing the heart and regulating conduct
arise from the loss of the Dào.
【Transcription】"Qíng xìng bù lí" is read as written.
It means not being separated.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, "qíng xìng" is written as "xìng qíng".
【一０】【Note】All these are transformations from simplicity to ornamentation,
abandoning the root to exalt the branch,
thereby damaging their innate nature,
rendering it impaired.
Although the world values them,
it is not what is truly valuable.
【Commentary】Patterns and colors originate from mutual contrast,
while the value of music lies in harmony.
If each color and each sound
does not highlight and enhance the others,
then the five notes and embroidered robes
would have no way to fulfill their functions.
This analogy is raised again
to reaffirm the previous point.
【一一】【Note】Artisans have the standards of compass and square,
while sages possess exemplary deeds to be revered.
【Commentary】This summarizes the preceding meaning.
Just as craftsmen ruin the substance of simplicity by creating ornate sacrificial vessels,
so sages destroy the Way of non-action through the traces of benevolence and righteousness.
Since the harm caused is the same,
the blame incurred should be equal.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "yǐ" and the character "fú" at the beginning of the annotation.
(2) The character "wèi" has been deleted in accordance with the Shuōwén.
(3) The Shìdétáng edition uses the character "zūn",
while this book has been revised following the Shìwén.
As for horses,
they live on land eating grass and drinking water,
when pleased they rub their necks together,
when angered they turn back to back and kick.
This is the extent of horses' knowledge.
But when the crossbar and yoke are imposed on them,
and the moon-shaped frontlet is used to control them,
then horses learn to break the yoke, twist out of the harness, smash the carriage front, spit out the bit, and chew through the reins.
Thus, causing horses to develop knowledge and crafty thieving behaviors
is the crime of Bó Lè.
【一】【Note】Mastering true knowledge,
riding upon what is natural,
then the journey of ten thousand miles can be reached,
and the nature of all horses remains intact.
【Explanation】Mǐ means
rubbing,
compliance.
Dì means
treading.
Yǐ means
cessation.
The joy and anger of creatures,
endowed by nature,
follow their instincts in action,
not arising from artificial pretense.
Thus, when joyful, they rub and comply neck to neck;
when angry, they turn their backs and tread upon each other;
and the understanding of horses is fully expressed in this,
eating grass and drinking water,
with happiness lying therein.
【Explanation】"Jiao Jing": Jing means
neck.
Pronounced as Juying,
also as Qiying.
"Xiang Mi": Read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Li says:
It means to rub.
Another interpretation:
It means affection.
◎ Qing Fan's note: Mi,
anciently read as mo,
hence interchangeable with mo.
(See Correct Tang Rhymes.
) In the Han Shu, the Biography of the Kings of Huainan and Hengshan, it is said that their customs corrupted the ministers,
gradually influenced to become so.
"Jian mi" is "jian mo".
In Xunzi's chapter "Human Nature is Evil," it says that one advances daily in benevolence and righteousness without realizing it,
is due to influence.
Mi here means mo.
(In the Book of Rites, Xue Ji, observing and learning from the good is called mo,
Zheng's note:
Mo means
to mutually refine and discuss.
) In the second year of Cheng in the Zuo Zhuan, the army reached under Mi Ji,
Mi is also pronounced mo.
In the Historical Records, the Biography of Su Qin, "to produce chuai mo,"
Zou Dan's version writes it as chuai mi.
Mi is read as mo.
Yuan dynasty Dai Tong's Six Scripts:
Mi and mo are interchangeable.
In this book, wherever it says "when close, they influence each other with trust,"
also read mi as mo.
"Xiang Ti": Pronounced as daji,
also as tudi,
also as tuqi.
Li says:
Ti means
to tread.
Guangya, Zi Yun, and Sheng Lei all agree.
Tong Su Wen says:
Light treading is called ti.
"Ma Zhi": Li pronounces it as zhi.
Same below.
【二】【疏】Héng,
is the horizontal bar in front of the carriage shafts.
È,
is the wooden piece that presses against the horse's neck.
Yuètí,
is placed on the forehead above the skull,
shaped like a moon.
Jiè,
means alone.
Nì,
means to look askance or sideways.
Yīn,
means curved.
Zhì,
means to resist.
Màn,
means to charge or thrust.
Guǐ,
means deceitful.
Qiè,
means to steal.
The true nature of horses
only delights in freedom and ease;
they do not seek adornments,
how could they crave glory and splendor!
Yet when adorned with yuètí,
and aligned with héng and è,
it goes against their innate nature,
making them unable to endure hardship and toil,
hence deceit and cunning begin to emerge,
they look askance, curve their heads, and twist the yoke,
resisting and charging at the handlers.
Qiè pèi means stealing off the bridle,
guǐ xián means spitting out the bit deceitfully.
It truly stems from the damage to their true nature,
that they display all sorts of feigned and artificial behaviors.
【Explanatory Text】"Héng È": yú gé fǎn.
Héng,
the horizontal wood in front of the carriage shaft,
used to bind the yoke.
È,
is what presses on the horse's neck.
"Yuè Tí": tú xī fǎn.
Sīmǎ and Cuī say:
It is a moon-shaped object on the horse's forehead.
"Jiè": Xú gǔ bā fǎn.
"Ní": Xú wǔ guī fǎn,
Guō wǔ dì fǎn.
Lǐ says:
Jiè ní,
is like looking askance.
Cuī says:
Jiè means protruding and looking sideways.
"Yīn": yīn yīn.
"Zhì": Xú chì èr fǎn,
Guō yīn zhì.
"Màn": wǔ bàn fǎn,
Guō wǔ jiàn fǎn.
Lǐ says:
Yīn,
means curved.
Zhì,
means to resist.
Màn,
means to thrust.
Cuī says:
Yīn è zhì màn,
means resisting the yoke and halting sluggishly.
Sīmǎ says:
It means bending the neck against the yoke to resist and thrust.
Another says:
Zhì màn,
means protruding sideways.
◎ Jiā Shìfù says:
The explanatory text quotes Lǐ as saying:
Jiè ní,
is like looking askance.
Yīn,
means curved.
Zhì,
means to resist.
Màn,
means to thrust.
Cuī says,
Yīn è zhì màn,
means resisting the yoke and halting sluggishly.
Sīmǎ says,
it means bending the neck against the yoke to resist and thrust,
another says:
Zhì màn,
means protruding sideways.
Now, considering the second year of Chéng in the Zuǒzhuàn: "They charged without armoring the horses,"
Dù Yù notes:
Jiè,
is horse armor.
Shuōwén says:
Bǐ,
means to benefit.
Ní,
means to assist.
This means the horse knows the armor is placed on its body.
In the Shǐjì, Jìn Shìjiā: "The horse was heavy and could not move."
Shuōwén says:
Zhì,
describes the horse's heavy appearance.
Yīn è,
is like saying trapped and restrained;
Zhì màn,
is like saying sluggish and heavy;
meaning the horse, armored, has blocked energy and滞滞 movement,
with worries of breaking the bit and reins,
Lǐ's interpretation of looking askance
is incorrect.
"Guǐ": jiǔ bǐ fǎn.
"Xián": the bit in the mouth.
Some say:
Guǐ xián,
means spitting out the bit.
"Qiè pèi": biting the reins.
Cuī says:
Guǐ xián qiè pèi,
means perverting the bit and rein,
stealing the harness and reins.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
Previously, "hén" was mistakenly written as "jiān",
now corrected.
Shuōwén says:
The leather in front of the carriage is called "hén".
【Three】【Comment】Horses have different natures, yet uniformly demand their utility,
hence some exhaust their strength while others feign capability.
【Commentary】Attitude refers to
deceit and cunning.
The horse's true knowledge
is suited to the open plains;
when galloped excessively,
crafty and deceptive thoughts arise.
The cunning and thieving demeanor
is a fault attributed to Bólè.
【Explanation】"態" is pronounced as tài, with the initial consonant "t" and the rhyme "ài".
【Collation】（一）The character 'rán' has been emended according to Wáng Shūmín's theory.
In the time of Héxūshì,
people dwelled without knowing what to do,
walked without knowing where to go,
chewed contentedly and played joyfully,
strolled with full bellies,
and the people were capable of living like this.
But when it came to the sages,
they bent and twisted rites and music to rectify the forms of the world,
and elevated benevolence and righteousness to soothe the hearts of the world,
and only then did the people begin to strive eagerly for knowledge,
competing in pursuit of profit,
which could not be stopped.
This too was the fault of the sages.
【一】【注】This is the true capability of the people.
【Shū】 means
"to go to."
Hèxū,
was an ancient emperor;
it is also said that he possessed illustrious virtue,
which made the people adhere to him,
hence the name Hèxū,
likely referring to Yándì.
In the era when the Way was practiced,
an age of non-action,
minds were free from worries and thoughts,
living peacefully without any forced actions;
they acted according to their nature,
moving about without any fixed destination.
Moreover, they held food in their mouths and played joyfully,
no different from infants;
with full bellies, they roamed freely,
indistinguishable from young children.
This was the age of utmost purity,
when the people could live in such a way.
【Explanatory Text】"Hè" may also be written as 赫,
pronounced with the sound "hū bái" in reverse.
"The Xū Clan" Simǎ comments:
Hèxūshì,
was an ancient emperor.
Another view states:
He possessed a virtue so illustrious,
that it made the people flock to him,
hence the name Hèxū,
likely referring to Yándì.
◎ Yú Yuè remarks:
The explanatory text cites Simǎ as saying,
Hèxūshì was an ancient emperor,
which is appropriate.
It also says,
another view holds that he had a virtue so illustrious,
that it made the people flock to him,
hence the name Hèxū,
likely referring to Yándì.
This interpretation is based on a superficial reading of the characters,
and is hardly credible.
Yándì,
is another name for Shénnóng.
In the "Qū Qiè" chapter, Hèxūshì is mentioned,
and Shénnóngshì is also mentioned,

【一】【Explanation】The title is named after the event.
To guard against thieves who rifle trunks, ransack bags, and break open boxes,
one must bind them with cords and ropes,
and secure them with locks and bolts.
This is what the world calls wisdom.
Yet when a great thief comes,
he shoulders the box, lifts the trunk, and carries off the bag,
fearing only that the cords, ropes, locks, and bolts might not be secure enough.
Then, does not the so-called wisdom of the past
turn out to be nothing but a stockpile for great thieves?

If one wishes to guard against them,

One must gather and secure chests and bags,

and firmly bolt and lock them,
so as not to be careless in storing things.
This is the shallow knowledge of the common world.

In ancient texts, when encountering repeated characters,

ensuring victory in every advance—
this is wisdom.

taking little and yielding much,
distributing goods fairly—
this is benevolence.

【Explanation】"Wú zhì" is pronounced as "zhí lì fǎn".
The same applies to "shǐ zhì" in the following text.
【Nine】【Commentary】It is not that the lips shrivel to chill the teeth, yet the teeth become chilled;
it is not that the wine of Lǔ was weak to besiege Hándān, yet Hándān was besieged;
it is not that the sage is born to give rise to great thieves, yet great thieves arise.
This is the natural way of mutual generation,
an inevitable trend.
Although the sage does not establish esteem for things,
they cannot prevent things from being esteemed either.
Hence, whether people are noble or base,
matters true or false,
if they imitate the sage's methods,
then the world will swallow their voices and submit in silence,
and this is precisely what Dào Zhí relies upon to accomplish his great thievery.
【Commentary】The Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuo Tradition state,
"When the lips are gone, the teeth feel the cold,"
which refers to the states of Yú and Guó.
Hándān,
is a city of Zhào.
Long ago, King Xuān of Chǔ held a court assembly with the feudal lords,
and Duke Gōng of Lǔ arrived late and the wine offered was weak.
King Xuān was angered,
and intended to humiliate him.
Duke Gōng said:
"I am a descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
I practice the rites and music of the Son of Heaven,
and my merits are recorded in the Zhōu court.
Now, offering wine is already a breach of etiquette,
yet you blame me for its weakness,
is that not excessive?"
Thereupon, he left without taking leave.
King Xuān was enraged,
and raised an army to attack Lǔ.
King Huì of Liáng had long desired to attack Zhào,
but feared that Lǔ would rescue it.
Now that Chǔ and Lǔ were in conflict,
Liáng then attacked Zhào and besieged Hándān.
This is also like when a sage is born,
it is not that they wish to give rise to great robbers, yet great robbers arise,
it is the circumstances that make it so.
【Translated Text】"The wine of Lǔ being thin and Hán" pronounced as hán.
"Dān" pronounced as dān.
Hándān,
is the capital of the state of Zhào.
"The Siege" When King Xuān of Chǔ held court with the feudal lords,
the Duke Gōng of Lǔ arrived late and his wine was thin,
King Xuān was angered,
and wished to humiliate him.
Duke Gōng did not accept the command,
and said:
"I am a descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
senior among the feudal lords,
practicing the rites and music of the Son of Heaven,
with meritorious service to the Zhōu house.
My offering of wine was already a breach of etiquette,
and now you blame its thinness,
is that not too extreme!"
So he left without taking leave.
King Xuān was enraged,
and sent troops to attack Lǔ together with Qí.
King Huì of Liáng had long wanted to attack Zhào,
but feared rescue from Chǔ.
Chǔ was preoccupied with Lǔ,
hence Liáng was able to besiege Hándān.
This shows how events are interconnected,
and also a case of cause and effect.
King Xuān,
named Xióng Liángfū,
was the son of King Dào.
Duke Gōng,
named Fèn,
was the son of Duke Mù.
Xǔ Shèn, annotating the Huáinánzǐ, said:
When Chǔ assembled the feudal lords,
both Lǔ and Zhào presented wine to the King of Chǔ.
The wine of Lǔ was thin while that of Zhào was strong,
the official in charge of wine for Chǔ requested wine from Zhào,
but Zhào did not give it.
The official, angered,
then exchanged Zhào's strong wine for Lǔ's thin wine,
and presented it.
The King of Chǔ, thinking Zhào's wine was thin,
therefore besieged Hándān.
◎Yú Yuè said:
This character "jié" should be read as the "jié" in "raising its tail."
The explanation of the character for pig in the Shuōwén states:
It raises its tail,
hence it is called a pig,
that is correct.
The original meaning of "jié" is to bear or lift,
"raising its tail" means lifting its tail.
Here, "lips raised"
refers to curling the lips upward.
【一０】【Note】The sage is
what the world esteems.
But if one were to abandon what is esteemed and preserve simplicity,
discard prohibitions and replace them with few desires,
this is how to criticize the sage while maintaining one's own simplicity intact,
and by releasing thieves and robbers, their wickedness will naturally cease.
Thus, the ancients had a saying:
"To guard against evil and preserve sincerity,
does not lie in keen observation;
to curb extravagance and eliminate ostentation,
does not lie in severe punishments;"
this is what it means.
【Commentary】Pǒu means
to strike.
The term "shèngrén"
refers to the traces of sages.
As for the sages,
their wisdom encompasses all things,
and their Way brings aid to the world.
Now, speaking of striking them
also signifies the intention to devalue benevolence and righteousness, to abolish sages and discard wisdom.
Not valuing goods that are hard to obtain,
thus releasing thieves and robbers,
without resorting to harsh punishments,
and the world will be at peace.
【Transcription】"Pǒu": pronounced as P'ou with the third tone.
"Jī": pronounced by Xú as Ku with the fourth tone.
"Zòng shě": shě is read as shě with the third tone,
the same applies to the annotations.
"Xián xié": xié is pronounced as sié with the second tone.
"Qù huá": qù is read as ch'ü with the third tone.
In the following annotations, "qù yù" and "qù qí" are all the same.
【一一】【Note】Draining rivers does not empty valleys, yet valleys become empty;
leveling hills does not fill abysses, yet abysses become full;
abolishing sages does not stop thievery, yet thievery ceases.
Thus, stopping thievery lies in eliminating desires,
not in promoting sage wisdom.
【Explanation】When wisdom and intelligence emerge, then deceit and falsity arise;
when the traces of the sages vanish, then great thieves cease.
It is like when rivers dry up and valleys become empty,
hills are leveled and abysses filled,
how could one impose their will?
It is the inevitable outcome.
Death,
means cessation.
【Explanation】"When the sage has died, great thieves will not arise" - Xiàng's commentary states:
Affairs and tasks renew daily,
what is new is considered alive,
what is old is considered dead,
hence it is said the sage has died.
Riding the correctness of heaven and earth,
mastering the changes of daily renewal,
obtaining the substance while diminishing its name,
returning to authenticity while forgetting its path,
then great thieves will cease.
【一二】【Note】Not only to stop theft,
the traces of rivalry and ostentation are thus all removed.
【Commentary】故 means affairs.
Abolish sagacity and discard wisdom,
and the world will be at peace.
People sing and strike the soil in joy,
thus there are no forced actions.
【Explanation】"Zhēng" as in contention and struggle.
The same applies hereafter.
【Collation】(1) The characters '佯' and '而' have been amended according to the original text of Shuō Yuàn.
(2) The character '臣' has been amended according to the original text of Guǎnzǐ.
(3) Yú's annotation was originally misplaced under the commentary text,
and has now been corrected following the standard format.
If the sage does not perish,
the great thieves will not cease.
Even if we honor the sage to govern the world,
it is actually benefiting Zhí the Robber.
【一】When bushels and tubs are made to measure things,
people steal even the bushels and tubs along with them;
when weights and balances are made to weigh things,
people steal even the weights and balances along with them;
when tallies and seals are made to establish trust,
people steal even the tallies and seals along with them;
when rén and yì are established to rectify conduct,
people steal even rén and yì along with them.
【二】How do we know this is so?
Those who steal a buckle are executed,
while those who steal a state become feudal lords;
within the gates of feudal lords, rén and yì reside—
is this not indeed stealing rén, yì, wisdom, and knowledge?【三】
Therefore, those who pursue great thievery,
proclaim themselves feudal lords,
and seize the benefits of rén, yì, bushels, tubs, weights, balances, tallies, and seals—
even the reward of carriages and crowns cannot encourage them otherwise,
nor can the threat of axes and executions restrain them.【四】
That such great profits embolden a robber like Zhí and make him unstoppable
is precisely the fault of the sages.【五】
【一】【注】The sage is valued for governing the world,
yet even the likes of Jié and Zhí rely on their methods.
What is relied upon is significant,
so the benefits derived cannot be trivial.
【Commentary】In the age of pristine simplicity,
when tranquility and non-action prevailed,
all things returned to their roots,
and all people restored their innate nature—
how could there be any need for teachings and traces to later attain obscurity!
But when sagely wisdom was not forgotten,
great thieves arose.
Even if we again honor the laws of the sages
to govern the world,
it is no different from multiplying the profits of Dào Zhí.
Why is this?
The reason why Xià Jié could unleash his harm and poison,
and Dào Zhí could indulge his greed and cruelty,
is because they relied on the traces of the sages.
Had there been no traces of the sages,
how could Xià Jié have occupied the imperial throne
to let his poison flow through the common people?
How could Dào Zhí have gathered thousands of followers
to run rampant across the world?
Since what they relied on was substantial,
the benefits they gained were not light.
From this we may deduce
that the fault lies with sagely wisdom.
【Explanation】"If the sage does not die, the great thief will not cease." Xiàng comments:
If the sage does not die,
it means adhering to the old ways without daily renewal,
clinging to names without creating substance.
The great thief not ceasing,
is that not fitting indeed!
【二】【注】What troubles the petty thief,
is what the grand thief capitalizes on and benefits from.
【Commentary】The hú is
what is now called a container,
used to measure the quantity of things.
The quán,
is the weight of a scale,
and the héng,
is the beam of a scale,
used to balance the weight of objects.
The fú,
is divided into two pieces,
which join together to form one,
similar to today's bronze fish tallies or wooden contracts.
The xǐ,
is the jade seal of the king,
held to summon and command the world.
Rén,
means benevolence;
yì,
means righteousness;
the king's benevolence covers all living beings,
following what is appropriate to establish rules,
thereby nurturing and caring for the common people.
These eight things,
are the sharp tools of the world,
and none can be without the others.
The sage establishes teachings to govern the state and family rightly,
yet Tián Chéng used them to usurp the state of Qí—
is this not harmful to petty thieves but beneficial to great robbers?
【Explanation Text】"Making dou and hu to measure them" Xiang comments:
From here onward,
all are meant to clarify that if it is not the right person,
even laws are of no benefit.
"Weights and scales" Li comments:
Quán,
is the weight of a steelyard;
héng,
is the beam of a steelyard.
Zhuì,
pronounced as zhí wèi fǎn.
"Tallies and seals" pronounced as xǐ.
"To forge" pronounced as jū biǎo fǎn.
【Three】【Discourses】The hook refers to
a belt hook.
The emergence of the sage's path
originally aimed to punish evil and encourage good.
Now, if one privately steals a hook and belt,
they will inevitably face punishment and execution;
yet publicly seizing the state of Qí,
one is crowned among the feudal lords;
where benevolence and righteousness do not exist,
there is no way to lead the masses.
Speaking from this perspective,
is it not akin to stealing the sage's path and plundering the state?
How do we know this is so?
It is a rhetorical question;
what follows about stealing
is a hypothetical answer.
【Translated Text】"Stealing a Hook" Hook,
refers to a belt.
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī says:
"cún yān" should be "yān cún".
Yān,
means "yúshì" (thereupon).
It means that benevolence and righteousness thereupon exist.
The annotation in the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū: Jì Chūn" chapter says:
yān,
is like "yú cǐ" (herein).
The "Pìn Lǐ Jì" says,
"and during the offering, the breath is emitted, yān filling the countenance,"
meaning the breath is emitted thereupon filling the countenance.
The "Yuè Lìng" says,
"the Son of Heaven yān begins to ride in a boat,"
(In current editions, the character yān is placed in the previous sentence under "nǎi gào zhōu qiè jù yú tiānzǐ zhī xià",
this is a reckless alteration by later people who did not understand the text's meaning.
Now corrected according to "Lǚshì Chūnqiū: Jì Chūn" and "Huáinán: Shí Zé".
) meaning the Son of Heaven thereupon begins to ride in a boat.
The "Jīn Yǔ" says,
"yān began to issue commands,"
meaning thereupon began to issue commands.
The "Sān Nián Wèn" says,
"therefore the former kings yān established moderation and regulated ceremonies,"
meaning the former kings thereupon established moderation and regulated ceremonies.
(In "Xúnzǐ: Lǐ Lùn", yān is written as ān,
Yáng Liàng says:
ān,
is a particle.
Sometimes written as ān,
sometimes as àn,
Xúnzǐ often uses this character.
Yān, ān, àn,
these three characters have the same meaning,
detailed in "Explanatory Words".
) The "Dàhuāng Nán Jīng" says,
"On the Cloud-Rain Mountain, there is a tree named Luán,
the group of emperors yān gather medicine,"
meaning the group of emperors thereupon gather medicine.
The "Guǎnzǐ: Kuí Duó" chapter says,
"when the people's wealth is sufficient,
then the ruler's levies yān are inexhaustible,"
meaning the levies thereupon are inexhaustible.
The "Mòzǐ: Fēi Gōng" chapter says,
"Heaven then commanded Tāng at Biāo Palace,
to receive the great mandate of Xià,
Tāng yān dared to lead his multitude toward the borders of Xià,"
meaning Tāng thereupon dared to attack Xià.
The "Chǔ Cì: Jiǔ Zhāng" says,
"yān adrift became a wanderer,"
and also says,
"yān express feelings and draw forth sincerity,"
meaning thereupon adrift became a wanderer,
thereupon express feelings and draw forth sincerity.
Also, in the 15th year of Duke Xī in "Zuǒ Zhuàn",
"Jìn yúshì hū instituted the yuán fields,"
"Jìn yúshì hū instituted the zhōu troops,"
the "Jìn Yǔ" writes as "yān instituted yuán fields,"
"yān instituted zhōu troops."
The "Western Zhōu Cè",
"What worry does the lord have yān,"
the "Shǐ Jì: Zhōu Běn Jì" writes as "What worry does the lord have yúshì."
This shows yān and yúshì have the same meaning.
In the 8th year of Duke Zhuāng in "Gōngyáng Zhuàn",
"I will on the jiǎwǔ day then offer sacrifices to arms yúshì,"
the "Guǎnzǐ: Xiǎo Wèn" chapter,
"and I observe that among the small state lords who do not submit, only Jǔ yúshì,"
this shows yúshì and yān have the same meaning.
These four lines rhyme "zhū" with "hóu",
"mén" with "cún",
their rhymes are all at the end of the lines.
The "Shǐ Jì: Yóu Xiá Zhuàn" writes as "Those who steal hooks are executed,
those who steal states become lords,
at the lords' gates,
benevolence and righteousness reside,"
this is clear evidence.
【Four】【Commentary】Carriages and crowns, axes and battle-axes,
are the most significant instruments of reward and punishment.
Heavy rewards and punishments are used to prohibit theft,
yet grand thieves pursue and steal them,
turning them instead to be used by thieves.
The very weight of what is employed
is precisely what enables the grand thieves.
A grand thief,
must act with benevolence and righteousness,
balance with scales and measures,
pledge trust with tallies and seals,
encourage with carriages and crowns,
intimidate with axes and battle-axes,
stealing these public instruments,
and only then can the feudal lords be subjugated and raised up.
Therefore, benevolence, righteousness, rewards, and punishments
are merely sufficient to punish those who steal hooks.
【Commentary】"Zhú" means
to follow.
"Quàn" means
to encourage.
"Jìn" means
to stop.
"Xuān" refers to
a carriage.
"Miǎn" refers to
a crown.
The establishment of the sage's traces
originally aimed to quell deceit and evil,
yet Tián Héng then used this way to usurp the state of Qí,
taking complete possession of
the authority, seals, and tallies,
swore oaths to the feudal lords,
and securely faced south as ruler.
How could one encourage him with carriages and crowns,
or intimidate him with axes and battle-axes!
The small one is called an axe,
the large one is called a battle-axe.
It is also said that gold adorns the axes and battle-axes.
【Explanation】"Jie": read as "qiè" or "liè" with two alternative pronunciations.
"Fǔ yuè": pronounced as "yuè".
◎Qìng Fān's note: In Huìlín's "Sound and Meaning in the Entire Canon" volume 95, "Correcting Slander Treatise III" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
The Xià held yellow battle-axes,
the Yīn held white axes,
the Zhōu, on the left wielded yellow battle-axes,
and on the right held white banners.
The explanatory text is missing.
"Néng jīn": pronounced as "jīn",
also read as "jū zhèn" alternatively.
The same applies to "bùkě jīn" below.
【Five】【Comment】The reason why theft cannot be prevented,
lies in the great profit gained from stealing.
The reason why the profit is great,
is because the sage does not belittle it.
Therefore, to eradicate theft, one must devalue goods,
not exalt the sage.
【Commentary】The reason why Dào Zhi was able to gather nine thousand followers and run rampant across the land,
was also due to relying on the five virtues.
Had there been no sage wisdom,
how could he have achieved this!
From this, we understand that driving horses to plunder people,
and being unable to be restrained or controlled,
originates from the fault of the sages establishing laws.
Therefore it is said:
"A fish should not be taken out of the deep,
and the sharp weapons of a state should not be shown to others."
Those so-called sages
are the sharp weapons of the world,
and should not be the means to enlighten the world.
Thus, when sageliness and wisdom are cast aside,
great robbers will cease to appear;
when jade is shattered and pearls are destroyed,
petty thieves will no longer emerge;
when tallies are burned and seals are broken,
the people will revert to simplicity and innocence;
when measures are smashed and scales are broken,
the people will no longer contend;
when the sagely laws of the world are utterly destroyed,
the people may begin to be reasoned with.
Confuse the six pitch-pipes,
break up the pipes and lutes,
stop up the ears of the music master Kuàng,
and for the first time the people of the world will hold their hearing within;
abolish ornate patterns,
scatter the five colors,
glue shut the eyes of Lí Zhū,
and for the first time the people of the world will hold their sight within;
destroy and discard the marking-line, the chalk-line, the compass, and the square,
break off the fingers of the artisan Chuí,
and for the first time the people of the world will possess their own skill.
Hence it is said, "Great skill appears clumsy."
Eradicate the conduct of Zēng and Shǐ,
gag the mouths of Yáng and Mò,
cast aside benevolence and righteousness,
and for the first time the virtue of the world will reach mysterious unity.
When people hold their sight within,
the world will not be dazzled;
when people hold their hearing within,
the world will not be encumbered;
when people hold their knowledge within,
the world will not be confused;
when people hold their virtue within,
the world will not be led astray.
Those like Zēng, Shǐ, Yáng, Mò, the music master Kuàng, the artisan Chuí, and Lí Zhū,
all set up their virtues externally and thereby bring chaos and confusion to the world,
are of no use to the law.
【一】【注】When fish lose their deep abode, they become prey to humans;
when sharp tools are exposed, they become assets for robbers;
therefore, they must not be shown to others.
【Commentary】To lose,
means to be deprived.
The sharp tool,
refers to the traces of the sage.
To show,
means to reveal.
If a fish loses water, it will be captured by creatures;
if a sharp tool is revealed, it will be seized by others,
hence it must not be done.
【二】【注】The sage,
truly capable of abandoning sageliness and discarding knowledge to return to the unity with the ultimate of things,
when all things reach their ultimate and become one,
then their traces are the traces of benefiting things.
Utensils are like traces,
what can be grasped and used is called an utensil.
【Commentary】The sages refer to figures like Yáo, Shùn, Wénwáng, and Wǔwáng.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
If one borrows the wisdom of the sages to reap benefits,
and all under heaven borrow and utilize it,
then it inherently becomes a sharp tool for the world.
When the world uses the sages as a sharp tool,
they fear others uncovering their hidden motives,
and thus none can truly understand it.
【Three】【Comment】Displaying sharp weapons to the world,
thereby supplies the robbers and thieves.
【Commentary】The sage governs the world,
responding to circumstances and adapting to the times.
Whether through ceremonial deference or armed conflict,
their actions and withdrawals are not fixed to one approach,
and they cannot be rigidly adhered to,
making this clear to all under heaven.
If one clings to and enforces a single way,
it is certain to lead to its flaws,
as exemplified by cases like Yān Kuài and Bái Gōng.
【Four】【Annotation】Remove the resources they rely on,
then without imposing a ban, they will cease on their own.
【Commentary】Rejecting sagely wisdom,
all things in the world abide by their proper roles,
and thievery naturally ceases.
【Five】【Comment】To devalue what they treasure,
then punishments need not be applied and troubles will cease on their own.
【Commentary】Concealing jade in the mountains,
hiding pearls in the rivers,
not valuing precious gems and jewels,
how could there be theft or excess!
【Transcription】"Tī yù" is pronounced as chí chì fǎn,
its meaning is the same as the character zhì.
Cuī shuō:
It is like throwing away.
Guō pronounces it as dū gé fǎn.
Lǐ shuō:
It means to carve.
【Six】【Annotation】Without the reliance on deceit and artifice,
there would be no means to carry out their cunning schemes.
【Commentary】Tallies and seals are,
symbols of sincerity and trust.
Deceitful and fraudulent individuals,
rely on and use them,
hence burning and destroying them,
can lead to a return to simplicity and purity, reverting to rustic and unadorned ways.
【七】【注】For, minor peace is what great unrest gives rise to.
【Commentary】The dou and heng measures are instruments
used to gauge volume
and weigh lightness and heaviness.
Once they fall into the hands of thieves,
they ironically become tools for theft.
Smashing and destroying them
aligns with the wisdom of the ancients in upholding integrity,
thus avoiding conflicts and disputes.
【八】【Note】When there is nothing to correct externally,
one preserves the simplicity of one's inner self entirely,
and thus avoids words that cause self-loss.
【Commentary】Dān means
to exhaust.
Cán means
to destroy.
The sacred laws
refer to the five virtues.
Having already destroyed the Three Sovereigns,
and ruined the Five Emperors,
all temporary lodgings are completely exhausted,
straw dogs are no longer displayed,
forgetting the trap and the snare,
things and self merge into the ultimate unity,
only then can one begin to discuss the realm of profound subtlety,
and deliberate on the far-reaching nature of the Dào and Dé.
【Explanation】"Dān" is pronounced dān,
meaning to exhaust.
【九】【注】Sounds and sights, the pleasures of Li Kuáng,
are what those with ears and eyes value.
Life is endowed with its allotted portion,
yet if one is drawn by what one values,
then life's destiny is lost.
But if one destroys what one values,
abandons that and trusts to the self,
then hearing and sight are each preserved whole,
and humans embody their genuineness.
【Commentary】"Zhuó" means
to pull out.
"Shuò" means
to melt away.
The yú resembles the shēng in shape,
both having pipes arranged inside a gourd,
with reeds attached at the ends of the pipes.
The sè is eight chǐ and one cùn long,
one chǐ and eight cùn wide,
with twenty-seven strings,
created by Fúxī.
When the ear becomes engrossed in the gōng and zhǐ notes,
it yearns for the keen hearing of Shī Kuàng;
when the eye is fixated on the dark and yellow hues,
it desires the sharp sight of Lí Zhū;
thus, the mind and spirit race,
and the ears and eyes are exhausted and lost.
Then, by breaking the pipes and cutting the strings,
melting the warps and severing the wefts;
destroying the melodies of Huánghuā,
abandoning the songs of Báixuě;
erasing the patterns of fǔfú,
scattering the brilliance of red and purple;
so, gluing shut the eyes of Lí Zhū,
removes the root of imitation;
plugging the ears of Gǔ Kuàng,
takes away the leader of chaos.
Afterward, everyone attains self-contentment,
and nothing in the world deprives me of myself,
reaching the limit of what the ear can hear, yet turning inward to hear silence,
indulging the eye's ability to see, yet looking inward to see no color,
the natural mechanism unfolds on its own,
achieving the ultimate state of non-action,
how could there be distinctions of clarity and obscurity, superiority and inferiority among them!
Therefore, the world is peaceful,
and all things share the same virtue.
Following one's own perceptions,
thus, people contain their keen senses.
"Contain" means
to nurture within.
【Interpretation】"Shuò jué" — Guō Xiàng and Lǐ Yí read it with a fǎnqiè spelling as "shī zhuó fǎn,"
Xiàng Xióng and Xú Wú pronounce it as "yào."
Cuī Màn states:
It means to burn and sever.
"Yú" — Xú Wú pronounces it as "yú."
"Sè" — the text also writes it as "shēng."
"Sāi Gǔ Kuàng" — Cuī Màn's version writes "sāi" as "dù,"
stating:
It means to block.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Current editions do not have the character "gǔ" (one).
"Jiāo" — pronounced as "jiāo,"
Xú Wú gives a fǎnqiè spelling as "gǔ xiào fǎn."
Lost indeed. (Xiè Làng's rebuttal.)
【一０】【Note】Even with the simplicity of spiders and dung beetles,
they spin webs and roll dung balls,
without seeking help from craftsmen—
thus, all things have their own capabilities.
Though their abilities differ,
if what they practice does not dare to vary,
then it may seem skillful but is actually clumsy.
Therefore, those skilled at employing people
let those capable of squares handle squares,
and those capable of circles handle circles,
each entrusted with what they can do,
so people settle into their natures,
without demanding from all the people the skill of Gōng Chuí.
Thus, various skills appearing incompatible may seem clumsy,
yet when all under heaven can act according to their own abilities, that is the greatest skill.
By utilizing their innate capabilities,
compass and square can be discarded, and the fingers of a master craftsman can be cast aside.
【Commentary】A hook is
curved;
a string is
straight;
a compass makes
circles;
a square makes
squares.
Gǒng Chuí was a craftsman under Yáo,
who created the methods of using the compass and square;
it is also said he was a minister of Shùn.
Lì means
to break,
to cut.
Gǒng Chuí, endowed with innate skillfulness,
employed hooks and strings,
cutting and carving to eliminate irregularities,
and by applying the compass and square,
consequently led the common people of the world,
to be enticed into imitating him,
abandoning their own nature to chase after external things—
this indeed stems from this.
If one were to discard the compass and square,
abandon hooks and strings,
break off Gǒng Chuí's fingers,
then everyone, following their inherent master,
would possess their own skill.
Just as a spider's web or a dung beetle's ball,
how could they involve the efforts of a craftsman?
It is as if the natural mechanism is skillful!
(The saying) comes from the classic of Lǎozǐ.
【Explanation】"攦": Guō gives the pronunciation as lǚ xì fǎn,
also lì jié fǎn,
Xú gives suǒ qǐ fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means to break.
Cuī says:
It means to tear.
"工倕": pronounced as chuí,
a skilled artisan during Yáo's time.
Another pronunciation is shuì.

【一一】【Note】Remove those who lead the disorderly masses,
and the world will each return to its proper place, aligning with the profound virtue.
【Explanation】To pare away means
to eliminate.
To clamp means
to shut.
To repel means
to reject.
The profound
is the origin,
the Way.
Zēng Shēn was of utmost filial piety,
Shǐ Yú was loyal and upright,
Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí
possessed a nature of grand eloquence.
Those four individuals,
with their innate dispositions,
thus caused the scholars of the world
to abandon themselves and imitate others,
leading to chaos among the masses,
losing their inherent nature.
Therefore, eliminate the practices of loyalty and trustworthiness,
clamp shut the mouths of frivolous debaters,
repel the strained benevolence,
and discard the forced righteousness.
Thereby, things do not lose their authenticity,
people all attain self-fulfillment,
follow their nature and preserve principle,
thus merging with the profound Way.

means to disperse and vanish.
Burdens,

It is solely because one flaunts their intelligence,
that such worries and calamities gather,
causing the common people to stumble and scatter.
If one can embrace wisdom within the inner self without showing it off outwardly,
then all things will find contentment and joy, free from worries and calamities.

【13】【Comment】If one can understand what lies within their bounds,
nurture virtue without dissipation,
they will surely tread the righteous path of the central harmony,
roaming the cosmos without confusion—
how could there be any inversion or depravity in between!
【Transcription】"Bù pì" pǐ yì fǎn.
【14】【Comment】These several individuals,
endowed with diverse talents,
thus cause the world to leap and imitate them.
Imitating them leads to the loss of self,
and the loss of self stems from them,
making them the source of chaos.
The great calamity of the world
lies in the loss of self.
【Commentary】The aforementioned individuals,
all endowed with extraordinary talents,
failed to conceal their brilliance and hide their radiance.
Instead, they stirred waves and agitated customs,
establishing their reputations outwardly,
drawing things toward themselves,
dazzling the multitude of beings.
Under heaven, virtue was lost and they did not return to the root,
losing the origin of the self—
this is the reason for it.
【Explanation】"爚" is pronounced by Xú as yào.

Sīmǎ and Cuī say:

【15】【Comment】As for the application of laws,
vision does not exceed what can be seen,
thus all eyes are clear-sighted;
hearing does not exceed what can be heard,
thus all ears are sharp;
tasks do not exceed one's capabilities,
thus all skills are masterful;
knowledge does not exceed what can be known,
thus all natures are content;
virtue does not exceed what is attained,
thus all virtues are appropriate.
Why then establish what lies beyond the inherent nature,
causing the world to rush about aimlessly without being able to return to themselves!
【Commentary】To act in accordance with one's nature,
all actions must stem from one's inherent character—
this is the subtlety of the method.
Yet followers like Zēng and Shǐ,
who impose their own views to guide others,
bring no benefit to the present age,
and instead cause harm for the future.
Even if such a method is established,
it ultimately proves to be of no use.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "瞽",
this book supplements it based on the explanatory text.
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "也".
(3) The character "失" has been emended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original explanatory text.
Are you alone unaware of the age of perfect virtue?
In ancient times, there were Róngchéng Shì, Dàtíng Shì, Bóhuáng Shì, Zhōngyāng Shì, Lìlù Shì, Líchù Shì, Xuānyuán Shì, Hèxū Shì, Zūnlú Shì, Zhùróng Shì, Fúxī Shì, and Shénnóng Shì.
During that era,
the people used knotted cords for recording,
found sweetness in their food,
beauty in their clothing,
joy in their customs,
and contentment in their dwellings.
Neighboring states were within sight of each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs could be heard from one to another,
yet the people grew old and died without ever interacting.
In such times,
there was perfect order.
But now it has come to the point where people crane their necks and stand on tiptoes saying,
"There is a worthy person in such a place,"
and packing provisions, they rush to him.
Thus they abandon their parents at home and neglect their duties to their rulers abroad,
their footprints connecting across the borders of feudal lords,
their carriage tracks intertwining a thousand miles away.
This is the fault of the rulers' fondness for knowledge.
【一】【注】Sufficient to record the essentials only.
【Commentary】The above twelve clans,
were all ancient emperors and kings.
At that time, since historical records had not yet existed,
their sequence and order remain unknown.
They carved wood to create tallies,
and knotted ropes to signify trust,
fostering harmony between rulers and subjects,
and a pure and simple human heart.
Therefore, the Yì Jīng states,
"In ancient times, governance was achieved through knotting ropes;
later sages replaced this with written contracts."
【Transcription】"Róng Chéng Shì" Sīmǎ states:

【二】【Note】What is familiar is always sweet,
what is fitting is always beautiful.
But if one indulges in extravagance and waste,
then there will never be satisfaction.

【Four】【Annotation】The ultimate of having no desires.
【Commentary】The settlements are adjacent to each other,
not far apart,
the sounds of chickens and dogs barking

Yet their natures are each self-sufficient,
with no need for the world,
they end their days following Heaven's decree,
without interacting with each other,
the ultimate in non-action.

embracing the Way and upholding virtue,
in such times as these,

If the ruler truly loves knowledge but lacks the Way,
then the world will fall into great chaos.
How do we know it is so?
When there is much knowledge of bows, crossbows, nets, arrows, and clever traps,
then birds become disordered in the skies;
when there is much knowledge of hooks, bait, nets, and fish traps,
then fish become disordered in the waters;
when there is much knowledge of snares, cages, and pitfalls,
then beasts become disordered in the marshes;
when there is much sophistry of cunning, poison, deceit, hard-and-white arguments, and disputes over similarity and difference,
then the common people are confused by debate.
Thus, the world repeatedly falls into great chaos,
and the fault lies in the love of knowledge.
Therefore, all under heaven know to seek what they do not know but do not know to seek what they already know;
they all know to condemn what they do not consider good but do not know to condemn what they already consider good;
this is why there is great chaos.
Thus, above, the brightness of the sun and moon is obscured;
below, the essence of the mountains and rivers is dissipated;
in between, the progression of the four seasons is disrupted;
even the timid, soft insects
and the delicate, fluttering creatures
all lose their inherent nature.
How extreme is the chaos caused by the love of knowledge in the world!
This has been the case since the Three Dynasties onward.
They abandon the simple, honest people and delight in the fawning, cunning ones;
they forsake calmness, detachment, and non-action and delight in the garrulous, meddlesome ways;
and this garrulous meddling has already thrown the world into chaos!
【First】【Memorial】If the ruler above cannot be non-active, tranquil and indifferent,
clear and empty to unite with the Dao,
but instead uses knowledge and ability to govern things,
things will inevitably become corrupted,
thus leading to great chaos.
Lǎojūn said that governing the state with knowledge
is the state's calamity.
【Èr Shū】posed hypothetical questions,

【Three】【Commentary】The more intensely one attacks,
the more skillfully one evades.
Thus, even birds and beasts cannot be fathomed through knowledge,
let alone humans!
Therefore, those who govern the world rely not on cunning,
for employing cunning yields no subtlety.
【Commentary】The net is small with a handle,

Jū fú,

Since governing affairs with cunning
inevitably leads to turmoil and calamities,
therefore, one who rules a state must not employ cunning.

【Five】【Explanations】Měiměi,
describes a state of darkness and confusion.
If one forgets personal concerns and lets things take their natural course,
then the world becomes clear and peaceful;
but if one clings to traces and employs cunning,
then the world falls into great chaos.
Thus, it is known that the darkness and confusion above and below,
arise from the love of cunning.

Méng being written as měi,
is like méng (rafter) being written as ●.
(In the Fāngyán, ● is called (●)〔●〕(seven),
Guō's annotation:
Nowadays the character is written as méng.
【Six】【Annotation】Not seeking to understand what one knows but pursuing what one does not know,
this is to abandon oneself and imitate others without stopping at one's proper limit.
【Commentary】What we know
lies within our bounds;
what we do not know
lies beyond them.
To abandon the inner and seek the outer—
is that not indeed delusion?
【Transcription】"Shě jǐ" is pronounced as shě,
the same applies in the following text.
【Seven】【Annotation】Each regards their own good as good,
thus arises contention and rivalry.
【Commentary】What is considered not good refers to
Jié and Zhí;
what is considered good refers to
the ways of the sages.
Robber Zhí acted immorally to seize Dōnglíng,
while Tián Héng followed the ways of the sages to usurp the state of Qí.
Thus, though Zāng and Gǔ pursued different occupations,
they ended up losing the sheep alike;
similarly, whether one acts like Bó Yí or Zhí, though their deeds differ,
the harm to their innate nature is the same.
Foolish and conventional people
arbitrarily pass judgments,
but what is deemed good or not good
truly cannot be definitively determined.
【八】【注】For fortune, misfortune, regret, and distress,
arise from action.
And the movement of knowledge,
truly can shake heaven and earth,
govern and command all living beings.
Therefore, the ruler of men,
how can he not be cautious about his knowledge!
【Commentary】Therefore,
it continues from the preceding text.
It is precisely because the previous use of cunning and adherence to traces
that the world fell into great chaos.
"Bèi" means
chaos.
"Shuò" means
melting away.
"Huī" means
destruction.
Creeping creatures on the ground are called "chuǎn ruǎn,"
while flying insects in the air are called "xiào qiào,"
both referring to small, insignificant beings.
Adhering to traces and employing cunning
inevitably leads to severe harm,
capable of stirring yin and yang,
shaking heaven and earth,
causing eclipses of the sun and moon,
making mountains and rivers collapse and dry up,
disrupting the order of heat and cold,
so that wind and rain do not come in their proper seasons.
Creatures that fly, walk, swim, or dwell on land
lose their inherent nature,
and the obsession with cunning poisons all things,
reaching such an extreme state.
【Explanatory Text】"Upper Eclipsed" Lǐ Guō states:
Must be read with the inner tone,
also pronounced as pèi.
Sīmǎ states:
It means eclipse.
"Lower Scorched" is pronounced with shī and yuē.
Cuī states:
It means to melt away.
Sīmǎ states:
It means to collapse and dry up.
Cuī and Xiàng's version writes it as lì,
same meaning.
Xú pronounces it as yào.
"Middle Fallen" is pronounced xǔ and guī,
meaning to destroy.
"Of the Spread" is pronounced shǐ and chǐ.
"Trembling" is also written as ● in some versions,
or as chuǎn,
pronounced chuān and yuǎn.
Xiàng pronounces it as chuǎi.
"Soft" is pronounced ěr and zhuǎn.
Cuī states:
It refers to wriggling insects.
Another interpretation:
trembling and soft,
means legless insects.
"Tiny Floating" is pronounced xiāo,
the lower character is pronounced qí and ráo.
Cuī states:
Tiny floating,
refers to plants.
Lǐ states:
It refers to the category of fluttering insects.
【Nine】【Annotation】Muttering incessantly,
to instruct others based on oneself.
【Subcommentary】"Zì" means
"from".
"Sāndài" refers to
the Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu dynasties.
"Zhǒngzhǒng" describes
simple and honest people,
while "yìyì" depicts
a frivolous and cunning appearance.
"Shì" means
to discard.
"Tūntūn" refers to
instructing others based on one's own views.
In the era of utmost purity in high antiquity,
during the age of simplicity and plainness,
people emulated the round heaven in its clarity and emptiness,
followed the square earth in its tranquility and stillness,
regarded all things as part of the same clan,
and were as unknowing as birds and beasts.
But when simplicity faded and purity was lost,
when they strayed from the Dào and turned against virtue,
the sagely traces of the Five Emperors had already become evident,
and the Three Dynasties employed wisdom even more excessively;
they abandoned the plain scholars of simplicity,
favored frivolous and cunning flatterers,
discarded the self-contentment of desirelessness,
and took pleasure in instructing others with deliberate intent,
thereby throwing the world into chaos—
is this not lamentable!
【Explanatory Text】"Zhǒngzhǒng" - Xiàng reads as zhāng yǒng fǎn.
Lǐ says:
Cautious and respectful appearance.
Another says:
Pure and sincere.
"Ér yuè" is pronounced yuè.
Same below.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current version writes it as yuè.
"Yìyì" - Lǐ says:
Cunning and sly appearance.
Another says:
A person who acts with purpose.
"Tián" is pronounced tú qiān fǎn.
"Dàn" is pronounced tú zàn fǎn.
Xú reads it as dà gǎn fǎn.
"Zhūnzhūn" - Lǐ reads it as zhī rùn fǎn,
also zhī chún fǎn.
Guō pronounces it dūn,
describing the manner of teaching others based on oneself.
Same below.
Sīmǎ says:
Appearance of little wisdom.
Xú reads it as xǔ péng fǎn,
also xǔ gāng fǎn.
Xiàng's version writes it as tūn,
pronounced hēng.
Cuī's version writes the previous phrase as hēnghēng,
meaning little knowledge and confusion.
Another says:
Hēnghēng,
a robust and healthy appearance.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
[In the current version] this and the following are both written as zhūnzhūn.
Note: The character with the component "xiǎng" can also be pronounced as hēng.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition has "喘".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition has "机" for "民",
while the Zhào edition has "民".
(3) The Shìdétáng edition has "网",
and this book follows the Shìwén in emending it.
(4) The original Shìwén lacks the character "音".
(5) The character "柞" is emended based on Zhèng's commentary to the Zhōulǐ.
(6) The character ● is emended based on the Huáinánzǐ.
(7) The character ● is emended based on the Fāngyán.
(8) The Zhào edition has "正" for "止".
【Chapter One】【Explanation of Terms】The chapter is titled by its meaning.

◎Qìng Fān's case: In the annotation of Xiè Língyùn's poem "Following Duke Sòng on the Double Ninth Festival at the Xìmǎtái Gathering to Send Off Official Kǒng" from the Wénxuǎn, it quotes Sīmǎ's commentary:
Zài means
to examine.
Yòu means
to be lenient.
The Explanation of Terms omits this.
I have heard of letting the world be and indulging it,
but not of governing the world.【一】
Letting it be is done
for fear that the world would corrupt its inborn nature;
indulging it is done
for fear that the world would deviate from its virtue.【二】
If the world does not corrupt its inborn nature
nor deviate from its virtue,
what need is there to govern the world?【三】
In ancient times, when Yáo governed the world,
he made the world joyful so that people were happy with their inborn nature—
this was lack of tranquility;
when Jié governed the world,
he made the world toilsome so that people suffered in their inborn nature—
this was lack of contentment.【四】
Both lack of tranquility and lack of contentment
are contrary to virtue.
Nothing that is contrary to virtue
can last long in the world.
【一】【注】To let things be at ease brings order,
while to govern them leads to chaos.
Humans are born upright,
and if nothing disturbs them,
their nature and destiny will not go astray,
and their desires and aversions will not err.
If those in power cannot act through non-action,
the people will all pursue what the rulers do,
thus giving rise to seductive cravings and desires, corrupting the people's innate nature.
Therefore, what is valued in a sage king
is not the ability to govern,
but the practice of non-action, allowing all things to act on their own.
【Commentary】Yòu (宥) means
leniency.
Zài (在) means
natural spontaneity.
Zhì (治) means
governing and controlling.
The fable states,
it is heard that the sages and worthies entrusted things to their own course,
allowing natural leniency and spontaneity,
and thus the world was peaceful and tranquil;
if one establishes teachings to govern the common people,
things lose their inherent nature,
just as Bólè managed horses.
【Explanatory Text】"Wén Zài Yòu" reads yòu,
meaning leniency.
"Zé Zhì" is pronounced zhí lì fǎn.
The following zhì luàn is the same.
"Yù Wù" is wū lù fǎn.
"Hào Yù" is hū bào fǎn.
【Two】【Shū】Nature is
the principle inherent in life;
virtue is
the name for meritorious conduct;
hence the discourse on allowing freedom exists
to prevent the fault of excessive indulgence.
If one does not follow their nature freely,
there is fear that things may lead to depravity and loss of innate nature.
If not lenient towards them,
there is further concern they might imitate others,
causing their virtue to shift and change.
【Three】【Annotations】Without governance, there will be no excess or indulgence.
【Commentary】When nature is upright and virtue is settled,
what need is there to laboriously implement governance and administration!
Having governance is not as good as having no governance,
having action is not as good as having no action.
【Explanatory Text】"Is there one who governs the world?" The Cuī version reads: "Is there one who governs the world? It is a failure of ability,"
stating:
"To forcibly govern it,
is a failure of ability."
【Four】【Annotation】Although Yáo governed the world with benevolence,
his methods still involved governance.
Though order and chaos differ in nature,
in terms of depriving later generations of tranquility and contentment,
causing beings to compete, revere, fear, and despise without attaining self-fulfillment, they are the same.
Therefore, praising Yáo and condemning Jié
