【Commentary】Tián means
tranquility.
Yú means
joy.
Cuì means
sorrow.
Yáo ruled people with virtue,
and people sang the "Jī Rǎng" song,
which went against their tranquil nature;
Jié harmed all things with cruelty,
causing them to suffer sorrow and distress,
which went against their joyful nature.
Though the governance of Yáo and Jié differed in this way,
both caused all things to lose their inherent nature equally.
【Explanation】"Rén lè" is pronounced with the sound "luò".
"Tián" is pronounced as "tú qiān" in reverse.
"Cuì cuì" is pronounced as "zài jì" in reverse,
meaning illness.
Guǎngyǎ states:
it means worry.
Cuī's version writes it as "zuì".
"Yú" is pronounced as "yú",
while Xú pronounces it as "yù".
"Gù yù" is pronounced as "yú".
【Five】【Note】Content and self-satisfaction,
can then last long.
【Commentary】Yáo failed to understand people,
Jié seized things without joy,
neither aligning with the pure and harmonious nature;
to desire longevity,
such a thing has never existed under heaven.
Does excessive joy
lean towards yang?
Does excessive anger
lean towards yin?
When both yin and yang are imbalanced,
the seasons do not arrive timely,
the harmony of cold and heat is disrupted,
and this instead harms the human form!
It causes people's joy and anger to lose their proper place,
their dwelling to be without constancy,
their thoughts unable to attain self-contentment,
and their midway path to lack coherent pattern.
Thereupon, the world begins to be filled with arrogance, resentment, and unruly behavior,
and thereafter appear the actions of bandits like Zhi and sages like Zeng and Shi.
Hence, employing the whole world to reward the good is insufficient,
employing the whole world to punish the evil falls short,
so the vastness of the world is inadequate for reward and punishment.
Since the three dynasties and below,
people have clamorously busied themselves with rewards and punishments as their main affair.
How could they have the leisure to settle the genuine condition of their innate nature and destiny!
【一】【疏】Pí,
means to assist.
Joy emanates from the hún,
anger arises from the pò,
humans are endowed with yīn and yáng,
sharing the same qì as heaven and earth.
When Yáo made the people joyful,
he aided yáng's warmth and expansion;
when Jié incited anger in people,
he bolstered yīn's harshness and severity.
If humans' joy and anger become excessive,
then heaven loses its regularity,
resulting in no heat in midsummer,
and no frost in deep winter.
Once harmony is disrupted,
compounded by natural disasters,
people suffer from numerous illnesses—
is this not ultimately harming the physical form?
One should not act or create rules arbitrarily,
as it will inevitably lead to ruin and injury.
【Translated Text】"Pí yú" is read as it is.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to assist.
Another interpretation says:
It means simultaneously.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
In the explanatory text,
"pí" is read as is,
Sīmǎ states,
it means to assist,
another interpretation says,
it means simultaneously,
yet the following text mentions,
"yīn and yáng are both pí,"
the four seasons do not arrive,
the harmony of cold and heat is not achieved,
then interpreting it as assistance is already untenable,
and interpreting it as simultaneous is even more mistaken.
In this case, the character "pí" should be read as the "pí" in "pí liú bào lè."
The "Ěryǎ Shìgǔ" states,
"pí liú,"
means "bào lè."
Combined, it is called "pí liú,"
separately, it may be referred to only as "liú,"
as in the line "luō cǎi qí liú" from the poem "Sāng Róu";
or only as "pí,"
here, "pí yú yáng, pí yú yīn" is an example.
"Bào lè,"
in Máo Gōng's commentary, is written as "bào shuò."
Zhèng Shī's annotation says:
When plucking and gathering, it becomes "bào shuò" and sparse.
Thus, "bào shuò" is like peeling off or falling away.
Great joy pertains to yáng,
great anger pertains to yīn,
so excessive joy harms yáng,
and excessive anger harms yīn.
"Pí yīn, pí yáng"
means injuring the harmony of yīn and yáng,
hence the four seasons do not arrive,
and the harmony of cold and heat is not achieved.
If following Sīmǎ's interpretation of "pí" as assistance,
then the following three clauses do not connect logically.
In the "Huáinánzǐ Yuándào Piān,"
it says, "Great anger in humans breaks yīn,
great joy collapses yáng,"
which aligns precisely with the same meaning here.
【二】【Note】These are all followers of Yáo and Jié,
who cause excessive joy and anger in things,
leading to such calamities.
Humans, situated between heaven and earth,
are most capable of disturbing all living beings and unsettling yīn and yáng with their intelligent awareness of joy and anger.
Hence, in the gap between gain and loss,
when joy and anger gather in the hearts of the common people,
the harmony of cold and heat is disrupted,
the rhythm of the four seasons goes awry,
all measures become confused and lost,
and myriad affairs fall into disarray.
【Commentary】Being mired in personal joys and angers,
thus causing the common people's planning and considerations to lose authenticity,
already violates the principles of statutes and regulations,
this is ruin indeed.
【Transcription】"Sīlǜ" is read as xī sì fǎn.
"Dàguò" is pronounced as tài.
【Three】【Annotation】The desire for rewards makes one good,
thus rewards cannot be sufficient.
【Transcription】"Qiáo" - Xiǎng reads as qīn xiāo fǎn,
or alternatively qù yāo fǎn,
Guō pronounces as jiǎo,
Lǐ pronounces as jiāo.
"Jié" - Lǐ reads as qù jí fǎn,
Xú reads as qǐ liè fǎn.
Cuī states:
Qiáojié
means unsettled intention.
"Zhuó" - chì jiǎo fǎn,
Guō reads as dīng jiǎo fǎn,
Xiǎng pronounces as ●.
"Zhì" - chì èr fǎn,
Lǐ reads as zhū lì fǎn,
Xiǎng reads as zhū lì fǎn,
also chì lì fǎn.
Cuī states:
Zhuózhì,
means uneven movement.
"Zhī xíng" - xià mèng fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Fear of punishment brings it to a halt,
thus punishment cannot prevail.
【Commentary】Qiáo,
means deceitful and false.
Jié,
means to question and blame.
Zhuó,
means solitary.
Zhì,
means fierce.
Thus, with deceit and falsehood, questioning and blaming,
standing aloof from the crowd,
uniquely harboring fierceness,
they lightly trampled upon others,
beginning with Yáo,
followed later by the wickedness of Dào Zhí,
the goodness of Zēng and Shǐ,
once good and evil were clearly manifested,
rewards and punishments were tied to them.
Aspiring for rewards, they practiced good;
fearing punishment, they refrained from evil.
Even if all the axes under heaven were used, it would not suffice to punish evil;
even if the treasures of the entire universe were exhausted, it would not suffice to reward good.
Jǐ,
means sufficient.
【Transcription】"Néng Shèng" is pronounced as "shēng".
【Five】【Memorial】If rewards and punishments are forgotten,
then the essence of authenticity lies in sufficiency.
【Six】【Annotation】Forgetting rewards and punishments yet becoming naturally good,
one's inherent nature then becomes fully satisfied.
Now, rewards and punishments
are what the sage kings used to correspond to merits and faults,
not to display encouragement or intimidation.
Thus, when principle is perfected, they are discarded,
after which the ultimate unity can be returned to.
However, from the Three Dynasties onward,
people then sought their traces and deeds,
hence clamorously competing with these traces,
ultimately taking what is relied upon as their main affair—
how could the true disposition of their inherent nature find leisure to be at peace!
【Commentary】"Xiōngxiōng" means
clamor and uproar,
which refers to competitive striving.
People fear the punishment of the axe and execution,
yet also covet the reward of high office and honors.
Their minds harbor countless worries,
and affairs arise in endless varieties.
They clamorously compete and strive without knowing when to stop.
Since the Xia and Yin dynasties,
this trend has gradually spread,
with rewards and punishments causing turmoil and disturbance,
leaving people in constant haste and confusion all day long.
How could there be any room for them to peacefully settle their lives and natures!
【Transcription】"Xiōngxiōng" is pronounced as xiōng.
【Collation】(1) The character 'wéi' is deleted according to the 'Various Scholars' Commentary and Discussions'.
(2) In the Zhào Jiànyì edition, 'shī' is mistakenly written as 'yāo',
while the Shìdétáng edition writes it as 'shī'.
Is it delight in beauty?
That is excess in form.
Delight in keen hearing?
That is excess in sound.
Delight in benevolence?
That is confusion in virtue;
delight in righteousness?
That is contradiction to reason.
Delight in ritual?
That is an aid to artifice;
delight in music?
That is an aid to dissipation.
Delight in sagacity?
That is an aid to craft;
delight in knowledge?
That is an aid to faultfinding.
If the world is to find peace for the inborn nature and its condition,
these eight things
may be preserved
or may be discarded;
but if the world is not to find peace for the inborn nature and its condition,
then these eight things
will begin to warp and constrict the world as they shove it into confusion.
And yet the world will honor them and cherish them!
Great is the delusion of the world!
They do not merely pass by them and then leave them behind,
but they prepare themselves with fasting and austerities in order to discourse on them,
kneeling formally in order to transmit them,
singing and drumming and dancing in order to applaud them
—what am I to do in the face of all this?
【一】【疏】explains,
it is attachment and defilement.
Lust,
is indulgence and fixation.
Yearning to depart and admiring the vast,
is being fixated on sounds and sights.
【Text】"而且" as in the character's pronunciation,
Xú reads it as zǐ yú in the opposite tone.
【Explanation】 Pronounced as yuè.
The same applies below.
【Two Perspectives】Virtue holds no aversion or favor,
yet partial affection disrupts virtue;
Principle knows no right or wrong,
yet judging faults contradicts principle.
To defy,
is to oppose.
【Interpretation】"Is悖" must be read internally as fan,
Xu reads it as Pu not fan.
【Three】【Memorials】Rites involve
bowing, kneeling, and bending in salute,
with elaborate or simplified protocols.
Music encompasses
the Xiánchí and Dàxià compositions,
the twelve pitches and eight tones.
Discussing rites only fosters superficial skills and artifice,
while indulging in music further amplifies seductive melodies of the pentatonic scale.
【Explanatory Text】"Shì xiāng" is read as xī liàng fǎn,
meaning to assist.
This applies to the following and annotations alike.
"Yú jì" is read as qí qǐ fǎn,
Lǐ pronounces it as qí.
Cuī agrees,
saying:
It means not upright.
【Four】【Annotation】When principles are beyond words,
speaking of them leads to the peril of excess and contradiction.
Xiàng means
to assist.
【Commentary】Expounding the traces of the sages,
aids the arts of the world;
cherishing wisdom and strategy,
remedies the flaws of right and wrong.
【Explanation】"Shuō zhī" is pronounced as "zhì".
"Yú cī" is pronounced with the initial "jí" and the final "sī".
【Five】【Annotation】Existence and non-existence have no fixed abode;
by accepting the portion one receives,
then life's course is secured.
【Commentary】The eight refer to
acumen, clarity, benevolence, righteousness, rites, music, sagacity, and wisdom.
It means that people are endowed with different dispositions,
and their inherent natures vary.
For individuals like Lí Kuàng and Zēng Shǐ,
who inherently possess these qualities,
preserving them is appropriate;
but for the masses, whose nature lacks them,
striving for them goes against authenticity,
so discarding them is fitting.
【Six】【Annotation】If one must preserve these eight things,
then one cannot follow nature freely,
hence it leads to being constrained and confined.
【Commentary】"Coiled and cramped" refers to
an appearance of being unable to stretch freely.
"Hurried and flustered" describes
a state of haste and agitation.
All living beings in the world,
only know to exceed their limits,
unable to remain content with their lot,
coil and cramp themselves in self-restriction,
boast and embellish their human affairs,
hurried and flustered in their rush,
racing and chasing after material things.
It is due to these eight aspects not being forgotten
that such flaws arise.
【Translated Text】"Luǎn" is pronounced as lì zhuǎn fǎn.
Cuī's version writes it as Luán.
"Juǎn" is pronounced as juǎn miǎn fǎn,
Xú pronounces it as jū ruǎn fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
Luǎn juǎn,
means a state of not stretching out comfortably.
Cuī agrees.
Another explanation:
It means pulling each other.
"Cāng" is pronounced as cāng.
Cuī's version writes it as qiāng.
"Náng" is read as is.
Cuī states:
Qiāng náng,
is like qiǎng rǎng.
◎Lú Wénchāo comments:
In current versions, cāng is written as chuàng.
【Seven】【Annotation】Unable to discard it,
is already a mistake.
Yet still further honor it as something precious,
is that not extremely deluded!
【Commentary】The preceding eight items are
principles that disrupt the world;
being unable to forget and discard them
is already a great delusion.
Yet further revering them
and using them as models
is profoundly lamentable.
【Explanation】"Nǎi fù": read with the pronunciation fú yòu.
【八】【Note】Not merely because it is entrusted and passed by,
but because it is treasured so dearly.
【Commentary】The meaning of the eight principles,
is like straw dogs—
once they have passed,
they should not be gathered again.
Sincerely prohibiting to achieve solemnity,
clearly stating the adherence to rites,
with the ruler and subjects kneeling and sitting,
taking turns to present offerings,
beating the songs of Jiǔsháo,
dancing to the melodies of Dàzhāng.
Treasuring the temporary dwelling,
to such an extent,
Zhuāngzǐ witnessed it,
yet had no way to change it.
【Explanation】"而去" begins with the pronunciation "lǜ" and is read as "fǎn".
"之邪" in Cui's edition only this character is written as "xié",
the rest are all written as "zhǐ".
"齊戒" in another version is also written as "zhāi",
same.
Pronounced as "cè jiē fǎn".
"跪" is pronounced as "qí guǐ fǎn",
Guo reads it as "wēi".
【Collation】(1) The character '邪' was amended according to the Shidetáng edition.
(2) The Shidetáng edition uses '愴',
with the annotation being the same.
The Zhào Jiànyì edition uses '傖'.
Thus when a gentleman finds it unavoidable to preside over the world,
nothing is better than non-action.
Through non-action, one can then settle the true state of his innate nature and destiny.
Therefore, if one values his person more than governing the world,
he can be entrusted with the world;
if one loves his person more than governing the world,
he can be given the charge of the world.
Hence, if a gentleman can refrain from dissipating his five internal organs,
and avoid displaying his keen senses;
if he remains as still as a corpse yet manifests like a dragon,
as silent as a deep abyss yet resounds like thunder;
if his spirit moves and Heaven follows;
if he is composed and non-active while all things evolve like swirling dust—
then what leisure would I have to govern the world?
【一】【注】"Non-action" does not mean
keeping one's hands folded and remaining silent;
rather, it means letting each thing act according to its own nature,
so that its innate qualities and life are preserved.
"Acting out of necessity" does not mean
being compelled by threats or punishments;
it means embracing the Dào and cherishing simplicity,
allowing things to follow their inevitable course to the fullest,
and the world will naturally submit.
【Commentary】The gentleman is
a sage.
When compelled to oversee the world,
he always remains in a state of non-action.
Although he again practices non-action,
it is not about remaining silent and idle;
his actions and stillness are without deliberate intent,
yet the essence of his nature and destiny has never been unsettled.
【Transcription】"Lì" is pronounced as lì,
and also as lèi.
◎Jiāshìfù said:
It means valuing one's own self more than the means to govern the world,
cherishing one's own self more than the means to govern the world.
Because of this valuing and cherishing,
therefore there is non-action.
【二】【注】As for those who would lightly risk their lives in pursuit of gain,
abandoning their own nature to sacrifice for material things,
they cannot even secure their own well-being—
how then could they possibly bring order to the world!
【Commentary】Valuing the self and belittling gain,
prioritizing the inner self over external matters,
preserving and cherishing one's essence and spirit,
without being swayed by worldly affairs—
such a person can thus be entrusted to sit above all things,
and entrust their transformation to the world.
【Three】【Notes】Excessive pulling out will cause injury.
【Commentary】The five viscera are the abode of the ethereal and refined spirits;
acuity is the function of the ears and eyes.
If one distinguishes the consciousness and emotions of the five viscera,
and highlights the use of acuity,
then the essence and spirit will rush about within,
and the ears and eyes will be exhausted and lost on the outside.
【Explanation】"No solution" as the character reads.
Another reading is xiè,
meaning to disperse.
【Four】【Annotation】Whether speaking out or remaining silent,
one should always do so without preconceived intentions and entrust everything to spontaneity.
【Commentary】The sage in stillness is like a corpse in tranquility,
in movement resembles a flying dragon in the heavens;
how could there be a distinction between stillness, movement, principle, and teaching?
Thus, stillness gives rise to movement,
residing like a corpse yet appearing as a dragon,
silent as the abyss yet resounding like thunder.
This aims to clarify that stillness and movement, movement and stillness,
principle and teaching, teaching and principle,
are neither identical nor different.
【Transcription】"Lóng xiàn": xián biàn fǎn.
Xiàng's and Cuī's editions have it as "xiàn",
Xiàng's pronunciation is "jiàn",
Cuī's pronunciation is "xiàn".
【Five】【Annotation】The spirit moves in harmony with things,
Heaven follows the principle in its course.
【Commentary】The term "spirit" refers to
that which wondrously governs all things and gives them expression,
being both movement and stillness simultaneously,
its virtue equal to the vast heavens,
compliantly following and giving life to all beings.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
It resides like a corpse yet appears like a dragon,
manifesting without being seen;
silent as the abyss yet resonant like thunder,
transforming without moving;
the spirit stirs and heaven follows,
accomplishing all through non-action.
【Six】【Annotation】Like the self-movement of drifting dust.
【Commentary】Accumulation,
is dust.
At ease and self-possessed,
acting without effort and empty in tranquility,
like the wind stirring fine dust,
resembling objects floating in the sky,
the yang energy drifts and sways,
merely following its course in coming and going.
【Transcription】"Cóng róng" is pronounced as seven róng fǎn.
"Chuī" is pronounced as chāng shuì fǎn,
and also chāng guī fǎn.
Some versions write it as "chuī",
with the same meaning.
"Lěi" is pronounced as liè wèi fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
"chuī lěi"
means like moving upward.
Xiàng and Guō explain:
it is like the self-movement of dust particles.
【Seven】【Annotation】Simply let things take their natural course.
【Commentary】When all things and the self blend into one,
united in spontaneity,
what need is there for effort or leisure,
much less for imposing methods of governance!
Cuī Qú asked Lǎo Dān, saying:
"If the world is not governed,
how can the people's hearts be kept in good order?"
Lǎo Dān said:
"You must be careful not to disturb the human mind.
The human mind represses what is lowly and advances what is lofty,
and in this up-and-down struggle it becomes imprisoned and destroyed.
It is soft and supple yet can overcome the hard and strong.
When sharpened and polished,
it becomes hot as a scorching fire,
and cold as freezing ice.
In the swiftness of a bow and rise, it can travel twice beyond the four seas.
In repose, it is deep and still;
in motion, it soars into the heavens.
Fierce and proud, it cannot be tethered—
is this not the human mind alone!"
【一】【注】To disturb it would harm its inherent goodness.
【Commentary】His surname was Cuī,
given name Jù,
but it is unknown where he was from.
He once asked:
"If governing through non-interference does not regulate people's hearts,
how can one practice goodness?"
The reply stated:
"To let them be and give them freedom
naturally aligns with their inherent principles;
to establish laws and regulate things
would instead disturb and agitate people's hearts."
[The matter of people's hearts] is discussed in the following text.
【Translated Text】"Cuī Qū" Xiàng's edition has Cuī written as Qú.
Pronounced as qiú zhū in reverse.
Cuī Qū,
is the name of a person.
"Lǎo Dān" is pronounced as tǔ lán in reverse.
"Nǚ Shèn" is read with the sound of rǔ.
"Yīng" is pronounced as yú yíng in reverse,
and also as yú yíng in reverse.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to lead.
Cuī says:
It means to bind or ensnare.
【二】【注】When pushed, it goes down;
when advanced, it rises up,
meaning it is easily swayed.
【Commentary】It is human nature to push others down
and elevate oneself above,
as is commonly the case.
【Text Explanation】"Pái" is read as pí jiē fǎn.
Cuī's edition writes it as "pái".
"Jìn shàng" is read as shí zhǎng fǎn.
The same applies to the annotations and below.
"Qí yì" is read as yǐ chì fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】There is nothing to promote or advance,
so it is merely safe and secure.
【Explanation】When the mind sinks into the highs and lows,
it becomes bound by external circumstances,
like a prisoner in confinement,
entangled in vexations and distress.
【Translated Text】"Imprison and destroy" read as written,
Xu reads it with the fanqie spelling of suǒ lì.
It means to imprison and destroy all things.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Above and below imprison and destroy,
meaning to deceive above and deceive below,
causing the mind to be confined and strangled,
without self-ease.
The tender and graceful are artificially shaped,
then the hard can be made soft,
the sharp and cutting are straightforward and direct,
cold and heat change a hundredfold,
water and fire are applied together,
disturbing it thus eventually leads to being unstoppable.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation is likely mistaken.
【Four】【Annotation】It means that if one can be pliant and yielding,
then those who are rigid and strong will become gentle.
【Commentary】Nàoyuē,
means soft and weak.
Feigning emotion through softness and weakness,
aims to subdue the strong and rigid.
【Transcription】"Nào" is read as chānglüè fǎn,
also as zhíjiǎo fǎn.
【五】【Note】The heat of a blazing fire,
the chill of frozen ice,
all arise from the accumulation of joy and anger.
If one neither carves nor polishes,
but preserves each in its natural simplicity,
then how could there be any ice or burning coals?
【Commentary】Lián (廉)
is the pursuit of reputation.
Guì (劌)
means to harm.
Carving and polishing one's reputation and conduct,
aims to stand out among others.
If anger arises against one's feelings,
it becomes colder than freezing ice;
if joy follows the heart's desires,
it grows hotter than scorching fire.
【Explanation】"Lián Guì": "jū wèi" pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to injure.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means sharp.
"Zhuó": "dīng jiǎo" pronunciation.
【六】【Note】It is the customs that move people.
【Commentary】The mind that follows the environment,
in the span of a single thought,
has already pervaded the ten directions;
how much more so in the time between a bow and rising,
could it not reach the four seas again!
【Seven】【Annotation】In stillness, one can be made as deep as an abyss,
in motion, one is connected to heaven and leaps with vigor.
【Commentary】The mind with desires
lacks a fixed standard.
Occasionally it becomes still,
like flowing water encountering a deep pool;
when it meets circumstances, it stirs,
akin to the high heavens suspended;
if it does not cease its stirring,
then it is bound to leap and surge like the sky.
【Explanatory Text】"Xuán ér tiān" is pronounced as xuán.
Xiàng's edition does not have the character "ér",
stating:
"Admiring the lofty and yearning for the distant,
hence it is called 'xuán tiān'."
【八】【Note】The changes in the human heart
know no bounds in action.
If allowed to flow freely,
it calms and naturally (two) connects;
if restrained and controlled,
it strains and rebels with arrogance.
Such arrogance
is an unstoppable force.
【Commentary】To push down those below and advance those above,
to delight in beauty and detest ugliness, to feel joy and anger,
to act recklessly with arrogance and conceit,
all that cannot be restrained or controlled—
does it not lie within the human heart!
【Explanation】"僨" is pronounced as Xiang Fenwen's fǎnqiè.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
It means to fall stiff.
Guǒ gives the pronunciation as bēn.
"驕" is read as its usual pronunciation,
and also as Jūbiǎo's fǎnqiè.
Guǒ states:
As for "僨驕,"
it refers to an uncontrollable force.
【Collation】(1) In the Shìdétáng edition, "藏" is written as "臧".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "自".
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor first disturbed people's hearts with benevolence and righteousness.
Yáo and Shùn then toiled until their thighs were without surplus flesh
and their shins without hair,
nourishing the forms of all under heaven,
tormenting their five organs to practice benevolence and righteousness,
and straining their vital energy to establish laws and standards.
Yet there were still those they could not subdue.
Yáo then exiled Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
cast out the Sānmiáo to Sānwéi,
and banished Gònggōng to Yōudū—
this was because he could not subdue all under heaven.
When this reached the time of the Three Kings, all under heaven were greatly alarmed.
Below there were Jié and Zhí,
above there were Zēng and Shǐ,
and both Confucians and Mohists arose in full force.
Thereupon, joy and anger mutually doubted each other,
foolishness and wisdom deceived one another,
good and bad denounced each other,
falsehood and truth ridiculed one another—
and all under heaven declined.
Great virtues diverged,
and innate natures became shattered.
All under heaven prized knowledge,
and the common people were exhausted in their pursuits.
Thereupon, axes and saws were used to cut,
ink lines to execute,
and chisels and awls to decide.
All under heaven fell into great chaos and disorder—
the crime lay in disturbing people's hearts.
Hence, the worthy hid in deep mountains and beneath steep cliffs,
while rulers of ten thousand chariots worried and trembled in their court halls above.
【一】【注】The Yellow Emperor did not act for the sake of benevolence and righteousness;
he simply became one with all things in obscurity,
and thus the traces of benevolence and righteousness naturally appeared.
Once these traces emerged,
the minds of later generations inevitably pursued them of their own accord,
which is also how the traces of the Yellow Emperor caused things to become entangled.
【Commentary】Huángdì established principles according to what was appropriate,
nurturing the people with compassionate love.
This was indeed different from one-sidedly emphasized benevolence
and the righteousness of censuring others.
The kings of later generations,
adhering to his tracks,
were called sages by the common people,
but the disturbance of people's hearts began from this.
The flaws arose from the later kings;
the fault does not lie with Huángdì.
【Explanatory Text】"Zì jiàn" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
The same applies below.
refers to white flesh.
When Yáo and Shùn followed Huángdì's path,
their bodies and minds became emaciated and exhausted,
their thighs thinned without white flesh,
their shins became bare without fine hair,
yet they nurtured the forms and appearances of the world,
and pacified the natures and dispositions of all things.
With worries and sorrows pent up inside their five organs,
and blood and energy strained solemnly on the outside,
they practiced benevolence and righteousness as their compass and square,
and established laws and standards as their models.
Even so, they still could not avoid banishing the vicious clans,
thus there were matters they could not overcome.
【Textual Explanation】"Gǔ" is pronounced as in ancient.
The base of the shank is called the thigh.
"Bá" is read with the sound pàn mò,
Xiàng gives the reading fù mò.
Lǐ offers the reading fú gài,
and says:
It refers to white flesh.
Some say:
The character should be written as "fú".
"Fú",
means a front apron.
Cuī states:
"Bá",
is ●.
"Jìng" is read as xíng dìng.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: To restrain one's vital energy and blood,
is similar to what Mèngzǐ means by tormenting one's mind and will.
"Jīn" here means
to torment,
as explained in the "Shì Yán" chapter of the Ěryǎ.
【Three】【Memorials】In ancient times, Emperor Hóng had an unworthy son,
whom the world called Hùndùn,
who was Huāndōu,
forming a faction with Gònggōng,
and was exiled to the southern border.
Jìnyún had an unworthy son,
whom the world called Tāotiè,
who was Sānmiáo,
serving as one of Yáo's feudal lords,
and was enfeoffed with the state of Sānmiáo.
The state was located with Dòngtíng Lake to the left,
Pénglí to the right,
residing in Yùzhāng,
near the Southern Mountain.
Sānwéi,
a mountain name,
is in the western border,
which is the land of the Western Qiāng in Qínzhōu.
Shǎohào had an unworthy son,
whom the world called Qióngqí,
who was Gònggōng,
serving as Yáo's water official.
Yōudū was in the north,
which is the land of Yōuzhōu.
The "Shàngshū" mentions the execution of Gǔn,
but this text does not cover it in detail.
These four individuals all harbored malevolence,
refusing to follow Yáo's transformation,
so they were cast out to the four borders,
which shows that Yáo could not overcome the affairs of the world.
The banishment of the Four Fiends was carried out by Shùn;
now when referring to Yáo,
it is because Shùn was acting in Yáo's position at that time.
【Transcription】"Huān" is pronounced as huān.
"Dōu" (below) [dīng] (three) hóu fǎn.
"Chóng Shān" is in the southern frontier.
In the sixtieth year of Yáo's reign,
Huāndōu was exiled to Chóng Shān.
"Tóu sānmiáo" - Cuī's version uses "kill" for "tóu",
while the Book of Documents uses "exile".
Sānmiáo refers to
the son of Jìnyúnshì,
namely Tāotiè.
"Sānwēi" is pronounced as wēi.
It is also written as "wēi".
Sānwēi is
a mountain in the western frontier,
now part of Tiānshuǐ.
In the sixty-sixth year of Yáo's reign,
Sānmiáo was exiled to Sānwēi.
"Gònggōng" is pronounced as gōng.
Gònggōng is
an official title,
namely Qióngqí.
"Yōudū" - Lǐ Yún states:
It refers to Yōuzhōu.
The Book of Documents records it as Yōuzhōu,
located in the northern frontier.
In the sixty-fourth year of Yáo's reign,
Gònggōng was banished to Yōuzhōu.
【四】【注】Yáo and Shùn are the names of emperors and kings,
all of which are merely their traces.
I entrust myself to these traces, but the traces are not me.
Thus, those who are astonished come from the world.
The more the world is astonished,
the coarser their traces become.
Coarseness and subtlety
depend on whether the path is smooth or perilous.
Does the traveler ever change their feet because of it?
Therefore, the sage is one,
yet there are differences like Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ.
To understand these differences,
they are merely names of the times and the world,
insufficient to name the reality of the sage.
Hence, Yáo and Shùn—
how could they be limited to just one Yáo and one Shùn?
Thus, although there may be a dignified and sorrowful appearance,
and traces of benevolence and righteousness,
the source of these traces remains whole.
【Commentary】Shī means
extension.
From the time of Huángdì until Yáo and Shùn,
the traces of the sages stagnated,
all things were disturbed and chaotic,
extending to the Three Sovereigns,
where the alarm and fear became even more intense.
【Explanation Text】"Extends to" is read with the sound of "zhì".
Cuī Zǐ states:
It means to prolong.
"Greatly startled" — startled,
means alarmed.
"More crude" is pronounced as "cū".
The same applies below.
【Five】【Memorials】 Jié and Zhí conduct themselves with the behaviors of petty men, which are considered base;
Zēng and Shǐ conduct themselves with the behaviors of noble men, which are considered superior.
【Six】【Exposition】It is said that Confucians and Mohists adhere to the traces [of the past],
and because of this, disputes over right and wrong arise.
【Seven】【Memorials】They delighted in what was right and were angered by what was wrong,
leading to mutual suspicion and distrust.
【Eight】【Neglect】Adorning wisdom to startle the foolish,
mutually deceiving and disrespecting each other.
【Transcription】"Yú zhì" is pronounced as wisdom.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【Nine】【Commentary】Good and not good,
each side condemns the other.
【一０】【Commentary】They deride the false and believe in the true,
ridiculing each other.
【一一】【Note】None can equal self-attainment.
【Commentary】Conflicts persist and entangle,
a sign of the universe's decline.
【一二】【Note】Establishing minor differences without stopping at division.
【Commentary】When joy, anger, right, and wrong,
blaze with excessive intensity,
one's natural lifespan is cut short prematurely,
and life becomes scattered and disordered.
Scattered and disordered,
means in disarray.
【13】【Comment】Knowledge is boundless, and if one delights in it,
there will never be enough to satisfy their demands.
【Commentary】The sage exhausts boundless knowledge,
how could the common people not deplete it!
【Transcription】"Hào zhì" pronounced as hū bào fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
【一四】【Note】Carving and polishing one's nature and destiny,
has led to this point.
【Commentary】The ink line and carpenter's square
straighten the crookedness of wood;
ritual and righteousness,
demonstrate the elevation and diminishment for people;
the mallet and chisel,
bore holes through wood;
penal laws,
sever the body and head of a person.
Craftsmen wield axes and saws to cut wood,
sages employ rituals and laws to harm the Way.
【Explanation】"釿" is pronounced as jīn,
originally also written as 斤.
"鋸" is pronounced as jù.
"制焉" refers to the application of the adze and saw for punishment,
meaning like corporal punishment.
"繩墨殺焉" is read with the characters' standard pronunciations.
Cuī states:
it refers to executing by exacting justice.
"椎" is pronounced with the retroflex initial and the rhyme of zhuī.
"鑿" is pronounced with the initial z and the rhyme of luò.
"決焉" is pronounced with the initial g and the rhyme of xué,
or alternatively with the initial k and the rhyme of xué.
Cuī states:
it is a corporal punishment,
hence the use of the mallet and chisel.
【一五】【注】If one entrusts things to spontaneity and resides in what is fitting,
then the worthy and foolish follow their innate dispositions, and the noble and humble tread their proper positions.
Sovereign and minister, superior and subordinate,
none fail to reach their ultimate principle,
and there are no calamities under heaven.
These traces, however,
end up disturbing the hearts of all under heaven,
causing them to race about uncontrollably.
Therefore, those of medium intelligence and below
all without exception adorn their natures outwardly to dazzle and confuse the masses,
detesting the straightforward and vilifying the upright,
gathering followers who draw one another in.
Thus, those who uphold authenticity lose their foundation,
while those who exalt falsity usurp the handle of power.
Thereupon, the ruler above is burdened with worries,
and the people below are trapped in hardship.
【Commentary】"Jǐjǐ" means
trampling upon one another.
Another interpretation suggests chaos,
a great disorder in the universe,
with the blame lying on the sages and the wise.
The way of the noble person wanes,
who retreats into obscurity in forests and marshes,
while the ruler, though in the court,
is constantly anxious and fearful,
lacking capable assistance,
fearing the state may collapse into peril.
【Explanatory Text】"Jí jí" is pronounced like jí,
with the pronunciation in the reverse of zài yì,
meaning trampling upon one another.
It is also written as yáo yáo.
The Guangya states:
yáo,
means chaos.
"Dà shān" is pronounced as tài,
or as per the common reading.
"Kān" is pronounced with the reverse of kǔ yán,
another pronunciation is kǔ xián reverse,
and also kǔ yán reverse.
"Yán" is pronounced as yán,
with the reverse of yǔ xián.
Another pronunciation is yán,
with the reverse of yǔ xián (and)
(eight).
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
The current edition writes it as "yán" (nine).
◎Yú Yuè states:
In the explanatory text,
"dà shān",
is pronounced as "tài",
but it can also be read with its original sound,
and it is correct to read it with its original sound.
This generally refers to a large mountain,
not necessarily the Eastern Peak, Tài Shān.
"Kān" should be "zhàn".
In the "Wénxuǎn", the text "Fēngshàn Wén" says "zhàn ēn wěi hóng",
Lǐ's annotation states:
"Zhàn",
means deep.
"Zhàn yán",
is like deep cliffs,
because it refers to mountain cliffs,
the character was changed from the water radical to the mountain radical.
"Shān" describes its size,
"yán" describes its depth,
the meanings correspond appropriately.
Scholars who do not understand its meaning,
and pronounce "dà" as "tài",
are mistaken.
In the "Tián Zǐfāng Piān", it says "its spirit passes through the great mountain without hindrance",
"enters deep springs without getting wet",
the explanatory text pronounces "dà" as "tài",
the error is the same as here.
In the "Wénxuǎn", "Fù of Wind" says "along the curves of Tài Shān",
an ancient poem says "tall, tall, the lone bamboo grows",
"its roots are anchored in the curves of Tài Shān",
but the wind's path,
and the bamboo's growth,
are not necessarily on Tài Shān.
The original text should have been written as "dà shān" in both cases,
generally referring to a large mountain.
Later people mistakenly read it as "tài",
and changed it to "tài".
"To dazzle" is pronounced "xuàn", universally reversed.
"Detest straightness" is pronounced "wù", with "lù" reversed.
"Luxuriant growth" is pronounced "fán".
【Collation】(1) In Zhào's advisory edition, the character is written as 太 in large script.
(2) Zhào's edition lacks the character 乎.
(3) The character 丁 has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original version of the explanatory text.
(4) In the Shìdétáng edition, 而 is written as 天,
and in Zhào's edition, there is the character 天 following 而.
(5) In Zhào's edition, 聖 is written as 至.
(6) In the Shìdétáng edition, 若 is written as 故.
(7) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character 遂.
(8) The character 反 has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original version of the explanatory text.
(9) The Shìdétáng edition writes it as 岩,
while this book has amended it based on the explanatory text.
In this age, those who die by execution lie pillowed upon each other;
those in cangues press against one another;
the punished and slain are seen everywhere.【一】
Yet the Confucians and Mohists begin to strut and bare their arms among the shackles and fetters.
Alas,
how extreme this is!
How profoundly they are without shame and know no disgrace!
【二】I do not know if sage wisdom is not the fastener for cangues and fetters,
or if benevolence and righteousness are not the mortise and tenon of shackles.【三】
How can we know that Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiū are not the heralds of Jié and Zhí?【四】
Therefore it is said, "Eradicate sagehood and discard wisdom, and the world will be greatly ordered.
【One】【Explanation】Shū (execution) refers to
the determination that one must die.
Hàngyáng are
instruments of restraint,
used to clamp the feet and neck,
all called hàngyáng.
During the time of the Six States and the declining era of the Zhou Dynasty,
it was truly due to the traces of the sages,
with punishments like tattooing and cutting off the nose among the five penalties,
that hàngyáng filled the streets,
the bodies of those executed lay piled upon each other,
and the mutilated crowded the roads.
Pushing and gazing upon one another,
it shows how numerous they were.
【Explanation Text】"Shūsǐ" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
Shū means
to sever.
Sīmǎ explains:
to decide.
Another interpretation says:
to execute.
The "Zìlín" states:
to die.
The "Shuōwén" concurs.
It further states:
According to a Hàn decree,
if a tribal chieftain is guilty,
they should be subjected to shū punishment.
Cuī's version writes it as "yāosǐ."
"Xiāng zhěn" uses the fǎnqiè spelling with "zhèn."
"Héng" uses the fǎnqiè spelling with "hù gāng."
Sīmǎ explains:
it is a long shackle for the feet.
"Yáng" is pronounced by Xiàng as "yáng."
Cuī states:
restraints that clamp the neck and shins
are all called héngyáng.
【二】【注】Because the pedantic Confucians clung to the superficial traces,
they brought about this disaster.
They did not consider abandoning these traces and returning to the essence,
but instead raised their arms to use the traces in an attempt to govern by them.
This can be said to be not only shameless but also the height of ignorance of shame.
【Commentary】"Lìqǐ" means
an appearance of exerting force.
The traces of the sages become tools that harm things,
while the Rú and Mò schools are again pushing beyond their bounds with bared arms,
exerting effort within shackles,
clinging to traces and enforcing teachings,
to remedy the ills of the current age.
How can such chaos ever reach its limit!
Hence, they sigh with lament,
obstinately persisting in their narrow views,
without shame and unaware of their disgrace.
【Interpretation】"Lí" is pronounced with the tone as in lìshì,
and also as lìzhì.
"Qǐ" is pronounced with the tone as in qiūshì,
and also as qiūchì.
"Rǎng" is pronounced as rúyáng.
"Zhì" is pronounced as zhīshí.
"Gù" is pronounced as gǔdú.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: "Líqǐ" corresponds to the meaning in Xúnzǐ's "Róngrǔ" chapter of distancing oneself and standing aloof in criticism,
referring to setting oneself apart from the crowd.
"Yì" is read with its standard pronunciation,
and also pronounced as yī.
"Wúkuì" is written as ● in Cuī's version.
"Fǔ" is pronounced as fǔ.
"Fāngfù" is pronounced with the tone as in fúyòu.
【Three】【Notes】Cangues use tenons and mortises as fastenings,
and shackles rely on carved joints for function.
Sagely wisdom and humaneness with righteousness,
distance one from the traces of crime.
When traces distance from crime, the people then esteem them;
esteeming them gives rise to affectation and deceit.
Once affectation and deceit arise, for tools to guard against wickedness not to be prepared—
such a thing has never existed.
Therefore, abandoning what is esteemed prevents affectation and deceit from arising;
without affectation and deceit, cangues and shackles become obsolete.
What need is there then for carved joints, tenons, and mortises!
【Commentary】Joining tenons and mortises,
are like mechanical wedges.
Boring,
creates a hole.
Inserting an object into a hole is called fitting a tenon.
Without wedges, mechanisms are not secure;
without holes, shackles are useless.
Similarly, laws and institutions cannot be established without the traces of sages;
Jié and Zhí cannot act without benevolence and righteousness.
The traces of sages are the source of entanglement and disturbance;
benevolence and righteousness are the root of harm and injury.
【Translated Text】"Jīe" Lǐ reads as the character itself,
Xiàng and Xú pronounce it as (qiè) (four),
Guō gives the fanqie as cí jiē.
"Xí" Guō and Lǐ pronounce as xí,
Xiàng and Xú give the fanqie as tú xiè.
Sīmǎ says:
Jiē xí,
are mechanical wedges.
Pronounced as xī jié.
Cuī's version writes it as ●,
and says:
read it as dié,
or sometimes written as the character xiè.
Jiē xí,
refers to the beams of shackles.
Huáinánzǐ says:
The larger ones are pillars and beams,
the smaller ones are jiē xí.
◎Qìng Fān's note: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Hépíngshū's "Jǐngfú Diàn Fù" quotes Sīmǎ [as saying:
] xí,
is a mechanical wedge.
This differs from the explanatory text.
(The explanatory text has the character jiē before xí,
and no character yě after wedge.
) "Záo" is pronounced as zài luò,
also as zài bào.
"Ruì" is pronounced as rén ruì.
Xiàng's version writes it as nèi,
with the same pronunciation.
Sāncāng says:
It is the tenon at the top of a pillar.
The mortise is fitted with wood,
like the tenon at the top of a pillar.
"Yuǎn yú" is pronounced as yú wàn,
the same below.
"禦" is pronounced as yú lǚ fǎn.
It is also written as "御" in some versions,
with the same pronunciation.
【Four】【Annotation】The whistling arrow,
the fiercest of arrows,
signifies that Zēng and Shǐ were utilized by Jié and Zhí.
【Commentary】The whistle arrow,
is an arrowhead that produces a fierce, roaring sound.
Sagely wisdom serves as a tool for usurping the state,
benevolence and righteousness become resources for cruelty and violence.
Figures like Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú are used by tyrants such as Jié and Zhí like sharp arrows,
hence the statement is made accordingly.
【Explanation】"焉知" is read as yú qián fǎn.
"嚆矢" is read as xǔ jiāo fǎn.
It is also written as "嗃".
Xiàng comments:
"嚆矢"
refers to an arrow that whistles.
Guǒ comments:
it means a fierce arrow.
The dictionary "Zìlín" states:
means to shout loudly.
Cuī's version writes it as "蒿",
explaining:
wormwood can be used to make arrows.
Some versions write it as "矯",
means to chirp.
Cuī's version adds below this: "The mutual generation of being and non-being is profound,
Zēng Shǐ and Jié Zhí are born from being and non-being,
how can they not interact with each other?"
totaling twenty-four characters.
【Five】【Annotation】Remove that which causes disturbance.
【Commentary】Eliminate the means to usurp the state,
discard the resources for cruelty and violence,
then the world will be peaceful and clear,
signifying great order.
【Transcription】"Dà zhì": pronounced as zhí lì fǎn.
"Qù qí": pronounced as qǐ lǚ fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The Shidetang edition reads "sī",
the Zhào Jiànyì edition reads "sī".
(2) The Zhào edition has "jiāo" instead of "jiǎo".
(3) The Shidetang edition reads "jiān".
(4) The character "qiè" is amended according to the Shidetang edition,
the original explanatory text also mistakenly wrote "xiè".
The Yellow Emperor had been established as the Son of Heaven for nineteen years,
and his decrees were implemented throughout the land.
Hearing that Guǎngchéngzǐ was on Mount Kōngtóng,
he therefore went to visit him,
saying:
"I have heard that you, my master, have attained the ultimate Way.
I venture to ask about the essence of the ultimate Way.
I wish to draw upon the essence of heaven and earth
to assist the five grains
and nourish the people.
I further desire to regulate yīn and yáng
so that all living beings may flourish.
How should this be done?"
【One】【Memorial】Virtuous edicts transforming through moral influence,
are widely implemented throughout the realm.
【二】【疏】Kōngtóng Mountain,
in the northern border of Liángzhōu.
Guǎngchéng,
is an alternative name for Lǎozǐ.
【Interpretation】"Guǎngchéngzǐ" is sometimes said to be:
that is, Lǎozǐ.
"Kōngtóng" Sīmǎ states:
it should be the mountain under the Northern Dipper.
The Erya says:
the north carries the Dipper's pole as Kōngtóng.
Another says:
it is thirty li east of Yúchéng in the state of Liáng.
【Three】【Cereals】 refer to the five grains,
namely millet, broomcorn millet, beans, hemp, and wheat.
The aim is to draw upon the profound principles,
the essence of heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng,
to assist in the growth of the five grains,
thereby nourishing all living beings.
【Four】【Explanations】Suì,
means to follow.
Wishing to emulate yīn and yáng in establishing offices and dividing duties,
to follow the nature of all living beings,
and to inquire into the reasons for it.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "山" was amended based on the missing text cited from Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition and Chéng's commentary.
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"What you wish to inquire about
is the essence of things;
what you wish to govern
is but the fragments of things.
Since you began governing the world,
clouds gather not yet fully before raining,
plants and trees fall not waiting for yellowing,
and the light of sun and moon grows increasingly dim.
With the narrow, petty mind of a flatterer,
how could you be worthy of discussing the ultimate Way!"
【一】【注】Inquiring about the essence of the ultimate Way,
can be said to be a matter of substance.
【Commentary】"Er",
means "you".
You wish to sow and plant the five grains,
and govern the two regulators (heaven and earth),
but your questions are crude and shallow,
not going beyond form and substance,
deviating from the profound and mysterious essence.
This is a reproach.
【Explanation】"Substance is" The Guangya says:
substance,
correctness.
【二】【注】Not allowing things to follow their natural course but instead attempting to govern them,
thus leads to harm.
【Commentary】If one merely wishes to establish offices and assign duties,
drawing all things to follow one's own will,
it would contradict the natural order of creation,
and inevitably lead to harm and destruction.
【Three】【Divisions】 of clans,
signify gathering.
To divide the hundred offices according to yin and yang,
and intentionally govern the myriad things,
will inevitably lead to ominous disasters.
Rain and wind become unseasonable,
heat and cold lose their proper rhythm,
clouds have not gathered yet rain falls,
trees are still green but leaves drop;
with comets and eclipses,
the three luminaries grow dim,
people's hearts are disturbed,
and the celestial phenomena fall into chaos.
【Explanation】"Clouds do not wait to gather before raining." Simǎ comments:
gather,
means to congregate.
Raining without first gathering
indicates scant moisture.
"Plants do not wait to yellow before falling." Simǎ comments:
This speaks of an abundance of destructive energy.
The Ěryǎ states:
fall,
means to die.
"Increase with" in Cuī's version is written as cover with.
【Four】【Petitions】Mean and petty,
a description of narrow-mindedness and inferiority.
You are a flattering and cunning person,
with a very narrow and inferior heart,
how can you speak of the ultimate way!

Guǎngchéngzǐ lay with his head to the south,
and Huángdì, crawling on his knees, advanced from below the wind.
Bowing twice and knocking his head on the ground, he asked:
"I have heard that you, my master, are well-versed in the ultimate Way.
I venture to ask,
how can one govern the body so that it may endure long?"
Guǎngchéngzǐ sprang up abruptly
and said:
"An excellent question indeed!
Come!
I will tell you of the ultimate Way.
The essence of the ultimate Way
is deep and darkly obscure;
the pinnacle of the ultimate Way
is dim and silent.
See nothing, hear nothing,
embrace the spirit in stillness,
and the body will naturally become upright.
Be still, be pure,
do not toil your body,
do not agitate your essence,
and you may thereby attain long life.
When the eyes see nothing,
the ears hear nothing,
and the mind knows nothing,
your spirit will guard the body,
and the body will thereby endure long.
Guard what is within you,
close off what is without,
for much knowledge leads to ruin.
I will guide you to the heights of great brightness,
to the source of utmost yang;
I will lead you through the gate of deep obscurity,
to the source of utmost yin.
Heaven and earth have their offices,
yin and yang their storehouses.
Carefully guard your own person,
and things will naturally flourish.
I hold fast to the One and abide in harmony,
thus I have cultivated myself for twelve hundred years,
and my body has never decayed."
【一】【Note】If everyone cultivates themselves and does not govern the world,
then the world will be well-governed,
hence it is considered good.
【Commentary】When people govern things,
things are bound to be troubled;
if each governs themselves,
the world will be clear and upright,
hence it is praised.

"Ah!
Nourish the heart!
If you abide in non-action,
things will transform themselves.
Cast off your physical form,
spit out your intelligence,
and forget all distinctions along with things;
blend completely with the primordial chaos,
untie the heart and release the spirit,
be blank and without a soul.
The myriad things in their multiplicity,
each return to their root,
each return to their root without knowing it;
in a state of undifferentiated chaos,
they never depart from it throughout their lives;
if they were to know it,
that would mean departing from it.
Do not inquire into its name,
do not spy into its reality,
for things are naturally self-generated."
【一】【注】When the heart is harmed by overuse,
then to nurture the heart,
is it not by refraining from using it?
【Commentary】The methods for nurturing the mind
are listed in the following text.
is "merely".
It means that by keeping the mind in a state of non-action, all things transform naturally.
【Three】【Commentary】Neither principle nor things are held in the heart,
yet silently entrusted to nature,
then through non-action, transformation occurs spontaneously.
【Commentary】Lún means
principle.
To discard physical form is
to forget the self.
To renounce intelligence is
to forget the mind.
When both body and mind are forgotten,
and both external things and self are set aside,
that is the cultivation of the mind.
【Translated Text】"墮" is pronounced as Xǔguī fǎn.
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī says:
"吐" should be "咄".
"咄" is the same as "黜".
(In the "Xú Wúguǐ" chapter, "黜" desires,
the Sīmǎ version uses "咄".
) Wéi Zhāo's commentary on the "Zhōuyǔ" states:
means to abolish.
"黜" and "墮",
have similar meanings.
In the "Dà Zōngshī" chapter, discarding limbs,
and abolishing intelligence,
is evidence of this.
In clerical script, the character "出" is sometimes abbreviated as "士" (like "﹄" abbreviated as "敖",
"●" abbreviated as "賣",
"●" abbreviated as "款", etc.
) Therefore, the character "咄" is sometimes written as "●",
its shape is similar to "吐",
and thus it is mistakenly written as "吐".
("咄" being mistaken for "吐",
is like "吐" being mistaken for "咄".
In the "Hànshū · Wàiqī Zhuàn", it says "must fear, detest, and spit out me",
the "Hàn Jì" mistakenly writes "吐" as "咄".
) Yú Yuè says:
"吐" should be "杜",
meaning to block one's intelligence.
【Four】【Annotation】Harmonizing with all things without boundaries.
【Comment】Míngxìng refers to the qi of spontaneity.
With vast and boundless body and mind in great unity,
one naturally becomes one with it.
【Translated Text】"Xìng" is pronounced with the character 戶頂反,
also pronounced as xìng.
"Míng" is pronounced with the character 亡頂反.
Sīmǎ explains:
Xìngmíng,
refers to the natural energy.
【Five】【Annotation】Sitting in oblivion and embracing solitude.
【Commentary】The soul,
is fond of knowledge and action.
To explain,
means to dispel and cleanse.
Being oblivious,
is without knowledge;
purifying the heart and spirit,
akin to dead ashes and withered trees,
is the unknowing soul.
【Six】【Annotation】To return without knowing it,
is the true return.
【Commentary】And so on,
it means numerous.
With numerous comings and goings,
birth and extinction do not depart from the natural,
returning to the root is clear,
how could one use knowledge and only then return to the root!
【Seven】【Annotation】Being in a state of chaos and ignorance, yet allowing it to naturally restore itself,
is how one can remain inseparable from their origin throughout life.
【Commentary】Chaos is without knowledge and follows its own course alone,
undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes,
yet never departing from the natural.
【Explanation】"Hún hún": read as hùn hùn.
"Dùn dùn": read as tún tún.
"Bù lí": read as bù lì.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【Eight】【Annotation】To know and return to it (one),
is to contradict the act of returning.
【Commentary】Using knowledge to yearn for the ultimate origin,
one then departs from the nature of spontaneity.
【Nine】【Annotation】To pry and inquire is to lose that which arises of itself.
【Commentary】The Dao transcends words and names,
the Principle is beyond emotions and thoughts.
If one seeks the Dao through names,
or peers into the Principle through emotions,
is that not far from the truth indeed!
Only by dispelling emotions and forgetting names,
entrusting oneself to solitary transformation,
can things attain their natural principle.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition uses "zhī".
Yún Jiāng said:
"Heaven bestowed virtue upon me,
and revealed to me the way of silence;
I sought it with my own person,
and now at last I have obtained it."
He bowed twice and knocked his head on the ground,
then rose, took his leave, and departed.
【一】【注】Knowing yet failing to remain silent,
often leads to self-loss.
【Commentary】He descended the words of the Dao and virtue,
demonstrating the conduct of profound silence;
since establishing himself in life,
only now has he come to realization.
People in the world
all delight in others agreeing with themselves and dislike others differing from themselves.
To desire those who agree with oneself
and not desire those who differ from oneself
is to harbor the intention of standing out from the crowd.
Now those who harbor the intention of standing out from the crowd,
how often do they actually stand out from the crowd!
Relying on the crowd to affirm what one has heard,
one's skills are far inferior to the collective skills of the multitude.
Yet those who wish to rule others' states
are grasping at the benefits of the Three Sovereigns while failing to see their troubles.
This is staking others' states on luck;
how many who rely on luck do not end up losing others' states!
As for preserving others' states,
the chance is less than one in ten thousand;
while losing others' states,
failure is certain with ten thousandfold losses remaining.
How lamentable
that those who possess lands remain unaware of this!
【One】【Memorial】Those who are tainted by habits,
having long been deluded and attached,
rejoice in those who agree with them,
and detest those who differ from them.
【Explanation】"而惡" is pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
【二】【Note】The mind desires to stand out from the crowd to become the most distinguished among the masses.
【Commentary】Those who affirm themselves and deny others,
who delight in conformity and detest divergence,
inevitably seek to showcase their own merits and fame,
aspiring to stand out from the masses.
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
One who stands out from the crowd
does so by surpassing others in talent and wisdom, and others all follow them.
Yet, do they not consider whether they themselves have emerged from the crowd,
or the crowd has emerged from them?
To conform because the crowd conforms,
and to diverge because the crowd diverges,
believing this to be aligning with the masses—
then, delighting in others' conformity and resenting their divergence
is still merely aligning one's own conformity or divergence with the crowd.
Thus, joy and anger are not truly rooted in oneself but in the crowd,
yet one clings to them as if they were one's own,
and this is the source of confusion.
【Three】【Annotation】All people take surpassing others (three) as their aim,
hence they remain ordinary individuals.
If I too desire to stand out from the crowd,
then I would be no different from the masses and unable to truly transcend them.
Since everyone strives to outdo one another,
while I alone harmonize without contention,
this makes me profoundly distinct from the multitude and thus qualified to lead them.
【Commentary】People harbor the intention to compete and stand out from the crowd,
which is the common vulgar sentiment of ordinary beings.
How could one alone transcend beyond the multitude?
Only by blending one's light with the dust,
can one truly stand out from the masses and become their paragon.
【Four】【Annotation】What one person alone hears
is not as much as the multitude of skills;
therefore, relying on the multitude brings peace.
If one does not rely on the multitude,
then even if there are thousands or tens of thousands of them,
they all become my enemies.
【Commentary】Utilizing the skills of the masses,
relying on their knowledge and observations,
eliminates disputes and competition.
This is what is meant by the clear-sighted providing vision,
and the wise offering counsel.
【Explanatory Text】"Relying on the multitude to pacify what is perceived" By entrusting and assigning tasks based on what the multitude hears and sees,
and delegating it to them,
one naturally achieves peace and security.
"Not as skilled as the multitude's abilities" Qí qǐ fǎn.
"The multitude is vast" If I exert my wisdom to reach the level of the multitude,
the skills of the multitude far exceed mine;
how can one avoid becoming trapped by this!
【Five】【Comment】Those who wish to govern a state for the people,
if they do not rely on the people acting for themselves but instead impose their own actions,
this is merely seeking the benefits that the Three Sovereigns gained from ruling all things while failing to see the troubles caused by their own interference.
So then, the benefits that the Three Sovereigns obtained,
did they really achieve them through deliberate action?
They simply followed the natural course of the world's self-governance and let things take their own course.
【Commentary】To govern a state with one's own biases and obstinacy
is merely to seek the benefits of the three sage-kings' rule over all things,
unaware that it becomes the great calamity leading to self-destruction.
【Explanation】"此攬" is pronounced as lǎn.
The original text also writes it as 覽.
【六】【疏】Jiǎo,
means to seek.
Those who use the benefits of the imperial kingdom to demand what is not their due,
seeking personal fortune,
have never failed to meet with ruin.
Not one in ten thousand survives,
hence it is said, how few are they?
【Interpretation】"僥" is pronounced as gǔ yáo fǎn.
Xú reads it as gǔ liǎo fǎn,
and the character is sometimes written as 徼.
"倖" is pronounced as xìng.
Another interpretation says:
"僥倖"
describes the appearance of incessantly seeking profit.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary states that 僥 means
to demand,
to seek.
The interpretation text sometimes uses 徼,
and 徼 also means to seek.
(See Gāo's annotation in the "Mín" chapter of Lǚ's Annals.
) "幾何" is pronounced as jū qǐ fǎn.
Guō Jù reads it as jī fǎn,
"不喪" is pronounced as xī làng fǎn.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【Seven】【Annotation】Oneself and the world under heaven,
are mutually dependent and formed together.
Now, if one uses oneself alone to monopolize control over the world under heaven,
then the world under heaven becomes blocked,
how could oneself be unobstructed then!
Therefore, not only will one's own self fail to achieve completion,
but all corners of the world will suffer excessive loss.
【Commentary】To harbor a mind of luck and chance as the ruler of an emperor,
in discussing survival, there is certainly not a single success,
and in speaking of downfall, there is more than enough failure.
【Transcription】"Wànfēn" as pronounced by its characters,
also read with the fǎnqiè spelling fú wèn.
【Eight】【Commentary】This line laments the ruler's ignorance of the dangers of relying on luck.
【Collation】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, which has "this" in place of "this because."
(2) The Shidetang edition lacks this sentence.
(3) The Shidetang edition omits the character "zhòng" (眾).
He who possesses territory,
possesses a great thing.
He who possesses a great thing,
must not be treated as a thing;
being a thing yet not being treated as a thing,
thus he is able to govern all things.
Understanding that the governor of things is not a thing himself,
how could his governance be limited to just ruling the empire and its people!
He moves freely throughout the universe,
wanders across the nine regions,
going and coming alone,
this is called solitary possession.
He who possesses solitude,
is called the noblest of all.
【One】【Memorial】The ninth and fifth positions are supremely honored and elevated,
the four seas are vast and immense,
thus they are called the great entities.
【二】【注】If one cannot utilize things but instead is used by things,
then one is merely a thing oneself.
How could one possibly master things!
If one cannot master things,
then one is inadequate to possess great things.
【Commentary】If one forcibly seeks the domains of the Three Sovereigns,
failing to let things act naturally,
one instead becomes used by things.
Since one is oneself a thing,
how can one master other things?
This is absolutely impermissible.
【Three】【Comment】One who utilizes things,
is not used by things.
Not being used by things,
this is to not be a thing;
not being a thing,
thus one can master all things under heaven,
enabling each to attain its own place.
【Commentary】It is not being used by things but using things.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
When there are things present,
and one perceives them as objects and treats them as such,
one remains bound to things for a lifetime.
The larger the perceived objects, the smaller the self becomes;
whereas by not perceiving objects, all things dutifully serve their purpose.
Since one does not even perceive the existence of objects,
how could the size of objects matter at all!
◎Yú Yuè commented:
Guō’s reading must not take the five characters "bù kě yǐ wù wù" as one phrase,
for that misses the correct parsing.
This should be read with "bù kě yǐ wù" as one phrase,
and "wù ér bù wù" as another.
【Four】【Annotation】Utilizing the world's self-directed actions,
thus galloping through all things without exhaustion.
【Commentary】The sage comprehends the natural order,
penetrates the workings of creation,
operates through the minds of the common people,
and utilizes the senses of all living beings.
Thus, it is understood that governing things is not about material things themselves.
How could it be limited to wearing the imperial yellow canopy,
sitting in Fényáng,
bearing the jade seal,
and ruling the world?
Truly, one should transcend the six directions,
soar above the supreme purity,
surpass the nine provinces,
and wander to Gūyè.
【Five】【Annotation】While others all set themselves apart, he alone mingles with the crowd,
this is the one who comes and goes alone.
To possess such solitude,
can indeed be called unique possession.
【Subcommentary】There are annotations.
【Six】【Commentary】To merge mysteriously with the masses,
is not to seek honor from them,
yet the masses cannot but honor one—
this is the ultimate honor.
If instead one holds to biased views and takes uniqueness as the goal,
then even if aligned in principle,
one remains merely an object among the common,
not a truly distinctive being.
Failing to achieve true distinctiveness,
yet craving to usurp high positions and honors,
presumptuously seizing what is not rightfully theirs—
how could the masses possibly follow such a one?
Thus, this is not the ultimate honor.
【Commentary】 (While others all consider themselves unique and only I mingle with the masses,
this is indeed one who comes and goes alone.
To possess this solitude,
can be called having true uniqueness.
(Second part)) Others desire to stand out from the crowd, yet only I wander freely;
the multitude lacks this ability,
hence it is named unique possession.
One who possesses such uniqueness,
the common people gladly support,
the hundred families bear and uphold.
Taking this as the foundation,
can be deemed the most honored and esteemed.
【Transcription】"Tāo" is pronounced as t吐刀反.
"Mào" is pronounced as m亡北反,
and also as m亡報反.
【Collation Note】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has the character "yě" (也) below it.
(2) The twenty-seven characters from "rén jiē zhì yǒu yǐ" (人皆至有矣),
which are commentary mistakenly incorporated into the text,
should be deleted.
The teaching of the great person,
is like form giving rise to shadow,
and sound producing echo (1).
When questioned, they respond,
exhausting all that is within their bosom,
becoming the counterpart of all under heaven.
They dwell where there is no echo,
and move where there is no fixed direction.
Leading you through the tangled complexities of return,
to wander in the boundless;
entering and exiting without reliance,
sharing with the sun a beginningless existence;
their praised form and body
conform to the Great Unity,
and in the Great Unity, they lose themselves.
Having lost themselves,
how could they possess possession!
Those who perceive possession
were the noble persons of old;
those who perceive non-possession
are the friends of heaven and earth.
【一】【注】The hearts of the common people are like form and sound;
the teachings of the great person are like shadow and echo.
What intention does the great person have toward the world?
It is merely like the way shadow and echo follow form and sound.
【Commentary】The great person is a sage.
They respond without deliberate intention,
acting not through conscious mind.
Thus, the hearts of the common people
are like forms and sounds;
the teachings of the great person
are like echoes and shadows.
【Explanation】"Yú xiǎng": Xǔ zhàng fǎn.
Also written as xiǎng.
Same for the annotations and below.
【Two】【Annotation】This allows each thing's inherent nature to fully express itself.
【Commentary】The sage's mind responds to the stimuli of things,
and this response is also called opportunity,
fully embracing the sentiments of all beings.
【Three】【Commentary】The questioner takes the primary role,
while the respondent accordingly serves as the counterpart.
【Commentary】Match,
means to pair,
the one who feels first is the host,
the one who responds is the pair.
【Four】【Annotation】Remain tranquil to receive all things.
【Commentary】Dwelling,
is stillness.
In times without sensation,
the heart is like a withered tree,
silent and without echo.
【Five】【Annotation】Transforming in accordance with things.
【Explanation】Action,
is responding to the opportunity.
Engaging with the opportunity is not fixed to a specific place.
【Six】【Annotation】Náonáo,
means self-movement.
To lead and guide all things,
enabling them to return to the nature of self-movement,
is the ultimate state of non-action.
【Commentary】Restless movement,
is self-initiated action.
Adapting to opportunities without fixed methods,
it further aims to uplift all of you diverse beings,
enabling you to return to your inherent nature,
thus attaining the state of non-action.
【Transcription】"Qiè" is pronounced as kǔ jié fǎn.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
to hold (also).
"Náo náo" is pronounced as ér xiǎo fǎn.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
Guō's annotation fails to grasp the explanation.
The "Ěryǎ Shìgǔ" explains:
shì,
means to go.
Therefore, shì fù,
is like going back and forth.
Náo náo,
means chaos.
The "Guǎngyǎ Shìgǔ" states:
náo,
means chaos.
Repeating it makes it náo náo.
The chaos of going back and forth,
is why ordinary people cannot come and go independently.
Only the great person can take hold of this chaotic going back and forth and roam with it in the boundless,
hence it is said, "Take hold of your chaotic going back and forth to roam in the boundless."
Originally, these two lines were just one sentence;
Guō failed to understand the explanation,
and also misread the text.
【Seven】【Comment】Moving with transformation,
thus having no beginning.
【Commentary】Roaming,
the mind wanders together with nature,
thus there are no traces of its beginning or end.
【Eight】【Annotation】Profound unity without external manifestation.
【Commentary】Moving in and out of the dust of life and death,
mysteriously united with the creator,
with no boundaries visible.
【九】【注】It accompanies the daily renewal,
thus having no beginning.
【Commentary】Renewing with each day,
thus it has neither end nor beginning.
【一０】【Note】His form and appearance are no different from that of Heaven and Earth.
【Commentary】（Eulogy）Ode,
〔Eulogy〕;
Discussion,
Sayings.
The sage's magnificent virtue and physical form,
are in harmony with the great way of the two primal forces,
externally not peering into the cosmos,
internally not possessing their own self.
【一一】【Note】Having a self prevents one from achieving great unity.
【Commentary】To unite with the two principles,
and align with the great Way,
is to forget both the self and external things.
【一二】【Note】Under heaven, the most difficult thing is to be without self.
Once the self is without,
then the multitude of beings are not worth possessing again.
【Commentary】Since the self is nonexistent,
how could things exist!
【Transcription】"Wù" is pronounced as wū.
"Zú fù" has the fǎnqiè spelling of fú yòu.
【一三】【Note】They are merely capable of embellishing their reputation.
【Commentary】Practicing benevolence and righteousness,
and observing the rites between ruler and minister,
does not depart from being a gentleman of action.
【一四】【Note】Upon seeing non-being, one allows it to exist in solitude.
【Commentary】Witnessing the wondrous principle of non-action,
beholding the true nature of spontaneity,
the two realms are non-existent,
all things are entirely empty,
turning from existence into non-existence,
thus it is called being a friend.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition has 響,
the Shìdétáng edition has 嚮,
the annotation is the same.
According to the explanatory text, it should be 嚮.
(2) The character 也 was changed based on the Shìdétáng edition.
Though lowly, they cannot but be employed—
things;
though humble, they cannot but be followed—
the people;
though concealed, they cannot but be done—
affairs;
though coarse, they cannot but be set forth—
laws;
though distant, they cannot but be abided by—
righteousness;
though intimate, they cannot but be extended—
benevolence;
though restrained, they cannot but be accumulated—
ritual;
though centered, they cannot but be elevated—
virtue;
though unified, they cannot but be transformed—
the Dào;
though divine, they cannot but be acted upon—
Heaven.
Thus, the sage observes Heaven but does not assist it,
achieves virtue but is not burdened,
emerges from the Dào but does not scheme,
embodies benevolence but does not rely on it,
adheres to righteousness but does not accumulate it,
responds to ritual but does not avoid it,
engages in affairs but does not decline them,
aligns with laws but does not cause disorder,
depends on the people but does not belittle them,
follows things but does not abandon them.
Things are not worth acting upon,
yet one cannot but act.
Those who do not understand Heaven
are not pure in virtue;
those who are not versed in the Dào
have no way to succeed;
those who do not comprehend the Dào—
alas for them!
【一】【注】Govern by following their nature, and there will be order;
oppose their nature and oppress them, and there will be chaos.
The reason why the common people and things are considered lowly and humble
is precisely because they are not governed according to their nature.
Thus, those who govern the humble become esteemed,
and those who follow the lowly become honored.
This is an inevitable correspondence.
【Commentary】Although the people reside in humble positions,
each possesses their own abilities and functions;
though objects may be light and lowly,
all bear their own material uses.
When no material is discarded as useless,
and no person is left unemployed,
then all may thrive and prosper.
【Explanation】"Zé zhì" is pronounced as "zhí lì" in the opposite tone.
【二】【注】When affairs are concealed by them,
they are thus hidden.
They each act on their own,
so one cannot but act,
only one must follow along accordingly.
【Explanation】To conceal means
to hide.
Matters may be evident or obscure,
abilities may be skillful or clumsy;
some are evident here,
while others are hidden there,
some are skillful in this,
while others are clumsy in that.
One should simply let them be,
and all matters will be accomplished.
【Explanation】"Nì ér" is pronounced as nǚ lì fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】The Dharma is the trace of wondrous matters,
how can one, because the traces are coarse, fail to present the wondrous matters!
【Commentary】The Dharma,
refers to verbal teachings.
Comparing teachings to the principle,
the principle is subtle while the teachings are coarse,
using the metaphor of traps and snares,
hence it is presented accordingly for explanation.
【Four】【Annotation】One should dwell in it,
thus achieving distance.
【Commentary】Although the meaning is far removed from the Way,
if it accords with reason,
it should be adopted for decision.
【Five】【Annotation】Affection leads to the suffering of partiality,
hence only through broadening can benevolence be achieved.
【Commentary】Affection, though it may be partial and narrow,
when extended universally as broad love,
becomes great benevolence.
【Six】【Annotation】As for ritual and moderation,
the concern lies in being constrained by singularity;
thus, embodying them in all things,
then they accumulate and become all-encompassing.
【Commentary】Accumulation means
substantiality.
Etiquette means
refinement.
As ritual values mutual respect,
yet human sentiments often become shallow,
therefore outwardly displaying courtesy
while inwardly cultivating profound substance
constitutes true ritual.
【Seven】【Annotation】In matters of lowly affairs,
even if fitting, they are not virtuous.
【Commentary】In the center,
it means compliance.
Those who cultivate the Way
blend their light with the world,
humbly yielding to all things,
yet their aspirations and conduct remain pure and lofty,
like being soaked in black dye but not turning black—such is their virtue.
【Explanation】"What is inherent yet must be elevated is virtue." Inherent means,
compliance.
To comply with one's nature and elevate it.
【Eight】【Annotation】In matters that are difficult,
even one deviation from the Way is problematic,
how much more so when there are many!
【Commentary】The wondrous origin is a single breath,
penetrating and giving life to all things,
so inherently simple and effortless,
is it not only the Dao that is thus!
【Transcription】"Not easy" pronounced with the fanqie spelling yǐ chǐ fǎn.
The annotation below follows the same.
【Nine】【Annotation】Firmly resolved not to act,
even a deity is not divine,
let alone one who is not a deity!
【Commentary】The divine work is unfathomable,
manifesting and concealing without fixed pattern,
responding to opportunities without obstruction,
in harmony with what is natural.
【一０】【注】Just follow its own way.
【Commentary】The sage observes the subtle principles of nature,
following the multitude of things in great harmony without interfering with their inherent dispositions.
The following explains the preceding text.
【一一】【Note】Naturally, one harmonizes with the sublime gathering.
【Commentary】It enables the realm and wisdom to merge indistinguishably,
and once the superior virtue is perfected,
naturally there will be no flaws or burdens.
【一二】【Note】Unplanned yet unified,
this is why it is considered easy.
【Commentary】The Way of Marvelous Oneness manifests itself,
how could it require explicit consultation before being spoken of!
【一三】【Note】Relying on it leads to narrow-mindedness.
【Commentary】The Classic of Lǎozǐ states,
"Act without relying on it."
Benevolence and extensive love
are valuable when applied appropriately,
hence there is no dependence.
【一四】【Note】Following one's nature to dwell in seclusion,
is not a matter of accumulation.
【Commentary】The ancient kings' temporary lodgings,
are not to be treasured as precious;
like straw dogs once displayed in rituals,
how could they be accumulated and preserved!
【Section 15】【Comment】It aligns with rites naturally,
not due to taboos.
【Commentary】The profound essence is serene and unchanging,
its manifestations respond to ritual,
how could it be bound by taboos!
◎Yú Yuè states:
"Huì" should be read as "wéi".
Both "wéi" and "huì" share the phonetic component "wéi",
hence the "Guǎngyǎ Shìgǔ" says:
"Huì"
means to avoid.
Wéi Zhāo, in his annotations to the "Zhōuyǔ" and "Jìnyǔ",
both state:
"Wéi"
means to avoid.
This shows the two characters are phonetically similar and semantically interchangeable.
To respond to ritual without "huì"
means not to violate it.
Guō Xiàng's annotation says,
"Naturally conforms to ritual,
not due to taboos,"
which is overly convoluted and misses the point.
