【一六】【Note】Engaging with matters according to reason,
one's capability or incapability is naturally assumed,
acting in response to stimuli,
without any refusal or yielding.
【Commentary】Mingling with the mundane and going with the flow,
engaging with matters and interacting with things,
responding to opportunities without grasping,
yet also without refusal or yielding.
【Interpretation】Yìngdòng: yì shēng fǎn.
【一七】【Note】Mastering the coarse with subtlety,
thus it does not become chaotic.
【Commentary】By following the nature of things,
and regulating them with laws,
thus there is no disorder.
【一八】【注】They rely on their own actions,
and do not employ them lightly.
【Commentary】The people are the foundation of the state,
only when the foundation is firm can the state be at peace,
hence one relies on them and dares not to use them lightly.
【一九】【Note】Thus, one takes up the position accordingly,
without departing from the foundation.
【Commentary】Following the hearts of the common people,
and accommodating the nature of all things,
even when applying laws and teachings,
one must not cause them to deviate from their fundamental nature.
【二０】【Comment】Does one act
merely because there is a reason to act?
One embodies this action in oneself,
hence it cannot be stopped.
【Commentary】All things receive their nature,
with functions and capabilities vastly different.
For instance, the dung beetle rolls its ball,
the spider weaves its web—
these actions arise from innate instinct,
not through acquired learning.
Therefore, what is fundamentally absent cannot be forced into being,
yet what is inherent in one's nature cannot be left undone.
【Explanation】"Things are not worth doing" refers to what lies beyond one's duty.
"Yet they cannot be left undone" refers to what lies within one's duty.
【二一】【Note】Not understanding spontaneity leads to deliberate action,
and deliberate action results in virtue not being pure.
【疏】Those who are ignorant of the natural principles
will find their shallow virtues impure.
【二二】【Note】If one cannot empty oneself to receive things,
then every matter will miss its proper timing.
【Commentary】Stagnating in the emptiness of the mysterious Dao-nature,
thus encountering affairs is like facing a wall,
indeed there is no way to proceed.
【二三】【疏】They were ignorant of the principles of Heaven and humanity,
confused about the duties between ruler and subject,
their actions were reckless and stumbling,
deeply lamentable and sorrowful.
【Collation】(1) The character 'zé' has been emended according to the commentary text.
(2) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character 'qí'.
(3) The character 'lǐ' has been emended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
What is the Dào?
There is the Way of Heaven,
and there is the way of humanity.
To act through non-action and be honored
is the Way of Heaven;
to act through action and be burdened
is the way of humanity.
The ruler
embodies the Way of Heaven;
the minister
embodies the way of humanity.
The Way of Heaven and the way of humanity
are far apart from each other,
and this cannot but be examined.
【一】【注】The sovereign is above and entrusts all things to act on their own.
【Commentary】To be without affairs and without action,
those who are honored and elevated above,
align with the natural way of Heaven.
【二】【Note】Those who are burdened by purposeful action
cannot follow their innate spontaneity.
【Commentary】Officials having duties to perform,
affairs burdened with numerous disturbances,
is the way of human relations.
【Three】【Comment】To be like Heaven in entrusting things,
then one naturally resides above all things.
【Commentary】The ruler governs all things from above,
aligning with the Way of Heaven through non-action.
【Four】【Notes】Each fulfills their respective role.
【Five】【Annotation】The ruler's position is non-action, entrusting all officials,
officials have their specific duties, and the ruler does not interfere.
Both achieve self-attainment through non-action,
thus the way of the ruler is leisurely,
the way of the ministers is laborious,
between labor and leisure,
they cannot be discussed on the same day.
【Commentary】The ruler's position is noble and lofty,
entrusting affairs to ministers and administrators;
the minister's path is humble and lowly,
devoting sincerity in serving the superior;
thus the way of the ruler is leisurely,
while the way of the minister is laborious,
and they cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
【Interpretation】"Not participating" is pronounced as yù.
【Six】【Annotation】If not examined, the positions of ruler and subject will fall into chaos.
【Commentary】The Way of Heaven acts as the ruler through non-action,
while the Way of Humanity serves as the minister through engagement.
With a clear distinction between noble and humble,
their toils and ease differ.
If each holds to their proper role,
then both ruler and minister may embody non-action.
But if one fails to grasp the underlying principle,
the balance of labor and rest is disrupted,
leading to chaos between ruler and minister.
(Now, the two primal forces generate and nurture,
undergoing endless transformations.
Among all forms and substances,
they are the most vast and encompassing.
With constant renewal and change,
and moment-to-moment evolution,
they maintain true equilibrium—
this is what is meant by "stabilizing and maturing" them.
【Collation Note】(1) The thirty-seven characters following "The Two Principles"
are a commentary from the beginning of the "Heaven and Earth" chapter in the second volume that has been mistakenly incorporated here,
and should be deleted.
【1】【Explanation】Titled after the event.
Though heaven and earth are vast,
their transformations are uniform;
though the myriad things are numerous,
their governance is one;
though the multitudes of people are many,
their ruler is the sovereign.
The sovereign originates in virtue and is perfected by heaven,
hence it is said:
the sovereigns of the most ancient times ruled the world
through non-action,
relying solely on heavenly virtue.
【一】【Note】All things transform naturally without deliberate action.
【Commentary】The two realms give birth and nurture,
covering and carrying without end;
among forms and substances,
they are the most vast.
Yet with constant renewal and transformation,
their appearance remains unchanged;
with every thought shifting and fading,
they are truly equal in essence,
which is what is meant by harmonizing them.
Hence it is said, Heaven and Earth and I are born together.
【Explanatory Text】"Tiāndì" Explanation of Terms states:
Tiān (Heaven),
means to manifest,
being lofty and manifest above;
also means level,
being level and extending high and far;
Dì (Earth),
means base,
its substance is low and beneath,
carrying all things.
Lǐtǒng states:
Tiāndì (Heaven and Earth),
are what generate the primordial qì,
the ancestors of all things.
Yì Shuō states:
When the primordial qì first separated,
the clear and light rose to become heaven,
the turbid and heavy sank to become earth.
【Two】【Comment】One governs through self-attainment.
【Commentary】All living beings in the four forms of birth and the myriad things,
their kinds are the most numerous,
yet when it comes to following their nature and attaining self-realization,
this principle is singular,
which is what is meant by unifying them.
Hence, it is further said that the myriad things and I are one.
【Transcription】"其治" reads as "zhí lì" with a rising tone.
The annotation is the same,
and the following "官治" along with its annotation are also the same.
【Three】【Comment】Under heaven, minds differ,
but the one without a mind is the ruler.
【Commentary】The black-headed masses and common soldiers,
though their numbers are many,
the one who rules as sovereign
is but a single person.
Without preconceptions, he relies on their service,
truly fitting for this position.
【Interpretation】"Rén zú" is read as zūn hū fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Taking virtue as the source,
nothing is left unattained.
What is attained is gained naturally,
hence there is no gratitude for the attainment,
and thus it fulfills the way of heaven.
【Commentary】Origin,
means foundation.
The ruler governs people and things,
and must take virtue as the guiding principle;
when all things attain their own fulfillment,
they thus fully realize their natural dispositions.
【Explanatory Text】"The Origin of the Ruler": Origin,
is the foundation.
【Five】【Annotation】Follow the movement of nature.
【Commentary】Xuán means
far-reaching.
The rulers of antiquity,
refer to the sovereigns before the Three Sovereigns.
It speaks of the sage rulers of the profound past,
who governed the world through non-action,
truly, what did they do?
This cites antiquity to validate the present,
completing the meaning of heavenly virtue.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition already reads as "止".
When viewed through the Dào, the rulers of the world are rectified,
when viewed through the Dào, the duties of sovereign and minister are clarified,
when viewed through the Dào, the officials of the world are well-governed,
when broadly viewed through the Dào, the responses of all things are complete.
Thus, what permeates heaven and earth
is Dé;
what operates through all things
is Dào;
what governs people from above
is affairs;
what enables one to master something
is skill.
Skill is subsumed by affairs,
affairs are subsumed by righteousness,
righteousness is subsumed by Dé,
Dé is subsumed by Dào,
Dào is subsumed by Heaven.
Hence it is said,
those who nurtured the world in ancient times,
through having no desires, the world was content;
through non-action, all things transformed;
through profound stillness, the common people were settled.
The record says:
Through the mastery of the One, all things are accomplished.
With a mind free from desires, even ghosts and spirits submit.
【One】【Annotation】Non-action means,
being the ruler naturally,
not through wicked means.
【Commentary】With the principle of emptiness and penetration,
observing the patterns of responding to things,
a ruler who acts through non-action and follows nature,
does not employ deceitful and crooked words.
Thus, the principle aligns with the correct path.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Words
are names.
Rectify the ruler's name,
and the world will naturally obey his commands.
Hence it is said that what is named must be speakable,
all ultimately conforming to the Dao.
【Transcription】"Fei xie ye" sounds like "jie" with a rising tone.
The original text also has it as "wei."
【Two】【Annotation】Each fulfills its role,
then non-action is the position above,
and action is the position below.
【Commentary】The way of the ruler is non-action,
while the way of the ministers involves affairs,
with distinctions in nobility and baseness, labor and ease,
for it is natural that their principles differ.
Just as the head resides above,
and the feet remain below,
when observed through the Dao,
their roles and duties are clearly defined.
【Three】【Comment】When officials each fulfill their capabilities according to their abilities, then order is achieved.
【Commentary】Offices have their high and low ranks,
abilities have their superior and inferior qualities,
when abilities match the positions, then things are not obtained through favoritism,
thus the officials of the world are well governed.
【Four】【Annotation】If one is non-active,
then the world will each respond to it with their own non-action.
【Commentary】The Great Way generates all things,
each with distinct dispositions and natures,
following their own inherent principles,
all are fully equipped.
Some run, some fly,
each responding to its function,
unaware of the reasons,
how could they deliberate with intention!
Thus, observing through universal principle,
all things are seen to correspond completely.
The Master said:
"The Way
covers and carries all things;
how vast and great it is!
The noble man must hollow out his heart for it.
Acting through non-action is called Heaven;
speaking through non-action is called Virtue;
loving people and benefiting things is called Humanity;
unifying differences is called Greatness;
acting without standing apart is called Broadness;
embracing all diversity is called Wealth.
Therefore, holding to virtue is called Discipline;
virtue's completion is called Establishment;
following the Way is called Completeness;
not letting external things break one's will is called Integrity.
When the noble man understands these ten aspects,
he stores them in the greatness of his cultivated heart,
and flows abundantly as he moves with all things.
Being thus,
he leaves gold in the mountains,
and pearls in the deep;
he does not profit from goods and wealth,
nor draws near to honor and riches;
he does not rejoice in long life,
nor grieve over early death;
he does not glory in success,
nor feel ashamed of poverty;
he does not monopolize the benefits of the world as his private share,
nor regards ruling the world as his personal prominence.
Prominence means clarity;
all things are one storehouse,
death and life share the same form."
【一】【注】Having a mind burdens its natural state,
so it should be hollowed out and removed.
【Commentary】The term "Fūzǐ" refers to
Lǎozǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ was a disciple of Lord Lǎo,
hence he is called "Fūzǐ."
"Kū" means
to remove,
to cleanse.
The Way, being empty and penetrating,
encompasses all without exception;
the two spheres (heaven and earth) rely on it for support and bearing,
and all things attain it to transform and come into being.
Is there anything not following this?
It is the ultimate root of all things.
Praising its vast and magnificent beauty and greatness,
to exhort the rulers of the time—
should they not emulate the non-action of the Way,
and wash away the burdens of having a deliberate mind?
【Explanatory Text】"The Master" Simǎ comments:
It is Zhuāngzǐ.
Another says:
It is Lǎozǐ.
These two instances of "The Master said,"
in the Yuánjiā edition are all separate chapters,
the Cuī edition is also like this.
"Cover and carry" is pronounced fǎn with initial f and final ù.
"Vast" is pronounced yáng,
also pronounced xiáng.
"Not hollowed out" is pronounced kǒu wú fǎn,
also kǒu hóu fǎn.
The Cuī edition uses 軒,
explaining:
an appearance of broad contentment.
"And depart" is pronounced qǐ lǚ fǎn.
【Two】【Comment】Not acting for this purpose,
yet this action acts on its own,
is the Way of Heaven.
【Explanation】Acting through non-action,
is to move in accordance with one's nature.
The heavenly mechanism unfolds spontaneously,
hence it is called heaven.
This is the act of non-action.
【Three】【Annotations】Not uttering these words,
yet these words speak themselves,
is true virtue.
【Commentary】Silent without speech yet responding without fixed method,
like a mirror suspended in a high hall,
when objects come, it reflects them,
whether speaking or silent, it is no different,
hence it is called virtue.
This is not speaking, yet speaking.
【Four】【Annotation】This is to let the nature of life take its own course.
【Explanation】Compassion is like clouds drifting,
love is like rain falling,
the heart holds no bias or obstinacy,
virtue and grace spread widely and universally,
thus establishing one's nature and life,
hence it is called benevolence.
【Five】【Annotation】All things and forms,
each abiding in their own place,
without drawing others to resemble oneself,
thus achieve greatness.
【Commentary】Now, carving and sculpting myriad forms,
each with distinct innate dispositions,
they follow their inherent nature,
all in harmony with the natural order,
allowing things to be without interference,
thus it is called greatness.
【Six】【Annotation】Mystically uniting self and other,
all things naturally accommodate each other,
hence there is abundance.
【Commentary】Concealing one's brilliance and obscuring one's traces,
blending with the common folk and drifting with the waves,
if cultivating virtue is no different from others,
how could establishing conduct be distinct from ordinary things!
Yet the heart knows no bounds,
like the waves spanning ten thousand qǐng,
a forest marsh nurturing all living beings,
this may truly be called magnanimous tolerance.
【Seven】【Annotation】I have no distinctions,
thus I alone can possess these multitudes.
【Commentary】Occupying the position of the ninth and fifth lines,
his authority surpasses that of ten thousand chariots,
he entrusts the myriad things despite their differences,
and accommodates the variations among the common people.
Thus, all natures are fulfilled,
enabling him to possess the wealth of the entire world.
【八】【注】Virtue is the essential principle of humanity.
【Commentary】One who can maintain the virtues cultivated previously
may be called the guiding principle for all beings.
【Nine】【Annotation】What is achieved without virtue,
cannot be called establishment.
【Commentary】Only after virtue and conduct are fully cultivated,
can one achieve merits and thereby aid all beings.
【一０】【注】The Way is not a partial thing.
【Explanation】Xún,
means to follow.
Being able to follow the emptiness and connection,
one's virtuous conduct is then sufficient.
【Transcription】"Xún" is pronounced as xún,
sometimes written as xiū.
【一一】【Note】It means finding contentment within oneself.
【Commentary】To thwart,
means to bend.
Unifying praise and blame,
blending honor and disgrace,
not bending one's principles for worldly matters,
one's virtue is complete.
【Transcription】"Cuò" is pronounced as "zuò wò fǎn".
【一二】【Note】The heart is vast,
therefore nothing in the world is beyond its embrace.
【Commentary】Tāo,
means to encompass.
When a gentleman or a virtuous person
fully cultivates the ten matters previously mentioned,
they can then embrace all affairs,
and their mind and nature become broad and magnanimous.
【Transliteration】"Tāo" is pronounced as tǔ dāo fǎn.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
It means to conceal.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
Guō's annotation did not capture the meaning of the character "shì".
"Shì xīn",
is akin to establishing the heart,
referring to the greatness of one's established heart.
In the "Jīao Tè Shēng" chapter of the "Lǐjì", Zhèng's annotation states:
"Shì",
means to establish.
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Shì",
is "zì";
"zì",
means to establish.
These serve as evidence.
According to Guō's annotation,
it would mean the heart is sufficient to accommodate affairs, not to establish the heart.
In the "Lùn Rén" chapter of "Lǚshì Chūnqiū",
it says "shì xīn hū zìrán zhī tú",
also using "shì xīn" together,
with the same meaning as here,
which sufficiently proves the error in Guō's annotation.
【一三】【Note】Virtuous grace overflows abundantly,
leaving all things to go their own way.
【Commentary】Shì (逝) means
"to go to."
With a broad and leisurely disposition,
and virtue and grace overflowing abundantly,
thus it becomes that all living beings turn to and go toward it.
【Explanatory Text】"Pèi" is pronounced as pǔ bèi fǎn.
The Zìlín states:
It means to flow.
"Wù shì" In Cuī's version, "shì" is written as "qǐ",
stating:
It means to open.
"Pāng pèi" is pronounced as pǔ páng fǎn.
【一四】【Note】Do not value rare goods.
【Commentary】If one acts as described above,
it is then non-action,
and since one does not covet glory and splendor,
one does not value precious goods.
Thus, pearls are born in water,
and without being sought, they remain hidden in the depths;
gold emerges from mountains,
and without being pursued, it stays concealed within the peaks.
【一五】【注】One can even forget oneself,
how much more so material possessions!
【Commentary】Even upon obtaining pearls and jade,
one still does not covet them to enrich oneself;
when routinely using goods and wealth,
how could one ever exploit them for profit!
【1.6】【Comment】They have always been but temporary lodgings,
for the mind often stays far removed from them.
【Commentary】Sending off and receiving,
without sorrow or joy,
thus externally distancing oneself from official carriages and crowns,
and internally not drawing near to wealth and honor.
【Explanation】"Bù jìn": jìn means to be near or close by.
【一七】【Note】This is what is called liberation from all ties.
【Commentary】If one's lifespan were extended indefinitely,
it would not be considered a joy;
if life were cut short prematurely,
it would not be regarded as sorrow.
【Translated Text】"Not enjoying" is pronounced as luò.
"Unraveling the suspension" has the upper character pronounced as xuán,
and the lower character pronounced as xiè.
【一八】【Note】Forget longevity and premature death in your heart,
how much more so the distinctions between adversity and success!
【Commentary】Wealth, nobility, glory, and success,
are not considered as splendor;
poverty, lowliness, obstruction, and hardship,
are not seen as shame or disgrace.
Longevity or premature death are not even matters of concern,
so how could feelings of honor or disgrace
possibly be allowed to dwell in the heart!
【One Nine】【Annotation】All are entrusted to the myriad things.
【Commentary】The light reaches the universe,
governing all under heaven,
the treasures of the four seas,
are all tied to one person's actions,
not benefiting from goods and wealth,
entrusting them to all nations,
how could it be permissible to restrict and take for oneself,
using them for private gain!
【二０】【Note】Suddenly unaware that honor is upon oneself.
【Commentary】He nurtured and cared for the common people,
ruled over the world,
yet attributed his achievements to others,
forgetting his own wealth and status,
thus not considering himself great or seeking glory and prominence.
【Translated Text】"Not using the title of king" is read with the pronunciation of Yú Kuàng.
The occurrences of "king's virtue" below are the same.
【二一】【Note】If not prominent, then remain silent (two).
【Explanation】Brightness means
to manifest.
Even if one sits in Fényáng,
losing their empire,
they must still display wisdom;
how can it be called concealing one's light!
【二二】【Note】Detached, with no fixed abode.
【Commentary】Forgetting the distinction between self and others,
thus all things can be unified as one storehouse;
merging with the process of transformation,
hence life and death share the same form.
Life and death bring no change to oneself,
how much less do matters of adversity, success, premature death, or longevity!
【Transcription】"Tuì rán" begins with the sharp initial,
also pronounced as yuè.
【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Jūn Fáng's edition, where "cáng" is written as "chén".
(2) In Zhào Jiàn Yì's edition, "yǐ" is written as "zhǐ".
The Master said:
"The Way is
profound like an abyss in its stillness,
clear like a flowing stream in its purity.
Without metal and stone,
there would be nothing to produce sound.
Thus although metal and stone possess the capacity for sound,
they do not ring unless struck.
Who among the myriad things can determine this!
The man of kingly virtue,
goes forth in simplicity and considers it shameful to be entangled in affairs,
establishes himself in the fundamental source and his understanding connects with the divine.
Therefore his virtue is vast,
when his mind expresses itself,
things respond to it.
Thus forms cannot exist without the Way,
and life cannot be illuminated without virtue.
To preserve form and fulfill life,
to establish virtue and illuminate the Way -
is this not the work of one with kingly virtue!
How expansive it is!
Suddenly emerging,
vigorously moving,
and the myriad things follow it!
This is what is called the man of kingly virtue.
He looks into the dark and obscure,
listens to the soundless.
In the midst of darkness and obscurity,
he alone sees dawn;
in the midst of silence,
he alone hears harmony.
Thus through depth upon depth he is able to perceive things,
through divinity upon divinity he is able to grasp the essence;
therefore in his interaction with the myriad things,
from utmost emptiness he supplies their needs,
constantly moving yet serving as their resting place,
whether great or small,
long or short,
far-reaching."
【一】【疏】The ultimate principle is profoundly mysterious,
comparable to an abyssal ocean,
serene and pure,
illuminating even the finest hairs and eyebrows.
The abyss is admired for its stillness and profound clarity,
while the serenity is praised for remaining pure even in motion.
Some versions also use the character "jūn" here.
【Translated Text】"Liáo" is given by Lǐ as yóu fǎn,
by Xú as lì xiāo fǎn,
in Guangya as xià qiǎo fǎn,
explaining:
a clear appearance.
【二】【注】Sound manifests through silence.
【Commentary】Sound is made manifest by silence,
and response arises from truth.
【三】【注】Hence it is used as a metaphor for those who embody the Way: they respond only after being stirred by things.
【Commentary】To strike is
to beat.
Within metal and stone,
there inherently lie musical tones;
if they are not struck,
they will never produce sound.
Similarly, in the heart of the ultimate person,
truly resides sagely virtue;
if things do not evoke it,
there is no way for it to manifest a response.
Previously, deep waters were used to illustrate the ultimate Way,
here, metal and stone are employed to reveal the sage's heart.
【Four】【Annotation】Response and perception are without fixed methods.
【Subcommentary】It is likened to a bright mirror,
compared to an empty valley,
when things come, it responds,
yet in responding, it is without a mind of its own.
Since things vary in length without end,
the responses also take on square or round forms without fixed pattern.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Within the depth of serene clarity,
the natural mechanism moves spontaneously.
Now, when the mechanism moves,
there is something that causes it to move,
yet the movement is not constant.
Metals and stones have no constancy,
yet from the Sháo, Xià, Huò, and Wǔ [ancient musical compositions],
music arises from what moves them,
that which causes them to move
cannot be fixed by any thing.
【五】【Note】To proceed with simplicity,
not to be fond of meddling in affairs.
【Commentary】Sù means
genuineness.
Shì means
to go.
The king's virtue is neither arrogant nor boastful,
he follows genuineness in his actions,
holding fast to simplicity and maintaining purity and loftiness,
thus feeling ashamed to engage in worldly affairs.
【Explanation】"Non-fondness" is pronounced with the sound "hào".
【Six】【Annotation】When the foundation is established, knowledge does not run counter.
【Commentary】Spirit is the
unfathomable function.
It constantly abides in principle,
going forth to respond to things.
The unfathomable spirit
knows and penetrates things,
and this subtle function
must be rooted in the fundamental.
To show that the fundamental can give rise to function,
the function does not contradict the meaning of the fundamental.
【Explanation】"而如" is pronounced as zhì.
The annotation is the same.
【Seven】【Annotation】When one's innate nature communicates with the divine,
it then expands even more broadly.
【Commentary】Being pure and simple, acting without deliberate action,
following one's true nature and proceeding forward,
with a spirit and wisdom that connects with all things,
yet always rooted in the fundamental origin,
so that its application does not contradict the essence,
and its movement does not harm the stillness.
With such virtue and conduct,
is this not the great Middle Way indeed!
【Eight】【Annotation】Things emerge only after being sought,
not by leading before the things themselves.
【Explanation】"Cǎi" means
"to seek".
The utmost sage embraces emptiness,
thus all things and self respond accordingly.
Unless things themselves seek the sage's virtue,
there is no way for the sage's mind to manifest.
The emergence of the sage's mind
truly arises from things' seeking.
It wishes to show harmony without initiating,
not acting before things do.
【九】【疏】The form is
the seven-foot body;
life is
a lifespan of a hundred years;
virtue is
the wisdom that can clarify;
the Way is
a realm that can be penetrated.
The Way can penetrate and give birth to all things,
hence without the Way, nothing is born;
virtue can illuminate the source of principles,
hence without virtue, nothing is enlightened.
The Lǎojīng says,
the Way gives them life,
and virtue nurtures them.
【一０】【Commentary】存，
means to entrust.
窮，
means to exhaust.
Entrusting the beauty or ugliness of appearance,
exhausting the longevity or brevity of life,
establishing great virtue to rectify the times,
using the ultimate Way to connect with all things.
One who can act thus,
is it not only Wáng Dé!
【一一】【Note】Hū,
bó,
both describe a manner of responding without intent.
Acting without premeditation,
thus all things follow it,
this is vast and boundless.
Therefore, one can preserve form and exhaust life's potential,
establish virtue, illuminate the Way, and achieve kingly virtue.
【Commentary】"Dangdang" is a term
denoting breadth and evenness.
"Hu" and
"bo"
describe a state of being without preconceived intention.
When things stir and move,
responding to opportunities as they arise,
following along and entrusting to things,
then things will comply.
Because it encompasses all virtues,
it is considered the virtue of a king.
【一二】【疏】The ultimate Dao is profoundly mysterious,
the sage's mind is concentrated and tranquil,
it is not of form and thus cannot be seen with the eyes,
it transcends sound and thus cannot be heard with the ears.
【一三】【Comment】If one relies on sight and hearing without anchoring them in stillness,
then there will be obscurity and disharmony.
【Commentary】Although it is dark and formless again,
it is capable of molding and shaping all phenomena;
it is said to be silent and without sound,
yet it can harmonize the eight tones.
This is intended to clarify that function arises from the essence,
and its capability is indeed like this.
【一四】【Note】Only by exhausting its origin can one master all things.
【Commentary】It is existence and yet non-existence,
it is stillness and yet response,
negating it again and again,
thus profound upon profound.
Having then exhausted principles and fully realized nature,
one is thereby able to master all things.
【一五】【注】Only by reaching the ultimate state of compliance can one fully embody subtlety.
【疏】Spirit is a name for the unfathomable.
【疏】Response and stillness are mutually inherent,
【疏】existence and non-existence are thoroughly transcended,
【疏】thus it is neither fathomable nor unfathomable,
【疏】nor is it not unfathomable either—
【疏】this precisely constitutes the essence of spirit's subtlety.
【16】【Comment】If I affirm this and leave everything to them,
then they will seek to provide for themselves.
【Commentary】Eliminating further eliminations,
one arrives at ultimate non-being.
Yet in engaging with phenomena, there is no fixed method;
it adapts according to circumstances and responds fittingly.
For the myriad distinctions and categories,
whatever is sought is immediately provided,
like a mirror suspended high in a hall,
reflecting everything that comes before it.
【Explanation Text】"而供" is pronounced as gōng,
originally also written as 恭.
"確" is pronounced with a bitter and learned tone.
The pronunciation is "sì" (as in "bestow"),
and it is also read as the common pronunciation.
【一七】【Note】All are indulged and left to their own devices,
until they reach their ultimate limits.
【Commentary】Chěng means
to let loose.
Sù means
to meet.
As for embodying the ultimate non-being,
it follows demands and suits the occasion,
thus it can comply with the times and adapt to circumstances,
responding to things in myriad ways,
the key is to converge without stagnating in one.
Therefore, sometimes large, sometimes small,
now short, now long,
even to the extent of long distances,
allowing those who come freely,
following their urgent affairs,
fully supplying their needs,
prescribing medicine according to the illness,
in principle, nothing is inappropriate.
The Yellow Emperor was traveling north of the Chìshuǐ River,
ascended the heights of the Kūnlún Mountains and gazed southward.
Upon returning,
he lost his Dark Pearl.
He sent Zhì to search for it, but it was not found;
he sent Lízhū to search for it, but it was not found;
he sent Chīgòu to search for it, yet it was still not found.
Then he sent Xiàngwǎng,
and Xiàngwǎng found it.
The Yellow Emperor exclaimed:
"How extraordinary!
Could it be that only Xiàngwǎng was able to find it?"
【一】【注】This elucidates the means by which one attains truth.
【Commentary】Red is the color of the southern direction,
the heart is the organ of the southern quarter.
The nature of water is to flow,
and its position is in the north.
This metaphor illustrates how the deluded mind attaches to external objects,
remaining in darkness without illumination,
hence it is said to be north of the Red River.
The Kunlun Mountains
represent the body.
The south is the direction of clarity,
"gazing" signifies the act of observation,
"mysterious" denotes something distant and obscure,
while the "pearl" symbolizes a precious treasure.
The intent is to clarify that all beings in the world
are deluded and mistaken in both body and mind,
chasing after attachments and indulgences,
lacking any awareness,
shrouded in darkness like the north,
restless as flowing water,
losing their true nature and the path,
all stemming from this.
Now, to return to the origin and source,
seeking the truth and inquiring about the Way,
thus gazing southward signifies illumination and introspection,
and returning symbolizes the restoration of one's innate nature.
Therefore, first, the place where the true nature is lost is clarified,
and then the method to attain the Way is revealed.
The methods to be revealed
are listed in the following text.
【Explanatory Text】"Chìshuǐ" Lǐ Yún states:
The water originates from beneath the Kūnlún Mountains.
"Huánguī" is pronounced as "xuán."
"Xuánzhū" Sīmǎ explains:
It is the truth of the Dào.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Liú Xiàobiāo's "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Chìshuǐ,
is a metaphorical name (for water),
Xuánzhū,
symbolizes the Dào.
This differs from the explanatory text.
【二】【注】Words and knowledge are insufficient to attain the truth.
【Commentary】Suǒ means
to seek.
Therefore, one cannot use the mind to seek when thoughts are cut off.
【Explanatory Text】"Shǐ zhī" is pronounced with the tone of "zhì".
The same applies to the annotations and the following instances.
"Suǒ zhī" is pronounced as "suǒ bái fǎn".
The same applies below.
【Three】【Subtleties】 are not forms,
and cannot be grasped with the eyes.
【Four】【Annotation】Cōngmíng chīgòu,
stray further from the truth.
【Commentary】Chī Gòu,
refers to the clarity of speech.
Without words, one cannot seek clarity.
【Translated Text】"Chī" is pronounced as kǒu xiè fǎn.
"Gòu" is pronounced as kǒu dòu fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
Chīgòu
means great strength.
◎ Jiāshìfù comments:
In the Guǎngyùn,
"chī"
is the same as ●.
refers to sound;
"gòu"
means anger,
and anger also relates to sound.
The Jíyùn states that chīgòu involves forceful arguing, which is correct.
The wise seek it with spirit,
Lí Zhū seeks it through form and shadow,
while chīgòu seeks it through sound and reputation,
thus the more they seek, the farther it becomes.
Xiàng Wǎng
seems to have form,
yet seems formless,
hence it is said to be obtained through intuition.
Seeking it through form yields nothing,
nor does seeking it by abandoning form.
The Shìwén quotes Sīmǎ as saying
chīgòu
means great strength,
which is incorrect.
【五】【疏】Wǎngxiàng,
means having no mind.
It detaches from sounds and forms,
severs thoughts and considerations,
thus knowledge and Lízǐ Zhū reach their limits and turn back,
Chīgòu's eloquence in debate,
exerts effort but loses the true essence,
only Wǎngxiàng, being mindless,
uniquely attains the mysterious pearl.
【Six】【Annotation】One who clearly attains the truth does not rely on deliberate effort,
for the formless and obscure is precisely the truth.
【Commentary】Lílóu, deluded in nature,
relied on his keen eyesight yet lost the Way;
Xuānyuán, enlightened to the principle,
marveled at obtaining the pearl through the formless.
Exhorting all students,
thus one may not abandon form and discard wisdom,
nor suppress hearing and destroy the body.
【Collation Notes】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "huán" is written as "xuán".
(2) The character "shuǐ" has been amended according to the Hú Kèběn version's commentary in the Wénxuǎn.
Yáo's teacher was called Xǔ Yóu,
Xǔ Yóu's teacher was called Niè Quē,
Niè Quē's teacher was called Wáng Ní,
Wáng Ní's teacher was called Pī Yī【1】.
【一】【疏】The above four individuals,
were all recluses during the time of Yáo,
who detested the filth and turmoil of the mundane world,
embraced the Way and upheld virtue,
maintained purity and integrity for themselves,
and were distinct from ordinary society.
Yáo recognized their worthiness,
and wished to abdicate the throne to them.
Zhuāngzǐ demonstrated that there was a lineage of transmission,
hence he fully listed their teachers and sources of learning.
【Explanatory Text】"Wáng Ní" Xú wǔ xī fǎn.
"Pī Yī" yīn pī.
Yáo asked Xǔ Yóu, saying:
"Can Niè Quē be matched with Heaven?
I am relying on Wáng Ní to invite him."
【一】【Note】Refers to being the Son of Heaven.
【二】【注】He intended to use their teacher to coerce and command them.
【Commentary】To match means
to harmonize.
To rely on means
to depend on.
Yáo said:
"Nièquē, being a worthy,
possesses the virtue that aligns with the heavenly position,
and it is hoped that by depending on Wángní,
he might be persuaded to come from afar."
As the matter remained unresolved,
he thus inquired of Xǔyóu.
【Transcription】"Yào zhī": Yī yáo fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
Xǔ Yóu said:
"How perilous is the world!
As for Niè Quē's character,
he is intelligent and wise,
quick and sharp,
his nature surpasses others,
yet he uses human effort to impose upon Heaven.
He is well aware of preventing faults,
but does not know how faults arise.
How could he be a match for Heaven?
He relies on human cunning and ignores the Heavenly way,
emphasizing his own form while treating others as different,
revering knowledge which races like fire,
being driven by trivial matters,
entangled by external things,
looking around and responding to everything,
trying to suit all circumstances,
changing along with things without constancy.
How could he be fit to be a match for Heaven?
Nevertheless,
he has a clan,
has ancestors,
he may serve as father to the multitude,
but cannot be father to the fathers.
Governance
is the source of chaos,
the curse of the minister,
the bane of the sovereign."
【一】【注】Jí,
means perilous.
【Commentary】Dài means
"near."
Jí means
"perilous."
Like Yǎo and Nièquē,
who declined the throne of ten thousand chariots,
the signs of peril and downfall
are not far off in their principles.
【Transcription】"圾" is also written as "岌",
pronounced as wǔ jí fǎn,
and also as wǔ hé fǎn.
Guō Xiàng and Lǐ Yí said:
It means perilous.
【二】【注】Being exceptionally intelligent and sharp,
one makes others look up to them,
yet repeatedly harms the people.
【Commentary】Ruì means
sagehood.
Jǐ means
nimbleness.
Mǐn means
swiftness.
When a sage governs the world,
the tassels of the crown veil the eyes,
and the yellow silk plugs the ears,
to block out sharp senses,
desiring not to see or hear too much.
Now, Niè Quē internally harbors sagely wisdom,
externally dazzles with cleverness,
his words are sharp and debates nimble,
his calculations vast and far-reaching,
his moral conduct and innate understanding,
all actions surpass others;
since his traces are so evident,
he is bound to be seen as a problem.
The signs of peril and downfall
are detailed below.
【Explanation】"給數" is pronounced as shuò.
【Three】【Annotation】Using wisdom to seek the restoration of one's natural state.
【Commentary】The loss of authenticity in things
has persisted for a long time.
To use the methods of intellect and cunning
to restore their original state
is to stray far from the natural disposition.
【Four】【Annotation】Faults arise from intelligence and knowledge,
and to use knowledge to suppress them
only makes the faults even greater.
Therefore, it is said,
the way to be without faults lies in letting go of knowledge,
not in forcibly suppressing it.
【Commentary】The origin of faults arises from,
knowledge.
It means that Niè Quē only knew how to strictly prohibit the faults and afflictions of the common people,
but did not know that afflictions originate from knowledge.
【Explanation】"Zài qù": Qǐ lǚ fǎn.
"Yú qiáng": Qí zhàng fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】If one were to bestow the world upon them,
they would then lead future generations to rely on cunning and lose their authenticity.
【Commentary】If one were to assume the position of Heaven,
commanding all living beings,
they would inevitably exercise their intellect and will,
acting against the natural order,
causing all things to lose their own essence,
and no longer preserve their inherent nature.
【Six】【Annotation】Taking the myriad things as fundamental,
then various changes can be unified and different forms can be harmonized.
This trace,
would ultimately lead later generations to control things according to themselves,
then the myriad things would become disordered.
【Commentary】"Fāng" means
"about to."
The sage has no personal mind,
but follows and entrusts things to their nature.
Now, Nièquē takes his own person as the foundation,
drawing things to make them return,
causing all under heaven with different forms
to follow his transformation.
The loss of things' inherent nature
truly stems from this;
the troubles of later generations
begin from this point.
【Explanatory Text】"Fāng qiě" is read as written.
Whenever "fāng qiě" is mentioned,
it means just about to undertake some action.
【Seven】【Annotation】When the virtuous are placed in front,
their wisdom and insight are revered thereafter,
and they race forward as swiftly as fire.
【Commentary】If one cannot forget wisdom to handle things,
but esteems knowledge to govern the world,
then one will follow in the footsteps of others,
abandon oneself to imitate others,
gallop and rush about,
as swift as fire.
【Eight】【Annotation】This will give rise to the beginnings of forced labor in later generations.
【Commentary】Xù (beginning),
means duān (starting point).
Shǐ (to employ),
means yì (toil).
Being unable to act through non-action,
and instead relying on knowledge to control things,
the toil and servitude of later generations
began from this starting point.
【Nine】【Annotation】This will consequently cause future generations to become constrained and manipulate things.
【Commentary】Gài,
means obstruction.
When one cannot use the Way to connect with others,
one instead relies on cunning to hinder things.
【Translated Text】"Wù gāi" - Xú reads it as hù gé fǎn,
Guǎngyǎ reads it as gōng cái fǎn,
saying:
to bind.
This aligns with Guō's interpretation.
Nowadays, the pronunciation from Guǎngyǎ is used.
◎ Jiā Shìfù commented:
The Shìwén quotes Guǎngyǎ saying,
gāi,
means to bind.
It is suspected that gāi should be gāi.
Guǎngyùn:
gāi,
means to prepare,
to encompass.
The Hànshū Lǜlì Zhì states "gāi cáng wànwù" (encompassing all things),
the Tàixuán Jīng mentions "wànwù gāi jiān" (all things are fully included).
As for the remnants,
their leftover threads are sufficient to command all categories.
As for "wù gāi,"
its mechanism is enough to embrace all things.
【一０】【Note】This would lead future generations to command and manipulate creatures,
compelling them to fulfill the tasks of their superiors.
【Commentary】He was about to survey the four directions,
pacify and secure all nations,
so that their common people
would respond to his transformative governance.
【Interpretation】"Lìng Yìng" is pronounced as lì chéng fǎn.
【一一】【Note】This will cause future generations not to forget goodness,
and to practice benevolence appropriately in response to circumstances.
【Commentary】Using one's own limited knowledge,
to respond to the appropriateness of all things,
is not without intention,
yet it inevitably leads to peril.
【一二】【Note】This will lead future generations to chase after external things,
unable to find fulfillment within themselves.
【Commentary】If I impose what I already know,
applying it to the multitude of beings,
and compel all things to follow this transformation,
then not only will the beings lose their nature,
but I too will have gained nothing.
【13】【Comment】These were all measures that fully suited the exigencies of their times.
However, those who today receive their benefits
will tomorrow inherit their drawbacks.
Hence it is said that there has never been constancy.
【Commentary】When governing affairs with cunning intellect,
with policies issuing from multiple sources,
earlier generations bear the burden of its virtue,
later ones suffer from its harms.
This already deviates from the pure ancient ways,
hence there is no constancy.
【14】【Note】Its affairs can be categorized and thus emulated through ancestral practices.
【Commentary】Clan
means a marshland.
Now, Niè Quē lived in seclusion among the mountain marshes,
holding his aspirations high,
unable to blend into the worldly tracks,
and thus insufficient to match Heaven.
Yet, within the mixed customs of society,
few are his peers,
so his lofty and far-reaching ambitions
are indeed worthy of emulation.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
A clan
is the trace of categorization.
An ancestor
is the origin of living beings.
Following this categorization to unite them,
then all things are unified into one,
and that which governs all things becomes the destination of all living beings;
seeking from the origin of living beings,
then all things begin from non-being,
and that which produces beings is but the branching flow of derivation.
Without fathoming the origin of living beings,
and hastily seeking unity through categorization,
order and chaos thereby arise,
and the calamities of ruler and minister thereby emerge.
【一五】【注】The multitude of fathers' father is
the means by which traces are left.
【Commentary】Father,
means ruler.
It says that Niè Quē was lofty and engaged in non-action,
not leveling himself with common customs.
Although his way can be narrated,
he is merely fit to be the father of the multitude,
yet cannot be the father of fathers.
The father of fathers
is Yáo.
Now Yáo, while dwelling as a host above all things,
had his mind racing towards the Gūyè Mountain.
When he went to see the four masters,
he was right in the land of Fényáng.
Thus, from stillness he moved,
and in moving he was still.
Non-action was action,
action was non-action,
being and non-being were simultaneous,
movement and stillness mutually inherent.
Therefore, he could be the ruler among rulers,
the father among fathers.
This is what is called exhausting principle and fulfilling nature,
mysterious and even more mysterious,
thus becoming the father of the multitude's fathers,
which is indeed fitting.
Hence, Guō Xiàng's annotation states,
"The father of the multitude's fathers is that by which traces are left."
【一六】【Comment】It means not only does it govern order,
but it also becomes the leader of chaos.
【Commentary】"Shuài" means
"to lead."
If one uses cunning to govern affairs,
though there may be order at the time,
chaos is certain to follow later.
Both approaches take cunning as the guiding principle.
【Text】"Zhì luàn": "zhì" reads as "lì" in reverse.
The annotation is the same.
"Zhī shuài": "shuài" is pronounced as "lǜ".
The annotation is the same.
Also pronounced as "sè lǜ" in reverse.
【一七】【Note】It was not that Jié and Zhòu were capable of killing virtuous ministers,
but rather that they relied on the traces of sagely wisdom to bring disaster upon them.
【Commentary】Jié and Zhòu relied on sagacious wisdom to kill virtuous ministers,
thus sagacious wisdom becomes the calamity of the northern throne.
【一八】【注】Tián Huán was not capable of killing the ruler outright;
instead, he used benevolence and righteousness as tools to harm him.
【Commentary】Tián Héng utilized benevolence and righteousness to assassinate his lord,
hence benevolence and righteousness are the tools of a usurper on the throne.
The annotation states,
Tián Héng was not inherently capable of killing a ruler;
rather, he relied on benevolence and righteousness to commit the crime.
【Explanation】"Shā jūn" is pronounced as shì.
It is also written as "shì",
with the same pronunciation.
【Collation】（一）The character above has been emended based on the Song edition.
Yáo looked towards Huà.
A border guard of Huà said:
"Ah,
a sage!
Please allow me to offer blessings to the sage."
【一】【疏】Huá,
is a place name,
now Huàzhōu.
Fēngrén,
refers to the person guarding the borders in the Huá region.
Xī,
is an exclamation of sigh.
The fēngrén saw that Yáo possessed the virtue of a sage,
shining upon the world,
and requested to wish for longevity and wealth,
as well as many sons.
【Transcription】"Huá" is pronounced as Húhuà fǎn,
also Húhuā fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is a place name.
The Border Official: Simǎ comments:
A person who guards the borderlands.
"Said, 'Ah'": pronounced as xī.
"Request a blessing": read with the fanqie of zhī and yòu,
also read with the fanqie of zhōu and liù.
"May the sage live long."
Yáo said:
"I decline."
"May the sage be wealthy."
Yáo said:
"I decline."
"May the sage have many sons."
Yáo said:
"I decline."
【一】【疏】Wealth, longevity, and many sons
indeed bring about numerous troubles,
yet those who can embody them
do not abandon non-action.
Therefore, by entrusting these two individuals,
the three afflictions are made clear.
The essence of declining and yielding
is set forth in the text below.
The border official said:
"Longevity,
wealth,
many sons -
these are what people desire.
You alone do not desire them,
why is this?"
【First】【Memorial】Regarding the three matters previously mentioned,
they encompass the greatest desires of humanity.
You alone have raised objections;
what is your intended meaning?
【Transcription】"Nǚ" is pronounced as "rǔ".
The same applies hereafter.
Yáo said:
"More sons mean more fears,
wealth means more troubles,
long life means more disgrace.
These three things
are not the means to cultivate virtue,
therefore I decline them."
【One】【Memorial】The Master's lineage flourishes and spreads,
bringing profound worries and fears;
wealth and goods are abundant and prosperous,
yet affairs and tasks are truly numerous;
life and longevity are prolonged,
but they bequeath hardships and humiliations.
These three are insufficient to nurture the virtue of non-action,
and instead can increase the burdens of action,
hence I decline them all.
The border official said:
"At first I thought you were a sage,
but now I see you are merely a gentleman.
Heaven gives birth to the multitudes of people,
and must assign them their duties.
If you have many sons and assign them their duties,
then what is there to fear!
If you are wealthy and let others share in it,
then what troubles could you have!
As for the sage,
he dwells like a quail and feeds like a fledgling,
moves like a bird without leaving traces;
when the world has the Way,
he flourishes together with all things;
when the world lacks the Way,
he cultivates virtue and retires into leisure;
after a thousand years, weary of the world,
he leaves and ascends to become an immortal;
riding on those white clouds,
he reaches the land of the Divine;
the three afflictions do not come near him,
his body is always free from calamity;
then what disgrace could there be!"
【One】【Exegesis】When I first spoke of you possessing the illumination of both being and non-being,
you were then a sage embodying the Way;
but now that you have abandoned being to dwell in non-being,
you have merely become a worthy gentleman.
【二】【Note】All things attain their proper place, and thus the will is settled.
【Commentary】Heaven and Earth create and transform all things,
each endowed with its own abilities.
Assigning positions according to one's talents,
what is there to worry or fear!
【Three】【Notes】Entrust it to the world,
thus there are no affairs.
【Commentary】The people are prosperous and well-provided,
the entire realm is affluent and substantial,
entrusting all things to the collective without acting out of self-interest,
this is the essence of non-action.
【Four】【Annotation】Without intention, yet expecting peace.
《Chún》 yīn chún.
《Jū》 Chún jū,
wèi wú cháng chù yě.
Yòu yún:
rú chún zhī jū,
yóu yán yě chǔ.
【Five】【Note】Looking up at things and feeling content.
【Explanation】The quail,
● a quail,
dwells in the wild without a fixed abode.
The nestling,
being the offspring of a bird,
must rely on its mother for sufficient food.
The sage sleeps and lives with frugality and simplicity,
likened to that ● quail;
his provisions are just enough to satisfy,
comparable to this nestling bird.
Since he has no inclination toward extravagance,
how could he harbor any attachment to flavors!
【Translated Text】"Kòu" is pronounced as kǒu dòu fǎn.
"Shí" according to the Ěryǎ says:
Those that are fed by mouth,
are called kòu.
The term "kòu shí zhě",
means relying on others for sustenance.
◎Lú Wénchāo comments:
The old text erroneously had "zhǔ" for "shēng",
now corrected.
【Six】【Annotation】Acting in accordance with one's nature,
is not the usual path.
【Explanation】Zhāng means
traces of writing.
The sage extinguishes his heart and annihilates his wisdom to merge with all things in obscurity,
just like a bird flying through the sky,
leaving no tracks to be seen.
【Seven】【Note】Reckless and presumptuous actions lead one to tread upon the great path.
【Commentary】When the times are peaceful and orderly,
one governs and cares for the millions of people;
when things come and affect me,
I respond timely and prosper.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation speaks of reckless and arbitrary actions,
which likely contradicts the intended meaning of the text.
【Eight】【Comment】Even the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ,
if they conformed to Heaven and responded to the people,
were not considered unattainable.
Therefore, those who act through non-action yet accomplish all things
are not unattainable either.
【Commentary】In times of turmoil and disorder,
one should blend with the common people and conceal one's brilliance,
cultivate virtue and hide one's traces,
preserve the path of one's life intact,
retreat gracefully to dwell in leisure,
roaming freely and withdrawing from the world.
This is what is meant by being at ease whether hidden or visible,
employing or setting aside actions according to the times.
【Transcription】"Jiù xián" is pronounced as xián.
The annotation is the same.
【九】【注】The ultimate person exhausts the length of their lifespan,
embraces the changes of exhausting (reason) [through] (one),
their life is a natural course,
their death is a transformation of things,
hence it is said they weary of the world and ascend to immortality.
【Commentary】The sage comprehends that life and death are not two different things,
and understands that transformation is one unified process.
Thus, they are able to fully accept the length or brevity of their natural lifespan,
and detest the clamor of worldly life to vanish and ascend.
Why must one seek the ascent at Dǐnghú,
to be uniquely considered an immortal?
Or why must one possess Ānqī's longevity,
to be called a thousand years old!
【Interpretation】"上僊" is pronounced as xiān.
【一０】【Note】When the qi disperses,
it goes everywhere.
【Commentary】The ethereal spirit ascends,
merging indistinguishably with the Great One,
riding clouds and harnessing the ether,
arriving at the realm of heaven and earth.
【一一】【Commentary】The three afflictions,
previously mentioned as wealth, longevity, and many sons.
For one who rides the Creator to come and go,
and mounts transformation to roam freely,
the three afflictions are fundamentally void and illusory,
the seven-foot body arises from non-existence.
Calamities and humiliations,
how could they ever be worth mentioning!
【Collation】（一）The character "tōng" has been changed according to Wáng Shūmín's explanation.
The border official left him.
Yáo followed him,
saying:
"May I ask a question?"
【One】
【一】【疏】After the petition was fully stated,
the border official then departed.
Yáo then realized his mistake,
and thus inquired further.
The border official said:
"Step back!"
【One】【Memorial】The doubts raised have been resolved,
you should promptly withdraw and return.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quēwù cites the Jiangnan ancient manuscript version, which already uses "jì".
Yáo ruled the world,
and Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo was established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
whereupon Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo resigned his position as a feudal lord and took up farming.
【一】Yǔ went to visit him,
and found him plowing in the fields.
Yǔ hurried to a lower position downwind,
stood, and inquired of him,
saying:
"In the past, when Yáo ruled the world,
you, sir, were established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to me,
yet you, sir, resigned as a feudal lord and took up farming.
May I ask,
what is the reason for this?"
【One】【Account】Bó Chéng Zǐgāo,
it is unknown from what place he hailed,
seemingly a man of the Way.
【Explanatory Text】"Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo" from the Tongbian Jing states:
Since the beginning of heaven and earth's creation,
my body has undergone one thousand two hundred transformations.
In later generations, the one who attained the Way
is Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo.
【Èr Shū】In the era of Táng Yú,
they faced south and called themselves sovereigns,
but by the time of the Xià dynasty,
they retreated to farm in the countryside.
Their positions and circumstances abruptly changed,
what was the meaning behind this?
Zǐgāo said:
"In ancient times, when Yáo governed the world,
he gave no rewards yet the people were diligent,
he imposed no punishments yet the people stood in awe.
Now you employ rewards and punishments, yet the people remain unvirtuous.
From this point, virtue shall decline,
punishments shall be established,
and the chaos of future generations shall begin.
Why don't you leave, sir?
Do not disrupt my work!"
He plowed intently without looking back.
【一】【疏】Rewards and punishments are means
to manifest encouragement and deterrence.
Yet Yáo governed through non-action,
whereby all things followed his transformation.
Thus, the common people needed no praise or rewards to voluntarily strive toward goodness,
nor required punishments to fear and refrain from evil deeds.
This reveals Yáo's divine wisdom,
whose virtue was such.
【Èr Shū】vigorously implemented rewards and punishments,
yet the common people remained unvirtuous.
When supreme virtue had already declined,
thus penal codes increasingly emerged.
Hence, it is known that the chaos of the future
began from this point.
【Three】【Commentary】In the time of Yǔ, the three sages succeeded one another,
governance was perfected and virtue complete,
their splendid achievements gradually faded,
thus historical records have nothing to document,
even Zhòngní could find no gap to criticize,
hence although they possessed the world, they did not interfere with it,
this is having it yet not possessing it.
Therefore, examining their era, Yǔ stands as the most excellent,
considering the individuals, though called three sages,
they are essentially one Yáo.
As there were no sages in that time,
the hearts of the world suddenly turned to Qǐ.
One who embodies ultimate impartiality and occupies the rightful position,
entrusts the world to the common people,
neither taking nor giving is for oneself,
thus when losing, one does not seek,
when gaining, one does not decline,
departing abruptly,
arriving freely,
hence receiving criticism from men of integrity yet being listed among the three sovereigns,
is not at all strange.
Zhuāngzǐ uses this to illustrate the flaws of Yáo,
flaws that originated with Yáo and conflicts that culminated with Yǔ,
how much more so in later ages lacking sages!
Entrusting distant traces to Zǐgāo,
then abandoning them without governance,
intending to end sageliness and return to oneness,
discarding knowledge to attain ultimate tranquility.
But its reality remains unheard.
The words of Zhuāngzǐ,
cannot be interrogated through a single approach,
sometimes using the traces of Huángdì to criticize the paths of Yáo and Shùn,
how could he solely honor Yáo and demean Yǔ!
Therefore, one should set aside what is entrusted,
and record his intent of abolishing sageliness and discarding wisdom.
【Commentary】"Hé" means
why not.
"Luò" means
to abandon.
"Yìyì" describes
the appearance of plowing the fields.
Bó Chéng referred to Yǔ as Fūzǐ.
"Fūzǐ, why don't you leave!
Do not abandon my farming work."
Thereupon, he exerted effort in plowing,
no longer looking around.
As for the three sages succeeding one another,
there were essentially no distinctions of superiority or inferiority,
but because the simplicity and refinement differed across eras,
therefore their traces were not the same.
Guō Xiàng's annotation says that problems arose with Yáo and conflicts were completed with Yǔ,
intending to clarify that having sages is not as good as having no sages,
and having action does not reach the level of having no action.
Therefore, he esteemed distant traces,
to make clear the idea of abolishing sages and discarding wisdom.
【Explanation】"He" is also written as 盍,
pronounced as Hú là.
"Wu luo": luo,
means to neglect.
"Yi yi": Xu reads it as yú zhí,
also as zhí lì.
Li says:
appearance of plowing.
Another says:
the appearance of a plowman walking.
Also pronounced as zhì,
and yú shí.
Zilin says:
appearance of bravery and strength.
"Zhi cheng": pronounced as zhí lì.
"Neng jian": jian meaning interposed.
"Bu yu": pronounced as yù.
"Tong": pronounced as dòng,
also as tóng.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is simply written as "使".
In the great beginning there was nothing,
which had neither being nor name.
From it there came the first existence;
the first existence had not yet bodily form.
Things got that by which they came into existence,
and were called their virtue.
What had not yet bodily form was divided,
and without intermission passed on,
and was called its lot.
The influences of the Yin and Yang operated on it, and things were produced.
When things were produced, there came the distinctive laws of their several kinds,
which were called their forms.
The bodies were charged with the powers that gave them their individuality,
each with its own peculiar manifestation,
which were called their nature.
When the nature has been cultivated, it returns to its virtue;
and the virtue at its highest point is the same as the Beginning.
That sameness becomes pure vacancy;
the vacancy becomes all-embracing.
Then the closing of the beak takes place;
the closing of the beak is like the union of heaven and earth.
That union may be seem as if stupid or dull.
It is what we call the mysterious virtue,
which is the same as the great Submission.
【一】【Note】There is nothing,
hence there is nothing to name.
【Commentary】Tài means
supreme;
chū means
beginning.
When the primordial energy first sprouts,
it is called Tàichū,
meaning that this energy is vast and great,
capable of being the origin of all things,
hence the name Tàichū.
At the time of Tàichū,
there was only this non-being,
and being had not yet come into existence.
Since being had not yet emerged,
how could names be assigned!
Therefore, there is neither being nor names.
【Explanation】"The Great Beginning," as explained in the Yì theory, states:
It is the inception of qì.
【二】【注】The One is
the beginning of existence,
the most subtle,
and because it is the most subtle,
it has not yet taken the form of physical principles.
The arising of the One
originates from the Ultimate One,
not from non-being.
Yet why does Zhuāngzǐ repeatedly refer to non-being at the beginning?
What is the reason?
The beginning means
not being born yet but attaining life;
the difficulty of attaining life
is such that it does not rely on non-being above
nor depend on knowledge below.
Suddenly and spontaneously, it obtains this life—
so why strive for life after it has already been born, thereby losing its self-generated nature?
【Commentary】One (should) [is] the Dào,
possessing the name of one but without the forms of the myriad things.
【Three】【Commentary】That which is non-being cannot generate things,
yet it is said that things attain their existence,
which serves to clarify that things come into being through self-attainment.
Allowing them to achieve this self-attainment,
this can indeed be called virtue.
【Commentary】Virtue (dé) means
attainment (dé),
referring to the attainment of this.
That by which things attain their existence,
externally does not rely on anything,
internally does not originate from the self,
neither non-existent nor existent,
neither self-caused nor other-caused,
unknowable in its origin of life,
thus it is called virtue (dé).
【Four】【Explanations】Although it has not yet taken form and substance,
it receives the vital energy and possesses inherent allotment.
Yet this allotment, whether long or short,
is so seamless and without the slightest gap
that it is called destiny.
【Explanation Text】"You fen" is read with the character 符 pronounced as 问 in the opposite tone.
"Wu jian" is read as the character's usual pronunciation.
◎Jiā Shìfù commented:
The alternation of yin and yang is called the Dao,
what continues it is goodness,
what completes it is nature.
When things attain their life,
it is what is referred to as the continuation being goodness,
before the concept of virtue has been named.
Upon solidifying into destiny,
and with nature inherent within it,
it is what is called the completion being nature.
With destiny established, each resembles its form;
actualizing the form then returns to nature.
Each has its norms and principles,
which is the function of fulfilling nature.
Zhuangzi here seems to have grasped its elusive essence as well.
【Five】【Explanations】To remain,
is to be still.
The active yang and the still yin,
ascend and descend in a misty fusion,
distributing throughout the three realms,
transforming and generating all things.
When things achieve completion,
their life principles are fully endowed,
this is called form.
【Translated Text】"Liú dòng" - Liú,
sometimes written as flow.
【Six】【Comment】Virtue, form, nature, and destiny,
are named according to changes,
yet in their spontaneity, they are one.
【Commentary】"Tǐ" refers to
substance;
"bǎo" means
to preserve.
One receives physical form,
and preserves the spirit.
In form, there is ugliness and beauty;
in spirit, there is foolishness and wisdom.
Following this, one should adhere to the natural course,
each being different,
with inherent nature fixed,
and no further changes,
hence it is called xìng (nature).
【Seven】【Annotation】Constantly achieving it without deliberate action.
【Commentary】By following this innate nature endowed,
one cultivates and restores the virtue of the primordial beginning,
thus arriving at the state of such virtue,
which aligns with the Great Beginning.
【八】【Note】Different from the beginning,
yet midway there is action,
thus within the bosom there is indeed something held.
Having something held, the virtue of accommodating and nurturing becomes small.
【Commentary】Being one with the Great Beginning,
the mind becomes empty and open;
once the mind is void and spacious,
it can thus encompass vastness.
【Nine】【Commentary】One who speaks without intent to speak,
harmonizes with the chirping of birds.
【Commentary】The beak,
is the mouth of a bird.
Since the mind is empty and void,
and actions merge with the obscure nature of things,
thus his words harmonize with the chirping of birds.
Just as the chirping of birds holds no intention for right or wrong,
how could the sage's words harbor emotions of hatred or love!
【Transcription】"喙" is pronounced as dīng dòu fǎn,
also as chōng ruì xǐ huì èr fǎn.
【一０】【Note】Heaven and Earth also move spontaneously without intent.
【Commentary】Words that harmonize with the calls of birds,
virtue also aligns with heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth have no intention in sheltering and carrying all things,
the sage has no intention in speaking,
thus they are in harmony with heaven and earth.
【一一】【Note】It is through sitting in oblivion that one spontaneously unites,
not by scrutinizing to achieve this union.
【Commentary】Mín means
to harmonize.
The sage internally aligns with the ultimate principle,
externally conforms to all living beings,
whether in traces or in essence,
nothing fails to harmonize,
hence it is called mín mín.
This is to blend with the common and ride the waves,
merging with the dust of all things,
appearing as if foolish and deluded,
yet also like dim and obscure.
Another explanation:
harmonizing with the chirping of birds,
and harmonizing with heaven and earth,
is also referred to as mín mín.
【Explanation】"Mín mín" is pronounced as wǔ jīn fǎn.
【一二】【注】Virtue is profound, and what it conforms to is vast.
【Commentary】Summarizing what came before,
it praises its magnificence and prosperity.
Such individuals
can be said to possess profound and mysterious virtues,
thus aligning with the Great Beginning,
and greatly harmonizing with all under heaven.
The Master asked Lǎo Dān, saying:
"There are those who cultivate the Way as if imitating each other,
making the unacceptable acceptable,
affirming the unaffirmable.
Disputers have a saying:
'Separating hardness and whiteness is as clear as the sky above.'
Can such people be called sages?"
【一】【注】If one imitates others,
forcing what is impossible to be possible,
treating what is not so as so,
this is distorting one's true nature.
【Commentary】He studied under Lǎo Dān,
hence he sought answers on every matter.
General discussions lack specific targets,
thus it is said there is someone.
Implementing governance and education,
making people imitate and follow,
using oneself to control things,
causes things to lose their nature.
Therefore, what is permissible for oneself,
may not be permissible for things;
what is so for oneself,
may not be so for things;
what is permissible or so for things,
applies to oneself in the same way.
【Explanation】"Fūzǐ" refers to Zhòngní.
"Xiàng fāng" is read according to the character's usual pronunciation,
and also has a reading of fǔ wǎng fǎn.
The text also has a variant written as fàng,
pronounced fǔ wǎng fǎn.
The commentary is the same (note 1).
"Qiǎng yǐ" is read as qí liǎng fǎn.
【二】【注】This means it is lofty and conspicuous, easily seen.
【Commentary】"Hardness and Whiteness",
was Gōngsūn Lóng's doctrine of defending whiteness.
Kǒng Chuān and his followers,
firmly upheld this doctrine,
standing unparalleled in their time,
unmatched under heaven.
Now the debaters say:
"We can dissect the theory of hardness and whiteness,
not considering it mere argumentation,
but making the arguments clear and distinct,
as if hanging the sun and moon in the firmament."
Therefore, Guǒ's annotation says this speaks of its prominence and clarity being easily seen.
【Explanation】"Xuán" is pronounced with the second tone.
"Yǔ",
Sīmǎ explains:
It clarifies clearly, like hanging a room in front of people.
"Yì jiàn" is read with the falling-rising tone.
【Third】【Memorial】Concludes the preceding question's intent.
"Can such a person
be considered a sage?"
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition reads "相放",

The original text reads "作方",

Lǎo Dān said:
"These are but people who, through their skills, become bound and toil in body and fret in mind.
A dog that is good at hunting becomes the target of thought,
and a nimble monkey is taken from the mountains and forests.
Qiū,
I tell you,
what you cannot hear and what you cannot speak of.
Many have heads and feet but lack a mind and ears;
few are those with form who coexist with the formless and shapeless.
Their movement
is but stillness;
their death,
life;
their downfall,
rise.
Yet this, too, is not the reason for it.
Governance lies in humanity;
forget things,
forget heaven,
and this is called forgetting oneself.
Those who forget themselves—
this is what it means to enter into heaven."
【一】【疏】Xū,
means mutual.
It refers to using right and wrong to alternately override each other,
employing this skill to bind oneself,
thereby exhausting the physical form,
and unsettling the mind with anxiety.
This addresses the previous question's intent.
As for the term "skill,"
some versions use the character for "branch,"
indicating that right and wrong are easily overridden,
branching out and diverging like leaves.
【Text】"技係" is read as "jì xì" with the pronunciation of "jì" as "qí qǐ fǎn".
【二】【注】This means all of these have lost their inherent nature.
"Chéng sī" should be an error for "lái tián";
"zì shānlín lái" is likely an error for "lái jí".
【Commentary】Yuán jū,
are macaques.
Dogs that catch foxes,
often get leashed for hunting,
lacking freedom,
thus they become sorrowful.
Monkeys originally dwell in mountain forests,
winding and unrestrained,
for leaping and seizing with agility,
thus they lose their usual abode.
Lí,
some texts write it as ●,
which is a bamboo rat.

Sīmǎ says:
● (three),
is a bamboo rat.
Another explanation:
a dog that is detained,

【Three】【Comment】Beginning and end,
is like start and finish.
Without mind and without ears,
speaks of its self-transformation.
【Commentary】"Ruò" (若) and
"ér" (而)
both mean "you."
"Shǒu zhǐ" (首趾)
refers to beginning and end.
Truth transcends verbal debate,
hence one cannot rely on hearing words.
Moreover, it cannot be grasped by mental deliberation,
nor perceived through the ear's faculty,
thus it is said to have no mind and no ear.
All sentient beings and insentient things
are spoken of in terms of beginning and end,
hence the reference to "the multitude."
None can convey it through speech,
none can comprehend it through thought—
why then do you so elaborately display monkey-like cleverness,
flaunt lofty debates suspended in abstraction,
compelling others to emulate yourself?
Is this not excessive!
【Four】【Comment】It is said that things with form are prone to change,
and cannot coexist with that which is formless and shapeless.
Therefore, those skilled in governing
do not cling to the old ways,
but instead follow and adapt to the ever-renewing transformations.
【Commentary】That which has form is
the body;
that which is formless is
the mind.
You say both mind and body exist,
but I, through the observation of principle,
perceive all of it as empty.
【五】【注】This speaks of how actions and stillness, life and death,
prosperity and decline, abolition and rise,
have never been constant,
all occurring naturally and spontaneously,
not because of any deliberate use that makes them so,
hence letting them be leads to self-attainment.
【Commentary】Times have movement and stillness,
beings have life and death,
affairs have rise and fall,
these six aspects,
are the principles of nature,
whose reasons are unknowable.
How could they be tied to human emotions and thoughts,
or achieved through imitation and effort!
One should merely trust and follow that things will naturally align themselves.
【Six】【Annotation】It does not lie in the ruler's self-reliance.
【Commentary】Each person acts according to their inherent nature,
with the natural mechanism unfolding on its own,
not governed by external doctrines.
【Seven】【Annotation】All things are forgotten,
not only forgetting oneself,
what else remains then?
【Commentary】Not only are worldly affairs empty,
but also the principles of heaven are non-existent.
Only when both matters and principles
are forgotten in these two aspects,
can one reach the ultimate state of neither existence nor non-existence.
【Text】"Fu He" reads as fú yòu fǎn.
【八】【注】What people cannot forget is
themselves;
if even the self is forgotten,
then what else is there to know!
This is to be unknowing and unlearned, merging into the natural state.
【Subcommentary】"Enter" means
to converge.
All that is difficult to forget in the world
is oneself,
and if even oneself can be forgotten,
then what thing in the world is worth preserving!
From this, we know that those who forget both things and self
thereby mysteriously converge with the Way of Nature.
◎ Jià Shìfù said:
Having a head and feet
is what humans and creatures share;
lacking a mind and thus unable to deliberate on affairs,
such as birds and beasts are;
lacking ears and thus unable to hear sounds,
such as insects and fish are.
Their movements and rest,
their death and life,
their decline and rise,
are all the transformative mechanism of Heaven and Earth.
The transformative mechanism within Heaven and Earth
is not exhausted by things,
having no form or shape;
what propels, shifts, and stirs within Heaven and Earth
is all the transformative mechanism.
Yet there is governance among humans,
how meddlesome humans are!
Forcing things to comply with governance
is not as good as forgetting oneself and leaving things to their spontaneous course.
◎ Qìng Fān's case note states: This means only those who forget themselves can unite in virtue with Heaven.
The Yǐn commentary on the Guǎnzǐ Báixīn Piān says:
Heaven and Earth
are those that forget form.
Those who can emulate Heaven and Earth—
is it not only those who forget themselves!
This conveys the same idea.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì version retains it as "māo".
(2) The character "●" is changed to "māo" based on the Shìwén version.
(3) The Shìdétáng version uses "māo",
this follows the original Shìwén version.
(4) The character "suǒ" is deleted based on the Zhào version.
Jiānglǘ Wǎn met Jì Chè and said:
"The ruler of Lǔ told me:
'I beg to receive your instruction.
'I declined but could not avoid the command,
and having already advised him,
I do not know if it was appropriate.
I venture to present it to you.
I said to the ruler of Lǔ:
'You must practice reverence and frugality,
promote those who are public-spirited and loyal without favoritism or partiality,
then who among the people would dare not be harmonious!'
【一】【疏】Recommendation,
means offering.
Jiǎng Lǘ and Jì,
are surnames.
Miǎn,
Chè,
are given names.
These two worthies are unknown as to their origins,
the source is not detailed.
The ruler of Lǔ,
refers to the Marquis of Lǔ,
a descendant of Bóqín,
it's uncertain exactly which duke it was.
The Duke of Lǔ met Miǎn,
and requested the methods for governing the state.
Although he repeatedly declined, he could not refuse the ruler's command,
so he informed the Duke of Lǔ about the way of governance.
At the time, it was done hastily,
fearing it might not be well-balanced,
I dare to present what was advised,
attempting to offer it to my worthy.
If it is unsuitable,
I hope for corrective guidance.
【Explanation Text】"Jiāng" in one version is written as Jiǎng.
"Lǘ" is pronounced with the initial "l" and the final "ü".
"Miǎn" is also written as ,
pronounced miǎn,
also pronounced wǎn,
Guō gives the pronunciation as wèn.
Jiāng Lǘ Miǎn,
is a person's name.
One theory says:
the surname is Jiāng Lǘ,
and the given name is .
Another theory says:
the surname is Jiǎng,
and the given name is Lǘ Miǎn.
"Jì Chè" is a person's name,
likely from the Jì clan.
"The ruler of Lǔ" some say:
refers to Duke Dìng.
"Zhì Zhòng" is pronounced with the initial "d" and the final "ong" in the fourth tone.
【二】【疏】Ah,
it means crooked.
孰,
means who.
輯,
means harmony.
The way of governance
first requires personally practicing reverence and respect,
frugality, simplicity, purity, and restraint,
then promoting fair and loyal individuals,
selecting honest and selfless scholars,
to advise on what is acceptable and reject what is not,
jointly governing the people,
so that the borders are secure without worries,
and the realm is peaceful and tranquil,
the people sing of the simplicity of life,
who would dare not be in harmony!
【Transcription】"Bù jí" is pronounced as jí.
The Ěryǎ says:
It means harmony.
Also read as zè lì fǎn.
Guō reads it as sī yú fǎn.
Jì Chè chuckled heartily and said:
"As for your words,
in terms of the virtue of emperors and kings,
they are like a mantis furiously stretching its arms to block a chariot's path—
then you are certainly not up to the task.
Moreover, if it were so,
then you would put yourself in a precarious position,
with many watchtowers of observation,
things would come to you,
and those following in your footsteps would be numerous."
【一】【注】One must practice reverence and frugality,
