not by forgetting frugality yet being frugal;
to elevate public loyalty,
is not by forgetting loyalty yet being loyal.
Therefore, even without favoritism,
it is still insufficient to overcome the burden of hypocrisy and deceit.
【Commentary】"Jú jú" means
bending over with laughter.
If one must be capable of reverence and frugality,
and rise above with public loyalty,
these are all artificial sentiments,
not those of one who has forgotten simplicity.
Therefore, to regard such words as the virtue of facing south [ruling],
how is it different from a mantis angrily raising its arms to block a chariot's wheel tracks!
Using the small to imitate the great,
thus it cannot bear the responsibility.
【Explanation】"Jú jú" is pronounced with the character "yù" as the initial.
Another interpretation:
The appearance of great laughter.
"Tángláng" is pronounced as táng láng.
"Chē yì" is pronounced as chē zhé.
◎Qìng Fān's note: The explanatory text gives "yì" as the pronunciation for "zhé",
which is correct.
"Zhé",
means the rut of a cart.
In ancient times, the character "zhé" was commonly written as "yì".
In the "Strategies of the Warring States," where it says "the extent reached by the cart's yì,"
the annotation:
"yì",
is pronounced as "zhé".
(The "Shuōwén" does not have the seal script for "zhé",
as "zhé" is actually "chè".
) In the "Records of the Grand Historian," the "Annals of Emperor Wen" mentions "jié yì on the road,"
and the annotation also pronounces it as "zhé".
The "Book of Han," "Annals of Emperor Wen" writes it as "jié zhé",
which serves as evidence.
"Bù shèng" is pronounced as bù shēng.
The annotation is the same.
【二】【Note】These all position themselves lofty and prominent,
as if towers and pavilions can be gazed upon.
【Commentary】Respect, frugality, impartiality, and loyalty
are not meant to forget simplicity,
but rather to display one's brilliance to dazzle the crowd.
When a person stands too high and in peril,
they are bound to meet with downfall and ruin,
just like a towering pavilion or observatory,
situated precariously on a height.
Although travelers may come to gaze upon it,
its collapse and destruction are not far off.
【Explanation】"Zì wèi jù" is read with the pronunciation according to its reference.
Another version writes it as "chǔ".
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current version writes it as "chǔ".
"Guān tái" is read with the ancient pronunciation of "guàn".
The annotation is the same.
【Three】【Annotation】This would cause things to not remain within the bounds of their inherent nature,
but rather to force and elevate themselves excessively to conform to it.
【Commentary】The observation tower stands lofty and remote,
people eagerly gaze upon it,
thus establishing conduct and esteeming themselves,
and all things vie to gather and align.
◎Jiǎshìfù remarked:
The abundance of observation towers
refers to making the people observe celestial phenomena and receive laws,
indicating the complexity of such affairs.
Guō Xiàng's punctuation by ending the sentence at "endangering their observation tower"
is likely mistaken.
【Four】【Annotation】Kicking one's feet and following in others' footsteps
is not being at ease with one's original stride.
【Commentary】When brilliance dazzles living beings,
they become restless and discontent,
hence many lift their feet to follow in the tracks,
and stand on tiptoe with eagerness.
Jiǎng Lǘ Miǎn looked startled and said in astonishment:
"Miǎn is utterly bewildered by what you have said, Master.
Nevertheless,
I wish you would speak of its general purport."
【一】【疏】Qùqù,
means a startled appearance.
Máng,
is to see nothing.
Suddenly hearing lofty discussions,
one is hastily startled and awed,
pondering without understanding,
hence becoming mángrán.
【Explanation】"Qù qù": pronounced xǔ nì fǎn,
also pronounced shēng zé fǎn.
Some say:
a look of alarm and fear.
"Máng ruò": some versions write it as "máng".
Pronounced wǔ gāng fǎn,
Guō pronounces it wǔ dàng fǎn.
is about teaching.
What I previously presented,
was deeply contrary to reason,
and I wish to speak one word,
hoping it may serve as a model for teaching.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
"Fēng" should be read as "fán",
meaning to speak of it in general terms.
"Fēng" originally derives its sound from "fán",
hence they can be used interchangeably.
Jì Chè said:
"When the great sage governs the world,
he stirs and moves the people's hearts,
causing them to form teachings and change customs,
entirely eradicating their thieving intentions and all advancing their unique aspirations,
as if it were their nature acting on its own,
and the people do not know how this comes about.
If it is so,
how could he regard Yáo and Shùn's way of teaching the people as an elder brother,
and muddledly treat them as a younger brother?
He desires to unite with virtue and settle the heart."
【一】【注】Each aspiration has its own inclination,
which cannot be imitated by others.
Therefore, if one sways it according to its natural swaying,
then even though it sways, it is not done intentionally;
if one swings it according to its inherent swinging,
then even though it swings, it is not set in motion by force.
Thus, harmful intentions vanish on their own,
and individual aspirations advance naturally.
When teaching is accomplished and customs transformed,
it happens silently without leaving a trace.
People follow their nature spontaneously, unaware of the reasons,
and all say, "It is our own nature."
meaning all) (一).
【Commentary】When sages govern the world,
they harmoniously comply with all living beings,
riding on their natural oscillations to establish laws,
and following their spontaneous fluctuations to form teachings;
thus, the teachings are accomplished without leaving visible traces,
customs transform without beings being aware,
all eradicate their harmful intentions,
and advance in cultivating the aspiration for self-transformation.
Unmoved by external things,
it thus seems as if it is the nature acting on its own;
acting in accordance with their nature,
they do not know the reason why it is so.
Jǔ,
means "all."
【Translated Text】"Jǔ miè" means all,
all.
"Mēn rán" is pronounced as mén.
【二】【Note】Míngxìng,
means highly esteemed.
Unwilling to overly praise Yáo and Shùn or elevate them as elder brothers.
【Commentary】Míngxìng refers to what is supremely noble.
If the methods of former ages
were used to teach the common people,
then governance would align with pristine antiquity,
and all things would attain their inherent nature.
Why then must we exclusively honor Yáo and Shùn
and exalt them as elder brothers?
This implies that the custom of yielding precedence
would not concede to Tángyú's era.
【Transcription】"Qǐ xiōng" is written as "qǐ zú" in the Yuánjiā version.
"Míng" is pronounced with a reverse of wáng and dǐng.
"Xìng" is pronounced with a reverse of hù and dǐng.
【Three】【Comment】To dwell means
not to be driven by external things,
for if the mind does not dwell, virtue will not be in harmony.
【Commentary】Residing means
achieving stability and tranquility.
When the mind races beyond its proper sphere,
it encounters all things as discordant and uneven;
but when empty, balanced, calm, and settled,
then the myriad realms become one.
Thus, the distinction between different realms
lies in the calmness or turmoil of the mind.
Therefore, for those who wish to align their virtue with Yáo and Shùn,
it is essential to stabilize and settle their minds.
【Collation Note】(1) The phrase "jǔ jiē yě" (meaning "all are") was mistakenly incorporated from the explanatory text;
it has been deleted according to the version by Councilor Zhào.
Zǐgòng traveled south to Chǔ,
and on his return to Jìn,
passing by the south bank of the Hàn River,
he saw an old man who was just tending his garden plots,
digging a channel to draw water from the well,
carrying a jar to pour it out for irrigation,
laboring strenuously with great effort but achieving little result.
【一】Zǐgòng said:
"There is a tool here,
which can irrigate a hundred plots in one day,
using very little effort but achieving much result,
wouldn't you, Master, desire it?【二】"
【一】【疏】The south side of a river is called yīn,
planting vegetables is called a pǔ (garden),
within ridges is called a qí (plot).
Suì,
means an underground passage.
Húhú,
describes the appearance of exerting effort.
Zhàngrén,
is a term for an elder.
Zǐgòng traveled south to the region of Jīngchǔ,
and on the road passed by the yīn side of the Hànshuǐ,
then engaged in a broad exchange of questions and answers with the zhàngrén.
The nuances of their rhetoric and tone,
are fully presented in the text.
Zhuāngzǐ thus used these two worthies to illustrate the praise of chaos.
【Transcription】"圃" is pronounced as bù hù fǎn,
also pronounced as bù,
meaning garden.
Lǐ Yí says:
Vegetable garden is called pǔ.
"畦" is pronounced as (kǒu)〔hù〕(èr) guī fǎn.
Lǐ Yí says:
Enclosed plots are called qí.
Shuōwén explains:
Fifty mǔ are called a qí.
"隧" is pronounced as suì.
Lǐ Yí says:
It means a path.
"甕" is pronounced as wū sòng fǎn.
The character can also be written as 瓮.
"搰搰" is pronounced as kǔ gǔ fǎn,
Xú and Lǐ pronounce it as kǔ huá fǎn,
Guō pronounces it as hū huá fǎn.
It describes the appearance of exerting force.
Another pronunciation is hú mò fǎn.
【二】【疏】A mechanism,
is a type of machine.
Since Zǐgòng observed that the old man expended great effort for little result,
he thus taught him the use of the machine,
hoping to achieve more with less effort.
I venture to offer my humble sincerity,
not knowing if it is desired or not?
【Explanation】"Yǒu xiè" is read with "hù" and "jiè" as the fanqie.
The Zìlín writes it as "xiè" (three).
Lǐ Yún says:
It means tools and implements.
"Jìn" is read with "zǐ" and "zhèn" as the fanqie.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to irrigate.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Junfang edition as having the character "機" below.
(2) The character "戶" was changed based on the Shidetang edition and the original version of Shi Wen.
(3) "械" is suspected to be a miswriting of the character "●".
The gardener looked up at him and said:
"What's this about?"
He replied:
"I've carved wood into a machine,
heavy at the back and light at the front,
lifting water as effortlessly as drawing silk,
swift as boiling water overflowing,
it's called a shàogāo."
The gardener flushed with anger and said with a scornful laugh:
"I've heard from my teacher that
those who have machines are bound to have machinations,
and those who have machinations are bound to have a scheming heart.
When a scheming heart resides in one's breast,
pure innocence is incomplete;
when pure innocence is incomplete,
the spirit becomes unsettled;
and an unsettled spirit
is not sustained by the Dào.
It's not that I don't know how to use it,
but I'd be ashamed to do so."
【一】【疏】How to manage it,
is like asking how,
(meaning) [requesting] the method for it.
【Explanation】"卬而" is pronounced as yǎng.
It is also written as 仰.
【二】【疏】The mechanism,
is a device.
It lifts the water,
irrigating as if drawing it up,
intending to discuss rapid movements,
resembling the boiling surge of hot water,
light in the front and heavy in the back,
which is the jiégāo in use today.
【Explanation】"挈水" is pronounced with the initial consonant of "kǒu" and the final of "jié".
"若抽" is pronounced with the initial consonant of "chì" and the final of "liú".
Lǐ Yí says:
It means to draw.
Sīmǎ and Cuī's versions use "流".
"數如" is pronounced with the initial consonant of "suǒ" and the final of "jiǎo",
while Xú reads it with the initial consonant of "suǒ" and the final of "lù".
"泆湯" is pronounced as "yì".
Some versions use "溢".
Lǐ Yí says:
It describes rapid movement like boiling water overflowing.
Sīmǎ's version uses "佚蕩",
also indicating swift back-and-forth movement like unrestrained flow.
"佚蕩"
means unrestrained and free.
"槔" is also written as "橋" in some versions,
or as "皋",
with the same meaning.
It is pronounced as "gāo",
while Xú reads it with the initial consonant of "jū" and the final of "qiáo".
Sīmǎ and Lǐ Yí say:
It refers to a well-sweep.
【Three】【Comment】That which is used in accordance with the times,
is pure and complete.
If a person desires to cultivate purity and completeness,
yet clings to oneness and adheres to antiquity,
they miss its true meaning.
【Commentary】Where there are devices with mechanisms,
there must be tasks that set them in motion;
where there are tasks that set mechanisms in motion,
there must be minds inclined to cunning changes.
When cunning changes reside in the heart's chamber,
then purity, simplicity, and unblemished whiteness are not fully perfected.
If purity, simplicity, and unblemished whiteness are not fully perfected,
then the spirit is suspended in a realm,
fluctuating and unstable.
Being unstable,
it cannot bear the ultimate Way,
hence one would feel ashamed and refrain from such actions.
This is because one has not yet embodied true cultivation,
thus clinging to unity and preserving whiteness.
【Explanation】"Our Master" refers to Lǎozǐ.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "卬" is written as "仰".
(2) The Quē Wù cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, where "為" is written as "桔".
Zǐgòng looked ashamed and embarrassed,
bowed his head and did not reply【一】.
【一】【疏】Mán,
is the appearance of shame and embarrassment.
Having lost what was said,
thus one does not know how to respond.
【Explanation】"Mán": pronounced as wǔ bǎn fǎn,
also pronounced as wáng ān fǎn.
The Zìlín states:
It describes the appearance of flat eye sockets.
Lǐ (written as ) pronounced as tiān diǎn fǎn,
meaning a look of shame.
Another pronunciation is mén,
also pronounced as wáng gān fǎn.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as "wǔ",
pronounced as wǔ.
Cuī's version writes it as "fǔ".
After a while,
the gardener said:
"What are you doing here?"
【一】【疏】A short while,
a moment.
Xi,
meaning why.
Asked Zǐgòng:
"Whose disciple are you?
What studies do you pursue?"
He said:
"I am a disciple of Kǒng Qiū."
【一】【疏】Answer,
Xuānní's disciple.
◎Qìng Fán's case: In the twenty-fifth volume of the Sound and Meaning of the Complete Scriptures, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Tú,
means disciple.
The explanatory text is missing.
The gardener said:
"Are you not one of those who, with broad learning to emulate the sages,
with ostentatious behavior to surpass the masses,
strum a solitary lute and sing mournful songs to sell your reputation throughout the world?
You should rather forget your spirit and energy,
cast off your physical form,
and then you might come close [to the Way]!
When you cannot even govern your own self,
how could you have the leisure to govern the world!
Go away now,
do not hinder my work!"
【一】【疏】Yúyú,
means being flattering and fawning.
It says that you are widely learned and well-informed,
imitating the sages,
using deceitful flattery and fawning,
to overshadow all others;
sitting alone, playing the qin and singing,
modulating tones in sorrowful sighs,
holding onto these traces of sageliness,
selling that reputation,
traveling extensively to various states,
journeying throughout the world.
【Explanation】"於于" are both read as they are.
Some versions write it as "唹吁",
with the same pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
an appearance of boastfulness and exaggeration.
Another explanation:
an appearance of practicing benevolence and kindness.
"以蓋眾" in Sīmǎ's version writes "蓋" as "善".
◎Jiāshìfù comments:
In "Responding to Emperors and Kings",
they lie down leisurely,
they wake up contentedly.
The "Shuōwén" dictionary states:
means "at" or "in",
resembling the ease of breath.
Thus, the characters "於" and "于" are similar,
"於于",
is akin to "于于".
【二】【Note】Without remembrance and without negligence,
there is no path to near-perfection.
【Explanation】Jǐ means
to be close.
If you forget and let go of your spirit and energy,
let your physical form deteriorate,
and once both body and mind are forgotten,
then you may come close to the Dào.
【Explanatory Text】"墮" is pronounced as xǔ guī fǎn.
【Three】【Neglects】 means,
you.
Lack,
means deficiency.
When all things govern themselves,
then the world is in order;
to impose one's own order on things,
then great chaos arises.
With Zǐgòng's virtue,
it is not sufficient to govern himself,
how could he possibly respond to the summons of the world!
It is appropriate to go quickly,
and not abandon my work.
【Transcription】"Wú fá" fá,
means abandoned.
Zǐgòng looked downcast and pale,
appearing disconcerted and ill at ease,
and only after walking thirty li did he gradually recover.
【一】【疏】Bēizōu,
describes the appearance of shame and embarrassment.
Xūxū,
describes the appearance of being disconcerted.
After being criticized and rebuked,
his countenance became disconcerted,
and he walked thirty li,
before he could return to normal.
【Translated Text】"Bēizōu" is pronounced as zǒu hóu fǎn,
while Xú reads it as cè liú fǎn.
Lǐ explains:
Bēizōu
refers to an appearance of shame and fear.
Another interpretation says:
it means the complexion shows unease.
"Xūxū" is also written as xùxù,
pronounced xǔ yù fǎn.
Lǐ explains:
it denotes a look of self-loss.
His disciple asked:
"Who was that man just now?
Why did you, Master, change countenance and lose color upon seeing him,
and remain unsettled throughout the day without returning to your normal self?
means to return.
Zǐgòng's disciples referred to Cì as their master.
"That person we saw earlier,
what art or skill has he cultivated,
that upon your first sight of him, sir,
your countenance lost its usual composure,
and throughout the day from dawn till dusk,
your spirit and energy have not returned?"
The disciples found it strange,
hence they posed the question.
【Explanatory Text】"Xiàng zhī" is pronounced with the characters Xǔ Liàng fǎn.
It is also written as "xiāng",
with the same pronunciation.
The same applies hereafter.
He said:
"At first I thought there was only one man in the world,
not knowing there existed another such person.
I have heard from my master that
in undertaking affairs we seek what is acceptable,
in pursuing achievements we seek success.
Using little effort
yet accomplishing much
is the way of the sage.
But now I see this is not so.
Those who hold the Way possess complete virtue,
those with complete virtue possess complete form,
those with complete form possess complete spirit.
Complete spirit
is the way of the sage.
They dwell among the people, walking with them yet none know where they are going
—how profoundly simple and perfectly complete!
Thoughts of merit, profit, and clever schemes must be forgotten in such a person's mind.
As for such a person,
they do not go where their will does not incline,
they do not do what their heart does not desire.
Though the whole world praises them,
calling them right,
they remain aloof and disregard it;
though the whole world blames them,
calling them wrong,
they remain detached and do not accept it.
The world's blame or praise
brings them no benefit or harm
—this is what we call a person of complete virtue!
As for me, I am but one of those tossed by winds and waves.
【一】【注】Refers to Kǒng Qiū.
【二】【疏】In the past, I came to receive learning,
and within the realm, only you, Master, stood alone;
now encountering you, Elder,
whose virtue and principles run even deeper and more profound,
thus I feel humble and ashamed, unable to attain such heights myself.
Since I have not yet grasped the essence of truth and falsehood,
I truly say you are wiser than Zhòngní.
【Explanation】"復有" is pronounced as "fú yòu" with the opposite tone.
"夫人" is pronounced as "fū rén".
The following "夫人" is the same.
【Three】【Comment】The way of the sage
is simply to use the hearts of the common people.
【Commentary】Actions are considered appropriate when they are timely,
and achievements are deemed successful when they can be accomplished.
Therefore, achieving great results with minimal effort
signifies the opportune moment for timely and successful action.
Zǐgòng recounted what he had learned in the past,
regarding it as the way of the sage.
【Four】【Annotation】This is the way of the sage kings,
not the way of ordinary people.
Zǐgòng, upon hearing his discourse on artificial cultivation, was convinced by it,
unaware that those of pure whiteness align with the world.
【Commentary】Now the elder asks me,
but it is not so.
It means that those who uphold the Way have no deficiency in virtue,
those with complete virtue have no impairment in form,
and those with complete form have concentrated spirit.
Those with complete spirit leave their traces in the human world,
are born into the same era,
and though they walk alongside all things,
they do not know where they are going,
obscure and profound,
immeasurable.
Thus, their conduct is pure and harmonious,
their virtue and Way are perfectly complete,
and one cannot speak to their hearts with utilitarian schemes or cleverness.
This is the Way of the sage,
not a method achieved through artificial cultivation.
Zǐgòng did not comprehend this,
and thus mistakenly offered such talk.
【Explanatory Text】"Vast and boundless" is pronounced with the initial 'm' and the rhyme 'ang'.
"The heart" refers to the heart,
sometimes written as 'the Way'.
【Five】【Annotation】These followers of Sòng Róngzǐ,
are not yet sufficient to be considered of complete virtue.
Zǐgòng's confusion and immersion among such people,
is akin to Lièzǐ's infatuation with Jì Xián.
【Commentary】"Áo" refers to an arrogant and disrespectful demeanor,
"tǎng" describes an appearance of indifference.
The elder's will and spirit are pure and simple,
he does not engage in cunning or artifice,
his heart harbors few desires,
and he does not strive for action.
Even if the whole world praises him,
calling him virtuous,
knowing it is of no benefit,
he does not even glance back;
if the whole world criticizes and slanders him,
causing him to lose his reputation,
understanding that it does no harm,
he pays it no heed at all;
since neither slander nor praise can sway him,
he can be called a person of complete virtue.
Although the nature of water is clear,
it stirs when encountering wind and waves;
if one's mind is not steadfast,
it resembles those turbulent waves,
hence such a person is called "a man of wind and waves."
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
these followers of Sòng Róngzǐ
are not yet sufficient to be considered of complete virtue.
Zǐgòng's confusion and immersion among such people
is like Lièzǐ's infatuation with Jì Xián.
【Explanatory Text】"Yù zhī" is pronounced as yú,
the same below.
"Áo rán" is pronounced with the initial wǔ and the final gāo.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as jǐng.
"Tǎng rán" is also written as dǎng in some versions.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as ●,
same.
Pronounced with the initial chì and the final dàng,
Guō reads it as tǔ gèng.
Returning to Lǔ,
he reported this to Confucius.
Confucius said:
"He is one who practices the art of Hùndùn's school in a superficial manner;
he knows one aspect,
but is ignorant of the other.
He cultivates his inner self,
but neglects the external world.
As for those who comprehend clarity and enter simplicity,
act through non-action and return to plainness,
embody their nature and embrace their spirit,
to wander freely within the mundane world—
would you truly be astonished by them?
Moreover, the art of Hùndùn's school,
how could you and I be sufficient to understand it!"
【一】【注】Because he turned his back on the present and looked toward the past,
feeling ashamed to engage in worldly affairs,
it is thus known that he was not truly like Hundun.
【Commentary】Zǐgòng traveled from Lǔ to Chǔ,
then returned to Lǔ,
and based on the circumstances he encountered,
reported to Kǒngzǐ.
The term "hundun" (primordial chaos)
refers to a state without distinctions.
Since he turned his back on the present and looked toward the past,
this is how we know it was not the true method of the Hùndùn school.
【Explanation】"Hún" is pronounced as Húběn fǎn.
"Dùn" is pronounced as Túběn fǎn.
"Bèi jīn" is pronounced as Bèi.
【二】【注】They only recognize the simplicity of ancient practices like carrying water and tending fields,
but do not understand the ease of adapting to the times and responding to circumstances.
【Commentary】To recognize only one aspect,
means adhering rigidly to antiquity without adapting.
To be unaware of the other aspect,
means failing to conform to the present and adjust to changes.
【Explanation】"Zhi Yi" is read with the pronunciation of "yǐ chǐ fǎn".
【Three】【Commentary】The true state of primordial chaos,
is entirely ungoverned.
How could it be that distinctions between internal and external lead to partial governance!
【Commentary】Embracing the Way and preserving simplicity
is governing the inner self;
being unable to adapt to the times and respond to changes
is failing to govern the external.
【Four】【Annotation】This is true chaos and simplicity,
thus one flows with the worldly currents without losing oneself,
so even while moving within the mundane world, one remains seamlessly traceless,
how could it be necessary to startle you!
【Commentary】When the mind is clear and enlightened,
it converges with the essence of simplicity;
through non-action and empty tranquility,
it returns to the origin of pristine purity.
One who comprehends the true nature and embraces essential purity,
mingling with the clamorous dust yet wandering through the mundane world,
should naturally become like rivers and seas to all living beings,
like forests and marshes to the myriad things,
where birds and beasts are not startled—
how could people be alarmed!
The statement "you will surely be alarmed"
actually clarifies that it is not necessarily so.
◎ Yú Yuè remarks:
"Gù" should be read as "hú."
Both "hú" and "gù" derive from the phonetic element "gǔ,"
hence they can be used interchangeably.
"How could you be alarmed?"
means that when you encounter true primordial chaos, you will not be startled.
Guō Xiàng's annotation states:
Therefore, flowing with the world yet not losing oneself,
even while moving through世俗, one remains seamlessly traceless—
how could it necessarily startle you!
This correctly captures the meaning.
In ancient texts, "hú" is sometimes written as "gù."
As in the "Chǐ Mí" chapter of the Guǎnzǐ:
"If you are about to depart,
why would I not see you off?"
And in the "Shàng Xián Zhōng" chapter of the Mòzǐ:
"Why not recognize that esteeming the worthy is the foundation of governance?"
Both are evidence of "gù" being used for "hú."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary in the "Āi Gōng Wèn" chapter of the Lǐjì states:
"Gù"
is equivalent to "gù" (meaning "why").
Thus, using "gù" for "hú"
is akin to using "gù" for "hú."
【Five】【Comment】Where there is that, there is that;
where there is this, there is this.
In the chaotic and profound unity,
who can truly recognize it?
What is recognized is often merely its traces.
【Commentary】Chaos is without intention,
profoundly transcending wisdom and deliberation.
Even if sages and worthies possess exceptional insight,
how could they fully comprehend it?
It elucidates the elusive and profoundly mysterious,
thus pushing it beyond the realm of emotion and thought.
Zhūnmáng was about to journey east to the great abyss,
when he happened to meet Yuànfēng on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Yuànfēng said:
"Where are you going?"
【一】【疏】Zhūn,
means pure.
Yuàn,
is a small breeze,
also said to be a great whirlwind.
Bīn,
is the shore;
the great chasm,
is the sea.
Zhūn Máng and Yuàn Fēng,
are both allegorical figures.
Zhuāngzi placed these two characters,
who understood the great Way,
thus fictitiously made them guest and host,
meeting by the seashore.
【Translated Text】"Zhūn" Guo's reading gives lún fǎn,
also shù lún fǎn.
"Máng" originally sometimes written as máng,
wǔ gāng fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
From afar it appears zhūn zhūn,
upon close inspection it seems máng máng,
hence called Zhūnmáng.
Another says:
It is a name.
Or it is said:
It refers to mist or vapor.
"Great Chasm" huǒ gè fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
Great Chasm,
is the Eastern Sea.
"Yuànfēng" originally also written as wǎn.
Xú gives yú ruǎn fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
Describes something small,
meaning wandering in the mundane world.
Another says:
Yuànfēng,
is a person's name.
Another says:
It refers to a strong, swirling wind.
"The shore" pronounced bīn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that the variant text also writes yuàn as wǎn,
yuàn and wǎn are the same character.
In Huáinánzǐ's "Chù Zhēn Piān," it says "the form is wǎn and the spirit is strong,"
Gāo Yòu annotates:
Wǎn,
means withered or sickly,
wǎn is read as the wǎn in Nányáng Wǎn.
【二】【疏】Xī,
What is it?
Zhī,
means to go.
I ask Chún Máng,
Where are you wandering off to?
Said:
"To the great abyss."
【One】【Memorial】Wishing to journey to the Eastern Sea.
He said:
"Why are you doing this?"
【One】【Memorial】Again asked what he sought to inquire.
He said:
"The great abyss as an entity,
pours into it yet it does not fill,
draws from it yet it does not exhaust;
I shall wander there.
【One】【Exposition】The ocean is vast and profound,
deep and boundless, difficult to fathom.
Hundreds of rivers flow into it, yet it does not overflow;
the Weǐlǘ drains it, yet it does not run dry.
This serves as a metaphor for the ultimate truth,
and its meaning is likewise.
Thus, though one may journey to the vast sea,
in truth, it is to roam the heart in the Great Dào.
【Interpretation】"Zhuó Yān" in one edition is written as "Qǔ Yān".
Yuàn Fēng said:
"Does the Master have no concern for the common people with horizontal eyes?
I wish to hear about sagely governance."
【One】【Memorial】 Among the five elements,
only humans have horizontal eyes,
hence they are called the horizontal-eyed people.
Moreover, Chún Máng traveled east,
arriving at the great ravine,
observing its depth and vastness,
to devise a method of governance.
Yuàn Fēng, having perceived this situation,
thus posed the following question:
Does the Master have no concern for the common people?
I wish to hear the methods of sage-like transformation.
【Explanation】"The people with horizontal eyes" Lǐ Yí said:
They are like insects,
wanting him to govern them.
"Wish to hear" some versions follow Sīmǎ's version as "ask",
same below.
"Sagely governance" pronounced with a direct official tone.
All below are the same.
Zhūnmáng said:
"What is sage-like governance?
Officials implement policies without losing their appropriateness,
promote people without overlooking their abilities,
fully understand the actual situations and act accordingly,
their actions and words are self-directed yet the world is transformed,
with a mere hand gesture or glance,
the people from all four directions all come forth,
this is what is called sage-like governance."
【One】【Memorial】Establishing decrees and setting up officials,
should be done appropriately and conveniently,
promoting and recommending individuals,
without missing out on talent and ability.
In this way, the world will be at peace,
the constant principles of human relations will be in order,
the method of sagely governance
lies herein.
【Explanatory Text】"Guān Shī" begins with the initial consonant "zhī" and the fanqie spelling,
also with the initial "zhì" and the fanqie spelling.
Sīmǎ explains:
implementing governance and spreading teachings,
each is carried out appropriately.
【二】【注】All are thus entrusted to their roles.
【Commentary】The ways in which matters go awry are numerous and varied,
arising from diverse causes and circumstances.
Thus, the methods and pace of governance differ with the times,
and the purity or decadence of customs shifts across eras.
Therefore, those who seek to govern must first rely on understanding the nature of things,
observing their true conditions and examining their actions.
Only then can one act in accordance with the way of things,
ensuring that nothing is mishandled.
【Three】【Comment】If one forces things to act,
then they will not transform.
【Commentary】All actions to be implemented,
teachings and decrees to be issued,
should allow things to follow their own course,
without forcing them to comply with oneself.
Acting in this manner,
all living beings under heaven will naturally follow and transform.
【四】【注】It means that with his gestures and glances, the people each realize their inherent nature,
because he lets them act on their own.
【Commentary】Náo means
to move.
It is said that by moving a finger to command,
and raising the eyes to look around,
then all directions sincerely submit,
and myriad states come to pay tribute.
The efficacy of sagely governance,
its meaning is like this.
Some versions have the character yí,
meaning to command using the chin,
and all directions submit.
Here, there are three types of individuals in total:
first, the sage,
second, the virtuous,
third, the divine.
The above refers to sagely governance,
the following sequentially lists the two individuals: virtuous and divine.
【Explanation】"Shǒu náo" is pronounced with the initial "r" and a rising tone,
also with the initial "r" and a falling-rising tone.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to move.
Another explanation:
It refers to directing commands to the four directions.
"Gù zhǐ" is read as its standard pronunciation.
Xiàng explains:
"Gù zhǐ" means
that by directing commands with a glance (or look), one can govern.
Sometimes it is pronounced as "yí".
The text also uses the character "頤",
pronounced with the initial "y" and a level tone,
meaning to raise the chin to give orders.
◎Qìng Fān's case analysis: "shǒu náo" and "gù zhǐ"
are two contrasting terms.
The commentary on directing commands relates to "shǒu náo",
while glancing around relates to "gù zhǐ",
hence the sub-commentary explains the four characters separately as moving the hands and raising the eyes.
If, as Xiàng says, "gù zhǐ" means directing commands with a glance,
it loses the original meaning.
"Gù zhǐ"
means to glance at someone and direct them with a gesture.
In Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú," seizing flags is like "gù zhǐ",
Liú Kuí annotates:
It means glancing and pointing as one wishes.
This mention of "gù zhǐ"
shares the same meaning as in the "Hànshū" biography of Gòng Yǔ, where it describes using eyes and breath to command.
(Shī Gǔ notes:
Moving the eyes to point at things,
exhaling to order people about.
【Collation】（一）The character '盼' has been amended according to the original version of the explanatory text.
"I wish to hear about the virtuous person."
【First】【Memorial】The previous sagely governance,
has already been elucidated;
the meaning of virtuous individuals,
is what I deeply wish to hear.
He said:
"The virtuous person
dwells without thought,
acts without worry,
and harbors no judgments of right and wrong, beauty and ugliness.
When all within the four seas share in the benefits, this is called contentment;
when all are provided for, this is called peace.
They are as sorrowful as an infant who has lost its mother,
as disoriented as a traveler who has lost their way.
Their wealth and resources are abundant, yet they do not know where they come from;
their food and drink are sufficient, yet they do not know their source.
This describes the demeanor of the virtuous person."
【一】【注】It is simply natural.
【Commentary】Marvelously uniting with the realm of the Way,
one attains what is without attainment,
hence called a person of virtue.
The virtuous person concentrates their spirit and sits upright with folded hands,
tranquil and without thought.
Even if responding to things and acting to transform them,
they remain entirely free of scheming or deliberation.
【二】【注】Harbor no right or wrong in the heart, and entrust them to the world.
【Commentary】Embracing the Way and upholding virtue,
one forgets both the self and the external world.
How could there be room to harbor judgments of right and wrong,
or to conceal good and evil within!
【Transcription】"Měi è" wū lù fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】There is no heart of selfishness.
【Commentary】The virtuous man's benevolent grace is vast and extensive,
reaching all beings universally.
Thus, wealth and goods shall be shared across the four seas,
and resources provided to the myriad people without distinction.
Therefore, the entire heaven rejoices and delights,
and all within the realm is peaceful and tranquil.
◎Qìng Fán's annotation states that "yuè" (delight) and "wèi" (for) form a parallel structure with "ān" (peace).
It means
that "wèi" is equivalent to "for."
In ancient usage, the characters "wèi" and "wèi" (another form of "for") were used interchangeably with the same meaning.
【Four】【Analogy】When an infant loses its mother,
its heart is desolate and has nothing to rely on;
when a traveler loses the way,
its spirit is bewildered and has nothing to hold onto.
These two examples
serve to illustrate the state of a virtuous person.
【Translated Text】"Chāo" is pronounced as chāo.
The Zìlín states:
It means disconsolate.
Xú gives the pronunciation as chǐ yáo fǎn,
while Guō pronounces it as tiáo.
"Tǎng" is pronounced as chì dǎng fǎn.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as ●.
【Five】【Annotation】Virtue is,
the trace of the divine person,
thus called demeanor.
【Commentary】Having few desires and knowing contentment,
thus wealth and resources are abundant;
not craving rich flavors,
thus food and drink are sufficient;
making no demands on life,
thus unaware of whence they come.
Summarizing the previous meaning,
thus it is said: such is the demeanor of a virtuous person.
【Translated Text】"The Appearance of the Virtuous Person" uses the pronunciation yǎng xiōng fǎn.
Some say:
According to the commentary, it should be kè.
"I wish to hear about the divine person."
【一】【注】I wish to hear the means by which it is traced.
【Commentary】Virtue is but the trace of the divine and human;
I wish to hear about the source of the trace.
He said:
"The supreme spirit rides on light,
and with the form vanishes —
this is called illuminating vastness.
Fulfilling destiny and exhausting emotions,
heaven and earth rejoice and all affairs melt away;
the myriad things return to their true nature —
this is called primordial darkness."
【一】【注】He who rides the light has no light.
【Commentary】"Chéng" means
to use.
"Guāng" means
wisdom.
The superior-grade spiritual person
uses wisdom to illuminate things,
and although their light is like the sun and moon,
it illuminates yet vanishes,
abandoning the body and silencing the senses,
discarding both mind and form,
thus perishing along with form.
【二】【Note】Without self and letting things be,
Empty and void, holding nothing within,
Is not darkness or blockage.
【Commentary】Wisdom encompasses all things,
brilliance surpassing the three luminaries,
no darkness remains unilluminated—
is this not profoundly vast!
【Three】【Notes】When emotions are exhausted and destiny arrives,
heaven and earth rejoice.
Matters do not hinder joy,
thus there are no matters to attend to.
【Commentary】He delved into the ultimate nature of life and destiny,
exhaustively explored the essence of transformation and existence,
hence, though dwelling in the world, he was always carefree and joyful.
Having realized the illusory nature of both self and things,
thus all worldly matters dissolved into nothingness.
【Translated Text】"Tiāndì Lè" the character "樂" is pronounced as "luò".
The same applies to the annotation.
"Xiāo Wáng" the character "銷" is pronounced by Xú as "xiāo".
【Four】【Annotation】Emotions return and blend into the profound mystery without a trace.
【Commentary】When one forgets illumination yet illuminates,
such illumination rivals the radiance of the three luminaries;
when one forgets life yet lives,
such life shares joy with the two primal forces.
Thus one can perceive the return of all things to their origin,
witness the rebirth of the four forms of life,
whereby chaos remains undivided and darkly merges into the single Way.
【Text】"Hùn Míng" Hú běn fǎn.
Mén Wúguǐ and Chì Zhāng Mǎnjī observed King Wǔ's army.
Chì Zhāng Mǎnjī said:
"It is not equal to the age of Yǒuyúshì!
Therefore we encounter this calamity."
【一】【疏】Mén and Chìzhāng,
are surnames.
Wúguǐ,
Mǎnjī,
are given names.
Twenty-five hundred men form a division,
division,
means a multitude.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
his troops crossed the Mèngjīn,
at that time, these two men observed together.
【Explanatory Text】"Mén Wúguǐ" is written as Wúwèi in the Sima edition,
stating:
Mén,
a surname;
Wúwèi,
is the courtesy name.
"Chìzhāng Mǎn" in some editions is written as Pú.
"Jī" is pronounced with the ancient sound, the reverse of xī.
Lǐ's commentary says:
Mén,
Chìzhāng,
are clan names.
Wúguǐ,
Mǎnjī,
are personal names.
【Èr Shū】departure,
is a calamity.
Yú Shùn used yielding and deference to govern his era,
while King Wǔ resorted to arms to save the world.
Yet yielding and arms,
their merits and demerits are vastly apart.
Judging by this measure,
there are even words of inadequacy.
And weapons are instruments of ill omen,
hence they bring the calamity of slaughter and destruction.
Mén Wúguì said:
"Was the world already well-ordered when Yǒuyú Shì governed it?
Or did he bring order only after it had fallen into chaos?"
【一】【注】This means both sages brought order because of chaos,
so the difference between yielding the throne and resorting to military force
is merely a matter of timing,
with no superiority or inferiority between them.
【Commentary】Jūn,
means level.
If the world were in great peace,
and all things were in order,
then why would there be any need for Yú Shùn to establish laws to govern it!
Truly, because Yáo's years were waning,
his virtue declining daily,
he thus yielded to Chónghuá,
ordering him to restore order.
【Explanatory Text】"均治" is read with the retroflex initial and the departing tone.
The following occurrences and the annotation for "均治" are the same.
"之與" is pronounced with the level tone.
Another version writes it as "邪".
"復何" is read with the voiced initial and the departing tone.
The annotation in the following chapter is the same.
Chì Zhāng Mǎnjī said:
"If the world were universally well-governed, that would be my wish,
why then should we consider Yǒuyúshì necessary!
Yǒuyúshì's method is like treating a sore:
only when one goes bald does he provide a wig,
only when one falls ill does he seek a doctor.
Though a filial son may prepare medicine to serve his kind father,
his countenance appears haggard,
and the sage would feel ashamed of this.
【一】【注】When all are governed equally, then everyone's wishes are sufficiently met,
so why bother to consider the virtue of Yǒuyúshì and promote him as ruler!
Xǔ Wúguǐ's words are correct.
【Commentary】When the world is peaceful and tranquil,
and everyone's aspirations are fulfilled,
why then would there be a need to consider the virtue of Yǒuyúshì and elevate him as sovereign!
This grasps the statement that there are no ghosts,
acknowledging its reasonableness.
【Two】【Annotation】All under heaven suffer from wounds and chaos,
thus they seek Yúshì's remedy.
【Commentary】Yáng,
refers to sores on the head.
When the body suffers from wounds,
one seeks medical treatment;
similarly, when the world encounters turmoil,
it requires a sage to govern it.
Thus, without illness, there would be no need for doctors,
and without chaos, there would be no need for sages.
【Explanation】"Yáng" is pronounced as yáng.
Lǐ Yún states:
It refers to a head sore.
Using the sore as a metaphor for chaos,
seeking the Yú family's medicine to cure it.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is a skin ulcer or sore.
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī comments:
"Yào" (medicine),
was anciently pronounced as yào,
(see explanation in Táng Yùn Zhèng.
) Its sound is close to "liáo" (cure).
In the Fāngyán (Regional Words):
"Yáo,"
means to treat or cure.
In the Jiāng-Hú region, treating an illness is called "yáo,"
or sometimes "liáo."
Annotation:
"Yáo,"
is pronounced yào.
It is interchangeable with the ancient character for "yào" (medicine).
Hence, the Shēn Jiàn Sú Xián Piān states:
"Yào" (medicine),
means to cure.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, the 31st year of Duke Xiāng, it says, "Better than if I had heard it and cured it."
The Jiāyǔ Zhèng Lùn Piān is the same,
with Wáng Sù annotating:
"Yào,"
means to cure.
In the Shī Dà Yǎ Bǎn Piān,
"beyond cure,"
the Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn writes "liáo" instead of "yào."
The characters for "yào" and "liáo,"
were anciently used interchangeably with the same meaning.
"Huàn chuāng" is pronounced with the initial sound chū and the rhyme liáng.
【Three】【Memorials】With hair like clouds,
no need for adornment;
fortunate to be free from ailments,
how could one rely on physicians!
This shows that under a clear and peaceful world,
there is no need for the great sage.
These two lines
summarize the preceding intent.
【Translated Text】"Tū" is pronounced as tùmù fǎn.
"Xì" is pronounced as dàxì fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means a wig.
Also pronounced as tǔdì fǎn.
Guō (two) sounds like máo.
Lǐ explains:
Máo,
refers to hair.
【Four】【Annotation】To bring order to the world under heaven,
is not for the sake of glory.
【Commentary】Cāo means
to hold.
Xiū means
to manage.
Jiāorán describes
a haggard appearance.
When a filial son cares for a kind father,
he does not boast of his achievements;
when a sage rescues from calamity and chaos,
how could he seek to flaunt his glory and prominence!
Acting out of necessity,
thus he feels ashamed of it.
【Interpretation】"Cǎo yào": pronounced as seven knife reverse.
"Jiāo rán": pronounced as jiāng yáo reverse,
also pronounced as qiáo.
【Collation Notes】(1) The *Quē Wù* cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, where "羞" is written as "所羞也".
(2) It is suspected that the two characters "作髦" are missing after "Guō".
In the age of perfect virtue,
they did not esteem the worthy,
nor employ the able;
the rulers were like the high branches [of a tree],
and the people like the wild deer;
they were upright but did not know it as righteousness,
loved one another but did not know it as benevolence,
were sincere but did not know it as loyalty,
acted appropriately but did not know it as trustworthiness;
they moved instinctively and served one another,
without considering it a favor.
Hence, their actions left no traces,
and their deeds were not transmitted.
【一】【注】The worthy are in their proper positions,
not because they are exalted.
【Commentary】The unworthy and the worthy
each fulfill their own roles,
not elevated to distinguish the worthy.
【二】【注】The capable act on their own,
not because they are made to do so.
【Commentary】Ingeniousness and clumsiness are matters of ingrained nature,
not to be boasted of or aspired to by one another,
nor are they promoted or enforced.
【Three】【Annotation】It emerges above things yet does not exalt itself.
【Commentary】The ruler resides above the people,
serene and detached, free from desires,
akin to the branches of a tall tree,
with no ambition for glory or rank.
【Interpretation of the Text】"Rú biāo": pronounced fāng xiǎo fǎn,
Xú gives fāng yáo fǎn,
also fāng miào fǎn.
It refers to the branches at the top of a tree, which naturally grow upward without intent.
"Jiào": pronounced hú xiào fǎn,
Lǐ reads it as jiào.
One version writes it as "zhī" (branch).
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
In the current edition, "jiào" is written as "zhī".
【Four】【Annotation】Let go and attain self-realization.
【Commentary】When those above practice non-action,
those below also remain pure and simple,
like wild deer in the wilderness,
free from the rituals of kings and lords.
【Five】【Expositions】To straighten one's heart,
refraining from evil deeds,
how could one understand the principle of discerning right from wrong!
Following the natural order,
drawing closer to one another,
how could one know the benevolence born of partiality!
【Six】【Annotation】Following one's inherent nature spontaneously,
it does not arise from knowledge.
【Commentary】Following one's nature to achieve sincerity,
one does not know this sincerity is loyalty;
acting genuinely in accordance with principle,
how could this be regarded as faithfulness!
【Seven】【Annotation】Employing its spontaneous motion,
Hence it moves without acknowledgment.
【Commentary】Bestowment,
is the reliance upon the ignorant.
Even the simplest creatures in motion,
which are the kinds with consciousness and vitality,
drive one another in turn,
a principle that is inherently natural.
Compare it to the limbs,
or to these eyes and ears:
since they are unintentional in their creation,
how could they have any intent in being relied upon by the ignorant!
Governing things through non-action,
its meaning is likewise.
【Transcription】"Chǔn" Guō chǔ yǔn fǎn,
means to move.
【八】【注】(Wáng) [Zhǔ] (èr) can let it act on its own,
thus leaving no trace.
【Commentary】The ruler and people were simple and unadorned,
there was harmony between high and low,
they acted according to their nature,
thus leaving no traces to record.
【Nine】【Annotation】Each abides in its own role,
thus not transmitting teachings to the other.
【Commentary】The head and limbs of governance,
each have their designated duties,
halting within their allotted roles,
without mutual instruction or practice.
Traces thus become obscure,
and matters likewise fade away.
【Explanation】"Wú zhuǎn" is read as zhàng zhuān fǎn.
【Collation Notes】(1) The character 'wú' was amended based on the Song edition and various other editions.
(2) The character 'zhǔ' was amended according to the Daoist Canon edition.
A filial son does not flatter his parents,
a loyal minister does not fawn upon his ruler—
this is the pinnacle of being a subject or child.
To approve of everything one's parents say,
and praise everything they do,
is what the world calls an unworthy son;
to approve of everything one's ruler says,
and praise everything he does,
is what the world calls an unworthy minister.
But is this necessarily so?
If one approves of whatever the world approves,
and praises whatever the world praises,
then one is not called a flattering or fawning person.
Does this mean the world is more revered than parents and more honored than the ruler?
If told they are flatterers,
people flush with anger;
if called sycophants,
they scowl in displeasure.
Yet throughout their lives,
they remain flatterers and sycophants,
using embellished speech and assembled analogies to gather followers—
this is a fundamental inconsistency from start to finish.
Draping robes,
adorning colors,
adjusting expressions
to charm the age,
without considering it flattery,
aligning with the crowd,
sharing their judgments,
yet not seeing themselves as common—
this is the height of folly.
Those who know their folly
are not utterly foolish;
those aware of their delusion
are not deeply deluded.
The deeply deluded
never break free;
the utterly foolish
never gain clarity.
If one of three travelers is lost,
the destination can still be reached,
for the lost are few;
if two are lost, they toil but never arrive,
for the lost prevail.
Now, with the whole world astray,
though I plead for direction,
it is unattainable.
Is this not sorrowful?
【一】【疏】To serve one's parents well is called filial piety.
Flattery
is deceitful.
Sycophancy,
is deception.
Not seeking others through proper means is called sycophancy.
As ministers or children,
serving fathers or rulers,
without sycophancy or flattery,
fulfilling loyalty and filial piety to the utmost,
this is the supreme virtue of ministers and children.
【Explanation】"Not flattering" is pronounced as yáng zhū fǎn,
Guō's reading is yí fù fǎn.
"Not fawning" is chì jiǎn fǎn.
【二】【Note】This is simply going against common customs to follow the sovereign and parents,
hence common people deem it unworthy,
without knowing where the utmost appropriateness truly lies.
【Commentary】Unworthy,
means not resembling.
The words and actions of the ruler or father,
without distinguishing good from evil,
directly follow the times,
never having the heart to admonish or oppose,
thus in worldly terms,
they are truly unworthy,
and it is unknown where the correct principle lies.
【Explanatory Text】"Bùxiào" is pronounced as "xiào".
【Three】【Annotations】It is said that when customs do not honor the dignity of rulers and parents, yet one follows those customs,
it is not considered flattery.
This illustrates that dignity alone is insufficient to command respect;
thus, what truly commands respect lies in conforming to customs.
Therefore, the sage has never sought to stand alone in opposition to the world,
but must adapt with the times,
so in the era of Huáng, they embody Huáng,
in the era of Wáng, they embody Wáng.
How could there be turning away from customs to assert oneself alone!
【Commentary】Yán means
reverence.
This clarifies that compliance and defiance are not fixed.
If worldly customs are deemed good,
then remonstrance and contention are appropriate.
Yet, to defy customs and follow one's parents
is called flattery,
while to defy one's parents and follow customs
is surely sycophancy!
Moreover, with defiance and compliance both present,
thus arise views of right and wrong.
But when both defiance and compliance are void,
it is unknown where correctness truly lies.
Furthermore, to defy one's parents and follow customs
can hardly be called honoring and revering the ruler and father!
"The Way" is pronounced as guidance.
The same applies below.
◎ Qing Fan's note: "Dao ren" means a flatterer.
In the "Fisherman" chapter, it is said,
"To anticipate others' intentions and guide one's speech is called flattery,"
where "guide" and "flattery" share the same meaning.
In Xunzi's "Not Being Deceitful" chapter, it refers to avoiding flattery and sycophancy,
and in Jia Yi's "Awakening First" chapter, it mentions that the ruler favors flatterers and dislikes straightforward advice,
while the Han Shi Wai Zhuan uses "guide and flatter" interchangeably.
"Chǎn" (flattery) and "dǎo" (guide),
are phonetic variations of each other.
"How could there be turning the back" is pronounced as carrying on the back.
【Four】【Annotation】The common world thus regards conformity as correctness,
hence it is called flattering the Way,
and they change countenance, unwilling to accept it.
【Transliteration】"则勃" is pronounced as bù hū fǎn.
"谓己谀人" is also written as zhòng rén in another version.
The same applies below.
Sīmǎ explains:
zhòng rén
refers to ordinary people.
"则怫" is pronounced as fú fú fǎn,
while Guō reads it as fū wèi fǎn.
【五】【注】Without inquiring into the principles,
the aim is simply to foster mutual goodwill.
【Commentary】Bó and
fú
both describe an angry countenance.
Dào,
meaning to achieve or reach,
refers to flattering and fawning to curry favor with rulers or elders.
It is said that worldly people,
when accused of being sycophantic,
immediately change their expression in anger,
refusing to accept such a label,
yet they engage in flattery and toadyism their whole lives,
and this is the case throughout the world.
【六】【注】Using combined analogies and embellished words,
one should be guilty of flattery and sycophancy,
yet the world again uses this to win people over and gather crowds, which is also a way of following the common practice,
and they are often not found guilty or punished for it.
【Commentary】When one harmonizes with analogies,
adorns with ornate phrases,
everyone eagerly rushes toward it,
thus gathering a multitude;
able to preserve its beginning and end,
unify its root and branches;
once the multitude follows,
therefore they do not implicate each other in guilt.
As for "analogy,"
some versions originally use the character "jade disc,"
meaning to match with jade tablets and discs.
【Transcription】"Mutual Implication" pronounced as cái wò fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
【Seven】【Annotation】The world is filled with utmost folly,
thus it is even more imperative to follow.
【Commentary】The Yellow Emperor established governance by instituting robes and skirts, bringing order to the world.
Upper garments and lower skirts
symbolized heaven and earth.
Colors like red and purple
were interwoven to create patterns.
Using such ornate decorations
to alter appearances
and charm an entire era—
those who are superficial and deceitful
do not consider it flattery of the Way,
but instead follow rulers with sycophancy and cunning.
This aligns them with the common crowd, forming factions,
mutually reinforcing each other,
sharing right and wrong indiscriminately.
They deem themselves superior to the masses,
which can be called the height of foolishness and ignorance.
【Explanation】"Yǔ fū" is pronounced as "yīn fú".
【八】【注】The sages share the same Way, yet the deeds of emperors and kings differ—
truly, the confusion of the mundane world cannot be unraveled,
so we follow and accept it as it is.
【Commentary】To understand is
to awaken.
Spiritual means
to know.
Those who are aware of their own foolishness and confusion
are sages.
Following and accepting it,
thus foolishness is not [true] foolishness or confusion.
The greatly foolish and confused
are ordinary people,
with minds obscure and vulgar,
encountering situations and giving rise to delusion,
therefore throughout their lives they never awaken.
【Explanation】"Not understanding" is pronounced like "crab" (xiè),
also read as jiā mǎi fǎn.
"Not intelligent" is also written as "without intelligence."
Sīmǎ explains:
"Intelligent" (líng)
means to comprehend.
【Nine】【Annotation】The world is all deluded,
even though I possess the desire to seek the ultimate Way, in the end, it cannot be attained.
Thus, Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
merely adapted to their times.
【Commentary】Shì means
to go.
Zhì means
to arrive.
Huò means
to be lost.
Qí means
to seek.
If three people travel together,
and one gets lost,
the direction they are heading
can still be reached,
because clarity outweighs confusion;
if two are lost, then the spirit is wearied and they cannot arrive,
because confusion prevails over understanding.
Now, all under heaven are lost,
and although Zhuāngzǐ seeks the true essence of the ultimate Dào,
there is no way to attain it,
hence it is lamentable.
【Transliteration】"Qí Xiàng" Xǔ Liàng fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
Qí,
means to seek.
◎Yú Yuè says:
The character Qí has no meaning here.
Sīmǎ says,
Qí,
means to seek.
Then it should simply say, "Although I seek direction, it is sufficient."
Guō's annotation says,
"Although I have the desire to seek and aspire to the ultimate Way,"
then it adds the character for "desire,"
which is likely incorrect.
Qí is suspected to be a miswriting of the character suǒ,
meaning the world is all deluded,
although I have something to aspire to,
it cannot be attained.
The characters Qí and suǒ have similar shapes,
hence the error.
The same applies below.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "dào" is written as "dǎo",
same below.
(2) The Quēwù cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, which has the character "zuì" following "xiāng".
Grand music does not enter the ears of village folk【一】,
but when they hear the songs "Zhé Yáng" and "Huáng Huā",
they chuckle with laughter【二】.
Thus, elevated discourse does not linger in the hearts of the masses【三】,
the highest words do not emerge,
while vulgar speech prevails【四】.
With two jars and a bell causing confusion,
one cannot reach the proper destination【五】.
And now the whole world is in such confusion,
even if I have prayers and aspirations,
how could they possibly be realized【六】!
To know it is unattainable yet force it,
is yet another delusion,
so it is better to let it go and not pursue it【七】.
By not pursuing it,
who would share the worry【八】!
When an ugly person gives birth to a child at midnight,
she quickly brings a light to look at it,
anxiously fearing it might resemble herself【九】.
【一】【注】It is not esteemed by the humble alleys.
【Interpretation】"The Great Sound" Simǎ comments:
It refers to the music of Xiánchí and Liùyīng.
【二】【Note】When common folk hear an intricate melody,
they all join in laughing at it.
【Commentary】The grand music,
refers to the melodies of the Xiánchí and Dàsháo,
not what is heard in the lower alleys and winding lanes.
The Zhéyáng and Huánghuā,
are likely the popular minor tunes of ancient times,
playful and rustic,
thus causing people to burst out,
laughing heartily in unison.
In the past, Marquis Wén of Wèi listened to ancient music,
and dozed off in a daze,
but upon hearing the new melodies of Zhèng and Wèi,
he became delighted and joyful,
which illustrates this very matter.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhé Yáng" is read with the pronunciation liè.
"Huáng Fū" is read with the pronunciation kuàng yú,
and also fǔ yú.
Another version writes it as "Huá",
pronounced huā.
Sima's version writes it as "Lǐ Huá".
"Kè rán" is read with the pronunciation xǔ jiǎ.
Li notes:
"Zhé Yáng" and "Huáng Huá",
are both ancient song titles.
Kè,
is the sound of laughter.
Another version writes it as "Yì",
pronounced wō miǎo.
Sima's version writes it as "Kē".
"Zé qǔ" is read with the pronunciation shì zé.
Another version writes it as "Kè".
【Three】【Annotations】Do not harbor in the heart.
【Commentary】The discourse on the most profound mysteries,
transcends worldly appearances,
hence it is called lofty speech.
It is fitting to be stored in the spiritual repository of all sages—
how could it be confined to the understanding of the common people?
Grand music does not enter the ears of the village folk,
and lofty speech certainly does not rest in the minds of the multitude.
【Four】【Annotation】This is why the world has never employed sages yet constantly relies on its own devices.
【Commentary】To emerge,
is to manifest.
The words of the ultimate Way,
are plain and without flavor,
not pleasing to the ears of the common alleys,
how could they halt in the hearts of the multitude!
Yet the words of prevailing customs,
adorned with rhetoric and floating in falsity,
are like the melody of "Plucking the Willow,"
enjoyed by many who delight in listening.
Since vulgar sayings hold sway on the main path,
the ultimate words remain hidden and obscure,
hence the "Equalizing All Things" states,
words are obscured by glory and flourish.
【Five】【Annotation】Each trusts in their own basis,
thus they do not know where to go.
【Commentary】Zhǒng,
means foot.
Those who have lost their direction,
point north as south,
and once these two confusions arise,
they halt their steps and do not proceed.
Not even one person can advance alone,
wishing to reach the destination ahead,
how could it be possible!
This further explains the earlier confusion.
【Explanation】"Using two fǒu zhōng": fǒu should be read as chuí,
zhōng should be read as zhǒng,
meaning dangling one's feet in the air,
inevitably lacking a destination to reach.
Sīmǎ's version writes "two chuí zhǒng",
stating:
zhǒng,
means focusing the mind.
"The destination reached" Sīmǎ explains:
means "to arrive".
◎Jiāshìfù comments:
The explanatory text says fǒu should be chuí,
zhōng should be zhǒng,
meaning dangling feet in the air,
inevitably having no destination to reach.
Sīmǎ's version writes "two chuí zhǒng".
Now, according to Shuōwén:
fǒu,
is an earthenware vessel,
used for holding wine or liquid.
Zhōng,
is a wine vessel.
Xiǎo Ěryǎ states:
two and a half fǔ make a sǒu,
two and a half sǒu make a fǒu,
two fǒu make a zhōng.
Both fǒu and zhōng are measuring vessels,
a fǒu holds four hú,
a zhōng holds eight hú.
"Being confused by two fǒu zhōng"
means failing to distinguish the capacity difference between fǒu and zhōng,
using them as measures,
one becomes bewildered and lacks direction.
The previous text mentions one person confused,
two people confused,
referring to people;
here, being confused by two fǒu zhōng,
refers to matters.
When everyone is confused,
who can bring clarity!
Handling measuring vessels while confused,
one cannot determine quantities.
With the entire world in confusion,
who can point out the way!
This distinguishes two meanings.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
The phrase "two fǒu zhōng"
is unclear in meaning.
The explanatory text says,
fǒu should be chuí,
zhōng should be zhǒng,
meaning dangling feet in the air,
inevitably lacking a destination to reach.
This does not match Zhuāngzǐ's intent.
"The destination reached",
refers to where one goes.
Guō's annotation states,
each holding to their own beliefs,
thus not knowing where to go,
which is correct.
According to Lù's explanation,
it takes "shì" as meaning satisfaction,
it should say "not achieving satisfaction",
not "the destination not reached".
Now, I believe zhōng should be zhǒng,
and "two" is a miswriting of "one",
while fǒu is a miswriting of "qǐ".
"Qǐ" is written with "zhǐ" below,
fǒu is commonly written as ●,
which also has "zhǐ" below,
the two forms are similar,
leading to the error.
Wénxuǎn's "Lament for the Departed" annotation quotes Zìlín:
qǐ,
means raising the heel.
Everything Classic Sounds and Meanings 15 quotes Tōngsúwén:
raising the heel is called qǐ.
Thus, "qǐ zhǒng" means raising the heel.
With one lift of the heel,
it's only a step away,
yet being confused by one heel lift,
one already loses their direction.
Hence, it says below,
"Now, with the whole world confused,
even if I have a direction,
how could it be attainable!"
"With the whole world confused"
emphasizes the vastness of the area;
"confused by one heel lift"
emphasizes the smallness of the area.
The earlier text says with two people confused, one toils without reaching the goal,
as the confused prevail.
"Now, with the whole world confused,
even if I have a direction,
it is unattainable."
Comparing the whole world to two people,
refers to the number of people;
here, comparing the whole world to one heel lift,
refers to the breadth of the area.
"One heel lift" mistaken as "two fǒu zhōng"
loses the original meaning.
【Six】【Commentary】When two people follow in each other's footsteps,
their destination is still hard to reach,
so how much more difficult when the whole world is lost,
how can one attain correctness!
Thus, even with a heart seeking direction,
its purpose surely cannot be achieved.
This explains the earlier lament—is it not sorrowful?
The grief and sighing run so deep,
hence the solemn emphasis.
【Seven】【Annotation】Then unite them as one.
【Commentary】To release means,
to let go.
When confusion runs deep,
it is hard to resolve in haste,
and to forcefully try to correct it
is yet another folly.
It is better to let go and not press further,
so that both things and self may be at peace.
【Transcription】"Ér qiáng" reads as qí zhàng fǎn.
The same applies to the annotation below.
【Eight】【Annotation】To let go or hold on
according to the appropriateness of the moment, without forcing understanding upon it,
then together we can be free from worries throughout our lives.
【Commentary】Compare,
means to associate.
If one entrusts matters to nature and resolves doubts,
discarding them without further deliberation,
then both self and others wander freely,
and with whom would worries and troubles be shared!
【Explanatory Text】"Bǐ Yōu" is pronounced as pí zhì fǎn.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as bí,
saying:
It means beginning.
"Qù Lìng" is pronounced as lì chéng fǎn,
the same applies below.
"Lìng Xiè" is pronounced as xiè.
【Nine】【Annotation】Lì,
are wicked people.
It means that no one in the world wishes to be evil,
but when they commit evil deeds,
some are compelled by harsh labor,
while others are deluded and lose their true nature.
However, the deluded naturally think of reforming,
and the wicked naturally think of doing good,
thus I take no action, and the world transforms of its own accord.
【Explanation】Lì,
refers to an ugly or sickly person.
Jù,
means swift.
Jíjí,
describes a hurried appearance.
It is said that an ugly person gives birth to a child at midnight,
quickly fetches a light to look at it,
with a rushed state of mind,
fearing that the child might resemble themselves.
And if the ugliness is extreme,
there is still hope to change the ugliness into beauty,
intending to illustrate that those who are foolish and confused,
how could they not detest their delusion and seek enlightenment!
If one lets it go without probing,
naturally there will be no worries or troubles.
【Explanatory Text】"Lì" is pronounced lài,
and also as the character's usual reading.
◎ Jiāshìfù said:
A person with leprosy gives birth to a child at midnight,
presenting another meaning to fully capture the idea above.
By aligning oneself with the customs,
one also delights when the customs align with oneself,
unaware that this is wrong.
The leper gives birth to a child,
and fears it will resemble them,
yet in this case, they do not seek similarity,
only because they are aware of their own leprosy.
However, their conformity to the customs,
is no different from forcing oneself to align with the leper,
and being ignorantly unable to distinguish the wrong,
is merely due to their lack of awareness.
"Jù" is pronounced with a strong, abrupt tone.
Some versions use "qú,"
with the same pronunciation.
"Jíjí" is pronounced jí.
"Oppressive labor" is pronounced hé.
【Collation】（一）The character 'shě' was altered according to Zhào Jiànyì's version.
A tree that has stood for a hundred years,
is split to make a sacrificial vessel,
adorned with green and yellow patterns,
while its discarded pieces lie in a ditch.
Comparing the sacrificial vessel with the discarded pieces in the ditch,
there is a distinction in beauty and ugliness,
yet in losing their innate nature, they are one and the same【一】.
Between Zhí and Zēng Shǐ,
there is a difference in their conduct of righteousness,
but they are equal in losing their innate nature【二】.
Moreover, there are five ways to lose one's innate nature【三】:
First, the five colors confuse the eyes,
causing them not to see clearly【四】;
second, the five sounds confuse the ears,
causing them not to hear acutely【五】;
third, the five odors assail the nose,
causing congestion and distress in the forehead【六】;
fourth, the five flavors corrupt the mouth,
causing it to lose its sensitivity【七】;
fifth, preferences and aversions扰乱 the heart,
causing the nature to become flighty and unsteady【八】.
These five aspects,
are all harms to life【九】.
Yet Yáng and Mò just begin to stride apart, thinking they have attained something,
but this is not what I call attainment【一０】.
If those who attain are troubled,
can that be considered attainment?
Then the turtledoves and owls in their cages
could also be considered to have attained something【一一】.
Moreover, with preferences and aversions, sounds and colors barricading their inner selves,
and leather caps, kingfisher-feathered headdresses, official tablets, and girdles constraining their outer forms【一二】,
their inner selves are stuffed full like a barricade of firewood,
their outer forms heavily bound with cords,
yet they gaze blankly within these bindings, thinking they have attained something—
then it would be like criminals with arms tied and fingers pressed in shackles, or tigers and leopards in cages and pens,
also being considered to have attained something.
【一三】
【One】【Explanation】Xī,
carved into the shape of a sacrificial ox,
to serve as a ritual vessel,
is called the xīzūn.
Jiàn,
means to distinguish.
Once carved into an ox,
and further adorned with blue and yellow patterns,
one piece is discarded into a ditch,
not put to use.
If these two pieces are compared,
then the beautiful and the ugly differ,
yet in losing their original wooden nature, they are the same.
This is to begin an analogy.
【Transcription】"Xī" is pronounced with the meaning of "ornamentation,"
also read as "sù hé" in reverse.
◎Qìng Fān's case: Máo's commentary states:
The Xī zūn has a sand-like decoration (see the Ode to the Bì Palace in the Book of Songs).
(See the annotation to the Ode to the Bì Palace in the Book of Songs.)
Zhèng Sīnóng said:
The Xī zūn is adorned with jadeite.
(See the annotation to "Zūn yí" in the Rites of Zhōu.)
Later, Zhèng commented:
"Xī" is read as "shā,"
(see the Correct Meaning of the Míng Táng Wèi in the Book of Rites.)
depicting the image of a phoenix carved on the zūn,
its feathers appearing gracefully swaying.
Wáng Niànsūn cited Gāo's annotation to the "Chù Zhēn" chapter of Huái Nán Zǐ, saying:
The Xī zūn
is like a zūn with openwork carving.
Thus, the Xī zūn
is carved and painted to represent various forms,
among the six types of zūn,
it is the most ornate.
Therefore, when the ancients spoke of lavish decoration,
they still referred to the Xī zūn.
Now, considering that some say it has a sand-like decoration,
some say it is adorned with jadeite,
some say it depicts the image of a phoenix carved on the zūn,
and some say it is a zūn with openwork carving,
although the explanations differ,
they all agree on the meaning of carving and engraving.
As for Ruǎn Chén's Lǐ Tú, which states:
The Xī zūn is decorated with an ox,
painting the shape of an ox on the belly of the zūn,
this is because "xī" is derived from "ox,"
interpreting the meaning based on the character's form.
"Qí duàn" is pronounced "tú luàn" in reverse.
The same applies below.
Some versions use "gù" instead.
【Two Departures】This is a combined analogy.
Whether it's the tyrannical cruelty of Jié and Zhí,
or the benevolent righteousness of Zēng and Shǐ,
although their deeds of good and evil differ,
in losing their true nature, they are actually the same.
【Three】【Categories】Confusion of emotions and loss of one's nature,
though varied in their manifestations,
can be summarized
into five types.
【Four】【Dissipations】The five colors are:
green, yellow, red, white, and black.
The vulgar are greedy,
using these to confuse the eyes,
unable to perceive the principle,
hence it is said they are not clear.
【Five】【Explanation】The five tones,
refer to gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
Indulging in stagnant vulgar sounds,
one cannot hear the Way,
hence it is said to be not perceptive.
【Six】【Explanation】The five odors,
refer to gamy, fragrant, aromatic, fishy, and rotten.
Blocked,
means obstructed,
indicating that it is severely clogged and impassable.
This speaks of the nose's connection to the five odors,
hence becoming blocked and impassable, thereby injuring the forehead.
External texts refer to fragrance as an odor.
Therefore, the Yi Jing says its odor is like orchids;
Taoist scriptures speak of the five fragrances,
hence the Xī Shēng Jīng states that fragrances and odors are sources of harm.
【Explanation】"Kùn" is read as it is.
Some versions have "kǔn",
with the same pronunciation.
"Zōng" is pronounced with the initial "z" and the final "ong".
Guō reads it as "jùn",
and also as "sù fèng".
Lǐ says:
"kùn zōng"
means as if carved and blocked, not flowing freely.
"Zhòng" is pronounced with the initial "d" and the final "ong".
"Sǎng" is pronounced as sāng dàng fǎn.
【Seven】【Dispersions】refer to the five flavors,
namely sour, pungent, sweet, bitter, and salty.
Lì,
means illness;
shuǎng,
means loss.
If one indulges in the five flavors,
it fouls and clouds the root of taste in the mouth,
eventually causing salty and bitter flavors to form ailments,
and the tongue to lose its sense of taste,
hence the term "lì shuǎng."
【Interpretive Text】"Zhuó kǒu" is also written as 噣,
with the same pronunciation.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes: In the "Dà Yǎ Sī Qí" annotation it says:
Lì,
means illness.
The "Yì Zhōu Shū·Shì Fǎ" chapter states:
Shuǎng,
means injury.
(Guǎngyǎ has the same definition.
) "Shǐ kǒu lì shuǎng,"
refers to the impairment and injury of taste.
(Seen in Huáinánzǐ's "Jīngshén" chapter.
Gāo Yòu's annotation writes it as "shuǎng shāng,"
while the Wénzǐ's "Jiǔ Shǒu" chapter writes it as "shǐ kǒu shēng chuāng,"
both are later arbitrary alterations by people.
【Eight】【Explanation】"Qu" means to take.
"Hua" means to disrupt.
When it aligns with the heart, one takes it;
when it goes against one's feelings, one discards it.
This confuses the mind,
causing the natural disposition to race restlessly,
becoming frivolous and impulsive,
hence it is called "flying and soaring."
【Explanatory Text】"Slippery Heart" Lǐ sounds like gǔ.
Originally also written as zhòu.
【Nine】【Admonitions】In summary, the aforementioned five matters,
are all blades that sever destiny,
axes that harm life,
and represent great calamities for the people.
【一０】【Commentary】"Líqǐ"
describes the appearance of exerting force.
It means that Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí,
each flaunting their own abilities,
lost their inherent nature and harmed their lives,
yet considered this as attainment.
Since this contradicts the principle of naturalness,
it is not what Zhuāngzǐ would regard as valid.
【Translated Text】"Lí" is pronounced lì zhì (yě) [fǎn] (three).
"Qí" is pronounced qiū chì fǎn.
【一一】【Commentary】Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and laws are constraints on the mind,
and are not the true nature.
Once the nature is falsified,
it encounters hardship and suffering.
If one considers this hardship as attainment,
how is it different from a caged owl or turtledove,
boasting of its contentment!
【一二】【疏】The leather cap is
a crown made of leather.
The snipe is
a bird's name,
resembling a duck,
of a dark reddish-blue color,
found in Yùlín;
its kingfisher feathers are taken to adorn the crown,
hence it is called the snipe crown.
This bird,
is worn as a crown by those who understand astronomy.
To tuck,
means to insert.
The tablet,
is like a jade scepter,
referring to inserting the tablet.
The sash,
is a large belt.
The long robe,
is a long skirt.
These are all used to adorn court attire.
Those who are superficial and deceitful,
make choices their occupation,
thus sounds, sights, and all worldly dusts clog their inner faculties,
while clothes, caps, inserted tablets, and sashes constrain their outer form,
turning away from the path of non-action,
and violating the nature of spontaneity,
considering this as attainment,
how is it different from the cuckoo and the owl!
【Translated Text】"Yù" is pronounced Yǐn bì fǎn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as shù.
Another version writes it as "Shù",
with the same pronunciation,
it is a bird's name.
Also called cuì,
resembling a swallow,
dark red in color,
found in Yùlín,
its feathers are taken to adorn hats.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: According to Shuōwén:
Yù,
is a bird that knows when rain is about to fall.
The case states that Yù is the cuì bird.
In the Lǐjì:
Those who know astronomy wear a Yù crown.
In Yùpiān, Ěryǎ, Shìwén, and the Hànshū Wǔxíngzhì,
Yù has both the pronunciations yù and shù.
Kuāng Miù Zhèng Sú says:
The case states Yù is a water bird,
it calls when rain is about to fall,
the ancients, knowing it understood the weather,
thus made a representation of this bird's shape,
and had those in charge of astronomy wear it as a crown.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
Also has the pronunciation shù,
hence the Lǐzhī Yīfú Tú and Cài Yōng's Dú Duàn refer to it as the Shù shì crown,
also (pronounced) [because] Yù's sound shifts to shù.
This Shìwén also writes Yù as "Shù".
The case in Hànshū Yúfúzhì quotes the record saying those who know heaven wear a shù,
Shuōyuàn Xiūwén Piān writes it as wearing a shù,
probably because Yù has the pronunciation shù,
hence sometimes written as "Shù",
or as shù,
or as shù.
"Hù" is pronounced hū.
"Shēn" is pronounced shēn,
meaning a belt.
【一三】【疏】Blockage means
obstruction.
Fullness means
repletion.
A fence means
a cage.
Twisted cords mean
ropes.
Wide-eyed means
the appearance of staring.
When choices and rejections obstruct and fill the inner treasury,
thus square firewood fences it;
sash and tablet bind and restrain the outer form,
likened to the ropes of a snare.
With both internal and external exhaustion and decay as such,
yet considering oneself to have attained success—
how is this any different from a guilty person,
arms crossed and fingers pressed,
bound backwards with ropes!
It is also akin to tigers and leopards caught in a trap,
confined within bags or cages,
where anxiety, peril, and hardship
reach their utmost severity;
to deem oneself successful in such a state—
how does it differ from this!
【Transcription】"Chái zhà" is pronounced as Chǔ gé fǎn,
Guō's reading sounds like cè.
"Wài zhòng" is pronounced as zhí lóng fǎn.
"Mò" sounds like mò,
"Zhuó" sounds like zhuó,
Guō's reading is gǔ diào fǎn.
"Huǎn huǎn" is pronounced as huán bǎn fǎn,
also hù guān fǎn.
Lǐ says:
A look of exhaustion.
Another says:
The appearance of closed eyes.
"Jiāo bì lì zhǐ" Sīmǎ says:
Crossed arms,
means bound behind the back.
Pointing through each,
resembles the appearance of passing through joints.
"Jiàn" is pronounced as hù lǎn fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The character 'yě' has been amended according to the original text of Máo Zhuàn.
