(2) The character 'zhī' has been amended based on Jīngyì Shùwén.
(3) Amended in accordance with the Shìdétáng edition and the original version of Shìwén.
【Chapter One】【Explanatory Notes】The chapter is titled based on its moral significance.
The Way of Heaven operates without accumulation,
thus all things are brought to completion.
The Way of the Emperor operates without accumulation,
thus the world turns to him.
The Way of the Sage operates without accumulation,
thus all within the seas submit.
One who understands Heaven,
comprehends the Sage,
and is thoroughly versed in the virtue of emperors and kings,
acts spontaneously,
and in obscurity, all is tranquil.
The Sage's tranquility is such that
it is not that he considers tranquility good,
and therefore is tranquil;
nothing among the myriad things can disturb his mind,
hence he is tranquil.
When water is still, it clearly reflects beard and eyebrows;
its levelness accords with the plumb line,
and the great carpenter takes it as his standard.
If still water is so clear,
how much more the quintessential spirit!
The Sage's mind in tranquility!
It is the mirror of Heaven and Earth,
the glass of the myriad things.
Emptiness, tranquility, blandness, silence, and non-action—
these are the level of Heaven and Earth, the perfection of the Way and its Virtue.
Therefore, emperors, kings, and sages rest herein.
Resting leads to emptiness,
emptiness leads to fullness,
and fullness leads to order.
Emptiness leads to tranquility,
tranquility leads to movement,
and movement leads to attainment.
Tranquility leads to non-action,
and non-action means those charged with affairs bear their responsibilities.
Non-action brings ease,
and ease means care and anxiety cannot dwell within,
so one's years and longevity are prolonged.
Emptiness, tranquility, blandness, silence, and non-action—
these are the root of the myriad things.
Understanding this and facing south,
Yáo became such a ruler;
understanding this and facing north,
Shùn became such a minister.
Abiding in the highest position by this,
is the virtue of the emperor, the Son of Heaven;
abiding in the lowest position by this,
is the way of the hidden sage and uncrowned king.
Retiring to dwell and wander idly by rivers and seas with this,
and the scholars of the mountains and forests submit;
advancing to act and pacify the age with this,
then achievements are great, fame is illustrious, and the world is unified.
Tranquil, one is a sage;
active, one is a king.
Through non-action, one is honored;
through simplicity, none in the world can contend with one in beauty.
One who clearly understands the virtue of Heaven and Earth—
this is called the great root and great ancestor,
being in harmony with Heaven.
That by which one evenly harmonizes the world
is being in harmony with humanity.
Being in harmony with humanity
is called human joy;
being in harmony with Heaven
is called heavenly joy.
【一】【疏】Yùn,
means movement,
and rotation.
Jī,
means stagnation,
and accumulation.
It speaks of the heavenly way's operation,
nurturing all living beings,
illuminating them with the sun and moon,
moistening them with rain and dew,
stirring and shaping them,
never stagnating or accumulating,
thus the four seasons revolve,
and all things come into being.
【Explanation】"Without Accumulation" refers to being blocked and obstructed, failing to flow freely.
【二】【疏】The heavens emulate the forms of heaven and earth,
governing and steering all beings,
dispersing without accumulation,
imparting transformation without fixed methods,
thus the six directions converge as one,
and the eight regions sincerely submit.
【Three】【Annotations】These three
all follow the nature of things without any constraints or obstructions.
【Commentary】The Way of the Sage refers to
the path of the mysterious sages and uncrowned kings.
They manifest according to circumstances,
establishing laws and setting up teachings,
serving as vessels for sentient beings,
saving and aiding endlessly,
their Way aligns with Heaven,
their virtue matches that of emperors.
Their roles and actions vary,
hence there are the two paths of emperor and sage.
Moreover, applying wisdom to rescue the times,
they act without obstruction or delay,
their compassionate deeds are vast and extensive,
thus the whole world submits to them.
【Four】【Annotation】Let it act on its own,
thus, even when connecting all six directions and opening to the four quarters, it remains unharmed by tranquility.
【Commentary】The six connections
refer to the four directions, above and below.
The four openings
refer to spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
Only by illuminating the non-action of the heavenly way,
and penetrating the sage's state of mind free from all concerns,
can one connect the six directions to generate and transform,
and follow the four seasons to act accordingly.
By thus governing the myriad chariots (the state),
this can be called the virtue of an emperor.
Letting things move spontaneously,
thus it is said to act naturally;
concealing one's traces and hiding one's light,
is like being in obscurity and darkness;
action that does not harm tranquility,
thus there is nothing that is not calm.
【Explanation】"Six Thoroughfares" refers to the six qi,
which are yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and brightness.
"Four Openings" (pí chì fǎn),
means the opening of the four directions.
"●" pronounced as mèi.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
The current version writes it as mèi.
【Five】【Annotation】When goodness is achieved, it becomes tranquil,
yet there are times when it moves.
【Commentary】The reason why the sage is empty and tranquil
is simply that his form resembles a withered tree,
his mind is like dead ashes,
and he does not even know that tranquility is the reason for being tranquil.
If one considers tranquility as good and beautiful and has an attachment to practicing tranquility,
then there will be times when one becomes agitated.
【六】【注】This is self-attainment.
【Commentary】The wondrous substance of the two principles is non-existent,
all realms are empty.
Therefore, one who partakes in transformation and mingles with the dust yet remains unperturbed,
attains tranquility not through forced discipline but naturally.
【Transcription】"Náo xīn" is read as nǎi xiào fǎn,
also as nǚ jiāo fǎn,
and another pronunciation is ér xiǎo fǎn.
【Seven】【Memorials】Water,
when in motion, flows in waves;
when still, becomes clear and calm.
Suspended as a mirror, it illuminates thoroughly,
impartial to all things.
Thus, it can brightly reflect even beards and eyebrows,
pure and centered in its correctness.
It governs all that is crooked and unjust,
serving as a standard and measure.
Even with the skill of Gōng Chuí,
one must still imitate water to achieve levelness.
Therefore, the Lǎozǐ says,
"The highest good is like water."
This illustrates the meaning through metaphor.
【Explanation】"Zhōng Zhǔn": Dīng Zhòng fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current edition writes it as "准" (four).
"Dà Jiàng": Some say:
It refers to the Son of Heaven.
【Eight】【Annotation】When one possesses the means and entrusts them to act on their own,
thus, all that is illuminated is thoroughly understood.
【Commentary】The sage's virtue aligns with the dual principles of heaven and earth,
and his wisdom pervades all things.
How could he be discussed on the same day as the unfeeling water!
When water is still, it can clearly reflect even beards and eyebrows;
how much more so when the spirit and mind of the sage are tranquil!
Thus, it is only fitting
that he mirrors the subtleties of heaven and earth
and reflects the profound mysteries of all things.
This is an appropriate analogy.
【Nine】【Annotation】All that is uneven and incomplete
arises from deliberate action.
【Commentary】Emptiness and tranquility, simplicity and detachment, stillness and silence, non-action—
these four are different names for the same reality.
To praise the beauty of non-action,
it is thus endowed with these four names,
and heaven and earth take this as their standard,
while the Way and its virtue use this as their ultimate principle.
【Explanation】"淡" is pronounced as "tán" with a falling-rising tone.
◎Qìng Fān's note: "至" (zhì) is equivalent to "质" (zhì).
"至" (zhì)
means "实" (shí).
In the "Lǐ Jì Zá Jì," it says "使某实" (shǐ mǒu shí),
with Zhèng's annotation:
"实" should be read as "至."
In the "Shǐ Jì Sū Qín Zhuàn," it states, "赵得讲于魏" (Zhào dé jiǎng yú Wèi),
reaching the noble son Yán,
Suǒyǐn comments:
"至" should be interpreted as "质."
In the "Hàn Shū Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn," it says "非至数也" (fēi zhì shù yě),
with Shī Gǔ's note:
"至" (zhì)
means "实" (shí).
The "Kè Yì Piān" correctly uses "道德之质" (dào dé zhī zhì).
【一０】【Note】It has never moved.
【Explanation】By calming one's thoughts,
one attains ultimate peace.
【一一】【Note】Lún,
means principle.
【Commentary】Having ceased deliberation and quieted the mind,
one then unites in virtue with the void;
uniting in virtue with the void,
one then converges with the true and real Way;
the true and real Way
is the principle of spontaneity.
【一二】【Comment】Not losing the means by which it moves.
【Commentary】The principle is empty, tranquil, and quiescent,
yet from quiescence, it can initiate movement,
this is how one attains it.
【13】【Comment】When there is non-action,
then all talents and myriad types
each undertake their affairs and naturally bear their responsibilities.
Hence it is said, "How majestic were Shùn and Yǔ in possessing all under heaven, yet not interfering with it,"
this expresses it.
【Commentary】"Ren shi" refers to
ministers,
meaning that each minister has their own assigned duties.
When the emperor employs wisdom,
remaining tranquil and non-interfering,
then the ministers undertake their responsibilities,
each managing their own areas of concern.
This means the ruler is non-interfering while the ministers are actively engaged,
hence the emperor lowers the ceremonial beads before his eyes and does not participate in affairs.
【Text Explanation】"Wēi wēi": read as yú guī.
"Bù yù": pronounced as yù.
【一四】【Note】Yúyú rán,
a manner of being composed and self-satisfied.
【Commentary】Yúyú,
is the appearance of being composed and harmonious in joy.
When there is deliberate action, it creates a state of stagnation,
and worldly burdens disturb one's mind;
when there is non-action, one attains natural ease,
and worries cannot occupy one's thoughts.
With yúyú harmony and joy,
thus one's years and longevity are prolonged.
【Translated Text】"Yú Yú" pronounced as yáng zhū fǎn:
The Guangya says:
It means joy.
Also pronounced as yù.
Cóngróng (cóng: the seventh tone, róng).
【一五】【Note】Tracing its origin, all stem from the state of non-action.
【Commentary】These four lines are the root of all things,
hence the previous words are reiterated,
to conclude their essence.
righteousness.
【一六】【疏】The beauty of yielding the throne,
has no greater example than Táng and Yú;
the height of sovereign and minister relations,
finds no predecessor before Yáo and Shùn;
thus these two rulers are cited to illuminate the four virtues,
though one faced south and the other north,
their impartiality reached the same ultimate standard.
【Transcription】"Nán Xiāng": Xǔ Liàng's annotation reads fǎn.
The original text also uses "xiàng".
【一七】【注】These are the ultimate expressions of non-action.
One who possesses the Way and is revered by the world yet holds no official rank—
this is what is called the Unadorned King who esteems himself.
【Commentary】Using this non-action to preside over all beings,
is the virtue of Emperor Yáo the Son of Heaven;
employing this emptiness and tranquility to reside among ministers,
is the way of the Mysterious Sage and Unadorned King.
Those who possess the Way but lack the noble rank,
are what is called the Mysterious Sage and Unadorned King,
who honor themselves,
namely Lǎojūn and Master Nǐ (Confucius) are such figures.
【Transcription】"Sù Wáng" wǎng kuàng fǎn.
Note same.
【一八】【Commentary】Retiring from public life,
means to conceal one's traces and live in seclusion.
Using this principle to withdraw from the world,
thus one can roam and enjoy the mountains and waters,
leisurely and at ease with joy.
Therefore, all the recluses under heaven submit willingly,
such as those like Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu are examples of this.
【Explanation】"而閒" is pronounced as xián.
【一九】【Note】This is yet the next level.
Thus, when retreating, they are like the company of Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu,
when advancing, they are akin to the ranks of Yī Yǐn and Lǜ Wàng.
Indeed, the substance of non-action is vast,
what in the world is not encompassed by non-action?
Hence, if the sovereign does not take on the duties of the prime minister,
then Yī Yǐn and Lǜ Shàng remain tranquil while overseeing administration;
if the prime minister does not control the responsibilities of the hundred officials,
then the hundred officials remain tranquil while managing affairs;
if the hundred officials do not dictate the tasks of the myriad people,
then the myriad people remain tranquil and secure in their livelihoods;
if the myriad people do not exchange what each is capable of,
then all under heaven, self and others, remain tranquil and attain fulfillment naturally.
Therefore, from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
and extending to insects,
who can achieve success through deliberate action?
Thus, the more one embraces non-action, the more revered one becomes.
【Commentary】Advancing in action,
means revealing one's traces to take up public office.
One who profoundly embodies non-action yet descends to mingle with the dust and leave traces,
thus can soothe the common people into benevolence and longevity,
and expand the ultimate virtue in the sacred court.
Establishing unfathomable achievements and fame,
manifesting the administrative accomplishments of an Āhéng.
Therefore, the world becomes greatly unified,
with uniform chariots and scripts sharing the same tracks,
reaching perfection and utmost beauty—
is it not only the likes of Yī and Wàng who achieve this!
【二０】【Comment】Act when the time is right to act,
and stop when the time is right to stop.
【二一】【Note】Nature is revered by all things.
【Subcommentary】When it corresponds to stillness,
it holds the dignity of the Mysterious Sage and the Unadorned King;
when it corresponds to movement,
it possesses the nobility of the ninth-fifth position and ten thousand chariots.
Through non-action, it is revered;
emerging, it becomes the Son of Heaven;
abiding, it becomes the Unadorned King.
Thus, knowing where the Way resides,
who would dare not honor it!
【二二】【Note】That which matches Heaven in beauty,
is only simplicity.
【Commentary】The genuine and unadorned essence,
the state of non-action and tranquil emptiness,
is truly the foundation of all things.
Thus, what is held in such high esteem,
who can contend with its beauty!
【二三】【Comment】Heaven and Earth take non-action as their virtue,
thus understanding their fundamental principle,
one will not oppose Heaven and Earth.
【Commentary】When the spiritual abode is clear and tranquil,
the divine reflection is pure and unsullied,
and virtue aligns with the dual forces of heaven and earth,
one can indeed become the master architect of all living beings,
the root and foundation of all existence,
silently merging with the Way of nature,
and harmonizing with heaven.
【二四】【Note】To follow Heaven is the means to respond to humanity,
thus when heavenly harmony arrives, human harmony is fully achieved.
【Commentary】Jūn means
equalizing.
Tiáo means
harmonizing.
Moreover, responding to stimuli without intention,
is like echoes and shadows;
equalizing all beings,
greatly harmonizing with the nature of things,
while blending traces and uniting with the dust,
thus achieving harmony with others.
【二五】【Note】When heavenly joy is sufficient, human joy is also fulfilled.
【Commentary】Bending to conform with worldly customs,
one temporarily partakes in the joys of human life;
looking upward to align with nature,
one then delights in the bliss of the heavenly way.
【Translated Text】"Rén lè" is pronounced with the tone luò,
the same applies below.

(2) The Quē Wù cites the Zhāng Jūnfáng edition as having the character 也 following 至.

Zhuāngzǐ said:
"My master!
My master!
You grind down all things yet are not cruel,
Your kindness extends to all ages yet you are not benevolent,
You are older than the highest antiquity yet are not aged,
You cover and support heaven and earth, carving all forms yet are not skillful -
this is called Heavenly Joy.
Therefore it is said:
'Those who know Heavenly Joy,
in life move with the way of Heaven,
in death transform with all things.
In stillness, they share the virtue of yīn,
in motion, they flow with the waves of yáng.'
Thus those who know Heavenly Joy
have no complaint against Heaven,
no blame from men,
no burden from things,
no reproach from ghosts.
Therefore it is said:
'In motion, they are like Heaven,
in stillness, they are like Earth.
With a single-minded focus, they rule the world;
ghosts do not haunt them,
their spirits do not weary,
with a single-minded focus, all things submit.'
This means extending emptiness and stillness to heaven and earth,
penetrating all things -
this is called Heavenly Joy.
Heavenly Joy -
it is the sage's mind,
with which he nurtures the world."
【一】【注】Change and intermingling,
hence it is called disorder.
It is the disorder itself,
not due to our teacher's tyranny.
【Commentary】Cuì,
means to crush.
Lì,
means violent.
Zhuāngzǐ takes the natural ultimate way as his teacher,
and repeatedly praises it,
admiring its virtue.
It says that the great way which I take as teacher,
nurtures and fosters living beings,
even if it crushes the myriad things,
it does so without intentional violent anger,
hence in plain autumn when things wither and fall, they bear no resentment.
This clarifies that even though it involves cutting and shaping, it is not out of righteousness.
【Explanation】"Zǐ xī" is the reverse pronunciation.
"Wèi lì" is the reverse pronunciation of lì jì,
meaning violent.
【二】【注】Benevolence is the name for universal love;
without love,
there is nothing to be called benevolence.
【Commentary】Benevolence is the manifestation of partial affection.
It is said that the Great Way opens and closes heaven and earth,
creates and transforms all living beings,
and bestows boundless compassionate grace without partial affection,
therefore it does not act with benevolence.
【Three】【Commentary】Longevity refers to
an extended period of time;
without such a period,
there is nothing to be called longevity.
【Commentary】Not only does it predate high antiquity,
but it also precedes the image of the divine.
Since it neither perishes nor is born,
how can there be any talk of premature death or longevity?
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
longevity
merely refers to an extended span of time.
【Transcription】"Cháng yú" is read with the pronunciation dīng zhàng fǎn.
The same applies to the end of the chapter.
【Four】【Annotation】Skillfulness lies in the subtlety of action;
it arises naturally,
hence there is no need to praise it as skillful.
【Commentary】The two primal forces carry and support all things,
carving and shaping the myriad creatures.
Yet the two primal forces excel in transformation and growth,
while the myriad creatures function through spontaneity.
Since transformation and growth do not rely on external means,
how could carving and shaping depend on others?
Thus, each thing fulfills its own capacity,
and every person follows their innate nature.
Then, the distinctions of skillful and clumsy vanish at this point.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
"Skillfulness
is but the marvel of acting naturally."
【Five】【Annotation】Forgetting music, yet joy is sufficient.
【Commentary】Wherever one is, one finds contentment,
forming the harmony of heaven.
【Translated Text】"Tiān Lè" the pronunciation is luò.
The same applies within the chapter.
【Six】【Exposition】Once it is understood that heavenly joy is not sorrow or joy,
it becomes clear that life and death are without birth or demise.
Thus, living aligns with the four seasons of the heavenly way,
and dying merges with the transformations of all things.
【Seven】【Dissertations】The wondrous essence is ethereal and congealed,
aligning the extreme yin with its serene stillness;
its manifestations coexist in the world,
merging with the great yang in its flowing waves.
【八】【疏】Virtue harmonizes with Heaven,
thus there is no grievance from Heaven;
conduct aligns with the world,
thus there is no blame from others;
I merge indistinctly with all things,
thus things do not burden me;
I bear no guilt toward the unseen or the visible,
so how could there be any reproach from ghosts!
【Nine】【Commentary】Movement and stillness, though distinct,
share the same essence of being without deliberate intent.
【Commentary】Heaven and Earth,
are used to illustrate the principle of being unmoved and without intention.
【一０】【Note】Constantly without a mind,
thus ruling the world without exhaustion or ailment.
【Commentary】When the realm and wisdom merge indistinguishably,
it is called oneness.
When external things cannot disturb it,
it is called stability.
Precisely because one attains stability in a single mind,
one can thereby reign over all states.
Since there are no condemnations from spirits,
what calamities or misfortunes could there be!
Active yet perpetually tranquil,
thus the spirit does not grow weary.
《而王》wǎng kuàng fǎn.
The notes and the following "wáng tiān" are the same.
《祟》suī suì fǎn,
Xú xī lèi fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means calamity.
【一一】【Commentary】One whose mind is concentrated resembles dead ashes;
stillness is the master of restlessness,
thus all things submit and follow.
【一二】【Note】My mind is constantly tranquil,
then the hearts of all things connect with it.
Connected, they submit;
disconnected, they rebel.
【Commentary】The reason why a focused mind brings all things into submission is that
it solely employs the wisdom of emptiness and stillness,
to deduce the principles of the two modes (yin and yang),
comprehend the nature of all things,
and adapt to the transformations of things without ever failing to be appropriate,
hence it is called the joy of heaven.
【一三】【注】What is it that the sage's heart uses to nurture the world?
It is nothing but the joy of heaven.
【Commentary】The reason why the sage descends to manifest traces like an ordinary person,
is to harmonize with the ultimate joy of heaven and earth,
intending to nurture all living beings,
and to foster the multitude of creatures.
【Transcription】"畜天" pronounced as Xù with the sixth tone.
Same for the annotation.
The virtue of emperors and kings
takes Heaven and Earth as its ancestor,
the Way and its Virtue as its master,
and non-action as its constant norm.
Through non-action,
they employ the world and have energy to spare;
through action,
they are employed by the world and find it insufficient.
Therefore the men of old valued non-action.
If those above practice non-action
and those below also practice non-action,
then those below share the same virtue as those above,
and if those below share the same virtue as those above, they are no longer subjects;
if those below take action
and those above also take action,
then those above share the same path as those below,
and if those above share the same path as those below, they are no longer rulers.
Those above must practice non-action in employing the world,
while those below must take action in being employed by the world -
this is an unchangeable principle.
Therefore the ancients who ruled the world,
though their knowledge encompassed Heaven and Earth,
did not deliberate themselves;
though their eloquence adorned all things,
they did not speak themselves;
though their abilities surpassed all within the seas,
they did not act themselves.
Heaven does not produce, yet all things transform;
Earth does not grow, yet all things are nurtured -
emperors and kings practice non-action, yet the world achieves merit.
Therefore it is said: nothing is more divine than Heaven,
nothing richer than Earth,
nothing greater than emperors and kings.
Hence it is said the virtue of emperors and kings matches Heaven and Earth.
This is what it means to ride Heaven and Earth,
gallop through all things,
and employ the masses of people.
【First】【Memorial】The king's lineage is rooted in heaven and earth,
thus encompassing all without intent;
the ruler is grounded in the Way and its virtue,
hence creating life without possessing it;
even amid countless changes and transformations, he remains naturally non-interfering.
Such is his magnificent virtue,
exemplified by Yáo as a sovereign.
【二】【Note】Having surplus means,
having leisure time.
【Three】【Commentary】Those who are insufficient,
are eagerly desiring to be of use to things.
Desiring to be of use to things,
thus they can be made subjects;
and when they become subjects,
they still have surplus.
【Commentary】"Insufficient" refers to
a state of urgency.
"Ample" means
a condition of leisure.
This explains that when the ruler governs through non-action,
his wisdom illuminates broadly and expansively,
ruling over the realm,
he remains at leisure with ample capacity;
whereas the ministers engage in action,
their thoughts and concerns are narrow and limited,
each holding specific duties,
employed by the ruler,
tirelessly devoted to public affairs,
yet still fearing insufficiency.
Thus, it is understood that non-action and active engagement
follow distinct paths of ease and toil.
【Four】【Annotation】The craftsman does nothing in carving the wood but acts in using the axe,
the ruler does nothing in handling affairs personally but acts in employing ministers.
The ministers can handle affairs,
the ruler can employ ministers;
the axe can carve the wood and (two) the craftsman can use the axe;
each fulfills their own capability,
then the natural order of heaven prevails,
it is not forced action.
If instead the ruler takes over the duties of the ministers,
then he is no longer a ruler;
if the ministers seize the ruler's authority,
then they are no longer ministers.
Therefore, each attends to their own responsibilities,
then both superior and inferior are properly fulfilled, and the principle of non-action is perfectly realized.
【Commentary】Non-action (wúwéi) is
the virtue of the ruler;
action (yǒuwéi) is
the way of the ministers.
If both superior and inferior practice non-action,
then ministers usurp the ruler's virtue;
if both superior and inferior take action,
then the ruler encroaches upon the ministers' way.
When the ruler encroaches upon the ministers' way,
he ceases to be a true sovereign;
when ministers usurp the ruler's virtue,
how can they be called ministers indeed!
Thereupon, superior and inferior become confused with one another,
ruler and ministers transgress and fall into disorder,
which, being contrary to the natural order,
is bound to invite peril and calamity.
Therefore, the saying about non-action
must be carefully examined.
Non-action
pertains to the ruler.
The ancients valued non-action.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation on this passage
is highly reasoned and eloquent.
【五】【注】The discourse on non-action,
must be carefully examined.
Those who govern the world,
also engage in actions as part of their role.
However, attaining this state of action naturally,
acting in accordance with one's innate nature,
is what is termed non-action.
Those who serve the world today,
likewise attain it naturally.
Yet, those in subordinate positions handle affairs directly,
so even Shùn and Yǔ as ministers,
are still said to be engaged in action.
Thus, in the relationship between ruler and subject,
the ruler remains tranquil while the ministers act;
comparing ancient and modern times,
Yáo and Shùn practiced non-action while Tāng and Wǔ undertook endeavors.
However, each employing their nature with profound spontaneity of heavenly mechanism,
then across ages and ranks, all is non-action—
who then can be said to be acting!
【Commentary】When positioned above as the ruler,
one must practice non-action and entrust affairs to others,
utilizing the talents of all under heaven;
when residing below as a minister,
one should also personally engage in action,
fulfilling the duties of one's assigned office;
then all under heaven will be transformed.
This is the unchanging way of all kings.
【六】【疏】It refers to the simple and ancient rulers of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Their wisdom was bright and penetrating,
encompassing the two realms of heaven and earth,
yet they ruled with folded hands and non-action,
entrusting matters to their ministers.
The wise offered counsel,
thus they did not deliberate on their own.
【Transcription】"Zhi Sui" is pronounced as zhì.
The lower and foolish have the same pronunciation.
【Seven】【Memorials】Eloquently debating like a flowing stream,
adorning all things,
entrusting them to governance,
yet never speaking of oneself in the end.
【Explanation】"自說" is pronounced as "yuè".
【八】【注】The ruler above
fears being unable to practice non-action and instead usurping the duties of his ministers.
If Gāo Yáo cannot exercise his wise judgments,
or Hòu Jì cannot apply his sowing and cultivation,
then all talents lose their roles, and the sovereign becomes burdened with toils.
Thus, the emperor lowers his beaded crown and entrusts affairs to the world;
the world all attains the ability to act by themselves,
this is non-action yet there is nothing that is not done,
so both superior and subordinate practice non-action.
However, the non-action of the superior lies in employing those below,
while the non-action of the subordinate lies in acting autonomously.
【Commentary】His artistic talent is unparalleled throughout the land,
yet he does not count himself among the capable assistants when entrusted with responsibility.
What, then, does he do?
He remains in profound silence.
Thus, the old classic states,
this is called employing the strength of others.
【Explanatory Text】"Jiù" is pronounced as gāo.
"Yáo" is pronounced as yáo.
"Míng duàn" has the fanqie reading of dīng luàn.
【Nine】【Annotation】What is called "self-so."
【Commentary】Heaven has no intention for creation, yet all things transform and come into being;
Earth has no mind for nurturing, yet all things mature and are cultivated.
Therefore, Guo Xiang's annotation states,
This is what is called spontaneity.
【一０】【Note】The achievement is completed by them.
【Subcommentary】The king, sharing in the nurturing of the two primal forces,
follows the four seasons to bestow life,
entrusts all things to act on their own,
thus the work of the world is accomplished.
◎Wáng Niànsūn states:
According to Guǒ's interpretation,
the word "work" requires the addition of "accomplished" for its meaning to become clear.
Yet it is not realized that "work" itself means "accomplished,"
signifying that through non-action, the world is perfected.
(The Doctrine of the Mean says,
"Without acting, it is accomplished."
) The Ěryǎ states:
"Work,"
means "accomplished."
The Dàdàilǐ's chapter "Shèng Dé" says,
"One who can perfect virtue and laws is considered to have achieved work."
In the Zhōuguān, the office of the Gǎorén,
then submits the work to the Director of Bows and Arrows and the Repairman,
with Zhèng's annotation stating:
"Work,"
means "accomplished."
The Guǎnzǐ's chapter "Wǔ Fǔ" says,
"Great officers hold office and discern affairs,
officials in charge undertake duties and uphold their responsibilities,
scholars cultivate themselves and accomplish their talents,"
where "accomplish their talents"
means to become fully formed in ability.
The Xúnzǐ's chapter "Fù Guó" says,
"The strength of the hundred surnames,
depends on it to then achieve work,"
meaning it depends on it to then be accomplished.
"All things transform,"
"all things are nurtured,"
"the world's work is done,"
are parallel in structure,
confirming that "work" here means "accomplished."
【一一】【疏】The sun and moon shine and darken,
clouds, thunder, wind, and rain
provide cover and shelter unpredictably,
thus nothing is more divine than heaven.
It encompasses rivers and plains,
contains mountains and valleys,
and bears an endless load,
thus nothing is richer than earth.
Occupying the position of the ninth and fifth,
with authority spanning ten thousand chariots,
illuminated by the sun and moon,
the sovereign rules alone,
with merits and virtues so great,
none precede the king.
Therefore, the Lǎojīng says,
within the realm, there are four greats,
and the king is one of them.
【一二】【Note】It aligns with the non-action of heaven and earth.
【Commentary】To match means
to unite.
It speaks of the virtue of the sage,
uniting with the non-action of heaven and earth.
【一三】【疏】Heaven and earth have no master in their vast coverage,
thus they ride and control the two realms;
following the comings and goings of transformations,
hence they can drive all things;
entrusting the talents of the common people,
this is the way to employ the masses.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks this character.
(2) The Dàozàng edition lacks the character 'ér'.
The foundation lies with the superior,
while the branches lie with the inferior;
the essentials rest with the ruler,
and the details with the ministers.
The deployment of the three armies and five weapons
is the branch of virtue;
rewards, punishments, benefits, and harms,
the regulations of the five punishments,
are the branch of education;
rituals, laws, measures, and calculations,
forms, names, comparisons, and details,
are the branch of governance;
the sounds of bells and drums,
the appearances of feathers and banners,
are the branch of music;
weeping, mourning garments,
and the distinctions in funeral attire,
are the branch of grief.
These five branches
require the movement of the essence and spirit,
the activation of the mind's techniques,
and only then can they be followed.
The root
is the Dàodé.
The branch
is Rényì.
It means that the purity and simplicity of the Dàodé
are the fundamental principles of governance,
practiced in ancient times;
while Rényì, being more superficial and diluted,
are the secondary aspects of governance,
practiced in later generations.
Hence it is said,
the root lies in the earlier era,
the branch lies in the later times.
【Explanatory Text】"The root lies above, the branch lies below" Lǐ Yí says:
The root,
is the Way of Heaven;
the branch,
is the Way of Humanity.
【二】【疏】Essential means
concise and simplified.
Detailed means
numerous and complex.
The way of the ruler is leisurely and essential,
while the way of the ministers is laborious and cumbersome.
Cumbersome,
thus they act to serve the superior;
essential,
thus they govern without action over the subordinates.
【Three】【Categories】of five weapons:
first the bow,
second the shū,
third the spear,
fourth the dagger-axe,
fifth the halberd.
Yùn,
means to move.
In the age of sage-like brilliance,
then arms are laid aside and culture is cultivated;
when virtue declines,
then culture is set aside and arms are taken up.
Setting aside culture and taking up arms,
then the five weapons stir chaos;
laying aside arms and cultivating culture,
then the four classes of people live in peaceful occupations.
The root and branch of virtue,
from this can be known.
【Four】【Explanations】Rewards,
such as carriages, official hats, glory, and splendor,
are thus benefits.
Punishments,
involving execution, mutilation, humiliation, and disgrace,
are thus harms.
"Pì"
means law.
The five punishments are:
first, cutting off the nose;
second, tattooing the face;
third, cutting off the feet;
fourth, castration;
fifth, execution.
When the Dào is lost and virtue declines,
and superficial falsehood grows daily,
then penal laws are established to govern the common people.
This already damages the fundamental principle,
and merely addresses the superficial aspects of education.
【Text】"Zhī Pì" is pronounced as pí chì fǎn.
【Five】【Commentary】Rites and laws refer to
the laws of the five rites.
Numbers refer to
calculation;
measures refer to
length and size;
forms refer to
appearance and demeanor;
names refer to
written taboos;
comparisons refer to
verification and alignment;
details refer to
determination and examination.
Using these methods to nurture the common people
governs deviations from pristine antiquity,
hence it is considered the lesser art of governance.
【Translated Text】"Bǐ Xiáng" is pronounced with the characters 毗 and 志.

comparing and examining in detail.
