【Six】【Commentary】Music is
harmony.
Feathers refer to
bird plumage;
fur refers to
animal hair;
this means gathering the feathers and fur of birds and beasts to adorn their instruments.
The reason why emperors and kings created music
was to harmonize yīn and yáng above,
and reconcile with the customs of the times below.
The ancients, upon hearing music, could discern the rise and fall of a state;
whether it was an era of order or chaos,
their sounds were distinct.
Thus, it is understood that great music resonates in harmony with heaven and earth,
and is not merely about feathers, fur, bells, and drums.
Since the three dynasties and below,
decadent waves have repeatedly surged,
favoring the licentious sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
while abandoning the elegant melodies of Yúnsháo.
Consequently, feathers and vibrant colors
became lavish adornments for appearances and ceremonies,
which were no longer the essence of Xiánchí,
but rather the dregs of Púshuǐ.
【七】【疏】The dié (mourning headband) signifies
substance.
The cuī (mourning garment) represents
grief.
The upper part is called the garment,
the lower part is called the skirt.
On the head and at the waist,
both have dié.
As for the degrees of intensity,
it refers to the five grades of mourning: zhǎncuī, zīcuī, dàgōng, xiǎogōng, and sīmá,
including weeping, garments, and attire,
each with its own gradations.
These are the external forms of ritual practice,
not emotions arising from the heart,
hence they are the lesser aspects of sorrow.
【Text Explanation】"衰" is pronounced as Cuī.
"絰" is pronounced as Tiéjié.
"隆殺" is pronounced as Suǒjiè.
【Eight】【Annotation】The essence, spirit, mind, and methods are
the foundation of the five branches.
By entrusting to naturalness and allowing movement,
then the ends of the five affairs will not need encouragement but will rise on their own.
【Commentary】Shù means ability;
what the mind is capable of,
is called the mind's methods.
The essence, spirit, and mental faculties
are the foundation of the five secondary aspects.
It means that these five secondary aspects
must be guided by the essence, spirit, and mind following their nature in action,
and only then can they align with the five affairs,
which are not acts of arrogance or pretense.
The lesser learners,
the ancients had them,
but they were not what took precedence【1】.
The lord precedes and the minister follows,
the father precedes and the son follows,
the elder brother precedes and the younger brother follows,
the senior precedes and the junior follows,
the man precedes and the woman follows,
the husband precedes and the wife follows【2】.
This precedence and subordination,
is the movement of Heaven and Earth,
thus the sage takes them as models【3】.
Heaven is lofty,
Earth is lowly,
such are the positions of the divine and the bright;
spring and summer precede,
autumn and winter follow,
such is the sequence of the four seasons【4】.
The myriad things transform and arise,
sprouting in distinct forms【5】;
the gradations of growth and decline,
are the flow of change and transformation【6】.
Now Heaven and Earth are supremely divine,
yet have an order of precedence and subordination,
how much more so the way of humans【7】!
In the ancestral temple, kinship is honored;
at the court, rank is honored;
in the village community, age is honored;
in conducting affairs, worthiness is honored;
this is the order of the great Way【8】.
To speak of the Way and deny its order,
is to deny the Way itself【9】;
to speak of the Way and deny the Way,
how can one obtain the Way【10】!
【一】【注】That which comes first is the foundation.
【Commentary】The people of old,
refer to the people of the Middle Ages.
"Xiān,"
means the root.
The study of the five branches,
existed in the Middle Ages,
matters that involve superficiality and falseness,
ultimately are not the root.
【Two Departures】The precedence of noble and humble,
is the movement of Heaven and Earth.
【Transcription】"Cháng xiān ér shǎo" shī zhào fǎn.
【Three】【Comment】This statement (three) indicates that although these sequences and priorities pertain to human affairs,
they all originate from the ultimate (four) principle,
and are not created by the sages.
【Commentary】The movement of heaven and earth,
means spring and summer come first,
autumn and winter follow,
as the four seasons proceed.
Although heaven and earth are vast,
they still have positions of honor and humility,
how much more so in human relations,
can there be no precedence!
Therefore, the sage emulates the creative transformation of the two realms,
observes the natural order of the four seasons,
thus able to uphold the great righteousness between ruler and subject,
and rectify the essential way between father and son.
【Four】【Expositions】Heaven is honored,
Earth is humble—
these are unalterable positions.
Spring and summer come first,
autumn and winter follow—
such is the natural order.
By citing these two principles,
one can sufficiently understand all things.
【Five】【Memorials】All things in the universe undergo transformation,
never pausing even for a moment;
they rise and fall,
emerge and perish abruptly,
in thousands of clans and myriad kinds,
their appearances and categories differ,
yet from their budding signs and distinctions,
each possesses its own form and shape.
【Explanation】"萌區" is pronounced as qū jù fǎn.
【Six】【Exposition】In spring and summer, there is abundant growth;
in autumn and winter, there is decline and withering.
Sometimes, change gives birth to life and brings about death;
at other times, transformation turns the old into the new.
This is the natural principle of things,
not a matter of deliberate intent.
Therefore, by following the flow and accepting things as they are, all that is created finds its proper place.
【Seven】【Annotation】It clarifies the sequence of honor and humility, priority and posteriority,
which inherently cannot be without among all things.
【Commentary】The two primal forces give birth and nurture,
possessing unfathomable merits,
among the myriad things,
they are the most divine and transformative,
yet there still exist honor and humility, precedence and succession,
how much more so in the principles of human relations!
【八】【注】This means it is not only valued in human relationships.
【Commentary】The affairs of the ancestral temple are of great importance,
and must follow the order of the zhao and mu positions,
with inheritance passing through the direct line,
hence the emphasis on kinship.
In the imperial court, official ranks determine honor and humility,
in the local community, age dictates precedence,
in conducting affairs, the virtuous and capable are selected for employment,
this is the inevitable principle,
thus it is called the order of the great way.
【Text】"Cháotíng" is pronounced with the direct and distant tones.
【Nine】【Annotations】Those who discuss principles without knowing the proper sequence,
though they may have words,
ultimately do not speak of the Way;
having lost the proper order,
they are unfit to govern affairs.
【一０】【Note】The reason for adopting the Way,
is because it possesses order (5).
【Commentary】Since one does not recognize the proper sequence,
even if words are spoken, they are not the Way;
from what, then, can one take the Way to act and govern affairs?
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Jūnfáng edition as having the character 也 after 神.
(2) The Que Wu cites the Wén Rúhǎi edition as having the character 哉 after 道.
(3) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character 言.
(4) The Zhào edition lacks the character 至.
(5) The characters 其 and 也 have been supplemented based on the Sòng edition and the Dàozàng edition.
The Shìdétáng edition reads as 為有序也,
lacking the character 其.
Therefore, the ancients who understood the great Way
first clarified Heaven, and only then did virtues and the Way follow【一】;
once virtues and the Way were clarified, humanity and righteousness followed【二】;
once humanity and righteousness were clarified, duties and responsibilities followed【三】;
once duties and responsibilities were clarified, forms and names followed【四】;
once forms and names were clarified, appointment according to ability followed【五】;
once appointment according to ability was clarified, examination and deliberation followed【六】;
once examination and deliberation were clarified, right and wrong followed【七】;
once right and wrong were clarified, rewards and punishments followed【八】.
When rewards and punishments were clarified, the foolish and the wise each found their proper place,
the noble and the humble occupied their respective positions【九】;
the benevolent and worthy, as well as the unworthy, followed their true natures【一０】,
their abilities were necessarily distinguished,
and they were necessarily guided by their titles【一一】.
Using this to serve superiors【一二】,
using this to nurture subordinates,
using this to govern affairs,
using this to cultivate oneself【一三】,
cunning strategies were not employed,
everything necessarily returned to its Heaven-endowed nature,
this is called great peace,
the pinnacle of governance【一四】.
【一】【注】Heaven is,
nature.
Once nature is understood,
then all things attain their proper way.
【Commentary】This reiterates the sequence of principles in the great Dao.
It means that the ancient sages who elucidated the great Dao
first clarified the principle of naturalness.
Because naturalness is the foundation of virtue and the Dao,
therefore, virtue and the Dao follow it in sequence.
【二】【注】When things attain their proper way, they harmonize;
principles naturally become fitting.
【Commentary】Virtue comes before benevolence,
benevolence before righteousness,
hence benevolence and righteousness follow in sequence.
【Three】【Annotation】Reason is fitting without losing its proper measure.
【Commentary】Having practiced the benevolence of universal love,
and clarified the righteousness of discerning what is wrong,
it then orders each to abide by their own duties,
without contending or seizing from one another.
【Four】【Annotation】By assigning scores, the names of all things correspond to their forms.
【Commentary】Form,
refers to the body.
Each keeps to their proper place,
without encroaching upon one another,
next is to encourage cultivating oneself,
to achieve reputation.
【Five】【Annotation】There is nothing further to amend.
【Commentary】Although it again encourages cultivating one's character to attain reputation,
one must follow their inherent disposition,
let things take their natural course,
and must not distort their nature or feign emotions to seek fame.
【Six】【Annotation】When each thing fulfills its own responsibility,
then blame and fault are eliminated.
【Commentary】Yuán means to
pardon and exempt;
shěng means to
remove and abolish.
Although it follows their inherent nature,
it does not mean there are no transgressions or faults.
Therefore, it is appropriate to bestow benevolent grace,
forgiving and exempting them from guilt.
【Explanatory Text】"Yuán shěng" is read with the pronunciation jǐng fǎn.
Yuán means
to remove;
shěng means
to abolish.
【Seven】【Annotation】Each considers what attains its nature as right,
and what loses its nature as wrong.
【Commentary】Although pardons and forgiveness for offenses are repeatedly granted,
the moral integrity of people gradually erodes,
making it necessary to clarify right from wrong,
to serve as a warning and lesson.
【八】【注】Rewards and punishments are the recompense for failures and successes.
The way of perfect governance fundamentally lies with Heaven,
and its ultimate manifestation reaches this.
【Commentary】When right and wrong are made clear,
praise and blame become apparent.
Therefore, reward the good and punish the wicked,
to encourage the common people.
【Nine】【Annotation】Officials (1) each correspond to their talents.
【Commentary】By employing these rewards and punishments,
following the previous sequence to establish governance methods,
the wisdom's clarity or obscurity,
allows each to find their appropriate place in peace,
and the talent's superiority or inferiority,
ensures that all, noble or humble, fulfill their rightful positions.
【一０】【Note】Each follows the natural disposition of their own capabilities.
【Commentary】The benevolent and worthy are wise;
the unworthy are foolish.
"Xí" means to employ.
When the ruler is sagely and enlightened,
and his transformative guidance is appropriate,
although the worthy and foolish differ in nature,
they all act according to their inherent dispositions,
ultimately never abandoning their own ways to imitate others,
nor boasting and flaunting to show off.
【One One】【Annotation】Do not exchange undertakings without form.
【Commentary】Each nature differs from the others,
every object is distinct in its kind,
skills and abilities are inherently varied,
talents and uses must be differentiated.
Employ them as tools,
and all will be harmoniously suited.
【Explanation】"Must divide" — Fǎng says: fǎn.
【一二】【Note】The name matches its reality,
thus through the name, the reality is not misrepresented.
【Commentary】Names are used to summon realities,
and because they correspond to realities, they are thus called names.
If realities do not arise from names,
then names would exceed their realities.
Now it is clarified that names and realities correspond to each other,
hence it is said that it must be through their names.
【一三】【疏】以，
means to use.
It means that by employing the aforementioned nine methods,
one can serve superiors as a minister,
govern subordinates as a ruler,
manage external affairs,
and cultivate oneself internally.
【一四】【Commentary】Being supremely silent and non-acting,
entrusting affairs to the multitude of subordinates,
blocking one's hearing and closing off one's wisdom,
returning to the natural state—
this can be called the sovereign of great peace,
the beauty of perfect governance.
【Translated Text】"Knowledge and Strategy" is pronounced as zhì.
"Great Peace" is pronounced as tài.
【Collation】(1) In the Shìdétáng edition, "official" is written as "speech."
(2) The two characters should be transposed according to the commentary.
Therefore the Book says:
"There are forms and names."
Forms and names
were possessed by the ancients,
but they were not considered primary.【一】
Those who spoke of the Great Way in ancient times
went through five transformations before forms and names could be raised,
and nine transformations before rewards and punishments could be discussed.【二】
To abruptly speak of forms and names
is to not know their root;【三】
to abruptly speak of rewards and punishments
is to not know their origin.【四】
Those who speak contrary to the Way,
or discourse in opposition to the Way,
are those who are governed by others;
how could they govern others?【五】
To abruptly speak of forms, names, rewards and punishments
is to know the instruments of governance,
but not the Way of governance;【六】
they may be employed by the world,
but are insufficient to employ the world.
Such persons are called sophists,
people of limited perspective.【七】
Rituals, laws, measures and standards,
comparisons and examinations of forms and names
were possessed by the ancients,
but these are what inferiors use to serve superiors,
not what superiors use to nurture inferiors.【八】
【One】【Memorial】First,
it is the root.
Speaking of laws such as form and name,
they are merely the traces of the sage's responses,
used out of necessity,
not the means by which traces are made.
As for the texts,
they are Taoist writings,
which suffered burning during the Qin dynasty,
and now, upon examination, there is no concrete evidence.
【Two】【Annotation】From the primordial heaven and earth onward,
through forms and names making five,
to rewards and punishments making nine,
this is the natural sequence of precedence.
【Commentary】The essence of governance
must adapt to the rise and fall of the times,
as eras vary in decadence and purity,
so governance too must have its leniency and urgency.
Thus, the five transformations and nine variations
can be enacted and discussed.
If the proper sequence is not lost,
then this is the ultimate peace and orderly rule.
【Three】【Explanations】Suddenness,
means frequency,
means swiftness.
People of the declining age,
do not understand the order of human relationships,
frequently discuss forms and names,
considering them as methods of governance,
yet fail to comprehend the nine transformations,
and take nature as their foundation,
only recognizing the branches,
without knowing the root.
【Four】【Memorials】Swiftly discussing rewards and punishments,
using this to manage the times,
one only sees the branches,
without knowing the root.
The beginning,
is also the root,
they are interchangeable names.
【Five】【Comment】Those who govern others must follow proper order.
【Commentary】Wǔ means
to oppose.
Not knowing the methods of governance,
unaware of proper order,
reversing the principles of reason,
contradicting the nature of things,
one would merely be governed by things—
how could one ever govern things!
【Explanation】"迕道" is pronounced as wù.
Simǎ explains:
It means to oppose.
"而說" is pronounced by Xú as yuè,
or it can also be read according to its original character.
【Six】【Annotation】In governing, the Way first illuminates Heaven,
not to discard rewards and punishments,
but to ensure the proper sequence of priorities is maintained.
【Commentary】Forms and names, rewards and punishments,
these are the instruments for knowing governance,
but they are not the essential way of knowing governance.
【Seven】【Annotation】He who governs the world must greatly comprehend the principles of proper order.
【Commentary】If one believes that forms, names, rewards, and punishments can be applied to the entire world,
they are insufficient to govern the world.
These are merely those who superficially adorn themselves with flowery rhetoric and drift aimlessly,
individuals with narrow perspectives and stubborn biases,
who have yet to comprehend universal principles,
or awaken to the Great Way.
【Eight】【Annotation】Entrusting this matter to the multitude of talents,
this is indeed nurturing subordinates.
【Commentary】Reiterating the previous statements.
The ancients had such practices,
yet they entrusted various talents without personally intervening,
which was indeed a strategy for ministers,
not the ruler's way of nurturing the people.
This summarizes the meaning of the chapter,
to clarify the fundamental purpose from beginning to end.
Long ago, Shùn asked Yáo, saying:
"How does the Heavenly King apply his mind?"
【One】【Memorial】The Heavenly King,
is akin to the Son of Heaven.
Shùn inquired of Yáo about the methods of being a sovereign,
as to how to apply one's mind to align with the great Way.
Yáo said:
"I do not look arrogantly upon those who have no one to turn to,
nor do I abandon the destitute people.
I grieve for the deceased,
delight in children and show compassion towards women.
This is how I apply my mind."
【一】【注】Those who have no one to appeal to are
what are called the stubborn people.
【Commentary】Ào means
to insult and slight.
Wúgào refers to
those who are extremely stubborn and foolish,
incapable of receiving admonition or instruction.
Yáo responded to Shùn, saying:
"Even if there are stubborn and foolish people
who cannot be admonished or instructed,
I shall still diligently teach and guide them,
without insulting, slighting, or abandoning them."
Therefore, the ancient classic states,
"To those who are not good, I also show goodness."
Some versions have the character for 'teach' instead of 'insult,'
but it is not adopted here.
【Translated Text】"Bù Ào" is read with the fifth tone in reverse.
【二】【注】Constantly bestowing kindness.
【Commentary】Among the common people, there are those who are impoverished,
and I have always provided relief and support to them,
never ceasing in this intention.
【Three】【Memorials】The term "rúzǐ",
refers to young children.
"Āi",
means to pity.
When there were people who had died,
he would grieve and console them.
Young children and infants,
women, orphans, and widows,
he treated them all with compassion, kindness, and provided for their care.
【Four】【Memorials】 finished,
that is all.
Summarizing what came before,
to respond to Shùn's inquiry.
"My efforts of heart,
end here completely."
Shùn said:
"Beautiful it is indeed,
but not yet great."
【一】【疏】He governs with great dedication,
which is admirable indeed,
yet his methods are narrow and flawed,
not worthy of being called great.
Having received Yáo's response,
he thus voiced this criticism.
Yáo said:
"Then what should be done?"
【One】【Memorial】Yáo, having been criticized,
thus sought further advice,
"The grand principles of governance—
what methods do they entail?"
Shùn said:
"Heaven's virtue manifests, and tranquility prevails.
The sun and moon shine, and the four seasons proceed,
as if day and night follow their constant course,
clouds move and rain falls."
【一】【注】Being in harmony with Heaven's virtue,
one remains tranquil even when active.
【Commentary】The method of nurturing and transforming,
aligns in virtue with the profound heavens;
though the traces are manifest and clear,
the heart remains ever tranquil.
【二】【注】These all occur spontaneously without deliberate action.
【Commentary】The classics embody constancy.
When the sun and moon shine in their full brilliance,
they illuminate all six directions of the universe.
The transition between spring and autumn,
the alternation of coolness and warmth,
the cyclical progression of the four seasons,
the succession of day and night with their twilight and dawn,
the movement of clouds and the falling of rain—
all these are manifestations of the great virtue of heaven and earth,
the constant way of nature.
Since they are devoid of intentional favoritism,
how could they possess deliberate nurturing emotions!
The way of the sovereign and the king,
its principle is likewise.
【Explanation】"Rain bestows" begins with the sound "shǐ chǐ" reversed.
Yáo said:
"How chaotic and tumultuous!
You,
are in harmony with Heaven;
I,
am in harmony with men."
【一】【Note】Feeling uneasy about having matters to attend to.
【Comment】Jīao jīao,
rǎo rǎo,
both describe appearances of disturbance.
Understanding these words,
one naturally feels ashamed of being meddlesome,
and further stirs up
to modestly restrain oneself here.
【Explanation】"Jiāo jiāo" is pronounced with the initial 'j' and final 'iao', in the third tone.
Simǎ comments:
It means harmonious.
"Rǎo rǎo" is pronounced with the initial 'r' and final 'ao', in the third tone.
Simǎ comments:
It means gentle.
According to the annotator's interpretation,
jiāo jiāo and rǎo rǎo
describe a state of turmoil and disturbance.
【Two Abdications】Yáo humbly effaced his own brilliance,
yielding the throne to Shùn,
thus it is said that the son's magnificent virtue
aligns distantly with the heavens above,
while my own intentions
closely correspond to human affairs.
As for the two sovereigns Yáo and Shùn,
their virtue knows no superiority or inferiority,
hence these two sages are invoked here to illustrate the principles of governance.
Heaven and Earth are,
what the ancients considered great【1】,
and what Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn collectively admired【2】.
Therefore, the ancient rulers of the world,
what did they do?
They simply followed Heaven and Earth【3】.
【One】【Memorial】From here onward,
are the words of Zhuāngzǐ.
Now heaven covers and earth supports,
giving birth to all living things,
among the four greats in the universe,
these two stand out.
Therefore, citing the ancient to prove the present,
he praises their virtue.
【二】【疏】Only Heaven is truly great,
and only Yáo modeled himself after it.
Thus we know that Xuān, Xù, Táng, and Yú
all considered it their glory to have virtue that matched Heaven and Earth.
【Three】【Memorials】 state: What were the ancient emperors who embodied the Way like?
They were those who,
without deliberate intent, followed the natural course of things,
and whose virtue harmonized with heaven and earth—that is all.
【Transcription】"Zhī wáng" wǎng kuàng fǎn.
Confucius was going to deposit his books in the western treasury of the Zhōu royal house.
Zǐlù advised him, saying:
"I have heard that among the officials in charge of the collected archives of Zhōu, there is one Lǎo Dān,
who has retired from his post and returned to live in seclusion.
If you, Master, wish to deposit your books,
then perhaps we could try to go and make use of his assistance."
【一】【疏】His surname was Zhòng,
his given name was Yóu,
his courtesy name was Zǐlù,
and he was a disciple of Xuānní.
Xuānní observed that the virtue of Zhōu had already declined,
beyond rectification and support,
so he intended to store the books he had compiled
in the archives of Zhōu,
hoping they might serve as methods for future rulers to govern and transform society.
Therefore, he discussed with his disciples,
deliberating in detail on its feasibility.
Lǎojūn,
whose surname was Lǐ,
given name Dān,
served as the Zhōu dynasty's official in charge of the archival collection,
akin to today's secretarial officer,
responsible for classical texts and records.
Witnessing the turmoil in the Zhōu court,
he resigned from his position,
returning to a life of quiet retirement.
Thus, Zǐlù advised Confucius,
suggesting he briefly attempt to visit,
and take the opportunity to inquire of him.
【Explanatory Text】"Cáng Shū" Sīmǎ says,
it stores the books he authored.
"Zhēng Cáng" pronounced as cái làng fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
Zhēng Cáng,
is the name of a repository.
Another explanation:
Zhēng,
means canonical.
"Shǐ" refers to the historian of the repository.
Lǎodān》 tǔ gān fǎn.
Some say:
Lǎodān was the title of Lǎozi during the time of Kǒngzǐ.
《Retired and Returned》 means that Lǎozi saw that the end of the Zhōu dynasty could no longer be rectified,
which is why he resigned and left.
Confucius said:
"Good."
He went to see Lǎodān,
but Lǎodān did not approve,
so he expounded the Twelve Classics in an attempt to persuade him.
【First】【Memorial】Lǎozi knew that the book he wished to conceal was like straw dogs used by ancient sages in sacrifices—
it could not be preserved for long,
fearing it would mislead later generations,
hence he said it should not be allowed.
【二】【疏】Confucius edited the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
established the Rites and Music,
compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and elucidated the Way of the Changes,
making these the Six Classics;
to which were added the Six Apocrypha,
combining to form the Twelve Classics.
He elaborated in detail,
hence explaining them repeatedly.
【Explanation Text】"繙" is pronounced as fān with the sound "敷袁反".
Xú further gives the pronunciation as pán,
and also as fán.
Sīmǎ [states]:
It means vexation and grievance.
Those who explain "The Twelve Classics" say:
The six classics are the Book of Songs, Book of Documents, Rites, Music, Changes, and Spring and Autumn Annals,
plus the six weft texts,
making twelve classics in total.
Another explanation says:
The upper and lower parts of the Classic of Changes along with the Ten Wings make twelve.
Yet another says:
It refers to the chronicles of the twelve dukes in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
"以說" is read according to its character,
or with the initial sound "始銳反".
This marks the end of the sentence.
Lǎodān, struck by his argument,
said:
"That is too vast and vague;
I wish to hear the essence of it."
【One】【Memorial】Those who agree with its argument,
acknowledge that it has reason.
As for the overly verbose,
they find fault with its excessive complexity and verbosity,
and request a method of brevity.
【Transcription】"Lǎodān zhōng": Dīng Zhòng fǎn.
"Qí shuō": rú zì.
Jué jù.
"Yuē dà": yīn tài,
Xú chì zuǒ fǎn.
"Màn": mò dàn fǎn,
Guō wǔ jiàn fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The Zhào Jiànyì edition has "tài" written as "dà".
Confucius said:
"The essence lies in benevolence and righteousness【one】."
【One】【Memorial】There are twelve classics,
which have become vast and abundant;
to discuss what is essential,
nothing comes before benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎodān said:
"Pray tell,
are benevolence and righteousness
part of human nature?"
【一】【疏】Question:
"Is this benevolence and righteousness in accordance with human nature?"
Confucius said:
"Indeed.
A gentleman cannot achieve his purpose without benevolence,
nor can he survive without righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness
are the true nature of a genuine person.
What else would one pursue?"
【一】【疏】Thus,
it is still so.
It speaks of benevolence and righteousness as the innate nature of humans.
Virtuous individuals and noble persons,
if not benevolent, cannot establish their reputation and conduct;
if not righteous, cannot uphold the way of life.
Therefore, it is understood that benevolence and righteousness are the true nature of humans.
So why should there be any doubt about this?
Lǎodān said:
"May I ask,
what is meant by benevolence and righteousness【一】?"
【One】【Memorial】The preface states that benevolence and righteousness are the true nature of humans,
and now there is a renewed inquiry,
requesting an explanation of the reasons behind this.
Confucius said:
"To have a heart in harmony with all things,
to love universally without selfishness,
this is the true essence of benevolence and righteousness."
【一】【注】This is what ordinary people call benevolence and righteousness,
hence it is entrusted to Confucius and Laozi to rectify it.
【Commentary】Kǎi means
joy.
With a loyal and sincere heart,
one wishes for all beings to be safe and happy,
showing compassionate love equally,
universally aiding without selfishness,
truly aligning with human sentiments,
it can serve as a teaching for the world.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhōngxīn wù" is also written as "wù".
"Kǎi" is pronounced as kāi dài fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means joy.
Lǎo Dān said:
"Alas,
you nearly come to speak afterwards!
That universal love,
is it not rather迂远 impractical?
To be without selfishness,
is itself a form of selfishness.
Do you, Master, wish to make the Son of Heaven not lose his shepherding of the people?
Then know that Heaven and Earth inherently possess constancy,
the sun and moon inherently possess brightness,
the stars inherently form their ranks,
birds and beasts inherently gather in flocks,
trees inherently stand upright.
You, Master, should also follow virtue in your actions,
proceed along the path of the Way,
and that would be sufficient;
why then must you so strenuously uphold benevolence and righteousness,
as if beating a drum to seek a lost child?
Alas,
you, Master, are disturbing human nature!"
【一】【注】The most benevolent person,
acts directly without partial affection.
【Explanation】"Yì" is
the sound of discontent.
"Jī" means
close to.
"Yū" means
crooked.
Words spoken after the fact,
bordering on superficial falseness,
thus evoke a sigh of discontent,
to express dissatisfaction.
The perfect person follows reason directly forward,
without mental deliberation,
yet you harbor feelings of universal love,
is that not indeed selfish and crooked!
【Explanatory Text】"Yue Yi": Regarding its contrary.
Sima says:
It is not a level tone.
The same applies below.
Almost pronounced as jī.
The Sima version writes it as qí,
saying:
Qí,
means tall,
later it is said again as tall.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In the old version, "later" is written as "again" (note 1),
details unknown.
"Yū hū" pronounced as yú.
【二】【Note】What the world calls selflessness
means abandoning oneself to love others.
However, loving others
with the desire for them to love oneself in return
is actually a profound selfishness,
not the forgetting of self-interest that constitutes true public-mindedness.
【Commentary】To love others inclusively
while wanting them to love oneself in return
is indeed a deep-seated selfishness—
how can this be considered public-mindedness at all!
【Three】【Explanations】Mù,
means to nurture.
To enable all the common people under heaven to fully realize their inherent nature,
nothing is better than for each person, high and low, to uphold their proper roles,
preserving themselves in tranquil cultivation,
then great order will be achieved.
Some texts have the character "fàng" instead of "mù,"
meaning that if the ruler simply allows the masses to follow their own course,
then peace will prevail under heaven.
【Explanatory Text】"Mù hū" Sīmǎ explains:
Mù,
means to nurture.
【Four】【Dissertations】Heaven and earth cover and carry all things,
the sun and moon shine upon them,
the stars are arrayed in the sky,
all of which are the natural order of things,
unrelated to human affairs.
How could it be only these three phenomena?
All things in the universe are like this.
We should simply let them be,
and nothing will be lacking.
Why trouble ourselves with deliberate intentions,
or engage in arrogant and artificial efforts!
【Five】【Annotations】All are already (two) self-sufficient.
【Commentary】Sentient birds and beasts,
insensate plants and trees,
each attain their existence and establishment,
each possess their social groupings and distinctions—
how could it be by relying on benevolence and righteousness
that they achieve this state!
【Six】【Annotation】One does not need to practice universal love.
【Commentary】To follow,
means to accord.
To let one's virtue roam free and wander through the world,
to align with the way of heaven and tread among humanity,
the ultimate sublime conduct in human life,
is nothing beyond this.
【Explanation】"Fàng dé" is pronounced with the initial "fāng" and the departing tone.
【Seven】【Annotation】There is no way to obtain it.
【Commentary】"Jié jié"
describes the appearance of strenuous effort.
"Jiē"
means to bear or carry.
"Wáng zǐ"
refers to a runaway person.
It is said that Kǒng Qiū exerted his body and mind,
shouldering benevolence and righteousness,
forcing their practice in the world,
to teach the common people.
How is this different from beating a large drum to search for a runaway?
Thus, the louder the drum sounds, the farther the runaway flees;
the more benevolence and righteousness are emphasized, the farther one departs from the Dào.
Therefore, there is no way to attain it.
【Explanation】"Jié" is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "iē" in the tone of "juē",
and also with the initial "q" and the final "iē" in the tone of "qiē".
Some say:
It describes the appearance of exerting force.
"Jié rén" is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "iē" in the tone of "jiē",
and also sounds like "jié".
【八】【注】When events arise and one loves,
if it aligns with righteousness then stop,
this is forgetting benevolence and righteousness;
constantly dwelling on them disrupts authenticity.
【Commentary】The lost child is not found,
the fault lies in beating the drum;
the true nature is not clear,
the error arises from benevolence and righteousness;
hence, a sigh of lament is expressed,
summarizing it all.
【Collation】(1) Both the original commentary text and the Shìdétáng edition read as "fù".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition already uses "yǐ".
Shì Chéng Qǐ went to see Lǎo Zǐ and asked:
"I have heard that you, sir, are a sage,
so I made no excuse to travel the long road, wishing to see you,
walking a hundred stages with calloused feet, not daring to rest.
But now as I observe you,
you are no sage.
There are leftover vegetables in the rat holes,
yet you abandon your sister—
this is unkindness;
both raw and cooked foods are not exhausted before you,
yet you accumulate and hoard without limit."
【一】【疏】His surname was Shì,
his courtesy name was Chéngqǐ,
and it is unknown where he was from.
The lodging
was an inn.
Jiǎn
refers to blisters and sores on the feet.
Chéngqǐ had long heard of Lǎozǐ's divine and sagely virtue,
so he did not shy away from hardship and difficulty,
aspiring to righteousness, he came from afar.
Passing through numerous inns,
he dared not rest even once,
and as the journey was long,
his feet developed severe blisters.
【Transliteration】"Shì Chéng Qǐ" as pronounced,
also read as yú zhǐ fǎn.
Shì Chéng Qǐ,
is a person's name.
"Yuàn jiàn" read as xián biàn fǎn.
Same below.
"Bǎi shè" Sīmǎ explains:
staying overnight for a hundred days.
"Chóng" read as zhí lóng fǎn.
"Jiǎn" read as gǔ xiǎn fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
callus.
Callus,
pronounced as zhì zhī qí fǎn.
Xǔ Shèn says:
injury to the middle of the toe joint is called jiǎn.
◎Qìng Fán's note: The transliteration quotes Xǔ's explanation,
originally from the annotation in Huáinánzǐ's Xiūwù Piān.
Huáinánzǐ quotes Zhuāngzǐ as writing chóng pián,
pián is a miswriting of the character jiǎn.
Gāo's annotation says:
jiǎn,
means calluses growing on the feet.
Jiǎn,
also read like jiǎn (cocoon).
In Jiǎzǐ's Quànxué Piān, it says bǎi shè chóng jiǎn,
in Sòng Cè, Mòzǐ says bǎi shè chóng jiǎn,
(Gāo's annotation:
chóng jiǎn,
means accumulated calluses.
) all use jiǎn (cocoon) as a loan for jiǎn.
【二】【Note】This speaks of his not sparing material goods.
【Commentary】In the past, relying on hearsay,
I believed him to be a supreme being;
but today, witnessing it firsthand,
I realize he lacks sage virtue.
I saw rat burrows in the earth
with leftover remnants of vegetables.
Disgusted by the filth and squalor,
hence I voice this criticism.
【Translated Text】"Yú shū" is read as suǒ jū fǎn,
also pronounced as suǒ.
Sīmǎ explains:
"shū" is read as "xǔ".
"Xǔ"
means grains.
Within the rat's burrow, there are leftover grains,
which are excessively filthy and foul.
Another explanation says:
like the mounds of soil from rats,
the surplus spills beyond the vegetables.
【Three】【Annotations】There is no favor in proximity,
hence it is called abandonment.
【Commentary】Mèi,
is akin to obscurity.
For those who are benighted and ignorant,
it is necessary to guide and advance them.
To abandon them without instruction,
how can that be called benevolent and kind!
【Translated Text】"Abandoning the Younger Sister" — In one edition, it reads "the elder of the younger sister."
"Lacking Benevolence" — The Explanation of Names states:
"Mèi" (younger sister)
means "mò" (end).
It refers to those who are late in learning,
who require compassionate guidance;
to be abandoned and neglected,
is the height of lacking benevolence.
【Four】【Annotations】Reaching the fullest extent,
thus always having a surplus.
【Commentary】Raw,
refers to grains and silk;
cooked,
refers to food and drink.
Beyond what is sufficient,
one should not harbor further concerns,
hence food, drink, and material resources
are left in disarray before one's eyes.
Moreover, the great sage is broad-minded and does not cling to minor details,
while Shì Chéng, being mediocre and petty,
considers this wrong.
In trivial matters,
to measure the true sage,
can be said to use a ladle to gauge the ocean—
how could one fathom its depth or shallowness!
【Explanation】"Shēng Shú" Sīmǎ states:
Shēng means
minced raw meat.
Another interpretation says:
Shēng shú
refers to likes and dislikes.
【Five】【Annotation】All things return to embrace,
those who come are accepted,
without setting the slightest boundary.
【Commentary】Possessing sagely virtue,
he is revered by all things,
thus provisions are gathered and stored,
seemingly without bounds,
vast and without intent,
accumulating or dispersing as matters dictate.
【Explanation Text】"ér jī" is read as zǐ yì fǎn,
Lǐ Zǐ reads it as cì fǎn.
"liǎn" is read as lì jiǎn fǎn,
Lǐ Zǐ reads it as lí yàn fǎn.
Lǎozi remained indifferent and did not respond.
【一】【注】Do not use his words to summarize the meaning.
【Comment】Words of dust and grime,
How could they ever have entered my ears!
Indifferently empty and detached,
Why should they be enough to trouble my mind!
Shì Chéng Qǐ the next day again saw [Lǎozi],
saying:
"Yesterday I had criticisms of you,
but today my heart is properly withdrawn from them,
what is the reason?"
【一】【注】I wonder at the heart's tendency to criticize and mock,
which is what leads to its corruption.
【Commentary】Què means
emptiness,
cessation.
When I first arrived yesterday,
I rashly produced criticism and satire,
but now upon reflection,
I realize my own faults.
Therefore, I admit my errors and reproach myself,
deeply feeling ashamed and apprehensive.
My heart is empty—
I do not know what it is.
【Explanation】"復見" is read as fú yòu fǎn.
"有刺" is read as (yú) [qiān] (yī) cì fǎn.
"正卻" is read as qù nì fǎn.
Some say:
It means to rest.
【Collation】(1) The thousand characters have been revised according to the original version of the Interpretations of Texts.
Lǎo zǐ said:
"As for those ingenious and sagely persons,
I consider myself free from such traits.
In the past, if someone called me an ox, I would answer as an ox;
if someone called me a horse, I would answer as a horse.
If the reality truly exists,
and one refuses to accept the name given by others,
they will bring double misfortune upon themselves.
My compliance is constant compliance,
I do not comply for the sake of appearing compliant."
【一】【Note】Tuō,
means the past.
【Commentary】Those who possess ingenious wisdom and divine sageliness,
are but traces,
not that which leaves the traces.
"You say I aspire to be a sage?
I have long been free from that here,
why do you still call me sage or non-sage?"
Lǎojūn wished to suppress Chéng Qǐ's critical mind,
hence he demonstrated letting go of traces and returning to the root.
Guǒ's annotation states,
"free,"
means to have passed by,
indicating that I have already transcended and moved beyond sagehood.
【Explanation】"Fu qiao": read with the "kǔ jiào" pronunciation,
or alternatively as the character's usual reading.
"Zhī": pronounced as "zhì".
"Wéi tuō": read with the "tú huó" pronunciation.
Same applies to the annotations.
【二】【Note】Named according to the object.
【Three】【Commentary】Having substance,
therefore one does not let slander or praise weigh on the mind.
【Explanation】"Praise and Blame": the pronunciation is yú,
the same below.
【Four】【Annotation】One slander and one praise,
if taken to heart,
will burden both reputation and reality,
this is why one suffers doubly from them.
【Commentary】Yesterday you called me an ox,
and I complied with you being called an ox;
you called me a horse,
and I also complied with you being called a horse—
I never resist.
Moreover, if there is the reality of being an ox or a horse,
that is one instance of naming.
When others give you a name,
to refuse it out of avoidance
is to bring double misfortune.
Words of ridicule and criticism,
even if not as severe as being called an ox or horse,
are still not avoided—
how much more so when they are not such!
【Five】【Annotation】Fú means
the demeanor of one's conduct.
Not allowing praise or blame to cause self-harm,
thus one can remain unchanged in demeanor.
【Commentary】Guō's annotation states,
"fú" refers to
the conduct and appearance.
Lǎojūn, the Great Sage who embodies the Dào,
is thus able to subdue his body and mind,
accepting all actions and appearances,
whether called an ox or a horse,
he follows only the nature of things.
This is a constant principle,
not achieved through deliberate intention.
【Transcription】"Róng xíng" is read as it is written.
【Six】【Comment】When action is taken with deliberate intent,
it cannot consistently command adherence.
【Commentary】It means I follow my nature and embrace authenticity,
accepting things naturally,
not through deliberate intention or effort,
yet achieving this state.
If one must exert effort,
it becomes a distortion of nature;
once there is artificial action,
how can it be called non-action!
Shì Chéngqì, like a wild goose in flight avoiding its shadow,
stepped forward respectfully and asked:
"How should one cultivate one's character?"
【一】【疏】Chéng Qǐ himself realized he had spoken improperly,
feeling ashamed in both mind and body,
so he walked obliquely like a goose in flight,
turning sideways to avoid his own shadow,
following behind Lǎozi,
not daring to step in his footprints,
yet slowly advancing to ask,
"What is the way to cultivate one's character?"
Lǎo zǐ said:
"With a countenance stern and imposing,
eyes piercing and direct,
a forehead broad and prominent,
a mouth gaping wide,
and a posture rigidly upright,
he resembles a horse tethered and halted.
In movement, he is restrained;
in action, swift as a triggered crossbow;
in observation, meticulous and discerning;
in wisdom and cunning, perceiving with an air of arrogance—
all these traits are deemed untrustworthy.
If there is such a person on the border,
his name is 'Thief'."
【一】【注】A restless and uneasy appearance.
【Commentary】"而" means
"you".
It refers to you adorning your appearance,
boasting to astonish others,
building your own cliffs and banks,
unable to be at ease.
【二】【Note】The appearance of dashing out.
【Commentary】The heart being unsettled,
the eyes also dart restlessly,
hence one glances left and right,
with a wild and agitated expression.
【三】【注】Gāo Lù's appearance is beautiful and radiant.
【Commentary】With a forehead high and prominent,
displaying ornate decorations,
maintaining such a demeanor,
one becomes arrogant and haughty toward others.
【Transcription】"Sǎng Kuí": the first character is read with the initial "xī" and the final "dǎng" in the fanqie spelling,
the second character with the initial "qù" and the final "guǐ" in the fanqie spelling.
It is also written as "Xiǎn",
pronounced as it is normally read.
Sima's version has it as ●.
【Four】【Annotation】The appearance of being fierce and expansive.
【Commentary】Guō's annotation states,
it describes a fearsome and imposing appearance.
This means a strong-willed and domineering disposition,
with powerful and fierce speech,
boasting and intimidating,
making others feel apprehensive.
【Explanation】"闞" is given by Guō as xǔ lǎn fǎn,
also huǒ zhǎn fǎn,
also huǒ zàn fǎn.
"虓" is huǒ jiāo fǎn.
"豁" is huǒ kuò fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】The appearance of straining to maintain self-control.
【Commentary】Righteousness means
what is appropriate.
Strutting with arrogance and pride
truly violates the rites and norms,
yet by cultivating one's appearance and demeanor,
it naturally becomes fitting.
【Text Explanation】"Tí" is pronounced as zhí shì fǎn.
"Qí" is pronounced as qù shì fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: Yì should be read as é.
Yì rán,
means é rán.
The detailed explanation is found in Yǔ Shì's commentary in the "Great Master" chapter.
Guō's annotation and Chéng's subcommentary both misinterpret it.
【Six】【Annotation】Aspiring to gallop.
【Commentary】Though the appearance is solemn and dignified,
the nature of the mind is restless and agitated,
like a spirited horse tethered,
its intent fixed on galloping away.
【Seven】【Annotation】Unable to freely express oneself.
【Commentary】The mind chases after external circumstances,
stirred by encounters with objects,
unable to follow spontaneity,
and constrained in every affair.
【Eight】【Annotation】Decisions on advancing or retreating are made swiftly.
【Commentary】Jī,
refers to the trigger of a crossbow.
The mind that clings and grasps,
when encountering circumstances, arises,
its arising is fierce and swift,
similar to a crossbow trigger.
【Nine】【Annotation】To clarify right and wrong.
【Subcommentary】Unable to empty and dismiss,
forgetting both opposition and compliance,
yet clearly discerning right and wrong,
focusing the mind to examine and determine.
【一０】【Note】Tài refers to
having more than one's inherent nature.
Being skilled at displaying excess
means being unskilled at embracing simplicity.
【Commentary】Tài means
"abundant."
Unable to forget cunning and forget knowledge,
one observes the single principle of non-action,
yet feigns knowledge and cunning,
perceiving the multitude of affairs in action.
【一一】【Note】All these ten matters,
are considered as not believing in destiny and being reckless about praise and blame,
none of which are the ways to cultivate one's character.
【Commentary】Xìn means
reality.
It is said that these ten matters,
are all acts of deceit and falsity,
not virtues of truth and authenticity.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Guǒ Xiàng stated,
all these ten matters,
are considered as not trusting in inherent nature but indulging in praise and slander,
which adds a twist to the text.
All that is deemed untrustworthy,
means all actions arise from affectation,
not corresponding with the natural disposition,
hence called untrustworthy.
The countenance,
the eyes,
the forehead,
the mouth,
the demeanor,
once there is restraint,
like tethering a horse to curb its galloping,
one cannot have confidence within the heart.
When moving and expressing,
uniformly responding to its mechanism,
and overcoming each other with cleverness,
one cannot have confidence externally.
Slightly distinguishing two meanings,
they do not amount to ten matters.
【一二】【Note】Just as (two) your actions,
are not those of an upright person.
【Commentary】Qiè (stealing),
means thievery.
In the border regions and territories,
there suddenly appears a person,
who does not fear the laws and regulations,
but only engages in theft.
Internally, it damages moral customs,
externally, it obstructs relations with the frontier tribes,
corrupts governance and harms the people,
nothing is more severe than this.
The actions of Chéng Qǐ,
are similarly base,
his behavior is arrogant and presumptuous,
just like this thief.
【Translated Text】"Border" is pronounced as jìng.
"There is a person whose name is called thief" refers to people from the remote frontiers,
who are unaware of the proper rites and music,
even if they speak,
occasionally coinciding with ancient texts,
all are gains from theft,
how can their ways be worth discussing!
Sīmǎ comments:
meaning that such people have long existed in distant lands.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "jìng" is written as "jìng".
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, "rú" is written as "zhī".
The Master said:
"The Way,
in the great does not end,
in the small does not omit,
thus all things are encompassed.
Vast and expansive, there is nothing it does not contain;
profound and deep, it cannot be fathomed.
Forms, virtues, humanity, and righteousness
are but the branches of the spirit;
who but the perfect person can establish them!
When the perfect person possesses the world,
is it not indeed great!
Yet it is not enough to burden him.
The world strives for power, yet he does not join them;
he examines the flawless and does not shift with profit.
He exhausts the truth of things,
able to guard their root.
Thus, he sets aside heaven and earth,
discards all things,
yet his spirit has never been troubled.
Penetrating the Way,
harmonizing with virtue,
he withdraws from humanity and righteousness,
sets aside rites and music;
the mind of the perfect person is thus settled."
【First】【Explanation】Zhuāng Zhōu studied under Lǎo Jūn,
hence addressing him as Fūzǐ.
End,
means limit.
Though the two primal forces are vast,
they still exist within the Dào,
unable to exhaust the measure of the Dào;
though an autumn hair is tiny,
it relies on it to form its substance,
thus nothing small is overlooked.
Since it can be both small and large,
it is known to be fully present in all things.
【二】【疏】Since it encompasses all things without exception,
penetrates even the minutest details,
threads through all creation,
and embraces both cosmic principles,
thus "guǎng guǎng" praises its vast breadth,
and "yuān" admires its profound depth.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: "guǎng guǎng"
is akin to saying "kuàng kuàng."
"Kuàng kuàng"
describes an appearance of emptiness and absence of human presence.
In the "Treatise on the Five Elements" of the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
it states that when troops are deployed beyond the appropriate time,
it is called "guǎng,"
Lǐ Qí explained:
"guǎng,"
is pronounced as "kuàng."
"Kuàng" and "guǎng,"
are interchangeable in meaning in ancient texts.
In the "Biographies of the Five Sons of Emperor Wu" in the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
"héng shù" (Xuē Zàn noted:
"shù,"
means road.
) "hé guǎng guǎng xī,"
Sū Lín commented:
"guǎng,"
is pronounced as "kuàng."
【Three】【Discourses】Form, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are
merely the traces of the spirit,
not the means by which these traces are made.
To remedy the flaws of things,
they are used only out of necessity.
Unless one is a supremely sagely and divine person,
who can determine their coarseness or subtlety!
【Four】【Commentary】Employing the world,
thus one does not worry about its greatness.
【Commentary】The sage's majesty spans ten thousand chariots,
the king possesses the world,
his position resides at the ninth and fifth rank—
is this not grand indeed!
Yet at Gūyè and Fényáng,
he forgets things and forgets himself,
where movement is stillness itself—
how could the four seas possibly burden him!
【Five】【Annotation】Be still and follow it.
【Commentary】Quán,
means power.
Jiē,
means to dwell.
When the state is overturned,
and the world collapses into chaos,
those who follow the times,
stirring with power,
must remain calm and guard themselves,
not competing with them.
【Explanatory Text】"Fèn bǐng" is pronounced as bǐng.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means authority and power.
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as chǒu lún fǎn.
One version writes it as dòng.
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying,
bǐng,
means authority and power.
Shuōwén states:
Bǐng,
is the handle.
Bǐng,
is sometimes written as bǐng.
In the Guǎnzǐ's "Shān Quán Shù" chapter, it says this is called state authority,
and this is called the ruler's power.
Managing the surplus and deficit of state affairs,
is called state authority.
Controlling the importance and triviality of human affairs,
is called the ruler's power.
Bǐng,
is what one relies on to control matters.
The greater it is, the more it controls major issues;
the lesser it is, the more it controls minor ones.
Rising together to take action in the world,
all have something to rely on.
Shuōwén states:
Jiǎ,
means to borrow.
Without anything to rely on, there is no action;
with no action, one becomes submissive and compliant,
turning into waves and currents,
and thus follows along with things as they change.
Without reliance and not moving with benefits,
this is called acting through inaction, yet achieving everything.
Guǒ Xiàng says,
follow authenticity and go straight forward,
but this is incorrect.
【六】【Note】Follow one's true nature and proceed directly.
【Commentary】His nature is tranquil and composed,
entrusting his fate to authenticity.
Since glory and status do not concern his heart,
how could wealth and profit sway him!
【七】【疏】The sage, with a spirit mirror that penetrates thoroughly,
exhausts principles and fulfills nature,
thus reaching the utmost truth of things.
Yet responding to stimuli without fixed method,
acting without harming tranquility,
is able to preserve the root.
【八】【疏】Although one may hold the chart and rule the realm,
governing all regions,
yet forgetting the external dual principles,
abandoning all things,
thus being without action,
affairs become without affairs,
the mind is at ease and the spirit reigns supreme,
how could there be any distress or exhaustion!
【九】【疏】A heart of indifference and simplicity,
penetrates to the ultimate Way;
a wisdom of emptiness and forgetfulness,
harmonizes with the highest Virtue.
This is the mutual convergence of realm and wisdom,
where ability and its object mysteriously align.
【一０】【Note】Advancing in virtue and morality.
【一一】【Note】It takes emotion and nature as the core.
【Commentary】Rejecting the superficiality of benevolence and righteousness,
advancing the purity and harmony of the Way and virtue,
discarding the ostentation of rites and music,
and upholding the emptiness and tranquility of non-action.
◎ Yú Yuè states:
"Bīn" should be read as "bìn" (to reject),
meaning to reject rites and music,
consistent with the previous line's rejection of benevolence and righteousness.
Guǒ's annotation says,
"Taking innate nature as the foundation,"
which interprets the character in its original sense,
making the meaning rather roundabout.
In the "Dá Shēng" chapter, it says,
"Rejected by the village,"
"Expelled by the local administration,"
this is evidence of "bīn" being used interchangeably with "bìn."
◎ Qìng Fán notes: Yú's interpretation is correct.
In ancient times, "bīn" and "bìn" had the same pronunciation,
and characters with the same pronunciation
were often used interchangeably.
In the "Zhōu Lǐ · Sī Yí,"
"the guest bows while presenting the gift,"
the "Shì Wén" explains:
"bīn"
is pronounced as "bìn."
In the "Xú Wú Guǐ" chapter of this text,
"to be a guest of the ruler,"
Sīmǎ's version writes "bīn" as "bìn,"
which serves as evidence.
【一二】【Note】It is settled in non-action.
【Commentary】Tranquil and non-active, yet its function does not contradict stillness,
settled indeed.
【Collation】(1) The Omission Correction cites the Jiangnan Ancient Repository edition with the character "chóng yuān" repeated.
What the world values in the Way is found in books.
Books are nothing more than words,
and words have value.
What is valuable in words is their meaning.
Meaning has something that follows it.
What meaning follows
cannot be conveyed in language.
Yet the world values language and transmits books.
Although the world values them,
I still do not consider them worthy of value,
because what is valued is not what is truly valuable.
Thus, what can be seen by looking
are form and color;
what can be heard by listening
are names and sounds.
Alas!
The world believes that form, color, names, and sounds are sufficient to grasp the true essence of things!
If form, color, names, and sounds are indeed insufficient to grasp their true essence,
then those who know do not speak,
and those who speak do not know.
How could the world understand this!
【一】【疏】The Way is spoken words;
speaking;
writing is
written characters.
Ordinary people,
with shallow understanding,
sometimes rely on speech to communicate their thoughts,
or use writing to express their ideas,
reciting and exchanging them back and forth,
considering them precious,
unaware that there is nothing worth speaking of.
【二】【疏】The reason for writing letters,
lies in valuing the expression through words,
and the reason for expressing through words,
lies in valuing the conveyance of meaning.
【Three】【Explanations】Suí,
means to follow.
What arises from the mind,
comes from the Dào,
and since the Dào is neither form nor sound,
it cannot be conveyed through words.
【Transcription】"Yán chuán" zhàng zhuān fǎn.
Hòu tóng.
【Four】【Annotation】Its nobility always lies beyond words and expressions.
【Commentary】Writing serves to record words,
words serve to convey meaning,
yet people of the declining age,
with their minds obscured and blocked,
thus value words and esteem writing,
unable to forget words and seek the underlying principle.
Therefore, although they value them,
I still deem them unworthy of value,
because words and writing are but dregs,
not things that can be truly prized.
Hence, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
what is truly valuable always lies beyond the expressions and words.
【Explanation】"Wèi qí" is pronounced as yú wèi fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】To grasp the essence of others' sentiments,
only those who transcend words and forsake writings can do so.
【Commentary】What the eyes can perceive
is nothing beyond forms and colors;
what the ears can hear
resides solely in names and sounds.
Yet worldly people,
failing to comprehend the ultimate principle,
claim that names, words, sounds, and forms
fully convey the truth of reality.
How could they know that the profound ultimate
cannot be reached by sight or hearing!
So foolish and deluded are they,
deeply worthy of lament.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
"To grasp the essence of that reality,
one must only forget words and discard writings."
【Six】【Annotation】This conveys the idea of abandoning learning and discarding knowledge.
【Commentary】Those who understand the Way forget words,
those who value virtue remain unknowing,
yet the deafened masses, foolish and deluded,
how could they ever realize and awaken!
Only the enlightened can truly embody this.
【Transcription】"The wise" is read as the character itself.
The same applies below.
Some read it with the pronunciation meaning wisdom.
"To discard the esteemed" is pronounced with the rising tone of the departing tone.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has the character zāi below it.
(2) The character zhī is supplemented based on the Sòng edition and commentaries.
Duke Huán was reading in his hall.
Wheelwright Biǎn was carving a wheel below the hall,
He set down his mallet and chisel and went up,
asking Duke Huán:
I dare to ask,
what words are those that Your Excellency is reading?"
【一】【疏】Duke Huán,
referring to Duke Huán of Qí.
Wheel,
means the wheel of a vehicle.
Biǎn,
is the name of a craftsman.
Zhuó,
means carving and chiseling.
Shì,
means to set aside.
The ruler of Qí was engrossed in reading,
while the wheelwright Biǎn was crafting a cart,
their statuses high and low differed,
their tasks varied,
so he set aside his tools,
and proceeded to question.
Wishing to clarify that the profound mystery of the ultimate truth,
cannot be transmitted through words,
thus, through the story of Duke Huán and the craftsman,
it briefly reveals the essence of forgetting words.
【Text】"Huán Gōng" Lǐ Yún said:
It is Qí Huán Gōng,
named Xiǎo Bái.
"Lún Biǎn" is pronounced as piān,
and also has a pronunciation of fú tiǎn.
Sīmǎ explained:
He was a wheel maker,
named Biǎn.
"Zhuó" is pronounced as zhí jiǎo.
"Chuí" is pronounced as zhí zhuī.
"Ér shàng" is pronounced as shí zhǎng.
【Collation】(1) The Shidetáng edition writes it as "者".
The Duke said:
"These are the words of a sage."
【一】【疏】It is said to model after King Wén and King Wǔ,
to follow the examples of Yáo and Shùn,
which are the words of the sage.
He asked:
"Is the sage present?"
【One】【Memorial】Another question:
"Is the Sage present now or not?"
The Duke said:
"He has already died."
【One】【Memorial】The reply stated:
"Although the sage has died,
his teachings still remain."
He said:
"Then what you, my lord, are reading
is merely the dregs of the ancients!"
【One】【Explanation】The dregs of wine are called zāo,
and soaked zāo is called pò.
Fine aged wine can be compared to the Way and Virtue,
while zāo and pò are likened to benevolence and righteousness.
Like straw dogs that have already been displayed in rituals,
how could they be worth mentioning!
【Transcription】"Zāo" is pronounced like zāo.
Lǐ Yí says:
It refers to the dregs of wine.
"Pò" is pronounced with the initial p and the final ò.
Sīmǎ Biāo says:
Rotten food is called pò.
Another explanation states:
The dregs becoming rotten is pò.
The text also uses the character 粕,
with the same pronunciation.
Xǔ Shèn explains:
Pò,
refers to the coarse dregs after filtration.
Some pronounce it as pò with the initial p and the final ò,
meaning the soul or spirit.
"Yǐ fú" is pronounced with the sound fú.
This is a full stop.
Or it can be read according to its regular meaning.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary on the transcription,
pò,
is also written as 粕,
which is Sīmǎ Biāo's version.
The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Lù Jī's "Wénfù" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Rotten food is called pò.
Duke Huán said:
"I, the solitary man, am reading books;
how dare a wheelwright offer his opinion!
If you have an explanation, it is acceptable;
if not, you shall die."
【One】【Memorial】The rites separate the noble and the humble,
making it improper to speak lightly;
yet a common, insignificant man
dares to voice opinions.
If his arguments hold reason,
he may be spared punishment;
but if he lacks justification,
he is certain to face the death penalty.
Wheelwright Biǎn said:
"Your servant judges by the way he practices his own craft.
In wheel-making,
if you work too slowly, the joinery seems sweet but won't be solid;
if too quickly, it's bitter and the parts won't fit.
Not too slow, not too fast—
you find it in your hands and respond with your heart,
the mouth cannot put it into words,
there is a subtle art residing within it.
I cannot make my son understand this,
nor can my son receive it from me,
thus I've reached seventy years of age still making wheels in my old age.
The ancient people and what could not be transmitted have perished,
so then what you, my lord, are reading
must be nothing but the dregs of the ancients!"
【One】【Explanation】Sweet,
signifies slowness.
Bitter,
signifies urgency.
Calculation,
signifies method.
If the carving of a wheel is done improperly, then...
Not] (one) firm,
if applied appropriately,
then the mouth cannot speak of it.
Moreover, the principles of teachings,
their meaning is also thus.
【Transcription】"Gān" is read as the character's standard pronunciation,
also pronounced as hān.
Sīmǎ explains:
"Gān" means
relaxed.
"Kǔ" means,
urgent.
"Yǒu shù" Lǐ explains:
pronounced with the initial sh and the final ù,
shù,
refers to a method or technique.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Considering that both before and after it is given as sh and ǔ,
this note's character is likely erroneous.
【二】【注】This means that all things have their own inherent nature,
and teaching cannot alter it.
【Explanation】"Yù" means
to enlighten.
The skill of Lún Biǎn,
could not be demonstrated to his son;
Lún Biǎn's son,
also could not receive his teaching,
so as he reached old age,
he could not avoid the toil of the axe.
Hence, it is known that each thing has its own nature,
and one should not imitate blindly.
【Three】【Commentary】The affairs of antiquity,
have already perished with the past.
Even if some are passed down,
how could they make the past exist in the present?
The past does not reside in the present;
present affairs have already changed.
Therefore, abandon learning and follow one's nature,
transforming with the times to attain fulfillment.
【Commentary】The sages established laws,
benefiting all things according to the times.
Since the times do not stand still,
the laws also change accordingly.
Thus, the ancient people and their laws have faded into the past,
while contemporary laws and people arise in the present.
There is no place for clinging to the traces of ancient sages in today's world.
Hence, it is understood that the books we read
are indeed mere dregs.
【Text】"Rén yǔ" read as the character's standard pronunciation,
also another reading yú.
"Kě chuán" pronounced with the retroflex initial and the final as in "zhuān".
The same applies to the annotations.
【Collation Notes】(1) The character '不' has been added based on the main text.
(2) In Zhào Jiànyì's version, '古' is written as '今'.
(3) In Zhào's version, '滅' is written as '減'.
【Chapter One】【Explanation】Named after its meaning.
Tiānyùn,
Sīmǎ [reads it as] Tiānyuán.
"Does Heaven revolve?
Does Earth stand still?
Do the sun and moon compete for their positions?
Who directs this?
Who maintains this?
Who, residing idly, pushes and sets it in motion?
Could it be that there is a mechanism forcing it, leaving no alternative?
Or does it revolve and spin, unable to stop itself?
Do the clouds bring rain?
Or does rain form the clouds?
Who exalts and bestows this?
Who, residing idly, indulges in pleasure and urges this on?
The wind rises in the north,
blowing now west, now east,
and ascends whirling about.
Who exhales and inhales it?
Who, residing idly, sweeps it back and forth?
May I ask, what is the reason for all this?"
【一】【Note】It moves on its own without being carried.
【Commentary】It is said that Heaven is endowed with yang qi,
which is clear and floats above,
moving spontaneously without intent.
【Interpretation】"Its Movement" The _Ěryǎ_ states:
Movement,
means shifting.
The _Guǎngyǎ_ states:
means turning.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: Movement,
in the variant text by Sīmǎ, is written as yuán,
the two characters yùn and yuán,
were used interchangeably in ancient times.
In the _Yuèyǔ_, "guǎng yùn bǎi lǐ",
Wéi's annotation states:
east-west is guǎng,
north-south is yùn.
The _Xīshān Jīng_ writes it as "guǎng yuán bǎi lǐ".
In the _Mòzǐ_, "Fēi Mìng Shàng Piān": "It is like standing at dawn and dusk upon a revolving potter's wheel,"
in the middle chapter, yùn is written as yuán.
Yùn,
in ancient times, was also read like yún.
Yún and yuán are interchangeable.
In the _Guǎnzǐ_, "Jiè Piān": "When the four seasons revolve, the myriad things transform,"
yún is the same as the character yùn.
The _Shuōwén_,
zhèn,
also known as yùn rì,
Liú Kuàng's annotation in the "Wǔdū Fù" writes yùn rì as yún rì.
Yún is the same as yuán.
In the _Shū_, "Tài Shì": "Although it is said so,"
the annotation in the _Hànshū_, "Wéi Xián Zhuàn", writes it as yuán rán.
In the _Shī_, "Chū Qí Dōngmén": "How it pleases me, yuán,"
the variant text states:
yuán,
originally written as yún.
In the "Shāng Sòng", "Jǐng Yuán Wéi Hé",
Zhèng's commentary:
yuán,
in ancient script, is written as yún.
All of these serve as evidence.
【二】【Note】It stops by itself without being placed.
【Commentary】The earth receives the yin energy,
which sinks turbidly below,
and without intent for tranquility, it naturally settles.
【Three】【Notes】It naturally replaces itself without contending for position.
【Commentary】It shines upon day and night,
rises and sets, comes and goes,
naturally just as it is.
Since it is without emotion in the succession of changes,
how could it have any intention to contend for a place!
【Four】【Explanations】Shú,
means "who".
"Shì zhě",
refers to the preceding text.
It speaks of the four seasons and eight solar terms,
clouds moving and rain falling,
nurturing all living beings,
fostering and refining all creatures,
who is the master that governs and executes these actions?
This sentence explains the movement of heaven.
【Five】【Annotations】All are self-so.
【Commentary】The mountains and hills produce and nurture,
the rivers and springs flow and pour forth,
embracing all things,
transporting and bearing without end,
spring gives birth and summer fosters growth,
surely without any error or deviation.
Who is it that maintains the order and principles,
thus enabling it to be so?
This one phrase explains the aspect of the earth.
【Six】【Annotation】Without it, there is nothing to infer;
with it, each has its own affairs.
Then, who is it that, without affairs, yet carries out this inference?
Each acts on its own.
【Commentary】The sun and moon alternate in succession,
the stars and constellations shine brightly,
each follows its own measured course,
all occurring spontaneously.
Who, residing in tranquility without affairs,
calculates and propels them forward?
This line explains the contention between the sun and moon.
The preceding three points,
all posed as hypothetical questions,
illuminate the profound subtleties.
Thus, it is understood that all things are as they are of themselves,
with no entity compelling them to be so.
【Interpretation of the Text】"推而" is read as per its standard pronunciation,
an alternative reading is with the reverse pronunciation of "吐回".
Simǎ's version writes it as "誰".
【Seven】【Explanations】Jī,
means a mechanism.
Jiān,
means to close.
In the profound winter's harsh and killing cold,
the night is dark and obscure;
by one's thoughts and estimations,
it is assumed there is a master in charge of opening and closing,
a matter of unavoidable necessity,
causing it to be so.
But by reasoning and deduction,
all things are naturally thus.
The square earth does not move,
and its principle is the same.
【Transcription】"Jian" is read as gǔ xián fǎn,
while Xú reads it as gǔ xiàn fǎn.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as "xián",
and explains:
It means to pull.
【八】【注】From then on,
it is therefore unknowable.
【Commentary】When the vitality of spring emerges,
all things come to life;
as day and night alternate with clarity,
the entire universe is illuminated.
The cyclical order of energies operates,
leading to this growth and reproduction.
Examining the underlying principle,
no external force compels it to be so.
The circular motion of the heavens,
its meaning is likewise.
【Nine】【Annotation】Neither can substitute for the other,
each remains as it is.
【Commentary】When vapor rises upward,
it forms clouds;
when clouds disperse downward,
they moisten and become rain.
However, tracing their beginnings and ends,
neither has a distinct origin,
thus it is understood that the two cannot create each other.
【Transcription】"For rain" is read as wèi yǔ fǎn.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
【一０】【Commentary】Lóng,
means to rise.
Shī,
means to cease.
It speaks of who raises the clouds and rain to pour down in torrents,
and who ceases the sweet showers to cause this severe drought.
【Transcription】"Lóng shī" is pronounced as chí,
with the fanqie spelling shì shì fǎn.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
This follows the previous discussion about clouds and rain.
"Lóng" should be read as "jiàng,"
meaning the descent and bestowal of this cloud and rain.
In the "Shangshu Dazhuan," there is "lóng gǔ,"
with Zhèng's annotation stating:
"Lóng" is read like the "jiàng" in "Páng jiàng."
This is because "lóng" derives its sound from "jiàng,"
and their ancient pronunciations were originally the same.
In the "Xúnzǐ·Tiānlùn" chapter, "lǐ lóng zūn xián ér wáng,"
the "Hánshī Wàizhuàn" writes "lóng" as "jiàng."
In the "Qí Cè," "suì bā yuè jiàng yǔ xià,"
the "Fēngsú Tōngyì·Sìdiǎn" chapter writes "jiàng" as "lóng."
These are evidences of the interchangeable use of ancient characters.
【一一】【Commentary】Who dwells in peace with nothing to do,
self-motivated to encourage others,
creating this excessive rain for pleasure?
The Sīmǎ version uses the character 'juàn'.
【Interpretation】"Pleasure" is pronounced luò,
also pronounced yuè.
"And encourage" in Sima's version, "encourage" is written as "weary",
stating:
read as "follow",
meaning who does nothing,
but follows Heaven in coming and going,
revolving endlessly.
【一二】【疏】Páng Huáng,
describes the appearance of circling and turning.
Xū Xī,
is like exhaling and inhaling.
Pī Fú,
is like fanning or stirring.
The northern yīn energy,
is where the wind originates,
hence it is called the north.
Now, the wind blows without intent.
It goes east or west as it pleases,
sometimes wandering and dwelling in the void,
sometimes exhaling and inhaling within the mountains,
brushing and lifting, rising and falling,
with hardly any fixed pattern.
Who, with nothing to do, engages in this?
It is simply nature.
【Explanation Text】"有上" is pronounced as shí zhǎng fǎn.

páng huáng,
means a whirlwind.

Guō pronounces it as fú fú fǎn.
"披拂",
