The Sīmǎ version writes it as fú.
【13】【Note】Posing the question to explain the reason for its being so.
【Comment】This sentence generally asks what the intention was before.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites Li's edition, where "施" is written as "弛".
(2) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition, where "有" is written as "在".
Wū Xiánzhào said:
"Come!
Let me tell you.
Heaven has six poles and five constants,
if emperors and kings follow them there is order,
if they oppose them there is calamity.
When the affairs of the nine domains,
are ordered and virtue is complete,
shining illumination reaches the lower realms,
all under heaven uphold them,
this is called the supreme sovereign."
【One】【Annotation】For matters close at hand,
one might know their reasons,
yet tracing their origins to the utmost,
they exist without cause, simply as they are.
Being as they are, there is no need to inquire into their reasons further,
but one should simply follow them.
【Commentary】Wū Xián was
a divine shaman,
who served as the chancellor to Emperor Zhòng Zōng of the Yīn dynasty.
"Tiāo" is
his name.
The "six extremities" refer to
the six directions,
namely the four cardinal points, above and below.
The "five constants" refer to
the five elements:
metal, wood, water, fire, and earth,
which are the constant nature of human relations.
This speaks of the principle of spontaneity,
which encompasses these six extremities and five constants.
As for the sun, moon, wind, and clouds,
all follow this pattern.
One should simply let them be,
naturally complete in themselves;
why impose deliberate intention upon them?
【Interpretive Text】"Wūxián Shào": Chìyáo's annotation,
Guō reads as "tiáo",
also read as "shào".
Lǐ says:
Wūxián,
was the minister of the Yīn dynasty.
Shào,
is a pseudonym.
"Wú yǔ": Yújù's annotation.
"Nǚ" is read as "rǔ".
The same applies hereafter.
"Liùjí": Sīmǎ explains:
the four directions, up and down.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
Liùjí wǔcháng,
is suspected to be the Wǔfú Liùjí from the Hóngfàn.
"Cháng" and "xiáng",
are interchangeable in ancient script.
In the Yílǐ Shìyú Lǐjì, it is recorded "recommend this constant matter",
Zhèng's note says:
in ancient script, "cháng" is written as "xiáng",
this is the evidence.
In the Shuōwén Jiězì, the radical "shì" section:
"xiáng",
means blessing.
Then, wǔcháng is wǔfú.
The following text says,
the affairs of the Jiǔluò,
governance accomplished and virtue complete,
does it refer to the nine categories of the Luòshū that Yǔ received!
【二】【注】For artificial learning can be altered,
yet inborn nature cannot be reversed.
【Commentary】The sovereign,
aligning with the heavenly way above,
and conforming to the common people below,
rules with effortless ease and non-action,
following and entrusting matters to the nature of things,
thereby bringing order to the world.
Yet, if they oppose the contentment of all nations,
disrupt the harmony of the dual forces of yīn and yáng,
and act with malevolence and perversity,
then calamity and chaos will arise.
【Three】【Explanations】The affairs of the Nine Luo,
refer to the matters of the nine regions' settlements.
It means that the king responds to heaven and conforms to all things,
ruling without deliberate intent,
thus bringing about peace under heaven,
where people sing and strike the soil in joy.
In the lands of the nine regions' settlements,
governance is stabilized and achievements are accomplished;
in the states of the eight wilds and barbarian tribes,
the Way is perfected and virtue is complete.
It aligns with the two modes (heaven and earth),
covering and carrying all things;
and equalizes the three luminaries (sun, moon, and stars),
shining upon the earth below.
◎ Jià Shìfù said:
This speaks of heaven's operation as entirely natural,
and the emperor follows this natural course,
responding with the Way,
so that heaven and earth also receive proper formation,
winds and rains are harmonized,
and the four seasons follow in order.
The affairs of the Nine Luo,
are the nine categories that Yǔ received.
Zhuāngzǐ speaks of the Way not being contrary to that of the sages,
and this is an example of it.
【四】【Note】It follows its own natural course, hence it is so.
【Commentary】The Way aligns with spontaneity,
virtues harmonize with creation,
thus all beings delight in upholding it without weariness,
the common people bear and support it without refusal,
which can be said to be returning to simplicity and purity,
the governance of the supreme sovereign.
The Grand Steward Dàng of Sòng asked Zhuāngzǐ about benevolence.
Zhuāngzǐ replied:
"Tigers and wolves
possess benevolence."
【一】【疏】The Song state inherited the legacy of Yin,
hence Shang refers to the state of Song.
The Grand Steward,
an official title,
was named Yíng,
with the courtesy name Dàng.
Wishing to resolve his own doubts,
he thus inquired about benevolence from Zhuāngzǐ.
【Explanation】"Shāng Dà" is pronounced as tài,
the same applies to the following "dà xī".
"Zǎi Dàng" Simǎ comments:
Shāng,
refers to Sòng,
Grand Steward,
is an official title,
Dàng,
is his courtesy name.
【Er】【Shū】benevolence is
the manifestation of affection.
Even fierce beasts like tigers and wolves
still understand mutual closeness,
which sufficiently demonstrates that all beings possess a benevolent nature.
He asked:
"What does that mean?"
【First】【Memorial】The Grand Steward, not yet grasping the profound sentiment,
inquired again, wondering what meaning was intended.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"When father and son are affectionate to each other,
why would that be considered not benevolent?"
【One】【Memorial】The affection between father and son,
arises from nature,
this is true benevolence,
why trouble to ask further!
He asked:
"May I ask about perfect benevolence?"
【First】【Memorial】The affection between tigers and wolves,
its principle is not yet fully understood,
hence I beseech the utmost benevolence,
hoping to hear its profound meaning.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Perfect benevolence has no kin."
【一】【Note】Lacking partiality
does not mean having meager virtue.
In the human body,
there is no inherent partiality;
yet the head naturally resides above,
the feet naturally remain below,
the organs dwell within,
and the skin and hair stay outside.
The external and internal, above and below,
the noble and humble, esteemed and lowly,
each in the body fulfills its ultimate role,
with no partial affection existing among them.
Thus, perfect benevolence is sufficient,
so the five relationships and six clans,
whether wise or foolish, distant or near,
do not lose their proper distinctions in the world—
this is the natural principle.
Why then should one seek to have partiality?
【Commentary】The one of utmost benevolence,
forgets personal concerns and eliminates thoughts,
unites with the great void as one body,
blends with all things to become a single entity,
how can distinctions of closeness or distance be discussed!
Calmly and without intention, they follow the world's natural affinities and distances.
【Transcription】"Fǔcáng" is pronounced as cái làng fǎn.
The Grand Minister said:
"Dǎng has heard that,
without kinship there is no love,
without love there is no filial piety.
To say that ultimate benevolence lacks filial piety,
can this be right?
【One】【Memorial】To lack love and kinship bonds,
is simply unfilial.
Claiming ultimate benevolence requires unfiliality,
how could this be logically sound?
Shāng Ràng failed to grasp the profound meaning,
and thus gave rise to shallow doubts.
Zhuāngzǐ explicitly refuted this for him,
with the argument laid out in the following text.
【Explanatory Text】"Dàng Wén Zhī" In one edition, "Dàng" is written as "Yíng,"
the Cuī edition is the same.
Some say:
Yíng
is the style name of the Grand Steward.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Not so.
The ultimate benevolence is supreme,
and filial piety is inherently insufficient to describe it.
This is not an overstatement of filial piety,
but rather falling short of describing it.
When traveling south one reaches Yǐng,
but looking north one cannot see Míng Mountain.
Why is this?
It is because the distance is too great.
Therefore it is said:
To be filial through respect is easy,
to be filial through love is difficult;
to be filial through love is easy,
to forget one's parents is difficult;
to forget one's parents is easy,
to make parents forget me is difficult;
to make parents forget me is easy,
to simultaneously forget the world is difficult;
to simultaneously forget the world is easy,
to make the world simultaneously forget me is difficult.
When virtue leaves Yáo and Shùn behind without striving,
benefits and grace extend for ten thousand generations,
yet the world remains unaware of it,
how could one merely sigh and speak of benevolence and filial piety?
Filial piety, fraternal duty, benevolence, and righteousness,
loyalty, trustworthiness, integrity, and purity,
these are all things one forces upon oneself to burden one's virtue,
and are not worthy of praise.
Therefore it is said,
the ultimate honor
discards even the ranks of state;
the ultimate wealth
discards even the treasures of state;
the ultimate aspiration
discards even fame and reputation.
Thus the Way remains unwavering."
【一】【注】It must be spoken in the realm where benevolence and filial piety are forgotten,
only then can it reach the ultimate.
【Commentary】The one of utmost benevolence,
forgets righteousness and forgets benevolence,
worthy of honor and esteem,
how can one use the superficial traces of love and respect to speak of their heart?
Truly, it is not sufficient to put into words.
【二】【Note】All names arise from inadequacy,
thus surpassing the names of benevolence and filial piety to enter the realm of the nameless,
and only then reaching it.
【Commentary】The questions from Shāng Rǎng,
are confined within worldly concerns,
while Zhuāngzǐ's responses,
transcend far beyond the ordinary realms.
Thus, it is understood that the essence of intimate affection,
does not surpass discussions on filial piety,
and adhering rigidly to repute and teachings,
falls short of the discourse on filial devotion.
【三】【注】The Dark Mountain lies at the North Pole,
yet one travels southward to observe it;
the ultimate benevolence resides in being unattached,
yet people speak of it through acts of kindness;
thus, though Yǐng is seen, the Dark Mountain grows ever more distant,
and though benevolence and filial piety are made evident, they drift further from the supreme truth.
【Commentary】Yǐng lies in the south,
while Míngshān is in the north.
Thus, Guǒ's annotation states,
"Míngshān is located at the North Pole;
journey southward to observe it."
Ultimate benevolence resides in being impartial,
yet people speak of it in terms of kindness and affection.
Therefore, though Yǐng is visible, it only makes Míngshān seem farther away;
though benevolence and filial piety are evident, they drift further from the ultimate Way.
This annotation is quite clear,
requiring no further explanation.
【Translated Text】"Yǐng" is pronounced with the jǐng initial,
also with the zhèng initial,
it is the capital of Chǔ,
located north of Jiānglíng.
"Míng Shān" Sīmǎ explains it as the name of a mountain in the northern sea.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that the Suǒyǐn in the Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Sū Qín, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Míng Shān is north of Shuòzhōu.
This differs from the explanation in the text.
"Yù yuǎn" is pronounced with the yù initial and wàn final.
【Four】【Expositions】Reverence lies in outward forms,
while affection springs from the inner heart.
The heart follows natural disposition,
hence it is difficult;
forms relate to human emotions,
hence they are easy.
【Text Explanation】"Xiào Yì" is pronounced with the initial "chǐ" and the final "yì".
The same applies to all instances below.
【五】【疏】Although loving filial piety is difficult,
it still remains within worldly bounds;
it is not as good as forgetting one's parents,
being serene and unattached.
Since forgetting surpasses loving,
there are superior and inferior aspects,
using this standard to measure,
the difficulty and ease become clear.
【Six】【Memorial】When the gibbon leaps and its intestines snap,
the old cow licks its calf,
kindness flows downward,
a constant nature of all beings.
Thus, for a child to forget a parent is easy,
for a parent to forget a child is hard.
Unless one has attained the ultimate Way,
who can act otherwise!
【Seven】【Comment】The one of utmost benevolence,
finds comfort in every joint,
yet remains unaware of it all day long.
When a sage reigns above,
it is not through deliberate action,
but by allowing all to attain self-fulfillment on their own.
Once each achieves their own way,
all affairs naturally fall into place,
every life is self-sufficient,
how could the world not forget the self, each in their own manner?
When all have forgotten themselves,
where then does the ruler reside?
This is what is called mutual forgetting.
【Commentary】One who completely forgets the world
discards an empire of ten thousand chariots as if taking off a sandal;
one who enables the world to also forget oneself
means the common people use it daily without knowing it.
To rule effortlessly at Fényáng while wandering in spirit to Gūyè,
the beauty of yielding the throne
lies in the emptiness of forgetting,
this is the one who completely forgets the world.
Compared to the former it seems difficult,
but relative to the latter it becomes easier;
nothing matches forgetting all in the ultimate Way,
ceasing intellectual efforts to follow nature,
aligning with the transformations of creation,
and uniting virtue with heaven and earth.
Thus one can indulge the innate nature of all things,
follow the actions of the common people,
ensuring both great and small attain their due,
where neither soaring nor sinking suffer loss,
benefits silently spread,
and all things follow their natural course,
the ruler like the highest branch,
the people like wild deer.
At such a time,
where would the ruler be?
This is how the world comes to forget the ruler entirely,
comparable to the era before Xuānyuán and Zhūanxū,
the pristine ancient sovereigns.
Their virtue remains unseen,
thus the world forgets them.
This progression moves from inferior to superior,
from coarse to subtle,
discarding even the discarding,
reaching the mystery within mystery.
【八】【Note】It is only after forgetting Yáo and Shùn
that the virtue of Yáo and Shùn becomes complete;
if one clings to them in the heart,
then it is not self-attained.
【Commentary】To forget means to
abandon and discard.
It speaks of the two rulers Yáo and Shùn,
whose majestic virtue was profound and far-reaching,
yet they also forgot their own virtue,
allowing things to take their course without interference.
This resolves the difficulty of simultaneously forgetting the world.
【Nine】【Annotation】Serenely and constantly at ease.
【Commentary】There are benefits and gracious favors,
that nourish and enrich all living beings.
Even after ten thousand generations,
their virtue does not fade,
and the supreme virtue subtly permeates,
felt daily without conscious awareness.
This explains how the world can universally forget the difficulty of self.
【一０】【Note】Having lost the vastness of rivers and lakes,
one then longs for the mutual moistening with mere spit.
【Commentary】A deep sigh,
is akin to lamentation.
Even with virtues as great as those of Yáo and Shùn,
one can still overlook them without self-display;
how much less would one need to sigh and speak of benevolence and filial piety,
or lament over historical traces!
【Explanation】"Rú mò" is pronounced as mò.
【一一】【疏】Brotherly respect,
means compliance.
Virtue is
the true nature.
Based on these eight matters above,
all are distortions of nature and artificial emotions,
forced efforts and exerted strength,
abandoning oneself to imitate others,
toiling and oppressing one's nature,
thus they are not worthy of much praise.
【Explanation】"Xiào tì" is pronounced as tì.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The old edition writes it as "xiào tì",
pronounced as dì.
This is a reckless alteration based on the modern edition using "tì".
If it is written as "tì",
then there is no longer a dual reading,
so why indicate the pronunciation?
This is similar to other volumes where "dào" is pronounced as dǎo,
and there are also instances inverted to "dǎo" pronounced as dào,
all resulting from later people's alterations and confusion,
now corrected.
【一二】【Note】"Bìng" means
to discard and abandon.
If one considers nobility to reside within oneself,
one may even forget one's own self,
how much more so the ranks bestowed by the state!
This is the ultimate form of nobility.
【Commentary】"Bìng" means
to discard and abandon.
Those who value noble ranks and emoluments

If even the self is forgotten,
how much more so noble ranks and emoluments!
This is the ultimate nobility.
【Transcription】"Bìng yān" bì lǐng fǎn.
Abandon,
means to remove.
Same as in the annotation.
【一三】【Comment】The wealthiest person is one who is
self-sufficient,
and thus removes the wealth of the world.
【Commentary】The wealthiest person is one who is content.
A contented person regards non-covetousness as a treasure.
Even if presented with the wealth of an entire nation,
they would discard it and not use it.
Therefore, the Laozi states,
"He who is content is rich."
This is what it means.
【一四】【Note】What one ultimately wishes for is contentment,
once content, the labels of benevolence and filial piety all fade away.
【Commentary】The ultimate aspiration
lies in nothing more than fulfilling one's inherent nature.
Once praise and blame are unified,
honor and disgrace are blended,
the self and external things are forgotten,
and right and wrong are obliterated,
then renowned reputation
is regarded as nothing more than tears and spittle.
【一五】【Note】It is because one discards the superficial and adopts the substantial.
【Commentary】渝 means
to change,
or to diminish.
Having forgotten wealth and honor,
and forsaken fame and reputation,
thus one's virtue and integrity become pure and profound,
not altering with external things.
【Text】"Qù Huá" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "Lǚ".

in its vastness and silence,

Zhāng,

Xián,

【Explanatory Text】"Běi Mén Chéng" is a person's name.
"Dòngtíng" is pronounced with the initial "t" and the final "ing".
signifies retreat and cessation.
卒，
means end.
復，

惑，

Unaware of the ultimate joy,
upon first hearing it,
one is fearfully startled;
hearing its sound again,
one gradually comprehends its musical essence,

finally hearing it,

【Explanation】"The fear" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.

【Three】【Annotations】Not attaining by oneself,
is what is called sitting in forgetfulness.
【Explanation】"Dangdang" refers to
a state of ease and simplicity.
"Momo" describes
an appearance of having no knowledge.
When the third person hears of it,
they comprehend the profound principles,
thus becoming "dangdang" and without bias,
"momo" and without knowledge,
sitting in oblivion as if in a daze,
where both the self and external things are forgotten,

The Emperor said:
"You are indeed frightened!
I played it through with human elements,
tested it with the heavenly principles,
performed it with ritual and righteousness,
and established it with the great purity.
Now the perfect music
first responds to human affairs,
follows the natural order,
proceeds with the five virtues,
corresponds to nature itself,
then harmonizes the four seasons,
and brings perfect harmony to all things.
The four seasons arise in succession,
all things follow their course of growth;
now flourishing now declining,
the civil and martial modes alternate in due order;
now clear now turbid,
yin and yang blend in harmony,
their flowing light becoming music;
when hibernating insects begin to stir,
I startle them with thunderclaps;
it ends as if without a tail,
it begins as if without a head;
now dying now living,
now falling now rising;
its constant changes are endless,
yet none can be anticipated.
That is why you were afraid.
【一】【注】From this perspective,
we know that the ultimate music
is not merely about sounds;
it must first accord with heaven,
respond to human nature,
be grasped in the heart and suit one's character,
only then is it expressed through sounds,
and performed in melodies.
Thus, the music of Xiánchí
could only be perfected after Huángdì's transformative influence.
【Commentary】Dài means
close.
Zòu means
respond.
Huī means
compliant.
Lǐyì refers to
the five virtues.
Tàiqīng is
the Way of Heaven.

embodied and comprehended the mysterious Way,

【Explanation】"Zhēng zhī" is read as it is pronounced.
Many ancient texts use "huī" instead.
"Dàqīng" is pronounced as tài.
【Èr Shū】, although they once again practiced the traces of ritual and righteousness,
forgot the root of naturalness.
This is the first argument.
【Three】【Explanations】Follow means
to comply;
order means
principle;
constant means

It speaks of spring, summer, autumn, and winter succeeding one another in turn,
all things coming into being in sequence;
summer flourishing and winter declining,

the principle of life and death,
the constancy of the Way of Heaven,

Turbid corresponds to
Earth.
Yin ascends and Yang descends,
the two energies harmonize,

Harmonious energy flows and spreads,
the light of the three luminaries shines,

the sound of no sound.
◎Jià Shìfù said:
In the Records of Music,

【Five】【Annotation】Utilize the cause of their movement as they act on their own.
【Commentary】In the second month of spring,

The startling clap of thunder

Where they begin,

where they end,

Life and death,

【Six】【Annotation】Revolving without limit.
【Commentary】Seeking the principles of nature,

【Seven】【Comment】Taking transformation as the constant,

【Commentary】Fèn means

Now, flourishing and decline, life and death,

If one takes transformation as the constant,

【Eight】【Annotation】Upon first hearing of the boundless changes,

【Subcommentary】The principle of ultimate unity,

I then played with the harmony of yīn and yáng,
illuminating it with the brightness of the sun and moon;
its sounds could be short or long,
soft or firm;
varied yet unified,
not adhering to old conventions;
in valleys, it filled the valleys,
in hollows, it filled the hollows;
blocking gaps and guarding the spirit,
taking things as their measure.
Its tones resounded broadly,
its fame shone brightly.
Thus, ghosts and spirits kept to their obscurity,
while the sun, moon, and stars followed their courses.
I halted it where there was an end,
and let it flow where there was no cease.
I wished to ponder it but could not comprehend,
to gaze upon it but could not see,
to pursue it but could not reach it;
I stood as if aimless on the path of the four voids,
leaning on a withered plane tree and sighing.
My vision exhausted what I desired to see,
my strength spent on what I wished to pursue,
I simply could not attain it!
My form filled with emptiness,
until I became yielding and adaptable.
You, being yielding and adaptable,
thus grew at ease.

Following along flexibly and following one's nature,

【Commentary】When the form fills the void,
it becomes equal in measure to the void;
yielding and following one's nature,
thus one aligns with all circumstances without a deliberate mind;
this is what is called abandoning the body and dismissing keen hearing,
departing from form and discarding wisdom.
Precisely because of yielding and following one's nature,
feelings of fear and apprehension cease.
This explains the second hearing of music.
【Explanatory Text】"Weǐ" is pronounced as yú wēi fǎn.
Xú reads it as the character's usual pronunciation.
"Shé" is pronounced as yǐ zhī fǎn.
Also written as "Shī",
Xú pronounces it as shī.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "fū" is written as "yǐ".
(2) The character above has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) In the Shìdétáng edition, "gǔ" is written as "kū".
I then played with the sound of non-indolence,
harmonizing it with the decree of nature.
Thus, it seemed to blend and chase, flourishing together;
a forest of music without form;
spread and wielded without drag,
dim and silent without sound.
It moves without a fixed direction,
residing in the deep and obscure;
some call it death,
some call it life;
some call it fruit,
some call it bloom;
flowing, dispersing, and shifting,
it does not adhere to constant tones.
The world doubts it,
and consults the sage.
The sage is one
who comprehends emotions and fulfills destiny.
The heavenly mechanism not deployed, yet the five senses are all complete—
this is called heavenly music,
wordless yet joyful in heart.
Hence, Yǒuyǎnshì praised it, saying:
'Listening, you hear not its sound;
gazing, you see not its form;
it fills heaven and earth,
enveloping the six extremes.
'You wish to hear it but cannot grasp it,
and thus are perplexed.
【一】【Note】When the mind has already become lax,
then again be without laxity,
this is its ultimate state.
【Commentary】Upon hearing the ultimate music again,
one follows one's nature and meanders freely,
the feelings of awe and fear
thus slacken and subside.
Although this surpasses the first hearing,
it still falls short of the later hearing,
hence the performance of the unremitting melody.
This is to eliminate weariness with non-weariness,
as Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states,
when the mind is already weary,
yet again becomes unwearying,
this is the pinnacle of it.
This is the third performance.
【二】【注】What is endowed by fate,
is not done through action,
but all occurs naturally.
【Commentary】"Harmonize" means
to blend.
All living beings
take spontaneity as their nature and destiny.
The reason for performing this music of Xiánchí
is precisely to harmonize the spirit of creation,
and to blend with the nature and destiny of spontaneity.
【Three】【Commentary】Blending without attachment,
following the multitude in arising.
【Explanation】Hùn means
identical.
Shēng means
to emerge.
It is identical to the movement of wind stirring things,
following the sounds produced from clusters of trees.
【Explanation】"Cóng shēng" pronounced as cái gōng fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】The ultimate joy.
lies in comfort alone.
Comfort resides within the body,
thus it has no distinct form.
【Commentary】The sounds from the thickets and forests, the pipes of earth,
form the highest music without intent,
merely fitting the nature of life;
how could they possess form again!
【Explanation】"Lín yuè" is pronounced with a falling tone for "yuè",
but it can also be read according to its regular character pronunciation.
【Five】【Note】From Bù'ěr.
【Commentary】It moves the four seasons,
scatters the myriad things,
each finding its proper place,
not by pulling or dragging.
【Explanation】"布揮" is pronounced as huī.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means to shake or vibrate.
【Six】【Annotation】What is called ultimate joy.
【Commentary】It means the ultimate joy is silent and vast,
transcending sight and sound,
hence it is obscure, dim, and without sound or echo.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
According to Shuōwén,
a dense growth of trees is called a forest.
"Forest music" refers to
a collective, communal enjoyment.
When the five tones blend intricately,
one cannot discern where the sounds originate from,
hence it is described as formless.
"Waving" means
to shake and uplift it,
as if cloth is being pulled and lengthened,
yet there is no one actually pulling it.
Forest music being formless
signifies the convergence of its sounds;
cloth waving without being pulled
signifies the lingering nature of its sounds;
obscure and dim without sound
signifies the subtlety of its sounds.
【Seven】【Annotation】Does movement indeed require a direction before it can occur?
【Commentary】The essence of supreme music,
though again without sound,
responds and moves in accordance with the times,
truly having no fixed direction or place,
this is stillness in motion.
【Eight】【Annotation】This is what is called the tranquility of the ultimate.
【Commentary】Although it responds to things and adapts to circumstances,
undergoing countless transformations,
its profound roots remain tranquil and ultimate,
eternally abiding in the deep and obscure,
this is movement within stillness.
【Text】"Yū Yǎo" is read as wū liǎo fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Follows the changes of things.
【Commentary】That which is born in spring dies in winter,
bears fruit in autumn and flourishes in summer,
as clouds move and rains disperse,
water flows and wind follows—
these are the principles of nature,
ever renewing their changes.
The way of ultimate joy
how could it be confined to constant sounds!
【一０】【Note】The sage responds to the world, not by initiating.
【Commentary】To delay,
means to linger.
As for the sage,
it is like the echo in a deep valley,
the reflection in a bright mirror:
when facing it, one does not know its origin;
when it ceases, one does not know its destination.
Things come, and it responds accordingly;
it responds but does not cling.
How could it be that one sets rules in advance and deliberately minds responding to the world!
Thus, whether moving, lingering, scattering, or shifting,
it does not adhere to constant sounds,
yet worldly people
groundlessly harbor doubts and confusion.
【Text】"Jī yú" is pronounced as gǔ xī fǎn.
【一一】【Note】Thus, all beings with emotions and life
depend on it without exception.
【Commentary】What is meant by "sage" is,
nothing other than this:
to comprehend the nature of all things,
and to follow the destiny of the natural order,
hence the term "sage."
【一二】【Comment】Forgetting music yet joy is sufficient,
it is not something that needs to be expanded upon to be complete.
【Commentary】Heavenly mechanism refers to
the natural pivot.
The five organs correspond to
the five viscera.
This means each of the five viscera has its own functions,
hence they are called officials.
The eyes see, the ears hear,
the hands grasp, the feet walk,
spreading webs or rolling pellets,
flying in the sky or running on the ground—
these are not learned through imitation
but are endowed by the Creator.
How could they require deliberate intent to perform!
Thus, the duties of the five viscera,
inherently complete and sufficient,
the beauty of heavenly joy
lies precisely in this.
【一三】【Note】The heart's delight lies in contentment,
not in words.
【Commentary】Embracing this heavenly harmony,
it does not arise from deliberate effort;
thus, the mind finds ease and joy, yet it transcends the reach of words.
【Transcription】"Xīn Shuō" is pronounced as yuè.
The annotation is the same.
【一四】【Note】This is the joy of no joy,
the ultimate joy.
【Commentary】Yǎnshì
refers to Shénnóng.
He admired this supreme music,
and composed odes for it.
The greatest sound is faint,
thus listening does not make it audible;
the greatest form is formless,
thus gazing does not make it visible;
the Dào is omnipresent,
hence it fills heaven and earth, the two realms;
its greatness encompasses all,
thus it embraces the six extremes.
The six extremes
mean the six directions.
Even if one intends to listen attentively,
it cannot be perceived through the faculty of hearing;
therefore, to embody this supreme music,
its principle is subtle and profound,
the mind must be free of discrimination,
and one appears as if ignorant and perplexed.
【Interpretation】"Yǎn shì": must be read as Bì Yáo's pronunciation.
Originally also written as Yán.
"Bāo guǒ": pronounced as Bāo.
Originally sometimes written as Bāo.

(2) The character "gù" has been supplemented based on the context.
Music begins with fear,
and fear gives rise to haunting spirits;
then I proceed with weariness,
and weariness leads to withdrawal;
finally, it ends in confusion,
and confusion brings about foolishness;
foolishness leads to the Way,
and the Way can be carried within and accompany one wherever one goes.
【一】【注】Filled with awe and trepidation upon hearing,
thus it is indeed a haunting,
not yet in great harmony.
【Commentary】The following further explains the meaning of the three performances and three hearings,
concluding the way of perfect music.
Upon first hearing perfect music,
one has not yet comprehended great harmony,
giving rise to fear in the heart,
unable to release and let go,
hence it brings misfortune and calamity.
【Explanation】"Suì" is read as suī suì fǎn.
【二】【Note】The traces gradually fade away.
【Commentary】After hearing it a second time,
the meaning gradually becomes clear,
so the fear in the heart subsides,
and its traces vanish into retreat.
【Three】【Commentary】To consider lack of knowledge as foolishness,
this is the ultimate foolishness.
【Commentary】Finally hearing the music,
the spiritual abode becomes pure and harmonious,
the mind free from distinctions,
akin to being in a state of ignorance and confusion.
Vast and silent,
resembling the foolish and lost.
Neither lax nor fearful,
it elegantly aligns with the true Way,
then, moving and carrying without intent,
it arrives together with all things.
Confucius traveled west to Wèi.
Yán Yuān asked Shī Jīn:
"What do you think of our Master's journey?"
【One】【Commentary】Wèi was originally the city of Kūnwú,
and also the fief of Kāng Shū.
Traveling from Lǔ to Wèi,
hence it is called journeying westward.
Shī Jīn,
the Grand Master of Lǔ,
whose name was Jīn.
Xī,
means "why" or "how."
It is said that the Master practiced the way of benevolence and righteousness to transform the Marquis of Wèi,
but it is unknown whether this method could be implemented effectively or not?
【Explanation】"Shī Jīn" Lǐ Yún said:
Shī,
refers to the Grand Tutor of Lǔ.
Jīn,
is his name.
Zhī Xíng, read as xià mèng fǎn.
Shī Jīn said:
"Alas,
how beleaguered is your master!"
【一】【疏】It states that Zhòngní was wise and astute, quick-witted,
with talents and wisdom worthy of admiration,
upholding the sacred legacy of the former kings,
adhering to the ancient ways of Yáo and Shùn,
which is why he frequently encountered hardships,
and repeatedly faced destitution.
Yán Yuān said:
"Why is that?"
【一】【疏】It inquires into the reason for poverty.
Master Jīn said:
"Before the straw dogs are displayed for sacrifice,
they are stored in bamboo boxes,
wrapped with embroidered cloths,
and the officiants fast and purify themselves to prepare them.
Once they have been displayed,
passersby tread on their heads and backs,
and grass-cutters gather them to burn as fuel.
If one were to again collect them to store in bamboo boxes,
wrap them with embroidered cloths,
and linger, dwell, sleep, and rest beneath them,
even if he did not have nightmares,
he would certainly be frequently disturbed.
Now you, Master,
also take up the straw dogs of the former kings that have already been displayed,
gather your disciples to linger, dwell, sleep, and rest beneath them.
Therefore, you had a tree cut down in Sòng,
your traces erased in Wèi,
were impoverished in Shāng and Zhōu—
is this not your nightmare?
Besieged between Chén and Cài,
for seven days without cooked food,
life and death becoming close neighbors—
is this not your disturbance?
【First】【Commentary】The following analogies
comprise six items in total:
first, the straw dog;
second, the boat and cart;
third, the well sweep;
fourth, the hawthorn and pear;
fifth, the monkeys;
sixth, the beautiful and ugly.
The straw (dog),
is made of grass,
meaning twisting grass into a dog shape for ritual purification.
The container,
is a bamboo box.
The priest,
is a shaman.
To escort,
means to send off.
It is said that before the straw dog is displayed,
it is placed in a box or basket container,
covered with an embroidered cloth,
to achieve purity and express sincerity,
displaying as if present to escort it off,
hoping for blessings,
valuing it in such a manner.
【Explanation】"Chú gǒu" Lǐ Yún states:
straw is tied to form a dog,
used by shamans and invokers.

【二】【注】Discarded objects,
when useless in their time,

Spine,

Cooking,

Nightmare,

It is said that before the straw dogs are displayed,
they are treated with utmost reverence.
After the sacrificial ceremony,
they are discarded on the roadside,
so passersby tread upon their heads and spines,
and gatherers collect them for fuel to cook with.
If one were to retrieve and value them again,
placing them in bamboo baskets,
covering them with embroidered cloth,
carrying them along while traveling or residing,
sleeping and resting beside them,
even if they do not cause nightmares,
they would surely frequently lead to hauntings.
Therefore, Guǒ's commentary states,
discarded objects,
useless at the time,
will instead attract other misfortunes.
【Explanation】"Su Zhe": Li Yún says:

【Three】【Explanations】This combines the analogy of straw dogs,
and also incorporates Confucius's exploration of righteousness.
The former kings,
referring to Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng,
were the emperors of previous eras.
Modeling themselves on Wén and Wǔ,
tracing back to Yáo and Shùn,
they established teachings and legacies,
thus gathering disciples,
roaming in the realm of benevolence and righteousness,
and resting in the land of ritual and trust.
Ancient laws cannot be rigidly held onto,
as matters are like straw dogs that have already been displayed.
The felling of the tree in Sòng:
Confucius once traveled to Sòng,
and was lecturing to his disciples under a large tree,
when Sīmǎ Huántuí wanted to kill the Master.
After the Master left,
Huántuí detested the place where he had sat,
and thus had the tree cut down.
"Xiāo,"
means to erase.
The Master once traveled to Wèi,
where the people of Wèi resented him,
so they erased his traces,
and he was not employed.
Shāng refers to the land of Yīn,
Zhōu is Eastern Zhōu,
Confucius traveled extensively on diplomatic missions,
and was once trapped there.
It was truly due to clinging to the traces of the sages,
that such drawbacks arose.
In such dire straits,
was it not like a nightmare!
◎ Yú Yuè said:

【Four】【Annotation】These all convey the idea of rejecting sages and discarding knowledge,
leaving no room for slight suspicion.
The ancient kings' canonical rites
were meant to suit the needs of the time.
If they are not abandoned when the era has passed,
they become evils for the people,
giving rise to the beginnings of hypocritical imitation.
【Commentary】At that time, King Zhāo of Chǔ invited the Master,
and the Master led his disciples to lodge in the territory between Chén and Cài.
The people of Cài, seeing the exceptionally large number of followers,
mistook them for bandits,
and thus raised troops to surround them.
After seven days had passed,
their food supplies were completely exhausted,
with no means to cook any more,
causing the followers to suffer from hunger and illness,
unable to rise.
In their sorrow and hardship,
they were on the verge of death.
Was this not a case of encountering the already discarded straw dogs and thus being haunted by misfortune?
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "qǔ" instead of "jù".
For traveling on water, nothing is better than using a boat,
and for traveling on land, nothing is better than using a cart.
If, because a boat can travel on water, one tries to push it on land,
then it will never go even a short distance.
Are not ancient and modern times like water and land?
Are not the Zhōu and Lǔ dynasties like boat and cart?
Now, to wish to implement the ways of Zhōu in Lǔ,
this is like pushing a boat on land,
laboring without achievement,
and one is bound to face calamity.
They do not understand the transmission without fixed directions,
which responds to things without exhaustion.
【一】【疏】Boats travel on water,
carriages move on land,
covering thousands of miles
is not considered difficult.
But if one pushes a boat on land,
seeking to transport goods with it,
even after a whole lifetime,
it would not have moved a few feet.
【Explanation】"Tui" Guo reads as tǔ huí fǎn,

how is this different from water and land!
Zhōu and Lǔ's lands are distinct,

【Three】【Commentary】Times change and the world shifts,
rituals too should adapt accordingly,
thus aligning with things without attachment,
this achieves effortlessness and effectiveness.
【Commentary】"Fang" means
constant.

The wisdom of a sage,
extends aid without fixed method,

Not knowing this way,
thus he encountered such misfortune.

And have you, sir, not seen the well-sweep?
Pull it and it bends down,
release it and it rises up.
It,
being pulled by others,
does not pull others itself,
thus in its bending and rising, it incurs no blame from people.
Hence, the rites, righteousness, laws, and measures of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
were valued not for their uniformity but for their ability to bring order.
Thus, to analogize the rites, righteousness, laws, and measures of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
they are like the pear, plum, orange, and pomelo!
Their flavors differ, yet all are pleasing to the palate.

When a person pulls it, it bends down;
when released, it rises up.
Bending and rising, up and down,
its pulling and releasing depend on the person,
submitting without its own will,
thus it bears no blame.
If a person can empty themselves,
the principle is the same.

while the one with the hand radical refers to the object for drawing water.

【Two】【Annotation】It aims only to be timely and appropriate,
and to align with the principles of governance.

As for the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
their paces differed with the times,
their rituals, music, and dignified ceremonies
were not passed down unchanged.
Excellence lies in adapting to the moment,
not in rigidly fixing standards,
nor in valuing conformity to the present to match antiquity.

though their eras varied in simplicity and refinement,

Thus, rituals, righteousness, laws, and regulations
are things that change with the times.
If you were to take a monkey and dress it in the robes of the Duke of Zhōu,
it would inevitably bite, tear, and rip them apart,

Observing the differences between ancient and modern times
is like the difference between a monkey and the Duke of Zhōu.
Thus, when Xī Shì, suffering from a heart ailment, frowned in her village,
an ugly woman from the same village saw it and found it beautiful,

When the wealthy people of the village saw her,
they firmly shut their doors and would not come out;
when the poor people saw her,
they took their wives and children and ran away.
She knew that frowning was beautiful but did not understand why it was beautiful.
Alas,
how impoverished is your master!
【一】【注】What one considers beautiful, another may deem ugly,
so it is fitting to adapt with the times,
thus ensuring everything finds its proper place.
【Commentary】The paths of emperors and kings,
indeed have no fixed standard,
they change according to the times,
and cannot be rigidly maintained.
How can one glue the pegs of a lute or carve marks on a boat to find a sword,
dwelling in the present yet acting according to antiquity!
means satisfaction.
The sage Duke of Zhōu,
represents the age of pristine simplicity;
the cunning macaques and crafty beasts,
symbolize times of contention and cunning.
Thus, though ceremonial robes are splendid,
macaques do not deem them beautiful;
and though the traces of sages are precious,
later generations do not honor them.
Therefore, only by discarding ceremonial robes
do macaques first feel content in their hearts;
only by abandoning the traces of sages
can the common people truly follow their nature.
