【Three】【Discourses】Xī Shī,
a beautiful woman of Yuè,
whose appearance was exceedingly lovely,
suffered from heartache,
and frowned in pain.
Yet, graceful individuals,
whose forms are often naturally elegant,
because of her frowning,
found her even more beautiful.
Therefore, when the villagers saw her,
they cherished her all the more.
An ugly woman from the neighborhood,
upon seeing this, imitated her,
frowning without being ill,
which doubled her ugliness.
So, the wealthy detested her and she did not go out,
while the poor abandoned her and fled far away.
To forsake oneself and mimic others,
the principle is naturally thus.
Erasing traces and cutting down trees,
all are the faults of learning to frown.
【Interpretation】"Ér pín" Xú fúzhēn fǎn,
yòu fú rén fǎn.
Tōngsú wén yún:
cù é yuē pín.
"Qí lǐ" jué jù.
"Pěng xīn" fū yǒng fǎn,
Guō yīn fèng.
"Qiè" kǔ jié fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】As for ritual and righteousness,
when applied at the appropriate time,
they are like Xīshī;
if not abandoned when the time has passed,
they become an ugly person (1).
【Commentary】"Suǒyǐ",
means "that by which" or "the means through which".
The reason why the frown is considered beautiful
comes from Xīshī's loveliness.
That unattractive person,
only admires the elegance of the frowning expression,
without realizing it stems from Xīshī's beauty.
【Five】【Commentaries】 collectively summarize the subsequent text,
concluding their main intent.
Exhaustively examining the events and deeds,
they are fully recorded within the chapters.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the characters for "kuàng fū" and the two characters "zé".
Confucius, at the age of fifty-one, had not yet understood the Way,
so he journeyed south to Pèi to see Lǎodān.
【一】【疏】Although Confucius led three thousand disciples,
was honored as the Unrowned King,
and widely practiced the Five Virtues,
he had not yet comprehended the Great Dao.
Therefore, he journeyed from Lǔ to Pèi,
traveling from north to south to meet Lǎojūn,
in order to inquire about the profound ultimate truth.
【Translated Text】"To Pei" is pronounced as Bèi.
Simǎ says:
Lǎozǐ,
was a person from Xiàng in the state of Chén.
Xiàng,
now belongs to Kǔ County,
which is near Pei.
Lǎo Dān said:
"Have you come?
I have heard of you,
a worthy man from the north.
Have you also attained the Way?"
Confucius said:
"I have not attained it."
【One】【Memorial】It is heard that Confucius possessed the virtue of a sage fit for the times,
yet it is unknown whether he attained the ultimate Way or not?
The reply stated he had not attained it.
From Chǔ looking toward Lǔ,
thus it is said to be north.
Lǎo zǐ said:
"How do you seek it?"
【One】【Memorial】Asked:
"Where does one seek the ultimate Way?"
【Explanation】"How can it be" is pronounced as wū,
the same below.
He said:
"I sought it through methods and calculations,
but after five years had not attained it【一】."
【One】【Explanation】Calculation,
is arithmetic.
Every three years there is an intercalary month,
a minor completion of the heavenly cycle,
every five years there are two intercalary months,
a major completion of the heavenly cycle,
hence the mention of five years.
The Way is not calculation,
thus it has not been attained.
Lǎo zǐ yuē:
"Zǐ yòu wū hū qiú zhī zāi?"
【One】【Memorial】Further inquired:
"By what method does one seek the Way?"
He said:
"I have sought it in the principles of yin and yang,
for twelve years and have not attained it."
【一】【注】This all employs the teachings of Confucius and Lǎozǐ to elucidate the meaning of transcending conventional learning.
【Commentary】Twelve years
complete one cycle of yīn and yáng.
Yet what remains unattained
clarifies that while the Way is approached through yīn and yáng,
the Way itself is not yīn or yáng.
Hence, the following text states,
"In the central kingdom, there are people
who are neither yīn nor yáng."
Lǎozǐ said:
"Indeed.
If the Dào could be presented,
then everyone would present it to their sovereign;
if the Dào could be offered,
then everyone would offer it to their parents;
if the Dào could be told to others,
then everyone would tell it to their brothers;
if the Dào could be given to others,
then everyone would give it to their descendants.
Yet the reason it cannot be done
is none other than this:
when there is no master within, it will not abide【一】;
when there is no correctness without, it will not proceed【二】.
What emerges from within,
if not received from without,
the sage does not bring forth【三】;
what enters from without,
if it finds no master within,
the sage does not harbor【四】.
Fame,
is a public vessel【五】,
and should not be excessively sought【六】.
Benevolence and righteousness,
were the temporary lodging of the former kings【七】,
fit for a single night's stay but not for prolonged dwelling,
for encountering them invites much blame【八】."
【一】【疏】The ultimate Dao is profoundly mysterious,
transcending words and forms in its subtlety,
neither non-existent nor existent,
neither self nor other.
Thus, it cannot be presented to rulers or parents,
how could it be told to disciples and children!
The reason for this
lies in no other cause.
Therefore, it is entrusted to the two sages, Confucius and Laozi, to elucidate the mystery within the mystery.
【二】【Note】If the heart lacks the substance to receive the Way,
then even upon hearing the Way, it will pass by.
【Commentary】If within the heart there is no master capable of receiving the Way,
even if one hears the teachings of the sages,
they will not remain fixed in the mind and heart.
Thus, it is understood there is no other reason.
【Three】【Commentary】If there is no master within,
then there will be nothing outside to rectify oneself either,
thus one has never been truly connected.
【Subcommentary】Since internally there is no mind receptive to the Way,
externally there is also nothing that can match with oneself,
therefore it cannot proceed.
◎Yú Yuè says:
"Zhèng" (正) is an error for "pǐ" (匹).
In the "Zī Yī" chapter of the Book of Rites,
"Only the gentleman can truly appreciate his match,"
Zhèng's annotation states:
"Zhèng" should be "pǐ,"
it is a scribal error,
which serves as an example here.
This text says, "Without a host within, it does not stop;
without a match outside, it does not proceed."
This resembles the meaning in the third year of Duke Xuān in the Gongyang Commentary: "What comes from outside does not proceed without a match;
what comes from within does not stop without a host."
The literary meaning is similar.
What comes from outside
does not stop without a host,
hence this text says, "Without a host within, it does not stop."
What comes from within
does not proceed without a match,
hence this text says, "Without a match outside, it does not proceed."
Because "pǐ" was mistaken for "zhèng,"
Guō's annotation then interpreted it as "correcting oneself,"
which is far from the intended meaning.
In the "Zé Yáng" chapter,
"What enters from outside has a host but is not clung to;
what emerges from within has a match but is not resisted,"
here "zhèng" should also be "pǐ,"
the error is the same as in this case.
【Four】【Annotation】What emerges from within
is the way of the sage;
it only comes forth when there is one capable of receiving it externally.
【Commentary】Yóu means
"to follow from."
That which emerges from within
refers to the sage manifesting traces to reveal teachings.
It is truly because beings can resonate with the sage,
that the sage reveals a response;
if external beings were incapable of receiving it,
the sage would ultimately not manifest teachings.
【Five】【Annotation】What enters from the outside
relies on learning to complete one's nature.
Although one's nature can be cultivated through learning,
it is essential to have an innate quality within,
for if there is no foundation in the heart,
then there is no means to harbor the way of the sages.
【Commentary】To conceal means
to store away.
What enters from the outside
is formed into nature through learning and practice.
When one externally receives the teachings of the sages,
it should be held within the heart.
If there were originally no mind receptive to such entry,
then there would be no storage of the sagely way.
◎ Jiā Shìfù said:
What emerges from within
is following one's own preconceived mind;
what enters from the outside
is learning the words of a single teacher,
being self-satisfied and narrow-mindedly pleased with oneself.
Following one's preconceived mind,
then externally one becomes unable to receive,
and even a sage cannot emerge to force acceptance upon it;
learning the words of a single teacher and being privately pleased,
then internally there is nothing to take as master,
and a sage cannot conceal within that heart to act as its master.
【Six】【Annotation】Names are
what all under heaven share in common.
【Commentary】Míng (name) means
míng (to sound).
Gōng (fair) means
píng (impartial).
Qì (vessel) means
yòng (to use).
There are two types of míng:
one is naming things,
the other is praise and blame.
What is discussed here
is the míng of praise and blame.
【Explanation】"Name is the tool of justice." The Shìmíng explains:
name,
means to sound.
Justice,
means fairness.
Tool,
means utility.
Yǐn Wénzǐ states:
Names have three categories:
first, names for designating objects,
such as square and round;
second, names for praise and blame,
such as good and evil;
third, names for descriptions and appellations,
such as love and hate.
Here, it refers to the names for praise and blame.
【Seven】【Annotation】Excessive adornment beyond reality,
leads to taking too much,
and taking too much brings chaos to the world.
【Commentary】Fine reputations and good names are
universally valued in the world.
If one must seek them excessively,
then affectation beyond truth arises and competition follows.
【Eight】【Annotation】It is like a relay station.
【Interpretation】"Qú" is pronounced qú.
Sīmǎ and Guǒ say:
Qú lú,
is like a relay station.
【Nine】【Commentary】Benevolence and righteousness are
the nature of human beings.
Human nature undergoes changes,
differing between ancient and modern times.
Therefore, when wandering and letting things pass, one remains obscure;
if stagnant and bound to one side, they become apparent.
When apparent, falseness arises;
with the rise of falseness, blame abounds.
【Commentary】Qú lú refers to
a temporary lodging or relay station.
Gòu means
to see,
and also implies a long duration.
Now, a Qú lú guesthouse
is not fit for long-term stay;
likewise, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
should be discarded once their purpose is served.
If a guest stays too long,
faults and disputes arise;
if traces of sages linger,
blame and criticism follow.
【Explanation】"Gòu" is pronounced as gǔ dòu fǎn,
meaning to see,
to encounter.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Zhang Jūnfáng edition cited in Quēwù has the character 者 following 名.
(2) The character 也 has been deleted based on the Zhào Jiànyì edition.
(3) In the Shìdétáng edition, 性可 is written as 由假.
The ultimate person of antiquity,
borrowed the path through benevolence,
lodged temporarily in righteousness,
to wander in the realm of carefreeness,
fed from the fields of simplicity,
and stood in the garden of non-lending.
Carefreeness
is non-action;
simplicity
is easy sustenance;
non-lending
means no expenditure.
The ancients called this the wandering of gathering the genuine.
【一】【注】It changes with the times,
leaving no constant trace.
【二】【疏】The true beings of antiquity,
harmonizing their radiance and descending to leave traces,
responded to opportunities by practicing universal love,
and adapted to things by mingling with the masses.
How is this different from borrowing a path,
entrusting oneself to a temporary lodging,
dwelling briefly in a transient abode—
indeed, it is not the ultimate reality.
Yet in action, they did not harm their tranquility;
in response, they never strayed from the true essence.
Thus, they always roamed freely in the realm of self-attainment,
wandering in the state of non-action.
【Transcription】"Zhī xū" is pronounced as xū.
Originally also written as xū.
【Three】【Explanations】Gǒu,
means careless.
Jiǎn,
means rough.
Dài,
means to give or bestow.
Knowing when to stop and being content,
one feeds on a field of carelessness and roughness;
without depleting one's own possessions,
one stands in a garden of no giving.
Mentioning field and garden
clarifies that these are the grounds where the sage nourishes life.
【Explanatory Text】"Gǒu Jiǎn" Wáng states:
Gǒu,
means temporary.
Jiǎn,
means brief.
Sīmǎ's version writes jiǎn as jiàn,
stating:
it means to differentiate.
◎Qìng Fán's note: Jiǎn,
in Sīmǎ's version, is written as jiàn.
The note indicates that jiàn is the same as jiǎn.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Yàolüè" chapter, it says "thus frugal with wealth and simple burials,"
jiàn fú arises there,
(jiàn fú,
means simple attire.
Jiàn fú,
refers to the three-month mourning attire.
) The annotations in Wénxuǎn [by Pān Ānrén] for Xiàhóu Chángshì's Lěi and the Hòu Jì of Lùshǐ quoting Huáinánzǐ,
both write it as jiǎn fú.
"Bù Dài" is pronounced chì dài fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
it means to bestow.
"Zhī Pǔ" is pronounced yīn bǔ.
【Four】【Annotation】To act with deliberate effort is contrary to benevolence and righteousness.
【Five】【Note】Moreover, following simplicity,
thus it is easy to nurture.
【Commentary】It is only because all burdens of carefree wandering are exhausted,
that one can be effortless and serene.
Simple and frugal,
being content with simplicity and plainness,
satisfied with what one has,
thus easily sustained.
【Transcription】"Yì Yǎng" is read with the pronunciation fǎn of chǐ.
The annotation is the same.
【Six】【Comment】Not giving means,
not harming oneself to cater to things.
【Commentary】Not diminishing myself to benefit others,
thus there is nothing to give.
These three sentences reiterate and explain the previous meaning.
【Interpretation】"To regard as a thing": read as yú wèi fǎn.
【Seven】【Comment】Roam and entrust it,
this is the true essence.
When the essence is true, then the colors are not false.
【Commentary】The sages of antiquity practiced methods of simplicity and frugality,
which were considered to be expressions of genuine spirit and authenticity without falsehood,
allowing them to wander freely and adapt, roaming in harmony with the transformations of nature.
【Collation Notes】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "xū" is written as "xū" (with a different character).
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, "sī" is written as "zé".
(3) Cǎi Zhēn followed the Shìdétáng edition in making the change.
Those who regard wealth as right
cannot yield their emoluments;
those who regard prominence as right
cannot yield their fame;
those who cling to power
cannot share authority with others.
Grasping it, they tremble;
relinquishing it, they grieve,
yet without any insight
to perceive what drives their relentless pursuit—
these are the condemned of Heaven.
Resentment and favor, taking and giving, admonition and instruction, life and death—
these eight
are the tools of rectification,
but only those who follow the great changes without obstruction can wield them.
Thus it is said,
"Rectification means correctness."
If one's heart deems it otherwise,
the gate of Heaven will not open.
【一】【注】There is no one in the world who burdens themselves with what they disapprove of,
yet each dedicates their life to what they affirm.
Those who devote their lives to what they affirm
do not stand in the garden of inexhaustible resources.
【Commentary】Those who affirm wealth and deny poverty,
and are greedy for goods and bribes,
how could they yield to others in wealth and emoluments!
Those who affirm prominence and deny seclusion,
and are obsessed with glorious positions,
how could they yield to others in fame and reputation!
Those who cherish power and authority,
and boast of their possessions,
how could they yield to others the handle!
The handle
means power.
Only those who detest the foulness of worldly dust,
and loathe the stench of glory and profit,
can thus discard them as if casting away refuse.
【二】【Note】The sorrow of abandoning it,
is the trembling that cannot be avoided when holding it.
【Commentary】To wield authority and power,
one fears losing them, hence trembles with anxiety;
to relinquish might and influence,
one grieves their absence, hence is filled with sorrow.
【Transcription】"Cāo zhī" is read with the initial consonant of qī and the final of dāo.
"Shě zhī" is pronounced as shě.
The same applies to the annotations.
【Three】【Comment】It speaks of knowing how to advance but not knowing when to stop,
thus (1) one's life is lost,
and that is why they are executed.
【Commentary】Those who are wealthy and crave power,
with minds dull and benighted,
are solely obsessed with fame and profit,
utterly lacking in discernment,
how could they possibly perceive profound truths and rest their hearts to cease intellectual striving!
Such individuals,
even if physical punishment has not yet been inflicted upon them,
are already tormented in their nature and disposition,
thus they are naturally condemned to suffer.
【Text】"Sāng" is pronounced with the tone of "xī" and "làng".
【Four】【Principles】Enemies must be slain,
favors must be repaid,
take what is rightfully yours,
give to others what is beyond your due,
ministers and sons remonstrate with their superiors,
rulers and fathers instruct their subordinates,
respond to spring by fostering growth,
follow autumn in executing punishments.
These eight are the tools of governance and rectitude,
and cannot but be employed.
【Five】【Annotation】If one holds fast to the old without change,
then one loses what is correct.
【Explanation】Xún means
to follow.
Yān means
to block.
Only by following human principles,
adapting to changes,
and understanding the nature of things without obstruction,
can one govern with the eight affairs.
Correctness and change align with the natural order,
hence it is said that correctness means being upright.
For those whose hearts cannot be like this,
the gate of natural instinct is blocked and does not open.
Tiānmén,
refers to the heart.
【Explanation】"Yān zhě" is pronounced as yīn.
Lǐ Yún:
It means blocked,
and also stagnant.
Guō pronounces it as yān,
and also gives the pronunciation as wū jié fǎn.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as yīn,
meaning doubtful.
Jiǎn Wén writes it as zhēn,
saying:
it means separated.
"Tiānmén" is said by some:
to refer to the heart,
and by others:
to the Great Way.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition does not have the character "zé".
Confucius visited Lǎodān and spoke of benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎodān said:
"When winnowing chaff blinds the eyes,
the heavens and earth and the four directions shift places;
when mosquitoes and gnats bite the skin,
one stays awake all night long.
Now this benevolence and righteousness irritate my heart,
causing the greatest chaos.
If you, my son, could make the world not lose its simplicity,
you too could follow the wind and move,
uphold virtue and stand firm.
Why then must you be so ostentatious, as if carrying a great drum to seek a lost child?
The swan does not bathe daily yet is white;
the crow is not inked daily yet is black.
The natural simplicity of black and white
is not something to argue about;
the spectacle of fame and reputation
is not something to spread widely.
When the spring dries up,
the fish are left together on the land,
moistening each other with their breath,
wetting each other with their saliva—
it would be better if they could forget each other in the rivers and lakes!"
【One】【Annotation】Even if external things add but a small burden,
the harm to one's nature is already great.
【Subcommentary】Zhòngní was confined by the traces of sages,
hence when he spoke, he discoursed on benevolence and righteousness.
Now, when chaff is scattered, it blinds the eyes;
with eyesight dimmed, one cannot distinguish east from west.
When mosquitoes and gnats bite the skin,
the pain keeps one awake all night.
Thus, though external things may be trivial,
the harm they cause is inevitably great.
How much more so when benevolence is not the natural principle,
righteousness does not follow innate nature,
abandoning oneself to imitate others,
thereby losing one's original nature—
the harm this causes
is far beyond mere eye-blinding or skin-biting!
"Zǎn"
means to bite.
【Text Explanation】"播" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "甫" and the final as in "佐" (fǎn),
also read with the initial as in "波" and the final as in "我" (fǎn).
"" is pronounced as "康".
The character is also written as "康".
"蚊" is pronounced as "文".
The character is also written as "".
"虻" is pronounced as "盲",
and the character is also written as "".
"噆" is pronounced with the initial as in "子" and the final as in "盍" (fǎn).
Guǒ reads it with the initial as in "子" and the final as in "合" (fǎn).
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to bite.
"通昔" refers to "昔",
meaning night.
◎ Qìng Fán's commentary notes that "昔"
is equivalent to "夕";
"通昔"
means all night long.
The "Rèn Dì" chapter of "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states,
"In the late part of the early summer,
when three leaves wither, harvest the barley."
(The "Tiānwén" chapter of "Huáinánzǐ" mentions "until the night of mid-spring,
then gather the stored items and seal off the cold,"
using "夕" directly.
) The "Dà Zhuàn" of the "Shū" says,
"the beginning of the month,
the middle of the month,
the end of the month,"
with Zhèng's annotation stating:
the first ten days are the beginning,
the middle ten days are the middle,
the last ten days are the end,
and the character is also written as "昔".
【二】【注】By esteeming it to enhance their nature,
thus chaos arises.
【Commentary】Benevolence and righteousness are more venomous
than mosquitoes and horseflies,
agitating our minds,
causing people vexation and distress,
and disrupting the nature of things—
nothing is greater than this.
Some versions also use the character "憒" for "agitating,"
but it is unclear which is correct.
【Explanation】"憯然" is pronounced with the initial "七感反".
"乃憤" is pronounced with the initial "扶粉反".
Another version is written as "憒",
pronounced with the initial "古內反".
◎Qìng Fān's commentary states that "憤",
in the explanatory text, another version is written as "憒",
and this should be followed.
The characters "賁" and "貴" are similar in shape,
so characters composed with "賁" and "貴" are often confused.
In the "Fú Chǐ" chapter of "Qián Fū Lùn", it reads "怀忧憒憒",
while in the "Wáng Fú Zhuàn" of "Hòu Hàn Shū", it is written as "愤愤" (note two),
which serves as evidence for this.
【Three】【Commentary】Integrity complete and benevolence-righteousness manifest.
【Four】【Commentary】The wind moves on its own and adheres to it,
virtue stands on its own and upholds it,
this is the way that is easy to maintain and easy to practice.
【Commentary】"Fàng" means
to indulge and let be.
To make the common people lose their simple and honest nature,
nothing is better than abandoning benevolence and righteousness,
so as to return to the profound origin of our being.
Zhòngní should also promote the teachings of non-action,
responding to things according to the situation and opportunity,
embracing the ultimate virtue of emptiness and non-attachment,
and establishing unfathomable divine achievements.
There is also an interpretation as "fàng" (four),
meaning going back and forth.
"Fàng"
means to rely on.
【Explanatory Text】"Yì fàng" is read as fang wang fan.
"Move with the wind" Simǎ comments:
fàng,
means to rely on.
It moves by relying on the wind of non-action.
"Easy to maintain, easy to practice" both are read with the yì fan.
【五】【注】To advocate benevolence and righteousness in order to reach the realm of morality,
is like beating a drum to pursue those who flee,
making it impossible to attain.
【Commentary】To establish,
means to strike.
Vigorously,
describes the appearance of exerting force.
To uphold benevolence and righteousness and hasten towards the land of morality,
how is it different from beating a large drum to seek a runaway child!
Thus, the louder the drum sounds, the farther the runaway child flees;
the more benevolence and righteousness are emphasized, the more morality is abandoned.
【Explanatory Text】"傑然" Guo's reading is jū jié fǎn,
also jū yè fǎn,
jù jié fǎn.
"夫揭" qí liè qí yè èr fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Each is naturally self-sufficient.
【Transcription】"Hú" is also written as "Hè",
same.
Pronounced as Hú Luò.
"Rì Qián" pronounced as Jù Yān,
Xú reads it as Qí Jīn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means black.
【Seven】【Annotations】All are natural,
without any partial preference.
【Commentary】Bathing means
washing.
Dyeing silk black is called qián.
Qián
means black.
Disputation refers to
distinguishing victory and defeat.
Now, swans are white and crows are black,
endowed by nature—
how could they need daily washing and dyeing
to become so!
Speaking of the nature of things,
the principle follows this pattern.
Black and white in their simplicity
are each sufficient in their allotted share;
what they encounter is thus fitting.
Therefore, being insufficient in one's share
is the basis for discussing victory and defeat.
It is also said:
Disputation
means change,
yet with black and white distinctly fixed,
one cannot change white into black.
【Eight】【Annotation】The perfectly content forget fame and reputation,
forgetting fame and reputation is what broadens the mind.
【Commentary】To cultivate fame and establish reputation,
attracting the attention of all things,
such narrow-mindedness and inferiority,
how could it be enough to boast about oneself!
Only by forgetting and discarding fame and reputation
can one be considered great.
【Explanation】"之觀" is read as gǔ luàn fǎn.
Simǎ's version writes it as 讙.
【Nine】【Annotation】The praise of benevolence and righteousness
all arises from insufficiency.
【Textual Explanation】"Spring dries up" is read as Hú Luò.
"Mutually breathing on" is read as Huàng Fù,
also as Huàng Yú.
"Moistening each other" is read as Rú Zhǔ,
also as Rú Yú.
"With foam" is pronounced as mò.
【一０】【Note】This is forgetting benevolence and yet being benevolent.
【Commentary】This summarizes the preceding text,
criticizing the drawbacks of benevolence and righteousness.
When the spring source dries up,
fish pass moisture to each other with their saliva to stay wet;
as simplicity scatters and purity departs,
benevolence and righteousness are practiced to aid all things.
But when rivers and lakes surge boundlessly,
each has enough to forget about the others;
as the Dào and virtue are profoundly mysterious,
attaining one's nature leads to emptiness and tranquility.
Since rivers and lakes are likened to the Dào and virtue,
and sharing saliva is compared to benevolence and righteousness,
using this standard to measure,
they indeed cannot be spoken of on the same day.
【Interpretation】"Xiāngwàng" both are read as their usual pronunciation.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Jūnfáng's edition as having the character 傑 repeated,
which is the same as in Zhào Jiànyì's edition.
(2) The character 憤 has been emended to 憤 according to the Hou Han Shu.
(3) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, the character 秉 is written as 乘.
(4) The character 放 is suspected to be an error for 倣.
Confucius saw Lǎo Dān and returned,
for three days he did not speak.
His disciples asked, saying:
"Our Master, you saw Lǎo Dān,
what advice did you give him?"
【One】【Memorial】Lǎozǐ is a great sage beyond the mundane world,
ever-changing and unpredictable,
immeasurable and unfathomable,
hence there is nothing to be discussed or said of him.
【Interpretation】"Bù tán" is also written as "bù yán".
【Èr Shū】's exact names are unknown,
simply referred to as disciples.
They were likely among those who had entered the hall,
collectively raising this doubt.
Having met Lǎo zǐ,
there should have been admonitions and teachings,
yet what did they hear that kept them from speaking for three days?
Confucius said:
"Only now have I beheld the dragon!
The dragon,
united forms its body,
dispersed forms its patterns,
riding the clouds and nourished by yīn and yáng.
My mouth hangs open yet cannot close,
how could I possibly offer counsel to Lǎodān!"
【一】【注】It is said that Lǎodān was capable of transformation.
【Commentary】The virtue of the dragon,
transforms without constancy.
It is used to illustrate how the ultimate person conceals or reveals without fixed form,
thus the essence unites to form a wondrous body,
the wondrous body profound and obscure;
the traces disperse and give rise to literary patterns,
the literary patterns radiant and brilliant.
【二】【注】It means that because there is no fixed method in governing,
it naturally becomes sufficient.
【Commentary】It is said that the ultimate person rides the clouds and ethers without a fixed mind,
following yīn and yáng to nurture all things.
【Three】【Memorials】Xié,
means to close.
When the heart is fearful and unsettled,
the mouth opens and does not close,
how then can there be any leisure to hear words of admonition and instruction!
【Explanation】"嗋" is pronounced as xiē jié fǎn,
meaning to close or join.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, with the following six characters after "xié": "the tongue raised but unable to restrain."
Zǐgòng said:
"Then can there indeed be a person who,
while still as a corpse, appears like a dragon,
thunders yet remains silent as the abyss,
and acts with the force of heaven and earth?
May I, Cì, also be permitted to witness this?"
【一】【疏】The perfected person, when dwelling in stillness, resides like a corpse in eternal rest;
when emerging into action, appears like a dragon-god's transformative manifestation;
when speaking, resonates like thunderclaps shaking the heavens;
when silent, resembles the voiceless profundity of dark principles.
Thus, through stirring divine mechanisms into motion,
they emulate the cosmic duality's life-generating power.
Yet whether dwelling or emerging,
speaking or remaining silent,
how could these distinctions in action and stillness create actual differentiation!
Therefore, the perfected person must possess the unspoken capability to harmonize action, withdrawal, silence, and speech—
which is why when Confucius witnessed this,
his mouth fell open and remained agape.
【Explanation】"Long xian" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
was Zǐgòng's name.
Zǐgòng wished to observe the manifestation of the dragon virtue of the ultimate person,
so he went to see him with Confucius's teachings as his guide.
【Interpretation】"Cì yì" is also written as "cì yě."
【Collation】(1) The Guan Error quotes the Jiangnan Guzang edition: above "rén" there is the character "zhì".
(2) The Que Error quotes Zhang Junfáng's edition: "hū" is written as "zāi".
Lǎo Dān was just sitting upright in the hall to receive him,
and said softly:
"My years and fortunes have passed me by.
What admonitions do you have for me?
【一】【疏】Arrogant,
means to sit with legs stretched out.
To move,
refers to the times.
Lǎo zǐ naturally attained ease,
thus he sat in the hall with pride and extravagance,
responding as things stirred him,
subtly expressing his words.
"My years are declining and advanced,
how can you instruct and admonish me?"
【Translated Text】"Jùtáng" is read as jū lǜ fǎn,
meaning standing on tiptoe.
Zǐgòng said:
"The ways in which the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors governed the world differed,
yet their connection to fame and reputation was the same.
But you, sir, alone consider them not to be sages,
how can this be?
【一】【疏】As the simplicity and refinement gradually diverge,
the methods and steps differ,
whether employing effort or military force,
the opposition and compliance thus vary,
hence it is said they are not the same;
yet reputation and renown,
are interconnected as one.
"You, sir, have dismissed the Three Sovereigns as unworthy sages—
what is the intent behind this,
may I hear it?"
【Transcription】"The Three Sovereigns" in some versions is written as the Three August Ones,
according to the commentary,
writing it as "Sovereigns" is correct.
The rest all refer to the Three Sovereigns.
【Collation】(1) The variant text has "king" written as "emperor".
(2) The variant text cites the Jiangnán ancient manuscript edition, with the character "yě" (也) present below "tiānxià" (天下).
Lǎo Dān said:
"Young man, step forward a little!
Why do you say they are different?"
【One】【Memorial】"You, step forward a little,
explain the reasons for the differing opinions."
He replied:
"Yáo handed it to Shùn,
Shùn handed it to Yǔ (note 1),
Yǔ used effort while Tāng used arms,
King Wén complied with Zhòu and dared not oppose,
King Wǔ opposed Zhòu and would not comply,
hence it is said they differed (note 1)."
【一】【疏】Yáo and Shùn, these two individuals,
are counted among the Five Emperors,
and from Xià Yǔ onward,
they are considered the Three Sovereigns.
Yáo yielded to Shùn,
Shùn yielded to Yǔ,
Yǔ controlled the floods through labor,
Tāng overthrew Jié by military force,
King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ yet submitted to Shāng Xīn,
King Wǔ crossed Mèngjīn to oppose Yīn Zhòu,
their differing circumstances
can be briefly described.
【Collation Note】(1) The Dunhuang manuscript writes these six characters as "Yáo yǔ ér Shùn shòu."
Lǎo Dān said:
"Young man, come closer!
I will tell you about the way the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors governed the world.
When Huáng Dì governed the world,
he made people's hearts uniform,
so that when people's parents died and they did not weep, no one criticized them.
When Yáo governed the world,
he made people's hearts affectionate,
so that people would make distinctions in mourning for their parents according to kinship, and no one criticized them.
When Shùn governed the world,
he made people's hearts competitive,
so that pregnant women gave birth after ten months,
and children could speak at five months old,
not yet reaching infancy but already beginning to recognize people,
and thus humans began to die prematurely.
When Yǔ governed the world,
he made people's hearts changeable,
so that people had cunning minds and weapons found justification,
killing robbers was not considered killing,
people formed their own factions throughout the world,
thus the world was greatly alarmed,
and both Confucians and Mohists arose.
At their beginning, there was some order,
but now it has come to women dominating affairs,
what more can be said!
I tell you,
the governance of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
though called governance,
could not have been more chaotic.
The wisdom of the Three Sovereigns,
above, contradicted the brightness of the sun and moon,
below, disrupted the essence of mountains and rivers,
and in between, ruined the functioning of the four seasons.
Their wisdom was more venomous than the sting of a scorpion's tail,
even tiny creatures
could not find peace in their natural dispositions,
yet they still considered themselves sages—
is this not shameful,
how shameless they were!"
【一】【Memorial】The Three Sovereigns are
Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Huángdì.
The Five Emperors,
are Shǎohào, Zhuānxū, Gāoxīn, Táng, and Yú.
The manner in which they governed the world
is detailed in the following text.
【Transcription】"Yú yǔ" yú jù fǎn.
Xià tóng.
【二】【注】If one disagrees with it,
then one forces a cry.
【Commentary】When the Three Sovereigns practiced the Way,
people's hearts were pure and unified.
They did not only care for their own parents,
nor did they only cherish their own children.
Therefore, when their parents died, they did not weep, yet the world did not criticize them.
If one were to necessarily criticize this,
then those who force themselves to weep would become numerous.
【Interpretation】"Zé qiáng" is read with the pronunciation of its characters.
【Three】【grades】 of mourning reduction,
signify diminution.
This refers to the diminishing of mourning rites based on closeness or distance of kinship.
【Commentary】The Five Emperors practiced virtue,
yet fell short of the Three Sovereigns,
leading fathers and sons, brothers to love one another more closely.
They established graded mourning garments to distinguish closeness and distance in kinship,
which both complied with human sentiments
and avoided improper criticism.
【Interpretation】"For its" is read with a false pronunciation.
"Diminish its diminishments" are both read with the same pronunciation,
meaning to reduce.
The annotation is the same.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
"Diminish its diminishments" means
the intention focuses on mutual affection;
rituals like morning and evening greetings,
the etiquette of bowing and kneeling,
all that stems from the superficial aspects of formalities
can be reduced.
Guǒ Xiàng said that closeness and distance have their reductions,
which is incorrect.
【Four】【Annotation】Teaching with speed.
【Commentary】Shùn was the last of the Five Emperors,
and the customs of the time gradually became decadent,
simplicity dissipated and purity faded,
the people's hearts grew restless and competitive,
leading to pregnant women
giving birth after ten months,
with their children able to speak by five months.
In ancient times, pregnant women
gave birth after fourteen months,
and their children
only began to speak at two years of age.
As the shift from purity to decadence had already occurred,
it thus differed from the ways of antiquity.
【Interpretation】"Pregnant" is pronounced with the sound of yǐn and zhèng.
【Five】【Annotation】"Shuí" refers to
the intentions of others.
Before even being able to choose people as an infant,
it speaks of competing to teach for rapid achievement.
【Commentary】Before understanding infant laughter,
one already discerns right from wrong;
the mind that discriminates
begins from this point.
【Transcription】"Hái": reading as hài cái fǎn.
The Shuōwén explains:
It means to laugh.
"Bié rén": reading as bǐ liè fǎn.
The same applies below.
【Six】【Annotation】If one cannot equate self and others,
then the mind competes over closeness and distance,
thus failing to live out one's natural lifespan.
【Commentary】The distinctions became so extreme,
that they did not complete their natural lifespans,
the beginning of premature deaths,
originated from Yú Shùn.
【Seven】【Annotation】This means that warfare has its proper order,
because there is already disorder in the world.
【Commentary】As they strayed far from the Way,
deceit and artifice grew daily,
causing the ignorant masses
to readily engage in calamitous uprisings.
Abandoning the traces of non-action,
they stirred the mindset of purposeful action,
rewarding the good and punishing the evil,
using this as their means of transformation.
Yet Yǔ, cherishing compassion and kindness,
still understood weeping for the guilty,
and when imposing the blade of war,
necessarily followed the Way of Heaven.
【Eight】【Comment】The thief deserved death,
killing him was justified,
hence it was not wrongful killing.
【Commentary】Thieves and robbers are guilty,
and it is reasonable that they should be executed.
This aligns with the natural order of autumn,
so even killing is not truly killing.
This illustrates that military action can be in accordance with righteousness.
【Nine】【Annotation】Unable to greatly harmonize all things, and people distinguish themselves individually,
thus each person becomes their own kind.
Inheriting the currents of a hundred generations and converging with the changes of the present era,
the degeneration reaching this point,
is not due to Yǔ,
hence it is said to be the world's own doing.
This means that the traces of sage wisdom do not themselves bring disorder to the world,
but the world inevitably possesses this disorder.
【Commentary】When turbulent waves have arisen,
distinctions grow increasingly severe day by day,
each person holds their own biased views,
unable to universally harmonize all things.
This explains why humans possess a discriminating mind.
The traces of sagely wisdom,
cause them to be like this,
yet it is not the fault of Yǔ,
hence it is said to be the world's affair.
【Transcription】"For the seed" Zhǎng Yǒng's rebuttal.
The annotation is the same.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
People form their own kinds to constitute the world,
thus there arises the distinction between good and evil,
and the differentiation of right and wrong.
Warfare,
is what goes against human nature and controls life and death.
Once there is a distinction between good and evil,
and a differentiation of right and wrong,
the use of warfare becomes frequent.
Thus, relying on this as justification,

【一０】【Note】This is a malady that has persisted for a hundred generations.
【Commentary】This comprehensively discusses the traces of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,

Subsequently, the hundred schools of thought vigorously emerged,

Thus we know that when the sages' traces first emerged,

The world is decadent and customs are shallow,

The author of the treatise expresses indignation and laments with sorrow.

【Commentary】The governance of the Three Sovereigns,

The traces of non-action,
arise from arising flaws,
so after a hundred generations,

The manifestations of flaws and chaos,

mountains and rivers to deviate and separate,

disrupting the four seasons,

Zǐgòng stood uneasy, looking flustered and restless.
【一】【注】Zǐgòng originally believed that Lǎozǐ exclusively rejected the Three Sovereigns,
thus intending to equate the Three Sovereigns with the Five Emperors.
Now, seeing Lǎozǐ further thoroughly disparage the Five Emperors,
and even extend to the Three Sovereigns,
he lost the basis for his argument.
【Commentary】Cùcù,
describes a startled and alarmed appearance.
Zǐgòng wished to emulate the Three Sovereigns,
and align with the Five Emperors;
now, seeing Lǎozǐ's lofty and distant tone,
rejecting the Five Emperors,
and reproaching the Three Sovereigns,
his mind and form were startled and alarmed,
losing his intended words,
hence he appeared cùcù,
though his posture remained erect,
his spirit was unsettled.
【Transcription】"Cù cù" is pronounced as zǐ liù fǎn.
Confucius said to Lǎodān:
"I have devoted myself to the Six Classics—the Book of Songs, Book of Documents, Rites, Music, Changes, and Spring and Autumn Annals—
believing it has been a long time,
and thoroughly understanding their principles;
yet I have presented myself to seventy-two rulers,
discoursed on the ways of the ancient kings and elucidated the deeds of the Zhōu and Shào dynasties,
without a single ruler employing my ideas.
How extreme it is!
Is it that people are hard to persuade,
or that the Way is difficult to make clear?"
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"How fortunate you are not to have encountered the sovereign of a well-governed age!
Now the Six Classics
are but the stale footprints of former kings,
and do not represent the means by which they made those footprints!
What you now speak of
is still but these footprints.
Now footprints
are made by the shoes that tread them,
but are the footprints the shoes themselves?
When white egrets gaze at each other,
their pupils do not move, yet they conceive by wind influence;
among insects,
the male calls from the windward side,
the female responds from the leeward side, and they conceive by wind influence;
each species has its own males and females,
and thus they conceive by wind influence.
Nature cannot be altered,
destiny cannot be changed,
time cannot be halted,
the Dào cannot be obstructed.
If one attains the Dào,
there is no situation in which one cannot proceed;
but one who loses it
has no situation in which one can proceed."
【一】【注】The means by which traces are left,
is the true nature.
To follow the true nature of things,
its traces are the Six Classics.
【Explanatory Text】"奸" is pronounced as gān.
The Sān Cāng states:
It means to offend.
"鉤用" — 鉤,
means to take.
"甚矣夫" — pronounced as fú,
same as at the end of the chapter.
"難說" — initial sharp, reverse tone.
"治世" — initial straight, official reverse tone.
【二】【Note】Moreover, people today's affairs,
regard nature as the shoe,
and the Six Classics as the footprints.
【Third】【Annotation】The goose gazes with its pupils.
Insects respond to each other with their calls,
both producing offspring without the need for mating,
hence it is called transformation by wind.
【Translated Text】"White Egret" is read as wǔ lì.

It is the cāng egret.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is a young bird.
"Their mutual gaze with pupils" is read as mào hóu.
"Without moving, they transform by wind" Sīmǎ says:
They rely on the wind's energy to transform and generate.
Another explanation:
They look at each other and form yīn and yáng.
"The male insect calls from the upper wind, the female responds from the lower wind, and they transform" one version reads "and transform by wind" (three).
Sīmǎ states:
The male,
belongs to the soft-shelled turtle category;
the female,
belongs to the turtle category.
【Four】【Annotation】Male and female of the same species
each possess the means to influence one another.
The variations in their interactions
are too numerous to exhaust,
but if they find their proper counterparts,
their transformation is not difficult.
Hence, there are instances of transformation through remote influence.
【Explanation Text】"Species naturally form male and female pairs, hence wind influences transformation." Some interpretations state:
various entities in the world,
are like plants and trees that, though of different kinds, belong to the same category.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas records:
on Dànyuán Mountain, there is a beast,
shaped like a wildcat but with hair,
named Shī Lèi;
on Dài Mountain, there is a bird,
resembling a phoenix in appearance,
with multicolored patterns,
called Qí Lèi,
all of which possess both male and female characteristics themselves.
"Can be surpassed" is pronounced as "shēng".
【五】【注】Thus, the ultimate sage all follow and penetrate it.
【Explanation】"壅" is pronounced as yǒng with the third tone.
【Six】【Annotation】Although transformation has no fixed method, all are possible.
【Seven】【Annotation】None of the locations are permissible.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Junfang edition, which has the character '感' (gǎn) after '下' (xià),
and the same applies to the following clause.
(2) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Junfang edition, which has the character '曰' (yuē) after '故' (gù).
(3) In the current text, '而' (ér) has been changed to '而風' (ér fēng) and then to '化' (huà).
Confucius did not go out for three months,
then he saw again and said:
"Qiū has attained it.
The crow and the magpie nurture their young,
fish transmit through foam,
the slender-waisted insects transform
when there is a younger brother, the elder brother cries
For a long time, I, Qiū, have not become a person with the transforming process!
Not becoming a person with the transforming process,
how can I transform others
【一】【注】This speaks of the natural state of things,
each having its own nature.
【Commentary】The magpie dwells in its nest,
mating to manifest yin and yang;
the fish in water,
exchange foam to serve as female and male;
the wasp takes the mulberry insect,
praying it becomes its own offspring.
Thus it is known that the natures of creatures differ,
bestowed by the great Dào,
as the natural state of things,
each possesses its own nature.
【Explanatory Text】"Fu jian" is read with the rising tone in "fu" and the departing tone in "jian."
Below, "xian" is read with the level tone,
and also as the character's usual pronunciation.
"Wū què rú" has "rú" read with the departing tone.
Lǐ Yí says:
It means to be born through nurturing.
"Yú fù" is pronounced with the sound "fù,"
and also with the sound "fū."
The original text also writes it as "chuán,"
read with the level tone in "zhí" and the rising tone in "zhuān."
"Mò" is pronounced as "mò."
Sīmǎ explains,
"passing on foam" means
nurturing each other with foam.
Another explanation says:
transferring foam from the mouth,
they give birth together.
"Xì yāo" has "yāo" read with the level tone.
"Those that transform" refers to the category of wasps.
Sīmǎ says:
They take mulberry insects and pray for them to resemble themselves.
According to the case, this is what the Book of Songs refers to as "the mulberry insect has offspring,
and the potter wasp carries them away."
◎Qìng Fān's case: In the explanatory text of the Liezi, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying above:
Young wasps with slender waists
take mulberry insects and pray over them,
making them resemble their own offspring.
This is more detailed than what is quoted in the explanatory text.
【二】【注】This means that human nature abandons the elder and turns to care for the young,
hence the crying.
【Commentary】When a younger brother is favored while the elder brother loses affection,
abandoning the elder and doting on the younger,
thus he weeps.
This shows that past circumstances cannot be clung to,
but one should simply follow along,
so that neither things nor self are burdened.
〔Guǒ Xiàng states,
〕It means that human nature, by neglecting the elder and favoring the younger, causes weeping.
【Transcription】"Shě" is pronounced as shě (to abandon).
"Zhǎng" is pronounced with the initial zh and the final ǎng.
【Three】【Comment】One who becomes human with transformation
entrusts them to self-transformation.
If one disseminates the Six Classics to explain, it becomes superficial.
【Collation】(1) The character "qīn" was emended according to the Daoist Canon edition.
Lǎo zǐ yuē:
"Kě.
Qiū dé zhī yǐ!"
【一】【Explanatory Text】Named the chapter based on righteousness.
Deliberately exalting conduct,
withdrawing from the world and differing from customs,
uttering lofty discourses of discontent and criticism,
is merely for the sake of being aloof;
this is what the mountain and valley scholars,
those who condemn the world,
and those who wither away or plunge into the abyss delight in.
【一】Speaking of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
of respect, frugality, deference, and yielding,
is merely for the sake of self-cultivation;
this is what the scholars of a peaceful world,
those who teach and instruct,
and itinerant or resident scholars delight in.
【二】Speaking of great achievements,
establishing great fame,
ordering the relations between ruler and subject,
rectifying the distinctions between high and low,
is merely for the sake of governance;
this is what the court scholars,
those who honor the ruler and strengthen the state,
and those who strive for merit and territorial expansion delight in.
【三】Seeking marshes and lakes,
dwelling in idle wilderness,
fishing and passing time in leisure,
is merely for the sake of non-action;
this is what the river and lake scholars,
those who avoid the world,
and those who cherish leisure and idleness delight in.
【四】Blowing and breathing,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
imitating the bear’s stretch and the bird’s extension,
is merely for the sake of longevity;
this is what the practitioners of Dǎoyǐn,
those who nurture the body,
and those who emulate Péng Zǔ’s long life delight in.
【一】【疏】To engrave means
to cut away.
Intention refers to
aspiration.
Kàng means
extremity.
Those who are biased and obstinate,
unable to grasp the underlying principles,
discipline their bodies and minds rigorously,
elevate their conduct to noble heights,
detach themselves from the world and diverge from customs,
standing aloof and unmatched by the crowd.
They engage in refined discussions of the ways of the Five Emperors,
and lofty debates on the teachings of the Three Sovereigns,
lamenting their talents going unrecognized,
condemning the unprincipled for their decadence and excess.
They harbor extreme aspirations amidst the forests and winds,
erasing their traces beneath cliffs and crags.
These are the recluses dwelling in mountain valleys,
not those who slander the current age.
In their emaciated state, they resemble figures like Bào Jiāo and Jiè Tuī;
in plunging into the abyss, they are akin to Shēn Dí and Biàn Suí.
Truly, they are individuals of narrow perspectives—
how could they be worthy of discussing the ultimate Way?
Yǐ means
to cease.
Their methods stop right here.
【Explanation】"Deliberation" Simǎ comments:
Deliberation means
to carve,
to make one's intentions lofty.
According to the case, it means carving the intentions to make them lofty.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
Intention
is will.
"Exalting Conduct" is read with the falling tone in the fourth tone.
"Withdrawing from the World" is read with the departing tone in the fourth tone.
"Lofty Discourse" is read with the level tone in the first tone.
"Resentful Criticism" is read with the rising tone in the third tone,
while Xú pronounces it as the level tone.
Lǐ comments:
Criticizing the world for its lack of principle,
and resenting one's own lack of opportunity.
"For the Lofty" is read with the falling tone in the fourth tone.
Lǐ comments:
Reaching the extreme of height is called lofty.
"Withered and Gaunt" is read with the falling tone in the third tone.
"Plunging into the Abyss" Simǎ comments:
Withered and gaunt,
like Bào Jiāo and Jiè Tuī;
plunging into the abyss,
like Shēntú Dí.
【Èr Shū】When expressing their thoughts and articulating their ideas,
they spoke of benevolence and righteousness,
using such methods as the foundation for self-cultivation.
These were scholars who governed the world in peaceful times,
people who imparted teachings and enlightened others.
This is like Zǐxià in Xīhé,
or Xuānní residing in Zhūsì,
some traveling to discuss and debate,
others settling down to lecture and explain.
These are indeed the pursuits favored by scholars,
but certainly not the priorities of Daoist practitioners.
【Explanation】"Suǒ hào" is pronounced with "hào" in the falling tone.
The same applies to the following text and annotations.
【Three】【Memorials】They established achievements that benefited the entire realm,
built a great reputation spanning past and present,
brought about the profound rites between ruler and subject,
upheld the paramount duty of the hierarchy,
brought peace and stability to the state,
made the constant way bright and illustrious,
then honored the sovereign and subdued distant lands,
strengthened the homeland and annexed rival states.
Are these not the scholars of the court,
the ministers of the imperial temple?
Such were the likes of Gāo Yáo, Yī Yǐn, and Lǚ Wàng.
【Explanation】"For governing": "吏" is pronounced with the retroflex initial, in the falling tone.
The same applies below.
"This court": "朝" is pronounced with the retroflex initial, in the rising tone.
【Four】【Hermits】They dwell in seclusion among mountains and marshes,
roam freely by lakes and wetlands,
live leisurely while engaged in fishing,
withdraw from the world to abide in non-action,
so that the Son of Heaven cannot make them his subjects,
and feudal lords cannot befriend them.
These are people of ease and leisure,
such as Cháofù, Xǔ Yóu, and Gōng Yuèxiū.
【Transcription】"Sǒu" is pronounced as sù kǒu fǎn.
"Chǔ xián" is read as yīn xián.

"Diào yú" is also written as 钓 in some versions,
same meaning.
Pronounced as diāo jiào fǎn.

In current editions, diào is written as 钓.
【五】【注】These several individuals,
though their preferences differ,
indulge in what they favor,
each going their own way,
thereby achieving a state of carefree wandering.
Yet this is merely their individual fulfillment—
how could it lead to establishing everything universally?
As for enabling all things to attain their proper roles without losing themselves,
it should indeed be entrusted to non-assertive action.
【Commentary】Exhale the old by blowing cool breath out,
Inhale the new by breathing warm air in,
Like a bear climbing a tree to stretch itself,
Resembling a bird soaring in the sky while extending its legs.
These are all methods to guide the spirit and energy,
To nourish the body and soul,
The way to prolong life,
The art of preserving one's form.
Thus Péng Zǔ lived eight hundred years,
Báishí reached three thousand years,
Those who enjoy longevity,
Are examples of this kind.
As for the several masters mentioned earlier,
Their aspirations and pursuits differed,
Each confined to one aspect,
Not achieving comprehensive excellence.
Only from those who do not force their intentions onward,
Can one truly grasp the profound and mysterious essence.
【Explanation】"Chuixǔ": reads as kuàng yú fǎn,
the character is also written as xǔ.
"Hūxī": reads as xǔ jí fǎn.
"Expelling the old and drawing in the new": Lǐ says:

"Xióng jīng": read as the character's usual pronunciation,
Lǐ gives the ancient reading as gǔ dìng fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
like a bear climbing a tree to stretch and guide the breath.

Guō pronounces it as xìn.
Sīmǎ says:
like a bird stretching and sighing.
"Dǎoyǐn": pronounced as dǎo.
The same below.

guide the breath to make it harmonious,

As for those who are lofty without deliberate effort,
cultivated without benevolence and righteousness,
governed without merit and fame,
leisurely without rivers and lakes,
long-lived without guiding the breath【一】,
they forget everything,
yet possess everything【二】,
serenely boundless, and all beauties follow them.
【三】This is the Way of Heaven and Earth,
the virtue of the sage【四】.
【一】【注】What is called natural.
【二】【Note】Forgetfulness,
thus enables possession;
if one consciously possesses it,
then one cannot save oneself from forgetfulness.
Therefore, what is possessed
is not possessed by actively holding onto it,
but by possessing it through forgetfulness.
【Commentary】Those who are profoundly attuned to transformation,
and individuals who silently embody truth and align with principle,
do not force their intentions, yet their Way is all the more lofty;
they lack conscious benevolence and righteousness but constantly cultivate themselves;
they forget achievements and fame, yet the world is greatly ordered;
they withdraw from rivers and lakes, yet remain serene and leisurely;
they practice no guided breathing, yet their lifespan is boundless.
Thus, they can regard all things and the self
as entirely forgotten,
and all things return to them,
so there is nothing they do not possess.
This is forgetting and yet having,
not having through conscious possession.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Benevolence and righteousness
are manifested in the interactions between people.
Loving is called benevolence;
loving based on others
inherently preserves the notion of others;
appropriateness is called righteousness;
acting appropriately based on others
still retains the notion of self.
If there is no notion of others or self preserved,
then the names of benevolence and righteousness need not be established,
and what is cultivated is true cultivation.

【Three】【Annotation】If one forces oneself to do it,
then it is impossible to avoid excess and thus various evils arise.
【Commentary】The mind is not confined to any single direction,
its traces mysteriously align with the five elements,
thus serene and boundless, its way is inexhaustible,
all virtues and beauties originate from within oneself.
【Transcription】"Dàn" is pronounced as dà zàn fǎn,

【Four】【Annotation】It is Heaven and Earth that do not act for the myriad things, yet the myriad things come into being of themselves;
it is the sage who does not act for the hundred deeds, yet the hundred deeds are accomplished of their own accord.
【Commentary】Heaven and earth have no intention of nurturing, yet all things are born;
the sage has no intention of educating, yet all virtues are perfected.
Thus, heaven and earth take generating without generating as their way,
the sage takes acting without acting to accomplish virtue.
Therefore, the Classic of Lǎozǐ states,
"Heaven and earth are not benevolent,"
"the sage is not benevolent."
【Transcription】"Bǎi Xíng" is read with the lower tone in the fourth tone for "Xíng".

Therefore it is said,

Thus it is said,
the sage rests in this and thereby attains simplicity,
and simplicity leads to tranquility.
With simplicity and tranquility,
worries and troubles cannot enter,
and perverse energies cannot assail,
so his virtue remains whole and his spirit unimpaired.
【一】【注】If not for the tranquility and non-action,
then one would endanger their peace and lose their essence.
【Commentary】Tranquility and serene solitude,
are the mind of concentrated clarity;
emptiness and non-action,
are the wisdom of quiescent function;
heaven and earth take this principle as the source of equilibrium,
the Way and its virtue take this principle as the foundation of substance and reality.
【Explanation】"Tiándàn": pronounced as dà zàn fǎn,

correct.

【Two】【Annotation】Rest in placidity and solitude,
repose in emptiness and non-action,
then even when encountering the changes of adversity and danger,
one remains consistently calm and free from hardship.
【Commentary】When one rests the mind in the realm of tranquility and indifference,
and stills the intellect in the sphere of emptiness and non-being,
then even treading through hardships becomes simple and easy,
and traversing dangers turns into a smooth and level path.
【Textual Explanation】"Human rest" is read as xū qiú fǎn,

【Three】【Commentary】Adversity arises from deliberate action,
and deliberate action also arises from adversity,
thus simplicity and tranquility mutually complete each other.
【Commentary】Is it only because the mind is at ease and tranquil that it becomes calm and untroubled?
Rather, it is through being calm and untroubled that one achieves tranquility and simplicity.
Thus, we know that calmness and tranquility mutually reinforce each other.
【Four】【Annotation】Vanished into obscurity, advancing together with the correct principle.
【Commentary】The mind being serene and tranquil,
and the conduct also plain and unassuming,
only when both the mind and conduct
are uniformly non-action,
can worries and burdens of care not enter his spiritual terrace,
and evil energies and ominous atmospheres not invade his internal organs.
Invade
means to enter,
which is used interchangeably in the text.
【Transcription】"Xié qì" sounds like "似嗟反".

【Five】【Comment】Is it only the body that is harmed by imbalance and lack of calm?
Both the spirit and virtue are lost within.
【Commentary】Those who are tranquil and non-active,
not only have an external form free from harm,
but also possess inner virtue that is complete and perfect.
Once both form and virtue are at peace,
then the spirit suffers no loss or deficiency.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition as having "休休焉" written as "休焉休".

Therefore it is said,
The sage's birth is a natural course of heaven,
and his death is a transformation of things;
In stillness, he shares virtue with yīn,
in movement, he flows in harmony with yáng;
He does not initiate blessings,
nor does he start misfortunes;
He responds only after being stirred,
acts only after being pressed,
and rises only when compelled.
He discards knowledge and artifice,
and follows the principles of heaven.
Thus, he incurs no heavenly disasters,
no burdens from things,
no blame from others,
no reproach from ghosts.
His life is like floating,
his death is like resting.
He does not ponder,
nor does he plan in advance.
He is bright yet does not dazzle,
faithful yet makes no promises.
He sleeps without dreams,
and wakes without worries.
His spirit is pure and unadulterated,
and his soul never wearies.
Empty, non-existent, calm, and tranquil,
he thus aligns with heavenly virtue.
【一】【注】Act in accordance with spontaneity and movement.
【二】【Note】Detached and free from all attachments.
【Commentary】The sage embodies the non-duality of labor and rest,
comprehending that departure and arrival are one and the same.
Thus, their life is like the operation of the heavenly way,
their death resembles the transformation of all things.
They entrust themselves to the forging and molding of the furnace,
harboring not the slightest concern in their heart.
【Transcription】"Tuì rán" is pronounced like shuì,
and also has the alternate reading shǐ ruì fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】Movement and stillness are without intention and are entrusted to yin and yang.
【Commentary】Concentrating the spirit and calming thoughts,
one shares the abundant virtue with the great yīn;
responding to stimuli and acting,
one shares the waves with the yáng energy;
movement and stillness follow the seasons,
being without deliberate intent.
【Four】【Annotation】There is nothing to chant.
【Commentary】Goodness acts as the precursor to blessings,
while evil serves as the origin of calamities.
Since both good and evil are simultaneously dismissed,
calamities and blessings are likewise both forgotten.
Responding only after being moved—
how could it be a matter of precursors or origins!
【Five】【Annotation】Movement occurs only when the gathering reaches its peak.
【Commentary】Pressing means,
reaching,
compelling.
Moving,
responding.
Harmonizing without initiating,
meeting the moment with response.
【Six】【Annotation】Acting according to reason,
I have no alternative but to do so.
【Commentary】"Ji" means
to stop.
When the stimulus (presses) urgently,
one cannot stop the matter but responds only after it arises,
not through premeditation.
【Seven】【Annotation】Heavenly principles are natural,
knowing thus to act without deliberate effort in their midst.
【Commentary】To follow means
to comply.
Internally, one removes intellectual knowledge;
externally, one forgets worldly affairs.
Like the primordial chaos acting without deliberate action,
it aligns with the wondrous principle of nature.
【Translated Text】"Qù zhì" is read with the rising tone of lǚ.
◎Qìng Fān's case states that gù means
deception.
In the Jìnyǔ, many such reasons are used to alter one's will,
Wéi's commentary says:
meaning to frequently employ schemes to change their will.
The Lǚlǎn's "Discourse on People" chapter advises abandoning cunning and guile,
Gāo's annotation:
qiǎo gù,
refers to falsehood and deceit.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "The Sovereign's Techniques" chapter, if the superior has many tricks, the subordinates will have much deceit,
Gāo's annotation:
gù,
means cunning.
These are all examples.
In the Guǎnzǐ's "Mind Techniques" chapter, it says to discard wisdom and guile,
Yǐn Zhīzhāng's annotation:
gù,
means affairs,
is incorrect.
【八】【注】Disasters arise from defying Heaven.
【Commentary】In harmony with Heaven,
thus there are no calamities.
【Nine】【Annotation】Accumulation arises from opposing things.
【疏】By following the nature of things,
one is thus free from burdens.
【10】【Note】Those who align with others,
will surely be affirmed by the masses.
【Commentary】Tóngrén,
thus nothing is not in accordance.
【一一】【Note】Being content in one's own attainment,
thus there is no blame.
【一二】【Note】Indiscriminately without any regret.
【Commentary】The sage acts and rests without personal intent,
unifies life and death as one,
hence their living is like the fleeting rise of a bubble,
changing in an instant;
their death is akin to resting from weariness,
truly without any attachment or longing.
【一三】【Note】Entrust it to the natural order.
【Commentary】The mind is like dead ashes,
severed from all connections and thoughts.
【一四】【Note】With the principle established, the response follows.
【Commentary】It is like a mirror hung high in the hall,
reflecting objects as they come,
never premeditating or anticipating affairs in advance.
【一五】【Note】It is by using the world's own light that
it is not I who shine.
【Commentary】The light of wisdom's illumination,
shines brighter than the sun and moon,
yet it conceals its radiance and obscures its traces,
thus it does not flaunt itself before the world.
【一六】【Note】To employ the confidence of all under heaven
is not what I aspire to.
【Subcommentary】Responding to opportunities and answering to feelings,
like a shadow following the form,
as reliable as the four seasons,
there is certainly no error or deviation.
Only when the opportunity comes is there a response,
without anticipation or expectation.
【一七】【疏】When one bonds with the true,
they become so tranquil and still that they do not dream;
when burdens are exhausted,
they are ever at ease and free from worries.
【Transcription】"其覺" is pronounced as gǔ xiào fǎn.
【一八】【Note】One has no desires.
【Commentary】Purity and refinement mean
being unadulterated.
Since there are no dreams and no worries,
one aligns with the truth and harmonizes with the Way.
Therefore, one's spirit and mind are pure and refined, without any gaps or impurities.

【One Nine】【Comment】Desire brings weariness.
【Commentary】Tranquil and detached, acting without deliberate effort,
the mind and spirit are leisurely and at ease,
thus one's essence and soul function effectively,
never growing weary in the end.
【Explanation】"Bù pí" is pronounced as pí.
【二０】【Note】Thus, one harmonizes with heaven and earth in their tranquil and serene virtue.
【Commentary】Praising this emptiness and nothingness,
it aligns its virtue with heaven and earth.

Therefore it is said,
Sorrow and joy
are perversions of virtue;
delight and anger
are transgressions of the Way;
likes and dislikes
are failures of virtue.
Hence the mind free from sorrow and joy
is the perfection of virtue.
To be unified and unchanging
is the perfection of stillness.
To be in conflict with nothing
is the perfection of emptiness.
To have no dealings with externals
is the perfection of blandness.
To show no dislike for anything
is the perfection of purity.
Hence it is said,
When the body is toiled without rest it will become worn out;
when the essence is employed without cease it will become fatigued,
and fatigue will bring exhaustion.
【One】【Exposition】To act against one's heart brings sorrow,
to follow one's desires brings joy,
but failing to understand when to resist or comply
is the depravity of virtue.
【Transcription】"Bēi Lè" is pronounced as luò.
The same applies below.
【二】【注】When the heart is content, there is joy;
when emotions are disturbed, there is anger.
If joy and anger are not forgotten,
it is the fault of the Way.
【Three】【Memorials】To have no preference yet create preference,
to have no aversion yet create aversion,
this deluded mind
is the transgression and fault of virtue.
【Text】"Hào wù" wū lù fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Perfect virtue is always in harmony,
thus emotions have nothing to restrain them.
【Commentary】Neither joyful nor angry,
free from worry and delight,
serene, detached, and unassuming—
such is a person of supreme virtue.
【Five】【Annotation】That which is tranquil and unified,
cannot be altered.
【Commentary】Embracing the mysterious Way of the True One,
blending with the clamorous dust yet remaining unchanged,
if not for the utmost tranquility,
who could be like this!
【Six】【Annotation】His mind becomes thoroughly clear and assured,
leaving not the slightest trace of doubt.
【Commentary】To oppose,
is to go against.
To greatly harmonize with all living beings,
without any conflict or opposition,
if not for the ultimate state of emptiness and openness,
who indeed could achieve this!
【Explanation】"於忤" is pronounced as wǔ with the fifth tone.
"確" is pronounced as què with the entering tone.
"纖介" is pronounced with jiè for the second character.
【Seven】【Annotation】Things come of themselves;
the most indifferent have no desire to engage with things.
【Commentary】Guarding one's lot with elevated sentiments,
not mingling with external matters,
having no needs or dependencies,
this is the pinnacle of tranquility and indifference.
【八】【Note】If mixed with turbid desires,
then there will be something that is not smooth.
【Commentary】With wisdom illuminating and clear,
utterly pure and without impurity,
thus it can blend and unite all things,
greatly harmonizing with the common people.
This discusses opposition and rebellion,
their principles are not different,
revealing the two meanings of emptiness and purity,
hence it is mentioned again.
【Nine】【Annotation】Everything has its proper place,
which must not be lost.
【Commentary】The physical form and spiritual essence
are endowed with finite capacity,
yet their exertion knows no bounds,
inevitably leading to the path of death.
Thus, to labor the body beyond its proper share,
unaware of the need for rest,
gives rise to exhaustion and decay.
When the spirit chases after things without knowing when to stop,
it is bound to become wearied and impaired,
and once impaired, the vital energy will wither and deplete.

The nature of water is such that
when unmixed, it becomes clear,
and when undisturbed, it becomes calm.
Yet if blocked and unable to flow,
it cannot remain clear.
This mirrors the virtue of Heaven.
Thus it is said:
Be pure and unadulterated,
serene and unchanging,
detached and non-acting,
moving in accordance with the way of Heaven.
This is the path to nurturing the spirit.
Those who possess swords from Gān and Yuè
store them in cases and keep them hidden,
not daring to use them lightly,
for they treasure them deeply.
When the spirit flows freely in all directions,
there is no place it does not reach.
Above, it touches the heavens;
below, it spreads across the earth.
It nurtures and transforms all things,
yet cannot be captured in form.
Its name is "Equal to the Divine Ruler."
【一】【注】Emulating the virtue of Heaven means
acting without conscious intent yet harmoniously aligning with it.
【Commentary】"Xiàng" means
to emulate and imitate.
It speaks of water's nature being clear and calm,
adept at reflecting things.
If it is muddied and mixed with impurities,
dammed up and blocked,
then it goes against its constant nature,
becoming unable to ripple and flow freely,
and also incapable of mirroring and illuminating objects.
Only when it remains unstirred and unblocked,
can it be clear and level,
penetratingly illuminating without bias,
serving as a standard for all things—
this is the image of heavenly virtue.
This is used to analogize how the sage's mind is pure and bright,
reflecting without selfishness,
emulating the natural order,
and harmonizing in virtue with the profound heavens.
Therefore, the Lǎozǐ says, "The highest goodness is like water."
【二】【Note】There is nothing that is not the most appropriate matter.
【Commentary】Although he once again harmonized his light with the dust of the world,
his spirit remained concentrated and profound.
This further explains the earlier statement about his spirit being pure and unadulterated.
【Three】【Annotations】He often resided at the imperial court.
【Commentary】Even if there are thousands of changes and transformations,
the mind remains constantly tranquil and unified.
This further explains the concept of being unified and unchanging.
【Four】【Annotation】To participate in the gathering together, that is all.
【Commentary】Even if one blends with the mundane and rides the waves,
it does not hinder emptiness and tranquility;
when interacting with things,
one also does not abandon non-action.
This explains the ultimate state of calmness and indifference mentioned earlier.
【Five】【Annotation】As for those who act driven by desires,
it is human conduct.
【Commentary】Moved by sensing things,
responding without conscious intent,
akin to the operation of the Heavenly Way,
which gives rise to all things without conscious intent.
【Six】【Treatise】summarizes the previous methods such as Tiānxíng,
which are techniques for governing the body,
and the way of nurturing the spirit.
【Seven】【Annotation】How dare one lightly employ one's spirit!
【Commentary】Gān,
is the name of a stream.
Yuè,
is the name of a mountain.
From Gānxī and Yuèshān,
both produced fine swords.
It is also said:
(Yú) [Gān],
refers to Wú.
This means the two states of Wú and Yuè,
both were renowned for their famous swords,
hence the name derived from them.
Now, possessing such a precious sword from Gān and Yuè,
stored and concealed in a case,
unless it is a major conflict with an enemy state,
one dares not use it lightly.
Treasuring and valuing it,
one goes to such lengths,
how much more so for those who cherish and protect their vital essence and spirit!
【Explanatory Text】"Gān Yuè's Sword" Simǎ comments:
Gān,

Wú and Yuè produced fine swords.
Lǐ comments:
Gān Stream and Yuè Mountain produced famous swords.
According to records, Wú had a stream named Gān Stream,
Yuè had a mountain named Ruòyē,
both yielded excellent iron,
which was cast into famous swords.

【八】【注】One who embodies the ultimate of heaven and earth and responds to the myriad things' principles to form their essence and spirit,
is thus as such.
Being as such and yet achieving the merits of transcending heaven and earth,
it is merely by following the course of nature,
not by acting lightly.
【Commentary】Flow means
to penetrate.
Those who cherish and nurture their spirit
can thereby reach out to the four directions,
flowing everywhere without obstruction.
Thence, below, it spreads extensively through the solid earth;
above, it extends to the dark heavens.
Across the four dimensions and all directions,
there is no limit it cannot reach,
active yet ever tranquil,
not one to be used lightly.

【Commentary】Transforming and guiding all living beings,
nurturing and fostering all things,
responding according to circumstances,
not confined to one direction,
thus it cannot be limited by form or boundaries.
【一０】【Note】It is the same as the Celestial Emperor's non-action.
【Commentary】Dì,
means to examine.
It summarizes what came before,
naming it the way of examining reality.
It is also said:
like the Celestial Emperor, it does not act.
