The way of purity and simplicity,
lies solely in preserving the spirit;
preserve it without loss,
and become one with the spirit【一】;
when this oneness is thoroughly understood,
it aligns with the natural order【二】.
There is a common saying:
"Most people value profit,
the incorruptible value reputation,
the worthy esteem high ideals,
the sage treasures essential purity【三】."
Thus, what is called simplicity
means being free from admixture;
what is called purity
means not impairing one's spirit【四】.
One who can embody purity and simplicity
is called a true person【五】.
【一】【Note】Always abide in utmost tranquility with pure simplicity and do not let the mind wander externally,
for that leads to profound obscurity.
【Commentary】The Way of pure essence and simple substance
lies solely in preserving the spirit.
By preserving the spirit without losing it,
the essence and spirit become concentrated and tranquil.
Then the body becomes like a withered tree,
the mind like dead ashes,
forgetting both the self and external things,
so that body and spirit become one.
【二】【Note】Essence is
the truth of things.
【Commentary】Lún,
means principle.
Since one has become united with the divine,
then the essence and intellect are unobstructed,
hence merging with the principle of nature.
【Three】【Comment】Being one with the spirit,
is not about guarding the spirit;
not distancing from its essence,
is not about valuing the essence;
yet in practice, it is still important to maintain this (one).
【Commentary】Zhuāngzǐ sought to evaluate human character,
yet aspirations and values differ,
so he broadly outlined general principles,
roughly categorizing them into four types,
still entrusting it to reclusive individuals
to illustrate that words lack absolute certainty.
Moreover, among the common multitude of people,
all value wealth and profit—
such are the followers of Dào Zhí;
those of integrity, purity, and simplicity
all value reputation—
such are Bó Yí and Jiè Tuī;
worthy men and noble persons,
lofty in principle and resolve,
unbending to worldly pressures,
such are Xǔ Yóu, Zǐzhōu, and Zhībó.
Only the sage who embodies the Dào,
free from all bias and obstruction,
is thus able to treasure his essence and spirit,
unswayed by external things.
Though he responds to change and adapts to the times,
he never loses his innate purity and simplicity.
【四】【注】If one takes lack of deficiency as purity,
then even if a hundred conducts are simultaneously upheld,
and myriad transformations are fully accommodated,
it is the ultimate purity;
if one takes lack of adulteration as simplicity,
then even with the elegance of a dragon and the grace of a phoenix,
displaying extraordinary splendor,
it is the ultimate simplicity.
But if one cannot preserve the natural substance and becomes adulterated with external adornments,
then even if it were the hide of a dog or sheep,
how could it be called pure and simple!
【Commentary】To blend into worldly affairs yet remain untainted by them
is the epitome of pristine simplicity;
to engage in the clamor and dust of change while preserving one's spirit intact
is the essence of utmost purity.
How could it be achieved solely by standing aloft on mountain peaks,
or folding hands amidst the whispers of the forest, claiming purity and simplicity?
Surely, it is not so!
This concludes the explanation of the earlier meaning of the Way of purity and simplicity.
【Transcription】"Qiàn hū" is read as qī liàn fǎn.

means understanding and realization.
Marvelously attuning to the principle of pure simplicity,
then everywhere is the true Way,
thus it can be said that one who attains the true Way is such a person.

Cultivating one's nature through vulgar customs,
and learning in order to restore one's original simplicity;
indulging desires in vulgar ways,
and thinking in order to attain clarity;
such a person is called a deluded and benighted individual.
【一】【Note】Having already cultivated one's nature according to customs,
and yet wishing to restore the fundamental essence of life and nature through worldly learning,
the means by which one seeks it increasingly deviate from the proper path.
【Commentary】"Cultivate" means to govern.
"Nature" means innate endowment.
"Custom" means habit.
"Origin" means foundation.
It speaks of humans receiving their nature spontaneously,
each preserving their innate lot,
following it in action,
naturally aligning with principle.
Yet now they form habits through artificial norms,
manipulating their genuine nature,
posturing and forcing it,
already exhausting and corrupting it.
Then further practicing the Confucian customary studies of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom,
seeking to return to their original nature,
thus gaining more custom yet losing more nature,
the closer the learning seems, the farther the Dào becomes.
【Transcription】"Shàn" is read with the pronunciation meaning good at warfare.
Cuī says:
It means to govern.
Some say:
It means good.
"Xìng" refers to nature,
the fundamental essence.
【二】【注】When the mind is already disordered by desires,
and one still strives to use thought to seek clarity,
the more refined the thinking becomes,
the farther one strays from the truth.
【Commentary】Slippery means
chaotic.
Attain means
to obtain.
Desires,
refer to things that can be coveted such as fame, profit, sounds, and sights.
It is said that the reason people's minds become dim and disordered
is because they covet worldly desires.
Now, if one instead employs a discriminating mind,
pondering and seeking through study,
hoping to attain the way of clear illumination,
it is certainly impossible.
Only by learning without learning
can one return to their origin;
by thinking without thinking
can one attain clarity.
Some versions also read "slippery desires among desires."
【Explanation】"Huá" is pronounced as gǔ,
meaning to disrupt.
Cuī states:
to govern.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
In the explanation,
"huá" is pronounced gǔ,
meaning to disrupt;
Cuī states,
to govern.
It is more appropriate to follow Cuī's interpretation here.
The preceding text mentions cultivating one's nature through common learning to seek the return to one's original state,
where Cuī's annotation also interprets "shàn" as governing.
Essentially, the two phrases share the same meaning;
"shàn" and
"huá"
both mean to govern,
hence the expressions "seeking to return to one's original state"
and "seeking to attain clarity."
If "huá" is interpreted as disruption,
it would not align with the meaning of "seeking."
The reason "huá" can mean to govern
is that "huá"
is similar to "gǔ."
In the "Shuōwén" water radical section:
"gǔ,"
means to govern water.
This is its meaning.
The "Yùpiān" hand radical section states:
"hú,"
is also the character "gǔ."
Thus, the relationship between "huá" and "gǔ"
is like that between "gǔ" and "hú."

【Three】【Commentary】As for enlightening the ignorant,
they must depart from worldly customs and renounce desires before they can approach it.

obstructed.

To return to the fundamentals through worldly learning,
and to seek clarity through contemplation,
such approaches as these
can be said to describe those who are obstructed and benighted.

Those in ancient times who cultivated the Dao
nourished their knowledge with tranquility;
knowledge was born yet not used for action,
which is called nourishing tranquility with knowledge.
When knowledge and tranquility mutually nourish each other,
harmony and principle emerge from one's nature.
Now virtue
is harmony;
the Dao
is principle.
Virtue that embraces all things
is benevolence;
the Dao that governs all principles
is righteousness;
when righteousness is clear and all things feel intimate,
that is loyalty;
when inner purity and sincerity return to one's true disposition,
that is music;
when sincere actions and dignified form comply with refinement,
that is ritual.
If ritual and music are universally imposed,
then the world falls into disorder.
When others are upright yet one imposes one's own virtue upon them,
virtue then becomes intrusive,
and intrusion inevitably causes all things to lose their nature.
【一】【注】Only after attaining tranquility does one know not to be unsettled,
and by knowing not to be unsettled, one does not lose one's nature.
【Commentary】Tián means
tranquility.
In ancient times, when sages governed themselves and the state with the Dào,
they invariably used methods of tranquility to nurture genuine wisdom,
ensuring it would not be dissipated externally.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhi dao" is read as it is,
also pronounced as "zhi" with the fourth tone.
"Yang zhi" is pronounced as "zhi" with the fourth tone.
The rest should be understood according to the context.
【二】【注】If one does not use knowledge to act but relies on self-awareness,
then even if one's knowledge encompasses all things, one remains serene and content.
【Commentary】To illuminate by following one's nature
is to know the nature of life;
to know without deliberate intent
is to refrain from using knowledge as a tool.
Proceeding by relying on knowledge,
yet refraining from forced action—
this is to know without conscious knowing,
to possess knowledge yet remain free from it,
not the knowing that comes through deliberate pursuit.
Thus, one may know all day long yet never consciously know,
nor ever be without knowing;
one may act all day long yet never consciously act,
nor ever be without action—
thereby nurturing this genuine knowledge through tranquility.
If it were not so,
how could one attain serenity?
【Three】【Commentary】To know without acting,
does no harm to tranquility;
to be tranquil and act naturally,
does no injury to knowledge;
this can be said to be mutual cultivation.
When the two mutually cultivate each other,
then the distinction of harmony and principle,
how could it arise from elsewhere!
【Commentary】If one cannot attain tranquility,
how then can genuine wisdom arise?
Without genuine wisdom,
how can one achieve such tranquility?
Thus, tranquility stems from wisdom,
enabling stillness;
wisdom relies on stillness,
thereby attaining genuine insight.
Therefore, wisdom and tranquility
mutually nurture each other.
This is the way of central harmony,
residing within the heart,
a natural principle,
emerging from innate nature,
dependent solely on oneself,
how could it concern anything external!
【Four】【Annotation】Harmony,
thus nothing is unattained;
the Way,
thus nothing is ungoverned.
【Commentary】Virtue extends to the people,
hence it takes harmony and balance as its meaning;
principles connect with all things,
therefore it is named the Great Way.
【Five】【Annotation】There is nothing it does not encompass,
not for the sake of benevolence,
yet the traces of benevolence are manifested through it.
【Commentary】The profound virtue is deep and far-reaching,
encompassing all without exception,
its compassion and love are vast and extensive,
thus the traces of benevolence are revealed here.
【Six】【Annotation】There is nothing that is not orderly,
not for the sake of righteousness,
yet the merit of righteousness becomes evident.
【Commentary】The Way can penetrate all things,
and each thing accords with its principle.
Since the principle is appropriate,
righteousness and merit become evident.
【Seven】【Annotation】If one understands righteousness but does not follow loyalty,
then things will become increasingly distant.
【Commentary】The principles are clear and evident,
with sincerity arising from within,
there is no pretense or affectation,
hence all beings draw near and adhere.
【八】【注】When benevolence and righteousness arise from within,
and one returns to follow one's innate disposition,
then the will is fulfilled;
the will is fulfilled,
and its manifestation is joy.
【Commentary】Since benevolence and righteousness originate from within,
the will and nature are pure and sincere;
even when interacting with external objects, they always return to genuine emotions.
What is achieved is harmony and appropriateness,
hence it is called music.
【Transcription】"Lè yě" is pronounced as luò.

【九】【注】When trustworthiness in conduct and demeanor conforms to the natural rhythms and patterns,
its manifestation is ritual propriety.
【Commentary】When trustworthiness and conduct are prominent,
and one's demeanor and appearance conform to norms without violating the rules of propriety,
such manifestations are indeed the essence of ritual.
【Transcription】"Xìn Xíng": Xià Mèng fǎn.

what one mind finds pleasure in,

The people of old,
amidst the primordial chaos,
lived their entire lives in tranquility and indifference.
At that time,
yīn and yáng harmoniously settled,
spirits and deities caused no disturbances,
the four seasons followed their proper course,
the myriad things remained unharmed,
and all living beings did not meet untimely deaths.
Though humans possessed knowledge,
they had no use for it.
This is what is called the state of perfect unity.
At that time,
nothing was done, yet everything constantly followed its natural course.
【One】【Memorial】It is said that before the Three Sovereigns,
in the profound antiquity, there were rulers without names or titles.
At that time, the pure customs had not yet dissipated,
so they dwelled in a state of chaos and obscurity, becoming one with the era and the world.
They were dark and without traces,
with no interaction between rulers and subjects, superiors and inferiors.
All attained the Way of tranquility, indifference, silence, and non-action.
【Transcription】"In Hun" is pronounced as Hú běn fǎn.
"Máng" is pronounced as Mò gāng fǎn.
Cuī says:
"Hun hun máng máng,"
refers to the time before differentiation.
"Dàn" is pronounced as Tú zàn fǎn.
【二】【注】Simply let things take their natural course.
【Commentary】This must refer to the era of primal chaos,
an age of pristine simplicity,
when the whole world was tranquil and serene,
and all beings embodied non-action.
Thus, yin ascended and yang descended,
the two energies harmonized in peaceful stillness;
spirits remained obscure and humans manifest,
each keeping to their station without disturbance.
Heat and cold followed in due order,
the four seasons observed their rhythms,
with neither calamity nor misfortune,
the myriad things remained unharmed,
all living beings fulfilled their natural lifespans,
ending without premature death.
Though humans possessed the capacity for knowledge and cunning,
through non-action,
they had no use for it.
【Explanation】"Bù rǎo" is read with a slight retroflex sound.
【Three】【Annotation】All things are spontaneous,
thus reaching the ultimate oneness.
【Subcommentary】Equalizing self and other through non-action,
blending right and wrong in serene indifference,
where things and self are not two,
thus it is called the ultimate oneness.
"Mò,"
means without.
Doing nothing yet accomplishing naturally,
is non-action;
not knowing why it is so yet it is so,
is spontaneity.
Therefore, at that time,
people embraced the virtue of non-action,
and things contained the way of spontaneity.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: "Zìrán,"
means self-completion.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
"Rán,"
means to complete.
The "Dà Dài Lǐ · Wǔwáng Jiànzuò Piān" says, "Do not say how can it be destroyed,
its calamity will 'rán',"
meaning the calamity will form.
The "Chǔcí · Yuǎnyóu" says, "Do not disturb your soul,
it will 'zìrán',"

【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition, where "de" is written as "ying".
When virtue later declined,
reaching the time of Suìrén and Fúxī who began to rule the world,
then there was compliance but not unity.
When virtue further declined,
reaching the time of Shénnóng and Huángdì who began to rule the world,
then there was stability but not compliance.
When virtue further declined,
reaching the time of Tángyáo and Yǔshùn who began to rule the world,
they initiated the flow of governance and transformation,
weakening purity and scattering simplicity,
departing from the Way in their goodness,
endangering virtue in their conduct,
only then abandoning their innate nature to follow their minds.
When mind and mind employed knowledge yet were insufficient to stabilize the world,
only then adding ornamentation to it,
supplementing it with erudition.
Ornamentation destroyed substance,
erudition drowned the mind,
only then did the people begin to be confused and chaotic,
unable to return to their innate disposition and restore their original state.
【一】【注】The reason why virtue declines is that,
since sages do not continue through generations,
those in high positions cannot embody non-action yet admire the traces of non-action,
thus leading to this flaw.
【二】【Note】The world has already lost its unity,
confusion cannot be resolved,
therefore, explain without delving deep,
and simply follow it as it is.
【Commentary】Dǎi,
means "to reach."
In ancient times, people ate raw meat and drank blood,
living among herds of deer.
It was not until Suìrén began to cook raw food,
and Fúxī tamed oxen and rode horses,
established kitchens,
drew the Eight Trigrams to create writing,
and imitated spiders to craft intricate nets.
Thereafter, cunning and deceit sprouted,
desires gradually arose,
eroding the heart of simplicity and purity,
scattering the way of non-action.
As virtue declined, they began to rule the world,
is this what it means!
This was顺应ing the hearts of the common people,
yet unable to blend them into ultimate unity.
【Transcription】"Suìrén" is pronounced as suì.
【Three】【Annotation】One should be content with what brings them peace.
【Commentary】As virtuous governance further declines,
the resulting malpractices grow increasingly severe.
Hence, Shénnóng launched the campaign against Gònggōng,
and Huángdì waged war against Chīyóu.
As baleful influences did not cease,
armed conflicts repeatedly arose.
Thus, eradicating tyranny and eliminating cruelty,
comforting the people and punishing the guilty—
even if temporarily seeking stability under heaven,
could not bring harmony to all living beings.
【Four】【Commentary】The sage has no personal intentions,
but lets the world form itself.
Whether it becomes pure or shallow,
neither is due to the sage.
The sage can only allow the world to attain its own state,
how could they make the world attain sagehood?!
Thus, the traces of emperors and kings
change along with the times,
yet the way of the sage has never been incomplete.
【Commentary】Now, Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn,
though positioned at the end of the Five Emperors,
rose to establish governance and propagate transformation,
standing at the forefront of the Three Sovereigns.
Thus, they instituted the Five Canons to regulate the Five Elements,
and established the hundred officials to harmonize and enlighten the common people.
Yet, the common people, because of this, became corrupt and deceitful,
and the Five Elements from then on fell into disarray and peril.
Branching streams and divided factions
have persisted up to this very day.
Is it not indeed the case that they destroyed purity and simplicity to create corruption and deceit,
scattering unadorned substance to produce flashy falsity?
【Explanatory Text】"Xingzhi" is read with the tone of an upright official.
"(Shuǐ Xiāo)" is pronounced as in ancient times.
It is also written as "Jiǎo".
"Chún" is also written as "Chún",
pronounced as pure.
【Five】【Annotation】The term "good" refers to
exceeding what is appropriate,
hence having goodness does not mean the Way is complete.
【Commentary】The Way that is empty and all-pervading
forgets both good and evil.
Now, abandoning oneself to imitate others,
boasting of reputation and striving for goodness,
such goodness already violates the principle,
hence it is called separation.
【Explanation】"Zhī chēng" is read with the initial "chǐ" and the final "zhèng" in reverse.
【Six】【Comment】The one who acts,
goes against their nature in action,
thus when actions are established, virtue does not become level.
【Commentary】"Perilous" means
hazardous and obstructed.
Being unable to follow one's true nature and act genuinely,
concealing one's traces,
but instead forcing one's disposition to establish conduct for the sake of gaining reputation,
truly arises from external actions and reputations being superficial and false,
thus causing inner virtue to be in danger.
How could there be any peace and tranquility!

This interpretation takes the words at face value,
and is not logically consistent.

meaning what is done is not the great Way,

The "Chù Zhēn" chapter of Huái Nán Zǐ states: Departing from the Way with artifice,
("zá" should be a miswriting of the character "lí".)
"wěi",
in ancient times, was the character "wéi",
and "wéi" also means to act.)
endangering virtue to act,
("jiǎn" and "xiǎn",
ancient characters are interchangeable.)
The "Běn Xiào" chapter of Zēng Zǐ says: not engaging in perilous conduct to seek luck,
the Hàn dynasty Shèn Lìng Liú Xiū inscription reads: acting from a perilous center,
in both cases "jiǎn" should be read as "xiǎn".)
The "Fù Guó" chapter of Xún Zǐ states: customs are perilous and the people are not unified,
Yáng Liàng's commentary:
"jiǎn" should be "xiǎn".)
which is based on this.
【Seven】【Annotation】When the mind enslaves itself,
then nature is lost.
【Commentary】Departing from the path of emptiness and penetration,
abandoning the virtue of purity and harmony,
then one discards the nature of spontaneity,
and follows the mind of discrimination.
【Eight】【Annotation】The minds of self and others,
vie to be the first to perceive,
no longer act according to their innate nature.
【Commentary】The minds of self and others,
mutually scheming and considering,
debating right and wrong, good and bad,
all strive to be the ones with foresight.
【Interpretation】"Xīn yǔ xīn shí" is read as written.
All versions are the same.
Xiàng's version writes "zhí",
stating:
"The minds of self and others,
compete to take precedence in duty."
Since Guō's annotation aligns with Xiàng's,
it should also be written as "zhí".
【Nine】【Annotation】Forget knowledge and follow one's nature,
this is stability.
【Subcommentary】When the mind clings to realms of existence,
and knowledge discriminates without bounds,
the six directions become as smoke and dust,
the eight wastelands surge and seethe,
the four seasons thus fall into disorder,
and the three luminaries thus comet and conflict.
This is the source of calamity and chaos,
how could it suffice to bring order to the world!
◎Jiāshìfù comments:
Guō Xiàng states,
"The minds of self and other,
vie to be the first to perceive,
no longer following their innate nature."
Various editions all punctuate "mind and mind's perception" as one phrase.
Xiàng Xiù's edition uses "duty",
saying,
"The minds of self and other,
vie to be the first in duty."
I suspect "mind and mind"
does not mean self and other have different minds,
but that the mind itself becomes differentiated.
The original state is one mind,
yet when drawn into activity, it becomes another mind.
Drawn into activity,
a single thought's awareness gives rise to perception—
in winter perceiving cold,
in summer perceiving warmth, this is it;
from awareness arises intention, yielding knowledge—
when eating, knowing to seek sweetness,
when dressing, knowing to seek warmth, this is it.
Buddhists divide consciousness into two realms.
Knowledge
is the expression of intention,
hence it is said: "Without perception or knowledge,
follow the rule of the Emperor."
Perception
is the clarity of the inner mind;
knowledge
is the communication of the outer mind.
When perception and knowledge arise together, chaos begins to flourish,
how could this suffice to bring order to the world!
◎Yú Yuè comments:
"Perception" and "knowledge" form a connected phrase.
The Book of Songs says,
"Without perception or knowledge,"
showing perception and knowledge share meaning,
hence they are connected as "perception-knowledge."
"Mind and mind's perception-knowledge" being insufficient to bring order to the world
clearly means one must be without perception or knowledge before one can speak of bringing order.
Other scholars all break at "perception" as the end of the phrase,
which is incorrect;
Xiàng's edition uses "duty",
which is even more incorrect.
【一０】【Note】Wén bó is the adornment of the heart's substance.
【Commentary】Previously, when one merely employed the mind to operate knowledge,
it was insufficient to bring stability to the world.
Therefore, later generations relied on documents and writings to rectify the times,
and with each era, increasing erudition to aid society.
They did not realize that substance is the foundation of refinement,
and that ornate refinement obscures and diminishes the plain substance.
Erudition is but a branch of the mind,
and extensive learning can submerge and drown the innate spirit.
Only by abandoning learning and discarding refinement
can one truly embody the beauty of non-action.
【Transcription】"Bó nì" is read as nǎi lì fǎn,
Guō reads it as nú xué fǎn.
【One One】【Annotation】At the beginning,
it refers to the root of nature and life.
【Commentary】When literary embellishment is obscured and extinguished by plain substance,
and extensive learning is submerged and drowned in the heart and mind,
then the ignorant masses begin to form chaos.
To wish to return to their tranquil and indifferent innate nature,
and restore their original state of natural simplicity,
how could it be possible!
Alas,
the mind recognizes the error of excessive literary refinement and broad knowledge!
【Collation】（一）The Shìdétáng edition has ● in place of ●.
（二）The character "yǐn" is supplemented based on the commentary text in the preceding sentence.
From this perspective,
the age has lost the Way,
and the Way has lost the age.
The age and the Way have mutually lost each other;
how can a person of the Way arise in the age,
and how can the age arise through the Way?
The Way has no means to arise in the age,
and the age has no means to arise through the Way.
Even if a sage does not dwell in the mountains and forests,
their virtue remains hidden.
【一】【注】The Way, by not being valued,
is thus able to endure in the world.
However, when the world endures, it values it,
and by valuing it,
the Way is thereby lost.
The Way cannot prevent the world from valuing it,
nor can the world refrain from valuing the Way,
thus they mutually cause each other's loss.
【Commentary】Sàng means to abandon.
It is to discard.
By observing from these events,
it is understood that the times have become shallow and superficial,
abandoning the way of non-action,
and likewise, because of the way of non-action,
the simple and harmonious age has been discarded and transformed.
Thus, it is known that the world and the way mutually abandon each other.
【Translated Text】"Shì sàng" is pronounced with "shì" as xì làng fǎn.
The following and annotations are all the same.
◎Qìng Fān's case: In the selection of literary works, Jiāng Wénchōng's miscellaneous style poem annotation quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
The world all follows different doctrines and loses the Dào,
the Dào does not favor the world,
hence it is called lost.
The explanation text is missing.
【二】【注】If not valued,
then they mutually arise together.
【Commentary】Therefore, the sage who embraces the Way,
transcends worldly customs with lofty steps,
unwilling to promote and govern the world,
and in an age of decadence and hypocrisy,
how could the people be inspired by the Way of the sage!
【Three】【Annotations】The reason they are not concealed now,
is because they have emotions to arise from.
How do they arise?
From having no nobility.
【Commentary】In the decadent age,
the Way could not be employed,
and the path of non-action
no longer prevailed in the world.
Even if a sage embodying the Way
descended into the dusty mundane world,
blending with the masses,
no one would recognize them.
Concealing their sagely virtue,
they could not be seen or employed.
Though dwelling in court or marketplace,
how would it differ from residing in mountain forests!
To conceal oneself,
is not originally to conceal oneself.
Those whom the ancients called reclusive scholars
did not hide their persons and refuse to be seen,
nor did they shut their mouths and refuse to speak out,
nor did they conceal their wisdom and refuse to express it.
It was because the times and fate were greatly awry.
When encountering the right time and fate to greatly act upon the world,
they would return to unity without leaving a trace;
when not encountering the right time and fate and being greatly constrained in the world,
they would deepen their roots and calm their utmost to wait;
this is the way to preserve one's life.
【一】【注】If one conceals oneself yet utilizes things,
then the Way and the world mutually flourish;
how can there be any concealment at all!
【Commentary】The times were beset by chaos and darkness,
thus the way of the sages could not prevail.
How could this mean they concealed their brilliance and hid their virtue away!
【二】【注】They do not know to return to the One to cease the traces, yet chase after the traces to seek the One.
The more they gain traces,
the more they lose the One.
This is a great fallacy.
Even if they rise to illuminate it,
speak out to express it,
or reveal knowledge to elucidate it,
how could these lead to mutual flourishing?
They only result in mutual loss.
【Explanation】Mistaken,
it means false and absurd.
It is not that they conceal themselves and remain unseen,
but even when seen, they do not disrupt the group;
it is not that they keep their words unspoken,
but even when spoken, they do not offend others;
it is not that they hide their wisdom and do not express it,
but even when expressed, they do not dazzle or confuse;
rather, it is because the times are fraught with falsehood and absurdity,
and fate encounters hardship and obstruction,
that they adapt to the world's fluctuations,
preserving their lives and avoiding harm.
【Transcription】"Not seen" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
"Only where" is pronounced as zhī.
【Three】【Comment】This is a time of tranquility and indifference.
【Four】【Annotation】By returning to the nature of things, their essence naturally becomes unified,
thus leaving no trace.
【Commentary】When the times meet with the Way,
and fate belongs to clarity and peace,
then virtue is spread and transformation broadened,
greatly practiced throughout the world.
Subsequently, each person returns to oneness,
and every thing reverts to its root,
where self and other mysteriously align,
hence leaving no trace of self.
【五】【Note】This is a time when one cannot remain indifferent.
【Six】【Annotation】Even in times of turmoil,
the sage has never ceased to be tranquil and detached.
Therefore, they establish deep roots and maintain utmost serenity, awaiting the natural course of events.
This is how the Way remains undiminished.
【Commentary】In times beset by unprincipled rule,
and fate met with decadence and indulgence,
when virtuous influence fails to prevail,
it brings great hardship across the land.
Yet by deeply rooting oneself in the foundation of spontaneity,
preserving the ultimate nature of tranquility,
adapting arrangements to follow the course of change,
and abiding in constancy while awaiting the end of one's years,
how could there be any room for concerns over adversity, success, joy, or sorrow?
【Seven】【Annotation】There has never been one whose self was preserved yet whose era did not flourish.
【Commentary】To be constantly joyful even in destitution and isolation,
to remain peaceful and secure even amidst peril and danger,
to accept the world's shifts between engagement and withdrawal,
this may be called the way of preserving one's self.
The ancients who cultivated their persons
did not use eloquence to adorn knowledge,
did not use knowledge to exhaust the world,
nor did they use knowledge to exhaust their virtue.
Composedly they stayed in their proper place and returned to their nature—
what more was there to do!
The Way is not meant for petty conduct,
virtue is not meant for petty knowledge.
Petty knowledge injures virtue,
petty conduct injures the Way.
Therefore it is said,
Just rectify yourself, that is all.
To find joy in wholeness is called attaining one's aim.
【一】【注】Simply follow one's genuine understanding.
【Commentary】The ancients valued reticence over eloquence,
esteemed actions above words.
Therefore, those who entrusted themselves to the ways of the ancients
would certainly not employ flashy rhetoric
or adorn petty wisdom of discrimination.
【二】【注】This is the sentiment of indifference to fame and fortune.
【Commentary】"Qióng" means
being trapped and burdened,
not indulging in the knowledge of poison and harm to cause suffering to the common people.
【Explanation】"Dàn": pronounced as dà zàn fǎn.
"Pò": pronounced as bó.
【Three】【Annotation】Maintain one's own virtue, that is all.
【Commentary】To know where to stop is to understand one's proper place,
so as not to burden one's self-attainment with boundless pursuits.
【Four】【Annotation】Wēi rán,
describes the appearance of standing alone and upright.
【Commentary】"Wēi" (危),
means "dú" (獨, solitary).
It speaks of dwelling alone amidst a chaotic world,
residing in peril yet finding peace and joy where one is,
acting without harming tranquility,
constantly returning to the natural disposition,
following one's nature in action,
what more is there to do?
This speaks of its non-action.
【Explanation】"危然" is read according to its standard pronunciation.
Guǒ Xiàng comments:
A solitary and upright appearance.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as "",
and states:
An appearance of standing alone.
The Cuī version writes it as "垝",
pronounced like the "垝" in "累垝".
"垝然"
means a self-possessed and stable appearance.
【五】【注】Traveling on a level road.
【Commentary】The Great Way is vast and boundless,
encompassing all without exception;
minor achievements obscure the Way,
thus they are not trivial practices.
【Explanatory Text】"於坦" is read as chì dǎn fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Vast and greatly penetrating.
【Commentary】The person of superior virtue,
with wisdom encompassing all things,
how could they dwell on judgments of right and wrong as a means of discernment!
【Text】"Kuài rán" kǔ duì fǎn.
【Seven】【Neglects】Small insights and minor knowledge,
impair the profound and mysterious great virtue;
trivial learning and petty actions,
damage the vast and penetrating great Way.
【Eight】【Annotation】To attain one's own aspirations,
to pacify one's heart in solitude,
and to be without the emotions of sorrow or joy,
this is the perfection of happiness.
【Commentary】When one's own person treads the path of righteousness,
then all actions become empty and penetrating.
Subsequently, there is neither compliance nor opposition,
forgetting both sorrow and joy,
all that is created is fitting,
this is the wholeness of joy.
The ultimate joy is complete,
and only then can one's will and nature be fulfilled.
【Transcription】"Lè Quán" is pronounced as luò.
The same applies to the annotations and the following instances.
【Collation】(1) In the Shìdétáng edition, "xíng" is written as "cún".
(2) The Quēwù cites the Zhāng Jūnfáng edition, which has the character "hū" following "wèi".
(3) For "the one who embodies music in its entirety,"
