What the ancients called the fulfillment of ambition
did not refer to carriages and official caps,
but meant that nothing could be added to their joy.
What modern people call the fulfillment of ambition
refers precisely to carriages and official caps.
Carriages and caps upon one's person
do not belong to one's innate nature
—they are accidental things that come
and are but temporary lodgings.
Being temporary lodgings,
their coming cannot be prevented,
nor can their departure be stopped.
Therefore, one should not be wanton in ambition because of carriages and caps,
nor should one conform to vulgar customs due to poverty and hardship.
One's joy remains the same in both circumstances,
thus simply being free from worry.
Nowadays when these temporary things depart, people become unhappy.
From this perspective,
even when they seem joyful,
it is not without turmoil.
Hence it is said:
"Those who lose themselves in material things
and forfeit their innate nature to vulgar customs
are called people who have inverted the fundamental order of things."
【一】【注】Fulfill the inner self and be content.
【Commentary】Yì means
to add.
Xuān refers to
a carriage.
Miǎn is
a ceremonial cap.
The ancients were simple and genuine,
embodying the Way through non-action.
Fulfillment lay in tranquility and simplicity;
joy was not found in carriages or ceremonial caps.
Their joy was already sufficient—
how could it depend on such additions!
【Èr Shū】People of the present age,
many are frivolous and superficial,
coveting fine honors and positions,
relying on these to satisfy their hearts.
Thus, wearing crowns and riding in carriages
is taken as achieving their ambitions.
【Three】【Discourses】Fortuitous things are
those that come unexpectedly.
High positions and glory,
are external possessions,
things that arrive by chance,
not part of my life's essence,
merely temporarily entrusted,
how could they last long!
【Text Explanation】"Tǎng lái" is pronounced with "tǎng" as in "tǎng" from "tǎngdǎng".
The Cui version writes it as "dǎng",
stating:
it means multitude.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that in the Cui version, "tǎng" is written as "dǎng",
and "dǎng"
is the ancient form of "tǎng".
"Dǎng"
is a word expressing possibility or uncertainty.
In the "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of the Marquis of Huáiyīn", it says "fearing that it might not succeed",
and in the "Book of Hàn: Biography of Wǔ Bèi", "perhaps one can hope for luck",
both using "dǎng" interchangeably with "tǎng".
In the "Xúnzǐ: Discourse on Heaven" chapter, it mentions "the strange stars' occasional appearance",
where Yáng's annotation explains "dǎng" as frequent,
but Wáng Niànsūn argues that this has no basis in ancient texts.
Huì Dìngyǔ, in "Ancient Meanings of the Nine Classics", said:
"dǎng jiàn" means what is seen.
He also interprets "dǎng" as "suǒ" (that which),
based on the commentary of the "Gōngyáng Tradition",
but this also seems inconsistent.
Cui states,
"dǎng",
means multitude,
which is particularly incorrect.
【Four】【Annotation】It lies in external things,
gain and loss are not of me.
【Commentary】When fortune comes by chance,
one may casually attain high office and honors;
when fate departs as if entrusted,
one serenely abandons glory and splendor.
Since there is no intention to resist or defend,
how could there be any attachment to holding on!
【Explanation】"Kě Yǔ" is pronounced as Yú Lǚ fǎn.
The original text also uses the character for "Yù".
【五】【注】Serene and composed as ever,
unaware of the parasite dwelling within.
【Transcription】"Bù wéi": yú wèi fǎn.
The following is the same.
【Six】【Annotation】Serenely content within oneself,
one does not perceive poverty as a personal burden.
【Commentary】Sì means
to express.
Qū means
to contend.
The ancients understood that poverty and success are fated,
and recognized that glory and decay are not of their own making.
Even if one held high office and wore courtly headgear,
it would not suffice to express one's aspirations and spirit;
if one were frugal and in dire straits,
how could one contend in the clamorous customs of the world!
【Seven】【Annotation】Each other,
referring to high rank and poverty.
【Commentary】That refers to
high rank and official carriage.
This refers to
poverty and humble circumstances.
Now, high rank and humble circumstances
both come by chance.
Since one delights in that high rank,
one must also accept this poverty,
for both are temporary lodgings,
and thus are the same.
【八】【Note】There is also no joy of delight.
【Commentary】Neither delighting in high positions and official hats,
nor suffering from poverty and hardship,
one accepts arrangements and transformations,
thus being free from worries.
【Nine】【Annotation】Those who are unhappy when what is entrusted departs,
become unsettled when it arrives,
this is to exchange the inner for the external.
【Commentary】People of the present age,
with shallow understanding,
thus when things come to them,
they rejoice with delight,
and when they depart,
they become despondent and unhappy.
How could they know that these matters arise fortuitously,
and that with each coming and going,
they constantly worry and rejoice?
Therefore, it is understood that even in joy, their minds are never free from turmoil.
【一０】【Note】To deplete the outside and damage the inside,
is to invert their proper positions.
【Commentary】When entrusting things to depart and arrive,
one feels both worry and joy,
sacrificing oneself to follow external matters—
how is this not a loss!
Whether in high chariots and crowns or in poverty and constraint,
matters revert to worldly dust.
If one treats common customs as the norm,
losing one's innate nature,
turning away from truth and betraying the Way,
this indeed is the cause.
The way one settles and positions oneself
is truly topsy-turvy.
【Explanatory Text】"The People Who Are Upside Down" Cuī Zǐ states:
They go against their innate nature and are not in harmony.
Xiàng Xiū states:
Exchanging the inner for the outer,
can be called being upside down.
【Collation Notes】(1) The "Zhī Yǒu" following "Mìng" in the Zhang Jūnfáng edition is cited in the Quē Wù.
(2) The character "Shì" has been emended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The character "Jiù" has been revised based on the original text of the Shǐ Jì.
(4) The four characters "Xúnzǐ Tiān Lùn" have been altered following Liú Wéndiǎn's Bǔ Zhèng edition.
(5) The inverted three characters "Qí Zhì Dǎo" have been corrected as per the Shìdétáng edition.
【One】【Explanatory Text】Borrowing objects to title the chapters.
When the autumn floods arrived,
all the streams poured into the Yellow River,
its swelling current so vast
that one could not distinguish an ox from a horse
across the banks, islets, and shores.
Thereupon the River Earl, overjoyed with himself,
believed all the beauty under heaven belonged to him alone.
Following the current eastward,
he reached the Northern Sea.
Gazing eastward,
he could see no end to the waters,
whereupon the River Earl began to change his expression,
and, looking out over the ocean, said to Ruò with a sigh:
"There is a saying among country folk,
'He who has heard a hundred doctrines thinks no one is equal to himself'—
this refers to me.
Moreover, I have heard those who belittle Confucius' learning and disparage Bóyí's righteousness,
and initially I did not believe them;
now that I have witnessed your boundless expanse,
had I not come to your gate, I would have been in peril,
and forever laughed at by those of great understanding."
【一】【Note】It speaks of its vastness.
【Commentary】The river,
refers to Mèngjīn.
"Flowing,"
means to pass through.
"Bank,"
is the shore.
"Boundary,"
is the edge.
"Islet,"
is a shoal,
meaning a place in the water where one can dwell is called a shoal.
Great waters arise in spring and flourish in autumn,
as the autumn's yin energy is intensely abundant,
often leading to continuous rains,
hence water levels rise in autumn.
Subsequently, all the hundred rivers and valleys,
pour into the Yellow River,
flowing through until full,
its waters become very great,
the banks and boundaries vast and wide,
the shoals and islets distant and remote,
thus making it hard to distinguish from across the water,
whether an object is an ox or a horse.
【Explanation Text】"Autumn Waters" Lǐ Yún states:
Water is born in spring,
and matures in autumn.
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
Water,
is the standard.
"Floods the River" pronounced as guàn hé.
"Flowing Streams" pronounced as jīng liú.
Sīmǎ explains:
Jīng,
means to flow through.
Cuī's version uses jìng,
stating:
Direct passage is called jìng.
It also says:
The character might be written as jīng.
"Two Banks" pronounced as sì,
meaning the shore.
"Zhǔ" Sīmǎ explains:
A place in the water that can be inhabited is called a zhǔ.
The Explaining Names says:
Zhǔ,
means to block,
with a high body,
it can block the water, making it flow around from the sides.
"Yá" can also be written as yá,
or as yá,
all are the same.
"Unable to distinguish ox from horse" biàn,
means to differentiate.
It speaks of vastness,
so from a distance, one cannot tell them apart.
【二】【疏】Hé Bó,
the river god,
surnamed Féng,
named Yí,
was a native of Tóngdī Township in Huàyīn,
who attained the way of the water immortals.
The river being vast and expansive,
he thus felt joyful and delighted,
believing that all the glory, splendor, and magnificent beauty under heaven
were entirely within himself.
【Explanatory Text】"Hé Bó" has the surname Féng,
given name Yí,
also known as Bīng Yí,
also known as Féng Chí,
already seen in the chapter "The Great and Venerable Teacher."
Another account says:
has the surname Lǚ,
given name Gōngzǐ,
Féng Yí is Gōngzǐ's wife.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary:
Wénxuǎn] Méi Chéng's "Qī Fā" annotation quotes Xǔ Shèn as saying:
Féng Chí,
is the Earl of the River.
Shìwén states:
The Earl of the River,
surname Féng, given name Yí,
also known as Féng Chí.
The characters chí and yí,
were used interchangeably in ancient times.
Huáinánzǐ's "Qí Sù Xùn" mentions Féng Yí attained the Way and submerged into the great river,
Xǔ's annotation:
Féng Yí,
is the Earl of the River,
a native of Dīshǒu Village, Tóngxiāng, Huáyīn,
who ingested eight minerals,
and became a water immortal.
In the "Sì Mǔ" chapter of the Shī Xiǎo Yǎ, "Zhōu dào wēi chí,"
the Hán Shī version writes it as wēi yí.
Yǎn Yòu's "Jiǎngsú Zhèngsú" states:
In ancient times, chí and yí were interchangeable,
this is the evidence.
Gāo's annotation to Huáinánzǐ's "Yuán Dào" chapter:
Féng Yí,
also called Féng Chí,
was an ancient who attained the Way and could command yin and yang.
"Wéi jìn" is pronounced jīn rěn fǎn.
【Three】【Explanations】Běihǎi,
now known as Láizhōu.
Gazing at the vast ocean,
it appears indistinct,
with the water and sun reflecting each other,
hence the term "gazing at the vastness."
Ruò,
is the sea deity.
Hé Bó followed the current eastward,
reaching the great sea,
casually glanced back,
but could not see the edges of the water,
only then did he turn his gaze,
looked up at Hǎi Ruò,
and sighed with emotion,
expressing it through rustic words.
Yet, even one in a hundred or ten thousand,
is truly not enough to feel self-satisfied,
thus claiming none could compare to oneself—
this is what Hé Bó meant.
This is but a crude tale,
not considered a comprehensive discourse.
【Explanatory Text】"Běihǎi": Lǐ Yún states:
It is north of the Eastern Sea.
"Miànmù máng": pronounced as mò gāng fǎn,
also read as páng,
and also as wàng.
Originally, one version writes it as wàng.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, máng is written as wàng.
"Yáng": pronounced as yáng.
Sīmǎ and Cuī state:
máng yáng,
is like wàng yáng,
describing the appearance of looking upward.
"Xiàng ruò": Xiàng, Xú pronounces as xiàng,
xǔ liàng fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
Ruò,
is the sea god.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The explanatory text cites Sīmǎ and Cuī's versions as writing máng yáng,
stating máng yáng is like wàng yáng,
describing the appearance of looking upward.
Now, it is considered that both yáng and yáng are borrowed characters,
their correct characters should be yáng.
In the "Gǔ Xiàng" chapter of Lùn Héng, King Wǔ wàng yáng,
meaning looking at the sun.
The sun is in the sky,
one should look up to observe it,
hence it is interpreted as looking upward.
"Wén dào bǎi": Lǐ Yún states:
It is one ten-thousandth part.
◎Jiā Shìfù states:
Lǐ Guǐ says:
hearing of a hundred ways,
is one ten-thousandth part.
Now, it is considered that the character wén (hear) contrasts with the following character dǔ (see).
Although one hears many ways, they do not know their boundlessness,
presuming their truth and confidently believing they have made progress,
until they see their boundlessness,
only then do they begin to feel disheartened and lost.
Bǎi (hundred),
is a term for multitude,
Lǐ's annotation is incorrect.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: Bǎi,
in ancient times, was read like bó,
rhyming with ruò.
In the "Zōu Yáng Biography" of the Hàn Shū, "zhì niǎo lěi bǎi",
rhymes with è.
In Cài Yōng's Dú Duàn, the lá zhù cí "suì qǔ qiān bǎi",
rhymes with zhái hè zuò.
【Four】【Annotation】Knowing one's smallness and not being able to make oneself great,
then the principles of one's lot are inherently plain,
and there is no room for feelings of envy or aspiration in between.
【Commentary】"Fang"
means the Way.
The world considers Confucius' editing of the Six Classics as evidence of extensive knowledge and broad learning,
and Bo Yí's yielding of the throne as pure and upright,
principles worthy of high regard.
Yet there are also learned and enlightened scholars
who engage in lofty discussions,
regarding Bo Yí's righteousness as insignificant
and Confucius' knowledge as limited.
Even if the River Earl had heard such claims,
I secretly find them hard to believe.
Now, witnessing the vastness and breadth of the great sea,
boundless and impossible to exhaust,
I realize that what I heard in the past
was indeed not unfounded.
Had the River Earl not reached the gate of the Sea God,
it would have been greatly perilous for his understanding.
If one's perspective remains narrow and inferior,
they will long be ridiculed by those who comprehend the great Way.
【Explanatory Text】"Now I behold" - the old pronunciation is dǔ.
According to Shuōwén,
dǔ (睹) is the modern character,
dǔ (睹) is the ancient character,
dǔ (睹)
means to see.
Cuǐ's version writes it as "now behold me",
saying:
dǔ (睹)
means to show.
"The Great Way's Master" - Sīmǎ comments:
It means the Great Dào.
"Pattern division" - read with the fǎnqiè fú wèn,
same hereafter.
【Collation】（1）The two characters "dǔ" have been emended according to the main text below.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"The reason one cannot discuss the ocean with a frog in a well
is that it is confined by its limited space;
the reason one cannot speak of ice with a summer insect
is that it is restricted by its season;
the reason one cannot talk about the Dao with a scholar of narrow learning
is that they are bound by their doctrines.
Now that you have emerged from the banks of your river,
beheld the vast sea,
and realized your own insignificance,
it becomes possible to discuss the great principles with you.
Among all waters under heaven,
none is greater than the sea.
Countless rivers flow into it,
yet never cease to make it full;
the Weǐlǘ drains it,
yet never exhausts its emptiness.
It remains unchanged through spring and autumn,
unaware of flood or drought.
Its capacity surpasses that of the Jiāng and Hé rivers,
beyond all measure and calculation.
Yet I have never prided myself on this,
for I recognize that I received my form from heaven and earth and my vital breath from yīn and yáng.
My existence between heaven and earth
is like a small stone or tiny tree on a great mountain.
Conscious of my own insignificance,
how could I possibly boast?
Consider the four seas within the expanse of heaven and earth—
are they not like anthills in a vast marsh?
Consider the Middle Kingdom within the four seas—
is it not like a grain of millet in a great granary?
When we enumerate all things, we call them 'the ten thousand',
and humanity occupies but one among them.
Wherever people dwell across the nine regions,
wherever grain grows,
wherever carts and boats can reach—
humanity occupies but one place.
Compared to the myriad things,
is this not like a single hair on the body of a horse?
All that the Five Emperors ruled over,
the Three Kings fought for,
the benevolent worried about,
the capable toiled for—
amounts to no more than this.
Bóyí declined rulership to gain fame,
Zhòngní discoursed to show erudition—
this is their self-importance,
is it not like your former pride in your river's abundance?"
【一】【注】All things are born and find their peace,
each having its own ultimate inclination.
【Commentary】The Sea God knew the River Earl was constrained and limited,
so he cited three analogies to illustrate this.
Now, a frog in a shallow well,
hearing that the great sea has towering waves a hundred feet high even without wind,
would certainly refuse to believe it,
because it is confined to its narrow domain.
An insect born in summer,
which dies by autumn,
upon hearing that in the depths of winter,
water freezes into ice,
and rain congeals into sleet,
would surely refuse to believe it,
because its mind is deeply attached to the summer season.
A person with narrow views,
or one who clings stubbornly to biases,
upon hearing of the utterly pervasive ultimate Way,
which transcends sages and discards wisdom,
regards Mount Tài as small and a hair-tip as large,
considers the short-lived youth as long-lived and Péng Zǔ as prematurely deceased,
and would certainly not believe it,
because they are bound by conventional teachings and doctrines.
And as for the River Earl, who had not reached the vast ocean,
nor encountered the Sea God,
yet prided himself on his greatness,
the principle is the same.
【Commentary】"To speak" is read as the character's standard pronunciation,
same below.
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī says:
"frog"
originally was written as "fish",
later people changed it.
Tàipíng Yùlǎn's sections on Seasons (seven), Scaly Creatures (seven), and Insects (one) quote this,
all stating "a well fish cannot be spoken to about the sea",
thus it is known the old version used "fish".
Moreover, the commentary does not list the character "frog" for this sentence,
only until the later phrase "the frog in the caved-in well",
does it begin to say "frog" is also written as "frog",
with pronunciation hù guā fǎn,
quoting Sīmǎ's commentary saying,
"frog",
is an aquatic creature,
shaped like a shrimp蟆,
thus it is clear this sentence used "fish" and not "frog".
If it were "frog",
then the hù guā pronunciation,
and the aquatic creature annotation,
should have appeared here first,
it shouldn't only appear later.
Further proven by two pieces of evidence:
In Huái Nánzǐ's "Yuándào" chapter,
"A well fish cannot be discussed with about greatness",
constrained by narrowness;
Liáng's Zhāng Wǎn's writing,
"A well fish does not recognize the vast sea",
"a summer insect does not see winter ice",
(Shuǐ Jīng Gànshuǐ annotation says:
merely recording strange hearsay,
to broaden the hearing of the well fish.
) all use Zhuāngzǐ's text,
thus it is even clearer that Zhuāngzǐ wrote "well fish".
"Well" hexagram nine three,
"in the well valley shooting a perch",
Zhèng's commentary says:
"the fish born there are not large fish,
only many perch fish."
(See Liú Kuí's annotation to Wūdū Fù.
) Kùn Xué Jì Wén (volume ten) quotes Yùlǎn's recorded Zhuāngzǐ saying,
"if one's intent is like a well fish,
I cast hook and line to catch them",
Lǚshì Chūnqiū's "Yù Dà" chapter says,
"in a well there are no large fish",
these are all evidence for "well fish".
Later people, because this piece has the phrase "frog in the caved-in well",
and Xúnzǐ also says "a frog in a pit well cannot be spoken to about the joy of the Eastern Sea",
(see "Zhèng Lùn" chapter.
) thus changed "well fish" to "well frog",
not knowing that wells naturally have fish,
no need to change it to frog.
Since this change,
the world then often speaks of "well frog and summer insect",
no longer knowing there was the metaphor of the well fish.
"On emptiness" sound xū.
Also originally written as xū (ruins).
Fēngsú Tōng says:
"xū (ruins)",
means empty.
Cuī says:
"constrained by the emptiness within the well."
◎Wáng Niànsūn says:
Cuī's annotation "constrained by xū" says,
"constrained by the emptiness within the well."
Case: Cuī explaining xū as empty is
incorrect.
Xū is the same as xū (ruins),
thus the commentary says,
"xū is also written as xū (ruins)".
Guǎngyǎ says:
"xū (ruins)",
is dwelling.
(Dwelling is the ancient character for residence.
) Wénxuǎn's "Xī Zhēng Fù" annotation quotes Shēng Lèi saying:
"xū (ruins)",
is the former dwelling place.
Where classics mention "mound ruins",
all refer to former dwelling lands.
Meaning the well fish is constrained by its dwelling,
thus does not know the sea's vastness.
The fish dwells in the well,
just as the River Earl dwells between the banks,
thus the text below says,
"now you have come out from the banks,
beheld the great sea,
then you know your insignificance."
"Summer insect" pronunciation hù jià fǎn.
◎Qìng Fán's case: Wénxuǎn Sūn Xìnggōng's "Tiāntāi Shān Fù" annotation quotes Sīmǎ saying:
"firmly believing in the season it sees."
Commentary missing.
◎Also case: Sīmǎ explains dǔ as firm,
Chéng's subcommentary "heart firm on summer time",
uses Sīmǎ's meaning.
This explanation is convoluted and hard to follow.
Ěryǎ Shìgǔ:
"dǔ",
means fixed.
Lúnyǔ "Tàibó" chapter "firm in belief and fond of learning",
means belief is fixed.
Lǐ "Rú Xíng" "steadfast in conduct and untiring",
means conduct is fixed.
Hòu Hàn's Yán Dǔ styled Shūjiān,
jiān (firm) also means fixed.
All crude and unenlightened are called fixed,
the summer insect is obscured by the season and cannot be spoken to about ice,
thus said "fixed in time".
"Dǔ" precisely matches the meaning of constraint in the context.
"Provincial scholar" Sīmǎ says:
a scholar from the rural countryside.
【二】【注】Because they understand their lot,
they can thus be spoken with about principle.
【Commentary】The River God, steering the waters and riding the currents,
soared beyond the banks' confines,
when he chanced upon Ruò of the Sea,
right there in the vast ocean's expanse.
He carefully observed the endlessness of the great abyss,
and thus scorned the narrow inferiority of his small river.
Having realized the limitations of his dwelling place,
he could then discuss the vast and unobstructed principles of the great truth.
【Three】【Drains】The Wěilǘ is
the place where seawater drains;
located east of the Bì Sea,
there is a rock formation there,
forty thousand lǐ wide,
forty thousand lǐ thick,
situated at the lower end of all rivers and serving as a drainage hub,
hence called Wěilǘ.
Seawater poured onto it instantly evaporates,
also named Wòjiāo.
The Shānhǎijīng states,
Yì shot down nine suns,
which fell and became Wòjiāo.
This account is fanciful and exaggerated,
so it is not recorded in detail here.
Spring rain is scarce while autumn rain is abundant,
Yáo faced floods while Tāng suffered drought.
Thus, the sea as an entity
receives all rivers yet never fills,
is drained by Wòjiāo yet never empties,
unchanging in volume through spring and autumn,
unaware of increase or decrease despite floods or droughts.
Considering its vastness,
it far surpasses the flow of the Jiāng (River) and Hé (River),
the disparity is immense—
how can one even speak of measuring its magnitude!
【Explanation Text】"Wěilǘ": Cuī's commentary states:
a river name east of the sea.
Sīmǎ's commentary states:
that which discharges seawater outward.
"Xiè zhī" is pronounced with the initial "x" and the rhyme "ie" in the departing tone,
also read with the initial "y" and the rhyme "i" in the departing tone.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: The commentary by Sīmǎ cited in the annotation of Jī Shūyè's "Essay on Nourishing Life" in the "Wénxuǎn" states:
Wěilǘ,
is where water flows out from beyond the sea,
also named Wòjiāo,
located in the eastern great sea.
"Wěi" (tail)
signifies being below all rivers,
hence called "tail."
"Lǘ" (gathering)
means to gather,
a place where water congregates,
hence called "gathering."
East of Fúsāng,
there is a rock,
forty thousand lǐ in circumference,
forty thousand lǐ thick,
seawater pouring into it all boils away without exception,
thus called Wòjiāo (Scorching Torrent).
This is more detailed than the explanation cited in the explanatory text.
"Liàng shù": pronounced with the departing tone "liàng."
This applies to the annotations and the following instances as well.
【Four】【Commentary】To exhaust the measure of all rivers and suspend them in the Yellow River,
the Yellow River is suspended in the sea,
the sea is suspended between heaven and earth,
thus each has its own measure.
Those who express such ideas
seem to suggest that observing the great can illuminate the small,
but upon examining their meaning, it is not so.
What the world worries about
is inequality;
hence, those of substantial size feel discontented, considering the small as lacking surplus,
while those of modest substance feel self-contained, regarding the great as perfectly sufficient.
This leads to mutual boasting and posturing between high and low,
causing confusion and self-loss in every gesture,
which is what perplexes the common people.
The perplexed seek correction,
and the best way to correct them is first to fully expose their disparities and then follow their own claims.
What they call great is deemed perfectly sufficient,
so not even the tip of an autumn hair can burden heaven and earth;
what they call small is considered without surplus,
thus heaven and earth cannot surpass an autumn hair;
only then can the perplexed find a path to return,
each understanding their own limits,
things resting content in their roles,
and the carefree wanderer using their innate steps to roam in the field of self-attainment.
This is why Zhuāngzǐ utters words of virtue.
If we follow the perplexed's argument,
turning to mutual comparison of small and large,
then such comparisons would be endless.
If one sees the great and feels uneasy about the small,
regards the little and considers oneself abundant,
they will race in the arena of victory and defeat, fueling the pride of the people under heaven—
how could this grasp the essence of Zhuāngzǐ's teaching!
【Commentary】"Cún" means
"to exist."
"Xī" means
"what."
Now, covering and carrying all things,
nothing is greater than heaven and earth;
spreading energy and transforming life,
nothing is greater than yīn and yáng.
Thus, if the sea god were to compare his form to heaven and earth,
there would be no hierarchy to place him,
and speaking of receiving energy from yīn and yáng,
then he is but one entity embodying yīn and yáng.
Therefore, using things as metaphors,
it is like small trees and stones on Mount Tài—
yet the sea god, in the natural order, is of little significance.
Each thing has its measure,
so how can any be sufficient to consider itself abundant!
【Explanatory Text】"而縣" is pronounced as xuán.
The same applies below.
"怏然" is pronounced with the fanqie 於亮反,
and also with 於良反.
"之竟" is pronounced as jìng.
【五】【疏】礨空，
is an ant hole.
稊，
is a grass similar to barnyard grass but with very fine and few grains.
中国，
refers to the Nine Provinces.
Now, the Four Seas lie between Heaven and Earth,
and the Nine Provinces reside within the Four Seas.
Is this not like an ant hole situated in a great marsh,
or a grain of tí rice in a vast granary?
This illustrates the vast disparity in size and significance between them.
【Translated Text】"Lěi" is pronounced lì zuì fǎn,
Xiàng agrees,
Cuī pronounces it as lěi,
Lǐ gives lì duì fǎn.
"Kōng" is pronounced kǒng.
Lěi kǒng,
means a small hole.
Lǐ says:
a small mound.
Another says:
an anthill.
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
The explanatory text cites Cuī saying,
lěi kōng refers to a small hole.
Lǐ Guǐ says,
a small mound.
Another says an anthill.
Now, the term lěi kōng inherently carries two meanings,
referring to the situation of high and low.
Lěi means,
suddenly elevated;
kōng means,
sunken and low.
In a great marsh,
some areas rise like mounds,
some are deeply depressed,
the undulating highs and lows,
are a natural tendency often interdependent,
hence called lěi kōng.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Shanglin Park" mentions qiū xū jué lěi,
similarly conveying this meaning.
Describing the terrain of hills and ruins,
some are dug into holes,
others piled into mounds.
"Tí mǐ" is pronounced tú xī fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
tí mǐ,
is a type of small grain.
Lǐ says:
tí grass.
According to Guō's annotation in the Erya,
tí resembles bài,
bài is pronounced pú mài fǎn.
"Dà cāng" is pronounced tài.
【Six】【Annotation】The distinction between small and large,
each has its own hierarchy,
cannot be equated.
【Explanation】"Hào" refers to
names and titles.
"Zú" means
the multitude.
The number of things in existence exceeds ten thousand,
yet in common parlance,
people often refer to them as "the myriad things,"
and humans are but one among these myriad entities.
Within the nine provinces of Zhōngguó,
where people gather in crowds,
all grains grow,
and boats and carriages come and go,
humanity is counted among the myriad things,
occupying just one place.
However, comparing humans to the myriad things,
and the nine provinces to the universe,
it is no different than a single hair on a horse's body—
hardly worth troubling one's mind over!
【Translated Text】"Rén zú" - Zūn hū fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
multitude.
Cuī zǐ xù fǎn,
states:
entirety.
◎Jiā Shìfù says:
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying,
zú,
means multitude,
Cuī says,
means entirety.
The case is, rén zú jiǔzhōu,
meaning the total population of the nine provinces.
Zú here,
is an exhaustive term.
The vastness of the nine provinces,
the multitude of people,
within the center of heaven,
essentially are but one among the myriad things.
Cuī's explanation is correct.
◎Yú Yuè says:
The two characters rén zú,
their exact meaning is unclear.
Sīmǎ interprets zú as multitude,
Cuī interprets zú as entirety,
both are untenable.
Moreover, below it says rén chù yī yān,
so here it should not refer to people.
Rén zú is suspected to be a miswriting of the two characters dà shuài.
In the chapter "Rénjiān Shì,"
shuài rán fǔ zhī,
the explanatory text says,
shuài sometimes written as zú.
This is evidence that shuài and zú are similar in form and easily confused.
Shuài mistaken for zú,
thus dà was changed to rén to match it.
According to the chapter "Zhìlè," rén zú wén zhī,
and the chapter "Dàozhì," rén zú wèi yǒu bù xīng míng jiù lì zhě,
these instances of rén zú,
exist in this book,
but applied here,
they are not tenable.
Dà shuài means,
a term for a general estimate.
Above it says jì sìhǎi zhī zài tiāndì zhī jiān yě,
and also jì zhōngguó zhī zài hǎinèi,
jì and dà shuài,
their meanings are exactly the same.
【Seven】【Annotations】do not go beyond one realm.
【Commentary】The Five Emperors succeeded one another through abdication and yielding,
while the Three Kings raised armies to contend and seize power.
Benevolent individuals deeply concerned themselves with the altars of soil and grain,
and capable officials toiled diligently in their official duties.
Although these four groups differed in their undertakings,
all exemplified the principle of exhausting the minutest details.
【Explanatory Text】"What the Five Constants Connect" Simǎ comments:
It refers to the continuity of benevolence and righteousness.
Cuī comments:
Connect,
means to continue.
Some versions also read as the Five Emperors.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
The current edition reads as the Five Emperors.
◎Jiā Shìfù states:
The Jiangnán ancient (Zhuāng) [Zàng] edition has "connect" written as "operate",
and it seems more appropriate to follow "operate".
"What They Strive For" is read with the side pronunciation of "plow".
"What the Capable Men Toil For" Lǐ comments:
Capable,
means able.
Toil,
means to serve.
【Eight】【Annotation】Things have their fixed realms,
which even the wisest cannot transcend.
Thus, the distinction between large and small arises,
to elucidate that the ultimate truth is beyond debate.
【Commentary】Bóyí declined the five ranks of nobility to establish his reputation,
Zhòngní discussed the Six Classics to demonstrate his erudition.
Using such trivial matters,
and holding onto these to boast of themselves—
how does this differ from the earlier River God boasting of his waters!
This connects with the previous analogy,
and explains the earlier passage about belittling Zhòngní's knowledge and disparaging Bóyí's righteousness.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "xū".
(2) In Zhào's edition, it is written as "yá".
(3) Zhào's edition lacks the character "yú".
(4) The character "yú" has been added based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(5) The "Quēwù" cites the Jiāngnán Gǔzàng edition, where "lián" is written as "yùn".
(6) The character "hé" has been emended according to the main text.
(7) The character "yàng" has been emended based on the "Shìwén" and the Shìdétáng edition.
(8) The character "zhī" has been added according to the main text.
The River Earl said:
"Then if I regard Heaven and Earth as great and the tip of a hair as small,
would that be acceptable?"
【一】【疏】The largest of forms
cannot surpass heaven and earth,
the smallest of substances
begins with the tip of a hair;
thus, whether considering the large or the small,
it is clear that inherent natures differ.
Hé Bó presented what he knew,
and inquired of Ruò of the Sea.
Further explanation:
If one considers self-satisfaction as greatness,
I could be greater than the two realms (heaven and earth);
if one regards nothing left as smallness,
I could be smaller than the tip of a hair.
Once Hé Bó grasped this,
all things and the self became equal,
so he expressed his enlightened mind,
inquiring whether this was acceptable.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"No.
For things,
their dimensions are boundless[Note 1],
their time is unceasing[Note 2],
their divisions are inconstant[Note 3],
and their ends and beginnings have no fixed cause[Note 4].
Therefore, the great wise observe both far and near,
hence what is small is not considered meager[Note 5],
what is large is not considered abundant[Note 6],
knowing that dimensions are boundless[Note 7];
verifying the present and the past[Note 8],
thus what is distant does not perplex,
what is near does not prompt striving[Note 10],
knowing that time is unceasing[Note 11];
examining fullness and emptiness,
therefore gain does not bring joy,
loss does not cause sorrow[Note 12],
knowing that divisions are inconstant[Note 13];
understanding the level path[Note 14],
thus life is not a cause for delight,
death is not a calamity[Note 15],
knowing that ends and beginnings cannot be fixed[Note 16].
If we reckon what humans know,
it does not compare to what they do not know[Note 17];
the time of their existence,
does not compare to the time before their birth[Note 18];
using their utmost smallness to seek to exhaust the realm of utmost greatness,
therefore they become confused and unable to attain self-realization[Note 19].
From this perspective,
how can we know that the tip of a fine hair is sufficient to determine the limit of the finest smallness!
How can we know that Heaven and Earth are sufficient to exhaust the realm of the utmost greatness[Note 20]!"
【一】【注】Each thing has its own measure.
【Commentary】Having acknowledged the doubts raised,
the response states it is not permissible.
For the capacity of things,
endowed natures differ;
following what they receive,
each finds its fitting state.
Yet with a thousand distinctions and myriad variations,
the categories are endless.
In the place of fittingness,
there is neither large nor small.
How can one rashly use what one knows
to suppress and fix it as a standard!
【二】【注】Death and life both follow the course of time.
【Commentary】Renewing ceaselessly without pause.
【Three】【Annotation】Gain and loss are both fated.
【Commentary】The endowed allotments of fate,
change according to the times.
【四】【注】Renewing daily.
【Commentary】Although it cycles from end to beginning again,
it is never not renewed.
【Five】【Annotation】Each is self-sufficient.
【Commentary】This section explains the inexhaustibility of measurement.
With the wisdom of the great sage,
one perceives distant principles,
and examines nearby matters.
Thus, even a tiny tip, though small,
is inherently complete in itself,
lacking nothing at all.
【Six】【Annotation】There is nothing more either.
【Commentary】Though heaven and earth are vast,
they should embody nothing beyond themselves,
hence they are not sufficient to boast of their own greatness.
Without boasting, there is no exaggeration;
without feeling lacking, there ceases to be striving.
【Seven】【Annotation】Gathering them for observation,
one understands that all things, whether distant or near, large or small, have their own measure.
【Commentary】With the wisdom of the great person,
one understands the capacity of things.
Though their sizes may differ,
each corresponds to its nature;
their rise and fall vary,
hence they are boundless.
This concludes the discussion on the boundlessness of things' capacities.
【Eight】【Annotation】Xiàng,
means bright.
Present and past,
is like ancient and modern.
【Commentary】This section explains the meaning that time has no cessation.
Xiàng,
means clarity.
Since it is understood that small and large are not truly small and large,
then it proves that past and present have no true past and present.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhèng Xiàng" is read as xǔ liàng fǎn.
Cuī states:
It means 'to go'.
Xiàng and Guō state:
It means 'to clarify'.
Also read as xū zhàng fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Yáo,
means long.
【一０】【Note】Duō,
means short.
【Commentary】Yáo means
long.
Duō means
short.
Since we know that ancient and modern have no distinction between ancient and modern,
then we understand that longevity and premature death have no true longevity or premature death.
Therefore, if one's years are long,
one never grows weary of life or feels depressed;
if one's allotted lifespan is cut short,
one also does not yearn for or aspire to long life;
following change and accepting transformation,
it is always me.
【Transcription】"掇" is pronounced as duō with a falling-rising tone.
Guǒ Xiàng notes:
It means short.
"而不跂" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
One version writes it as "企".
The annotation below is also the same.
◎ Jiā Shìfù comments:
In Guǒ Xiàng's annotation,
means long,
while "掇"
implies short.
According to Shuōwén,
means to pick up.
In the Yì commentary:
"troubles come as if picked up,"
like gathering things by hand,
indicating they are near and can be easily taken.
is as in Lǎozi's "its governance is muddled,"
meaning unclear.
refers to what is used for walking.
In Huáinánzǐ's "Yuándào Xùn," it mentions creatures that walk on tiptoe and breathe through beaks,
and in the "Horses' Hooves" chapter, it talks about forcing oneself for benevolence,
straining for righteousness,
implying toil and trouble.
Knowing that time does not stop,
one should simply go with the flow.
Thus, the past is not distant,
and should not be ignored;
the present is not near,
and should not be forced.
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation is not satisfactory.
【一一】【Note】It demonstrates the constancy from ancient to modern times,
knowing that change does not stop at life and death,
thus not being distressed by longevity,
nor striving anxiously due to brevity.
【Commentary】This concludes the preceding discussion on the inexhaustibility of time.
【一二】【Commentary】The following explains the meaning of impermanence in division.
Since the Way of Heaven has its waxings and wanings,
how could human affairs lack gains and losses!
Therefore, by observing the changes of waxing and waning,
and understanding the principles of gain and loss,
thus if one gains unexpectedly,
it is due to timing,
and not worthy of joy;
if one loses occasionally,
it is due to fate,
and not worthy of sorrow.
【13】【Comment】Observing its alternating fullness and emptiness,
one understands that possession is not constant,
thus enabling the forgetting of joy and sorrow.
【Subcommentary】This concludes the preceding section on the meaning of impermanence.
【一四】【Note】Life and death are
the true path of daily renewal.
【Commentary】This section explains the meaning of having no fixed beginning or end.
Tǎn means
level.
Tú means
path.
Not considering death as death,
not considering life as life,
because there is no separation between life and death.
One who understands the great path of tǎnrán equality is like this.
【Explanatory Text】"Tǎn" is pronounced as tǔ dàn fǎn.
【15】【Commentary】Those who understand the serene and open way,
find their birth not a cause for joy,
nor their death a reason for calamity.
Having realized the non-duality of life and death,
how can there be any talk of worry or delight?
【Explanation】"Does not speak" is read as "yuè" (pleased).
【16】【Note】It clarifies that each day's renewal marks the end and the beginning,
thus understanding that the past cannot be clung to or retained.
Therefore, one encounters the new without surprise,
and leaves the old without alarm,
seeing the transformations of life and death as one and the same.
【Commentary】This concludes the previous discussion on the principle of beginning and ending without cause.
【Transcription】"Bù è": wǔ gè fǎn.
"Shě gù": yīn shě.
【一七】【Note】What each knows has its limits.
【Commentary】Those who force knowledge deviate from the truth,
while those who do not know unite with the Way.
Judging by this,
it is indeed better not to know.
【一八】【Note】Each life has its own allotted years.
【Commentary】Before birth,
there is no joy, hence no sorrow;
after coming into existence,
there is affection, hence there is aversion.
【一九】【Comment】Nothing is better than being content with the lot one has received.
【Commentary】The ultimate smallness is
the intellect;
the ultimate greatness is
the realm.
Now, with the limited small intellect,
one seeks the boundless great realm,
yet before the boundless realm is fully encompassed,
the limited intellect is already lost.
Therefore, one remains confused and disordered throughout life,
with no means to return to the origin,
losing oneself in pursuit of external things without attaining self-realization.
【二０】【Note】Seeking the great through the small,
one ultimately fails to grasp the principle;
if each remains in its proper place,
then both large and small are fully sufficient.
If the tip of a hair does not seek the achievements of heaven and earth,
then the remainder of its entire form
becomes discarded matter;
if heaven and earth do not appear larger than an autumn hair,
then observing their shapes and images,
they are merely self-sufficient;
how then can one know that the fine is truly fine,
and the great is truly great!
【Commentary】All things receive their allotted nature,
each differing from the others.
Though their sizes vary, all achieve fitting satisfaction.
If the small aspire to be large,
they become confused and lose their inherent nature.
If each remains content with its own allotment,
then all equally attain carefree freedom.
Thus, though the tip of a hair is small,
its nature being sufficient allows it to be called great;
though heaven and earth are vast,
having no excess allows them to be called small.
From this perspective,
the ultimate boundary of the minuscule
need not necessarily lie at the tip of a hair!
The realm of the supremely great
surely cannot be conceptually exhausted by heaven and earth alone!
【Explanation】"Zhī Ní" is read as wǔ wù fǎn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as yì.
Guō gives it as wǔ mǐ fǎn.
The same applies below.
【Collation Notes】(1) The character 'háo' was amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(2) The character 'tǐ' was revised based on the memorial text.
(3) The character 'qí' was supplemented in accordance with the following sentence.
The River Earl said:
"Those who discuss the world all say:
'The most refined has no form,
the greatest cannot be encompassed.'
Is this truly the case?"
【一】【疏】Belief,
is about truth.
In worldly discussions,
without distinguishing right from wrong,
it is commonly said that the most refined things have no form or substance,
and the vastest cannot be encompassed.
It is unknown whether this reasoning pertains to the reality or illusion of emotions and intellect.
Hé Bó had not yet grasped this,
hence he harbored such doubts.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"Looking from the small toward the great, one cannot see the whole;
looking from the great toward the small, one cannot discern clearly.
The minute is the smallest of the small;
the colossal is the largest of the large;
thus they differ in convenience.
This is a matter of inherent tendency.
The refined and the coarse
are confined to things that have form.
What is without form
cannot be divided by numbers;
what cannot be encompassed
cannot be exhausted by numbers.
What can be discussed in words
is the coarseness of things;
what can be conceived in thought
is the refinement of things;
what words cannot discuss
and thought cannot grasp
has nothing to do with refinement or coarseness.
【一】【注】The eyes have constant limits to what they can see,
unable to perceive without end.
Thus, for the vast, there are aspects they cannot fully encompass,
and for the minute, there are details they cannot clearly discern.
It is simply that the eyes cannot reach everything.
Both the subtle and the vast are not nonexistent;
how then can we know what is formless and cannot be encompassed?
【Commentary】When viewing a vast object with a minute form,
one is bound to fail to grasp its full breadth and distance,
hence it is said to be immeasurable.
Conversely, when observing a minute form with a vast perspective,
one is bound to lack clarity and distinction,
hence it is said to be without shape or substance.
Both of these perspectives still do not transcend the realm of existence;
how could this be the meaning of ultimate non-being!
【Two】【Annotation】Their sizes differ,
so their conveniences cannot be the same.
【Commentary】Jīng means
something minuscule.
Fú means
something vast and grand.
This aims to clarify the smallest within the small,
the largest within the large.
Although the endowments of vital breath differ,
none are detached from having form (note 2).
Their natural mechanisms operate spontaneously,
each having its own appropriateness.
【Transcription】"垺" Lǐ reads as pū huí fǎn.
Xú pronounces it as fú,
meaning abundant.
Guō reads it as fāng yóu fǎn,
Cuī pronounces it as póu.
"之殷" Yīn,
means multitude.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary states Yīn,
means great,
hence the annotation says the greatest within the great,
and should not be interpreted as multitude.
"異便" reads as bì miàn fǎn.
Xú reads it as fú miàn fǎn.
The annotations are all the same.
【Three】【Comment】If it is formless and cannot be encompassed,
then there is no such advantage of differing suitability.
【Commentary】Since their sizes differ,
their appropriate uses also vary;
thus, it is understood that this situation has not transcended the realm of existence.
【Four】【Notes】There is essence and coarseness,
thus it cannot be without form.
【Commentary】When discourse touches upon the refined and the coarse,
it is necessarily confined to the realm of forms and names,
and fails to transcend the surface of words and appearances.
【Transcription】"Jīng cū" qī hú fǎn.
Xià tóng.
【Five】【Treatise】That which is formless and cannot be encompassed,
is the Dào.
The ultimate Dào is profound and mysterious,
transcending both mind and form,
thus it cannot be distinguished by names or categories,
nor can it be exhaustively measured by quantity or extent.
【Explanation】"Néng fēn" is read as the character itself.
【六】【注】It is simply nonexistent,
how could there be any distinction between refined and coarse!
Words and ideas exist,
but what is spoken of and intended is nonexistent.
Therefore, seek beyond words and ideas,
and enter the realm without words or intentions,
only then can one reach it.
【Commentary】What can be articulated through debate and discourse
pertains to the coarse methods of things;
what can be apprehended through the mind's intent
pertains to the subtle and refined aspects of things;
but that which the divine mouth cannot express,
and the sage's heart cannot discern,
is the profound principle.
One must seek it beyond words and meanings,
how could it be confined to the realm of the refined and the coarse!
【Transcription】"Bù Néng Lùn" may also be written as "Bù Néng Yù".
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition, which has the character 'ear' (耳) after 'convenience' (便).
(2) The character 'form' (形) is amended based on the main text below in the phrase "expecting there to be form."
(3) The character 'that which' (所) is supplemented according to the preceding sentence.
Therefore, the conduct of the great person,
does not involve harming others,
nor does it excessively emphasize benevolence and kindness;
actions are not driven by profit,
nor does it despise gatekeepers and slaves;
there is no contention over goods and wealth,
nor excessive emphasis on polite refusals;
in handling affairs, they do not rely on others,
nor do they overly depend on labor for sustenance;
they do not look down upon greed and corruption;
their actions differ from the common customs,
yet they do not excessively pursue eccentricities;
their behavior follows the crowd,
but they do not disdain flattery and sycophancy;
the ranks and emoluments of the world are insufficient to encourage them,
and punishments and shames are not enough to humiliate them;
they know that right and wrong cannot be distinctly separated,
and the fine and the great cannot be clearly defined.
It is said:
'The person of the Way is not heard of,
the one of utmost virtue gains nothing,
the great person has no self.'
This is the pinnacle of restrained distinctions.
【一】【注】The great person,
acts naturally without intention.
Every step they take lands in an auspicious place,
how could they tread on paths that harm others!
【Commentary】The great man responds to things,
akin to the movement of heaven,
operating without intent,
thus casting all into auspicious places.
His words benefit all beings,
and ultimately bring no harm to anyone.
【二】【注】He does no harm and does not boast of his kindness.
【Commentary】His benevolent grace is like the spring sun,
yet he does not widely dispense favors.
【Three】【Comment】Act in accordance with reason,
and reason inherently brings no harm.
【Commentary】Acting in response to opportunities,
one does not confine the mind in benefiting others.
【Translated Text】"For profit" pronounced as yú wěi fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】He was placed in this position based on his abilities,
not because he was looked down upon that he was assigned to this post.
【Commentary】Blending honor and disgrace,
unifying poverty and success,
thus even gatekeepers and slaves
are not considered lowly.
【Explanation】"故措" is read as qī gù fǎn.
【Five】【Annotations】Each is assigned a specific division.
【Commentary】Having few desires and knowing contentment,
maintaining one's place without greed,
thus towards those goods and wealth,
there is truly no contention.
【Six】【Annotation】Just right is enough.
【Commentary】He was naturally modest and amiable,
accepting or declining in accordance with circumstances,
never feigning emotions to the end,
and often yielding with embellished words.
【Seven】【Annotation】Each is to assume their own responsibility.
【Commentary】Foolishness and wisdom follow one's nature,
skill and clumsiness are inherited from one's disposition,
ultimately never borrowing from others,
nor seeking endeavors beyond one's allotted capacity.
【Eight】【Annotation】Sufficient and that is all.
【Commentary】Eating within one's allotted portion,
being content with sufficiency,
not greedily seeking more,
so as not to exhaust the mind and strength.
【九】【注】Principle is inherently without desire.
【Commentary】One who embodies and comprehends the profound Way,
is therefore free from emotional desires.
It is not merely about valuing purity and integrity,
or despising greed and corruption.
【一０】【Note】One alone has neither that which must be nor that which must not be,
thereby standing apart from the common ways.
【Commentary】Blending the light and merging with the dust,
there is nothing that cannot be done,
yet remaining unstained amidst the stains,
thus one's conduct differs from the common ways.
【Explanatory Text】"Xíng shū": read as xià mèng fǎn.
The actions of Xià, Yáo, and Jié are the same.
【一一】【Note】It naturally differs by following principles (二).
【Commentary】He abides in correctness and embodies the Way,
thus he does not engage in much wickedness or deviation,
but greatly conforms to all living beings,
hence there has never been any discord or divergence.
【Transcription】"辟異" is pronounced pì yì fǎn.
【一二】【Note】Follow the actions of the multitude.
【Commentary】The perfect person has no fixed mind,
never clings to personal views,
thus in all actions and endeavors,
strives to follow the multitude.
【一三】【Annotation】Naturally upright.
【Commentary】By nature loyal and steadfast,
they do not tread the path of heresy,
not because they despise flattery and sycophancy and only then become upright.
◎ Jiāshìfù said:
The conduct of a great person encompasses five matters:
fundamentally not harming others,
yet not for the sake of benevolence;
having no regard for noble or base status, nor wealth or profit in their heart,
how could there be any need for polite refusal?
Not leading others to pursue profit,
how could there be any greed or corruption?
Acting differently from common customs,
yet not for the sake of being unconventional;
following the masses in compliance,
yet not for the sake of flattery.
In affairs, they do not rely on others,
as Xǔ Xíng spoke of plowing together and governing,
cooking meals and eating together;
not excessively consuming through labor,
as Lǎozǐ said, "I am free from action, and the people prosper on their own;
I am free from desire, and the people remain simple of their own accord";
those who are greedy and corrupt cease on their own,
without the need to despise them.
Guǒ Xiàng's commentary fails to make this clear.
【一四】【注】External affairs do not connect to the heart.
【Commentary】High office and generous salary,
the world considers glorious;
punishment, execution, dismissal, and demotion,
the world considers shameful.
Yet once one realizes that prosperity and decline do not define the self,
and comprehends that advancement and obstruction occur in their own time,
then their arrival is insufficient to encourage or spur,
and their departure is insufficient to humiliate or disgrace.
◎Jià Shìfù remarked:
When worldly ranks and emoluments are inadequate as incentives,
and penalties and shames are inadequate as disgraces,
following the above,
it speaks of governing through non-action so the people naturally transform.
Benevolence and deference find no place to apply,
greed and flattery have no means to be employed,
so what use are ranks, emoluments, penalties, or shame then!
Guǒ Xiàng said external matters do not lodge in the heart,
which is mistaken.
【一五】【Note】Thus, they are mysteriously united.
【Comment】Each holds to their own right and wrong,
thus right and wrong cannot be fixed as absolute standards;
they mutually define what is large and small,
so how can the fine and the coarse have definite boundaries?
This is precisely what is meant by "the universe is but a tiny blade of grass"!
【16】【Comment】By entrusting things to their nature, their essence naturally becomes understood,
thus achievements and fame are attributed to the things themselves,
hence they are not heard of.
【Commentary】The sage who embodies the Way,
harmonizes with the light yet conceals their brilliance,
attributes achievements to others,
leaving no reputation or fame to be known.
By lodging these in others,
it is said that they are heard of.
【一七】【Note】Gain is born from loss;
if all things had no loss,
then the name 'gain' would vanish.
【Commentary】"Attainment" refers to
the name for not losing.
But those who have reached the ultimate state,
are equal in gain and loss,
since there is nothing lost,
there is also nothing gained.
Therefore, the Lǎojīng states,
the highest virtue is not virtuous.
【一八】【Note】It merely follows the nature of things.
【Commentary】The great sage,
responding to all that stirs feeling,
adapts to things whether square or round,
thus having no self.
【Explanatory Text】"Wújǐ" is pronounced as jǐ.
【One Nine】【Comment】By restraining it to its utmost limit,
thus it becomes obscure,
for only what is extremely formless and cannot be encompassed is truly so.
【Commentary】Yāo means
to rely upon.
Fèn means
a limit.
The great man benefits all things,
and indeed there are many ways to do so,
but in essential terms,
nothing comes before relying on one's proper limits.
If one sees only what the eyes can see,
hears only what the ears can hear,
and knows only what the understanding can know,
thus confining oneself within the bounds of one's proper limits,
this is the perfection of virtue.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's version, which has the three characters "zhī tú yě" after "rén".
(2) Zhào Jiànyì's version lacks the character "ér" and the character "yě".
(3) The character "wèi" is emended according to the original text of the Lǎo Zǐ.
(4) The Shìdétáng edition writes "qī",
while Zhào's edition does not contain this sentence.
The River Earl said:
"When it comes to the exterior of things,
or the interior of things,
by what standard do we distinguish between noble and base?
By what criterion do we differentiate between small and large?"
【One】【Explanation】Whether outside of things,
or inside of things,
refers to the internal and external aspects of the nature of things.
"Wù" (why),
what does it mean?
It speaks of the distinctions between nobility and baseness,
the boundaries between small and large,
whether they lie within the nature of things,
or outside the inherent nature,
and where exactly do these distinctions exist?
Hé Bó had not yet understood their origin,
hence he posed this question.
【Explanation】"Wicked" is pronounced as wū.
The same applies below.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"From the perspective of the Dào,
things have no nobility or baseness【note 1】;
from the perspective of things themselves,
each considers itself noble and others base【note 2】;
from the perspective of common customs,
nobility and baseness lie not within oneself【note 3】.
From the perspective of differences,
if we deem large what is inherently large,
then nothing under heaven is not large;
if we deem small what is inherently small,
then nothing under heaven is not small;
knowing that heaven and earth can be as small as a grain of rice,
and the tip of a hair can be as large as a mountain,
then the relativity of measurements is perceived【note 4】.
From the perspective of function,
if we affirm what is inherently functional,
then nothing lacks function;
if we deny what is inherently non-functional,
then nothing possesses function;
knowing that east and west are opposite yet cannot exist without each other,
then functional distinctions are determined【note 5】.
From the perspective of inclinations,
if we approve what is inherently approvable,
then nothing is not approvable;
if we disapprove what is inherently disapprovable,
then nothing is not disapprovable;
knowing that Yáo and Jié each naturally disapproved of the other,
then the relativity of inclinations and conduct is perceived【note 6】."
【一】【注】Each is self-sufficient.
【Commentary】The Way is the subtle principle of emptiness and penetration;
things are the coarse matters of material obstruction.
When viewing the subtle through the coarse,
there arises distinction between great and small;
when observing the coarse through the subtle,
there is no hierarchy of noble and base.
【二】【Note】This trifling matter,
is what the Way intricately weaves and harmonizes (1).
【Commentary】When human sentiments are inverted,
confusing right and wrong,
everyone desires to elevate themselves and belittle others,
while others likewise value themselves and look down upon them in return.
With mutual misunderstanding between both sides,
hence it is spoken of as mutual delusion.
【Three】【Annotations】This is what is called inversion.
【Subcommentary】The splendor of glory and the shame of execution
are matters that come unexpectedly,
yet those among the vulgar crowd
groundlessly generate joy and sorrow.
Thus, what is bestowed is considered noble,
and obtaining it is thereby seen as favor;
what is taken away is deemed lowly,
and losing it is thereby regarded as disgrace.
This shows that favor and disgrace depend on external things—
how could nobility and baseness lie within oneself!
【Four】【Commentary】What is considered large,
is so because it is sufficient;
what is considered small,
is so because it lacks surplus.
Thus, by following its nature to deem something large,
then a hair's tip and a mountain hill cannot differ in their designation;
by following its lack of surplus to call something small,
then heaven and earth and a grain of rice do not vary in their description.
If one observes differences without following this principle,
then the varying measures accumulate,
the subtleties clash against each other,
and it becomes impossible to fully discern them.
【Commentary】Chà (差) means
distinction.
If one considers self-sufficiency as greatness,
then a hairtip and a mountain
are equally great;
if one considers nothing beyond as smallness,
then heaven-earth and a grain of rice
are equally small.
Therefore, based on the hairtip as greatness,
nothing in the myriad things is not great;
based on heaven-earth as smallness,
nothing in the myriad things is not small.
Hence, although there are thousands of differences and myriad distinctions,
with varying quantities and measures,
viewing them from this perspective,
the principle becomes evident.
◎ Jiā Shìfù (家世父) said:
Dào (道) is
that which connects self and others;
wù (物) is
what the mind relies on to judge others;
sú (俗) is
what follows customs to determine nobility and baseness;
chà (差) is
the gradations among the myriad things;
gōng (功) is
achievements that serve both self and others;
qù (趣) is
the guiding purpose of a single mind.
Amidst profusion and confusion,
upholding them all follows a dào,
hence discussing them all has a basis.
Nobility and baseness, greatness and smallness,
with debates and reversals,
thus the world becomes tumultuously complex.
【Explanation】"其稱" is read with "chēng" in the fourth tone.
"可勝" is pronounced as "shēng".
【Five】【Annotation】Under heaven, none do not interact with one another as self and other,
and both self and other desire to act for themselves,
this is like east and west being opposites.
Yet self and other interact like lips and teeth,
and though lips and teeth do not consciously act for each other,
when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.
Therefore, when the other acts for itself,
the benefit to me is vast,
this shows how opposites cannot exist without each other.
Thus, if we deny their achievements because they act for themselves,
then under heaven, no achievement would be acknowledged;
if we recognize their achievements because they cannot exist without each other,
then under heaven, all achievements would be acknowledged.
If instead we forget their achievements in acting for themselves and dwell on the favor of mutual assistance,
the more diligently favors are given, the more hypocrisy and superficiality grow,
under heaven loses its proper functions, and human nature becomes dissipated,
thus the merit and portion can never be fixed.
【Commentary】East and west are different directions,
their meanings are opposite,
yet without the east, the west cannot be established,
showing that they cannot exist without each other.
If we take examples from the human body,
the eyes see and the ears hear,
the hands grasp and the feet walk,
the five viscera and six bowels,
the four limbs and all body parts,
each have their own functions,
all endowed with fixed roles,
how could the eyes see for the ears or the feet walk for the hands?
The notion of mutual substitution in function
is thus negated here.
This is to negate based on what they lack,
then nothing in the world is without absence.
However, if the feet do not walk, the limbs become weak and sluggish,
if the eyes do not see, the whole body becomes obstructed and stagnant,
and while each part performs its own duty,
without intention to act for others,
the effect of aiding one another
is naturally achieved,
this is to affirm based on what they possess,
then nothing in the world is without presence.
From this perspective,
functions indeed exist,
and roles are distinctly assigned.
If one forgets their inherent contributions and dwells on the idea of mutual favors,
then both self and others lose their nature, and right and wrong become confused and chaotic,
how could this be the intention of Zhuāngzǐ!
【Explanatory Text】"Zì wèi": read as "zì wèi" with the pronunciation of "wèi".
In the annotations, both "zì wèi" and "xiāng wèi" follow the same reading.
The rest are read according to their original pronunciation.
【Six】【Annotation】All things are naturally so,
hence there is nothing that is not so;
all things contradict each other,
hence there is nothing that is not contradictory.
When nothing is not contradictory,
then there is no "so";
when nothing is not so,
then there is no "contradictory."
One who is neither "so" nor "contradictory"
is Yáo;
one who is both "so" and "contradictory"
is Jié.
However, these two rulers,
each received their innate nature from heaven,
and could not exchange roles,
so by observing Yáo and Jié, one can see the inclinations and conduct of the world—
it becomes evident that they could not exchange roles.
Commentary: "Ran"
means "this is so."
All things consider themselves right,
hence there is nothing that is not right;
all things deem each other wrong,
hence there is nothing that is not wrong.
When nothing is not wrong,
then there is nothing right in the world;
when nothing is not right,
then there is nothing wrong in the world.
Therefore, observing from the perspectives and inclinations of things,
because each considers itself right,
then nothing in the myriad things is not right;
because they deem each other wrong,
then nothing in the myriad things is not wrong.
The most extreme opposites in the world
are Yáo and Jié,
hence citing these two rulers, Yáo and Jié, clarifies the dual meanings of right and wrong.
Thus, Yáo regarded non-action as right,
and having desires as wrong;
Jié regarded non-action as wrong,
and having desires as right;
hence it is said, "Know that Yáo and Jié naturally deem each other wrong."
From this perspective,
the inclinations and principles
of all things in the world can be understood.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has the character 者 below it.
(2) The character 以 has been added based on the following sentence.
In ancient times, Yáo and Shùn abdicated and became emperors,
while Zǐ Kuài abdicated and met his end;
Tāng and Wǔ contended and became kings,
while Bái Gōng contended and was destroyed.
From this perspective,
the rituals of contention and abdication,
the conduct of Yáo and Jié,
the nobility and baseness,
vary with the times and cannot be taken as constant norms.
A massive beam can batter down city walls,
but cannot be used to stop up a hole—
this illustrates differences in utility;
steeds like Qíjì and Huáliú
can gallop a thousand lǐ in a day,
yet at catching mice they are no match for a wildcat—
this illustrates differences in skill;
the owl can pick up fleas at night
and discern the tip of a hair,
yet in daylight it stares wide-eyed without seeing a hill—
this illustrates differences in nature.
Hence it is said:
Should one only follow what is right and avoid what is wrong,
only embrace order and reject chaos?
Such a view fails to comprehend the principles of heaven and earth,
the inherent nature of all things.
It would be like following heaven and ignoring earth,
embracing yīn and excluding yáng—
its impracticality is evident.
Yet if one still speaks of it incessantly,
they are either foolish or deceitful.
Emperors and kings abdicated differently,
the three dynasties had distinct successions.
Those who act contrary to their time
and go against the customs of their age
are called usurpers;
those who act in accordance with their time
and follow the customs of their age
are called righteous followers.
Be silent, oh Hébó!
How could you comprehend the gateway to nobility and baseness,
the abode of small and great!
【一】【疏】Monarchs of different eras,
contended and abdicated in different times.
When Yáo knew the Mandate of Heaven would shift,
he abdicated to Shùn;
Shùn recognized the dynastic fortune was about to change,
and in turn yielded to Yǔ.
Táng and Yú are counted among the Five Emperors,
hence it is said they abdicated and became emperors.
(Zǐ) Zhī,
was the chancellor of Yān named Zǐzhī.
Kuài,
was the name of the King of Yān.
Zǐzhī,
was the son-in-law of Sū Qín.
Qín's younger brother Sū Dài,
on a mission from Qí to Yān,
used the ancient tale of Yáo offering the throne to Xǔ Yóu to persuade King Kuài of Yān,
urging him to abdicate in favor of Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī thus accepted.
The people resented his acceptance of the abdication,
and none submitted to Zǐzhī,
leading to three years of state chaos.
King Xuān of Qí, adopting Sū Dài's strategy,
raised an army to attack Yān,
resulting in the killing of King Kuài of Yān in the suburbs,
the execution of Zǐzhī in the court,
and the destruction of the state of Yān.
Was this not a case of imitating the old paths of Yáo and Shùn, yet bringing disaster to such an extent!
【Translated Text】"Zhī Kuài" is pronounced as kuài,
also read as gǔ mài fǎn,
and also as gǔ huì fǎn.
Zhī refers to
the prime minister of Yān, Zǐ Zhī.
Kuài,
is the name of the king of Yān.
Sīmǎ comments:
King Kuài of Yān was unskilled in strategy,
following the advice of Sū Dài,
imitated Yáo and Shùn by abdicating the throne to Zǐ Zhī,
and within three years, the state fell into chaos.
【二】【Note】Those who receive the world by complying with Heaven and responding to the people,
their actions are the traces of contention and yielding.
Those who seek their traces
lose the means by which the traces were made,
thus they are cut off and extinguished.
【Commentary】Yīn Tāng conquered Jié,
Zhōu Wǔ overcame Zhòu,
these two rulers,
both received the Mandate of Heaven,
thus bringing peace and prosperity throughout the land,
with all states coming to pay tribute.
Therefore, they succeeded the Three Sovereigns,
hence it is said they contended and became kings.
When the times called for military force,
Yáo and Shùn were the appropriate response.
When the times required yielding and deference,
Yáo and Shùn were the fitting examples.
Thus, through countless changes and transformations,
one responds to things according to the times.
The traces of yielding and contending
cannot be rigidly adhered to.
Bái Gōng, named Shèng,
was the grandson of King Píng of Chǔ,
and the son of Crown Prince Jiàn.
King Píng, following the advice of Fèi Wújí,
took a woman from Qín as his consort and distanced the crown prince.
The crown prince fled to Zhèng,
married a woman from Zhèng and fathered Shèng.
The Grand Tutor Wǔ Shē was executed,
his son Wǔ Xū fled to Wú,
and Shèng followed him into exile in Wú,
farming in the fields with Xū.
The Chǔ Prime Minister Zǐxī welcomed Shèng back to the state,
enfeoffed him in the territory of Bái,
where he presumptuously declared himself a duke.
Shèng, because the people of Zhèng had killed his father,
requested troops to seek revenge.
Repeated requests were denied,
so he raised an army in rebellion.
Chǔ dispatched Lord Yè, Zǐgāo, to attack and annihilate him,
hence it is said Bái Gōng contended and perished.
【Explanation】"Ér Wáng" is read as wǎng kuàng fǎn.
"Bái Gōng" was named Shèng,
grandson of King Píng of Chǔ,
served as county magistrate of Bái,
usurped the title of Gōng,
and died in rebellion.
The event is recorded in the sixteenth year of Duke Āi in the Zuǒzhuàn.
【Three】【Memorials】 contend and yield,
are civil and military affairs.
Yáo and Jié,
are right and wrong.
If governing the world,
then belittle the military and value the civil;
if quelling disasters and chaos,
then belittle the civil and value the military.
Thus, the ways of civil and military,
their value or belittlement depend on the time,
and the practice of right and wrong,
how can their use or abandonment be fixed!
Therefore, the rites of contending and yielding,
in the times of Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ are valued,
but in the times of Zhī Kuài and Bái Gōng are belittled,
they cannot be constant.
【Four】【Explanations】Liáng,
refers to the roof beam.
Lì,
refers to the ridgepole of the house.
Chōng,
means to strike.
Zhì,
means to block.
This means that beams and ridgepoles are large,
and can be used to attack city walls,
but cannot be used to block a mouse hole,
illustrating that the utility of tools varies with their size.
【Interpretive Text】"Liáng Lì": Sīmǎ [Lǐ] reads it as lǐ,
another reading follows the standard pronunciation.
Sīmǎ states:
Liáng Lì
is a small boat.
Cuī states:
It is a roof beam.
◎Qìng Fán's commentary: The Chūxué Jì volume 25 quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Lì,
is a small boat.
This differs slightly from the interpretive text.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Sīmǎ states,
"Liáng Lì is a small boat,"
while Cuī says it is a roof beam.
However, neither a small boat nor a roof beam
is suitable for assaulting city walls.
The poem "Huáng Yǐ" in the Shījīng mentions "with you, the lín and chōng,"
Máo's commentary states:
"Lín,"
refers to the lín chariot,
"chōng,"
refers to the chōng chariot.
The Correct Meaning states:
Military texts include methods for constructing lín and chōng chariots,
and Mòzǐ has a chapter on defending against chōng chariots,
confirming that both lín and chōng are types of chariots.
Thus, the statement here that it "can be used to assault city walls"
clearly refers to such a chariot.
In the "Xú Wúguǐ" chapter, "you must also not display crossbow troops between the Lì Qiáo,"
Guō's annotation states:
"Lì Qiáo,"
refers to a tall tower.
Sīmǎ states:
"Lì Qiáo,"
is the name of a tower observatory.
What is referred to here as Liáng Lì
is likely a chariot with a tower,
similar to what the Zuǒzhuàn calls a "tower chariot."
In the Wénxuǎn's "Biàn Wáng Lùn," "chōng péng ceased in the northern wilds,"
Lǐ Shàn's annotation states:
The character is abbreviated as ●,
meaning a tower,
which serves as evidence that chōng chariots could have towers.
◎Qìng Fán's commentary: Sīmǎ's interpretation of Liáng Lì as a small boat
is incorrect.
Yú's view that it is a tower chariot
also seems forced.
Examining the Lièzǐ's "Tāng Wèn" chapter, "Yōngmén performed songs,"
with lingering sounds winding around the liáng lì,
not fading for three days.
Liáng lì
is precisely what is referred to here as Liáng Lì.
In the "Lì Mìng" chapter, "dwellings are connected by lì,"
and in the Wénxuǎn's "Shànglín Fù" by Sīmǎ Chángqīng, "intertwined and winding lì guǐ,"
[Sīmǎ Biāo's] annotation:
"Lì guǐ,"
means supporting (pillars) [stacked in layers].
"Lì" means attached,
while "guǐ" means intersecting.
"Lì" is the same as "lì."
The Guǎngyùn states:
"Lì,"
means to attach.
The Yǔpiān states:
"Lì,"
means to pair.
Paired pillars are called "lì,"
and beams and pillars attached to each other are also called "lì,"
precisely referring to elements like rafters and pillars.
Thus, Cuī's interpretation is superior.
For Liáng Lì, it must be made of large timber,
hence it can be used to assault city walls,
and should not be rigidly interpreted.
"Zhì" is pronounced zhēn xī fǎn.
The Ěryǎ states:
It means to block.
Cuī and Lǐ agree.
The Shuōwén gives the pronunciation as dū jié fǎn.
【五】【疏】Qíjì Huáliú,
were both fine horses of ancient times.
To catch,
is to seize.
Líshēng,
are wild cats.
Now, fine horses with swift hooves,
can gallop a thousand miles in a day,
yet in catching small mice,
they are not as good as wild cats.
This shows that skills differ,
and one cannot judge all by the same standard.
【Text Explanation】"Qí" is pronounced as qí.
"Jì" is pronounced as jì.
"Huá" is pronounced with the initial consonant h- and the final -uā.
"Liú" is pronounced as liú.
Lǐ Yí says:
Qíjì huáliú,
are all fine horses.
"Bǔ" is pronounced as bù.
Another version also writes it as bó.
Xú pronounces it as fù.
"Lí" is pronounced with the initial consonant l- and the final -ī.
"Shēng" is pronounced as xìng,
Xiàng agrees.
Also pronounced as shēng.
Cuī's version writes it as yòu,
pronounced as yóu or yòu.
"Shū jì" is pronounced with the initial consonant q- and the final -ǐ.
【Six】【Annotation】By entrusting each according to its uniqueness,
then nothing in all creation fails to find its proper place.
【Commentary】The chī
is the xiūliú,
also known as the zhīhú,
a type of earth owl.
By day, its eyes are dim,
but by night, they are sharp,
enabling it to catch fleas and lice at night
and discern the finest details.
When it ventures out by day, it stares wide-eyed
yet cannot see the shape of a hill.
This shows that the natures of creatures differ,
and not just the chī and xiūliú alone!
Thus, by accommodating their inherent traits,
all things can find their proper place.
【Interpretation】"Chī" is pronounced chǐ yí fǎn.
Cuī states:
Chī
refers to xiūliú;
it is the same as wěi xiāo.
Night gathering" is pronounced with seven strokes.
The Cui edition writes it as "most,"
with the same pronunciation.
"Flea" is pronounced as early.
Shuowen:
A jumping insect that bites people.
Huáinánzǐ,
the owl gathers fleas at night,
discerning the finest details.
Xǔ Shèn states:
The owl gathers and eats fleas and lice at night without missing any.
The Sīmǎ edition writes it as "wén,"
pronounced as wén,
stating:
The owl,
xiūliú,
captures wén to eat at night.
Nowadays, the Guō edition also has versions written as wén.
The Cui edition writes it as "claw,"
stating:
The xiūliú gathers human claws in its nest at night.
◎ Wáng Yǐnzhī says:
The character "xiū,"
is redundant due to its appearance in the explanatory text as "chī xiū liú."
(The Běi Yǎ quotation of this is already erroneous.
) According to the explanatory text,
chī,
is pronounced chǐ yí fǎn,
Cuī states,
chī xiū liú,
but does not provide a pronunciation for the character "xiū,"
thus it is clear that the original text did not include the character "xiū."
The Huáinánzǐ's "Zhǔ Shù Piān" also says the owl gathers fleas at night.

Gāo's annotation in the Huáinánzǐ's "Zhǔ Shù Piān":
Chī,
is the chīxiū,
called the old hare,
it calls on human rooftops at night.
At night, its eyes are sharp,
it gathers human claws to place in its nest,
hence it is said to discern the autumn down;
during the day, it sees nothing,
