Xǔ's annotation states:
The owl gathers and eats fleas and lice at night without missing any.
The theory of gathering fleas,
Xǔ and Gāo have differing views.
Wáng Yǐnzhī says,
considering the matter logically,
Xǔ's annotation should be considered elegant and refined.
"Chēn" is pronounced chǐ yí fǎn,
Xiàng pronounces it as chù chén fǎn.
Sīmǎ states:
To open wide.
Cuī pronounces it as xuàn,
also as shī shèn fǎn.
Some versions write it as "míng."
◎ Qìng Fān's case: In the explanatory text,
chēn is sometimes written as míng.
It is suspected that writing it as míng is correct.
Shuowen:
Chēn,
means glaring in anger.
Míng,
means closing the eyes.
Closing the eyes means seeing nothing.
In clerical script, ● is sometimes written as zhēn,
míng is sometimes written as ●,
they are similar in shape and thus mistaken.
In the Guǎnzǐ's "Xiǎo Wèn Piān," Duke Huán glared and looked,
Zhù Fú yǐ (cī) [bì] (four),
in the Hánzǐ's "Shǒu Dào Piān," glaring, gnashing teeth, and straining ears,
in the Huáinánzǐ's "Dào Yìng Piān," glaring fiercely,
baring arms and drawing a sword,
in current editions, chēn is mistakenly written as míng,
all are examples of this.
【七】【注】The principle of heaven and earth,
the nature of all things,
considers gaining the self as right,
and losing the self as wrong,
following one's nature as order,
and losing harmony as chaos.
Yet things have no fixed limit,
and the self has no constant suitability.
With diverse natures and different conveniences,
right and wrong have no master.
If one takes what the self deems right,
then others cannot be wrong;
this is knowing the self but failing to see others.
Therefore, from the perspective of the Dào,
there is no fixed standard for right and wrong.
Entrust them to the heavenly balance,
let both sides proceed freely,
then different directions and diverse kinds
will all equally attain their fulfillment.
【Commentary】"Gài" is a word that
does not exhaust the meaning.
"Shī" means
following one's own mind.
All things follow their own
stubborn minds,
arbitrarily clinging to biases,
considering themselves to be right,
unaware that others see them as wrong;
viewing themselves as orderly,
unaware that others see them as chaotic.
Thus, by following their own minds as right,
they fail to see the wrongs above themselves;
by following their own minds as order,
they claim their own persons are free from chaos.
How could they know that order and chaos share the same origin,
and right and wrong have no fixed master!
Therefore, the shared origin of order and chaos
is the principle of heaven and earth;
the absence of a fixed master for right and wrong
is the nature of all things.
Being ignorant of this truth,
【Transcription】"Shī Shì" some say:
Shī,
means to follow.
"Shī Zhì" read with the pronunciation zhí lì fǎn.
The annotations are all the same.
【Eight】【Memorial】Heaven and earth, yin and yang,
exist in opposition to each other.
If there were heaven without earth,
then all things would not be formed;
if there were yin without yang,
then living beings would not be established.
From this, it is clear that
following only what is right and rejecting what is wrong,
or adhering solely to order and avoiding chaos, is certainly unworkable.
【Nine】【Commentary】Heaven and earth, yin and yang,
are paired in existence;
right and wrong, order and chaos,
are mutually present;
so which should be discarded?
【Commentary】If one takes what is right as the teacher and denies what is wrong,
takes heaven as the teacher and disregards earth,
and yet speaks of this without ceasing,
then unless such a person is utterly foolish,
they must be intentionally deceptive.
【Transcription】"Bù shě" is pronounced as shě.
The same applies below.
【一０】【Commentary】Dì refers to the
Five Emperors.
Wáng refers to
the Three Sovereigns.
The Three Dynasties are
Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
Shàn means
to hand over.
Jì means
to continue.
Some were passed down within the same clan,
while others were yielded to different surnames,
hence the term "different successions."
Some were inherited from father to son,
while others seized power through rebellion or assassination,
hence the term "different inheritances."
Some were too slow or too hasty,
not aligning with the timing of heaven;
some were not accepted by the common people,
contrary to human affairs.
Thus, Zhī and Kuài admired Yáo and Shùn but ended their lineage,
Bái Gōng imitated Tāng and Wǔ but brought about his own destruction.
Such examples as these
are called usurpation.
【Transcription】"Cuàn fū": initial sound is the fǎnqiè "chū huàn fǎn",
meaning to seize.
The lower part is read as its usual pronunciation.
【一一】【Comment】Arms and courtesies,
their deeds differ,
their use or abandonment depends on the time,
and one cannot rigidly adhere to either.
As for Tāng and Wǔ raising armies,
or Táng and Yú yielding the throne,
they aligned with the heavenly way above,
and harmonized with human hearts below.
Such actions as these
are called righteousness.
【一二】【Note】What the common people value
may at times be deemed worthless;
what things consider great,
the world might belittle.
Therefore, following the traces of things,
one cannot avoid differences,
which is why the Five Emperors and Three Kings were not alike.
【Commentary】The River Earl failed to grasp the principle,
so the Sea Spirit reproved him to forget speech,
to remain silent and not utter a sound,
hoping he would refrain from wasteful words.
For small and great have no fixed master,
noble and base have no set gate,
yet perceptions of things are topsy-turvy,
and judgments of good and bad are recklessly made.
So how can you, by chasing after distinctions, know the gateways of noble and base, great and small?
This means you do not understand.
【Explanation】"Nǚ" is pronounced as "rǔ".
The same applies hereafter.
"Xià" is pronounced as "wū".
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Jūnfáng edition, which has the character 'zhī' following 'cuàn'.
(2) The character 'zhī' is supplemented based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The two characters 'chóng lěi' are emended according to the Wénxuǎn annotations.
(4) The character 'bì' is revised based on the Guǎnzǐ.
The River Earl said:
"Then what should I do,
and what should I not do?
In matters of accepting and declining, advancing and retreating,
how should I ultimately proceed?
【一】【疏】What is to be done?
It is like asking "how".
Although the River Earl acknowledges the lofty principle,
he has not yet grasped the intended meaning.
Therefore, I further request a resolution to my doubts,
awaiting your explanation.
I wish to dwell and move among human society,
preserving my health and cultivating the Way.
In what matters may I engage?
In what matters should I not engage?
As for declining and accepting,
advancing and retreating,
and the multitude of worldly affairs,
how should these matters be handled?
I hope you will bestow your instruction,
which I shall uphold and follow for life.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"From the perspective of the Dào,
what is noble and what is humble?
This is called reversal and extension.
Do not constrain your will,
lest you greatly obstruct the Dào.
What is little and what is much?
This is called alternating transformation.
Do not act with a fixed bias,
lest you become inconsistent with the Dào.
Be as dignified as a ruler of a state,
showing no personal favoritism.
Be as serene as the altar of the land in sacrifice,
granting no personal blessings.
Be as boundless as the four directions, limitless and endless,
with no fixed boundaries.
Embrace all things impartially,
then who is to be specially supported?
This is called having no fixed direction.
All things are one and equal,
so what is short and what is long?
The Dào has no beginning or end,
while things have life and death,
yet do not rely on their completed forms.
Now empty, now full,
they do not maintain a fixed shape.
Years cannot be held back,
time cannot be stopped.
Decline and growth, fullness and emptiness,
end only to begin again.
This is how to speak of the principles of great righteousness,
and discuss the patterns of all things.
The life of things
is like a gallop, like a swift run,
with no movement that does not bring change,
no moment that does not involve shift.
What then should one do,
and what should one not do?
For they will naturally transform by themselves."
【一】【注】The way of nobility and baseness,
alternates in cycles.
【Commentary】Fǎnyǎn means
reversal and transformation.
Nobility and baseness
arise from deluded attachments.
Now, when illuminated by the principle of emptiness and interconnectedness,
the noble become base and the base again become noble,
hence it is called fǎnyǎn.
【Explanatory Text】"Fǎn Yǎn" is read according to the character's standard pronunciation,
and also pronounced with the reading of "zhàn".
Cuī's commentary states:
Without distinctions of nobility or baseness,
it instead becomes something beautiful.
The text also appears as "pàn yǎn",
Lǐ's commentary states:
Like "màn yǎn", merging into one family.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: The commentary to Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" in the "Wén Xuǎn" quotes Sīmǎ's version as "pàn yǎn",
stating:
"Pàn yǎn",
is like "màn yǎn".
The explanatory text is missing.
"Fǎn Fù" is pronounced with "fāng" and "fú".
【二】【Note】By restraining oneself, one does not align with the Way.
Commentary: "Er",
means "you".
Those who cultivate the Way,
should be unrestrained,
yet you cling stubbornly to your will,
proud and holding fast,
thus conflicting with the principle of emptiness and connection, obstructed and not smooth.
【Explanation】"Yǔ Dào Dà Jiǎn" Xiàng jì niǎn fǎn,
Xú jì yǎn fǎn.
Some versions have "Yǔ Tiān Dào Jiǎn".
Cuī's version has jiǎn written as huàn,
saying:
It means to harmonize.
【Three】【Annotations】Follow its portion,
thus the application is without constancy.
【Explanation】Xiè,
means substitution.
Shī,
means application.
Things may gather little to become much,
or disperse much to become little,
hence application and substitution,
are without constant fixity.
【Explanatory Text】"Xiè Shī" is read as written.
Sīmǎ explains:
Xiè means
to substitute.
Shī means
to use.
Cuī explains:
Not substituting one's virtue,
this is called Xiè Shī.
【Four】【Annotations】If one cannot adapt to change,
then one will not align with the Way.
【Commentary】The alternation of application,
whether more or less, should suit the occasion,
adapting to changes as they arise,
thus enabling the harmonization of all things.
If one rigidly adheres to a single course of action,
it will not align with the underlying principle.
【Transcription】"Cān": initial sound lín, fanqie.
"Chā": initial sound yí, fanqie.
【Five】【Annotation】The Duke should be just and that is all.
【Commentary】The person who embodies the Way,
appears dignified when observed,
sits uprightly ruling over ten thousand chariots,
serves as a model for all things,
unifies those myriad states,
with all revering one sovereign,
nurtures and governs the common people,
surely without any personal favoritism.
【Transcription】"Yán hū" is read as yú jiǎn fǎn,
and also as the regular pronunciation.
【Six】【Annotation】What all under heaven equally seek.
【Commentary】Yáoyáo,
● is the appearance of being long and continuous.
It is like when the multitude of people offer sacrifices to the gods of soil and grain,
yet the gods of soil and grain do not grant personal blessings to anyone.
【Explanation】"Yóu Yóu" is pronounced as yóu.
【Seven】【Comment】Drifting aimlessly without a fixed abode.
【Commentary】"Extensive" refers to
an appearance of universality.
The supreme person establishes their resolve,
encompassing all without bias,
aiding all living beings,
loving broadly and equally.
It is like the east, west, south, and north,
vast and boundless without end,
their capacity akin to the empty sky—
how could there be boundaries or limits!
【Explanatory Text】"Fàn fàn" is pronounced fú jiàn fǎn.
The character is also written as fàn.
"Zhěn" is pronounced zhī rěn fǎn.
Yù was forced to rebel,
Jiù was targeted to rebel.
【Eight】【Annotation】To shelter and govern all living beings,
returning them to their inherent duties and pacifying their comings and goings,
how could it be through favoring some and supporting others!
【Commentary】Huái means
to harbor.
Shú means
who.
This means the great sage, with compassion,
embraces all beings impartially,
treating them with equality,
ultimately without partiality or favoritism.
Who, then, would have the intention to rescue, receive, support, and assist them?
【Nine】【Notes】have no fixed method,
thus they can take all things as their method.
【Commentary】Like a bright mirror,
compared to this secluded valley,
it responds to opportunities in countless ways,
never fixed to one direction.
【一０】【Note】There is none that is not fully sufficient.
【Commentary】All things vary in form,
yet their nurturing is unified;
Ducks' legs are short, cranes' legs long,
each sufficient by nature, thus equal.
【One】【Comment】Life and death are
but the endless transformations,
not the ultimate beginning and end.
【Commentary】The Way of empty penetration,
has neither end nor beginning;
that which is attached and obstructed
falsely speculates on death and life.
Therefore, the Classic of Lǎozǐ states:
Meeting it, one does not see its head;
following it, one does not see its back.
【一二】【Note】Completion has no fixed place.
【Commentary】Responding to things without fixed methods,
transcending all and transforming independently,
how could it rely on opposition to generate existence!
【13】【Comment】Not taking form as position,
and guarding it without change.
【Commentary】Just like the principles of yīn and yáng,
spring gives birth and autumn brings death,
fullness and emptiness shift and transform,
flourishing and withering follow their seasons—
how could one cling to physical form and stubbornly hold onto fame and status?
【一四】【Note】Wishing to raise it up and make it depart, yet unable to do so.
【Explanation】"Lìng qù" is read as lì chéng fǎn.
【一五】【Note】Wanting to stop it yet unable to make it cease.
【Commentary】The brevity or longevity of one's years,
the swiftness or slowness of time,
arise from the natural order,
and are not governed by human will.
Thus, when they come, one cannot lift them to make them depart;
when they leave, one cannot halt them to make them stay.
Both should be accepted as they are,
for from the beginning, they are not separate from the self.
【1.6】【Comment】Change and renewal occur daily,
never adhering to the old.
【Commentary】As yin wanes and yang waxes,
summer fills and winter empties,
the sequence of qi cycles in a loop,
ending only to begin anew;
the way of primordial unity,
transforms and renews daily,
following principle straightforwardly,
requires no deliberate effort.
The previous discussion on the words of Hǎi Ruò,
precisely addresses the proper principles of the Great Way,
and expounds on the profound truths of all things.
【一八】【Note】Simply make use of it as is.
【Commentary】The flow of life and cessation,
ceaselessly moving and changing,
is as swift
as a gallop or a dash.
It is like a hundred years passing in an instant;
why should it trouble the heart!
【One Nine】【Annotation】Thus, it cannot be held onto and preserved.
【Commentary】The flow and transformation of all things,
the shifting of eras and times,
are as swift as a passing glance,
as sudden as a glimpse through a crack.
Thus, there has never been discussion of movement without change,
nor mention of time without transition.
【二０】【Note】If one acts with deliberate intent in between,
it will disrupt the natural transformation.
【Commentary】All things in their chaotic diversity
share the same endowment from nature.
If one remains tranquil and lets them be,
they will inevitably transform on their own.
Why trouble the mind with deliberate action or non-action?
【Collation】（一）In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as '汎'.
（二）In Zhào's edition, there is one character below '之'.
The River Earl asked:
"What, then, is the value of the Way?"
【一】【注】Because it transforms of itself.
【Commentary】If acting and not acting were merged into one,
then the principles of the ordinary and the sage would be equalized.
Since one entrusts oneself to the naturalness of transformation,
what value would there be in the ultimate Way?
Hé Bó raised this question again,
expressing his lingering doubts.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"Those who comprehend the Way are sure to penetrate the principles;
those who penetrate the principles are sure to understand adaptability;
those who understand adaptability do not allow external things to harm themselves.
Those with perfect virtue
cannot be burned by fire,
cannot be drowned by water,
cannot be harmed by heat or cold,
cannot be injured by birds or beasts.
This is not to say they make light of these things,
but that they discern safety and danger,
remain calm in fortune and misfortune,
are cautious in advancing and withdrawing,
so nothing can harm them.
Therefore it is said:
Heaven lies within,
human effort manifests without;
virtue resides in Heaven.
Understanding the actions of Heaven and humanity,
rooted in Heaven,
positioned in attainment;
advancing and retreating with flexibility,
returning to the essence and speaking of the ultimate."
【一】【注】Those who understand the Dao
know that it has no capability;
having no capability,
how could it then give birth to me?
I am born spontaneously,
and thus my four limbs and all parts of the body,
the five organs and the essence-spirit,
are already accomplished without any deliberate action—
so how could there be any intention after life is formed?
Those who comprehend this principle
are sure to dismiss excessive knowledge,
relinquish emotions that strain life,
and ride along with change, responding flexibly.
Thus, they do not let the external injure the internal,
nor allow things to harm themselves, and so remain ever whole.
【Commentary】One who can comprehend the Way of empty penetration,
must grasp the profound and mysterious true principle;
one who grasps the profound and mysterious true principle,
must be clear about the expedient wisdom in responding to things.
Since one is clear that expedience and truth have no fixed method,
thus one can accept arrangements and let go of transformations.
Life and death bring no change to oneself,
so how can external things cause harm!
This addresses the doubts of Hé Bó,
then clarifies the preciousness of the ultimate Way.
【Transcription】"Wǔ Zàng" cái làng fǎn.
【二】【注】When the heart is at peace,
danger cannot imperil it;
when the mind is entirely content,
hardship cannot cause suffering.
【Commentary】The one with ultimate virtue refers to a person who has attained the ultimate Way.
Although they blend their light with the world,
and live among customs, mingling with the dust,
they are not invaded by the four seasons,
nor harmed by the three calamities.
Having grasped it within,
thus external forces cannot harm them.
This clarifies the preciousness of understanding the Way.
【Three】【Annotations】Even if the heart finds it acceptable,
one must not allow it to be violated.
【Commentary】"Bó" means
"to slight."
The reason why water and fire do not invade,
and birds and beasts do not harm,
lies solely in the peace of the mind.
Thus, what could harm cannot harm,
as one neither avoids them
nor lightly offends them.
【Explanation】"Its thinness" is read according to its literal pronunciation.
Cuī Zǐzhēn says:
It means to attach it with the body.
【Four】【Annotation】He knew he could not escape it.
【Commentary】The reason harm cannot inflict harm,
is precisely because one carefully examines safety and danger,
follows it and cannot escape,
abides in it and always remains at ease.
【Five】【Annotation】Be at peace with the circumstances fate has bestowed.
【Commentary】Níng,
means peace.
Huò,
means hardship and blockage.
Fú,
means smoothness and attainment.
A person of utmost virtue,
adapts only to changes,
understands that hardship and smoothness are fated,
realizes that misfortune and fortune have no fixed gate,
thus their joy does not lie in hardship or smoothness,
and whatever they encounter is always peaceful.
【Six】【Annotation】To discern that the decision of whether to depart or stay is not one's own.
【Commentary】Carefully considering that departure and approach have no fixed rule,
examining that acceptance and rejection have their proper timing,
even though one follows things in shifting and moving,
yet one constantly abides in the utmost appropriateness.
【Seven】【Annotation】Not considering harm as harm,
thus nothing can harm one.
【Commentary】Being unified in safety and peril,
oblivious to calamity and fortune,
moving along with the transformations,
thus nothing can harm him.
This summarizes the earlier meaning of being unharmed.
【Eight】【Annotation】What is natural lies within,
while what conforms to the natural exists externally.
Hence, the Great Ancestral Teacher states,
"To know what pertains to Heaven and humanity is the ultimate knowledge,"
clarifying that distinctions between inner and outer are not acts of deliberate doing.
【Commentary】Natural disposition
is stored within the heart;
human affairs that follow order
manifest in external actions;
none of these are forced.
By letting things follow their natural course,
nothing in the world can harm them.
【九】【注】If one allows people to rely solely on their knowledge,
they will drift and lose their inherent simplicity.
【Commentary】The excellence of ultimate virtue
lies in its naturalness.
If one indulges in human cunning and knowledge,
it will lead to the dissipation of innate nature.
【一０】【Note】This is the natural understanding,
which acts on its own without exceeding its inherent portion,
so even when it manifests outwardly,
it always remains rooted in heaven and positioned in attainment.
【Commentary】This is true knowledge.
Position,
refers to one's dwelling place.
Applying true knowledge and acting in the world,
even when involved with things through countless transformations,
one always takes spontaneity as the foundation,
abiding in utmost emptiness without losing one's nature,
moving yet remaining tranquil.
【Transcription】"Zhi Xing" is read as it is written.
【一一】【Note】Corresponding with the opportunity,
there is this change.
【Commentary】Hesitant pacing,
is the appearance of being unsettled in advancing or retreating.
The ultimate person responds to the world,
following the rise and fall of things,
sometimes yielding, sometimes extending,
never holding fixed positions,
their choices and rejections mysteriously align,
to suit what is appropriate to the occasion.
【Explanation】"Zhi" is pronounced with the rhyme "zhang yi",
also with the rhyme "chi ge".
"Zhu" is pronounced with the rhyme "zhang lü",
also with the sound "zhuo".
"Qu Shen" is pronounced as "shen".
【一二】【Note】Though knowledge encompasses heaven and earth,
and affairs connect with all things,
one must never lose sight of the essential principles,
thereby achieving the complete integration of the heavenly and human ways.
【Commentary】Although he once again mingled among people, his mind remained constantly tranquil and still,
often dwelling at the pivotal core while returning to the origin and source.
All his utterances
emanated from the void and the ultimate,
his actions never contravening stillness,
his words never contradicting silence.
【Explanation】"Fǎn Yào" is pronounced as "fǎn" in "miào".
【Collation】（1）The Que Wu cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, where "tiān" is written as "hū".
He asked:
"What is meant by Heaven?
What is meant by man?"
【一】【疏】The River God, not yet comprehending the profound mysteries,
raised this doubt again,
inquiring about the Way of Heaven and humanity,
hoping for an answer in the future.
The Spirit of the Northern Sea said:
"That oxen and horses have four feet
is called the natural;
to put a halter on a horse's head,
to pierce a bullock's nose,
is called the artificial.
Hence it is said,
'Do not let the artificial obliterate the natural;
do not let purposeful actions obliterate destiny;
do not let gains sacrifice reputation.
Guard this carefully and do not lose it,
and you will return to the innate nature."
【一】【注】In the life of humans,
can they do without harnessing oxen and riding horses?
To harness oxen and ride horses,
must they not pierce and bridle them?
Oxen and horses do not refuse being pierced and bridled because
it is inherently decreed by Heaven's mandate.
If it aligns with Heaven's mandate,
then even though it is entrusted to human affairs,
its foundation lies with Heaven.
【Commentary】Oxen and horses receive from Heaven
the natural possession of four legs,
which is not a matter of human intervention,
hence it is called heavenly.
Bridling a horse's head
or piercing an ox's nose
comes from human intention,
hence it is called human.
Yet an ox's nose can be pierced,
and a horse's head can be harnessed,
without knowing why it is so,
unable to discern the reason.
Although these acts depend on human circumstances,
the principle ultimately returns to the Creator.
To reveal the unity of Heaven and humanity,
the two creatures, the ox and the horse, are thus employed.
【二】【Note】It is acceptable to have minor lapses,
but if one acts excessively,
and loses moderation in conduct,
then the natural order is destroyed.
【Commentary】When human effort is applied in accordance with natural principles,
it is acceptable to bridle and harness.
But if one were to pierce a horse's nose or yoke an ox,
it would violate the natural order of creation.
This can be said to pursue the artificiality of human desires,
extinguishing the spontaneity of heavenly principle.
【Three】【Commentary】Not acting according to one's own will but deliberately forcing actions—
where then does destiny find its place of peace!
【Commentary】To act in accordance with one's nature is to move,
and if movement does not exceed its proper measure,
then a thousand miles can be reached and the heavenly mandate is fully preserved.
But if one uses a jade horse to spur a steed and drives it without restraint,
this is to destroy the heavenly principle with human affairs and worldly matters,
leading to peril and demise in no time.
How then can fate remain secure?
This applies not only to horses and oxen,
but to all things in the world.
【Four】【Annotation】What one gains has its constant portion;
to sacrifice for fame is excessive.
【Commentary】The names one may pursue are boundless,
while what one's nature can attain is limited.
If one uses the limited gains to chase after the boundless names,
then the natural principle is extinguished and life's essence is lost.
【Five】【Annotation】Truth lies within the nature's bounds.
【Commentary】Folly and wisdom, premature death and longevity,
poverty and success, honor and disgrace,
are endowed by nature,
each having its own lot.
One should only firmly guard and maintain
without chasing after material things,
to attain what is within one's lot without losing the Way—
this is called returning to the origin and source,
restoring one's true nature.
This sentence summarizes the profound and subtle principles discussed earlier.
Kuí pities the millipede,
the millipede pities the snake,
the snake pities the wind,
the wind pities the eye,
the eye pities the heart.
【一】【疏】"Lian" is a term denoting affection and admiration.
Kuí is a one-legged beast,
its form resembling a drum,
with feet like human feet,
but with heels bent forward.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states,
within the Eastern Sea,
there is Liúbō Mountain,
on which resides a beast,
shaped like an ox,
of a bluish-gray color,
hornless,
moving on one leg,
its voice like thunder,
named Kuí.
In ancient times, Huángdì battled Chīyóu,
using Kuí's skin to cover a drum,
whose sound could be heard for five hundred lǐ.
Xián,
is the centipede,
Kuí, with its few legs, yearns for many,
thus it pities Xián;
Xián, having legs, envies the legless,
thus it pities the snake;
the snake, being small, aspires to largeness,
thus it pities the wind;
the wind, being dark, admires brightness,
thus it pities the eyes;
the eyes, being external, long for the internal,
thus they pity the heart.
This aims to clarify that all things in heaven and earth
are endowed with their natural states,
be it brightness or darkness, existence or non-existence,
there is no need to yearn or envy,
but to let go and allow things to be,
naturally aligning with the profound Dào.
Those who are misguided,
deludedly aspire and admire,
hence the crude examples of Kuí and others are cited,
to illuminate the subtle principle of natural endowment.
Another interpretation:
"Lián"
means compassion.
Kuí, hopping on one leg,
pities Xián for the toil of its many legs;
Xián, walking securely with legs,
sympathizes with the snake for its hardship without legs;
the snake, having form and thus ease,
commiserates with the wind for its lack of substance and obscurity;
the wind, drifting freely,
pities the eyes for being confined to form and stagnation;
the eyes, being external and clear,
pity the heart for being internal and obscured.
This aims to reveal how emotions towards things are inverted,
giving rise to misguided compassion,
hence the use of Kuí and Xián to remedy such afflictions.
【Text Explanation】"Kuí" is pronounced as qiú guī fǎn,
a one-legged beast.
Lǐ Yí says:
When the Yellow Emperor was on the throne,
the feudal lords obtained a strange beast at Liúshān in the Eastern Sea,
its appearance like an ox,
bluish in color,
without horns,
one-legged,
able to run,
entering and exiting water would bring wind and rain,
its gaze like the sun and moon,
its voice like thunder,
named Kuí.
The Yellow Emperor killed it,
took its skin to cover a drum,
the sound could be heard for five hundred lǐ.
"Lián" is pronounced as lián.
"Xián" is pronounced as xián,
also pronounced as xuán.
Sīmǎ says:
the horse-xián insect.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
qū qú horse-xián.
"The xián pities the snake, the snake pities the wind, the wind pities the eyes, the eyes pity the heart." Sīmǎ says:
Kuí,
has one foot;
xián,
has many feet;
snake,
has no feet;
wind,
has no form;
eyes,
their form is fixed here,
but their light flows to there;
the heart, however, is inherently obscure,
and travels externally as the spirit.
Kuí said to Xián:
"I manage to walk by hopping on one foot,
and there's nothing more I can do.

Xián said:
"Not so.
Have you not seen one who spits?
When he sputters, the larger droplets are like pearls,
the smaller ones like mist,
and those mingled as they fall are too many to count (note 1).
Now I move by my natural mechanism,
without knowing how it is so."
[Note 1]
【First】【Commentary】When one spits and sprays,
it is truly without intention towards size,
yet the substance of large and small naturally distinguishes itself;
thus, the large ones are like pearls and gems,
the small ones like fine mist,
scattering and falling mixed together,
their numbers hard to count.
Now, the multitude of legs of the millipede,
is a natural mechanism,
moving and walking,
unaware of the reason why,
unintentionally stretching on their own,
similar to spraying spit.
Kuí raised the question based on human reasoning,
while the millipede answered directly with innate nature,
the inevitable logic
becomes clear here by itself.

The millipede said to the snake:
"I walk with many feet,
yet I cannot keep up with you who have no feet.
Why is that?"
【One】【Argument】The millipede with many legs moves slowly,
while the snake with no legs moves swiftly.
Yet, whether slow or fast, having or lacking,
is endowed by the creator's design.
To clarify this principle,
this question is thus raised.
The snake said:
"The movements of the heavenly mechanism,
how can they be altered?
What need have I for feet!"
【一】【注】The birth of things,
is not because they know how to be born that they are born (一).
Thus, the course of life,
how could it be because they know how to proceed that they proceed?!
Therefore (二), the feet do not know why they walk,
the eyes do not know why they see,
the mind does not know why it knows,
yet they naturally attain their functions with ease.
The pace of speed or slowness,
the discernment of hearing and sight,
whether capable or not,
are none of them my own doing.
But the deluded, because they wish to possess their bodies and boast of their abilities,
thereby go against their natural mechanism and harm their divine instruments (三).
The perfect person knows that the natural mechanism cannot be altered,
so they discard cleverness,
abandon knowledge and scheming,
placidly forget what they do and let things follow their own movement,
thus nothing fails to roam in carefree ease.
【Commentary】The natural mechanisms,
possess such movements and functions,
whether slow or fast, existent or non-existent,
cannot be altered.
Acting spontaneously without deliberate intent,
what need is there for feet!

The serpent said to the wind:
"When I move my spine and ribs to travel,
it appears as if I have form.
But now you, billowing up from the Northern Sea,
billowing into the Southern Sea,
seem to have no substance at all.
Why is this?"
【One】【Explanation】Xié,
means ribs.
Péng péng,
is the sound of wind,
also describes the appearance of dust stirring.
Since a snake has no feet,
it must move by flexing its spine and ribs.
Sì,
means to resemble.
Although a snake has no feet,
it has a form and image,
while wind has no form or image,
yet it stirs and moves without fixed direction,
from north to south,
striking and lifting the vast sea,
formless yet powerful.
I secretly have some doubts,
hence I present this question,
hoping to hear a later response.
【Explanatory Text】"Peng peng": pronounced as bù dōng fǎn,
Xú pronounces it as fú gōng fǎn.

The Wind said:
"Indeed.
I blow gustily from the Northern Sea and enter the Southern Sea,
yet pointing at me overcomes me,
and treading on me also overcomes me.
Nevertheless,
the breaking of great trees
and the toppling of large houses
—this only I can accomplish.
Thus, by not prevailing in numerous small matters, I achieve great victory.
As for achieving great victory,
only the sage is capable of it."
【一】【注】Indulging in their natural instincts,
having nothing to contend with,
this is the minor victory (一).
Yet, by riding on the actions of all things and directing the multitude of talents,
enabling each talent to find its own place,
and allowing all things to act according to their own nature,
then under heaven, none will not (二) roam freely,
this is precisely (三) how the sage achieves the great victory.
【Commentary】Although the wind travels from north to south,
whipping up the vast sea,
if a person points a finger against the wind,
the wind cannot break the finger;
if one steps on the wind with a foot,
the wind likewise cannot break the foot—
this is its minor incapability to prevail.
Yet when a sudden gale arises,
a whirlwind abruptly surges,
then grand towers are sent flying by it,
and the Li shrine is torn apart by its force—
this is its major capacity to prevail.
Analogously, the perspicacious scholar,
who stirs waves in murky traces,
blends wisdom and folly among the petty crowd,
and extinguishes right and wrong within the clamorous dust—
this is his minor incapability to prevail among the multitude.
Yet in nurturing all living beings,
creating and transforming the realm,
matching the sky and earth in sheltering and supporting,
equaling the sun, moon, and stars in illumination—
this is his major capacity to prevail.
It is not something the ordinary can comprehend,
only the sage alone can achieve it.

where the people of Sòng surrounded him several layers deep,
yet he did not cease playing the zither and singing (1).

Confucius said:
"Come!
Let me tell you.
I have long sought to avoid poverty,
yet cannot escape it —
such is fate;
I have long pursued success,
yet cannot attain it —
such is timing.
In the eras of Yáo and Shùn,
no one in the world suffered poverty —
not because they gained wisdom;
in the eras of Jié and Zhòu,
no one in the world achieved success —
not because they lost wisdom.
It was simply the circumstances of the time.
Those who travel by water unafraid of serpents and dragons
possess the courage of fishermen;
those who journey on land unafraid of rhinoceroses and tigers
possess the courage of hunters;
those who face crossed blades before them
and regard death as life
possess the courage of martyrs;
those who understand poverty is fated,
success is timed,
and face great adversity without fear
possess the courage of sages.
【一】【注】To clarify that the timing of fate is inherently just,
it is thus entrusted to the pursuit of concealment.
【Commentary】To shun,
means to avoid,
to resist.
Adversity,
is obstruction and blockage.
Prosperity,
is smoothness and attainment.
The Master instructed Zhòng Yóu to come,
and spoke of the ultimate principle, saying:
"I avoid adversity and hardship,
yet cannot escape them—
is this not the mandate of Heaven!
I have long sought prosperity,
yet cannot attain it—
it is because I have not encountered an enlightened era.
As for timing and fate,
when they come, one cannot resist them;
when they depart, one cannot retain them.
Therefore, accept them with peace,
and there will be no situation where one does not find ease."
The Master wished to illuminate this principle,
so he used the metaphor of avoiding adversity,
though in reality, there is no adversity to avoid.
【Explanatory Text】"吾語" is read as yú jù fǎn.
【二】【注】Do not trouble your mind with matters of adversity and success.
【Commentary】When living in the times of Yáo and Shùn,
the world was peaceful and prosperous,
treating people like vessels,
allowing them to fulfill their inherent roles,
thus there were no obstructions or blockages.
In the times of Jié and Zhòu,
the world was tyrannical and chaotic,
all things lost their nature,
thus there were no enlightened individuals.
It is merely that the era was marked by peril and adversity,
circumstances made it so,
not due to the workings of fate or knowledge,
that such gains and losses occurred.
【Three】【Comment】Each feeling finds its own peace.
【Commentary】When the heart finds solace, it forgets its fears.

Gōngsūn Lǒng asked Wèi Móu, saying:
"I studied the way of the ancient kings in my youth,
and when I grew up, I understood the practice of benevolence and righteousness;
I unified similarity and difference,
separated hardness and whiteness;
affirmed what is not so,
approved what is not acceptable;
I confounded the knowledge of the hundred schools,
exhausted the arguments of numerous mouths;
I thought myself to have reached the ultimate understanding.
【一】Now that I have heard Zhuāngzǐ's words,
I am bewildered and find them strange.
I do not know whether my reasoning falls short,
or my knowledge is inferior?
Now I have no way to open my beak,
I dare to ask the method."
【一】【疏】His surname was Gōngsūn,
named Lóng,
a man of Zhào.
Wèi Móu,
a prince of Wèi,
embraced the Way and upheld virtue,
weary of the defilements of the mundane world.
The former kings,
were the traces of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng.
Benevolence and righteousness,
were the practices of the five virtues.
Sūn Lóng was endowed with innate intelligence,
leading with talent and broad debate,
authored the theory of "Defending Whiteness,"
and became renowned for his erudite argumentation.
Thus, he could unite differences into sameness,
and separate sameness into differences;
making the impossible possible,
and the unacceptable acceptable;
he challenged the writings of the hundred schools, leaving them all confounded,
and exhausted the arguments of many mouths, causing all to yield.
Born in the declining Zhōu era,
he stood alone in his time,
with disciples like Kǒng Chuān,
who revered and learned from him.
He dominated fame in his era,
with none able to contend against him.
Thus it is said,
proud of this knowledge,
he reached the utmost subtleties,
yet when he suddenly encountered Zhuāngzǐ,
he was like a frog at the bottom of a well.

Prince Mou leaned on his desk with a deep sigh,
looked up to the sky and laughed, saying:
"Have you alone not heard of the frog in the sunken well?
It said to the turtle of the Eastern Sea:
'How happy I am!
I leap and jump upon the railing of the well,
rest within the broken rim of the bricks when I enter;
when I dive into the water, it reaches my armpits and holds my chin,
when I tread in the mud, it covers my feet and submerges my insteps;
looking back at the shrimp crabs and tadpoles,
none can compare to me.
Moreover, to command the waters of this one gully,
and straddle the joy of this sunken well,
this is the utmost indeed.
Why don't you come in sometime to see for yourself?'
The turtle of the Eastern Sea had not yet inserted its left foot
when its right knee got stuck already.
Thereupon it hesitated and retreated,
and told the frog about the sea, saying:
'A distance of a thousand miles
is not enough to convey its vastness;
a height of a thousand fathoms
does not suffice to fathom its depth.
In the time of Yǔ, there were nine floods in ten years,
yet the waters did not increase;
in the time of Tāng, there were seven droughts in eight years,
yet the shores did not diminish.
Not shifting with the brief or long,
not advancing or retreating with the much or little—
this is the great joy of the Eastern Sea.'
Thereupon, the frog in the sunken well, upon hearing this,
was startled and astonished,
and in bewilderment, felt lost within itself.
【一】【疏】The nobleman embodies the Way with purity and loftiness,
transcending worldly affairs,
recognizing the shallow arguments of Sūn Lóng,
discerning the profound words of Zhuāngzǐ.
Thus, he gazes at the sky, sighs, and scoffs,
raising two analogies of the frog and the turtle
to clarify the victory and defeat between the two masters.

while swimming, I cradle my armpits and chin,
and when stirring the mud, it submerges my insteps and feet;
looking back at creatures like shrimp and crabs,
glancing down at the likes of tadpoles,
carefree and joyful,
none are as content as I."

The frog called the turtle "Fūzǐ,"
saying:
"I alone monopolize the water of this one gully,
and am content with the joy of a pit well.
The utmost satisfaction in the world
is nothing greater than this.
Though the place is humble,
one can wander and wade here.
Fūzǐ, why not temporarily descend your steps
and enter to see this lowly town?"
With this, he prided himself,
boasting to the turtle.
【Translated Text】"To monopolize" is to engage in market warfare,
meaning to specialize.
"One valley" refers to a single ravine.
【Three】【Commentary】It is not that the great takes no pleasure in roaming through the small,
but rather, it is not by choice.
【Commentary】"Zhí" means
to be restrained.
The sunken well is narrow and small,
while the sea turtle is enormous.
To contain the large within the small,
is logically untenable,
hence, as soon as the right knee lowered, it was already constrained.
【Transcription】"已縶" pronounced as zhū lì fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
to detain.
The Sān Cāng states:
to hobble.
"非樂" pronounced as yuè,
also read as wǔ jiào fǎn.
【Four】【Shu】Qūnxún,
means unhurried and calm.
Seven chǐ is called a rèn.
The turtle, with its left foot not yet entered,
and its right knee already bent,
then hesitated and retreated,
telling the frog about the state of the great sea.
Now, people who consider a thousand lǐ as far,
are not yet qualified to speak of the sea's vastness;
those who regard a thousand rèn as high,
are also insufficient to fathom the sea's utmost depth.
Speaking of the sea's depth and greatness,
it is beyond human measurement,
to consider a pit in the ground as the ultimate,
is that not inferior indeed!
【Explanation】"Qūn" is pronounced as qī xún fǎn.
【Five】【Commentary】A moment,
is a short period of time.
Long,
is a lengthy duration.
Shifting and moving,
refers to change and alteration.
Yáo encountered a great flood,
appointed Yǔ to manage it, and he achieved success,
hence it is referred to as the time of Yǔ.
Yet during Yáo's ten-year reign,
nine years were plagued by floods;
in the eight years of Yīn Tāng,
seven years suffered from drought.
(However) during the drought, the cliffs did not diminish,
nor did the waters increase during the floods,
this clearly shows the vastness of the surging waves,
the profound and boundless depths,
unaffected by the brief or long passage of time,
how could they be influenced by the ebb and flow of quantity!
The joy of the Eastern Sea,
lies herein!
【Translated Text】"Jiǔ Lǎo" pronounced as lǎo.
"Fú Wèi" with the pronunciation according to Yú Wèi's interpretation.

"Qǐng Jiǔ" Simǎ explains:
It means early and late.
【Six】【Annotation】By coveting what is greater,
one thus loses oneself.
【Commentary】Tìtì (startled),
describes a look of shock and terror.
Guīguī (disoriented),
depicts the appearance of being at a loss.
The frog, monopolizing the beauty of its sunken well,
claimed there was nothing surpassing it in the world.
Suddenly hearing the sea turtle's discourse,
it was bewildered and lost what it had asserted,
hence tìtì and guīguī,
startled and disoriented.
As for Gōngsūn Lǒng, who studied the ways of the ancient kings,
was devoted to the practice of benevolence and righteousness,
perplexed by the knowledge of the hundred schools of thought,
exhausted the arguments of many mouths in debate,
upon suddenly hearing Zhuāngzǐ's words,
it was just like the well frog encountering the sea turtle.
【Transcription】"Shìshì": initial reading chì fǎn,
alternative reading zhàng gé fǎn,
Guō's reading tù dí fǎn.
"Guīguī": read as standard pronunciation.
Alternative reading xū yì fǎn,
Lǐ Xú's reading jì shuì fǎn.
Shìshì,
guīguī,
both describe the appearance of being startled, gazing, and losing self-composure.

Moreover, one who does not know the boundaries of right and wrong,
yet still wishes to observe the words of Zhuāngzǐ,
is like making a mosquito carry a mountain
or a marsh insect race across a river
—they will certainly be unequal to the task.
Furthermore, is not one who does not know how to discuss the most profound teachings yet finds self-satisfaction in temporary gains
just like the frog at the bottom of a well?
Moreover, he treads upon the nether springs and ascends to the great empyrean,
neither south nor north,
freely released in all four directions,
submerged in the unfathomable;
neither east nor west,
beginning in the dark obscurity,
and returning to the great thoroughfare.
Yet you rigidly seek to understand it through scrutiny
and probe it with argumentation—
this is truly like viewing the sky through a tube
or measuring the earth with an awl.
Is that not petty indeed!
Be gone now!
And have you not heard of the youth of Shòulíng who went to Hándān to learn how to walk?
He failed to acquire the skills of that state,
yet also lost his original way of walking,
so he could only crawl back home.
Now if you do not leave,
you will forget what you originally had
and lose your own vocation."
【一】【Note】Each thing has its allotted role,
and one should not forcibly emulate others (1).
【Commentary】The shāngjù,

also called qiěqú.
Although Sūn Lóng possessed intelligence and understanding,
it was merely worldly knowledge,
not true wisdom.
Thus, knowing that he was unable to exhaust the realm of right and wrong,
and yet wanting to observe Zhuāngzǐ's words of ultimate principle,
how is this any different from making a mosquito carry a mountain,
or having a shāngjù race across rivers and seas?
With strength too weak for the heavy burden,
and wisdom too small for grand schemes,
it is certain that he would be unequal to the task.

Shāngqú,

how could he discuss Zhuāngzǐ's words that probe the subtlest and most wondrous depths?
He could only debate right and wrong,

To take this as the Way,
is he not indeed a frog at the bottom of a well!

【Three】【Annotations】This speaks of its all-encompassing presence.
【Commentary】To tread upon,

The Great Sovereign,

Xuánmíng,

The words of Zhuāngzǐ,

to tread,

【Four】【Annotation】Those who roam the boundless are not
understood through scrutiny and argumentation.
【Explanation】"Suǒ zhī" is pronounced as suǒ bái fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】If one is not suited for the position,
it is permissible to remove them.
【Commentary】Guīguī describes the appearance of meticulous planning.
To seek the Way through observation and examination,
and to express sincerity through eloquent debate,
even if one applies one's mind with utmost care,
still remains far from attaining it.
It is like looking at the sky through a tube—
how could one know the vastness or narrowness of the heavens!
Or probing the earth with an awl—
how could one measure the depth or shallowness of the land!
Zhuāngzǐ's Way harmonizes with the two primal forces,
while Sūn Lóng's virtue is akin to the tube and awl.
The disparity in wisdom and capability is so vast;
since he falls so short,
it is fitting that he should quickly withdraw.
【Six】【Annotation】Using this to imitate that,

Hándān,

Sūn Lóng, though his arguments were vast and extensive,

Thus, to study Sūn and discuss Zhuāng

If it gives rise to a mind of longing and admiration,

This is the combined metaphor.

Gōngsūn Lóng's mouth gaped open and would not close,

Fleeing,

Previously hearing Zhuāngzǐ's discourse,

Internally distinct and externally separated,
it was beyond what Sūn Lóng could comprehend.
Thus, the mouth gaped open but could not close,
the tongue lifted but could not lower,

Zhuāngzǐ held his fishing rod without turning his head,
and said:
"I have heard that in Chǔ there is a sacred turtle,
which died three thousand years ago.
The king wrapped it in cloth, stored it in a bamboo box, and enshrined it in the ancestral temple.
Now,
would this turtle rather die and leave its bones to be honored,

【一】【疏】The turtle possesses divine marvels,

The question is:

dragging its tail in the muddy paths?
Or does it wish to be hollowed out, leaving its bones behind for fame,
to be honored in the temple above?"
Therefore, Zhuāngzǐ deeply understood this sentiment,
hence he leisurely disregarded it.

stored it in a bamboo box,

Zhuāngzǐ went to see him,
and said:
"In the south there is a bird,
its name is Yuānchú,
do you know it?
Now this Yuānchú,

Huìzǐ said:
"You are not a fish,
how do you know the joy of fish【一】?"
【一】【疏】Huì Shī failed to comprehend the nature of things,
raising baseless doubts,
Zhuāngzǐ was not a fish,
how could he know the joy of fish?
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"You are not me,
how do you know that I do not know the joy of the fish【一】?"
【一】【注】This aims to illustrate the idea that we can recognize each other's differences yet cannot fully understand one another.
You are not me,
yet you can still know that I am not a fish;
similarly, I am not a fish,
but I can also know the happiness of the fish.
【Commentary】If because I am not a fish,
I cannot know the fish,
then since you are not me,
how can you know me?
If you, not being me,
can still know me,
then although I am not a fish,
why should I be hindered from knowing the fish?
This is turning the question back to challenge him,
making it impossible for him to raise objections.
Huìzǐ said:
"I am not you,
so of course I do not know you;
you are certainly not a fish,
so your not knowing the happiness of fish
is perfectly clear."
【一】【注】He abandoned the fundamental principles and resorted to sophistry to raise objections.

so he could not understand Zhuāngzǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ was certainly not a fish,
how could he know the joy of fish?

yet abandoning its fundamental principle,
he resorted to sophistry to raise objections.

means to trace or seek.

The meaning of following the root
is presented in the text below.
【二】【注】Examining the fundamental argument of Huìzǐ, it states:
"If one is not a fish, then one has no basis to know it.
Now you are not me,
yet you say 'How do you know the fish are happy?'
This shows you know that I am not a fish.
If you know that I am not a fish,
then all who understand each other
can indeed use this to know that,
without needing to be a fish first to know fish.
Therefore, following your 'how do you know' statement,
you already know what I know.
Yet you still ask me again -
I precisely know it from the Háo River's banks,
why must I enter the water!"
Now, what creatures are born with and are content in,
heaven and earth cannot change their place,
yin and yang cannot alter their nature;
thus, using what land-dwellers are content with
to know what water-dwellers enjoy
is hardly sufficient to be called profound.
【Commentary】"The Master said" refers to
Zhuāngzǐ's rebuttal to Huìzǐ's argument.
When Huìzǐ stated, "You are not a fish, how do you know the fish are happy?"
it sufficiently demonstrates that Huìzǐ was not Zhuāngzǐ,
yet he knew that Zhuāngzǐ did not know the fish.
Moreover, since you are not me but know me,
and knowing me, you question me,
why should it hinder me, though not a fish, from knowing the fish,
and knowing the fish, from admiring them?
The natures of things differ,
as water and land have distinct characteristics,
but those who comprehend their principles understand their essence.
Thus, wandering by the Háo River,
one knows the fish's contentment and joy;
reflecting upon all beings,
must one enter the water?
Therefore, the two sages Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ are used as examples
to illustrate the essence of the debate.
【Transcription】"Fāng fù" is read as fú yòu fǎn.
"Qí chù" is read as chāng lǜ fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfáng's version with the character "且" present above.
【Chapter One】【Explanatory Notes】The chapter is titled based on its meaning.
The "Yuè" (Music) is pronounced as "luò".
Is there perfect happiness in the world or not?
Are there means to preserve one's life or not?
What should one do and what rely on?
What avoid and what dwell in?
What pursue and what abandon?
What delight in and what detest?
【One】【Commentary】Only by forgetting joy can one attain perfect contentment,
and only with perfect contentment can one preserve one's true self.
Should one consider this as having joy?
Yet the highest joy is devoid of mere pleasure;
or should one consider this as having no joy?
Yet with the self preserved, there is no sorrow.
【Commentary】This is a hypothetical inquiry.
"Ultimate,"
means the extreme.
"Joy,"
means happiness.
It asks whether in the entire universe,
there might be some ultimate happiness
that can sustain and nurture one's life and existence, or is there none?
【Explanation】"Zhì Lè" is pronounced as luò.
The same applies throughout the chapter where not otherwise indicated.
Zhì,
means ultimate.
Lè,
means joy.
【二】【注】Choosing among these eight options,
none suffices to preserve one's life;
only by making no choice and accepting whatever one encounters can one achieve wholeness.
【Commentary】Xī means
"what".
Now, if one wishes to practice the Way of ultimate joy to preserve one's life,
what actions should one undertake,
what principles should one rely on,
what should one avoid,
where should one find peace,
what should one follow,
what should one abandon,
what should one delight in,
what should one detest,
to align with the Way of ultimate joy?
This poses a hypothetical question,
which will be clarified in the following discussion.
【Interpretation】"Xī wù" is read as wū lù fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has the character 者 after 遇,
while the Zhào Jiànyì edition does not.
What the world honors are
wealth, rank, longevity, and fame;
what it delights in are
bodily comfort, rich flavors, fine clothes, beautiful sights, and sweet sounds;
what it looks down upon are
poverty, low station, early death, and ill repute;
what it suffers from are
the body's lack of comfort,
the mouth's lack of rich flavors,
the form's lack of fine clothes,
the eyes' lack of beautiful sights,
the ears' lack of sweet sounds;
if these cannot be obtained,
then great worry and fear arise.
Is this not foolishness in caring for one's physical form?
【一】【疏】What the world holds in high regard
is nothing more than abundant wealth and treasures,
noble prosperity and glory,
a long and extended lifespan,
a good reputation and fine renown;
what brings joy and pleasure
is flavors that delight the palate,
elegant attire that honors the body,
vibrant colors that please the eyes,
harmonious music that entertains the ears.
If one attains these,
then they can settle into enjoyment.
【Ershu】 poverty and low status,
premature death and ill repute,
the world considers these to be inferior.
【Three】【Comment】All these,
losing them does no harm to the form, yet gaining them damages the nature;
now, on the contrary, they worry over not obtaining them,
hence, they are foolish.
【Commentary】All the matters mentioned above,
bring no benefit to people,
yet common customs consider their absence as suffering,
which does not suit one's disposition,
leading to worry, sorrow, fear, and anxiety.
To cultivate the body in such a manner,
is it not extremely foolish!
The wealthy ones,
toil their bodies and labor diligently,
accumulating much wealth yet unable to use it all,
thus their care for their physical form is also external.
The noble ones,
working night and day,
ponder over what is good or not,
thus their care for their physical form is also neglected.
Human life,
is born together with worries,
the long-lived are muddled and confused,
long troubled yet not dying,
how bitter it is!
Thus their care for their physical form is also distant.
Martyrs are seen as good by the world,
yet it is not enough to keep themselves alive.
I do not know if this goodness is truly good,
or truly not good?
If it is considered good,
it is insufficient to preserve one's life;
if considered not good,
it is sufficient to save others.
Therefore it is said,
"If loyal advice is not heeded,
withdraw and do not contend."
Thus, Master Wǔ Zīxū contended and thereby mutilated his body;
had he not contended,
his fame would not have been established either.
Is there truly such a thing as goodness or not?
【一】【Note】To keep one's form within,
it is enough to know contentment (1).
【Commentary】The wealthy and affluent households,
exhaust their spirits and toil their thoughts,
exerting their physical strength to the utmost,
amass vast sums of wealth,
hoarding it without dispersing it,
how could they ever use it all!
Those who nurture their inner selves,
would they ever be like this!
【二】【注】Therefore, those who cherish their form,
find contentment within their own being.
【Commentary】Those in high positions ponder far-reaching matters,
with heavy emoluments come deep worries.
Thus day and night they deliberate,
proposing what is advisable and rejecting what is objectionable,
toiling their bodies and distressing their minds,
without a moment's rest.
As for their physical form,
is this not indeed neglectful?
【三】【注】Only by relinquishing attachment to life can one forget sorrow,
only by forgetting sorrow can life become enjoyable,
only when life is enjoyable can the body be truly possessed by oneself,
wealth be truly one's own,
and honor be truly one's glory.
【Commentary】Those endowed with a stubborn and foolish disposition,
born into sorrow and distress,
even if they live long lives,
their spirits remain dull and obscured.
Lingering in sorrow without dying
turns into sheer misery.
To exist in such a form,
is it not far removed
from the ultimate joy?
Is that not a grave error!
【Transcription】"惛惛" pronounced as hūn,
also pronounced as mén.
【Four】【Annotation】Goodness should be appropriate,
thus not universally aiding.
【Commentary】Sincerity means
truthfulness.
Those who are loyal and heroic,
sacrifice themselves for their principles,
and their names are passed down through the ages,
are seen as virtuous in the world.
However, it is unknown whether this virtue is genuine or false.
If virtue is genuine,
it may not be enough to preserve one's life;
if virtue must be false,
it should not sustain the common people.
Relying on remonstrance and counsel brings about peace,
which is sufficient to preserve people's lives;
being loyal and heroic yet suffering execution,
this is not enough to preserve one's own life.
【五】【注】Only the virtue of the Mean is such.
【Commentary】Dūn xún,
means compliance and following.
The principle for being a minister is,
if the ruler is without virtue,
one should remonstrate with a loyal and sincere heart;
if the ruler does not listen,
then one must dūn xún and cease,
for if one argues forcefully against the grain like stroking the scales the wrong way,
one will inevitably suffer punishment or death.
【Explanatory Text】"Crouch" is pronounced as qīxún fǎn.
Guō's reading is cún,
also pronounced as qùyǔn fǎn.
"Follow" is pronounced as xún,
also pronounced as chún.
"Do not contend" refers to the contention in fighting.
Same below.

means to retreat.

【Six】【Annotation】Therefore, one should follow the central path as the constant principle.
【Commentary】King Fúchāi of Wú,
was debauched and unprincipled,
while Wǔ Zǐxū, through loyal remonstrance,
met a cruel death.
Had he not admonished,
his reputation for loyalty would not have been established.
Therefore, whether to remonstrate or not,
and what is good or not good,
truly cannot be definitively determined.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, this sentence reads as "thick form knows contentment."
(2) The characters "dāng" and "wǎn" have both been emended according to the Hànshū.
As for what the common people do and what pleases them,
I truly do not know whether such pleasure is indeed pleasure,
or indeed not pleasure.
Observing what the common people find pleasurable,
they all flock toward it in crowds,
clamoring as if driven by necessity,
and all call it pleasure—
this is not what I find pleasurable,
nor do I find it unpleasurable.
Does genuine pleasure truly exist or not?
I consider non-action to be true pleasure,
yet it is what the common people greatly suffer over.
Hence it is said,
"The ultimate pleasure is without pleasure,
the ultimate honor is without honor.
【一】【疏】Fruit,
is not yet determined.
The common people take greed and attachment as their heart,
and find pleasure in forms and sounds.
Do they know whether this pleasure is true pleasure?
With such an inverted heart,
it cannot be called faith.
【二】【注】When the masses chase after what they delight in,
they do not even avoid death.
【Commentary】"Hěng hěng"
describes the appearance of rushing toward death.
"Yǐ"
means to stop.
All people in the world,
gathering in crowds and competing eagerly,
what they delight in
is nothing beyond the five desires,
greedily seeking them until death,
yet unable to cease from them.
【Explanation】"Hēng hēng" is pronounced with the initial "h" and the final "eng" in the second tone,
while Xú reads it with "k" and "eng" in the first tone,
and there's also a reading with "h" and "ing" in the third tone.
Lǐ says:
It describes the appearance of hastening toward death.
Cuī says:
Taking what is right as wrong,
and what is wrong as right.
"Hēng hēng,"
in some versions, is also written as "jìng jìng."
【Three】【Comment】Act without intention and let things take their own course.
【Commentary】Ordinary people of the world
all consider sensual pleasures as the highest joy,
while Zhuāngzǐ embodied the Way and forgot about blandness,
thus he did not perceive their joy,
nor did he perceive their lack of joy.
【四】【注】The joy of non-action,
is simply being free from worry.
【Commentary】For those who take pleasure in colors and sounds,
it is uncertain whether such pleasures are truly assured.
If we speak in terms of Zhuāngzǐ's philosophy,
then using emptiness, tranquility, and non-action constitutes the most genuine form of joy.
【五】【Note】Customarily, resounding and clanging are considered music,
excellence and goodness are deemed praise.
【Commentary】Common customs consider wealth, honor, splendor, the clinking of gold, and the chiming of jade as the highest joy,
using flattering words and sycophantic praise as fine reputation,
while viewing non-action, tranquility, simplicity, solitude, and emptiness as sorrow and suffering.
Thus, it is understood that the ultimate joy takes no joy as its joy,
and the ultimate reputation takes no reputation as its reputation.
【Transcription】"Kēng" is read as kǔ gēng fǎn.
"Qiāng" is read as qī yáng fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, where "未之俱" is written as "未知之".
The Zhao Jianyi version writes it as "未知".
(2) The Que Wu cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, where "诚乐" is written as "而诚者为乐".
The world's right and wrong truly cannot be determined.
Even so,
non-action can settle right and wrong.
【一】Perfect joy preserves one's life,
and only through non-action can it be nearly maintained【二】.
Allow me to attempt to explain this.
Heaven is clear because of its non-action,
Earth is tranquil because of its non-action,
【三】thus when both act through non-action in harmony,
all things are transformed【四】.
Vast and dim,
yet they seem to emerge from nowhere【五】!
Dim and vast,
yet they appear without form【六】!
All things in their multitude,
proliferate from non-action【七】.
Hence it is said Heaven and Earth do nothing yet leave nothing undone【八】,
so who among humans can attain such non-action【九】!
【一】【注】I do nothing and leave the world's rights and wrongs to themselves,
for when each person takes responsibility for their own rights and wrongs, they will be settled.
【Commentary】When one acts with purposeful attachment,
one clings to "right" and contends over "wrong,"
yet right and wrong have no fixed master,
so they cannot be settled.
Through non-action, emptiness, and simplicity,
one forgets both right and wrong,
and thus, without distinctions of right and wrong, right and wrong are settled.
【二】【注】If the common people are prosperous (two), then my own existence is nearly preserved.
【Commentary】Jǐ means
near.
Cún means
to exist.
The ultimate joy is without joy,
constant contentment is without worry,
it can nurture body and mind,
fulfill one's natural lifespan,
only that non-action,
is near and contained within it.
【Explanatory Text】"Jìn" means to be close to.
【Three】【Annotations】All arise from clarity and tranquility,
not attainable through deliberate effort.
【Four】【Comment】Without acting yet naturally in harmony,
thus all are transformed;
if there is intent in the acting,
then at times it becomes stagnant.
【Commentary】Heaven has no intention to be pure, yet is naturally clear and void;
Earth has no intention to be tranquil, yet is naturally peaceful and still.
Thus, Heaven and Earth act without deliberate action,
the two primal forces interact in harmony,
rising and falling bring calamity and fortune, and all things transform and come into being.
If they were to act with intention,
it would be impossible to sustain this process.
【Five】【Notes】All emerged from within themselves,
none were produced through deliberate effort.
【Explanation】"Mǎng hū": Lǐ reads it as huāng,
also pronounced as hū huǎng.
Same below.
"Wù hū": pronounced as hū.
Same below.
【Six】【Annotation】There is no appearance of deliberate action.
【Subcommentary】The dual forces of creation and transformation,
generate things without intent,
elusive and obscure,
irregular and hard to fathom;
tracing their origins,
none know whence they come;
observing their forms and appearances,
ultimately find no shape or likeness.
Further discussion of "máng hū"
merely interchanges the phrasing.

This is the evidence.
【Seven】【Annotation】All are self-propagating.
【Commentary】"Zhí zhí" means
a profuse and abundant appearance.
Now, spring gives birth and summer fosters growth,
and all things are numerous and diverse.
Who causes it to be so?
They all come into being spontaneously.
Tracing their origins and course,
they follow from non-action in planting and cultivating.
Since there is no action in planting and cultivating,
how could there be any deliberate action!
【Explanation Text】"The myriad things are bustling about." Simǎ comments:
bustling about,
is like being numerous and dense.
Lǐ comments:
a flourishing and proliferating appearance.
According to the Ěryǎ,
"zhí"
means to be in charge.
This refers to each having its own role and being distinguished.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
The old text mistakenly wrote "zhí" as "chí,"
now corrected.
【八】【Note】If there is action, then there is also failure to accomplish (four).
【九】【注】Attaining non-action means that even without seeking joy, joy arrives of itself.
【Commentary】Shú means
"who".
Now heaven and earth are clear and tranquil,
acting through non-action, empty and vast in their rising and falling,
generating and transforming without exception through non-action.
Ordinary people,
with minds obscured and dull,
are addicted to and stuck in desires—
who can attain this non-action!
To speak of one who can
is to refer to the ultimate endeavor.
If one attains it,
then one's virtue aligns with the two realms (heaven and earth),
and silently accords with the highest joy.
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì version lacks the character 'zhě'.
(2) In the Zhào version, 'zú' is written as 'dìng'.
(3) The Shìdétáng version writes it as 'zhí'.
(4) In the Shìdétáng version, 'jì' is written as 'qí'.
When Zhuāngzǐ's wife died,
Huìzǐ went to offer his condolences.
Zhuāngzǐ, however, was squatting on the ground, drumming on a pot and singing.
【One】【Condolence】Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ were long-standing friends of pure acquaintance;
now that one has passed away,
it is only proper to pay a condolence visit.
【二】【疏】Sitting with legs stretched out and apart,
letting both feet hang down like the shape of a winnowing basket.
Basin,
refers to an earthenware pot.
Zhuāngzǐ understood that life and death are not two separate things,
and realized that sorrow and joy are one and the same.
Therefore, when his wife passed away, he did not weep,
but instead beat the basin and sang,
sitting with legs stretched out and apart,
proudly enjoying himself.
【Explanation】"Jī Jù" is pronounced as jù.
"Pén" refers to an earthenware jar.
Huìzǐ said:
"Living with someone,
watching your children grow up and yourself grow old,
not crying at death is already enough,
yet you drum on a bowl and sing—
isn't that going too far【一】!"
【一】【疏】They share a dwelling with their wives,
nurturing their children and grandchildren.
Yet when their wives grow old and pass away,
they do not mourn or weep,
acting contrary to human principles.
This is enough to show their lack of affection,
and even adding drumming and singing—
how excessively extreme this is!
【Explanation】"Zhǎng" in "eldest son" is pronounced with the falling-rising tone, dǐng zhàng fǎn.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Not so.
When she first died,
how could I alone not feel sorrowful?
Reflecting on her beginning, she was originally without life;
not only without life but originally without form,
not only without form but originally without vital energy.
In the midst of the nebulous chaos,
transformation produced vital energy,
vital energy transformed and produced form,
form transformed and produced life,
and now another transformation has brought death,
this is like the progression of spring, autumn, winter, and summer - the four seasons.
She lies peacefully sleeping in the great chamber,
while I wail and weep following after her,
considering myself unenlightened about destiny,
therefore I cease."
【一】【疏】Indeed,
it is still like this.
All people in the world rejoice in life and detest death,
grieve over death and delight in life.
Therefore, when I first heard of death,
how could I alone not have sighed in astonishment!
【Explanation】"Wú gài": ancient pronunciation fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to feel.
Also pronounced as gǔ,
appearance of sorrow and chaos.
【二】【疏】Zhuāngzǐ, the sage,
profoundly understood the fundamental truth,
thus observing that at the very beginning, there was originally no birth,
and before birth, there was also no form or substance,
and before the absence of form and substance, there was also no vital energy.
From non-existence comes existence,
temporarily combined to form it,
hence knowing that this body is not worth clinging to.
【Three】【Discourses】The Great Dao resides within the realm of indistinctness,
in the midst of chaotic and obscure creation,
blending the pure and the turbid,
transforming into the two energies of yīn and yáng;
these two energies congeal and solidify,
changing to take on form;
once form is fully realized,
it transforms to generate and nurture life.
Moreover, from non-being emerges being,
transforming into life;
from being returns to non-being,
transforming into death.
Thus, life comes and death goes,
in a cyclical process of transformation,
much like spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
the four seasons succeeding one another in order.
Therefore, the enlightened observer contemplates this,
how can there be room for sorrow or joy?
【Four】【Annotation】To sigh before understanding,
to stop upon achieving comprehension,
this is the way to teach sentient beings,
so that they may infer the ultimate principle to dispel their burdens.
【Commentary】Yǎnrán,
refers to a state of peaceful rest.
Jùshì,
means the space between heaven and earth.
Moreover, death brings me rest,
lying within the realm of heaven and earth,
likening it to the alternation of heat and cold,
how can one follow with sorrow and lamentation!
Realizing one's failure to comprehend the mandate of heaven,
thus ceased weeping and drummed on the pot instead.
【Explanatory Text】"The Grand Abode" Grand,
means great.
Sīmǎ comments:
It takes heaven and earth as its abode.
"Jiào jiào" is pronounced as gǔ diào fǎn,
also as gǔ yáo fǎn.
"Jiāng lìng" is pronounced as lì chéng fǎn.
