now they change again and proceed to death,
stating:
after "transform" there is the character for "life,"
also written as "have."
Zhīlí Shū and Huájiè Shū were viewing from the hill of Míngbó,
the ruins of Kūnlún,
where Huángdì once rested.
Suddenly, a wart grew on his left elbow,
and he appeared startled and disgusted by it.
【One】【Disjointed】 means fragmented and scattered,
referring to the limbs being separated and dismembered,
to illustrate forgetting the physical form.
Huá Jiè,
is akin to bony and rugged,
meaning the bones stand out prominently,
to signify forgetting wisdom.
To reveal the decadence and deceit of a declining age,
hence named Shū (Uncle).
Míng,
means dark or obscure.
Bó,
means elder or leader.
Kūnlún,
refers to the human body.
It speaks of the profound obscurity of divine wisdom,
capable of leading all things;
Kūnlún is mysterious and distant,
yet close within the human body;
hills and mounds are uneven,
bowing to conform with worldly customs;
and the Yellow Emperor, a sage ruler,
illuminated the realm,
resting his mind and ceasing his intellect,
dwelling among the ordinary.
This shows that the ultimate way is deep and mysterious,
its principles are not far away,
hence entrusting the two Uncles to elucidate its meaning.
【Translated Text】"Zīlí Shū and Gǔ" Gǔ pronounced with a guttural sound.
The Cuī version writes it as ●.
"Jiè" pronounced as jiè.
"Shū" Lǐ Yún says:
Zīlí forgets his form,
Gǔ Jiè forgets his wisdom,
meaning these two gentlemen understood transformation.
"Míngbó's Hill" Lǐ Yún explains,
the name of a hill,
symbolizing profound obscurity.
"Kūnlún" pronounced with a forceful gate sound.
"The Ruins" pronounced as xū.
"Where they rested" rest,
means to repose.
【二】【疏】startled and alarmed,
a look of being shocked.
The willow (grows),
a tree that sprouts easily;
trees,
symbolize coffins and outer burial containers;
this is an omen of impending death.
Èr Shū journeyed to Kūnlún,
observed the transformations,
and in a brief moment,
a willow sprouted from his left arm,
causing him to startle in alarm,
as if he were repulsed by it.
【Translated Text】"Left Elbow" Zhú jiǔ fǎn.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as fū,
pronounced fū,
stating:
fū,
refers to the upper part of the foot.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Shuōwén:
liú,
means swelling.
Yùpiān:
liú,
is polypous flesh.
Guǎngyùn:
liú,
a disease where flesh protrudes.
Shuōwén also defines xī as parasitic flesh.
The growth of a liú on the body,
is a borrowed existence;
the existence of human life,
is also a borrowed existence;
both are like dust and grime adhering to objects.
The characters for willow and liú,
are a phonetic shift.
"Stumbling" Jì wèi fǎn,
means movement.
"Dislike It" Wū lù fǎn.
The same applies hereafter.
Zhīlí Shū said:
"Do you detest it?"
【One】【Memorial】Together observing the transformations,
the essence lies in emptying the mind and forgetting.
Suddenly startled and moved,
as if there is aversion and dislike.
Huà Jièshū said:
"Not at all,
why should I loathe it?
Life is but a borrowed form;
what is born through this borrowing
is mere dust and grime.
Death and life are like day and night.
Moreover, you and I observe the transformations, and now transformation has reached me—
why then should I loathe it?"
【一】【疏】Lost,
means non-existent.
The principle of observing transformation,
lies in forgetting oneself,
I originally have no self,
so how can there be anything to dislike!
【Two Departures】It is through the interaction of the two energies and five elements,
the temporary union and aggregation of the four limbs and hundred parts,
that a body is formed by borrowing.
Thus, we know that life is but a dusty, impure burden,
not a true, enduring entity.
【Interpretation】"Gòu yě" is pronounced as gǒu.
【Three】【Memorials】To regard life as day,
to regard death as night,
thus heaven cannot be without day and night,
how can humans be without life and death!
【四】【Note】These all first show sentient beings,
then seek the ultimate principle to dispel them.
If one says I originally have no emotions,
therefore can be without sorrow,
then those who have emotions
would cut themselves off from the vast and open realm,
and be lost and trapped in the realm of sorrow and joy.
【Commentary】You and I wander together,
observing the transformations,
and when transformation reaches me,
this indeed is...
Reason dictates that one should await the end,
so what aversion or loathing could there be?
Since one has transcended the transformation of life and death,
thus one attains supreme joy.
【Interpretation】"Zhī jìng" is pronounced as jìng.
Zhuāngzǐ went to Chǔ,
and saw an empty skull,
bleached yet still holding its shape.
He poked it with his horse whip,
and then asked it,
saying:
"Was it, Sir, due to a life of greed and loss of principle
that you came to this?
Or was it because of the affairs of a fallen state,
the execution by axe and halberd,
that you came to this?
Or was it due to some misconduct of yours,
bringing shame upon your parents, wife, and children,
that you came to this?
Or was it the hardship of freezing and starvation
that brought you to this?
Or did your years simply reach their natural end,
leading you to this?"
【一】【疏】It means to strike,
fittingly.
Dry and withered,
lacking moisture or luster.
To strike,
means to hit.
A horse whip,
is like a horse cane.
Zhuāngzǐ went to Chǔ,
encountered a skull,
an empty bone without flesh,
a decayed skeleton without moisture,
so he struck it with a horse cane,
and thus questioned it.
Wishing to clarify that the principles of life and death are equal,
he therefore used the skull's fable to answer the inquiry.
【Transliteration】"髑" pronounced dú.
"髏" pronounced lóu.
"髐" read with the initial k and the final iáo,
Xú also gives the reading with the initial x and the final iáo,
Lǐ gives the reading with the initial h and the final iāo.
Sīmǎ and Lǐ say:
It describes the appearance of white bones having a withered form.
"撽" read with the initial k and the final iào,
also read with the initial g and the final í.
In the Shuōwén it is written as ●,
saying:
To strike from the side.
"馬捶" read with the initial zh and the final uǐ,
also read with the initial zh and the final uì,
meaning a horse whip.
【Two Hermits】Did the gentleman's greed for material sustenance,
lead him astray from the proper path,
causing his life to be cut short prematurely,
and his bones to end up like this?
【Third】【Memorial】Is it because there are signs of a nation's downfall and the occurrence of warfare,
with executions carried out on the battlefield using axes and battle-axes,
that this is being done?
【Four】【Statements】If one commits acts of adultery, theft, or other wicked deeds,
despised by the world,
shamed by human ethics,
leaving disgrace for their parents,
feeling ashamed to face their wife and children,
would they not die in humiliation and disgrace because of this?
【Transcription】"Kui Yi" is read as wéi jì fǎn.
【Five】【Explanations】něi,
means hunger.
Some travel to study in other lands,
where their clothing and provisions run out,
suffering from hunger and cold,
would they die from this?
【Explanation】"Dòng": pronounced dīng gòng.
"Něi": pronounced nú zuǐ.
【Six】【Memorial】The Spring and Autumn Annals,
are like chronological records.
Will you, my lord, reach the age of yellowed hair,
the longevity of the elderly,
ending by Heaven's decree,
concluding here?
With these words concluded,
he picked up the skull,
laid it under his head as a pillow and slept.
At midnight,
the skull appeared to him in a dream and said:
"The way you spoke makes you seem like a debater.
From what you've said,
it's all the burdens of the living,
which cease to exist after death.
Would you like to hear about the state of death?
【一】【疏】Zú,
means end.
Yuán,
means to pull.
Initially encountering dried bones,
he took a horse staff and struck them;
once the conversation was over,
he pulled the skull close and used it as a high pillow.
【Transcription】"Yuán" is pronounced as Yuán.
"Zhěn ér" is pronounced with the initial zhèn.
【二】【疏】Upon witnessing this,
all that you have spoken pertains to the burdens and afflictions of the living.
If one wishes to discuss the way of death,
then such worries and anxieties do not exist.
You are among the living;
do you have any desire to hear about the perspective of the dead?
Zhuāngzǐ, in his sleep, was stirred by this dream.
【Interpretation】"See Dream" is pronounced as xián biàn fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition with the character 向 above.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Yes."
【One】【Memorial】So,
he addressed the skull,
wishing to hear the tale of its death.
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'wén' has been supplemented according to the main text above.
The skull said:
"In death,
there are no rulers above me,
no subjects below me;
nor are there the affairs of the four seasons,
serenely I take heaven and earth as my spring and autumn,
even the joy of a king facing south on his throne,
cannot surpass this."
【One】【Memorial】As for the deceased,
their ethereal spirit ascends to the heavens,
while their flesh and bones return to the earth.
Since they are no longer subject to the changing seasons of heat and cold,
how could they still bear the burdens of ruler and subject, high and low?
At ease, they no longer experience life and death,
thus sharing the longevity of heaven and earth;
even if one were to face south and declare sovereignty,
the pleasures of kings and nobles could not surpass this.
【Transcription】"Cóng rán" is read as qī róng fǎn,
meaning composed and unhurried.
Lǐ Xú reads it as zǐ yòng fǎn,
signifying unrestrained and free-spirited.
【Collation】（一）The missing text cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, where "cóng" is written as "fàn".
Zhuāngzǐ did not believe it,
and said:
"If I were to have the Director of Fate restore your body,
reconstitute your bones, flesh, skin, and complexion,
and return you to your parents, wife, children, neighbors, and acquaintances,
would you desire this?"
【One】【Memorial】Zhuāngzǐ did not believe the words of the skull,
and further spoke of the affairs of the living.
Wishing to have the ghost of the Director of Fate
restore flesh and bones,
return wives and children,
and bring one back to the hometown—
would one truly desire this?
【Transcription】"Fù shēng" is pronounced as fú,
also read as fú with an alternative pronunciation.
The skull deeply frowned and knitted its brow, saying:
"How could I abandon the joy of a king facing south and return to the toils of the human world?"
【一】【注】The old theory claims that Zhuāngzǐ rejoiced in death and detested life,
but this theory is mistaken!
If that were the case,
how could one speak of equanimity?
What is meant by equanimity is
being at peace with life while living,
and being at peace with death when dying.
Once the emotions toward life and death are balanced,
there is no need to worry about death while alive.
This is the essence of Zhuāngzǐ's philosophy.
【Commentary】Deep frown and furrowed brow,
is the appearance of worry and sorrow.
Having heard that the Director of Destinies could restore the form,
and return to one's hometown,
then one would worry and frown with sorrow,
not adopting these words.
Who would then again undertake the toils of the living and abandon the joy of a king facing south!
【Explanation】"Deep frown" pronounced as pín.
"Cù" also written as顣,
and also as,
same meaning.
Pronounced zǐ lù fǎn.
"È" pronounced yú gě fǎn.
Lǐ Yún said:
Frowning and wrinkling,
is an expression of worry.
"Ér fù" pronounced fú yòu fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The textual variant cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's version, which originally read "in the human world" as "among the living."
Yán Yuān went east to Qí,
and Confucius had a worried expression.
Zǐgòng stepped down from his mat and asked:
"May your disciple dare to ask,
since Yán Huí has gone east to Qí,
why does our Master have a worried expression,
what is the reason?"
【One】【Memorial】Yán Huí journeyed from west to east,
traveling from Lǔ to the state of Qí,
intending to impart the Way of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to the Marquis of Qí.
Fearing the timing might not be opportune,
the Master, Confucius, wore a worried expression.
Thereupon, Zǐgòng rose from his mat,
humbly referring to himself as a junior,
and ventured to ask the Master the reason for his concerned countenance.
Confucius said:
"Excellent is your question!
In the past, Guǎnzǐ had a saying,
which I greatly admire,
stating:
'A small bag cannot hold large objects;
a short rope cannot draw from deep wells.'
If this is so,
it is because destiny has its formations and forms their suitability,
which cannot be increased or diminished.
I fear that when Yán Huí speaks to the Marquis of Qí about the ways of Yáo, Shùn, and Huángdì,
and further elaborates with the words of Suìrén and Shénnóng,
he will look inward to himself and fail to comprehend,
and failing to comprehend, he will become confused,
and when a man is confused, he may perish.
【一】【疏】A bag,
is for containing.
A bosom,
is for harboring.
A rope,
is a well-drawing cord.
A vessel that holds small things,
cannot store large objects;
a short rope,
cannot draw from a deep well.
This saying comes from the book of Guǎnzǐ,
which Kǒng Qiū praised,
hence it is cited here as an analogy.
【Translated Text】"Chǔ xiǎo" is pronounced as zhū xǔ fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary in the Yùpiān:
Chǔ,
means to pack clothes.
The character is sometimes written as ●.
The Yīqièjīng Yīnyì quotes the Tōngsúwén as saying:
Packing clothes is called ●.
The Shuōwén Xìzhuàn states:
Chǔ,
is a bag for clothes.
The Jíyùn defines it as:
a sack.
The character is sometimes written as ●.
According to the Shuōwén,
is a ●,
used to carry and hold rice.
It also says:
is a container for carrying rice.
The Xìzhuàn notes:
● is also a sack.
In the third year of Duke Chéng in the Zuǒzhuàn,
a merchant from Zhèng hid someone in a chǔ to smuggle them out,
indicating that a chǔ can hold objects,
and can also conceal a person.
"Gěng" is pronounced as gé měng fǎn,
meaning a well rope.
"Jí" is pronounced as jū jí fǎn.
【二】【注】Thus, it should simply be entrusted to them.
【Commentary】Human beings receive their nature from the Mandate of Heaven,
and each, whether foolish or wise, achieves something in their own way;
they receive their forms from the Creator,
and their affections and preferences all manifest according to what suits them;
just as one cannot lengthen a duck's legs or shorten a crane's,
thus one should let things take their course, and nothing will be unfit.
【Translated Text】"Suǒ Shì" Shì,
sometimes written as tōng.
【Three】【Commentary】If one fails to find it within,
they will seek it outside.
To abandon the inner search and seek externally,
is that not delusion indeed!
【Commentary】Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn
are among the Five Emperors.
Suìrén and Shénnóng
are among the Three Sovereigns.
It is feared that Yán Huí would expound the ways of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to the Marquis of Qí.
Yet, their paces and eras differed,
and the simplicity or refinement of their times varied.
Clinging to the traces of the sages
without adapting to the opportune moment,
when the Marquis of Qí heard these grand words,
he could not comprehend them.
Seeking within himself,
he found no understanding.
If he failed to grasp it,
doubt would arise in his heart,
and then, resenting Yán Huí's superiority over himself,
he would inevitably kill Yán Huí.
【Explanation】"Huángdì" refers to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
The Sīmǎ version has "Huángdì".
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
The current version has "Huángdì".
The case is that "huáng" and "huáng" were used interchangeably in ancient times,
Lù Shì referred to them as the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
which is incorrect.
"Ér zhòng" is pronounced with a direct and reversed tone.
"Shě nèi" is pronounced as "shě".
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'zǎi' has been added based on the Shuōwén.
(2) The character 'yì' has been added based on the Xìzhuàn.
Additionally, the character ● was incorrectly carved as ● in the original edition,
now corrected.
And have you alone not heard of this?
In the past, a sea bird alighted in the outskirts of Lǔ,
The Marquis of Lǔ welcomed it and entertained it with a banquet in the ancestral temple,
Had the Jiǔsháo performed for music,
And prepared the Tàiláo sacrifice as its meal.
The bird then became dazed in sight, distressed and sorrowful,
Dared not eat a single morsel,
Dared not drink a single cup,
And died after three days.
This was nourishing the bird with what nourishes oneself,
Not nourishing the bird with what nourishes birds.
Now, to nourish a bird with what nourishes birds,
One should let it roost in the deep forests,
Wander over plains and mounds,
Float on rivers and lakes,
Feed on schools of fish,
Follow the formations in movement and rest,
And dwell in leisurely contentment.
It is only the sound of human speech that it detests to hear,
So why all that clamorous noise?
The music of Xiánchí and Jiǔsháo,
When played in the wilderness of Dòngtíng,
Birds hearing it would fly away,
Beasts hearing it would run off,
Fish hearing it would dive deep,
Yet when people finally hear it,
They gather around and watch it.
Fish thrive in water,
But humans die in water.
They surely differ from each other,
Hence their likes and dislikes are inherently different.
Therefore, the former sages did not uniform their abilities,
Nor did they make their affairs the same.
Names stop at reality,
Righteousness is established according to suitability,
This is called orderly attainment and sustained blessing.
【One】【Commentary】Outside the city walls is called the suburbs.
"Yù" means
to welcome.
"Jiǔ Sháo" is
the name of Shùn's music.
"Tàiláo" refers to
ox, sheep, and pig.
In the past, there was a sea bird,
named Yuánjū,
extremely large in appearance,
its head eight feet tall,
that arrived to avoid the wind,
and stopped in the eastern suburbs of Lǔ.
It was actually an ordinary bird, yet mistakenly considered auspicious;
Zāng Wénzhòng sacrificed to it,
thus earning a reputation for lack of wisdom.
Thereupon, they played the Sháo music,
set out the Tàiláo sacrifice,
and welcomed it in the ancestral temple to toast and feast it.
This was Zāng Wénzhòng treating it as a divine bird,
unrelated to the Marquis of Lǔ,
but since the bird was feasted in the Lǔ temple,
it is said that the Marquis of Lǔ toasted it.
【Explanation】"And you" is read as "rǔ".
The same applies hereafter.
"Sea bird" Simǎ comments:
According to the "Guóyǔ", it is the yuánjū.
It perched outside the eastern gate of Lǔ for three days,
Zāng Wénzhòng had the people offer sacrifices to it;
it does not mention the Marquis of Lǔ.
Yuánjū,
also known as záxiàn,
raises its head eight feet high.
Fán Guāng annotates in the "Ěryǎ":
Its shape resembles a phoenix.
◎Qìng Fán's commentary: The annotation in Jiǎng Wéntōng's "Miscellaneous Style Poems" in the "Wénxuǎn" quotes Simǎ as saying:
The sea bird,
is the yuánjū.
(The "Tàipíng Yùlǎn" volume 925 quotes with the character "jí" after "bird",
and writes yuánjū as yuánjū.
) It is not as detailed as the explanation in the text.
"Welcome" is read as "yà".
"Toast" is read as "shāng".
"In the temple" Simǎ comments:
Toasting it in the temple.
"Nine Sháo" is read as cháng yáo fǎn.
The name of Shùn's music.
【二】【疏】The Sháo music and the grand sacrifice,
are indeed beautiful and good,
but when presented to the yuánjū bird,
it is not what it can consume or hear,
hence it becomes dizzy-eyed and heart-sickened,
dying after several days.
This is just like the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
whose ways are lofty and far-reaching,
but when applied to the Marquis of Qí,
it is not what he can comprehend.
【Explanatory Text】"Xuàn": pronounced as xuán biàn fǎn.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as "xuán",
sounding like "xuàn".
"Shì": read as the character's usual pronunciation.
Xú pronounces it as shì zhì fǎn.
"Luǎn": pronounced as lǐ zhuǎn fǎn.
【Three】【Memorials】 Sháo music and sacrificial offerings,
are tools for nurturing people,
not objects for rearing birds.
Similarly, Yán Huí used his own learning to instruct the Marquis of Qí,
but it was not what he delighted in.
【Four】【Explanations】Tánlù,
refers to the islets in lakes.
Ní,
means muddy sediment.
Fù,
refers to white fish roe.
Wēiyí,
describes being relaxed and content at ease.
The method of raising birds
should involve perching in dense forests,
releasing them on the islets,
feeding them fish roe,
letting them float on rivers and lakes,
follow the flock in flight,
and be free and unrestrained naturally;
this is the way of raising birds by nurturing them as birds.
It is also like the Marquis of Qí following his own conduct,
carefree and content,
without any envy or longing.
【Translated Text】"Tán" is pronounced as dà dān fǎn.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as chán,
pronounced as dàn,
and explains:
it refers to water and sandbanks.
"Shí zhī" is pronounced as sì.
"Tiáo" is pronounced as tiáo,
also pronounced as yōu (two),
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as tú yóu fǎn,
another pronunciation is yóu.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
In the current version, it is written as also pronounced xiǎo.
"Suí xíng" is pronounced as hù gāng fǎn.
"Wěi" is pronounced as yú wēi fǎn.
Shé, pronounced with the initial consonant "zhī" as a variant reading,
and also read as the common pronunciation.
【五】【疏】Xī,
means "why".
Rào,
means clamorous noise.
Xiánchí,
is the music of Yáo.
Dòngtíng zhī yě,
refers to the space between heaven and earth.
Huán,
means to circle around.
Xiánchí and Jiǔsháo,
only humans love and enjoy them,
while fish, birds, and other creatures detest hearing their sounds.
If they love them, they circle around to watch;
if they detest them, they fly high or dive deep.
Since there is both liking and disliking,
what is the use of the eight tones of music!
【Explanation】"Náonáo" is pronounced as nǎojiāo fǎn.
"Xiánchí" is the name of Yáo's music.
"Zhī yuè" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
"Rén zú" is pronounced as cùn hū fǎn.
Sīmǎ gives the pronunciation as zǐ hū fǎn,
and says:
It means the multitude.
"Huán ér" is pronounced as yīn huàn,
alternatively xuán miàn fǎn.
【Six】【Sparse】Fish love water and detest land,
while humans love land and detest water.
Those humans and fish,
endowed with distinct natures,
have different likes and dislikes,
hence their life and death differ accordingly.
Is it only these two kinds?
All things in the world are like this.
【Explanation】"Its fondness" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling "hū bào fǎn".
【Seven】【Notes】Each according to its circumstances.
【Commentary】The ancient sages of old,
following the inherent nature of things,
treated people like vessels,
not standardizing their abilities,
allowing each to suit their disposition,
and differing in their affairs.
Thus, it is known that using the Way of the Three Sovereigns to persuade the Marquis of Qí
was profoundly inappropriate.
【Eight】【Annotation】Being substantial and fitting,
thus it flows smoothly;
with nature constantly fulfilled,
thus blessings are maintained.
【Commentary】Names are established based on reality,
and names are used to summon reality,
therefore names should correspond to reality,
without seeking names beyond reality.
Righteousness is what is appropriate,
applied according to circumstances,
simply suiting one's nature,
without abandoning oneself to imitate others.
Such a way,
can be said to be systematic and penetrating,
and supported by blessings and virtue.
【Collation】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan ancient manuscript version, which has "故異也" (thus they differ) written as "好惡異" (likes and dislikes differ).
(2) The Shide Tang edition uses "筱",
this follows the original version of the Shì Wén.
Lièzǐ was traveling and eating by the roadside,
when he saw a century-old skull.
Pushing aside the weeds and pointing at it, he said:
"Only you and I know that we have never truly died,
nor have we ever truly lived.
Are you indeed content?
Am I indeed joyful?"
【一】【注】Each finds joy in what they encounter.
【Commentary】Qiān means
to pull out.
Cóng means
alongside.
Liè Yǔkòu was distressed by his journey,
eating by the roadside,
and then saw a dried-up skull,
its appearance and color seeming ancient.
Mentioning a hundred years
is to state a rough estimate.
The skull was hidden beneath overgrown weeds,
so he pulled away the weeds,
and thus pointed and spoke to it.
However, the skull regarded life as death,
and death as life,
while Lièzǐ regarded life as life,
and death as death.
Each held firmly to one side regarding life and death,
which is insufficient to be definitive,
thus it has never truly died,
nor has it ever truly lived.
【Explanation】"Dào cóng" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
"cóng"
means the side of the road.
Some versions alternatively write it as "tú".
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Yīn Jìngshùn's commentary on the "Tiān Ruì" chapter of the Lièzǐ says:
In the Zhuāngzǐ, "cóng" is written as "tú".
Sīmǎ explains:
"tú",
means the side of the road,
some versions alternatively write it as "cóng".
This differs from the current version.
◎Qìng Fān's analysis suggests that "dào cóng" should be an error for "dào tú".
The characters "cóng" and "tú" are similar in shape,
hence "tú" was mistakenly written as "cóng".
The "Tiān Ruì" chapter of the Lièzǐ correctly writes it as "shí yú dào tú".
"Qiān" is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "iǎn",
Xú reads it with the initial "j" and the final "iǎn",
and also with the initial "q" and the final "iān".
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to pull out.
Some pronounce it as "jué".
"Péng" is pronounced with the initial "b" and the final "ōng",
Xú reads it with the initial "f" and the final "ōng".
◎Qìng Fān's analysis notes that "qiān"
is correctly written as "●".
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
means to pluck or take.
"Qiān" is a borrowed form of "●",
hence Sīmǎ interprets it as "to pull out".
It is also commonly written as "qiān".
As in the Lí Sāo: "In the morning, I pluck the magnolia on the hill."
(The Shuōwén dictionary quotes this line, correctly using "●".
) The Ěryǎ dictionary states:
"mào",
means to pluck.
Fán Guāng explains:
"qiān",
still means to pull out.
The explanation text says:
"qiān",
is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "iǎn".
In the Hànshū, the biography of Jì Bù records several instances of "plucking flags",
Lǐ Qí's annotation also states:
"qiān",
still means to pull out.
【二】【Note】The substance of joyful nourishment,
has no fixed abode.
【Commentary】"You delight in the obscure and profound,
but does such profundity truly bring nourishment?
I take pleasure in human relationships,
yet are they certainly a source of joy?"
Depending on the circumstances one encounters,
these cannot be definitively determined.
【Translated Text】"Ruǒ guǒ" one edition writes as Rǔ guǒ,

"Yǔ guǒ" in the Yuánjiā edition writes as Zǐ guò.

Ěryǎ Shìgǔ:
Yàng,
means worry.
Are you indeed worried?
Am I indeed joyful?
Yàng and huān are contrasted,
just as worry and joy are contrasted.
This means that your death is not a sorrow,
and my life is not a joy.
Yàng and yǎng,

In the poem "Èr Zǐ Chéng Zhōu" it says "center heart yǎng yǎng",
the commentary interprets yǎng as worry,

The Sīmǎ edition writes yǎng as mù,
which is a character error.

How many kinds of seeds are there?
When they encounter water, they become jì (a continuation organism).
At the water's edge, they become duckweed-like garments.
Growing on hillocks, they become plantains.
When plantains obtain putrid soil, they become crowfoot plants.
The roots of crowfoot turn into grubs,
and their leaves become butterflies.
Butterflies soon transform into insects,
born beneath the stove,
their appearance as if molted,
named qúduō insects.
After a thousand days, the qúduō insects become birds,
called gānyúgǔ birds.
The foam of gānyúgǔ birds becomes sīmí insects,
and sīmí insects turn into vinegar flies.
Yílù insects are born from vinegar flies,
huángkuàng insects arise from jiǔyóu molds,
and màoruì gnats emerge from rotten melon worms.
Yángxī fungi combine with old bamboo that has no shoots to produce qīngníng insects;
qīngníng insects give birth to chéng creatures,
chéng creatures generate horses,
horses give rise to humans,
and humans again return to the cosmic mechanism.
All things emerge from the mechanism,
and all return to the mechanism.
【一】【注】The varieties of transformations,

【Commentary】Yīn and yáng create all things,

【One-Seven】【Comment】This speaks of one qi giving rise to myriad forms,
having transformations but no death or life.
【Commentary】"Jī" refers to that which initiates movement,
what is called the transformative process of creation.
This transformative process,
is fundamentally non-being.
Humans are born from non-being into being,
and in turn return to enter back into non-being.
This is not only true for humans,
all things are like this.
Sometimes the non-sentient transforms into the sentient,
[or] the sentient transforms into the non-sentient,
sometimes the non-sentient transforms into the non-sentient,
sometimes the sentient transforms into the sentient,
in thousands upon thousands of changes and transformations,
there has never been an end.
And this exiting, entering, and mechanistic transformation,
is called death and life.
Since we know that transformation and change are endless,
how can we still delight in life and dread death?
To embody this meaning and purpose,
is called the ultimate joy.
◎ Yú Yuè says:

"Rén jiǔ fǎn rù yú jī" means,
that when a person becomes old, they return to enter into the mechanism.
The "Lièzǐ · Tiān Ruì piān" correctly writes "rén jiǔ rù yú jī".

Jiǔzhú gives birth to Qīngníng.
(3) The character "xiē" has been emended according to the original version in the Textual Explanations.
【Chapter One】【Explanatory Notes】The chapter is titled based on its moral significance.
One who comprehends the true nature of life
does not strive for what life cannot provide.【一】
One who understands the true essence of fate
does not pursue knowledge of what fate cannot change.【二】
To nurture the body, one must first have material means,
yet there are cases where materials abound but the body remains unnourished.【三】
To preserve life, one must first not be separated from the body,
yet there are cases where the body remains but life has perished.【四】
When life comes, it cannot be refused;
when it departs, it cannot be detained.【五】
Alas!
People of the world believe that nurturing the body is sufficient to preserve life;
【六】yet if nurturing the body truly proves insufficient to preserve life,【七】
then what in this world is worth doing?【八】
Though it may not be worth doing, there are things one cannot avoid doing—
such actions are inescapable.【九】
【一】【Note】What life has no means to achieve
are external things.
【Explanatory Text】"Dáshēng": Dá means
smooth,
unimpeded.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
Shēng means
to emerge.
【二】【注】That which knowledge has no means to deal with,
is a matter of destiny.
【Commentary】In human life,
each person has their inherent lot,
whether it be the comeliness or ugliness of form,
the length or brevity of lifespan,
as well as poverty or wealth, honor or lowliness,
foolishness or wisdom, hardship or success—
even the slightest detail beyond a hair's breadth
is all determined by fate.
Thus, those who comprehend the principles of nature and destiny,
with their spirits bright and illuminating,
ultimately do not covet what lies beyond their portion,
nor trouble themselves with affairs that are not their own.
For all that life bestows upon one,
is beyond the reach of wisdom and strategy to alter.
【Three】【Annotations】Knowing when to stop at one's proper limit,
things correspond to their nature,
such a life is sufficient,
having more than enough brings harm.
【Commentary】Material goods refer to resources, goods, clothing, and food—
the necessities for daily life.
To nourish and sustain the body,
one must first rely on material goods;
yet these goods have their limits
and cannot be pursued without bounds.
Thus, among the common and vulgar folk,
there are indeed those who accumulate more than enough
yet fail to adequately nourish and protect themselves.
【Text】"Wù chēng" chǐ zhèng fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Preserving form excessively,
thus life perishes.
【Commentary】Since there exists such a fleeting life,
yet one cannot transcend physical form and abandon intellect,
loving the body excessively,
thus losing the way to preserve life in its entirety.
Instances like these,
are found in the world.
【Explanation】"No Departure" is read with the initial "li" and the rhyme "zhi" in the opposite tone,
the same applies below.
"Excessive" is pronounced as "tai".
【五】【Note】What is not under my control,
then there is no reason to harbor thoughts about it.
【Commentary】Life and death, coming and going,
are entrusted to the Creator.
Having profoundly understood this fundamental principle,
thus there is nothing to resent.
【Six】【Annotation】Thus, the more one nurtures it, the more one loses it.
【Commentary】Life span, whether long or short, its departure and arrival,
are not within one's own control.
Yet ordinary people in the world,
fail to comprehend this principle,
greedily amassing abundant wealth and goods,
lavishly nourishing their bodies,
mistakenly believing it sufficient to preserve life,
which is profoundly lamentable.
【Seven】【Comment】The more generously one nurtures it,
the more closely death approaches.
【Commentary】By lavishly nourishing the body,
one hastens death all the more,
so such determination is insufficient to preserve life.
【Eight】【Annotation】It is best to let go and allow things to follow their natural course.
【Commentary】Rushing after material things,
was originally meant to sustain life.
Since life is not preserved through such nourishment,
we understand that worldly affairs and material pursuits,
what are they worth doing!
【Nine】【Annotation】That which each individual's innate nature and lot independently brings about,
all originates from the ultimate principle,
and thus cannot be avoided.
Therefore, those who are skilled in nurturing life
follow and accept it.
【Commentary】Matters beyond one's duty
are not worth pursuing;
matters within one's duty
must not be neglected.
The abilities of the eyes to see, ears to hear, feet to walk, and mind to understand
are endowed by natural principle.
Even if one acts through non-action,
one should not strive to avoid these inherent duties.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Hongmingji's Zhengwu Lun quotes zhi as ming.
(2) The Shidetang edition lacks the character yi.
(3) The large character is emended based on the Shiwen and the Shidetang edition.
To avoid being burdened by the body,
nothing is better than abandoning the world.
Abandoning the world brings no troubles,
no troubles lead to uprightness and peace,
uprightness and peace enable one to renew with others,
and renewal brings one close to the Way.
Why should affairs be abandoned and life forgotten?
Abandoning affairs keeps the body from toil,
forgetting life prevents the essence from being depleted.
When the body is whole and the essence restored,
one becomes one with Heaven.
Heaven and Earth
are the parents of all things;
their union forms bodies,
their separation marks new beginnings.
When form and essence remain undamaged,
this is called the capacity to transform;
refining the essence to its utmost purity
allows one to assist Heaven in return.
【一】【注】Gēngshēng means
daily renewal.
Entrust it to daily renewal,
then life's potential is fully realized.
【Commentary】Jǐ means
to exhaust.
Renewal,
is daily renovation.
For those who wish to act and nurture their form,
nothing surpasses abandoning the extraneous affairs of the world.
Abandoning the world then brings no worries or burdens,
no worries or burdens then aligns with the true and impartial Way,
impartial and correct then merges with the transformation of daily renewal,
thus one can exhaust the profound mystery of the Way.
【Explanation】"Then almost" Xú reads it as yī with a rising tone.
【二】【注】This is why he abandoned them.
【Commentary】The world of men is illusory and empty,
why must one renounce it?
Life is but a fleeting illusion,
why must one forget it?
Therefore, by abandoning worldly affairs, the body is at ease and free from toil;
by forgetting the course of life, the spirit is concentrated and remains undiminished.
【Three】【Annotations】None of them are done.
【Commentary】When the form remains whole and undisturbed,
it can thus preserve the Mandate of Heaven intact;
when the essence is firm and undiminished,
it thereby returns to the origin and reverts to the source;
with both form and spirit wholly secure,
they thus unite with the virtue of the Mysterious Heaven.
【Four】【Annotation】Without any bias or partiality,
thus it can nurture all things.
【Commentary】The two primal forces, without intent, give birth to and transform all things;
thus, those who align their virtue with heaven and earth
become the parents of all living beings.
【Five】【Annotation】Achievement is possible everywhere,
with no fixed place.
【Commentary】When yin and yang merge and combine,
they form physical substance;
when the vital breath disperses and separates,
it returns to the state before birth.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Union is
the mechanism of growth,
and the gradual process of dissolution;
dispersion then leads to a return to its origin,
and within this, the mechanism of growth begins anew,
hence it is said to complete the beginning.
With an end, there is a beginning,
such is the movement of Heaven,
which enables transformation,
not adhering to fixed patterns, thereby achieving its great constancy.
【Transcription】"Cháng Chǔ" is read as Chāng Lǜ with a rising tone.
【Six】【Annotation】To be in harmony with transformation.
【Commentary】"Transference" refers to
the concept of shifting and transforming.
One who does not labor the body,
nor deplete its essence,
can thus follow changes and undertake transformations, moving along with all things.
【Seven】【Annotation】It also assists in its natural state.
【Commentary】Xiàng means
to assist.
To eliminate it again and again,
is called refining it to the utmost,
thus returning to the origin and reverting to the source,
in order to support the way of nature.
【Translated Text】"Xiāng Tiān" is pronounced as xī liàng fǎn.
Zǐ Lièzǐ asked Guān Yǐn, saying:
"The perfect man walks without obstruction,
treads on fire without feeling heat,
and travels above all things without fear.
May I ask how one attains to this?"
【一】【Note】Because his mind is empty,
it can thus command all realities.
【Commentary】The ancients called their teachers "Zǐ",
which was also an honorable title for virtuous individuals.
Possessing these two meanings,
hence he was called Zǐ Lièzǐ,
referring to Liè Yùkòu.
[Guān Yǐn],
whose surname was Yǐn,
given name Xǐ,
courtesy name Gōngdù,
served as the guardian of Hángǔ Pass,
thus was called Guānlìng Yǐn Zhēnrén;
he was a disciple of Lǎozǐ,
embodying the Way and upholding virtue,
which is why Yùkòu consulted him.
"Zhì"
means to block.
The ultimate sage,
harmonizing light and concealing brilliance,
moves covertly through the world,
blending traces and merging with the dust,
unobstructed by material circumstances,
thus likened to an empty room,
void and unblocked.
Some versions also use the character for "empty".
【Explanatory Text】"Guǎn Yǐn" Lǐ Yún said:
Guānlìng Yǐn Xǐ yě.
"Bù zhì" zhēn xī fǎn.
【Two】【Comment】Reaching the ultimate state of suitability,
thus there is nothing that cannot be accommodated,
not because things are made to conform to it.
【Commentary】Being indifferent to cold and heat,
thus fire cannot bring disaster;
being unified in both high and low,
thus the heart holds no fear.
【Transcription】"Tàohuǒ" is read as tú bào fǎn.
【Three】【Memorials】This summarizes the meaning of the previous questions.
Guān Yǐn said:
"This is the preservation of pure energy,
not something that belongs to the categories of knowledge, skill, or courage.
Sit,
and I will tell you!
All that have form, appearance, sound, or color
are things,
and how can things differ greatly from one another?
What enables one to reach the forefront?
It is merely due to their forms.
Thus, things are created without form and cease without transformation.
Those who attain this and exhaust its principle—
how can things stop them!
They will abide in the measure of excessiveness,
and conceal themselves in the boundless continuum,
wandering where all things begin and end,
unifying their nature,
nurturing their energy,
harmonizing their virtue,
thereby penetrating the source of all things.
One who is like this
keeps their heaven intact,
their spirit without gaps—
how can things find a way in!"
【One】【Memorial】To remain unharmed by external matters,
one must preserve the pure and harmonious energy,
nurturing it through a tranquil and detached heart to achieve this,
not by exhausting the mind and intellect,
distinguishing clever deceptions,
or through bravery, decisiveness, and boldness.
【Explanation】"Fei Zhi" is pronounced with the tone for wisdom.
"Zhi Lie" is pronounced with the tone for example.
Some versions write it as "example".
【Èr Shū】ordered Yù Kòu to sit back down,
and said, "I shall impart to you the ultimate truth."
【Transcription】"Yǔ yǔ" read as yú jù fǎn.
"Nǚ" pronounced as rǔ.
Same hereafter.
【三】【注】Only those without a deliberate mind can truly distance themselves.
【Explanation】"Xiàng yuǎn": yú wàn fǎn.
【Four】【Comment】They are merely things of form and color alike,
not sufficient to take precedence over one another.
【Commentary】Forms, appearances, sounds, and colors,
which can be seen and heard,
are all material things.
Yet since they are all material,
how can they be sufficient to transcend,
or sufficient to arrive first?
This is because they are merely sounds and colors.
Only what is beyond form and sound,
beyond sight and hearing,
can transcend the realm of appearance and image,
and exist prior to all things.
【Five】【Annotation】Often roams to the utmost.
【Commentary】That which is without color and without form,
is thus capable of creating all forms and colors;
that which is without change and without transformation,
is thus capable of transforming all things in the world.
Therefore, all beings receive their forms from the Creator,
and rely on the wondrous foundation of all transformations.
【Six】【Annotation】That which is the ultimate,
is not constrained by things.
【Commentary】One who attains the profound root of creation,
the wondrous essence of nature,
and exhaustively investigates principles and fulfills innate nature—
how could the myriad things of the world
ever be halted or controlled by them!
Thus, they should come and go alone,
appearing and disappearing freely,
riding correctness and mastering discernment—
what could they possibly depend upon!
【Explanation】"Yān dé": Yú Qián's annotation.
【Seven】【Annotation】Cease at the limits of what one has received.
【Commentary】Those sages who have attained the Way,
are about to set their minds in emptiness and tranquility,
their capacity is vast and broad,
ultimately not lingering in the mundane world.
【八】【Note】Silently aligning with the transformations that renew each day.
【Commentary】The Great Way has neither beginning nor end,
neither start nor finish.
It uses this chaos as its guiding principle,
hence the sage conceals his mind and obscures his traces in the realm of the indistinct.
【Nine】【Commentary】The beginning and the end represent
the ultimate of all things.
【Commentary】The beginning and end of all things,
refers to the work of creation.
This means that life and death, beginning and end,
are all part of creation's work.
Thus, things inherently regard their beginning and end as the process of creation.
And the sage lets go freely within the realm of spontaneity,
roaming through the domain of creation.
【一０】【注】Embellishment then becomes twofold.
【Commentary】Acting in accordance with one's nature,
thus there is no duality.
【一一】【Note】Not to direct it with the mind.
【Commentary】Exhaling and inhaling to achieve emptiness and tranquility,
thus nurturing the primal energy.
【一二】【Note】Do not let external things cause the nature to deviate.
【Commentary】Holding fast to the One without departing,
thus one constantly merges imperceptibly with the profound virtue.
【一三】【Comment】All things come into being of their own accord.
【Commentary】That which creates all things
is nature itself.
Since one's nature is in harmony with virtue,
and corresponds with all beings,
thus one can comprehend the origin of the ultimate Way,
and penetrate the foundation of nature.
【一四】【Commentary】This refers to
criticizing the sages of the past.
“Zì” means
“from.”
If so,
they preserve the Way of nature,
complete and undamaged,
their spirit and mind concentrated and illuminated,
without the slightest gap,
so how could worldly affairs
ever enter the spiritual abode!
【Explanation】"Wú Xì" is read as "qù nì fǎn".
【Collation Notes】(1) The Que Wu cites the Jiangnan Guzang version with the character 形 above 色.
(2) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Junfang edition which only uses 正.
A drunken man falling from a carriage,
though injured, does not die.
His bones and joints are the same as others', yet the harm he suffers differs—
it is because his spirit is whole.
He is unaware of riding,
unaware of falling;
life, death, alarm, and fear do not enter his breast.
Therefore, he encounters things without fear.
If one can achieve such wholeness through wine,
how much more so through Heaven?
The sage hides in Heaven,
thus nothing can harm him.
An avenger does not break the Moyé sword,
and even a resentful heart does not blame a falling tile.
Hence, the world is balanced and fair.
Thus, there are no disorders of attack and war,
no punishments of slaughter and execution—
all because of this Way.
【First】【Explanation】From here onward,
there are three analogies in total,
illustrating how the sage acts alone without conscious intent.
The first is the drunken man,
the second is the sharp sword,
the third is the drifting tile,
and this is the initial one.
When a drunken man rides in a carriage,
he may suddenly fall and tumble,
yet even if he suffers injury,
he is certain not to die.
This signifies that his mind is free from attachments and worries,
his spirit remains focused and intact,
so that he is unaware of the fall,
and death and life do not penetrate him,
thus he encounters external things without fear or dread in his emotions.
【Textual Explanation】The character "之墜" is sometimes written as "隊",
same meaning.
Pronounced as "zhùi" with a falling tone.
The same applies hereafter.
◎ Jiā Shìfù commented:
Begin by preserving the vital energy and ultimately nurture the spirit,
which is what Daoism refers to as refining qi to return to the spirit.
"乘亦" is pronounced as "shéng",
also read as "shéng zhèng" with a falling tone.
"遻" is pronounced as "wù",
Guō reads it as "è".
The "Ěryǎ" states:
means to oppose.
Guō's annotation says:
It refers to offending or provoking.
◎ Lú Wénchāo noted:
The current edition writes it as "".
"不慴" is pronounced as "zhé" with a falling tone,
meaning to fear.
Lǐ and Guō pronounce it as "xí".
【二】【注】It is due to drunkenness that one loses one's awareness,
not because one is naturally without a mind.
【Three】【Discourses】That drunken person,
bound by the effects of wine,
can still temporarily remain calm and detached,
unharmed by external things.
How much more so for a sage of perfect virtue,
who is immersed in the Way of spontaneity!
Nothing can harm him,
as is fitting.
【Four】【Annotation】Not peering beyond one's innate nature,
hence it is called hidden.
【Commentary】The sage illuminates equally the three luminaries,
his wisdom encompasses all things,
yet he conceals his light and veils his wisdom in the realm of naturalness,
thus nothing in the world can harm him.
【五】【注】The swords Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
though employed by an enemy,
are not broken by the avenger,
for they bear no ill intent.
This is the second analogy.
Gānjiàng and Mòyé
were both fine swords of antiquity.
Although they were used to kill and harm,
thereby creating enmity,
those who sought revenge
would ultimately not become angry at these swords and break them.
Because they were without intent,
thus nothing could harm them.
【Transcription】"Mò" is pronounced as mò.
Originally also written as mò.
"Gān" Lǐ Yún states:
Mòyé and Gànjiàng,
are both names of ancient sharp swords.
The Annals of Wú and Yuè records:
King Hé lǘ of Wú ordered Gànjiàng to forge swords,
the swords came in two forms,
one called Gànjiàng,
the second called Mòyé.
Mòyé,
was the name of Gànjiàng's wife.
【Six】【Annotation】A falling tile,
even if it hits someone,
no one holds a grudge against it,
because it is without intent.
【Commentary】A falling tile,
which accidentally injures someone,
even a resentful and narrow-minded person
will ultimately not hold a grudge,
because the tile is an inanimate object.
This is the third analogy.
【Explanation】"Zhì xīn" is read with the initial "zh" and the final "i" in the fanqie method,
Guo and Li pronounce it as "zhī".
It means to harm.
According to the character dictionary:
It means cruel.
"Piāo wǎ" is read with the initial "p" and the final "iáo" in the fanqie method,
Guo and Li say:
It means to fall.
"Suī fù" is read with the initial "f" and the final "òu" in the fanqie method.
The same applies in the following chapter.
"Zhōng rén" is read with the initial "d" and the final "òng" in the fanqie method.
【Seven】【Annotation】All that is unjust,
arises from sentient beings.
【八】【Note】The Way of Non-Emotion is vast indeed.
【Commentary】When the realm is clear and peaceful,
distant lands are tranquil and still,
there are no conflicts of attack or warfare in the wilds,
and no punishments of execution or slaughter in the court,
it is all due to this Way of non-action,
and the sage who is without deliberate intent,
that such a state is achieved.
Thus, we know the principle of being without deliberate intent is of great significance.
【Collation】（一）"Yù" and "Yù" are ancient characters that are interchangeable,
yet in the commentary texts, the character for analogy is consistently written as "Yù".
Do not open the human-made nature (1),
but open the nature of Heaven
Opening the nature of Heaven gives rise to virtue
while opening the human-made nature gives rise to harm
Do not be weary of Heaven's way,
nor neglect the human aspect
and the people will almost attain their genuineness
【一】【Note】Knowing without deliberation,
is the opening of Heaven;
knowing and then feeling,
is the opening of humanity.
Thus, the opening of Heaven
is the movement of nature;
the opening of humanity,
is the application of knowledge.
【Commentary】Guǒ's annotation states:
Knowing without deliberation
is opening the heavenly;
knowing and then perceiving
is opening the human.
Thus, opening the heavenly
is the movement of nature;
opening the human
is the function of knowledge.
Guǒ has grasped it,
no need for further explanation.
【二】【Note】For the nature that is active,
when encountering things and being sufficiently satisfied, it forgets the surplus,
thus virtue is born.
【Three】【Comment】One who knows how to use it,
follows desires in pursuit,
ceaselessly without end,
thus harm arises.
【Commentary】To act in accordance with one's nature,
and in action remain constantly tranquil,
thus virtue arises.
To employ cunning in governing the world,
brings about profound harm,
thus calamity arises.
As the Classic of Lǎozǐ states,
"To govern a state with cunning is the state's calamity;
to govern a state without cunning is the state's virtue."
【Four】【Annotation】If one acts according to their innate nature,
then human principles will naturally be fully realized.
【Commentary】Constantly employing the nature of spontaneity,
one does not oppose Heaven;
relying on wisdom to illuminate things oneself,
this is not neglecting humanity.
【Transcription】"Bù yàn" Lǐ yú yàn fǎn,
Xú yú zhān fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】What the people suffer from,
the emergence of falsity,
often lies in the knowledge of application,
not in the stirrings of their nature.
【Commentary】Jǐ means
to exhaust.
By relying on heaven and employing humans,
nature moves and wisdom is applied,
then humans and heaven become indistinguishable,
knowledge and application are not different,
thus all under heaven are entirely genuine,
and the common people are without falsity.
【Transcription】"Jīhū" is pronounced as jī,
or sometimes as qí.
【Collation】(1) The textual variant citation quotes Liú Déyī's version which has "人" in place of "天".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition has "勸" in place of "".
Zhòngní went to Chǔ,
and as he was walking through a forest,
he saw a hunchback catching cicadas,
as easily as if he were picking them up.
【One】【Explanation】Hunchbacked,
the appearance of an old man bending his waist.
Catching cicadas,
is capturing cicadas.
To pick up,
means to gather.
When Confucius was visiting Chǔ,
walking through the forest's rustling sounds,
he encountered an old man using a pole to catch cicadas,
as if bending down to pick up blades of grass from the ground,
without missing a single one.
【Interpretation】"Gōu": Guǒ gives the pronunciation as yú fǎn,
Lǐ Xú gives it as jū jù fǎn,
also read as qí yǔ fǎn.
"Lǚ": Guǒ pronounces it as lǚ,
Lǐ Xú as liáng fù fǎn.
"Chéng": one version writes it as měi.
◎Qìng Fān's note: Chéng should be read as zhěng,
(in Shuōwén, it is written as ●.
) Zhěng,
means to pull and take.
In the Gen hexagram, the second six line, "not zhěng its following,"
Yú Fān said:
Zhěng,
means to take.
The interpretive text writes zhěng as chéng,
(the Tōngzhìtáng [edition] changes chéng to zhěng.
) saying it is pronounced like the zhěng in zhěngjiù.
(Fù)
Huàn (Hexagram 59): (1) Initial Six: Using a strong horse to rescue brings good fortune.
Explanation of Text:
Zǐxià's version writes "zhěng" as "●";
means to retrieve.
In the "Yellow Emperor" chapter of the Lièzǐ, it says, "He made his disciples wade into the stream and retrieve it."
The explanation notes that "chéng" is pronounced as "zhěng,"
citing the Fāngyán: "to rescue from drowning is called chéng."
(The current edition of Fāngyán writes it as "zhěng."
) In the twelfth year of Duke Xuān in the Zuǒzhuàn, it is said,
"Looking into a dry well and rescuing him,"
the explanation writes "zhěng" as "chéng,"
noting it is pronounced as "zhěng."
All these convey the meaning of retrieving.
"Tiáo" is pronounced with the second tone,
meaning cicada.
"Yóu duō" has "duō" pronounced with the retroflex initial and the entering tone,
meaning to pick up.
【Collation】（一）The character "huàn" has been emended according to the variant readings in the "Yì".
Zhòngní said:
"Are you skillful!
Do you possess the Way?"
He said:
"I have my way.
In five or six months, when I can stack two pellets without dropping them,
I miss very few cicadas;
when I can stack three without dropping them,
I miss only one in ten;
when I can stack five without dropping them,
it's as easy as picking them up.
I position my body
as if it were a rooted stump;
I hold my arm
like a branch of a withered tree;
though heaven and earth are vast,
and all things are numerous,
I am aware only of the cicada's wings.
I do not turn or shift,
nor let anything distract me from the cicada's wings.
How could I not succeed?"
【一】【疏】I marveled at how exquisitely clever it was to such a degree,
so I asked about the method.
The reply said there is a way.
【Two】【Annotation】Placing two balls atop the pole's end,
this is to ensure the hand's steadiness and precision.
Hence, (two) in catching cicadas,
the margin of error is no more than a hair's breadth.
【Commentary】Zīzhū refers to the smallest units of weight measurement.
When first learning to catch cicadas,
after practicing for half a year,
one's hand movements become steady and precise,
thus resulting in few misses.
【Explanation of the Text】"Fifth and Sixth Months": Simǎ comments:
It is the time when cicadas stick.
"Piling Balls": pronounced as "liè bǐ fǎn".
Same below.
Simǎ comments:
It means piling them on the tip of a pole.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The explanation of the text in Lièzǐ quotes Simǎ as saying:
"Léi huán",
refers to piling balls on the tip of a pole.
Slightly different from the explanation of the text.
"Those Zī": pronounced as "cè qí fǎn".
"Shū": pronounced as "shū".
【Three】【Commentary】The less one loses, [the better].
【Commentary】The season has been especially long,
and the accumulated pellets have increased in number,
so among the cicadas caught, one in ten is lost.
【Four】【Annotation】The ultimate of halting deliberation,
thus there is nothing further to lose.
【Commentary】Stacking five balls atop a pole,
none falling off,
the intent of focused stillness
reaches such a state,
thus catching cicadas becomes as effortless as bending down to pick something up.
【Five】【Annotation】The ultimate state of immobility.
【Commentary】"拘" means
to cut and trim the withered branches of a tree.
"执" means
to use.
I settle my body and mind,
as if they were a withered tree.
Using my arms to hold a pole,
like the branches of a dried-up tree,
I remain still and composed,
reaching the ultimate state of immobility.
These words convey the Way,
and this is what is meant by it.
【Explanatory Text】"若厥" is sometimes written as 橛,
same meaning.
Pronounced as "其月反".
"株" is pronounced as "誅".
"拘" is pronounced as "其俱反",
Guo Xiang pronounced it as "俱".
Li Yi said:
means upright,
standing like a tree stump.
◎Lu Wenchao noted:
The character "也" was not carved,
added according to the Song edition.
◎Jia Shifu said:
In the Liezi·Huángdì chapter, it is written as "若橛株駒",
with the annotation stating:
"株駒"
means a broken tree.
In the Shānhǎijīng·Hǎinèijīng,
(建)木 has nine twists,
below which are nine bends.
Guo Pu annotated:
refers to branches that twist and turn,
refers to roots that are gnarled and intertwined.
Shuōwén Jiězì explains:
means the root of a tree.
Xú Xuàn said:
Below the soil, it is called the root,
above the soil, it is called the stump.
"株枸" refers to
the area near the roots where they are gnarled and intertwined;
"厥" means
a broken tree used as a stake.
The body is like a broken stump,
the arms like the branches of a withered tree,
both conveying the idea of being solid and unmoving.
"若槁" is pronounced as "苦老反".
【Six】【Exposition】The two realms are extremely vast,
and the myriad things are exceedingly numerous,
yet in employing wisdom and focusing the mind,
one attends only to the cicada's wing.
Beyond the cicada's wing,
there is no other object of contemplation.
【Seven】【Annotation】Losing that, one gains this.
【Commentary】"Turning and twisting"
means change and movement.
Externally ceasing to grasp at conditions,
internally concentrating the mind in stillness,
even though the myriad things are numerous,
they cannot snatch away the knowledge of the cicada's wings,
thus handling affairs is like picking up a blade of grass,
how could one not succeed!
【Collation】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition has it as "橛".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "故".
(3) The character "少" is amended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(4) The character "建" is amended according to the original text of the Classic of Mountains and Seas.
Confucius turned to his disciples and said:
"When one's will is undivided,
it becomes focused like a spirit,
this describes the hunchbacked old man, does it not!
【One】【Memorial】When one focuses the mind and applies the will,
maintaining unwavering concentration,
thus stacking balls and catching cicadas,
the skill astounds spirits and ghosts.
And Confucius encouraged his disciples,
hence referring to the hunchbacked old man.
【Explanation Text】"Not divided" is read as written.
◎Yú Yuè says:
"Níng" should be "yí".
In the following text, Zǐqìng carved wood to make a bell stand,
when the stand was completed,
those who saw it were astonished as if by ghosts or spirits,
which is precisely what is referred to here as "seeming like the divine".
The "Yellow Emperor" chapter of the Liezi indeed uses "yí",
Zhàng Zhàn comments:
"When the mind is wholly focused, it resembles the divine."
This can be used as evidence for correction.
Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní, saying:
"I once crossed the Shāngshēn Abyss,
where the ferryman handled the boat with divine skill.
I asked him,
saying:
'Can boat-handling be learned?'
He replied:
'Yes.
Good swimmers can master it quickly.
As for expert divers,
they can handle boats skillfully even without having seen one before.'
I inquired further but he told me nothing more.
May I ask what this means?"
【一】【疏】Shāngshēn,
is the name of a deep pool.
Its shape resembles a cup,
hence it was named accordingly,
located in the state of Sòng.
The ferryman,
refers to the person operating the ferry.
Cāo,
means to handle.
Yán Huí once traveled on a journey,
crossing this deep pool,
and the ferryman handled the boat,
with great ease,
his dexterity and cleverness,
were as marvelous as that of gods or ghosts,
Yán Huí found it strange,
so he asked the Master.
【Transcription】"Cāo Zhōu" qī cáo fǎn.
Same for the following chapter.
【Two】【Annotation】This means that although things have their inherent nature,
they still require repeated practice before they can achieve their potential.
【Commentary】Yán Huí asked:
"Can it be learned?"
The reply was:
"Those who enjoy traveling across waters,
with repeated practice will master it."
Although all things receive their nature from the natural order,
there are also those who form their nature through practice.
【Explanation】"Shuò Néng" is pronounced as shuò.
Note: The same applies below.
【Three】【Notes】Mò rén,
meaning capable of diving and submerging underwater.
The commentary states,
it means diving to the bottom of the water.
Wù,
refers to a duckling.
It describes a ferryman skilled in water,
submerging underwater,
just like a duck diving into the water,
and thereby seizing the boat.
【Transcription】"Wù" is pronounced as mù,
meaning duck.
Zhòngní said:
"Those who are skilled at swimming can do so through repeated practice,
forgetting about the water.
As for those expert divers who have never seen a boat yet can handle it with ease,
they look upon abysses as if they were hills,
and view the capsizing of a boat just like the backing up of a carriage.
Countless instances of capsizing and backing up are arrayed before them, yet none can enter their minds,
so how could they ever be flustered!
When betting with tiles, one is skillful;
when betting with belt hooks, one becomes apprehensive;
when betting with gold, one is bewildered.
The skill is the same in all cases,
but when there is something at stake,
one values external things.
Whenever external things are overvalued, the inner self becomes clumsy."
【一】【注】Habit becomes second nature,
making it seem innate.
【Explanation】He delights in swimming in water,
and through repeated practice masters the skill,
his heart harbors no fear or caution,
forgetting the water's presence.
【二】【注】They view the abyss as if it were a hill,
so they see a boat capsizing in the abyss
just as a cart retreating on a slope.
【Commentary】Frequent swimming in the waters,
practiced until it becomes second nature,
thus makes one regard deep pools,
as if they were hills and plains.
Even if the boat were to capsize,
it would be like a carriage retreating on a slope.
【Explanation】"之覆" is pronounced as fāng fú fǎn.
Same for the annotations below.
"猶其車卻也" — the Yuánjiā edition does not include the character for "chē" (vehicle).
【Three】【Commentary】Although there are many setbacks and rejections, one still does not take them to heart,
because it is in their nature to be at ease with them.
【Commentary】The "abode" refers to
the mind.
Following the boat's advance and retreat,
with countless methods of expediency,
arrayed before one's eyes,
yet not affecting the heart's embrace.
Since one can forget the water,
how could the mind be troubled!
◎ Yú Yuè states:
The character "wù" (物) is missing after "wàn" (萬).
The original text should read "fù què wànwù" (覆卻萬物) as one phrase,
and "fāng chén hū qián ér bù dé rù qí shè" (方陳乎前而不得入其舍) as another.
"Fāng" (方) means
"side by side."
The original meaning of "fāng" is two boats placed side by side,
hence it carries the meaning of "alongside."
In the "Zhì Shì" chapter of the Xúnzǐ, it says, "Mò bù míng tōng fāng qǐ yǐ shàng jìn yǐ,"
Yáng Liàng comments:
"Fāng qǐ" means
"arising together."
In the Hànshū, in the biography of Yáng Xióng, it states, "Suī fāng Zhēng Qiáo yǔ Wò Quán xī,"
Shǐ Gǔ annotates:
"Fāng"
means "to proceed together."
These are all evidence.
"Fāng chén hū qián"
means the myriad things are arrayed side by side before one.
Now, the character "wù" is missing from the previous phrase,
and "fāng" is mistakenly attached to the preceding reading,
so what exactly does "arrayed before" refer to?
Guō Xiàng's annotation says:
"Though the overturnings and rejections are many,
one still does not take them to heart,"
indicating that the version he relied on included the character "wù."
The main text should read "wànwù" (萬物),
hence it speaks of "many."
If it were "wànfāng" (萬方) as in the current version,
it should refer to vastness,
not to multitude.
The Lièzǐ, in the "Huángdì" chapter, correctly states, "fù què wànwù fāng chén hū qián ér bù dé rù qí shè,"
which can be used for correction.
【Four】【Annotation】All encounters are moments of leisure.
【Commentary】Steering a boat by following its nature,
swimming by embracing one's innate spontaneity,
with a heart free from pride and attachments,
where would one not find ease and leisure?
This is not only true for steering a boat,
but also for learning the Way.
If one can simply forget and let go,
that in itself is attaining a liberated life.
【Explanation】"Wicked" pronounced as wū.
"Leisure" pronounced as xián.
【Five】【Annotation】The more important the demands placed upon him,
the more arrogant his heart becomes.
【Commentary】Note:
It refers to archery.
When using cheap earthenware vessels as stakes in a betting game of shooting,
since the mind holds no attachment or reluctance,
one becomes skillful and hits the target.
When betting with belt hooks,
because the object is somewhat valuable,
there is fear of missing the target,
leading to anxiety in the mind and failure to hit.
When betting with gold,
as it is an extremely precious item,
one becomes attached and reluctant to lose it,
causing the mind to become confused and miss the target.
Thus, the ferryman, by forgetting external concerns, achieves a divine-like skill,
while the archer, due to attachment to the object, becomes disoriented.
Therefore, attachment leads to clumsiness,
while forgetting leads to skill.
I urge all learners
to bear this in mind earnestly.
【Explanation】"瓦注" is read with a retroflex initial and a rising tone.
Lǐ Yún says:
It means to strike.
"憚" is read with an initial "d" and a level tone,
also pronounced as "dān",
and also with an initial "zh" and a falling tone.
It means to detest or loathe.
Another interpretation is difficult.
"(歹昏)" is read with an initial "m" and a rising tone,
also pronounced as "hūn",
and also as "mén".
The original text also writes it as ●.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
means confusion.
The Yuánjiā version writes it as "hūn".
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
In current editions, ● is written as ●,
and the old text "confusion" was mistakenly written as "restraint",
which is an error.
Now it is corrected according to the original text.
◎ Qìng Fān's commentary on ●,
means swift.
Also, in the "Qu Yóu" chapter of the Lǚshì Chūnqiū, "using gold to cast causes doubt."
Doubt,
means suspicion,
(see the annotation in the fourth year of Duke Xiāng in the Gōngyáng Zhuàn.
) also conveys the meaning of confusion.
The term for casting with gold is not separately attested elsewhere.
The annotation by Gāo in the Lǚshì Chūnqiū also states there is no evidence.
The "Huáng Dì" chapter of the Lièzǐ uses "tossing with tiles" for ●,
and the "Shuō Lín" chapter of the Huáinánzǐ uses "stumbling when using gold",
both borrowing from the Zhuāngzǐ but not using the character for casting.
"所要" is read with a level tone on the first character and a rising tone on the second.
【Six】【Annotation】To nurture life and preserve the inner self,
one must simply harbor no arrogance or self-importance.
【Commentary】The archer's mind,
whether skilled or clumsy, is fundamentally the same;
but when burdened by external matters,
the heart becomes strained.
It is only because of valuing gold too highly
that the inner mind becomes confused and inept.
This is not only true in archery—
all endeavors are likewise.
【Collation Note】(1) The Textual Discrepancies states:
The annotation in the Lǚ's Annals reads as "殶",
the rest is the same.
Tián Kāizhī paid a visit to Zhōu Wēi Gōng.
Wēi Gōng said:

and you, sir, have associated with Zhù Shèn.
What have you learned from him?"

【Explanatory Text】"Tián Kāi zhī" Lǐ Yún:

Duke Wēi said:

The way of nurturing life,

without the need for modesty.

【One】【Memorial】Not yet comprehending Tián Kāi's words,

Tián Kāizhī said:
"In Lǔ there was one Shàn Bào,
who dwelt among cliffs and drank from streams,
did not share profits with the common people,
and at seventy still had the complexion of an infant;
unfortunately he encountered a starving tiger,
the starving tiger killed and devoured him.
There was one Zhāng Yì,
in every high gate and low curtain,

yet at forty he died of an internal fever disease.
Bào nurtured his inner self but a tiger consumed his outer form,
Yì nurtured his outer form but illness assailed his inner self.
These two men
both failed to attend to what followed."
【一】【疏】His surname was Shàn, given name Bào,
a recluse of the state of Lǔ.
He dwelled among cliffs and drank only water,
contending for neither fame nor profit.
Although he had grown old in years, his appearance and complexion did not fade;
having long resided in the mountain forests,
he was suddenly devoured by a starving tiger.
【Explanatory Text】"Shàn Bào" is pronounced as Shàn.
Lǐ Yí says:
Shàn Bào

"Ér shuǐ yǐn" in the Yuánjiā edition is written as yǐn shuǐ.
【Èr Shū】was surnamed Zhāng and named Yì,
also a person of Lǔ.
High gates,
signify a wealthy and noble family.
Thin curtains,
refer to hanging blinds.
It is said that Zhāng Yì was a man of worldly customs,
chasing after worldly gains,
visiting high gates and grand residences,
with vermilion doors and hanging blinds,
he would gallop to pay his respects without fail,
rushing about to offer congratulations or condolences,
until his body grew weary and his spirit weakened,
exhausted yet without rest,
thus internal heat erupted on his back and he died.

【Three】【Commentary】Those who adhere rigidly to one-sided affairs to the point of exceeding reason,
fail to reach the appropriateness of comprehensive understanding.
Whipping those who lag behind,
means eliminating their inadequacies.
【Commentary】Shān Bào, with his few desires and purity of emptiness,
cultivated his inner virtue, yet a tiger devoured his outer form.
Zhāng Yì engaged with the noble and powerful of the world,
nurturing his physical body, yet illness attacked him from within, leading to his death.
These two individuals each clung to one extreme,
failing to achieve balance,
and thus neither could be held up as a model to follow.
【Transcription】"Qù qí" is read as qǐ lǚ fǎn.

Zhòngní said:
"Do not enter and hide away,
nor emerge and show off,
but stand firm like deadwood in the center.
If you attain these three,
your name will surely reach its pinnacle.
As for dangerous roads,
where one in ten travelers is killed,
fathers and sons, brothers warn each other,
and must gather a large company before daring to set out—
is this not wisdom!
Yet what people should truly fear
lies in the intimacy of beds,
and in the indulgence of food and drink;
but failing to be cautious about these
is a fault."
【一】【注】When the storehouse is already internal,
and yet one enters further into it,
this is an excess of entering.
【Commentary】The note says,
having already entered,
and then concealing oneself.
Being overly confined to one place,
this is Shàn Bào.
【二】【Note】When yang is already external,
and yet it is further emitted,
this is an excess of emission.
【Commentary】Yáng,
means to manifest.
Having already emerged,
yet further revealing it.
To be excessively attached to emerging,
this is Zhāng Yì.
【Three】【Comment】Like a withered tree without a mind, yet centered and at ease,
this is the state of standing.
【Commentary】Chái is
wood.
Not clinging to emergence,
not clinging to abiding,
both emergence and abiding are simultaneously relinquished,
like withered wood devoid of emotion,
wondrously abandoning the two extremes,
and standing alone in the path of the Middle Way.
【Four】【Annotation】The name reaches its limit and the substance corresponds appropriately.
【Commentary】Through names, principles are explained,
and from principles, names arise.
If one comprehends the meaning of the preceding three statements,
then the principles are exhausted and names are fully understood.
It is also said:
One who attains these three is called a person who has reached the ultimate.
is the road.

they greatly fear it;

The ceremonial official, in formal attire, approached the animal pen,
and addressed the pig, saying:
"Why do you detest death?
I will nurture you for three months,
observe abstinence for ten days,
fast for three days,
spread white rushes,
and place your shoulders and rump upon an ornate sacrificial stand—
would you then choose this?"
When planning for the pig,
it's said that it would be better to feed it with chaff and bran and leave it in the pen.
But when planning for oneself,
if in life one can have the dignity of a high carriage and official hat,
and in death be laid on an ornamented carriage and encoffined in a decorated burial vault, one would opt for it.
For the pig, such choices are rejected;
for oneself, they are embraced.
What, then, is the difference between us and the pig?
