(Explanatory text:
"Quán",
is read as shì zhuān fǎn,
or shì zhuǎn fǎn.
) The commentary on the lower part of the Shì Sāng Lǐ Jì says:
It is the hearse.
In the Zhōu Lǐ, it is called the "shèn" carriage,
in the Zá Jì, it is called "tuán",
sometimes written as "quán",
or as "tuán",
all with similar sounds and readings.
The carriage's frame is like a bed,
with a central shaft,
extending front and back,
and front and back yokes are set.
The frame has four sides,
with axles at the front and bottom,
using "quán" as wheels.
Xǔ Shūzhòng explains,
having spokes is called a wheel,
without spokes is called "quán".
"Quán",
"chuán",
"tuán",
"tuán",
are all different characters with the same meaning,
here written as "zhuàn",
the meaning is also the same.
"Shǔn" is read as "chūn",
also referring to the hearse.
The Tán Gōng says:
For the Son of Heaven's encoffining,
it is coated and adorned with a dragon "chūn" and an outer coffin.
It also says:
The Son of Heaven uses a dragon "chūn" with an outer coffin and shroud,
feudal lords use a "chūn" and set a shroud.
The Sāng Dà Jì says:
The ruler's encoffining uses a "chūn",
Zhèng's commentary says:
For the Son of Heaven's encoffining,
the coffin is placed on a dragon "chūn",
feudal lords use a "chūn" without painted dragons,
great officers do not use a "chūn".
The commentary on the lower part of the Shì Sāng Lǐ says:
"Gǒng",
is shaped like a long bed,
pierced with a crossbar,
with metal fittings at the front and back and a pivoting axle,
for great officers and feudal lords and above, it has four sides,
called "chūn".
(This refers to what is used when presenting at the temple.
) "Chūn" and "shǔn",
are interchangeable in ancient script.
The commentary in Zá Jì says,
the coffin is carried on a "shǔn",
which is evidence of this.
"Jù lǚ",
refers to the decorations on the hearse.
It is where many ornaments gather,
hence called "jù lǚ";
also because its shape is high in the center and low on the sides,
hence the term "lǚ".
The commentary in Zá Jì says:
When about to bury,
the decorations on the coffin carriage are called "liǔ".
In the Zhōu Guān, the Féng Rén,
prepares materials for the "shà" and "liǔ" coverings,
the commentary says:
"Liǔ" means to gather,
where various ornaments come together.
Liú Xī's Shì Míng says:
The carriage that carries the coffin,
its cover is called "liǔ".
"Liǔ",
means to gather,
where many ornaments gather,
and its shape is also curved.
The Tán Gōng says:
Set the "lóu shà".
The Xúnzǐ Lǐ Lùn Piān says:
Without curtains, silk, or tassels,
the "shà" and its hangings resemble thin curtains and coverings.
"Liǔ",
"lóu",
"lǚ",
"lǚ",
are all different characters with the same meaning.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū Jié Sāng Piān says "lǚ shà" to oversee it.
The character is also written as "lǚ".
The alternative explanation quoted in the explanatory text,
taking "lǚ" as "lóu shà",
is correct.
The other explanations are all mistaken.
◎ Jiā Shìfù says:
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying,
"zhuàn",
is like a seal script pattern,
"shǔn",
is like a table,
"jù lǚ",
is the name of a vessel,
now made in tomb pits.
I suspect "shǔn" is the same as "chūn",
"zhuàn shǔn",
is the painted "chūn",
which is what the Sāng Dà Jì refers to as using a "chūn" for burial.
"Jù lǚ",
is the curved mat,
what the Xúnzǐ calls the mat vessel,
and what the Sāng Dà Jì refers to as the parched grains,
for the ruler, eight baskets,
for great officers, six baskets,
for gentlemen, four baskets.
The "chūn",
is what carries the coffin,
hence "on the zhuàn shǔn";
baskets and containers are placed outside the coffin but inside the outer coffin,
hence "within the jù lǚ";
all are burial ornaments for great officers and above.
【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Junfang edition, which reads "huàn" for ●.
(2) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Qianfu edition, which has the character "qí" above "suǒ".
(3) In the Zhao Jianyi edition, "xián" is written as "wèn".
(4) The two characters "xià piān" are supplemented based on the following text.
The lower part of the Shì Sāng Lǐ is the Jì Xī Lǐ.
(5) The character "zhū" is emended according to the Dú Shū Zá Zhì.
(6) The character "jūn" is emended according to the Sāng Dà Jì.
Duke Huán was hunting in the marshes,
with Guǎn Zhòng driving his chariot,
when they saw a ghost there.
The duke grasped Guǎn Zhòng's hand and said:
"What does Father Zhòng see?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Your subject sees nothing."
【一】【疏】The Duke,
namely Duke Huán Xiǎobái,
was hunting in the wild marshes,
and had Guǎn Yíwǔ drive his chariot.
The Duke then saw a ghost,
felt fear in his heart,
and, grasping Guǎn's hand, asked him about it.
He replied:
"I see nothing."
This chapter illustrates that all ailments and afflictions
often arise from deluded attachments.
The duke returned,
suffering from melancholy and delirium,
and did not emerge for several days.
A scholar of Qí named Huángzǐ Gào'áo said:
"Your Grace has harmed himself;
how could a ghost harm you?
When pent-up anger and stagnant energy
disperse and fail to return,
it leads to deficiency;
if it rises but does not descend,
it makes one prone to rage;
if it descends but does not rise,
it makes one prone to forgetfulness;
if it neither rises nor descends,
lodging in the middle of the body at the heart,
then it causes illness."
【一】【疏】Yíyí,
is the appearance of laziness and slackness,
and also the look of being vexed and depressed.
Having seen a ghost,
he returned worried and fearful,
and consequently fell ill,
which is why he did not come out.
【Transcription】"Qù fǎn" one edition reads as gōng fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current edition reads as gōng fǎn.
"Āi" is pronounced with the fǎnqiè yú dài,
Guō reads it as xī.
The Shuōwén states:
It is a detestable expression.
Lǐ reads it with the fǎnqiè hū gāi,
another reading is āi.
"Yí" is pronounced with the fǎnqiè tǔ dài,
Guō reads it as yí,
Lǐ reads it as tái.
Sīmǎ explains:
An appearance of weariness.
Lǐ explains:
Āi yí,
means losing one's soul and spirit.
"Shuò rì" is pronounced with the fǎnqiè suǒ zhǔ.
Sīmǎ's edition reads as shuò yuè.
【二】【疏】姓皇子，
字告敖，
是齐国的贤人。
听说您生病了，
前来探望，
说道：
“您是心中有妄念纠缠，
自己招致了伤病。
鬼有什么力量，
能伤害您呢！”
这是想用正理来驱除他的邪病。
【Interpretive Text】"Huángzǐ Gào'áo" is read as written.
Simǎ comments:
Huáng
is the surname;
Gào'áo,
is the courtesy name;
he was a virtuous scholar of Qí.
◎ Yú Yuè states:
In the "Guǎngyùn," the annotation for the character "zǐ" in the sixth rhyme group "zhǐ"
lists eleven compound surnames,
and the "Zhuāngzǐ" mentions Huángzǐ Gào'áo.
Thus, Huángzǐ is considered a compound surname.
At the end of the "Tāng Wèn" chapter in the "Lièzǐ," the tale of the Kūnyú sword and the fire-washing cloth is recorded,
stating that Huángzǐ believed such things did not exist,
likely referring to this same person.
"Guǐ wù" is pronounced as wū.
【Three】【Manifestations】When a person is filled with anger, it accumulates perverse energy;
thereupon, the essence and soul scatter and disperse,
no longer returning to the body.
This leads to a heart that is empty and impaired, offending the spirits,
because the Way is insufficient.
【Explanation】"Fèn" is pronounced fú fěn fǎn,
Lǐ (Li) reads it as fáng fěn fǎn.
"Chù" is pronounced chì lù fǎn.
"When the vital energy scatters and does not return, it results in insufficiency." Lǐ (Li) says:
Fèn means
fullness.
Chù means
accumulation and gathering.
If the spirit is contrary,
then yin and yang knot internally,
and the hun and po souls scatter externally,
hence it is called insufficiency.
【Four】【Syndromes】When pathogenic qi rises but does not descend,
it then attacks the head,
causing a person to feel fearful in the heart,
depressed and prone to anger;
when it descends but does not rise,
with yáng subdued and yīn dispersed,
the spirit becomes disoriented,
thus leading to a tendency to forget.
Now, the heart is
the ruler of the five zàng organs and the dwelling of the spiritual essence,
so when qi is contrary to the body and heart, it results in illness.
【Text】"Shàng": read as shǎng zhǎng fǎn.
Same below.
"If it rises but does not descend, it makes a person prone to anger; if it descends but does not rise, it makes a person prone to forgetfulness": read as wáng shàng fǎn.
Lǐ Yí says:
When yang scatters and yin congeals,
it causes anger;
when yin stirs and yang lies dormant,
it causes forgetfulness.
"Neither rising nor descending, in the middle": read as dīng zhòng fǎn.
"If it affects the body at the heart, it becomes an illness": Lǐ Yí says:
When above and below are not harmonious,
then yin and yang contend and attack the heart.
The heart,
being the master of spirit and essence,
thus becomes ill.
【Collation】（一）The character 'shì' has been supplemented based on the 'Píngyì of Various Masters'.
Duke Huán said:
"So, do ghosts exist?"
It is said: "There are
in swamps, there is Lǚ;
in hearths, there is Jì;
in the dusty corners inside doors,
Léitíng dwells;
in the lower parts of the northeast,
Bèi'ā Guīlóng leaps about;
in the lower parts of the northwest,
then Yìyáng resides;
in waters, there is Wǎng Xiàng;
on hills, there is Shēn;
in mountains, there is Kuí;
in the wilds, there is Pánghuáng;
in marshes, there is Wēiyí."
【One】【Memorial】The Duke inquired about the cause,
and the reply mentioned there was a ghost.
【二】【疏】The submerged one,
lies in the muddy silt under the water,
where there is a ghost called Lǚ.
The kitchen god,
appears like a beautiful woman,
dressed in red clothes,
named Jì.
【Translated Text】"Shen has Li": The Sima edition writes "Shen has Lou",
stating:
Shen is muddy water sediment.
Lou,
is the name of a spirit.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Sima says:
Shen,
is muddy water sediment.
Then it should follow sentences like "water has Gang Xiang,"
and should not come after "stove has Ji."
Shen should be Chén.
Chén is pronounced from the radical Shèn,
while Shěn is pronounced from Yín,
the two sounds are similar.
In the poem "Dang," the line "its mandate is not Chén,"
the Shūowén dictionary's heart radical section quotes as "heaven's mandate is not Chén";
in "Cháng Dì," the phrase "harmonious and joyful, and deeply so,"
the Lǐjì's Zhōngyōng chapter quotes as "harmonious and joyful, and indulgent";
these serve as evidence.
Chén being interchangeable with Shěn,
is like Chén being interchangeable with Chén,
and Zhàn being interchangeable with Dān.
In "Bái Huá," the line "I warm by the Chén,"
Máo's commentary says:
Chén,
is a stove.
Thus, Chén and stove are of the same category,
hence they are mentioned together as "Chén has Li, stove has Ji."
Zhèng Bì Chén's courtesy name is Zào,
Chén here is a borrowed character for Chén;
the Hànshū's "Table of Ancient and Modern Persons" writes as Bì Zhàn,
Zhàn is also a borrowed character for Chén.
Lǐ Shàn annotates in the Wénxuǎn's "Zōu Yáng's Letter to the King of Wú":
Zhàn,
is the modern character Shěn;
and in annotating "Reply to a Guest's Mockery," he says:
Zhàn,
is the ancient character Shěn.
Therefore, taking Shěn as Chén,
is equivalent to taking Zhàn as Chén.
The stove has a Jì. Pronunciation: jié,
Xú gives the pronunciation as hújié,
Guō pronounces it as jié,
Lǐ pronounces it as jí.
Sīmǎ says:
Jì,
is the stove god,
dressed in red clothes,
appearing like a beautiful woman.
◎Qìng Fān's case: the Suǒyǐn of the Historical Records, Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaowu, quotes Sīmǎ,
writing Jì as Hào,
saying:
Hào,
is the stove god,
like a beautiful woman,
clad in red.
【Three】【Excreta】Within the filth of the household gates,
there dwells a ghost,
named Léitíng.
【Explanation】"Tíng" is pronounced as tíng,
also pronounced as tǐng,
and also read as dìng in the reverse spelling.
【Fourth】【Memorial】In the northeast corner under the wall of a person's house, there is a ghost,
named Bèi'ā Guīlóng,
leaping in form like a small child,
one chi four cun tall,
wearing black clothes and a red headscarf,
carrying a sword and holding a halberd.
【Explanation】"倍" is pronounced as Péi,
Xú gives the pronunciation as fú lái fǎn.
"阿鮭" is also written as 蛙 in some versions,
pronounced as hù guā fǎn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as hú jiā fǎn.
"蠪" is pronounced as lóng,
and also as lōng.
"躍之" Sīmǎ comments:
Bèi Ā,
is the name of a deity.
Guī Lóng,
has the appearance of a small child,
one chi four cun in height,
dressed in black clothes, wearing a red headscarf and a large hat,
carrying a sword and holding a halberd.
【Five】【Descriptions】With a leopard's head and a horse's tail,
it is named Yìyáng.
【Explanation】"Yìyáng" is pronounced as yì.
Sīmǎ says:
Yìyáng
has the head of a leopard and the tail of a horse,
some versions say the head of a dog.
Another explanation:
It is the name of a deity.
【Six】【Commentary】 states (three),
its form resembles a small child,
black in color,
wearing red clothes,
with large ears,
long arms,
named Wǎng Xiàng.
【Transliteration】"Wǎng Xiàng" is read as written.
In Sīmǎ's version, it is written as "Wú Shāng",
and it says:
It looks like a small child,
reddish-black in color,
with red claws,
large ears,
and long arms.
Another version says:
It is the name of a water deity.
【Seven】【Shū】It looks like a dog,
has horns,
and its body is adorned with patterns.
【Transcription】"Shèn" is also written as "Shēn".
Pronounced with the initial "sh" and final "in",
also pronounced as "zhēn".
Sīmǎ explains:
Its appearance resembles a dog,
has horns,
and a body patterned with five colors.
【Eight】【Shū】As large as an ox,
shaped like a drum,
it walks on one foot.
【Transcription】"Kui" is pronounced as qiú guī fǎn.
Simǎ states:
Its appearance resembles a drum with one foot.
【Nine】【Shū】 Its form is like a snake,
with two heads,
and five colors.
【Text Explanation】"Fāng" is pronounced as páng.
Some versions also write it as "fǎng",
with the same meaning.
"Huáng" in some versions is also written as "huáng",
with the same meaning.
Sīmǎ explains:
Fǎnghuáng,
shaped like a snake,
with two heads,
and five-colored patterns.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Modern editions write it as fǎnghuáng.
【Collation】(1) The character 罔 was amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(2) The character 汙 was supplemented based on the Shìwén.
(3) Current editions lack this annotation,

The Duke said:
"May I ask,
what is the appearance of the Wēi Yí?"
【Part One】【Memorial】Duke Huán encountered a ghost,
originally in the marshes,
and upon hearing of the winding serpent,
inquired about its form.
【Transcription】"Weǐ" is pronounced with the yúwēi fǎnqie,
and also as the character's regular reading.
The prince said:
"The Wēiyí,
as large as a hub,
as long as a shaft,
wears purple clothes and a vermilion crown.
As a creature,
it detests hearing the sound of thunderous chariots,
then holds its head and stands.
One who sees it is nearly destined to become a hegemon."
Duke Huán gave a hearty laugh and said:
"This is exactly what I have witnessed."
Thereupon, he straightened his robe and cap and sat with him,
and before the day was over, he realized his ailment had vanished.
【一】【疏】Chěn,
is the appearance of joyous laughter.
Dài,
means near.
As if seeing the winding path,
approaching to become the hegemon.
Duke Huán heard the explanation,
laughed heartily and exclaimed:
"What I saw was exactly this."
【Translated Text】"Zhū Guān" in Sīmǎ's version is written as Yú Guān,
saying:
It is the headwear of the Yú state,
its shape resembles a spiral shell.
"È Wén Léi" is pronounced with the initial "wū" and the final "lù" in reverse.
"Pěng" is pronounced with the initial "fāng" and the final "yǒng" in reverse.
"Qí Shǒu" is the same in Sīmǎ's version.
One edition writes it as "shǒu".
"Chěn" is pronounced with the initial "chì" and the final "yǐn" in reverse,
Xú gives another pronunciation as "chì yī" in reverse,
and also "chì sī" in reverse.
Sīmǎ says:
Appearance of smiling.
Lǐ says:
Appearance of laughing heartily.
【二】【Note】This chapter says that when worries come and burdens arise,
it is due to lack of clarity;
when troubles depart and one's nature is attained,
it is due to understanding the principles.
【Commentary】Having heard of the tale of Wēiyí,
one's heart feels unburdened and at ease,
so one straightens their attire and headdress,
engages in conversation and discussion,
and before the day ends, the heart's burdens are lifted,
not knowing from where the illness has vanished.
Jì Shěngzǐ raised fighting cocks for the king【1】.
【One】【Narrative】Surname Jì,
given name Shěngzǐ,
also written as Xiāo,
read it according to the character.
He raised chickens for the King of Qí,
intending them for fighting.
This chapter illustrates that it is not necessary to possess innate knowledge of natural principles;
there are also those who develop their nature through accumulated practice.
【Translated Text】"Jì Shěng" is pronounced as suǒ jǐng fǎn,
while Xú reads it as suǒ xìng fǎn.
It is a person's name.
One version writes it as Xiāo.
"Wèi" is pronounced as yú wèi fǎn.
"Wáng" according to Sīmǎ,
refers to the King of Qí.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
The "Huáng Dì" chapter of the Lièzǐ also records this event,
stating that Jì Shěngzǐ raised fighting cocks for King Zhōu Xuān,

After ten days he asked:
"Is the chicken ready?"
The reply was:
"Not yet,
it is still vainly arrogant and relies on its vigor."
【One】【Memorial】After nurturing it for ten days,
"Is it ready for combat?"
The reply said:
"Initially, its nature was arrogant and conceited,
relying on its own spirit and will,
thus it is not yet ready."
【Explanation】"Xū jiāo": pronounced as jū qiáo,
also pronounced as jù xiāo.
Lǐ Yún:
Means lofty.
Sīmǎ Yún:
Means holding the head high and looking upward.
Ten days later, he asked again,
saying:
"Not yet.
Still responding to echoes and shadows."
【One】【Memorial】Seeing or hearing other chickens,
they still respond to each other like forms and echoes, shadows and reflections.
【Explanation】"Yìng" means the response in dialogue.
The same applies below.
"Xiǎng" is pronounced as xǔ zhǎng fǎn.
It is also written as "echo."
"Yǐng" is pronounced as yú lǐng fǎn,
or as the common reading.
Lǐ Yún said:
Respond like an echo,
Look back at the shadow while walking.
Ten days later, he asked again,
and said:
"Not yet.
He still glares fiercely and is full of arrogance."
【One】【Memorial】Looking around swiftly and sharply,
with a vigorous and robust spirit,
the mind and heart are still agitated,
thus not yet fit for it.
After ten more days, he asked again,
and the reply was:
"Almost there.
Even when other crows crow,
it shows no change
and appears like a wooden rooster.
Its virtue is complete.
No other rooster dares to confront it,
and they all turn and flee."
【One】【Explanation】Ji,
means to exhaust.
Without any arrogance or conceit,
the mind and spirit are calm and stable.
Although the rooster crows,
there is no longer any fear or alarm.
The essence of raising chickens,
its principle is fully contained herein.
【二】【注】This chapter speaks of nurturing oneself to achieve completeness,
such that one remains unmatched externally,
how much more so in achieving self-wholeness!
【Commentary】The spirit is at ease and composed,
the appearance calm and settled.
From a distance,
it resembles a wooden rooster,
unmoving and unstartled,
its virtue complete and intact.
Other people's roosters,
upon seeing it, turn and flee.
Unrivaled under heaven,
who would dare to challenge it?
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites versions by Wén Hǎi and Liú Déyī, where the character "zhě" is preceded by the character "jiàn".
Confucius was observing at Lǚliáng,
where the hanging waters measured thirty fathoms,
and the rushing foam extended for forty miles,
a place where giant turtles, alligators, fish, and softshell turtles could not swim.
He saw a man swimming in it,
thinking he was suffering and intended to die,
so he sent his disciples to rescue him along the current.
After several hundred paces, the man emerged,
with disheveled hair, singing and swimming by the embankment below.
【一】【疏】Lǚliáng,
is the name of a river.
Interpreters differ,
some say it is at Héhuáng County in Líshí of Xīhé, where the Yellow River is cut off,
called Lǚliáng;
some say two hundred lǐ from Púzhōu there is Lóngmén,
where the river water passes through,
cascading down as a waterfall,
also named Lǚliáng;
some say it is the Lǚliáng in Péngchéng County of the state of Sòng.
Eight chǐ make a rèn,
calculating its height as twenty-four zhàng and hanging down.
Now, this water,
said to be named for its height in cascading,
is likely a fable,
exaggerating its reality.
Yuán,
resembles a biē but is larger in shape;
tuó,
is like a fish but has feet.
This water's waterfall being so high,
with swift and steep flowing waves,
thus causes turbulent rapids and churning foam for forty lǐ,
as for aquatic creatures,
still cannot swim,
let alone land animals,
how could they possibly wade across!
【Explanatory Text】"Lǚliáng" Sīmǎ's commentary states:
It is a place where the river water has a rock barrier.
Nowadays, west of Líshí in Xīhé, there is such a steep cliff,
commonly known as Huángliáng.
Huáinánzǐ says:
In ancient times, before the Dragon Gate was chiseled,
the river emerged above Mèngmén.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: Tàipíng Yùlǎn, volume 183, quotes Jùnguó Zhì, which in turn quotes Sīmǎ's commentary:
Lǚliáng is the Dragon Gate.
However, it is not as detailed as the explanatory text.
"Xuán shuǐ" is pronounced as xuán.
"Thirty rèn" rèn is pronounced as rèn,
with seven Chinese feet making one rèn.
Flowing foam. "Foam" is pronounced mò.
"Yuán" is pronounced yuán.
"Tuó" is pronounced tuó duō fǎn,
or sometimes pronounced tán.
"Biē" is also written as 鱉,
pronounced bì miè fǎn.
【二】【疏】The torrent surged and boiled furiously,
unfit for any human to swim in.
Suddenly, they saw a man,
whom they believed was drowning and in distress,
so they ordered their disciples to follow the current and rescue him.
【Explanation】"Having bitterness" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means illness.

Confucius followed and asked him,

singing as he walked with composure,

"I thought you were a ghost or deity,
but upon closer observation, you are actually a human.
You are able to tread in deep waters—
do you possess some art of the Way or not?"
He said:
"No,
I have no special way.
I began with what was innate,
grew with my nature,
and perfected through destiny.
I enter together with the whirlpool,
and emerge together with the surge,
following the way of water without imposing my own will.
This is how I tread upon it."
【One】【Memorial】He replied:

indulging freely and unrestrained,
thus aligning with the natural decree of heaven."

like the rotation of a millstone's core,
is called "qí";
the churning and overflowing that reverses and surges outward,
is called "gǔ".
Since it harmonizes with the water,
and aligns with the mandate of heaven,
therefore, whether entering as "qí" or emerging as "gǔ",
it remains entirely unburdened.
Guō Xiàng's annotation mentions "the mill's hub entering,"

When I am about to make a bell stand,
I never dare to waste my vital energy,
but must fast to still my mind.
After three days of fasting,
I no longer harbor thoughts of celebrations, rewards, titles, or emoluments;
after five days of fasting,
I no longer harbor thoughts of praise, blame, skill, or clumsiness;
after seven days of fasting,
suddenly I forget I have four limbs and a body.
At that moment,
I lose awareness of the court,
my skill becomes focused and external distractions dissolve;
then I enter the mountain forest,
to observe the natural disposition of trees;
when the perfect form appears,
then the completed bell stand becomes visible to me,
only then do I apply my hand;
if not, I cease.
Thus, I match Heaven with Heaven,
and the reason why my instruments are suspected to be divine
must be this!"

there is one method I follow.

nor deplete my spirit and energy.
I must fast and purify to calm my heart and soul."

Now, examining the "Ultimate Joy" chapter, it states:
Those who raise birds in the way birds should be raised
ought to let them perch in deep forests,
roam over open plains,
float on rivers and lakes,
feed them with small fish,
follow their natural formations and rest,

and let them dwell in a leisurely, winding way;

【Commentary】Being capable implies action,

it is still like humans being unable to govern humans perfectly,
or geese being unable to fully harmonize with geese.

and still carries such afflictions and burdens.

【Transcription】"Wúxíng Jù" pronounced as jù.
Sīmǎ explains:
Do not be arrogant in one's demeanor.
"Zhì" is pronounced zhí shí fǎn,
also known as zhī lì fǎn.
"Ài" is wǔ dài fǎn.
【二】【注】To remain and dwell,
means to stagnate and hold fast.
【Commentary】Following things and accepting their course,
without clinging to glorious views.
【Explanation】"Wú liú jū" Sīmǎ explains:
Do not linger and settle in one's dwelling.
【Three】【Annotations】When form and things are leveled,
and mind transforms along with things,
this is entrusting oneself to things for self-conveyance.
The lord said:
"That path is dark and remote, with no people;
With whom shall I be neighbors?
I have no provisions,
I have no food,
How can I reach there?"
【一】【疏】Not having comprehended solitary transformation,
one cannot forget external things.
【Interpretation】"I have no food" — one version writes "I" as "hungry."
Shìnánzǐ said:
"Reduce your expenditures,
lessen your desires,
and though you have no provisions, you will yet have enough.
You should cross the river and float upon the sea,
gazing until you no longer see its shore,
and the farther you go, the less you know where it ends.
Those who see you off will all turn back from the shore,
and from here, you will go far away!
Thus, to possess people is a burden,
to be possessed by people is a worry.
Therefore, Yáo did not possess people,
nor was he possessed by people.
I wish to remove your burdens,
relieve your worries,
and wander alone with the Dào in the land of great emptiness.
If you are crossing the river in a boat
and an empty vessel comes and bumps into it,
even a narrow-minded person will not get angry;
but if there is someone in that boat,
then you will shout to them to steer away;
if you call once and they do not hear,
call again and they still do not hear,
and then you call a third time,
you will surely follow it with harsh words.
Previously, you were not angry, but now you are angry;
previously, it was empty, but now it is occupied.
If a person can empty themselves to wander the world,
who can harm them!
【一】【注】This means that knowing contentment leaves nothing unfulfilled.
【Commentary】It means that the Way does not rely on things to be complete,
but is merely tranquil and detached.
【Two】【Expanses】The river,
signifies wisdom;
the sea,
signifies the Way.
Wading into the river of supreme goodness,
roaming in the sea of the great Way.
【Three】【Annotations】To distance oneself from desires and passions.
【Commentary】How could one know the ultimate limit!
【Four】【Annotation】When the ruler's desires are extinguished,
the people will each return to upholding their proper roles.
【Commentary】Sending off the lord on his journey afar,
reaching the land of virtue and morality,
the people return to their true nature and abide by their simple station.
Yá,
means division.
【Five】【Annotation】It stands aloof and independent above all things.
【Commentary】Zì means
"from."
The ruler, from this sentiment, is lofty,
and his virtue and Dao are profound and far-reaching.
【Six】【Annotation】To possess others means
to have them as one's own private gain.
【Commentary】When a ruler governs the state of Lǔ,
abundant in wealth and talented individuals,
considering them as his own possessions,
it deeply becomes a source of affliction and burden.
【Seven】【Annotation】Being perceived by others means
being employed and utilized by people.
【Commentary】It speaks of being unable to forget Lǔ,
being recognized by others,
hence revering ghosts and honoring the worthy,
showing compassion to people and caring for the masses,
toiling for the people,
how could this not be distress and hardship!
【八】【注】Although possessing the world,
it is entrusted to all officials,
delegated to all things without personal involvement—
this is not having people;
relying on the people and utilizing things without burdening oneself,
this is not being seen as having people.
【Commentary】Guō Xiàng's annotation states:
Although possessing the empire,
one entrusts all affairs to the hundred officials,
delegates all matters to the myriad things without personal involvement—
this is not because one possesses others;
by relying on the people and utilizing things without exhausting oneself,
this is not because one is seen as being possessed by others.
【Text】"Bù yǔ" is pronounced as yù.
【Nine】【Annotation】To make one feel utterly devoid of any attachment to the state.
【Commentary】Dà mò,
means great nothingness,
signifying that nothing in the world can adulterate it.
【Transcription】"Dà Mò" means mò,
which is "none" or "without."
【一０】【疏】Two boats side by side are called a fāngzhōu.
【Interpretation】"Fāng Zhōu" Sīmǎ comments:
Fāng means
parallel.
【一一】【Commentary】Biǎn,
means narrow-minded and impatient.
The reason for not getting angry
is because the boat is empty.
【Transcription】"Biǎnxīn" must be read with the initial consonant 'b' and the final 'iǎn'.
The Erya says:
It means urgent.
【一二】【疏】Evil words,
mean cursing and insulting.
《则呼》 pronounced with fire radical and ancient sound.
Same below.
《张歙》 pronounced with aspiration and urgent sound,
Xu Xuzhe's pronunciation,
Guo Shulie's pronunciation.
Zhang,
means to open.
Xi,
means to close.
【13】【Comment】Though the world changes,
the principle of humbling oneself to avoid harm
remains the same.
【Commentary】Emptying oneself means
having no mind.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "惼" is written as "褊".
Běigōng Shū
and built an altar outside the outer city gate.
Within three months, the bell stands for both the rulers and the subjects were completed.
【One】【Shū】His surname was Běigōng,
and his given name was Shē.
He resided at Běigōng,
hence he adopted it as his surname.
He was a senior official of Wèi.
【Explanation】"Běi Gōng Shē": Lǐ Yún said:
A senior official of Wèi,
resided at the Northern Palace,
hence he was known by this title.
Shē,
was his name.
【Èr】【Shū】 bell,
is the name of a musical instrument.
It means that before casting the bell, a sacrificial ceremony must be set up,
which is why an altar is built.
【Explanatory Text】"For the Wei" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
"Tax levy" is read as lì yàn fǎn.
"Building the altar" is read as dàn dān fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
It is a sacrifice;
praying to it,
hence the building of the altar.
【Three】【Strings】 harmonize high and low,
the eight tones are complete,
hence it is called the chime.
【Explanation】"The Suspended Instruments Above and Below" is pronounced as xuán.
Sīmǎ explains:
When the eight kinds of musical instruments are fully prepared and suspended, their sounds vary in pitch.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì saw him and asked,
saying:
"What technique have you set up?"
【One】【Memorial】Qìng Jì,
son of the King of Zhōu,
a senior official of Zhōu.
He spoke of seeing an exquisitely crafted bell altar,
and, finding it strange, inquired about it.
【Explanation】"Wángzǐ Qìngjì": Lǐ Yún states:
He was of royal lineage.
Qìngjì,
was a senior official of Zhōu.
He found it strange that it was so brief and swift,
hence he inquired about it.
◎Yú Yuè remarks:
In the Huang commentary of the Analects,
Wángsūn Gǔ,
was a grandson of King Líng of Zhōu,
named Gǔ,
at that time served in Wèi as a senior official.
If so, this Wángzǐ Qìngjì,
is suspected to also be a prince of Zhōu who served in Wèi.
There was also a Wángzǐ Chéngfù in Qí,
as seen in the eleventh year of Duke Wén in the Zuǒzhuàn.
Shē said:
"In the briefest moment,
I dare not impose any artifice.
I have heard it said,
'Once carved and polished,
it returns to simplicity.'
Be simple, as if without knowledge;
be detached, as if hesitant and doubtful;
be gathered yet indistinct,
sending off the departing and welcoming the arriving;
do not hinder those who come,
do not stop those who go;
follow the strong and forceful,
accompany the crooked and compliant,
adapt to their self-imposed limitations.
Thus, even with daily levies and collections, not a hair is harmed,
how much more so for those who follow the great way!"
【一】【注】Serenely embracing unity,
not daring to fabricate assumptions to augment affairs.
【Commentary】Guō Xiàng's annotation states:
It is simply embracing oneness with tranquility,
not daring to fabricate assumptions to augment affairs.
【Explanation】"Bó rán" is pronounced as bù gè fǎn.
【二】【注】It still employs its inherent nature.
【Commentary】Guō's annotation states,
one returns to use their inherent nature.
【三】【注】Simply let it remain pure and unadorned.
【Explanation】Tǒnghū,
an expression of being without affectation.
It simply follows its innate simplicity and genuineness.
【Explanation】"Tǒnghū" is read with two pronunciations: tòng and chìdòng,
meaning an ignorant appearance.
The Zìlín states:
a grand appearance.
Another reading is tòng.
【Four】【Annotation】There is no direction to go.
【Commentary】If,
there is no concern.
Lazy,
means retreat.
It refers to matters of doubt and deliberation,
all of which have been removed.
【Transcription】"Tǎng" is pronounced as chì dàng fǎn.
【五】【注】There is nothing to delight in.
【Commentary】Cuì,
means gathering.
It speaks of things gathering together,
being dimly unaware,
neither knowing the coming and going of things,
nor welcoming or sending them off,
here below, each follows its own nature.
Moreover:
in a state of obscurity and vagueness,
the mind has no fixed focus,
it follows along with the welcoming and sending,
allowing things to come and go.
【Explanation】"Cuì hū" is read with the initial in the manner of "zuì" (in the falling tone).
"Máng hū" is read with the initial in the manner of "mò" (in the level tone).
"Xīn yuè" is pronounced as "yuè".
【Six】【Annotation】It means to let things be as they are.
【Commentary】The common people who cherish coming are not prevented,
and those who leave are not emotionally detained either.
【七】【Comment】It accords with the multitude.
【Interpretation】"Qiángliáng" means great strength.
【Eight】【Annotation】It is without attachment.
【Commentary】Transmit,
pronounced as Zhāng liàn fǎn.
For those who are strong-willed and difficult to assign,
follow and entrust them;
for those whose human feelings are subtly conveyed,
adapt and comply with them.
【Explanation】"Qū Fù" is pronounced as "fù".
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to follow those who attach themselves to one.
Some versions have "zhuàn",
pronounced as "zhàng liàn" in reverse.
【Nine】【Annotation】Employ it because it cannot be otherwise.
【Commentary】It is because the people are allowed
to fully express their individual circumstances (4).
◎Jiǎshìfù remarked:
Levying taxes to cast a bell,
is similar to the record in the Zuo Zhuan, 29th year of Duke Zhāo, where the state of Jìn levied a "gǔ" of iron to cast a penal cauldron.
It is called levying taxes but allowing the people to contribute voluntarily,
hence it is said to rely on their own exhaustion.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
"Exhaustion" (qióng)
means the extreme.
This means to use up all one has to deliver as payment.
Only by not daring to employ schemes to seek,
and purely relying on spontaneity,
will the people also respond with spontaneity.
In today's tax levies,
the use of schemes is excessive,
yet there is no way to counter the people's clever evasion of such schemes!
Therefore, it is said,
after carving and polishing,
return to simplicity.
【一０】【Note】Thus, there is no loss.
【Commentary】Although taxes and levies were established,
there was never any oppressive measure,
each followed their nature,
hence there was virtually no harm or loss.
【Interpretation】"Bù cuò" is read with the pronunciation zǐ wò fǎn.
【一一】【Note】Serene and unattached,
utilizing the world's own actions,
this is the great thoroughfare's path,
hence it is said: "Measure it and plan it,
and in no time it is completed."
【Commentary】Tú means
the Way.
Directly entrusting things to their nature,
one suffers no harm oneself,
let alone relying on the great Way,
where spiritual transformation operates through non-action.
Achieving completion in three months—
what is there to marvel at!
【Collation Notes】(1) The character "傅" has been emended based on the Textual Variants and the Shidetang edition.

Kǒngzǐ was besieged between Chén and Cài,
and for seven days had no cooked food.
【First】【Commentary】King Zhāo of Chǔ summoned Confucius,
and Confucius traveled from Lǔ to be a guest in Chǔ,
passing through the region between the two states of Chén and Cài.
As Confucius had a large following of disciples,
the people of Chén and Cài mistook Confucius for Yánghǔ,
and therefore raised troops to surround them.
The disciples suffered from hunger and starvation,
going without cooked food for seven days,
experiencing dire distress and hardship.
Dàgōng Rèn went to offer condolences and said:
"Were you nearly dead?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Do you detest death?"
He replied:
"Yes."
【One】【Annotation】It is aligning oneself with personal likes and dislikes,
whereas the sage has no likes or dislikes.
【Commentary】Tàigōng,
is how an elderly person is addressed.
Rèn,
is a name.
Jī,
means near.
Rán,
means like this.
Since Nǐfù was surrounded,
Tàigōng condoled and asked him:
"Are you near death?"
He replied:
"It is so."
[Tàigōng] said:
"Do you detest it?"
He answered:
"It is so."
【Text Explanation】"Dà" is pronounced as tài.
"Gōng Rèn" is read as written.
Lǐ's commentary states:
Dàgōng,
refers to a senior official.
Rèn,

Same throughout the chapter.

Rèn said:
"I have previously spoken of the way to avoid death.
In the Eastern Sea there is a bird,
whose name is Yìdài.
As a bird,
it appears sluggish and clumsy,
seemingly incapable;
it flies only when led by others,
and perches only when pressed by the flock;
when advancing, it dares not take the front,
when retreating, it dares not stay at the rear;
when eating, it dares not be the first to taste,
but always follows the leftovers.
Therefore, it is never rejected by its flock,
and outsiders ultimately cannot harm it,
thus it avoids calamity.
Straight trees are felled first,
sweet wells are drained first.
You, in your intentions, adorn your wisdom to startle the foolish,
cultivate yourself to expose others' flaws,
shining brightly as if carrying the sun and moon while walking—
that is why you cannot avoid trouble.
Long ago, I heard from a greatly accomplished person:
'Those who boast of their achievements have no merit;
those who accomplish deeds face ruin;
those who gain fame suffer loss.'
Who can renounce achievement and fame to return and merge with the masses?
The Dào flows but remains obscure;
dwelling in virtue and action without claiming status;
pure and ordinary,
one resembles a madman;
erasing traces and abandoning power,
not seeking merit or fame;
thus, one does not blame others,
and others also do not blame them.
The ultimate person is unknown to the world—
why do you delight in this?"
【一】【注】He was both grand and composed in his demeanor,
and his mind was never bound by constant attachments.
【Explanation】Speaking of the way to longevity,
it is illustrated by the example of a seabird.
Fēn fēn zhì zhì,
describes its slow and unhurried appearance, unable to fly high.
When it flies, it must lead its companions,
not daring to take off first;
when it perches, it must fold its wings close to its body,
drawing near to the flock.
【Explanation】"Fēnfēn" is pronounced as fēn.
The character is sometimes written as ●.
"Zhìzhì" is pronounced as zhì,
and some read it as zú.
The character is sometimes written as ●.
Simǎ comments:
Fēnfēn zhìzhì
describes a leisurely and unhurried appearance.
Another interpretation:
it refers to not flying high in appearance.
Lǐ notes:
it is the sound of wings.
"Perching close and constrained" Lǐ explains:
not daring to roost alone,
but squeezing among the flock of birds,
just enough space to accommodate the body for resting,
as an extreme measure to avoid harm.
【二】【注】He often comported himself with ease while in the court.
【Text】"Cóngróng" is read with the seventh tone and the róng sound.
【Three】 【Annotation】 It lies in following things and nothing more.
【Commentary】Advancing and retreating while maintaining balance,
is the ultimate way to avoid harm;
feeding and pecking in accordance with one's actions,
must follow a proper sequence.
【Explanation】"Its remnants" — remnants,
refers to the sequence or leftover.

remnants,

【Four】【Comment】To be together with the multitude.
【Explanation】"Row" is read as hù gāng fǎn.

"Not reprimanding" is pronounced as chǐ.
【Five】【Annotation】Troubles and harms arise from employing wisdom in the pursuit of competition.
【Commentary】Because of its humble and gentle nature,
it does not contend with other creatures,
thus flocks of birds form orderly rows,
and it is not singled out for rejection.
Moreover, outsiders cannot harm it rashly,
and so it avoids the calamities of the human world.

【六】【注】Talent brings harm.
【Commentary】Straight trees with useful timber
are the first to be felled;
sweet wells from which people come to drink
have their streams exhausted first.
When a person flaunts their talents and wisdom,
the principle is the same.
【Seven】【Annotation】To scrutinize minor differences
is to oppose the multitude;
to blend into grand unity
is to lack uniqueness in the world.
Thus, that which is brilliantly clear
is but the trace of profound obscurity.
Intending to convey words while leaving traces behind,
hence, through Chén and Cài, one expresses intent.
【Commentary】This means that Zhòngní intended to adorn his wisdom and talent,
to astonish the ignorant masses;
to cultivate and polish his mind and body,
revealing others' impurities;
with clear and sharp discernment,
flaunting his own abilities;
as if lifting the sun and moon to walk with them,
thus he could not avoid calamity.
【Explanation】"Adorning Knowledge" is pronounced as zhì (智).
"Exposing Filth" is pronounced as wū (污).
"Carrying" has two readings: qíliè and qíyè.

"Carrying"

【八】【注】Those who rely on their achievements and reputation as if they were complete
have never attained perfection in them.
【Commentary】The one of great accomplishment,
refers to Lǎozi.

generating and nurturing all beings,
hence he is called the one of great accomplishment.
"Fá" (伐)
means to claim.
"Huī" (墮)
means to fall or fail.
For those who take credit for their abilities achieve no merit,
and those who do not withdraw after success are bound to fall and fail,
those whose fame and reputation are prominent, if they do not conceal their brilliance, will inevitably face ruin and disgrace.
【Explanation】"Zhuì" is pronounced as xǔ guī fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】Achievement is accomplished by the masses,

【Commentary】Who is capable of establishing great achievements,
building a grand reputation,
yet not dwelling on the success once accomplished,
instead attributing the merit to external factors?
Who can act in such a manner?
Is it not only the sage!
【Explanation】"Qù gōng" is read with the rising tone of lǚ.
【一０】【Note】Unaware, they proceed on their own.
【Commentary】The Dao and its virtue flow forth,
permeating all under heaven,
yet they conceal their radiance and hide their brilliance,
hence it is said they are not manifest.
【一一】【Note】They all naturally and contentedly followed this path,
not because of reputation that they then abided by it.
【Commentary】Though one possesses virtue and principles,
and their influence spreads widely in the world,
they conceal their name and obscure their traces,
thus not dwelling in fame.
【Translated Text】"Jū dé xíng" is read as written,
also pronounced with the lower tone of mèng.
The annotations are the same.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Dé,
is like virtue.
Jíyùn:
virtue,
is the attainment of action.
It means that the Way circulates throughout the world,
yet does not overtly reside in it,
the practice of its virtue,

Guǒ Xiàng appears to have naturally attained this practice,

【一二】【Note】It is because the movement is without intention.
【Commentary】Purity refers to unadorned substance,
constancy refers to blending with the mundane,
since there is no pretense or affectation,
it resembles even more the nature of a mad person.
【13】【Comment】The achievement was accomplished by them,
so the authority does not lie with me,
and both reputation and traces fade away.
【Commentary】Erasing the traces of sages,
abandoning power and influence,
how could one harbor attachment to achievements,
or fix attention on fame and reputation!
【一四】【Note】By indulging their feelings and leaving them to their own devices,
thus each of them bears their own responsibility accordingly.
【Commentary】For this reason, there is no fame or reputation.

others likewise do not hold me accountable.
【一五】【注】Serene and tranquil, free from concerns,
is the ultimate person.
【Commentary】The person of utmost virtue,
does not show off in the world,
since you are a sage and wise,
why do you delight in fame?
【Translated Text】"Pò" is pronounced as bù gè fǎn.

Confucius said:
"How commendable!"
He bid farewell to his companions,
left his disciples behind,
and retreated into the vast marshlands;
clad in coarse garments of animal hides,
he ate acorns and chestnuts.
When entering among beasts, he did not disturb their herds;
when entering among birds, he did not disrupt their flocks.
If even birds and beasts did not despise him,
how much less would people!
【一】【注】He took from abandoning the pleasures of the human world.
【Commentary】Confucius, having received the admonition,
found merit in the words spoken,
and thus took leave of his companions,
parted from his disciples,
dispersed his followers,
and alone fled into the mountains and marshes,
discarding his wide-sleeved robe for coarse garments,
forsaking rich foods to eat acorns and chestnuts.
【Textual Explanation】"Yì Qiú": yú jì fǎn.
"Hè": hù gē fǎn.
"Shù": shí rǔ fǎn,
also pronounced xù.
【二】【注】Like plants and trees that have no consciousness,
they are therefore not feared by birds and beasts.
【Three】【Commentary】This is to express through words the ultimate extension of the utmost sincerity and trustworthiness,
entrusting oneself to all things without falling into a position of harm.
【Commentary】Being as tranquil as dead ashes,
and as emotionless as plants and trees,
even flocks of birds and beasts are not startled,
how much less would human relations harbor evil!
Kǒngzǐ asked Zǐsāng Hù (1) saying:
"I was twice driven out of Lǔ,
had trees cut down upon me in Sòng,
had my tracks erased in Wèi,
was impoverished in Shāng and Zhōu,
and was besieged between Chén and Cài.
Having encountered these numerous troubles,
my close associates have become increasingly distant,
my disciples and friends increasingly scattered.
Why is this?
【One】【Distant】His surname was Sāng,
his name was ●,
a recluse.
When Confucius served as the Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
the people of Qí heard about it,
so they selected female musicians and decorated horses to present to the ruler of Lǔ,
creating a rift with the ruler of Lǔ,
leading to his expulsion.
Sòng was the descendant of Yīn.
Confucius was in Sòng and Zhōu,
yet he was not employed,
hence it is said he was in dire straits.
Faced with such adversities,
his relatives and close friends,
became even more distant,
his disciples and friends,
became even more scattered,
why was it like this?
【Explanation】"Zǐ Sāng Hù": pronounced as hù.
Another version writes it as ●,
pronounced as yú.
Lǐ's commentary says:
Sāng is the surname;
● is the given name;
a recluse.
Another opinion states:
the surname is Sāng Hù,
and the given name is Yǐn.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Suspected to be Zǐ Sāng Hù from the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter.
Hù is pronounced as hù,
thus indeed identical to Zǐ Sāng Hù.
The variant written as ● is actually the character yú.
According to Shuōwén,
yú is sometimes written as ●.
I believe that Cǎi Sāng Yǔ in the "Table of Ancient and Modern Figures" is Zǐ Sāng Hù,
as discussed in the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter.
Yǔ might be a corrupted form of ●.
"Felled trees in Wèi": one version writes felled trees in Sòng,
erased traces in Wèi.
◎ Lú Wénchāo notes:
In current editions, Wèi is written as Sòng,
Lù shì (believes) that Sòng and Wèi in the following sentence should be interchanged.
"These several": the pronunciation is shuò.
"What concern": yú is pronounced as yú.
The same applies below.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "雽" is written as "雩",
while in the Shìdé Táng edition, it is written as "虖".
Zǐ Sāng Hù said:
"Have you alone not heard of the flight of the people of Jiǎ?
Lín Huí abandoned a jade disk worth a thousand pieces of gold,
but carried an infant on his back and fled.
Someone asked:
'Was it for the cloth?
The infant's cloth is meager;
【一】Was it because of the burden?
The infant's burden is great;
To abandon a jade disk worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and carry an infant on your back to flee,
Why is that?
【二】' Lín Huí said:
'That was joined by profit,
this is connected by Heaven.'
Those joined by profit,
when pressed by poverty, calamity, harm, or distress, abandon each other;
those connected by Heaven,
when pressed by poverty, calamity, harm, or distress, embrace each other.
The difference between embracing and abandoning is indeed vast.
【三】Moreover, the friendship of a noble person is as mild as water,
while the friendship of a petty person is as sweet as rich wine;
the noble person is mild yet intimate【四】,
the petty person is sweet yet severed【五】.
Those who come together without cause,
will part without cause【六】."
【一】【Note】Cloth,
refers to wealth and silk.
【Translated Text】"Jiǎ" is pronounced in ancient elegant speech as gǔ yǎ fǎn.
Lǐ Yí says:
It is a name of a state.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Wáng Zhòngbǎo's "Chǔ Yuān Bēiwén" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Jiǎ,
is the name of a state.
The explanatory text is missing.
"Lín Huí": Sīmǎ says:
The name of a fugitive from Yīn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Liú Xiàobiāo's "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Lín Huí,
is a person's name.
Slightly different from the explanatory text.
◎Yú Yuè says:
In the text above, "the flight of the people of Jiǎ,"
Lǐ's annotation:
Jiǎ,
is the name of a state.
Then Lín Huí should be a fugitive from Jiǎ.
It seems that Jiǎ perished and its people fled,
hence Lín Huí carried the infant and hurried away.
Yīn is a mistake for the character Jiǎ.
"Wèi qí" is read as the character's original sound.
The same below.
Also all read as yú wèi fǎn.
"Bù yǔ": Bù,
refers to goods and wealth.
【Èr】【Shū】 Jiǎ,
a state's name,
is a lower town of Jìn.
The surname is Lín,
the given name is Huí,
a worthy person of Jiǎ.
Bù,
refers to wealth and goods.
When Jiǎ suffered destruction by Jìn,
the common people fled into exile,
Lín Huí discarded and threw away his precious jade,
and carried his child on his back to escape.
Someone asked him about it,
saying it was for the wealth and goods,
yet considering it as wealth, it meant little wealth,
and considering it as a burden (heavy), it meant much burden.
Lightening the little but increasing the much,
not knowing why it was so?
【Three】【Discourses】Treasure jade discs,
are united by profit.
An infant,
is connected by kinship.
Kinship,
even in urgent distress still gathers together;
profit-based unity,
in extreme misfortune then abandons each other.
The sentiments of abandonment and gathering,
are far apart from each other.
◎Qìng Fān's case: In the annotation of Wáng Zhòngbǎo's "Epitaph for Chǔ Yuān" from the Wénxuǎn, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Shǔ,
means to connect.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Four】【Annotation】No gain thus indifferent,
aligned in principle thus intimate.
【Transcription】"Dàn" is read as it is,
also read as tú zàn fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】Adorned with profit, thus sweet;
profit cannot be constant,
thus there are times when it ceases.
【Commentary】No benefit thus indifference,
Dao in harmony thus intimacy,
with benefit thus sweetness,
benefits exhausted thus severance.
【Six】【Commentary】When there is no reason yet they come together naturally,
it is a connection ordained by heaven.
If the union does not arise from a cause,
then no cause can sunder it.
However, if they join due to a cause,
they will inevitably separate due to a cause as well.
【Commentary】Those who come together without cause or reason
refer to the natural bond between father and son,
which thus cannot be separated without reason.
When Confucius spoke of the traces left by the former kings,
being close to friends,
it was not a natural bond,
as they all came seeking fame and profit,
which means they came together for a reason;
when they saw the tracks erased and trees cut down, they departed,
which means they parted for a reason.
It was not a natural bond,
where closeness occurs without cause,
and separation happens without reason.
Confucius said:
"I respectfully heed your command!"
He slowly walked back with measured steps,
abandoned his studies and discarded his books,
yet his disciples felt no less devotion before him,
and their affection only grew deeper.
【一】【注】It is because they abandoned adornment and embraced simplicity.
Hearing the lofty decree,
he leisurely strolled back,
soaring freely and unrestrained,
carefree and self-content.
He abandoned the studies of purposeful action,
discarded the books of sage traces,
did not practice the teachings of ornate rhetoric,
thus eliminating the rituals of bowing and yielding.
Solely possessing reverence and affection,
he daily advanced in virtue.
【Explanatory Text】"Wú Yì" is pronounced as yī.
Lǐ's commentary says:
It means having nothing to hold onto.
"Qù Shì" is pronounced with the rising tone in qǐ and the third tone in lǚ.
【Collation】(1) The Dunhuang manuscript writes "ài" as "shòu."
Another day,
Sāng Hù said further:
"When Shun was about to die,
he earnestly instructed Yǔ, saying:
'Take heed!
For the body, nothing is better than following natural connections;
for emotions, nothing is better than sincerity.
Following natural connections, one will not become alienated;
being sincere, one will not be wearied;
neither alienated nor wearied,
one will not seek ornamentation to adorn the form;
not seeking ornamentation to adorn the form,
one naturally does not depend on external things.
【一】【注】Follow emotions according to one's nature,
without correcting them for the sake of profit.
【Commentary】Yuán means
to follow.
Forms must conform to things,
emotions must follow the inner nature.
In the past, when Yú Shùn was nearing his end,
he used this true teaching to command Dà Yǔ,
ordering him to be cautious and vigilant,
to follow the words and obey in action,
hence Sāng ● quoted it to inform Confucius.
There are also those who write it as the character líng,
líng means
to enlighten,
indicating that Shùn was enlightening Dà Yǔ with his true words.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhēn" is written as "zhí" in Sīmǎ's version.
"Líng" is pronounced as líng.
"Yǔ" Sīmǎ states:
Líng,
means to enlighten,
referring to using the true way to enlighten and speak to Yǔ.
Líng,
is sometimes written as mìng,
and also as lìng.
Mìng,
is like teaching.
◎Wáng Yǐnzhī says:
The explanatory text states,
zhēn,

líng,

Sīmǎ states,
líng,
means to enlighten,
referring to using the direct way to enlighten and speak to Yǔ.
Líng,
is sometimes written as mìng,
and also as lìng,
mìng,
is like teaching.
According to the case, zhí should be ●.
is the ancient form of the character nǎi,
written as nǎi in clerical script.

Mìng and lìng,

【二】【Note】Form is not artificial,
thus always whole;
emotion is not contrived,
thus always at ease.
【Commentary】When form is compliant, it is always in harmony with things;
when nature is guided, its function is without harm.
【三】【注】To act with simplicity and straightforwardness.
【Commentary】Acting in accordance with one's nature,
proceeding straightforwardly with simplicity,
how could one ever seek to borrow literary traces and rely on adornments to embellish their innate character!
【四】【注】Simple and sufficient.
【Commentary】Since one does not seek literary traces to adorn one's form,
it is understood that each is inherently sufficient in their own capacity,
and does not rely on external things.

Zhuāngzǐ, wearing a coarse cloth patched up,
with his sash properly tied and shoes secured, passed by the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi said:
"Why is the gentleman so weary?"
【一】【疏】Coarse cloth,
is still rough fabric.
Zhuāngzǐ's family was poor,
so he wore coarse cloth for clothing and mended it.
Xié,
refers to a shoelace,
also said to be a waistband.
His shoes were worn out, so he tied them with a rope.
The King of Wèi,
is King Huì of Wèi.
Bèi,
means sick or weary.
Dressed in coarse cloth and wearing worn-out shoes,
he straightened his waistband to meet the King of Wèi.
The king saw his impoverished state,
and thus asked:
"Sir, why are you so poor and sickly like this?"
【Translated Text】Zhuāngzǐ wore a garment made of coarse cloth.
"Coarse cloth" Sīmǎ explains:
It is rough cloth.
"Straightening the hem" is pronounced xián jié fǎn,
also kǔ jié fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is a belt.
"Tying the shoes" Lǐ explains:
The shoes were worn out,
hence they were tied.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"Hem,"
means a belt.
The term "hem" for a belt,
lacks other evidence,
and straightening a belt to tie shoes,
also cannot be considered as being in distress.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
"Xié,"
is one end of hemp.
[Xié] is interchangeable with the character "hem,"
meaning to arrange one end of the hemp,
to thread and bind the shoes with it.
The shoes had no decorative band,
tied with hemp,
hence described as distressed.
"Passing by" is pronounced gǔ hé fǎn.
"King of Wèi" Sīmǎ explains:
It is King Huì.
"Distressed" is pronounced pí bài fǎn,
also bó jì fǎn.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as "ill."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"It is poverty,
not exhaustion.
When a scholar possesses the Way and virtue but cannot put them into practice,
that is exhaustion;
wearing tattered clothes and shoes full of holes,
that is poverty,
not exhaustion.
This is what is called not encountering the right time.
Have you, King, not seen the leaping monkeys?
When they are among the nán, zǐ, yùzhāng trees,
they swing from branch to branch and reign supreme among them,
even Yì and Péng Méng could not take them lightly.
【一】But when they find themselves among the thorny bushes of zhè, jí, zhǐ, and gǒu,
they move cautiously and glance sideways,
trembling with fear;
this is not because their sinews and bones have become tighter and less flexible,
but because the situation is unfavorable,
and they cannot fully display their abilities.
【二】Now, living in an era of foolish rulers and chaotic ministers,
and wishing to avoid exhaustion,
how could it be possible?
This is the evidence of Bǐgàn's heart being cut out!
【一】【注】When encountering the right time and favorable terrain,
one can fully display their exceptional skills,
so even the finest archers of ancient times
could not harm them.
【Commentary】Nán, zǐ, and yùzhāng,
are all fine woods that are upright and straight.
Lǎn màn,
means to grasp and hold.
Wáng zhǎng,
means to be self-satisfied.
Yì,
was a skilled archer in ancient times.
Péng Méng,
was Yì's disciple.
Pì nì,
means to look askance.
The character can also be written as miǎn,
and it should be read accordingly.
It is said that when a virtuous or worthy person,
encounters the right time and place,
it is like a monkey finding a straight tree,
then it leaps and jumps freely,
and even if there is a skilled archer,
they dare not raise their eyes to look sideways,
let alone draw a bow!
【Transcription】"Téng" is pronounced as téng.
Originally also written as téng.

wáng,

Yì,

【二】【疏】The cudrania, brambles, medlars, and trifoliate oranges
are all thorny, undesirable trees.
When monkeys encounter such thorny trees,
they cannot display their agility and skill,
hence they feel sorrowful and tremble inwardly,
moving cautiously and glancing sideways,
not because their physical strength differs from before,
but because the circumstances are unfavorable.
Scholars facing a chaotic era
must also act accordingly.

◎Wáng Niàn Sūn said,
in ancient times, the place where one lived was called chǔ shì,
as in the Shǐjì biography of Cài Zé, "the kingfisher, swan, rhinoceros, and elephant,

occupies genuine earth,

【Three】【Comment】When the situation is unfavorable yet one forces action,
they will suffer execution.
【Commentary】This is a comprehensive discussion.
At that time, the Zhōu court was weak and feeble,
while the six states flourished and thrived,
leading to a situation where the rulers above were benighted,
and the ministers below were in chaos.
Zhuāngshēng, embracing the Way and upholding virtue,
was unable to be employed,
so he concealed his traces to avoid harm,
hence he uttered these words.
In the past, when King Zhòu of Shāng was unprincipled,
Bǐgān loyally admonished him,
only to have his heart cut out and die—
is this not clear proof!
Citing the past to validate the present,
it serves as a bright mirror for future generations.
