Confucius was stranded between Chén and Cài,
for seven days without cooked food,
leaning on a withered tree with his left hand,
and striking a dried branch with his right,
while singing the ballads of the Biāo clan.
He had the instruments but not the rhythm,
he had the sounds but not the musical notes.
Yet, the sounds of the wood and the human voice
struck a clear resonance in people's hearts.
【一】【疏】Yǎnshì,
refers to Shénnóng.
Confucius, being a sage,
was content with both poverty and success.
Although he encountered hardship in Chén and Cài,
he did not abandon non-action.
Thus, with his left hand striking dried wood,
and his right hand leaning on a withered branch,
he was serene and self-satisfied,
singing of the pure customs of Yǎnshì.
Wood is one of the eight musical tones,
yet striking it produces no melody;
without sound, it is merely hitting wood—
how could it possess the notes of gōng or shāng!
However, the singing and the sound of wood,
distinct and subtly pure, yet harmoniously correct,
resonated within the heart,
fitting perfectly with human emotions.
【Transcription】"Gǎo Mù" kǔ lǎo fǎn.
The following is the same.
"Biāo Shì" bì yáo fǎn.
Refers to the ancient inactive emperors.
"Lí Rán" lì xī fǎn,
also lì zhī fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
Lí rán,
means as if trembling.
"Yǒu Dàng" dīng làng fǎn.
Yán Huí stood upright with hands clasped, turning his gaze to observe.
Zhòngní feared that he might amplify his own concerns to greatness,
or, out of self-love, create sorrow.
He said:
"Huí,
it is easy not to suffer the harms of heaven,
but hard to refuse the benefits of men.
There is no beginning that is not also an end;
man and heaven are one.
Now, who is it that sings this song?"
【First】【Memorial】When Yán Shēng saw Zhòngní striking wood and singing,
he straightened his posture and turned his gaze to look.
Fearing that he had not yet understood,
Zhòngní worried he might form misguided speculations,
such as thinking Zhòngní was boasting of his own virtue and ambition for high position,
or lamenting his personal hardships by composing a sorrowful tune.
Concerned that it might be so,
he summoned him to offer guidance.
【Explanation】"Huán mù" is pronounced as xuán.
"Ér kuī" Xú reads it as qǐ guī fǎn.
"Zào dà" Sīmǎ explains:
Zào,
means to go to.
【二】【注】Only because of its tranquility, it is easily managed.
【Transcription】"Sǔn Yì" uses the sound of chǐ.
Note: The same applies below.
【Three】【Commentary】Things that come by chance,
cannot be forbidden or resisted.
【Commentary】The principle of nature
has the detriment of exhaustion and blockage,
yet when one comprehends the mandate of the times,
accepting it becomes easy.
The way of human relations
has the benefit of rank and emolument,
which come unexpectedly as if entrusted,
yet relinquishing them proves difficult.
This clarifies that although Zhòngní strummed wood and sang,
he harbored no sorrow or resentment in his heart.
【Four】【Annotation】What is considered a beginning today,
was an ending yesterday,
thus what is called a beginning is essentially an ending.
This speaks to the boundlessness of change.
【Commentary】"Cù" (卒) means
"end."
What is now the beginning
was the end of yesterday.
This aims to clarify that there is no beginning and no end,
no birth and no death.
Since there is no death and no birth,
how can there be grief over any blockage or hardship!
【Five】【Annotation】All are natural.
【Commentary】The so-called "Heaven diminishes and humans augment,"
is still a teaching expressed through words.
But when it comes to the point of congealing principle,
all is spontaneous,
hence there is no duality.
【Six】【Annotation】If one lets things take their natural course,
then the singer is not the self.
【Commentary】The great sage empties his mind and forgets,
losing both self and others.
Since I am not myself,
whose song is this song!
I have no body,
where then can the song be placed!
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'jué' (爵) has been supplemented based on the subsequent main text where 'jué' (爵) and 'lù' (禄) appear together.
Yán Huí said:
"May I ask about the ease of not being harmed by Heaven."
Zhòngní said:
"Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat,
being trapped in困境 and unable to advance,
are the workings of heaven and earth,
the flow and release of all things.
This means to journey alongside them.
As a subject serving a ruler,
one dare not depart from this path.
If this is how one upholds the way of a subject,
how much more should it be so in how one responds to heaven!"
【一】【注】It is inescapable.
【Commentary】The previous section briefly indicated the names,
and what follows explains their meanings.
"Blockage"
means obstruction.
When one's destiny reaches its end and is obstructed,
and the Way and its virtue cannot be practiced,
this is like the earth's emptiness and fullness,
the turning of the four seasons,
moving all things,
and releasing the qi and climatic phases.
The reality of "exhaustion and fetters" is reversed.
◎Jià Shìfù said:
When exhaustion and fetters impede progress,
it means hunger, thirst, cold, and heat are enough to shackle a person,
causing them to lose comfort.
Yet driven by hunger and thirst,
and moved by cold and heat,
one cannot resist without accepting it;
one merely goes along with them.
"Movement of things," Sīmǎ comments:
Movement
means to act.
"The discharge" is pronounced with a breathy separation.
Sīmǎ says:
It means to release.
Xú pronounces it with a worldly tone.
【二】【注】This means being unaware and unknowing, yet following the principles of the Emperor.
【Commentary】Together,
means both.
To pass away,
means to go.
Since one has realized the impermanence of the movement of things,
therefore, one goes along with the changes,
without delight or aversion in the midst of them.
【Explanatory Text】"Yán yǔ zhī" yán,
means "I".
【Three】【Annotations】Wherever one is, all is at peace.
Not considering loss as loss,
thus one awaits Heaven and does not suffer its harm.
【Commentary】As a subject serving his lord,
one dare not evade the commands of the ruler.
Upholding the way of a minister,
(thus)
Even so it is,
how much more for the transformations of adversity and success,
one must await the principle of spontaneity;
how could one oppose it!
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan ancient manuscript edition, where "物" is written as "化".
"What is meant by 'not receiving benefits from others is difficult'?"
Zhòngní said:
"At first, when employed, one's influence reaches everywhere,
ranks and emoluments come in abundance without end.
The benefits brought by material things,
however, are not truly one's own;
I say these are external to one's destiny.
A noble person does not engage in robbery,
a wise person does not resort to theft.
If I were to take them,
what would that make me!
Therefore, it is said,
among birds, none is wiser than the swallow,
where the eye should not linger,
it does not dwell to look;
even if it drops the fruit it holds,
it abandons it and flies away.
Though it fears humans,
it nests among their dwellings,
for the altars of the land and grain are there, and thus, it finds its place to survive."
【一】【注】Sensing and responding extends in all directions, reaching through to the four thoroughfares.
【二】【注】Being versatile and interconnected,
thus one can master the grand and lofty.
【Three】【Annotation】It is not something one seeks and acquires by oneself.
【Commentary】"Shǐ" means
origin.
"Nǎi" means
appropriate.
The wondrous origin is empty and tranquil,
its traces and functions respond to opportunities,
connecting widely to the four directions,
and its concentrated radiance illuminates the nine regions.
Since it does not covet high positions,
its virtue and resources are boundless.
All things benefit and seek it,
which is indeed appropriate.
【Four】【Annotation】Human life,
must externally have the destiny of interacting with things,
unlike tiles and stones,
which are limited to mere form and substance.
【Commentary】Confucius, being a sage,
stood out by the Mandate of Heaven,
exercised his exceptional virtue,
to rescue the common people,
was not of the substance of tiles or stones.
【五】【注】Theft refers to
taking something privately.
Now when worthy men and gentlemen obtain ranks and emoluments,
it is not taking them privately,
but rather receiving them.
【Commentary】Even worthy men and noble individuals,
would not engage in theft,
let alone Confucius, a great sage—
how could he possibly defy heaven and reason to privately seize ranks and emoluments?
If they came to him unsought and were entrusted to him,
he accepted them and that was all,
for he had no selfish intent.
【Six】【Annotation】Swiftly evading calamity.
【Commentary】The yì'ér,
is a swallow.
Shí,
means to eat.
With the intelligence to avoid harm and preserve oneself,
among birds, none surpass the swallow.
It flies into human dwellings,
intending to build a nest,
and if it briefly observes that the location is not suitable,
it does not wait to thoroughly inspect the surroundings,
but immediately flies far away.
Even if it drops the food it is carrying to the ground,
it quickly abandons it and flees,
never returning to retrieve it,
such is its swiftness in avoiding calamity.
【Explanation】"Mò zhī" is pronounced with the tone of "zhì".
"Yì" is pronounced as "yì".
"Ér" is pronounced as "ér".
Some say:
Yì'ér,
is a swallow.
"Mù zhī suǒ bù yí chù" has the pronunciation "chāng lǚ fǎn".
This means it is not a suitable place to stay,
the eyes have already perceived it through observation,
thus it is abandoned.
【Seven】【Annotation】There has never been one who distanced themselves from others yet was preserved by them.
Fearing people, they enter human dwellings,
which is why this bird is praised for its wisdom.
【Explanation】Invasion means
entering.
Swallows, fearing humans yet relying on them to dwell,
enter people's houses,
and build their nests there.
Therefore, people cherish and become familiar with them,
allowing them to avoid harm.
Similarly, the sage harmonizes their light within the world,
blending into human society,
remaining vigilant against disasters and dangers,
without sinking into the dusty realm.
The common people gladly support them without aversion,
thus enabling them to endure long and live fully (1).
【八】【注】As for the ultimate person,
they mysteriously unite with the world,
thus the world joyfully supports them without weariness,
jointly establishing them as the foundation of the state.
This is the reason why not receiving benefits from others is considered difficult.
【Commentary】The sage's virtue spreads far and wide,
all beings delight in upholding it,
the preservation of the state,
is thus fitting indeed.
What is called the benefit to humanity,
this refers to it!
◎Jiàshìfù remarked:
Having land thus gives rise to the altar of the soil,
having fields thus gives rise to the altar of grain.
The altar of the soil,
is that by which one dwells;
the altar of grain,
is that by which one is nourished.
Birds too have their dwellings,
birds too have their sustenance,
the swallow nesting among humans,
does not borrow from humans for dwelling but instead creates its own abode,
does not borrow from humans for sustenance but instead finds its own nourishment.
【Collation Note】(1) The character for "life" has been emended according to the Lǎozǐ.
"What is meant by 'there is no beginning that is not also an end'?"
Zhòngní said:
"Transforming all things without knowing who succeeds them,
how can one know their end?
How can one know their beginning?
One simply rectifies oneself and awaits it, that is all."
【一】【注】No one perceives its transformation.
【Commentary】Chan means succession.
The Dao permeates and gives birth to all things,
transforms all realms,
operates without cease,
constantly renews and alters,
yet in daily life, people are unaware of it,
hence none perceive its process of renewal and decay.
Since there is daily renewal and change,
how can there be any fixed beginning or end!
【Interpretation】"其禪" is pronounced as shì zhàn fǎn.
Simǎ explains:
It means to bestow.
【Two】【Comment】Day and night alternate,
without beginning or end,
thus one should face it with uprightness and await it,
without harboring any concerns.
【Commentary】Where there is an end, there is a beginning;
where there is a beginning, there is an end.
So how can one fix what is beginning and what is ending?
Since there is neither end nor beginning,
there is neither death nor life.
Therefore, one follows change and lets transformation take its course,
finding appropriateness in whatever is encountered,
holding fast to the true and the upright,
and simply awaiting what the Creator brings.
【Transcription】"Yān zhī" yú qián fǎn.
The same below.
"What is meant by the unity of man and Heaven?"
Zhòngní said:
"There are people,
due to Heaven;
there is Heaven,
also due to Heaven.
That humans cannot possess Heaven
is due to their inherent nature.
The sage peacefully embodies the passing of things and thus ends his life!"
【One】【Comment】All that is referred to as Heaven,
signifies clarity of non-action and spontaneity.
【Commentary】All human relations and the myriad things,
are inherently natural;
since love extends to this natural state,
thus humans and heaven are not separate,
and the myriad things are blended into one.
【二】【注】To speak of the natural is indeed natural,
but how can humans deliberately possess this naturalness?
It is simply natural,
hence it is called nature.
【Commentary】As for what is natural,
it is that which acts without knowing why it does so,
simply by its own accord,
without deliberate action.
How could it be something possessed by anyone!
If one claims it is possessed,
then it is no longer natural.
Hence, it is understood that what is natural is inherent nature,
not something humans possess.
This explains the earlier meaning of "having heaven."
【三】【注】Serenely without pride,
the body moves in harmony with change.
【Commentary】"Yàn rán" means
tranquility.
"Shì" means
to depart.
The sage comprehends the non-duality of beginning and end,
understands life and death as one,
thus able to peacefully relinquish the body,
following transformation as it goes,
floating freely without beginning,
accepting change until the end.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Mèngzǐ said,
the mouth's desire for flavors,
the eyes' for sights,
the ears' for sounds,
the nose's for smells,
the limbs' for ease and comfort,
are nature,
yet there is destiny in them.
Zhuāngzǐ's statement that humans cannot possess Heaven
corresponds to what Mèngzǐ called "nature yet with destiny."
Zhuāngzǐ regards those with material desires as human, and spontaneity as Heaven,
hence cutting off sounds and sights,
eliminating smells and tastes,
separating Heaven and humanity into two.
His saying "humanity and Heaven are one"
is akin to abandoning humanity to approach Heaven.
The sage fulfills nature to know Heaven,
his effort not beyond daily use, eating and drinking.
Nature has destiny,
yet it is not called nature alone;
destiny has nature,
yet it is not called destiny alone;
this is what is meant by Heaven and humanity being one.
Zhuāng Zhōu was wandering within the hedges of Diāolíng,
when he spotted a strange magpie coming from the south.
Its wings spanned seven feet,
and its eyes were a full inch in diameter.
It brushed against Zhuāng Zhōu’s forehead and alighted in a chestnut grove.
Zhuāng Zhōu said,
"What kind of bird is this?
Its wings are broad, yet it does not fly away;
its eyes are large, yet it does not see."
He lifted his robe and strode quickly,
grasping a catapult to wait for it.
Then he noticed a cicada,
which had just found a fine shade and forgotten its own safety;
a mantis, hiding behind a cover, was about to strike it,
seeing its prey but forgetting its own form;
the strange magpie followed to take advantage of them,
seeing the gain but forgetting its true nature.
Zhuāng Zhōu, startled, said,
"Alas!
Things indeed entangle one another,
and different kinds attract each other!"
He discarded his catapult and turned to leave,
but the gamekeeper chased after him and berated him.
【一】【疏】Diāolíng,
is the name of a chestnut garden.
Fán,
means a fence,
referring to wandering within the fence of the chestnut garden.
Yùn,
means round.
Gǎn,
means to touch.
Sǎng,
means the forehead.
An extraordinary magpie,
coming from the south,
with wings spanning seven feet,
eyes an inch round,
suddenly struck Zhuāngzǐ on the forehead,
and then perched within the chestnut forest.
【Textual Explanation】"Diāo" - Xú (the commentator) pronounces it as diāo.
The text also writes it as diāo.
"Líng zhī Fán" - Fán is pronounced as fán.
Sīmǎ (commentator) says:
Diāolíng,
is the name of a hill,
Fán,
means a hedge or fence,
referring to wandering inside the fence of a chestnut garden.
Fán,
sometimes written as Yě.
Yě,
is the ancient character for yě (field/wilderness).
"Yì Guǎng" - Guǎng is pronounced with a broad tone.
"Yùn Cùn" - Sīmǎ says:
It can revolve one cùn.
◎ Wáng Niànsūn comments:
Sīmǎ Biāo stated,
"yùn cùn,"
means it can revolve one cùn.
I note that Sīmǎ interpreted yùn as the revolving movement,
which is incorrect.
"Yùn cùn" contrasts with "guǎng qī chǐ" in the text,
if guǎng means width, then yùn means length.
"Mù dà yùn cùn,"
is akin to saying the eye has a diameter of one cùn.
In the Yuèyǔ,
it says the land of Gōu Jiàn was guǎng yùn bǎi lǐ,
Wěi's annotation states:
East-west is guǎng,
north-south is yùn.
This shows yùn means length.
In the Xīshān Jīng,
it says this mountain is guǎng yuán bǎi lǐ.
Yuán is the same as yùn.
In the Zhōuguān Dàsītú,
it mentions knowing the guǎng lún measurements of the nine provinces;
the Shìsāng Lǐjì records,
guǎng one chǐ,
lún two chǐ;
Zhèng's annotation in both cases says:
lún,
means length.
Lún and yùn,
are similar in sound and meaning,
guǎng lún is the same as guǎng yùn.
"Gǎn Zhōu zhī Sǎng" - Sǎng is pronounced with a rising tone.
Lǐ (commentator) says:
Gǎn,
means to touch.
【二】【疏】Yīn,
means great.
Shì,
means to go.
Jué bù,
is like walking swiftly.
Liú,
means to wait upon.
Wings large but unable to fly far,
eyes large but unable to see far.
Zhuāng Shēng found it strange that it was like this,
and then immediately conceived the idea to seek it out,
soon after, he strode swiftly,
holding a slingshot and lying in wait.
【Explanation】"The wings large yet not turning, the eyes large yet not seeing." Simǎ comments:
Yīn means
large,
bending and turning is called shì.
Lǐ comments:
With large wings, turning is difficult;
with large eyes, vision is sparse;
therefore, one does not see others.
"Jiǎn" is pronounced with "qǐ qiān" as the reverse.
"Jué" by Lǐ is pronounced with "qū bì" as the reverse,
while Xú pronounces it with "jiǔ fù" as the reverse.
Simǎ comments:
It means walking swiftly.
According to the case, it is as in the Analects where it is said, "The feet moved swiftly."
Holding the pellet — "dàn" is the pronunciation.
"Detaining it" — "liù" is the pronunciation.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to wait and observe for an opportune moment.
【Three】【Comment】Holding a leaf to hide himself from the cicada,
he forgot that his form was visible to the strange magpie.
【Explanation】"螳" is pronounced táng.
"蜋" is pronounced láng.
"執翳" is read with the fanqie spelling yú jì fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
Holding grass to conceal oneself.
"搏之" is pronounced bó according to Guō,
and fù according to Xú.
"之見乎" uses the fanqie spelling xián biàn fǎn.
【四】【注】Eyes can see,
wings can fly away,
this is the true nature of the bird,
but now, upon seeing gain,
it thus forgets it.
【Commentary】To seize,
means to capture.
The true essence,
refers to one's life.
Zhuāngzǐ held a slingshot, not yet released,
when suddenly he spotted a cicada in between,
hidden among the tree leaves,
enjoying the fine shade,
unaware of its own existence;
a mantis, using a leaf to conceal itself,
intended to catch the cicada,
unaware that its form was spotted by a strange magpie;
the strange magpie, following behind the mantis,
took advantage of its convenience in catching the cicada,
focused on gaining benefit,
unaware of the danger to its life,
this is what is called forgetting one's true essence.
【Interpretation】"Qí zhēn" Sīmǎ says:
Zhēn,
means the body.
【Five】【Annotation】Those who act for mutual benefit,
will always burden each other.
【Commentary】Having witnessed the cicada and the magpie pursuing gain and forgetting self-preservation,
one becomes suddenly alarmed and vigilant,
and then emits a sigh of lamentation.
Thus, it is understood that when creatures benefit each other,
there must inevitably be burdens and worries.
【Explanation】"Chù rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "zhào" and the rhyme as in "lǜ".
【Six】【Annotation】Those who have desires for things,
will also be desired by things in return.
【Commentary】Those who desire things from others
will find that others also desire things from them.
Thus, cicadas and magpies are both creatures of the world,
where benefit and harm mutually attract,
which is inevitably so.
【Seven】【Annotation】Suì,
means to question.
【Commentary】Juān means
to discard.
Yú rén,
is the Yúhòu who oversees the chestnut grove.
Suì,
means to question.
Having realized that gains and losses follow each other,
he discarded his slingshot and turned to flee.
The Yú rén suspected him of stealing chestnuts,
so they pursued and questioned him.
【Explanatory Text】"Sui zhi" is also written as "xun,"
pronounced as xin,
meaning to inquire.
Sima says:
Taking Zhou as the thief of grain.
【Collation】(1) The erroneous character is written as "qiān",
stating:
The Zhāng edition uses "jiǎn".
(2) In the Zhào Jiànyì edition, "xiāng" is written as "cháng".
Zhuāng Zhōu returned home,
and for three months remained secluded.
Lìn Jū followed him and inquired:
"Why has the master been so withdrawn of late?"
【One】【Memorial】Zhuāng Zhōu, upon seeing a magpie, forgot about his own person,
was suspected of stealing chestnuts,
returned home ashamed,
and did not step outside his gate.
His surname was Lìn, his name Qiě,
a disciple of Zhuāngzǐ,
found it strange that his master had recently shut his door,
and therefore followed him to inquire about it.
【Interpretive Text】"Three months without tíng" — one edition reads "three days."
Sīmǎ comments:
He did not come out to sit in the courtyard for three months.
◎Wáng Niànsūn states:
The interpretive text says,
"three months without tíng,"
one edition reads "three days."
Sīmǎ comments:
He did not come out to sit in the courtyard for three months.
According to Sīmǎ's explanation,
then the character "out" must be added to "courtyard" for the meaning to become clear.
The text below says,
"Why has the master been so 'not tíng' recently?"
If "so not tíng" is taken to mean "so not coming out to the courtyard,"
then it especially does not form coherent speech.
Now, in my opinion, "tíng" should be read as "chěng."
"Not chěng"
means not happy;
"very not chěng"
means very unhappy.
Forgetting one's own person,
forgetting one's true self,
and being humiliated by the gamekeeper,
this is the reason for the unhappiness.
The "Fāngyán" says:
"Chěng,"
"xiǎo,"
means happiness.
East of the pass,
some say "xiǎo,"
some say "chěng";
in the region between Jiāng, Huái, Chén, and Chǔ, it is called "chěng."
In the sixth year of Duke Huán in the Zuǒzhuàn, "Now the people are starving, and the ruler is indulging his desires,"
and in the Guóyǔ, "The Duke of Guó exhausted the common people to indulge his transgressions,"
the annotations by Wěi and Dù both state:
"Chěng,"
means to indulge or be happy.
The character "chěng" was anciently pronounced like "chéng,"
its sound being similar to "tíng,"
hence it was interchangeably written as "tíng."
(In Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on Contemplating the Mysterious," "Resenting the plain intent's lack of fulfillment,"
it rhymes with words like emotion, fame, camp, level, towering, sacrifice, cry, glory, peace.
The "Shuōwén" explains:
"Chěng,"
is composed with the radical ,
and pronounced as "chéng."
In the twenty-third year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒzhuàn, "Indulging in excessive punishments,"
the interpretive text writes "chěng" as "chéng."
The "Fāngyán":
"Chěng,"
means to resolve.
The "Guǎngyǎ" writes it as "chéng."
) "Three months without tíng,"
one edition reads "three days,"
which is correct.
The text below says the master has been "so not tíng" recently,
if it were for as long as three months,
it could not be described as "recently."
"Lìn" is pronounced as lì xìn fǎn.
One edition writes it as .
"Qiě" is pronounced as zǐ yú fǎn.
Sīmǎ comments:
Lìn Qiě,
is a disciple of Zhuāngzǐ.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The commentary in Wénxuǎn, Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"Qǐng,"
means a long time.
Xiè Língyùn's poem "Entering Huázǐ Cave, the Third Valley of Máyuán" commentary quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"Qǐng,"
means constantly long.
The interpretive text omits this.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang version, with the character "宫" (palace) included after "入" (enter).
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"I was guarding the form but forgot the self【一】,
gazing at the turbid water yet lost in the clear abyss【二】.
Moreover, I have heard from the Master:
'Enter a custom,
follow its decrees【三】.'
Now I wandered in Diāolíng and forgot myself,
a strange magpie brushed against my forehead,
roaming through the chestnut grove I forgot my true nature,
the keeper of the chestnut grove took me for an offender,
this is why I am not at ease【四】."
【一】【Note】The body resides in the human world,
where times may be peaceful or perilous.
If one applies the principles of ease and simplicity to this era without considering what is appropriate for it,
then one is preserving the form but neglecting the essence of existence.
【Transcription】"Yí Yì" uses the pronunciation with a rising tone.
【Bù Dù】 is pronounced with a falling tone.
【二】【注】When one sees others but lacks clarity,
one then relies on them to see oneself,
nearly forgetting the principle of reflecting inward.
【Commentary】I see profit and pursue material things,
loving to preserve my physical form,
yet benefit and harm call to each other,
causing one to forget oneself.
Having witnessed the magpie and cicada,
I return home and do not step beyond the courtyard,
doubting and reproaching myself.
This is what is called observing turbid water,
thereby becoming confused by the clear spring.
Although it does not align with the original truth of one's nature,
it still preserves the path of introspection.
【Explanation】"Zì jiàn" is read with "xián" as the initial sound.
【Three】【Annotation】Do not violate its prohibitions and orders.
【Commentary】Zhuāng Zhōu studied under Lǎo Dān,
hence he referred to Lǎo Zǐ as "the Master."
Those who are enlightened blend with the dust and enter into customs;
when there are prohibitions in society,
they follow and abide by them.
Now that he has wandered into that Diāolíng,
he was suspected of stealing chestnuts,
lightly violating the legal code.
These are words of regret and self-reproach.
【Four】【Annotation】He considered being questioned as an insult.
Now, Zhuāngzǐ advocated equality throughout the world,
so he often conveyed his ideas through allegorical words,
thus criticizing Zhòngní,
belittling Lǎodān,
attacking the Three Sovereigns above,
and lamenting his own plight below.
【Commentary】His attention was fixed on the strange magpie,
thus forgetting the prohibition of the chestnut grove,
which is to forget oneself.
The character is also written as the character "zhēn,"
read it according to the character.
The gamekeeper accused me of stealing chestnuts,
thus forming such shame and humiliation for oneself,
hence he did not go to court.
Now, Master Zhuāngzǐ, a great man,
concealed himself in a lowly position,
wandered in the state of Sòng,
nurtured his nature in the Lacquer Garden,
how could he be one to dazzle his eyes in clear waters,
or fix his mind on gain and loss?
Truly, he wished to evaluate the natures of all beings,
even to the point of damaging his own body.
【Transcription】"Shàng pǒu" pǔ kǒu fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The character '令' has been emended according to the version by Chéng Xuányīng cited in Quēwù,
as Guǒ Xiàng's commentary also uses '令'.
(2) In Quēwù, the citations from the versions by Wén Rúhǎi and Zhāng Jūnfáng both have '栗林' written as '□□'.
(3) The version by Zhào Jiànyì omits the three characters '言以出'.
Yáng Zǐ went to Sòng,
and lodged at an inn.
The innkeeper had two concubines:
one was beautiful,
the other was ugly.
The ugly one was honored, while the beautiful one was treated with contempt.
Yáng Zǐ asked the reason for this,
and the young innkeeper replied:
"The beautiful one is conscious of her beauty,
but I do not recognize her beauty;
the ugly one is conscious of her ugliness,
but I do not recognize her ugliness."
【一】【疏】His surname was Yáng,
his given name was Zhū,
his courtesy name was Zǐjū,
and he was from the state of Qín.
"Nìlǚ"
means an inn.
When he traveled to the state of Sòng,
he stayed at an inn in Zhōngdì.
The beautiful rely on their beauty,
so people forget their beauty and remain unaware of it;
the ugly humble themselves and acknowledge their ugliness,
so people forget their ugliness and remain unaware of it.
【Translated Text】"Yáng Zǐ" Sīmǎ comments:
Yáng Zhū.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Liu Deyi's original text as reading "zhi" for this character.
Yángzǐ yuē:
"Dìzǐ jì zhī!
Xíng xián ér qù zì xián zhī xíng,
ān wǎng ér bù ài zāi!"
【一】【注】Speaking of the way of self-proclaimed worthiness,
there is no time when it is acceptable (一).
【Commentary】One who cultivates virtue and establishes conduct, thereby eliminating a self-important and dismissive attitude toward others—
where would they not be loved and respected?
Hence, the disciples were instructed to record this saying.
【Transcription】"而去" begins with the Lǚ sound.
"之行" is pronounced with the lower Mèng sound.
【Collation】(1) The version by Councilor Zhào has the character 也 (yě) below that can be added.
【One】【Explanatory Text】Named after a person.
Tián Zǐfāng was attending and sitting with Wèi Wénhóu,
and repeatedly praised Xī Gōng.
【一】【疏】His surname is Tián,
named Wú Zé,
styled Zǐ Fāng,
a worthy man of Wèi,
and a teacher to Lord Wén.
Lord Wén was the seventh-generation descendant of Bì Wàn,
and the father of Lord Wǔ.
His surname was Xī,
named Gōng,
also a worthy man of Wèi.
【Explanatory Text】"Tián Zǐfāng" Lǐ Yún states:
He was the teacher of Wèi Wénhóu,
named Wú Zé.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The explanatory text quotes Lǐ Yún,
Tián Zǐfāng,
named Wú Zé.
Wú Zé should be Wú Yì.
Both "Yì" and "Zé" derive from the phonetic component "Yì",
ancient interchangeable characters.
The "Dàyǎ·Sīqí" in the Book of Songs says, "The ancient people had no Yì (weariness)",
Zhèng's annotation uses "no Zé".
Shuōwén Jiězì states:
Yì,
means to be weary of,
or to end.
Not being weary implies constancy,
hence his courtesy name is Zǐfāng.
(The "Tángōng" chapter in the Book of Rites, Zhèng's annotation says:
Fāng,
means constant.
) "Shuò chēng" is pronounced with a double-angle fanqie,
and also as suǒ zhǔ fanqie.
The same applies below.
"Xī" is pronounced as xī,
and also as xí.
Sīmǎ's version uses "jī".
"Gōng" Lǐ Yún states:
Xī Gōng,
was a virtuous person.
The Marquis of Wén inquired:
"Is Xī Gōng
your teacher?"
Zǐfāng said:
"That is not so.
He is a fellow villager of Wú Zé;
his judgments were often appropriate,
therefore Wú Zé praised him.
【One】【Explanation】 Xī Gōng was a fellow villager of Zǐ Fāng,
who spoke of the Way,
and his words often aligned with reason.
Therefore, Wú Zé praised him,
but he was not a teacher.
Wén Hóu said:
"Then you have no teacher?"
Zǐfāng said:
"Yes."
Said:
"Who is your teacher?"
Zǐfāng said:
"Dōngguō Shùnzǐ."
The Marquis of Wén inquired:
"Then why, Master, have you never praised him?"
【一】【疏】He resided east of the outer city walls,
and thus took that as his surname,
with the personal name Shùnzǐ,
being the teacher of Zǐfāng.
Since he was the teacher of the master,
why is he not spoken of?
Zǐfāng said:
"His way of being is genuine,
with a human appearance yet heavenly in nature,
adapting effortlessly while preserving truth,
pure and accepting of all things.
When things lack the Way,
he rectifies his demeanor to enlighten them,
causing people's misguided intentions to dissipate.
How could I, Wú Zé, be worthy enough to praise him!"
【一】【Note】There is no need for pretense.
【Commentary】This refers to a genuine practitioner of the Way.
【二】【注】Although his appearance is the same as that of others,
he alone embraces what is natural.
【Commentary】Although his appearance conforms to human norms,
his heart is in harmony with nature.
【Three】【Annotations】Empty and compliant with things,
thus the true nature is not lost.
【Commentary】Yuan means
to follow.
To empty the mind and follow things,
while constantly preserving the true essence,
is to act while remaining ever tranquil.
【Explanation】"Bǎozhēn" is pronounced as bǎo.
It is also written as bǎo.
【四】【注】Those who are pure worry about being overly immaculate,
but now purity accommodates all things,
in harmony with heaven.
【Commentary】Guō Xiàng's annotation states,
"The pure are troubled by excessive cleanliness,
but now purity accommodates all things,
harmonizing with Heaven."
【Transcription】"Dà" is pronounced as Tài.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Guō's annotation takes the four characters "rén mào ér tiān" as a single phrase,
which likely misinterprets the reading.
This should instead read "rén mào ér tiān xū" as the phrase.
"Rén mào tiān xū"
forms a parallel in meaning.
"Yuán ér bǎo zhēn" is the phrase,
paralleling "qīng ér róng wù" in meaning.
"Xū" here
refers to the orifices.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Fàn Lùn Piān," it says "as if following xū to exit and enter,"
with Gāo's annotation stating:
"Xū,"
means the orifices.
Interpreted as orifices,
hence it also refers to the heart/mind.
In "Chù Zhēn Piān," "xū shì shēng bái,"
the annotation says:
"Xū,"
means the heart/mind.
In Tài Xuán's "Duàn Chū Yī," it says "cut off the heart and destroy the axe,"
and in "Shī Chū Yī," "pierce xū and destroy the blade."
"Destroy the blade" is similar to "destroy the axe,"
and "pierce xū" parallels "cut off the heart,"
so in "Gǔ Chū Yī," it says "embody authority and fill xū,"
meaning to fill the heart/mind.
Details are explained in Tài Xuán Jīng.
Here, "rén mào ér tiān xū" means "human in appearance but heavenly in heart,"
indicating that one's appearance is human,
but their heart is of heaven.
Scholars who do not grasp the meaning of "xū"
mistakenly attach it to the following phrase,
resulting in the phrase "rén mào ér tiān" being incomplete in meaning.
The following two phrases, originally parallel, then become uneven.
In "Yǎng Shēng Zhǔ Piān," "yuán dū yǐ wéi jīng,"
the transcription quotes Lǐ as saying:
"Yuán,"
means to follow.
"Yuán ér bǎo zhēn" means
to follow and preserve authenticity.
Attaching "xū" above would render it meaningless.
【Five】【Annotation】Expansively clear and empty,
rectify oneself and that is all,
then the evils of things will naturally dissipate.
【Commentary】In the world, there are unprincipled things and
deviant, eccentric individuals.
Dōng Guō rectifies his own demeanor,
to enlighten them,
so that their confused and disordered thoughts naturally dissipate.
【Explanation】"Wù yé" is read as sì jiē fǎn.
【Six】【Memorial】The master's profound virtue,
so deep and mysterious,
leaves no room for my mediocrity and shallowness to select,
how could it be worthy of praise!
When Zǐfāng had departed,
Marquis Wén remained dazed the whole day without speaking.
He summoned the courtiers standing before him and said to them:
"How far-reaching,
the nobleman of perfect virtue!
I used to believe that the words of sagely wisdom and the conduct of benevolence and righteousness were the ultimate,
but having heard the teachings of Zǐfāng's master,
my body feels unbound and I do not wish to move,
my mouth feels sealed and I do not wish to speak.
What I have learned is merely worthless clay figurines,
and indeed, the state of Wèi has become nothing but a burden to me!"
【一】【疏】Trǎngrán,
the appearance of being at a loss.
Upon hearing about Shùnzǐ's virtue,
he was trǎngrán and without foundation,
naturally losing what is called,
thus he did not speak all day.
Thereupon, he summoned the minister standing in attendance before him,
and conversed with him,
sighing over Dōngguōzǐ's Way,
profound and difficult to comprehend,
truly a person of complete virtue,
who can be a gentleman to all things.
【Explanation】"Tǎng rán" is read with the pronunciation chìdàng.
Sīmǎ explains:
It describes a dejected appearance.
"Yǔ" is read with the pronunciation yújù.
【Two】【Annotation】He himself realized it was close.
【Explanation】"Shèng zhì" is pronounced with the tone for wisdom.
"Zhī xíng" has a lower, stronger tone.
"Xíng jiě" is pronounced with a rising tone.
"Kǒu qián" has a sharp, high tone,
and (the rest) [Xú] (one) with a deep, firm tone.
【Three】【Annotation】It is not a genuine object.
【Commentary】In my early years of study,
I employed the sagely words of the ancient kings,
and practiced the benevolent and righteous deeds of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
believing them to be the ultimate in exhausting principles;
now, having heard of the teachings of Zǐfāng's master,
whose Way is vast and profound,
it has caused my form to feel dissolved,
unable to move or halt,
my tongue to be clamped and constrained,
with no words to speak,
I realize that what I have learned,
is merely like a clay figure,
which crumbles upon encountering rain,
and is not the true substance.
A clay puppet refers to
a clay figure.
【Explanatory Text】"Straight" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Some editions also write it as "true,"
and the following phrase is the same.
The Yuánjiā edition writes this as "true,"
and the following phrase as "straight."
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
Modern editions write it as "true."
"Clay figure" is pronounced with a more forceful tone.
Sīmǎ explains:
A clay figure,
is a human form made of earth,
which crumbles when exposed to rain.
◎ Qìng Fān's annotation: The commentary in Wénxuǎn, Liú Xiàobiāo's "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
A figure,
is a crude earthen form.
The Yīqiè Jīng Yīnyì, volume twenty, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
A clay figure,
is a wooden figure made of earth,
also a wooden human form;
when earth and wood are paired,
it means using materials to resemble a human shape,
all are called effigies.
This differs from the explanatory text.
【Four】【Annotation】One who understands the utmost nobility
considers human ranks to be burdens.
【Commentary】Having heard the true Way,
one discards physical form and sits in oblivion,
thus realizing that noble ranks and ceremonial altars
are merely burdens of worry.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "Xú" was amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Wēn Bó Xuězǐ was going to Qí,
and stopped in Lǔ.
A man of Lǔ requested to see him,
and Wēn Bó Xuězǐ said:
"That cannot be.
I have heard that the gentlemen of the Central States
are well-versed in ritual and righteousness but shallow in understanding the human heart.
I do not wish to see them."
【一】【疏】His surname is Wēn,
given name Bó,
courtesy name Xuězǐ,
a man of Huáidào in the state of Chǔ.
The Central States,
refer to the state of Lǔ.
"Lòu" means
awkward or unskilled.
Traveling from Chǔ to Qí,
he passed through Lǔ
and stayed at his host's residence.
The man of Lǔ was a disciple of Confucius,
who heard that Wēn Bó Xuě was a virtuous man
and requested to meet him.
Wēn Bó declined,
saying:
"I have heard that the people of the Central States
are well-versed in rituals, righteousness, and the ways of the sages,
but awkward in understanding the human heart.
Therefore, I do not wish to meet."
【Explanation】"Wēn Bó Xuězǐ" Lǐ says:
A virtuous man of the southern states.
When he arrived in Qí,
and returned to lodge in Lǔ,
this man again requested an audience.
Wēn Bó Xuězǐ said:
"Previously he sought to see me,
and now he again seeks to see me,
this must mean he has something to enlighten me with."
【One】【Memorial】Wēn Bó arrived in Qí,
returned and lodged in Lǔ,
being the person from before,
again wished to request an audience.
【二】【疏】Qí,
means to seek.
Zhèn,
means to move or stir.
In the past, when I went to Qí,
he sought an audience with me.
Now that I have returned to Lǔ,
he comes again seeking to see me.
There must be a particular reason for this,
hence he intends to move or stir me to come.
【Transcription】"Qí" is pronounced as qí.
He went out and met the guest,
then came back in and sighed.
The next day he met the guest,
and again came back in and sighed.
His servant said:
"Every time you meet this guest,
you always come back in and sigh,
why is that?"
【One】【Memorial】Before and after meeting guests,
he frequently sighed to himself,
and Wēn Bó's servant,
finding it strange, inquired about it.
He said:
"I had indeed told you:
'The people of the Middle Kingdom,
are well-versed in rites and righteousness but deficient in understanding the human heart.'
Those who formerly came to see me
advanced and retreated with perfect compass-like precision,
with perfect square-like correctness,
their composure now like a dragon,
now like a tiger,
their admonishments to me resembled a son's,
their guidance of me resembled a father's,
therefore I sighed."
【一】【注】He circles around in his steps,
winding and meandering in his tracks.
【Commentary】Lifting, kneeling, bowing, and yielding,
advancing, retreating, square, and round,
winding like a dragon,
circling like a tiger.
【Textual Explanation】"Cóng róng" is pronounced as qī róng fǎn.
"Pán pì" is pronounced as bì yì fǎn.
"Yí" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
Another version writes it as wēi,
pronounced yú wēi fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In the current version, yí is written as wēi.
"Shé" is pronounced yǐ zhī fǎn.
【II】【Comment】The decay of ritual and righteousness
gives rise to such artifice.
【Explanation】"Its way" is pronounced as dǎo.
【Three】【Memorials】To admonish and remonstrate with me,
as a son serves his father;
to instruct and guide me,
like a father teaching his son.
Now, whether distant or near, noble or humble,
there are natural affections and duties,
yet since they are not innate,
why such earnestness!
Thus, I realize the flaws of saintly deeds,
have led to such affectation,
and hence I sigh over it.
【Collation】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan ancient manuscript edition, where "dào" is written as "dǎo".
Confucius saw him but did not speak.【一】
Zǐlù said:
"Our master has long wished to see Wēn Bó Xuězǐ,
yet upon seeing him, you did not speak.
Why is this?【二】"
【一】【注】We have already understood his heart.
【Two】Two men were so pleased,
that they forgot their words.
Zhòng Yóu found it strange,
hence he raised the question.
Zhòngní said:
"In the case of such a person,
with a single glance, the Way is present,
and there is no room for words either."
【一】【Note】The gaze is set to go forward,
the intention has already been conveyed,
leaving no room for virtuous words.
【Commentary】To strike means,
to move.
Those who embody enlightenment,
forget words and grasp the principle,
where with just a movement of the eye, the profound Way is present,
there is no need to further expend words,
nor to allow for verbose explanations.
【Explanatory Text】"Fūrén" is pronounced as "fú".
"When eyes meet, the Way is present" Simǎ comments:
Upon seeing his eyes move, the spiritual essence is already manifest.
"Jī"
means to move or act.
Guǒ notes:
As soon as the eyes glance over,
the intention is already conveyed.
Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní:
"When you walk slowly, I also walk slowly;
when you walk quickly, I also walk quickly;
when you run, I also run;
but when you dash away leaving no dust behind,
then I, Huí, can only stare blankly, falling behind!"
The Master said:
"Huí,
what do you mean?"
He said:
"When the Master walks,
I also walk;
when the Master speaks,
I also speak;
when the Master hastens,
I also hasten;
when the Master debates,
I also debate;
when the Master gallops,
I also gallop;
when the Master speaks of the Way,
I, Huí, also speak of the Way;
but when he dashes away leaving no dust behind and I, Huí, can only stare blankly from behind,
it is because the Master gains trust without speaking,
achieves universal connection without partiality,
and though possessing no official position, the people naturally gather before him -
I simply do not understand how this comes to be."
【一】【疏】"奔逸绝尘" means
running swiftly.
"瞠" refers to
the appearance of staring straight ahead.
It describes moving so fast that the dust is left behind,
making it impossible to catch up,
hence one can only stare as it moves ahead.
"器" here denotes
official rank or nobility.
The Master, without speaking, is trusted by others;
without intentionally drawing close, he interacts smoothly with all things.
Though he holds no sovereign position, people naturally gather before him in crowds.
It happens without knowing how or why,
simply by being as he is,
which is what is meant by "奔逸绝尘."
【Explanatory Text】"Ben Yi" in Sima's [edition] is also (in one edition) (one) written as "Che".
"Cheng" is pronounced with the retroflex initial and Geng rhyme,
also (Yin) [Chou] with Lang rhyme.
The character dictionary "Zi Lin" states:
Appearance of staring straight.
Another reading is with the Du initial and Geng rhyme,
also with the retroflex initial and Meng rhyme.

◎Qing Fan's note: In the annotations to the Biographies of Hermits in the "Book of the Later Han" and the annotations to Fan Ye's "Discourse on Biographies of Hermits" in the "Selections of Refined Literature",
both quote Sima as saying:
It means unreachable.
The explanatory text is missing.
"Bu Bi Er Zhou" uses the Pi initial and Zhi rhyme.
"Tao Hu Qian" uses the Tu initial and Dao rhyme.
It means lacking the capacity of a ruler,
with crowds gathering before him.
Another reading is with the Du initial and Gao rhyme.
【Collation Note】(1) This character and the character "chǒu" have been emended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Zhòngní said:
"Alas!
How can one not examine this!
There is no sorrow greater than the death of the heart,
and physical death comes next.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the western extreme,
all things follow this pattern,
those with eyes and feet
depend on this to accomplish their tasks,
when it appears they exist,
when it disappears they perish.
All things are like this,
some depend on it to die,
some depend on it to live.
Once I receive this formed body,
I do not transform but wait for its end,
responding to things and moving with them,
day and night without interval,
yet not knowing its final destination;
vaguely it takes form,
I therefore daily move forward with it.
【一】【注】If the heart considers death as death,
it only hastens its own demise;
the swiftness of this death
arises from sorrow leading to self-loss.
Without sorrow, it ceases;
when there is sorrow and the heart dies,
that is the greatest of sorrows.
【Commentary】To be united without forming cliques,
to be trusted without speaking,
this surely stems from an open mind that顺应物性,
how could it be without reason!
How can one not keep in mind reflection and illumination,
and calmly examine one's heart!
Among the burdens of emotions,
none surpass the fickleness of the heart,
its changes, birth, and extinction,
are deeply lamentable,
and to grieve over life and death
is secondary to that.
【Explanation】"Wicked" is pronounced as wū.
"Observing and" is pronounced as yú.
The following "mourning and" is the same.
"Self-loss" is pronounced with a rising tone on sàng.
The same applies to the following chapter.
【Two】【Annotations】All are visible.
【Commentary】The darkness of night and brightness of day,
the sun rising in the east and setting in the west,
are like humans entering seclusion and emerging into prominence,
dying and being reborn.
Thus, we understand that human life and death
are analogous to the sky's day and night.
Using this metaphor for comparison,
why should there be any regret?
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
When the sun rises,
it rides on its motion;
when it sets,
people then rest,
all due to its light.
Things that depend on light to act
cannot escape this principle;
they rely on light to move,
on qi to live,
merely following it.
If one cannot control qi to sustain life,
then one also cannot forcibly grasp the light to act.
The light of the past
is like the light of today,
yet we cannot hold today's light
to precisely match it with the past.
To seize today's light and try to conform it to the past
is to lose it even as we cross paths.
That has its own pace and steps,
this has its own pace and steps.
Resemblance
lies in the pace and steps,
but what enables resemblance
is not the pace and steps themselves.
Only when both forget each other in the midst of their paces and steps
can they greatly accord with the Dào.
Only by being able to forget
can that which is not forgotten thereby persist.
If one does not rely on others' paces and steps at all,
it is like riding the sun's light without knowing to act—
this is called human death;
if one forcibly strives to match others' paces and steps,
it is forgetting today's light and seeking it in the past—
this is called the death of the heart.
Death
means adhering without transformation,
clinging without change.
Zhuāngzǐ's words are profound,
and should only be grasped through spiritual comprehension.
【Three】【Annotations】The eyes achieve merit through observation,
the feet achieve merit through action.
【Commentary】"Zhǐ" means
foot.
All parts of the human body,
originate from yīn and yáng,
the eyes see and the feet walk,
relying on the act of creation,
if not for these,
how could accomplishments be achieved!
Thus we know life and death are not matters determined by humans.
【四】【注】Simply because it was not seen, it was considered lost,
but in the end, it was not lost.
【Commentary】Seeing the sun rise is called existence,
watching the sun set is called extinction,
these are but the arbitrary attachments of ordinary sentiments,
not the profound perspective of the enlightened sage.
【Five】【Comment】Awaiting concealment is called death,
awaiting manifestation is called life,
ultimately there is no death or life.
【Commentary】The concealment and manifestation of all things
depend on the workings of creation.
Concealment is called death,
manifestation is called life.
Since the sun's rising and setting involve neither preservation nor perishing,
how can the concealment and manifestation of things involve life and death?
【Six】【Annotation】What exists cannot transform into non-existence,
thus once it receives form,
its transformation continues endlessly.
【Commentary】My physical form and nature,
bestowed by the Creator,
whether bright or dull, beautiful or ugly,
have already been distinctly formed.
Once fixed,
they undergo no further changes,
only remaining upright to await the end,
passing the years in this manner.
Since beauty and ugliness are not within my control,
life and death should likewise be left to fate.
【Seven】【Annotation】It is from having no mind.
【Commentary】The supreme sage, in his emptiness and stillness,
responds as soon as he is moved,
acting in accordance with the movement of things,
yet remains without deliberate intent.
【八】【Note】Constant transformation renews things.
【Commentary】Transformation renews daily,
seamlessly and without gaps.
【Nine】【Annotation】Not regarding death as death.
【Commentary】Following it, one does not see its rear.
【一０】【Note】Warm and natural, self-formed,
what more is there to do!
【Commentary】Xūn rán,
describes the appearance of spontaneous movement.
Xūn rán means receiving qi to take form,
with nothing causing it to be so.
【Explanation】"Xūn rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "Xǔ" and the rhyme as in "yún".
【一一】【Note】Not tied to the past,
moving along with change,
hence it is said to pass by.
【Commentary】Cú,
means to go.
Being attuned to the changes of the times,
one cannot pre-establish fixed patterns;
embodying daily renewal,
thus one progresses together with transformation.
【Explanation】"Rì cú" is read as written.
The Sīmǎ version has it as "jū",
saying:
It means illness.
I have been with you all my life, yet we passed by each other and lost one another,
is that not lamentable?
You are likely fixated on what I am fixated on.
That has already vanished,
yet you seek it as if it exists,
which is like searching for a horse in an empty market.
What I receive from you is easily forgotten,
and what you receive from me is also easily forgotten.
Even so,
why should you worry?
Though you may forget the former me,
there remains something of me that is unforgettable.
【一】【注】Change and transformation cannot be grasped and detained.
Thus, even if one holds onto another's arm to keep them close, it cannot make them stay.
If one mourns the dead,
then this too is worthy of mourning.
Yet people today do not consider this a cause for sorrow;
why then mourn death alone!
【Commentary】Confucius and Yán Huí,
two sages of virtue and wisdom,
cultivated themselves together,
as if standing side by side;
yet change renews daily,
the flow of time swift,
even holding firm and guarding steadfastly,
cannot pause it momentarily.
In the span of an arm's grasp,
suddenly it has passed away;
as the new has already advanced,
thus the old is lost.
If one grieves over the loss of the past,
this is profoundly lamentable.
【Transcription】"Néng lìng" is read as lì chéng fǎn.
The same applies to the annotations in the following chapter.
【二】【Note】The Tang marketplace,
is not a place to tether horses.
It speaks of seeking what was there before,
which can no longer be regained.
Human life,
is like a horse passing through a marketplace,
never pausing for even a moment.
The succession of the new and the old,
does not cease day or night.
Zhù,
means to perceive.
It says that you nearly saw that by which I am perceived.
That by which I am perceived,
is renewed daily,
so the old has already vanished.
How could you possess it!
【Explanation】Dài means
near.
Zhù means
to appear.
Táng is
a road;
sì is
a market.
What I have seen
are changes and transformations renewing daily.
Yán Huí and Confucius,
conversing face to face,
the words spoken earlier,
their principles are not far,
hence it is said they are nearly apparent.
Those past events,
have already vanished by now,
yet you still seek the existence of that time,
thinking it remains in the present,
which is called seeking a horse at a táng sì.
A táng sì is not a place where horses are tethered;
earlier, a horse was seen,
passing along the market road,
but if you search for it now,
the horse has already moved on.
Similarly, the traces of the past have already faded away,
seeking them in the present,
the things have already changed.
Thus, it is understood that the new ceaselessly does not linger,
and movement continuously shifts and transforms.
【Translated Text】"Nǚ" is pronounced as "rǔ" (meaning 'you').
"Dài zhù hū wú suǒyǐ zhù yě" — Guō's annotation: "zhù" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling "zhāng lǜ fǎn".
The note is the same.
Another pronunciation is "zhāng lüè fǎn".
Sīmǎ's commentary says:
What I manifest externally is my outward transformation,
and you are nearly at this stage.
But there is one part of me that does not transform,
which is beyond your reach.
"Shì qiú mǎ yú táng sì yě" — Guō's note says:
A "táng sì" is not a place to stable horses.
Lǐ's interpretation is the same.
It also says:
"Táng"
means a pavilion.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as "guǎng sì",
explaining:
It means a broad courtyard,
and seeking a horse in a market's broad courtyard
is not the right place for it.
"Mǎ chǔ" — "chǔ" is pronounced with the fanqie "chāng lǜ fǎn".
"Kě fù" — "fù" is pronounced with the fanqie "fú yòu fǎn".
"Bù shě" — "shě" is pronounced as "shě" (meaning 'to abandon').
【Three】【Annotation】To ponder means
to keep in thought.
Quickly forgotten,
refers to the swiftness of the past.
It says your departure was sudden,
and thinking of it always feels insufficient.
【Commentary】To reflect (thrice) means
to engage in contemplation.
The you of the past,
has by now faded away,
and as I ponder it again,
I too have ultimately forgotten it.
【Four】【Notes】All are so,
regardless of whether one is worthy or sage,
none have been able to halt it.
【Commentary】Change and renewal occur daily,
without distinguishing between the worthy and the sage.
How could this apply only to you,
but also to me.
Your thoughts of me,
thus the matter too will fade.
【Five】【Annotation】What is not forgotten endures,
meaning it is renewed daily through continuation.
Although the old self is forgotten, the new self has already arrived;
it has never not been me,
so why should I worry about it!
Thus, one can transcend worldly customs, break free from dust, and merge seamlessly with all things.
【Commentary】The way of transformation
never ceases for a moment.
Though the old self is lost, the new self still remains;
thus, there exists that which is not forgotten.
Therefore, it has never not been me—
why should you worry?
【Explanation】"Lí Sú" is read with the tone "lì zhì fǎn".
The following chapter's text is the same.
【Collation】(1) The Tang manuscript lacks the character 故.
(2) Wáng Shūmín states:
"执臂 should be written as 交臂."
(3) Liú Wéndiǎn states:
"复 should follow the main text and be written as 服."
Confucius saw Lǎo Dān,
who had just bathed,
and was about to let his hair hang down to dry,
looking so still as if he were not human.
Confucius stepped aside and waited for him.
After a short while, he approached and said:
"Was I dazzled,
or was it truly so?
A moment ago, sir, your body stood as rigid as a withered tree,
as if you had forsaken things and left humanity behind, standing in solitude."
【一】【注】Utmost tranquility and serenity.
【Translated Text】"被髮" pronounced as pí jì fǎn.
"而干" in some versions written as 乾.
◎ Lú Wénchāo said:
Modern editions use 乾.
"慹" pronounced as nǎi dié fǎn,
also dīng lì fǎn.
Sīmǎ explained:
Appearance of not moving.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
To be terrified.
"泊" pronounced as bù bó fǎn.
【二】【疏】Having just washed their hair anew,
they let it dry under the sun,
their spirits tranquil and still,
motionless as if in a trance,
stiff like withered wood,
thus appearing almost inhuman.
When Confucius saw them,
he dared not approach to disturb,
so he moved to another place,
waiting quietly for the right moment.
【Transcription】"Convenient and wait" — 'wait' is sometimes written as 'serve'.
【Three】【Annotations】Without one's own mind and body,
then external things can be set aside.
【Commentary】In a moment's time,
he entered to see Lǎozi,
and said:
"Qiū, upon meeting you, Sir,
my eyes were dazzled,
I forgot and cast aside physical form and intellect,
truly believing you to be a sage;
thereafter, I became detached from others,
abandoned all things,
lost in the unfathomable and immersed in solitary transformation."
【Explanation】"See" is pronounced as xián biàn fǎn.
"Dizzy" is pronounced as xuán biàn fǎn.
"And" is pronounced as yīn yú.
The same applies below.
"Dig like" is pronounced by Xú as qū.
"Withered wood" is pronounced as kǔ lǎo fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) The character '掘' has been amended in accordance with the main text.
Lǎo Dān said:
"I let my mind wander in the origin of all things."
【One】【Commentary】Initially, there was nothing, and then suddenly there was existence;
thus, by wandering at the beginning of things,
one then understands that things exist not by deliberate action but by their own nature.
【Commentary】"Chū" (初) means
the origin.
The Dào (道) permeates and gives birth to all things,
therefore it is called the initial state of existence.
When the mind wanders in this primordial state,
it becomes concentrated on the wondrous foundation,
causing the form to resemble a withered tree,
and the mind to be like dead ashes.
【Interpretation】"而欻" is pronounced as "xū fú fǎn".
Confucius said:
"What do you mean by 'evil'?"
【一】【疏】Although I have heard the sage's words,
I do not yet understand their meaning.
He said:
"When the mind is perplexed and cannot comprehend,
when the mouth is shut and cannot speak,
let me try speaking to you of its general principles.
Extreme yin is solemnly cold,
extreme yang is fiercely bright;
the solemn cold emanates from heaven,
the fierce brightness issues from earth.
The two interact, achieving harmony, and thus things are born.
Perhaps someone serves as the regulator of this, yet no form is seen.
Growth and decline, fullness and emptiness,
now dark, now bright,
daily changing, monthly transforming,
each day there is some action,
yet no achievement is seen.
Birth has its place of sprouting,
death has its place of return,
beginning and end oppose each other without origin, and none know where they end.
If it were not this,
then who could be the ancestor of it all!"
【One】【Annotation】To compel Zhòngní to seek beyond the expressions and meanings.
【Commentary】The "gap" refers to
an open mouth that does not close.
It is not that the sage's mind is incapable of knowing,
but rather that there is no fixed method by which to know;
it is not that the mouth is incapable of debate,
but rather that there is no fixed method by which to debate.
To debate it would violate its essence,
to know it would lose its truth.
Thus, it is understood that the ultimate Way is profoundly mysterious,
transcending the realm of words and thoughts.
Therefore, one is left perplexed and speechless.
【Translated Text】"Mouth puckered" must also be pronounced with the opposite tone.
Simǎ explains:
Puckered,
means curled and not open.
Also pronounced as bì yì fǎn,
Xú pronounces it as fū chì fǎn.
【二】【Note】Attempting to discuss yīn and yáng to analogize the formless aspects of direction,
I dare not be certain of it.
【Commentary】The ultimate principle is profoundly mysterious,
beyond what words and thoughts can fully elucidate.
I shall attempt to discuss yīn and yáng for you,
aiming to approximate the Great Dào.
Although this serves as an imitation and semblance,
it is not yet the truth itself.
【Explanation】"Cháng wèi": read as yú wěi fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】This speaks of their interaction.
【Commentary】Sùsù,
signifies the chill of yin energy;
hèhè,
represents the heat of yang energy;
approaching the yang within yin,
and the yin within yang,
speaks of their harmonious interaction.
【Four】【Annotation】Do not perceive the form that governs it,
clarifying that it is so of itself.
【Commentary】The yang qi descends,
the yin qi ascends,
the two qi communicate,
thus achieving harmony and union,
and through this harmonious qi, things are born.
Although the four seasons alternate in heat and cold,
governing all things,
each transforms on its own,
so the form of governance is not seen.
【Five】【Annotation】Never adhering to the old ways.
【Commentary】Yin wanes and Yang waxes,
summer is full and winter is empty,
night is dark and day is bright,
the sun moves and the moon shifts,
renewing without ceasing,
thus each day has its own activity.
【Six】【Annotation】Thus, from the beginning, there is no merit.
【Commentary】The profound work subtly aids,
thus none perceive who accomplishes it.
【Seven】【Annotation】It sprouts before it gathers.
【Commentary】It sprouts from nothingness.
【Eight】【Annotation】It returns to dispersion.
【Commentary】Returning to the state before birth.
【Nine】【Comment】This is what is meant by: when you face it, you cannot see its head;
when you follow it, you cannot see its tail.
【Commentary】Life and death, beginning and end,
cycle back and forth in succession,
having neither starting point nor thread,
who can fathom their ultimate limit!
Thus, the consummate person comprehends thoroughly,
and lets transformation take its course.
【一０】【Comment】If it were not for the Way that is empty, penetrating, and generative,
who could be the ancestral foundation of the myriad things!
All things in their multitude
must rely on the Way.
【Transcription】"And who" is read according to the character's usual pronunciation.
Formerly, it was read as zǐ yú in the reverse tone.
Confucius said:
"May I ask about wandering in this."
【一】【疏】I inquire:
"To let the mind wander in the Way,
what is the method?
If one must wander in this,
what power and benefit are gained?"
Lǎo Dān said:
"To attain this
is the ultimate beauty and joy.
To attain the ultimate beauty and wander in the ultimate joy,
is called the ultimate person【one】."
【一】【注】The ultimate beauty has no beauty,
the ultimate joy has no joy, for that reason.
【Commentary】One who attests to the profound Way,
finds beauty in it and rejoices,
and thus attains the beauty of non-beauty while dwelling in the joy of non-joy,
can be called the ultimate person.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhìlè" is pronounced with a falling tone (luò).
The same applies below and in the annotations.
Confucius said:
"I wish to hear your method."
【一】【疏】A method,
is akin to a path.
Let me speak of the path to ultimate beauty and joy.
He said:
"Grazing beasts do not fret over changing pastures,
water-dwelling insects do not fret over changing streams,
for minor alterations do not disrupt their fundamental constancy.
Joy, anger, grief, and pleasure do not enter their breast.
Now this world of ours
is the unity of all things.
Having attained this unity and identified with it,
then one's four limbs and hundred joints will become as dust and grime,
and life, death, beginning, and end will become as day and night, unable to cause confusion—
how much less could the distinctions of gain, loss, calamity, and blessing!
To cast off attachments is like discarding mud,
knowing that the self is more valuable than attachments.
What is valuable lies within me and is not lost through change.
Moreover, the myriad transformations have never reached an extremity—
what then could trouble the mind!
Those who have embodied the Way understand this."
【一】【注】Life and death are but minor transformations.
【Explanation】"Jí" means
"to worry about."
"Yì" means
"to change."
For beasts that feed on grass,
they do not worry about moving from one marsh to another;
for aquatic insects,
they do not worry about changing ponds or swamps;
as long as there is grass and water,
they do not lose the great constants,
whether going east or west,
it is merely a minor change.
Similarly, when humans dwell within the great Dào,
following change and accepting transformation,
it has never been not oneself,
this is not losing the great constants,
the changes of life and death,
are also but minor matters.
【Transcription】"Xíng xiǎo" is read with the lower tone in Mèng's commentary,
and also as in the original character.
【二】【注】He knows there are minor changes but does not lose the great constancy.
【Commentary】Joy follows compliance,
anger opposes it,
delight comes with life,
sorrow accompanies death.
These four are matters of the realm of existence.
Yet, if life and death bring no change to oneself,
how could joy and anger enter the heart!
【Explanation】"Xiōngcì" Lǐ Yún said:
Cì,
means the center.
【Three】【Annotations】The less, the less to worry about.
【Commentary】Heaven and earth and all things,
their substance is not dual,
one who comprehends this principle,
thus can blend and unify.
Therefore, both things and self are empty,
the hundred parts of the body will become dust and filth;
death and life are illusory,
their end and beginning are equal to day and night.
Death and life cannot cause confusion,
let alone matters of gain and loss, fortune and misfortune in the course of life!
They are even less worthy of being taken to heart.
【Explanation】"Néng huá": ancient pronunciation as "gǔ mò fǎn".
"Suǒ jiè": pronounced as "yīn jiè".
【Four】【Annotation】Knowing that one's body is more noble than a slave,
therefore one discards it as if leaving behind dust.
If one understands that the transformation of life and death resides within oneself,
then nobility is eternal.
【Five】【Comment】What is valued is the self,
and as I change along with transformations,
thus there is no loss.
【Commentary】Abandoning servants and slaves,
is akin to discarding mud and dirt;
thus, it is understood that value lies within oneself,
not in external things.
Since I will change along with them,
therefore, there is nothing lost.
【Six】【Annotation】What is called the release from bondage.
【Commentary】The things of the world are in constant flux,
never reaching an ultimate state.
To follow change and embrace transformation—
who then would let their heart be burdened?
Only by cultivating the Way and understanding human nature
can one resolve this matter.
【Transcription】"Xiè hū" is read with the pronunciation hù mǎi fǎn.
The same applies to the annotations.
【Collation】（一）The character "也" was amended according to Zhào Jiànyì's version.
Confucius said:
"The Master's virtue matches heaven and earth,
yet he still borrows profound words to cultivate his mind.
Among the ancient noblemen,
who could have dispensed with this?"
means to harmonize.
脫，
means to be free from.
Lǎozǐ's virtue harmonized with the two cosmic forces,
his brightness equaled the three luminaries,
thus he should have forgotten words and returned to principle,
with sage wisdom being natural.
Now, however, there is much talk of profound teachings to cultivate the mind,
so then, among the ancient gentlemen,
who could abandon speech and be free from cultivation and practice?
Lǎodān said:
"Not so.
Take water's gushing forth,
it does nothing yet its nature emerges spontaneously.
The perfected person's virtue,
requires no cultivation yet nothing can separate from it,
like heaven's natural height,
earth's natural thickness,
sun and moon's natural brightness -
what need is there for cultivation!"
【一】【注】Without cultivation or action, one attains it naturally.
【Commentary】Zhuó,
refers to water that is clear and deep.
The clarity and depth of water,
its nature is spontaneous,
drawing from it brings benefit and enrichment,
not through cultivation or learning.
The profound virtue of the ultimate person,
its meaning is likewise,
sitting upright in the courtly halls yet nothing can depart from him,
his grace covers all beings,
used daily without being known.
Like the sky being high and the earth thick,
the sun and moon shining brightly,
what need is there for deliberate action?
It is simply natural.
【Translated Text】"Zhuó" is pronounced as zhuó,
also read as shàng ruò fǎn.
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as yǐ lüè fǎn.
Lǐ says:
It means to take.
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
According to Shuōwén, zhuó,
is the sound of gushing water;
a well that sometimes has water,
sometimes has none,
is called jì zhuó.
This is quoted from the "Explaining Water" section of the Ěryǎ.
Guō Pú annotated the Ěryǎ,
citing the Shānhǎijīng that Tiānjǐng has water in summer and none in winter,
which is of this type.
Zhuó refers to
water naturally gushing forth,
unlike a spring that has a source,
or the confluence of streams and brooks that flow together.
Shuōwén states:
jī,
is water obstructed, deflected, and rapidly forming waves.
It means being obstructed and thus deflecting out swiftly,
hence producing sound.
The gushing of water
also resembles being agitated and making a sound.
It is effortless and naturally endowed,
meaning there is nothing channeling it.
The "Explained Text" cites Lǐ as saying,
zhuó,
means to take.
This is incorrect.
Confucius went out,
and told Yán Huí, saying:
"As for me with regard to the Way,
am I not like a vinegar-fly?
Had it not been for the master's lifting the covering from me,
I should not have known the grand completion of Heaven and Earth.
【一】【Note】The vinegar fly is,
a midge within a jar.
【Explanation】"Xī jī": Xǔ Xī fǎn,
Guǒ says:
Xī jī,
are the midges in the jar.
Sīmǎ says:
like the midges on wine.
◎Qìng Fán's note: Tàipíng Yùlǎn 395 quotes Sīmǎ saying:
Xī jī,
are the flying gnats on wine.
Slightly different from the explanation text.
"Wèng zhōng": Wū nòng fǎn.
"Miè": Wáng jié fǎn.
"Měng": Wú kǒng fǎn.
【二】【注】Compared to me, Lǎodān is complete,
just like a jar compared to heaven and earth.
【Explanation】The vinegar fly,
a midge in a vinegar jar,
often gets the jar covered by objects,
so it cannot see the two realms (heaven and earth).
Similarly, Zhòngní (Confucius) was obscured by the traces of sages,
unable to perceive the principles of things.
If not for Lǎozi uncovering the veil for him,
he would have never known the full extent of heaven and earth,
nor the wondrous way of emptiness and interconnectedness.
Zhuāngzǐ went to see Lǔ Āi Gōng.
Āi Gōng said:
"In Lǔ there are many Confucian scholars,
but few who practice your methods, sir."
【一】【疏】Method,
is a technique.
Zhuāngzǐ was a person from the Warring States period,
contemporary with King Huì of Wèi and King Wēi of Qí,
one hundred and twenty years after Duke Āi of Lǔ.
Thus, the mention of seeing Duke Āi of Lǔ
is likely a fable.
However, Lǔ was indeed the descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
and should have been a land of refined culture.
Moreover, since Confucius was born in Lǔ,
where the teachings of the five virtues flourished,
hence his three thousand disciples
embraced Confucian attire,
with long robes and wide sleeves.
Such styles must have been common in the land of Lǔ,
while the study of non-action,
its practitioners were few there.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhuāngzǐ appears" is read with the character 賢 pronounced as biàn in reverse tone,
and can also be read according to its usual pronunciation.
"Lǚ Āigōng" Sīmǎ comments:
Zhuāngzǐ was contemporary with King Wèi Huì of Wèi and King Qí Wēi of Qí,
living about one hundred and twenty years after Āigōng.
Zhuāngzǐ yuē:
"Lǔ shǎo rú."
【One】【Memorial】Clothing serves to symbolize virtue,
which does not change with the individual;
Zhuāngzǐ grasped this principle,
hence he ridiculed the Confucians for their shortcomings.
Duke Āi said:
"If the entire state of Lǔ wears Confucian robes,
how can you call that few?"
【First Memorial】Duke Āi, mediocre and dim-witted,
failed to discern the true Way,
merely judging by attire and appearance,
mistakenly claimed there were many Confucian scholars.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"I have heard that
Confucian scholars who wear round caps
understand the timings of heaven;
those who tread in square-toed shoes
know the forms of the earth;
those who leisurely wear jade pendants
decide when matters come to them.
A gentleman who possesses the Way
does not necessarily wear its garments;
one who wears its garments
does not necessarily know its Way.
【一】Since you, Duke, firmly believe this is not so,
why not proclaim throughout the state:
'Whoever lacks this Way yet wears these garments
shall be guilty of a capital crime!
【One】【Shū】 phrase,
means square.
The huǎn,
is a five-colored silk cord,
threaded through a jade jué to adorn the girdle.
Jué,
means decision.
Some versions also use the character shòu.
Heaven is round, earth is square,
and attire is used to symbolize virtue.
Therefore, those who wear a round crown to symbolize heaven
then know the fortunes and misfortunes of the three symbols;
those who tread in square shoes to emulate the earth
then know the waters and lands of the nine provinces;
those who trail a sash and wear a jué
make decisive judgments when matters arise.
Thus, those who embody the Way
do not necessarily do so through attire,
and those who adopt the attire
do not necessarily embody the Way.
That kind of person,
has existed in both ancient and modern times,
hence Zhuāngzǐ used allegories and debates to explain.
【Transcription】"冠" is pronounced as in ancient times, "guàn".
"圜冠" is pronounced as "yuán".
"履句" is pronounced as "jǔ",
with Xu's alternative reading being "qí jù".
Li says:
It means square.
"屨" is given by Xu as "jū jù".
"緩" is pronounced "huǎn".
Sima's version writes it as "绶".
"佩玦" is pronounced "jué".
◎ Qing Fan's note: In the Shuowen, the characters ● and  explain each other,
"缓" means
loose and spacious.
The Jin Shu mentions a loose belt and light fur coat,
where "loose belt"
is like a broad belt.
"缓佩玦"
means that what is worn is a "玦",
attached to the belt,
leaving it loose and spacious with room to spare.
The transcription cites Sima's version as "绶",
which is an error.
"而断" is pronounced "duàn".
Thereupon, Duke Āi lamented for five days,
and in the state of Lǔ, no one dared to wear Confucian robes anymore【1】,
except for one man standing in Confucian attire at the duke's gate.
The duke immediately summoned him and inquired about state affairs,
and through a thousand twists and myriad changes, his responses were inexhaustible.
【One】【Memorial】Those who are in mourning yet act without virtue,
their crimes warrant the severest punishment.
Since the laws are strict,
none dare to violate them.
After five days of proclamation,
not a single scholar remained.
【Explanation】"Hào yú guó": hào means
to issue commands.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"In the state of Lǔ, there is only one true Confucian scholar,
can that be considered many?"
【一】【注】One whose virtue is full within
does not adorn themselves outwardly.
【Commentary】One person,
refers to Confucius.
Confucius, being a sage,
observes opportunities and expresses wisdom,
like a mirror reflecting,
transforms endlessly,
in the whole state, one person
is not considered excessive.
Bǎilǐ Xī did not let rank and emolument enter his mind,
so he fed the ox and the ox grew fat,
causing Duke Mù of Qín to forget his lowly status,
and entrusted him with governance.
Yǒuyúshì did not let life and death enter his mind,
thus he was able to move others.
【One】【Biography】His surname was Mèng,
his courtesy name was Bǎilǐ Xī,
a worthy man of Qín.
Originally a man of Yú,
when Yú was destroyed by (Qín) [Jìn],
he subsequently entered the state of Qín.
Initially, he was not employed,
and in poverty and lowliness, he herded cattle.
Content with herding cattle,
his body became very plump and cheerful,
forgetting about wealth and honor,
thus titles and emoluments did not enter his heart.
Later, Duke Mù recognized his worthiness,
entrusted him with state affairs,
and never harbored suspicion,
hence it is said that he forgot his lowly status.
【Transcription】"Gù fàn" is read as fán wǎn fǎn.

【二】【注】One who is content within,

whose surname was Guī,

He endured hardships caused by his stepmother,
frequently facing setbacks and stumbles,

moving heaven and earth.

When Sòng Yuán Jūn was about to have a painting made,
all the court artists arrived,
received his greeting and stood aside;
licking their brushes and mixing ink,
half of them remained outside the hall.
One artist arrived late,
unhurried and without hastening his steps,
received the greeting but did not stand aside,
and then went directly to his quarters.
The lord sent someone to check on him,
and found him disrobing and sitting cross-legged and naked.
The lord said:
"Excellent,
this is a true painter.
【一】【疏】The ruler of the state of Sòng,

so painters gathered in response,
receiving the sovereign's command,
bowing and standing ready,
mixing vermilion and ink,

Zāng,

King Wén inspected the state
and found that the ranked scholars had disbanded their factions and dispersed their groups,
officials in charge did not flaunt their virtues,

The ranked scholars disbanding their factions and dispersing their groups

Yǔ,

the ruler and ministers followed the Way,

the halls for remonstrance letters were dismantled,
harmony prevailed above and below,
the virtues of the high officials were not flaunted,
near and far followed the same path,
and measures did not enter the four borders.
