evasively declining,
receiving the order in the morning but fleeing by night,
remaining unknown for the rest of his life【note 1】.
【1】【Note】When achievements are not attributed to oneself,
thus upon accomplishing the task, one inevitably must withdraw from position;
upon achieving the goal, one inevitably must relinquish fame.
By renouncing fame and stepping back from personal prominence,
one can then truly benefit the entire world (1).
【Commentary】In the span of a moment,
he was appointed as a mentor,
and they served him with the utmost respect,
inquiring about his governance strategies.
Unconcerned with glory and favor,
he thus declined vaguely;
his hidden intent was to fade into obscurity,
hence he remained silent and unresponsive.
Due to achieving fame and then withdrawing,
attributing achievements to others,
he had no desire to involve himself in worldly affairs,
thus he escaped into anonymity.
However, Lü Shang assisted the Zhōu dynasty,
was enfeoffed in Qí,
and upon examining historical records,
there is ultimately no trace of his flight.
The claim that he fled by night
is likely an allegory from Zhuāngzǐ's writings.

how could he have dreamed?

【二】【注】In a brief moment,
the sentiments of the common people,

King Wén was a sage,

You should remain silent

complying with the hopes of the common people.
In the moment of seeking to enlighten those not yet awakened,
within the brief interval of advancing or retreating,
he thus entrusted a dream to reveal their innate nature—
this is nothing to be surprised about.

Jiānwú asked Shūsūn Áo, saying:
"You have served three times as Prime Minister without feeling honored or glorious,
and have been removed from the position three times without showing any sign of worry.
At first, I doubted you,
but now I see your nostrils breathing calmly and contentedly.
How is it that you alone manage your mind this way?"
【First】【Commentary】Jiānwú,
was a recluse.
Shū'áo,
was a virtuous man of Chǔ.
Xǔxǔ,
describes an appearance of joy and ease.
Those who are enlightened remain unmoved by praise or blame,
unshaken by honor or disgrace.
Hence, Sūn'áo held office three times without feeling honored or glorious,
and was dismissed three times without showing any sign of worry.
Jiānwú initially heard his words,
and still harbored doubts,
but upon further observing his demeanor,
he appeared joyfully content,
as if by some special state of mind,
he alone had achieved such equanimity.
【Explanation】"Xǔ xǔ" is pronounced as kuàng fǔ fǎn.
Sūn Shū'áo said:
"How am I superior to others!
It is because I recognize that what comes cannot be refused,
and what goes cannot be stopped.
I consider that gain and loss do not depend on me,
and thus remain free from anxious expressions.
How am I superior to others!
Moreover, I do not know whether it lies with them,
or whether it lies with me.
If it lies with them,
then nothing depends on me;
if it lies with me,
then nothing depends on them.
I am just wavering in uncertainty,
just looking around in all directions,
how would I have leisure to care about others being noble or base!"
【一】【疏】High chariots and glorious splendor,
are but things that come by chance;
thus, when they arrive, one cannot send them away,
and when they depart, one cannot stop them.
Poverty and prosperity, gain and loss—
how could they be up to me!
Understanding this coming and going,
one thus wears no worried expression;
how could there be any art surpassing others then!
【二】【Note】Being carefree and unburdened,
mysteriously uniting the other and the self,
then for the other, it is not solely perishing,
and for the self, it is not solely surviving.
【Commentary】To lose (wáng) means
to be without.
Moreover, one does not know whether glory and splendor truly lie in that person,
or truly lie in oneself?
If they lie in that person,
then to me it is a loss;
if they lie in myself,
then to that person it is a loss.
But since that person and I are mysteriously one,
gain and loss naturally vanish.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: Both that person and I are without,
meaning it is not in me,
nor in that person.

【Three】【Comment】Hesitating and looking around in all directions,
expressing that there is nothing definite that must or must not be done.
【Commentary】Hesitation signifies complacency and self-satisfaction,
while looking around in all directions means gazing loftily at the eight points of the compass.
Just as one is about to roam freely among all things,
command the cosmos at will,
how could there be any room or leisure to concern oneself with human affairs,
or pay attention to the distinctions between nobility and baseness?
Therefore, one departs without a trace of worry.
【Transcription】《Chóu》 zhí liú fǎn.
《Chú》 zhí yú fǎn.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"The true person of antiquity,
could not be persuaded by the wise,
could not be seduced by the beautiful,
could not be robbed by thieves,
and could not be befriended by Fúxī or Huángdì.
Life and death are indeed great matters,
yet they bring no change within oneself,
let alone titles and emoluments!
Being such a person,
their spirit traverses Mount Tài without hindrance,
enters deep springs without getting wet,
dwells in lowly and humble places without weariness,
fills heaven and earth,
and having given to others,
they themselves become even more abundant."
【一】【注】Fúxī and Huángdì are merely
titles for achievements,
not the actual means of achieving them.
Therefore, comparing the titles for achievements to the actual means of achieving them,
the distance between them is vast,
so their names are insufficient to befriend the actual individuals.
【Commentary】Confucius heard Shū'Áo's words and admired his virtue,
thus citing ancient sages to validate this man.
The true persons of antiquity,
whose subtlety reached the ultimate and whose marvel touched the sublime,
even if there were those with clever words,
could not engage them in debate;
even with captivating beauty,
could not lead them to indulgence;
and as for bandits and thieves,
how could they possibly rob or plunder them?
Not even the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
would have been worthy to be their companions.
【Transcription】"Dé jié": jū yè fǎn.
The Yuánjiā version writes it as què.
"Fú xì": pronounced as xī.
【二】【疏】Though people renew themselves daily,
life and death are profoundly significant,
yet they remain unchanged within oneself;
how much more so for ranks and emoluments—
how could they ever occupy one's heart!
【Three】【Commentary】To sacrifice one's own flesh and skin for the sake of the world
results in loss for both others and oneself;
to enable everyone to attain self-fulfillment
is to give to others without harming oneself.
One's divine spirit fills heaven and earth,
thus being acceptable everywhere,
acceptable everywhere,
hence not harming oneself for external things but residing in the realm of self-fulfillment.
【Explanation】"Jiè" means
obstruction.
"Jì" means
exhaustion.
The true person enters fire without being burned,
enters water without getting wet,
passes through great mountains with spirit unimpeded,
stoops to dwell in lowliness and humility,
yet their Way remains undiminished,
their virtue aligns with the two realms (heaven and earth),
thus filling heaven and earth,
not diminishing themselves for external things,
hence they become even more abundant.
【Transcription】"Dàshān" is pronounced as tài.
"Wújiè" is pronounced as jiè.
"Bùbài" is pronounced with the fanqie pí bài.
"Yǐwéi" is pronounced with the fanqie yú wèi.
The same applies below.
【Collation】（一）The character,
the Yuán engraved diagram interlinear commentary edition, the Míng Shìdétáng edition, and the Dàozàng Jiāo Hóng edition all read as "yú",
while the Sòng edition reads as "qí".
Wáng Shūmín states:
It should be "yú".
The King of Chǔ sat with the Lord of Fán,
and after a short while,
the attendants of the King of Chǔ three times mentioned the fall of Fán.
The Lord of Fán said:
The loss of Fán,
is not enough to obliterate my existence.
Now, 'the loss of Fán is not enough to obliterate my existence,'
then the survival of Chǔ is not enough to ensure survival.
From this perspective,
it follows that Fán never truly perished and Chǔ never truly existed.
【一】【Note】There are three signs of perdition.
【Commentary】King Wén of Chǔ sat together with Marquis Fán of Fán,
discussing matters of forming alliances and convening meetings.
Fán is the name of a state,
descended from the Duke of Zhōu,
located within the boundaries of Jí Commandery,
and what is now called Fánchéng.
The three points
refer to: not revering spirits, honoring the worthy, and nurturing the people.
Since Chǔ was large and Fán small,
Chǔ harbored intentions to annex the smaller state,
thus the attendants were made to influence with words.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
There were three attendants of the King of Chǔ who spoke of Fán's downfall.
Guō's annotation states that there were three signs of its downfall,
which is incorrect.
【Interpretation】"Fán Jūn" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Sīmǎ states:
Fán,
a state's name,
located in Gòng County of Jí Commandery.
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Fán
was descended from the Duke of Zhōu.
In the seventh year of Duke Yǐn,
the Son of Heaven sent Fán Bó to conduct a diplomatic visit.
Common editions include after this the two chapters "Confucius Impoverished between Chén and Cài" and "Confucius Speaks to Yán Huí,"
which are identical to those in the "Yielding the Throne" chapter.
Various commentators have provided phonetic notations for them in the "Yielding the Throne" chapter.
Upon examination, these two chapters lack Guō Xiàng's commentary,
suggesting they may be duplicates.
Ancient editions do not include them,
and it is correct to consider their absence appropriate.
【二】【Note】It is because of abandoning the ordinary and the old.
【Commentary】Having attained the workings of nature,
he remained serene and unafraid,
truly one could say that after the Duke of Zhōu,
each generation has not lacked worthies.
【Three】【Comment】If one who abandons it does not regard loss as loss,
then possession is also insufficient to be considered possession.
Vast and without pride,
that is eternal preservation.
【Four】【Annotation】Survival and demise depend entirely on where the heart is directed,
thus, in the world, there ultimately is no fixed survival or demise.
【Commentary】Existence and demise are matters of gain and loss for the conscious mind.
Once one is oblivious to gain and loss,
then what is lost may not truly be lost, but rather, what is lost becomes preserved;
what exists does not merely exist alone, but rather, what exists becomes lost.
【Collation Note】(1) The character '措' was amended according to the Ming Shidetang edition.
【一】【Explanation】The chapter is titled based on its meaning.
Zhì traveled north to the banks of the Xuánshuǐ River,
ascended the Yǐnfèn Hill,
and there happened to meet Wúwéiwèi.
Zhì said to Wúwéiwèi:
"I wish to ask you some questions:
What thinking and what pondering lead to understanding the Dào?
What dwelling and what practice bring peace with the Dào?
What following and what path result in attaining the Dào?"
Three times he asked, and Wúwéiwèi did not answer.
It was not that he refused to answer,
but that he did not know how to answer.
【One】【Commentary】This chapter employs fabricated names,
using allegories to elucidate principles.
The north represents the realm of darkness,
while water symbolizes the obscure direction.
In concealment, it is profound and difficult to comprehend;
in manifestation, it is vividly perceptible.
To clarify that the ultimate Dao is mysteriously transcendent,
with appearances and disappearances being unpredictable,
these words are borrowed to illuminate its meaning.
【Interpretive Text】"Zhī Běi Yóu" is read with zhì (wisdom) pronunciation,
and also read according to its regular character pronunciation.
"Upon the Xuán Shuǐ" Lǐ Yí says:
Xuán [Shuǐ],
a river name.
Sīmǎ and Cuī's versions have "shàng" (upon) written as "běi" (north).
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Current editions read "Xuán Shuǐ, a river name."
Based on the example of Bái Shuǐ below,
the duplicated character is correct.
"Yǐn Fèn" is pronounced with fǎn according to Fú,
also pronounced fēn,
and also with fǎnfēn pronunciation.
Lǐ Yí says:
concealed emergence and rising mound,
the appearance of a hill.
you also.
This clarifies that by exercising utmost sincerity in seeking the Way,
through the hypothetical roles of guest and host,
it is called non-action.
【Three】【Inquiries】This hypothetical method asks,
how to operate wisdom to inquire about the Way.
If one engages in contemplation,
what should one ponder,
to then know the ultimate Way?
If one devotes effort diligently,
in what place or context,
can one then settle the mind and unite with the Way?
What should one rely on and follow,
what should one speak of or expound,
to thereby attain the Way?
【Four】【Explanations】To know,
is to differentiate.
These three questions were posed,
yet not a single answer was given.
It's not that Wú Wéi Wèi was reluctant to answer out of sentiment,
but rather that the principle inherently lacks differentiation,
thus he did not know how to respond.
Knowing he could not ask,
he returned south of the Báishuǐ River,
ascended the heights of Húquè,
and there beheld Kuāngqū.
Zhì then used these words to ask Kuāngqū.
【一】 Kuāngqū said:
"Ah!
I know it,
and would tell you,
but in the midst of speaking, I forget what I intended to say【二】."
【一】【疏】White is the color of purity and simplicity,
South is the direction of clarity and brightness,
the fox embodies doubt and hesitation,
while emptiness signifies tranquility and absence.
When questions remain unresolved,
one reflects upon the southern side of the clear waters,
abandoning the tangible to return to the intangible,
yet fox-like doubts fail to exhaust the truth.
Then, acting with reckless abandon,
withered like a dried-up tree,
to express this meaning,
it is thus called "wild and bent."
【Explanation】"Báishuǐ" is the name of a river.
"Húquè" is pronounced as kǔ xué fǎn.
Sīmǎ and Lǐ Yún stated:
Húquè,
is the name of a hill.
"Ér dǔ" is pronounced as dīng gǔ fǎn.
"Kuángqū" is pronounced as qiú wù fǎn,
and Xú also gives its pronunciation as qí shù fǎn.
Sīmǎ, Xiàng, and Cuī's versions write it as "qū".
Lǐ Yún said:
Kuángqū,
refers to being deceitful and arrogant,
appearing human-like but not truly so.
◎Qìng Fān's case: the explanatory text quotes Lǐ Yún,
Kuángqū,
deceitful and arrogant,
appearing human-like but not truly so.
In the Wénxuǎn's "Gānquán Fù," it mentions driving away kuí and xū,
and subduing the mad and arrogant.
Kuángqū is equivalent to being mad and arrogant.
Sīmǎ and Cuī's version writes it as "qū",
which is incorrect.
"Yǐ zhī yán" Sīmǎ stated:
zhī,
means "this" or "correct."
【Èr Shū】Āi,
the echo's response.
Initially intending to speak,
midway forgetting it,
this art of forgetting,
is the way of introspection.
【Transliteration】"Āi" is pronounced as in the character for sorrow.
Xú gives the pronunciation as in the character for crow coming.
Lǐ reads it as xī,
saying:
It is a responsive sound.
"Yǔ ruò" is pronounced with the tone as in the character for fish according to.
Knowing he could not get an answer,
he returned to the emperor's palace,
and saw Huángdì to ask him.
Huángdì said:
"Only by neither thinking nor scheming can one begin to understand the Dào,
only by neither abiding nor practicing can one begin to be at peace with the Dào,
only by neither following nor speaking of it can one begin to attain the Dào."
【One】【Memorial】Xuānyuán embodied the Way,
profoundly comprehending mysterious words,
thus using one "non-being" to respond to the three inquiries.
Zhì Wèn Huángdì said:
"You and I know it,
but those others do not,
so who is right?"
Huángdì said:
"That Wúwéiwèi is truly correct,
Kuángqū approximates it;
you and I never come close.
Those who know do not speak,
those who speak do not know,
therefore the sage carries out wordless teaching.
The Way cannot be obtained,
virtue cannot be reached.
Benevolence can be practiced,
righteousness can be compromised,
ritual is mutual pretense.
Thus it is said,
'When the Way is lost, then comes virtue;
when virtue is lost, then comes benevolence;
when benevolence is lost, then comes righteousness;
when righteousness is lost, then comes ritual.
Ritual is
the flower of the Way and the beginning of disorder.'
Thus it is said,
'Those who cultivate the Way daily diminish,
diminishing and further diminishing until reaching non-action,
through non-action, nothing is left undone.'
Now having become things,
to desire to return to the root—
isn't it difficult!
As for its ease,
that belongs only to the great man!"
【一】【注】Let it act on its own,
this is the teaching without words.
【Commentary】The genuine ones are unaware,
the semblable ones forget within,
those who do not approach do so because they know it.
To practice the teaching without words,
this is cited as evidence from the Lǎozǐ's scripture.
【Explanation】"Bù jìn": jìn means to be close to.
【二】【注】The Way lies in spontaneity,
not something that can be attained through words.
【Commentary】Attainment means
obtaining.
The profound Dao cannot be obtained through words;
if it is obtained through words, it is not the Dao.
【Three】【Comment】Not losing virtue, thus it is called virtue,
called virtue but not reaching it.
【Commentary】The highest virtue does not appear as virtue;
if one acts with deliberate virtue,
it is not the ultimate virtue.
【Four】【Memorials】The utmost benevolence knows no partiality,
yet those who practice biased benevolence today
can only act with purpose and nothing more.
【Five】【Dispersion】Now, to cut is not to sever completely;
it merely results in damage and impairment,
not the Great Whole.
The Great Whole
simply lets things live as they are.
【Six】【Memorial】For propriety emphasizes reciprocity,
which leads to mutual superficiality and falseness,
where flowery rhetoric confounds virtue,
and is not genuine.
【Seven】【Annotation】Rites have constant norms,
thus giving rise to the means by which correction and emulation are practiced.
【Commentary】Abandoning the fundamental and pursuing the trivial,
scattering simplicity into superficiality,
the Way is lost and purity diluted.
When it comes to practicing rituals,
thus the Laozi is quoted to substantiate its meaning.
【八】【Note】It diminishes ostentation and falsity.
【九】【注】When the ornate is removed and the simple is preserved,
then even in action, it is non-action.
【Commentary】The person who cultivates the Way,
daily diminishes embellishment and falsity,
first diminishing existence,
then diminishing non-existence,
discarding both existence and non-existence,
thereby reaching the non-action of neither existence nor non-existence,
tranquil and unmoving,
through non-action, there is nothing that is not accomplished.
This quotes the Laozi to reiterate its meaning.
【一０】【Note】When things lose their proper place,
thus there arise actions for things.
【一一】【Note】The ease of returning to the root
is found only in the great person.
The great person embodies and unites with transformation,
thus transforming things is not difficult.
【Subcommentary】Such reversals of order,
with frivolous falsity occupying the mind,
pursuing the trivial while forgetting the root,
treating the Dào as a mere object—
even if one indulges desires while seeking to return to the root and resume one's destiny,
how could it be attainable!
Now, considering that returning to the root is not difficult,
it lies solely with the great sage.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
What humans receive to live is
qì.
Once having obtained it to sustain life,
then qì daily flows within the great transformations,
while we, lump-like, receive our formed shapes,
with no means to return the qì and merge with the vast indistinct.
The flowering of the Dào becomes ritual,
just as the flowing qì becomes human beings—
neither are what they inherently are.
Penetrating life and death as companions,
wholly accepting the gathering and dispersion of qì without our involvement,
then there is non-action.
When the Dào reaches non-action,
the names of benevolence, righteousness, and ritual may remain unestablished—
this is called returning to the root.
【Transcription】"Its Change" uses the fanqie spelling "yi fan".
The annotation is the same.
【Collation Notes】(1) "Cái" is not doubtful; it is an error for "cái zhì".
(2) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "xiào" is written as "fàng".
Life is the follower of death,
death is the beginning of life,
who knows their pattern!
Human life,
is the gathering of vital energy;
gathering then there is life,
dispersing then there is death.
If death and life are followers,
what have I to worry about!
Thus all things are one,
what they consider beautiful is magical and wondrous,
what they detest is foul and rotten;
the foul and rotten again transforms into the magical and wondrous,
the magical and wondrous again transforms into the foul and rotten.
Therefore it is said, 'Throughout the world, it is but one vital energy.
'Thus the sage values oneness."
【一】【注】Those who understand the way of transformation
do not regard life and death as different.
【Two】【Comment】Taking turns to be the beginning,
then it is unknown which dies and which lives.
【Commentary】When qi gathers, life comes into being,
yet this still belongs to the category of death;
when qi scatters, death occurs,
yet this is the very origin of life.
Birth and death, beginning and end—
who can comprehend their guiding principles?
Gathering and scattering, coming and going,
their transformations are unfixed.
【Transcription】"Gēng xiāng" is pronounced as gēng.
【Three】【Notes】All are gatherings,
All are dispersions.
【Four】【Annotation】Trouble arises from difference.
【Commentary】When qi gathers, it is life;
when qi disperses, it is death.
Although gathering and dispersing differ,
they are both qi in essence.
Thus, life and death, gathering and dispersing,
can be considered companions in flux;
since there is no real distinction between them,
why should one wear a worried expression!
【Five】【Expositions】Since life and death are fundamentally non-dual,
all things in principle should return to oneness.
【Six】【Annotation】Each regards what they find beautiful as divine and marvelous,
and what they detest as foul and rotten.
However, what they find beautiful,
I may find detestable;
what I find beautiful,
they might detest.
Thus, in essence, both share the divine and marvelous,
and both share the foul and rotten.
How then can death and life, them and us, be fundamentally different!
【Commentary】Things themselves have no inherent beauty or ugliness, but human inclinations lean toward or against them.
Thus, what one's feelings find beautiful is deemed divine and extraordinary,
while what one's feelings detest is called foul and rotten.
This reversal of essence and triviality
reaches such an extreme.
Yet, the nature of things varies,
and preferences differ among individuals.
What one finds beautiful,
another may despise;
what one despises,
another may consider beautiful.
Hence, Máo Qiáng and Lì Jī,
whom people admire as beauties,
cause fish to dive deep upon seeing them,
and birds to soar high.
This shows that foulness and divinity,
divinity and foulness,
along with judgments of right and wrong, beauty and ugliness,
have no fixed standard!
Thus, it is understood that all things under heaven
share the same harmonious essence.
【Transcription】"Suǒ wù" is pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
"Fù huà" is pronounced as fú yòu fǎn.
The following is the same.
【Seven】【Dissertations】The sage who embodies the Dao,
with wisdom encompassing all transformations,
thus values this true oneness,
and silently unites with all realms.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Dunhuang manuscript lacks the character "復".
(2) The Quē Wù cites Liú Déyī's version, where "天下" is written as "天地之".
(3) The characters "死生" have been added based on Wáng Shūmín's argument.
(4) The character "今" has been deleted following Liú Wěndiǎn's revised and corrected edition.
Zhī said to Huángdì:
"I asked Wúwéiwèi,
and Wúwéiwèi did not respond to me.
It was not that he wouldn't respond to me,
but that he didn't know how to respond to me.
I asked Kuángqū,
and Kuángqū inwardly wanted to tell me but did not tell me.
It was not that he wouldn't tell me,
but that while inwardly wanting to tell, he forgot what to say.
Now I ask you,
and if you know the answer,
why is it still not within reach?"
Huángdì said:
"That is truly so,
because of their lack of knowledge;
this resembles it,
because of their forgetting it;
you and I will never come close to it,
because of our knowledge of it."
Kuáng Qū heard this,
and considered Huángdì's words to be wise.
【一】【注】It is clear that what is natural
is not something that can be known through words,
so one should remain in the obscure realm beyond speech.
Therefore, first, the standard of non-speaking is raised,
and then understanding is entrusted to Huángdì,
so that the profound nature of things
can generally be perceived and seen.
【Commentary】That Wúwéiwèi wonderfully embodies non-knowledge,
thus truly being the Way.
This Kuáng Qū reflects and dismisses words,
inwardly forgetting what to tell,
resembling the Way but not truly so.
Zhī and Huángdì, these two individuals,
employ wisdom to explain principles,
hence they do not approach the true Way.
Kuáng Qū, upon hearing from afar,
and considering this evaluation,
stated that although Huángdì had not approached the true,
he could merely understand profound discourse, and that was all.
【Transcription】"Zhī biāo" must be read as yáo fǎn.
Heaven and Earth possess great beauty yet speak no word;
the four seasons follow clear laws yet hold no debate;
all things have fixed principles yet give no explanations.
The sage,
tracing the beauty of Heaven and Earth to comprehend the principles of all things,
thus the ultimate person takes no artificial action,
the great sage initiates no arbitrary creations,
for they observe and follow the way of Heaven and Earth.
【一】【注】This is why Confucius said, "I wish to speak no more."
【Commentary】The heavens and earth provide cover and support,
their merit is most beautiful;
the four seasons follow in succession,
each has its clear pattern;
all things are born and grow,
all rely on the principle;
yet they never speak,
nor do they engage in discussion.
【Explanation】"The Great Beauty" refers to the beauty of covering and carrying all things.
【二】【注】Let it act on its own, that is all.
【Commentary】The sage,
unites with the support and covering of heaven and earth,
harmonizes with the generation and growth of all things,
therefore speaks nothing with the mouth,
and acts on nothing with the heart.
【Three】【Annotations】Only by following along.
【Four】【Annotation】Observe its form and appearance,
embody the essence of things,
which is no different from heaven and earth.
【Commentary】The great sage, the ultimate person,
neither acts nor creates,
observes heaven and earth's sheltering and supporting,
emulates the utmost Way's giving birth and completing,
acting without action, speaking without words,
this is what is meant.
Now, those divine spirits are of the utmost essence,
and with them, all transformations occur.
Things have their death and life, their square and round,
yet none can know their root.
Abundantly, the myriad things have existed firmly since ancient times.
The six directions are vast,
yet they do not escape its confines;
the autumn hair is tiny,
but depends on it to take form.
Under heaven, nothing fails to sink and float,
lifelong without repetition;
yin and yang, the four seasons, proceed in their course,
each attaining its proper order.
Dimly, it seems as if non-existent yet present,
fluidly, without form yet divine,
the myriad things are nurtured by it unknowingly.
This is called the fundamental root,
through which one can observe heaven.
【一】【注】All things transform themselves, yet the divine intelligence is not usurped.
【Commentary】That divine sage is luminous and numinous,
supremely refined and profoundly subtle,
harmoniously blending with all things,
transforming and flowing with the currents,
now gathering, now dispersing,
never showing joy or sorrow.
Now, when we speak of hundreds, thousands, and myriads,
it is merely to cite the general numbers.
【二】【注】The dead have died by themselves, and the living have lived by themselves;
the round have become round by themselves, and the square have become square by themselves;
there is no one who acts as their root,
thus none can know it.
【Commentary】Things may live or die,
appear square or round,
transforming naturally,
with none knowing their origins.
【三】【注】How could it exist only after being acted upon!
【Commentary】"Bian ran" means
the appearance of universal growth.
It speaks of all things fluttering into existence,
following the seasons to be born and nurtured,
from ancient times to the present,
necessarily having existed inherently,
how could they come into being only after deliberate intention!
【Transcription】"Biǎn" is pronounced as piān,
and also as fān.
【Four】【Annotation】Considering the six directions within the boundless, they appear crude indeed.
【Transcription】"Wèi lí" is read with the initial "lì" and the final "zhì" in reverse.
"Qí nèi" means unable to emerge from self-transformation.
【Five】【Annotation】Though the autumn hair is minute,
without non-existence, there is also no means to contain its substance (two).
【Commentary】The six directions,
are heaven, earth, and the four cardinal points.
When beasts encounter the autumn scenery,
the tips of their fur grow fine hairs,
which are extremely minute,
referred to as autumn hairs.
Vast,
means great.
Although the six directions are immense,
they still reside within the ultimate Dào,
and though the hairs are tiny,
they rely on the Dào to form their substance.
【Six】【Annotation】It renews daily.
【Commentary】All things in the world,
none do not float and sink,
rise and fall, live and die,
come and go without ceasing,
move unceasingly,
continuously renewing one after another,
never holding to the old.
【Seven】【Annotation】There is no need to act upon it.
【Commentary】The two energies mingle in harmony,
the four seasons revolve in succession,
spring and autumn, cold and heat,
follow their natural order,
how could they require deliberate action to proceed!
【八】【Note】（Zhao）〔Zhāo〕（Three） So clear it seems to exist, yet it is lost.
【Commentary】Dazed as if in darkness,
seeming absent yet present.
【Transcription】"Hūn rán" pronounced as hūn,
also pronounced as mǐn.
【Nine】【Annotation】If it is clean and has form, then it is not divine.
【Commentary】Spirit is what is spoken of as subtly pervading the myriad things.
It flows freely without attachment,
revealing no form or image,
yet its divine function knows no bounds.
【Explanatory Text】"Yóurán" is pronounced as yóu,
meaning without any reluctance to give.
【一０】【Note】To nurture them without grasping the root of their inherent nature,
thus one does not know the means by which to nurture them.
【Commentary】Nurturing all living beings,
rearing and cultivating the myriad things,
yet its mysterious workings subtly pervade,
used daily without awareness,
this true power,
is the very root of the ultimate Way.
【Explanation】"Wù Chù" is also written as "Chù",
same.
Pronounced as "chì lù fǎn".
Same for annotations.
【一一】【Note】Observing together with Heaven.
【Commentary】"Guān" means
to see.
"Tiān" refers to
nature.
One who can comprehend principles and penetrate mysteries,
understand origins and know the root,
may be said to observe the ultimate way of nature.
【Collation Notes】(1) According to the Que Wu, quoting Liú Déyī's edition, now written as "合".
(2) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, there is the character "也" following "质".
(3) The character "昭" has been amended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
Niè Quē asked Dào of Bèi Yī,
Bèi Yī said:
"If you correct your form,
unify your gaze,
heavenly harmony will arrive;
restrain your knowledge,
unify your measures,
the spirit will come to dwell.
Virtue will be your beauty,
the Dào will be your abode,
you shall appear as innocent as a newborn calf without seeking the reasons of things!"
【一】【疏】Niè Quē,
was a disciple of Wáng Ní;
Bèi Yī,
was the teacher of Wáng Ní.
Your appearance is dignified and elegant,
do not engage in wickedness,
keep your sight and hearing pure and unified,
do not grasp at many external things,
and naturally harmony and principle will return to your being.
【Explanation】"Bèi yī" is pronounced as pī,
originally also written as pī.
【二】【疏】Gather and restrain your private thoughts,
make them impartial and even,
focus your will and demeanor,
so that there is no negligence,
and your spirit will naturally come to reside.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
"Focus your demeanor" should be "correct your demeanor."
These four lines vary in wording to form the expression,
but they actually convey the same meaning.
"Restrain your perceptions,"
means to focus your vision,
so that what you see is concentrated,
and thus what you perceive is gathered and restrained.
"Correct your demeanor,"
means to correct your form,
"demeanor"
is akin to form.
Both the "Dào Yìng" chapter of Huáinánzǐ and the "Dào Yuán" chapter of Wénzǐ read as "correct your demeanor,"
which can be used as evidence for emendation.
Profound and mysterious is the supreme virtue,
Abundant beauty resides in you,
The boundless Great Dao,
Dwells within your heart.
【Four】【Negligences】Pupils wide open,
appearing ignorant and staring straight ahead.
Affairs,
refer to matters.
Since the mind is empty and at ease,
the gaze is also level and direct,
thus like a newborn calf,
having no desires for worldly matters.
【Explanation】"Tóng" is pronounced as chì hóng fǎn.
Guō gives the pronunciation as tù jiàng fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
It describes a state of having no knowledge.
Before the words were finished,
Niè Quē fell asleep.
Bèi Yī was greatly pleased,
and went away singing,
[One]
saying:
"His form is like a withered skeleton,
his heart like dead ashes.
Truly, he possesses real knowledge,
and does not hold fast to past ways.
Dim and obscure,
without a mind, he cannot be consulted.
【一】【疏】Before the discourse on the profound had concluded,
this person had already attained enlightenment,
sitting in oblivion and aligning with the Way,
akin to the state of slumber.
Thereupon, Bèi Yī leaped with joy,
praising his swift comprehension,
and walked upon the great path,
singing as he departed.
【Explanation】"Niè Quē slept deeply": his body inclined as previously described,
he feared his senses and thus slept.
He received the Way swiftly,
hence Bèi Yī was pleased.
"Greatly delighted" reads as "yuè" (pleased).
【二】【Note】It changes along with transformation.
【Commentary】The body is like the skeleton of a withered tree,
the mind resembles the soil of dead ashes,
it follows the genuine knowledge of pure simplicity without emotional attachment,
and does not hold onto self-importance in worldly affairs.
【Explanation】"若槁" is pronounced as kǔ lǎo fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】It is self-transformation.
【Commentary】Dim and obscure,
extinguishing illumination and dismissing brightness,
forgetting the mind and forgetting knowledge,
it cannot be discussed or deliberated.
It is not something ordinary people can comprehend,
hence it is said, "What kind of person is that?"
From "the form like withered bones" onward,
these are all the lyrics of Bèi Yī's song.
【Explanation】"Méiméi" is pronounced like mèi,
also read as wǔ péng fǎn.
"Huìhuì" is pronounced like huì.
Lǐ Yún says:
Méiméi,
means a dim appearance.
Shùn asked Chéng, saying:
"Can the Dào be possessed?"
【一】【疏】Chéng,
an enlightened Daoist of ancient times,
was a teacher of Shùn.
The ultimate Dao is empty and all-pervading,
generating and nurturing all living beings and plants.
Yet, do we know whether within our own bodies,
this Dao exists or not?
Since we have encountered a master,
it is fitting to seek guidance.
【Explanation Text】"Cheng" is read as the character itself.
Lǐ Yí says:
He was Shùn's teacher.
Another explanation states:
In ancient times, there were four assistants,
with the front one resolving doubts and the rear one supporting,
which was likely an official title.
He said:
"Your body is not your possession,
so how can you attain the Way?"
【一】【Note】The body is not something you can possess;
it exists of its own accord, a mere lump.
If the body is not yours to own,
how much less so is the Way!
【Commentary】The Dao is something that
the four propositions cannot attain,
and the hundred negations cannot elucidate.
Your own body is not even something you can truly possess,
so how could you possibly possess the Dao?
【Translated Text】"Yǒu fū" is pronounced as fú.
"Kuài rán" is pronounced as kǔ duì fǎn.
Shùn said:
"My body is not my own,
who possesses it then?"
【一】【疏】Not yet comprehending that life arises from spontaneity,
and forms are shaped by creation,
thus it is said, "This body is not mine to possess—
then whose could it be?"
He said:
"This physical form is but a temporary lodging bestowed by Heaven and Earth;
your life is not your own possession,
it is the harmonious essence entrusted by Heaven and Earth;
your innate nature is not your own possession,
it is the harmonious compliance bestowed by Heaven and Earth;
your descendants are not your own possession,
they are the molted skin left by Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, when walking one knows not where to go,
when dwelling one knows not what to grasp,
when eating one knows not the true flavor.
All is but the vigorous energy of Heaven and Earth,
so how could one possibly possess it!"
【One】【Comment】If the body were truly yours,
then beauty, ugliness, life, and death
should be under your control.
Yet when the vital energy gathers and life begins,
you cannot prevent it;
when the vital energy disperses and death comes,
you cannot stop it.
This shows that it forms and exists on its own,
and is not truly yours.
【Commentary】Wěi,
means to gather and accumulate.
Now, the heavens and earth, yīn and yáng,
gather and accumulate the qì of firmness, softness, harmony, and compliance,
forming your body, nature, and life.
Thus, when gathered, it is life;
when scattered, it is death.
Death and life, gathering and scattering,
are not up to you;
from this, know that your body,
how can it be said to be yours?
【Explanatory Text】"Entrusted Form" Sīmǎ comments:
Entrusted,
means to accumulate.
◎Yú Yuè states:
Sīmǎ says,
entrusted,
means to accumulate.
This does not align with the meaning.
In the Strategies of the Warring States, Qí Cè, it says "wish to entrust it to you,"
Gāo's annotation states:
Entrusted,
means to hand over.
In the second year of Chéng in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, "the king sent to entrust to the three officials,"
Dù's annotation states:
Entrusted,
means to assign.
"The form entrusted by heaven and earth"
refers to the form assigned and handed over by heaven and earth.
The following three instances of "entrusted" have the same meaning.
【二】【Note】The qi naturally gathers and then sheds like a cicada.
【Commentary】When yin and yang converge and unite,
offspring are thus produced,
formed through spontaneous transformation,
much like a cicada shedding its skin.
【Text】"Weituì": pronounced as tǔ wò fǎn,
also read as yuè,
also as chì wài fǎn,
also as shǐ ruì fǎn,
also as shǐ liè fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】all originate from within oneself,
thus one does not know.
【Commentary】Actions, stillness, flavors of food,
all follow spontaneity;
if one traces back to their origins,
none can know from whence they come.
So who is it that acts in action,
who is it that rests in stillness,
who is it that eats in eating,
who is it that tastes in flavor?
All are unaware of their source, yet everything arises of itself.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
Daily we see there is action but ultimately do not know where it goes;
daily we see there is dwelling but ultimately cannot maintain it by ourselves;
daily we see there is eating but ultimately do not know what makes it flavorful.
Thus, its going
is not something I can control;
its persistence for decades
is not something I can retain;
its eating and knowing flavor
is not something I can discern;
it is the movement of the qì of heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng that causes it so,
all of which cannot be possessed.
【Four】【Annotation】Qiángyáng,
is akin to movement.
Understanding this principle,
one may then transcend the body and forget life.
【Commentary】Qiángyáng means
movement.
Hú means
why.
As for forms, natures, and descendants,
they are all formed by the gathering and consolidation of the moving qi of heaven and earth's yīn and yáng,
so how could one possess this body on one's own!
【Interpretation】"The vigorous energy of heaven and earth." Guǒ Xiàng states:
Vigorous energy,
is akin to movement.
The commentary says that even heaven and earth are in constant motion,
how much more so the life force that gathers as breath?
How could one possibly grasp and detain it!
【Collation】(1) The erroneous text cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition which has "grandchildren" instead of "Master Sūn".
Confucius inquired of Lǎo Dān, saying:
"Today, at leisure in the evening,
I venture to ask about the ultimate Way【one】."
【一】【疏】Yàn,
means peace.
Confucius learned from Lǎozi,
hence he took advantage of a peaceful and leisurely moment to inquire about the profound Way.
【Transcription】"Yàn" is read as yù jiàn fǎn,
Xú reads it as yù xiǎn fǎn,
also yù jiàn fǎn.
"Xián" is pronounced as xián.
Lǎo Dān said:
"You must fast and purify yourself,
clear and open your heart,
wash and cleanse your spirit,
and break down your knowledge!
As for the Dào,
it is profound and difficult to speak of!
I shall give you an outline of its broad contours.
【一】【疏】疏洒，
means to cleanse and wash.
Purification through bathing,
signifies refinement and purity.
而，
refers to you.
Striking down,
means to break apart.
崖，
denotes division or boundary.
If you wish to inquire about the Way,
you must first purify your heart and traces,
be cautious and sincere,
cleanse your body and mind,
purify your spirit and consciousness,
shatter sagely wisdom,
and wash away emptiness and tranquility.
However, the profound Way is deep and obscure,
difficult to articulate and debate,
so I will outline its boundaries for you,
speaking in broad terms.
【Translated Text】"Fast and Abstain" pronounced as cè jiē fǎn.
"Yào" sounds like yào.
Some say:
It means to soak.
Pǒu: pronounced as pǒu,
Xú Fānggǒu's pronunciation.
Zhì: read as zhì.
Yǎo rán: pronounced as yǎo.
Jiāng wèi: read as wèi.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition has "zhāi".
The clearly manifest is born from the dark and obscure,
the ordered arises from the formless,
spirit and essence are born of the Dào,
and physical forms originate from this essence.
All things generate one another through their forms,
hence beings with nine orifices are born from wombs,
while those with eight orifices hatch from eggs.
Their coming leaves no trace,
their going knows no bounds,
with neither gate nor chamber,
they roam freely through the four directions.
Those who attain this state
have robust limbs,
thoughts that flow unimpeded,
keen ears and sharp eyes,
their minds never weary,
and their response to things knows no fixed method.
Heaven cannot but be high,
Earth cannot but be vast,
sun and moon cannot but move,
and all things cannot but flourish—
such is the Dào, is it not!
【一】【注】All these are meant to clarify that it exists independently without relying on anything.
【Explanation】"Formless" refers to the Great Beginning.
【二】【注】All proceed from the essence to the gross.
【Commentary】Lún means
order or principle.
Those things that are clear and manifest
are born from the depths of obscurity;
the affairs of human relations and purposeful actions
arise from within the formless;
the mind with its refined wisdom and spiritual awareness
is born from the Way of profound mystery;
all things with form, substance, and vital energy
fundamentally originate from the subtle and minute.
【Explanation】"Form originates from essence" refers to the eternal Dao.
【Three】【Comment】This speaks of how all things, though they give birth through form,
are all spontaneous in nature.
Thus, fetuses and eggs cannot exchange their kinds to be born,
illustrating that divine energy cannot be artificially contrived.
【Commentary】The formless Dao
can give birth to things with form;
things with form
then generate one another through their physical attributes and energetic categories.
Thus, humans and beasts, with nine orifices, are viviparous;
birds and fish, with eight orifices, are oviparous.
This is endowed by nature,
and cannot be interchanged.
【Explanation】"Nine orifices" pronounced with a bitter and hanging tone.
"Born from eggs" pronounced with a force and tube tone.
"Easy to propagate" pronounced with a chapter and brave tone.
【四】【注】One who follows the nature of spontaneity,
traveling on paths without traces,
releases the physical form between heaven and earth,
and entrusts the spirit beyond the eight directions;
thus, without doors or rooms,
reaching out in all directions majestically,
roaming freely throughout the six directions,
and walking in harmony with transformation.
【Commentary】Huáng means
great.
Taking non-coming as coming,
though it comes, it leaves no trace;
taking non-going as going,
though it goes, it has no boundaries.
Thus, exiting and entering have no gateway,
coming and going have no edges or sides.
Therefore, it can broadly reach the four directions,
greatly connecting with all things.
【Five】【Annotation】When a person is born and encounters this Way,
their innate nature is preserved and their spirit becomes settled.
【Commentary】Yāo means
to encounter.
Xún means
to penetrate.
When one encounters the Way and unites with the true principle,
then all parts of the body are peaceful and healthy,
the four limbs are strong and robust,
thoughts and considerations flow unimpeded,
vision and hearing become sharp and clear,
the mind without a mind
functions without weariness,
the response without deliberate response
acts without fixed direction or location.
【Explanation】"Yāo yú": ancient reading with the sound of Yáo.
◎Yú Yuè says:
The Shuōwén dictionary does not have the character "yāo",
in the "chì" radical section:
"jiǎo",
means "to follow".
This is the modern character "yāo".
It also says:
"xún",
means "to act in accordance with".
Therefore, "yāo" also means "to accord with",
"yāo yú cǐ" means
the same as "to accord with this".
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation says "human life encounters this path",
thus interpreting "yāo" as "encounter",
the meaning is forced and indirect,
and lacks evidence in ancient exegesis,
this is likely incorrect.
"Sī lǜ": read with the sound of "sì".
"Xún dá": pronounced as "xún".
【Six】【Annotation】This means all these are inevitable and spontaneous by nature,
not that the Dào causes them to be so.
【Commentary】The two realms rely on emptiness and interconnection to be lofty and vast,
the three lights depend on the mysterious Way to operate and move,
all things attain it to flourish and prosper,
this is the efficacy of the great Way.
Thus, the Lǎojīng states,
Heaven attains the One and thereby is clear,
Earth attains the One and thereby is tranquil,
the myriad things attain the One and thereby live,
this is what it means.
【Translated Text】"Heaven cannot but be high" means that without attaining the Way,
it would be unable to be high.
"Dào yǔ" is pronounced as yú.
The same applies to the following instances.
【Collation】（一）The Shìdétáng edition reads as "zhī".
Moreover, breadth of learning does not necessarily imply understanding,
nor does eloquence necessarily imply wisdom—
the sage has already determined this.
As for that which cannot be increased by addition
nor diminished by reduction—
this is what the sage preserves within.
Profound, it resembles the sea;
majestic, it ends only to begin again,
conveying and measuring all things without exhaustion.
If this is the way of the noble person,
is it something external to them?
All things resort to it for sustenance without depletion—
this is indeed the Way!
【一】【注】Abandon wisdom and entrust everything to nature.
【Commentary】Extensive reading of the classics
does not necessarily lead to true understanding;
eloquent and embellished speech
does not necessarily reflect wisdom.
Therefore, the Lǎozǐ states:
"The good do not debate,
the debaters are not good;
the wise are not erudite,
the erudite are not wise."
This is why the sage discards them.
【Explanation】"Being learned does not necessarily mean being wise" refers to reading unusual books to gain broad knowledge.
"To judge" is pronounced with the initial sound "duǎn" and the final sound "guǎn" in reverse.
The annotation is the same.
【二】【注】Let each preserve their proper role,
hence there is no need to employ wisdom and cunning.
【Commentary】Broad knowledge and eloquent wisdom
do not enhance one's clarity;
remaining silent and facing a wall
does not increase one's deficiency;
this is what is called neither increasing nor decreasing,
neither diminishing nor benefiting,
the sage's wondrous embodiment,
thus preserved and cherished.
【Three】【Annotations】Boundless in appearance and demeanor.
【Commentary】The Weǐlǘ drains it yet it does not diminish,
all rivers pour into it yet it does not increase,
its depths are clear, profound, and vast,
thus it serves as a metaphor for the Mysterious Dào.
【Four】【Annotation】One who accompanies transformation,
accumulates endless eons,
can be called majestic.
【Commentary】"Weiwei" (巍巍),
describes a majestic and lofty appearance.
The Dao,
far surpasses the Great One (Tàiyī),
and near transcends the Two Forms (Liǎngyí),
encompassing the boundless,
hence it is praised as "weiwei."
Ending then beginning again,
this clarifies that it has neither end nor beginning,
transforming and renewing daily,
making it impossible to follow or meet.
【Transcription】"Wei Wei": read as yú wēi.
"Ze Fu": read as fú yòu.
【Five】【Annotation】Using things without being enslaved by them,
thus there is no exhaustion.
【Explanation】"Yùnliàng" is pronounced with the tone liàng.
"Wànwù ér bú kuì" uses the pronunciation qiú wèi fǎn.
It means allowing things to operate spontaneously,
so that each and every thing is sufficiently measured.
【Six】【Annotation】Each draws from oneself and finds sufficiency.
【Commentary】The Way of the sage and noble person
transports and carries all things,
contains and measures all living beings,
covertly bestows endlessly without exhaustion.
This is not far away,
but close within the heart;
since it does not rely on external endowment,
how could it be external!
【Seven】【Annotation】It still utilizes [ten thousand] (three) things,
therefore I am not lacking.
This clarifies that the Way's provision for things,
lies in not providing,
and by not providing, things attain themselves naturally,
hence it is said, "Is this the Way?"
It speaks of the ultimate Way's lack of merit,
and it is this lack of merit that is truly worthy of being called the Way.
【Commentary】Beings with consciousness and things without sentience,
all receive this mysterious Dao;
and though its workings are subtly bestowed,
they never become depleted.
Yet the Dao and things are neither identical nor different,
and apart from the Dao there are no things,
hence it is said, "Is this not the Dao?"
【Transcription】"Zhī Shàn" is read with the pronunciation shè yàn.
The same applies below.
【Collation】(1) "Wei Wei" was changed according to the Shidetang edition,
the annotations and commentaries also read as Wei.
(2) In the "Que Wu" text, the versions by Wén Rúhǎi and Liú Déyī both have "yí" instead of the character "kuì".
(3) The character "wàn" was added based on Liú Wéndiǎn's argument.
In China there is a person,
neither yin nor yang,
dwelling between heaven and earth,
merely existing as a human for now,
yet destined to return to the ancestral source.
Viewing from the fundamental perspective,
life
is but a murky and turbid entity.
Though there are differences in longevity and premature death,
how far apart are they truly?
It is merely a matter of a fleeting moment.
How can it suffice to determine the rights and wrongs of a Yáo or a Jié!
Fruits and melons follow their inherent patterns,
and human relations, though complex,
are arranged accordingly in order.
The sage encounters them without resistance,
passes through them without clinging.
To harmonize and respond to them
is virtue;
to align and correspond with them
is the Way;
this is what the emperors promoted,
what the kings established.
【一】【Note】It means without any bias.
【二】【注】Proudly letting oneself roam free,
finding contentment wherever one encounters,
completely devoid of fame and achievement.
【Commentary】Zhōngguó,
refers to the Nine Provinces.
It speaks of the Way that humans are endowed with,
which is neither yīn nor yáng,
neither soft nor hard,
neither short nor long.
Therefore, it transcends the four propositions,
and detaches from all negations.
Dwelling between heaven and earth,
one is simply placed as a human,
without any bias or attachment.
Some versions also use the character "zhí,"
meaning residing within the cosmos,
encountering the state of being human,
completely free from any ties.
【Explanation】"Straight and" is read as the character's standard pronunciation.
Formerly, it was read as zǐ yú in reverse.
【Three】【Annotations】Do not chase after the trivial.
【Commentary】Since there is no biased attachment,
one can be appointed to any role,
thus enabling a return to the origin and restoration of the fundamental,
ultimately reverting to the ancestral core.
【Four】【Annotation】It is to directly gather the qi.
【Commentary】The root,
is the Way.
Yīnyì,
refers to the gathering of qi.
When viewed from the perspective of the Way and its principles,
it is thus understood that life is a phenomenon of gathered qi,
so why should it be worth clinging to!
【Explanation】"喑" is pronounced like 蔭,
Guǒ pronounces it as 闇,
Lǐ pronounces it as 飲,
another pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè spelling 於感.
Yì》 yú jiè fǎn,
Guō yú gǎn fǎn,
Lǐ yīn yì,
yī yīn tā gǎn fǎn.
Lǐ Guō jiē yún:
Àn yì,
jù qì mào.
【Five】【Annotation】Life and death are not yet sufficiently distinct,
how much less the difference between longevity and premature death!
【Commentary】In the span of a lifetime,
within a hundred years,
even if one's longevity is long or short,
how much difference can there truly be?
It is but a fleeting moment,
a brief instant in discourse,
hardly enough to praise Yáo and condemn Jié, making distinctions among them!
【Text Explanation】"Geometry" is read with the character 居 (jū) in the rising tone and 豈 (qǐ) in the falling tone.
【Six】【Annotation】All things have their inherent order,
one should simply follow it.
【Explanation】"Fruit and Melon" Xú Lìguǒ fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】Human relationships undergo changes in wisdom and intelligence,
making them difficult.
However, their wisdom and intelligence naturally align in order,
so we should simply follow and trust in that.
【Commentary】What grows on trees is called fruit,
what grows on the ground is called melon.
Such things as peaches and plums,
or types like gourds and squashes,
whether born from trees or vines,
all have their inherent order.
Humans living in the world,
face dangers and hardships,
with distinctions of nobility and baseness, honor and humility,
taking their turns in sequence like teeth,
one should simply accept them,
and naturally align with the Way,
just like those fruits and melons,
where an inherent order exists.
【八】【Note】Comply with whatever one encounters.
【Nine】【Annotation】It is appropriate to pass when it is time to pass.
【Commentary】When encountering high rank and carriage,
one follows without opposition;
once having passed through it,
one also does not linger or dwell.
【一０】【Note】Tiáoyǎ means harmony and union.
【Commentary】Harmonizing all things,
complying and responding to them,
is the virtue of the superior;
encountering the situation at hand,
seizing the moment to respond to matters,
is the way of the sage.
【一一】【Note】Just like this, that's all.
【Commentary】When emperors and kings arise,
they respond to the needs of all living beings from above,
by nothing more than harmonizing with the times appropriately,
and adapting to circumstances to connect with all things.
Humans live between heaven and earth,
like a white steed galloping past a crack,
gone in an instant.
Surging and thriving,
all things emerge;
flowing and fading,
all things return.
Having transformed into life,
they transform again into death.
Living beings grieve over it,
humankind mourns it.
They shed their heavenly sheath,
cast off their heavenly casing,
swirling and curling away.
When the ethereal soul departs,
the body follows it—
this is the great return!
From formless to formed,
from formed back to formless—
this is what all people commonly understand,
yet not what those approaching the ultimate strive for.
This is what the multitude commonly discusses.
Those who reach the ultimate do not discuss it;
those who discuss it do not reach it.
Clear sight misses the mark;
argument falls short of silence.
The Dào cannot be heard;
hearing it is inferior to blocking it out.
This is called the great attainment.
【一】【注】Then it is not worth regretting.
【Commentary】The white steed,
a swift horse,
also symbolizes the sun.
A crack,
is an opening.
Humans dwell in the world,
in the briefest of moments,
their existence is as pressing and hurried
as a galloping steed passing through a narrow gap,
vanishing in an instant,
how can it ever be considered sufficient to speak of!
【Explanation】"White Steed" some say:
it means the sun.
"Passing by the Gap" is read as 'qu ni fan'.
It is also written as 'xi'.
'Xi',
means a hole.
【二】【注】"Going out and coming in" refers to
transformation and change,
meaning that nothing under heaven remains unchanged.
【Commentary】The note "bó" describes the appearance of emerging into life,
while "yóuliáo" depicts the state of entering death.
It means that all things in the world,
interacting without constancy,
none fail to follow transformation to be born,
and conform to change to die.
【Explanatory Text】"Bórán": bù hū fǎn.
"Yóurán": yīn yóu.
"Liáorán": yīn liú,
Lǐ yīn lì.
【Three】【Annotations】All are transformations.
【Four】【Annotation】Lifeless things do not mourn.
【Five】【Annotation】The dead do not grieve.
【Commentary】Life and death, coming and going,
are but transformations,
entrusted to the Creator—
why should they be clung to!
Thus, at one's death,
living things and humans alike
share in the duties of sorrow and grief,
but what is not of their kind or not alive
feels no sorrow, no grief.
◎Jià Shìfù remarked:
Living things mourn it,
and they know how to mourn
only because they are alive,
yet they do not know that life alike ends in extinction.
Humans grieve over it,
and they know how to grieve
only because humans possess consciousness,
yet they do not know that human consciousness likewise ends in extinction.
【Six】【Annotation】Solitary detachment.
【Commentary】Tāo refers to
concealing in a pouch.
 means
tying the pouch.
It speaks of people clinging to their own right and disputing others' wrong,
rejoicing in life and detesting death,
thus being bound by the constraints of life and death.
Now that they have unified what is right and wrong,
forgotten life and death,
they therefore shed and loosen the natural tāo.
【Transcription】"Tiān tāo" chì dāo fǎn.
Zìlín yún:
gōng yī yě.
"Duò qí" xǔ guī fǎn.
"Tiān ?" chén bǐ fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】Transformed and misty.
【Explanatory Text】"宛乎" is pronounced as yú ruǎn fǎn.
"絪" is pronounced as yīn.
It is also written as 煙,
pronounced as yīn.
"縕" is pronounced as yú yún fǎn.
It is also written as 熅,
with the same pronunciation.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current version writes it as 煙熅.
【八】【Note】Do not exert the mind in between.
【Commentary】"Fenlun wanzhuan"
describes the appearance of dispersal and dispersion.
The hun and po ascend to heaven,
the flesh and bones return to the earth,
the spirit and qi scatter and depart,
drifting and turning freely,
transitioning from existence to non-existence,
which is the great return.
【Nine】【Notes】 do not take form,
form then becomes complete;
if one gives them form,
(form) (one) then ruins their form.
【Commentary】Before a person is born,
they originally do not have a form,
hence they come from formlessness;
when qi gathers, they acquire form, and when qi disperses, they return to formlessness.
【Transcription】"Zé bài" bǔ mài fǎn.
【一０】【Note】Although one may know it,
one cannot allow it to take shape on its own but instead shapes it,
which is why failure often occurs.
【一一】【Note】Without diligence, one will not reach the goal.
【Commentary】That from formlessness forms arise,
and from having form they return to formless substance,
is what all people commonly know.
These are merely mundane matters,
not the profound concerns of those who have reached the ultimate principle.
【一二】【Note】Although it is discussed,
yet it cannot but be pursued,
which is why it is not achieved.
【Commentary】Whether form and substance exist or not,
the coming and going of life and death,
are topics that ordinary people,
commonly discuss together.
【一三】【Note】Unaware and oblivious, thus reaching the ultimate.
【Explanation】"Mèn rán" is pronounced with the initial "wáng" and the final "běn" in reverse.
【一四】【疏】Those who are supremely sagely,
forget words and attain the principle,
thus have nothing to discuss or explain;
if they were to discuss or explain it,
then it would not reach the Way.
【一五】【Note】It is only when darkness reaches its peak that one encounters it.
【Commentary】"Zhí" means
to encounter or meet.
If one can shut off knowledge and block out hearing,
then one can silently unite with the profound principle;
if one clearly reveals what is seen and heard,
one will not meet with the truth.
【一六】【Comment】Silently closing it off,
then there is nowhere to rush and chase,
hence achieving greatly.
【Commentary】Eloquence adorned with rhetoric,
drifts far from the truth;
forgetting words and embracing tranquil silence,
brings one closer to the profound Way.
Thus, the Way cannot be sought through extensive learning,
for such pursuit is no better than ignorance and obstruction.
If one can profoundly understand this principle,
it may be said they have deeply grasped the great truth.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
The Way has no form;
upon perceiving it and considering it the Way,
it seems as if by chance it is encountered,
yet in reality, there is no such encounter.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
"encounter"
means to place or arrange.
If one cannot lift and apply it,
then what is seen here is one Way,
what is seen there is another Way,
leading to endless debates that cannot be resolved.
Hence, it is said that debate is not as good as silence.
【Collation】(1) The character for "form" has been deleted according to the Shidetang edition.
Dōngguō Zǐ asked Zhuāngzǐ, saying:
"The so-called Dào,
where does it exist?"
【一】【疏】He resided in the eastern outer wall,
hence was called Master Dōngguō,
being Wú Zé's teacher, Dōngguō Shùnzǐ.
He asked Zhuāngzǐ:
"The so-called empty and penetrating ultimate Way,
where does it exist?"
【Explanatory Text】"Dōng Guō Zǐ" Lǐ Yún said:
He lived in the eastern outer wall.
"Wū Hū" is pronounced as wū.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"It is present everywhere."
【一】【疏】The Way permeates all without exception,
present everywhere it exists.
Dōngguō Zǐ said:
"Only after a set time is it permissible."
【One】【Annotation】Intending to have Zhuāngzǐ indicate the specific location.
【Commentary】Guō Xiàng's annotation states:
He wished to have Zhuāngzǐ specify the location.
【Explanation】"Yù lìng" is pronounced as lì chéng fǎn.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"In ants and crickets."
Said:
"How lowly is this?"
He said:
"In the tares and weeds."
Said:
"Why does it descend even lower?"
He said:
"In the tiles and bricks."
He said:
"Why is it even more severe?"
He said:
"In the piss and shit."
Dōngguōzǐ did not respond.
【一】Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Your question,
after all, does not touch the essence【二】.
When Zhèng Huò asked the market inspector about treading on pigs,
he found that the lower he went, the more evident it became【三】.
Only if you refrain from insisting on specifics,
nothing can escape from things【四】.
The ultimate Dào is like this,
and so are great words【五】.
The three terms 'Zhōu,' 'Biàn,' and 'Xián,'
though named differently, share the same reality,
their meaning is one and the same【六】.
【一】【疏】The Great Dao is omnipresent,
yet it exists nowhere,
thus it is present everywhere,
without distinction of filth or lowliness.
Dōngguō had not grasped this essence,
believing the Dao to be lofty and pure,
considering even tiles and bricks too humble for it,
and upon hearing of excrement and urine,
he frowned and did not respond.
【Transcription】"蝼" is pronounced as lóu.
"蚁" is pronounced as yǐ.
"在" is pronounced as dà xī.
It is also written as "稊".
"薜" is pronounced as bì.
It is also written as "稗",
pronounced as pú mài.
Lǐ Yún says:
"" and "薜"
are the names of two types of grass.
◎ Lú Wénzhāo states:
The current version writes them as "稊" and "稗".
"瓦甓" is also written as "",
pronounced as bù lì.
"屎" is pronounced as shī zhǐ,
previously read as shī zhǐ.
Some versions use "矢" instead.
"溺" is pronounced as nǎi diào.
【二】【Note】When pointing out its essential quality,
it is said to be omnipresent,
yet one still finds this strange,
this is failing to grasp the essence.
【Commentary】Substance,
is reality.
It means the Way is omnipresent,
how could it be limited to mere tares and weeds!
Thus, the answer to the disciple's question
still falls short of the truth.
【Three】【Comment】Xī,
means a large pig.
The market inspector steps on the pig to know its fatness or leanness,
the more he steps on the parts that are hard to fatten,
the more he grasps the key to the pig's fatness.
Now, when inquiring about the whereabouts of the Way,
and repeatedly assessing it through the lowly and humble,
then it is certain that the Way does not evade things.
【Commentary】Zhèng,
an official title,
is what is now called the market administrator.
Huò,
is a name.
Jiān,
the chief of the market,
is what is now the butcher.
Xī,
means pig.
Generally, when inquiring about the method of buying pigs from a butcher,
it is said:
by stepping on the pig's thigh and leg areas,
the parts that are difficult to fatten,
one can better understand the condition of the pig's fatness or leanness.
Why is that?
If there is meat in the lower, hard-to-fatten areas,
it is sufficient to know that the easily fattened areas are rich in fat.
This is similar to how if there is a path in the lowly places of waste and filth,
then the clear and empty lands are all traversed as well.
【Text Explanation】"Zhèng Huò's inquiry to the market inspector" - ancient pronunciation: gǔ xián fǎn.
"Treading on pigs in the market" - pronunciation: xū qǐ fǎn.
"The lower it goes, the clearer it becomes" - Lǐ's commentary says:
Zhèng,
is a local constable;
Huò,
is his name.
Market inspector,
is the market chief.
Pig,
is a large swine.
Tread,
means to step on.
When the market chief treads on a swine,
he steps on its thighs and legs,
where pigs are least likely to be fat,
thus knowing if the swine is fat.
Inquiring about the Way also means understanding it by examining the lowly and humble.
"Lean" - pronunciation: sè jiù fǎn.
"Of that place" - pronunciation: chāng lǜ fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】If one insists that there is nothing that can escape from things,
then the Dao would not be all-encompassing,
and if the Dao is not all-encompassing,
then it is not sufficient to be called the Dao.
【Commentary】"Wú" refers to
the non-action of the Dào.
The great Dào is vast and boundless,
encompassing all things without exception.
You must not say that the ultimate Dào abandons or flees from things.
If it truly fled from things,
how could it be all-pervading!
【Five】【Annotation】The enlightened path does not evade things.
【Explanation】The ultimate Way is principle;
grand speech is teaching.
Since principle does not escape from things,
teaching is also universal and impartial.
【Six】【Comprehensive】Thorough and universal,
all possess the Way.
This reiterates that the ultimate Way does not evade things,
even though there are differences in the three names,
in reality, their principles and purposes converge into one.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhōubiàn" is pronounced as "biàn".
【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites the editions of Zhāng Jūnfáng and Chéng Xuányīng, which must have the character "謂" below "必".
We once wandered together in the palace of nonexistence,
discoursing in unity,
with no end or limit!
We once practiced non-action together!
How placid and tranquil!
How indifferent and pure!
How harmonious and leisurely!
My will was vast and empty,
going nowhere without knowing its destination.
Leaving and returning without knowing where it rests;
I have come and gone without knowing its final end.
Roaming in the vast emptiness,
great wisdom enters yet knows not its boundaries.
That which makes things things has no boundary with things;
when things have boundaries,
it is what we call the boundaries between things.
The boundaryless boundary
is the boundary of the boundaryless.
Speaking of fullness and emptiness, growth and decline—
that which causes fullness and emptiness is not itself fullness or emptiness,
that which causes growth and decline is not itself growth or decline,
that which forms root and tip is not itself root or tip,
that which creates accumulation and dispersion is not itself accumulation or dispersion."
【One】【Annotation】If one wanders in what exists,
then one cannot be all-encompassing and complete.
Therefore, by unifying and synthesizing them in discussion,
only then can one understand that the Dào is omnipresent.
Understanding that the Dào is omnipresent,
only then can one be open-minded and free from attachments, wandering in that boundless realm.
【Subcommentary】The Palace of Non-Existence,
refers to the abode of the profound Dao;
where not a single thing can be possessed,
hence it is called "Non-Existence."
As for the three—universality, pervasiveness, and all-inclusiveness—
they roam together in the realm of the ultimate Dao,
their essential meaning being unified,
discussed through convergence,
silently aligning with the profound principle,
thus having no beginning, end, or ultimate limit.
【二】【注】This is all because of non-action.
【Comment】This generally praises the magnificent virtue and abundant capabilities of the three functions of universal penetration and inclusiveness.
Having roamed in the homeland of the ultimate Way,
and dwelling in the realm of non-action,
thus one can be serene and tranquil,
solitary and pure in emptiness,
gentle and harmoniously attuned,
relaxed and at ease with leisure.
【Explanation】"Dan er" is read as tú zàn fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's case states: Mò ér qīng,
mò also means clear,
as the ancients naturally used repetitive expressions.
The "Ěr Yǎ" says:
mò,
chá,
means clear.
Fán's annotation:
mò rán,
describes a clear appearance.
Mò can also be written interchangeably as mò,
as in the Zuǒ Zhuàn from the 28th year of Zhāo: "virtue upright, response harmonious is called mò,"
Dù's annotation:
mò rán means tranquil and clear.
"Ér jiān" is pronounced as xián.
【Three】【Annotation】Vast and empty.
【Commentary】The profound sage who attains the Way,
aligns with the principle and merges with the truth,
with a nature and will empty and serene,
existing in stillness and solitude alone.
【Interpretation】"Liáo" is pronounced as liáo.
【四】【注】If the will is truly tranquil,
then there is nowhere to go;
having nowhere to go,
thus one goes without knowing where one arrives;
if there is somewhere to go,
then before the principle has moved, the will has already been startled.
【Transcription】"已驚" is read as written.
Some versions also write it as "騖",
pronounced as "wù".
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that according to Guō Xiàng's annotation,
when there is an intention to go,
the principle has not yet moved, but the will has already raced ahead,
the character "驚" is rather difficult to interpret,
the meaning should follow the transcription version using "騖",
which is correct.
"騖" has the same meaning as "馳",
the annotation says the will has already raced ahead before any movement occurs,
the will cannot be described as "驚" (startled).
The characters "驚" and "騖" have similar shapes,
hence the error.
(In Huáinánzǐ, "驰骋若惊" [galloping as if startled],
"惊" was again mistakenly written as "騖".
【Five】【Annotation】This is to comply with it.
【Commentary】When the will is in profound tranquility,
it therefore does not engage in coming and going.
Even if it goes without going,
comes without coming,
ultimately there is no destination reached,
nor any place of rest.
【Six】【Comment】It is merely that the comings and goings do not arise from conscious knowledge,
yet this does not mean they do not come and go.
These comings and goings
are the constant principle of spontaneity—
how could they ever have an end!
【Commentary】Even if one were to come and go with the Creator,
traverse life and death,
follow transformations and entrust to change,
one still would not know the beginning or the end.
【Seven】【Comment】Féng Hóng refers to
the concept of vast emptiness.
Great wisdom roams through the boundless expanse,
freely following wherever transformations lead,
hence it remains unknowable.
【Commentary】"Páng huáng" is the name for unrestrained freedom,
"Píng hóng" is the appearance of vast emptiness,
meaning to enter into harmonious union.
It is said that the sage who possesses great knowledge
can unite with the principle of silent solitude and boundless emptiness,
thus being carefree and self-content,
unrestrained and limitless.
【Text】"Pǎng" is pronounced as páng.
The text also has it as "páng".
"Huáng" is pronounced as huáng.
"Féng" is read with the initial consonant "pí" and the final "bīng",
also read as "pǔ gēng",
and also as "bù gēng".
"Hóng" is pronounced as hóng.
Lǐ Yǐ explains:
Féng and Hóng
both mean vastness.
Guō Xiàng explains:
It refers to emptiness and vastness.
【八】【Note】It clarifies that the thing which things things,
is no thing, and things thing themselves.
Since things thing themselves,
they are thus obscure.
【Commentary】"Jì" means
the edge or boundary.
One who can master things without being mastered by them
is the sage.
The sage silently merges with all realms,
thus with things there is no boundary of self and other.
【Nine】【Annotation】Things have boundaries,
hence they cannot always merge into obscurity with one another,
which is truly what is meant by having boundaries.
【Commentary】The inclinations of beings are diverse,
with countless choices and rejections,
hence there arises the interaction between self and others.
【一０】【Note】That which has no boundaries,
although it bears the name of thing-ing things,
merely clarifies that things are things in themselves.
The thing that things things,
ultimately has no substance,
so where could its boundaries lie!
【Commentary】Regarding the non-boundary as boundary
is the sage's enlightened perspective;
Regarding the boundary as non-boundary
is the commoner's stagnant sentiment.
【一一】【Note】Since it is clear that the thing which makes things into things is itself not a thing,
and it is also clear that things cannot make themselves into things,
then who is it that does this?
It is all suddenly and spontaneously so.
【Commentary】Wealth and honor are considered fullness,
poverty and lowliness are considered emptiness;
old age and illness are seen as decline and diminishment,
beginning and end are regarded as root and tip;
coming to life is accumulation,
passing away is dispersion.
That which makes things into things is not a thing itself,
so what is it that gives birth to things?
This clarifies that both the maker of things and the things made
are not material entities.
Since things are not truly things,
how can one speak of fullness and emptiness, decline and diminishment!
Thus, it is understood that what are called fullness and emptiness are not truly so.
Therefore, the Xī Shēng Jīng says,
if you can comprehend this,
what seems to be is actually the opposite.
【Transcription】"Shuāi shā" is read with the initial consonant of the color radical,
and Xú's reading follows the pattern of the example.
The same applies below.
【Collation Notes】(1) The character "jīng" was emended based on the Interpretive Texts, the Shìdétáng edition, and Guō Qìngfān's commentary.
Only the reprinted Sòng edition uses "zhì".
(2) The character "zhì" was emended according to the main text.
(3) The character "yóu" was emended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
Hé Gān and Shénnóng studied under Lǎo Lóngjí.
Shénnóng was leaning on his desk with the door closed, dozing during the day,
when Hé Gān pushed the door open at noon and entered, saying:
"Lǎo Lóng has died!"
Shénnóng rose, leaning on his staff,
then with a clatter dropped it and laughed,
saying:
"Heaven knew I am narrow-minded and indolent,
so it abandoned me and let him die.
It is over, my master!
He has died without ever uttering those profound words to enlighten me!"
【One】 【Shū】 His surname is Shū,
and his courtesy name is Hégān.
The Shénnóng mentioned here,
is not the Shénnóng of the Three Sovereigns,
but rather a figure from a later period.
The two studied together under Lǎolóngjí.
Lǎolóngjí is also a title.
【Transcription】"" is pronounced as hé in the sense of river.
"Hègān" is read with the sound of hé.
Some versions alternatively write it as "苛".
"Lǎolóngjí" according to Lǐ's commentary:
He was a man who embraced the Way.
【二】【疏】Hidden,
means to lean on.
Close,
means to shut.
Open,
means to open,
also to push aside.
Those who study the Way,
with their spirit and mind concentrated and tranquil,
close their doors and recline on a table,
maintaining silence and closing their eyes.
Since Hègān heard of his teacher's passing,
he therefore pushed open the door to inform.
【Transcription】"Leaning on the armrest" pronounced as yǐn jī.
The same below.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
Modern editions write it as jī.
"Closing the door" pronounced as hé hù.
"Daytime nap" pronounced as zhòu mián.
"To open wide" according to Guō, pronounced chù yě,
also read as shē,
while Xú pronounces it dū jià,
and also chù yè.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to open.
【Three】【Annotations】He rose and realized that death is not something to be startled by,
so he put down his staff and laughed.
【Commentary】"Bó rán" is
the sound of dropping a staff.
Shénnóng, upon hearing Jí's death,
thus grasped his staff in shock;
but upon reconsidering that death is not worthy of mourning,
he therefore put down his staff and laughed.
◎ Yú Yuè remarks:
Since it is said he grasped his staff and rose,
it should not then mention leaning on a table.
It is suspected that the characters for "leaning on a table" were mistakenly duplicated from the earlier text where Shénnóng leaned on a table and closed the door for a daytime nap.
【Explanatory Text】"Bó rán" is pronounced like bō,
also read as fú miǎo,
and also as fú mào.
Lǐ Yí says:
It is the sound of dropping a staff.
"Tóu zhàng" is also written as fàng zhàng in some versions.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Modern editions use fàng zhàng.
【Four】【Annotation】From Jiānwú downward,
all regarded the ultimate discourse as madness and did not believe it.
Therefore, unless one is among the likes of Lǎolóng and Liánshū,
none are worthy to converse with.
【Commentary】The Master,
referring to Lǎo Lóng Jí,
is said to have possessed a natural virtue,
hence addressed as "Heaven."
"Wild words,"
meaning ultimate discourse,
are beyond the comprehension of ordinary people,
thus such profound speech is termed wild.
And the teacher, knowing my narrow-mindedness and ignorance,
my negligence and lack of dedication,
abandoned our group,
ceased his activities and passed away.
With the wise man gone,
the ultimate discourse is cut off,
no longer can metaphysical teachings be imparted,
enlightening my mind.
【Text Explanation】"Pì" is pronounced pì yì fǎn.
"Màn" is pronounced wǔ bàn fǎn,
Xú pronounces it as wú jiàn fǎn,
Guō reads it according to its original character.
