"Yí" is pronounced tú dàn fǎn,
Xú pronounces it as tú jiàn fǎn,
Guō reads it as dàn.
"Yǐ yǐ fū" is pronounced as fú.
Yǎn Gāng Diào heard of this,
and said:
"Those who embody the Way
are what the noble persons of the world rely upon.
Now, regarding the Way,
if one hasn't attained even one ten-thousandth of the tip of an autumn hair,
yet still knows to conceal his wild words and die,
how much more so for those who embody the Way!
Look for it - it has no form;
listen for it - it has no sound.
What people discuss,
calling it obscure and vague,
is merely what is used to talk about the Way,
but is not the Way itself."
【一】【注】One who embodies the Way is
the master of humanity.
【Explanation】"Yǎn" is pronounced as yǎn.
"Gāng" is pronounced as gāng.
"Diào," according to Lǐ Yí:
Yǎngāng,
is a person who embodies the Dào;
Diào,
is his name.
"Attached to him" means being the one to whom all things turn and entrust themselves.
【二】【注】The tip of an autumn hair is minute,
yet it doesn't even amount to one ten-thousandth of what they've grasped.
【Three】【Commentary】It is clear that the ultimate Way cannot be attained through words,
but only through self-attainment.
【Commentary】His surname is Yǎn,
given name Gāng,
a recluse.
"Xì"
means "to belong to."
Upon hearing of Lóng Jí's death,
he offered a commentary alongside:
"Those who embody the Dào
are universally revered in the world;
virtuous individuals and noble persons
affiliate with and rely upon them.
Now, even Old Lóng, in relation to the profound Dào,
had not grasped even one ten-thousandth part of a hair's tip,
yet he knew to conceal his unrestrained simplicity,
abide in accordance and pass away.
How much more so for those with sublime enlightenment—
would they ever be willing to reveal their words and teachings!"
This shows how exceedingly rare are those who deeply comprehend the profound mysteries of the Dào
and, forgetting words, align with the principle.
【四】【Note】Even the profound and obscure still does not conform to the Way,
illustrating that the Way is nameless.
【Commentary】The mysterious Way is empty and vast,
its subtle essence rare and imperceptible,
neither form nor sound,
beyond sight and hearing.
Therefore, for those who study and discuss it,
it is said that calling the obscure "obscure"
still falls short of the true Way.
【Transcription】"Yóu Fù" fú yòu fǎn.
Thereupon Tàiqīng asked Wúqióng, saying:
"Do you know the Way?"
Wúqióng said:
"I do not know."
【一】【疏】Tài,
means great.
The ultimate Way is vast and boundless,
tranquil and serene, pure and empty,
encompassing the limitless,
hence it is named Tàiqīng Wúqióng (Great Purity, Without End).
Then Tàiqīng asked Wúqióng about knowledge,
to which Wúqióng replied that he did not know,
intending to illustrate that the Way transcends form and sound,
and thus cannot be sought through verbal knowledge.
He further inquired of Wúwéi.
Wúwéi said:
"I know the Way."
He asked:
"Your understanding of the Way,
does it also have a method?"
He said:
"Yes."
He asked:
"What are the numbers?"
【One】【Memorial】Since you are versed in the Way,
do you have some knowledge of its enumeration?
How is this enumeration structured,
please provide a brief account.
Wúwèi said:
"I know that the Way can be noble,
can be base,
can be concentrated,
can be dispersed,
this is how I understand the nature of the Way."
【One】【Exposition】Noble as an emperor,
humble as a servant,
gathering marks life,
dispersal signifies death,
numbers are without limit.
This is stated briefly,
to clarify that which is not named yet named,
not numbered yet numbered.
Tàiqīng, using these words, asked Wúshǐ, saying:
"If so,
then the unknowing of the boundless and the knowing of the non-active,
which is right and which is wrong?"
【一】【疏】The ultimate Way is mysteriously pervasive,
silent and non-active,
unpredictable in its responses and approaches,
without end or beginning,
thus it is designated by the concepts of boundlessness and beginninglessness.
Boundless and non-active,
whether unknowing or knowing,
who is right and who is wrong?
I request a judgment on what is commendable or blameworthy.
【Interpretation】"Yǔ wú wéi zhī zhī" are all read according to their literal characters.
Wúshǐ said:
"Not knowing is profound,
knowing is shallow;
not knowing is inward,
knowing is outward."
【一】【疏】Not knowing aligns with principle,
hence it is profoundly mysterious and resides within;
knowing deviates from the Way,
therefore it is coarse, shallow, and estranged without.
Thereupon Tàiqīng sighed and said:
"Is it that not knowing is actually knowing?
And knowing is actually not knowing?
Who can understand the knowledge that comes from not knowing?"
【一】【注】What is attained not through knowledge,
is due to obscurity.
【Commentary】Tàiqīng attained the Middle Way and sighed in admiration,
realizing that not knowing is true knowledge.
Who understands the knowledge of not knowing?
This clarifies how exceedingly rare true knowledge is.
【Interpretation】"Zhōng ér tàn" — In Cuī Běn, "zhōng" is written as "áng".
Wúshǐ said:
"The Way cannot be heard;
what is heard is not It.
The Way cannot be seen;
what is seen is not It.
The Way cannot be spoken;
what is spoken is not It.
Do you know that which gives form to forms is itself formless?
The Way does not admit of names."
【一】【注】Thus, in the realm of what is neither heard nor seen, one attains it through silent completion.
【Commentary】The Way is without sound,
it cannot be heard by the ear,
for what is heard by the ear is not the Way;
the Way is without form,
it cannot be seen by the eye,
for what is seen by the eye is not the Way;
the Way is without name,
it cannot be spoken of in words,
for what is spoken of in words is not the Way.
【二】【注】Forms are merely forms themselves,
the one that forms forms ultimately has no substance.
【Commentary】That which can give form and appearance to all things,
is inherently without form or appearance itself,
hence it is said: "What gives form is itself formless."
【Three】【Comment】There is a name for the Way, yet ultimately it has no substance,
hence the name cannot truly correspond to it.
【Commentary】Names lack the merit of attaining the Way,
and the Way lacks the substance that matches names,
hence naming the Way is not the Way.
【Collation】（1）Wáng Shūmín and Liú Wéndiǎn both stated that after "not seen," there should be the two characters "not speak."
Wúshǐ said:
"One who responds when asked about the Dào
does not know the Dào.
Even the one asking about the Dào
has likewise not heard the Dào.
The Dào cannot be questioned,
and questioning cannot be answered.
To question what cannot be questioned
is to exhaust inquiry;
to answer what cannot be answered
is to lack inner substance.
Using this lack of substance to address exhausted inquiry—
one who does this
outwardly does not observe the cosmos,
inwardly does not know the Great Beginning,
therefore cannot pass beyond Kūnlún,
nor wander in the Great Void."
【一】【注】Asking without genuine ignorance,
and receiving an answer upon inquiry,
is not the Way.
If there is no response, it is not something the questioner can obtain;
thus, even if one asks,
in the end, one will not hear it.
【Commentary】The Way transcends verbal description,
and cannot be addressed through questions and answers.
Therefore, when asked about the Way or responding about the Way,
one remains entirely unknowing.
【二】【Note】It means abandoning learning and discarding teachings,
returning to the essence of nature.
【Commentary】Embracing the Dao transcends words,
what need is there for questions and responses!
All such statements
serve to elaborate on the preceding text.
【Text】"Qù jiào" is pronounced with the rising tone from Lǚ.
【Three】【Comment】This is what is called the emptiness of accountability.
【Commentary】To exhaust means,
to be empty.
When there is no reasonable basis for questioning yet one forces a question,
that is demanding emptiness.
【Four】【Annotation】Responding to what is actually nonexistent but seemingly existent pertains to the external.
【Subcommentary】When principle offers no response yet one forcibly responds to it,
it results in divergence from the external.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
The Dào does not pose questions;
to speculate about the Dào and question it
is to first confine oneself,
hence it is called "questioning confinement."
The Dào does not [respond;
to speculate about the Dào and] respond to it
is to follow the external,
hence it is called "lacking inwardness."
【Five】【Explanations】The four directions of heaven and earth are called space,
the continuum from ancient past to coming future is called time.
The Great Beginning,
is the root of the Way.
If one uses a mind detached from principle to approach the wisdom within emptiness,
it can be said that externally, they do not recognize the six directions and the cosmos,
and internally, they do not know the wondrous origin of their own being.
【Transcription】"Dàchū" is pronounced as Tài.
【Six】【Annotation】As for those who roam the vastness of heaven and earth,
journey through the void and traverse the distant,
entering into the profound darkness,
they simply do not respond.
【Commentary】Kūnlún represents the lofty and distant mountains,
while Tàixū signifies the profound and mysterious principle.
If one remains attached to names and words,
still holding onto questions and answers,
it shows they have not yet traversed the lofty and distant,
nor wandered through the profound and mysterious.
【Explanation】"Lán luò": pronounced as lì hán fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "shè" is written as "bù".
Guāngyào asked Wúyǒu, saying:
"Do you, sir, exist?
Or do you not exist?
【一】【疏】Guāng Yào refers to
the intelligence capable of seeing.
Wú Yǒu refers to
the realm that is observed.
Because intelligence can illuminate and examine,
it is provisionally named Guāng Yào;
because the essence of the realm is empty and tranquil,
it is provisionally named Wú Yǒu.
However, intelligence has brightness and darkness,
while the realm has no depth or shallowness,
so when intelligence questions the realm,
does it exist or not?
Guāngyào, unable to get an answer,
gazed intently at its form and appearance:
deep and hollow,
all day looking at it but not seeing it,
listening to it but not hearing it,
grasping at it but not catching it【one】.
【一】【疏】The wondrous realm is formless and silent,
beyond sight and sound,
thus to examine its appearance,
it is but stillness and emptiness.
◎Yú Yuè remarks:
In the "Dào Yìng" chapter of the Huáinánzǐ, before "Guāng Yào could not ask," there are the five characters "yǒu wú yǒu fú yìng yě,"
which should be followed.
Only because there was no response to "having and not having,"
hence Guāng Yào could not inquire.
Here, the omission of these five characters
renders the meaning incomplete.
【Explanatory Text】"Yǎo rán" is pronounced as wū liǎo fǎn.
"Bó zhī" is pronounced as yīn bó.
Guāng Yào said:
"Perfect!
Who could attain this!
I can possess nothingness,
but cannot yet attain the nothingness of nothingness;
when I reach the state of non-being having being,
how could I ever get to this point!"
【一】【注】This expresses the idea of transcending learning.
By cutting it off from the Way,
then the learner actually comes from the root.
Therefore, the best kind of learning
is perhaps not learning at all!
【Subcommentary】Its radiance shines brilliantly,
yet its wisdom is still shallow,
capable only of attaining non-being while abandoning being,
unable to transcend both being and non-being.
Therefore, it sighs at the profound depth of non-being,
asking who can reach such mystery!
When speaking of non-being,
it is not merely the absence of being,
but also the absence of non-being itself;
the four propositions and hundred negations
are all subsumed under non-being.
With the single word "non-being,"
there is nothing that is not negated;
concise in expression yet vast in principle,
hence it is called non-being.
The question of how to reach this state
refers to the realm of non-being,
which exhausts principle and fully realizes nature.
Unless one is a superior person of profound virtue,
who can embody it?
Thus, those with shallow learning and petty wisdom
have no means to attain it.
The hammerer of hooks in Dàmǎ,
though eighty years old,
never missed by even a hair's breadth.
Dàmǎ asked him:
"Are you skillful?
Or is there a Way to it?"
【一】【Note】(niān)〔diǎn〕(two) The lightness or heaviness of the hammered hook,
without the slightest discrepancy.
【Commentary】Dà Mǎ,
an official title,
refers to the Grand Marshal of Chǔ.
Chuí,
means forging by hammering.
Gōu,
refers to a waist belt.
In the household of the Grand Marshal, there was an artisan
who, from a young age, excelled at forging belt hooks.
Having lived to the age of eighty,
his skill in hammering hooks became even more refined.
He concentrated his mind and focused his thoughts,
thus achieving not the slightest error.
Gōu,
here refers to a steelyard hook,
meaning he could skillfully hammer steelyard hooks,
discerning the weight in jīn and liǎng,
with not the slightest error.
【Translated Text】"The hook-forger of the Grand Marshal, though eighty years old, never missed by a hair's breadth."捶，
Guō's pronunciation is given as dīng guǒ fǎn，
Xú's as zhī lèi fǎn，
Lǐ's as zhī shuì fǎn。
Grand Marshal，
refers to Sīmǎ。
(Sīmǎ) Guō states：
捶 means，
adjusting the weight of the hook without missing a hair's breadth。
Another explanation says：
in the regions of Jiāngdōng and Sān Wèi, people all call forging as 捶，
with the same pronunciation and character，
Guō erred on this。
Now, this explanation is not followed。
◎Lú Wénchāo says：
玷捶钩，
old editions have 玷捶铁，
now corrected according to the Sòng edition (three)。
Other editions are the same。
"玷" is pronounced dīng tián fǎn。
"捶" is pronounced dīng guǒ fǎn。
【Èr Shū】Sīmǎ wondered at his advanced age yet his forging skills grew ever more refined,
believing his craftsmanship must involve some unique art or technique.
【Explanation】"Qiǎo yǔ" is pronounced as yú.
The same applies below.
【Collation】(1) The Tang manuscript has "háo" written as "gōu".
(2) The character "diǎn" has been amended according to the Interpretations of Texts and the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The Shìdétáng edition uses "gōu".
Said:
"I have something I preserve.
At the age of twenty, I became fond of forging hooks,
paying no attention to other things,
and would observe nothing but hooks.
This means that what is employed
borrows from what is not employed to long maintain its usefulness—
how much more so for that which employs everything!
What thing would not draw support from it?"
【一】【疏】There is no other method,
only something to uphold and maintain.
Since my youth,
I have focused intently and loved this,
beyond forging hooks,
I observed nothing else,
practice made it nature,
thus it has come to this.
◎Wáng Niànsūn said:
"Shǒu" is actually the character "dào".
In the "Dáshēng" chapter, Zhòngní said:
"You are skillful!
Do you have the Way?"
He replied:
"I have the Way."
This is the evidence.
The character "dào" was anciently pronounced like "shǒu",
hence it interchanges with "shǒu".
(In the Nine Classics where rhyming is used,
the character "dào" is always pronounced like "shǒu",
the "Chǔcí" and various philosophers like Lǎo and Zhuāng are the same.
In the Qín inscription on the Kuàijī stone, "zhuī dào gāomíng",
the "Shǐjì: Qín Shǐhuáng Běnji" writes "dào" as "shǒu",
"shǒu" and "shǒu" are homophones.
"Shuōwén Jiězì" states:
"Dào",
follows the radical ,
with "shǒu" as its phonetic.
The reason modern editions lack the phonetic character
is that the two Xú did not understand ancient phonetics and deleted it.)
【Explanation】"而好" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling "呼報反".
【二】【注】If one is entirely without attachments in the heart,
then one can respond to all things as they come.
【Commentary】The reason why one can maintain the use of hammering hooks until old age is,
because it relies on not paying attention to other things.
If relying on non-use can lead to usefulness,
one can even sustain it throughout the year,
how much more so for the sage who embodies the Dào,
who neither uses nor does not use,
thus able to achieve great usefulness,
with all things drawing from it—
is that not fitting indeed!
【Explanation】"以長" is read as dīng zhàng fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The character "zhī" has been added based on the "Reading Notes Miscellany."
Rǎn Qiú asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Can it be known what existed before Heaven and Earth?"
Zhòngní said:
"Yes.
The past is like the present."
【一】【注】It speaks of heaven and earth enduring perpetually,
meaning there was never a time when they did not exist.
【Commentary】His surname was Rǎn,
his name was Qiú,
a disciple of Zhòngní.
The teacher initiated the discussion,
asking whether the state before the two primal forces existed could be known.
Since transformation and renewal occur daily,
there is neither present nor past,
the past is just like the present,
hence the reply was that it can be known.
Rǎn Qiú withdrew having asked a question incorrectly,
the next day he came to see again,
saying:
"Previously I asked, 'Can we know about the time before heaven and earth existed?
' You, Master, said:
'Yes.
The past is just like the present.
【一】' Yesterday I understood clearly,
but today I am confused,
dare I ask what this means?【二】"
【一】【疏】Missing the intent of the question,
he then retreated and returned.
Having followed the response to the query,
he proceeded to use the corresponding answer.
【Transcription】"Míng Rì Fù" reads fú yòu fǎn.
"Jiàn" reads xián biàn fǎn.
【二】【疏】In the past, when first consulted,
the mind was clear and discerning;
now, in later leisure,
thoughts and concerns have become obscure and dim.
I venture to ask: the clarity before and the obscurity now,
what does this signify?
Zhòngní said:
"In the past, clarity
was first received by the spirit【一】;
now, in obscurity,
is it because we seek through the non-spiritual【二】?
There is neither ancient nor modern,
neither beginning nor end【三】.
To have descendants before having descendants,
is that possible【四】?"
【一】【注】With an open mind awaiting the mandate,
thus the spirit receives it.
【二】【注】Continuously seeking more only leads to endless complications.
【Commentary】Initially, when one has not yet attained enlightenment,
they sharpen their spirit and intellect,
applying their mind diligently to seek understanding,
thus achieving clarity and lucidity.
Later, when comprehension dawns,
they no longer exert their spirit and intellect,
but simply abide in natural authenticity,
with nothing to seek or request,
thus becoming obscure and seemingly dull.
The phrase "seeking wrongly"
means actually not seeking at all.
【Transcription】"You wei" is read as yú wèi fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】Not only does non-being invariably transform into being,
but being also cannot transform into non-being.
Therefore, that which is the entity of being,
though it undergoes countless changes and transformations,
can never become non-being.
Since it cannot become non-being,
it has eternally existed from ancient times without ever having a moment of non-existence.
【Commentary】Renewal brings change,
thus there is no beginning and no end,
no present and no past,
hence we know there is no time before heaven and earth existed.
【Four】【Annotation】It means generations without end.
【Commentary】Speaking of descendants being born in succession,
generation after generation without end,
it is said that heaven, earth, and all things
all had no origin and no time of existence.
Is this acceptable?
It is said that it is not acceptable.
【Explanation】"There was no grandson before there was a grandson" means that essentials have their origins,
they cannot exist without cause;
thus, through generations, there come to be sons and grandsons,
one cannot have a grandson without first having a son.
In this way,
heaven and earth could not have previously not existed and now exist.
◎Lú Wénchāo comments:
In current editions, "grandson" is also written as "sons and grandsons."
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
Heaven and earth operate without ceasing,
sons and grandsons succeed each other without end.
Gradually, there come to be sons and grandsons;
to seek before there were sons and grandsons
is to confuse oneself from the start.
The operation of the great transformation of heaven and earth
has no beginning and no end.
Before heaven and earth existed,
from what could one seek them!
Therefore, it is said that antiquity is like the present,
together forming an endless discourse.
【Collation】（一）The character 'fū' has been emended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Rǎn Qiú did not respond.
Zhòngní said:
"Enough,
no need to answer!
Do not use life to give birth to death,
nor use death to extinguish life.
Are life and death interdependent?
They are both part of a single entity.
Is there a thing that existed before heaven and earth?
That which creates things is not itself a thing.
Things cannot precede the existence of things,
just as there are things.
Since there are things,
there is no end.
The sage's love for others never ends,
and this is also derived from this principle."
【一】【注】The deceased transforms independently and thus dies,
it is not that the living give birth to this death.
【二】【Note】That which is born also undergoes solitary transformation in being born.
【Commentary】"Yǐ" means
to cease.
"Wèi" means
nonexistence.
Gathering and dispersal, life and death,
all transform independently and renew daily,
never relying on anything,
how could they depend on each other!
Thus, life does not rely on generating death,
nor does death rely on ending this life.
While Rǎn Qiú had not yet responded,
Zhòngní stopped him and instructed no reply,
for the principle is fully expressed here—
what more could be said?
【Three】【Annotations】Self-transformation suffices.
【Four】【Annotation】Death and life each form their own entities.
【Commentary】Death is
a solitary transformation;
how could it become another entity!
Since death does not depend on life,
we know that life likewise does not depend on death.
Death, life, gathering, and dispersion
each form their own distinct reality,
thus there is nothing that relies on anything else.
【Five】【Commentary】Who could precede all things?
I consider yīn and yáng as preceding things,
yet yīn and yáng are precisely what we call things.
Who then precedes yīn and yáng?
I take zìrán (nature/spontaneity) as preceding them,
yet zìrán is simply the self-so of things.
I regard the supreme dào as preceding it,
yet the supreme dào is ultimately wú (non-being).
Since it is wú,
how could it precede anything?
Then what truly precedes all things?
If there still exist things,
without end,
it illuminates that things are zìrán,
not made to be so by anything else.
【Commentary】That which can make things into things,
is not itself a thing.
Therefore, what is not a thing has no before or after;
once a thing emerges, it is a thing,
and there can be nothing prior to this thing.
How do we know this is so?
Because it is still a thing itself.
By this reasoning,
there is ultimately nothing that precedes things.
Then what could possibly precede things?
It clarifies that things are spontaneous,
and spontaneity has no beginning or end.
Thus we know that heaven, earth, and all things
have existed firmly since ancient times,
with no time when they did not exist.
【Transcription】"You Xian" is read as Xī Jiàn fǎn.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
What precedes heaven and earth is the Dào.
Once it is called a birth,
then this Dào is also a thing.
Once it is called a thing,
then what is it that gives birth to this thing that precedes things?
Things transform into one another without end,
and tracing back to the beginning of things,
to find what gives birth before things,
can this thing ever have an end?
If it has an end,
then something might initiate and precede it;
if it has no end,
what could initiate and precede it?
Therefore, it is said that things cannot precede things.
【Six】【Annotation】It is derived from its own nature,
thus kindness flows through a hundred generations without being abandoned.
【Commentary】The sage who attains the Way,
with compassionate love shelters and nurtures,
whose grace flows through a hundred generations without cease,
truly because their virtue aligns with heaven and earth,
marvelously embodying spontaneity,
thus can empty themselves in relation to others,
forget their own involvement in nurturing,
show no partiality to the myriad things,
treat all living beings as straw dogs,
it is based on this principle that they act thus.
【Collation Note】(1) In the Tang manuscript, the character "物" is absent after "者".
(2) Regarding the phrase "猶其有物也",
Liú Dé's version does not repeat it.
Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Huí once heard from the Master:
'Do not escort anything off,
do not welcome anything in.'
May Huí ask about the practice of this?"
【One】【Memorial】Requesting the Master's words.
To send off,
means to see off.
The sage is like a mirror,
neither seeing off nor welcoming,
Yán Huí heard this and said,
not yet understanding the principle,
therefore inquired of Confucius,
asking the reason for it.
Zhòngní said:
"The people of old
were transformed outwardly but not transformed inwardly【一】,
while people today
are transformed inwardly but not transformed outwardly【二】.
Those who transform along with things
maintain one unchanging aspect【三】.
How to be transformed and how not to be transformed【四】,
how to smoothly interact with them【五】,
must involve not exceeding them【六】.
The garden of Xīwéishì,
the park of Huángdì,
the palace of Yǒuyúshì,
the chamber of Tāng Wǔ【七】—
men of virtue,
such as the masters of the Rú and Mò schools,
thus clashed over right and wrong,
let alone people today【八】!
The sage dwells among things without harming them【九】.
One who does not harm things
cannot be harmed by things either【一〇】.
Only those who are entirely unharming
can interact with others harmoniously【一一】.
The mountain forests!
The marshy plains!
How they make me joyful and delighted【一二】!
But before the joy is complete,
sorrow follows upon it【一三】.
The coming of joy and sorrow
I cannot ward off,
nor can I stop their departure.
Alas,
the people of this world are but inns for things【一四】!
They know what they encounter but not what they do not encounter【一五】,
they know the abilities they have but not the abilities they lack【一六】.
Lack of knowledge and inability
are inevitably unavoidable for humans【一七】.
To strive to avoid what is unavoidably human
is indeed pitiable【一八】!
The ultimate speech is without speech,
the ultimate action is without action【一九】.
To equate all knowledge as known
is shallow indeed【二〇】."
【一】【注】By aligning the heart with the form, the form naturally transforms.
【Commentary】The ancients were pure and simple,
many were in harmony with the Way,
thus they could let their forms follow things outwardly,
while their inner minds remained tranquil and still.
【Two】【Annotation】Using the mind to command the body.
【Subcommentary】Internally using connections to penetrate,
transformations arise from ignorance,
externally the form becomes discordant and erroneous,
unable to comply with things.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
External transformation means harmonizing with things,
internal transformation means the mind finding contentment.
When the mind finds contentment, it transforms along with things yet cannot pinpoint what is being transformed.
Transforming along with things,
merely means mutual attrition.
Failing to recognize what is being transformed while engaging in welcoming and sending,
there exists excess attachment to things.
The garden of Xīwéi,
the vegetable plot of Huángdì,
the palace of Yǒuyúshì,
the chamber of Tāngwǔ –
the deeper one goes inside them,
the more obstructed the exterior becomes.
《Shuōwén》 explains:
"Yuàn"
means a garden enclosed by walls.
Growing vegetables is called "pǔ".
《Shìmíng》 states:
"Gōng"
means vaulted,
a house whose walls appear arched overhead.
《Shuōwén》 says:
"Shì"
means substantial.
Following and embellishing these matters,
daily increasing welcomes and send-offs,
daily confusing right and wrong,
hence Confucians and Mohists simultaneously arose,
each using their own concepts of right and wrong to harmonize with others;
yet together studying one master's words,
revering him as teacher,
adopting his so-called rights and wrongs,
sending away what they deny,
welcoming what they accept,
this is what is called being transformed internally but not externally.
【Three】【Commentary】Constantly without a mind,
thus the One does not transform;
the One does not transform,
and only then can it be in harmony with the transformation of things.
【Four】【Annotation】Whether transformation occurs or not,
is entirely left to it,
this is being without a deliberate mind.
【Commentary】"Ān" means
to accept.
The sage has no fixed mind,
but follows the flow of things.
Therefore, whether transformation occurs or not,
he accepts it as such.
Since there is no discrimination,
he never imposes his own intentions.
【Five】【Annotation】It is simply without intention and lets everything follow its own transformation,
not by forcing or welcoming but by complying effortlessly.
【Explanation】Mǐ means
compliance.
The reason why both the transformed and untransformed are all left to their own accord,
is to avoid opposing the common people,
allowing them to mutually comply with each other.
【Six】【Comment】Not welcoming nor seeing off,
one stops when it is sufficient.
【Commentary】Although once again conforming with all things,
it does not overly indulge in benevolence or kindness;
each remains within their proper bounds,
with no harm done to either side.
【Seven】【Annotation】It speaks of being without a mind and entrusting to transformation,
which is where all the sages roam and dwell.
【Commentary】Xīwéi, Xuānyuán, Yú Shùn, Yīn Tāng, and Zhōu Wǔ
were all sagely and enlightened kings.
The way of being unselfconscious and in harmony with things
was precisely the park where Xīwéi roamed freely,
the garden where Xuānyuán wandered at leisure,
the palace chambers where Yú Shùn cultivated virtue,
the empty chamber where Tāng and Wǔ delighted their spirits—
these were the places where the multitude of sages wandered and dwelled.
【Transcription】"The park" is pronounced as yòu.
"The garden" is pronounced as bù wǔ fǎn,
and also as bù.
【八】【注】Harmony,
is about accord.
The masters of Confucianism and Mohism,
are the most difficult in the world to reconcile,
yet one who is without preconceptions can still harmonize them;
how much more so for ordinary matters!
【Explanation】Harmony,
means concord.
The masters of the Rú and Mò schools,
constantly dispute each other's views,
are among the most difficult in the world to reconcile.
Yet the sages and noblemen,
can still follow along and harmonize them.
How much more so for people of the present age,
who are not masters of the Rú and Mò schools,
to adapt and be transformed by it—
is that not fitting indeed!
【Explanation】"Xiāngxī" is read with the characters 子兮 as a phonetic reversal,
meaning harmony.
The masters such as Xīwéi, Huángdì, Yǒuyú, Tāng, Wǔ, the Confucians, and the Mohists,
all failed to fully comprehend the Way of inner non-transformation,
thus they ended up using right and wrong to oppose each other,
indicating that they still had disputes over right and wrong.
Just as the five flavors must contend with one another before they can achieve harmony,
hence it is called "xiāngxī" (mutual opposition leading to harmony).
【Nine】【Annotation】It signifies utmost compliance.
【Commentary】Dwelling in the mundane world while harmonizing with its radiance,
benefiting without causing harm,
thus one remains unharmed.
【一０】【Note】It all depends on me.
【Commentary】Like an empty boat and drifting tiles,
they greatly comply with all living beings.
All living beings gladly support them,
hence they dwell without harm.
【一一】【Note】Being without a deliberate mind leads to ultimate harmony,
and ultimate harmony enables one to neither send off nor welcome, yet righteousness prevails over all acts of sending and welcoming.
【Commentary】Only by safely entrusting all beings,
without harm to self or others,
can one interact with things and achieve clarity without actively welcoming yet welcoming all.
【Interpretation】"Yì Guān" is pronounced as Gǔ Luàn in the reverse spelling method.
【一二】【Note】The mountains, forests, and marshlands
are not inherently good to me,
yet I find joy in them;
this is to be joyful without a cause.
【Transcription】"Forests and Mountains with" pronounced as yú.
The same applies below.
"And Enjoy" pronounced as luò.
This applies to the annotations and the following instances.
【13】【Comment】There is no reason for joy,
and likewise no reason for sorrow.
Thus, all that is joyful is not truly worthy of joy,
and all that is sorrowful is not truly worthy of sorrow.
【Commentary】Ordinary emotions, when obstructed and fixated,
give rise arbitrarily to delight and aversion.
Suddenly beholding high mountains and dense forests,
divine plateaus and profound lands,
one feels spontaneous admiration and yearning,
considering it a source of joy.
Yet before this joyful sentiment lasts long,
sorrow follows in its wake.
As feelings shift with circumstances,
grief and pleasure thus transform.
This is to be joyful without cause,
and sorrowful without cause.
Hence we understand that the world's grief and joy
are not worth reckoning.
【一四】【Note】Unable to sit in oblivion and attain self-realization,
thus becoming a vessel for sorrow and joy.
【Commentary】An inn,
is a guesthouse.
The arrival of adversity and success,
cannot be resisted or warded off;
the departure of sorrow and joy,
cannot be prevented or stopped.
Yet ordinary people,
unaccustomed to this principle,
are like that guesthouse,
detained by external things,
mistaking the false for the true,
deeply lamentable and pitiable.
【Explanatory Text】"Able to resist" is read as yú lǚ in reverse.
【15】【Comment】What knowledge encounters is known,
what knowledge does not encounter remains unknown.
【16】【Comment】What one is incapable of,
one cannot force to be capable of.
From this perspective,
whether one knows or does not know,
whether one is capable or incapable,
is not determined by oneself,
but should be left to nature.
【Commentary】Wisdom has its clarity and obscurity,
ability has its skill and clumsiness,
each endowed with innate disposition,
which cannot be forced.
Thus, within the scope of one's allotment,
what can be known is known,
but what lies beyond cannot be known;
within the capacity of one's nature,
what can be done is done,
but what is inherently impossible
cannot be accomplished.
Consider birds flying and fish swimming,
spiders weaving webs and dung beetles rolling balls—
these follow their natural tendencies.
How could they not be innate!
◎ Jiàshìfù remarked:
Each has what they know,
each has what they can do,
with no need to force one another;
each has what they do not know,
each has what they cannot do,
with no need to surpass one another.
Forcing one's knowledge to comprehend the unknown,
forcing one's abilities to achieve the impossible,
and then claiming it as knowledge,
claiming it as ability,
imposing uniformity upon the world—
right and wrong become entangled,
sorrow and joy grow rampant.
Therefore, forgetting what one knows,
knowledge naturally finds its ease;
forgetting what one can do,
ability naturally finds its ease.
The ultimate speech is without speech,
the ultimate action is without action.
If even the self is forgotten,
how could there be leisure to uniformize the world!
To uniformize knowledge based on what is known
is to impose one's limited understanding forcibly upon the world.
【Explanation】"Qiáng" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "zhàng" and the tone as in "fǎn".
【一七】【Note】Each life receives its own allotted portion.
【Commentary】Since they are not sages,
they cannot possess wisdom that encompasses all things.
Therefore, in what they know and do not know,
what they can and cannot do,
their innate endowments differ,
and their inherent capacities vary.
Yet ordinary people
inevitably cling stubbornly to what they cannot avoid.
【一八】【Commentary】What people cannot avoid
are matters beyond their innate abilities and wisdom.
Yet those of common and shallow nature cannot remain content with their lot,
thus they intently delude themselves with purity,
striving solely for personal exemption.
Such extreme foolishness and delusion
is profoundly lamentable.
【一九】【Note】All attain self-realization.
【Commentary】The discourse of ultimate truth,
has no words that can be spoken,
hence words are abandoned.
The action of ultimate truth,
has no deeds that can be done,
hence action is abandoned.
【二０】【Note】What is acquired through knowledge
is merely borrowed by the learner,
hence it is shallow.
【Commentary】Seeing the virtuous and aspiring to emulate them,
abandoning oneself to imitate external things,
relying on learning to seek truth,
applying knowledge to inquire about the Way—
these are but superficial approaches;
how can they be called profound understanding!
【Transcription】"Qí zhī zhī": cái xì fǎn,
yòu rú zì.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Dunhuang manuscript has "rén" for "wǒ".
(2) The Quēwù cites the Jiangnan Guzang manuscript, which includes the four characters "yǔ wǒ wú qīn" before "shǐ".
(3) The Dunhuang manuscript lacks the character "zhī".
(4) The character "yóu" has been emended according to the Shidetáng edition.
【一】【Explanation】Named after a person's name.
Some versions have "Gēngsāng Chǔ".
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
Current texts include the character "Chǔ".
Lǎo Dān had a disciple named Kǎng Sāng Chǔ,
who partially grasped Lǎo Dān's Dào,
and dwelled north in the Wèilěi Mountains.
His ministers who were ostentatiously knowledgeable left him,
his concubines who were conspicuously benevolent distanced themselves;
he lived alongside the uncouth and unrefined,
and employed the rough and untutored.
After residing there three years,
Wèilěi greatly prospered.
The people of Wèilěi said to one another:
When Gēngsāng Zǐ first arrived,
I was astounded and found him extraordinary.
Now, when I tally by the day, it seems insufficient,
but when reckoned by the year, it proves abundant.
Is he not nearly a sage?
Why do you not join in honoring him as a master and offering prayers,
establishing him as the guardian of the altar and the land?"
【一】【疏】His surname is Gēngsāng,
his given name is Chǔ,
a disciple of Lǎojūn,
and he is a recluse.
"Yì"
is how disciples are referred to;
in ancient times, people served their teachers,
carrying out their tasks and errands,
without fearing hardship or danger,
hence the term "yì."
And Lǎojūn, being a great sage,
had many disciples,
among his followers,
Gēngsāng Chǔ was the most outstanding,
thus he is said to have particularly excelled.
【Explanatory Text】"Lǎo Dān's Disciple" Sīmǎ comments:
Disciple,
refers to a student follower.
The Guangyǎ states:
Disciple,
means one who is employed.
"Gēng Sāng Chǔ" Sīmǎ comments:
Chǔ,
is the given name;
Gēng Sāng,
is the surname.
The Records of the Grand Historian writes it as Kàng Sāng.
◎Qìng Fán's case study: the Suoyin of the Biographies of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzǐ in the Records of the Grand Historian quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Gēng Sāng Chǔ,
is a person's name.
This slightly differs from the explanatory text.
◎Yú Yuè states:
In the chapter "Zhòngní" of the Liezi, among Lǎo Dān's disciples is one named Kàng Cāngzǐ.
Zhàng Zhàn's annotation pronounces it as Gēng Sāng.
Jiǎ Kuí's Survey of Surnames states:
In Wú commandery, there is the surname Gēng Sāng,
counted among the seven clans.
So, could Gēng Sāngzǐ be from Wú?
"Partially Attained" Xiàng pronounces it as "piān".
【二】【Note】Posing as wise with ostentation,
and adorning knowledge;
acting with affected grace,
and priding oneself on benevolence.
【Commentary】Wèilěi is
the name of a mountain,
located in the State of Lǔ.
"Chén" refers to
male servants or slaves,
while "qiè" means
to receive or connect;
it signifies that people use benevolence and wisdom as their servants,
but Gēngsāngzǐ entirely discards benevolence and wisdom to serve the nobleman.
Since Chǔ secluded the recluse,
dwelling in the mountain wilderness,
his emotions were sincere and plain,
and his heart despised superficiality and extravagance;
the local men and women nearby
vied to become his servants,
so those who ostentatiously [adorned] (1) their wisdom to show off
were repelled and driven away;
those who [held] themselves aloof, priding themselves on benevolence and seeking to differ from others,
were made to keep their distance.
【Explanation】"Wei" may also be written as ,
or as 猥,
with the same meaning.
Pronounced as wū zuì fǎn,
Xiàng gives yú guǐ fǎn.
"Lei" in Cuī's version is written as 纍,
with the same meaning.
Pronounced as lì zuì fǎn,
Xiàng gives liáng péi fǎn.
Lǐ says:
Wèilěi,
is the name of a mountain.
Some say it is in Lǔ,
others say it is in Liángzhōu.
"Huà rán" is pronounced as huò.
"Zhī zhě" is pronounced as zhì.
The same applies to the annotations.
The "Qiè" version is also written as "Qì,"
same.
Pronounced as kǔ jì fǎn.
Xiàng comments:
It means knowledge.
Also pronounced as kǔ jié fǎn.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means to carry.
"Yuǎn zhī" is pronounced as yú wàn fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to people using benevolence and wisdom as servants,
while Gēngsāng entirely discards benevolence and wisdom.
【Three】【Annotations】Lumpy and gnarled,
signifies simplicity.
【Explanation】"Yōng" is pronounced as yǔ yǒng fǎn.
"Zhǒng" is pronounced as zhāng yǒng fǎn.
This character is also written as zhǒng.
【Four】【Comment】Yǎngzhǎng,
self-satisfied.
【Commentary】"Yǒngzhǒng yāngzhǎng"
both describe the appearance of natural simplicity and self-contentment.
Rejecting benevolence and wisdom,
serenely returning to genuineness,
thus the pure and simple scholars dwell with them,
and those who follow their nature serve under their command.
【Translated Text】"Yǎngzhǎng" is read with the pronunciation yāng zhǎng,
Guǒ Xiàng states:
yōngzhǒng,
means simplicity;
yǎngzhǎng,
signifies self-contentment.
Cuī Yǎn states:
yōngzhǒng,
describes an ignorant appearance;
yǎngzhǎng,
implies a lack of benevolence.
Xiàng Xiù states:
these two phrases,
refer to the concept of simplicity and burden,
Sīmǎ Biāo states:
both describe ugly appearances.
【五】【Note】It differs in discarding wisdom and embracing foolishness.
【Translated Text】"Dà rǎng" is read with the pronunciation of "rǎng" in reverse.
The original text also uses the character "穰".
Cuǐ Běn's version is the same,
and it is also pronounced like "yáng" in reverse.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means abundant.
◎ Lú Wénchāo said:
According to the "Tiān Ruì" chapter of the "Lièzǐ", "壤" is also used interchangeably with "穰".
"Sǎ rán" is pronounced "sù tiǎn" in reverse,
and also "xī lǐ" in reverse.
Cuǐ Běn and Lǐ Yí say:
It means a startled appearance.
Xiàng Sū (jù) [hěn] (sān) in reverse.
【Six】【Annotation】Those who align with the four seasons achieve no immediate results.
【Commentary】"Great abundance" means
bountiful harvest.
"Startled"
describes a slight expression of surprise.
After residing for three years,
the mountains experienced a great harvest,
and the people of Wěilěi all privately said:
When Gēngsāngzǐ first arrived,
we were slightly surprised and doubtful.
Now, if we calculate by the day,
the benefits seem insufficient to mention;
but if we calculate by the year,
his achievements are more than ample.
This is because the sage,
aligning with the rhythm of the four seasons,
shows no immediate gains hence the daily calculation seems insufficient,
yet possesses enduring virtue thus the yearly calculation proves abundant.
Every three years, there is an intercalary month,
marking a minor completion in the way of heaven,
therefore after three years of dwelling, Wěilěi achieved great abundance.
【Translation】"Counting by days, it is insufficient" Xiang's commentary says:
There is no small profit in the short term.
"Counting by years, it is abundant" Xiang's commentary says:
Following the seasons brings great harvests.
【七】【疏】Shù,
means to admire.
Jǐ,
means to be close to.
Shī,
means to preside over.
Gēngsāng was a man of great virtue,
who admired and drew near to the sage's virtue.
Why not together honor him as sovereign,
to preside over the affairs of ruling,
establish the altars of land and grain for him,
build his ancestral temple,
and perform sacrifices according to the rites?
Would that not be excellent!
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'shì' has been amended according to the commentary text.
(2) The character 'shì' has been amended based on Liú Wěndiǎn's revised and corrected edition.
(3) The character 'hěn' has been amended according to the Yùnhuì,
the Shìdétáng edition mistakenly writes ●.
Gēngsāng Zǐ heard this,
and facing south he remained unsettled.
His disciples found it strange.
Gēngsāng Zǐ said:
"Why do you find me strange?
When the spring energy arises, all grasses grow;
just as with the arrival of autumn, the myriad treasures mature.
Spring and autumn,
could they be without cause and yet be so?
The Way of Heaven is already in motion.
I have heard of the ultimate person,
who dwells inactive in a room surrounded by earthen walls,
while the common people run wild, not knowing where to go.
Now, the petty folk of Wèilěi are furtively wishing to place me among the wise with sacrificial honors,
am I then to be a target for others?
This is why I am unsettled by Lǎo Dān's words."
【一】【疏】Suddenly hearing that the people of Wèilěi had established him as their ruler facing south,
this already deviated from the way of non-action,
so he felt displeased and let it go.
His disciples did not understand this inclination,
hence they found it strange and regarded it as unusual.
【二】【注】The Spring and Autumn Annals were born from qi and completed,
all attaining the natural Way,
thus they act without deliberate action.
【Commentary】The sprouting in spring and fruiting in autumn
are constants of yin and yang;
the growth in summer and storing in winter
are natural regularities of all things.
Thus, do spring and autumn intentionally bestow upon the myriad fruits?
The way of nature already operates of its own accord,
hence forgetting the virtue of their life-giving existence.
Some versions write "treasure" for "fruit,"
meaning the two primal forces regard all things as treasures,
thus they mature upon encountering autumn.
【Translation】"It is precisely in autumn that all treasures are accomplished." Heaven and Earth consider all things as treasures,
which reach completion in autumn.
The Yuánjiā version writes "all fruits" instead of treasures.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
The character "dé" (得) is suspected to be redundant,
the original text probably read "precisely in autumn all treasures are accomplished."
As stated in the "Explaining the Trigrams" of the Yìjīng,
Duì represents the exact autumn.
It is what all things delight in,
the subcommentary explains:
"In exact autumn, all things delight and are accomplished."
This directly references the present text,
serving as evidence.
The character "dé" likely mistakenly carried over from the next line, "Could spring and autumn occur without reason?"
thus erroneously becoming redundant.
With the spring energy emerging, all grasses grow;
in exact autumn, all treasures are accomplished.
The meaning is already complete,
there is no need to add "dé" to parallel the previous line.
"The Great Way has already been put into practice." Some versions read "Tiāndào" (the Way of Heaven) instead (note two).
【Three】【Comment】It was simply going straight there oneself,
not due to knowledge.
【Explanation】Surrounded by a wall on all four sides,
it is called a walled enclosure,
which is what is referred to as the one-zhàng-square room.
As still and tranquil as a dead corpse,
hence the term "corpse-dwelling."
【Explanation】"Huán" is read as its common pronunciation.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means round.
"Dǔ" is pronounced with the initial D and the final ǔ.
Sīmǎ explains:
One zhàng is called a dǔ.
A huán dǔ refers to
each side being one zhàng,
indicating smallness.
【Four】【Annotation】Not wishing to be a standard for things.
【Commentary】Whispering discussions,
are private conversations about public affairs.
The sacrificial stand (zǔ),
is a table for cutting meat;
the ritual vessel (dòu),
is a container for holding dried meat;
both are ceremonial utensils.
"When a flock of dragons has no leader,"
is an ancient sage's dictum;
"nurturing simplicity through concealed virtue,"
is the path followed by later worthies.
Now the common people in their trivial concerns,
whispering and deliberating,
wish to honor me as a worthy,
revere me as their master,
this would make me a conspicuous marker,
how can this be called living in seclusion!
【Transcription】"Zǔ Dòu" is pronounced cè lǚ fǎn.
Cuī states:
Zǔ Dòu,
means feeding me among the crowd.
"Sháo" Guō pronounces as dí,
also pǐ mō fǎn,
and another pronunciation diào.
Guǎngyǎ says:
the tip of a tree.
Guō explains:
it serves as the marker for things.
Wáng explains:
this is because oneself becomes the standard for others.
Xiàng states:
the Mǎ family writes it as "diào",
pronounced dí.
"Biāo" is pronounced bì yáo fǎn,
another pronunciation bì xiǎo fǎn.
【Five】【Annotation】Lǎo Dān said,
"When achievements are completed and matters settled,
the common people all say it happened naturally by itself.
Now Wèilěi runs counter to this,
hence I cannot feel at ease."
【Commentary】Lǎojūn said:
When the task is accomplished, do not dwell on it;
guide without controlling.
Since Chǔ had devoutly received the master's instruction,
yet Wèilěi acted contrary to this,
therefore he could not be at ease.
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'chéng' was emended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(2) Modern editions read as 'Tiāndào'.
The disciple said:
"Not so.
In an ordinary ditch,
a giant fish has no space to turn its body,
yet it becomes a domain for the mudfish;
on a hillock only a few feet high,
a massive beast cannot conceal its form,
yet it proves auspicious for the stealthy fox.
Moreover, honoring the worthy and appointing the capable,
prioritizing the virtuous and bestowing benefits,
has been the way since the times of Yáo and Shùn in antiquity,
how much more so for the people of Wèilěi!
You should comply, Master!"
【一】【注】The disciple implies that a great man must have abundant emoluments.
【Commentary】Eight chǐ is called a xún,
double xún is called a cháng.
Six chǐ is called a bù,
seven chǐ is called a rèn.
The ní,
a small fish with feet,
is not the kūn, a great fish.
"Zhì"
means to monopolize.
How could the small ditches of xún and cháng
be where the kūn and whales roam!
Yet the ní, a small fish,
is instead considered beautiful;
the hills of bù and rèn,
are not where large beasts hide,
yet the bewitching fox,

Gēngsāngzǐ said:

yet if waves toss it out of water,

Thus, birds and beasts dwell in high mountains,

Even fish and birds act this way,

Nánróng Chú said:
"As for the eyes and their form,
I do not know how they differ,
yet the blind cannot see by themselves;
as for the ears and their form,
I do not know how they differ,
yet the deaf cannot hear by themselves;
as for the mind and its form,
I do not know how they differ,
yet the mad cannot attain by themselves.
Form with form should indeed be open to each other,
but perhaps things come between them,
so that though wishing to seek each other they cannot attain each other?

embrace your life,

【一】【Note】Eyes and eyes,

though they possess the same ears and eyes as ordinary people,

and the deaf cannot hear sounds;
the insane individuals,
though they resemble the sane in appearance,
lose their inherent nature,
unable to attain self-mastery.

failing to understand that the words of the ultimate Way are no different from the blindness and deafness of those,
hence the Inner Chapters state,

but wisdom also has its own deafness and blindness."

Lǎozi said:
"The principles of preserving life—
can you embrace the One?
Can you not lose it?
Can you know fortune and misfortune without divination?
Can you stop?
Can you cease?
Can you forsake others and seek within yourself?
Can you be carefree?
Can you be simple?
Can you be like an infant?
An infant cries all day without its throat becoming hoarse—
this is the perfection of harmony;
it clasps its hands all day without them cramping—
this is the constancy of its virtue;
it gazes all day without its eyes blinking—
because its focus is not directed outward.
It moves without knowing where it goes,
it rests without knowing what it does,
it follows things smoothly
and rides their waves.
These are the principles of preserving life."

shares sustenance with others from the earth and shares joy with them in heaven【二】,
not allowing the gains and losses of people and things to disturb them,
not joining others in creating strangeness,
not conspiring with them,
not engaging in affairs with them【三】,
going forth freely,
and coming simply.
This is called the principle of preserving life.
【一】【Note】Capable indeed,
it is clear that it is not so by itself.
【Commentary】Nán Róng had been constrained by benevolence and righteousness,
for a long time indeed.
Now, upon hearing the sage's teachings,
he began to understand the nurturing of life.
Like winter ice
meeting the spring sun,
his stubborn and stagnant mind
dissipated at this moment.
This was an awakening achieved through learning,
not a spontaneous natural occurrence.
Capable as it may seem,
it is not truly genuine.
These are Lǎo Zǐ's words in response to Chū.
【Interpretation】"Ice melts" is pronounced as xiè.
【二】【Note】Since they themselves have no mind of their own,
they all share with things.
【Commentary】The ultimate person is without personal emotions,
responding to things as they arise with feeling,
thus able to partake in the common people's sustenance from the earth,
and share in the multitude's joy in heaven.
"Jiāo"
means to share.
【Explanatory Text】"Jiao Shi" Cui comments:
Jiao,
means both.
Li comments:
means together.
"Jiao Le" pronounced as luò.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
Guō's annotation states,
from having no mind of one's own,
all are shared with things.
The explanatory text quotes Cui as saying,
Jiao,
means both.
Li says,
means together.
These all fail to understand the meaning of the character Jiao.
In the chapter "Xú Wú Guǐ" it is said,
I with him seek pleasure from heaven,
I with him seek food from earth.
This text differs in wording but shares the same meaning.
Jiao is equivalent to yāo,
in ancient characters, it was written only as jiǎo.
In the second year of Wén in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, "Our ruler wishes to seek blessings from Zhōu Gōng and Lǔ Gōng."
Here it says seeking food from earth,
seeking pleasure from heaven,
the phrasing and meaning are quite similar.
Using yāo is a later evolved character,
using jiāo is a borrowed character.
In the poem "Sāng Hù" it says, "That is not arrogant in interactions,"
the Hàn Shū's "Treatise on the Five Elements" writes it as "not seeking, not arrogant,"
which serves as an example.
【Three】【Explanations】Yīng,
means to disturb and confuse.
The ultimate person empties their mind and conforms to the world,
flowing along with all things,
thus able to quell peculiarities among the multitude,
and eliminate schemes and plans from the common people.
By not treating affairs as affairs,
how can profit and harm disturb them!
【Explanation】"相攖" is pronounced as yú yíng fǎn,
and Xú also reads it as yīng.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means chaos.
Cuī says:
It is like threading through.
【Fourth】【Exposition】Reiterates the preceding text,
concluding its meaning.

He said:
"Is this then the ultimate?"
【一】【注】Do you think you can attain these words so easily?
【Commentary】It means that upon hearing these words,
one can reach the ultimate.
Nán Róng, being unwise,
inquired again of Lǎo Jūn.
He said:
"Not yet.
I have always told you:
'Can you be like an infant?'
【一】 An infant moves without knowing what it is doing,
walks without knowing where it is going,
its body is like the branch of a withered tree and its heart like dead ashes【二】.
Being thus,
calamity does not come,
nor does fortune arrive.
Without calamity or fortune,
how could there be human-caused disasters?
【一】【注】It is not that these words are not profound,
but those who can hear and learn
do not arrive at it on their own.
If one does not arrive at it on their own,
then even if they hear the most profound words,
they can only treat them as scriptures,
how could they possibly attain the ultimate?
Therefore, those who learn do not attain,
and those who attain do not learn.
【Commentary】The term "capable" is,
an expression of encouragement and exhortation.
Although these words reach the ultimate,
they are still just a trap or a snare.
Since it is said "I tell you,"
it relies on imparting learning.
However, those who learn do not reach the ultimate,
and those who reach the ultimate do not learn.
It is like the trap being different from the fish,
hence it is said "not yet."
This is Lǎo Zǐ's repeated response to Nán Róng.
【Èr Shū】Empty and yielding, concentrated and serene,
Solitary and devoid of emotion,
Like withered wood that does not flourish,
Resembling dead ashes that have forgotten to glow.
Since both body and mind are equally relinquished,
How can one know of any action or movement?
This is the essence of preserving life.
【Transcription】"若槁" is read as kǔ lǎo fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】Misfortune and fortune arise from loss and gain,
human calamities stem from love and hatred.
Now, withered wood and dead ashes,
being utterly without emotion,
thus have no basis for love, hatred, loss, or gain to come from.
【Commentary】Misfortune and fortune arise from gain and loss,
human calamities stem from beauty and ugliness.
Now, with a form like withered wood,
a heart as dead ashes,
having forgotten both gain and loss,
and dismissed both beauty and ugliness,
there is not even the blame of obscurity,
so how could there be any human calamity?
【Explanation】"Wù yǒu" is pronounced as wū.
"Ài wù" is pronounced with the wū lù fǎnqie.
The same applies below.
One whose cosmic breath is serene
emanates a heavenly radiance.
He who emanates a heavenly radiance
shows his inner self to others,
Things are seen as they truly are.
(1) When a person cultivates themselves,
only then do they attain constancy [three];
those who have constancy,
people dwell with them,
and Heaven assists them [four].

those whom Heaven assists

【一】【注】When one's virtuous nature is serene and stable,
then what emanates from it is the light of heaven,
not human brilliance.
【Commentary】The body is the dwelling of the spirit,
thus the sage serves as the vessel of the Way and Virtue.
Moreover, when the abode of virtue is tranquil and stable,
one's enlightened mind illuminates all things,
through the natural light of wisdom.
【Explanatory Text】"Yǔ Tài Dìng" Wáng Yún:
Yǔ,

meaning that when one's bearing is composed and serene, it becomes tranquil and settled.

An empty room gives rise to brightness,
auspiciousness settles upon stillness,
the human mind naturally reveals its clues and heavenly light shines forth,
spontaneously and cannot be concealed,
cultivate what is natural and the mechanism responds to it.
Each person cultivates themselves,
each sees for themselves,

【二】【注】When the light of heaven shines forth spontaneously,
people see themselves as they are,
things see themselves as they are,

unable to fathom the sage,
merely see them mingling among the masses,
unaware of the heavenly radiance shining from afar.
【Three】【Comment】When a person cultivates their humanity,
they attain self-realization,
thus maintaining constant peace.
【Commentary】Héng means

Although principle transcends learning,
the Way still relies on seeking,
hence there are genuine cultivators
who can comprehend the congealed constant Way.
【Four】【Annotation】Chángtài,
thus can reside in my abode in return and naturally (two) obtain assistance.
【Commentary】For a person who embodies constancy,
actions are met with auspicious encounters,
becoming the refuge for the common people,
and receiving the blessings and aid of the August Heaven—
is this not fitting indeed!
【Five】【Comment】When in office, he is the Son of Heaven;
when in seclusion, he is a subject of Heaven.
Both of these states are attained with great tranquility and self-contentment,
not acquired through deliberate striving.
【Commentary】When in public, they serve their sovereigns and lords;
when in private, they bring ease to the people;
all because they embody the Way and adhere to constancy,
thus achieving such merits.

A learner is one who learns what cannot be learned;
a practitioner is one who practices what cannot be practiced;
a debater is one who debates what cannot be debated【一】.
To know to stop at what cannot be known is the ultimate achievement【二】;
if there is one who does not follow this, the heavenly balance will thwart them【三】.
【One】【Annotation】All that one is capable of,
even if acted upon, is not considered doing;
even if practiced, is not considered learning;
even if spoken, is not considered debate.
【Commentary】When one acts within their inherent duties,
even if they act, it is as if they do not act;
thus, even if they learn, it is as if they do not learn;
even if they practice, it is as if they do not practice;
even if they debate, it is as if they do not debate.
How could they then engage in matters beyond their duties,
or learn what cannot be learned?
【Explanation】"The learner learns what they cannot learn" means that everyone wishes to learn what they do not yet know.
As for all that one is capable of,
it is inherently mastery within one's abilities.
To be capable within one's capabilities
means that even if practiced, it is not truly practice.
【二】【Note】What cannot be known,
should not be forced to know,
hence stopping here is the ultimate (principle).
【Commentary】To pursue what one is capable of,
and stop within one's proper bounds,
without forcing knowledge of
what lies beyond one's abilities—
this is the utmost subtlety in approaching learning.
【Three】【Annotations】Although the mind may wish to act,
those who act are bound to fail,
for in the end, principle cannot be forced.
【Commentary】If one has the intention to go beyond what is proper,
and does not regard what is within one's proper bounds as right,
such a person is one who damages their natural disposition.
【Transcription】"Defeat it" is read as bǔ mài in the reverse tone.
Some versions write it as zé.
The Yuánjiā edition writes it as zé.
【Collation】（一）The Shìdétáng edition includes the character 也 (yě).
Prepare things to nurture the body,
store away anxieties to cultivate the mind,
revere the inner self to connect with others.
If despite this all manner of evils befall,
it is all due to Heaven,
and not to human actions.
They are not sufficient to disrupt one's accomplishments,
nor can they be allowed entry into the spiritual terrace.
The spiritual terrace has its support,
yet one does not know what it supports,
and it is something that cannot be forcibly maintained.
【一】【注】It follows its own preparedness and conforms to its formed nature.
【Commentary】"Jiāng" means
to follow.
The great furnace of creation,
provides all things in abundance;
one merely follows to take form,
and inquires into learning through principle.
【Explanation】"Preparing things to accord with the form": "Preparing" means
to have ready.
"Accord with" means
to follow along.
【二】【Note】It arises from the mind itself,
not from anticipation that it emerges.
Anticipation means
conjecture.
【Commentary】The perfect person is without personal emotions,
yet responds when stimulated by things,
harboring sagely wisdom within,
and gives rise to thoughts upon encountering matters,
never planning or speculating in advance.
【Explanation】"Yì Duó": Pronounced as dài luò fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】Principle naturally reaches the other,
not by being negligent internally while reverent externally.
【Explanation】"Zhong" (inner),
refers to internal wisdom.
"Bi" (that),
refers to external circumstances.
Respect and revere spiritual wisdom,
dare not lightly defile it;
once wisdom becomes concentrated and tranquil,
circumstances naturally become empty and interconnected.
【四】【注】The principle of heaven inherently has its vicissitudes.
【Five】【Note】It is humans who act with intent and thus bring about evil.
【Commentary】Like King Wén's confinement in Yǒulǐ,
or Confucius being besieged by the people of Kuāng,
their wisdom was not unenlightened,
their virtue was not unsagely,
yet they encountered such extreme adversity and dire straits—
this was due to the workings of heavenly timing and fate,
how could it be the doing of men!
【Six】【Comment】Accept it as destiny,
thus its completion remains undisturbed.
【Commentary】Slippery means
chaotic.
Embodying the Way and uniting with the genuine,
being content with the times and understanding destiny,
even if encountering myriad evils,
is not enough to disturb the heart of great accomplishment.
【Explanatory Text】"To slip" is pronounced with a bone-like sound.
【Seven】【Annotation】Língtái refers to
the heart,
which is clear and smooth,
thus worries and troubles cannot enter.
【Commentary】Nèi means
to enter.
The Spiritual Tower,
refers to the heart.
Its essence is empty and tranquil,
thus worldly things cannot enter this Spiritual Tower.
【Explanation Text】"Líng Tái" Guō notes:
It is the heart.
The case states that the heart possesses spiritual intelligence capable of abiding and sustaining.
Xǔ Shèn states:
Above the human heart,
is where the energy comes and goes.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
The characters "wàn è" should precede "bù kě,"
as the preceding text says, if such conditions lead to all evils arriving,
it is all due to heaven,
and not due to humans,
insufficient to disrupt completion,
the text is already complete.
All evils cannot enter the Líng Tái,
then it further introduces the following idea.
The following text states,
the Líng Tái has something to hold onto,
yet one does not know what it holds and cannot hold it,
all continuing from this.
Readers who do not examine the meaning in detail,
mistakenly think that "cannot enter the Líng Tái" and "insufficient to disrupt completion" are two consecutive clauses,
hence they deleted the two characters "wàn è."
In the "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn" of the Wén Xuǎn, Lǐ Shàn's annotation quotes this text,
precisely as "wàn è bù kě nèi yú Líng Tái."
【八】【Note】One who holds fast,
means being unmoved by external things,
yet in truth, it is not holding fast.
【Commentary】Only the noble can maintain this heart,
yet ultimately do not know the reason why.
【Nine】【Annotation】If one knows what they uphold, then they uphold it.
【一０】【注】To grasp is to lose.
【Comment】If one intentionally clings to it,
one will stray far from it,
and thus it is not permissible.

each action will be inappropriate.
When external matters enter and do not depart,
each change leads to further loss.
Those who do wrong in the open and clear,
people can punish them;
those who do wrong in secrecy and solitude,
ghosts can punish them.
Being clear about people,
and clear about ghosts,
only then can one walk alone.
【一】【注】This is an erroneous occurrence.

【二】【注】If one acts without sincerity from within,
how can it ever be appropriate!
【Commentary】Previously, it was shown that those who have attained the Way possess wisdom that illuminates brightly.
From here onward, it explains how those who have lost their true nature harbor deluded minds that contradict reason.
"Chéng"
means "truth" or "reality."

【Three】【Annotation】Affairs do not reside within their proper boundaries.
【Commentary】Yè,
means affairs.
The disturbances of worldly affairs,

thus one cannot abandon and cease them.
【Four】【Annotation】It is only when it arises from one's own sincerity,

【Commentary】Whenever one recklessly gives rise to thoughts,

yet instead lose their true nature.
【Five】【Memorials】Though humans and ghosts exist in the hidden and visible realms,
which are said to be different paths,
when it comes to upholding sincerity and practicing faithfulness,
the principles remain without separation.
If one deviates from this and loses authenticity,
retribution is inevitable;
mutual animosity stirs reactions,
leading to the suffering of punishment,
as seen in cases like Dù Bó and Péng Shēng.
【Explanation】"Yōu Xián" is pronounced as xián.
【Six】【Annotation】Being without shame in one's heart towards both the hidden and the visible,
one can walk alone without fear.
【Commentary】The paths of the hidden and the manifest,
are clearly without fault,
not offending against things,
thus walking alone without fear.

The Way is all-pervading,

What is considered completion here,

Having annihilated and blocked the way of pure simplicity while outwardly chasing after shallow and insubstantial realms,

Hence, it is said to be one aspect of being a ghost.
【Seven】【Annotation】Although possessing this form,

Vast and self-forgetting,

【Four】【Annotation】Words spoken inherently possess substance,
yet their origin lacks roots or apertures from which to emerge.
【Commentary】When something appears to exist yet lacks any aperture or cavity,
from a common perspective,
it is considered to have substance,
but in reality, it does not exist.
【Explanation】"That which comes into being must have a source."
"Yet it is non-being." This clarifies that the source is non-being.
Since it is non-being,
how could it have a source?
"An opening implies substance." Since there is mention of an opening,
an opening must have substance;
if substance cannot be found,
then the opening is also non-existent.
【Five】【Note】Space is that which

yet the four directions and above and below have no finite extent.
【Commentary】Yǔ (space) refers to
the four directions, up and down.
When living things come into existence,
it is said they have substance,
yet searching throughout space,
ultimately there is no place of origin.
Since space itself is unreal,
how could there truly be a location!
【Explanation】"That which has substance but no fixed location is space." The Three Cang Dictionary states:
"The four directions and up and down constitute space."
Although space has substance,
it has no fixed location that can be sought.
【Six】【Annotation】Zhòu refers to
the span of ancient and modern times,
and the span of ancient and modern times is limitless.
【Commentary】Zhòu refers to
the past coming to the present.
The passage of time is vast and long,
which we call the present and the past.
When we seek to trace the sequence of eras,
we ultimately find no beginning or end.
Since Zhòu itself is nonexistent,
how could there be a beginning at all!
【Explanation】"That which has length but no beginning or end is Zhòu." The Three Cāng dictionaries state:
"From the ancient past to the coming present is called Zhòu."
The Shuōwén dictionary says:
"The utmost reach covered by boats and carriages is Zhòu."
"Length"
means increase.
"Beginning"
means start.
Although Zhòu has increase in length,
one still does not know where its start and end reach.
【Seven】【Annotation】Death and life, coming and going,
all occur abruptly and spontaneously,
with no cause,
hence their forms remain unseen.
【Commentary】"Going out and coming in,"
(refers to) life and death.
It is said that one goes out and comes in through life and death,
hence there is the term "going out and coming in."
Delving into the principles of nature and reason,
ultimately, there is no visible form of a place from which one goes out or comes in.
【八】【Note】Tiānmén is
the collective name for all things.
Calling it the Gate of Heaven
is like saying the gate through which all wonders pass.
【Commentary】Heaven refers to what is natural;
what is natural
means having no origin.
It is said that all beings have no source,
their reason is unfathomable,
thus nature serves as the gateway to creation.
【Nine】【Annotation】Death and life, coming in and going out,
all occur suddenly and spontaneously,
with no one acting as their agent.
Yet there is gathering and scattering, concealment and manifestation,
hence the names of coming in and going out exist;
these are merely names,
ultimately without actual coming in or going out,
so where is the door to be found?
Therefore, non-being is taken as the door.
Taking non-being as the door,
then there is no door.
【Commentary】The principle of natural spontaneity,
the gateway of creation and transformation,
merely possesses a name,
yet ultimately lacks substance.
However, all things in existence
arise from this gateway.
Hence, Guǒ Xiàng's annotation states: "Regard non-being as the gateway."
To regard non-being as the gateway
is to have no gateway at all.
【一０】【Note】Before existence comes into being,
by what means does it come to be?
Therefore, it must inherently possess itself,
how could existence be something that existence itself can possess!
【Commentary】If existence already exists,
how can it be capable of having existence?
Before existence came into being,
who gave birth to this existence?
Delving into the nature of this existence,
ultimately, there is no existence at all.
【一一】【Note】This clarifies that being cannot be made into being but exists of itself,
not that non-being can create being.
If non-being could create being,
how could it be called non-being!
【Commentary】That which has already come into being and that which has not yet come into being
are both non-existent.
This existence emerges from non-existence,
but it is not to say that this non-existence can generate existence.
If non-existence were to generate existence,
how could it be called non-existence?
【一二】【Note】If there were truly nothing, then nothing would persist.
Nothingness persists as nothing,
thus it becomes clear that existence arises abruptly on its own.
【Commentary】Without inquiring into the hundred negations and the four propositions,
all is nonexistent,
hence it is called "utterly without being."
【13】【Comment】Allow it to live naturally without forcing life.
【Commentary】The sage of profound virtue,
who silently aligns with truth and principle,
conceals his spirit and hides his wisdom—

【七】【注】In the ancestral temple, it is used for feasting and banquets;
behind the screen or in the restroom, it serves for relieving oneself.
When one relieves oneself there,
then the purpose of the ancestral temple is shifted to the screen or restroom.
Thus, the shift of right and wrong,
now here, now there,
who can hold it constant!
Therefore, the perfect person, by following and riding along with it, achieves balance.

◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Having life,
is like dust;
is the accumulation and retention of dust;
then to exchange life for death,
is it not called shifting this?
Although,
once life exists,
like the mutual attachment of the spleen and calf,
if dispersed, death ensues,
and thus it inherently cannot be dispersed;
those who have life also have death,
like the ancestral temple having its resting place,
they rely on each other to form;
and this is called shifting this,
thus considering life as disturbance,
death as return,
is seeing oneself as a burden.
Those who equate life and death,
have no more talk of right and wrong, name and reality.
Considering life as a burden,
inevitably there remains a view of self,
and riding on this to establish right and wrong, name and reality,
then disputes over wisdom and folly, honor and disgrace arise in chaos.
Shifting this,
ultimately there is what cannot be shifted,
which is why life becomes ●.
"Sōu" is read with a retained pronunciation.

Let us often speak of shifting "this."
It takes life as its foundation [one],
and knowledge as its teacher [two],
thereby riding upon right and wrong [three];
indeed, there are names and realities [four],
and it takes oneself as the substance [five];
it makes others consider it their integrity [six],
and thereby uses death to repay integrity [seven].
If it is so,
then it regards employment as wisdom,
and non-employment as folly,
thorough understanding as reputation,
and poverty as disgrace [eight].
Shifting "this"—
it is the people of today [nine],

【一】【注】The transformations of things,
at no moment are they not generating life,
and where life exists, all is rooted in the fundamental.
【Commentary】Those who can forget life and death,
are without right and wrong.
It is only because of clinging to life
that they insist on what is right.
If one must be able to renounce life,
then where can "right" be placed?
Thus, we know that shifting "right" is rooted in life.
【二】【Note】Though what is known differs,
each follows their own understanding.
【Three】【Comment】Those who ride upon right and wrong,
have no right and wrong.
【Commentary】Because of the mind that knows through learning,
the mind employs the function of distinguishing right from wrong.
How could one know that those who invert right and wrong through learned knowledge actually have no sense of right or wrong at all!
【Four】【Annotation】The names and realities of things,
indeed each possesses its own.
【Commentary】All things in their multitude,
are entirely illusory;
like straw dogs, the myriad phenomena—
how can names and realities be applied!
Those who are misguided
claim that names and realities are definitively existent.
【Five】【Annotation】Zhì,
is the master.
Each thing considers itself to be right,
and sufficient (two) to be the arbiter of right and wrong.
【Explanation】Zhì,
means lord.
Deludedly clinging to names and realities,
one then uses oneself as the arbiter of names and realities and contends over right and wrong.
【Six】【Annotation】Everyone considers themselves to be right,
thus none can communicate.
【Commentary】Integrity is
the ultimate moral conduct.
Since people are confused about names and realities,
and also mired in disputes over right and wrong,
it leads to those without true understanding
stubbornly clinging to empty reputations as their integrity.
【Seven】【Annotation】When one holds fast to it,
it is not true liberation.
【Commentary】They uphold their sense of right and wrong to form their aspirations and integrity,
steadfast and unyielding,
determined to hold fast to them even unto death.
【Explanatory Text】"Thus using death to repay integrity" Cháng Liàng's commentary.
The Guangya states:
"repay,"
means to require,
to reciprocate.
It is considered that one kills oneself to establish a reputation,
integrity is achieved and the body perishes,
hence it is said to use death to repay integrity.
【Eight】【Annotation】Unable to be at peace with whatever situation one encounters.
【Commentary】To regard ostentation as wisdom,
and concealment of one's traces as folly,
thorough understanding as honor and fame,
and poverty and obscurity as shame and disgrace—
if it is so,
how can one unify poverty and success, honor and disgrace?
【Explanatory Text】"For knowing" is pronounced as zhì.
【Nine】【Annotation】The people of the primordial age,
had neither right nor wrong,

【Commentary】Those who stubbornly cling to names and realities,
shift and stagnate in right and wrong,
embody the superficial deceit of a decadent age—
such are the people of the present time.
How could they be the sincere, harmonious, and unadorned scholars of high antiquity!
【一０】【Note】They share in common what they agree upon.
【Commentary】The cicada and the sparrow, two creatures,
regard the overgrown weeds as correct.
The two creatures share the same correctness,
yet this does not constitute universal insight.
Those who shift their correctness,
are thus of the same kind.
The cicada agrees with the dove,
the dove agrees with the cicada,
hence it is said: agreement in agreement.

If you tread on a stranger's foot in the market,
you apologize with polite excuses;
if it's your elder brother, you show affection with a gentle demeanor;

the highest ritual is not treating others as outsiders,
the highest righteousness is not distinguishing between things,
the highest wisdom does not involve scheming,
the highest benevolence shows no partiality,

【Six】【Annotation】Knowledge comes after contemplation,
