Eliminate the turmoil of aspirations,
untangle the delusions of the mind,
remove the burdens of virtue,
and clear the obstructions of the Way.
Nobility, wealth, prominence, dignity, fame, and profit—these six are
the turmoil of aspirations.
Appearance, movement, expression, reasoning, temperament, and intention—these six are
the delusions of the mind.
Aversion, desire, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—these six are
the burdens of virtue.
Withdrawal, approach, acceptance, giving, knowledge, and ability—these six are
the obstructions of the Way.
If these four sets of six do not stir within the breast, one becomes upright;
upright, one becomes tranquil;
tranquil, one becomes clear;
clear, one becomes empty;
empty, one becomes non-active and yet there is nothing that is not done.

To act out of inevitability is called virtue;
to act without anything not being of the self is called order;
names are opposite, but realities are in accord.

【13】【Comment】The eye's ability to see is not

then such knowing is artificial.

such is his prowess.

Thus, being honored brings him no joy,
being insulted stirs no anger—
only those in harmony with Heaven’s essence achieve this.
When anger emerges yet no anger is felt,
then anger arises from non-anger;
when action emerges yet no action is taken,
then action springs from non-action.
To desire tranquility, one must calm the breath;
to embody spirit, one must follow the heart—
this is purposeful practice.
To act appropriately, one must act through inevitability;
the category of inevitability
is the path of the sage.
【一】【注】Makeup,
is used to adorn one's appearance.
Since the appearance of those punished by amputation is already damaged and incomplete,
they no longer harbor concerns about beauty or ugliness in their hearts,
therefore they discard and abandon it.
【Commentary】Jiè means
amputation.
Yí means
to discard.
Huà means
adornment.
Adorning with solemn attire and ornaments
originally serves for dignified appearance.
For a person who has suffered amputation,
with a maimed and damaged form,
matters of praise and blame, honor and disgrace
no longer remain in their heart,
hence they discard and abandon them.
【Explanation Text】"介" is pronounced as jiè.
Guǒ's commentary states:
It means amputation of the feet.
Another pronunciation is gǔ xiá fǎn.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means solitary.
Cuī's version writes it as wù.
"拸画" is pronounced chǐ huà fǎn,
also pronounced tā,
and also yǔ zhǐ fǎn.
The original text also writes it as yí.
Sīmǎ's commentary states:
Huà,
refers to tools for adorning appearance;
without feet,
thus no longer caring for them.
Another interpretation:
Yí,
means to depart from.
Cuī's commentary states:
Yí huà,
means not constrained by rules and standards.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Guǒ's annotation says,
huà,
is used to adorn appearance,
since the appearance of an amputee is already damaged,
they no longer hold beauty or ugliness in mind,
hence discarding and abandoning it.
However, speaking of being indifferent to praise or blame,
it seems inappropriate to refer to appearance.
Cuī's commentary states,
chǐ huà,
means not constrained by rules and standards.
This should be followed.
In the "Hànshū" biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, it says "tān yǐ lùlí,"
with Shǐ Gǔ's annotation:
Tān,
means to indulge oneself freely.
This is the meaning of the character "拸".
In the sixth year of Duke Huán, the "Gǔliáng Zhuàn" says "yǐ qí huà wǒ,"
while the "Gōngyáng Zhuàn" writes it as "huà wǒ,"
with Hé Xiū's annotation:
Acting beyond propriety is called huà.
This is the meaning of the character "画".
It seems that once a person has their feet amputated,
they no longer care for themselves,
indifferent to both criticism and praise,
hence not constrained by rules and standards.
"不复" is pronounced fú yòu fǎn.
【二】【注】Having nothing to cling to in life,
one thus does not fear death.
【Explanation】Xūmǐ are
those who are conscripted for labor.
The children of wealthy families naturally value their own lives,
while servants and slaves do not hold their lives in high regard.
Since they do not cherish themselves,
they climb to dangerous heights without fear.
【Explanation Text】"Xūmǐ" Simǎ states:
a person punished with penal servitude.
Another says:
a person with a disability.
Cuī states:
castration punishment.
【Three】【Comment】They do not recognize what others hold dear.
【Commentary】"餽",
some versions also use the character "愧",
and it is read according to the character used.
Returning to one's inherent nature,
all things are accomplished through mutual assistance,
without abandoning oneself to imitate others,
thus neglecting the expression of gratitude and apology,
which is to forget the principles of human relationships.
Take, for example, the hands and feet,
or various utensils,
which serve and support each other—
how could there be a need for gratitude or reliance among them!
【Transliteration】"Fù" is pronounced as fú,
while Xú pronounces it with fú and yòu as the initial and final.
"Xí" is pronounced as xí.
"Bù kuì" has the pronunciation of qí and kuì as initials.
According to the Guangya dictionary,
it means to give or leave behind.
Another pronunciation is kuì.
The Yuánjiā version writes it as kuì.
"And forgetting others" refers to
the concept of reviewing or warming up.
Xí means
to be accustomed to or familiar with.
For someone who is accustomed to something,
even if it's a minor matter,
they hold it dear.
Now, when one reviews what others are familiar with,
and has already gained it,
but does not return or give it back,
this is the utmost foolishness of not acquiring what others are accustomed to.
Without the sentiment of mutual interaction,
it is called forgetting others.
◎Jiā Shìfù commented:
Fēiyù,
commonly interpreted as praise and blame.
This refers to criticizing its simplicity.
External praise and blame,
disregarding life and death,
is forgetting oneself;
reviewing and being accustomed without giving back,
is forgetting others.
The Shuowen dictionary states:
Zhé,
means to lose one's breath in speech.
Xí,
refers to speech that is trembling or fearful.
Fù xí,
means when someone speaks in a submissive manner to lower themselves before me, and I respond in kind.
Zhèng Kāngchéng's annotation on the Shiyu Rites:
Kuì,
is akin to returning,
and giving objects to spirits or people is called kuì.
Giving objects to people is called kuì,
and using words to address someone is also called kuì.
Reviewing and being accustomed without giving back,
is forgetting distinctions of nobility and baseness.
Forgetting others and forgetting oneself,
then one harmonizes with the natural balance.
The interpretation that pronounces it as xí,
meaning to be accustomed to,
is incorrect.
【Four】【Annotation】Without human emotions,
one naturally becomes a heavenly person.
【Commentary】Following the nature of the Heavenly Way,
forgetting the emotions of the human way,
thus harmonizing with the principle of naturalness.
【五】【注】Those with maimed bodies or in bondage still share in the harmony of heaven,
how much more so does the natural harmony of heaven itself!
【Commentary】Being in harmony with the heavenly equanimity,
one forgets both adversity and favor.
Thus, when treated with respect, one does not feel joy;
when insulted or slighted, one does not feel anger.
【Explanation】"Wǔ zhī": wǔ is pronounced as wáng fǔ with a reverse tone.
【Six】【Annotation】This is the idea that non-being cannot produce being, and being cannot give birth.
【Commentary】Those who can express anger or take action,
are not those who do not act or feel no anger,
hence they arise from a state of no anger and no action.
Therefore, it is understood that action is fundamentally non-action,
and anger is fundamentally non-anger.
One who can embody this principle,
thus endures insults without becoming angry.
【Seven】【Annotation】When the vital energy is balanced, one attains tranquility;
when principles are fulfilled and the heart is compliant, the ultimate spiritual achievement is reached;
acting out of inevitability ensures that all actions are appropriate.
Therefore, the sage takes this as the Way,
how could one seek inaction beyond the realm of the indistinct and elusive!
【Commentary】Yuán (緣) means
to follow.
To still the grasping mind,
one must regulate will and breath;
the divine transformation of spiritual work
begins with surrendering to the heart's nature.
To harmonize with the realm of action and align with principle,
one must further yield to unavoidable circumstances.
Unavoidable circumstances refer to
responding only after being stirred—
matters within one's inherent duty.
Examples like these
are why the sage employs them as the correct path.
【Collation Note】(1) The characters "謵" and "讋" were originally mistakenly reversed,
and have been corrected according to the Shuōwén.
【Chapter One】【Explanatory Text】Named after a person.
Xú Wúguǐ, through Nǚ Shāng, had an audience with Wèi Wǔhóu.
Wǔhóu consoled him, saying:
"You must be weary, sir!
Having suffered the toils of the mountain forests,
you have thus deigned to visit me."
【一】【疏】His surname is Xú,
his courtesy name is Wúguǐ,
and he is a recluse.
The woman's surname is Nǚ,
her given name is Shāng,
and she is a chief minister of Wèi.
Marquis Wǔ,
the son of Marquis Wén,
is the tenth-generation descendant of Bì Wàn.
Wúguǐ wished to admonish Marquis Wǔ,
so he relied on the chief minister to gain an audience with him.
【Explanation】"Xú Wúguǐ" was a man from Mínshān,
a recluse of the state of Wèi.
The Sīmǎ version writes "Mínshān rén Xú Wúguǐ."
"Nǚ Shāng" is a person's name.
Lǐ's commentary says:
Wúguǐ and Nǚ Shāng
were both favored ministers of Wèi.
"Wèi Wǔhóu," named Jī,
was the son of Wénhóu,
and governed Ānyì.
【二】【疏】Having long dwelled in the mountains and forests,
enduring hardship, poverty, and illness,
they suddenly could humble their aspirations,
blending into the mundane world,
their hearts joyful,
there is comfort and relief.
【Explanatory Text】"Wǔhóu láo zhī" is read with the retroflex sound.
Only the character "láo" in "shānlín zhī láo" is read with its original pronunciation,
all others in this and the following chapter are read with the retroflex sound.
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"It is I who have toiled for you,
what toil have you had for me!
If you were to fill your cravings and desires,
and amplify your likes and dislikes,
then the true nature of life would be afflicted;
if you were to suppress your cravings and desires,
and restrain your likes and dislikes,
then your ears and eyes would be afflicted.
It is I who am to toil for you,
what toil have you had for me!
"Marquis Wǔ looked disconcerted and did not reply.
【一】【Note】Desires, preferences, likes, and dislikes,
have no distinction between internal and external.
【Commentary】"Chù" means
to depose and dismiss.
"Qiān" means
to pull back and retreat.
If the ruler is filled with excessive desires,
and his likes and dislikes grow unchecked,
then his life force and spirit will suffer from illness;
if the ruler banishes and dismisses his desires,
and withdraws from his likes and dislikes,
it will no longer bring comfort,
thus his ears and eyes will be troubled.
Therefore, I will console and comfort the ruler,
how could the ruler have any leisure to trouble me!
【Explanation】"Yíng Qí" is pronounced with the initial "shí" and tone "zhì".
The same applies below and in the annotations.
"Cháng" is pronounced with the initial "dīng" and tone "zhàng".
好: pronounced as hǔ bào fǎn.
Same for the annotations below and the following chapter.
恶: pronounced as wū lù fǎn.
Same for the annotations below and the following chapter.
黜: pronounced as chì lǜ fǎn,
meaning to dismiss or retreat.
Another version writes it as 出,
with the same pronunciation.
Simǎ's version uses 咄.
掔: pronounced as kǔ tián fǎn,
or alternatively kǒu xián fǎn.
According to the Ěryǎ,
it means firm.
Cuī states:
to lead away.
Simǎ states:
to pull or drag.
【Èr Shū】This reiterates the previous meaning.
【Three】【Comment】Do not speak of his words.
【Commentary】Chāo means
disappointed.
Since it did not meet his expectations,
he was therefore disappointed and did not respond.
【Explanation】"Chāorán" Sīmǎ [Zhuāng] says:
It means as if disheartened.
"Bù yuè" is pronounced as yuè.
The same applies to the "dà yuè" mentioned later in the text.
After a short while,
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"I have told you before,
I am skilled at judging dogs.
The lowest quality is content with a full belly and stops there,
which is the nature of a wildcat;
the medium quality appears as if gazing at the sun,
the highest quality seems to have lost itself.
My judgment of dogs,
however, is not as good as my judgment of horses.
When I judge horses,
the straight ones match the plumb line,
the curved ones match the hook,
the square ones match the square,
the round ones match the compass,
these are national-grade horses,
but they are not as good as world-class horses.
World-class horses possess innate talent,
appearing anxious as if lost,
as if having lost themselves,
horses like these
leap beyond and leave no dust behind,
one cannot tell where they are going."
Marquis Wǔ was greatly pleased and laughed.
【One】【Memorial】Having noticed the Martial Marquis was disheartened and displeased,
I attempted to speak of dogs and horses,
hoping to somewhat please his heart.
【Transcription】"Yǔ jūn" is read as yú jù fǎn.
"Wú xiàng" is read as xī xiǎng fǎn.
The following are all the same.
【二】【疏】They hold fast to their emotions and will,
only craving to eat their fill,
such is their physical form and nature,
their virtue comparable to that of a fox,
a dog of the lowest grade.
【Transcribed Text】"The inferior's substance" In one edition, the character "substance" is absent.
"Stops when full" Simǎ breaks the sentence after the character "catch,"
saying:
"The ability of the inferior to catch game."
"This is the virtue of a lí" Means greedy like a fox.
◎Yú Yuè says:
In the "Guǎngyǎ·Shì Shòu":
"Lí,"
means cat.
When a cat catches mice,
it stops once full,
hence it is said "this is the virtue of a lí."
The "Qiūshuǐ" chapter states:
Steeds like Qíjì and Huáliú,
can gallop a thousand lǐ in a day,
but cannot catch mice as well as a lí or shēng.
This is evidence from the text that "lí" refers to a cat.
The "Imperial Readings" quotes Shīzǐ saying:
Using an ox to catch mice
is not as swift as using a cat or shēng.
Zhuāngzǐ mentions "lí shēng,"
while Shīzǐ says "cat shēng,"
which are the same.
The "Shìwén" states,
"the virtue of a lí,"
means greedy like a fox,
but this misses the true meaning.
【Three】【Dispatches】With lofty and far-reaching spirit,
his gaze is like looking at the sun,
such is his physical constitution,
a dog of medium grade.
【Explanatory Text】"Shì rì" is pronounced as shì.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as shì,
stating:
"Shì rì" means gazing into the distance.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The current text writes it as "shì rì".
The old pronunciation was shì,
but it was mistakenly written as shì,
now corrected.
【Four】【Characteristics】First,
the body.
When the spirit and energy are settled and composed,
as if losing one's own body,
it is a top-grade dog.
【Interpretation】"As if losing their one" one,
refers to the body;
meaning the spirit does not stir,
as if without their own body.
【Five】【Memorial】Dogs have three grades,
horses have several ranks,
yet the skill of judging dogs
is not as good as judging horses.
Wǔhóu was mediocre and shallow,
so he used this to seize the moment,
hoping to delight him,
in the hope that he might return to the right path.
【六】【疏】refers to the front teeth of a horse.
【Seven】【Shū】Refers to the horse's neck.
【Eight】【Shū】Refers to the horse's head.
【九】【疏】refers to the eye of a horse.
【Explanatory Text】"Straight ones match the marking line" - Dīng Zhòng's annotation.
The following are all the same.
Sīmǎ says:
Straight,
refers to the horse's teeth;
curved,
refers to the back;
square,
refers to the head;
round,
refers to the eyes.
【一０】【Comment】The appearance matching the superior grade,
is referred to as the top-tier horses of the feudal lords' states.
【一一】【疏】Talent and virtue are inherently formed,
without the need for practice,
this is the finest steed in the world,
fit for the Son of Heaven to drive.
【Explanatory Text】"Chéngcái" is also written as 才.
It means that nature is already sufficient,
and there is no need for teaching or practice.
【一二】【疏】With eyes looking back at itself,
it appears both anxious and concerned,
its hooves moving slowly and sparsely,
yet also as if galloping away swiftly,
observing its divine aura,
it seems to forget its own body,
a talent such as this,
is the steed of the Son of Heaven.
【Explanation】"Ruò Xù" is pronounced as xù.
"Ruò Shī" is pronounced as yì.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as yì.
Lǐ's commentary says:
Xù and shī,
both describe being startled and alarmed as if flying away.
"Ruò Sàng" is pronounced with sàng.
The same applies to the note in the following chapter.
"Qí Yī" means losing one's counterpart.
【一三】【疏】Zhuó yì,
means to surpass.
It runs swiftly,
outstripping the herd of horses,
as fast as a gust of wind,
leaving dust far behind,
not trained by teaching,
thus its origin remains unknown.
【Explanation】"Chāo Yì": Lǐ gives the pronunciation as yì,
Xú gives the reverse reading as tú liè.
Cuī says:
It means to penetrate.
The "Guǎng Yǎ" says:
It means to surpass.
【一四】【Note】How could the words of a true person be modest?
Only what things themselves favor is acceptable.
【Commentary】The words hit the mark,
so laughter and joy ensued.
Xú Wúguǐ came out,
Nǚ Shāng said:
"What alone did you, sir, use to please my lord?
What I use to please my lord,
if speaking broadly, is with the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music;
if speaking specifically, is with the Metal Plates and Six Bows.
Those who served him and achieved great merits are too numerous to count,
yet my lord has never shown a smile.
Now what did you, sir, use to please my lord,
making my lord so delighted like this?"
【一】【疏】The deliberation of matters concluded,
he took his leave and departed.
Nǚ Shāng found it strange that the ruler was so cheerful,
hence he inquired whether there were no ghosts.
【Explanatory Text】"To explain" as the character reads,
also pronounced with the initial sharp sound.
The following are all the same.
Sīmǎ's version uses "yuè".
【二】【疏】The Poetry, History, Rites, and Music,
the Six Classics.
The "Jīnbǎn Liùtāo,"
a chapter title from the Zhōushū,
some say it is a secret prophecy.
Originally, some versions use the character "tāo,"
read according to the character used,
it is said to be the military strategies of Tàigōng,
referring to the six tāo of civil, military, tiger, leopard, dragon, and dog.
Héng,
means distant;
cóng,
means near.
Wǔhóu loved martial affairs and disliked civil arts,
hence he considered military strategies as cóng (near),
and the Six Classics as héng (distant).
【Translated Text】"Cóng Shuō" is pronounced as zǐ róng fǎn.
"Jīn Bǎn" is also written as "bǎn",
pronounced as bó bǎn fǎn,
and also read as the regular character.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Now it is written as "bǎn".
"Liù Tāo" is pronounced as tù dāo fǎn.
Sīmǎ and Cuī state:
Jīn Bǎn and Liù Tāo,
are both chapter titles from the Zhōu Shū.
Some say:
they are secret prophecies.
It is also written as Liù Tāo,
referring to the Tài Gōng Liù Tāo,
namely Wén, Wǔ, Hǔ, Bào, Lóng, Quǎn.
【Three】【Comment】This is merely amusing the quail with bells and drums,
hence the sorrow.
◎Qìng Fān case: Wénxuǎn Guō Jǐngchún's "Yóuxiān Shī" annotation quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
to open the teeth,
means to laugh.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Transcription】"Lè" is pronounced as luò.
Same at the end of the chapter.
"Yàn" is read with the first tone in the fourth tone.
【Four】【Memorials】 Serving Lord Wǔ,
he exhausted loyalty and integrity,
sometimes advising on what to adopt or reject,
his achievements were clearly manifest.
Such individuals,
are too numerous to count,
yet our lord never opened his mouth to offer a slight smile.
Now, what method do you possess,
that has finally made our lord so delighted and pleased?
【Explanation】"Our Lord's Delight" is pronounced yuè.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "讖" has been amended according to the original version of the Interpretive Text.
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"I merely told him about my skill in judging dogs and horses."
【One】【Memorial】Medicine knows no distinction of noble or base;
healing an ailment makes it good.
Hence, I straightforwardly inform even dogs and horses,
with no other explanation.
Nǚ Shāng said:
"Is it really so?"
【One】【Memorial】Would one address dogs and horses directly like this?
I found his method shallow,
hence this question.
He said:
"Have you not heard of the exiles of Yuè?
After being away from their country for a few days,
they rejoice upon seeing anyone they know;
after being away for ten days or a month,
they rejoice upon seeing anyone they had previously seen in their country;
and after a full year,
they rejoice upon seeing anyone who merely resembles a human.
Is it not true that the longer they are away from people,
the deeper becomes their longing for them?
As for those who flee into desolate places,
where weeds grow thick along the paths of weasels,
and they tread through the empty spaces,
they rejoice at the sound of human footsteps;
how much more would they rejoice
at the voices of their own brothers and relatives beside them!
【一】【注】Each reflects on what their innate nature delights in.
【Commentary】Having traveled far from the state,
there are those who have been exiled—
some for violating laws and regulations,
others for suffering under harsh governance.
Having just left their homeland,
only a few days into the journey,
they suddenly encounter an acquaintance,
how could their joy and relief be in doubt!
This is the beginning of the analogy.
【Explanation】"The Exile of Yuè": Yuè means
distant.
Sīmǎ explains,
an exile is
someone guilty who is seen being banished.
"Shù rì": the pronunciation is as indicated.
【二】【疏】As days and months passed by,
the longing for home gradually deepened.
Though they were not acquaintances,
having seen an old friend from their homeland in a foreign land,
they rejoiced upon meeting them.
【Three】【Notes】When each obtains what they desire, there are no thoughts;
no thoughts then one forgets the reason for their joy.
【Commentary】Having been away from the state for a full year,
as the distance from home grows,
one naturally feels joy upon seeing someone who resembles a fellow villager.
Is it not because the farther one is from home, the deeper the longing becomes?
This is analogous to Wǔhóu's fondness for dogs and horses,
having long been detached from affairs of governance.
It is like a person far from home
suddenly hearing familiar chatter and laughter.
【Explanation】"And the period" pronounced as jī.
【Four】【Annotation】Having attained the ultimate joy,
one is greatly delighted.
【Commentary】"柱" means
to block up.
"踉" refers to
a good person.
"跫" is
the sound of footsteps.
In times of violent turmoil,
when famine prevails,
fleeing from the turbulent waves,
one takes refuge in deserted gardens and dwellings,
where only wild grasses and weeds remain,
blocking the gates and courtyards,
with monkeys, apes, weasels, and other creatures
making paths through them.
As for the halls and human dwellings,
they stand empty and vast, silent and still.
At such moments,
the longing for home grows ever stronger,
and if one suddenly hears the footsteps of another person,
it brings spontaneous joy.
How much more so if it were the laughter and conversation of brothers and close relatives!
This is to draw another analogy.
【Transcription】"Fú táo" is written as "xún yě" in the Simǎ version.
"Xū kōng zhě" Simǎ states:
An old collapsed tomb site is considered empty and void.
"Lí" is pronounced lì xī fǎn.
"Huò" is pronounced tú diào fǎn.
Some versions have ●,
same.
柱》诛矩反。
司马云：
塞也。
《乎鼪》音生，
又音姓。
《鼬》由救反。
《之逕》本亦作径。
司马云：
径，
道也。
本又作迹。
元嘉本作迭，
徐音逸。
崔云：
迭，
迹。
◎庆藩案藜，
蒿也。
藋即今所谓灰藋也。
尔雅拜商藋，
郭注：
商藋，
似藜。
案藜藋皆生于不治之地，
其高过人，
必排之而后得进，
故史记仲尼弟子传曰排藜藋。
此言柱乎鼪鼬之逕，
亦极谓其高也。
《良位其空》司马云：
良，
良人，
谓巡虚者也。
位其空，
谓处虚空之间也。
良，
或作踉，
音同。
◎卢文弨曰：
今书良作踉。
◎家世父曰：
释文良位其空，
司马云，
良人，
谓巡虚者也。
良或作踉。
据秋水篇跳梁乎井干之上，
一本作跳踉。
潘安仁射雉赋已踉蹡而徐来。
玉篇：
疾行。
此云藜藋鼪鼬之逕，
有空隙焉，
跄踉处乎其中。
说文：
跄，

【One】【Memorial】My life has been one of poverty and lowliness,

how could I desire to covet food and drink merely to sustain myself?

Rather, I intend to toil for Your Majesty.
The lord said:

He said:

【One】【Memorial】Desires and cravings know no satiety,

The Marquis Wǔ said:

【One】【Memorial】Asked about what he said,
what meaning was intended.
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"Heaven and earth nourish all as one.
Being on high does not make one tall,
nor does being below make one short.
You alone, as the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
cause suffering to the people of the whole state,
to indulge your ears, eyes, nose, and mouth.
The spirit does not consent to this.
The spirit
prefers harmony and detests excess;
excess
is a malady,
thus it brings toil.
Yet you alone are afflicted by this malady—

【一】【注】He did not consider him a ruler and thus allowed him to be unrestrained without limit.
【Commentary】Heaven and Earth, the two primal forces,

things rely on them for sustenance,
universally and without bias,
not so that rulers may indulge in extravagance.
These are all expressions denying that spirits would trouble a ruler.
【二】【注】In this way,
it violates the balance of heaven and earth.
【Commentary】To ascend to high positions and become a gentleman,
one should not take pleasure in it as a lasting state;
to dwell in lowly status as a commoner,
one should not endure hardship as a brief phase.
Yet, to boast solely of the might of ten thousand chariots,
and inflict suffering upon the people of this nation,
greed for colors, sounds, fragrances, and flavors,
to indulge the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth—
this already goes against the will of Heaven and Earth,
and I privately believe that you, sir, should not adopt such ways.

Xú Wúguǐ said:
"It will not do.
Loving the people
is the beginning of harming them;
advocating righteousness and ceasing warfare
is the foundation of creating warfare.
If you proceed from this, my lord,
you will likely not succeed.
All accomplishments of good
are instruments of evil;
though you practice humaneness and righteousness,
it will almost certainly be artificial!
Forms inevitably create forms,
accomplishments inevitably bring boasting,
change inevitably leads to external conflict.
You must not deploy your troops in grand arrays between watchtowers,
nor station foot soldiers and chariots in the palace courtyards,
do not harbor rebellious thoughts in your gains,
do not use cleverness to overcome others,
do not use schemes to overcome others,
do not use warfare to overcome others.
As for killing other people's soldiers and citizens,
annexing other people's lands,
to nourish our selfish desires and our spirits—
in such warfare, who can be said to be good?
Wherein lies the victory?
If you, my lord, cannot desist,
then cultivate the sincerity within your breast,
respond to the disposition of heaven and earth without disturbing it.
Then the people will already be freed from death—
what use would you have, my lord, for the cessation of warfare?"
【一】【注】The traces of loving the people,
are esteemed by the people.
Esteeming it as love,

【Two】【Commentary】To act for righteousness makes one's reputation prominent,

and competition arising leads to the loss of genuineness.
Between father and son, ruler and subject,

【Commentary】The benevolence of partial affection,
the righteousness of judging what is wrong,
the achievements of halting military actions,
the endeavors of cultivating culture—
once these traces become evident,

begin from this point.
【Three】【Annotation】It is only by acting through non-action that accomplishment is achieved.

"Dài" means

【Four】【Annotation】When excellence is established beforehand,

【Commentary】When good deeds are accomplished beforehand,
and their beautiful traces become evident,
then people will vie to follow them,
thus becoming instruments for eliminating evil.
【五】【Note】The people will then follow with pretense,

【Six】【Annotation】Benevolence and righteousness have forms,

【Seven】【Annotation】Achievement then becomes manifest.

【Eight】【Annotation】Losing its inherent constancy.

but is a change forced by circumstances.
Since there is already artificial self-praise,
how can there not be conflict!

【二】【注】At sunrise, I venture out;
at sunset, I rest.
【Subcommentary】Within the six directions,
it refers to the realm of clamor and dust.
Dizziness ailment,
refers to vertigo, confusion, and disorientation.
It says that I have traveled little into the realm of the ultimate Way,
dwelling with my heart beyond the dust and grime,
yet I suffer from dizziness,
and have not been able to embody the truth.
Fortunately, the sage teaches me to cultivate the Way,
working by day and resting by night,
riding the sun to roam freely,
thus settling peacefully and wandering carefree in the world.
Originally, some wrote it with the character "zhuān,"
meaning to ride the renewal of the sun to transform.
【Explanation】"予少" is read as shī zhào fǎn.
"瞀" is read as mò dòu fǎn,
Guō's pronunciation is wù.
Lǐ says:
It describes the appearance of dizziness.
Sīmǎ says:
瞀,
should be read as ●,
meaning dizziness and ●.
"長者" is read as dīng zhàng fǎn.
"乘日之車" Sīmǎ says:
It means using the sun as a chariot.
In the Yuánjiā edition, "車" is written as "居".
【Three】【Comment】To govern the world,
nothing surpasses allowing oneself to act freely;
once one acts freely,
how can things disturb them?
Thus, I do nothing, and the people transform themselves naturally.
【Commentary】Recovery means
removal.
The illness of falsehood and delusion,
has long been cured,
allowing one to roam the mind beyond material things,
whether governing the self or the state,
how could there be any difference!
Things and the self merge into one,
hence there is no need for action.
【Explanation】"Shǎo quán" is pronounced with the initial "qī" and final "quán" in reverse.
Lǐ Yún states:
It means to remove.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: The commentary in Wénxuǎn by Pān Ānrén in "Xiánjū Fù" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"Quán,"
means to remove.
The explanation text is missing.
"Qiě fù" is pronounced with the initial "fú" and final "yòu" in reverse.
Huángdì said:
"Governing the world
is truly not something for someone like you.
Nevertheless,
I ask you about governing the world."
The young boy declined.
【一】【注】Affairs arise from the people.
【二】【注】Allowing the people to attain
must have a way.
【Commentary】To govern and nurture the common people,
is truly not the primary concern of the sage.
Although the principle is such,
it is still requested to be shown with essential words.
【Three】【Memorials】There is nothing to be said.
Huángdì asked again.
The young lad said:
"Governing the world—
how is it any different from herding horses?
Just get rid of what harms the horses, that's all!"
【一】【疏】Earnestly inviting the young boy.
【二】【注】Horses suffer harm from excess.
【Explanation】Harming the horse refers to matters beyond one's proper duties.
In governing oneself, nothing takes precedence over maintaining one's proper role,
hence the methods of herding horses
can be applied to nurturing the people.
Since the question was earnestly posed,
I offer this response in brief.
【Transcription】"Qù qí" is pronounced with the rising tone of Lǚ.
The same applies below and in the annotations.
Huángdì bowed twice and kowtowed,
addressed him as the Celestial Master, and withdrew.
【一】【注】If the master of heaven acts naturally and removes his excess,
then the Great Wěi will arrive.
【Commentary】Suddenly comprehending the sage's words,
thus the body and mind feel love and reverence,
withdrawing from what is beyond one's duty,
reaching the Great Wěi,
it is the decree of the natural Way,
is it not in our master!
Knowledgeable scholars find no joy without the changes of thought and consideration,
eloquent scholars find no joy without the order of discourse and debate,
discerning scholars find no joy without matters of scrutiny and inquiry,
all are confined by external things.
【一】【疏】In an era fraught with perils,
times beset by calamities and upheavals,
those with wisdom and strategies
ponder and deliberate deeply.
If circumstances do not align with their ideals,
they find no joy in it.
【Explanation】"Zhi Shi" is pronounced with the meaning of wisdom.
"Bu Le" is pronounced as luò.
The following "Bu Le" and its annotation are the same.
【Èr Shū】Their arguments were as diverse as the rivers and streams,
their words flowed as smoothly as a greased wheel;
without the threads of discourse,
there was no joy or delight.
【Three】【Memorials】The astute and the discerning,
those with keen insight,
if not allowed to exchange inquiries between host and guest,
with words sharp and overwhelming,
would find no pleasure in it.
【Explanatory Text】"The Scrutinizing Scholar" Lǐ Yún states:
Scrutinizing,
means to discern.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
In the Book of Rites, chapter on Village Drinking Ceremonies, it says "to scrutinize according to the time,"
Zhèng's annotation states:
Scrutinize,
is like being meticulous,
a stern and severe appearance.
In Laozi, "the common people are meticulous,"
Héshàng Gōng's annotation states:
Meticulous,
means urgent and hasty.
Thus, scrutinizing carries a connotation of strictness and urgency,
hence taking delight in being overbearing and interrogative.
Lǐ Yún states,
scrutinizing,
means to discern,
which overlaps with the preceding mention of the knowledgeable scholar.
"Overbearing" Lǐ Yún states:
Refers to being domineering.
"Interrogative" is pronounced as xìn.
Guǎngyǎ states:
It means to inquire.
Also pronounced as suì,
and also as jùn.
One version uses "explain."
【Four】【Commentary】When one cannot find contentment within and instead seeks joy in external things,
they can thus be confined (two).
Therefore, if each is confined by what they delight in,
then all things will come of their own accord without being summoned,
not by force.
【Subcommentary】These several individuals,
each had their own biases and obstructions,
failing to comprehend the great principles,
and were all confined by material things.
【Transcription】"Jiē Yòu" pronounced as yòu.
"Fēi Qiáng" with the pronunciation qiáng according to the fǎnqiè spelling.
【Collation Notes】(1) The quoted text in the Que Wu edition, as well as the accounts by Wén Chéng and Zhāng Sān, all use the word "decline".
(2) Zhào Jiàn Yì's edition lacks the four characters "gù kě yòu yě" (hence can be confined).
Those who summon the world rise at court,
those who benefit the people glory in office,
those with sinewy strength take pride in overcoming difficulties,
the courageous exert themselves in times of calamity,
warriors delight in battle,
recluses cling to fame,
legalists broaden governance,
ritualists reverence demeanor,
and advocates of benevolence and righteousness value social interactions.
If farmers have no fields to tend, they feel unsettled;
if merchants have no market affairs, they feel unsettled.
Commoners are diligent when they have daily work;
artisans are vigorous when they possess skillful tools.
If wealth is not accumulated, the greedy worry;
if power and influence are not supreme, the boastful grieve.
Those obsessed with power and material things delight in change;
encountering their time, they find their use,
unable to remain inactive.
These all follow along with the times,
not transcending change through detachment from things.
They drive their bodies and natures,
submerging them among the myriad things,
never turning back their entire lives—
alas, how pitiable!
【一】【疏】To recommend the loyal and virtuous,
to attract men of talent and character,
is how the court may flourish.
【Transcription】"Xīng cháo" is read as zhí yáo fǎn.
【Èr Shū】governed the four classes of people,
being very capable of striking a balance,
such individuals with astute competence and proper boundaries
are fit to bring honor to official positions.
【Explanation】"Zhōng Mín" Lǐ Yún said:
It means governing the people well.
【Three】【Memorials】The outstanding and stalwart men,
possessing strength like tigers,
encounter times of calamity,
are devoted to aiding the world.
【Explanation】"Jīnnán" is read as nǎi dàn fǎn.
【Four】【Memorials】The warriors of martial prowess,
the resolute and decisive individuals,
rise with vigor and heroism,
to cleanse and eliminate calamities.
【Five】【Categories】Those whose passions delight in arms and warfare,
whose ambitions lie with blades and weapons,
such individuals
find joy in waging battles.
【Six】【Neglect】Coarse food and plain hemp garments,
a haggard appearance,
with no care for rest or lodging,
focusing solely on reputation.
【Explanation】"枯槁" is pronounced with "苦老" as the fanqie.
Same applies in the later chapter.
means accumulated over time.
Wáng explains:
Those who are withered and austere take this as their lifelong amusement,
what they rest and dwell on
is merely fame.
◎Yú Yuè says:
"宿" should be read as "缩".
In the "Guóyǔ: Chǔyǔ", it says "缩於財用則匱",
and in the "Zhànguó Cè: Qín Cè", "缩劍將自誅",
with Wéi Zhāo and Gāo Yòu both annotating:
means to take.
Thus, "枯槁之士缩名"
means to take fame.
The explanation text says,
means accumulated over time,
which does not fit well with the meaning.
It further quotes Wáng saying "其所寢宿唯名而已",
which is even more convoluted.
This is because it fails to recognize that "宿" is a borrowed character for "缩".
【Seven】【Memorials】Those who practice criminal law,
are attentive to statutes and regulations,
punishing evil and encouraging good,
their governance (method) [broad] (second) is extensive.
【Transcription】"Guǎng Zhì" is read with the tone "zhí lì fǎn".
【Eight】【Disciplines】The rituals that regulate refinement,
cultivate a dignified and respectful demeanor.
【Nine】【Annotation】Scholars differ to such an extent,
that those who take on their roles must not alter their principles.
【Commentary】When the world is in turmoil,
and the times meet with opportunity,
one should practice benevolence and righteousness to establish a reputation for meritorious deeds in such moments.
【Explanation】"Guì jì" refers to matters of alliances and meetings.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
"Guì jì"
means mutual interactions,
where the application of benevolence and righteousness operates within the context of these interactions.
Zhèng Kāngchéng's annotation on the Doctrine of the Mean in the Book of Rites states:
"rén" (person),
is read as in "xiāng rén ǒu zhī rén" (the 'rén' in mutual human connection),
meaning words of mutual inquiry and care with human intent.
Thus, when people come together, benevolence becomes apparent,
which is why men of benevolence and righteousness value social interactions.
The explanation in the text,
"guì jì",
referring to matters of alliances and meetings,
is incorrect.
【一０】【Note】When abilities align, affairs align,
thus they can be compared.
【Commentary】Compare,
harmonious joy.
In ancient times, markets were established around wells,
hence they were called marketplaces.
If one deviates from their fundamental duties,
emotions will inevitably become discordant.
【Translated Text】"Not compare" is read as pí zhì fǎn,
the same below.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Compare,
is interchangeable with manage.
The commentary on the Zhou Guan Sui Shi states:
the earlier Zheng interpretations all treat it as manage.
This is correct.
In the Discourses of the State of Lǔ, it says, "You will manage the administration of the Jì family,"
and also says,
"At night, manage his household affairs,"
Wěi's annotations both state:
Manage,
means to govern.
Farmers only govern matters of weeding and clearing,
hence if there are no weeding and clearing tasks, they do not manage;
merchants only govern market affairs,
hence if there are no market affairs, they do not manage.
Guō's annotation says,
"If abilities are the same, then affairs are the same,
therefore they compare."
This interprets it according to the original character's reading,
which is incorrect.
"Merchants" is pronounced as gǔ.
【One One】【Comment】When one's undertakings align with their aspirations, they are thus encouraged.
【Commentary】The multitude of people each have their duties,
day and night expressing their true feelings,
thus they encourage themselves.
【一二】【Note】If the task is not done skillfully, one becomes negligent.
【Commentary】Strong,
means flourishing.
The various artisans and their skills,
each have their tools and implements,
if one can follow their nature,
then affairs will flourish.
【Explanation】"Then vigorous" Lǐ Yí said:
vigorous,
means swift.
"Then lazy" pronounced as tuò.
【一三】【Note】Things find joy in obtaining what they desire.
【Explanation】"Desired" is pronounced with the tone "shì zhì fǎn".
"And enjoyed" is pronounced with the tone "yīn luò".
【一四】【疏】尤，
means extreme.
Those who are greedy and competitive,
must amass wealth to satisfy their nature;
those who are boastful and vain,
rely on power and influence to please their hearts;
if matters go against their feelings,
then sorrow and grief arise from this.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The annotations to Jiǎ Chángshā's (i.e., Jiǎ Yì's) "Rhapsody on the Owl" and Ruǎn Sìzōng's (i.e., Ruǎn Jí's) "Yǒng Huái Poems" in the Wénxuǎn both quote Sīmǎ's explanation:
夸 (kuā),
means empty reputation.
The explanatory text is missing.
【一五】【Note】Power arises from changing circumstances.
【Commentary】When calamity arises, power and influence become particularly prominent,
thus those who rely on force to bully others delight in turmoil and disaster.
【16】 【Comment】 All these scholars,
had their times to be employed;
when the time came for their use, they could not but act.
If they did not encounter the right era,
then even if they wished to employ themselves,
how could it be possible!
Therefore, nobility and lowliness are not constant.
【Commentary】The various scholars of former times,
encountering the mandates of their era,
found their sentiments shifting with circumstances,
thus they could not remain inactive.
【一七】【Note】The capabilities of scholars,
each have their limits,
just as the four seasons cannot be altered.
Therefore, when things are in their proper time,
and follow their natural order,
then each has its use.
Thus, following the year ensures the sequence of seasons,
altering nature leads to the loss of things' essence,
and treating things as things yet not truly recognizing them as such—
how is this not destruction!
【Commentary】These four,
are in sequence.
As for the conduct of scholars,
it can have strengths and weaknesses,
their employment or dismissal depends on the times,
all have an order,
comparable to the seasonal progression of heat and cold,
which does not change the nature of things.
Not changing things,
means still not altering the inherent nature of things.
【一八】【Note】Not adhering to the ability of a single school,
but going to all directions to seek timely advantages,
hence there are those who crawl back in submission,
which is the reason for sorrow.
【Commentary】Rushing and exhausting one's body and mind,
submerging oneself in external circumstances,
to the point of losing one's life,
unaware of turning back,
such obstinate foolishness,
is profoundly lamentable indeed!
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
Those confined by material things
are tools for practical use,
activated from within;
sometimes there is a use for them,
resources awaiting employment,
responding from without.
Nature has its dependencies,
talent has its biases,
inner and outer aspects rely on each other to form capability,
thus form and nature race together without return.
【Textual Explanation】"Yǐ yào" is read with the first tone and the second tone.
"Pú" is pronounced as fú,
and also as pú.
"Fú" is pronounced as fú,
and also with the pronunciation pú běi.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "jiào" as "yuè".
(2) The character "guǎng" is emended according to the main text.
(3) The character "xiāng" is supplemented based on the Dàozàng edition.
(4) The character "bǐ" is emended according to the main text.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"If an archer hits the target without aiming beforehand,
and we call him skilled,
then everyone under heaven would be a Yì,
is that acceptable【一】?"
【一】【注】Hitting the target without aiming,
is called an accidental hit,
not skillful archery.
If one considers mistaken hits as skillful archery,
then everyone in the world could be called Yì,
is that acceptable?
It is said to be unacceptable.
【Commentary】Aim,
refers to having a precise target.
If one shoots without any aim or target and accidentally hits something,
and is then called a skilled archer,
if this is considered skilled archery,
can it be deemed acceptable?
【Transcription】"而中" is read as Dīng Zhòng fǎn,
with the same note.
Huìzǐ said:
"It is acceptable."
【One】【Memorial】states that all under heaven are like Yì.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"If the world had no universally recognized right,
and each considered their own views to be right,
then everyone in the world would be a Yáo,
is that acceptable?"
【一】【注】If one says that hitting the mark by chance makes one an Yì,
then those who privately consider themselves right could also claim to be Yáo.
Zhuāngzǐ uses this to illustrate that accidental hitters are not Yì and self-approvers are not Yáo.
【Commentary】Each holds their own as right,
thus there is no universally accepted right.
Yet Táng Yáo was a sage,
and considered right in contrast to Jié.
If each deems their own as right,
then all would be sages,
is that acceptable?
It is said it is not.
Huìzǐ said:
"It is permissible【one】."
【一】【疏】Each advocates their own correctness,
the whole world would be like that of Yáo's reign,
such a principle exists,
yet Huì Shī's arguments are stagnant,
having words without substance.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Then the four schools of Rú, Mò, Yáng, and Bǐng,
together with you, Master, make five.
After all, which one is correct?
Or are they like Lǔ Jù?
His disciple said:
'I have acquired the Dào of our master,
I can cook with a cauldron in winter and make ice in summer.'
Lǔ Jù said:
'This is merely using yáng to summon yáng,
using yīn to summon yīn,
not what I call the Dào.
Let me show you my Dào.'
Thereupon he tuned two sè zithers,
placing one in the hall,
and one in the inner chamber.
When he plucked the gōng note on one, the gōng string on the other moved;
when he plucked the jué note, the jué string moved,
for their tones were in harmony.
But if he adjusted one string to a different pitch,
so that it didn't correspond to any of the five notes,
and plucked it,
all twenty-five strings would vibrate,
not differing in sound from before,
yet this note had become the master of all tones.
And are you perhaps like this?"
【一】【注】If all were like Yáo,
then why would the five sons have opposed each other?
【Commentary】Rú,
surnamed Zhèng,
given name Huǎn.
Mò,
given name Dí.
Yáng,
given name Zhū.
Bǐng,
styled Gōngsūn Lóng.
These four masters,
all renowned for surpassing ordinary understanding,
were world-renowned debaters.
Adding Huì Shī makes five,
each disputing the others' views,
with no certainty as to whose principles should be adopted.
If all under heaven were like Yáo,
why would these five still contend against one another?
【Text】"復相" reads as fú yòu fǎn.
【Èr】【Shū】's surname was Lǔ,
his given name was Jù,
and he lived during the early Zhōu dynasty.
It is said that in winter, he would take thousand-year-old dry ashes to bank a fire,
and within moments, flames would emerge,
capable of heating a tripod for cooking;
in the height of summer, he would fill an earthenware jar with water,
boil it in hot water,
then suspend the jar in a well,
and within moments, it would turn into ice.
Yet, the deluded customs of the masses,
who affirm themselves and deny others,
are no different from those of Lǔ.
【Explanatory Text】"Lǔ Qú" is pronounced with the rising tone "qú",
and also has an alternative reading as "qí jù".
Lǐ Yí says:
Lǔ Qú,
is a person's name.
Another source states:
he was a person from the early Zhōu dynasty.
"Cuàn" is pronounced as "qī luàn",
and also as "qī duān".
【Three】【Arguments】A thousand-year-old ashes are yang,
fire is also yang,
this is using yang to summon yang;
a well is yin,
water is also yin,
this is using yin to summon yin.
Lǔ Jù's statement here does not refer to his disciple.
【Four】【Annotation】All also use yang to summon yang, yet obstinately consider themselves correct.
【Commentary】To set aside,
means to place.
Place one se zither in the hall,
and another se zither inside the chamber.
When the gōng and jué notes are played on the one in the hall,
the strings of the one in the chamber resonate and vibrate.
This is because the five tones and six pitches share the same sound,
just as yáng summons yáng.
【Explanation】"Wéi zhī": read as yú wèi fǎn.
"Fèi yī": fèi means
to set aside.
【Five】【Note】Altered according to the tune.
【Commentary】If one string is retuned in the hall,
the sound inside the room no longer resonates in response,
which must be due to the pitch standards not matching.
【Explanatory Text】"改調" is pronounced as tú diào fǎn.
The annotations are all the same.
"無當" is pronounced as dīng làng fǎn,
meaning to combine.
【Six】【Annotation】Without sound, there would be no means to interact;
with sound, if not in harmony, there would be no response.
Now, altering this one string causes all twenty-five strings to change,
it is through tension and relaxation that tuning is achieved.
【Commentary】Only the gōng and jué notes should respond subtly,
when all twenty-five strings are set in motion,
those sharing the same pitch and temperament will all resonate and move.
【七】【注】Lǔ Jù used this to boast to his disciples,
yet it was merely a case of like responding to like,
not that he alone possessed such a unique ability.
【Commentary】Beyond the principles of sound and rhythm,
what other extraordinary techniques could there possibly be!
Although the responses and movements may vary,
they are all governed by the five notes.
Since there are no other techniques,
what is there to boast about!
【Eight】【Annotation】The five masters each held their own views and affirmed what they considered right,
yet this was no different from Lǔ Jù boasting about his disciples,
as they were unable to surpass one another.
【Commentary】Huìzǐ's words,
each holding fast to their own correctness,
strive to boast and overpower others,
no different from Lǔ Jù,
hence it is said to be like this.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition lacks the character "fù".
(2) The character "wèi" in the Shìdé Táng edition is placed below "dú néng",
while in the Zhào Jiànyì edition it is below "yì yǐ".
Huìzǐ said:
"Now the Confucians, Mohists, Yángists, and Bǐngists,
are about to engage in debate with me,
clashing with words,
suppressing with rhetoric,
yet they have never proven me wrong—
so what does that signify?"
【一】【Note】Those who have never found fault with me,
each consider themselves correct.
Huìzǐ thus wished to take this as the ultimate truth.
【Transcription】"Xiāng fú" fú fú fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "拂" as "排".
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The man of Qí who abandoned his son in Sòng,
appointed a gatekeeper not for his integrity【一】,
sought a xíngzhōng vessel yet bound it tightly【二】,
searched for his lost son but never left his domain,
truly left behind his kind【三】!
As for the man of Chǔ who lodged elsewhere yet offended the gatekeeper【四】,
fighting with the boatman in the dead of night when none were around,
had not yet left the riverbank but already created enmity【五】."
【一】【Note】When entrusting someone to a foreign state,
and having the gatekeepers guard them,
once they leave, even if it's with their own child, they cannot ensure their complete safety.
This shows the lack of parental affection in the people of Qí,
yet they still consider themselves right,
hence they act this way.
【Commentary】The gatekeeper,
is the one who guards the door.
A person from Qí abandoned their child in Sòng,
yet still gave them this name,
is that not considering us?
【Explanation】"蹢" is pronounced as chí yì fǎn,
meaning to cast away.
Sīmǎ comments:
A man from Qí despised his son,
abandoned him in Sòng,
had a gatekeeper guard him,
causing his body to be incomplete,
yet he considered himself right.
【二】【注】Instead, it is right to cherish the bell vessels,
binding them up,
fearing they might break or get damaged.
【Explanation】"Xíng Zhōng" is pronounced xíng,
with Xú giving the reverse reading hù tǐng.
Also, the Zìlín states:
The xíng resembles a small zhōng but has a long neck.
It further says:
It is like a hú but larger.
"Bound with restraints" — Guǒ explains:
fearing it might break or get damaged.
According to this, it means valuing the xíng over the child,
considering oneself correct in doing so.
【Three】【Commentary】Táng,
means loss.
Having lost his son,
yet unable to search far and wide,
he abandoned those of his own kind,
and never once considered himself at fault.
When humans are self-righteous,
such errors arise.
【Subcommentary】Xíng,
is a small bell.
Táng,
means lost.
Searching for a lost child,
without leaving the territory;
binding the xíng bell,
fearing it might be damaged;
valuing the vessel over the child is unkind,
abandoning one's own kind,
also says that I am.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
"There are those who abandon their kind,"
should connect with the following word "fú" to form the sentence.
"There are those who abandon their kind, alas!"
