Nánbó Zǐqí leaned on his armrest and sat,
gazing at the sky and exhaling slowly.
Yánchéng Zǐ entered and, upon seeing him, said:
"Master,
you are the epitome of things.
Can the body truly be made to resemble withered bones,
and the mind truly be made to resemble dead ashes?"
【One】【Commentary】This is still Nánguō Zǐqí from the "Discussion on Making All Things Equal" in the Southern Branch.
The meanings such as leaning on the armrest,
are all explained in the inner chapters.
◎Qìng Fán's case note: Nánbó Zǐqí,
in the "Discussion on Making All Things Equal" is written as Nánguō Zǐqí.
The ancient pronunciations of "Bó" and "Guō" are similar,
hence the characters are used interchangeably.
Tángyùnzhèng:
"Bó",
was anciently pronounced like "Bó".
In the Rites of Zhou, "Sī Jǐ Yán" mentions its cypress mat uses reeds,
also borrowing "Bó" for "Guǒ".
(Zheng's annotation considers "Bó" as a remnant of the worn-out character "Guǒ",
which is incorrect.
See "Jīngyì Shùwén" for explanation.
【Explanation】"Yǐn": pronounced as yú jìn fǎn.
"Xū": pronounced as xū.
【Two】【Disciples】Yán Chéng,
a disciple of Zǐ Qí.
Yóu,
means extremely.
Every time I look up and sigh at the Master's profound understanding of things,
it must be that his form is like withered bones,
and his heart resembles dead ashes.
Yearning for virtue with earnestness,
thus I have this sighing verse.
【Translated Text】"Rù jiàn" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
"Fū wù zhī yóu yě" has the pronunciation fú.
One version writes it as fūzǐ,
then it is read according to the character's usual pronunciation.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current texts, there is the character zǐ below fū.
He said:
"I once dwelt in a mountain cave.
At that time,
as soon as Tián Hé caught sight of me,
the multitudes of Qí State congratulated him thrice.
I must have put myself forward first,
thus he came to know of me;
I must have sold myself,
thus he came to trade upon me.
Had I not possessed such qualities,
how could he have come to know of me?
Had I not sold myself,
how could he have come to trade upon me?
Alas!
I grieve for those who lose themselves,
and I also grieve for those who grieve for others,
and I further grieve for those who grieve over the grieving of others,
thereafter becoming more distant with each passing day."
【一】【注】I consider it an honor to have met Zǐqí.
【Commentary】The mountain cave is located in the southern mountains of Qí.
Tián Hé was the name of the King of Qí.
Zǐ Qí lived in seclusion in the mountain cave,
and his virtuous reputation spread far and wide.
When the King of Qí briefly saw him,
he considered the meeting an honor.
This is why the people of the entire state celebrated three times.
【Explanatory Text】"Within the mountain cave" is the same as in Simǎ's version.
Lǐ Yún states:
It refers to the mountain cave on the southern hills of Qí.
One version writes it as "the mouth of it."
"Tián Hé" was the ruler of Qí.
He honored virtue,
thus the people of the state celebrated him.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
That is, Tàigōng Hé of Qí.
【二】【疏】My reputation preceded me,
thus things knew of me;
I was indeed selling myself for fame,
hence Tián Hé saw and traded upon it.
【Explanation】"Yù zhī" is read as yáng liù fǎn.
【Three】【Memorials】If I were to conceal my brilliance and hide my traces,
without having any reputation,
how would the people of that world come to know me?
If my name and worth were not esteemed,
how could they see me and trade me?
It is only because I cannot erase my traces and conceal my clues
that I am sold and bartered by things.
【Transcription】"The wicked" is pronounced as wū.
The same applies below.
【Four】【Losses】 of mourning,
are like being lost or gone.
Zǐ Qí laments the people of the world,
who abandon themselves to admire others,
thus losing their own way.
【Text】"Zì sàng" is pronounced with the tone of "sàng" as in "sàng" (喪).
【Five】【Commentary】The Way knows neither gain nor loss, yet beings experience sorrow and joy.
Therefore, to grieve over others' self-inflicted losses is itself a cause for sorrow.
【Six】【Annotation】Zǐqí understood that acting would not suffice to save others but would only harm oneself,
therefore he used non-sorrow to grieve for it,
so that his sorrow gradually faded away,
and he became placid and heartless,
withered in form,
thereby distancing himself further each day.
【Commentary】The profound Dao is empty and formless,
neither loss nor joy exists,
thus those who grieve for others' losses and those who are grieved for,
although the depth of sorrow may vary in degree and expression over time,
all fail to align with the Dao,
and hence are also lamentable.
Sorrow upon sorrow,
dispelling it again and again,
once the teaching becomes clear,
the mystery within mystery principle is thus revealed,
in harmony with all wonders,
so it grows ever more profound and far-reaching.
【Transcription】"Ér bó" bù gè fǎn.
【Collation】（一）In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "kǒu".
When Confucius went to Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ hosted a banquet for him.
Sūnshū Áo stood holding a wine vessel,
while Shìnán Yìliáo received the wine and offered a libation, saying:
"O people of ancient times!
Upon this occasion, let us speak of them."
【一】【Note】The ancients spoke,
always at gatherings.
【Commentary】Shāng,
is the general term for wine vessels,
meaning to feast with wine.
Jué is also a wine vessel,
holding one shēng.
The ancients, when about to drink,
must first make offerings to their ancestors.
Yì Liáo poured wine for the offering,
hence he toasted the sage,
wishing to engage in discourse with Confucius here.
【Explanation】"Shāng zhī" is pronounced as shāng.
Lǐ Yí says:
It is a general term for wine vessels.
"Sūn Shū Áo holds the jūé" — According to the Zuǒzhuàn, Sūn Shū Áo was the chancellor of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
before Confucius was born.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Āi,
after Zhòngní's death,
Báigōng caused a rebellion.
Yìliáo never held office in Chǔ.
Also, in the twelfth year of Duke Xuān in the Zuǒzhuàn,
there was a Xióngxiàng Yìliáo in Chǔ,
who was a contemporary of Shū Áo,
far removed from the time of Confucius.
This is likely an allegorical narrative.
Said:
"Qiū has heard of the speech that is without words,
yet has never spoken of it,
and here speaks of it.
Shìnán Yìliáo juggled balls and the conflict between two families was resolved,
Sūnshū Áo rested peacefully holding a feather fan and the people of Yǐng laid down their arms.
Qiū wishes he had a three-foot-long beak."
【一】【注】The sage has no words;
what they speak
are merely the words of the common people,
hence it is called wordless speech.
If one regards speech as non-speech,
then even though words come from the mouth,
it is as if nothing had been spoken.
【二】【注】Now, I will speak here of wordlessness.
【Commentary】When principle is present, teaching speaks without words;
when teaching occurs, principle has never actually spoken.
Thus, the sage mysteriously embodies this essence,
and so speaks all day without ever having spoken.
When Yìng Yīliáo made his request to Confucius,
he therefore also spoke here through wordless expression.
【Three】【Annotation】These two gentlemen quelled the dispute through silence,
maintaining their composure in tranquility,
and thus the military conflict resolved itself.
【Commentary】His surname was Xióng,
his courtesy name was Yìliáo,
a worthy man of Chǔ,
and also a brave warrior who was reserved and taciturn.
He lived south of the market,
hence he was called Shìnánzǐ.
When Báigōng Shèng of Chǔ intended to instigate a rebellion,
he planned to kill the Prime Minister Zǐxī.
Sīmǎ Zǐqí said that Xióng Yìliáo was a brave warrior,
and if he could be obtained,
he would be a match for five hundred men.
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to enlist him.
Yìliáo was calmly juggling balls in a playful manner,
and did not speak with the envoy.
The envoy then threatened him with a sword,
yet Yìliáo showed no sign of fear or alarm.
He neither complied with the command,
nor said anything else.
Since Báigōng failed to secure Yìliáo,
his rebellious plan did not succeed.
Hence it is said that the conflict between the two families was difficult to resolve.
His surname was Sūn,
his courtesy name was Shū'áo,
the Prime Minister of Chǔ,
a man of great virtue and worth.
Yǐng,
was the capital of Chǔ.
"Tóu" means
to rest.
Shū'áo possessed profound knowledge and genuine wisdom,
reclining on a high pillow in carefree leisure,
comprehending principles beyond words,
holding a feather fan in self-satisfaction.
Thus, he caused enemy states not to invade,
repelling threats a thousand miles away.
The people of Chǔ were free from troubles,
cultivating literary virtue,
and resting their military strategies.
Highlighting that these two men had such capabilities,
they were thus worthy of conversing with Zhòngní,
praising the profound Dào.
【Interpretive Text】"The conflict between the two families" nǎi dǎn fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
"Xiè" is pronounced xiè,
the annotation is the same.
Sīmǎ says,
Yí Liáo,
was a brave warrior of Chǔ,
skilled at juggling balls.
When Bái Gōng Shèng of Chǔ was about to stage a rebellion,
intending to kill Prime Minister Zǐ Xī.
Zǐ Qī and Shí Qǐ said:
"In the southern market, there is one named Xióng Yí Liáo,
if we can get him,
he could be worth five hundred men."
So they went to inform him,
but he did not consent.
They threatened him with a sword,
yet he remained unmoved,
continuing to juggle balls as before,
and said:
"I will not betray you either."
Bái Gōng then killed Zǐ Xī.
Zǐ Qī sighed,
the conflict between the two families had ended,
and Yí Liáo was not involved in their disaster.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The Tàipíng Yùlǎn, volume 279, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Yí Liáo was skilled at juggling balls,
Bái Gōng coerced him,
but he continued juggling as before.
This is somewhat briefer than the interpretive text.
"Gān qǐn bǐng yǔ" is read as is,
also pronounced hé.
Sīmǎ's version writes it as ●,
saying:
read as hé.
Some versions write it as chì,
what the rain dancers hold.
Cuī's version writes it as yì.
"Yǐng rén tóu bīng" Sīmǎ says:
meaning Shū Áo wished to rest peacefully and sleep soundly,
cultivating virtue in the court,
repelling the enemy a thousand miles away,
so that hostile states dare not invade,
the people of Yǐng would lay down their weapons,
with no need for attack or defense.
Yǐng,
was the capital of Chǔ.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The Tàipíng Yùlǎn, volume 279, quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Sūn Shū Áo held feather dances,
so the people of Yǐng had nothing to attack,
hence they laid down their weapons.
This is somewhat briefer than the interpretive text.
◎Fān also notes: Sūn Shū Áo resting peacefully and holding feathers led to the people of Yǐng laying down their weapons,
which aligns with the meaning in Huáinánzǐ's "Zhǔ Shù Piān" that in the past, Sūn Shū Áo lay peacefully and the people of Yǐng had no use for their weapons.
Laying down weapons,
means they had no use for them.
Gāo's annotation says:
merely resting peacefully to cultivate virtue,
repelling the enemy a thousand miles away,
so that hostile states dare not invade.
This is the basis for Sīmǎ's annotation.
(Wáng Niàn Sūn said:
The three characters "hài qí fēng" [harm its edge]
do not logically connect in meaning.
"Hài" should be a miswriting of "yòng" [use],
meaning there was no use for their edge.
In clerical script, "hài" is written as ●,
its upper part resembles "yòng".
Note that Huáinánzǐ often draws from Zhuāngzǐ,
here mentioning laying down weapons,
also means they had no use for them.
) Wáng's correction of the character "hài" is quite precise.
【Four】【Annotation】If what is spoken does not pertain to oneself,
then even if one speaks for a lifetime,
it is as if one has never spoken.
Thus, having a beak three feet long
is not enough to be called long;
when ordinary people keep their mouths closed,
it does not mean they are not speaking.
【Commentary】Huì,
means mouth.
If one's words are appropriate,
then there is no need for further speech.
Even if I had a beak three feet long,
how would it differ from keeping my mouth shut?
Therefore, I wish to possess it.
【Explanation】"Huì" is pronounced as xǔ huì fǎn,
also as dīng dòu fǎn,
or chāng ruì fǎn.
"Three Chǐ" refers to three chi,
meaning length.
Sīmǎ says:
Huì,
means breath or sigh.
Yì Liáo juggled balls to avert disaster,
Shū Áo removed defenses to thwart the enemy,
Qiū also wished to possess,
sighing over its three chi.
Three chi,
is a dagger or sword.
【Collation Note】(1) The thirty-four characters below the case of Qìng Fān were originally mistakenly incorporated into the commentary text below.
That is called the Way of no Way,
this is called the argument beyond words,
thus virtue encompasses what the Way unifies.
And speech rests where knowledge cannot reach,
that is the ultimate.
What the Way unifies,
virtue cannot equal;
what knowledge cannot know,
argument cannot demonstrate;
names like Rú and Mò bring misfortune.
Thus the sea does not refuse the eastern flow,
being the ultimate greatness;
the sage embraces heaven and earth,
his benefaction reaches all under heaven,
yet none know whose house he belongs to.
Therefore in life he holds no rank,
in death receives no posthumous title,
accumulates no wealth,
establishes no fame,
this is called the great person.
A dog is not considered good for being skilled at barking,
a person is not considered wise for being skilled at speaking,
how much less for being great!
Trying to be great is insufficient to achieve greatness,
how much less for cultivating virtue!
Now what is perfectly great,
none surpasses heaven and earth;
yet what do they seek,
that they are perfectly great?
One who knows perfect greatness
seeks nothing,
loses nothing,
abandons nothing,
and does not alter himself for external things.
Turning inward without exhaustion,
following antiquity without wearing down,
this is the sincerity of the great person.
【One】【Annotation】Them,
referring to the two individuals.
【Commentary】That,
refers to the principle being explained.
Speaking without speaking of the Way,
means it is neither the Way nor not the Way.
【二】【注】This refers to
Zhòngní.
【Commentary】This refers to the teaching that can express meaning.
Speaking without speaking,
neither speaking nor not speaking.
Zǐ Xuán then said this refers to Zhòngní,
but this annotation is crude and shallow,
missing the mark by far.
Not speaking of the ineffable,
this is to explore the subtle and seek the hidden,
exhaust principles and fully realize nature—
how could it be within the capacity of those two men!
If resting peacefully and juggling balls can be called settling disputes through silence,
then silence and speech are worlds apart—
how could Qiū have a three-foot beak?
Therefore, it is not acceptable.
Moreover, this chapter
extensively discusses profound ultimate principles,
and judging by its literary style,
it is clearly unrelated to Sūn Xióng.
【Explanation】"That refers to this refers to": Guǒ's commentary states:
"That"
refers to the two masters;
"this"
refers to Zhòngní.
Sīmǎ's commentary states:
"That"
refers to sleeping peacefully;
"this"
refers to juggling balls.
【Three】【Commentary】Although the Way encompasses all without confinement,
yet summarizing its ultimate essence,
it is nothing beyond attaining self-realization,
hence it is one.
【Text】"Zǒng" is pronounced as zǒng.
【Four】【Annotation】Speaking of stopping at one's proper limit,
how could it not be the ultimate state!
【Commentary】The realm of the ultimate Way,
the domain of profound mystery,
is beyond the comprehension of a sage's mind,
and ineffable even for a divine tongue.
If one seeks truth through words and knowledge,
they will stray far from it.
Therefore, what virtue encompasses,
and where words fall silent,
lies in the one path of utmost subtlety.
【Five】【Note】Each attains it in their own way,
not identical,
yet the Way is one.
【Commentary】The Way is one, empty and mysterious,
with no bounds or measure.
Yet virtue has its higher and lower levels,
(who) cannot be all-encompassing.
Some texts have the character for "same,"
meaning that virtues have their superiority and inferiority,
and cannot be identical to the Way.
This explains the oneness of the Way mentioned earlier.
【Transcription】"Cannot be the same" in one edition is written as "mutually the same."
【Six】【Annotation】It is not within his proper role,
thus he cannot accomplish it.
【Commentary】The wise grasp the profound Way,
which is said to transcend all verbal description,
and thus cannot be fully conveyed through debate or discourse.
This explains the earlier statement about what the wise do not know.
【七】【Note】The Confucians and Mohists sought to unify what could not be unified,
and to promote what could not be promoted,
hence they met with misfortune (1).
【Subcommentary】Those who cling to their own rightness and contend against others' wrongness,
and whose names align with the Ruists and Mohists,
will inevitably encounter calamity.
◎ Jiā Shìfù remarked:
The reason the Ruists and Mohists face misfortune
lies in having the labels of Ruist and Mohist.
By hoisting the names of Ruist and Mohist to provoke contention,
when virtues cannot be unified,
they force the Way to conform to one standard;
when debates cannot be resolved,
they compel knowledge to reconcile differences,
each affirming their own correctness,
and thus the reach of the Way and knowledge becomes quite limited.
In life, they hold no rank,
in death, no posthumous title,
not even occupying themselves with substance,
so what use have they for names!
【八】【Note】To clearly receive without declining
is the means to achieve greatness.
【Commentary】All rivers compete in pouring forth,
flowing eastward unceasingly,
yet the great sea accommodates them,
never declining or fearing.
This is based on the Eastern Sea as an example,
and indeed it represents the ultimate in vastness and breadth.
【Nine】【Annotation】All matters are entrusted with complete nonchalance.
【Commentary】Previously, the sea was used as an analogy,
and what follows here draws a parallel with the analogy.
The sage's virtue aligns with the dual principles of yin and yang,
thus encompassing heaven and earth;
his benevolence extends boundlessly,
so his grace reaches all under heaven;
he achieves success without claiming it,
thus none know who accomplished it;
he attributes the merit to others,
hence no one recognizes his clan or lineage.
【一０】【Note】Having it yet treating it as if not having it.
【一一】【Note】Posthumous titles serve to designate achievements,
achievements not being one's own,
thus even with a posthumous title, it is not personally possessed.
【Commentary】A person exists in the world,
alive with name and status,
and upon death is assigned a posthumous title,
all to manifest their true essence.
Since the sage, while living, already attributed achievements to others,
in death, there is nothing left to confer a posthumous title upon.
【一二】【Note】So that all things know contentment.
【Commentary】Even if one possesses wealth and virtue,
they should distribute it all among others.
【一三】【Note】The achievement was not made by oneself,
hence the credit is attributed to others.
【Commentary】Names are meant to summon realities;
since the realities do not gather,
where then can the names be anchored?
【一四】【Note】If one acts with purpose to possess it,
then it becomes small.
【Commentary】This summarizes what came before.
Those who are forgotten among the renowned and posthumously titled,
can be said to be people of great virtue.
【一五】【Note】Virtue stems from one's nature,
not from what words can achieve.
【Commentary】Shàn,
means to like.
A dog does not necessarily bark,
so how could a virtuous person speak excessively!
【Explanatory Text】"Shàn Fèi" is read as fá fèi fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It barks incessantly without distinguishing between guests and its owner.
"Shàn Yán" Sīmǎ explains:
It speaks endlessly, having lost the essence and chasing after trivialities.
【一六】【Note】Great healing cannot be achieved through deliberate effort.
【Commentary】To consider fondness for speech as virtuous,
is still unacceptable,
how much more so when deluding the mind to make choices in matters of great importance!
【一七】【Note】Only what is natural constitutes virtue.
【Commentary】A heart of love that is vast and extensive is called 'greatness';
silently aligning with the profound Way is called 'virtue'.
Now, to intentionally seek greatness
still contradicts the principle;
how much more so is it impossible
to cultivate virtue with deliberate intent.
【一八】【Note】Heaven and earth are fully equipped,
not sought by human effort.
【Commentary】"Bèi" means
to be fully equipped.
The two cosmic forces cover and support,
nurturing without intent;
the four seasons cycle through,
giving life to all beings.
What method is there,
yet all things are fully provided for?
【Chapter 19】【Commentary】Those who know they are self-sufficient
do not abandon themselves to seek things,
hence they have no seeking, no loss, and no abandonment.
【Commentary】One who embodies the vastness of natural principles and possesses all things inherently,
can thus remain detached and forgetful of distinctions between self and others.
Hence, there is no grasping or rejecting,
no loss or deprivation,
no proof or attainment,
and one does not allow external circumstances to alter their own mind.
【Interpretation】"Bù shě" is pronounced as shě.
【二０】【Comment】By returning to guard my own principles,
my principles naturally become clear.
【Commentary】It is solely for the sake of broad completeness,
that it accords with the ultimate principle.
Subsequently, returning to the origin and reverting to the source,
one converges with the wondrous ultimate within oneself, which is boundless and inexhaustible.
【二一】【注】It naturally arrives by following the constant nature,
not through polishing or wiping.
【Commentary】Xún means
to follow.
To follow the nature of things,
without any intention to alter or create,
how could one then polish and adorn them to boast!
【Explanatory Text】"Following antiquity without wearing away" one version has "grinding."
Guǒ Xiàng comments:
"Mó,"
means to wipe.
Wáng Bì states:
"Mó,"
means to vanish.
Though constantly interacting with things, one does not lose oneself;
though managing the present,
one always follows the ways of antiquity.
From ancient times to the present,
its name does not wear away or vanish.
"Wiping" is pronounced "shì."
【二二】【Note】Achieving without deliberate action,
thus it is called sincerity.
【Commentary】Sincerity,
is reality.
Returning to the origin and reverting to the root,
following the course of all things—
this is the inherent virtue of the great sage, embodying truth within oneself.
【Collation】（一）The Zhào Jiànyì edition has the character "yě" (也) below "xiōng" (凶).
Zǐqí had eight sons,
lined up before him,
and summoned Jiǔfāng Yīn, saying:
"Physiognomize my sons for me,
which one is auspicious?"
【One】【Explanation】Zǐ Qí,
was the Sīmǎ of Chǔ, Zǐ Qí.
Chén,
means battle formation.
Zhū,
means "at" or "in."
Jiǔfāng,
is a surname;
Yīn,
is a given name.
Shú,
means who.
Xiáng,
means good.
Jiǔfāng Yīn,
was skilled in physiognomy.
He lined up his sons in front of the courtyard,
and ordered Fāng Yīn to read their faces,
among the eight sons,
who would be the auspicious and good one.
【Explanation】"Jiǔfāng Yīn" is pronounced as Yīn,
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as wūjī fǎn,
also pronounced as Yān,
a person skilled at judging horses.
Huáinánzǐ writes it as Jiǔfāng Gāo.
"Wèi wǒ" is pronounced as yú wèi fǎn.
"Xiàng wú zǐ" is pronounced as xī xiàng fǎn.
Jiǔfāng Yīn said:
"Kǔn is an auspicious sign."
【一】【疏】Kǔn,
is the name of a son.
Among the eight sons,
Kǔn is the most virtuous and benevolent.
【Translated Text】"Kǔn" is pronounced as kùn,
also read as kǒu běn fǎn,
the name of Zǐ Qí's son.
Zǐqí looked up in joyful surprise and said:
"How so?"
The reply was:
"Kǔn will share meals with the ruler all his life."
【One】【Explanation】Startled,
an expression of pleasant surprise.
Upon hearing of your auspicious news,
hence the countenance shows joyful astonishment,
inquiring about the favorable appearance and demeanor.
【Explanatory Text】"Jù rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant of Jì and the final of Jù.
Sīmǎ explains:
An expression of joy.
The original text also uses the character "矍",
pronounced as Xū Fù.
The Zìlín states:
A wide-eyed appearance.
Lǐ Yí explains:
A startled gaze.
◎Qìng Fān notes that this "jù rán" and the "jù rán" in the Gēngsāngchǔ chapter
both describe a look of shock and alarm.
The character "瞿",
in the Shuōwén is written as ●,
and it says:
Raising the eyes in a startled ● manner.
In the Hànshū, the Biography of Wúwáng Bì states that Jiāoxīwáng looked "jù rán" in terror,
with Yán Shīgǔ annotating:
"Jù rán",
means a look of being unsettled.
Also, in the Biography of Zōu Yáng, Chángjūn said fearfully, "What should be done?",
Yán Shīgǔ annotates:
"Jù" should be read as "jù",
and "jù rán"
means a look of being unsettled.
In the Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò, it says, "Then Wúwáng looked fearful and changed countenance",
Yán Shīgǔ annotates:
"Jù rán",
means a look of losing composure.
Note that Yán Shīgǔ interprets "jù" and "jù" as a look of losing composure or being unsettled,
based on the Máo Commentary of the Qífēng, "The East is Not Yet Bright" chapter, which describes a madman as "jù jù".
However, it is not understood that the commentary refers to the two phrases about failing to keep the night watch,
hence interpreting "jù jù" as being unsettled,
which differs from "jù rán".
"Jù rán" should correctly follow Lǐ Yí's interpretation as given here.
Zǐqí shed tears freely and said:
"Why has my son come to such an extreme state!"
【One】【Explanation】Desolate and dreary,
describes the appearance of shedding tears.
Fāng Yīn's insight was shallow and narrow,
considering the consumption of meat as auspicious.
Zǐ Qí, however, discerned the profound and mysterious,
knowing it was not a blessing.
Therefore, he pitied its extreme ominousness,
and sorrowfully shed tears.
【Explanatory Text】"Suǒ rán" is pronounced as xì gè fǎn,
and also as sè bái fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It describes the appearance of tears flowing.
Jiǔfāng Yīn said:
"To share meals with the ruler of a state,
brings blessings to three generations of one's clan,
how much more so to one's parents!
Now that you, Master, weep upon hearing this,
this is to ward off blessings.
You yourself may be auspicious,
but your father will be inauspicious."
【One】【Explanation】The three clans,
refer to the paternal clan,
and the maternal clan.
To resist,
means to ward off or defend against.
Those who share meals with the state ruler,
enjoy honor, glory, wealth, and nobility,
with kindness extending to the three clans,
how could it be limited to just the two parents!
The son enjoys auspicious blessings,
while the father instead weeps with tears,
this is indeed resisting fortune and virtue.
【Explanation】"Yù Fú" is pronounced yú lǚ fǎn,
meaning to resist,
to oppose.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has the character 於 following 況.
Zǐqí said:
"Yīn,
how could you be sufficient to understand it,
and deem Kǔn auspicious?
It exhausts itself in wine and meat,
entering the nose and mouth,
yet how could you be sufficient to know from where they come?
I have never herded, yet a ewe was born in the corner of my room;
I have never enjoyed hunting, yet a quail was hatched in the recesses of my house.
If you find this not strange,
why is that?
That with which I wander with my son,
is wandering within Heaven and Earth.
I with it seek joy from Heaven,
I with it seek sustenance from Earth;
I do not with it engage in affairs,
do not with it form plans,
do not with it pursue the strange;
I with it ride the sincerity of Heaven and Earth and do not use things to entangle with it;
I with it wholly follow the natural course and do not with it engage in what affairs deem appropriate.
Now, however, there is a worldly reward!
Generally, those who have strange omens
must have strange conduct.
Perilous indeed!
It is not the fault of me and my son,
nearly it is Heaven that bestowed it!
I therefore weep."
means "from."
The petty shaman Fāng Yīn,
whose discernment does not reach far,
when observing signs of fortune,
perceives nothing beyond the taste of wine and meat entering the nose and mouth.
Fāng Yīn's methods and arts,
their principles are exhausted in this,
how could he know the origins of wine and meat,
from where they come.
【二】【注】The reason for surprise,
stems from it being unexpected.
【Commentary】Zāng,
is a sheep.
Ào,
the southwestern corner is the Wèi position,
the place of the sheep;
Yǎo,
the southeastern corner is the Chén position,
Chén corresponds to the quail's place;
hence it is said that the sheep and quail are produced.
Now, sheep require herding and rearing,
quails are obtained through hunting;
if one's emolument depends on meritorious service,
only then can wealth and nobility be achieved.
Now, Kǔn has not been heard of accomplishing any deeds,
yet he dines alongside the ruler of the state;
how is this different from having sheep without herding,
or obtaining quails without hunting!
Without herding or hunting,
how strange it is!
【Interpretation of Text】"Wèi cháng" is read according to its basic pronunciation.
Some versions write it as "zēng",
pronounced with the initial consonant "c" and the final "ái".
"Ér zāng" is pronounced with the initial "z" and the final "āng".
According to the Ěryǎ:
It refers to a female sheep.
"Yú ào" is pronounced with the initial "w" and the final "ào".
It denotes the southwestern corner, associated with the Wèi direction.
One interpretation says:
It is a pigpen.
"Hào tián" is pronounced with the initial "h" and the final "ào".
"Yú yǎo" has a variant character written as ●,
pronounced with the initial "w" and the final "iào",
and Xú reads it as "wū liǎo".
Sīmǎ explains:
It is the northeastern corner.
Another interpretation says:
The southeastern corner is associated with the Chúnhuǒ direction,
where quails are born.
Yet another says:
It is a burrow.
Guō pronounces it as "tú hū",
and the character is composed of "quǎn" under "xué".
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
Referring to the Ěryǎ's "Shì Gōng" chapter:
The southeastern corner is called "yǎo" (note two).
The northeastern corner is actually "yí".
Also, according to the Shuōwén:
denotes the sound of a door pivot,
and refers to the southeastern corner of a room.
"Yǎo" only means deep.
◎Jiā Shìfù states:
Where the female sheep comes from,
is herding;
where the quail comes from,
is hunting.
If a female sheep appears without herding,
or a quail appears without hunting,
arriving unexpectedly,
appearing suddenly,
it is considered an ill omen.
An omen,
is a strange sign;
to receive worldly rewards by riding on the sincerity of heaven and earth,
this too is a strange sign.
【Three】【Annotations】Not acting with ulterior motives.
【Translated Text】"Wandering in Heaven and Earth" Simǎ's version has "earth" as "gǔ,"
stating:
It means chaotic.
Cuī's version is the same.
【Four】【Annotation】Follow what one encounters in heaven and earth.
Yāo,
means to encounter.
【Commentary】Yāo means
to encounter.
Heaven and earth
have no intention.
Zǐqí embodies the Way,
empties forgetfulness and follows things,
is self-sufficient within the bounds of his nature,
roams freely between heaven and earth,
all that he creates is fitting,
not awaiting joy and pleasure,
whatever he encounters, he eats—
how could he rely on rich flavors!
【Translated Text】"Yāo" is pronounced as in ancient "Yáo",
meaning to encounter.
"Lè" is pronounced as luò.
【Five】【Annotation】Strange,
means extraordinary.
Following the norm and acting according to one's nature,
naturally and spontaneously so.
【Commentary】Forgetting material things,
thus not engaging in affairs;
forgetting wisdom,
thus not making plans;
following constancy,
thus not creating anomalies.
【Six】【Annotation】This is not to be done.
【Commentary】Sincerity means
genuineness.
Riding on the true way of the two principles,
following all things to roam freely,
thus not contending or disturbing with things further.
【Seven】【Annotation】This is pleasing to the ear,
with no need for selection.
【Commentary】Wēi yí (委蛇) means
to follow along with things.
When mind and reality are non-dual,
one accommodates and follows the nature of things.
Since affairs are ultimately non-affairs,
how could there be any fixed "ought" to be pursued!
【Eight】【Annotation】When one has merit towards things,
things will repay them.
If I do not act for merit yet am compensated for it,
why is that?
【Commentary】To repay merits and recompense virtue
is a worldly concern.
If one embodies the Way and entrusts matters to things,
without establishing merits or fame,
what need is there to recompense merits!
【Transcription】"Zhi cháng": Shí Liàng's rebuttal,
also pronounced as shǎng.
【Nine】【Annotation】Now, there are no strange behaviors but there are strange omens,
thus it is known that this is the Mandate of Heaven.
【Commentary】Dài means
peril.
Jī means
close.
One who behaves strangely
must have strange omens.
Now, you have not acted strangely but have strange signs,
and are bound to encounter peril,
which is close to being a disaster sent by Heaven,
not your fault.
【Transcription】"Strange Conduct" is read with the lower tone of Mèng.
The annotation is the same.
【一０】【Note】What happens because one acts,
ceases if one refrains from acting.
What comes without one's doing,
leaves no choice but to accept it,
hence the weeping.
【Commentary】If the fault lies with humans,
they might still amend their ways;
but since it pertains to the Mandate of Heaven,
therefore, he weeps.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Yin cites the Jiangnan Guzang edition, below which there is the character "也" (yě).
(2) The Erya Shìwén writes it as ●,
stating:
also written as "窔" (yào),
same.
The Shuōwén writes it as ●.
Not long after, he sent Kǔn to Yān,
and on the way, robbers captured him.
Selling him whole would have been difficult,
whereas amputating his feet would make it easier【一】.
Thus, they amputated his feet and sold him in Qí,
where he happened to serve on Qú Gōng's street,
yet he lived on meat till the end of his life【二】.
【一】【注】He feared the slave might escape entirely,
so he thought it better to amputate his feet to make him easier to sell.
【Commentary】Not long after,
meaning in a brief moment.
A Chǔ envoy named Kǔn was dispatched to Yān,
on the road,
was captured by bandits,
who seized Kǔn and made him a slave.
To sell him intact,
fearing he might flee,
would make guarding difficult;
thus, they amputated his feet,
so they wouldn't worry about his escape,
making him easier to sell.
【Text Explanation】"Wú jǐ": pronounced with the character jū qǐ fǎn.
"Yú Yān": Yān pronounced as yān.
"Quán ér yù zhī": Yù pronounced as yù,
with a full stop.
Another version writes it as yù zhī nán.
"Yuè": pronounced as yuè,
also read as wǔ guā fǎn.
"Yì": pronounced with yǐ chì fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
"Shòu yě": Shòu also pronounced as shòu yòu fǎn.
【二】【疏】Qú Gōng,
a wealthy man of Qí,
served as a street administrator.
Kǔn, having suffered the punishment of foot amputation,
was sold to a rich merchant's family in the state of Qí,
and took his master's place on the street,
eating meat for the rest of his life.
The character is also written as "shù,"
and it is said:
Qú Gōng,
was a butcher,
sold Kǔn to a butcher's household,
together with his master practiced the craft of slaughtering,
and ate meat for the rest of his life.
【Explanation Text】"Jú Gōng": Some say:
Jú Gōng,
a wealthy family of Qí,
served as a street official,
bought Kǔn to replace himself,
and ate meat until his death.
Another version says:
Jú Gōng was a butcher,
who ate meat together with Kǔn as ruler and subject.
"Zhī jiē" is pronounced as "zhuī".
One version writes it as "shù".
"Rán shēn shí ròu zhōng": some versions mistakenly write "shēn ròu shí zhě".
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current texts, there is the character "ér" before "zhōng".
Niè Quē encountered Xǔ Yóu,
and asked:
"Where are you going?"
【One】【Narrative】Niè Quē encountered Xǔ Yóu,
and asked where he intended to go.
He said:
"I intend to flee from Yáo."
【One】【Memorial】The reply stated:
I intended to flee from Emperor Yáo.
Said:
"What do you mean by that?"
【One】【Memorial】Asked what his intention was.
He said:
"Yáo,
with his laborious benevolence,
I fear he will be laughed at by the world.
In later ages, might people even end up eating each other!
The common people,
are not hard to gather;
love them and they will draw close,
benefit them and they will come,
praise them and they will be encouraged,
inflict what they detest and they will scatter.
Love and benefit stem from benevolence and righteousness,
yet those who renounce benevolence and righteousness are few,
while those who exploit them are many.
The practice of benevolence and righteousness,
not only lacks sincerity,
but also provides tools for the greedily predatory.
Thus, for one man's decisions to benefit the world,
is like trying to see everything in a single glance.
Yáo knew that worthy men benefit the world,
but did not realize they also harm it.
Only those who look beyond worthiness understand this."
【一】【注】This is the reason why benevolent individuals contend for supremacy.
【Commentary】Chùchù,
describes a flourishing appearance.
When the practice of partial benevolence flourishes,
it violates the virtue of pure harmony.
Fearing that scholars within the realm who have lost the Way might become even more degenerate than in an age of decline,
future generations would follow in their footsteps,
leading to famine among the common people,
with granaries emptied,
the people would inevitably resort to cannibalism,
hence the flight.
【Explanation】"畜畜" is pronounced Xùxù with the sound Xǔliù fǎn,
Guō gives the pronunciation Tāliù fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
It describes the appearance of practicing benevolence.
Wáng Yún:
It depicts a demeanor of compassion, love, and diligence.
"其人與" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
"人相食與" is pronounced Yú with the sound yú.
This means they will rush about for benevolence and righteousness,
no longer engaging in farming,
and when hungry, they will resort to eating each other.
【二】【疏】The people,
when nurtured with love, become close;
when benefits are offered, they come forth;
when praised, they encourage one another;
when faced with what they detest, the multitude scatters and disperses.
Thus, the gathering and scattering of the common people
is indeed not difficult.
【Transcription】"Yù zhī" pronounced as yú.
"Suǒ wù" with the pronunciation wù.
【Three】【Annotation】Once benevolence and righteousness are put into practice,
one will feign them to act accordingly (two).
【Commentary】To benefit the common people,
to cherish and nurture all beings,
to achieve merits and gather the masses,
nothing comes before benevolence and righteousness.
However, those who truly practice benevolence and uphold righteousness,
and selflessly devote themselves from the heart are few,
while many exploit the traces of sages to seek fame and profit.
Therefore, those who act with benevolence and righteousness
often force their nature and feign their feelings,
lacking sincerity and truthfulness.
【Transcription】"之行" is read with the lower tone of the Meng initial.
【Four】【Annotation】When benevolence and righteousness are made visible,
then the greedy will exploit these tools to achieve their ambitions.
【Commentary】The vessel,
is the trace of the sages.
Moreover, those who are greedy for fame and profit,
more treacherous than beasts,
must necessarily borrow benevolence and righteousness as their vessel.
【Explanatory Text】"Moreover, lending tools to those covetous as beasts" Simǎ comments:
The greed of beasts knows no bounds in killing and harming,
the greed for benevolence and righteousness causes endless injury.
【Five】【Annotation】If benevolence and righteousness each arise from one's genuine feelings,
then the judgment and decision do not rest with a single individual alone.
【Commentary】Those who chase after glory and profit,
betray benevolence and righteousness,
indulge in their venomous schemes,
and arbitrarily control the world.
Had there been no traces of the sages,
how could this have been so!
【Six】【Annotation】Piē,
means to cut.
All things have myriad forms,
and if one were to cut them with a single measure,
then there would be harm.
【Explanation】Piē,
means to cut.
If one person were to subdue the entire world,
it would be like using one knife to cut all things,
causing much harm to both sides.
【Explanation】"覕" Guo Xiang's annotation: read as bó jié fǎn,
meaning:
to cut.
Xiang Xiu's annotation: read as fāng shé fǎn.
Sima Biao's annotation:
appearance of a brief glimpse.
Also read as fǔ xié fǎn,
also as pǔ jié fǎn,
and as chū lì fǎn.
"劑" read as zǐ suí fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】When outsiders are deemed worthy, then the worthy do not feign.
【Commentary】The traces of sages and worthies,
though beneficial for their time,
after ten thousand generations,
are bound to give rise to harm and thievery.
Only those who can forget the external traces of sages and worthies understand this.
【Collation】（一）The Shìdé Táng edition reads as "fū".
（二）The Zhào Jiàn Yì edition has the character "yě" below it.
There are those who are self-complacent,
those who are self-satisfied,
and those who are toil-worn.
【One】【Outline】This is a brief outline,
explained in detail below.
【Explanation】"暖" is pronounced with a sighing aspiration and the "爰" sound,
also with a sighing aspiration and the "晚" sound,
meaning a soft appearance.
"姝" is pronounced with a rising tone and the "朱" sound,
indicating a bewitching appearance.
"濡" is read as "rú",
also as "rú",
meaning peace.
"需" is read as "xū".
"濡需",
refers to stealing a moment of peace for just an instant.
"卷" is read as "quán".
"婁" is read as "lǚ".
"卷婁",
is akin to being constrained and cramped.
The so-called self-complacent ones,
having learned the words of one master,
then become smugly self-satisfied and privately pleased,
considering themselves to be sufficient,
yet unaware that there has never been any real substance [to their learning],
this is why they are called self-complacent.
【一】【Note】Exhausting form in teaching,
how could they know that I alone transform in the realm of profound darkness!
【Commentary】Warmly self-satisfied,
is the appearance of self-approval.
Those with shallow insight,
whose learning is scanty and superficial,
find contentment in their own...
From this point,
it is said that one has delved into the subtlest and most profound mysteries,
yet how could they know that what they have learned does not amount to a single thing worth mentioning?
Therefore, they are called the self-satisfied,
which concludes the preceding statement.
【Explanation】"Zì shuō" is pronounced as yuè.
"Zhī jìng" is pronounced as jìng.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "zì" has been added based on the main text.
Those who are content with temporary ease
are like the lice on a pig.
They choose the sparse bristles
and consider them a vast palace and great park.
In the curves of the hooves, the crevices of the body,
between the udders and the thighs,
they deem themselves to be in a safe and advantageous abode.
Little do they know that once the butcher raises his arms, lays out the straw, and lights the fire,
they will be scorched along with the pig.
This is advancing within a confined space,
and this is retreating within a confined space.
【一】【疏】"Rú xū" refers to
a complacent and boastful appearance.
"Shǐ" means
pig.
It describes how lice inhabit a pig's body,
selecting the sparse, long hairs of its mane,
intending to make them into grand palaces and gardens.
In the crevices of the hooves and legs,
between the thighs and near the udders,
(they) use these as warm and convenient spots.
How could they know that the butcher might suddenly bring boiling water and fire,
roll up his sleeves, lay down straw, and kill them!
Thus, they and the pig both end up scorched and rotten.
(This) metaphor illustrates those with shallow knowledge in common customs,
who indulge in desires and passions,
no different from the complacent lice on the pig.
【Text Explanation】"Shī" is pronounced as sè.
"Kuí" is pronounced with the initial k and the final uí as in the fanqie spelling.
It is also written as "kuí" (睽).
"Qū wēi" has "wēi" pronounced with the initial w and the final ēi as in the fanqie spelling.
Xiàng (Xiu) states:
It refers to the area between the thighs.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: Qū wēi,
means the inner part of the crotch.
Whenever "wēi" is mentioned,
it all refers to names for inner parts.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Lǎn Míng" chapter, it says fishermen do not compete for the "wēi,"
Gāo's annotation:
"Wēi,"
refers to the deep, curved places,
where fish gather.
In the Lièzǐ's "Huáng Dì" chapter, "What curves in the deep 'wēi',"
Yīn Jìngshùn said:
"Wēi,"
is a bend in the water.
In the 25th year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, "The Qin people passed by Xī wēi,"
Dù's annotation:
"Wēi,"
is a hidden and secluded place.
Therefore, it is understood that when "wēi" is mentioned,
it all refers to inner, curved, and deep areas.
Xiàng Xiù said,
"Wēi,"
is the area between the thighs,
which is suspected to be incorrect.
"Nuǎn shì" has "nuǎn" pronounced with the initial n and the final uǎn as in the fanqie spelling,
also pronounced with the initial x and the final uān as in another fanqie spelling.
One version writes it as "ān shì."
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
Now the text writes it as "ān shì."
"Cāo" is pronounced with the initial q and the final āo as in the fanqie spelling.
【二】【疏】Domain,
refers to the realm of boundaries.
Just as lice on a pig thrive or perish with the pig,
so do people rise to glory or fall into joy according to their circumstances.
Therefore, it is called the domain of advancement and retreat.
【Three】【Comment】Those who are not endowed with the talent to navigate changes and transcend their era, but instead seek temporary ease and profit,
are all like lice on a pig.
【Commentary】This is the conclusion.
◎Jiāshìfù said:
Advancing with the crowd,
retreating with the crowd,
means following the likes and dislikes of the masses to advance or retreat with them.
Those who are self-satisfied,
are confined by their knowledge;
those who are complacent,
are stuck in outward forms;
those who are toil-worn,
are exhausted by constant adaptation.
These three share the same flaw,
which is why Zhuāngzǐ escaped and distanced himself from them.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition as having the two characters "long hair" after "mane."
The toil-worn one is
Shùn.
Mutton does not attract ants,
but ants are drawn to mutton,
because of its pungent odor.
Shùn had a magnetic character,
which pleased the common people,
so he moved three times and each time formed a capital,
until at the ruins of Dèng there were a hundred thousand households.
Yáo heard of Shùn's worthiness
and raised him from a barren land,
hoping to benefit from the favor of his coming.
Though Shùn was elevated from the barren land,
by then his years were advanced,
his hearing and sight had declined,
yet he could not retire and return home,
hence he is called the toil-worn one.
【一】【疏】卷娄者，
谓背项俯曲，
向前挛卷而伛偻也。
夫羊肉膻腥，
无心慕蚁，
蚁闻而归之。
舜有仁行，
不慕百姓，
百姓悦之。
故羊肉比舜，
蚁况百姓。
【Explanation】"Mutton does not attract ants" is read with a rising tone for "yú" and a falling-rising tone for "qǐ".
Lǐ says:
With advancing age and a weary heart,
one lacks the will for joy and pleasure,
which is like mutton not attracting ants.
"The smell of mutton" is read with a level tone for "shè" and a rising tone for "rán".
"Conduct like the smell of mutton" is read with a falling tone for "xià" and a falling tone for "mèng".
【二】【疏】Shùn avoided Dānzhū,
and also did not wish for crowds to gather,
so he fled three times,
moving and relocating to evade them.
The common people admired his virtue,
and a hundred thousand followers joined him.
Wherever he resided,
naturally formed into cities and towns.
They reached Dèngxū,
which is a place name.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhì Dèng" Xiàng comments:
Name of a town.
"Zhī Xū" pronounced as xū.
Also written as xū in some versions.
【Three】【Explanations】Land without grass or trees is called barren soil.
Yáo heard that Shùn had the virtue of a sage,
and gave him his daughters Éhuáng and Nǚyīng in marriage,
promoting him to succeed himself,
yielding the empire to him.
He lived on unproductive land,
enduring trials and hardships,
hoping that neighboring regions would follow his example,
so the common people might receive blessings.
【Translated Text】"Barren Land" is read as it is,
also pronounced as Dù.
Xiàng comments:
Barren Land,
refers to land without grass or trees.
【Four】【Annotation】The physical form of the sage is
no different from that of ordinary people,
hence the functions of their ears and eyes decline;
however, when it comes to their spirit,
it remains complete and constant from beginning to end (two).
If it were immature in youth,
and then declined upon reaching adulthood,
then the sage's sageliness would not even last a single morning—
how could that be possible?
【Commentary】Having ascended the throne as the sovereign,
his majesty spanned across ten thousand chariots,
yet he compassionately thought of the common people,
worrying and pitying the ordinary masses.

yáng means

Shǐlíng,

Even to the extent of seeing with the eyes,

they remain unaware of it.

the strategist ministers inevitably relied on their achievements,
believing there would be no future worries, yet they faced execution.
Thus, it is known that things that benefit each other will inevitably also harm each other.

existence and disappearance do not cease.
What existed yesterday

Mountains and boats shift and vanish,
but the ignorant are unaware.
This is the meaning of it.
