【Subcommentary】The seven great elements discussed above,
all originate from their own spontaneity.
【二】【注】By following it, one becomes enlightened,
with no need for deliberate action.
【Commentary】Xún means
shùn (to follow).
Simply follow what is natural,
and wisdom will illuminate by itself.
【Three】【Commentary】The ultimate principle has its limit,
one should simply immerse in it deeply,
and then grasp its essential pivot.
【Commentary】The principles of the profound and obscure,
inherently possess their own pivotal mechanisms,
and in applying them, there is no need for deliberate effort.
【Explanation】"Shū" is pronounced chǐ zhū fǎn.
【四】【注】It is they who began it,
therefore I transmit rather than create.
【Commentary】Guō's annotation states,
"It was they who first possessed it,
hence I transmit rather than create."
【Five】【Commentary】When one releases responsibility to others,
they will resolve matters on their own;
thus, the act of resolving appears effortless,
as if nothing was resolved at all.
【Commentary】One comprehends by learning from others,
but if discipline does not form one's nature,
then it appears as though one does not understand.
【Six】【Annotation】It clarifies that they possess knowledge.
【Commentary】Being able to forget one's knowledge,
thus appearing as if unknowing.
【Seven】【Annotation】If I do not know, then they know and act on their own;
they know and act on their own,
then there is none under heaven who does not know.
【Commentary】Not knowing yet knowing,
knowing yet not knowing,
is not knowing through knowledge;
thus, it is only after not knowing that one truly knows,
and this is genuine knowledge.
【八】【Note】Responds to things appropriately without fixed methods.
【Nine】【Annotations】Each according to their portion.
【一０】【Note】Though the myriad things are diverse and intricate,
each and every thing possesses its own reality.
【Commentary】Jiéhuá,
means dissimilarity. The myriad things are in chaotic turmoil,
jiénhuá and dissimilar,
yet when unified and governed,
all rely on the true Dào.
【Explanation】"Xié": Xú gives the pronunciation as xiàjié fǎn.
"Huá": hūbā fǎn.
Xiàng states:
Xiéhuá
means confusion and disorder.
【One by one】【Comment】Each has its own reason,
and cannot substitute for one another.
【Commentary】The past exists in its own past,
not extending from the past to create the present;
the present exists in its own present,
nor does it generate the past from the present;
each thing has its own nature,
and the new and old cannot substitute for one another.
【一二】【Note】Each should fulfill their respective duties.
【Commentary】When the times do not interact,
and the laws do not change or trade,
how can one rely on the past to serve the present!
【13】【Comment】To weigh and elevate it,
is to have a great limit.
【Commentary】As to the questions raised above,
the Way is vast and great,
could it not be said that it elucidates the wondrous principles and discusses them with solid reasoning!
【Explanation】"Yáng què" is pronounced as "què" (角),
also read as "kǔ xué" (苦學反).
The Sān Cāng states:
"què" (搉)
means to oppose.
Xǔ Shèn explains:
"Yáng què" (揚搉)
refers to a rough method or principle.
Wáng comments:
It means to highlight and make evident through simplification.
◎Qìng Fān's analysis: The explanatory text cites the Sān Cāng as saying,
"què" (搉),
means to oppose.
"Oppose" should be corrected to "knock" (敲).
The Shuō Wén dictionary states:
"què" (搉)
means to strike or knock.
In the Hàn Shū's "Treatise on the Five Elements," it says "què its eye,"
with Shī Gǔ's annotation explaining:
"què" (搉)
refers to knocking out its essence.
The confusion between "oppose" and "knock" arises from their similar written forms.
【14】【Comment】If one inquires about the general principle,
then all things have their ultimate distinctions,
so the principle of forgetting oneself and entrusting to things can be understood and known;
why be so bewildered like this!
【Commentary】Hé,
means why not.
Xī,
means what.
Beings without knowledge are like wandering at night,
why not inquire of the sages!
As for their being lost since youth and so bewildered and distressed, what is the reason for this!
【15】【Comment】When delusion cannot be resolved,
valuing great non-delusion
is the utmost of folly.
Therefore, the sage follows and entrusts them,
which is why emperors and kings have different traces,
adapting their names according to the times.
【Commentary】Not being deluded by sagely wisdom,
one is deluded by ordinary sentiments.
Using the words of sagely wisdom to distinguish ordinary delusions,
forgetting gains and returning to the root,
restoring the true foundation,
yet failing to grasp the meaning and forget the words, instead clinging to the traces of the sages,
valuing and esteeming clear expressions,
regarding non-delusion as paramount,
this is revering non-delusion,
but how can it eliminate delusion!
This again dismisses the concept of non-delusion.
【Text Explanation】"Huò jiě" is read as jiā mǎi fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
"Fù yú" is pronounced as fú,
also read as fú yòu fǎn.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "不亦" is also written as "亦不".
(2) In the Táng dynasty manuscript, there is a character "也" after "惑".
【One】【(Pronunciation and Meaning)〔Explanatory Text〕】Named after a person.
Zé Yáng traveled to Chǔ,
Yí Jié spoke of him to the king,
but the king did not grant him an audience,
and Yí Jié returned.
【One】【Brief Account】His surname is Péng,
his given name is Yáng,
his courtesy name is Zéyáng,
and he is from the state of Lǔ.
He traveled to serve various feudal lords,
later entered the state of Chǔ,
intending to serve King Wén of Chǔ.
【Explanatory Text】"Zé Yáng": Sīmǎ comments:
His given name was Zéyáng,
and his courtesy name was Péngyáng.
Another account states:
His surname was Péng,
his given name was Zéyáng,
and he was a figure from the early Zhōu dynasty.
【Èr】【Shū】 Yí Xìng,
míng Jié,
Chǔ chén yě.
Zé Yáng yù shì yú Chǔ,
gù yīn Yí Jié chēng yán yú wáng,
wáng jì guì zhòng,
gù yóu wèi zhī jiàn yě.
Yí Jié suǒ jìn wèi suì,
gù bà cháo ér guī jiā.
【Explanation】Yí Jié was a minister of the state of Chǔ.
Péng Yáng saw Wáng Guǒ and said:
"Why does the Master not speak of me to the King?"
【一】【疏】Wáng Guǒ,
was a virtuous senior official of the state of Chǔ.
Tán,
means to discuss or narrate,
and some versions use the characters for speech and conversation.
Previously, due to Yí Jié,
he had not been able to see the king,
but later he persuaded Wáng Guǒ,
hoping he would talk about and recommend him.
【Explanatory Text】"Wáng Guǒ": Sīmǎ explains:
A virtuous person of Chǔ.
"Tán": pronounced as tán.
The text also has it as tán.
Lǐ explains:
It means to discuss.
Guō gives the pronunciation as tú kān fǎn,
Xú gives it as tú àn fǎn.
Wáng Guǒ said:
"I am not as good as Gōng Yuèxiū."
【First】【Memorial】Ruò,
means "like".
Gōng Yuè Xiū,
is the name of a recluse.
Wáng Guǒ was a worthy man,
who disliked Péng Yáng's haste in coveting glory,
therefore he highly praised recluses,
in order to curb his ambitious heart.
【Translated Text】Gōng Yuèxiū was a recluse.
Yuè,
pronounced as yuè.
Péng Yáng said:
"What kind of person is Gōng Yuè Xiū?"
【一】【疏】Xī,
means "why".
Since it mentions Gōng Yuèxiū,
saying that I am not as good as him,
therefore, I ask for the reason,
hoping to hear the explanation.
He said:
"In winter, I spear turtles in the river;
in summer, I rest by the mountain slopes.
If someone passing by asks,
I say:
'This is my dwelling place.'
"【一】Even Yí Jié could not manage it,
let alone me!
I am not even as capable as Yí Jié.
As for Yí Jié's character,
he lacks virtue but possesses cunning,
does not hold himself to high standards,
and uses this to mystify his social connections,
becoming utterly lost in the realm of wealth and status,
It is not to assist him with virtue,
but to help dissipate it.
Just as the freezing person borrows clothing from spring,
the one suffering from heat longs for winter's cold wind.
Now, the King of Chǔ as a man,
has a dignified appearance and is severe;
when it comes to offenses,
he shows no mercy, fierce as a tiger;
if not for the eloquent man of true virtue,
who could possibly bend him?
【一】【注】This statement is made,
to curb Péng Yáng's eagerness for advancement.
【Commentary】Chuò means
to pierce.
Fán means
alongside,
and also refers to a dense forest.
In the deep winter, he pierced turtles,
roaming freely on the river islets;
in the height of summer, he returned to rest,
reclining in the dense forest to find comfort;
since there were no encircling corridors,
he thus designated the mountain's edge as his dwelling.
This briefly recounts the deeds of Yuán Xiū.
【Explanation】"Chuò" is pronounced with the initial sound "ch" and the rhyme "jiao" in the fanqie system,
also read as "chì jiǎo" in another fanqie.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to stab.
Guō gives the pronunciation as "chù",
Xú offers "dīng lǜ" in fanqie,
another reading is "zhuō".
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
The old character for "zhuō" was mistakenly written as "cù",
which is an error.
Now it has been corrected.
◎ Qìng Fān's commentary notes that the "Guǎngyùn" cites Sīmǎ as saying:
"Chuò biē" means
to stab a turtle.
This slightly differs from the explanation in the interpretive text.
"Fán" is pronounced as "fán".
Lǐ explains:
It means beside or next to.
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to the shady side.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
It means edge or border.
"Yǔ zhái" Sīmǎ explains:
It signifies making oneself prominent by living in seclusion on the northern side of the mountain.
【二】【注】This means that I am not like Yí Jié's fondness for wealth and honor,
his ability to form connections,
his intent to exhaust form and name,
and his reliance on knowledge to seek favor with those above.
【Commentary】"Diānmíng"
means being lost and submerged.
This says Yí Jié's social connections are firm,
but his intent lies in glory and splendor;
he is toppled and confused,
his nature greedy for wealth and honor;
in truth, he lacks genuine virtue,
yet possesses worldly knowledge;
he cannot embrace emptiness and tranquility to follow the divine,
but prefers to rely on cunning to interfere with his superiors.
Repeatedly acting in this manner,
he still cannot succeed himself,
let alone someone like me who adheres to simplicity,
how could I be fit to recommend him!
This is Wáng Guǒ's humble and modest words.
【Explanation】"Having knowledge" is pronounced with the tone for wisdom.
The annotation is the same.
"Dianming" is pronounced as "mian".
Simǎ comments:
Dianming,
means being confused.
It refers to associating with rulers,
with emotions driven by wealth and status.
【Three】【Notes】If one advances by improper means,
then virtue becomes shallow and reputation fades.
【Commentary】消，
means to destroy or damage.
This means that Zé Yáng relied on me to speak of himself before the king,
which could only ruin his reputation and conduct,
and certainly would not benefit his great virtue.
【Four】【Annotation】It is said that I have followed the arrangements of the four seasons,
and thus cannot rush to Péng Yáng's urgent aid.
【Commentary】A person suffering from freezing,
will feel warm upon receiving clothing;
one afflicted by heatstroke,
will revive upon encountering water.
Yet to await the warm sun to thaw the ice,
or rely on a cold breeze to relieve heatstroke,
though contrary to human efforts,
truly follows the natural order.
Those who tread the path and attain enlightenment,
embody a nature devoid of immediate favors,
not advancing like Péng Yáng,
and the principle here is the same.
【Explanation】"Yē" is pronounced like "yē".
The Zìlín states:
It means suffering from heatstroke.
"Zhī shī" is pronounced with "shī" as "shǐ".
The same applies below.
【Five】【Memorials】His demeanor possesses the dignity of one who faces south as ruler,
his awe and sternness rest upon the nobility of commanding a thousand chariots.
In his blazing fury, he carries out venomous acts,
akin to a raging tiger,
slaughtering and humiliating the common people,
with no pardon or forgiveness assured.
Unless one is a person of great cunning,
they cannot bear to serve under him.
As for those who walk the path of righteousness and embrace virtue,
who could bend their will and serve him?
【Interpretation】"Néng náo": pronounced as nǎi xiào fǎn,
also pronounced as hū máo fǎn.
Wáng explains:
Only by upholding correct virtue can one subdue others with the highest principles,
while cunning individuals use talent and sophistry to seize control,
hence they are capable of muddying and distorting them.
Thus the sage,
in poverty makes his family forget their hunger,
in success makes nobles forget their ranks and become humble.
Towards things,
he finds joy in them;
towards people,
he delights in their understanding while preserving himself;
thus sometimes without speaking, he quenches others with harmony,
standing alongside people, he transforms them.
The proper bond between father and son,
he peacefully returns to dwell in it,
and effortlessly applies it.
So far-reaching is his effect on people's hearts.
Hence it is said: await Gōng Yuèxiū."
【一】【注】With a placid heart free from desires,
finding contentment in whatever one encounters,
not valuing extravagance and luxury,
but taking pride in virtue and morality,
thus, one's family does not recognize poverty as something to suffer.
【Commentary】Yù Kòu resided in Zhèng,
Lǎo Lái dwelled in Chǔ,
their wives and children lived in poverty yet found joy within.
If virtuous scholars were thus,
how much more so the true sages,
this is forgetting poverty.
【Explanation】"淡然" is pronounced as tú zàn fǎn.
【二】【注】They esteemed lightly titles and emoluments but valued highly the Way and virtue,
transcending to sit in forgetfulness,
unaware that glory resided in their persons,
thus causing kings and dukes to lose their grounds for claiming superiority.
【Commentary】Concealing one's brilliance is considered obscurity,
while manifesting one's traces is regarded as prominence.
Duke Āi esteemed Confucius as a virtuous friend,
and Xuānyuán humbly walked on his knees before Guǎngchéng.
These examples illustrate that when the Way is entrusted, it commands respect,
unrestricted by rank or destiny.
Thus, it can transform the hearts of kings who command ten thousand chariots
and rulers of the five noble ranks,
turning their lofty and noble minds into humble and lowly actions.
【Explanation】"Transforming through Humility" means occupying a high position yet taking humility as the foundation.
Some versions read as transforming through humility toward others.
【Three】【Comment】He did not allow external matters to cause himself suffering.
【Commentary】Engaging with the world's dust and affairs,
being selfless with all things,
everything encountered is fitting,
thus there is never a time without joy.
【Four】【Annotation】Communicate with others without losing oneself.
【Commentary】He blends into the human world without obstruction,
though interacting with things, he does not lose his self,
his actions do not harm his tranquility, and he constantly abides in his true nature.
【Text】"Not lost" is read as xī làng in the reverse tone.
【Five】【Annotation】Each person attains their own fulfillment,
thus harmony is imbibed,
how could it depend on words!
【Commentary】Sheltering all living beings,
merging indistinguishably with the vast heavens,
the way of central harmony,
allows each to attain their heart's content,
returning with fulfilled hearts,
how could there be any need for laborious verbal instruction!
【Explanation】"To drink" is pronounced as yù zhèn fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Seeing his demeanor and submitting to it.
【Commentary】Blending the light and mingling with the dust,
this is how they coexist;
each returning to their true nature,
this is how people are transformed.
【七】【注】So that fathers and sons each fulfill their proper roles.
【Commentary】Although it blends and equalizes the noble and the humble,
the order of human relations remains intact;
thus, fathers and sons, rulers and subjects,
each occupy their proper positions,
without encroaching upon one another's roles—
is this not indeed fitting!
【八】【Note】His actions align with the virtue of heaven and earth,
thus he remains tranquil and undivided.
【Commentary】All acts of bestowing kindness,
align with the rhythm of the four seasons,
never failing to be leisurely and composed,
where movement and stillness are one.
【Explanatory Text】"一閒" is pronounced as xián.
【九】【疏】The sage's application of mind,
as fully described above,
thus reveals its purity, loftiness, profundity, and far-reaching nature.
◎Jià Shìfù comments:
The proper relationship between father and son,
follows from the family forgetting their poverty.
The son,
is the one who supports the father;
the father,
is the one who relies on the son for support;
this is what is meant by "proper."
Returning to dwell in seclusion,
refers to the aforementioned winter fishing for turtles and summer resting in the mountain groves.
Explaining the term:
"leisure,"
means simplicity.
It refers to differentiating what one applies in order to seek self-sufficiency,
not making the family forget their poverty,
but forgetting it oneself.
This is what distances it from the human heart.
【一０】【注】He wishes him to abandon the King of Chǔ and follow Yuàn Xiū,
intending to use the tranquil and serene demeanor to calm his restless heart.
【Comment】This is the concluding summary.
【Collation】(1) The character 'ér' was altered according to the Shìdétáng edition.
The sage comprehends intricate connections,
and is thoroughly united with all things,
yet does not know how this is so—
it is his nature.
In returning to his destiny and responding to actions, he takes Heaven as his guide,
and people consequently designate him as such.
How troubling it is to rely on knowledge, for what one practices often does not last long—
if it were to cease, what could be done about it!
【一】【注】This is what is called profound and all-encompassing understanding.
【Commentary】Chóumóu means
to bind and tie.
The sage who has attained the Way,
transcends and is liberated,
realizing that the material world is illusory—
how could they be ensnared by the dust-laden net!
Although Yuè Xiū had not yet reached the ultimate state of the Way,
it was thus entrusted to him to explain it.
【Explanation】"Chóu" is pronounced as zhí zhōu fǎn.
"Móu" is pronounced as wáng hóu fǎn.
Chóumóu,
means entangled or lingering.
It is also said:
profound and abstruse.
【二】【注】There is no distinction between external and internal (一) and all are equally illuminated.
【Commentary】When wisdom encompasses all things,
one exhausts principles and fully realizes nature,
so that self and others are not separate,
thus blending into a single unity.
【Explanation】"Zhou Jin Yi Tǐ" refers to the thoroughness of observation and reflection,
penetratingly discerning both the refined and the coarse,
hence it is said to be all-encompassing and unified as one body.
One body,
is Heaven.
【Three】【Comment】If it is not knowing how it is so and yet being so naturally,
how could it not be nature!
【Commentary】When the perceiver and the perceived correspond,
the object and the wisdom merge indistinguishably,
one does not know the reason,
nor can one discern how it is so,
thus it accords with the true nature.
【Four】【Comment】The swaying sways by itself,
the acting acts by itself,
all ultimately return to their destiny and follow what is natural.
【Commentary】Returning to the true root,
reverting to the fundamental destiny,
even though there is movement again,
it acts in accordance with things,
with no deliberate intent in motion or stillness,
it aligns with heaven and earth,
thus learning from the two realms.
【Explanation】"Returning to Destiny and Stirring into Action": Stirring means
movement.
All things move, act, grow, and live,
each possessing its inherent nature,
thus returning to their destiny.
【Five】【Annotation】This is not pursuing fame to elevate one's deeds.
Leading by following one's nature and acting accordingly,
one's deeds naturally become lofty,
thus others cannot belittle their reputation.
【Commentary】Mìng means
name.
The sage who embodies the Way
originally had no name;
because there exists pure dust worthy of admiration,
people later ascribed a name to them.
【Explanation】"Mìng zhī yě" means mìng,
which is to name.
【Six】【Comment】Relying on knowledge and acting arbitrarily,
then worries and calamities follow one after another.
【Commentary】When one relies on knowledge to manipulate things,
worries and troubles thus arise.
The mind is easily swayed,
and what one accomplishes is but little.
Clinging to attachments and thoughts,
how could there ever be a moment of stillness!
Even if it were the divine Yǔ,
there would be nothing he could do about it!
【Transliteration】"Yōu hū zhì" pronounced as zhì.
"Ér suǒ xíng héng wú jǐ" jū read as qǐ.
When will it ever cease? What can be done about it?" Wáng states:
Worrying about wisdom,
means that those who act worry when their form and wisdom fall short.
They do not know that employing wisdom inevitably leads to loss,
and after loss, they further worry about lacking wisdom.
By the time the application of their wisdom brings harm instead of aid,
thus their worries and troubles follow one another without a moment's rest.
Hence it is said, constantly, there is hardly any time when it ceases.
Unable to discard wisdom and rid themselves of worry,
how can it not be deemed worthy of worry!
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition reads as "nèi wài".
(2) The character "shuài" has been emended based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The character "ér" has been emended based on the Zhào Jiànyì edition.
One who is born beautiful
is given a mirror by others;
if not told, they do not know they are more beautiful than others.
As if knowing it,
as if not knowing it,
as if hearing of it,
as if not hearing of it,
their likability never ceases,
and others' fondness for them also never ceases—
this is due to their nature.
When a sage loves others,
people bestow a name upon them;
if not told, they do not know they love others.
As if knowing it,
as if not knowing it,
as if hearing of it,
as if not hearing of it,
their love for others never ceases,
and others' contentment with them also never ceases—
this is due to their nature.
【一】【Note】A mirror,
is a looking glass,
reflecting objects without partiality,
hence people praise it.
Now, as for the mirror,
does it know it's a mirror and thus reflects?
Being inherently capable of reflection,
people then call it a mirror;
if no one informs it,
it would not know it is praised by people.
This is like a sage,
to whom people ascribe the name.
【Explanation】A mirror is,
a looking glass.
To inform,
means to speak.
Heaven bestows clear illumination,
shining upon all things without bias,
and people admire it,
hence it is named a mirror.
If people did not communicate with each other,
the bright mirror would originally have no name.
This is the beginning of the analogy.
【Interpretation】》Then one would not know that it is more beautiful than humans》From birth, there is the beauty of seeing things without intention,
humans create names and mirrors for it,
hence people find it beautiful.
If not informed,
one would not know that it is more beautiful than humans.
【二】【注】The reason a mirror is admirable,
lies in its lack of emotion.
Regardless of whether it knows or does not know,
hears or does not hear,
when something comes, it reflects it immediately,
thus never ceasing.
If the mirror acted based on hearing or knowing,
then there would be times when it would cease to function.
【Commentary】"Cease" means
to stop.
When a mirror reflects objects,
its principle lies in being impartial;
regardless of resentment or intimacy,
its reflection remains consistently equal.
If it neither hears nor perceives,
the mirror does not reflect,
but once there is hearing and perception,
the mirror can reflect it.
This implies that matters involve interruption and deprivation,
sometimes ceasing and becoming inactive;
how could it reflect perpetually!
It is only because of its endless, concentrated reflection
that it is cherished by people.
◎Qìng Fān's case notes: Wáng Shì Niàn Sūn stated:
"Never ceasing" means
"never,"
signifying "ultimately,"
ultimately without a time of cessation.
【Three】【Annotation】If it is not by nature one's preference,
how could one endure long illumination!
【Commentary】The mirror's ability to reflect
arises from its inherent nature,
just as human preferences
stem from the creations of nature.
Since neither is artificially imposed,
they are thus inexhaustible.
【Transcription】"Hǎo zhī": pronounced as Hào with the fourth tone.
Same for the annotation.
【四】【注】The sage is without love, like a mirror.
Yet his actions benefit all things,
so people give him this name.
If people did not inform one another,
none would know of his love for others.
【Commentary】The sage's grace blankets all living beings,
his kindness flows through myriad generations.
All things bear his virtue,
and people bestow upon him a name.
They pass it on to one another in conversation,
thus giving rise to this laudable title.
Were it not so,
how could the name of a sage exist!
【Five】【Comment】Vast and impartial, treating the people as straw dogs,
yet the Way aligns with loving others,
hence able to be selfless.
If love arises from knowledge and perception,
then it may wane over time.
【Commentary】The sage's virtue is vast and far-reaching,
interacting with all things without partiality,
nurturing and sustaining all living beings,
treating the common people as straw dogs,
how could it be that only after knowing them does one come to love them!
It is solely because compassionate salvation is without bias,
that virtue is inexhaustible.
This is an analogy.
【Six】【Annotation】What is at ease with one's nature,
thus can endure long.
【Commentary】"Ān" means
settled.
When still, it shares virtue with yīn;
when moving, it shares waves with yáng.
Thus, it has no deliberate intent in stillness or motion.
Therefore, it can remain constant even when a sudden thunderbolt splits the mountains,
and stay unshaken when a great gale stirs the sea.
This is following one's true nature.
If one distorts nature with artificial emotions,
there will be times of agitation.
Hence, Wáng Bì stated,
"Without making emotions true to nature,
how can one long practice what one aspires to!"
The old country, the old capital,
one gazes at it and is cheered.
Even if the hills and mounds, plants and trees are tangled and overgrown,
so that nine-tenths of it is obscured,
one is still cheered by it.
How much more so when one sees what is to be seen and hears what is to be heard,
like a terrace ten fathoms high suspended before the crowd!
【一】【Note】To regain the old is still liberating,
how much more so to attain one's true nature!
【Commentary】The state capital,
(metaphorically) represents one's true nature.
For when one loses their homeland in youth,
and wanders displaced in foreign lands,
gazing back toward their native mulberry and catalpa trees,
they feel profoundly joyful.
Moreover, having long been estranged from the Way,
and chasing after trivialities for an extended period,
now that they have returned to the origin and recovered the root,
it is therefore said to be profoundly joyful.
【Explanation】"Chàng rán" means a joyful appearance.
【二】【注】Mín,
means to combine.
【Explanation】"之緡" is pronounced as mín with the people's endurance sound,
Xú gives the pronunciation as hūn.
Guǒ says:
It means to combine.
Sīmǎ says:
It means flourishing.
【Three】【Comment】Seeing what one has seen before,
hearing what one has heard before,
yet still feeling exhilarated—
how much more so when embodying its essence and applying its nature!
【Commentary】Mín means
to combine.
An old state or ancient capital,
long fallen into ruin,
with rugged hills and perilous defiles,
overgrown with dense vegetation;
entering and visiting within,
nine out of ten people are recognized,
seeing what one has seen before,
hearing what one has heard before,
the feelings of cherishing life,
bring forth spontaneous joy and delight.
How much more so for one who has long lost the Way,
adrift in the cycle of life and death,
suddenly returning to the origin,
meeting that true source,
returning to the realm of profound mystery,
beholding the state of the ultimate Dao—
the joy of this,
how could it be easily expressed!
【Explanation of the Text】"Nineteen" means seeing ten and recognizing nine.
"Seeing the seen and hearing the heard" refers to seeing what is seen,
and hearing what is heard.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
The character "mín",
the "Explanation of the Text" quotes Sīmǎ as saying it means abundant,
while Guō's annotation says it means to combine,
both interpretations are reasonable in meaning.
"Nineteen enter it",
the "Explanation of the Text" says it means seeing ten and recognizing nine,
but this does not capture the true meaning.
"Enter" here
means entering into the concealment of hills, trees, and plants.
If nineteen enter it,
then those that emerge and can be seen are only one in ten,
yet one still feels joyful and delighted,
hence it is followed by "how much more so for seeing the seen and hearing the heard."
Guō's annotation says,
seeing what one has seen before,
hearing what one has heard before,
and still feeling joyful,
then the phrase "how much more so for seeing the seen and hearing the heard" becomes inexplicable,
so he added, "how much more so for embodying one's substance and employing one's nature,"
which does not align with the original meaning of the Zhuāngzǐ.
【Four】【Annotation】What the multitude is accustomed to,
even in peril, remains at ease;
how much more so the sage, who is without peril!
【Commentary】Seven chi is called a rèn.
The terrace stands seventy feet high,
which can be considered perilously steep,
yet when people ascend it repeatedly,
they gradually feel no fear.
Habit becomes second nature,
bringing a sense of ease and familiarity;
how much more so when one attains the true way,
where is there that cannot be a place of peace?
【Explanatory Text】"Tái xiàn" is pronounced as "xuán".
"Zhòng xián" is pronounced as "xián".
The same applies to the annotations.
The Yuánjiā version uses "xián".
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
This follows from what is seen and heard.
A platform ten ren high is suspended amidst the ears and eyes of the crowd,
something that everyone sees and hears together,
unlike the hills and vegetation where nine out of ten blend in unnoticed,
its clarity is thus evident.
Guǒ's annotation states,
what the masses are accustomed to,
even if perilous, seems at ease.
This mistakenly reads "jiàn" as "xián",
making little sense in meaning.
Likely due to misunderstanding the preceding text,
hence missing the essence here as well.
◎ Jiā Shìfù comments:
According to Shuōwén:
"jiàn",
means a gap.
In the Rites of Zhōu, terms like well spacing, formation spacing, and shared spacing,
all empty spaces are called "jiàn",
even the empty space in a house is called "jiàn".
A platform ten ren high,
suspended in the midst of the crowd,
stands out prominently,
what is seen and heard cannot be concealed.
By grasping the central pivot to follow along with completion,
not displaying it outwardly but attaining it within oneself,
one can then respond to the infinite.
Rǎn Xiàng shì attained the pivot of the circle to follow completion,
with things having neither end nor beginning,
neither limit nor time.
One who daily transforms with things,
is one who does not transform,
so why ever abandon it!
To emulate Heaven yet fail to emulate Heaven,
and to perish along with all things—
how can one regard this as proper conduct?
The sage has never recognized Heaven,
never recognized humanity,
never recognized beginning,
never recognized things,
yet walks with the age without deviation,
perfectly practices without excess—
how does such harmony come about?
Tāng found his director of officials, Mén Yǐn Dèng Héng, to serve as his tutor,
following the teacher without being confined;
he attained this following completion.
He entrusted him with overseeing his reputation;
this reputation overflowed into methods,
attaining dual manifestation.
Zhòngní exhausted his thoughts
to transmit it for him.
Róng Chéng shì said:
"Without days, there are no years;
without inner, there is no outer."
【一】【注】Rǎn Xiàngshì,
was a sage king of antiquity.
Dwelling in emptiness and following things,
things naturally accomplished themselves.
【Commentary】Rǎn Xiàngshì,
was a non-action sovereign before the era of the Three Sovereigns.
"Huán" refers to
the emptiness within a circle.
It means that the ancient sage kings,
having attained the true path of emptiness,
embodied the subtlety of the center of the circle,
thus their way harmonized with all living beings,
and they seamlessly integrated all things.
【Explanation】"Rǎn Xiàng" is pronounced with "xiàng" as "xiàng" with the fourth tone.
The annotation is the same.
Guǒ (Guo Xiang) says:
Rǎn Xiàngshì,
an ancient sage king.
◎Yú Yuè (Yu Yue) states:
The "Lù Shǐ · Xún Fēi Jì" contains Rǎn Xiàngshì.
【二】【注】Suddenly, one journeys together with it.
【Commentary】Without beginning,
there is no past;
without end,
there is no future;
without moments or time,
there is no present.
Embodying transformation and merging with change,
moving along with all things,
thus there are no three periods of time.
【Three】【Commentary】Day by day transforming with things,
thus constantly without self,
constantly without self,
therefore constantly not transforming.
【Commentary】Being compliant with daily renewal,
and transforming along with all things,
one is active yet constantly tranquil,
thus unifying in the way of serene stillness,
standing firm and unchanging.
【Four】【Annotation】 It says that those who act,
why not try to abandon what they are doing?
【Commentary】Hé means
"how" or "why".
It speaks of one whose body is empty,
merging with the creator of things,
undergoing myriad transformations and journeying along with change,
never parting from it even for a moment!
【Transcription】"Cháng shě" is pronounced as shě.
The annotation is the same.
【Five】【Comment】Only when there is no teacher to follow,
can one learn from Heaven.
【Commentary】"Shī" means the name for imitation;
"tiān" refers to what is natural.
When the great creator makes things,
they act according to their inherent nature.
If one intentionally sets out to imitate and learn,
it goes against the natural way,
and thus cannot be achieved.
【Six】【Comment】Even taking Heaven as one's teacher still cannot avoid being driven by external things,
how could it be worth following!
Taking Heaven as a teacher is still not worthy of being called true practice,
how much more so when one does not even take Heaven as a teacher!
【Commentary】Xùn (to sacrifice) means
to pursue,
to seek.
When one intentionally imitates the Creator and goes along with things,
this is not following one's inherent nature;
how could it suffice for cultivating one's endeavors!
There is still something being sought,
hence it is xùn (sacrificial pursuit).
Even a teacher may be referred to with the term xùn,
let alone abandoning oneself to chase after external things—
what can be done about it!
【Transcription】"皆殉" is pronounced as cí jùn fǎn.
◎Jiā Shìfù remarked:
That which has its cessation,
is what communicates with destiny;
That which is taken as an affair,
is what responds to things;
That which is abandoned,
is the exhaustion of nature and return to destiny,
blending self and others to transform them.
Saying "how about this"
is the way of being thus.
【Seven】【Treatises】The sage who attains the mean,
reaches the ultimate principle,
thus can dismiss both humanity and heaven,
forget both things and self.
Since it is said there is no end,
how could there ever be a beginning!
Following nature to unite with the Way,
no longer emulating heaven.
【Eight】【Annotations】all absent,
then darkly unite.
【Commentary】To replace means
to abolish,
to obstruct.
To blend with human affairs,
and move alongside the world,
interacting with things according to the times,
never experiencing neglect or deficiency.
However, the ups and downs of human life,
they have been fully experienced,
yet without ever being obstructed,
wherever encountered, they flow through,
unintentionally learning from a master,
naturally aligning with the Way,
how could deliberate imitation
hope to attain truth?
It is certainly impossible.
【Explanatory Text】"The conduct is complete and does not overflow." Pronounced as yì.
Guǒ's pronunciation is xǔ's counter,
Lǐ's is xū yù's counter,
meaning to overflow.
Wáng states:
It means to ruin or decay.
Acting without deliberate intent,
there is no destination not reached,
hence it is said all are devoted.
The conduct is complete and neither things nor self are harmed,
thus there is no ruin or decay.
【九】【注】Entrust it to the hundred officials and do not interfere with it.
【Commentary】His surname was Mén,
and his given name was Yǐn.
It is also said:
Mén Yǐn,
was an official title;
his surname was Dēng,
and his given name was Héng.
Yīn Tāng, being a sage,
set aside personal concerns and followed the natural course of things,
thus he obtained excellent ministers to manage affairs.
Once they served as his tutors,
he remained serene and poised, doing nothing yet achieving everything.
【Explanation】"Mén Yǐn Dēng Héng" Xiàng comments:
Mén Yǐn,
an official title,
Dēng Héng,
a person's name.
"Wéi zhī" is read with the pronunciation yú wèi fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Fù zhī" is pronounced as fù.
The same applies below.
"Bù yǔ" is pronounced as yù.
【一０】【Note】Let them gather on their own,
not confining them;
allow them to disperse freely,
not releasing them.
【Explanation】Cóng,
means to entrust.
Yòu,
means to gather.
Being empty and tranquil, acting without striving,
entrusting matters to the mentor,
ultimately never accumulating achievements for one's own credit.
【一一】【注】The officials in charge of charioteering and such,
are also able to follow the natural course of things,
and Tāng obtained this ability,
hence his name is entrusted to things, and the merit does not lie with himself.
【Commentary】A virtuous minister receives his commission,
and accomplishes tasks in accordance with the nature of things.
He attributes achievements to the officials in charge,
ensuring that the credit does not rest with himself.
【一二】【Note】Names and laws are
merely traces of what has already passed (two),
not the actual steps themselves.
Therefore it is said,
one who is empty and without a mind
entrusts governance to the various officials,
then their names and traces will both appear there.
【Commentary】Yǐrán means
having no intention.
It appears.
It is manifest.
The names that complete things,
the methods of the sage's traces,
are all passed down through teaching without personal involvement.
Therefore, the two matters of names and methods,
are both revealed in that,
yǐrán, leisurely and unrestrained,
achieving success without claiming credit.
【Translated Text】"之名嬴" is pronounced as yíng (盈).
"法得其兩見" is read as xián biàn fǎn.
The annotation is the same.
Attaining its way of following and achieving to oversee its name,
name and reality establish the law,
hence achieving dual manifestation,
akin to the mutual reflection of a person and a mirror.
◎Jiā Shìfù commented:
"Following and achieving" means
complete and natural formation;
"dual manifestation" refers to
mutual opposition.
According to Shuōwén,
"fǔ" means
mutual.
This implies the meaning of assisting.
Following and achieving,
one can serve as a minister.
Zhòngní's exhaustive consideration,
is also a form of assistance,
and this too is a form of opposition.
"Overseeing" means
to observe.
The flourishing of names,
is the deficiency of laws.
Ěryǎ Shìgǔ explains:
"law" means
constant.
Lǎozǐ said, "The name that can be named is not the eternal name."
Observing the traces of names allows one to know their formation,
hence it is called dual manifestation.
"寄治" is read as zhí lì fǎn.
【一三】【Comment】Zhòngní said:
What is there in the world to ponder or worry about!
All worries have already been exhausted,
If there were even the slightest worry,
How could one remain tranquil and unmoving,
Responding to stimuli endlessly,
Thereby assisting the natural state of all things!
【Commentary】Fu (輔) means
to assist.
Jin (盡) means
to eliminate.
Confucius, being a sage,
emptied his mind and eliminated thoughts,
thus he could enlighten the multitude,
assisting them in following their natural dispositions.
If he harbored even a speck of intention,
how could he sit in oblivion and respond to stimuli!
【一四】【Note】The reason we have years and keep track of days now,
is because there is life and death.
If there were no death and no life,
then the reckoning of years and days would be eliminated.
【Commentary】Róng Chéng was
a sage king of antiquity.
"Year" and "day" are
merely names for the sequence of time.
Because we calculate by time,
there is birth and death.
When birth and death cease to exist,
then "year" and "day" are eliminated.
【Interpretive Text】Róng Chéng was the teacher of Lǎo Zǐ.
◎Yú Yuè states:
In the "Treatise on Literature" of the Book of Hàn, the Yin-Yang school includes the fourteen chapters of Master Róng Chéng,
while the sexual arts school also has the twenty-six volumes of Róng Chéng's Yin Dào,
this being the teacher of Lǎo Zǐ.
In the "Tāng Wèn" chapter of the Liè Zǐ, the Yellow Emperor resided with Master Róng Chéng atop Mount Kōngtóng,
observing a joint fast for three months.
This must be a different person.
In the "Běn Jīng" chapter of the Huái Nán Zǐ, during the time of the Róng Chéng clan,
wild geese lined the roads in rows,
infants were left in nests,
surplus grain was placed at the head of the fields,
tigers and leopards could be followed,
vipers and snakes could be trodden upon,
yet no one knew how this came to be.
This should refer to a sovereign of high antiquity,
namely the Róng Chéng clan mentioned in the "Qū Qiè" chapter of the Zhuāng Zǐ,
listed alongside clans such as Dà Tíng, Bó Huáng, Zhōng Yāng, and Lì Lù.
However, Gāo Yòu's commentary states,
the Róng Chéng clan,
were creators of the calendar during the Yellow Emperor's time,
thus regarding them as ministers of the Yellow Emperor.
This explanation, applied to the Róng Chéng clan in the "Tāng Wèn" chapter of the Liè Zǐ who lived with the Yellow Emperor at Kōngtóng,
is appropriate,
but not for this Róng Chéng.
Considering all these accounts together,
there are three Róng Chéng clans:
a sovereign of the Yellow Emperor's era,
the first;
a minister of the Yellow Emperor,
the second;
the teacher of Lǎo Zǐ,
the third.
However, the exact year of Lǎo Zǐ's birth remains unverifiable,
and his teacher might indeed be the minister of the Yellow Emperor,
which cannot be ruled out.
【一五】【Note】Without self and other, there is no distinction between inner and outer.
【Commentary】Inner,
refers to the self.
Outer,
refers to external things.
Because of calculating life and death,
hence the term "inner" is used.
As the years and days pass by,
what can be imposed upon things and the self!
【Collation Note】(1) The character 'zhī' is deleted based on the Song dynasty reprinted edition and Wáng Shūmín's explanation.
(2) In the Shìdé Táng edition, 'ěr' is written as 'ér'.
Wèi Yíng made a pact with Tián Hóu Móu,
but Tián Hóu Móu betrayed it.
Wèi Yíng was enraged,
and intended to send someone to assassinate him.
【一】【疏】Yíng,
is the name of King Huì of Wèi.
Tián Hóu,
refers to King Wēi of Qí,
named Móu,
the son of Duke Huán,
a descendant of Tián Héng,
hence called Tián Hóu.
The two states of Qí and Wèi,
made a covenant and established an alliance,
agreeing not to attack each other.
Not long after the alliance,
King Wēi violated it,
so the Marquis of Wèi became enraged,
and intended to send someone to assassinate him.
This alliance took place in the twenty-sixth year of King Wēi of Qí,
and the eighth year of King Huì of Wèi.
【Text Explanation】"Wèi Yīng": The Guǒ version writes it as Yīng,
pronounced like the yīng in polishing jade.
Most current editions write it as Yīng.
Pronounced with the second tone and gēng initial.
Sīmǎ comments:
This refers to King Huì of Wèi.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
In older versions, the use of Yīng and Yīng was interchanged,
making the text rather inconsistent.
Moreover, most current texts actually use the character Yīng,
so it has now been corrected.
The historical records table lists the name of King Huì of Liáng as Yīng.
"Yǔ Tián Hóu": One edition writes it as Tián Hóu Móu.
Sīmǎ comments:
Tián Hóu,
refers to King Wēi of Qí,
named Móu,
son of Duke Huán.
According to the Records of the Grand Historian,
King Wēi's name was Yīn,
not Móu.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
Note that current texts include the character Móu.
The Records of the Grand Historian states King Wēi's name was Yīnqí,
and the Strategies of the Warring States also agrees.
◎ Yú Yuè states:
The Records of the Grand Historian lists King Wēi's name as Yīnqí.
None of the rulers of Tián Qí were named Móu;
only Duke Huán was named Wǔ,
which resembles the character Móu.
Móu might be a miswriting of Wǔ.
However, Duke Huán of Qí, named Wǔ, and King Huì of Liáng were not contemporaries.
"Bèi zhī": Pronounced as pèi.
"Cì zhī": Pronounced with the qī initial and cì tone.
Xīshǒu (Gōngsūn Yǎn) (1) heard of this and felt ashamed, saying:
"You are the ruler of a state with ten thousand chariots,
yet you seek revenge like a common man!
I, Yǎn, request to lead two hundred thousand armored troops,
to attack them for you,
capture their people,
and round up their cattle and horses,
(2) making their ruler burn with such inner fever that it erupts on his back.
Then we will seize their state.
When Jì flees in exile,
we shall strike his back,
and break his spine.
【一】【疏】Xīshǒu,
is an official title,
similar to something like Hǔbēn nowadays.
It refers to Gōngsūn Yǎn, who held this position.
In the states of the feudal lords,
with ten thousand chariots of war,
thus he is called a lord.
A common man,
refers to someone without an official position, a husband and wife paired together.
Pursuing vengeance,
is like seeking revenge.
A ruler,
with one outburst of anger can cause corpses to fall and blood to flow,
yet now orders a common man to carry out an assassination,
sending a lone envoy to exact revenge,
this is not the affair of a state with ten thousand chariots,
hence it is shameful.
【Explanation】"Xī Shǒu" is an official title in Wèi.
Sīmǎ comments:
It is like today's Tiger Tooth General,
Gōngsūn Yǎn held this position.
The Yuánjiā edition writes it as "Chǐ Shǒu".
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: In the "Strategies of the Warring States" Volume Three, Bào's note quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Xī Shǒu,
an official of Wèi,
is like today's Tiger Tooth General.
This is more concise than the explanation text.
"Wàn Shèng" is pronounced with shéng as the initial and zhèng as the final.
【二】【疏】General Sūn Yǎn,
requested to be solely commanded and receive the battle-axe,
leading armored soldiers two hundred thousand in number,
to attack their city of Qí,
certain to achieve victory.
Thereupon, they plundered the common people,
rounded up cattle and horses,
recorded merits and bestowed rewards,
and distributed the troops accordingly.
【Transcription】"For the ruler": pronounced as wèi, with a falling tone.
The following instances of "for the ruler" share the same pronunciation.
【Three】【Memorials】His surname is Tián,
given name Jì,
a general of Qí.
"Chì" and "zhé"
mean to strike.
With the state destroyed and people lost, he harbored wrath,
thus hot energy accumulated in his heart,
leading to boils erupting on his back.
Once the state had fallen,
and its commander was captured,
they then struck his back,
breaking his waist and spine,
and the army returned triumphantly.
Wasn't that satisfying indeed!
【Explanatory Text】"Jì fled in fear." Jì, being afraid, ran away.
Some say he was besieged.
In the Yuánjiā edition, Jì is written as Wáng.
"Chì" is pronounced as chì with one variation.
According to the Sān Cāng:
It means to strike.
Guǒ states:
Zhì,
also pronounced as zhū lì with a variation.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In old texts, zhì was still written as chì,
which is erroneous.
Now, the phonetic and meaning annotations included in the book use zhì,
so I tentatively follow that.
Some suspect it might be dié,
but that does not mean to strike either.
"Break its" is pronounced as zhī shé with a variation.
【Collation Notes】(1) The three characters "Gōngsūn Yǎn" have been added based on the commentary text and the Zhào counsel version.
(2) The character "guān" has been added following the Bào annotation in the Strategies of the Warring States.
Jìzǐ heard of it and felt ashamed, saying:
"To build a city wall ten ren high,
and when the wall is already ten ren high,
then to destroy it again—
this is what troubles the convict laborers.
Now, no wars have arisen for seven years;
this is the foundation of the king's rule.
Yǎn is a troublemaker;
his words should not be heeded.
【一】【疏】Jì is the surname;
zǐ is an
honorific for one
with virtue;
he was a worthy minister of Wèi.
Xūmǐ refers to
convict laborers.
Jìzǐ, embracing the Way,
did not resort to military campaigns,
and upon hearing Xīshǒu request troops,
felt ashamed and offered his remonstrance.
For a city wall of seventy zhàng,
the labor expended was not little;
once the wall was completed,
to tear it down without cause,
this would mean the convict laborers suffered hardship in vain.
This is the analogy he raised.
【Translated Text】"Jìzǐ" was a minister of Wèi.
◎Yú Yuè said:
The two characters below,
are suspected to be a miswriting of the character for seven.
If the city wall has already reached seven rèn,
then although it hasn't reached ten rèn, it is not far from it,
so its destruction would be regrettable.
If it had already reached ten rèn,
then it could simply be said to be completed,
and it wouldn't be appropriate to say it has already reached ten rèn.
The text below says,
now the troops have not been raised for seven years,
this is the king's foundation,
clearly using seven rèn as a metaphor for seven years,
there is no doubt that it is a miswritten character.
《又壞》pronounced as guài.
【二】【疏】The weapons of war have been laid to rest,
for seven years already,
with military affairs ceased and culture cultivated,
the king's grand foundation.
Xī Shǒu is just beginning to stir up calamity and chaos,
and must not be heeded.
Huá Zǐ heard this and was disgusted, saying:
"Those who eloquently advocate attacking Qí
are troublemakers;
those who eloquently oppose attacking
are also troublemakers;
those who claim that both attacking and not attacking are the acts of troublemakers,
are themselves troublemakers again."
【一】【疏】Huá,
a surname;
zǐ,
an appellation for one of virtue;
also a worthy minister of Wèi.
Those skilled in advocating the attack on Qí,
meaning to mobilize arms and troops,
are thus the ones who bring calamity and chaos,
this refers to Gōngsūn Yǎn.
Those skilled in advising against the attack,
their intent lies in the king's grand foundation,
surpassing that of rival states,
harboring certain expectations,
are thus troublemakers,
this is Jìzǐ.
To say that both advocating for and against attacking are troublemakers,
is because they fail to forget words and practice the Way,
still holding right and wrong in mind,
thus they too cannot avoid being troublemakers,
this is Huázǐ's own explanation.
【Explanation】Huá Zǐ was also a minister of Wèi.
The lord said:
"Then what should be done?"
【一】【疏】Huá Zǐ's mind was profoundly detached and untrammeled,
the king could not fathom the reason for this,
so he inquired about the meaning of his words,
wondering what his intentions and inclinations were.
He said:
"You need only seek the Way!"
【One】【Memorial】The Way is pure, void, and serene,
forgetting both self and things,
thus I urge seeking it,
hoping to reduce desires,
so that one can surely tread the path,
and contention will naturally vanish.
Huìzǐ heard of this and went to see Dài Jìngrén.
Dài Jìngrén said:
"There is what is called a snail,
do you know it, my lord?"
【一】【疏】Dài Jìnrén,
was a worthy man of Liáng.
His surname was Dài,
and his courtesy name was Jìnrén.
Huì Shī, upon hearing Huá Zǐ's profound discourse,
still feared that the King of Wèi might not have understood,
so he summoned Dài Jìn
in hopes of resolving the doubts.
【Explanation】"Huìzǐ" refers to Huì Shī.
"Ér jiàn" is pronounced xián biàn fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Dài Jìnrén" was a worthy man of the state of Liáng,
recommended by Huì Shī to the King of Wèi.
He said:
"Yes."
【一】【注】The snail is extremely minute,
yet it possesses two horns.
【Commentary】The wō is
a type of insect,
resembling a small spiral shell;
commonly called huángdú,
also known as wōniú,
with four horns.
Does the lord know it?
He said yes,
King Wèi replied:
"I recognize it."
【Explanation】"Snail" is pronounced as guā,
Guō pronounces it as gē.
Lǐ Yún says:
The snail insect has two horns,
commonly called the snail.
Sān Cāng states:
It is the small ox spiral.
Another says:
commonly known as the yellow calf.
"There was a state on the left horn of a snail called Chùshì,
and a state on the right horn called Mánshì.
They often fought over territory,
leaving tens of thousands of corpses,
and pursued the defeated for fifteen days before returning."
【一】【Note】If one truly understands that the matters being contended over are as trivial as this,
then there would be no contention in the world.
【Commentary】On the two horns of a snail,
two states exist.
Mánshì and Chùshì
frequently wage war against each other,
causing no small number of casualties,
and their advances and retreats also take a long time.
This is an analogy.
【Explanation of Text】"数万" is pronounced with the initial "sè" and the final "zhǔ" in the opposite tone.
"逐北" is read as per its character,
and also pronounced as "pèi".
When an army flees, it is called "běi".
The lord said:
"Alas!
Are these empty words?"
【First】【Memorial】The words spoken are bizarre and deceitful,
far removed from human sentiment,
hence provoking sighs of astonishment,
and casting doubt on their truthfulness.
【Explanation】"Yuē yī": pronounced as yú qí fǎn.
"Yán yǔ": the sound is yú.
He said:
"I ask to verify it for you, my lord.
Does my lord believe that the four directions, above and below, have limits?"
【一】【疏】If you insist on dismissing these as empty words,
allow me to present the factual records.
【Two Theories】Do you, sir, by your own reasoning, surmise whether the four directions, above and below, have limits or not?
Based on this principle to manage affairs,
I further questioned Marquis Wèi.
The lord said:
"Boundless."
【One】【Memorial】The Marquis of Wèi replied, saying:
"Above and below, the four directions,
truly have no end."
He said:
"Knowing to let the mind wander in the infinite,
yet returning to dwell in the accessible realm,
does it seem to exist or not to exist?"
【一】【注】Where human footprints reach is considered accessible,
meaning the entire world within the four seas today.
【二】【疏】Human traces reach what is considered accessible and clear.
Existence,
is being.
Non-existence,
is nothingness.
Roaming the mind in the boundless infinite,
and comparing within the nine provinces,
speaking of their size,
it can be said to be as if there is and as if there isn't.
The lord said:
"Indeed."
【一】【注】Now, considering the vastness of the four seas as immense,
yet in the scheme of the boundless,
it seems both existent and non-existent.
【Explanation】"然" means
"like this".
It indicates that the statements presented are not false.
He said:
"Within the vast realm there is the state of Wèi,
within Wèi there is the city of Liáng,
and within Liáng there is a king.
Is there any distinction between this king
and the ruler of the Mán tribe?"
【一】【注】It means the state of Wèi is located at the center of the four seas.
【Èr Shū】In the past, they were in Hédōng,
the state was named Wèi,
Wèi was pressured by the powerful Qín,
and moved its capital to Liáng.
Liáng came into existence because of Wèi,
hence it is said that within Wèi there was Liáng.
【Three】【Memorials】argue,
distinguishing them.
A king's single state,
situated within the universe,
if one wishes to discuss its size,
it is as if it exists and as if it does not.
Compared to that of the Mán clan,
what difference is there?
This is an analogy that brings them together.
The lord said:
"Do not argue."
【One】【Annotation】The King of Wèi and the Mán clan,
are both limited entities (1).
Being limited,
then regardless of size,
neither can be compared with the boundless,
even though Heaven and Earth coexist within the boundlessness,
they are still insignificant.
How much more so the state of Liáng within Wèi,
and the King within Liáng,
are they worth contending over!
【Commentary】Realizing that one's own struggles are no different from those over the horns of a snail.
【Explanation】"Suī fù" reads as fú yòu fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The Zhào Jiànyì edition does not have the character "ear".
After the guest departed, the lord appeared lost, as if having forfeited something.
【一】【注】Lamenting that what was contended was trivial.
【Commentary】Chǎngrán,
means a countenance of regret and remorse.
After the man from Jìn finished speaking,
he bid farewell and departed.
The ruler realized his own faults,
feeling chǎngrán, full of regret and remorse;
his heart grieved,
as if lost in a daze.
【Transcription】"Chǎng" is pronounced as chǎng.
The Zìlín states:
It means perplexed.
Also read as tǔ dàng fǎn.
The guest left,
Huìzǐ appeared.
The ruler said:
"The guest,
is a great man,
even a sage would not be worthy of matching him."
【一】【疏】The Sage,
refers to Yáo and Shùn.
What the people of Jìn discussed,
its principle was vast and profound,
the conduct of Yáo and Shùn was insufficient to match it.
Huìzǐ said, "When one blows on a pipe,
there is a loud sound;
but when one blows on the hilt of a sword,
it's just a faint hiss.
Yáo and Shùn
are praised by people;
yet to speak of Yáo and Shùn before Dài Jìngrén
is like that faint hiss.
【一】【注】It is not even worth hearing.
【Commentary】Hè,
is a loud sound;
xuè,
is a faint sound.
When blowing through a bamboo pipe,
the sound is still loud and grand;
but blowing on a sword guard,
the sound is then minuscule.
The praises from the common folk in Táng Yáo's time,
if one were to grandly discuss this way before the people of Jìn,
how would it differ from the sound of blowing on a sword guard,
truly not worth hearing at all!
【Transcription】"筦" is pronounced as guǎn.
The text also uses the character 管.
"嗃" is pronounced with the fanqie 許交反,
meaning the sound of a pipe.
The Yùpiān gives the fanqie 呼洛反,
and also 呼教反.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
It means to chirp or cry.
"劍首" Simǎ explains:
It refers to the small hole in the ring at the end of a sword's hilt.
"吷" is pronounced as xuè,
and also with the fanqie 呼悅反.
Simǎ explains:
It describes a sound like the wind passing by.
"所譽" is pronounced as yú.
Confucius traveled to Chǔ,
and lodged at the cottage of Yǐqiū's beverage seller.
His neighbors had a couple with their servants climbing to the rooftop,
Zǐlù asked:
"What are these bustling people doing?"
【一】【疏】Yǐqiū,
is the name of a hill.
Jiāng,
refers to a household that sells fermented rice water.
Zhòngní was on his way to Chǔ and served as an envoy,
resting by the roadside at the home of those selling fermented rice water,
whose residence was at the foot of the hill,
hence the hill was named after it.
【Translated Text】"Yǐ Qiū" is read as yú qǐ fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
Yǐ Qiū,
a mountain's name.
"Zhī Jiāng" Lǐ Yún says:
a household selling jiāng (a fermented drink).
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to a lodging place covered with gū jiǎng grass.
【二】【疏】extreme,
meaning high.
"Total total,"
refers to a large gathering of people.
Kǒng Qiū accepted the invitation for employment,
his disciples were very numerous,
with carriages, horses, and majestic demeanor,
astonishingly different from common customs.
Therefore, the neighbors, men and women from the beverage seller's household, gathered in crowds,
all climbed up to sell drinks,
to watch Zhòngní.
Zǐlù did not recognize this,
hence he asked in surprise.
【Explanatory Text】"Ascending the Ridge" Sīmǎ comments:
Ridge,
refers to the roof beam,
one climbs it to observe.
Another explanation:
Ridge,
is a flat-roofed house.
"Zǒng zǒng" is pronounced as zǒng,
the character is also written as 總.
Lǐ comments:
It means a gathering appearance.
The original text also uses 稷.
One version uses 稷,
with the initial pronunciation as chū lì fǎn.
◎ Lú Wénchāo says:
The two characters 稷 are suspected to have one that is erroneous.
Zhòngní said:
"This is a sage's attendant.
He buries himself among the people,
hides himself in the fields.
His voice fades away,
yet his aspirations are boundless;
though his mouth speaks,
his heart has never uttered a word.
He is at odds with the world and disdains to go along with it.
This is a man submerged on dry land—
could this be Shìnán Yìliáo?"
【One】【Memorial】In ancient times, virtuous gentlemen and noble individuals,
were all referred to as sages,
hence Confucius named Yì Liáo as a sage.
Those who claim that servants and concubines ascend the throne and gather multitudes
are but the slaves and subordinates of Shìnán Yì Liáo.
【Explanation】"The Sage's Servant" refers to one who harbors sage virtue yet conceals himself among servants and slaves.
Sima's version writes "servant" as "unhewn,"
meaning the sage is like uncarved simplicity.
【二】【注】Share with the people.
【Three】【Commentary】Advancing without glory and splendor,
retreating without withering and decay.
【Commentary】He concealed his tracks in the mud and filth,
blending in with the common dust of the mundane crowd,
not displaying his virtue,
thus burying himself among the people;
advancing, he did not seek glory and splendor,
retreating, he did not wither away,
in the transitions between hiding and appearing, advancing and withdrawing,
he thus concealed himself in the fields.
【Explanation】"Hidden at the Field Borders" King said:
Cultivating the work of farming,
is to be hidden at the field borders.
【Four】【Annotation】Sǔn (one) is its name.
【Transcription】"Xiāo" is pronounced as xiāo.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means small.
"Juān qí" is also written as sǔn in some versions.
◎ Lú Wéncháo states:
Nowadays, the text writes it as sǔn.
【Five】【Annotation】Guidance is the beginning of life.
【Commentary】Sound,
is reputation.
To vanish,
means to perish.
Unifying honor and disgrace,
thus destroys one's reputation;
merging with the ultimate Way,
therefore the mind becomes boundless.
【Six】【Annotation】What is spoken are all worldly words.
【Commentary】The mouth responds to the human world,
while the mind remains constantly in tranquil stillness.
Thus, without speaking, it speaks;
what is spoken has never truly been spoken.
【七】【Note】The mind differs from the world.
【Commentary】The Way stands in opposition to the mundane,
and thus inevitably contradicts the world.
With an empty mind free from attachments,
it does not align with material things.
This is a state where both the mind and its traces are distinct.
【Explanation】"Bù xiè": xiè means
purity,
not being pure in the world.
Some versions use "kěn" instead.
【Eight】【Annotation】The recluse among men,
is like sinking without water.
【Commentary】Desolate and void,
it is like sinking without water,
meaning land sinking.
【Explanation】"Lù Chén" Simǎ explains:
One should be prominent but instead withdraws into obscurity,
as if sinking without water.
【Nine】【Shū】His surname is Xióng,
his courtesy name is Yìliáo,
and he resided in the southern part of the market,
hence he was called Shìnán Yìliáo.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "sǔn" is written as "juān".
(2) In Zhào's edition, "guī" is written as "shì".
Zǐlù requested to go and summon him.
【First】【Memorial】Having heard that Yíliáo was a reclusive virtuous scholar,
I requested to go to his residence to summon him.
Confucius said:
"Enough!
He knows that I am well-informed about him,
and that I am going to Chu.
He thinks I will certainly cause the King of Chu to summon him,
and he probably regards me as a sycophant.
If that is the case,
he would be ashamed to hear the words of a sycophant,
let alone meet him in person!
So why should I go to see him?"
【One】【Memorial】Finished,
cease it.
They certainly will not come,
hopefully stop and do not summon.
【二】【注】To annotate means
to clarify.
【Three】【Memorials】That person,
is Yì Liáo.
To write,
is to make clear.
Knowing that Qiūmíng recognized Yì Liáo as a reclusive virtuous scholar,
and also knew that upon going to Chǔ, he would certainly recommend and summon him to the King of Chǔ,
in this case, then using Qiū would make him a flattering and fawning person.
【Four】【Memorials】A person who has withdrawn from the world,
by nature sincere and straightforward,
when it comes to wickedness and flattery,
feels ashamed even to hear such words,
let alone examining their own form,
truly finds it undesirable.
【Five】【Annotation】It is better to let go and follow their aspirations.
【Commentary】Ér,
means rǔ (you).
Cún,
means zài (to exist).
Concealing one's shadow and silencing one's voice,
one should have fled long ago to evade,
why do you, rǔ, request a summon,
claiming that it still exists?
Zǐlù went to see him,
but his house was empty.
【一】【注】He indeed fled away.
【Commentary】Zhòng Yóu lacked foresight,
and did not heed his teacher's words,
so he went to that house,
hoping to witness great virtue.
But the refusal of the invitation was so earnest,
Yí Liáo had already fled,
and the house was empty.
Chángwú's border official asked Zǐláo:
"In governing, do not be rough and careless;
in managing the people, do not be hasty and negligent.
In the past, when I grew grain,
if I plowed the land roughly,
the harvest would repay me with roughness in return;
if I weeded hastily,
the harvest would repay me with negligence in return.
The following year, I changed my methods,
plowing deeply and carefully tilling the soil,
and the grain grew lush and abundant,
so that I had plenty to eat all year long."
【一】【注】To act rashly and destructively,
carelessly and superficially,
without fulfilling one's duty.
【Commentary】Chángwú is a
place name,
so called because there are tall paulownia trees in the area,
hence the name.
Fēngrén refers to
the person guarding the border in this area.
Zǐ Láo,
a disciple of Confucius,
surnamed Qín,
was a minister of the state of Sòng.
"Wéi zhèng" means
to implement governance.
"Zhì mín" refers to
administering the people.
"Lǔ mǎng" indicates
not applying one's mind.
"Miè liè" means
being frivolous.
The people are the foundation of the state;
when the foundation is firm, the state is tranquil.
One must focus on nurturing the people,
and must not lightly cause them disturbance.
The border guard had the Way,
hence he admonished Zǐ Láo.
【Explanation】"Chángwú Border Guard" - Chángwú is a
place name.
"Border guard" refers to
a person who guards the border territory.
"Zǐláo" - Simǎ comments:
this is Qín Láo,
styled Zǐláo, a disciple of Confucius.
◎Qìng Fān notes: Qín Zhāng,
a disciple of Confucius,
does not appear in the classics or commentaries as Qín Láo or Zǐláo.
Only in the "Family Sayings of Confucius" among the disciples is Qín Zhāng mentioned.
Also named Láo,
styled Zǐkāi,
also styled Zhāng,
from the state of Wèi.
Thus, Qín [Zhāng] first appears in the "Family Sayings",
a book forged by Wáng Zǐyōng,
and cannot be relied upon.
Jiǎ Kuí and Zhèng Zhòng's annotations to the "Zuǒ Zhuàn"
identify Qín Zhāng as Zhuānsūn Shī.
Fú Qián refutes this, saying:
Zǐzhāng was over forty years younger than Confucius,
and Confucius was forty at that time,
so it is known that Zǐzhāng could not have existed then.
Zhào Qí's annotation to the "Mèngzǐ"
also identifies Qín Zhāng as Zǐzhāng,
stating:
Zǐzhāng was skilled at playing the qin,
hence called Qín Zhāng.
(This is likely a forced interpretation based on a few phrases in the "Book of Rites" about Zǐzhāng after the mourning period.
) It is particularly unfounded.
Qín Zhāng and Zǐláo
are originally not the same person;
Simǎ's claim here is incorrect.
The "Hànshū" table of ancient and modern figures lists Qín Láo,
which was also altered by superficial scholars based on the "Family Sayings".
If the "Hànshū" had Qín Láo,
then Jiǎ, Zhèng, and Fú would have long cited it to explain Láo as Qín Zhāng.
The same applies to Zhèng's annotation in the "Analects", Zhào Qí's in "Mèngzǐ", and the "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
"Lǔ" is pronounced as lǔ.
"Mǎng" is pronounced as mò gǔ fǎn,
or as the character's usual reading.
"Mièliè" means short grass.
Lǐ comments:
It refers to being unripe.
Guō comments:
"Lǔmǎng mièliè"
implies being careless and superficial,
not fulfilling one's duty.
Simǎ comments:
"Lǔmǎng"
means coarse or rough.
It refers to shallow plowing and sparse planting.
"Mièliè"
means cutting the grass.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Note: "cū"
is pronounced qiān nú fǎn;
"cū"
is pronounced cái gǔ fǎn;
these two characters were often used together in ancient times.
For example, the "Chūnqiū Fánlù" Yù (yǔ) [xù] (yī) chapter states:
starting with the coarse and rough,
ending with the refined and subtle.
The "Lùnhéng" Zhèng Shuō chapter says:
briefly correct the topic with rough explanations,
to illuminate the subtle text within the chapter.
There are many other instances where "cūcū" is used together,
meaning coarse and rough.
Some wish to change it to "cūshū",
hence this correction.
【二】【疏】refers to planting crops,
just like sowing grain.
Weeding,
is pulling out the grass.
If the plowing of the land is not deep,
and the hoeing is not thorough,
by the time of the autumn harvest,
the fine yield will not be abundant,
all due to negligence.
Hence, this outcome follows.
【Transcription】"Yún" is pronounced as yún,
meaning to remove weeds.
【Three】【Annotation】Fulfill one's duty to the utmost,
reaching the pinnacle of non-action (two).
【Explanation】"Biàn Qí": "Qí" is read with the pronunciation of "cái" and the tone "xì".
Sīmǎ reads it according to its original character,
saying:
It means to change,
referring to altering what is being followed.
"Qí",
means the same.
"Yōu": pronounced as "yōu".
Sīmǎ says:
It means a hoe.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
It means to push.
The "Zìlín" says:
It is a tool for leveling the fields.
【Four】【Explanations】Change,
means to alter.
Plowing,
means to cultivate.
Harrowing,
means to weed.
Last year's fields,
repeatedly suffered from famine and hunger,
this year's planting,
therefore altered methods to deep plowing.
Since the plowing and tilling were deep,
and the hoeing and harrowing were thorough,
thus the seedlings grew lush and dense.
The grains flourished abundantly,
ensuring a year of ample food,
so it was appropriate.
【Explanation】"厭" is pronounced as Sūn.
Another version writes it as 飧 (three).
【Collation】(1) The character '序' has been emended according to the Fanlù text.
(2) The Shidetáng edition reads as '無所不至',
while the Zhào Jiànyì edition has '所' written as '為'.
(3) The current edition uses the character '飧'.
Zhuāngzǐ heard this and said:
"People nowadays in cultivating their bodies
and ordering their minds,
often resemble what the border official described:
they evade their Heaven[-given nature],
depart from their inherent character,
extinguish their genuine emotions,
and obliterate their spirit,
conforming to the multitude.
Thus those who treat their nature recklessly
find the sprouts of desires and aversions
growing like reeds and rushes in their nature -
at first sprouting to support our physical form,
but soon tearing at our inherent nature;
when they erupt like bursting boils and leaking sores,
discharging indiscriminately,
manifesting as running ulcers, scabies, feverish rashes,
and internal heat with turbid urine - such are the consequences."
【One】【Memorial】People of the present age,
are frivolous and shallow,
chasing after the realm of desires,
weary yet never resting,
when it comes to governing their minds and bodies,
for instance, as the border official once said.
Zhuāng Zhōu, hearing this,
thus discussed it.
【二】【注】It is because of the multitude that fleeing and perishing
are brought about.
If each reaches their utmost,
then what worry is there?
【Commentary】Those who flee from the natural principles,
scatter their pure and harmonious nature,
extinguish their genuine feelings,
and lose the way of nurturing the spirit—
all do so because they pursue what lies beyond their lot,
and are excessively mired in deliberate action.
【Explanation】"Li qi" is pronounced with "li" as "lì" and "zhi" as "zhì".
The same applies below.
"Yi zhong wei" is read as the characters are.
Wáng explains:
It refers to all matters that can be acted upon.
Escaping from and avoiding destruction and demise,
all stem from the actions of the multitude.
The actions of the multitude,
are what is called reckless and crude.
The Sīmǎ version writes it as "wei wei".
【Three】【Annotation】Reeds and rushes harm the millet and grain,
desires and aversions injure the true nature.
【Commentary】Huánwěi,
is reed.
The mind of desires and aversions,
often gives rise to calamities.
Huánwěi harms the millet crops,
desires and aversions injure the true nature,
all arise from recklessness and superficial falseness,
hence leading to such outcomes.
【Explanation of Text】"Desire and aversion" - read as wù lù fǎn.
The same applies to annotations.
"The calamity" - read as yú liè fǎn.
Huán is pronounced as wán,
a type of reed.
Wěi is pronounced as yú guǐ fǎn,
meaning bulrush.
【Four】【Annotation】When the form is neglected, the spirit and vital energy are harmed.
【Commentary】Jiānjiā,
is also a type of reed.
When vile weeds first sprout,
they are still easy to remove and cut down;
but once they grow lush and abundant,
they will inevitably harm the millet and grain.
Similarly, when desires first arise in the heart,
they are still easy to suppress and cease;
yet when one becomes deluded and immersed in them,
it is crucial to guard against them in their subtle beginnings.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said,
"It is easy to plan for what has not yet shown signs."
【Translated Text】"Jiān" is pronounced as in ancient times with the sound "tián",
meaning reed.
"Jiā" is pronounced as "jiā",
also referring to reed.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
The nature of huán wěi jiān jiā,
these six characters form a sentence.
Guō commented below huán wěi, saying,
huán wěi harm the millet crops,
desires and evils injure the true nature.
This misses the correct reading.
At first, they sprout to support my form,
gradually they pluck out my nature.
"Gradually" and "at first" are contrasted in meaning,
"gradually" implies a slow progression.
In the "Treatise on Sacrifices" of the Book of Hàn, it says it slowly reached Tài Shān,
Jìn Zhuó commented:
"Gradually",
means the idea of proceeding onward.
"At first, they sprout to support my form",
means that initially, they seem sufficient to assist my form;
"gradually they pluck out my nature",
means that after a slow progression over time, they uproot my nature.
Guō explained "support my form" as,
if the form is overly spread out, the spirit and energy are harmed,
which is also a misinterpretation.
【Five】【Note】Using desires and aversions to guide one's nature,
does not stop at what is appropriate.
【Commentary】"Xún" means
to entice.
"Zhuó" means
to uproot.
By using matters of desire and aversion to lure their minds,
it ultimately causes the uprooting of their true nature,
preventing them from resting in what is appropriate.
【Six】【Annotation】This is the retribution for recklessness.
Therefore, those who cultivate their nature,
how can they not align with their utmost destiny!
【Explanation】Ulcerating sores refer to

Boils and carbuncles refer to

the discharge of essence through urination.
Indulging in material desires,
drowning in sensual pleasures,
thus leads to mental confusion,
physical weakness and emaciation,
triggering various illnesses,
without regard to where they manifest.

Bǎijǔ studied under Lǎodān,
and said:
"I ask to travel throughout the world."
【一】【疏】Bǎi,
is the surname;
Jǔ,
is the given name.
He was a scholar who embraced the Way,
a disciple of Lǎozǐ.
He requested to travel throughout the world,
to observe customs and transformations,
and to examine the nature of things.
【Explanation】Bǎi Jǔ was a man of the Way.
Lǎo Dān said:
"Enough!
The world is still the same."
【One】【Memorial】Lǎozǐ stopped him,
not permitting him to go,
saying that the nature of things in the world
is no different from this place.
He asked again,
and Lǎodān said:
"Where will you begin?"
【First】【Memorial】With solemnity and earnestness,
the requests were incessant,
only then did I inquire about the itinerary, asking which country you intended to visit first.
He said:
"It began in Qí."
【一】【Memorial】Bǎi Jǔ was a man of Lǔ,
bordering Qí to the near,
where the people of Qí were without virtue,
and he wished to take the lead in action.
Arriving in Qí,
he saw a condemned criminal there.
He pushed and straightened him,
took off his court robe and covered him with it,
then cried out to heaven and wept for him, saying:
"Alas, alas!
Under heaven there are great calamities,
and you alone have first encountered them,
saying 'Do not be robbers!
Do not be murderers!'
When honor and disgrace are established,
then we see what people worry about;
when goods and wealth are accumulated,
then we see what people contend for.
Now establishing what people worry about,
accumulating what people contend for,
pushing people's lives into hardship without rest -
wanting to avoid reaching this point,
is it possible?
【One】【Memorial】While traveling to Qí,
to observe the customs and transformation,
I suddenly saw a criminal,
executed and deceased.
Thereupon, I approached and compelled him,
had him lie straight,
took off my court robe,
and covered him with it like a shroud.
【Explanation Text】"Gū" means

"Gū" means to wither,

"Zhé"

【Two】【Annotation】Great calamities of killing people,
refer to the events from here onward.
Once great calamities have occurred,
even if warned against doing them,
how could they possibly be stopped!
【Commentary】"Lí" means
"to suffer."
"Zāi" means

Crying out to heaven,
weeping in sorrow,
lamenting the injustice and excess,
hence the repeated exclamation "zǐ hū."
Committing robbery and murder—
these are great calamities in the world.
What crime have you alone committed,
to encounter such suffering beforehand?
The specifics of great calamities
are listed below.
Another explanation:
The so-called guilty persons
are the court officials.
It speaks of them forcefully deferring to one another while wearing court attire,
layering nets to ensnare the common people,
hence crying out to heaven in lament,

The preemptively spread net

【Explanation】《Hào Tiān》Hào is pronounced with the initial "h" and the final "ao" with a rising tone.
《Dà Zāi》Zāi is pronounced as "zai".
