【Three】【Commentary】When each attains their own fulfillment, there is neither honor nor disgrace.
Gains and losses become entangled and numerous,
hence honor and disgrace are established.
Once honor and disgrace are established, people boast of what they call honor and strive for what they deem glorious.
Rushing about between boasting and striving,
how could it not be an affliction!
【Commentary】Considering chariots and crowns as glory,
and execution and disgrace as shame,
rushing about to pursue or abandon things,
how could this not be a malady!
【Four】【Annotation】If one regards contentment as wealth,
then what is there to contend for!
【Commentary】Treasures accumulate in abundance,
thus stirring up the race for competition.
【Five】【Annotation】When those above have their preferences,
then those below cannot remain content in their proper roles.
【Commentary】Rewarding them with high carriages and official caps,
indulging them with pearls and jades,
thus causing all ranks to rush about,
exhausted yet never ceasing,
how could it be possible to make each abide by their original station
and achieve peace?
【Text】"Suǒ hào" is pronounced with the tone of hū bào.
The rulers of antiquity,
attributed achievements to the people,
and took failures upon themselves;
credited the people with righteousness,
and shouldered their own errors;
thus, whenever there was any flaw in governance,
they would retreat and blame themselves.
But now it is not so.
They conceal affairs and deem those unaware ignorant,
create great difficulties and punish the timid,
impose heavy burdens and penalize the incapable,
set distant journeys and execute those who fail to arrive.
When the people's wisdom and strength are exhausted,
they resort to deceit to cope;
as deceit becomes rampant daily,
how can the common folk avoid turning to deceit themselves!
For when strength falls short, deceit follows;
when wisdom is lacking, deception arises;
when wealth is insufficient, theft ensues.
As for these acts of theft and fraud,
upon whom should the blame rightly fall?
【一】【注】If the ruler has no faults,
then the people will naturally be content.
【Commentary】Attributing achievements to external factors,
thus the credit lies with the people;
accepting the nation's misfortunes,
thus the blame rests on oneself.
【二】【注】If the ruler does not bend them unjustly,
then the people will naturally be upright.
【Explanation】Non-action entrusts matters to things,
the correctness lies with the people;
attributing faults and blaming oneself,
the error lies with oneself.
【Three】【Commentary】Why do the forms and natures of things become lost?
It is all because rulers disturb them, leading to such calamities.
Therefore, they should blame themselves (Part One).
【Commentary】People receive different endowments of vital energy,
and their innate dispositions vary accordingly.
If each is allowed to exercise their abilities,
then all things will attain their natural fulfillment.
Should any single thing lose its proper place,
impairing its form or nature,
one should attribute the fault to oneself,
stepping back to reflect on personal responsibility.
In ancient times, King Tāng of the Shāng dynasty cut his own hair
as a plea for rain that came across a thousand lǐ,
exemplifying this principle.
【Four】【Memorials】The methods differ with the times,
and customs vary across eras,
so those who govern today no longer act in this manner.
【Five】【Comment】To go against one's nature is to conceal it;
to conceal it,
to use one's nature is to reveal it;
to reveal it,
thus, when revealed by things, all are recognized.
【Commentary】The statutes and regulations they enacted,
all went against the nature of things,
concealed crimes and accusations,
and were foolishly ignorant,
hence those accused of crimes were numerous.
【Translated Text】"Nì" is pronounced as nǚ lì fǎn.

In "Yànzǐ Chūnqiū Wài Piān", "shèng wéi shēngyuè yǐ yín yú mín",

Previously, it was thought that following the explanatory text and using "yù" was more appropriate,
but now, considering Yú's view that it is a miswriting of "guò",
his explanation is even more precise.
The characters "guò" and "yù",
were often mistaken for each other in ancient times.
In this book's "Yú Fù Piān", "jīn zhě qiū dé guò yě",
explanatory text:
"guò" is sometimes written as "yù".
In "Ràng Wáng Piān", "jūn guò ér yí xiānshēng shí",
explanatory text:
"guò" is also written as "yù".
This is evidence that the two characters are similar in shape and often mistaken.
"Bù shí" means going against the nature of things and forcing recognition.
【Six】【Annotation】When swayed by material things, all become reckless.
【Commentary】Since laws are difficult to establish,
and their implementation is not easy,
therefore, those who deliberately violate them
shall be punished for this offense.
【Explanation of the Text】"Making things excessively difficult and punishing those who dare not attempt them." Wáng remarked:
In all endeavors,
if one utilizes the inherent capabilities of things,
then nothing would be difficult, and people would dare to act.
Yet, intentionally creating great hardships,
issuing demands that cannot be fulfilled,
so that things or people become unwilling to attempt them,
and then punishing them for it.
"Suǒ yì" is pronounced with "yì" in the falling-rising tone.
【Seven】【Annotation】If one lightens the responsibilities of their posts, then all will prevail.

【八】【Note】When their foot strength is adequate, then all will arrive.

【九】【注】This is to evade punishment.
【Commentary】When one's wisdom and strength are exhausted,
one cannot avoid punishment and penalty.
Fearing punishment and in dire straits,
thus, deception follows.

【Commentary】The trend of deceit and artifice,

how can one attain truth from this!

deceit and artifice inevitably arise;
when taxes and levies become increasingly harsh,

If one can relinquish attachments and abandon selfishness,
not valuing rare treasures,
the responsibility lies with those above—
how can the common people below be blamed!

【一】【Note】It is also capable of conforming to the world without being bound by self and others.

and he was a virtuous senior official of Wèi.
His abundant virtue and lofty brilliance,
illuminating and understanding the truth of emptiness,

transforming with the passing years.

【二】【注】Following things smoothly leads to unimpeded flow,
as such is the nature of changes in the feelings of things.
【Commentary】At the beginning of the year when one first treads upon it,
it is deemed correct;
when the year has fully passed and faded away,
it is deemed incorrect.
Within a single year, correctness and incorrectness frequently alternate,
thus what was considered correct at the start,
ultimately bends and becomes incorrect.

【Three】【Comment】The transformations in the nature of things
have never had a limit.
【Commentary】Thus the old transforms into the new,
and the new is taken as right;
the old has already faded away,
so the old is considered wrong.
If so, then what was wrong last year
becomes right today;
what is right this year
will be wrong next year.
From this, we know that those who cling to right or wrong,
who stagnate in the new or hold fast to the old,
are people with inverted views.
Therefore, Róngchéng Shì said,
"Without days, there are no years,"
and Qú Yuàn understood this,
thus he followed the transformation of things.
【Four】【Commentary】Without root or gate,
suddenly and naturally,
thus none can perceive it.
Only those who cease their existence and forget their emergence
are able to glimpse its gate and fathom its root.
【Commentary】It arises following change,
with no root or origin to its arising;
it emerges according to transformation,
with no gateway or door to its emergence.
Since it is said to have no root and no door,
we thus know there is no arising and no emerging.
With no gateway for arising and emerging,
the principle is such as this—
how could any year or age be used to represent it!
【五】【Note】What I do not know,
there are things that possess knowledge of it.
Therefore, utilizing the knowledge of things,
then there is nothing one does not know;
relying solely on my own knowledge,
the knowledge is very limited.
Now, if one does not depend on things for knowledge,
but instead esteems only one's own knowledge,
then things will not inform me,
is this not a great delusion indeed!
【Commentary】What is known
is worldly knowledge;
what is unknown
is true knowledge.
Ordinary people
all esteem discriminative knowledge,
fervently pursuing and rejecting,
yet none can rely on their knowledge of non-discrimination to illuminate the true source,
truly they are people of great delusion.
【Six】【Note】If one cannot employ that,
then there is no place to lodge one's body.
【Explanation】"Cease,"
means to stop.
If one fervently pursues gains and losses,
without knowing when to rest,
they are bound to encounter calamities,
with nowhere to hide from the consequences.
【Seven】【Annotation】What one considers to be so,
the world may not acknowledge as such.
【Commentary】Each affirms what they affirm,
each approves what they approve,
with self and others in opposition,
who then is right and who is wrong?

Líng is thus the posthumous name for those without virtue.
This is because of his lack of virtue,

【Collation】(1) The variant text cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition where "làn" is written as "jiàn".
(2) The character "yì" has been emended based on the reprinted Sòng edition and Wáng Shūmín's interpretation.
Xī Wéi said:
"When Duke Líng died,
divination for burial in his ancestral tomb was inauspicious,
but divination for burial at Shā Qiū proved auspicious.
They dug several fathoms deep,
and found a stone outer coffin there.
After washing and examining it,
they found an inscription,
which said:
'Not relying on his son,
Duke Líng seized it and was buried here.'
Duke Líng had long been destined to be named 'Líng'
—how could these two men have understood this!"
【一】【注】Zǐ,
referring to Kuǎikuì.
It means not relying on his son,
as Duke Líng was about to seize your position.
All things have their predetermined fate first,
hence future events can be known.
Therefore, all that is done,
must be done;
all that is not done,
cannot be done;
yet foolish people think it lies within their control,
is that not delusional!
【Explanatory Text】"故墓" in one edition is written as "大墓".

"數仞" is pronounced with the initial "所" and final "主".
"洗而" is pronounced with the initial "西" and final "禮".
"不馮" is pronounced as "憑".

Sīmǎ reads with a stop after the character "子",

It means that the descendants are not sufficient to rely on,

【二】【注】They merely recognize events that have already occurred,
unaware that what has occurred arises from spontaneity.
【Commentary】Shāqiū,
is a place name,
located north of the Mèngjīn River.
Zǐ,
refers to Kuǎikuì.
It aims to clarify that a person's name and posthumous title are determined before any signs appear,
not subject to changes based on worldly sentiments,
hence the stone coffin at Shāqiū already bore the inscription beforehand.
How could it be that only by relying on Kuǎikuì
could the burial be seized!
Tāo and Chángqiān,

【Interpretation】"之見" is read as xián biàn fǎn.

Shǎo Zhì asked Dàgōng Diào,
"What is meant by the discourse of the village?"
【One】【Exposition】With limited and shallow wisdom,
it is called having little knowledge.
"Tài"
means great.
"Gōng"
means just.
With virtue vast and great,
impartial and selfless,
and further able to harmonize all beings,
hence he is called Tài Gōng Diào.
Two figures are hypothetically set up
to discuss the principles of the Way.
【Translated Text】"Tàigōng" is pronounced as Tài.
The same applies below.
【二】【疏】In ancient times, ten households formed a qiū,
and twenty households constituted a lǐ.
Villages, neighborhoods, qiū, and lǐ
had different customs,
hence hypothetical questions and answers were used to debate them.
【Explanatory Text】"Qiūlǐ zhī yán" Lǐ Yún said:
Four jǐng make a yì,
four yì make a qiū,
five families make a lín,
five lín make a lǐ.
In ancient times, lín, lǐ, jǐng, and yì
had different local customs,
just as nowadays villages and hamlets each have their own regional practices,
and things are not uniform.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
The old version had "tǔ" instead of "shì",
now the phonetic and meaning annotations in the book use the character "shì",
so I follow that.
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "tài".
The same applies below.
Dàgōng Diào said:
"A village community
unites ten families and a hundred individuals to form its customs,
combining differences to create unity,
and dispersing unity to reveal differences.
Now, if you point to the hundred parts of a horse, you do not get the horse itself;
but when the horse is tethered before you,
it is by standing together that its hundred parts are called a horse.
Thus, hills and mountains accumulate the low to become high;
rivers and seas gather streams to become vast;
the great person unites all to achieve impartiality.
Therefore, what comes from without,
though it has a master, is not clung to;
what emerges from within,
though it has correctness, does not resist.
The four seasons have different climates,
yet Heaven shows no favoritism,
thus the year is completed;
the five offices have different duties,
yet the ruler shows no partiality,
thus the state is well-governed;
civil and military matters receive no special endowments from the great person,
thus virtue is perfected;
the myriad things have different principles,
yet the Dào shows no partiality,
thus it is nameless.
Being nameless, it is non-acting;
non-acting, yet there is nothing it does not do.
Time has its beginnings and endings,
the world undergoes transformations.
Fortune and misfortune ebb and flow,
reaching points of conflict yet also of harmony;
each pursues a different direction,
having correctness yet also deviation.
Compare it to a great marsh:
all materials find their measure there;
observe a great mountain:
trees and stones share the same platform.
This is what is called the discourse of the village community."
【一】【疏】Gather ten clans,
select a hundred names,
combine and discuss them,
to understand the customs.
【Explanatory Text】"Ten Surnames, Hundred Names": One surname represents ten people,
ten surnames represent a hundred names,
thus there are differences and similarities,
so they are combined or separated to determine them.
【二】【疏】If they adopt the words of the villages to form customs,
this is uniting differences to create uniformity;
if one person establishes teachings,
adapting to the locality and complying with things,
this is dispersing uniformity to create differences.
It is also like pointing to the hundred parts of a horse,
the head, tail, waist, and spine,
which no longer constitute a horse—
this is dispersing uniformity to create differences;
yet when tethered before us, there is a horse—
this is uniting differences to create uniformity.
【Three】【Annotations】Being impartial towards all under heaven,
then the customs of all under heaven become unified.
【Commentary】Accumulating earth and stones forms hills and mountains,
gathering small streams creates rivers and seas,
just as the sage has no fixed intention,
but applies teachings according to the circumstances.
Thus, they can unite all directions,
harmonize the world under one principle,
so that both Huá and Yí peoples tread together,
with no partiality between near and far.
【Explanation】"Accumulating the lowly" is read as written,
also pronounced bì.
"Combining waters" one version writes combining flows.
◎Yú Yuè says:
"Water" is an error for the small character.
Lowly and noble, small and great,
form parallel expressions.
"Uniting them to form the public" means gathering the names of all small things to create the one ultimate public.
【Four】【Explanations】Zì,
means "from."
It refers to the teachings of the sage,
entering from the outside,
emerging from within,
following along with the nature of things,
thus residing as the master without any attachments.
【Five】【Comment】What comes from the outside
is the transformation by the great person;
what emerges from within
is the nature of the people and creatures.
When each nature attains its correctness,
the people have no rebellious hearts;
when the transformation is inevitably impartial,
the ruler holds no prejudices.
Thus, it is possible to unite villages and merge the world,
unifying all things and leveling diverse differences.
【Commentary】"You" (由)
also means "to follow."
It refers to all living beings and the common people,
each having their own inherent nature,
acting from the heart,
receiving the imperial influence,
which aligns with the nature of things,
hence they comply without resistance.
【Six】【Annotation】Distinct energies inherently exist,
thus they can endure perpetually;
if they were originally absent and bestowed by heaven,
then there would be times when they cease.
【Commentary】To bestow,
is to give.
The warmth of spring and the heat of summer,
the coolness of autumn and the cold of winter,
are endowed by nature.
Thus, the sequence of the seasons is established;
if it were up to heaven to grant it,
it would sometimes cease to function.
【Translated Text】"Heaven does not bestow" bestow,
means to give.
【Seven】【Annotation】Each position has its own required talent,
thus they are appointed accordingly,
not out of personal favoritism.
【Commentary】The Five Offices,
refer to the ancient practice of establishing officials according to the Five Elements.
The Spring Office and the Autumn Office,
each had their specific duties,
the ruler remained profound and silent,
delegating responsibilities without bias,
thus achieving peace throughout the realm,
and tranquility and prosperity for the state.
【Text】"Guó Zhì" is read with the pronunciation of "zhí lì" in reverse.
【Eight】【Annotation】Literary talent manifests itself,
military prowess asserts itself,
not bestowed by the great person.
If it were acquired through bestowal,
then there would be times of lack.
How could this apply only to literary and military abilities?
All innate natures are like this.
【Commentary】Civil officials and military generals,
are assigned positions according to their abilities,
each entrusted with their own capabilities,
not due to the sage's favor.
Impartial towards all things,
thus the virtue and way are perfectly fulfilled.
【Nine】【Commentary】All creatures are not the same,
each follows its own nature with differences;
some nest in trees or dwell in caves,
some roam the earth or soar the skies,
yet they are nurtured and sustained,
all able to provide for themselves.
Each thing attains its own principle,
thus there is no need for forced intervention.
【一０】【注】Names correspond to realities,
thus there is non-action;
realities each act on their own,
thus there is nothing that is not done.
【Commentary】The merit is attributed to things,
thus acting through non-action,
not clinging to this (non-)action and thereby leaving nothing undone.
【一一】【Note】Thus, one without preconceptions follows along naturally.
【Commentary】Time,
refers to the four seasons succeeding one another in a cyclical pattern.
The world,
refers to human affairs changing and shifting unpredictably.
【One Two】【Comment】The currents flow and reverse.
【Commentary】Chún chún,
describes the appearance of flowing movement.
Now, the cold and heat of seasonal weather,
flow and change without constancy;
the fortunes and misfortunes in human affairs,
how could they remain fixed for long!
Therefore, the ancient Classic says,
misfortune is that upon which good fortune depends,
good fortune is that in which misfortune lurks.
【Transcription】"Chún chún" as pronounced according to the character.
Wáng states:
Flowing, a flowing appearance.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The two "flowing" characters are suspected to have one duplicated.
"Fǎnfù" is pronounced fān fú.
【13】【Note】What is considered perverse here,
may be deemed appropriate there.
【Commentary】Opposition means
going against.
The inclinations and aversions of things' nature
indeed have no fixed standard,
so what is contrary here
may be appropriate there,
hence the person who comprehends the Way does not cling to adversity or favor.
【Explanatory Text】"Suǒ fú" is read as fú fú fǎn,
meaning perverse.
Also pronounced as fú,
and also as bì.
【一四】【Note】Each is confident in their own correctness,
unable to depart from it.
【Explanation】To contend is,
to pursue.
To face,
is to orient.
Now, the rights and wrongs between one another,
are stubbornly adhered to in confusion,
thus each pursues their own view and their orientations differ.
【Explanation】"Self-devotion with different orientations": The Guangya says:
"Orientation" means
direction.
It refers to each person's heart being different and thus following their own path.
With distinct directions and personal devotion,
right and wrong are not separated by nature,
so what is correct in one aspect may be flawed in another.
"Lí" is pronounced with the initial "lì" and the final "zhì" in reverse.
【一五】【Note】What is correct in this aspect,
may be erroneous in that one.
【Commentary】What is considered correct and fixed here,
may be erroneous or deviant there,
this illustrates how the nature of things is inverted,
due to differing orientations.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
Fortune and misfortune flow continuously,
if accepted with a mind free of intent,
even if contrary to others, one naturally attains what is fitting.
When each pursues their own direction,
and is forced into divergent paths,
it is called rectifying, yet in reality, both sides have already erred.
【16】【Comment】Do not discard any talent.
【Commentary】Bǐ means
analogy.
Duó means
measurement.
The vast marshes and highlands,
with forests and sounds in abundance,
are used according to their material and measured for purpose,
ensuring nothing is discarded.
The great person takes things,
and the principle is the same.
【Transcription】"Compared to the great marsh," another version also reads as dwelling.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In current texts, "yú" is written as "yū".
"All materials are accommodated," accommodate,
means to dwell.
Although separated into different areas and locations,
they all take the great marsh as their dwelling;
though wood and stone differ in nature,
they both use the great mountain as their altar.
This can be considered as the words of the hill village.
【一七】【Note】Combining differences to form unity.
【Commentary】The altar,
is the foundation.
Stones may be large or small,
wood may be thick or thin,
yet they gather together on the great mountain to form the base,
this is uniting differences to create unity.
【一八】【Note】Speaking of the village community,
one can then understand the world.
【Comment】This summarizes the preceding meaning.
【Collation Notes】(1) The large characters have been amended according to the Shidetang edition.
(2) The two characters "tóng yǐ" have been supplemented based on the following sentence.
Shǎozhī asked:
"Then is calling it the Way
sufficient?"
【One】【Argument】To name it with the Way,
naming the Way through principle,
is it said to be insufficient?
Wishing to clarify that the ultimate Way has no name,
hence this question is raised.
Dàgōng Diào said:
"Not so.
Now when we count the number of things,
they exceed ten thousand,
yet we conventionally call them 'the ten thousand things'
because we use this large number as a general term to refer to them.
Therefore, heaven and earth
are the largest in form;
yin and yang
are the greatest in energy;
and the Dào is what encompasses them all.
It is acceptable to use these grand terms to designate and speak of them,
but having these designations already,
how could one compare them to lesser things?
If we try to argue in this manner,
it would be like comparing dogs to horses -
they fall far short indeed."
【一】【注】For things that have a number,
they still do not stop at ten thousand,
so how much more for numbers without limit?
Can we say that the Dào is sufficient?
【Commentary】A period is a
limit.
A designation is
speech.
As for tangible things,
they are indeed endless.
When people today speak of them,
limiting them to ten thousand things,
this is mentioning them by their major categories.
It is also like the profound Way and subtle principles,
originally nameless in themselves,
but based on their functions,
forcibly named as the Way,
a name that is insufficient for the principle.
【Explanation】"Ér dú" Lǐ Yún says:
dú,
is like speaking.
【二】【注】Things attain their passage,
passing through things without partiality,
yet we forcefully term it the Way.
【Commentary】Heaven covers and Earth supports,
yin and yang give birth and nurture,
thus they are the greatest among forms and energies.
The Way of Heaven can connect all things,
govern and nourish living beings,
impart transformations without partiality,
therefore it is called impartial.
【Explanation】"Qiáng" is pronounced with the initial "j" and the final "iàng".
【Three】【Comment】That which can be spoken of is the Way.
【Commentary】The Great Pervasion encompasses all things,
generating and transforming the multitude of beings.
Speaking of its primordial origin,
it is truly nameless;
yet based on its functional designation,
it may also be called "The Way."
【Four】【Annotation】The name is already established,
so how could there be nothing to compare it with!
【Commentary】Because of its function and utility,
it already possesses the name of the Dao,
one cannot compare this named entity to the principle of the nameless.
Using this as a basis for comparison,
the distance between them is vast.
【五】【Note】The debate over names today is nonexistent,
falling far short of the profound,
hence it is said that the Way is still insufficient;
one must reach the realm of namelessness and wordlessness to attain it fully,
even if names exist,
none can compare to it.
【Commentary】To compare by speaking of the two creatures, dogs and horses, alone,
is not only due to their difference in size,
but also because of the distinction in their nobility and baseness.
Now, comparing the named Way with the nameless principle,
it is not just that the coarse and the subtle differ,
but also that their depths and shallows are distinct,
hence it falls far short.
【Collation】（1）The Quē Wù cites Liú Déyī's version, where "dà" is replaced by "guǎng".
Shǎozhī asked:
"Within the four directions,
inside the six directions,
from where do all things arise?"
【一】【注】The question here arises,
perhaps suggesting that the Dào is capable of generating them.
【Commentary】Within the six directions,
between heaven and earth,
all things, moving and stationary,
from what do they arise?
Shǎozhī poses the question,
wishing to discern their origin.
【Explanation】"Wicked" is pronounced as wū.
Dàgōng Diào said:
"Yin and Yang reflect, cover, and regulate each other;
the four seasons alternate, generate, and extinguish each other.
Desires and aversions, approaches and withdrawals thus abruptly arise;
the pairing of male and female thus commonly occurs.
Safety and danger exchange places;
misfortune and fortune produce each other;
slowness and urgency rub against each other;
gathering and scattering thereby complete each other.
These are nameable realities that can be recorded,
subtle essences that can be noted.
Following the sequence of mutual regulation,
the abrupt movements of mutual influence—
when exhausted, they reverse;
when ended, they begin again.
This is what all things possess,
what language can fully express,
what knowledge can reach—
merely the limits of things.
Those who perceive the Dào
do not trace what has perished,
nor inquire into what arises—
this is where discussion ends."
【一】【Note】This means that all of these come about naturally on their own,
not that they arise from nothing.
【Commentary】The three luminaries shine upon each other,
the two modes (yin and yang) harm each other,
wind and rain govern each other,
heat and coolness alternate with each other,
spring and summer generate each other,
autumn and winter destroy each other.
How could this involve emotional deliberation?
It is the natural principle of things.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
"Gài" should be read as "hài."
In the "Explaining Words" chapter of the Ěryǎ:
"Gài"
means to cut and split.
The explanatory text says:
"Gài,"
in Shě Rén's version, is written as "hài."
This shows that "gài" and "hài" were interchangeable in ancient texts.
Yin and yang may harm each other
or govern each other,
just as the following sentence says the four seasons alternate, generate, and destroy one another.
【二】【Note】All these events, actions, pursuits, and choices,
arise proximately from the mutual illumination of yīn and yáng,
and the succession of the four seasons.
【Commentary】"Jiǎo" means
the appearance of arousal.
"Yōng" means
constancy.
When favorable, one approaches and desires;
when adverse, one dislikes and departs.
This speaks of how all things within the transformations of yīn and yáng,
harbor these emotions and considerations,
opening and closing in interaction,
taking this as the constant principle.
【Translated Text】"Yù wù" is read as wū lù fǎn.
"Qiáo qǐ" is read as jū biǎo fǎn.
The same applies below.
Also pronounced as gāo.
Wáng explains:
High and vigorous,
meaning the swiftness and forcefulness of its initiation.
"Piàn hé" is pronounced as pàn,
or as the character's usual reading.
【Three】【Dissertations】When encountering prosperity, there is peace;
when meeting adversity, there is peril;
peril leads to calamity,
peace brings fortune;
the gradual results in longevity,
the hasty leads to premature death;
dispersion means death,
while gathering signifies life.
All these matters
arise from the friction and interaction of creation,
much like the four seasons changing and shifting in turn—
how could they be tied to human emotions or concerns?
【Four】【Comment】Beyond this point,
one reaches the natural.
The reasons of the natural,
who can know their causes!
【Commentary】Zhì means
to record.
Within the realm of yīn and yáng,
between heaven and earth,
entities have actual names,
thus they can be categorized and documented.
Even if they are subtle and minute,
they can still be described and recorded.
However, when it comes to the profound and mysterious principles,
which transcend form and names,
they cannot be sought through words or images.
【Five】【Note】All are what things inherently possess,
occurring naturally of themselves,
not something that can be had from nothing.
【Commentary】The four seasons cycle in succession,
governing in turn,
the five elements move and operate,
driving and compelling one another in sequence.
When things reach their extreme, they reverse,
ending only to begin again.
All things in existence
find their principle fully expressed herein.
【Explanatory Text】"The Sequence of Following" refers to changes that follow one another,
having an order.
"Sequence",
sometimes written as "origin",
one version uses "enjoy".
"The mutual influence of alternating operations" — alternating operations
means taking turns to replace and arrive abruptly,
ordered to interconnect logically,
alternating operations to mutually control and direct.
【Six】【Annotation】Beyond the realm of things, there is nothing more to exist,
hence it is said that knowledge does not extend beyond the limits of things.
【Commentary】The profound mystery of the ultimate truth,
transcends words and knowledge.
If one attempts to explain it through debate,
or employs knowledge and contemplation,
one may at best reach the realm of tangible things,
but certainly cannot attain the state of profound profundity.
【Transcription】《Suǒ Fù》fú yòu fǎn.
【Seven】【Annotation】Rise and fall both originate from themselves,
with nothing to follow from the past.
【Eight】【Annotation】The ultimate lies in being so of itself,
thus there is nothing to debate.
【Commentary】To perceive,
is to see.
To follow,
is to pursue.
Those who have seen the Way,
profoundly enlightened individuals,
concentrate their spirit beyond material forms,
and illuminate serenely within the cycle of existence,
embodying the mystery in all realms,
recognizing the non-existence of the four kinds of living beings—
how could they still linger on every object and chase after the causes of decay and arising?
This is what is called where the path of language is cut off,
and all discussion ceases.
Shǎo Zhī said:
"Jì Zhēn's doctrine of non-action,
Jiē Zǐ's doctrine of some agency,
the arguments of these two schools—
which is correct in its essence,
which is comprehensive in its principle?"
【One】【Annotation】Jìzhēn says,
the Dào does not act.
Jiēzǐ says,
the Dào perhaps directs.
"Perhaps directs" means
it has the function of directing things.
【Commentary】Jìzhēn and Jiēzǐ,
both were virtuous men of Qí,
studied together at Jìxià,
thus these two worthies are cited to elucidate principles.
Mò means
non-being.
Shǐ means
action.
Jìzhēn considered non-action as the Way,
while Jiēzǐ claimed the Way possesses the function of acting upon things,
each adhering to one school of thought,
yet neither constitutes a comprehensive discourse.
Now Shǎozhī inquires about this to determine right and wrong,
regarding the fundamental nature and subtle principles, questioning which is correct and which is biased.
【Translated Text】"Jìzhēn and Jiēzǐ" Lǐ Yún states:
Two worthy men.

year 30 of Xī, "Zhèng Bó jiē zú,"
the Zuǒ and Gǔ versions both write it as "jié."
) Also, in the case of the Suǒyǐn of the Shǐjì's "Biographies of Mèngzǐ and Xúnqīng," it says:
Jiēzǐ,
is the name of an ancient author.
"Shú biàn" is pronounced as "biàn,"
Xú pronounces it as "piān."
Dàgōng Diào said:
"The crowing of cocks and the barking of dogs
are what people know;
even with great wisdom,
one cannot use words to describe their spontaneous transformations,
nor can one fathom with intention what they are about to do.
To analyze this,
the minute reaches the point of being without comparison,
the vast reaches the point of being immeasurable.
Some attribute it to a driving force,
others to non-action,
yet both unavoidably involve things and ultimately fall into error.
'A driving force' implies substance,
'non-action' implies emptiness.
Having name and substance
is the dwelling of things;
having neither name nor substance
lies in the emptiness of things.
What can be spoken of or conceived,
the more it is spoken of, the further it drifts away.
The unborn cannot be prevented,
the dead cannot be obstructed.
Death and life are not distant,
yet their principle cannot be seen.
'A driving force'
and 'non-action'
are grounds for doubt.
I observe the root,
its past is endless;
I seek the tip,
its future is boundless.
Endless and boundless,
to speak of it as non-existent
is in accordance with the nature of things;
'a driving force' and 'non-action,'
as foundational concepts in speech,
coexist with things from beginning to end.
The Dào cannot be possessed,
and what is possessed cannot be non-existent.
The name 'Dào'
is borrowed for its operation.
'A driving force' and 'non-action'
only grasp one aspect of things;
how can they represent the great method?
If words are sufficient,
then speaking all day will exhaust the Dào;
if words are insufficient,
then speaking all day will only exhaust things.
At the ultimate of Dào and things,
neither speech nor silence is adequate to convey it;
neither speech nor silence—
in discussion, there is a limit."
【1】【Comment】Things have their own nature,
which cannot be achieved by deliberate action.
From this perspective,
Jìzhēn's words are indeed correct.
【Commentary】What the eye sees and the ear hears,
the rooster's crow and the dog's bark,
arise from the workings of nature,
known alike by the foolish and the wise.
Thus, even the greatest sage or the most profound intellect
cannot use intention to fathom their actions,
nor employ words to explain their reasons.
The crowing and barking occur naturally—
how could it be that any principle compels them to be so!
From this, we know that Jiēzǐ's statement
is not appropriate in principle.
【Transcription】"Fèi" is pronounced fú fèi fǎn.
"Dà zhì" is read as dà zhì.
【Two】【Annotation】Both occur spontaneously without deliberate action.
【Commentary】Even if subtle things lack order and sequence,
and massive things cannot be measured by circumference,
by applying this principle to deduce and analyze them,
there is not a single phenomenon that is not spontaneously self-transforming.
【Three】【Annotation】Things have mutual influences,
all of which occur naturally,
thus what is not deliberately acted upon
is not necessarily non-existent.
All things in their multiplicity,
pass by through non-action (three).
【Commentary】Not conforming to the Way,
thus one is not free from material things;
each clings to one extreme,
hence ultimately becomes a source of faults and calamities.
【Four】【Annotation】It was indeed made to do so by itself.
【Commentary】It is because of stagnation and attachment.
【Five】【Annotation】There is nothing that causes it.
【Commentary】Drowning is without cause.
【Six】【Annotation】Refers to the location of name and reality.
【Seven】【Annotation】Where things exist,
their essence is supremely void.
【Commentary】If emotions are fixated on existence,
then everything perceived becomes material objects;
if emotions revere non-existence,
then everything perceived becomes emptiness;
thus it is understood that existence and non-existence reside in the mind,
not in the external environment.
【八】【注】Thus, one must seek beyond the words and meaning to reach it.
【Commentary】That which can be expressed in words,
can be comprehended through thought,
is all the more distant from the Way.
Therefore, one must seek beyond words and thoughts to reach it.
【Nine】【Commentary】Suddenly arising on their own,
Their control does not lie with me,
I cannot restrain them.
【一０】【Note】Suddenly died of its own accord,
I cannot defy it.
【Commentary】Jì means
prohibition.
Zǔ means
obstruction.
Life arises suddenly,
and cannot be forbidden or prohibited;
death comes abruptly,
so what obstruction is there!
One should only follow change and accept transformation,
finding peace wherever one is.
The character is also sometimes written as jǔ,
meaning resentment.
Dying while in accord with the natural course,
thus there is no resentment or mourning.
【Interpretation】"Cannot Cú" in one version is written as "zǔ".
【一一】【Note】It is close within the body itself,
yet one fails to see its natural state and instead worries about it.
【Commentary】Toil and rest, gathering and dispersal,
are matters close at hand within one's own person,
yet their principles are profound and obscure,
which the unwise fail to perceive.
【One Two】【Annotation】These two matters,
are what the world finds most doubtful.
【Commentary】The two attachments to existence and non-existence
are not the mind of the enlightened,
but arise from the biased sentiments of the doubtful,
thus giving rise to debates.
【一三】【Note】The principles of things are boundless,
hence knowledge and discourse are limitless,
only then can one align with the inherent logic of all things.
【Commentary】The root,
is the past.
The tip,
is the future.
The past has already gone by,
giving rise to transformations endlessly,
its origin cannot be fathomed,
how can it be grasped by thought!
Even if one extensively discusses non-existence,
that is already one-sided and stagnant,
and does not escape from things,
thus sharing the same principle with things.
【一四】【Note】Constantly acting without deliberate action, it naturally becomes so.
【Commentary】The fundamental,
means the beginning.
Those who hold onto one side as the root,
still cannot avoid the distinction between the fundamental and the incidental,
thus, sharing the same beginning with things,
yet ultimately departing from them.
【一五】【Note】The Way inherently cannot cause things to exist,
yet what exists is always so of itself.
【Commentary】The ultimate Way is inexhaustible,
neither existent nor non-existent,
thus clinging to either existence or non-existence
is both unacceptable.
【一六】【Note】Things follow it to proceed,
thus it is provisionally named the Way.
【Commentary】The Way is vast and nameless,
so we forcibly name it the Way.
By relying on this named teaching,
we diligently practice it.
【One seven】【Note】Upon mentioning one corner, the rest can be inferred.
【Commentary】Hú,
means "why".
Fāng,
means "the Way".
Whether acting or refraining from action,
if one has not yet ascended to the subtlety of emptiness,
this is merely one mundane thing among others,
a person of biased and limited views.
How could such a one be sufficient to attain the profound mystery,
or speak of the Great Way?
【一八】【Note】Seeking the Way beyond words and ideas is sufficient.
【一九】【Annotation】If one cannot forget the words and preserve the meaning, then it is insufficient.
【Explanation】Sufficiency means
perfect universality.
Insufficiency means
obstruction and stagnation.
If one can forget words and comprehend the principle,
it is said that speech has never spoken,
fully aligning with the profound Dao.
If one clings to words and fails to resonate with the principle,
it deviates from the path of emptiness and penetration,
thus becoming entirely obstructive and hindering things.
【二０】【Note】The ultimate principle of things,
is always such that it acts not yet naturally exists,
regardless of being spoken or unspoken.
【Commentary】When the Way reaches the ultimate state of things,
it is neither the Way nor things,
thus speech and silence cannot fully convey it.
【二一】【Note】It reaches the ultimate of being so of itself,
not through speech or silence that it is discussed.
【Commentary】Silence is not mere silence,
deliberation is not mere deliberation,
one must seek beyond the four propositions,
and only then can one reach the gate of all mysteries.
【Collation】(1) In the Zhào Jiànyì edition, "cú" is written as "zǔ".
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, "yǒu suǒ" is written as "qí yǒu".
(3) In the Zhào edition, below "qù" there is the character "suǒ".
(4) The character "zhī" is deleted according to the Shìdétáng edition.
【1】【Explanation】Titled based on its meaning.
External things cannot be predetermined.
Thus Lóng Féng was executed,
Bǐ Gàn was slain,
Jīzǐ feigned madness,
È Lái died,
and Jié and Zhòu perished.
Rulers all desire loyalty from their ministers,
yet loyalty does not necessarily earn trust.
Hence Wǔ Yún's body was cast into the river,
Cháng Hóng died in Shǔ,
his blood stored for three years before transforming into jade.
Parents all desire filial piety from their children,
yet filial piety does not necessarily earn affection.
Thus Xiàojǐ grieved and Zēng Shēn sorrowed.
When wood rubs against wood, it ignites;
when metal abides with fire, it melts.
When yīn and yáng stray from their course,
heaven and earth are greatly shaken.
Then there is thunder and lightning,
fire in the midst of water,
burning the great locust tree.
Some, deeply troubled, are trapped between dual perils with no escape,
tossed in uncertainty without resolution.
Their hearts hang as if between heaven and earth,
stifled in gloom and distress.
As gain and harm clash against each other,
much inner fire is kindled.
The masses burn up their inner harmony,
for the moon (calm nature) surely cannot overcome the fire (agitation).
Thus they collapse in ruin as their Way is exhausted.
【One】【Memorial】Being stubbornly fixated in one's thoughts,
claiming it to be inevitable.
Yet, among human affairs and matters,
complexities and variations are endless.
Only by embracing great harmony,
can one remain open and unimpeded wherever they are.
If instead, one goes against the nature of things and clings to personal biases,
they are bound to encounter misfortune and harm.
【Explanation Text】"External Things" Wáng notes:
Those who forget themselves and their concerns,
are naturally without opposition in the world,
and then there is no need to insist on external things.
If there are those who cling to actions,
indeed, they will never attain subtlety.
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
In the Song edition, "insist" is written as "heart."
◎ Qìng Fān's case: the annotation in Jī Shūyè's "Essay on Nourishing Life" from the "Wénxuǎn" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"Things,"
refer to affairs.
Loyalty and filial piety,
are internal matters,
and external affairs are all not trusted or accepted.
The explanation text is missing.
【二】【注】The outcomes of good and evil,
are both not inevitable.
【Commentary】Lóng Páng and Bǐ Gàn,
have already been explained in the Outer Chapters.
Jīzǐ,
was a paternal uncle of King Zhòu of Yīn,
who, when his loyal remonstrance was not heeded,
feared that Zhòu would harm him,
and therefore feigned madness,
yet ultimately could not escape execution.
È Lái,
a sycophantic minister of Zhòu,
devotedly followed Zhòu to the end,
and thus perished together with him.
【Three】【Annotation】Utmost sincerity.
【Commentary】"Bì" refers to
jade.
Regarding Zǐxū and Chánghóng,
the Outer Chapters have already explained them.
The phrase "flowing in the river"
refers to his loyal remonstrance with Fūchāi,
who then had him killed,
took horse hide to make a bag,
shaped it like an owl,
filled it with Wǔ Yuán's corpse,
and set it afloat on the river,
hence it is said "flowed in the river."
Chánghóng suffered from slander,
was exiled back to Shǔ,
resented his loyalty being met with false accusations,
and thus slit his own belly to die.
The people of Shǔ, moved by him,
used a box to collect his blood,
which after three years transformed into green jade,
demonstrating the ultimate power of sincere devotion.
【Interpretation】"Transformed into Jasper" According to the Annals of Lü Bùwéi, his blood was stored for three years,
and transformed into jasper.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The Taiping Imperial Encyclopedia, volume 809, quotes Sīmǎ as saying;
Cháng Hóng was loyal and thus executed,
therefore his blood did not decay but transformed into jasper.
The interpretation text is missing.
【四】【注】Thus, the ultimate person responds to things without a set mind,
adapting solely to change.
【Commentary】Xiàojǐ was
the son of the Shāng dynasty's Gāozōng.
He suffered the misfortune of having a stepmother,
and died from grief and hardship.
As for Zēng Shēn, who was extremely filial,
his parents detested him,
and he was often beaten by them,
nearly to the point of death.
Hence, he wept bitterly.
Now, the bond between father and son is innate,
and the duty between ruler and minister is weighty,
yet even the most loyal and filial
can still face lack of affection and understanding.
How much more so in the myriad affairs of the world—
what can one insist on holding fast to?
One should only forget the distinctions between self and others,
and thus be fit to preserve one's life and avoid harm.
【Interpretation】"Xiàojǐ" Lǐ Yún said:
The crown prince of Emperor Gāozōng of the Yīn dynasty.
"Zēng Shēn" Lǐ Yún said:
Zēng Shēn was extremely filial,
yet was hated by his father,
once he was cut off from food and later revived.
【五】【疏】Wood generates fire,
fire overcomes metal;
the energies of the five elements
follow the natural order.
Thus, when wood rubs against wood, fire is produced;
when fire envelops metal, the metal melts.
Therefore, those who stubbornly cling to sincerity and insist on external matters
face the ruin of being consumed and destroyed.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
The "Yuandao" chapter of Huáinánzǐ also states that two pieces of wood rubbing together ignite.
However, when two pieces of wood rub against each other,
one does not see them ignite.
The next sentence says that when metal and fire coexist, they flow;
I suspect this sentence should also read "wood and fire."
The text below states,
"There is fire within water,"
which then burns the great locust tree;
it also says,
"Profit and harm rub against each other,"
producing much fire;
"the masses burn up harmony,"
and "the moon certainly cannot overcome fire."
Since this chapter frequently discusses fire,
it further confirms that this passage should refer to "wood and fire."
Indeed, both wood and metal fear fire,
hence they are cited to illustrate
the great harm that fire can cause.
【Six】【Annotation】What is meant by acting in a disordered manner.
【Commentary】Fire within water,
is lightning.
It burns the great locust tree,
that is the thunderclap.
When yin and yang are in disarray,
and the five elements are not in harmony,
thus the thunder roars in wrath,
startling all beings.
If humans deviate from harmonious energy,
ruin and damage likewise ensue.
【Explanatory Text】"Dà hái" is pronounced like "hài",
also pronounced like "gāi",
and also read as "hú dài fǎn".
"When there is fire in water, it burns the great locust tree" Simǎ explains,
fire in water
refers to lightning.
Burning,
means when thunder strikes, it ignites large trees.
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
The great functions of heaven and earth
are merely water and fire.
Water,
though of yang nature,
operates with yin;
fire,
though of yin nature,
operates with yang.
In human life, the interplay of yin and yang,
with joy, anger, worry, and happiness,
love, hatred, life, and death,
contends and grinds against each other,
much like water and fire.
"Liǎng xiàn" refers to
the overflow of water and fire.
"Chén" should be read as "dōng".
The "Ěryǎ" explains celestial phenomena:
"Dìdōng",
is a rainbow.
"Chén dūn",
is akin to saying rainbow and secondary rainbow.
The Huáinánzǐ's "Shūoshān Xùn" states that two qi form a rainbow in the sky.
These two qi
are the mutual pressure of yin and yang.
When they press against each other and both strive for dominance,
even the rainbow cannot form.
The conflict of water and fire in the human heart,
with yang often easing in gradually,
and yin often striking fiercely and violently.
All discontent in the heart
arises from the release of yin qi,
hence it is said that much fire is generated.
Kǎn represents the moon,
the moon
is the essence of water qi,
embodying yang but functioning as yin.
When fire arises and water cannot overcome it,
that is why one is trapped between both with no escape.
【Seven】【Annotation】If one cannot forget the physical form,
then one will follow whatever the form encounters and sink into sorrow or joy,
with no appropriateness in either direction.
【Subcommentary】Unable to empty the will and forget the form,
confined in mind and stubbornly attached,
thus the emotions gallop between the two realms of honor and disgrace,
sinking into the two extremes of worry and joy,
with nowhere to escape the form.
【Explanatory Text】"Liǎng Xiàn" Sīmǎ explains:
Liǎng,
refers to the heart and gallbladder.
Xiàn,
means to break.
Fear of thunder and lightning causes great anxiety,
leading to the rupture of the heart and gallbladder.
"Yōu Lè" is pronounced as luò.
【八】【注】The more one esteems it heavily,
the more difficult it becomes to act,
not knowing what to abide by,
thus failing to achieve success.
【Commentary】Chéndūn,
means apprehension and fear.
Unable to detach from emotions,
one harbors undue attachment and concern,
thus, despite exhausting the body and troubling the mind, ultimately achieves nothing.
【Explanation】"螴" is pronounced by Guǒ as Chén,
also read as chǔ yǔn,
while Xú pronounces it as chì jǐn.
"蜳" is pronounced by Guǒ as Dūn,
also read as zhù yǔn,
Xú pronounces it as chì zhuǎn,
and Lǐ pronounces it as yú zhǔn.
Sīmǎ explains:
"螴蜳",
read as chōng róng,
referring to the breath of fear,
overflowing with anxiety and unrest,
indicating a state of unease and instability.
【Nine】【Annotation】What is hoped for is lofty and broad.
【Commentary】The mind pursues purposeful action,
lofty and far-reaching,
racing with emotions and chasing after material things,
connecting with the entire universe.
【Explanation】"Ruò xiàn" is pronounced as xuán.
【一０】【注】It is not clear, calm, level, and smooth.
【Commentary】When following one's heart, there is comfort and joy;
when going against one's will, there is confusion and gloom;
encountering situations leads to deep immersion;
touching upon things results in hardship and stagnation.
Since it is neither clear nor smooth,
how could it be peaceful and unimpeded!
【Explanatory Text】"Wèi mǐn": "wǔ jīn" is the pronunciation.
Lǐ reads it as "hūn",
and also as "mǐn".
"Wèi"
means depressed.
"Mǐn",
means distressed.
"Shěn tún": "zhāng lún" is the pronunciation.
Sīmǎ says,
"Shěn",
means deep.
"Tún",
means difficult.
【一一】【Note】It is due to internal heat.
【Commentary】Where there is benefit, there must be harm,
as seen with the cicada and the magpie.
Entangled between benefit and harm,
the heart within constantly burns,
thus giving rise to many flames.
【一二】【Note】When the multitude disregards profit, there is harmony;
but if gains and losses occupy their hearts,
then that harmony is consumed by fire.
【Commentary】"Fén" means
to burn.
The multitude of people
refers to ordinary individuals,
who are unable to maintain their inherent nature and act without artificial effort,
instead constantly chasing after gains and losses,
causing internal heat like fire,
thus scorching their balanced inner nature.
【13】【Comment】Being vast yet obscure leads to many burdens,
being small yet clear allows for understanding one's role.
【Commentary】The moon, though large, has a perfectly round light;
fire, though small, brightly illuminates.
(This) illustrates that having grand ambitions yet being overly greedy
is not as good as being cautious and content with one's lot.
【一四】【Note】Only by being utterly unassuming,
forsaking physical form to attain self-contentment,
can the Way be fully realized.
【Commentary】Tuǐrán,
refers to the appearance of being unrestrained and without conceit.
Forgetting the concerns of gain and loss,
remaining indifferent and without pride,
the profound and mysterious principles
are fully expressed herein.
【Interpretation】"Tuí" is pronounced like "tuī,"
also read as "huāi" in another pronunciation.
Guǒ Xiàng notes:
It means compliant.
【Collation】(1) "Mǐn" was originally miswritten as "Hūn",
corrected according to the Shìdétáng edition.
The explanatory notes below are the same.
(2) In the Shìdétáng edition, "zhī" is written as "zhī".
Zhuāng Zhōu's family was poor,
so he went to borrow grain from the Guardian of the River.
The Guardian of the River said:
"Certainly.
I am about to receive the tax revenue from my fief,
and then I will lend you three hundred gold coins.
Will that do?"
【First】【Memorial】Superintendent of Rivers,
who was Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Zhuāngzǐ, being of lofty and simple character,
did not engage in active pursuits,
and as his household livelihood had become impoverished,
he thus came to borrow grain.
【Translated Text】"Lending Grain" pronounced as tè,
or alternatively pronounced with the phonetic spelling tā dé.
"Jiānhé Hóu" with the pronunciation gǔ xián.
In Shuō Yuàn, it is recorded as Wèi Wén Hóu.
Èr Shū promised,
meaning "to agree."
Types such as copper and iron
are all referred to as metal,
but this is not gold.
Wait until the end of the year for me,
when I receive the commoners' rents, taxes, and fiefdom goods, then I will lend them to you.
【Translated Text】"Jiāng Dài" is pronounced as tā dài fǎn.
Zhuāng Zhōu flushed with anger and said:
"Yesterday when I was coming,
there was a voice calling from the roadside.
I looked down into the wheel rut,
and there was a perch fish there.
I asked it:
'Hey there, perch fish!
What are you doing here?'
It replied:
'I
am a wave official of the Eastern Sea.
Would you happen to have a bucketful of water to keep me alive?'
【一】I said:
'Alright.
I'm going south to visit the kings of Wú and Yuè,
and I'll stir up the waters of the Western River to welcome you -
will that do?'
【二】The perch fish flushed with anger and said:
'I've lost my constant companion,
and have nowhere to settle.
If I could just get a bucketful of water I could stay alive.
But since you say this,
you might as well go look for me earlier in the dried fish market!'
【One】【Memorial】A humble minister amidst the waves,
trapped in the rut of a cart,
might Your Majesty have some water to rescue me?
【Explanation】"而呼" is pronounced with a fire radical and ancient sound.
"鮒" is pronounced as fù.
The Guangya dictionary states:
it is a jì fish.
Jì,
pronounced as jī.
"波臣" Simǎ explains:
it refers to a minister of the waves.
【Two】【Shū】Xī Jiāng,
is Shǔ Jiāng.
There are many rivers,
most flow northward,
only Shǔ Jiāng comes from the west,
hence it is called Xī Jiāng, which is correct.
【Transcription】"Jī Xī" is pronounced as "gǔ dí fǎn".
【Three】【Comment】This means that if it accords with principle, nothing is too small;
but if it is improper,
then no matter how grand, what benefit is there?
【Commentary】Suǒ means
to seek.
Sì means
marketplace.
The common practice of seawater for perch fish,
when waves cause them to lose their usual habitat,
a mere bucket of water
can sustain their lives.
Yet to stir up the Western River
is not appropriate.
Since it cannot save them in the moment,
it is better to seek me in the dried fish market.
This saying illustrates that matters, regardless of size,
have their opportune moments.
If one fails to act at the right moment,
even great efforts will be of no benefit.
【Translated Text】"Zǎo Suǒ" is read as suǒ bái fǎn.
"Kū Yú" Lǐ Yún says:
It means dried fish.
【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Jūnfáng's version, with the character "shuō" present after "yóu".
Lord Rén crafted a giant hook with a massive black line,
using fifty oxen as bait [note 1],
crouched upon Kuàijī Mountain,
and cast his rod into the Eastern Sea [note 2].
Day after day he fished,
yet for a full year he caught no fish.
Eventually, a gigantic fish swallowed the bait,
pulling the enormous hook down deep,
submerging and darting fiercely (revised) [note 1],
then leaping and thrashing its fins,
creating white waves like mountains,
causing the sea waters to tremble and surge,
with sounds rivaling ghosts and deities,
terrifying and awe-inspiring for a thousand lǐ [note 3].
When Lord Rén caught this fish,
he cut it apart and dried it as salted meat,
and from the region east of the Zhì River
to north of Cāngwú,
there was no one who did not feast on this fish [note 4].
Later, generations of mediocre talents and gossipers
were all astonished and spread the tale [note 5].
Those who lift a tiny rod and thin line,
hurry to small ditches (revised) [note 2],
and aim for minnows and carps,
will find it hard to catch a great fish [note 6].
Those who embellish trivial tales to seek petty fame
are far from achieving great understanding [note 7].
Thus, those who have never heard of Lord Rén's ways
are also far from being able to manage worldly affairs [note 8].
【一】【疏】Rèn,
a state's name,
the prince of the state of Rèn.
Jù,
means large.
Zī,
is a black rope.
Jiè,
is a castrated ox.
Ěr,
is the meat on the hook's head.
Since it was a giant hook,
therefore a large rope was used,
suspending fifty oxen as bait.

【Three】【Commentary】The Book of Songs and Rites are

If they are not in the hands of the right person,
the Way does not operate in vain.
Therefore, when Confucian scholars use them to commit treachery,
it shows that these traces are not reliable (two).

Gathering their hair at the temples,

while Confucian scholars recited the Book of Songs and the Book of Rites to rob tombs.

Lǎo Láizǐ's disciple went out (once) to gather firewood,
encountered Zhòngní,
and upon returning reported it,
saying:
"There was a man over there,
with a long upper body and short legs,
hunched at the shoulders with ears set back,
whose gaze seemed to encompass the four seas,
but I do not know whose son he might be."
【一】【疏】Lǎo Láizǐ.
A virtuous recluse of Chǔ.
He often hid in Méng Mountain.
The King of Chǔ, knowing his virtue,
sent an envoy to summon him to be chancellor.
His wife was returning from gathering firewood,
and saw carriage and horse tracks in front of the door.
The wife asked the reason,
Lǎo Lái said:
"The King of Chǔ has summoned me to be chancellor."
The wife said:
"One who accepts from others
is bound to be controlled by others,
and I cannot be controlled by others."
The wife then discarded (the firewood) and left.
Lǎo Lái followed her,
the husband carrying on his back, the wife bearing on her head,
they fled to the south of the river,
none knew where they went.
"Going out to gather firewood"
means to collect firewood.
Having met Confucius,
he returned and reported to his teacher.
【Explanation】Lǎo Láizi was a man of the state of Chǔ.
【Gathering Firewood】Means going out to collect firewood.
【二】【Note】To honor the superior and hasten the subordinate.

Lǐ Yún:

【Translated Text】"To gaze as if overseeing the four seas" refers to those who exhaust their bodies and intellect to cope with worldly affairs,
losing their natural state.
Hence, Yáo had the metaphor of the soaring dragon,

and Zhòng Ní compared to a fleeing dog—
how could these not hold some truth!

Lǎo Láizǐ said:
"Those who cannot bear the grief of one generation bring calamity upon ten thousand generations to come.
Is it because they are inherently impoverished,
or because their strategies fall short?
To seek favor through pleasing others is disgraceful,
a lifelong shame.
The conduct of mediocre people advances only to this level:
they attract each other with reputation,
and bond through shared secrets.
Rather than praising Yáo and condemning Jié,
it is better to forget both and cease such judgments.
To oppose is invariably injurious.
To act is invariably misguided.
The sage hesitates before initiating affairs,
thus often achieving success.
How can one remain perpetually self-important in such endeavors!"
【一】【Note】If one generation acts in a certain way,
then its traces will bring calamity for ten thousand generations,
hence it must not be taken lightly.
【Commentary】The wisdom and benevolence of the sages
may remedy the wounds of an era;
yet later generations, clinging to them deceitfully,
create calamities for ten thousand ages.
Those who rely on the traces of the sages to act arrogantly—
such are the followers of Chén Héng.
There are also those who interpret it as "galloping" (pronounced wù),
meaning to drive ten thousand generations ceaselessly,
which also conveys the idea of rushing headlong.
【Transcription】"而驁" is also written as 敖 in some editions,
same.
Pronounced as wǔ bào fǎn.
Same below.

【Interpretation】"Poor" is pronounced as qí jǔ fǎn.
【Three】【Annotations】If directly entrusted with it,
then the people's nature will not be impoverished and all will possess self-sufficiency,
with virtually no matters left unaccomplished.
【Subcommentary】Losing one's inherent nature,
neglecting the path of life,
thus failing to reach the true Way.
◎Jiāshìfù remarked:
Unwilling to bear the sorrows of one generation, yet bequeathing calamities for ten thousand generations,
they consider themselves capable of governing the world,
unaware that their minds lack accumulated preparedness.
Lacking accumulated preparedness is called destitution,
and their wisdom and strategies fall short as well.
Guǒ Xiàng stated,
If directly entrusted, the people's nature would not be destitute and all would possess self-sufficiency,
with virtually nothing beyond their reach,
which seems to miss Zhuāngzǐ's original intent.
◎Qìng Fān's case note: "Wáng" should be read as "wú" (without).
"Wáng qí,"
is a transitional expression.
In the "Biographies of Fàn Jū and Cài Zé" from Records of the Grand Historian:
Is it that those who speak of me are lowly and unfit for use?
(Suǒyǐn:
"Wáng,"
meaning to belittle or despise,
but this interpretation is not coherent.
) In the "Àn Lèi" chapter of Mr. Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals: Is it that failing to obtain Sòng and acting unrighteously still warrants attacking it?
In the Strategies of Hán: Or is it that practicing your methods and abandoning your petitions?
Thus, whenever "wáng qí" is mentioned,

【Four】【Annotation】When favored, one is joyful;
without favor, one is disgraced.
However, favor cannot last long,
thus a single favor leads to a lifetime of disgrace.
【Commentary】Those who take delight in bestowing favors,
cannot make their favors reach all,
hence those who are neglected and treated with disdain are many.
Thus, to win people through favors,
only turns into a repository of resentment,
and thus leads to lifelong disgrace and shame.
【Five】【Annotation】It means it is easy to advance,
so one must not recklessly bestow favors upon it.
【Transcription】"之行" is read with the lower tone of Meng.
"其易" is read with the tone of Yi.
【Six】【Annotation】Concealment,
encompass;
advancing (three) is what is meant.
【Commentary】Those of supreme wisdom and the utterly foolish
have natures difficult to alter,
while those of average disposition
are easily swayed to advance or retreat.
Thus, upon hearing of Yáo's virtues,
they are drawn to emulate for fame and gain;
upon hearing of Jié's vices,
they bond over concealment and complicity.
【Interpretation】"Forming bonds through yǐn": Guǒ notes:
Yǐn means
to correct and guide.
Lǐ states:
Yǐn refers to
affliction or ailment.
Even if drawn together by reputation,
it is forming bonds through affliction.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
Lǐ says,
yǐn means
affliction.
However, affliction is not a means to form bonds.
Guǒ's annotation says,
yǐn means
to straighten;
it implies advancement.
Yet, straightening is for correcting crooked wood,
and also not a means to form bonds.
Yǐn should be interpreted as private or personal.
In the "Yuándào" chapter of "Lǚshì Chūnqiū," with roles fixed, subordinates do not conceal from each other,
Gāo's annotation states:
Yǐn means
private.
In "Rhapsody on the Red-White Horse" from "Wénxuǎn," kindness yǐn is deeply generous,
Lǐ Shàn cites the "Guóyǔ" annotation saying:
Yǐn means
private.
"Forming bonds through yǐn"
means forming bonds through personal favors.
The old interpretations are all incorrect.
【Seven】【Annotation】Closure means,
blockage.
【Commentary】Praising the virtuous ways of Yáo,
and condemning the wicked deeds of Jié,
by engaging in such pursuits,
one loses much of their innate nature.
Therefore, it is better to forget both good and evil,
and shut out praise and blame,
so that the nature of things remains intact.
【Transcription】"Praising Yáo" is pronounced as yú.
"But closing" in one version, both the text and commentary use the word "door."
【八】【Note】Follow it and you will be preserved whole,

【Commentary】To act contrary to the nature of things,
inevitably causes harm and damage,
disturbs the mind and spirit,
and is never the right way.
【Explanation】"Acting contrary to reason inevitably causes harm" means going against,
opposing principles.
"No action is free from evil" resembles a sigh of opposition.
It refers to acting arrogantly based on this.
【Nine】【Annotation】Affairs do not stray from their roots.
Therefore, their success is often achieved.
【Commentary】Hesitating with ease,
the sage has no fixed mind,
but acts in response to the moment,
initiating endeavors
always with natural composure.
By not opposing the nature of things,
thus his achievements often succeed.
【Explanatory Text】"Shèngrén chóu" is pronounced as chóu.
"Chú" is pronounced with the initial zhí and final jū.
"To initiate affairs and often achieve success" means,
frequently accomplishing success.
Hesitation refers to,
acting with ease.
When initiating affairs with ease,
even if success is achieved,
if the sage is not present,
it can still lead to flawed outcomes.
The harm may last for a hundred generations.
How much more so if one constantly prides on good deeds and carries them out without cease!
"Bù yuǎn" is pronounced with the initial yú and final wàn.
【一０】【Note】Arrogance cannot be borne,
thus it is discarded and not possessed.
【Commentary】Nài hé,
means "how can it be".
How can one cling to the traces of benevolence and righteousness,
disturb the minds of all things,
carry oneself with solemn dignity,
and never cease throughout life!
These are Lǎo Lái's words criticizing and reproaching Confucius.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
Fǎn,
is like rectifying a chaotic world and returning it to order.
Where there is reversal, there must be harm;
where there is action, there must be deviation.
Its reversal,
is the contentious heart holding onto pride;
its action,
is the proud heart carrying it forth.
Let things transform by themselves,
then there will be no harm;
do nothing, and nothing is left undone,
then there is no deviation.

Ā.

宰路，
is the name of an abyss by the river.
姓余，
名且，
is a person who catches fish.
【Explanatory Text】"Zǎi Lù" Lǐ Yún says:
the name of an abyss,
where turtles dwell.
"Yǔ wéi" read as the character's standard pronunciation,
also pronounced with the yú wèi reversal.
"Shǐ hé" with the shǐ lì reversal.
"Yú zhě" pronounced as yú.
"Yú" pronounced as yù.
"Qiě" with the zǐ yú reversal.
The surname is Yú,
and the given name is Qiě.
◎Yú Yuè states:
In the Historical Records' Biographies of Turtle and Divination Stalks, it is written as Yù Qiě.
◎Qìng Fān's case notes: the characters Yù and Yù are the same.
Yuán Jūn awoke,
and had someone divine it,
who said:
"This is a divine turtle."
The lord asked:
"Is there a fisherman named Yú Qiě?"
The attendants said:
"Yes."
The lord said:
"Command Yú Qiě to attend the morning assembly."
【一】【疏】Fate,
means summons.
Summoned to court,
to inquire about what was gained.
【Transcription】"Jiào" is read as gǔ xiào fǎn.
"Lìng" is read as lì chéng fǎn.
"Huì cháo" is read as zhí yáo fǎn.
The same applies below.
Tomorrow,
I shall go to court.
The lord asked:
"What has the fisherman obtained?"
He replied:
"Just now, in the net, I caught a white turtle,
its circumference is five chǐ."
The lord said:
"Present the turtle of Ruò."
The tortoise arrived,
and the ruler twice wished to kill it,
twice wished to spare it,
his mind doubtful,
he divined about it,
and the result said:
"Kill the tortoise to divine for auspiciousness."
So he cut open the tortoise,
seventy-two drillings yet without an unfulfilled prophecy.
【First】【Memorial】The heart is doubtful and hesitant,
deciding between life and death repeatedly,
then killed Jí,
and proceeded to cut open a turtle for divination.
【Èr】【Shū】 calculated the sequence of events,
delving through a total of seventy-two classics,
divining auspicious and inauspicious outcomes,
never once missing the mark.
【Translated Text】"Hollow out" is pronounced as kǒu gū fǎn.
"Drill" is pronounced as zuǒ duān fǎn,
and also as zuǒ luàn fǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's case: in the commentary on Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" from the "Wén Xuǎn," Sīmǎ notes:
drilling,
commanding the divination,
refers to burning it for the matter being divined.
[The explanatory text is missing].
"Discarding the divination stalks" is pronounced as chū gé fǎn.
Zhòngní said:
"The divine turtle could appear in a dream to Yuánjūn,
yet could not avoid the net of Yúqiě;
its wisdom enabled it to be divined seventy-two times without a single miscalculation,
yet it could not escape the calamity of having its belly cut open.
Thus,
it is clear that wisdom has its limitations,
and divinity has its shortcomings.
Even with the utmost wisdom,
one needs the counsel of ten thousand people.
Fish do not fear the net but fear the pelican.
Discard petty wisdom and great wisdom will shine forth,
relinquish conscious goodness and natural goodness will arise.
An infant is born without a learned teacher yet learns to speak,
for it dwells among those who can speak."
【一】【注】Thus it is seen that reliance on the wisdom of the spirits is insufficient;
only those who quietly abide in their abilities without seeking external pursuits can achieve wholeness.
【Commentary】Spiritual intelligence is something
one cannot rely upon.
Therefore, when the ultimate person lives in the world,
they forget physical form, spirit, and intellectual concerns,
becoming like a withered tree that bears no blossoms,
equating themselves with dying embers in their stillness and tranquility,
letting things merge darkly with the creator's transformations.
Thus, even Confucius, the great sage,
discussed this accordingly.
【Interpretation】"Appearing in a dream": xián biàn fǎn.
"Wisdom and ability": zhì is pronounced as zhì,
the same applies below and in the annotations.
"Knowledge has its perplexities" in one edition is written as "knowledge has its differences."
【二】【Note】Not employing one's own wisdom but utilizing the counsel of the multitude.
【Explanation】"Zhi Zhi" is pronounced as "zhì".
The same applies to the following text and annotations.
【Three】【Notes】The net is merciless,
thus it catches fish.
【Commentary】The net, though without emotion, catches fish;
this illustrates that the sage, without personal intent,
causes all under heaven to turn to him.
【Transcription】"Tí" is pronounced as tí xī fǎn.
"Hú" refers to the pelican,
a water bird,
also known as the scooping river.
【Four】【Commentary】The small-minded are self-centered,
the great-minded entrust themselves to all things.
【Commentary】The lesser wisdom makes distinctions in the mind,
while the greater wisdom is without discrimination.
By dispelling the sentiments of contention and usurpation,
one thus achieves non-discrimination,
and then the greater wisdom shines brightly.
【Transcription】"Qù xiǎo" qǐ lǚ fǎn.
The following and annotations are the same.
【五】【注】If goodness is removed, then there is nothing to admire in goodness,
and if there is nothing to admire in goodness,
then those who are good will become good without pretense and of their own accord.
【Commentary】Dispelling the petty mind of self-importance,
and uniting with the great goodness of nature,
thus the previous text states:
"Departing from the Way to pursue goodness,
and endangering virtue through action."
Furthermore, the Lǎojīng says:
"When all under heaven know beauty as beauty,
there is already ugliness."
【Transcription】"Bù jiǎo" - jū biǎo fǎn.
【Six】【Comment】To be capable without prior practice naturally,
is not to strive and learn from others.
【Commentary】The nature of an infant is such that,
without relying on teachers or masters,
as they gradually grow older, they naturally learn to speak.
It is not because they intentionally study it;
by being with their parents
and following their innate disposition,
they naturally become capable of speech.
From this, we understand that all things in the world
do not come about through acquired knowledge
or learning to achieve them.
【Explanation】"Shí Shī": Shí is the name
of a craftsman.
It means there is no one to serve as a teacher or master to instruct him.
One version writes it as "suǒ shī",
and another as "shuò shī".
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
"Your words are useless."
【一】【疏】Zhuāngzǐ,
was a profound man.
He illuminated both emptiness and existence,
his words were vast and broad,
yet they did not align with common minds,
thus Huì Shī criticized them as useless.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Only when one understands the useless can one begin to discuss the useful with them.
Heaven and earth are indeed vast and great,
yet what humans use is merely enough space for their feet.
But if one were to dig away the ground around their feet down to the yellow springs,
would the space for their feet still be useful?"
Huìzǐ said:
"It would not be useful."
【One】【Argument】For if something is useful, it shares the same fate as premature death;
if it is useless, it preserves its entire existence.
Thus, it is known that only through uselessness can one speak of its usefulness.
means to excavate.
Within the six directions of the universe,
nothing is vaster than the earth,
yet what humans utilize
is merely enough to accommodate their feet.
If, beyond where one stands,
one were to dig all the way down to the Yellow Springs,
then a person would tremble and be unable to move.
This illustrates that useful things
rely on the useless to achieve their purpose.
【Translated Text】"Cè Zú" is pronounced as zè,
also pronounced as cè.
"Diàn" is pronounced as diàn in the reverse spelling.
Sīmǎ and Cuī say:
It means low or lower.
The character is also written as qiàn,
pronounced as qiàn in the reverse spelling,
meaning to dig.
"Zhì Huángquán" means zhì,
which is to reach.
The original text also uses zhì.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Thus, the usefulness of the useless is also clear."
【一】【注】The sage responds from within,
acting appropriately as events arise;
he expresses it outwardly,
to fully convey the situation.
When feelings flow freely, affairs proceed smoothly;
when the external is clear, the internal becomes effective,
for such is the principle of mutual dependence.
【Commentary】If one only has space exactly for placing one's feet,
it would be impossible to walk.
One must rely on additional space
in order to move one's feet.
The principle of the usefulness of the useless is clear here,
hence, as quoted from Lǎo Zǐ:
"Having something brings benefit,
but it is the absence that creates its usefulness."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"If a person is capable of wandering freely,
how could they not wander?
If a person is incapable of wandering freely,
how could they wander?
The will that flees from the world,
the conduct that severs all ties—
alas!
are these not the burden of the highest wisdom and profound virtue?
They fall into ruin yet do not turn back,
rush forth like fire yet do not look back.
Though some may be rulers and others subjects,
it is but a matter of timing.
When ages change, there is no basis to despise one another.
Therefore, it is said the perfect person leaves no trace in their actions."
【One】【Annotation】What one's nature is capable of,
one cannot but do;
what one's nature is incapable of,
one must not force to do;
therefore, the sage only refrains from restraining them,
so all equally attain without knowing how they attain.
【Commentary】People are endowed with different natures,
and their aptitudes vary accordingly.
Some naturally understand words as swiftly as shadows follow form and echoes respond to sound,
while others are so intellectually dull they cannot distinguish beans from wheat.
Therefore, for those with inherent abilities,
their actions must stem from their nature;
for those lacking such innate traits,
they should not be forced to engage in them.
If each remains within their proper sphere,
then nothing in the world will be lost.
【Interpretation】"Dé qiáng" pronounced with the character's sound as "zhàng".
【二】【Note】Without utmost integrity, one cannot bear the weight of their aspirations and actions, nor trust in their exceptional abilities.
【Commentary】Drifting and chasing after things,
fleeing and not returning,
resolute in cutting off and extinguishing,
stubborn and unyielding,
such aspirations and conduct,
are the height of foolishness and baseness,
how could they be employed by the profound and subtle true knowledge and deep virtue!
Zhuāngzǐ's intent
is to say that it is like this.
【Transcription】"之行" is read with the lower tone of Měng.
The same applies to the annotations.
"任與" is pronounced as yú.
【Three】【Comment】What people are fond of,
they do not avoid right and wrong,
risking life and death for it.
【Commentary】Those who are foolish and deluded,
hold their will steadfastly,
even if their families are wiped out,
and they themselves suffer downfall,
they still do not know to repent and turn back.
They chase after worldly desires,
as urgently as smoke and fire,
yet do not know to look back.
They drift away and sever themselves decisively,
thus ending up in such a state.
【Explanation】"覆墜" is pronounced with the direct sound "zhí" and the category sound "lèi".
"所好" is pronounced with the exhalation sound "hū" and the report sound "bào".
【Four】【Annotation】This is why it is called the Great Equality and Unity (Three).
【Commentary】Those who are virtuous according to the times become rulers,
while those whose talents do not meet the era's needs become ministers,
as seen with Shùn and Yǔ, who succeeded each other as ruler and minister in accordance with their time.
Thus, when the world undergoes change and upheaval,
one should not demean or belittle others based on their roles as ministers or rulers.
Those who are lost in delusion
fail to understand this matter.
【Five】【Annotation】Only by following what one encounters and adapting to it,
can one thus move in step with the transformations.
【Commentary】As the world experiences rise and decline,
one should adapt and move with it,
hence the enlightened person never remains stagnant.
