【Collation】(1) The Tang manuscript lacks the character "yuē".
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì version lacks the character "zé".
(3) The Shìdétáng version reads "suǒyǐ wéi rén qí tóng".
The Zhào version reads "suǒyǐ wéi rén qí".
"Qí"
means "tóng".
To honor the ancient and belittle the modern
is the tendency of scholars.
Moreover, if we observe the present age from the perspective of the Xīwéi shì lineage,
who could avoid being swayed?
Only the ultimate person can wander in the world without being eccentric,
comply with others without losing oneself.
Their teachings need not be learned,
and by embracing the intent, one does not become like them.
【一】【Note】The ancients had nothing to revere,
the moderns have nothing to belittle,
yet scholars revere the ancients and belittle the moderns,
losing the essence of it all.
【Commentary】Pacing and running differ with the times,
simplicity and refinement vary across eras;
the sentiments and affairs of past and present,
undergo transformations and are not the same.
Yet to value antiquity and disdain the present
deeply violates the principle of far-sighted discernment,
merely fostering petty views in scholarship—
how can this be called clear and comprehensive understanding!
【二】【注】Adapting to the times and following the nature of things,
one achieves perfect harmony.
【Commentary】Xīwéi was the imperial title before the era of the Three Sovereigns.
To apply the ways of remote antiquity to the present age,
when the contrast between simplicity and ostentation is already evident,
who can avoid being stirred by waves without losing their true nature?
This is due to the flaw of venerating the past and belittling the present.
【Transcription】"Xǐ" is pronounced as xū qǐ fǎn.
"Bù bō" bō,
describes a high and low appearance.
【Three】【Comment】Responding to affairs of the time,
wherever one is, that is the right course (two).
【Interpretation】"Bù pì" is pronounced with the initial consonant "p" and the same rhyme as "yì".
【Four】【Annotation】Fundamentally there is no self,
so what have I lost!
【Five】【Annotation】Teaching adapts to their inherent nature,
thus it is not mere learning.
【Six】【Annotation】Their intentions are spontaneous,
thus by accepting and utilizing them,
all things can each fulfill their own selves.
【Commentary】Only those with supreme virtue,
follow the times to transform others,
not through learning but with innate nature fully complete,
it does not come from acquired study.
To receive the meaning without being swayed by others,
is to inherit the teachings to guide one's nature,
while the true path is inherently perfect,
not relying on external instruction.
【Collation Note】(1) The Tang manuscript lacks the character 乃.
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì version correctly uses 政 instead.
When the eyes are clear, they see;
when the ears are clear, they hear;
when the nose is clear, it detects scents;
when the mouth is clear, it tastes flavors;
when the heart is clear, it gains wisdom;
when wisdom is clear, it becomes virtue.
Generally, the Way should not be obstructed,
for obstruction leads to blockage,
and if blockage persists, it causes turmoil,
and turmoil gives rise to numerous harms.
Beings endowed with awareness rely on their breath;
if it is not abundant,
it is not the fault of Heaven.
Heaven pierces through them,
unceasing day and night,
yet humans block up their apertures.
The womb has layered chambers,
the heart has its heavenly wanderings.
If a house lacks emptiness,
then wives and mothers-in-law quarrel;
if the heart lacks heavenly wanderings,
then the six apertures conflict with each other.
That vast forests and hills benefit humans
is also because the spirit finds them overwhelming.
【一】【疏】Penetration,
means thorough understanding.
As for the term "rancid,"
it refers to pungent and foul matters.
When the six senses are unobstructed,
there is penetration;
when wisdom and clarity are not dissipated externally,
it constitutes virtue.
【Explanation】"Chàn" is pronounced as shū yán fǎn.
【二】【Note】When what should flow freely is blocked,
then principles fail to be released and trample over one another.
【Explanation Text】"Gěng" is pronounced with the initial "gēng" and final "měng" sound,
meaning blockage.
"Niǎn" is pronounced with the initial "nǚ" and final "zhǎn" sound.
Guǒ Xiàng notes:
It means to tread upon.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
To step on,
or to stop.
Some versions write it as "niǎn",
which is the same.
◎ Wáng Niànsūn comments:
Guǒ's annotation,
suggesting that when something should flow freely but becomes blocked,
then principles that do not dissipate may lead to trampling upon one another,
is explained in the interpretive text:
"niǎn",
pronounced with initial "nǚ" and final "zhǎn".
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
To tread upon,
or to stop.
Some versions write it as "niǎn",
which is the same.
I note that the meanings of treading and blockage
are not logically connected.
Guǒ's statement about principles not dissipating and trampling upon one another
is what is called a forced interpretation;
writing it as "niǎn" in some versions
is also incorrect.
Now, I propose that "niǎn" should be read as "niǔ".
"Niǔ"
means perverse or contrary.
This means if blockage does not cease,
it leads to mutual conflict,
and mutual conflict gives rise to various harms.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
"Niǔ" means "lì".
(Here, "lì" is the same as "lì" meaning perverse.
) The "Fāngyán" says:
"Zhěn",
means perverse.
Guǒ Pú annotated:
It means to twist or pervert mutually.
In the "Mèngzǐ·Gàozǐ" chapter, the phrase "twist one's elder brother's arm to snatch food",
Zhào Qí explains:
"Zhěn",
means to twist or pervert.
Here, it says if blockage does not cease, then it leads to "niǎn",
a meaning consistent with "niǔ".
【Three】【Annotations】life,
means to arise.
【Four】【Annotation】All root-born beings lack consciousness,
and also do not rely on breath.
【Commentary】Heaven endows the six senses,
none of which can be dispensed with.
The ears hear, the eyes see,
the nose smells, and the mind perceives—
these functions are within their natural roles,
and though used, there is no fault.
But if the eyes linger on the allurements within the mulberry groves,
the ears indulge in the sounds of the Pú River's banks,
the nose revels in the fragrance of orchids and musk,
and the mind engages in boundless desires,
then the principles of Heaven are extinguished—
how can this be called true understanding?
Therefore, when the six senses are thoroughly understood,
the vital energy flows freely, and the essence of life is preserved.
【Five】【Annotation】Yīn,
means appropriate.
Breathing does not arise from consciousness,
it is through consciousness that one then loses appropriateness,
losing appropriateness and then becoming obstructed,
thus consciousness relies on breathing,
but breathing does not rely on consciousness.
However, the use of conscious desires,
is controlled by humans,
and is not a sign of inevitability.
【Commentary】Yīn means
appropriate.
Some indulge the six senses,
chasing after external objects;
others have blocked orifices,
harming the path of life;
both types of conduct,
are unreasonable.
These are faults of human disposition,
not inborn transgressions.
【Transcription】"Bù yīn" is read as it is,
another reading is with the pronunciation yìn, following the fǎnqiè spelling yú jìn fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】The universal principle operates with constant motion.
【Commentary】"Jiàng" means
"to stop".
The principle of nature
penetrates all things,
from day to night,
never ceasing.
◎ Jià Shìfù said:
The consciousness of beings relies on breath,
breath is qì,
yet qì varies in richness, purity, and mixture,
Heaven cannot force them to be the same.
The "Ěryǎ·Shì Yán" states:
"Yīn" means
"to align",
and "to center".
Alignment leads to centrality,
but when they cannot be aligned,
it is something Heaven cannot control.
Yet Heaven has endowed them with a hundred bones and nine orifices to function on their own,
and given them a mind to transform themselves,
focusing solely on opening and connecting.
The "Shuōwén" explains:
"Chuān" means
"to penetrate".
Vast and ample, there is enough space for self-preservation, thus it is connected.
The "Yùpiān" states:
"Jiàng" means
"to subside".
This means the movement of accumulated qì never stops or subsides.
Guō Xiàng's annotation,
interpreting "Yīn" as
"to correspond",
is mistaken.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
"Jiàng"
should be read as "●",
which is the ancient form of "lóng" (blockage).
The "Sùwèn·Xuānmíng Wǔqì Piān" states that bladder dysfunction causes "lóng",
and the "Wǔcháng Zhèng Dàlùn Piān" mentions illnesses of "lóng" and blockage.
"Day and night without ●"
means without such blockages.
【Seven】【Annotation】Devoid of emotion, one entrusts to Heaven,
then the gate of enlightenment opens.
【Commentary】The opening,
is a passage.
Common people,
contrary to the natural order,
block their fundamental openings,
causing stagnation and obstruction.
【Explanatory Text】"其竇" is pronounced as dòu.
【八】【注】Làng,
means vast and empty.
【Commentary】Làng,
means empty.
It refers to the emptiness inside a person's abdomen,
thus accommodating the stomach and intestines;
when the stomach and intestines are empty,
they allow the passage of qi and fluids.
【Explanation】"胞" is pronounced pū jiāo fǎn,
meaning a fetus in the womb.
"有重" is pronounced zhí lóng fǎn.
"閬" is pronounced làng.
Guǒ's commentary says:
It means empty and vast.
【Nine】【Comment】To wander,
is to be unbound.
【Commentary】Void.
Thus, the way of nature roams within it.
【Explanation】Bó xì,
means contention and fighting.
When the house is not empty,
it cannot accommodate,
hence mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law contend for space,
with no regard for seniority or juniority.
【Explanation】"Bóxī" is pronounced xī.
Bó means
to contend.
Xī means
emptiness.
Sīmǎ explains:
Bóxī
refers to perverse conflict.
Without emptiness to accommodate one's selfishness,
then perversity and conflict lead to mutual contention.
【一一】【Note】Rǎng means
to oppose.
【Commentary】To bore,
means a hole.
To resist,
(then) means to oppose.
The way of nature,
if one's mind does not wander through it,
then the six senses oppose,
and do not accord with principle.
【Explanation】"Liù záo" is pronounced with the initial "zài" and the final "bào".
"Xiāng rǎng" is pronounced with the initial "rú" and the final "yáng".
Guǒ says:
It means to oppose.
Sīmǎ says:
It refers to the six emotions contending with each other.
◎Qìng Fān notes: In the commentary on the "Āigōng" chapter of the Xúnzǐ, it quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
The six emotions contend with each other.
This has one more "xiāng" character than the explanation in the text.
【一二】【Note】It is the principle of nature
that things communicate through their connections.
【Commentary】It is the principle of nature that
there are things which convey meaning through their lodging.
◎Jiàshìfù remarked:
The virtue of great forests, hills, and mountains for humans,
means that the reason for delighting in great forests, hills, and mountains
lies in their vastness accommodating the growth of all things.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
Shén (神),
is the celestial deity that draws forth all things.
Xú Qiǎn said:
"Shēn" (申) means to draw out.
"Shén zhě bù shèng" (神者不胜),
means that in generating all things,
it is inexhaustible and beyond measure.
【Collation】(1) The Quēwù cites two editions by Zhāng Wén, where both have "Lín" written as ●.
(2) In the Táng manuscript copy, the character "shèng" is followed by the character "yě".
Virtue overflows because of reputation,
reputation overflows because of contention,
plans are deliberated due to urgency,
wisdom emerges from disputes,
obstinacy arises from stubbornness,
official affairs are accomplished through collective appropriateness.
When the spring rain falls in its season,
the grass and trees vigorously grow,
and so the weeding tools begin to be prepared,
yet over half of the plants that are transplanted upside down thrive without anyone knowing why.
【一】【注】For when fame is exalted, the benefits run deep,
thus those who cultivate virtue often exceed the proper measure.
【Explanation】Excess means
depth.
The five virtues of benevolence and righteousness,
when practiced excessively,
are due to the pursuit of fame and competitiveness.
【二】【注】To prohibit violence makes one's reputation more beautiful than virtue.
【Commentary】Bào (暴) means
to cruelly harm.
Now, reputation is the tool of contention;
when reputation becomes excessive,
it inevitably leads to mutual harm.
The Inner Chapters state:
"Reputation is that by which people crush one another."
◎Jiāshìfù (家世父) said:
In the Shuōwén (說文),
bào (暴)
means to dry in the sun.
In Mencius, "exposing it to the people and the people accept it,"
and in Xúnzǐ's "Enriching the State" chapter, "reputation is sufficient to expose and scorch them,"
both convey the idea of displaying or exposing.
"Virtue overflows due to reputation"
means that virtue becomes abundant
because of reputation;
"reputation overflows due to exposure"
means that reputation becomes abundant
through display to achieve it.
These five phrases all convey the same meaning.
Guǒ Xiàng (郭象) stated,
"To prohibit violence makes reputation more beautiful than virtue,"
which is likely mistaken.
【Three】【Comment】Xián,
means urgency.
Act urgently and then examine the strategy.
【Commentary】Jī means
to investigate.
Xián means
urgency.
In matters of urgent difficulty,
only then are strategies and plans deliberated.
【Explanatory Text】"誸" is pronounced as xián.
Guǒ's annotation gives the pronunciation as xuán,
meaning urgent.
Xiàng's version writes it as "弦",
and states:
it signifies firmness and correctness.
【Four】【Annotation】When peace prevails, there is no use for wisdom.
【Commentary】When one employs cleverness and knowledge to go beyond boundaries,
then conflicts and struggles will surely arise.
【Five】【Annotation】Chái,
means to block.
【Commentary】Chái means
to block.
Shǒu means
to hold fast.
When emotions are held fast and stubbornly, what one creates does not flow freely.
【Explanation】"Chái" means
to accumulate.
Guǒ states:
to block.
【Six】【Annotation】What is suitable for the multitude is not uniform,
hence official duties are established.
【Commentary】Establishing government offices
and setting regulations
must align with what is suitable and convenient for the people.
If one seeks to oppose this,
then calamity and disorder will arise.
◎Yú Yuè said:
In the Analects, chapter "Zǐlù," it states that actions must be decisive,
Huáng Kǎn's commentary explains:
Decisive
means accomplished.
Only when the people have what is suitable can official duties be accomplished,
hence it is said that official duties are accomplished through what is suitable for the people.
【Seven】【Annotation】All things that come into being have their causes.
【Commentary】Yáo,
is a type of sì.
Nòu,
is a hoe.
During the spring season,
on days of timely rain,
all kinds of plants and trees,
sprout and grow,
and only then are farming tools first repaired.
This illustrates acting in accordance with the seasons,
and not going against the nature of things.
【Explanation】"Tiáo" is read as qī yáo fǎn,
meaning to pare.
It is capable of piercing and paring.
Also read as tā yáo fǎn.
"Nòu" is read as nǎi dòu fǎn.
Resembling a hoe,
it is a farming tool.
【八】【注】For matters arise from principle,
thus one is unaware (one).
【Commentary】Zhí,
means to grow.
Once the spades and hoes are prepared,
and the reeds and rushes are weeded out,
fortunate to encounter the spring days,
after hoeing, growth arrives.
This is truly due to the season making it so,
and cannot be measured by human sentiment.
Thus, it is known that establishing laws and teachings
must follow the timing.
【Explanation】"Dào zhí": read as "shí lì fǎn",
also pronounced as "zhí",
meaning to stand.
Originally also written as "zhì".
Sīmǎ explains:
"Chú bá fǎn zhī gēng shēng zhě yuē dào zhí" refers to what grows again after being uprooted and overturned.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
"Dào",
is the ancient character for "dǎo" (倒).
【Collation Note】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "Qí".
Tranquility can restore health,
rubbing the eyes can relieve aging,
and calm can halt haste.
Even so,
if this is the case,
these are the concerns of the toiling,
not what the carefree have ever bothered to inquire about.
The sage's way of startling the world—
the spiritual person has never bothered to inquire about it;
the worthy's way of startling the age—
the sage has never bothered to inquire about it;
the gentleman's way of startling the state—
the worthy has never bothered to inquire about it;
the petty person's way of conforming to the times—
the gentleman has never bothered to inquire about it.
In Yǎnmén, there was one whose parent died,
and through skillful grieving, he was ennobled as an official master;
half of his fellow villagers died from excessive grief.
Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
but Xǔ Yóu fled from it;
Tāng offered it to Wù Guāng,
and Wù Guāng was angered by it;
Jì Tā heard of this,
led his disciples and settled by Kuǎnshuǐ,
and feudal lords condoled with him;
three years later,
Shēntú Dí consequently drowned himself in the river.
The fish trap exists for the sake of fish—
once the fish is caught, the trap is forgotten;
the rabbit snare exists for the sake of rabbits—
once the rabbit is caught, the snare is forgotten;
words exist for the sake of meaning—
once the meaning is grasped, the words are forgotten.
How can I find someone who has forgotten the words and speak with them!"
【一】【注】It is not that he is not ill.
【Commentary】For those afflicted with irritability and restlessness,
simplicity and tranquility can serve as a cure.
【二】【注】It is not that they do not age.
【Commentary】Trimming the hair and beard,
alters one's appearance.
The look of aging and decline,
is thus cleansed through bathing.
【Text Explanation】"Zì" is pronounced zǐsī fǎn,
Xú gives the pronunciation as zǐzhì fǎn.
Also written as "jiǎn",
pronounced zǐqiǎn fǎn.
The Sān Cāng states:
"jiǎn"
means to cut off.
The Yù Piān says:
It means to eliminate.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: Xiāo Gāi's Hàn Shū Yīn Yì quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"zì",
means to look.
This is missing in the explanatory text.
"Miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)" is also written as "miè",
pronounced miè.
Another pronunciation is wǔqí fǎn.
The Zì Lín states:
It means ●.
is pronounced qiānmǐ fǎn.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The old text has "mǐ" written as "wèi",
now follows the Sòng edition.
◎Jiā Shìfù says:
The explanatory text "zì miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)" can mean to rest in old age,
"miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)",
is also written as "miè".
The Guǎng Yùn:
"miè",
means to press,
to rub.
It seems to refer to massaging the canthus with both hands,
but this does not match the context of the preceding and following sentences.
"Zì miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)",
should mean the inability to glance sideways with the inner and outer corners of the eyes,
allowing one to close the eyes and nourish the spirit,
hence it is said to rest in old age.
Another note:
"miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)" is interchangeable with "miè",
"zì",
refers to the corner of the eye,
"zì miè (hand radical changed to woman radical)",
is like saying the eyes are sunken.
【Three】【Annotations】It is not without haste.
【Commentary】Jù means
swift and rapid.
For those whose minds and dispositions are anxious and hurried,
tranquility can be used to calm them.
【Four】【Annotation】If there is still toil,
then the idle remain aloof and unconcerned.
【Commentary】To calm restlessness through stillness,
to cure agitation with tranquility—
these are methods of counteractive treatment,
matters that belong to those of shallow learning,
who toil and tax their spirit and intellect.
How could they be the heart of those who embody the Way,
of leisurely and carefree individuals,
free from toil and ailment!
Their demeanor is pure and lofty,
thus they have never briefly passed by and inquired about such things.
【Explanation】"Non-indulgence" is pronounced as yì.
【五】【Note】The divine person is the sage,
the sage refers to the external aspect,
the divine refers to the internal aspect.
【Commentary】Hài means
to startle.
Shén is the term
for the unfathomable;
shèng is the name
for the manifestation of traces;
because they disseminate teachings to move people,
they are not excessively questioned.
【Explanation】"To startle" is pronounced with the character 戶 and 楷, giving the sound.
King explains:
It means to change what the common people see and hear.
Xú gives the sound as jiè,
meaning the ruler does not consult with the subjects.
【Six】【Commentary】To verify emptiness is to be virtuous,
to illuminate all is to be sagely,
moving from depth toward shallowness,
thus it is not questioned.
【Seven】【Memorials】How is it that the gentleman of character and integrity startles and moves the states of the feudal lords?
The virtuous man abandons possession,
Therefore, he does not inquire.
【Eight】【Note】Each pace has its own measure,
each height its own rank.
【Commentary】Those petty men who chase after worldly trends,
temporarily conforming to the times,
such as the followers of Tián Héng,
are not worthy of esteem;
hence, virtuous gentlemen disdain and disregard them.
【Nine】【Annotation】Filial piety driven by the desire for rewards
strays far from authenticity,
this is the fault of exalting the worthy.
【Commentary】[Yǎn mén],
refers to the eastern gate.
Some texts write it as "Yín",
which should be read according to the character used.
The filial piety from the eastern gate,
originated from genuine feelings,
yet it manifested in external expressions of grief and physical deterioration.
Only the ruler of Sòng praised his utmost filial devotion,
and thus conferred upon him a noble rank and appointed him as a minister.
The people of his hometown,
upon hearing that he achieved nobility through filial piety,
then forced themselves to weep and feign distress,
distorting their nature and fabricating emotions.
As a result, those who died
amounted to half of them.
【Transcription】"Yǎnmén" is named after a rebellion by a virtuous person.
It is the name of a city gate in Sòng.
【一０】【Commentary】Yáo recognized Xiǔ's worthiness,
and offered him the throne through abdication.
Xiǔ washed his ears and declined,
fleeing to evade to Jīshān.
When Tāng approached Wù Guāng,
Wù Guāng refused to accept,
scolding and fuming with anger,
he distanced himself to the deep forests.
These all followed their innate nature,
detesting the stench of glory and emolument,
unrelated to feigning hypocrisy in pursuit of fame.
【一一】【Note】Their unrest and agitation harm their nature,
thus leading to this point.
【Commentary】His surname was Shēntú,
and his given name was Dí;
another had the surname Jì,
with the given name Tuó;
both were recluses.
Hearing that Tāng had yielded the throne to Wùguāng,
they feared it might extend to themselves,
so they squatted by the water's edge with their disciples.
The feudal lords, upon learning of this,
esteemed their integrity and simplicity,
and occasionally went to console them,
worried they might drown.
When Dí heard of this matter,
he admired their lofty reputation,
and thereupon threw himself into the Long River,
drowning to death.
The waves tossed him, causing him to lose his nature,
and so he ended up in this state.
【Explanatory Text】"Jì Tā": pronounced as tuó hé.
"Ér cún": pronounced as cún.
The Zìlín states:
It is the ancient character for squatting.
Xú gives the pronunciation as qī xún,
also pronounced as zūn.
"Kuǎn shuǐ": pronounced as kuǎn,
also pronounced as kē.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is the name of a river.
"Diào zhī": Sīmǎ explains,
fearing he might drown himself,
hence they condoled with him.
"Bó": Xú gives the pronunciation as fāng fù,
and pǒu.
The Zìlín states:
It means to fall stiffly.
Lǐ explains:
It means to stumble.
Guō gives the pronunciation as bó bēi.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
Between the two pronunciations,
there should be the character "yòu" (also).
Similar instances below are not all indicated.
【一二】【疏】Quán,
is a fish trap,
made of bamboo,
hence the character includes bamboo.
There are also those associated with grass,
(meaning) quán (筌) [荃],
a fragrant herb,
which can be used as bait for fish,
placing the fragrance among firewood, trees, and reeds to catch fish.
Tí,
is a rabbit snare,
also a rabbit trap (弶),
used to bind a rabbit's foot,
hence it is called tí.
These two things,
are analogies.
【Interpretation】"Quán" is read as qī quán fǎn,
Cuī pronounces it as sūn,
it is a fragrant herb,
which can be used to bait fish.
Some say;
it involves piling firewood in the water,
so that fish gather around and feed on it.
Another explanation:
it is a fish trap.
◎ Lú Wénchāo comments:
According to what some say,
this is qián.
See the "Odes of Zhōu" in the Shījīng.
"Tí" is read as dà xī fǎn,
it refers to a rabbit snare.
Also said:
it is a rabbit trap,
which ties its feet,
hence called tí.
The character ● is pronounced gǔ xiàn fǎn.
Jiàng,
is pronounced jù liàng fǎn.
【一三】【疏】This is a combined analogy.
The meaning,
is the wondrous principle.
For catching fish and hares originally relies on traps and snares,
yet traps and snares are truly different from fish and hares;
similarly, the profound principle depends on speech and explanation,
but speech and explanation are truly not the profound principle itself.
Once fish and hares are obtained, the traps and snares are forgotten;
once the profound principle is understood, words and names cease.
【一四】【Note】As for the two sages having no intent,
they thus had nothing to say at all.
【Commentary】Those who grasp the principle by forgetting the words,
and perceive the Way with a single glance,
are truly rare individuals,
hence such difficulties arise.
【Explanation】"Dé Fū" is pronounced as "yīn fú".
【Collation】(1) The Que Wu cites the Zhang Jūnfáng edition, where "xiū" is written as "mù,"
the same as in the Gāoshān Temple edition.
(2) The Zhào Jiànyì edition uses "quán,"
and the same applies below.
(3) Liú Wéndiǎn's Corrections and Supplements states:
It should be written as ●.
(4) The character "jiàng" has been amended according to the Shi Wen.
【One】【Explanatory Text】The chapter is titled based on its meaning.
Fables make up nine-tenths of it,
weighty words seven-tenths,
with goblet words poured out daily,
harmonized by the Heavenly Equality.
【一】【Note】Entrust it to others,
then nine out of ten words will be trusted.
【Commentary】Allegory means
to entrust.
People in the world are foolish and deluded,
engaging in baseless suspicions and jealousies.
When they hear a doctrine from someone they know,
they become doubtful and wary.
But if it is entrusted to another person to convey,
then out of ten statements, they will believe nine.
Therefore, figures like Hóng Méng, Yún Jiàng, Jiān Wú, and Lián Shū
are all merely allegorical devices.
【Explanation】"Fables Constitute Nine-Tenths": Fables are a means of
entrusting one's words.
Because people do not believe oneself,
one therefore entrusts them to others,
so that nine out of ten statements gain credibility.
【二】【Note】What the world values highly,
then ten words will be trusted in seven.
【Commentary】Repeated words,
refer to the respect held for elders within the village community.
The words of the elderly,
are still about seventy percent trustworthy.
【Explanation】"Zhòng Yán" refers to the words of those esteemed by others.
◎Jiā Shìfù commented:
The character "重",
should be pronounced as "zhòng" (直容切).
According to the "Guǎngyùn":
means repetition.
This refers to Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
which can be annotated endlessly without exhaustion,
and quoted continuously without depletion.
Guǒ Xiàng interpreted it as what the world values,
pronouncing it as "zhòng" (柱用切),
which is incorrect.
【Three】【Comment】The wine vessel,
when full, tilts;
when empty, leans back;
it does not maintain a fixed posture.
Applied to speech,
it adapts to things and follows changes,
solely conforming to their nature,
hence it is called "daily emergence."
Daily emergence
means daily renewal;
daily renewal then exhausts its natural allotment,
and when the natural allotment is exhausted, there is harmony.
【Commentary】A zhī,
is a wine vessel.
The sun rising,
signifies daily renewal.
Tiānní,
refers to the natural distinctions.
Hé,
means to harmonize or unite.
Now, when the zhī is full, it tilts,
when the zhī is empty, it leans back,
its fullness or emptiness depends on what is put in it,
its tilting or leaning follows the person handling it.
Words without preconceived intent,
are what is called zhīyán,
thus, by not speaking,
or speaking without attachment to tilting or leaning,
one aligns with the natural distinctions.
Another explanation:
Zhī,
means to branch or diverge.
To make one's words fragmented,
so they lack precise direction,
hence they are referred to as zhīyán.
【Interpretive Text】The term "Zhī Yán" is also written as 卮,
pronounced as "zhī".
The character annotation states:
"zhī",
is a round wine vessel.
Lǐ gives the pronunciation as "qǐ yí fǎn".
Wáng explains:
The vessel zhī,
tips when full,
tilts up when empty,
changes according to what it holds,
not one that stubbornly adheres to the old;
applied to speech,
it follows others and adapts to changes,
with no constant stance of its own.
Sīmǎ comments:
It refers to fragmented, incoherent speech without beginning or end.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
"zhī",
was formerly written as 卮.
According to Shuōwén, it is written as ●,
with the lower part from ●,
now often simplified to 卮.
If written as 卮,
then there would be no need to say "also written as".
"Tiān Ní" is pronounced as "yí",
Xú gives the pronunciation as "yì".
Nine out of ten fables
borrow external perspectives to convey their messages.
A biological father does not act as matchmaker for his own son.
When a father praises his child,
it carries less weight than when others do so;
this is not my fault,
but human nature's flaw.
We echo what aligns with our views,
and oppose what diverges from them;
approving what matches our own stance,
condemning what differs from it.
【一】【注】Words spoken from oneself,
are often not accepted by the common folk,
hence they borrow external means.
Figures like Jiānwú and Liánshū,
are all among those borrowed (1).
【Commentary】Jié means
to borrow,
a means to entrust it to others.
When nine out of ten statements are credible,
it is because they are attributed to the discourse of outsiders.
【Explanation】"Jiè" Guǒ notes:
Jiè,
means to borrow.
Lǐ notes:
means to rely on.
【二】【注】Though a father's admonitions to his son
are often met with disbelief,
there are times when they are credible,
yet they are frequently doubted due to habitual suspicions;
hence, external discussions are used to support them.
【Commentary】Méi,
means to arrange a match.
When a father praises his own son,
people often do not believe it;
but when others commend him,
many more will trust it.
【Transcription】"Praise it" is pronounced as yú.
The annotation is the same.
【Three】【Comment】Even if one is trustworthy oneself,
those who habitually harbor doubts still do not accept it;
yet when entrusted to another person, they believe it.
Such is the burden of human perception.
【Commentary】I,
being the father,
am not speaking of my son untruthfully;
rather, it is the listeners who groundlessly raise doubts,
leading to the fault of disbelief.
【Four】【Annotations】They refute each other.
【Commentary】Common people are confused and mistaken,
arbitrarily making judgments of right and wrong.
If others share their views, they respond and affirm them as correct;
if others differ from them, they oppose and deem them wrong.
【Five】【Annotation】Three differences coexist in the same place,
while two of them dispute over what they claim,
this must mean that those who do not dispute are all different as well,
yet one solely believes in what they deem right,
how can it be without relying on external factors!
【Commentary】When one is deluded and clings to sameness and difference,
false views of right and wrong arise.
Once sameness and difference are empty,
right and wrong vanish.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character 者 below 借.
Repeating words makes up seventy percent of speech,
which serves to put an end to arguments,
and this is characteristic of the aged and venerable.
If one is older in years,
but lacks the guiding principles and fundamentals to match that seniority,
then he cannot be considered a true elder.
If a person has nothing to surpass others,
they lack the way of humanity;
if a person lacks the way of humanity,
they are called an obsolete person.
【一】【注】Because of his advanced age,
it was customary for everyone to hold him in high esteem;
even if his words did not rely on external authorities,
people would still trust about seventy percent of what he said.
【Commentary】Qí'ài is
a term for those who are elderly and long-lived.
Having spoken for themselves,
without relying on external validation,
as respected elders,
they are therefore esteemed and trusted,
yet common people
hold such delusions and misconceptions.
【Explanation】"耆艾" is pronounced with the initial "wǔ" and the final "gài" in reverse.
【二】【注】The year is prior to things,
while the rest from root to branch,
cannot be used to await others,
thus it is not that by which one takes precedence.
To expect,
is to await.
【Subcommentary】Expectation means
to await.
Vertical and horizontal form the warp,
while lateral connections are called the weft.
This means that this person is simply placed first due to old age,
yet lacks the wisdom of fundamentals and details,
so they are treated with the respect due to an elder,
not because their virtue entitles them to precedence.
◎ Jiāshìfù said:
What has been spoken before,
is spoken again after having been mentioned earlier.
The "Ěryǎ·Shìgǔ" states;
qí and ài,
mean elder.
Ài,
signifies experience.
Guō Pú's annotation:
Elders have undergone many experiences.
The "Shìmíng" says;
at sixty, one is called qí;
qí,
means to point,
indicating matters and directing others.
This is the principle of qí and ài taking precedence over others.
The warp and weft, fundamentals and details,
are what give one precedence,
and people likewise expect this of them.
Repeating words tirelessly,
reminding and cautioning,
the way of humanity resides in this.
【Three】【Comment】It's merely about people who are accustomed to the old ways,
yet the common folk readily believe in them,
which is why society tends to stick to the familiar and follow conventions.
【Commentary】They lack propriety and righteousness to guide others,
and are devoid of the principles of human relationships.
They are merely people of long-standing vulgarity,
hence they are regarded with disdain.
The common world lacks discernment,
to such an extent as this.
【Collation】（一）The characters for this year in the Kōzan-ji version are written as "lái".
Goblet words emerge daily,
harmonized with the heavenly grindstone,
thereby extending boundlessly,
thus exhausting the years.
Without speech, there is uniformity;
uniformity and speech are not uniform,
speech and uniformity are not uniform either,
hence it is said: there is no speech.
Speaking without speech,
one may speak a lifetime,
yet never have spoken;
one may remain silent a lifetime,
yet never have been silent.
Some things are acceptable for their own reasons,
some unacceptable for their own reasons;
some are so for their own reasons,
some not so for their own reasons.
Why are they so?
They are so because they are so.
Why are they not so?
They are not so because they are not so.
Why are they acceptable?
They are acceptable because they are acceptable.
Why are they unacceptable?
They are unacceptable because they are unacceptable.
All things inherently have their "so",
all things inherently have their "acceptable",
there is nothing that is not so,
nothing that is not acceptable.
If not for goblet words emerging daily,
harmonized with the heavenly grindstone,
who could attain their endurance?
All things are seeds,
passing on through different forms,
beginning and ending like a circle,
none can grasp their order,
this is called the heavenly balance.
The heavenly balance is the heavenly grindstone.
【一】【注】For nature has its distinctions, yet right and wrong have no fixed master;
having no fixed master, they spread boundlessly—
who can determine them!
Therefore, be open-minded and free from concerns,
follow along and let things be,
so that each may live out their natural lifespan.
【Commentary】Meandering and extending,
it is without deliberate intent.
Following the daily renewal of changes and transformations,
it aligns with the natural boundaries and distinctions,
thus it can follow along with all things,
engaging with objects without deliberate intent;
this is how it exhausts the natural lifespan of creation,
reaching the distant longevity of existence.
【Transcription】"Mànyǎn" is read as yǐ zhàn fǎn.
【二】【疏】The principle resides in wordlessness,
for speech disrupts harmony.
Thus, by simply refraining from speech, all things naturally achieve equality.
◎Jiàshìfù remarked:
Without words, there is uniformity,
meaning to employ goblet words,
letting them flow freely to exhaust the years,
akin to saying nothing.
The words of goblet speech
follow speech when there is speech,
and follow silence when there is none;
having words yet fundamentally being wordless,
being wordless yet fundamentally not without words—
this is what is called the Heavenly Equality.
【Three】【Disparities】are aligned,
yet not spoken.
Not speaking and speaking,
since they are not the same,
therefore they are not aligned.
【Four】【Annotation】Entrust it to things and then utilize their words,
then the rights and wrongs of this and that,
naturally become equalized.
If one cannot rely on that to establish words and thereby equalize them,
then I and the myriad things will again be unequal.
【Transcription】"Fu bu" is pronounced as fú yòu fǎn.
The same applies below.
【五】【Note】What they say,
therefore, even though there are words, I ultimately do not speak.
【Commentary】Using words to dispel words,
words will be endless;
even if a hundred negations are added,
they still fail to reach the subtlety.
Only by contemplating the sage with unwavering focus,
whose wisdom merges movement and stillness,
whether in action or repose, silence or speech,
their essence remains unified.
Thus, they can speak without speaking,
and speak as if not speaking.
How can there be a distinction between speaking and not speaking,
or a difference between harmony and discord?
Hence it is said: words are without words.
【Six】【Annotation】Though spoken by my mouth,
they are all his words.
【Seven】【Annotation】It originates from my mouth.
【Commentary】This further explains the meaning of the previous statement about non-speech.
【Eight】【Explanations】Each holds to their own views,
hence there is affirmation and denial.
Since both self and others are empty,
affirmation and denial thus vanish.
【Nine】【Annotation】Self.
It is due to.
Due to the bias between self and others,
thus there is what is acceptable and what is not.
【Commentary】"Wūhū" means
"at what" or "where."
When both self and others are empty,
and things and I are illusory,
at what place can there be right or wrong?
At what place can there be affirmation or denial?
By reasoning this through to the end,
such distinctions naturally cease.
This further explains the earlier meaning of inherent affirmation and possibility.
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
The same applies below.
【一０】【Note】Each is so of itself,
each is acceptable.
【One One】【Comment】Speaking in general terms,
there is nothing that must be done or must not be done,
and it is through this that one arrives.
【Commentary】Those who are among the vulgar and hold inverted views
insist on what is naturally so where there is no basis for it,
and cling to what is acceptable where nothing can be accepted.
【一二】【Note】Only one who adapts speech according to circumstances and follows the natural distinctions of things,
can avoid premature demise.
【Commentary】Unless one follows the ever-renewing changes of the day,
and comprehends the principles of nature,
who can attest to the way of longevity and enduring vision?
This speaks of the utmost attainment of those who have realized it.
【13】【Comment】Although transformations succeed one another,
their fundamental energy remains one.
【Commentary】Alternation,
means replacement.
All things in their multitude,
endowed by the Creator,
receive the same vital energy yet differ in form and substance,
continuously flowing and changing, replacing one another in succession.
【Transcription】"皆種" is read as zhǒng with the pronunciation given by Zhāng Yǒng.
【一四】【Note】What is considered a beginning today,
was already an end again by yesterday.
【Commentary】The exchange of things,
is likened to a cycle,
where death gives way to life,
ending only to begin again.
This describes the pattern of dynastic succession.
【一五】【Note】The principle is naturally so,
thus it cannot be grasped.
【Commentary】Lún,
means principle.
Seeking the way of change,
ultimately finds no principle that can be attained.
【16】【Comment】Is uniformity and equality merely arbitrary?
All are natural distinctions.
【Commentary】Jūn means
qí (equal).
This summarizes the meaning of the previous chapter,
referring to the Way of natural equality,
which is this principle of equal distribution,
also called the natural allotment.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
It speaks of mutual generation as all things succeeding one another.
All things have seeds,
growing and developing endlessly,
yet one cannot hold onto a single form as they succeed one another.
It means that from seeds, they extend and evolve infinitely,
and one cannot fix a single word as the beginning.
Beginning and end have no traceable boundaries,
this is what is called the Heavenly Equality.
【Collation】（一）The Gāoshānsì edition has the character 'yán' following 'yuē'.
（二）The character 'ér' is supplemented based on the preceding sentence.
Zhuāngzǐ said to Huìzǐ:
"Confucius, having lived sixty years, transformed sixty times.
What he initially affirmed,
he ultimately denied.
We cannot know whether what he now calls right might not have been considered wrong when he was fifty-nine."
【一】【Note】It evolves with the times (1).
【Commentary】The cycles of operation never cease,
as the new continuously flows and fades,
thus, at the age of sixty, one changes along with the passing years.
However, when Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ met,
they delighted in discussing profound principles,
hence they distantly invoked Confucius to illustrate the methods of transformation.
【二】【注】Times change, and worldly sentiments change with them.
Those who ride on the course of things to let their minds wander freely—
how could they differ from the common customs?
【Three】【Comment】Change never ceases,
thus constancy is unattainable.
【Commentary】Human lifespan is measured by years,
but since the years themselves are not fixed,
how can there be a definite measure?
Thus, what was considered right last year
is now considered wrong.
Therefore, we know that what is right this year
was actually wrong last year;
and what is wrong this year
may be considered right next year.
Hence, Róngchéng Shì said,
"Without days, there are no years."
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is also written as "huà".
Huìzǐ said:
"Confucius diligently pursued his aspirations and devoted himself to knowledge."
【一】【注】It is said that Confucius understood only after diligently setting his will and embracing it with heartfelt devotion,
and was not capable of letting it transform naturally.
This clarifies how far Hui Zi fell short of the sage's profound charm.
【Commentary】服 means
to use.
Huì Shī did not comprehend,
but surmised about Confucius,
saying that he exerted his will and diligently practiced,
applying his mind to learn the Way,
thus attaining such wisdom,
rather than being one who follows natural transformation.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Confucius has repented of it,
yet he never spoke of it.
Confucius said:
'One receives talents from the Great Root,
and returns to the numinous to be born.
'When singing, it matches the pitch pipes;
when speaking, it matches the laws.
When profit and righteousness are laid out before one,
likes and dislikes, rights and wrongs, merely compel people's mouths.
To make people be convinced in their hearts,
and dare not obstinately stand against it,
this establishes the stability of the world.
Enough, enough!
How could I ever reach that!"
【One】【Annotation】The transformations occur spontaneously,
not wrought by knowledge or effort,
thus one follows the times and entrusts to things without crafting words.
【Commentary】Xiè,
means to replace.
Ér,
means you.
Wèi,
means without.
This says that Nǐfǔ's diligent and devoted heart has long been replaced,
you should restore your spirit,
and no longer speak recklessly.
【二】【注】If one employs their talents and wisdom without returning to their fundamental spirit,
then life is lost.
【Commentary】Human beings receive their intelligence and abilities from the profound origin of the Great Dao,
and return to their spiritual nature to live out their lives.
How could one toil one's will and exhaust one's mind,
acting contrary to the Creator!
This is Zhuāngzǐ recounting Kǒng Qiū's words to criticize Huì Shī.
【Explanation】"才知" is pronounced with the tone of "zhì".
【Three】【Comment】The chirping of birds,
arises from the natural order;
the words spoken,
emerge from the principles of law;
and these laws and principles,
are shaped by the collective will,
which the sages then apply and utilize,
thus ensuring they are always appropriate,
yet they never claim to have originated them,
nor to have created them themselves.
【Commentary】Míng means
sound.
Dāng means
center.
Master Nǐfǔ, being a sage,
harmonized his virtue with yīn and yáng,
thus his graceful bearing resonated with bell tones and pitch pipes,
and his teachings served as a model for examination and emulation!
means to use.
I have no words of my own,
what I speak,
merely employs the mouths of others,
the presentation of likes and dislikes, right and wrong, benefit and righteousness,
has never originated from my own mouth.
【Commentary】Benevolence, righteousness, advantage, and harm,
likes, dislikes, rights, and wrongs,
provoke those prior opportunities,
responding timely to present them in discourse.
Although the words again come from one's mouth and follow the predecessors,
it is precisely using the mouths of the multitude.
【Explanation】"Hào" is pronounced with the fanqie "hū bào fǎn."
The same applies to the annotations.
"Wù" is pronounced with the fanqie "wū lù fǎn."
The same applies to the annotations.
【Five】【Annotation】The mouth is the means to express the heart;
since the mouths of the multitude are employed,
then the hearts of the multitude are utilized.
If I align with the collective will,
then the collective will trusts me.
Who would dare to oppose and stand against it?
I follow the natural stabilization of the world to establish order,
so what more is there to do?
【Commentary】Follow what is suitable for the multitude,
employ their minds and wisdom,
since teaching adapts to things,
things comply with it,
like grass bending with the wind,
not daring to stand against it,
because of their inherent tranquility,
settle them in accordance with their nature,
thus establishing the stability of the world.
【Transcription】"Wù" is pronounced as wù,
also read as wǔ gè fǎn,
meaning to oppose.
【Six】【Comment】By thus riding upon it,
there is nothing that is not reached.
【Commentary】"Cease,"
means to stop.
"He,"
refers to Confucius.
Repeatedly urging Master Huì,
to stop and not speak,
our abilities are mediocre and shallow,
unable to reach and match his.
This is Zhuāngzǐ's words of admiration and praise for Xuānní.
Zēngzǐ held office twice and his feelings changed twice.
He said:
"When I held office while my parents were alive,
even with a salary of three fu, my heart was joyful;
later when I held office,
even with three thousand zhōng but it could not reach them (my deceased parents),
my heart was sorrowful."
【One】【Explanation】His surname was Zēng,
his given name was Shēn,
a disciple of Confucius.
The principle of serving in office twice,
is detailed in the following text.
【二】【注】Jì,
means "and" or "to reach."
【Commentary】Six dou and four sheng is called a fǔ,
six hú and four dǒu is called a zhōng.
Jì,
means "and" or "to reach."
Zēng Shēn was extremely filial,
seeking an official salary to support his parents.
Therefore, when he previously held office while his parents were alive,
though his salary was meager, he was joyful;
later, when he served after his parents had passed away,
though his salary was ample, he grieved;
this is what is referred to as the transformation twice,
where sorrow and joy shifted his heart,
all because he could no longer care for his parents.
【Explanation Text】"Three Fǔ": The Xiǎo Ěr Yǎ states:
Six dǒu and four shēng are called a fǔ.
"Heart's Joy": pronounced as luò.
The same applies to the annotations below.
"Not Reaching": pronounced as qì qì fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the character "ér".
A disciple asked Zhòngní:
"Can one like Shēn
be said to have no crimes for which to be condemned?"
【One】【Annotation】Attachment,
means connection.
It refers to participating in official service for the sake of one's parents,
without the guilt of being tied to a salary.
【Commentary】"Xiàn" means
"to be bound by."
Among the disciples,
there is no specific name recorded,
likely referring to those within the Four Disciplines and Ten Philosophers.
Zēng Shēn was benevolent and filial,
seeking an official salary for his parents,
and although he experienced both sorrow and joy,
he should not have been bound by guilt.
The disciples doubted this,
so they consulted Zhòngní about it.
【Explanation】"Cān" is read as suǒ jīn fǎn.
"Wú suǒ xuán" is pronounced as xuán.
The same applies below.
"Qí zuì hū" xuán,
means to tie or bind.
The heart is transformed again by the official salary,
what remains is closeness.
Although tied to the salary, one is not bound by guilt.
Yǐwéi, pronounced as Yúwèi fǎn.
He said:
"Since it is already something to be concerned about.
For those who have nothing to concern themselves with,
can there be grief?
They regard three bushels or three thousand bushels of grain,
as merely watching sparrows and mosquitoes pass before their eyes."
【一】【注】It is tied to the official salary for sustenance.
【Transcription】"To nourish" is read as yǎng, with the pronunciation yáng shàng fǎn.
The same applies below.
【Two】【Annotation】In nurturing parents to their comfort,
one does not inquire about the means.
If one can remain unattached,
then distinctions of nobility or baseness do not trouble the heart,
leading to tranquility, harmony, and joy,
thus fully embodying the proper way of caring with a pleasant countenance.
【Commentary】A filial son serves his parents,
focusing on appropriateness,
regardless of the amount of salary,
but rather on providing for them with a cheerful demeanor.
Thus, there are those who, despite menial labor, are praised as filial sons,
while others who have held multiple official posts may still be deemed unfilial.
Since Shēn harbors grief and joy in his heart,
how can he avoid the fault of being attached to his salary?
Only those who are unattached
can therefore remain free from sorrow and joy.
【Three】【Comment】That,
means being unattached.
Those who are unattached
regard glory and emolument as if they were gnats, flies, birds, or sparrows passing before their eyes,
how could there be sorrow or joy in such matters!
【Commentary】"Bi" (that),
refers to a person who is unattached.
The large bird and sparrow,
serve as a metaphor for a thousand zhōng (a large salary),
while the small mosquitoes and gnats,
represent three fǔ (a meager income).
A person who has attained the Way,
has no mind attached to emoluments;
whether it be a thousand zhōng or three fǔ,
they perceive no difference in amount.
It is like birds, sparrows, mosquitoes, and gnats flying past in front of them—
they simply let them pass by,
how could they be attached to them!
【Textual Explanation】"Like the stork" was also written as "observe",
same.
Pronounced as "guàn".
◎ Lú Wénchāo said:
Nowadays, it is written as "observe".
"Mosquito" is pronounced as "wén".
"Horsefly" is pronounced as "méng gēng".
Sīmǎ commented:
Observing sparrows flying swiftly,
passing by mosquitoes,
suddenly unaware.
Wáng commented:
The stork and mosquito illustrate a vast difference in size,
metaphorically comparing three fu and three thousand zhōng in quantity.
The Yuánjiā version reads "like the stork and mosquito",
without the character for horsefly.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
The character "sparrow" is redundant.
The textual explanation states.
The Yuánjiā version reads "like the stork and mosquito",
without the character for horsefly.
Thus, the version Lù referred to did not yet have the redundant "sparrow" character,
hence the Yuánjiā version reads "stork and mosquito".
Lù only mentioned the absence of the horsefly character,
not the absence of the sparrow character.
However, the stork and the mosquito/horsefly,
one being a bird and the other an insect,
make for an incongruous metaphor.
Wáng said,
referring to the vast difference in size,
metaphorically comparing three fu and three thousand zhōng in quantity.
This is not the case.
For the sage's view of things,
it is but a fleeting glance,
how could they bother with the quantity of three fu or three thousand zhōng,
and insist on distinguishing between a stork and a mosquito!
Now, examining the textual explanation,
"stork" was originally written as "observe".
It is suspected that the ancient version was like this.
The text likely said,
"He views three fu and three thousand zhōng,
as if observing mosquitoes and horseflies passing before him."
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Chù Zhēn Piān", praise and blame towards oneself,
are like a passing mosquito or horsefly.
The meaning is the same as here.
Because "observe" was mistakenly written as "stork",
then the three characters stork, mosquito, and horsefly became incongruous,
leading some to delete the horsefly character,
making the mosquito and stork correspond,
as in the Yuánjiā version;
others added a sparrow character,
making the stork-sparrow and mosquito-horsefly correspond,
as in the current version.
Both are not the original form of Zhuāngzǐ.
【Collation】（一）The Zhào Jiànyì version has "guàn" instead of "guān".
The Quē Wù concurs,
citing Zhāng Jūnfáng's version which states:
"Guàn què" is written as "guān niǎo què".
Yánchéng Zǐyóu said to Dōngguō Zǐqí:
"Since I heard your words,
in one year I became rustic【一】,
in two years I became compliant【二】,
in three years I became penetrating【三】,
in four years I became one with things【四】,
in five years things came to me【五】,
in six years the ghost entered【六】,
in seven years nature was perfected【七】,
in eight years I knew not death,
knew not life,
【八】in nine years I reached the great mystery【九】."
【一】【注】External rights.
【Commentary】He resided in the eastern part of the outer city,
hence the name Dōngguō,
much like Nánguō Zǐqí from the chapter "Discourse on the Equality of Things."
Zǐyóu,
was a disciple of Zǐqí.
Yě,
signifies simplicity and naturalness.
After hearing the Way for a year,
his mind in learning was not yet mature,
but he could somewhat embrace simplicity,
moving away from superficiality.
【Explanation】"Zǐ Qí" is pronounced as "qí".
【二】【Note】Not acting on one's own authority.
【Explanation】To conform to the customs.
【Three】【Annotation】Connecting the other and the self.
【Commentary】Not clinging to the external realm.
【Four】【Annotation】Harmonizing with all things.
【Commentary】It is in harmony with all things.
【五】【Note】Self-attainment.
【Commentary】It is for the multitude to return to.
【Six】【Annotation】To transcend the physical form and body.
【Commentary】The spirit comprehends and governs all things.
【Seven】【Annotation】There is nothing more to be done.
【Commentary】It harmonizes and naturally forms.
【Transcription】"Suǒ fù" fú yòu fǎn.
【八】【Note】All encounters are fitting and bring peace.
【Commentary】Wisdom merges with the creator,
spirit aligns with the natural,
thus one becomes unaware of the differences between life, death, gathering, and dispersion.
【Nine】【Annotation】Wonderful,
means good.
Good and evil are the same.
Therefore, there is no place not in darkness.
This saying means that having long heard of the Dào,
one knows the naturalness of the heavenly sounds,
and will suddenly forget oneself,
then daily shed defilements and burdens until they are completely gone.
【Commentary】"Subtle" means
"exquisitely refined."
Having long heard of the Way,
the mind of learning gradually becomes evident,
thus enabling one to transcend the four propositions,
cut off the hundred negations,
reach the ultimate of profound mystery in meaning,
exhaust the multitude of subtleties in principle,
with knowledge and illumination vast and extensive,
hence it is called "great."
【Interpretation】"Tiānlài" is read with the sound lì dài fǎn.
Life has its purposeful actions,
and death has its determinations.
I advise the lord,
regarding his certain death,
that there are reasons for it;
whereas being born into the world of the living,
has no apparent cause.
But is it truly so?
Where does one find suitability?
Where does one find unsuitability?
Heaven has its calendrical calculations,
Earth has its human occupations,
how should I seek to understand them?
No one knows their final end,
how then can it be said there is no fate?
No one knows their beginning,
how then can it be said there is fate?
If there are correspondences in response,
how can it be said there are no ghosts?
If there are no correspondences in response,
how can it be said there are ghosts?
【一】【注】To act with purpose from birth is to lose one's life.
【Commentary】Being in the state of human existence,
one sinks into the realm of action,
only to ultimately face death and extinction.
【Text】"Ze sang" is pronounced with the tone "xi làng" in reverse.
【二】【注】Self,
refers to cause.
Because there is action,
therefore death occurs;
because of selfishness in life,
hence there is action.
The reason for advocating selflessness now,
is due to the fact that death stems from selfishness.
【Commentary】Gōng means
impartiality.
Zì means
from or due to.
The reason why people, though born, move toward the land of death,
is because they selfishly cherish their lives,
failing to be impartial and just.
Hence, this is to advise and guide them.
【Three】【Comment】The yang of life,
thus, with its cessation of traces and non-action, suddenly exists alone,
not arising from any cause.
【Commentary】Stirred by the yang energy, thus comes this life;
since it arises from no particular origin,
it is therefore not something to be possessed privately.
【Four】【Shū】Fruit,
means determination.
The yang energy generates things,
it is determined to be so.
【Five】【Comment】Thus truly so,
therefore, without going or not going, all eventually go,
and by all going, they arrive.
【Commentary】When qi gathers, there is life,
yet life is not worthy of joy;
when qi scatters, there is death,
yet death is not worthy of sorrow.
Since life and death are equalized,
sorrow and joy thus vanish.
Therefore, where is there a place that can be suitable,
and where is there a place that cannot be suitable?
Everywhere is suitable.
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
The same applies below.
【Six】【Annotations】All are already self-sufficient.
【Commentary】The degrees and numbers of stars and calendars,
the mysterious phenomena adorn the heavens;
the nine regions and four extremities,
are where people and things rely;
within the creation of nature,
all are fully present—
where then should I seek beyond this?
【Interpretation】"Heaven has its calendar" in one edition is written as Heaven has its calendar and cycles.
【Seven】【Annotation】Principle necessarily concludes on its own,
not through knowledge,
if not fate, then what?
【Commentary】Heaven and earth, day and night,
the life and death of people and things,
if one seeks their origins and causes,
none can know their ultimate beginnings or ends.
When the time comes and fortune departs,
if not fate, then what is it!
Those who claim there is no fate
are in fact speaking of fate's existence.
【八】【注】Not knowing why it is so, yet it is so,
is called mìng (destiny/fate),
as if it had intention,
therefore, the name mìng is again employed to clarify that it is spontaneous,
and only then is the principle of mìng fully understood.
【Commentary】Death is but a departure and life a return.
Just as spring and autumn, winter and summer,
have neither true beginning nor end,
how could there be such a thing as fate?
To speak of fate's existence
is to declare its non-existence.
This again refutes the notion of fate.
【Nine】【Annotation】Principle necessarily has its response,
as if divine spirits bring it about.
【Commentary】Ghost,
is the consciousness of spirits.
The ears and eyes respond to sounds and sights,
the mind and intellect respond to objects and environments,
the principle is similar to shadows and echoes,
how could there be no spirituality?
Those who claim there are no ghosts,
are actually saying that they exist.
【一０】【Note】Principles naturally correspond with each other;
this correspondence does not arise from causes,
thus even when corresponding, there is no animating spirit.
【Commentary】When a person is asleep,
they are unaware of external things;
although they have eyes and ears,
they do not respond to sights and sounds.
If they possessed consciousness,
how could they not respond?
As for the claim that there are ghosts,
it is to say that there are none.
This again dismisses their existence.
【Collation】（一）The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's version, which has the character '私' below it.
Many penumbral spirits asked the shadow,
"Why is it that you were bowing before but are now looking up,
had your hair tied before but now wear it loose,
were sitting before but now stand,
were walking before but now halt,
what is the reason?"
【一】【疏】Wǎngliǎng,
is the faint shadow outside the shadow.
This is a fable.
Ruò,
means you.
Fǔ,
means to lower the head.
Cuō,
means to tie the hair.
Your sitting, rising, walking, and resting,
only follow the form,
by this measure,
it must exist because of the form.
Speaking without dependence,
the reasoning behind it is not detailed.
Setting up this question and answer,
is to illuminate the concept of spontaneous transformation.
【Explanatory Text】"Jǐng" is pronounced as yǐng,
and also read according to its original character.
Some versions alternatively write it as yǐng.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The character yǐng was created by Táo Hóngjǐng,
and is not an ancient character.
"Guā" is pronounced as gǔ huó fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It refers to tying up the hair.
"Pī fà" is pronounced as pí jì fǎn.
【Collation】(1) In the Zhào Jiànyì edition, "jǐng" is written as "yǐng",
same below.
(2) The character "cuō" is added based on Chéng Xuánshū and the erroneous citation from Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition.
Jǐng said:
"It's all random searching!
Why bother asking further?
I possess it but do not know the reason why.
I am
like the cicada's cast-off shell,
the snake's sloughed skin,
resembling the original but not truly being it.
With fire and sunlight,
I gather;
in shade and night,
I fade away.
Are those what I depend on?
How much more so for that which has nothing to depend on!
When they come, I come with them;
when they go, I go with them;
when they move vigorously, I move vigorously with them.
Since it's just vigorous movement, what more is there to ask about?"
【One】【Annotation】The movement is spontaneous,
with no need for any inquiry.
【Commentary】Sǒusǒu,
describes the appearance of moving without intention.
Xī,
means "why."
Jǐng replied, saying:
I move without intention,
serene and self-content,
having nothing to wait for,
transforming independently to come into being.
You know nothing of this,
why trouble yourself to ask?
【Transcription】"Sōusōu" is also written as "sǒu",
same.
Pronounced as sùkǒu fǎn,
also sùdāo fǎn,
also pronounced as xiāo.
Xiàng comments:
A moving appearance.
【二】【注】Since then,
it is thus unknown why.
【Commentary】Yǔ,
means "I".
All my actions and inactions,
follow the course of creation,
are all without knowing the reason why,
and entirely unable to discern their causes,
how could there be any deliberate intent!
【Three】【Annotation】A shadow resembles a form but is not the form itself.
【Commentary】The "cicada shell"
refers to the exoskeleton of the cicada.
The "snake slough"
is its shed skin.
Now, when a grub transforms into a cicada,
or a snake sheds its skin from within,
both do so without conscious awareness.
As the grub vanishes beforehand,
the cicada naturally emerges afterward—
it is not that the cicada exists because of the grub,
nor does the cicada rely on the grub to come into being.
The principle of the snake's skin
is likewise so.
From this, we understand that all phenomena in existence
have no interdependent causation,
each transforms independently,
and all are said to be spontaneous.
Hence, the shadow says:
"My dependence
is like the snake's slough or the cicada's shell—
it appears to rely on form but in truth does not depend on it."
【Interpretation】"蜩甲" is pronounced as tiáo.
Sīmǎ explains:
"蜩甲"
refers to the cicada shedding its skin.
"蛇蛻" is pronounced as shuì,
also read as tuò,
and also as shuì.
【Four】【Explanations】Tún,
means to gather.
Dài,
means to fade away.
When there is fire or sunlight,
shadows immediately gather;
when encountering night or overcast conditions,
shadows then fade away.
If it is because of the form that there is a shadow,
then it should not depend on fire or sunlight.
In darkness or night, there is form but no shadow,
from this we know that shadows certainly do not depend on form,
and the principle of independent transformation becomes evident.
【Translated Text】"Wú tún" is read as tú mén fǎn,
meaning to gather.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: In the annotations of Wén Xuǎn, Xiè Língyùn's poem "Roaming the South Pavilion" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
Tún,
means to gather.
When the sun is bright, shadows appear,
hence it is said "we gather";
in darkness, shadows are not visible,
hence it is said "we take turns."
Taking turns at night,
refers to allowing rest.
The explanatory text is missing.
【Five】【Explanations】That which I depend upon,
is the fire and the sun.
If it does not take form,
even the fire and the sun cannot produce a shadow,
therefore, the shadow does not depend on the fire and the sun either.
【Six】【Annotation】Extending this to its utmost,
then what is now called the three dependencies (all)
When one reaches the state of non-dependence,
the principle of self-transformation becomes evident.
【Commentary】Moreover, that which relies on something is form;
without the necessity of fire or sun,
form cannot produce shadow either,
for it does not depend on form.
The birth of form
does not require fire or sun;
the birth of shadow,
how could it depend on form then!
Thus, using fire and sun as analogies,
it becomes clear that shadow does not rely on form.
Even form and shadow do not depend on each other,
let alone other things!
From this, we know that all phenomena
arise independently through self-transformation.
◎Jiā Shìfù commented:
When fire or sun appears, shadows are born;
in the darkness of night, shadows lie hidden.
"Tún" (屯) refers to
the initial growth of plants and trees;
"dài" (代) means
change,
replacement,
and when there is something to replace, I naturally rest.
Shadows and forms depend on each other,
yet they also rely on fire or sun to move,
and on the darkness of night to rest.
That on which we depend
in turn depends on something else.
Because there is dependence,
one does not precede things,
responding immediately when relied upon,
thus also avoiding conflict with things.
Shadows follow forms,
each mirroring the emotions and postures of the person,
adapting emptily and flexibly.
This is the essential philosophy of Zhuāngzǐ for engaging with the world.
【Seven】【Annotation】It is merely the movement of vigorous yang,
following along as it comes and goes,
without intention,
and cannot be questioned.
【Commentary】That refers to
form.
Strong Yang,
is the appearance of movement.
The coming and going in motion,
form and shadow coexist in time,
since there is no dependency,
all rely on self-transformation.
The principle of self-transformation,
transcends words and descriptions,
yet through verbal questions and answers,
it is fully expressed.

Confucius said to Yán Huí:
"Huí,
come!
Your family is poor and you live in humble circumstances,
why not take up an official post?"
Yán Huí replied:
"I do not wish to take office.
I have fifty mǔ of farmland beyond the outer wall,
sufficient to provide congee;
ten mǔ of land within the outer wall,
sufficient for silk and hemp;
playing the qin is enough to amuse myself,
and what I have learned of the Master's Way is enough to bring me joy.
I do not wish to take office."
Confucius looked startled and changed countenance, saying:
"How excellent is your thought, Huí!
I have heard it said,
'Those who know contentment are not burdened by profit;
those who truly find self-contentment do not fear loss;
those who cultivate inner virtue feel no shame without official rank.'
I have long recited these words,
but only now in Huí do I witness them embodied,
and this is my gain."

Through Huí's reflection,
thus it is said that Qiū has understood it.

Confucius was stranded between Chén and Cài,
for seven days without cooked food,
having only coarse soup without grain,
his countenance greatly fatigued,
yet he played the lute and sang in his room.
Yán Huí was selecting vegetables,
while Zǐlù and Zǐgòng said to each other:
"Our master was twice driven from Lǔ,
his tracks erased in Wèi,
trees were felled over him in Sòng,
he was impoverished between Shāng and Zhōu,
besieged here between Chén and Cài.
Those who would kill our master go unpunished,
those who insult our master go unrestrained.
Yet he plays the lute and sings,
never ceasing the music -
can a gentleman's lack of shame be like this?"
【一】【疏】The events in Chén and Cài,
have already been explained in the outer chapters.
Having encountered famine and starvation,
with no cooked meals in camp,
only a soup of wild herbs,

the sage who comprehends the Way
does not regard such matters as significant.

Confucius said:
"What kind of talk is this!
A gentleman is considered accomplished when he comprehends the Way,
and is considered destitute when he fails in the Way.
Now I, Qiū, embrace the way of benevolence and righteousness yet encounter the calamities of a chaotic age—
how can this be considered destitution!
Therefore, through introspection I do not fail in the Way,
and facing difficulties I do not lose my virtue.
When the cold of heaven arrives,
and frost and snow have fallen,
I thereby know the luxuriance of the pine and cypress.
The hardship in Chén and Cài—
for me, Qiū, is it not a blessing!"
【一】【疏】When the year grows cold, we distinguish the trees;

The ancient ones who attained the Way,
were joyful even in adversity,
and joyful in prosperity.
Their joy did not lie in adversity or prosperity,

Shùn offered the empire to his friend Běirén Wúzé,

A scholar-official who aspires to benevolence
may sacrifice his life to achieve benevolence,
but never seeks to preserve his life at the expense of benevolence.
Those who uphold pure and lofty ideals,
with noble character transcending the mundane world,
stand in stark contrast to those who greedily pursue profit at the cost of their lives—
such is the distinction decreed by Heaven and Earth.

was a friend of Shùn.

if there is nothing they value,

Being detached and unbound,
they thus float along with the multitude,
with neither gain nor loss weighing on their hearts—
why would they choose to cast themselves into death?

they may be seen as sacrificing for fame or yearning for loftiness,
but they cannot be said to have transcended the world.

Long ago, when the Zhōu dynasty was rising,
there were two noblemen dwelling in Gūzhú,
named Bóyí and Shūqí.
The two said to each other:
"We have heard that in the west there is a man
who seems to be one possessing the Dào.
Let us try going to observe him."

making a covenant with them that said:
"We shall increase your wealth by two ranks,
and appoint you to official positions of the first grade."
They smeared the blood of a sacrificial animal and buried the covenant.

The two men looked at each other and smiled, saying:
"Ah,
how extraordinary!
This is not what we call the Way.
In ancient times, when Shénnóng ruled the world,
he offered sacrifices with utmost reverence but did not pray for blessings;
towards his people,
he governed with loyalty and trustworthiness without making demands.
He delighted in governance when it was time to govern,
and delighted in order when it was time to bring order,
never building his own success upon others' ruin,
never elevating himself by others' humility,
never seeking personal gain from fortuitous circumstances.
Now the Zhōu dynasty, seeing the chaos in Yīn, hastily seizes power,
employing stratagems above and trafficking in favors below,
relying on military force to maintain authority,
cutting sacrificial animals to make covenants as signs of trust,
flaunting their actions to please the masses,
engaging in slaughter and conquest to pursue profit—
this is replacing violence with chaos!
We have heard that scholars of antiquity,
when encountering orderly times, did not shirk their responsibilities,
and when meeting chaotic times, did not seek mere survival.
Now the world is dark,
the virtue of Yīn has declined,
rather than joining with Zhōu to defile ourselves,
we would better withdraw to purify our conduct."
The two men traveled north until they reached Shǒuyáng Mountain,
where they eventually starved to death.

when it came to wealth and honor,
even if they could have obtained them,
they would certainly not have relied on them.

they took pleasure in their own ideals alone,
not serving the worldly affairs—
such was the principle of these two scholars.

【四】【注】The Analects state:
Bóyí and Shūqí starved at the foot of Shǒuyáng,
but do not mention their death.
Yet here it is said they died there,
intending to clarify that they maintained their starvation to the end,
not necessarily that they died of starvation.
The main idea of this chapter
is to initiate a trend of noble yielding and distant retreat.
Therefore, those touched by this trend,
even greedy and ambitious individuals,
riding the celestial thoroughfare,
entering the purple court,
may still occasionally sigh with emotion midway on their path,
how much more so the ordinary people!
Hence, figures like Bóyí and Xǔyóu
are sufficient to match Jì and Qì,
and stand alongside Yī and Lǚ.
Those who dwell in mountain valleys yet influence the world,
though not all become sage assistants,
are they not still higher than those covered in dust?
Their deeds may be hard to accomplish,
but their influence has few drawbacks,
thus they can be passed down.
It is asked:
What are the drawbacks of Bóyí and Xǔyóu?
The answer:
The drawback of Xǔyóu
leads people to feign humility to seek advancement,
ultimately resulting in cases like Zhī and Kuài;
the influence of Bóyí
allows tyrannical rulers to unleash their cruelty without anyone daring to resist;
the drawbacks of Yī and Lǚ
enable greedy and ambitious heroes in the world to dare commit usurpation and rebellion;
only the sage leaves no trace,
hence has no drawbacks.
If considering Yī and Lǚ as the traces of the sage,
then Bóyí and Shūqí are also traces of the sage;
if considering Bóyí and Shūqí not as traces of the sage,
then the deeds of Yī and Lǚ are also not those of a sage.
The sage follows the natural course of things,
thus leaving no trace.
Therefore, what is called a sage,
inherently leaves no trace,
so things obtain their traces,
and upon obtaining traces, they are forcibly named sage,
thus the sage is but a name for having no trace.

Táng commentary says:
Some ask:
In the chapter "Ràng Wáng,"
most sections emphasize valuing life,
yet figures like Wù Guāng and others threw themselves into the water—
why is that?
The answer is:
The essence of Zhuāngzǐ's writings
lies in returning to the root,
and the means to return to the root
begins with renouncing glory;
thus, the chapter "Ràng Wáng" clarifies
the lofty aspiration of transcending the world,
aiming not to lower oneself to reform customs,
nor to prioritize the body to preserve life wholly.
Therefore, while there are occasional expressions valuing life,
they ultimately convey the intent to abandon honor,
deeply criticizing the harms of worldly affairs.
As for those of lesser attainment,
even if they wear coarse clothes and sip gruel,
they merely preserve their lives.
But those who fully embody the Dào, esteemed and transcendent, find freedom in detachment,
preferring to plunge into the clear, cold waters
rather than submit to worldly burdens.
This old collection includes pronunciations,
and I have casually recorded them here,
though they may not align perfectly with the meaning.

【Chapter One】【Explanation】Named after a person.
Confucius was a friend of Liǔxià Jì.
Liǔxià Jì had a younger brother,
named Dào Zhí.
Dào Zhí led a following of nine thousand men,
rampaging across the land,
invading and oppressing the feudal lords.
They broke into houses and forced open doors,
drove away people's cattle and horses,
seized their women,
were greedy for gain and forgot their kin,
disregarded parents and siblings,
and did not sacrifice to their ancestors.
In the cities they passed through,
large states guarded their walls,
small states took refuge in their fortresses,
and the myriad people suffered from them.

Confucius said to Liǔxià Jì:
"A person who is a father,
must be able to instruct his son;
a person who is an elder brother,
must be able to teach his younger brother.
If a father cannot instruct his son,
and an elder brother cannot teach his younger brother,
then there is no value in the kinship of father and son or brothers.
Now you, sir,
are a talented scholar of the age,
yet your younger brother is the robber Zhí,
a scourge to the world,
and you are unable to teach him.
I, Qiū, am privately ashamed for you, sir.
I request to go and persuade him on your behalf."
Liǔxià Jì said:
"You claim that a father must be able to instruct his son,
and an elder brother must be able to teach his younger brother.
But if the son does not heed his father's instruction,
or the younger brother rejects his elder brother's teaching,
then even with your eloquence, sir,
what can be done about it?
Moreover, as for Zhí's character,
his mind is like a gushing spring,
his thoughts like a whirlwind.
His strength is sufficient to resist enemies,
his rhetoric enough to gloss over wrongs.
He rejoices when his will is followed,
rages when it is opposed,
and easily insults others with words.
You must not go, sir."
Confucius did not listen,
with Yán Huí as the charioteer,
and Zǐgòng as the right-hand attendant,
they went to see Robber Zhì.
Robber Zhì was then resting his followers on the southern side of Mount Tài,
feasting on sliced human livers.
Confucius descended from the carriage and approached,
addressing the announcer, saying:
"I, Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ,
having heard of the general's lofty righteousness,
respectfully request an audience through you."
