Confucius said:
"I have heard that
under heaven there are three virtues:
to be born tall and stately,
of unparalleled beauty and grace,
so that all—young and old, noble and humble—rejoice at the sight,
this is the highest virtue;
knowledge encompassing heaven and earth,
the ability to discern all things,
this is the middle virtue;
courage, fierceness, decisiveness, and boldness,
gathering multitudes and leading troops,
this is the lowest virtue.
Any person possessing even one of these virtues
is fit to face south and claim sovereignty.
Now, General, you embody all three:
your stature is eight feet two inches,
your face radiates light,
your lips are like vibrant cinnabar,
your teeth like aligned shells,
your voice resonates with the huángzhōng pitch,
yet you are named Dào Zhí—
I privately consider it a disgrace for a general and find it unacceptable.
If you are inclined to heed my counsel,
I propose to journey south as your envoy to Wú and Yuè,
north to Qí and Lǔ,
east to Sòng and Wèi,
west to Jìn and Chǔ,
to have them build for you a great city spanning hundreds of miles,
establish a domain of hundreds of thousands of households,
honor you as a feudal lord,
initiate a new beginning with all under heaven,
cease warfare and rest your soldiers,
nurture your siblings,
and jointly honor your ancestors.
This is the conduct of sages and men of talent,
and the aspiration of all under heaven."

Huángzhōng,

Robber Zhi was greatly enraged and said:
"Come forward, Qiū!
Those who can be swayed by profit and persuaded by words—
are merely what we call foolish and ignorant common folk.
Now, being tall, grown, and handsome,
so that people are pleased upon seeing me—
this is the virtuous legacy left by my parents.
Even if you, Qiū, do not praise me,
do I not know it myself?"
Moreover, I have heard it said,
those who are fond of praising others to their faces
are also fond of slandering them behind their backs.
Now, you, Qiū, offer me great cities and numerous people,
intending to tempt me with profit and treat me as an ordinary person to be kept,
how can that last long!
When it comes to the greatness of cities,
none is greater than the entire world.
Yáo and Shùn possessed the world,
yet their descendants did not have even a place to set an awl;

【Three】【Memorials】Yīn Tāng and Zhōu Wǔ,
who governed all state affairs,
saw their descendants
all fall victim to usurpation and regicide.
Was it not the weight of the empire's interests that led to this!
Moreover, I have heard that
in ancient times, when beasts were numerous and people were few,
the people all dwelt in nests to avoid them.
By day they gathered acorns and chestnuts,
by night they roosted in the trees,
and thus they were called the people of Yǒu Cháo Shì.
In ancient times, the people did not know clothing.
In summer they accumulated great stores of firewood,
and in winter they burned it for warmth,
thus they were called the people who knew how to sustain life.
In the age of Shén Nóng,
they slept soundly and awoke serene,
the people knew their mothers
but not their fathers,
and dwelt together with deer.
They plowed for their food,
wove for their clothing,
and had no thought of harming one another.
This was the height of perfect virtue.
Yet Huáng Dì could not attain this virtue.
He fought Chī Yóu in the wilds of Zhuōlù,
till blood flowed for a hundred miles.
Yáo and Shùn arose,
appointed hosts of ministers.
Tāng exiled his sovereign,
and King Wǔ slew Zhòu.
From that time onward,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few.
From Tāng and Wǔ onward,
all have been troublemakers.

and found no place for yourself in the world.
You taught Zǐlù, yet he met such a calamity;

What the world holds in high esteem,
none more so than Huángdì,

Yáo was not compassionate,

and King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ.
These six individuals,
revered by the world,
upon closer examination,
all confused their true nature with profit and forcibly contradicted their innate dispositions,
their actions thus being utterly shameful.

Those whom the world calls worthy gentlemen,
are Bó Yí and Shū Qí.
Bó Yí and Shū Qí declined the throne of Gūzhú and starved to death on Mount Shǒuyáng,
their bones left unburied.
Bào Jiāo, cultivating his conduct and condemning the world,
died clinging to a tree.
Shēntú Dí remonstrated but was not heeded,
so he tied a stone to his back and threw himself into the river,
where he was eaten by fishes.
Jièzǐ Tuī was supremely loyal,
cutting flesh from his own thigh to feed Duke Wén.
When Duke Wén later turned his back on him,
Zǐ Tuī angrily left,
and was burned to death while clinging to a tree.
Wěi Shēng arranged to meet a woman under a bridge,
but the woman did not come.
When the water rose, he would not leave,
and died clinging to a bridge pillar.
These six individuals
are no different from dismembered dogs, drowned pigs, or beggars carrying bowls—
all are obsessed with reputation and treat death lightly,
never considering the foundation of nurturing their own lives.
【One】【Account】Two men died destitute on Shǒu Shān,
leaving no descendants to bury them.
The surname was Bào,
given name Jiāo,
a recluse of the Zhōu dynasty.
He cultivated conduct to criticize the age,
preserved his own integrity and purity,
carried a shoulder pole to gather firewood,
and collected acorns to satisfy his hunger.
Hence, he had no descendants,
did not serve the Son of Heaven as a minister,
nor befriended the feudal lords.
Zǐgòng encountered him
and said to him:
"I have heard that one who condemns its governance does not tread upon its land,
and one who defames its ruler does not accept its benefits.
Now you tread upon its land,
and eat from its benefits,
how can this be justified?"
Bào Jiāo replied:
I have heard that honest officials value advancement over retreat,
and virtuous men are easily shamed and hold life lightly."
Thereupon, he embraced the tree and stood there until he withered away.
【Èr Shū】Shēntú zì chén,
qián piān yǐ shì.
Jiàn ér bù tīng,
wèi xiáng suǒ jù.
Cuī Jiā suī jiě,
wú dì jiàn cí.
【Translation】"Carrying a Stone and Casting Himself into the River" Shēntú Dí was about to throw himself into the river,
when Cuī Jiā stopped him, saying:
"I have heard that sages and benevolent men are like parents to the people.
If one merely wets their feet for the sake of it,
without actually saving a drowning person,
can that be considered right?"
Shēntú Dí replied:
"Not so.
In the past, Jié killed Lóng Páng,
Zhòu killed Bǐ Gān,
and they lost the empire;
Wú killed Zǐ Xū,
Chén killed Xiè Yě,
and their states were destroyed.
It was not that the sages were not benevolent,
but that their counsel was not heeded."
Thereupon, he sank into the river and died.
【Three】【Narratives】Jìn Wéngōng Chóng'ěr,
having encountered the disaster caused by Lí Jī,
fled to another state.
On the journey, he suffered from hunger and exhaustion,
and Jiè Zǐtuī cut flesh from his own thigh to feed him.
After the duke returned three days later,
he rewarded his followers,
but forgot Zǐtuī.
Zǐtuī then composed the "Song of the Dragon and Snake,"
wrote it on the gate of his camp,
and fled in anger.
The duke later felt ashamed and apologized,
pursuing Zǐtuī to Jièshān.
Zǐtuī hid to avoid him,
so the duke set fire to the mountain,
hoping he would come out.
When the fire reached him,
Zǐtuī embraced a tree and was burned to death.
【Explanation】"To feed" is pronounced as "sì".
"Burned to death" is pronounced as "fán",
meaning to burn.

they then enclosed the mountains around Miánshàng and sealed them off,

After thoroughly examining the classics and commentaries,
there is no record of Jiè Tuī being burned to death.

Jiè Zǐ Tuī stood and withered.)
Zhuāng Zǐ wrote about being burned to death,

) and both Dōngfāng Shuò's Seven Remonstrances and the Hàn Shū's biography of Bǐng Jí inherited this error.
Now it should be corrected based on Zuǒ Zhuàn and Lǚ Lǎn.
【Four】【Commentaries】The six individuals refer to Bó Yí, Shū Qí, Bào Jiāo, Shēn Tú, Jiè Tuī, and Wěi Shēng.
It is said that these six people,
not aligning with the profound Way,
forced their emotions and adorned their conduct,
merely to stand out among the common customs,
using this to gain fame,
which was passed down to later generations.
How is this any different from stretching out a dead dog,
casting it into the water,
or a poor and sick person,
holding a gourd to beg for alms?
Such figures in this world,
should not be seen or heard of.
The actions of these six individuals,
are similar to this,
all valuing reputation over life,
not considering returning to the root and nurturing life,
thus exhausting their lifespan decreed by heaven.

The reason why Qiū speaks to me,
if he tells me about ghostly matters,
then I cannot understand them;
if he tells me about human affairs,

Excluding times of illness, emaciation, death, mourning, sorrow, and distress,
the days when one can open one's mouth to laugh
amount to no more than four or five days in a month.
Heaven and earth are endless,
yet human life has its limit.
To hold this limited existence within the boundless span
is as fleeting as a steed galloping past a crack—gone in an instant.
Those who cannot fulfill their aspirations and intentions
or nurture their allotted lifespan
are not those who comprehend the true Way.
What you, Qiū, have said,
is all that I reject.
Quickly leave and return,
and speak no more of it!
Your way,
is recklessly hurried and anxious,
a matter of deceitful artifice and falsehood,
incapable of preserving genuineness.
How is it worth discussing!"
【One】【Memorial】The eyes see and the ears hear,
the mouth discerns and the will fills,
acting in accordance with one's nature,
endowed by the Creator—
how could this be done through forced emotions?
When done within one's proper role,
the Way is present therein.
【Transcription】"To explain" is read as usual,
also pronounced with the initial sharp sound.
【二】【疏】Heaven is eternal and earth enduring,
yet the realm of extremity gradually recedes,
human life and death,
their time limits press urgently.
With a finite body,
entrusted to an infinite realm,
how is it different from a steed galloping past a crack in the wall!
【Explanation】"Shòu" is pronounced with the meaning of longevity,
and also according to its literal reading.
The same applies below.
"Shòu" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling sè yòu.
◎Wáng Niànsūn says:
In the explanatory text,
"shòu",
is given the fanqie sè yòu.
I argue that "shòu" should be "yǔ",
a mistake in the character.
"Yǔ",
also means illness.
Sickness and ailment form one category,
death and mourning form another,
and worries and hardships form yet another.
The character "yǔ" originally was written as "yù".
The Ěryǎ says:
"Yù",
means illness.
In the Xiǎoyǎ, the "Zhēngyuè" chapter says, "Why make me ill,"
Máo's commentary agrees with the Ěryǎ.
The Hànshū, "Annals of Emperor Xuān" records, "Now some of the imprisoned either from torture or from hunger and cold fall ill and die in prison,"
Sū Lín says:
means illness,
when prisoners fall ill,
the law terms it 'yǔ'."
Shī Gǔ says:
"Yǔ",
is pronounced like 'yǔ',
and the character is sometimes written as 'yù'.
The "Table of Prince Marquises" says:
Marquis Lóng of Fù was imprisoned (yǔ) [...
Yǔ (second) died.
【Three】【Explanations】Jí,
means urgent.
Kuángkuáng,
means losing one's true nature.
Jíjí,
means insufficiency.
The way of the sages' traces,
the practice of benevolence and righteousness,
is like that temporary lodging,
comparable to these straw dogs.
Clinging to them without letting go
only increases their drawbacks.
Frantically losing authenticity,
anxiously insufficient,
such hypocritical matters,
are hardly worth discussing!
【Explanation Text】"Néng shuō" is pronounced as yuè.
"Jí qù" has the fanqie spelling jí lì fǎn,
meaning urgent.
Some versions write it as jí.
"Wú fù" has the fanqie spelling fú yòu fǎn.
"Kuáng kuáng" is read with its usual pronunciation,
also pronounced as jiǔ kuàng fǎn.
"Jí jí" is also written as jí in some versions,
pronounced as jí,
also pronounced as jí.
"Zhà qiǎo" has the fanqie spelling kǔ xiào fǎn,
and also read with its usual pronunciation.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it is written as "伋伋".
(2) The character "瘐" has been emended based on the Hàn Shū.
Confucius bowed twice and hastened away,
went out the gate and mounted his carriage,
three times dropped the reins from his hand,
his eyes dazed and unseeing,
his complexion like ashes of the dead,
leaning against the front rail and bowing his head,
he could not catch his breath.
Returning to the east gate outside Lǔ,
he happened to meet Liǔxià Jì.
Liǔxià Jì said:
"Nowadays, after being absent for several days without seeing you,
your carriage and horses bear the marks of travel,
could it be that you went to see Zhí?"
【一】【疏】Shì,
the crossbar in front of a carriage,
is what one leans on to sit.
The heroic robber Zhí,
eloquently discussed the principles of things,
causing Confucius to tremble with fear,
and thus it came to this.
Wēi,
means "none" or "without."
【Translated Text】"Shàng chē": shí zhǎng fǎn.
"Sān shī": xī zàn fǎn,
also read as the character's usual pronunciation.
Vast and boundless — "mò" is pronounced as "gāng" in reverse.
"Having action" is read according to its literal pronunciation.
Confucius looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"Indeed."
【One】【Dissipated】so,
thus it is.
Liǔxià Jì said:
"Could it be that Zhí has gone against your expectations as before?"
Confucius said:
"Indeed.
What I did was like cauterizing myself without being ill,
running headlong to tweak a tiger's head,
and tugging at a tiger's whiskers—
I nearly could not escape the tiger's jaws!"
【One】【Memorial】If preceding this,
then at the beginning of the chapter, Liǔ Xià states:
"To oppose his heart is to anger him,
is it not that going against your will is as I said before?"
Confucius replies:
"It is indeed as you have said."
【二】【注】This chapter conveys that by following what the masses wish to abolish, one can abolish it,
even a King Zhòu can be removed;
if one does not follow the masses but solely relies on oneself,
even a Dào Zhí cannot be controlled.
【Subcommentary】"Jī" means
"to approach."
One who recklessly touches a tiger's head and tugs at its whiskers
will soon be devoured by the tiger.
Now, when Zhòngní went to persuade Dào Zhi,
treading into such peril,
it was no different from this.
Speaking of the main idea of this chapter,
it rejects the traces of the sages,
and scorns fame and profit.
Thus, in rejecting the sages' traces, it reprimands Yáo and Shùn;
in scorning fame and profit, it belittles Bóyí and Shūqí.
Therefore, it uses Kǒng[zǐ] and Zhi to convey this intention.
As for Guō Xiàng's annotation,
it misses the mark by far.
【Transcription】"Self-moxibustion" is read as jiǔ with a rising tone.
"Swiftly walking and gauging" liáo is pronounced as liāo.
"Flat tiger" biǎn is read as biān,
also pronounced with a rising tone as pián,
and Xú reads it as fú with a rising tone.
Some versions write it as "braid,"
with the same pronunciation.
"●" One version writes it as gauging the head and braiding the tiger's whiskers.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Nowadays, it's written as braiding the tiger's whiskers.
Older versions also used "whiskers,"
but now we follow the Song edition using ●.
"Almost not" jī is read as qí.
"Can leave" qù is pronounced with a rising tone as qǔ.
Zǐ Zhāng asked Mǎn Gǒu Dé, saying:
"Why not cultivate virtuous conduct?
Without conduct, one will not be trusted;
without trust, one will not be appointed;
without appointment, one will not gain benefits.
Therefore, considering reputation,
calculating advantages,
righteousness is truly essential.
If one discards fame and profit,
and turns inward to examine one's heart,
then for a scholar's cultivation of conduct,
can it be neglected for even a single day!"
【First】【Commentary】Zǐzhāng,
was a disciple of Kǒngzǐ,
whose surname was Zhuānsūn,
given name Shī,
courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
a person who practiced the deeds of the sages.
The surname Mǎn,
given name Gǒudé,
is fabricated as a name,
meaning to greedily obtain whatever satisfies one's desires,
representing a person who seeks profit.
Hé,
means why not.
Why not practice benevolence and righteousness?
This advises him to abandon the pursuit of fame and profit.
【Explanation】"Mǎn Gǒu Dé" is a person's name.
"Hé" is pronounced as hú là.
"Wéi Xíng" is pronounced as xià mèng.
The following and annotations are the same.
Hé,
means why not.
It advises why not cultivate moral conduct.
【二】【疏】If one does not practice benevolent and righteous deeds, then one will not be trusted or employed,
if not trusted or employed, then one will have no official position,
if without an official position, then one will have no salary or benefits.
Therefore, with virtuous conduct comes reputation,
with reputation comes profit,
considering and evaluating appropriately,
benevolence and righteousness are truly good things,
and it is fitting to practice them.
【Three】【Memorials】 returned,
going against propriety.
If one discards fame and profit,
it goes against my heart's desires,
therefore, in establishing oneself as a scholar,
one cannot go a single day without practicing benevolence and righteousness.
Mǎn Gǒudé said:
"The shameless become wealthy,
the highly trusted become prominent.
Those who achieve great fame and profit
almost always do so through shamelessness and trustworthiness.
Thus, when considering reputation
and calculating gain,
being trustworthy is truly the way.
If one were to abandon fame and profit,
and turn inward to examine one's heart,
then would the conduct of a scholar
embrace their true nature!"
【一】【疏】Trusting too much,
is like speaking too much.
For recognizing integrity and knowing humility leads to poverty,
while being shameless, greedy, and cruel leads to wealth;
being modest, gentle, quiet, and retiring leads to obscurity,
while speaking too much and boasting leads to prominence.
Therefore, when observing reputation and calculating profit,
nothing takes precedence over speaking too much,
as speaking too much is the foundation of fame and gain.
【二】【疏】To embrace,
is to guard.
Heaven,
is naturalness.
Those who cultivate the Way,
establish their person and conduct,
discard fame and profit,
thus go against worldly desires,
embrace and guard their innate genuineness,
which in turn aligns with the principles of emptiness and mystery.
Zǐ Zhāng said:
"In ancient times, Jié and Zhòu were honored as Sons of Heaven,
possessing the wealth of the entire realm.
Now if you tell a servant or laborer
that his conduct resembles that of Jié and Zhòu,
he will show a shameful expression (note 1),
and feel resentment in his heart -
this is because even base people despise such behavior.
Whereas Zhòngní and Mò Dí,
though impoverished commoners,
if you tell a prime minister today
that his conduct resembles that of Zhòngní and Mò Dí,
he will change countenance and modestly claim inadequacy -
this shows true nobility of scholars.
Therefore, one's status as Son of Heaven
does not necessarily confer nobility;
one's condition as a commoner
does not necessarily mean baseness;
the distinction between nobility and baseness
lies in the goodness or badness of one's conduct (note 2)."
【一】【疏】Jié, Zhòu, Kǒng, Mò,
are all explained previously.
Zāng,
refers to zāng huò (slaves).
Jù,
refers to theft,
that is, petty thieves and lowly persons.
Comparing the Son of Heaven to a slave,
one would feel ashamed and unwilling to accept;
comparing a prime minister to a common man,
one would change expression and be pleased;
thus, it is understood that what is valued lies in conduct,
not in position.
【Explanation】"Zāng Jù": Sīmǎ comments:
refers to people who are slaves, thieves, corrupt, or secretly gather.
"Yǒu Zuò": pronounced as "zuò".
"Zǎi Xiàng": the fanqie spelling is "xiàng".
The following "xiàng" is the same.
【Èr Shū】This further explains the previous meaning.
【Collation Note】(1) The Kōzanji version reads "zé zuò sè" (then changed countenance),
the Quē Wù cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's version as reading "zé yǒu zuò sè" (then had a change of countenance).
Mǎn Gǒudé said:
"Petty thieves are arrested,
while great thieves become feudal lords.
At the gates of feudal lords,
righteous men reside.
In the past, Duke Huán Xiǎobái killed his elder brother and took his sister-in-law as wife, yet Guǎn Zhòng served as his minister;
Tián Chéngzǐ Cháng murdered his sovereign and stole the state, yet Confucius accepted gifts from him.
In speech they condemn such acts as base,
but in action they lower themselves to serve.
This means the reality of their words and deeds are locked in combat within their breasts—
is this not perverse!
【一】Therefore, the texts say:
'Which is ugly, which is fine?
The successful become the head,
the unsuccessful become the tail.
【一】【疏】Bèi means
to rebel against.
Fú means
to oppose.
Duke Huán of Qí, named Xiǎo Bái,
killed his elder brother's son Jiū,
and took his sister-in-law as his wife.
Guǎn Zhòng, a virtuous man,
served as his minister and assisted him,
ultimately achieving the feat of uniting the feudal lords nine times,
and bringing order to the entire realm.
Tián Chéngzǐ Cháng killed Duke Jiǎn of Qí,
yet Confucius bathed and went to court,
accepting his gifts of silk and valuables.
Now, killing one's brother and taking his wife,
assassinating a ruler and usurping a state—
no evils in human relations are greater than these.
Yet Yí Wú served as a minister,
and Confucius accepted the gifts.
In speech and discussion, they are deemed base and lowly,
but in emotion and action, they are served with submission.
Is this not a conflict within the heart,
a contradiction between words and deeds?
【Transcription】"Rù sǎo": xiān zǎo fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
Taking the sister-in-law as wife.
"Wéi chén": chén,
sometimes written as xiàng.
"Shā jūn": shēn zhì fǎn.
"Lùn zé": lì dùn fǎn.
"Bèi zhàn": bù nèi fǎn.
"Yì fú": fú fú fǎn.
【二】【疏】Those who succeed become leaders,
and rulers serve them;
those who fail become followers,
and are criticized and slandered.
From this perspective,
it only discusses success and failure,
how could it relate to virtue or lack thereof?
Thus, it is unclear where true goodness and evil lie.
The books that were referenced
were all destroyed by fire,
and now none of the original texts remain.
Zǐ Zhāng said:
"If you do not cultivate conduct,
then close and distant relations will lack proper order,
the noble and humble will lack righteousness,
the elder and younger will lack sequence;
the five constants and six social positions,
how shall they be distinguished?"
【一】【疏】Qī means
kin.
Lún means
principle.
The five cardinal relationships refer to
grandfather and ancestors,
oneself and descendants,
and also denote the five elements of metal, wood, water, fire, and earth,
as well as the five virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and fidelity.
The six positions refer to
ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife,
and also mean parents, siblings, and spouses.
Zǐzhāng said:
"If one does not practice acts of benevolence and righteousness,
then there will be no principle to distinguish between close and distant relatives,
no righteousness to differentiate the noble from the humble,
no order to sequence the elder and the younger,
and no way to distinguish the five cardinal relationships and the six positions."
【Explanation】"Zhǎng Yòu" is pronounced with "Zhǎng" as dīng zhàng fǎn.
"Wǔ Jì": Sīmǎ comments:
year, day, month, stars and planets, calendar calculations.
"Liù Wèi": ruler, subject, father, son, husband, wife.
◎Yú Yuè says:
Regarding Wǔ Jì,
Sīmǎ states it refers to year, day, month, stars and planets, and calendar calculations,
but this does not align with the concepts of distant and close relations, nobility and lowliness, seniority and youth,
so it is likely incorrect.
Now, examining the case, Wǔ Jì is actually Wǔ Lún,
and Liù Wèi is Liù Jì.
The "Sān Gāng Liù Jì" chapter in Bái Hǔ Tōng states:
Liù Jì refers to
paternal uncles, brothers, clansmen, maternal uncles, teachers and elders, and friends.
These are all distinctions for distant and close relations, nobility and lowliness, seniority and youth.
Not calling it Wǔ Lún but Wǔ Jì,
and not calling it Liù Jì but Liù Wèi,
is merely a difference in ancient people's language.
In the "Rù Guān" chapter of Jiā Yǔ, it mentions the relationships among various servants,
with Wáng Sù annotating:
"Lún"
means "Jì".
Thus, "lún" and "jì" can be used interchangeably.
For "parting," the pronunciation is bié, with the initial consonant as b and the rhyme as ié.
The same applies below.
Mǎn Gǒudé said:
"Yáo killed his eldest son,
Shùn exiled his maternal brother,
so is there order between close and distant relatives?
Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ slew Zhòu,
so is there righteousness between noble and base?
Wáng Jì became the heir,
the Duke of Zhōu killed his elder brother,
so is there sequence between elder and younger?
The Confucians use hypocritical speech,
the Mohists advocate universal love,
so will the five relationships and six social positions maintain distinction?
【一】【疏】Yáo deposed his eldest son Dānzhū,
not granting him the heavenly throne,
hence it is said to be execution.
Shùn enfeoffed his maternal brother Xiàng in the state of Yǒubì,
appointing officials to govern his state,
collecting tributes and taxes,
hence it is said to be exile.
Deposing a son and exiling a brother,
how can there be any principle of closeness or distance?
【Explanation Text】"Yáo Killed His Eldest Son" Cuī's commentary states:
Yáo killed his eldest son, whose name was Kǎojiānmíng.
"Shùn Exiled His Maternal Brother" The brother,
refers to Xiàng.
Exiled,
means banished.
Mèngzǐ states:
Shùn enfeoffed Xiàng at Yǒubì,
but he was not allowed to govern in his state,
the Son of Heaven appointed officials to administer his state,
and collected tribute taxes from him.
Therefore, it is said that he was banished.
【二】【疏】Yīn Tāng exiled Xià Jié at Náncháo,
Zhōu Wǔ killed Yīn Zhòu in Jíjùn.
Between ruler and subject, noble and base,
where lies the principle of righteousness?
【Three】【Memorials】Wáng Jì,
the common-born son of Zhōu Tàiwáng named Jì Lì,
was the father of King Wén.
Tàibó and Zhòng Yōng yielded the throne and did not take it,
so the young son Jì Lì became the heir.
Guǎn and Cài,
elder brothers of Zhōu Gōng,
were executed despite his tears,
hence it is said he killed his brothers (three).
Deposing the heir to establish a common-born,
a younger brother killing his elder brothers,
in terms of respect and humility, elder and younger,
is there any proper order?
【Explanation】"For appropriateness" - Dīng lì fǎn.
【Four】【Dissertations】The Confucians often speak,
forcibly establishing names and positions;
the Mohists advocate universal love,
comprehensive and impartial;
the five relationships and six social roles,
what distinctions do they have?
【Collation】(1) The character "gù" was emended according to the subsequent text.
(2) "Nà qí" was emended based on the Mèngzǐ and the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) The character "xiōng" was emended according to the main text.
You are precisely for fame,
I am precisely for gain.
The reality of fame and gain
does not accord with principle,
nor does it reflect the Dào.
I daily plead with Wú Yuē on your behalf, saying:
'Petty men sacrifice themselves for wealth,
noble men sacrifice themselves for fame.
The ways in which they alter their true feelings
and change their innate nature
may differ;
yet when it comes to abandoning what they should do
and sacrificing themselves for what they should not,
they are the same.'
Therefore I say:
Do not be a petty man—
turn back and follow your heaven;
do not be a noble man—
follow the principles of heaven.
Whether crooked or straight,
look to the heavenly standard;
turn your face to the four directions,
and with the times wax and wane.
Whether right or wrong,
hold fast to the round pivot;
alone complete your intention,
and wander with the Dào.
Do not obstinately persist in your conduct,
nor rigidly adhere to your righteousness—
you will lose what you ought to do.
Do not rush after wealth,
do not sacrifice for success—
【一】【疏】Supervision,
means clarity,
means insight.
Zǐzhāng's inner motives
lie precisely in fame;
Gǒu dé's inner motives,
lie precisely in profit.
Moreover, both paths of fame and profit,
are not true realities,
since they deviate from the ultimate truth,
how could they bring clarity and insight into the profound Dao!
【Interpretation】"And if you, sir, are indeed pursuing fame" is a hypothetical expression.
For "pursue,"
the pronunciation is according to the reverse spelling yú wèi.
The same applies to "pursue profit" below.
"Not to mirror" is also written as "to reflect,"
with the same meaning.
【二】【疏】Disputation,
refers to argumentation and discourse.
Covenant,
refers to agreements and oaths.
Abandoning what one does,
is to forsake oneself;
sacrificing for what one does not do,
is to chase after external things.
Those who sacrifice for profit are called petty persons,
those who sacrifice for reputation are called noble persons;
profit and reputation differ,
yet the sacrifice is the same.
If Zǐzhāng were to gain improperly,
all would discuss profound words on the principle of non-action,
solidifying an unbreakable bond.
【Textual Explanation】"Wú rì" is read with the character's meaning reversed.
"Wú yuē" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
Xú gives the pronunciation as yú miào reversed.
【Three】【Memorials】Thus,
it is you.
Since you neither chase after profit,
nor sacrifice for fame,
you can follow your nature and return to the root,
aligning with the natural way.
【Four】【Spread】Assist,
aid also.
Without questioning crooked or straight,
follow the natural way,
observe and illuminate the four directions,
wax and wane with the four seasons.
【Five】【Dispersions】 wandering and hesitating,
signifies the transformation of intentions.
The pivot of completeness,
is like the center of a circle.
By holding to the way of the circle's center to respond to right and wrong,
and employing the heart of self-transformation to fulfill one's intentions,
thus one can deeply embody the principle of emptiness and interconnectedness,
becoming one who transforms endlessly.
【Six】【Dispersions】 are what constitute
the true nature.
Do not divert your intent
to pursue the path of sagehood;
do not solidify your heart
to learn the way of benevolence and righteousness;
abandoning yourself to imitate others,
you will lose your true nature.
◎Wáng Niànsūn said:
"Do not divert and act,"
where "divert" should be read as "focus."
As the "Shān Mù" chapter states,
"like a dragon or a snake,
they change with the times,
and are unwilling to focus on action."
This is what is meant by not focusing on action.
This follows the previous text about advancing and retreating with the times,
and swaying with the Dào,
meaning one should follow the times and the Dào and not rigidly adhere to benevolence and righteousness.
If one focuses on action,
solidifying it into righteousness,
then one will lose what is essential.
Hence, the text below says,
"correcting their words,
insisting on their actions,
thus they suffer the consequences,
and encounter disaster."
"Insisting on their actions"
is what is referred to here as focusing on action.
The "Qiū Shuǐ" chapter says, "not acting as one,"
which is at odds with the Dào.
"One" also means focus.
Not focusing on action
is akin to saying not acting as one.
"Focus" and "divert"
are interchangeable in ancient characters.
It is also interchangeably written as "tuán."
In the Shǐjì, "Biography of Wúwáng Bì," it says, "the King of Yān tuán led Hú troops into Xiāo Guān,"
the Suǒyǐn commentary states:
"tuán,"
pronounced as "zhuān,"
means exclusively commanding Hú soldiers.
The Hànshū writes "tuán" as "zhuǎn."
【Seven】【Admonitions】Do not rush towards wealth and honor,
nor sacrifice yourself in the pursuit of success.
If one must rush and sacrifice,
then it goes against the natural disposition.
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfang's edition as reading "rì" (day) as "xī" (former).
Bìgān had his heart cut out,
Zǐxū had his eyes gouged,
such are the calamities of loyalty【one】;
Zhígōng bore witness against his father,
Wěishēng drowned to death,
such are the perils of trustworthiness【two】;
Bàozi stood dried up,
Shēnzi did not plead his own case,
such are the harms of integrity【three】;
Kǒngzǐ did not see his mother,
Kuāngzǐ did not see his father,
such are the failures of righteousness【four】.
These are what have been passed down from ancient times,
and are spoken of in later ages,
believing that scholars should correct their speech,
and stand firm in their conduct,
thus they suffer these misfortunes,
and encounter these disasters【five】.
【一】【疏】Bǐ Gàn loyally remonstrated with Zhòu,
who said,
"I've heard that a sage's heart has nine apertures."
Thereupon, he cut open Bǐ Gàn's heart to examine it.
Wŭ Zīxū loyally remonstrated with Fū Chāi,
who had him executed.
Wŭ Zīxū declared:
"After my death,
gouge out my eyes and hang them on the eastern gate of Wú's capital, so I may witness Yuè's destruction of Wú."
These are instances of utmost loyalty meeting with tragic ends.
【Text】"Gouge out the eye" - wū xué fǎn.
【Èr Shū】's father personally stole a sheep,
and his son testified against him.
Wěi Shēng had an appointment with a woman,
and he died holding onto the bridge.
These are all cases where keeping faith led to their misfortunes.
【Three】【Memorials】Bào Jiāo was incorruptible and upright,
yet he encountered Zǐgòng's ridicule,
and he embraced a tree, standing until he withered and died.
Shēnzǐ,
who was Shēnshēng, the crown prince of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
encountered the disaster caused by Lì Jī,
wrongfully suffered slander and calumny,
did not defend himself,
and hanged himself to death.
【Explanation】"Bào Zǐ Lì Gàn" Sīmǎ comments:
Bào Zǐ,
named Jiāo,
was a person from the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
who disdained the rulers of his time and did not serve in office,
instead gathering vegetables to eat.
Zǐgòng saw him,
and said to him:
"Why do you not take office and receive an official's salary?"
He replied:
"There is no one fit to serve."
Zǐgòng said:
"You disdain the rulers of the time and do not eat their salary,
you detest their governance and do not tread upon their land.
Now you detest their ruler,
yet dwell on his land,
and eat his vegetables—
how contradictory are your principles and actions?"
Bào Jiāo then discarded his vegetables and starved to death.
The Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn records the same.
It also says:
he withered away by the Luò River.
"Shèng Zǐ (Èr) Zì Lǐ" one edition writes lǐ as 俚.
Another version also writes it as Shēn Zǐ zì mái.
Some say:
it refers to Shēntú Dí embracing a jar and drowning in the river.
One edition writes it as Shēn Zǐ bù zì lǐ,
referring to Shēn Shēng.
【Four】【Critiques】Confucius was so immersed in the traces of sages,
traveling through states in response to appointments,
that when his mother was on her deathbed,
Confucius did not see her.
Surname Kuāng,
given name Zhāng,
a man of Qí,
remonstrated with his father,
but his father did not comply,
and he was disliked by his father.
So he wandered to another city,
also immersed in benevolence and righteousness,
studying and reading until he forgot to return,
and when his father was on his deathbed, Zhāng did not see him.
These are all cases of being bogged down in benevolence and righteousness,
having such faults.
【Explanation Text】"Confucius Does Not See His Mother" Lǐ Yún says:
Have not heard of it.
"Kuāng Zǐ Does Not See His Father" Sīmǎ says:
Kuāng Zǐ,
named Zhāng,
a person from Qí,
admonished his father,
was driven out by his father,
and never saw his father for the rest of his life.
This matter is recorded in the Mèngzǐ.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Suspects that the two characters for mother and father should be interchanged.
【五】【Note】This chapter says that if conduct is esteemed, then conduct becomes artificial;
if scholars are honored, then scholars become hypocritical.
Therefore, disregard conduct and devalue scholars to preserve their inner integrity,
and only then will conduct be lofty and scholars be truly honored.
【Commentary】From Bǐgàn downward,
and Kuāngzǐ upward,
all were loyal, trustworthy, incorruptible, and steadfast, yet they suffered calamities.
These are all tales passed down from ancient times,
spoken of in later ages.
Therefore, those who are loyal and sincere,
incorruptible and faithful,
who correct their words to admonish their rulers,
and uphold their conduct to serve their lords,
none fail to encounter such disasters,
and submit to such misfortunes.
Those who follow the Way should deeply take caution and be prudent.
【Transcription】"Suǒ chuán" zhàng zhuān fǎn.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "shèng" instead of "shēn",
the explanatory text also uses "shèng".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition includes the character "bù" after "zǐ".
(3) The Zhào edition uses "shàng" instead of "shàng".
Wú Zú asked Zhī Hé, saying:
"Among men, there are none who do not pursue fame and chase after profit.
When one is wealthy, others flock to him;
flocking to him, they defer to him;
deferring to him, they honor him.
To be deferred to and honored
is the way to nurture life, comfort the body, and delight the mind.
Now you alone have no desire for this—
is it because you know it is insufficient?
Or is it that you know it but lack the strength to act?
Or do you deliberately uphold correctness without forgetting it?"
【One】【Argument】Wúzú,
refers to a greedy person,
one who is never content.
Zhīhé,
refers to someone who embodies the understanding of the Way of Central Harmony,
a person who maintains their duty and is pure and honest.
These two hypothetical figures are used to illustrate the misfortunes and blessings of greed and integrity.
Wúzú says:
There is no one in the world who does not aspire to fame and pursue wealth and rank.
If one possesses riches, people will flock to them;
and when they flock, they will humble themselves and honor the wealthy.
Those who receive such humility and honor from others
find their emotions pleased,
their nature satisfied,
their physical constitution at ease, and thus live long lives.
Do you alone lack the desire for wealth and honor?
Is it because you understand that insufficiency should not be sought?
Or is it that your mind can comprehend this,
but your strength cannot act upon it,
so you adhere to righteous principles,
keeping your aspirations firm and unwavering,
thereby dismissing the heart of greed and refraining from taking such paths?
【Transcription】"Wú Zú" in one edition is written as Wú Zhī.
"Zé Xià" is pronounced with the characters Xiá and Jià.
The same applies below.
"Lè Yì" is pronounced as Luò.
The same applies below.
"Zhī Bù" is pronounced as Zhì.
The same applies to the following instances of knowledge and strategy.
◎Qìng Fān's note: Yì,
is a function word,
read like "yì".
"Yì" and "yì" were interchangeable in ancient script.
In the Analects, chapter "Xué Ér", the phrase "yì yǔ zhī yǔ",
the Han stone classics write "yì" as "yì".
In Mozi's "Míng Guǐ" chapter, "qǐ rǔ wéi zhī yǔ",
"yì bào wéi zhī yǔ".
These are all evidence.
"Gù Tuī Zhèng Bù Wàng Xié" (Commentary) Wàng,
sometimes written as wàng,
meaning if the ruler and ministers only pursue the correct path without forgetting,
then is it because they do not use wealth and status?
Or is it because their wisdom and strength are insufficient,
that they do not use them?
Zhī Hé said:
"Now such people consider those born in the same era as themselves,
and living in the same region,
to be men who have transcended the ordinary and surpassed the age;
this is because they lack a fixed foundation,
by which to observe the timing of past and present,
and the distinctions between right and wrong,
they conform with vulgar customs.
The world abandons what is most important,
and discards what is most honored,
to pursue what they themselves do;
this is how they discuss the way to long life, physical comfort, and joyful contentment—
is it not far off the mark!
The pain of acute suffering,
the ease of tranquil pleasure,
do not manifest in the body;
the fear of alarm and dread,
the joy of delight and gladness,
do not manifest in the mind;
they know they act but do not know why they act.
Thus, though they may be honored as the Son of Heaven,
and possess all under heaven as their wealth,
they cannot avoid calamity."
【一】【疏】This person,
refers to the wealthy and noble.
Common folk,
meaning those lacking knowledge,
driven by greed for profit,
if born in the same era as the noble,
or residing in the same village as the rich,
would still consider themselves superior to the masses,
surpassing the people of the world;
how much more so if they themselves enjoy wealth and nobility!
These are the foolish ones,
without a master within their hearts,
not treading the path of righteousness,
unaware of the eras of past and present,
unable to discern the boundaries of right and wrong,
yet competing with the dusty world in turmoil,
changing with the trivial and shifting trends,
how could they possibly understand the course of fortune and misfortune!
【Interpretation】"The Scholar Who Surpasses the World" speaks of how the human heart is easily swayed.
Yet, when one is born alongside virtuous individuals,
one naturally considers oneself superior to ordinary people,
let alone those who personally attain wealth and high status!
【Two essentials】 are of utmost importance:
life,
and the most revered,
the Dào.
Those who follow vulgar customs
abandon life and turn their backs on the Dào,
their actions always being like this;
thus, regarding the path to longevity,
they are far from it.
【Three】【Memorials】 of sorrow and grief,
express sadness.
Peace and joy,
express happiness.
Now, sadness, joy, delight, and fear,
are all matters external to the body,
thus they cannot illuminate the sage's nature,
nor shine into the heart and soul,
yet the foolish recklessly act upon them.
【Transcription】"Cǎn" is pronounced as qī gǎn fǎn.
"Dá" is pronounced as dān dá fǎn.
"Zhī kǒng" is pronounced as qiū yǒng fǎn.
【Four】【Explanations】To act for the sake of acting is
to act with intention;
the reason for acting
is to act without intention.
If one only knows to act with intention,
but does not understand that the source of action comes from acting without intention,
such a person,
even if honored to manage myriad affairs,
wealthy enough to possess the four seas,
will still not avoid the anxieties and other troubles.
Wú Zú said:
"Wealth, for a person,
brings benefit in all things,
exhausting beauty and mastering influence—
what even the perfect person cannot attain,
what the worthy person is unable to reach.
It borrows others' courage and strength to become awe-inspiring power,
wields others' knowledge and strategy to gain clear-sightedness,
relies on others' virtue to appear worthy and good.
Without ruling a state, one commands respect like a sovereign or father.
Moreover, sounds, sights, flavors, and authority—
the heart delights in them without waiting to learn,
the body finds comfort in them without needing example.
Desiring and disliking, avoiding and pursuing—
these truly require no teacher,
for they are human nature.
Though the world may criticize me,
who can refuse them!
【一】【疏】Poverty,
means exhaustion.
To be able to exhaust all that is good and beautiful in the world,
and to fully possess the authority and power among humans—
is it not only wealth and nobility that can achieve this?
Therefore, even individuals of utmost virtue,
and wise and philosophical scholars,
cannot surpass this.
【Explanation】"Qióng měi": Qióng,
means to exhaust.
"Jiū shì": Shì is pronounced as shì.
It is also written as shì.
Another pronunciation is yì,
meaning to investigate thoroughly.
【Two Recluses】For those who possess wealth and status,
many people attach themselves,
so the brave defend for them,
the wise strategize for them,
the virtuous assist them.
Although they do not rule over states,
their authority and dignity are akin to that of a sovereign or a father,
all of which is brought about by wealth and profit.
【Interpretation】"Xiárén" is pronounced as xié.
【Three】【Memorials】The ears delight in sounds,
the eyes love colors,
the mouth savors flavors,
and authority and power suit their dispositions—
these bring joy to the heart without awaiting teaching,
so how could adhering to laws and models bring physical comfort?
It is simply the nature of things.
【Four】【Memorials】If one desires something, they approach it;
if they detest it, they avoid it.
This is the constant nature of humans and creatures,
not something that requires a teacher's instruction to act upon.
Thus, even if the world lacks nothing,
who alone would argue over such matters?
【Transcription】"Yù wù" wū lù fǎn.
【Collation】(1) In the Shìdétáng edition, "virtuous" is written as "sage."
Zhī Hé said:
"The actions of the wise
are always aligned with the common people,
never transgressing their own measure.
Thus they are content and do not contend,
and having no desires, they do not seek.
It is because of insufficiency that one seeks,
contending everywhere yet not considering oneself greedy;
it is because of surplus that one declines,
renouncing the world yet not considering oneself upright.
The substance of uprightness and greed
does not stem from external pressures,
but from turning inward to examine one's own measure.
Though positioned as the Son of Heaven, one does not use nobility to傲慢对待他人;
though possessing the wealth of the world, one does not use riches to amuse oneself at others' expense.
Considering the potential harm,
reflecting on the possible reversals,
and deeming them detrimental to one's nature,
thus one declines and does not accept—
not for the sake of seeking fame and reputation.
Yáo and Shùn ruled as emperors with harmony,
not because they benevolently governed the world,
but because they did not let beauty harm their lives;
Shàn Juǎn and Xǔ Yóu could have become emperors but declined,
not out of empty courtesy and refusal,
but to avoid letting affairs harm themselves.
These all pursued what was beneficial,
declined what was harmful,
and thus the world praised them as worthy.
One may possess such qualities,
but they did not do so to build a reputation.
【First】【Commentary】The wise person,
with an open mind responds to things,
hence in actions and movements,
they take the people's heart as their own heart.
The people follow them,
and do not transgress their laws and norms either.
Reaching the ultimate within the heart,
thus there is no contention;
without use and without action,
therefore there is no seeking and no awareness.
【二】【疏】in four places,
refers to the four directions.
Now, the distinction between the ordinary and the sage,
separates greed from integrity,
hence some strive greedily for the four directions,
galloping across the eight extremes,
unaware of their own greed;
while others abandon the ten thousand chariots,
decline the imperial throne,
yet remain unaware of their own integrity and frugality.
【Three】【Explanations】Supervision,
means reflection.
Integrity and greed are inherent in one's nature,
not merely forced by external things,
but rather reflected inwardly,
each endowed with different measures.
【Four】【Memorials】Those who do not take pride in high status and wealth,
nor find amusement in money and possessions,
do so because they consider the disasters and troubles
that would worry and harm their true nature.
Thus, they decline the great treasure and do not accept it,
not because they seek fame and reputation.
【Transcription】"Yào míng" yī yáo fǎn.
【五】【疏】Yōng,
means harmony.
The transformation during the times of Táng and Yú,
which brought peace throughout the land,
was not due to an intentional display of benevolence and kindness,
but rather because they did not let superficial beauty harm life.
Shàn Juǎn and Xǔ Yóu declined the throne when it was offered to them,
not out of pretense in refusing and yielding,
but to avoid letting worldly affairs harm themselves.
These actions were all for the benefit of preserving their own lives,
and to steer clear of the dangers of usurpation and regicide.
Therefore, the world praised them for their wisdom and capability,
which can be said to stem from this intention of avoiding harm,
while in reality, they had no desire for fame or reputation.
Wú Zú said:
"If one must cling to reputation,
tormenting the body and forsaking sweetness,
restricting nourishment to sustain life,
then they are but one who, though long ill and endlessly distressed, does not die."
【一】【疏】If one must persistently strive to cultivate and enhance their reputation,
tormenting their physical form,
depriving themselves of sweetness and delights,
living in austerity and restraint for nourishment,
and rigidly preserving their life,
how is this any different from suffering a chronic, stubborn illness,
enduring long hardships without dying,
where even on the days they are alive,
it feels as if they are already dead!
These are insufficient words
to challenge the understanding of harmony.
【Transcription】"Cháng'è" is pronounced as è,
also read as wū mài fǎn.
【Collation】（一）The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan ancient manuscript edition, which also includes the character "yóu" below.
Zhī Hé said:
"Peace is bliss,
excess brings harm—
this holds true for all things,
and wealth is the most extreme case.
Take the wealthy of today:
their ears are consumed by the sounds of bells, drums, pipes, and flutes;
their mouths savor the flavors of fine meats and wines;
such sensations stir their minds,
making them neglect their proper duties—
this can be called chaos.
They drown in arrogant pride,
as if carrying a heavy load up a slope—
this can be called suffering.
Greed for wealth brings anxiety;
greed for power exhausts them;
in idleness they sink into indulgence;
in physical comfort they grow arrogant—
this can be called sickness.
In their pursuit of riches and profit,
they amass wealth like a wall yet do not avoid its perils,
clinging stubbornly without release—
this can be called disgrace.
Wealth piles up unused,
yet they cling to it obsessively,
their hearts filled with worry and agitation,
ceaselessly seeking more—
this can be called distress.
At home, they fear the treachery of greedy servants;
abroad, they dread harm from bandits and thieves;
within, they fortify their homes with layered walls;
outside, they dare not walk alone—
this can be called terror.
These six conditions
are the gravest harms in the world,
yet all are overlooked and unexamined.
When calamity strikes,
even pleading to sacrifice all their wealth
for a single day of peace cannot be attained.
Thus, seeking fame brings no recognition,
pursuing profit yields no gain.
To entangle mind and body in such struggles—
is this not delusion?"
【One】【Memorial】Equality brings its blessings and goodness,
surplus attracts its disasters and harms—
this is the natural principle of heaven.
All things are like this,
and wealth is the most extreme case.
【二】【疏】谦逊，
被称为适度。
管籥，
属于箫笛之类的乐器。
那些富贵人家的人，
放纵情感，过度沉溺，
口中贪享美酒佳肴，
耳边充斥着纷繁音乐，
取舍之间扰乱心神，
接触事物便易受触动。
本性因此昏昧不明，
正业被遗忘，
毫无觉察，
这难道不是混乱吗！
【Explanation】"筦" is pronounced as guǎn.
Some versions also write it as 管.
"籥" is pronounced as yuè.
In one edition, "筦籥" is written as "壎".
"口嗛" is pronounced with 苦 as kǔ and 簟 as diǎn.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that 嗛 means satisfaction.
It signifies contentment.
According to Shuōwén,
嗛
refers to something held in the mouth (originally "satisfaction with" but corrected to "holding in the mouth").
In the Zhào Cè, "the food's satisfaction in Wèi,"
and Duke Huán of Qí not being satisfied with Yì Yá at midnight,
Gāo's annotations both state:
嗛
means contentment.
In Xúnzǐ's "Róngrǔ" chapter, "smelling it without satisfaction in the nose,"
Yáng Liáng read 嗛 as qiè,
explaining it as disgust.
This is incorrect.
"醪" is pronounced as láo.
【Three】【Manifestations】Fèng qì,
refers to pent-up frustration.
When desires for greed are numerous,
toil and hardship lead to exhaustion,
the heart becomes obstructed and stifled,
sinking into deep-seated resentment and discontent,
much like carrying a heavy load uphill.
Such weariness and distress,
is it not indeed a state of bitter hardship!
【Interpretation】"Gāi nì": Xú's pronunciation is ài,
wǔdài fǎn,
also hù gāi fǎn.
Food and drink reaching the throat is called gāi.
Another explanation:
pervasive.
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
The interpretation that food and drink reaching the throat is gāi
unduly forces a meaning to connect it.
Shuōwén:
qí gāi,
means extraordinary.
Yángzǐ's Fāngyán:
extraordinary things are called gāi shì.
Gāi nì,
is like saying deeply sunk or addicted.
"Yú píng qì": Píng,
pronounced fèn,
means full of indignation.
Same below.
Refers to the accumulation of blocked and indignant energy.
◎Wáng Niànsūn said:
The interpretation states,
píng qì,
píng pronounced fèn,
meaning full of indignation.
Refers to the accumulation of blocked and indignant energy.
According to the case, píng qì
means abundant energy.
In Zuǒzhuàn, the fifth year of Zhāo, "Now the lord rouses like thunder and lightning, píng nù,"
Dù's annotation says:
Píng,
means abundant.
In Chǔcí's Lísāo, "Píng bù yàn hū qiú suǒ,"
Wáng's annotation says:
Píng,
means full,
people of Chǔ call full píng.
This shows píng has the meaning of abundant and full,
there is no need to change the reading to fèn.
"Ér shàng": shí zhǎng fǎn.
【Four】【Indulgences】Greedily seizing wealth and treasures to gratify one's heart,
enticing and flattering those in power to exhaust one's emotions and thoughts,
in quiet and leisurely living, the body sinks into indulgence,
when the body's energy is pleased and smooth, resentment and distress arise,
whether in action or stillness, there is hardship and suffering—
is this not an affliction!
【Explanation】"取慰" – 慰 can also be written as 畏.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: 慰 should be understood as interchangeable with 蔚.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Chù Zhēn" chapter, it says "the five viscera lack 蔚氣",
Gao's annotation states:
蔚,
means illness.
In the "Miù Chēng" chapter, it mentions "dwarfs and blind musicians",
are people in distress and ailment,
Gao's annotation states:
慰,
means illness.
This shows that the two characters 蔚 and 慰,
were used interchangeably in ancient exegesis.
【Five】【Shū】Dǔ,
is a wall.
Those who desire wealth and pursue profit,
their feelings are like deep valleys and steep walls,
akin to that wall,
built up to the brim,
their hearts filled with resentment and frustration,
clinging greedily without letting go,
unaware of avoiding harm,
is this not a disgrace indeed!
【Transcription】"Bù shě" is pronounced as shě.
The same applies below.
【六】【疏】"Qī jiào" means vexation and distress.
Vexation and distress.
When one accumulates without dispersing,
clings without letting go,
greedily seeks without satisfaction,
vexation fills the heart,
if we deliberate and discuss it,
is it not indeed worry and suffering!
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: "Holding firm without letting go"
means the same as "clinging without letting go" mentioned above.
"Holding firm" means to rely on.
In the "Wén Xuǎn," the "Eulogy for the Meritorious Officials of Emperor Gaozu of Han" has "relying on the chest but still lacking."
(In the "Wén Xuǎn," "chest" is mistakenly written as "response."
Lǐ Shàn's annotation mistakenly interpreted it as relying on auspicious responses,
which is incorrect.
In ancient times, "response" and "chest" were homophones and used interchangeably.
In the "Kāng Gào," "respond to and protect the people of Yīn,"
in the "Zhōu Gào," it is "uphold and protect the people's virtue."
In the "Odes of Lǔ·Bì Gōng" poem, "the Róng and Dí are to be repelled,"
in the "Records of the Grand Historian," "Tables of Enfeoffed Ministers Since the Jiànyuán Era," "repelled" is written as "responded."
In the "Mèngzǐ·Téng Wéngōng" chapter, "the Róng and Dí are to be repelled,"
the "Yīnyì" says:
in the Dīng version, "repelled" is written as "responded."
) "Holding firm" as "relying on the chest"
is like "leaning on the carriage rail" as "relying on the rail,"
(In the "Records of the Grand Historian," the "Biography of Lì Shēng" says, "leaning on the rail, he subdued seventy cities of Qí,"
while the "Book of Hàn" writes it as "relying on the rail."
) "Bending over the qin" as "relying on the qin,"
(In the "Records of the Grand Historian," the "Hereditary House of Wèi" mentions "Zhōng Qí relying on the qin,"
the "Suǒyǐn" says:
the "Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ" writes it as "bending over the qin."
) "Cushion resting" as "cushion relying."
(In the "Records of the Grand Historian," the "Biographies of Cruel Officials" says, "never dared to share the cushion rest,"
while the "Book of Hàn" writes it as "cushion relying."
)"Qī jiào" is pronounced with the fanqie spelling "zài yáo fǎn."
Lǐ Yún says,
it means "distress."
Also pronounced as "zǐ miào fǎn."
【Seven】【Windows】Doubt,
is fear.
To request,
is to seek.
A common man is not guilty,
but possessing a precious jade becomes his crime.
Thus, at home, he fears the disaster of thieves seeking wealth,
and when traveling outside, he dreads the harm of bandits and rampant theft.
Therefore, around the courtyard walls,
windows and towers are built with openings,
open to both inside and out,
causing fear in comings and goings,
and one dares not walk alone.
Such hardships,
are they not out of fear indeed!
【Transcription】"疑" is pronounced as Xǔ Yè fǎn,
also as Qǔ Yè fǎn.
"Inner encircling towers and open corridors" Lǐ Yún explains:
Multiple layers of towers winding internally,
with open verandas connecting externally,
referring to the setup of defensive equipment.
【Eight】【Disasters】The six refer to chaos, suffering, sickness, disgrace, sorrow, and fear.
They are the ultimate harms under heaven,
often overlooked and unexamined.
When a great thief suddenly arrives,
life hangs by a thread;
all the greed and pursuits of a lifetime
are wiped out in an instant.
Every treasure one possesses
is exhausted at that very moment.
To wish to return to a day of simple poverty—
how could that be possible?
【Transcription】"Cái dān" is pronounced as dān.
Some versions have it as "qí",
pronounced as qí.
◎ Jiā Shìfù said:
The transcription states that the original text has "dān" as "qí",
pronounced as qí,
but now I consider the transcription incorrect.
"Dān" should be taken as "dǎn".
In the "Shǐjì·Lì Shū", it says "dān yān",
with Cuī Yīn's annotation:
"dān yān",
also written as "dǎn ān".
The characters "dān" and "dǎn" are interchangeable.
In the "Hànshū", the character "dàn" is often written as "dǎn".
In the "Jiǎ Yì Zhuàn", it says "not merely hanging upside down",
and in the "Yáng Xióng Zhuàn", "merely exhausting one's spirit on this".
The "Shuōwén" states:
"dàn",
means to bare.
Thus, "dàn" itself means to bare, and "chán" serves as "dàn".
"Dān" is used to express "merely for the sake of returning for a day without reason",
similar to saying "dàn" to mean "merely for the sake of returning for a day without reason".
The "Yùpiān" says:
"dān",
means one.
"One",
implies alone or solitary,
and its meaning is close to that of the character "dàn".
【Nine】【Commentary】This chapter speaks of how those who know contentment are always satisfied.
【Commentary】"Liáo" means
to entangle.
When a great thief arrives,
one's body is no longer one's own.
At that moment,
how could one still perceive fame and gain!
Yet the common people
are profoundly misguided,
their emotions entangled in fame and gain,
their hearts resolute in pursuit of contention.
Judging by this,
is it not the height of delusion!
【Explanation】"Liáo" is pronounced as liǎo,
and also has a reading of yú diào fǎn.
It means to manage.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "筦" is written as "管".
(2) The character "阪" has been emended according to Chéng's commentary.
Quēwù cites Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition as reading "阪",
which is the same as "阪".
(3) In Zhāng Jūnfáng's edition, "慰" is written as "辱".
(4) The two characters "銜也" have been emended following the annotation in the Strategies of the Warring States.
【一】【Explanation】Titled after the events described.
Long ago, King Wén of Zhào delighted in swordsmanship,
and swordsmen flocked to his gate as guests, numbering over three thousand.
Day and night they dueled before him,
with casualties exceeding a hundred each year,
yet his fondness for it never waned.
This continued for three years,
leading to the state's decline,
and the feudal lords plotted against him.
【First】【Memorial】King Huì of Zhào,
named Hé,
was the son of King Wǔlíng of Zhào.
He favored men skilled at swordplay,
kept three thousand retainers,
and his desires knew no satiety.
His state fell into decline and distress,
so the feudal lords, knowing his lack of virtue,
conspired together,
intending to launch an attack against him.
【Explanatory Text】"King Wén of Zhào" Simǎ comments:
It is King Huìwén,
named Hé,
son of King Wǔlíng,
350 years after Zhuāngzǐ.
Dòng Jì states:
In the seventeenth year of King Nǎn of Zhōu,
it was the first year of King Huìwén of Zhào.
Another source says:
According to calculations using the long calendar, King Huìwén's reign coincided with Zhuāngzǐ's time,
so Biāo's statement is likely mistaken.
"Loves swords" is pronounced xǐ jiàn with the initial sound as in "xǔ" and the rhyme as in "jì".
The same applies below.
"Flanking the gate" is read by Guō and Lǐ as xié,
alternatively as gǔ qià.
"Is fond of" is pronounced hǎo with the tone as in "hū bào".
The same applies below.
"Never satisfied" is pronounced wú yàn with the tone as in "yú yán",
or alternatively as "yú yàn".
◎ Lú Wénchāo states:
Nowadays, the text reads as "not satisfied".
Prince Kuì was troubled by this,
and offered a reward to his attendants, saying:
"Whoever can persuade the king to stop the swordsmen
will be rewarded with a thousand pieces of gold."
The attendants said:
"Zhuāngzǐ would surely be able to do it."
【一】【疏】Kuī,
is the name of the crown prince of Zhào.
He detested his father's fondness for warfare,
so he wished to offer a thousand in gold to recruit persuaders.
Zhuāngzǐ, being a great worthy,
should be able to halt the swords.
【Transcription】"Kui" is pronounced as kǔ huí fǎn,
the crown prince's name.
◎Yú Yuè says:
After King Huìwén came King Xiàochéng named Dān,
so this crown prince probably was not enthroned.
"Mu" is pronounced as mù,
also pronounced as wù.
"Shuō wáng" is read according to its character,
meaning to explain.
Also pronounced as yuè.
The crown prince then sent someone to present Zhuāngzǐ with a thousand pieces of gold.
Zhuāngzǐ did not accept it,
but went together with the messenger
to see the crown prince, saying:
"What instructions does the crown prince have for Zhōu,
that you bestow upon Zhōu a thousand pieces of gold?"
The Crown Prince said:
"Having heard of your wisdom and sagacity,
I reverently present a thousand pieces of gold as gifts for your attendants.
Since you decline to accept,
what more dare Kuī say!"
【一】【疏】What matter do you wish to teach me,
that you bestow a thousand pieces of gold?
Since I saw the large amount of gold,
I therefore ask.
The Crown Prince said:
"I have heard that you, Master, are virtuous, wise, and sagely,
therefore I present a thousand pieces of gold to supply the silk and goods for your followers."
【Explanatory Text】"Yǔ shǐ" is read as suǒ lì fǎn.
"Yǐ bì cóng" is read as cái yòng fǎn.
One version writes it as "yǐ bì cóng zhě".
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The old text erroneously has "jūn",
now corrected.
The current text includes the character "zhě".
【Collation Note】(1) The Que Wu cites Zhang Junfáng's version, where "shàng" is written as "dāng".
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"I hear that what the Crown Prince wishes to use me for,
is to put an end to the King's preferences.
If I were to persuade the King above and go against his wishes,
and fail to meet the Crown Prince's expectations below,
then I would suffer physical punishment and die—
how then could I still have any use for gold?
But if I persuade the King above,
and satisfy the Crown Prince below,
what in the state of Zhào could not be obtained!"
The Crown Prince said:
"Indeed.
What our king sees,
are only swordsmen."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Very well.
I, Zhōu, am skilled at swordsmanship."
The Crown Prince said:
"Yet the swordsmen our king has seen,
all have disheveled hair, bristling sideburns, and drooping hats,
coarse tassels,
garments short in the back,
glaring fiercely and speaking with difficulty—
it is these that please the king.
Now if you, sir, insist on wearing Confucian robes to see the king,
the matter will surely go greatly awry.
【一】【疏】Hair disheveled like overgrown reeds,
sideburns protruding sharply,
an iron crown,
hanging down to reveal the face.
The coarse tassels of the Mánhú style,
refer to the wrapped neck and forehead covering.
Garments with short backs,
designed for ease in martial affairs.
Eyes wide with glaring anger,
the demeanor of a brave warrior,
chest filled with fury,
hence the voice is hoarse and strained.
Such is the appearance and attire of a swordsman.
【Explanation Text】"Shàng" is read as its standard pronunciation,
also pronounced with the initial "sh" and the rhyme "ui" with a sharp tone.
The same applies below.
"Péng" is pronounced with the initial "b" and the rhyme "u" in the level tone, followed by "gōng" in the level tone.
Some versions write it as ●,
which is the same.
"Tóu" refers to disheveled hair,
meaning wearing a helmet.
It has fur,
hence resembling péng grass.
"Tū bìn" is pronounced with the initial "b" and the rhyme "in" with a sharp tone.
Simǎ's version writes it as "bīn",
and states:
"bīn" should be read as "bìn".
"Chuí guān" means when about to fight,
the cap is tilted low.
"Màn hú" is pronounced with the initial "m" and the rhyme "an" in the level tone, followed by "hú" in the level tone.
Simǎ states:
"Màn hú's tassels",
refer to coarse tassels without pattern.
"Duǎn hòu zhī yī" is for convenience in action.
"Chēn mù" has two pronunciations: one with the initial "ch" and the rhyme "i" in the level tone, and another with the initial "ch" and the rhyme "en" in the level tone.
"Yǔ nán" is read as its standard pronunciation.
It means difficulty;
the warrior's angry energy accumulates in the chest,
making speech not fluent.
Also pronounced with the initial "n" and the rhyme "an" with a sharp tone,
meaning speaking in anger,
being feared and avoided by others.
Simǎ states:
it describes the appearance of clashing.
"Nǎi shuō" is pronounced as "yuè".
The same applies to "dà shuō" below.
Zhuāngzǐ said:

After three days of preparing the sword attire,
he then went to see the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince then took him to see the King,
who bared a gleaming blade awaiting him.
Zhuāngzǐ entered the palace hall without hastening his steps,
and upon seeing the King, did not bow.
The King said:
"What do you intend to teach me,
that you had the Crown Prince precede you?"
【One】【Memorial】Those who are self-content,
have no fear within their hearts,
and thus do not rush about.
【Explanation】"With see" is pronounced as xián biàn fǎn.
The following jiàn see is the same.
Also read as the common pronunciation.
"King's removal" one version writes as shuō,
same.
Pronounced as tǔ huó fǎn.
【Èr Shū】What method do you intend to use to admonish me,
and have the crown prince speak to me first?
He said:
"I have heard that Your Majesty delights in swordsmanship,
and so I have come to see you with my sword."
The king asked:
"What power does your sword possess to enforce prohibitions?"
Said:
"My sword,
with ten steps, one man falls;
across a thousand miles, none can impede its course."
King Wáng was greatly pleased,
saying:
"Invincible under heaven!"
【One】【Sword】Its blade slays one at ten paces,
departs a thousand miles away,
moves without lingering,
so sharp and swift,
could there be any match for it!
【Interpretation】"A thousand lǐ without leaving a trace of passage" Sīmǎ explains:
Within ten steps, when engaging in combat with one person,
they are invariably killed,
hence over a thousand lǐ, there is no lingering passage.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
Within ten steps,
invariably killing one person,
then traversing a distance of a thousand lǐ,
the number killed is vast,
yet the sword's edge does not dull,
and what it encounters does not bend it,
this is what is meant by ten steps one person,
a thousand lǐ without leaving a trace of passage,
extremely emphasizing the sharpness of the sword.
"Passage" refers to the sword,
not to the person,
as the following text mentions "passage in autumn and winter" confirms this.
Sīmǎ explains,
within ten steps, engaging in combat with one person and invariably killing them,
hence over a thousand lǐ, there is no lingering passage.
This does not capture the intended meaning.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"In the art of swordsmanship,
one shows emptiness,
opens with advantage,
follows with a delayed strike,
yet arrives first.
I wish to test this【one】."
【一】【疏】The Way of swordsmanship lies in,
thus forgetting oneself and emptying the mind,
opening up to benefit all things,
responding only after being moved,
perceiving opportunities before they manifest in things—
this is Zhuāngzǐ's application of the sword.
The king said:
"May the Master rest and retire to his quarters,
await the command to set up an entertainment for the Master."
【One】【Memorial】The wording is pure and far-reaching,
moving the king's heart,
so he ordered a rest,
humbly settling into the guesthouse,
awaiting the arrangement of swordplay entertainment,
before then extending an invitation.
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhāng Jūnfáng edition does not have the character "lìng".
The king then tested the swordsmen for seven days,
resulting in over sixty casualties,
and selected five or six men.
He had them present their swords beneath the palace hall
and then summoned Zhuāngzǐ.
The king said:
"Today, I shall have the men test their swords with vigor."
【One】【Test】Dùn,
means to cut.
Try displaying swordsmen,
and have them compete in cutting to determine superiority and inferiority.
【Explanatory Text】"Nǎi jiào" Sīmǎ comments:
It means examining and selecting the superior one.
Jiào,
some versions have it as jiāo.
"Shì dūn" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
Sīmǎ comments:
Dūn means
to sever,
to test by having them use swords to strike and cut each other off.
Another pronunciation is dīng huí fǎn.
◎Jiā Shìfù says:
The explanatory text quotes Sīmǎ as saying,
dūn means
to sever.
To test by having them use swords to strike and cut off.
In the annotation of the Odes of Bèi, "wáng shì dūn wǒ,"
dūn
is like throwing.
In the annotation of the Odes of Lǔ, "dūn shāng zhī lǚ,"
dūn
means to govern.
Dūn jiàn means the intention to govern the sword.
Shuōwén explains:
Dūn
means anger,
one interpretation is to question or challenge.
Questioning or challenging
is like saying no one can do anything to me,

Mutual comparison
thus leads to anger.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"I have long been looking forward to this."
【First】【Memorial】I have been looking forward to this for a long time,
and I request an early trial of it.
The king asked:
"The staff that you, Master, wield,
how long is it?"
He said:
"All that Your Majesty commands, I can fulfill.
However, I possess three swords,
for the King to choose from as he wishes.
Allow me to describe them first before putting them to the test."
means to use.
It is said that Zhuāng Zǐ was skilled at sword fighting,
hence he was asked about it.
【Explanatory Text】"Yùzhàng" is read with the pronunciation zhí liàng fǎn.
"Suǒ fèng" is written as suǒ zòu in the Sīmǎ version.
The king said:
"I wish to hear about the three swords."
He said:
"There is the sword of the Son of Heaven,
there is the sword of the feudal lords,
and there is the sword of the common people (1)."
【Collation Note】(1) In the Kōzan-ji manuscript, the three instances of the character "sword" all have the character "之" above them.
The king asked:
"What is the Son of Heaven's sword like?"
He said:
"The Son of Heaven's sword,
has Yānxī and Shíchéng as its point,
Qí and Dài as its edge,
Jìn and Wèi as its spine,
Zhōu and Sòng as its hilt,
Hán and Wèi as its guard;
it is enveloped by the four barbarian tribes,
wrapped by the four seasons;
encircled by the Bó Hǎi Sea,
girded by the Cháng Shān Mountains;
governed by the five phases,
deliberated through punishments and virtues;
opened through yīn and yáng,
upheld through spring and summer,
and wielded through autumn and winter.
This sword,
when thrust forward, nothing stands before it,
when raised, nothing is above it,
when pressed down, nothing is below it,
when swung, nothing is beside it;
above, it cleaves floating clouds,
below, it severs the earth's fabric.
Once this sword is employed,
it rectifies the feudal lords,
and the whole world submits.
This is the Son of Heaven's sword."
【One】【Explanation】Fēng,
is the tip of the sword.
È,
is the blade.
Yānxī,
is in the state of Yān;
Shíchéng,
is a mountain beyond the frontier;
this place is located in the north,
and is considered the sword's tip.
The Dàiyuè of the state of Qí is in the east,
and serves as the sword's blade.
【Translated Text】"Yān" is pronounced as yān.
"Xī" refers to Yānxī,
a place name,
located in the state of Yān.
"Shíchéng" is situated beyond the frontier.
"È" is pronounced with the initial "wǔ" and final "gè".
Sīmǎ explains:
it means the blade of a sword.
Another explanation:
it refers to the edge of a sword.
The two Shu swords,
have rings.
The states of Jìn and Wèi were close to the territory of Zhào,
therefore they are used for the spine.
The states of Zhōu and Sòng were near the south,
therefore they are used for the rings.
【Translated Text】"Tán" is pronounced as yín.
The Sān Cāng states:
It is pronounced with the reverse of tǎn,
meaning the mouth of a sword.
Xú gives the reverse as tán,
and also the reverse as tuò,
referring to the sword ring.
Sīmǎ explains:
It is the sword ear.
【Three】【Shū】Jiá,
means handle.
The states of Hán and Wèi are to the west of Zhào,
hence they are considered the handle.
【Translated Text】"Wéi jiā" is pronounced as gǔ xié fǎn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means to grasp.
One version writes it as "jiá",
which is the same.
Another explanation says:
The guard,
extends from the ridge toward the back;
the blade edge,
extends from the ridge toward the cutting edge.
【Four】【Dissemination】Embrace the four barbarians with virtue,
accord with the four seasons to foster growth and transformation.
【Explanatory Text】"Wrapped in" is pronounced guǒ.
【Five】【Regions】Bóhǎi is
Cāngzhōu.
Chángshān is
the Northern Mountain.
Within the creation of nature,
it uses mountains and seas to anchor the land.
【Six】【Categories】 are the five phases,
metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
Xíng,
means punishment;
dé,
means moral transformation.
Using these five phases,
to govern and regulate the world,
discussing their punishments and virtues,
to rule all living beings.
【Seven】【Memorials】The opening and closing of yīn and yáng,
the sustenance of spring and summer,
the stern execution of autumn and winter,
are the way of nature.
【Explanation】"Acting in autumn and winter" means following the way of heaven to advance or rest.
【Eight】【Explanations】Using the Dao as a sword,
it encompasses everything without exception.
Thus, it connects above and below, unimpeded in all directions;
nothing can obstruct it.
Floating clouds and the earth's order,
how could they even be worth mentioning!
Since it takes creation itself as its function,
therefore, there is nothing it does not subdue.
【Collation】(1)(2) In the Kōzanji version, "Wèi" is written as "Wèi".
King Wén looked bewildered and lost,
asking:
"What about the sword of the feudal lords?"
【One】【Memorial】When one's talent is small but hears of grand matters,
unable to comprehend them,
then one is bewildered as if crossing the sea,
losing grasp of what is meant,
akin to King Wèi Huì of Wèi hearing the Sháo music.
【Explanation】"Máng rán" is pronounced with the initial consonant "mò" and the final "gāng" in reverse.
He said:
"The sword of the feudal lords
has wise and brave men as its tip,
has incorruptible and upright men as its edge,
has virtuous and capable men as its spine,
has loyal and sagacious men as its guard,
has heroic and outstanding men as its hilt (1).
This sword,
when thrust forward, nothing stands before it;
when raised, nothing is above it;
when pressed down, nothing is beneath it;
when swung, nothing is beside it;
above, it models after the round heaven to follow the three luminaries;
below, it models after the square earth to follow the four seasons;
in the middle, it harmonizes with the people's will to pacify the four regions (1).
Once this sword is put to use,
it is like the rumble of thunder:
within the four borders,
there is none who does not submit and obey the ruler's commands.
This is the sword of the feudal lords (2)."
【One】【To Govern】 the four regions,
is akin to the four directions.
One who can emulate heaven and earth and understand the nature of all things,
is said to be what sets the feudal lords apart.
If one can wield this sword accordingly and rule over the states,
they will be invincible throughout the land.
【二】【疏】Why is the Zhen hexagram used to represent the feudal lords?
Thus, thunder and lightning are the swords of the feudal lords.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "virtuous and good" is written as "virtuous and sage,"
in the Shidetang edition and Zhào's edition, "loyal and sage" is written as "loyal and victorious,"

The king asked:
"What about the commoner's sword?"
He said:
"The commoner's sword
involves disheveled hair, bristling sideburns, and drooping hats,
coarse tassels,
garments short in the back,
with glaring eyes and contentious speech.

striking upward to sever necks,

unparalleled throughout the ages,

【Transcription】"Liver and lungs": fāng fèi fǎn.
"Secretly for": yú wèi fǎn.
The king then led him up to the hall.
The cook presented the meal,
and the king circled around it three times.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Great king, please sit calmly and steady your breath,
the matter of the sword has already been fully presented."
意为环绕。
国王意识到自己的过错，
内心深感羞愧与厌恶，
便命庄子登殿以表达愧疚之情，

Thereupon, King Wén did not leave his palace for three months,
and all the swordsmen died in their places (note 1)【note 1】.
【One】【Memorial】He no longer accepted rewards,
hence he died of resentment.
【Explanation】"Fú bì": bì is pronounced with a shì initial.
Sīmǎ explains:
Resentful at not receiving proper courtesy,
they all took their own lives.
【Collation】（一）The Gāoshānsì version and the scroll version both read "fú bì qí chù yǐ" for "fú bì qí chù yě".
【Chapter One】【Explanatory Text】Named after a person.
Confucius was wandering in the Forest of Zīwéi,
and rested sitting on the Apricot Altar.
His disciples were reading,
while Confucius played the zither and sang, strumming the qín,
but before the melody was halfway through.

means black.
When Fùzǐ traveled throughout the land,
reading and expounding on the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents,
he would sometimes stop by the riverbank,
resting amidst the forest's murmurs.
The forest was lush and dense,
shading the sun and casting deep shadows,
with leaves spread wide and branches hanging low,
resembling a curtain or canopy,
hence it was called the Forest of the Zīwéi.
Tán,
refers to an elevated area within a marsh.
That place was abundant with apricot trees,
so it was named the Apricot Terrace.
The qín,
symbolizes harmony,
capable of harmonizing the heart and nurturing one's nature,

There was an old fisherman,

with his beard and eyebrows both white,
his hair disheveled and sleeves fluttering,

and stopped upon reaching the high ground,
his left hand resting on his knee,
his right hand supporting his chin as he listened.

and both of them responded to him.

changed his name,

the one whom Qū Yuán encountered.
