where he was called Chīyí Zǐ;
reached Lǔ,
where he was called Báiguī Xiānshēng;
reached Táo,
where he was called Zhū Gōng.
He concealed his traces and hid his brilliance,
adapting to the times and changing form,
and subsequently sent a letter to Minister Wén Zhǒng.
Yú,
means to wave.
Mèi,
means sleeve.
Yuán,
means high plain.
Jù,
means to reach.
Hair and eyebrows both white,
is the appearance of a long-lived person;
loose hair without a cap,
is the look of a rustic man.
Thereupon, gazing afar at the plain,
he waved his sleeves with his hand,
reaching the high land,
moored the boat and stopped,
rested his chin on his knees,
to listen to the zither and songs.

both.

The guest said:
"Like attracts like,
and similar voices answer each other;
this is indeed the principle of Heaven.
Let me explain what I possess and thereby analyze your concerns.
What you concern yourself with
are human affairs.
When the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, high officials, and common people
—these four categories—each maintain their proper positions,
it represents the pinnacle of governance.
Should these four deviate from their positions, no disorder could be greater.
When officials attend to their duties
and people mind their own affairs,
then nothing will be transgressed.
Thus, fields lying barren and houses exposed,
insufficient clothing and food,
taxes and levies not being paid,
wives and concubines not living in harmony,
and the absence of order between elders and youth—
these are the worries of common people;
inability to fulfill one's responsibilities,
official duties not being properly managed,
conduct not being pure and upright,
subordinates being negligent and idle,
lacking any commendable achievements,
and being unable to maintain one's rank and emolument—
these are the worries of high officials;
the court lacking loyal ministers,
the state being in turmoil and disorder,
crafts and techniques not being refined,
tribute offerings not being excellent,
falling behind in spring and autumn court audiences,
and not showing deference to the Son of Heaven—
these are the worries of feudal lords;
the yīn and yáng forces being imbalanced,
cold and heat occurring unseasonably,
thereby harming all things,
feudal lords engaging in violent rebellions,
arbitrarily attacking one another,
thus bringing harm to the people,
rituals and music not being properly regulated,
financial resources being exhausted and depleted,
human relationships not being properly maintained,
and the common people indulging in debauchery and disorder—
these are the worries of the Son of Heaven and his officials.
Now, you neither possess the authority of the sovereign, feudal lords, or officials above,
yet you presumptuously adorn rituals and music,
select human relationships,
in order to transform the ordinary people—
is this not excessively meddlesome!"
【One】【Memorial】When the tiger roars, the wind races;
when the dragon rises, the clouds spread—
such is the natural principle,
and indeed it is so!
Thus, the Fisherman, a great worthy,
and Xuānní, the ultimate sage,
worthies and sages resonate with each other,
as like voices respond in harmony.
Therefore, I relinquish my Way beyond the mundane world
to manage your affairs within the secular realm.
【Explanation】"As for the reason why the classics and masters..." The classics,
refer to planning and management.
Sīmǎ explains:
the classics,
mean to organize or manage.
【Two】【Neglects】 encroachment,
also leads to chaos.
Matters of human relations,
indeed are multifaceted,
but in essence,
none surpass these four.
If these four maintain their positions,
then governance and education flourish splendidly,
but if superiors and inferiors infringe upon each other,
then no chaos is greater than this.
Therefore, all officials should attend to their respective duties,
and the common people should mind their own affairs,
without encroaching upon or disrupting each other,
this is the unchangeable way.

elders and youngsters lack any proper sequence,
these are the worries and hardships of the common people.

Moreover, people have eight flaws,
and affairs have four perils,
which must not go unexamined.
To meddle in matters not one's own is called
overreach;
【I】to press forward when none heed you
is called obsequiousness;
to echo others' wishes in speech
is called flattery;
to speak without distinguishing right from wrong
is called sycophancy;
to delight in speaking of others' faults
is called slander;
to sever friendships and estrange kin
is called treachery;
to praise deceit and falsehood to ruin others
is called villainy;
to ignore good and bad,
accommodating both sides with duplicity,
and stealthily advancing one's own desires
is called cunning.
These eight flaws
bring chaos to others externally
and harm to oneself internally,
making the noble person shun such friendship
and the enlightened ruler reject such servitude.
The so-called four perils are:
fondness for managing great affairs,
altering established norms,
to clutch at merit and fame—
this is called greed for glory;
monopolizing knowledge and controlling matters,
encroaching on others while self-assertive—
this is called avarice;
seeing errors but not correcting them,
hearing admonitions and growing worse—
this is called obstinacy;
approving only those who agree with oneself,
and rejecting those who differ,
deeming even good as not good—
this is called arrogance.
These are the four perils.
Only when one can rid oneself of the eight flaws
and avoid practicing the four perils
may one become fit for instruction."

Confucius looked sorrowful and sighed,

"I, Qiū, was twice driven out of Lǔ,
had my tracks erased in Wèi,
trees were felled because of me in Sòng,
and I was besieged in Chén and Cài.
I do not know what faults I committed,
yet why have I encountered these four slanders?"

a countenance of shame and awe.

The guest, with a sorrowful change of countenance, said:
"How profoundly you are difficult to enlighten!
There was a man who, fearing his shadow and disliking his footprints, tried to run away from them.
The more he lifted his feet, the more footprints he created;
the faster he ran, the closer his shadow clung to him (note 1).
Thinking himself still too slow,
he raced on without rest,
exhausting his strength until he died.
He did not know that by staying in the shade, he could rest his shadow,
and by remaining still, he could cease his footprints.
How exceedingly foolish he was!
You scrutinize the boundaries of benevolence and righteousness,
examine the distinctions between similarity and difference,
observe the transformations of movement and stillness,
adjust the measures of giving and receiving,
regulate the emotions of likes and dislikes,
and harmonize the rhythms of joy and anger,
yet you are nearly unavoidable [in hardship] (note 1).
Diligently cultivate your own person,
carefully guard your authenticity,
and return things to others,
then you will have nothing to burden you (note 2).
Now, if you do not cultivate yourself but make demands of others (note 2),
is that not focusing on the external? (note 3)"
【一】【疏】Lingering between benevolence and righteousness to attract followers,
observing the nuances of similarities and differences to await opportune moments,
watching the shifts in movement and stillness,
hoping for a stroke of luck,
adjusting the measure of giving and receiving,
aspiring for fame and achievement,
managing the feelings of likes and dislikes,
yet stubbornly holding onto right and wrong,
harmonizing the rhythm of joy and anger,
using it as a means to attain the Way,
teaching others based on oneself,
priding oneself on correcting innate nature,
approaches the unavoidable.
【Translated Text】"Difficult to Speak" yú jù fǎn.

Confucius looked solemn and said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'the genuine'?"
【一】【疏】To stand in awe of oneself.
The guest said:
"Authenticity is
the ultimate of essential sincerity.
Without essence and sincerity,
one cannot move others.
Thus, forced weeping may sound sorrowful but lacks grief,
forced anger may appear stern but lacks awe,
forced affection may smile but lacks harmony.
True grief is soundless yet mournful,
true anger unexpressed yet awe-inspiring,
true affection unsmiling yet harmonious.
When authenticity resides within,
the spirit manifests outwardly—
this is why authenticity is valued.
Applied to human relations,
it brings tender devotion in serving parents,
loyal steadfastness in serving rulers,
joyful merriment in drinking,
and heartfelt sorrow in mourning.
Loyal steadfastness prioritizes achievement,
drinking prioritizes pleasure,
mourning prioritizes grief,
serving parents prioritizes appropriateness—
the perfection of accomplishment
leaves no uniform traces.
Serving parents with appropriateness
doesn't debate the methods;
drinking for pleasure
doesn't select the utensils;
mourning with grief
doesn't question the rites.
Rites are
creations of worldly customs;
authenticity is
what is received from Heaven,
inherent and unchangeable.
Thus, the sage emulates Heaven and values authenticity,
unconstrained by customs.
The foolish do the opposite.
Failing to emulate Heaven while fretting over human opinions,
ignorant of valuing authenticity,
they busily accommodate worldly changes,
thus remaining unfulfilled.
Alas,
that you were steeped early in human artifice and learned the great Way so late!"
【One】【Memorial】What is genuine is not false,
what is pure is not mixed,
and what is sincere is not feigned.
Therefore, those who feign emotions and falsify their nature
cannot move others.
【二】【疏】The Way is omnipresent,
and wherever it exists, it connects all things.
Therefore, when applied to human relationships,
it manifests in these four matters.
The meaning of these four matters
is detailed in the text that follows.
【Explanation】"故強" is pronounced as "qí zhàng fǎn".
The same applies below.
"歡樂" is pronounced as "yīn luò".
The same applies below.
【Three】【Memorials】Constancy is the backbone of affairs,
and thus takes achievement as its core;
drinking wine mellows and stirs the disposition,
hence it takes joy as its essence.
Therefore, merit lies in its beauty,
and so one cannot treat these deeds as one and the same.
【Four】【Explanations】This further elucidates the four meanings discussed earlier.
【Five】【Expositions】The rituals that regulate refinement and ornamentation,
are established by worldly customs.
The genuine nature,
is endowed from the Great Simplicity,
and is so of its own accord,
thus it cannot be altered.
【Six】【Dissertation】Emulating nature,
treasuring the true Way,
thus not being constrained by worldly rituals.
means to worry.
祿祿，
describes a noble appearance.
Foolish and deluded individuals,
contrary to the ways of the sages,
are unable to follow nature to achieve ease,
or value the Dao and virtue to wander freely.
Instead, they drown in human affairs and anxieties,
stagnate in the noisy dust and change restlessly,
pursuing material things without satisfaction,
thus their hearts are perpetually discontent.
【Explanation】"Lù lù" is read as it is,
also pronounced as lù,
meaning the form appearing as ritual.
Sīmǎ says:
Lù,
is to oversee and record.
◎ Qìng Fān's note: Lù in Sīmǎ's version is written as lù.
The annotation of Liú Gōnggàn's miscellaneous poems in Wěnxuǎn quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
To oversee (lù) [record] (lù) also.
The character (lù) [record] is not present above overseeing,
differing from the explanation text.
【八】【疏】Alas, Confucius with his heroic talent,
long deluded by the traces of the sages,
indulged in the vain falsities of the human world,
and did not early hear of the mysterious Way.
【Textual Explanation】"蚤" is pronounced as zǎo.
The character is also written as 早.
"湛" is pronounced as dān nán fǎn,
the same applies below.
【Collation Notes】(1) In the Kōzan-ji version, "bēi" is written as "jí".
(2) Also, "wèi fā" is written as "bù yán".
(3) Also, "wèi" is written as "bù".
(4) Additionally, below "lùn" there is the character "qí".
(5) The Shidetáng edition does not have the character "rén".
(6) Both instances of "lù" have been emended according to the Wénxuǎn.
Confucius bowed twice again and rose, saying:
"Today, I, Qiū, have been granted this encounter,
as if by heavenly favor.
You, sir, do not disdain to treat me as one of your attendants,
and personally instruct me.
I venture to ask where your dwelling is,
so I may receive your teachings and complete my study of the great Way."
One】
【一】【疏】Confucius was overjoyed,
sighing at his own fortune,
having encountered the Fisherman,
as elated as ascending to heaven.
Surely he would not disdain the instruction,
and soon would devote himself to diligent service,
hoping to become a disciple,
personally receiving teachings,
inquiring about the dwelling place,
to ultimately study the great Way.
【Explanation】"Qiū dé guò yě" means having faults or errors.
Guò,
sometimes written as yù (note 2).
◎Qìng Fān's commentary: The variant reading where guò is sometimes written as yù is correct.
The characters for yù and guò are similar in shape,
leading to their frequent mistaken interchange,
as discussed previously.
"Ér bǐ" is read with the standard pronunciation,
meaning to personally meet and be counted among.
Also read with the bǐzhì pronunciation.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Kōzanji version does not have the character 为 below.
(2) The current text writes it as 遇.
The guest said:
"I have heard that
those with whom you can journey, journey with them,
reaching the wondrous Way;
those with whom you cannot journey,
who do not understand the Way,
carefully avoid accompanying them,
and your person will be free from blame.
Strive diligently, my friend!
I take my leave of you,
I take my leave of you!"
Then he punted the boat and departed,
winding his way through the reeds.
【一】【疏】To transition from confusion to enlightenment is the path forward.
The wondrous Way,
is the true essence.
Knowledge,
is discrimination.
If one encounters a person of superior wisdom,
one can speak with them about the wondrous essence;
if one meets a person of inferior capacity,
one cannot discuss the profound ultimate with them.
Observe the opportunity and radiate illumination,
only then will there be no flaw.
【Èr Shū】 admonished Confucius,
urging him to exert himself.
They lingered among the reeds.
Repeatedly advising him to depart,
they earnestly instructed and encouraged him.
【Transcription】"Nà cì" qī yì fǎn.
Yán Yuān turned the carriage around,
Zǐlù handed over the reins,
but Confucius did not look back,
waiting until the water ripples calmed,
and not hearing the sound of oars before daring to mount the carriage【一】.
【一】【疏】After Confucius had encountered the extraordinary man who imparted the ultimate Way to him,
he therefore revered him even more profoundly,
with joy and fear intermingling in his heart.
His disciples handed him the carriage strap,
yet he did not even glance back.
Only when the boat was far and the waves had calmed,
and the sound of oars could no longer be heard,
did he dare to mount the carriage.
【Explanation】"Bō Dìng" Lǐ Yún said:
It means the battle is like waves.
According to the case, it means the boat's movement causes water waves,
and when it goes far away, the waves calm down.
Zǐlù reined in the carriage and asked:
"I, Yóu, have had the privilege of serving you for a long time,
yet I have never seen you treat anyone with such deference.
Lords of ten thousand chariots,
rulers of a thousand chariots,
when meeting you have always shared the courtyard as equals in ceremony,
yet you still maintained a dignified and reserved demeanor.
Now this old fisherman stands holding his paddle facing you,
yet you bend your waist like a chiming stone,
respond with bowed words and gestures,
is this not excessive?
All your disciples find your behavior strange—
how does this fisherman deserve such treatment?
【First】【Commentary】The Son of Heaven commands ten thousand chariots,
while the feudal lords possess a thousand chariots.
Kàng,
means to face each other.
They are positioned separately in the courtyard,
setting rituals facing one another,
their status and prestige being similar,
with no hierarchical distinction.
When Zhòngní encountered the Son of Heaven or feudal lords,
he still harbored an attitude of pride,
yet upon meeting a fisherman,
he bent his waist fully in courtesy,
accepted his words,
responded with bows,
such was the fisherman's authority and dignity,
that it reached this extent.
Kǒng Qiū valued the ways beyond the mundane world,
whereas Zǐlù was a man of the secular realm,
hence he was startled and doubtful,
and asked from beside the carriage.
【Text Explanation】"Páng chē" reads as bù làng fǎn.
"Wàn shèng" reads as shéng zhèng fǎn.
The same applies below.
"Jù" sounds like jù.
"Áo" reads as wǔ bào fǎn.
"Qǔ yāo" reads as yī yáo fǎn.
"Qìng zhé" reads as zhī shè fǎn.
Confucius leaned on the carriage rail and sighed, saying:
"How persistent are Yóu's difficulties in being transformed!
He has been immersed in ritual and righteousness for some time,
yet his crude and vulgar heart has not been shed to this day.
Come forward,
let me tell you!
To encounter elders without respect
is to fail in propriety;
to see the virtuous without honoring them
is to lack benevolence.
If one is not a perfect man,
one cannot humble oneself before others;
if such humility is not genuine,
one cannot attain the truth,
thus often harming oneself.
Alas!
For a person to lack benevolence,
no misfortune is greater,
and Yóu alone excels in this.
Moreover, the Way
is that from which all things arise.
When creatures lose it, they perish;
when they attain it, they live.
In undertaking affairs, to oppose it leads to failure,
while to follow it brings success.
Therefore, wherever the Way resides,
the sage honors it.
Now, as for the old fisherman's relation to the Way,
he may be said to possess it.
How dare I not respect him!"
【One】【Memorial】Profoundly versed in rites and righteousness,
enduring through time indeed long,
alas for their vulgar clumsiness,
thus leaning on the carriage rail, I sigh over it.
【Transcription】"Zhàn yú" Zhàn,
sometimes written as qí.
【二】【疏】Summoned Zǐlù to come forward,
showing him how to advance and approach,
for if one encounters elders without respect,
then one fails in etiquette and propriety;
if one sees the worthy without honoring them,
then the heart lacks benevolence and love.
Unless one is a person of utmost virtue,
then one cannot make others humble and deferential;
if humility and deference are not sincere,
then one does not reach the profound ultimate.
Without benevolence and love,
lies the foundation of disaster and ruin.
Alas, Zǐlù,
how you erred in this regard!
【Transcription】"Xià rén": xiá jià fǎn.
Xià and the annotation are the same.
【Three】【Comment】This chapter speaks of those who attain leisure without retreating to rivers and seas,
yet are capable of humbling those who do retreat to rivers and seas.
Now, what Confucius allowed himself in freedom,
was it merely the Fisherman's way?
He would roam through the six voids,
penetrate everywhere without exclusion,
so that all creeping beings
could fully express their innermost thoughts,
and by exhausting principles and fulfilling destiny,
(thus) [truly] (two) he embodied the Way of the Perfect Man.
【Commentary】Yóu means
"to follow."
Shù means
"multitude."
The Way gives birth to all things,
thus it is called the Way.
Therefore, it is understood that the multitude is born from following the Way.
Hence, those who comply and attain it will live and flourish,
while those who oppose and lose it will die and perish.
Things have no inherent nobility or baseness;
wherever the Way resides, there is honor.
Since the Old Fisherman embodied the Way,
how could Confucius not respect him!
【Textual Explanation】"而閒" is pronounced as xián.
"蝡" is pronounced as in ruǎn with a rising tone.
【Collation Notes】(1) In the Kōzan-ji manuscript, "xián" is written as "guì".
(2) The character "gù" has been amended according to the Shidetáng edition.
【一】【Explanation】Named after a person.
Some versions do not have the character "liè".
Liè Yùkòu was going to Qí,
but halfway there he turned back,
where he met Bóhūn Màorén.
Bóhūn Màorén asked,
"What made you turn back?"
【First】【Memorial】Bó Hūn,
a virtuous scholar of Chǔ,
was known as Bó Hūn Mào Rén,
one of the reclusive kind.
Yù Kòu, having studied under Hú Zǐ,
also served Bó Hūn.
Just as he was about to go to Qí,
walking on the path of transformation,
he became alarmed at his own shallow practice,
and turned back midway.
It was then that he encountered Mào Rén,
who asked him the reason.
【Transcription】"Mào rén" pronounced as mào,
also pronounced as wù.
【二】【疏】Fāng,
means the Way.
Xī,
means what.
By what Way do you proceed?
To which direction do you wish to go?
This asks the reason for turning back midway.
【Explanation】"Xī Fāng" Lǐ Yún said:
Fāng means
the Way.
He said:
"I was startled."
【One】【Memorial】Realizing one's own faults,
being alarmed and fearful, then turning back,
this briefly addresses the previous question's intent.
【Interpretation】"I was startled by it" Lǐ Yún said:
Upon seeing someone moved by oneself, one immediately becomes startled and distances.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
The old text had 'moved' written as 'confused',
which is erroneous.
Now the textual notes say that upon seeing someone moved by oneself, one immediately deviates from the path,
hence the startle.
This seems to have omissions or errors.
He said:
"Why are you startled?"
【First】【Memorial】Repeatedly inquired about the origins of the bandit suppression campaign, startled by what events.
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
He said:
"I once ate at ten congee shops,
and five of them served me first."
【一】【注】The family that sells fermented rice drink.
【Translated Text】"Ten Jiāng (water radical changed to food radical)" Zǐ Xiáng's pronunciation.
Originally also written as jiāng.
Sīmǎ explains:
Jiāng (water radical changed to food radical) is read as jiāng,
meaning ten households all selling jiāng.
【二】【注】This speaks of their respect for oneself.
【Commentary】"Kuì" means
to give as a gift.
"Ten beverages"
refers to there being ten households selling drinks.
Lièzǐ, while walking and thirsty,
came upon ten inns selling drinks,
and five of them gave to him first.
Upon seeing his appearance and demeanor,
they competitively arose with a respectful heart,
unable to blend in unobtrusively,
hence causing alarm and fear.
【Translated Text】"Five households' offerings are presented first." Presented means,
to give,
referring to five out of ten households being the first to give.
Wáng explains,
that all are first offered to oneself.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "浆" (water radical) is written as "浆" (food radical),
same below.
(2) The character "敬" has been amended according to the commentary text.
Bó Hūn Màorén said:
"If so,
then why do you startle yourself?"
【First】【Memorial】Further inquiring into the causes of alarm,
hoping to present my own faults.
He said:
"When inner sincerity remains unresolved,
outward demeanor forms an aura,
using this to stabilize people's hearts,
making them disregard the respect due to elders,
thereby accumulating potential troubles.
Those who sell soup only provide food and broth as goods,
with no substantial surplus profit,
their profits are meager,
their influence is slight,
yet they still face such situations,
how much more so for the ruler of ten thousand chariots!
The body toils for the state and wisdom exhausts itself in affairs,
he will assign me tasks and evaluate me by achievements,
this is why I am alarmed."
【一】【注】Externally priding oneself on embellishments.
【Commentary】He was aware that his inner true wisdom
had not yet attained effortless liberation,
and because he was revered by others,
he became alarmed and returned.
【Explanation】"Not understanding" is pronounced as xiè.
Sīmǎ pronounces it as xiè.
【二】【Note】Through graceful movements and demeanor, one achieves a radiant presence.
【Explanation】"形諜" is pronounced as tú xié (徒協反).
Guǒ's commentary says:
It means flattering and fawning.
The Shuōwén dictionary states:
It means to create distance.
"成光" Sīmǎ's commentary says:
When one's inner feelings are revealed through outward demeanor,
it creates a radiant splendor.
"便辟" is pronounced as bì pì (婢亦反).
【Three】【Comment】His inner substance is truly insufficient to command respect from others.
【Commentary】Dié,
is an appearance of being fawning and ingratiating.
Zhèn,
means to subdue.
With a demeanor that is fawning and ingratiating,
one's actions become radiant and splendid.
Using this external appearance,
one subdues and controls people.
【Four】【Annotation】If the calming of things stems from inner substance,
then it deepens people's reverence and affection for the elderly.
【Explanation】"Guì Lǎo" means that Zhòng Yùkòu surpassed the elderly.
【五】【注】Words that use beauty to move creatures,
then the trouble of disorder arises.
【Explanation】●,
signifies disorder.
Unable to blend with the common and merge with the dust, yet becoming a conspicuous standard for things,
leads others to respect and value oneself while looking down upon the elderly.
Truly, it is feared that calamities and troubles will arise from this disorder.
【Transcription】"Ér" is read as zǐ xī fǎn,
meaning disorder.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
The old version had ●,
which is erroneous.
Now corrected.
The same applies throughout the volume.
【Six】【Commentary】With authority light and profits meager,
one can (three) have no need to seek from others.
【Explanation】"Wei shi" is pronounced as sì.
"Ying" is pronounced as yíng.
【七】【疏】"Tè" means
"alone."
"Yíng" means
"profit."
Those who sell soup,
only have broth and food as their goods,
the surplus they gain,
is indeed not much.
Since the profit is meager,
their influence is also not significant,
yet they still respect themselves,
eagerly running to offer soup.
How much more so for a monarch,
with high authority and abundant profits,
to hasten towards honor and nobility—
is that not fitting indeed!
【Explanation】"Wàn shèng" is pronounced with the rhyme group Shéng and the initial Zhèng.
【Eight】【Memorial】The ruler of men,
whose position oversees all affairs,
whose authority spans the four seas,
thus exhausts himself personally for the state,
and exhausts his mind with concerns for worldly matters.
Then he thirsts for the worthy to share his burdens,
and must assign me duties to test my achievements.
Yet in pursuing external matters, he loses his inner self,
chasing the artificial and forgetting the genuine.
The reasons for my alarm
are fully presented as above.
【Explanation】"效" is read as it is pronounced.
Some versions also write it as "校",
pronounced with the ancient sound "gǔ xiào fǎn".
【Collation Note】(1) The character "wú" was added based on the missing text cited from the Jiangnán ancient Tibetan edition and the editions of Wén Rúhǎi and Zhāng Jūnfáng.
According to Chéng's commentary, the character "wú" should indeed be present.
In the Shuōwén dictionary, it is written as ●.
(3) Zhào Jiànyì's edition does not include the character "kě".
Bó Hūn Màorén said:
"How excellent is your way of observation!
If you conduct yourself thus,
people will come to rely on you!
【First】【Exposition】You are able to observe your own self,
examine and understand gains and losses,
commendable for this self-awareness,
hence the praise: "Excellent!"
【Two】【Comment】If one does not abandon form,
then wherever they are, they will be preserved.
Preservation means
gathering and guarding.
【Commentary】Bǎo means
to guard.
If you can settle yourself securely,
without forgetting me,
it is like manifesting virtue through form,
becoming the gathering point for all things.
When disciples seek further instruction,
they gather and guard it.
【Translated Text】"Bǎo Nǚ" Sīmǎ explains:
Bǎo means
to attach.
【Collation Note】(1) The Quē Wù cites the Jiangnan Guzang edition and the Lǐ's edition, both of which are pronounced as "jì".
Not long after, he went there,
and found the shoes outside the door already filled.
Bó Hūn Màorén stood facing north,
resting his chin on his upright staff,
stood for a while,
and went out without saying a word.
【一】【疏】Not long after,
meaning not much time had passed.
In a short while,
Bó Hūn went to the place where Liè Yùkòu was,
and happened to see shoes taken off outside the door,
with bare feet ascending the hall,
there were many seeking to learn more.
【Transcription】"Wú jǐ" jū qǐ fǎn.
【二】【疏】Dūn,
is to stand upright.
Leaning on a staff supporting the chin,
listening to their discourse,
standing idly for a long while,
forgetting the words and returning home.
【Explanation】"Dūn zhàng" is pronounced as dùn.
Sīmǎ explains:
It means upright.
"Cù zhī" is pronounced as zǐ lù fǎn.
The visitor reported this to Lièzǐ,
Lièzǐ picked up his shoes,
ran out barefoot,
reached the gate,
and said:
"Since you have come, sir,
have you no medicine of instruction to offer me?"
【一】【疏】The term "guest" refers to
one who communicates with visitors.
Yùkòu, hearing the master had long stood,
departed without a word,
whereupon he became anxious, ashamed, and vigilant,
having no time to put on his shoes,
ran barefoot,
and reached the gate just in time (to catch up).
Since the eminent one had come,
he hoped to receive acupuncture and moxibustion treatment,
but before he could even begin to administer the remedies,
he was abandoned and left to return.
With sincere heart, full of admiration and thirst (for guidance),
hence this firm insistence.
【Interpretation】"The宾者" is also written as 儐 in some versions,
with the same meaning.
Pronounced as bì rèn.
Refers to the person who receives guests.
"The跣而" is pronounced xiān diǎn.
"The暨乎" is pronounced qí qì.
"The发药" is read according to its usual pronunciation.
Simǎ's version writes it as 废,
explaining:
to set aside.
◎Qìng Fān's annotation: 发,
Simǎ writes as 废.
发 and 废,
are ancient characters used interchangeably due to similar sounds.
The Ěr Yǎ states:
废,
税,
means to rest.
The Fāng Yán says:
发,
税,
means to stop the carriage.
Thus, 发 is the same as 废.
In the Hàn Shū's "Biographies of Traders," Zǐ Gòng fā zhù yù (则)〔财〕 between Cáo and Lǔ,
the Shǐ Jì writes it as 废.
(Xú Guǎng notes:
著,
is pronounced like 贮.
) In the Xún Zǐ's "Discourse on Rites," when the great marriage has not yet fā qí,
the Shǐ Jì's "Treatise on Rites" writes 发 as 废.
In the Shǐ Jì's "Biography of Biǎn Què," the complexion fèi and pulse in disorder,
Xú Guǎng notes:
one version writes it as 发.
All are examples of this.
He said:
"Enough!
I had warned you that people would put their trust in you,
and indeed they have.【一】
It is not that you can make people trust you,
but that you cannot stop them from trusting you【二】,
so why should you display such unusual delight about it【三】!
You must have stirred their feelings,
shaking your innate nature【四】,
which is utterly meaningless.【四】
Those who wander with you offer you no admonition;
their trivial words
are all poison to people.【五】
No one awakens or enlightens others—
how can they truly understand one another【六】!
The skillful toil and the knowledgeable worry,
while the incapable seek nothing,
eating their fill and wandering freely,
adrift like an unmoored boat,
emptying their minds and roaming at ease.【七】"
【One】 【Memorial】 finished,
cease it.
I had already firmly told you before,
you could not conceal your brilliance and hide your traces,
and were bound to become the refuge for all things.
Now indeed I see your disciples filling the room,
as I said to you in the past,
surely it was not empty words.
You should cease your request,
and not trouble with verbose excuses.
◎ Qìng Fān's case protects you,
meaning to rely on you.
In the second year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, "bǎo yú nì lǚ,"
Dù's annotation:
"bǎo,"
means to rely on.
In the Shǐ Jì, "Běn Jì of Zhōu," the common people cherished him,
and many followed and "bǎo guī" with him.
"Bǎo guī,"
means to rely on and return to.
Sīmǎ explains "bǎo" as to attach,
and to attach also means to rely on.
Wáng Yì's annotation in "Qī Jiàn" says:
"to rely,"
means to protect.
【Two】【Comment】Acting impartially and transforming,
then there is no feeling and no seeking,
no feeling and no seeking,
thus not preserving each other.
【Commentary】Manifesting traces outwardly,
thus people protect him;
being unable to forget virtue,
therefore he cannot be without self-guarding.
【Three】【Commentary】Bestowing favors before things occur,
favors do not depend on others,
preparing in advance makes it different.
【Commentary】"Er",
means "you".
"Yān",
means "what".
When both things and self are forgotten,
why would one need things to stir oneself!
Only when an opportunity necessarily arises,
should one respond after being stirred,
without the trouble of putting forth unusual views beforehand,
or bestowing favors ahead of things.
【Explanation】《而焉》yú qián fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】There will surely be a response,
then it stirs in accordance with one's inherent nature.
【Commentary】Yáo means
to move.
It necessarily arises from being inherently compelled by a stimulus,
following its intrinsic nature,
it stirs and responds accordingly,
erasing traces and concealing origins—
what designation could there be for it!
【Explanation】"Yáo ér běn cái" — one version has "cái" written as "xìng".
◎Jiā Shìfù said:
The explanation in the text,
one version has "cái" written as "xìng".
Guō Xiàng's annotation states,
there must be something that triggers a response,
then it stirs along with the inherent nature.
What triggers is the human heart/mind,
and what is triggered in turn arises from the heart/mind that triggers the human heart/mind.
The Ěryǎ Shìgǔ explains:
"Yáo"
means to act or create.
"Yáo ér běn cái"
refers to abandoning the natural state of one's original heart/mind and acting to impose upon it.
"Yòu wú wèi yě" — shaking the inherent nature to pursue something,
is also not what is meant by the Dào and virtue.
【五】【注】Subtle and intricate words that penetrate people's hearts are considered minor speech.
【Commentary】Though I journey with you,
and our conduct and understanding are similar,
if I only engage in superficial arguments and cunning words,
flattering others,
all such acts become like venomous poison—
how could I then use the true Way to guide you!
【Explanation】"Minor Words" refers to speech that does not enter into the Way,
hence it is called minor words.
"Human Toxin" is so named because it brings many troubles,

When the Creator rewards a person,

【一】【注】From this point onward,
it is Zhuāngzǐ's text.
The effort of accumulated practice is to reward,
to reward one's nature,
not to reward one's actions.
Thus, the achievement of learning's effort,
is merely to complete one's nature,

【Commentary】The Creator is

capable of fashioning all things,
hence it is called the Creator.
The intelligence and abilities of beings

not acquired through learning from a teacher.
Therefore, by means of learning,
one assists the Way of nature,
nurturing their innate nature,
not attributing it to human effort.
Thus, it is known that Dí has the nature of Mò,

【二】【注】They possess their own nature,

【Commentary】That Dí (Xiān) had an innate nature for ink,

learning will ultimately not succeed.

【Three】【Annotations】Yǎn Huǎn prided himself on his Confucianism,
claiming that he had achieved the merit of accumulated learning,
unaware that it was his innate nature.

those who disregard themselves to pacify their nature

【Commentary】This means that Huǎn relied on his own scholarly achievements,
which set him apart from ordinary people,

reach such a point!
【四】【注】Digging a well serves to connect with the spring,

focusing only on the superficial achievements of digging and chanting.
Thus, they boastfully claim possession of them—

【Commentary】Beneath the earth lie springs,

To bore through and form a well,

How deeply deluded are the people of the world,
who only know the trivial task of boring and studying,
yet fail to comprehend the naturalness of the spring's innate quality.
They boast of it as their own achievement,
and thus all in the world are like the man from Huǎn.
A man from Qí drilled and obtained a well,

The well's owner guarded the water,

Zhuāng Shēng heard of this

It metaphorically describes Huǎn not knowing that Dí's ink is natural and resenting it.
alternatively pronounced as "zǐ huì fǎn".

Confucius said:
"Human hearts are more treacherous than mountains and rivers,
and harder to understand than the heavens;
the heavens at least have the cycles of spring and autumn, winter and summer, dawn and dusk,
but humans conceal their true feelings behind thick appearances.
Thus, some appear sincere yet are arrogant,
some seem virtuous yet are unworthy,
some appear compliant yet are resolute and accomplished,
some seem firm yet are hesitant,
some appear gentle yet are harsh.
Therefore, those who pursue righteousness as thirstily as drinking
may abandon it as hastily as fleeing heat.
Thus, the gentleman tests loyalty by assigning distant tasks,
tests respect by assigning close duties,
tests ability through complex assignments,
tests wisdom through sudden questioning,
tests trustworthiness through urgent deadlines,
tests benevolence through entrusting wealth,
tests integrity through informing of dangers,
tests restraint through inebriation with wine,
and tests character through mixed-gender gatherings.
When these nine examinations are complete,
the unworthy person is revealed."

he is a vulgar person.
The various fathers,
refer to uncles.
Ordinary men are fiercely competitive for official positions,
with one appointment, they become arrogant and boastful of their glory,
with a second appointment, they grasp the carriage ropes and dance with joy,
with a third appointment, they grow self-important and haughty,
calling their uncles by their first names.
Yet Kǎo Fù's humility and others' boastfulness differ,
when assessing their merits and flaws,
who could match the style of Táng Yáo and Xǔ Yóu, who practiced effortless abdication!
【Explanation Text】"Ér Fū": Guǒ Xiàng's note says:
refers to an ordinary man.
"Lǚ Jù": describes an arrogant appearance.
◎Jiā Shìfù comments:
In the explanatory text,
"Lǚ Jù"

I suspect this should not be taken as arrogance.
The "Fāngyán" dictionary states:
● and Lǚ
mean "long";
in Eastern Qí it is called ●,
in Sòng and Lǔ it is called Lǚ.
The "Shuōwén" dictionary explains:
Jù
means very hard or strong.
It is also interchangeable with "jù" (巨),
meaning "great" or "large".
"Lǚ Jù"
refers to considering oneself grand and superior,
and should imply a sense of self-importance and exaggeration.
To interpret it as arrogance
is incorrect.
"Shú Xié Táng Xǔ": "Xié"
means "to be the same as" or "to harmonize with".
"Táng"
refers to Emperor Táng Yáo;
"Xǔ",
refers to Xǔ Yóu:
both were figures who esteemed humility and yielding.
This phrase questions whether Kǎofù and Ér Fū
could be compared to Táng Yáo and Xǔ Yóu.
◎Lú Wénchāo notes:
The old text read "xié" as "same as",

◎Jiā Shìfù comments:

states that "Táng" refers to Yáo,
and "Xǔ" refers to Xǔ Yóu;
meaning, between Ér Fū and Kǎofù,
who could be likened to the deeds of Táng and Xǔ.
Now, considering that "Shú Xié Táng Xǔ" and "Shú Gǎn Bù Guǐ" form parallel phrases,
it suggests that someone like Ér Fū
would hardly know how to compare himself to Táng and Xǔ!
Guǒ Xiàng's annotation is mistaken.
There is no greater harm than virtue having a mind of its own【一】 and the mind having eyelids【二】.
Once it has eyelids, it looks inward,
and looking inward leads to ruin【三】.
There are five harmful virtues,
among which the central virtue is the foremost【四】.
What is meant by the central virtue?
The central virtue is
that which makes one self-satisfied and despises what one does not do【五】.
【1】【Note】To have the intention to act virtuously
is not true virtue.
For true virtue is
a spontaneous attainment whose origin one does not even realize.
【Commentary】To employ wisdom and toil with concern,
having the mind set on virtue,
this is the utmost form of harm.
【二】【注】To follow one's heart in cultivating virtue,
may still be acceptable;
but to force one's heart in the subtleties of expression,
is already excessive in its artificiality.
【Explanation】"睫" is pronounced as jiē.
◎ Yú Yuè says:
Guō's annotation states,
"To exert the mind between the eyebrows and eyelashes,
then artifice is already extreme."
However, the main text speaks of the mind having eyelashes,
not of exerting the mind on the eyebrows and eyelashes.
Guō's annotation is incorrect.
The mind having eyelashes
means using the mind as eyelashes.
When a person encounters something the eyes do not directly see,
yet estimates it with intention,
assuming it to be so,
this is the mind having eyelashes.
The sage does not anticipate deceit,
nor suspect disbelief.
How could they be like this?
Therefore, it is said: "There is no greater harm than virtue having a mind and the mind having eyelashes."
The text below says,
"When it comes to having eyelashes, it looks inward,
and looking inward leads to failure."
Thus, the mind having eyelashes precisely refers to looking inward.
Looking inward
does not mean closing the eyes and turning the hearing inward,
but rather not using the eyes to see but using the mind to see.
Later Confucian scholars clung to one principle to judge all matters under heaven,
which is close to the mind having eyelashes.
【Three】【Commentary】If one seeks to probe into the obscure and hidden,
taking depth as their endeavor,
then both the mind and the matter will fail.
【Commentary】To let the mind be enslaved,
employing one's mental energy on trivial matters,
chasing after external circumstances with thoughts and worries,
unaware of when to rest,
leads to great danger and downfall.
【Explanation】"Tàn shè" is read as "shí yì" with a reverse tone.

It is said that these five roots,

The five roots are the masters of calamity,
and central virtue is being without a heart.
is to criticize.

If within there is no self-approving sentiment,
then one allows all things to be as they are,

and thus all under heaven would think to follow them.

means to criticize.
Using what one prefers in one's heart to consider oneself correct,
and criticizing and denouncing those who differ from oneself.
Believing that what one holds in one's heart is right is considered virtuous,
hence it is called "inner virtue."

There are eight extremes of distress,
three necessities for success,
and six repositories in form.
Fine beards, tall stature, robust beauty, and courage—
these eight qualities all surpass others,
yet because of them, one meets distress.
Following circumstances,
yielding adaptively,
and appearing timid as if inferior to others—
these three qualities all lead to success.
Wisdom and intelligence that reach outward
breed resentment through bold actions,
while benevolence and righteousness invite many reproaches.
One who comprehends the essence of life is magnanimous;
one who is versed in knowledge is insignificant;
one who understands the great destiny follows it,
while one who understands the minor destiny endures it.
【One】【Memorial】The eight directions and three necessities are explored through poverty and success,
just as the human body has its six treasuries.
They are listed in the text below.
【二】【注】They are exhausted by being subjected to servitude.
Yet, the world has never been exhausted by its shortcomings,
but is often trapped by its own strengths.
【Explanation】Měi means

Rán refers to
beard and sideburns.
Cháng means
Dà indicates

Possessing these eight qualities,
one surpasses ordinary people,
(loved) [received] (three) many duties and labors,
thus leading to poverty and hardship.

The stooped and hunchbacked,

The distressed and fearful,

Since these three types are not entrusted with tasks,
they are instead to be assisted and supported,
hence they must be understood.

Having these three traits makes one inferior to ordinary people,

【Commentary】Great destiny,

If one were to live as long as Péngzǔ,

Zhuāngzǐ said:
"There was a man by the river who was so poor he made his living by weaving reeds.
His son dove into the deep pool
and obtained a pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold.
The father said to his son:
'Bring a stone and smash it!
For a pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold
must have come from under the chin of the black dragon at the bottom of the nine-layered abyss.
That you could obtain the pearl
was only because the dragon was asleep.
Had the black dragon been awake,
how could you have come back with even a fragment of your body!'
【一】Now, the depth of the state of Sòng
is no less than a nine-layered abyss;
the fierceness of the King of Sòng
is no less than that of the black dragon.
That you were able to obtain the chariot
was only because you caught him in his sleep.
Had the King of Sòng been awake,
you would have been ground to powder!"
【One】【Explanation】Wěi,
means reed.

selling them to provide food.
Duàn,

Lí,
is a black dragon,
under whose chin lies a pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold.
This metaphor satirizes those who obtain carriages.

【二】【注】To attain wealth and status,
one must align with the people's aspirations.
Those who employ unconventional theories,
ride on the celestial thoroughfare,
to captivate the ruler's mind—
such individuals are not accepted by enlightened sovereigns.
Therefore, if there is to be praise,
it must be tested.
When it does not contradict the will of these people,
and all unanimously recommend someone,
uniting the hopes of the multitude,
this is how the Three Dynasties proceeded with integrity and straightforwardness.
【Commentary】Those who move their sovereign with loyalty and integrity
are bound to receive extraordinary rewards.
But those who employ unorthodox methods,
using flattering words to curry favor with the ruler,
and seeking wealth and status by luck,
thus develop an arrogant and childish demeanor.
How is this any different from obtaining a pearl by encountering a sleeping dragon!
For further details, refer to the annotations.

Someone sent an envoy to invite Zhuāngzǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ responded to the envoy, saying:
"Have you seen the sacrificial ox?
It is clothed in embroidered silk,
fed with hay and beans,
but when it is led into the grand temple,
though it may wish to be a lone calf,
could it possibly do so?"
【一】【疏】It is an allegory,
not clearly stating the surname and clan of the hired person,
hence the use of "perhaps" in the statement.
【二】【疏】A sacrificial ox,
is raised.
The king prepares and raises the ox three months in advance for offering at the ancestral temple, which is called the sacrificial ox.
【Transcription】"其使" is read as suǒ lì fǎn.
【Three】【Commentary】Lè Shēng feared being a sacrificial ox and declined the invitation,
the skull frowned upon hearing about life,
this shows that the circumstances of life and death differ and each has its own appropriateness.
【Commentary】Chú,
means grass.
Shū,
means beans.
When sacrificial animals are raised in abundance and well-provided,
on the day of the sacrifice, seeking a solitary calf cannot be achieved.
Moreover, those who live on official salaries,
often die prematurely,
while those who excel in reclusion,
are just the ones who preserve their lives fully.
Zhuāngzǐ, being noble and pure,
laughs at those who chase fame and profit.

Zhuāngzǐ was nearing death,
and his disciples wished to give him a lavish burial.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"I take heaven and earth as my inner and outer coffins,
the sun and moon as paired jades,
the stars and constellations as pearls,
and all things in creation as funeral offerings.
Are my burial accoutrements not already complete?
What could possibly surpass this!
【一】【疏】Zhuāngzǐ profoundly understood the mysterious Way,
treating his physical form as a temporary lodging,
thus taking heaven and earth as his inner and outer coffins,
the forging furnace of the two primal forces,
the pearls and gems as the stars,
transforming with the three luminaries,
having all provisions for his journey prepared.
His disciples gave him an elaborate burial,
which deeply contradicted the Creator's intent.
【Transcription】"Zhūjī" is pronounced as qí,
also pronounced as jī.
Another pronunciation is qíjì fǎn.
"Jī" is pronounced as zī.

zǐyì fǎn.
The disciple said:
"I fear that the crows and kites will eat our master."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Above, to be eaten by crows and kites;
below, to be eaten by mole crickets and ants.
To take from one and give to the other,
how partial is that!"
【一】【疏】The kite,
is a type of hawk.
The disciples, bearing the profound kindness of their master,
intended to bury him with rich offerings,
to avoid his body being taken by kites and crows.
Who would have known that a lavish burial would instead attract ants and termites!
Driven by their affection,
they acted out of partiality and selfishness.
【Transcription】"Yuān" is read with the initial "y" and the final "uan".
"Lóu" is pronounced as "lou".
"Yǐ" is read with the initial "y" and the final "i".
To use the uneven to even things out,
the result is not truly even.
To use the unproven to prove things,
the proof is not truly proven.
The clever are driven by their actions,
while the spiritual perceive the truth.
That the clever cannot surpass the spiritual has long been the case,
yet the foolish rely on their limited views to impose on others.
Their efforts are superficial—
is that not lamentable!
【一】【注】Using one standard to level all things
is not as good as letting all things level themselves.
【Commentary】To be impartial in granting and taking without personal feelings,
and to entrust duties with fairness,
this is true impartiality.
If one operates with emotional considerations,
attempting to equalize all things,
the moment one begins to stir such thoughts,
it is already not impartial.
【二】【注】Zhēng,
is response.
Not following the natural responses of all things but wanting to impose one's own views to respond to them,
then there will inevitably be discrepancies.
【Commentary】The sage has no deliberate mind,
responding only when stimulated,
which is the true response.
If one deliberately seeks to respond to things,
one cannot truly respond.
Zhēng,
means response.
【Three】【Comment】Holding fast to one's own views,
one has already received numerous influences,
how can one then master things!
【Commentary】Boasting of one's own intelligence,
emotions responding to affairs,
being driven by external things—
how can one possibly command others!
【Four】【Annotation】Only by entrusting to the spirit can one reach ultimate harmony,
thus there is no situation that does not receive a response.
【Commentary】The spirit is without a mind,
quiescent and unmoving,
yet capable of responding to all things.
【Five】【Annotation】The reach of vision,
does not extend beyond the physical form;
when utmost harmony is achieved, there is no distinction between near and far, hidden and deep,
everything attains its own fulfillment.
【Commentary】When conscious, one has a mind that responds to affairs,
being driven by external matters;
whereas the spirit is mindless,
responding to stimuli without fixed direction.
The conscious cannot match the mindless,
and deliberate response falls short of spontaneous response—
this can be understood through comparison.
【Six】【Annotation】When utmost compliance is achieved, then function arises from others and is stored within things.
If one relies on what they have seen,
clings to their own correctness,
even if they wish to enter into others,
their efforts remain external (1).
【Commentary】Those who respond to things with a mind free of attachments
act without claiming ownership,
achieve merits without dwelling on them.
The foolish and deluded,
clinging to their own usefulness,
usurp others' achievements,
attributing them to themselves.
Though they wish to boast and flaunt,
their merits remain external.
Confused (forgetting)〔
To be so deluded,
how profoundly lamentable it is!
【Collation】(1) The Shidetang edition reads "其功之外也".
【I】 【Explanation】 Named after righteousness.
There are many in the world who practice the arts of governance,
and all believe that what they possess cannot be improved upon.
As for the Dao arts spoken of in ancient times,
where, indeed, do they reside?
The answer is:
"They reside everywhere."
Then comes the question:
"From where does the divine descend?
From where does enlightenment emerge?"
"The sage has that from which they are born,
the king has that from which they are accomplished,
all originating from the One."
【一】【注】If one acts for the sake of having actions,
then it is genuine action;
but if one acts for the sake of genuine action,
then it becomes inaction.
What more is there to add!
【Commentary】Fāng means
the Way.
From the time of Xuānxū onward,
up until Yáo and Shùn,
the methods of governance and arts,
were numerous.
All followed the nature of existing things,
complied with their inherent characteristics,
allowed all beings, whether moving or stationary,
without imposing external standards or measures,
thus, though teaching, it was not teaching,
though acting, it was not acting.
【Two Departures】The Daoist arts practiced by the Three Sovereigns of high antiquity,
following things and entrusting to transformation,
were simple, unadorned, and non-active.
Where, then,
does this method reside?
This is posed as a hypothetical question
to elucidate profound principles.
【Explanation】"Wū hū" is pronounced as wū.
【Three】【Memorials】Reply states:
The mysterious Way of non-action,
exists wherever it may be,
from ancient times to the present day,
there is no place it does not pervade.
【Four】【Annotation】The divine spirits emerge and descend in response to events.
【Commentary】"Spirit" is the name for that which subtly encompasses all things;
"intelligence" means wisdom that is all-encompassing.
If one could already comprehend the sagely way through emptiness and penetration,
and this has existed throughout past and present,
then why would there be a need for those spiritual figures to manifest such brilliant wisdom,
establishing rituals and creating music to guide all beings?
【Five】【Commentaries】The profound Way, being empty and concentrated,
gives birth to all things through their responses;
the sage emperors and enlightened kings
manifest their traces by accomplishing their merits—
how could this be without reason!
【Six】【Annotation】Causing all things to return to their roots,
embracing the One and nothing more,
without adornment on the outside,
this is how the sage king fosters and nurtures life.
【Commentary】Origin,
is the foundation.
One,
is the Dào.
Although repeatedly descending with divine spirit to engage with beings,
blending traces and harmonizing light,
responding to things without departing from true constancy,
is to embrace the One and return to the foundation.
【校】（一）趙諫議本其所作以其。
Those who do not depart from the ancestral foundation,
are called Heavenly persons.
Those who do not depart from the essence,
are called Spirit persons.
Those who do not depart from the genuine,
are called Perfect persons.
Taking Heaven as their ancestral foundation,
taking virtue as their root,
taking the Way as their gate,
revealing themselves in transformation and change,
are called Sage persons.
【一】 Using benevolence to bestow kindness,
using righteousness to establish principles,
using ritual to guide conduct,
using music to foster harmony,
radiating warmth and compassionate benevolence,
are called Noble persons.
【二】 Using laws to define duties,
using titles as standards,
using comparison as verification,
using investigation for decisions,
their methods follow the sequence one, two, three, four【三】,
officials accordingly arrange themselves in order,
taking affairs as their constant occupation【四】,
focusing on food and clothing as primary,
promoting propagation, accumulation, and storage【五】,
with concern for the old, weak, orphaned, and widowed (一),
ensuring all are provided for,
this is the principle for the people【六】.
【One】【Annotation】All these four names,
refer to one person,
differing only in how they are spoken.
【Commentary】To unite with the fundamental source of the dark and profound,
is called spontaneity.
To be pure and unadulterated,
is called divine wonder.
To be steadfast and uncontrived,
is called the ultimate.
Taking spontaneity as the guiding principle,
the highest virtue as the foundation,
and the mysterious Way as the gateway,
observing the subtle signs of change,
and adapting along with the transformations of things—
such a one is called a sage.
The four types mentioned above
are essentially one and the same,
but according to their different functions,
they are given four distinct names.
【Transliteration】"Bù Lí" lì zhì fǎn.

which the worthy and noble uphold firmly.
Spreading benevolence as grace,
applying righteousness to judge wrongs,
practicing propriety as the foremost conduct,
moving with music to harmonize nature,
compassionate light shines upon the nine realms,
the wind of humanity fans across the eight directions,
like the fragrance of lán and huì orchids,
their scent permeates far and wide,
this can indeed be called virtuous.

using these four methods to arrange them in order of precedence,
so that the affairs between rulers and subjects

【Five】【Memorials】What cannot be neglected in affairs are
farming and weaving;
what cannot be disregarded for sages are
clothing and food.
Thus, the state takes the people as its foundation,
and the people regard food as their heaven.
Therefore, multiplying and nurturing life,
accumulating and storing reserves—
these are all methods for nourishing the people.

The ancient people were indeed perfect!
They aligned with the divine and luminous,
harmonized with heaven and earth,
nurtured all things,
brought peace to the world,
their beneficence reached the common people,
they were clear about the fundamental principles,
and connected to the detailed regulations.
They were thoroughly versed in all directions and seasons,
in matters small and large, refined and coarse,
their influence was present everywhere.
What was clear and embodied in regulations and measures
was largely preserved in the old laws and histories passed down through generations.
What was contained in the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music
was well understood by the scholars and gentlemen of Zōu and Lǔ.
The Odes express aspirations,
the Documents record events,
the Rites guide conduct,
Music promotes harmony,
the Yì reveals the principles of yīn and yáng,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals clarifies titles and duties.
These principles, scattered throughout the world and established in the Central States,
were occasionally mentioned and discussed by the various schools of thought.
【一】【注】The ancient people refer to the aforementioned four names.
【Commentary】Providing for the elderly and comforting the frail,
showing compassion to orphans and caring for widows,
from the Five Emperors onward,
all have practiced these virtues.
合也。
The sage emperor has no personal intent,
but follows the nature of all things,
thus able to unite with the wondrous principle of the divine,
align with the pure essence of heaven and earth,
nurture the common people within the universe,
and harmonize all beings in the world.
【Explanation】"Chún" is pronounced as shùn lún fǎn.

【Commentary】The fundamental principles refer to

The secondary regulations refer to
names and laws.
The sage's mind nurtures with compassion,
extending grace to the common people,

is the law.

is to connect.

The world is in great chaos,
the wise and sage are not illustrious,
the Way and its virtue are not unified,
and many in the world grasp a single aspect of it, considering it sufficient for their own satisfaction.
Just like the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth,
each has its own clarity,
yet they cannot interchange their functions.
It is akin to the various skills of the hundred schools,
each possessing its own strengths,
and at times proving useful.
Nevertheless,
they are neither comprehensive nor all-encompassing,
being scholars of a narrow perspective.
They divide the beauty of heaven and earth,
dissect the principles of all things,
scrutinize the wholeness of the ancients,
yet few are able to embody the beauty of heaven and earth
or match the countenance of divine intelligence.
Therefore, the Way of inner sagehood and outer kingship
remains obscure and unillumined,
stifled and unexpressed.
The people of the world each follow their own desires, taking them as their personal methods.
Alas,
the hundred schools proceed without turning back,
and are bound not to converge!
Scholars of later generations
unfortunately do not witness the purity of heaven and earth,
the grand essence of the ancients.
The art of the Way is about to be fragmented across the world.

They did not indulge in extravagance for later generations,
nor did they waste resources on myriad things,
nor did they glorify rules and measures,
but disciplined themselves with strict principles to meet the urgent needs of the world.
Among the ancient Daoist arts, there were those that embodied this.
Mò Dí and Qín Gǔlí heard of this tradition and delighted in it,
but they carried it to excess,
and moderated it too rigidly.
They advocated the rejection of music,
and called for the frugal use of resources;
in life, they did not sing,
and in death, they wore no mourning garments.
Mòzǐ promoted universal love and mutual benefit while condemning strife,
and his way opposed anger;
moreover, he was fond of learning and broad in knowledge,
not seeking distinction,
yet not in agreement with the ancient kings,
and he rejected the ancient rituals and music.
【一】【注】Diligence and frugality lead to exhaustion,
thus they do not shine.
【Commentary】Extravagance means
lavishness.
Opulence means
splendor.
Shining means
brightness.
To teach future generations,
one should not permit luxury and extravagance,
making both things and oneself utterly frugal,
never indulging in ornate beauty.
This already goes against the nature of things,
and the teachings and methods cannot be implemented,
hence the rites and regulations of the former kings cannot be made manifest and clear in the world.

【八】【注】Since one considers oneself to be in the right,
one then desires to make all things conform to oneself.
【Commentary】Mòzǐ was also fond of learning,
extensively mastering the ancient classics.
Since he himself was diligent and frugal,
he wished for all things to be the same.
【Nine】【Annotation】The ancient kings allowed their various differences to flourish,
then they all achieved unity without knowing how they achieved it.
【一０】【Note】Disapproving of its extravagance.
【Commentary】The rites involve the elaboration and reduction of ceremonial forms,
and music entails the use of bells, drums, and feathered ornaments.
There is concern that these may lead to extravagance and luxury,
hence they are discarded and not employed.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "xùn" instead of "shùn".
(2) The Shìdétáng edition has "ér" instead of "gù".
(3) The character "huá" was emended based on the reprinted Sòng edition.
Huángdì had the Xiánchí music,
Yáo had the Dàzhāng,
Shùn had the Dàsháo,
Yǔ had the Dàxià,
Tāng had the Dàhuò,
King Wén had the music of the Pìyōng,
King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu composed the Wǔ music.
In ancient funeral rites,
the noble and the humble had their rituals,
the high and low had their ranks:
the Son of Heaven had seven layers of inner and outer coffins,
the feudal lords had five layers,
the high officials had three layers,
and the scholars had two layers.
Now Mòzǐ alone advocated no singing in life,
no mourning garments in death,
and a three-inch thick tong wood coffin without an outer shell,
taking this as the standard.
To teach people with this
is feared to show no love for others;
to practice this oneself
certainly shows no love for oneself.
Although Mòzǐ's doctrine is not defeated,
nevertheless,
singing without true singing,
crying without true crying,
and rejoicing without true joy—
do these truly align with human nature?
His living was arduous,
his dying meager,
and his path exceedingly harsh;
it causes people worry,
it brings them sorrow,
his practices are hard to follow,
and it is feared they cannot serve as the way of the sages.
Opposing the heart of the world,
the world cannot endure it.
Even if Mòzǐ alone could bear it,
what can he do for the world?
Alienated from the world,
he is far removed from the path of true kingship.
【一】【疏】The above are the names of the music of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
【Transcription】"Yǒu Xià": hù yǎ fǎn.

【Èr Shū】From the Son of Heaven down,
to the officials and commoners,
there were all rituals and norms,
each having their ranks and grades,
this is the ancient rite.

【Three】【Commentary】All things are cherished when they fulfill their functions and satisfy natural inclinations,
but now, enforcing diligence and frugality to an extreme degree,
even with the intention to enrich the world,
is no longer an act of true care.
【Commentary】The master, in his traces of Yǔ,
was excessively diligent and frugal,
which above contradicted the ways of the Three Sovereigns,
and below went against the will of the myriad people.
Thus, in life and death, he toiled to the point of exhaustion,
unable to nurture external things,
his appearance haggard and withered,
making it impossible to cherish even his own body.
【Four】【Annotation】But it is not the Way and its Virtue.
【Commentary】Wèi means
"not have."
It refers to Dí Xìng Yǐn Lǎo's intention.
【Explanatory Text】"Wèi bài": bài,
sometimes written as huǐ.
"Mòzǐ" is the orthodox school of one family,
therefore it cannot be considered a failure.
Cuī states:
It has not corrupted its doctrine.
【五】【注】Although it uniquely forms the ink, it does not resemble the nature of all things.
【Commentary】For the living to sing and the dead to weep
is the constant principle of human relations;
mourning for misfortune and rejoicing in good fortune
is the fundamental sentiment of worldly affairs.
Now, if one acts contrary to this,
it is indeed unlike the norm.
【Explanation】"Feī Gē" means life should involve singing,
yet Mòzǐ regards singing as wrong.
"Lè ér" is pronounced as "luò ér".
This applies similarly to the annotations below.
◎ Jiā Shìfù said:
Mòzǐ's intention
primarily lies in advocating frugality.
In his essay "Feī Yuè," he mentions heavily taxing the myriad people
to make large bells, sounding drums,
qín, sè, yú, and shēng instruments,
stating that today's kings, dukes, and great men engage in music,
depriving the people of the time for food and clothing,
seizing the resources for their sustenance.
His three essays argue that the more elaborate the music,
the less orderly the governance becomes.
Zhuāngzǐ also debates his opposition to music and simple burials,
tracing it back to the root of frugality,
saying that the reason Mòzǐ's doctrine has not yet failed
is that today's singing is indeed not true singing,
today's crying is indeed not true crying,
today's music is indeed not true music.
Compared to Mòzǐ's words,
are they truly similar,
or truly not similar?
Therefore, what follows only records the reality of his diligence and hardship,
to clarify the original intent of Mòzǐ.

【Commentary】Dry and harsh,
lacking in enrichment.
In life, they toil diligently in body and mind,
and in death, their burials are frugal and sparse.
Their way is parched and harsh, devoid of enrichment.

【Seven】【Annotation】The way of the sage,
delights in guiding the people,
when the people attain joy in their nature, they are pleased,
and when pleased, there is nothing difficult under heaven.
【Commentary】The Way of the Sage,
wins the joyful hearts of the common people.
Now, if it causes beings to grieve,
its practice is difficult to sustain,
and it lacks enrichment,
thus it cannot be used to teach the world.

【八】【Note】The ruler must harmonize the joyful hearts of all under heaven and proceed in unison with all beings.
【Commentary】One who rules the world
must empty his mind and forget himself,
greatly accommodating the multitude of living beings.
Now, to destroy the laws of the sovereign kings
and go against the nature of the common people
—is this not far from
the proper way of governing things?

Mòzǐ praised him, saying:
"In ancient times, when Yǔ channeled the floodwaters,
dredged the rivers to connect the four barbarian regions and nine provinces,
there were three hundred major mountains,
three thousand tributary streams,
and countless smaller ones.
Yǔ personally wielded the spade and plow to interconnect the rivers of the world;
his calves were stripped of flesh,
his shins devoid of hair,
he bathed in torrential rains,
combed by fierce winds,
and established ten thousand states.
Yǔ was a great sage, yet he toiled physically for the world to such an extent."
This led later generations of Mòists
to often wear coarse leather and cloth for clothing,
use wooden clogs and straw sandals as footwear,
work ceaselessly day and night,
taking self-imposed hardship as the ultimate standard,
saying:
"If one cannot be like this,
they do not follow Yǔ's way,
and cannot be called a Mòist."
means to block.
In ancient times, when Yáo encountered the great flood,
he appointed Yǔ to manage the waters.
Yǔ built embankments to contain the floods,
dredged rivers to channel the flow,
thereby rescuing the people from severe disasters,
and enabling the cultivation of the nine grains.

【Three】【Commentary】Mòzǐ only saw Yǔ's physical toil,
but did not witness the harmony of his nature.
【Commentary】He channeled all rivers,
settled myriad states,
hearing his son Qǐ's cries,
had no moment to spare a glance,
passing thrice by his gate,
yet unable to see his child.
He relied on sudden rain to wash his hair,
used swift winds to comb it,
toiling diligently and bearing hardships,
his appearance haggard and worn,
till the flesh of his calves vanished,
and the hair on his shins was gone.
Even a great sage like Yǔ
endured such toil and hardship—
how much more should we, ordinary folk,
not strive and labor diligently!

and deviate from the Way of Yǔ,

The disciples of Xiànglǐ Qín such as Wǔ Hóu,
and the Mohists of the south like Kǔ Huò, Yǐ Chǐ, and Dènglíng Zǐ and their followers,
all recited the Mohist Canon,
yet their interpretations diverged and differed,
each calling the others "heterodox Mohists";
they criticized one another with debates on hardness and whiteness, similarity and difference,
and responded to each other with arguments of odd and even, incompatible and incompatible;
they regarded the Grand Masters as sages,
and all wished to be their presiding successors,
hoping to carry on their legacy for future generations,
yet to this day, the disputes remain unresolved.

"Běi",

Shuōwén states:

Rú Chún says:
Generally, energy above the [sun],
(the sun) forms a crown or cap,
directly opposite on the sides are "ěr",
on the sides like a half-ring,

"jué",

like two people turning their backs to each other.
To interpret "jué" as energy piercing the sun

Mò Dí and Qín Gǔlí's intentions were correct,
but their actions were wrong.
They would have later generations of Mohists
compete in self-inflicted hardship with callus-free calves and hairless shins.

Mòzǐ truly had the world's best interests at heart,

never abandoning it even when withered and worn.

even if withered and dry, do not give up,
is what's described as grinding one's head and heels to the ground,
doing it for the benefit of the world.
Guō Xiàng's annotation did not capture this.

【Seven】【Annotation】Unmatched.
【八】【Note】That is why it is considered truly good.
【Commentary】In all the world, those who truly cherish frugality
are but one person alone.
Seeking for their kind,
one ultimately cannot find any.
Being so,
they never cease or abandon it,
following their genuine nature out of true fondness,
not as an affectation.
【Explanation】"Kūgǎo": read as kǔ lǎo fǎn.
"Bù shě yě": pronounced as shě.
Same for the following chapter.
【Nine】【Annotation】It is not due to virtue.
【Commentary】Fú,
is an exclamation.
To go against things and harm one's nature,
is truly not the way of sages and worthies,
but rather the path of diligent and frugal individuals who strive to save the world with their talents.
【Collation】(1) The ancient manuscript from Gāoshānsì has the character "者" after "好".
Unburdened by vulgar customs,
unadorned by material things,
not meticulous in dealings with others,
not envious of the multitude,
they wished for the world to be peaceful and tranquil so that the people’s lives could be preserved,
and for the sustenance of both others and themselves to be sufficient and then to stop.
With this, they purified their hearts,
and among the ancient arts of the Way, there were those who dwelt in this.
Sòng Xíng and Yǐn Wén heard of this legacy and delighted in it.
They fashioned Mount Huà-style caps to express themselves,
and in interacting with all things, they took distinguishing biases as their starting point.
They spoke of the heart’s capacity,
naming it the heart’s conduct.
With harmony, they sought to unite joy,
and to harmonize all within the seas.
They requested that this be established as the guiding principle.
They regarded being insulted as no disgrace,
sought to rescue the people from strife,
prohibited aggression and ceased arms,
and aimed to save the world from war.
With this, they traveled throughout the world,
persuading those above and teaching those below.
Even if the world did not accept them,
they insisted tirelessly without ceasing.
Thus, it is said they were disliked by both high and low yet still forced themselves to appear.
【一】【注】Zhì,
means to oppose.
【Commentary】Free from worldly burdens,
without artificial adornment in dealing with things,
without negligence in interactions with others,
without defiance or envy among the multitude,
one establishes reputation and conduct to nurture all living beings.
【Explanatory Text】"Zhi" is pronounced as chì,
meaning to oppose.
Sīmǎ and Cuī say:
it means to harm.
The dictionary says:
it means to be ruthless.
Also pronounced as zhī,
Wéi Zhāo pronounces it as jì.
【二】【注】I dare not hope for anything more.
【Three】【Memorials】Each time I wish for peace within the realm,
to aid and sustain the common people,
to practice frugality for both things and self,
to know contentment with one's lot,
to follow these teachings in action,
and to purify one's heart,
the ancient methods are preserved,
passed down without interruption.
【Explanatory Text】"Bái Xīn" Cuī states,
to make one's heart clear.
Bái,
sometimes written as rèn.
【Four】【Dissertations】The surname is Sòng,
the given name is Xíng;
the surname is Yǐn,
the given name is Wén;
both were people during the time of King Qí Xuān,
and they studied together at Jìxià.
Sòng authored one book,
Yǐn authored two books,
both were teachers to the common people and became renowned for it.
Their nature harmonized with their teachings,
hence people admired and loved them upon hearing of their influence.

Xú gives the fanqie as hú lěng,
while Guō pronounces it as jiān.
Regarding "Yǐn Wén," Cuī states:
He was a person from the time of King Xuān of Qí,
