In the "King Mù of Zhōu" chapter of the Lièzǐ, Lǎo Chéngzǐ studied metaphysics under Master Yǐn Wén,
though it is uncertain if this refers to the same individual.
The "Yìwénzhì" of the Hànshū records one book by Yǐn Wénzǐ,
categorized under the School of Names.
Shǐgǔ notes:
Liú Xiàng said,
he traveled together with Sòng Xíng to Jìxià.
【Five】【Note】Huàshān is uniformly level from top to bottom.
【Commentary】Huàshān,
its form is as if carved,
uniformly level from top to bottom,
and Sòng Yǐn's aspirations were pure and lofty,
hence it was used as a crown to signify the uniqueness of his virtue.
【Explanation】"The Crown of Huàshān" The Huàshān mountain is uniformly level from top to bottom,
and they made a crown to resemble it,
to express their own hearts being equally balanced.
【Six】【Annotation】Not wanting them to conflict with each other.
【Commentary】Yòu,
means a region or area.
Shǐ,
means the root or origin.
Establishing names and teachings,
to respond to and interact with the human world,
and to distinguish all things,
this is the foundation used for it.
【Explanatory Text】"To distinguish" is read with the pronunciation 'bié',
and also as the common reading.
"To pardon as the beginning" means beginning,
is the foremost.
Cuī Zǐshū says:
In order to differentiate good from evil,
pardon does not reach that point.
【Seven】【Explanations】Mìng,
is a name.
Speaking and uttering words,
often enables the mind to embrace all things,
thus naming this capacity for acceptance as the mind's conduct.
【Eight】【Annotation】Forcibly using their ways to make them blend,
harmonizing to make them accord.
【Translated Text】"聏" is written as ● in Cui's version,
pronounced as ér,
Guo pronounces it as ěr.
Sima says:
It describes a rich complexion.
Cui, Guo, and Wang state:
It means harmony.
● harmonizes all things,
when things are united, there is joy.
Another interpretation:
It means to adjust.
"合驩" uses the Way to transform things,
harmonizing and adjusting them,
when intentions align, there is joy.
◎ Jiāshìfù comments:
Using ● to unite joy,
some versions write it as 聏,
the Zhuāngzǐ Quēwù cites it as 胹.
The Shuōwén dictionary's meat radical section:
胹,
means thoroughly cooked.
The Fāngyán dictionary:
胹,
means ripe.
Using 胹 to unite joy,
implies the idea of softness and ripeness.
The Tàixuán Jīng mentions ● in the center,
● at the knee,
● in the hollow,
Sima Guang's collected annotations:
The character ● is the same as 軟 (soft).
This also conveys the same meaning.
The Quēwù's use of 胹 is correct.
"強以" is read with the pronunciation of its components,
the same applies below.
"令合" is read with the pronunciation of its components,
the same applies below.
【Nine】【Annotation】The two gentlemen requested to have someone like this established as the master of all things.
【Commentary】Ér,
means harmony.
Using this doctrine to harmonize the four seas,
so as to unite all and win joyful hearts,
establishing this person as the master of all things.
【一０】【Note】His priority lies in saving the people's lives.
【一一】【Note】This is what is called harmonizing and mediating.
【Commentary】To rest,
means to cease.
To prevent and prohibit attacks and campaigns,
to stop and put an end to warfare,
the intention lies in harmonizing,
not permitting battles and conflicts.
Even if subjected to bullying and humiliation,
it is not considered a disgrace,
as the aim is to save the world,
and that is the reason for it.
【一二】【Note】The principle of harmony and regulation is indeed so.
【Commentary】Using these teachings as a guide,
he spread transformation throughout the nine provinces,
persuading rulers above,
and instructing the common people below.
Although things were not adopted,
he still vigorously urged and clamored,
never abandoning or giving up on his own.
【Explanation Text】"Shàng shuō" reads shuō as yuè,
or according to its regular pronunciation.
"Xià jiào" shàng,
refers to the ruler of the state,
meaning the ruler delights in instructing those below.
Another interpretation says:
shuō,
is akin to teaching.
The superior teaches and instructs the subordinates.
"Guō" is pronounced according to gǔ huó fǎn,
meaning to forcefully chatter in their ears and speak to them.
【一三】【注】This is what is meant by not being disgraced.
【Commentary】Even though all things are despised and held in low regard,
one still strives to appear and encourage others,
which is what is called being slighted and insulted by others without feeling ashamed or disgraced.
【Explanation】"見厭" is read as yàn,
Xu reads it as yàn.
Although,
they do too much for others,
and too little for themselves;
saying:
"We only ask to be firmly provided with five *sheng* of rice, which is enough,
though the master may fear he will not be full,
and the disciples, though hungry,
do not forget all under heaven."
They toil day and night without rest,
saying:
"We must thus manage to live!"
How arrogant they are in their aims to save the world!
They say:
"The superior man does not be censorious in his examination of things,
and does not allow himself to be a mere instrument for other things;"
thinking that to do what is of no use to the world,
it is better to stop and not pursue such inquiries.
They make the prohibition of aggression and the cessation of war their outer rule,
and the reduction of the desires to few and small their inner rule.
In regard to the great and the small, the subtle and the coarse,
their conduct only went so far and stopped.
【一】【注】If one does not follow their natural transformation but forcefully consoles them,
then the effort becomes too burdensome.
【Commentary】The sage who comprehends the Way
responds only after being moved,
first establishing it within oneself,
then establishing it in others.
Now, to laboriously force advice upon others,
only to be met with constant aversion,
until one's own self is withered and exhausted—
is this not too little regard for oneself!
【Transcription】"For others" is read with a feigned tone.
Below, it is the same as for oneself.
【二】【Note】This shows that he did too little for himself.
【Three】【Commentary】Sòng Xíng and Yǐn Wén referred to the world as the teacher,
and called themselves disciples.
【Commentary】Sòng Yǐn addressed the common people as "Xiānshēng" (teachers/elders),
while referring to themselves as "dìzǐ" (disciples),
thus prioritizing others over themselves.
Through their open and sincere conduct,
their intent lay in diligence and frugality.
They prepared five shēng of rice,
as a day's ration,
fearing only that the common people might go hungry,
without worrying about their own starvation.
Never forgetting the world,
with this as their guiding principle,
their diligence and frugality served to nurture the masses.
Adopting this method,
they toiled ceaselessly day and night.
【Four】【Annotation】It means the people must repay oneself.
【Five】【Annotation】Majestic and lofty in appearance.
【Commentary】Arrogant and aloof,
describes a lofty and imposing demeanor.
It speaks of one who endures humiliation with great strength,
aiding and supporting the common people,
though not entirely in accordance with the Way,
can be considered a savior of the age.
【Explanation】"Tú ào" is pronounced with the fifth tone.
【Six】【Annotation】Strive for magnanimity and forgiveness.
【Commentary】The virtuous and noble person,
being forbearing and tolerant towards oneself,
ultimately refrains from employing a mindset of discrimination to hastily scrutinize things.
【Textual Explanation】"Kē chá" is pronounced as hé.
One edition writes it as "gǒu".
◎Qìng Fān's case: One edition writes "kē" as "gǒu",
which is incorrect.
In ancient texts, characters with the radicals "jù" and "kě",
often became corrupted due to clerical script changes,
writing "kē" as "gǒu",
is also an error due to similar shapes.
On the stele of Bājùn Prefecture Governor Zhāng Nà, "àn wú jū xiè zhī rén",
"jū" is written as ●,
"qú rěn mán yí",
"qú" is written as .
On the stele of Jìzhōu Attendant Guō Jūn, "diāo kē shuāng róng",
the character "kē" is written as "gǒu",
the explanation of the character ● in Shuōwén quotes from Jiǔgào saying "jìn zhí ●",
in current editions ● is written as "jū".
In the Kǎogōng Jì, "fén hú zhī gǎn",
note:
the old book writes "gǎn" as "gǒu",
Dù Zǐchūn says:
"gǒu" should be written as "gǎn".
In the Guǎnzǐ Wǔfǔ Piān, "shàng mí cán kē ér wú jiě shě",
"kē",
in current editions is erroneously written as "gǒu".
These are all clear evidence.
【Seven】【Annotation】One must exert one's own strength.
【Commentary】One should establish oneself through self-reliance,
without needing to rely on external things to gain fame.
【Eight】【Annotation】This is why they are considered saviors of the world.
【Commentary】"Cease" means
to stop.
To torment one's mind and exhaust one's body,
acting contrary to the Way and opposing the nature of things,
brings no benefit to the world;
it is clear that it is better to stop and not proceed.
【Nine】【Kindnesses】 are for benefiting others,
an external practice.
【一０】【疏】It is for self-benefit,
an internal practice.
【一一】【Note】Unable to traverse the void and cross the vast expanse.
【Commentary】Benefiting oneself and benefiting others,
internal and external practices,
though they may differ in scope,
and vary slightly in refinement and coarseness,
the fundamental principles and guiding framework
ultimately aim at nothing beyond this.
【Transcription】"其行" is read with the lower tone as mèng fǎn,
and also as the regular character reading.
【Collation Note】(1) The character "必" has been emended according to the Zhào Jiànyì version.
Impartial yet not aligned,
easygoing yet without selfishness,
decisive yet without fixed views,
drawn to things without duality,
unconcerned with worries,
unswayed by knowledge,
making no distinctions among things,
moving along with them all,
such were the ancient arts of the Way that existed in this.
Péng Méng, Tián Pián, and Shèn Dào heard of this tradition and delighted in it,
taking the equalization of all things as their foundation,
saying:
"Heaven can cover them but cannot support them,
Earth can support them but cannot cover them,
the Great Way can encompass them but cannot differentiate them.
Knowing that all things have their affirmations
and their negations,
thus it is said: selection leads to incompleteness,
teaching leads to inadequacy,
but the Way leaves nothing behind."
【一】【注】Each acts according to their own nature.
【Commentary】Impartial and without factional bias,
equitable and without partiality,
making judgments based on principle,
without arbitrary control,
what is referred to as law,
lies precisely in this.
【Explanatory Text】"Bù dàng": pronounced dīng làng fǎn.
Cuī's edition writes "dǎng",
stating:
Utmost impartiality has no factions.
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
Writing "bù dǎng" is correct.
"Yì ér": pronounced yǐ chì fǎn.
【二】【Note】Things attain their delight,
hence they are unified.
【Commentary】The intent lies in the principle's essence, yet it does not differentiate between things.
【Three】【Memorials】Act according to reason and apply the law,
without regard for past or future,
making fair and upright judgments,
with no fear or concern,
nor employing cunning,
nor scheming beyond the law,
proceeding by upholding the law,
harsh and indiscriminate.
【Explanation】"於知" is pronounced as zhì (meaning wisdom).
The following instances of discarding "知" are the same.
【Four】【Memorials】Since the era of the Five Emperors,
there have been those who used law as a method of governance,
hence traces worthy of admiration still exist in the world.
【Five】【Disciples】Surnamed Péng,
named Méng;
surnamed Tián,
named Pián;
surnamed Shèn,
named Dào;
all were recluses of Qí,
who studied together at Jìxià,
each authoring several books.
Their natures aligned with the law,
hence upon hearing of their ethos, one would admire and cherish them.
◎Yú Yuè said:
According to the text below,
Péng Méng should have been Tián Pián's teacher.
Yìlín quotes Yǐn Wénzǐ as saying Péng Méng remarked:
When pheasants and hares are in the wild,
everyone chases them,
because their ownership is undetermined;
when chickens and pigs fill the market,
no one has designs on them,
because their ownership is settled.
【Text】《Tián Pián》 Bótián fǎn.
He was a man of Qí,
studied at Jìxià,
and authored fifteen books.
Shènzǐ states:
his given name was Guǎng.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
The "Bibliographic Treatise" of the Book of Hàn records the Daoist work Tiánzǐ in twenty-five chapters,
with the personal name Pián,
a man of Qí,
who studied at Jìxià,
and was nicknamed "Heaven's Mouth [Pián]" (note two).
The "Esteeming Uniformity" chapter in the Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi mentions Chén Pián's emphasis on uniformity,
referring to Tián Pián.
The "Human World" chapter in Huáinánzǐ recounts how Tángzǐ spoke against Chén Piánzǐ to King Wēi of Qí, etc.,
which pertains to the facts about Tián Pián,
and also illustrates one aspect of his doctrine of "esteeming uniformity."
【Six】【Annotation】Dūyòng nǎi Zhōu.
【Commentary】Heaven covers and earth supports,
each has its own capabilities.
The great Way embraces all,
yet never argues or explains.
Thus we know that among all things, some are acceptable and some are not,
following their inherent natures and allotments.
We should simply let them be as they are.
If we try to pick and choose,
we will inevitably fail to encompass everything.
【Interpretation】"Bù biàn" is pronounced as "biàn".
【Seven】【Annotation】To fully realize one's nature is to reach the ultimate.
【Explanatory Text】"Not Arriving" in one edition is written as "Not Ruling."
【八】【疏】（異）〔萬〕物不同，
endowed with distinct natures, each unique,
using one to teach another
is far from the ultimate method.
If guided by the profound Way,
then all things achieve self-realization without loss.
【Transcription】"Wú Yí" is read as it is written.
Another version is written as "guì".
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, it should read as "dǎng".
(2) The binome character has been supplemented based on the Hànshū.
Therefore, Shèn Dào discarded knowledge and self, following only what is unavoidable,
letting things take their natural course as the principle of the Way.
He said that to know what cannot be known
is to belittle knowledge and then come close to harming it.
Being remiss and unfit for office, he laughed at the world's esteem for worthies;
being unrestrained and without conduct, he criticized the great sages of the world.
He would hammer and round off corners,
turning and adapting along with things.
Setting aside right and wrong,
he merely sought to avoid blame.
He did not follow knowledge or forethought,
unaware of what came before or after,
standing tall and that was all.
Pushed, he would then move;
pulled, he would then go.
Like the whirl of a gusting wind,
like the spin of a feather,
like the grind of a millstone,
he remained whole and without fault,
in motion or at rest never erring,
and never incurred blame.
Why is this?
Because unconscious things
have no worry of establishing themselves,
no burden of employing knowledge;
their motion and stillness do not depart from principle,
hence throughout life they receive no praise.
Thus it is said, one should become like an unconscious thing,
with no use for sages or worthies;
even a clod of earth does not lose the Way.
The heroes and stalwarts laughed at him together, saying:
"Shèn Dào's Way
is not the conduct of the living but the principle of the dead—
truly it deserves to be called strange."
【一】【Note】Língtài,
means to let go and follow along.
【Commentary】Língtài,
means selection and refinement.
Cease deliberation and discard knowledge,
forget the self and abandon the ego,
act only when compelled by necessity,
respond only after being stimulated,
sift and refine right and wrong,
base judgments on laws and make decisive rulings,
Shèn Dào adhered to this,
employing it as his guiding principle.
◎ Yú Yuè said:
In the "Biographies of Mèngzǐ and Xúnzǐ" in the Records of the Grand Historian, Shèn Dào,
a man of Zhào,
wrote twelve treatises.
The "Bibliographic Treatise" of the Book of Hàn lists the Legalist school's Shènzǐ in forty-two chapters,
his name being Dào,
predating Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi,
and both Shēn and Hán spoke of him.

hence despising it and then also harming it (二).

means near.

thus one should keep their knowledge modest and shallow;
even with such modest knowledge, one may still not be able to forget it entirely,
hence it remains close to harming the principle.

and each member of the multitude is capable in their own right,
then there is no need to excessively honor the worthy.
【Commentary】Xìkē,
means an appearance of uncertainty.
Following things and complying with feelings,
without definite employment of talents,
each thing attains its own fulfillment,
not esteeming the worthy and capable,
hence they laugh at it.

forgetting and discarding past traditions,
thus they are not sages within the realm.

it still has its rough edges,
thus not yet achieving perfect harmony.

means to pat.
This implies merely striking and patting,
without using piercing or stabbing;
merely cutting off,
without employing sharp edges;
thus, it is a way to manage and control things while adapting flexibly to them.
【Six】【Negligence】Not stubbornly adhering to right and wrong,
but merely seeking to avoid the ways of the contemporary world.
【Seven】【Annotation】Unable to discern right from wrong,
past from future,
they blindly indulge their nature,
merely to evade the troubles of their time.
【Commentary】Not following one's preconceived mind,
not employing knowledge and deliberation,
nor looking ahead and behind,
correcting one's nature and artificial emotions,
directly upholding the grand principles,
simply following the nature of things.
【Explanation】"Not learning from knowledge" (zhì is pronounced with the meaning of wisdom).
【八】【Note】Acting willfully and independently.
【Commentary】Wèi rán,
describes an unmoving appearance.
Although again dwelling in the mundane world and mingling with the dust,
yet it stands wèi rán and independent.
【Transcription】"Wei ran" is read as yú wēi fǎn,
Lǐ reads it as wǔ huí fǎn.
【Nine】【Annotation】This is what is meant by acting out of necessity.
【Commentary】Pushing and pulling it,
following what is unavoidable,
responding only after being stirred,
not initiating first.
【一０】【Commentary】Grinding,
is milling.
Revolving,
is turning.
Like the whirl of a swift wind,
like the spiral of a falling feather,
akin to the rotation of a millstone.
These three are without intent,
thus they can fully attain their nature,
hence there is neither right nor wrong,
neither fault nor transgression,
being dispassionate and letting things be,
thus such a state is achieved.
【Explanatory Text】"Ruò piāo" is pronounced with the initial consonant as in "bi" and the final as in "yáo,"
another reading gives the initial as in "bì" and the final as in "yáo."
The "Ěryǎ" states:
"A whirlwind is called piāo."
"Zhī huán" is pronounced as "xuán,"
another reading as "huán."
"Ruò mò" is pronounced with the initial as in "mò" and the final as in "zuǒ,"
or read as the common pronunciation.
"Shí zhī suì" is pronounced as "suì,"
meaning to revolve.
Xú reads the sentence break here,
while another reading breaks the sentence at the character "quán."
"Quán ér wú fēi" refers to what the whetstone sharpens;
the coarseness or fineness entirely depends on the person,
meaning that when virtue is complete, there is no occasion for blame or reproach,
indicating a state of being free from deliberate intent.
【一一】【Comment】A hypothetical question is posed to demonstrate his ability.
【一二】【Note】Trouble arises from praise,
praise arises from achievements.
【Commentary】All beings are prone to clinging to their own selves,
establishing achievements and fame,
exerting their intellect and awareness,
and drowning in external circumstances.
Now, the millstone and the like,
act or rest in accordance with the nature of things,
moving or still without deliberate intent,
constantly abiding in profound principle,
thus cutting off afflictions and burdens.
Therefore, they fulfill their heavenly mandate,
free from blame and praise.
【Explanation】"Not leaving" is read as lì zhì fǎn.
【一三】【注】Only the sage is capable of discarding knowledge and artifice,
following the principles of Heaven.
Thus, the foolish and the wise each find their proper place,
the noble and the humble are appropriately positioned,
the virtuous and the unworthy act according to their true nature.
Yet to claim that there is no use for sages and worthies
is to show ignorance of the Way.
【一四】【Note】Intending to make one abandon knowledge like a clod of earth.
It also means that all things in their multitude,
have no means to attain the Dao,
for the Dao is not pervasive in all things.
【Commentary】They valued and esteemed ignorance,
their disposition was like tiles and stones,
they had no use for sages and worthies,
they were as benighted as one wandering at night,
thus becoming like clods of earth,
yet claimed to have grasped the truth.
Such was the delusion of Shèn Dào,
and this is an example of it.
【Transcription】"Fū kuài" kǔ duì fǎn,
or kǔ wěi fǎn.
"Yù lìng" lì chéng fǎn.
【一五】【Note】Only by abandoning knowledge and following one's inherent nature
can one's spirit attain profound clarity,
which is what makes a sage worthy and holy.
Yet to claim that a clod of earth does not lose the Way,
implying that a person should be like a clod of earth—
if so, what is that if not death!
This is why the heroic and outstanding laugh at it.
【Commentary】The sages who have attained the Way,
illuminate all things without a self-centered mind,
their virtue aligns with the dual principles of heaven and earth,
and their brilliance matches the three luminaries.
Yet now, to regard a clod of earth as the Way,
how is it any different from death!
Since it lacks any divine function,
it is not the conduct of the living.
Therefore, the wise Confucian scholars with broad knowledge,
and the profoundly insightful heroes,
recognizing its deviation from reason,
thus ridicule it.
【16】【Comment】Not yet in harmony with the ultimate Way,
thus appearing bizarre and uncanny.
【Commentary】What does not conform to the ultimate Way
is precisely what becomes strange.
【Collation】(1) The ancient manuscript scroll edition has the character 也 following 圣.
(2) The two characters 又焉 are emended based on the Shidetang edition.
(3) The five characters including 确也 are supplemented according to the original text of the *Shìmíng*.
Tián Pián was likewise,
studied under Péng Méng,
and attained the teaching of non-instruction.
Péng Méng's teacher said:
"The ancient men of the Way
reached the point where nothing was affirmed and nothing was denied, and that was all.
Their influence was like a sudden gust,
how could it be expressed in words?"
They often opposed conventional views,
did not engage in observation,
yet could not avoid being arbitrary.
What they called the Way was not the true Way,
and their statements of what was right inevitably fell into error.
Péng Méng, Tián Pián, and Shěn Dào did not understand the true Way.
Nevertheless,
they were all ones who had some general acquaintance with it.
【一】【注】It is the way of self-reliance.
【Commentary】Tián Pián and Shèn Dào,
studied under Péng Méng,
indulged in unrestrained and unconventional behavior,
with no teachings to impart.
【二】【注】This means to regard the equalization of all things as the foremost principle.
【Three】【Annotation】The sound stirred by an adverse wind.
【Commentary】Huò rán,
describes a swift appearance.
In ancient times, those who followed the Way,
embraced emptiness and forgot the self,
identified with heaven and earth,
and no longer distinguished right from wrong.
Their customs and teachings passed swiftly,
moving with the times,
so how could one preserve their sage traces
and cling to them in speech?
【Text Explanation】The character "Huì" is also written as 罭,
and also as 閾,
pronounced as "huàng bī fǎn",
and also as "huǒ mài fǎn".
Xiàng Guǒ states:
The sound of against the wind.
"È kě" is pronounced as "wū".
【Four】【Annotation】It goes against the people's expectations.
【Commentary】He was unable to bring all beings into great harmony,
and often acted contrary to people's hearts,
thus he could not earn the common people's admiration and expectation.
【Interpretation】"Bù jiàn guān" in one version is written as "bù jù guān".
【五】【Note】Although laws are established, their judgments are without sharp edges.
【Commentary】Huǎn duàn,
describes a state without sharp edges or corners.
Although laws are established and teachings are implemented,
they fail to fully harmonize all things,
hence one cannot avoid being huǎn duàn.
【Explanation】"於鯇" is pronounced with the fanqie 五管,
and also with the fanqie 五亂.
"斷" is pronounced with the fanqie 丁管.
Guǒ Xiàng notes:
"鯇斷"
means lacking sharp edges or corners.
One edition does not include the character "斷".
【六】【注】Wěi,
means "correct."
【Comment】Wěi,
means "correct."
What Shèn Dào called the Way is not the true Way,
and what he claimed to be correct is not correct,
hence it inevitably falls into error.
【Transcription】"Wěi" is pronounced as yú guǐ fǎn,
meaning "correct" or "so it is."
【Seven】【Comment】The Dao is omnipresent,
yet to claim that a clod of earth does not lose the Dao
is therefore considered ignorance.
【Commentary】Although they repeatedly practice and uphold the forgetting of emptiness,
taking non-mind as the Way,
they have not yet attained perfect illumination,
and thus remain unknowing.
【Eight】【Annotation】But it does not reach that point.
【Commentary】Those like Péng Méng,
although they had not yet embodied the truth,
aspired to value non-knowing,
roughly grasped the main points,
followed and revered one another as masters,
all receiving and inheriting teachings,
not merely making arbitrary judgments,
thus they had indeed heard of it.
【Explanation】"Gài hū" is pronounced as in ancient times with the sound "ài".
【Collation Note】(1) The Zhào Jiànyì edition appears to have the character "聚".
They regarded the fundamental as the essence,
considered things as the coarse,
viewed accumulation as insufficiency,
and serenely dwelt alone with the divine intelligence.
Among the ancient arts of the Way, there were those who embraced this.
Guān Yǐn and Lǎo Dān heard of this tradition and delighted in it.
They established it with the constant non-being and being,
and centered it on the Great One.
They took gentleness, humility, and deference as the outward expression,
and emptiness, non-destruction of all things as the substance.
【One】【Explanation】The root,
is non-being.
Things,
are being.
To use non-being is subtle,
the Dào is the essence;
to use being is action,
things are the coarse.
【二】【Note】Entrust it to the world,
then there will be surplus.
【Three】【Admonitions】To be greedy yet hoard possessions,
the heart is often unsatisfied.
Knowing contentment means stopping at one's lot;
thus, purity, integrity, emptiness, and tranquility,
transcending dependence, standing alone, and refining the spirit—
the Dao is present everywhere,
and has existed since ancient times.
【Explanation】"Dànrán" is pronounced as tú zàn fǎn.
【Four】【Explanations】His surname was Yǐn,
his given name was Xǐ,
his courtesy name was Gōngdù.
He served as the magistrate of Hángǔ Pass during the reign of King Píng of the Zhōu dynasty,
hence he was called Guān Yǐn.
His surname was Lǐ,
his given name was Ěr,
his courtesy name was Bóyáng,
and his alternative courtesy name was Lǎodān.
This refers to Lǎozi, the teacher of Yǐn Xǐ.
The teacher and disciple exchanged teachings and responses,
aligning with the principles of the Dào,
so when Yǐn Xǐ heard of the way of non-action, he delighted in it and cherished it.
【Explanation】"Guān Yǐn" refers to Guānlìng Yǐn Xǐ.
Some say:
Yǐn Xǐ's courtesy name is Gōngdù.
"Lǎo Dān" is pronounced with the characters "tā" and "gān" in reverse,
referring to Lǎozi.
He wrote nineteen chapters for Xǐ.
◎Yú Yuè comments:
The "Treatise on Literature" in the Book of Hàn records nine chapters of Guān Yǐnzǐ under the Daoist school,
with an annotation stating:
his name was Xǐ,
and he served as a border official.
Some take Yǐn Xǐ as a surname and given name,
which is incorrect.
Additionally, according to the explanation text:
Lǎozi wrote nineteen chapters for Xǐ.
Examining the book of Lǎozi,
the "Treatise on Literature" lists four chapters of Lín Shì's classic and commentary, thirty-seven chapters of Fù Shì's classic interpretation, and six chapters of Xú Shì's classic interpretation,
but there is no record of a version with nineteen chapters.
In the "Bù Èr" chapter of the Annals of Lǚ, Guān Yǐn valued clarity,
with Gāo's annotation:
Guān Yǐn,
was a border official,
named Xǐ,
who authored nine chapters of Daoist texts,
capable of divining winds,
and knew that a divine being would arrive when Lǎozi came.
Xǐ was pleased by this,
and requested the writing of the "Shàng Zhì Jīng" in five thousand characters.
The title "Shàng Zhì Jīng"
is not seen in other texts.
【Five】【Comment】What can Non-being establish?
By establishing it through constant non-being,
then it becomes clear that things establish themselves.
【Six】【Annotation】From heaven and earth down to all things,
each attains its own nature and that is all,
without adding embellishments from others.
Is this not governing through the Supreme Oneness!
【Commentary】"Grand" is a name denoting vastness and greatness,
"One" is called so for its undivided nature.
It speaks of the Great Way being expansive and boundless,
with nothing it does not encompass and encircle,
gathering all things within its fold,
connecting them to become one,
hence it is called the Grand One.
When establishing teachings and doctrines,
it often takes constancy and the absence of things as its foundation,
understanding its essential meaning,
with emptiness and connection to the Grand One as the core.
This is about preferring frugality to toil the physical form,
which cannot be used to teach others,
nor is there any need to undermine its methods and principles.
The seven remonstrances and memorials,
are external.
They take gentleness, weakness, humility, and harmony as the external practice of expedient wisdom,
and emptiness, benevolence, perfection, and clarity as the inner virtue of true wisdom.
【Explanatory Text】"以濡" pronounced as in "ruǎn" with the third tone,
alternatively read as "rú".
"謙下" pronounced as "xià" with the fourth tone.
Guǎn Yǐn said:
"If within oneself there is no fixed stance,
then forms and things will manifest themselves.
In movement, be like water;
in stillness, be like a mirror;
in response, be like an echo.
Vague as if disappearing,
silent as if clear,
harmonizing with others brings accord,
grasping for gain leads to loss.
Never strive to be ahead of others but always follow them."
【一】【注】When things come, respond;
respond without retaining,
thus achievements depart with the things.
【Commentary】Achieving success without claiming credit,
attributing the merit to others,
thereby using this principle to cultivate oneself.
【二】【注】Not asserting oneself but entrusting all things,
thus the forms of things each manifest distinctly.
【疏】Entrusting all things to their own devices,
without boasting of one's achievements,
thus their forms and natures each become clearly manifested.
【Three】【Comment】Constantly without emotions.
【Commentary】Movement is like flowing water,
stillness is like a suspended mirror,
its response to opportunity resembles an echo answering a sound,
movement and stillness are without deliberate intent,
hence the spiritual function is swift.
【Text】"Ruò Xiǎng" Xǔ zhàng fǎn.
【Four】【Annotation】Those who are constantly complete do not know what they have gained.
【Commentary】Wù (Vague)
means hū (indistinct).
Wáng (Nonexistent)
means wú (without).
The Dào is neither existent nor non-existent,
neither clear nor turbid.
Therefore, dim and indistinct, it seems non-existent,
yet its substance is not non-existent;
tranquil and still, it appears clear.
Thus, it has already transcended both clarity and turbidity,
harmonizing with the shallow views of the common people.
Consequently, to regard this clarity, emptiness, and non-action as virtue
is to lose the Dào.
【Explanation】"Hu" is pronounced as hū.
【Five】【Dissipation】Harmonious yet not leading.
Lǎodān said:
"Knowing the masculine,
but guarding the feminine,
one becomes the ravine of the world;
knowing the white,
but guarding the disgrace,
one becomes the valley of the world."
All others strive to be first,
but he alone chooses to be last,
saying, 'I accept the disgrace of the world';
all others seek substance,
but he alone takes emptiness,
not storing, thus having abundance;
standing firm, yet having abundance.
In his conduct of life,
he is unhurried and without waste,
acting through non-action and laughing at skill;
all others seek blessings,
but he alone bends to preserve wholeness,
saying, 'Thus I avoid blame.'
Taking depth as the root,
and restraint as the guideline,
he says, 'What is hard will be destroyed,
what is sharp will be blunted.'
Always tolerant toward things,
and not encroaching upon others,
he may be said to have reached the ultimate.
【One】【Annotation】When all things abide by their own allotment,
they remain silent and still,
without displaying prowess or prominence.
Now, what is prowess and prominence?
Is it not the pursuit of superiority and self-display?
To chase superiority and flaunt oneself,
is that not indulging in excessive knowledge to the detriment of one's life?
Therefore, the ancients did not follow boundless knowledge,
but held fast to what was within their allotment.
Thus, their nature remained whole.
With their nature whole,
they could then extend to the world;
able to reach the world,
they were then embraced by it like rivers flowing into valleys (3).
【Commentary】Heroes and outstanding figures,
meet premature death due to their aggressive haste;
while those who are yielding, gentle, humble, and submissive,
achieve longevity through withdrawal and tranquility.
Therefore, one should abandon the dazzling glory of that path,
and embrace the hidden disgrace of obscurity here.
This is the pivotal principle of learning the Way,
hence it is regarded as the valley of the world.
Now, both "xī" (brook) and "gǔ" (valley) refer to river channels and ravines,
but "xī" is small while "gǔ" is large,
hence the repetition for emphasis.
【Transcription】"Xī" is read as kǔ xī fǎn.
【Two】【Comment】Not contending with all things for supremacy,
then the world gladly supports without weariness,
hence putting oneself last.
【Commentary】Common people all strive to prevail and rush ahead,
while the great sage alone remains humble and stays behind.
Therefore, the Classic of the Way states,
"By putting oneself last, one becomes first."
【Three】【Annotation】Meekness, disgrace, inferiority, and the like,
are all what are considered filth in things.
【Explanation】Withdrawing oneself to a position behind others,
and yielding precedence to all things,
such is the one who accepts disgrace and humiliation.
【Explanation】"Zhī Gòu" is pronounced as gǒu.
【Four】【Annotation】They only know that having something brings benefit,
but do not yet understand that not having something serves a purpose.
【Commentary】It means coveting wealth and goods.
【Five】【Annotation】Maintain emptiness and tranquility to await the multitude of realities.
【Commentary】To preserve emptiness and tranquility.
【Explanation】"Chōng Bó" is pronounced as bù gè fǎn.
【Six】【Annotation】Entrust all things to maintain themselves,
thus there is no worry about their scarcity.
【Commentary】To store is
to accumulate.
Knowing contentment and maintaining one's lot,
distributing without hoarding,
thus there is surplus.
【Seven】【Annotation】It means being independent and self-sufficient.
【Commentary】Kuī rán means
standing alone.
It speaks of being pure and maintaining personal integrity,
being extremely rare among things,
only the sage is without a mind of his own.
【Interpretation】"Kuī" is pronounced as qù guǐ fǎn,
and also as qù lèi fǎn.
Originally, it might be written as Wèi.
【八】【Note】Act according to what benefits the people,
follow the four seasons to accomplish things,
always abide by the principles of the Way,
thus there will be no harm and no waste.
【Commentary】Fèi means
to diminish.
Those who have attained the Way,
do not seek immediate favors or benefits,
cultivate simple and unadorned fields,
establish gardens that require no borrowing,
move with ease and elegance,
and ultimately do not diminish themselves for external matters,
thus nurturing their lives through such conduct.
【Text】"Bù fèi" fāng wèi fǎn.
【Nine】【Comment】The clever take action,
thereby harming the self-formation of the divine vessel;
hence, those who practice non-action
follow things' spontaneous birth,
let them achieve self-completion,
so all beings can act according to their own nature.
Even spiders can weave webs,
showing that everyone has their own inherent abilities,
without valuing the artisan Chuí.
【Commentary】Acting in accordance with one's nature,
simple and unadorned, doing nothing artificial,
they laugh at those worldly people,
for their cunning minds and crafty deceit.
【Transcription】"Zhī" is pronounced zhī.
"Zhū" is pronounced zhū.
"Gōng Chuí" is pronounced chuí.
【一０】【Note】By submitting to the ultimate principle, one remains perpetually whole;
thus, there is no need to seek blessings,
for blessings are already sufficient.
【One by one】【Comment】Following things,
thus things cannot find fault.
【Commentary】Jiu means
calamity.
Ordinary people are foolish and deluded,
clinging obstinately to their actions,
only knowing how to seek blessings,
without the ability to consider calamities.
Only the great sage maintains an open mind,
adapts flexibly to circumstances,
preserves the way of life,
and thereby avoids disasters.
【一二】【Note】（Principle）〔Buried〕（Four）roots at the utmost of the great beginning,
it cannot be called shallow.
【Interpretation】"Dàchū" is pronounced as Tài.
【一三】【Comment】Eliminate excess and extravagance.
【Commentary】Taking profundity and mystery as the root of virtue,
taking frugality and restraint as the guiding principles of conduct.
【Explanatory Text】"Qù shèn": Qǐ lǚ fǎn.
【一四】【Note】When in perfect compliance, even metal and stone show no hardness;
when in opposition, even water and vapor show no softness.
Perfect compliance leads to preservation,
opposition leads to destruction,
this is the correct principle.
【Explanation】"迕逆": pronounced as wǔ nì with the fifth tone.
"無軟": pronounced as rú ruǎn,
some versions write it as 濡,
with the same pronunciation.
◎Lú Wénchāo comments:
In modern texts, it is written as 無耎.
【一五】【Note】Advancing rashly without bounds is considered sharpness.
【Commentary】It damages the firm and unyielding conduct,
and halts the greedy and aggressive heart.
Therefore, the Dao De Jing says: "Blunt the sharpness."
【Explanation】"Cuò" is read as "zuò wò fǎn".
【16】【Comment】Each keeps to their own role,
then there is naturally ample room for accommodation.
【一七】【Note】To preserve its inherent nature.
【Commentary】Retreating oneself with humility and harmony,
thus being tolerant towards things;
knowing contentment and keeping to one's lot,
thus not encroaching upon or exploiting others.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Kōzanji manuscript lacks the character "容".
(2) The Kōzanji manuscript reads "雖未",
with the same annotation in the Quēwù,
stating:
The Jiangnán ancient Tibetan edition and the editions of Wén and Lǐ both read "可謂至極".
(3) Zhào Jiànyì's edition lacks the character "也".
(4) The character "埋" has been emended based on the Sòng edition.
(5) In the Shìdétáng edition, "軟" is written as "耎".
Guān Yǐn and Lǎo Dān!
How vast and genuine were the sages of old!
【One】【Memorial】Guǎn Yǐn and Lǎo Zǐ,
the great sages of antiquity,
delved into the subtle and mastered the wondrous,
merging with truth and uniting with the Dào;
their teachings were vast and profound,
their principles extensive and deeply mysterious.
Zhuāng Zǐ nearly attained this,
hence his sigh of admiration.
Vague and without form,
transforming without constancy,
death and life,
heaven and earth together,
the divine and luminous moving with them!
Vast and obscure, where do they go?
Sudden and fleeting, where do they head?
All things are encompassed,
yet none suffice for a return.
The ancient art of the Way existed in this.
Zhuāng Zhōu heard of its tradition and delighted in it.
With absurd and far-fetched theories,
extravagant and boundless words,
and expressions without beginning or end,
he often indulged freely without partiality,
not presenting a one-sided view.
He regarded the world as sunk in turbidity,
unfit for solemn discourse.
He used "goblet words" to flow endlessly,
"repeated words" to convey truth,
and "imputed words" to broaden understanding.
Alone, he communed with the essence of heaven and earth, yet did not arrogantly disdain the myriad things.
He did not condemn right and wrong,
but dwelt with the世俗 world.
His writings, though magnificent and intricate, are without harm.
His words, though varied and uneven, are strikingly remarkable.
His fullness is inexhaustible,
soaring to roam with the Creator,
and descending to befriend those who transcend life and death, without beginning or end.
As for the root,
it is vast and penetrating,
profound and expansive.
As for the essence,
it may be said to be harmoniously attuned and reaching the heights.
Nevertheless,
in responding to transformation and unraveling things,
his principles are inexhaustible,
their origins never shedding their source,
obscure and dim,
never fully exhausted.
【一】【注】It follows things.
【Commentary】The wondrous origin is formless,
hence it is silent and still;
its traces follow the transformation of things,
therefore it is impermanent.
【Explanation】"Wù" is written as "jì" in the Yuánjiā edition.
"Mò" is pronounced as mò.
【二】【注】Entrust to transformation.
【Commentary】Taking life and death as day and night,
thus the two realms are equated;
following the transformations of creation,
thus one journeys with the divine.
【Transcription】"Death and" pronounced as yú.
The same below.
【Three】【Annotation】Lacking in interest.
【Commentary】Entrusting oneself to nature's transformations,
Roaming freely with the subtle and imperceptible,
Without attachment to choices or rejections,
One follows destiny to wherever it leads.
【Translated Text】"Vast and boundless" is pronounced with the initial "mò" and the rhyme "gāng," with a rising tone.
The same applies below.
【Four】【Annotation】Thus, the capital's appointments were established.
【Commentary】It encompasses all things,
contains the universe within,
never departing from the Way,
so where could it return to its root?
【Five】【Annotation】Not eager to make things reveal their intention.
【Commentary】Mistaken means
empty.
Far-reaching means
distant.
Absurd means
vast (originally "heaven," corrected to "great").
Unrestrained means
like letting go.
Awkward means
not aligned.
And Zhuāngzǐ, born to respond to the world,
silently united with the mysterious Way,
thus could produce theories of emptiness, distance, depth, and breadth,
talks without boundaries or ends,
letting go according to the time without bias or faction,
harmonizing energy and blending with the common,
never awkward or aloof.
【Interpretation】"Miùyōu" refers to that which seems to forget the true reality.
"Huāngtáng" refers to that which is vast and without boundaries.
◎Qìng Fán's note: "Wúduānyá,"
is akin to having no edges or limits.
In the Huáinánzǐ's "Yuándào" chapter, it mentions a gate without edges or limits,
with Xǔ's annotation on "yín'è" (the citation mistakenly writes "鄂" as "鍔"
) stating:
it means boundaries or cliffs.
(See the annotation in Wénxuǎn, Zhāng Héng's "Xījīng Fù.")
Gāo's annotation states:
it has no form or shape.
In Shuōwén, the "Tǔ" section:
"yín,"
means the edge of the earth.
In the Chǔcí, Wáng's annotation:
"yín,"
refers to the bank or cliff.
In Wénxuǎn, "Gānquán Fù," Lǐ Shàn's annotation:
means the edge or boundary.
"Ér tǎng": Dīng gives the pronunciation as "dàng fǎn."
Xú gives it as "chì dàng fǎn."
◎Lú Wénchāo says:
In the current text, "shí zìzòng ér bù tǎng" includes the character "bù."
"Jī": pronounced as "jī,"
Xú gives the pronunciation as "qǐ yí fǎn."
【Six】【Annotation】Burdened by forms and names,
they regard Zhuangzi's words as madness and do not believe them,
hence they do not associate with him.
【Comment】Zhuàng yǔ,
means grand words.
The common people within the realm,
sunk in stagnation and darkness,
are all immersed in petty arguments,
and cannot be spoken to with grand words.
【Explanation】"Zhuang yu" are both read according to their usual pronunciation.
Guǒ Xiàng states:
Zhuang,
refers to Zhuāng Zhōu.
Another interpretation says:
Zhuang,
means upright and correct.
One version writes it as zhuàng,
pronounced with the side-light tone,
meaning grand or great.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary notes that zhuāng and zhuàng,
were phonetically and semantically interchangeable in ancient usage.
In the "Posthumous Names" chapter of the Lost Books of Zhōu: "Frequently raising armies and armor is called zhuāng,"
"Wisely defending and overcoming is called zhuāng,"
"Defeating enemies with strong will is called zhuāng,"
"Dying in the open fields is called zhuāng,"
"Repeatedly campaigning and killing is called zhuāng."
Zhuāng here conveys the sense of zhuàng (strength/majesty).
In the Chǔ Cí's "Far Roaming": "Refined and beginning to be strong,"
it rhymes with xíng, xiāng, yáng.
In the annotation to "The Gentlemen Grow Old Together" in the Yōng Fēng section of the Shī Jīng, "the dignity of countenance,"
the explanation text states:
Zhuāng,
is also written as zhuàng in another version.
In the Lǐ Jì's "Tán Gōng" chapter: "Weì had a grand historian named Liǔ Zhuāng,"
the Hàn Shū's "Table of Ancient and Modern Persons" writes it as Liǔ Zhuàng.
"The world cannot be spoken to with zhuāng language,"
the explanation text states:
Zhuàng,
is written as zhuàng in one version.
These are all clear evidence of this.
【Seven】【Expositions】Goblet speech,
is unfixed.
Spreading widely,
is without preconception.
Reverence,
honors the aged.
Lodging,
is entrusting.
For when a goblet is full, it tilts;
when empty, it rights itself,
hence the goblet vessel is used to analogize the ultimate discourse.
And the talks of the elderly,
embody much truth and sincerity,
entrusted to others,
their principles are profound and vast,
such are the likes of Hóng Méng, Yún Jiāng, and Hǎi Ruò.
【Explanation】"Yǐ zhī" is pronounced as "zhī".
【Eight】【Annotation】His words penetrate the ultimate principle,
rightly aligning with the nature and destiny of all things.
【Commentary】Being arrogant and disdainful
means being prideful and conceited.
Embracing the wisdom of true essence,
wielding unfathomable divine power,
dwelling within the realm of existence,
coming to life and departing in death,
being humble and harmonious while complying with all things—
one is inherently not prideful or conceited.
【Translated Text】"Not Proud" is pronounced as wǔ bào fǎn.
" Ní" is pronounced as yì.
【Nine】【Annotation】Having no right or wrong of one's own,
Thus allowing things to proceed freely.
【Transcription】"Bù qiǎn" is read as qiǎn with the sound of zhàn.
【一０】【注】Forms gather in objects.
【Explanation】To reproach,
means to blame.
Right and wrong have no fixed master,
so one cannot exhaustively assign blame,
thus enabling one to blend into the world and ride the waves,
dwelling amidst the dust and customs of society.
【一一】【Note】Returning and uniting with things,
thus there is no harm.
【Commentary】Magnificent and extraordinary,
means grand and imposing.
Harmonious and blended,
means well-integrated and unified.
The writings of Zhuāngzǐ,
their essence is lofty and far-reaching,
yet the words still touch upon the mundane,
thus harmonizing with all things without harm.
【Transcription】"Guī" is pronounced as gǔ huí fǎn.
"Wěi" means guīwěi,
extraordinary.
"Lián ●" is also written as "biàn",
same.
Pronounced as fāng yuán fǎn.
Also pronounced like "huān",
and also fū wǎn fǎn.
Lǐ Yún says:
All are appearances of winding and turning.
Another interpretation:
the appearance of following along,
meaning not opposing but following along with things,
hence there is no harm.
【一二】【Note】Not only does it respond to the immediate tasks of the time,
hence the discrepancies.
【Commentary】"Uneven" means
sometimes empty and sometimes solid,
not uniform in its words.
"Whimsical and witty,"
is like being humorous.
Although it conveys ideas through allegories and entrusted events,
with timelines that are inconsistent,
its whimsical wit and humor
are highly enjoyable to read.
【Transcription】"Cān": initial sound lín, fanqie.
Same for the annotation.
"Chā": initial sound yí, fanqie.
"Chù": initial sound shū, fanqie.
【一三】【Note】It means having much of everything.
【Commentary】"Yǐ" means
"to stop."
The books he authored,
with their refined language and profound reasoning,
encompass a vast scope without being hollow,
rich in content and inexhaustible,
thus they do not reach an ultimate limit.
【一四】【Commentary】Riding the transformations to roam freely,
befriending nature as a companion,
thus one can blend life and death into one,
and obscure the distinction between beginning and end.
The essence is subtle, its traces coarse,
hence the mention of high and low.
【一五】【疏】闢，
means to open.
弘，
means great.
閎，
also means great.
肆，
means to extend.
遂，
means to reach.
This speaks of the fundamental depth and greatness,
extending and opening freely,
the true essence harmoniously adjusted,
ascending to reach the profound Way.
【Textual Explanation】"而辟" is pronounced as bì, with the same pronunciation as 婢 (bì).
"深閎" is pronounced as hóng.
"稠適" — 稠,
is pronounced as tiáo.
This character is also written as 调.
【一六】【Commentary】This says that Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
though again strange and extraordinary,
respond to opportunities with transformation,
explaining the nature of things,
and none surpass them.
【一七】【Commentary】To shed,
is to cast off and abandon.
The subtle principle is empty and profound,
responding without exhaustion,
yet when opportunities arise and touch oneself,
one ultimately does not shed and discard it.
【Transcription】"Bù Tuì" is pronounced as yuè,
Xú gives the initial reading as ruì,
and another reading is chuài.
【一八】【Note】Zhuāngzǐ universally explains himself with impartial intent,
no different from explaining others.
Examining his words, they are clearly vast and profound;
Yǔ likewise bowed to the wise words,
so why should there be any aversion to this!
【Commentary】Mángmèi (vast and obscure),
is akin to yǎomíng (profound and dim).
It means that Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
are subtle and far-reaching,
vast, obscure, and elusive,
making it hard to distinguish between seeing and hearing,
so if one seeks to grasp them through words and images,
one will never fully comprehend their essence.
【Interpretation】"Wāng Wāng" is pronounced as wū huáng fǎn.
【Collation】(1) In Zhào Jiànyì's edition, "wù" is written as "jì".
(2) In Zhào's edition, "tǎng" is written as "dǎng".
(3) In Zhào's edition, "chóu" is written as "diào".
(4) The character "duān" has been moved upward according to the Shìdétáng edition and the original commentary text.
(5) The character "ér" has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
(6) The character "bài" has been amended according to the Shìdétáng edition.
Huì Shī was a man of many methods,
his writings filled five carts,
but his doctrines were contradictory and inconsistent,
and his words missed the mark.
In examining the principles of things,
he said:
"The largest has nothing beyond it—
this is called the Great One;
the smallest has nothing within it—
this is called the Small One.
What has no thickness
cannot be accumulated,
yet its size extends a thousand li.
Heaven and earth are equally low,
mountains and marshes are equally level.
The sun is just at noon when it is declining,
things are just being born when they are dying.
Great similarities differ from small similarities—
this is called small similarities and differences;
all things are entirely similar and entirely different—
this is called great similarities and differences.
The south has no limit yet has a limit,
today I set off for Yuè and arrived yesterday.
Interlocking rings can be separated.
I know the center of the world
lies north of Yān and south of Yuè.
Love all things universally,
for heaven and earth are one body."
【一】【疏】Discrepancy,
means divergence.
Refutation,
means mixing and blending.
Since there are many methods and techniques,
and books fill five carts,
the principles become exceptionally varied and impure,
and the arguments, though eloquent, lack appropriateness.
【Explanatory Text】"Huì Shī": Shī,
is Master Huì's given name.
"Five Carts": pronounced chǐ shé fǎn,
also pronounced as jū.
"Chuǎn": pronounced chuān yuǎn fǎn,
Xú gives chǐ yǔn fǎn.
"Bó": pronounced bāng jiǎo fǎn.
◎Qìng Fán's note: Sīmǎ's version uses "chuǎn bó".
The commentary in Wénxuǎn, Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wèi" quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
"chuǎn" is read as "chuǎn";
"chuǎn"
means contradictory;
"bó"
refers to a mixture of colors that are not the same.
The explanatory text is missing.
◎Fán also notes that "chuǎn bó"
should be "chuǎn bó".
Also (quoting Sīmǎ's note here) it is written as "chuǎn chí".
In Huáinánzǐ's "Chù Zhēn" chapter, it says "the two alternate and run counter to each other".
In the "Shuō Shān" chapter, it says "flow in separate and opposing directions".
(Yùpiān quotes it as "● chí".
) In the "Fàn Lùn" chapter, it says "what is seen and heard runs counter externally".
In the preface to Fǎyán, it says,
"The various masters each let their knowledge run counter".
This serves as evidence.
("Chuǎn", "chuǎn", "●",
are different characters but share the same meaning.
) "Not fitting": pronounced dīng zhòng fǎn.
【Èr Shū】Their minds roamed among all things,
and through experience, they discerned and debated them.
【Explanatory Text】"Lì" is the ancient character for calendar.
It is also written as "lì".
"The meaning of things" is to differentiate and elaborate on them in detail.
【Three】【Explanations】It encompasses everything without exclusion,
which is called greatness;
it enters into the infinitesimal without gaps,
which is called smallness;
although these differ in name as great and small,
their principle ultimately returns to non-duality,
hence it is said to be one.
【Explanatory Text】"That which is so great that nothing lies beyond it is called the Great One; that which is so small that nothing lies within it is called the Small One." Sīmǎ's commentary states:
Having nothing beyond, it cannot be unified;
having nothing within, it cannot be divided;
hence it is called the One.
What the world calls large and small are not forms;
what it calls one and two are not ultimate names.
The ultimate form is formless;
the ultimate name is nameless.
【Four】【Treatises】The principle is already subtle and refined,
intangible when grasped for,
transcending form and appearance in its wondrousness,
how could there be any thickness to it!
Thus, it cannot be accumulated or piled up.
Not only does it not exist,
but it is also not non-existent;
existence and non-existence give rise to each other,
hence it spans a thousand miles.
【Explanation】"What has no thickness cannot be accumulated, yet it extends a thousand li." Sīmǎ's commentary states:
When speaking of things, having form is considered existence,
what lies beyond form is non-existence.
Formlessness and existence
serve as inner and outer aspects to each other.
Therefore, the thickness of formed things
is fully contained within the absence of thickness.
Absence of thickness and existence
share the same substance.
That which possesses thickness and magnitude
also has absence of thickness that is equally great.
Height is established through breadth,
existence accumulates through non-existence.
Thus, what can be accumulated
depends on what cannot be accumulated.
If it could truly be accumulated,
why would it be limited to merely a thousand li!
【Five】【Commentary】When things are perceived through emotions,
the heavens appear lofty and the earth lowly,
the mountains towering and the marshes low-lying.
But when viewed from the perspective of the Dào,
then mountains and marshes are level and equal,
and heaven and earth are one and the same.
As the Qí Wù states,
nothing is greater than the tip of an autumn hair, and Tàishān is considered small—
this captures its meaning.
【Explanatory Text】"Heaven and Earth are level" is read according to the character's usual pronunciation,
also pronounced as bì.
"Mountains and marshes are level" Lǐ Yí says:
Comparing Earth to Heaven,
then Earth is lower than Heaven;
but considering the height of the cosmos,
both Heaven and Earth are low,
since both Heaven and Earth are low,
then mountains and marshes are level.
【Six】【Explanation】Nì (睨)
means to look sideways.
For those residing in the west, it is called the center;
for those in the east, it is called the side—
thus, there is no fixed center or side.
It is like life and death:
the living consider death as death,
while the dead consider life as death.
Just as the sun's position (center or side) is not fundamentally different,
so too are things in life and death not distinct.
【Explanation】"The sun is at its zenith and simultaneously declining" — "nì" is pronounced yì.
"Things are being born and simultaneously dying" — Lǐ Yí says:
"nì" means
to look sideways.
It refers to the sun being at its zenith while its shadow has already shifted to the west,
to the shadow having just shifted west while the light has already vanished,
to the light having just vanished while brightness has already risen again.
All zenith and decline,
like a pivot turning in cycles,
mutually become each other's front and back,
with no distinction between beginning and end,
so how different are existence and extinction, life and death from this!
【Seven】【Dissimilarities】The conditions of things are differentiated,
and their appearances have similarities and differences,
which are the minor similarities and differences.
【Eight】【Explanations】Life and death alternate in succession,
cold and heat take turns in changing,
forms and natures are different,
yet the principles of their substance are without difference,
this is the great similarity and difference.

【Explanation】"When there is similarity with minor differences, this is called minor similarity and difference; when all things are entirely similar or entirely different, this is called major similarity and difference." When entities share the same substance but differ in aspects,
this is termed minor similarity and difference.
Life and death, fortune and misfortune,
cold and heat, day and night,
movement and stillness, transformation and change—
though all are debated, none are identical,
representing the utmost in difference.
Yet all differences converge in a single entity,
representing the utmost in similarity.
Thus, the similarity and difference among all things are unified.
Take hardness and whiteness, for example:
they are never inseparable,
nor are they ever completely apart.
Just as fire contains yīn,
and water contains yáng,
the yīn within fire differs from that in water,
and the yáng within water differs from that in fire.
Consequently, water differs from water itself,
and fire differs from fire itself.
The utmost difference distinguishes what is similar,
and the utmost similarity unifies what is different.
Hence, it is called major similarity and difference.
【Nine】【Dispersions】Knowing the four directions are boundless,
yet there will be things.
Forms do not exhaust forms,
colors do not exhaust colors,
forms and colors exhaust each other;
knowledge does not exhaust knowledge,
things do not exhaust things,
exhaustion and things exhaust each other;
only because it is without thickness,
thus it cannot accumulate.
Speaking solely of the southern direction,
raising one corner,
the other three can be known.
【Explanation Text】"The South is boundless yet bounded" Simǎ comments:
The four directions are boundless.
Lǐ notes:
Since the four directions are boundless,
therefore there are no fixed directions.
Neither above nor below can be considered their limit,
yet they ultimately have boundaries.
Another interpretation states:
Understanding the boundlessness of the four directions
thereby eliminates the concepts of boundlessness and boundedness.
Forms do not exhaust forms,
colors do not exhaust colors,
forms and colors mutually complete each other;
knowledge does not exhaust knowledge,
things do not exhaust things,
knowledge and things mutually complete each other.
Mentioning only the South
serves as an example of one corner.
【一０】【Commentary】If we observe the past from the present,
it is because of the present that the past exists;
if we observe the present from the past,
it is because of the past that the present exists.
Yet if the present were not itself the present,
how could there be a past?
If the past were not itself the past,
how could there be a present?
Since there is neither past nor present,
thus it can be said: "Arriving in Yuè today, one came yesterday."
【Interpretation】"Today I set out for Yuè, yet arrived yesterday." When wisdom adapts to things,
and things adapt to wisdom,
form has its limits,
wisdom has its course of action,
wisdom has its steadfast principles,
form has what it follows,
thus form and wisdom come and go,
mutually serving as inns for each other.
A mirror reflects an image, yet the mirror itself also has an image;
when two mirrors reflect each other,
then layered images become endless.
All things enter into one wisdom, and wisdom becomes seamless;
all things merge into one substance, and substance becomes without gaps.
If heaven is within the heart, then the body is beyond heaven;
if the heart is within heaven, then heaven is beyond the heart.
Those who long for their kin from afar are going;
those who think of their kin when ill are coming.
Wisdom in things becomes the things;
things in wisdom become wisdom.
Sīmǎ comments:
That day is like this day,
then seeing this is like seeing that.
If that is seen as this,
then people of Wú and Yuè see each other interchangeably.
◎Lú Wéncháo states:
In current texts,  is written as 眹.
Note that  is the same as 瞬 (blink),
while 眹 means the essence of the eye,
neither meaning fits.
It seems it should be 朕 as in 朕兆 (omen).
【一一】【Commentary】The mutual linking of rings occurs
through their hollow centers,
not through the rings themselves.
Thus, two rings linked through emptiness
do not interfere with each other,
each rotating freely,
hence they can be separated.
【Explanatory Text】"The Interlocking Rings Can Be Untangled" Simǎ comments:
All things are exhausted by their forms,
beyond the exhaustion of forms,
there are no things.
What the interlocking rings penetrate,
penetrates the ringless,
not the rings themselves.
If two rings do not interpenetrate,
then even if they are interlocking rings,
they can indeed be untangled.
【一二】【Commentary】The two states of Yān and Yuè,
being far apart from each other,
have customs that are firmly entrenched,
each esteeming its own region.
Thus, Yān in the north and Yuè in the south
can each be considered the center of the world.
【Explanation】"I know the center of heaven is north of Yān and south of Yuè." Sīmǎ comments:
The distance between Yān and Yuè is finite,
yet the expanse of north and south is boundless.
Viewing the finite from the perspective of the boundless,
then between Yān and Yuè, there has never been a distinction.
The world has no fixed direction,
thus wherever one is becomes the center;
it cycles without end,
so wherever one is becomes the beginning.
【13】【Commentary】All things are one with me,
hence I love them universally;
the two primal forces and I are born together,
hence we share the same substance.
【Transcription】"Fàn" is pronounced fāng jiǎn fǎn.
"Loving all things, Heaven and Earth are one body." Lǐ Yǐ says:
The sun and moon can be seen, yet the eye itself cannot see itself;
love emanates from the self, but what is loved lies in external things.
Consider Heaven and Earth as the head and feet,
and all things as the five organs.
Thus, the distinction between the liver and gallbladder
unites within a single person;
the distinctions within a single person
unite into one body.
【Collation Notes】(1) The Kōzan-ji edition does not have the character "也".
(2) In the Zhào Jiànyì edition, "厤" is written as "歷".
(3) The Shìdétáng edition does not have the character "下".
Huì Shī took these as grand principles,
surveyed the world and enlightened the debaters【一】,
and the debaters of the world delighted in them together【二】.
An egg has hair【三】,
a chicken has three legs【四】,
Yǐng contains the whole world【五】,
a dog can be considered a sheep【六】,
a horse has eggs【七】,
a tadpole has a tail【八】,
fire is not hot【九】,
mountains emerge from the mouth【一０】,
a wheel does not tread on the ground【一一】,
the eye does not see【一二】,
a point cannot be reached,
and if reached, it is not exhaustive【一三】,
a tortoise is longer than a snake【一四】,
a square cannot be truly square,
a compass cannot make a perfect circle【一五】,
a mortise does not enclose a tenon【一六】,
the shadow of a flying bird never moves【一七】,
a swift arrow has moments when it neither moves nor stops【一八】,
a puppy is not a dog【一九】,
a yellow horse and a black ox make three【二０】,
a white dog is black【二一】,
an orphaned colt never had a mother,
a one-foot long staff (1),
taking half of it each day,
will never be exhausted in ten thousand generations【二二】.
The debaters used these propositions to respond to Huì Shī,
engaging in endless discourse throughout their lives.
【一】【疏】Huì Shī employed this principle,
considering himself the foremost,
observed the world,
to enlighten and debate with others.
【Transcription】"For the Great Observation" is read in ancient pronunciation as "luàn".
"Throughout the World" refers to what is called considering oneself the foremost.
"Enlightened in Debate" the Zìlín states:
"Biàn",
means wisdom.
【Èr Shū】Since their passions and preferences were aligned,
and their temperaments resonated with each other,
thus the eloquent scholars within the region delighted in learning from them.
【Interpretation】"Lè" is pronounced as "luò".
【Three】【Treatises】Existence and non-existence are but two names,
both returning to emptiness and tranquility.
Mundane attachments cling to appearances,
claiming an egg has no feathers.
Since names are inherently empty,
saying it has feathers is also acceptable.
【Explanation】"Eggs Have Feathers" Sīmǎ comments:
The birth of embryos and eggs,
must involve fur or feathers.
When a chicken incubates a swan's egg,
the egg does not become a chicken,
thus the born creature resembles the swan.
The energy of fur forms fur,
the energy of feathers forms feathers,
although the embryo or egg is not yet born,
the nature of fur or feathers is already evident.
Therefore, hawk-like shoulders and wasp-like eyes,
are manifestations of inherent influences,
dragon-like forehead and tiger-like beak,
are signs of majestic and spiritual energy.
The spirit guides clarity,
energy forms substance,
the aspects subdued by substance are like windows,
the distinction between light and dark is as day and night.
By nature, they are close,
through habit, they drift apart,
thus the clarity and distance in nature,
are influenced by habits in life.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
"Yuǎn" (far),
was previously written as "dǎi",
now it is written as "yuǎn",
follow this.
◎Qìng Fān's case: In Xúnzǐ's "Not Being Improper" chapter, Yáng's annotation quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
The birth of embryos and eggs,
must involve fur or feathers.
When a chicken incubates a swan's egg,
the egg does not become a chicken,
thus the born creature resembles the swan.
The energy of fur forms fur,
the energy of feathers forms feathers,
although the embryo or egg is not yet born,
the nature of fur or feathers is already evident,
hence it is said that eggs have feathers.
This is more concise than the explanation in the commentary.
【Four】【Sparse】The origin of numbers arises from emptiness, following non-being,
from non-being proceeding to being,
whereupon the three names are established.
Thus, knowing two and three
ultimately lacks substantial form,
hence a chicken's two feet can be called three.
Since this is so for chicken feet,
it is evident in all things.
【Explanation】"A chicken has three legs." Sīmǎ's commentary states:
A chicken has two legs,
which are used for walking but are not the source of movement itself.
Thus, walking is initiated by the legs,
but movement is governed by the spirit.
Now although a chicken has two legs,
it requires the spirit to move,
hence it is said to have three legs.
【Five】【Memorial】Yǐng,
the capital of Chǔ,
is located seventy lǐ north of Jiānglíng.
All places where things reside,
have their four directions,
hence Yān in the north and Yuè in the south,
can be considered the center of heaven,
thus Chǔ established its capital at Yǐng,
with a territory spanning a thousand lǐ,
why should it hinder being the center of the world!
【Explanation】"Yǐng Possesses the World" Yǐng,
the capital of Chǔ,
is located seventy lǐ north of Jiānglíng.
Lǐ Yún states:
Within the Nine Provinces,
it is not even one ten-thousandth part of the cosmos.
Therefore, when referring to the entire world,
it serves as a metaphor to show that what is considered complete and called great is not truly great.
If each points to what they have and speaks of its insufficiency,
even though Yǐng is only a thousand lǐ square,
it could still be said to possess the world.
【Six】【Argument】Names do not possess the power to secure objects,
and objects lack the reality that corresponds to names.
When names and realities are not fixed,
one could call a dog a sheep.
The people of Zhèng referred to uncarved jade as "pú,"
while the people of Zhōu called an unsalted rat also "pú."
Thus, the form resides in the object,
but the name depends on the person.
【Explanation】"A dog can be considered a sheep" Simǎ comments:
Names are used to designate things,
but are not the things themselves.
The names "dog" and "sheep",
are not the actual dog or sheep.
If what is not a sheep can be named "sheep",
then a dog can also be named "sheep".
The Zhèng people call uncut jade "pú",
while the Zhōu people call undried rats also "pú".
Hence, form resides in the object,
while naming resides with people.
【Seven】【Arguments】All beings born from womb, egg, moisture, or transformation,
are distinguished by human emotions,
but when viewed from the perspective of the Dào,
they are fundamentally no different.
If a bird's egg can be said to have feathers,
why should a beast's womb-born fetus not be named an egg!
【Explanation】"Horses Have Eggs" Lǐ Yí says:
What physical forms rely on,
what names are ascribed to,
are all provisional,
not real.
Hence dogs and sheep have no fixed names,
womb-birth and egg-laying have no fixed forms,
so birds can have womb-birth,
and horses can have eggs.
Another explanation says:
Minor differences share major similarities,
between dogs/sheep and womb-birth/egg-laying,
there is no distinction for birds and horses.
【Eight】【Commentary】The people of Chǔ call the frog "dīng zǐ".
Now, it is universally known that frogs have no tails,
a fact understood by all under heaven.
This pertains to the nature of things,
not to the ultimate truth.
From the perspective of the Dào,
the absence of form does not equate to nothingness.
If what is not nothing can still be called nothing,
then why should what is not existent
not be named a tail?
【Explanation】"Dīngzǐ Has a Tail" Lǐ Yí said:
All things have no fixed form,
and forms have no fixed designation.
What is above is called the head,
what is below is called the tail.
People commonly say that a right-curving stroke is a tail,
but now the two characters for "dīngzǐ,"
although having left-curving strokes,
are also considered tails.
【九】【疏】Fire is hot and water is cold,
arising from the nature of things,
but when viewed according to principle,
they are neither cold nor hot.
Why is that?
In the south, there are beasts that consume fire,
while sages can enter water without getting wet.
From this perspective,
it is certainly not a matter of cold or heat.
Another example: when a stick strikes the body, pain arises in the person;
the person feels pain, but the stick does not.
Similarly, when fire touches the body, heat is felt by the person;
the person feels the heat, but the fire itself is not hot.
【Explanation】"Fire is not hot" Simǎ comments:
Wood is born from water,
fire is born from wood,
wood is moistened by water,
fire is illuminated by wood.
Metal is colder than water but hotter than fire,
yet cold and heat intermix endlessly,
while the natures of water and fire have limits.
To say fire is hot and water is cold
is a one-sided assertion,
and if one-sided, then claiming water is hot and fire is cold would also be permissible.
Another explanation says:
Just as metal and wood can cause pain when applied to a person,
the pain originates from the person,
but metal and wood themselves are not the pain.
Like birds that dwell in fire,
or insects born in fire,
then fire is not hot to them.
◎Lú Wénchāo states:
The old text had "dwell in water" instead of "dwell in fire",
which is an error,
now corrected.
【一０】【Commentary】The mountain originally had no name;
the mountain's name comes from people's mouths.
If it is so with the mountain,
then all phenomena are likewise.
【Interpretation】"The Mountain Has a Mouth" Simǎ comments:
Form, sound, breath, and color
combine to create things.
Musical pitches use sound to incorporate form,
dark and yellow use color to embody substance.
When a call is made to one mountain,
the entire mountain responds,
the sound of the mountain enters the ear,
form and sound proceed together,
this is how the mountain can be said to have a mouth.
【一一】【Commentary】The movement of a cart,
with wheels turning ceaselessly,
the previous tracks have already passed,
the path ahead has not yet been reached,
excluding both front and rear,
there is no moment when it truly treads on the ground.
Thus, although the wheels are in motion,
ultimately, they do not tread upon the earth.
It is as stated in the Zhào Lùn:
"The whirlwind topples mountains yet is ever still,
rivers compete in their flow yet do not move,
the wild horses drift and stir yet remain unmoved,
the sun and moon traverse the heavens yet do not revolve."
So what is there to marvel at?
So what is there to marvel at?
【Explanation】"The wheel does not crush the ground" is also written as "tread upon" in another version,
pronounced as niǎn.
Regarding "the ground," Sīmǎ explains:
If the ground is level and the wheel is round,
then what the wheel travels over leaves a trace.
【一二】【Explanation】The eye's perception of objects,
must rely on conditions.
Since these conditions are inherently empty,
it is thus understood that the eye cannot truly see them.
【Interpretation】"The Eye Does Not See" Simǎ comments:
When looking at fish in water,
one must first see the water;
when observing objects in light,
one must first see the light.
The moist scales of the fish are not the exposed scales,
different from exposed scales,
thus one sees the moistness.
The way light illuminates form differs from when it does not illuminate,
then one sees the illuminated form,
not the form itself.
The eye not seeing at night is not due to darkness,
seeing during the day is not due to brightness,
but depends on conditions,
that which enables sight is illumination.
If the eye does not rely on light to become clear,
it has no means to see the light,
therefore, the eye regarding objects,
has never truly seen them.
【一三】【Commentary】Using a finger to point at an object is not the object itself,
thus the pointing does not reach the actual thing.
Yet by pointing to oneself, one grasps the essence,
so the reaching never ceases.
【Explanatory Text】"The Finger Does Not Reach, Yet the Reaching Is Unceasing" Simǎ comments:
When the finger takes an object,
it cannot reach by itself,
it must borrow an object to reach it,
yet borrowing an object stems from the finger's unceasing action.
Another explanation:
The finger uses tongs to take fire,
an awl to stab a rat,
thus it relies on objects,
so the finger itself does not reach.
【一四】【Comment】When long and short are compared,
there is neither long nor short.
To say that snakes are long and turtles are short
is merely a rigid perception of things.
Now, to dispel such confusion,
it is therefore said that turtles are longer than snakes.
【Explanation】"The tortoise is longer than the snake" Simǎ comments:
The snake's form, though long, has a short lifespan;
the tortoise's form, though short, has a very long life.
◎ Yú Yuè remarks:
This conveys the same idea as "nothing is larger than the tip of an autumn hair, yet Mount Tài is small."
Simǎ states:
The snake's form, though long, has a short lifespan;
the tortoise's form, though short, has a very long life,
thus it speaks not of physical form but of longevity,
truly making the tortoise long and the snake short,
which entirely misses the original meaning.
【一五】【Comment】The standards for roundness and squareness,
have existed for a long time.
Yet their names and definitions are not fixed,
and the essence of square and round is not substantiated,
thus it cannot be accepted.
【Explanation】"The square cannot be square, nor the compass round." Sīmǎ's commentary states:
The square, though it makes squares, is not itself square;
the compass, though it makes circles, is not itself round;
just as the marking line, though it defines straightness, is not itself straight.
【一六】【疏】A zuò is a hole.
A ruì is the wood that fits inside the hole.
However, when the ruì enters the zuò,
the wood passes through the empty space without engaging,
so it cannot be enclosed.
This is similar to the meaning of how interlinked rings can be separated.
【Explanation】"Záo" is pronounced as Cáo bào fǎn.
"Bù wéi ruì" is pronounced as rú ruì fǎn.
Sīmǎ says:
The chisel and the tenon are of different natures,
yet they join to form one shape.
If the chisel accumulates against the tenon,
then the chisel and the tenon have different circumferences,
and the mirror and the tenon have different circumferences,
meaning they do not encircle each other.
【One Seven】【Commentary】The past has already vanished,
the future has not yet arrived,
beyond past and future,
there is no time in flight,
only the bird and its shadow,
stand still and unmoving.
Thus it is known that the world in its essence is entirely tranquil,
hence the Treatise by [Zhào] states,
yet the four phenomena gallop like the wind,
the celestial pivot rolls like lightning,
grasping the subtlety of their intent,
though they shift, they do not turn.
This is what is called the non-migration of things.
【Interpretation】"The shadow of a flying bird" is pronounced as yǐng (shadow).
"It has never moved" Simǎ comments:
The bird blocks the light,
just as the fish blocks the water.
When the fish moves and blocks the water, the water does not move;
when the bird moves, the shadow appears,
and as the shadow appears, the light disappears.
Disappearance does not mean it has gone away,
appearance does not mean it has come.
Mòzǐ said,
"The shadow does not move."
【一八】【Commentary】The arrowhead,
is the tip of an arrow.
Although the mechanism's release is swift,
it does not depart from the three times;
no different from a wheel's motion,
how unlike a bird's shadow.
[The wheel] neither crushes nor moves,
so how could the arrowhead have stopping or moving!
It is also like a sharp knife cutting three strands of silk—
among them, there are also those of the past, future, and present.
【Translated Text】"Zú" is read as Zǐmù's pronunciation,
Guō pronounces it as zú,
Xú gives Zhū Jué's pronunciation.
The Three Cang dictionaries state:
It is the arrowhead.
◎Qìng Fān's case: zú,
Guō pronounces it as zú,
which is incorrect.
Zú is a miswriting of the character ●.
Hóu,
in clerical script is written as ,
the character shapes are similar,
hence the character for hóu arrow,
