is often mistaken as zú.
(Also often mistaken as zhuī.
The character zhuī in clerical script is written as ●,
also mistaken due to similar shape.
Seen in Huainanzi's "Military Strategies" chapter: swift as zhuī arrows.
The Strategies of Qí also mistakenly writes it as zhuī arrows.
Gāo's annotation considers zhuī arrows as small arrows,
which is incorrect.
) The Erya says: metal-tipped with trimmed feathers is called ●.
The Shuowen agrees.
The Fangyan says:
Jiàn,
in the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers is called hóu.
The Greater Odes: "Four hóu are evenly balanced,"
the Zhou Official's "Archery Arrows" mentions shā arrows and hóu arrows,
the Artificers' Record "Arrow Maker" says:
hóu arrows, three parts.
(The character hóu is also written as hóu.
The "Rites of Mourning" says:
one chariot of hóu arrows.
) Therefore, it is known that zú is a miswriting of hóu.
(In the Heguanzi's "Worldly Soldiers" chapter: released like zú arrows.
Zú might originally be written as ●,
and it should also be correct to follow hóu.
) "An arrow's speed has moments when it neither moves nor stops" Sīmǎ explains:
Form determines stopping,
momentum determines movement;
when form is distinct, movement is slow,
when momentum is distinct, movement is swift.
The eye sees no form,
division has no stopping point,
then its speed is seamless.
An arrow's speed having gaps
is due to pauses within,
its substance thin and separable,
containing elements that cannot be reached.
【一九】【Commentary】Gǒu and quǎn,
are two names for one thing.
Since names are empty,
therefore gǒu is not quǎn.
Gǒu and quǎn share the same reality but have different names;
when name and reality correspond,
then what is called gǒu over there,
is called quǎn here;
when name and reality separate,
then what is called gǒu over there,
differs from quǎn.
Mòzǐ said:
Gǒu,
is quǎn,
yet gǒu is not quǎn.
【Explanation】"A Dog Is Not a Hound" Simǎ comments:
Dogs and hounds are the same in substance but differ in name.
When name and substance correspond,
then what is called a dog there,
is called a hound here;
when name and substance diverge,
then what is called a dog there,
differs from a hound.
【二０】【Commentary】Form is not color,
color is not form.
Thus, one horse and one ox,
taken as two entities,
adding the color of the horse can make three.
Call it a yellow horse,
call it a black ox,
call it yellow and black,
the forms become three.
This is similar to one and the word making two,
two and one making three.
【Textual Explanation】"Huáng mǎ lí" is read with the initial "lì" and the final "zhì" in the fanqie method,
also pronounced as "lí".
"Three of oxen" Simǎ comments:
Oxen and horses make two into three.
Speaking of oxen,
speaking of horses,
speaking of oxen and horses,
these are three in terms of form.
Speaking of yellow,
speaking of black,
speaking of yellow and black,
these are three in terms of color.
Speaking of a yellow horse,
speaking of a black ox,
speaking of a yellow horse and a black ox,
these are three in terms of both form and color.
Hence it is said that one with speech makes two,
and two with one makes three.
◎Qìng Fān's case: The annotation in Liú Xiàobiāo's "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn" from the Wénxuǎn quotes Simǎ as saying:
Oxen and horses make two into three,
combining and differentiating.
Speaking of horses,
speaking of oxen,
these are three in terms of form.
Speaking of yellow,
speaking of black,
these are three in terms of color.
Speaking of a yellow horse,
speaking of a black ox,
these are three in terms of both form and color.
This slightly differs from the textual explanation.
【二一】【Comment】Names and designations are unreal,
forms and colors are all empty;
to reverse clinging attachments,
thus, white is called black.
【Explanation】"A White Dog Is Black" Simǎ comments:
If a dog's eye is blind,
it is called a blind dog;
if a dog's eye is large,
it is not called a large dog;
this is a case of one being right and the other wrong.
Then, a white dog with black eyes
could also be considered a black dog.
【二二】【Commentary】"Chuí" means
a rod.
"Qǔ" means
to break.
The question asks:
A one-foot rod,
if broken in half this morning,
by the evening,
five inches remain.
Between two days,
the rod should be exhausted.
This matter is evident—
is this not the meaning of depletion?
The reply states:
Names correspond to substance,
substance corresponds to names.
Thus, using the name to seek the object,
the object cannot be concealed.
Therefore, holding the name to demand the reality—
if it is named a foot-long rod,
and each time a foot is taken from it,
how could there be an end?
If it is broken at five inches,
that violates the principle of the name.
Then it would be called a half-foot rod—
how could that mean a one-foot rod?
【Explanation Text】"An orphaned foal never had a mother." Lǐ Yí states:
A foal is born with a mother,
but calling it orphaned means it has no mother.
Once the term 'orphaned' is established, the mother's designation is removed.
The mother once was the foal's mother,
hence an orphaned foal never had a mother.
Some versions do not include this sentence.
"One foot" – one version omits the character 'one'.
"Of the staff" – pronounced with the zhāngfǎn.
"Taking half of it every day, it will never be exhausted in ten thousand generations." Sīmǎ explains:
The staff,
is a cane.
If it can be divided,
then there are always two parts;
if it cannot be divided,
the one part always remains.
Therefore, it is said to never be exhausted in ten thousand generations.
【Collation】(1) The Shìdétáng edition has "棰" instead of "捶".
Huán Tuán and Gōngsūn Lóng were among the debaters,
who adorned people's minds,
and altered their opinions.
They could overwhelm others in speech,
but could not convince their hearts—
such is the limitation of debaters.
Huì Shī daily used his knowledge to engage in debates with others,
deliberately creating oddities with the debaters of the world;
this was the essence of his approach.
One was named Huán,
called Tuán;
another was named Gōngsūn,
called Lóng;
both were from Zhào,
and were skilled debaters,
who traveled as guests in the household of Lord Píngyuán.
Gōngsūn Lóng authored the "Essay on Defending Whiteness,"
which circulated in the world.
Using arguments like "a foot is not a length" and "a rod is not long,"
they responded to each other in harmony,
thus passing their years in this manner,
without ever reaching an end.
【Explanatory Text】"Huán Tuán" Lǐ Yún said:
A person's name.
Xú reads it as tú wán.
【二】【疏】With such profound arguments,
they adorned people's minds,
employing these elegant words,
to transform people's thoughts.
【Three】【Arguments】When arguments surpass the substance of things,
they can thus overcome people's words;
when speech does not align with reason,
it thus fails to convince people's hearts.
Yet followers of argumentation
use this as their domain.
Another explanation:
domain,
means a bounded area.
Huì Shī's words,
not deeply grasping the principles,
the scope of what they explain,
does not extend beyond this.
【Explanation】"The Royal Park" is pronounced as yòu.
【四】【疏】"Tè" means
"alone/solitary",
and the character is sometimes written as "jiāng".
"Guài" means
"strange/different".
"Dǐ" means
"substance/essence".
Huìzǐ daily employed the knowledge of distinctions,
engaging in debates with others,
uniquely considering himself as fundamentally different from Heaven and Earth.
Although his arguments were endlessly cunning and varied,
their fundamental substance never went beyond this.
◎ Yú Yuè comments:
"The debates with others" -
this meaning is not coherent,
probably the character "zhī" is a redundant duplication from the following phrase "the debaters of the world".
"Dǐ" is interchangeable with "dǐ".
The Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Qín Shǐhuáng states: "Dà dǐ jìn pàn Qín lì",
the Correct Meaning commentary says:
"Dǐ"
means "roughly/approximately".
"This is its dǐ"
means "this is the gist/outline of it".
The examples above - "eggs have feathers",
"chickens have three legs" and what follows - all illustrate this.
【Explanation】"其柢" is pronounced as dīng jì fǎn.
【Collation Note】(1) Zhī Wěichéng's version originally lacked the character 'zhī',
aligning with Yú's interpretation.
Yet Huì Shī, in his oral discourses,
considered himself the most worthy,
declaring, "How magnificent are Heaven and Earth!"
Huì Shī preserved his vigor but lacked method.
In the south, there was an eccentric named Huáng Liǎo,
who asked why Heaven and Earth do not fall or collapse,
and the causes of wind, rain, thunder, and lightning.
Huì Shī responded without declining,
answered without deliberation,
expounded on all things universally,
spoke without cease,
prolifically and endlessly,
yet still thought it insufficient,
adding strangeness to it.
He took contradicting others as substance and sought fame through overcoming them,
thus he was incompatible with the multitude.
Weak in virtue,
strong in material pursuits,
his path was obscure and tortuous.
Viewing Huì Shī's abilities through the way of Heaven and Earth,
they are like the toil of a single mosquito or fly.
What use are they to the world of things!
To fulfill one principle might still be acceptable,
but to claim to honor the Dào more highly,
that is nearly it!
Huì Shī could not find peace in this,
scattered among the myriad things without tiring,
and ultimately gained a reputation for skilled debate.
Alas!
Huì Shī's talent,
vast and unrestrained yet unattainable,
chasing after the myriad things without return,
this is like trying to exhaust an echo with sound,
or a form racing with its shadow.
How lamentable!
【一】【疏】Thus,
it is still like this.
It is said that Huì Shī explained principles,
second only to Zhuāng Shēng,
and moreover, his eloquence was the most outstanding among the multitude,
how could he be like the others, merely engaging in straightforward debate!
【Two】【Arrogance】 is "zhuàng",
meaning "great".
"Shù",
refers to the "Way".
It says that heaven and earth are born together with me,
which is not enough to be called great.
The intent lies in being heroic and outstanding,
transcending the world and surpassing others.
Since it is neither humble nor gentle,
it therefore lacks the true Way.
And speaking of its "zhuàng",
it is like being uniquely strong.
【Explanation】"Heaven and Earth are so magnificent!" Simǎ comments:
Huì Shī considered only Heaven and Earth to be mightier than himself.
"Shī preserved his prowess but lacked method." Simǎ comments:
His intention was to surpass others,
yet he possessed no art of principle.
【Three】【Memorials】dwelled in the southern regions,
surnamed Huáng,
named Liáo,
who did not conform to the mundane,
stood apart from ordinary people,
roamed beyond the confines of the world,
was a man of wisdom and virtue.
Having heard of Huì Shī's intelligence and eloquence,
he came to pose questions,
inquiring about the enduring nature of the two realms (heaven and earth),
the winds, rains, thunder, and lightning,
the origins of movement and stillness,
and from what beginnings they arise.
【Interpretation】"倚人" may also be written as 畸,
with the same meaning.
Pronounced as jǐ yí fǎn.
Lǐ Yí states:
It means different/extraordinary.
◎Qìng Fān notes: 倚 should be 奇,
倚人,
refers to an extraordinary person.
Wáng Yì's commentary on the Nine Declarations says:
Different.
Since 倚 shares the phonetic component with 奇,
thus in ancient script, 倚 and 奇 were interchangeable.
In the "Explaining the Trigrams" chapter of the Book of Changes, "参天两地而倚数,"
the Shǔ Cái version writes 倚 as 奇.
In the Spring Offices, the Grand Invocator's "奇●,"
Dù Zǐchūn said:
奇 should be read as 倚.
In the Gǔliáng Commentary's 33rd year of Duke Xī, "a single horse and a leaning wheel, none returned,"
the explanatory text:
倚,
pronounced jū yí fǎn.
That is, an extraordinary wheel.
The character may also be written as 畸.
In Xúnzǐ's "Discourse on Heaven," "Mòzǐ saw the uniform,
but not the irregular,"
Yáng's annotation:
畸,
means not uniform.
Not uniform conveys the meaning of difference/extraordinariness.
(In the "Great and Venerable Teacher" chapter, "dare to ask about the 畸人,"
Lǐ Yí said:
畸,
means extraordinary and different.
) "Huáng Liǎo" is pronounced liǎo,
Lǐ gives the pronunciation ér xiǎo fǎn,
stating:
a virtuous person.
"不墜" is pronounced zhí lèi fǎn.
"霆" is pronounced tíng,
also pronounced tǐng.
【Four】【Eloquence】With a heroic and outstanding spirit,
eloquent in speech and debate,
thus responding to opportunities without bidding farewell or declining,
answering without the need for contemplation.
【Five】【Expositions】extensively expound the origins of all things,
and debate the reasons for the two principles and thunderclaps,
never ceasing,
still finding simplicity inadequate,
thus adding marvels to display their prowess.
【Explanatory Text】"Bian wei" is pronounced as "bian",
below, the reverse is "yu wei".
【Six】【Negations】Taking opposition to human emotions as the true path,
always seeking to surpass all beings,
harboring the ambition to stand out from the crowd,
with intentions fixed on fame and reputation,
thus one cannot harmonize and adapt to the world.
【七】【疏】Coating,
is the Way.
Its virtue and methods are very weak,
yet its transformative power is extremely strong,
claiming that its principles are exceptionally profound and abstruse.
【Explanation】"隩" is pronounced as wū bào fǎn.
Lǐ Yún:
It means profound,
referring to the depth of the Way.
【Eight】【Explanation】Yóu,
means to follow.
Yōng,
means to use.
Following the way of creation by the two principles,
observing Huì Shī's ability to transform things,
it is no different from a gadfly flying in the air,
flapping its wings and making a clamor,
merely tiring itself out,
how can it be worth mentioning!
Such discourses on things,
thus become useless.
【Transcription】"Yī wén" pronounced as wén.
"Yī méng" pronounced as Mèng Gēng fǎn.
means near.
As for Huì Shī's arguments,
they elucidate principles without grandeur,
among the myriad things,
they can merely fill one count.
Yet to keenly aspire to value the Way,
and adorn intentions to approach truth,
to assess and discuss it,
is truly not acceptable.
【Explanation】"Yù Guì": Yáng Zhǔ's rebuttal.
Lǐ Yún said:
He himself believed that what he admired became increasingly noble and closer to the Way.
【一０】【Comment】"Zu"
means "end."
Unable to use this profound Way to attain self-tranquility,
instead, they scatter their spirit and mind,
engaging in lofty discussions about all things,
ultimately failing to embody the Way in what they see and encounter,
and end up merely with the reputation of being skilled debaters.
【一一】【Note】In the past, before I had read Zhuāngzǐ,
I often heard debaters contending over the meaning of the "foot-long whip" and "interlocking rings" arguments,
and all claimed these were Zhuāngzǐ's words,
thus regarding Zhuāngzǐ as one of the sophists.
Examining this chapter's evaluation of various masters,
reaching this section,
it states that their ways are contradictory and flawed,
their words miss the mark,
thus realizing how hearsay damages truth.
I also believe they lack the substance for governing a state,
truly what is called useless talk.
However, for the sons of the wealthy,
equally indulging in leisurely amusement,
some may tire of classical texts,
yet can debate names and analyze principles,
to express their vitality,
to anchor their thoughts,
flowing down to later generations,
preventing their nature from becoming depraved,
is this not still better than gambling and board games?
Therefore, I preserve it without further discussion,
leaving it for the curious.
【Explanation】Dài means
unrestrained.
It deeply laments that Huì Shī had talent but lacked the Way,
indulging in unrestrained rhetoric and debate,
failing to grasp the true origin,
chasing after the superficial aspects of all things,
unable to return to the wondrous foundation.
Now, attaining principle is best achieved by forgetting knowledge,
and returning to the foundation is most effectively done by ceasing debate.
Yet Huì Zǐ exhausted his mental faculties in pursuit of the Way,
unleashing a torrent of words to seek truth—
how is this any different from trying to escape an echo by raising one's voice,
or attempting to avoid one's shadow by running swiftly?
With such great talent,
it is profoundly sorrowful indeed.
【Explanatory Text】"Dài" is pronounced by Lǐ as dǎi.
"Dàng dài" means,
to let loose,
being unrestrained and unattainable.
◎Qìng Fān's commentary:
The annotation in Wénxuǎn, Xiè Xuánhuī's poem "Directly in the Secretariat Province," quotes Sīmǎ as saying:
dàidàng,
is like being scattered and free.
The explanatory text is missing.
"Bēi fū" is pronounced as fú.
"Lùn zhě" is pronounced as lì kùn fǎn.
"Jiào" is pronounced as jiǎo.
"Píng" is pronounced as bìng.
"Bù zhōng" is pronounced as dīng zhòng fǎn.
"Huò juàn" is also written as  in some versions,
with the same meaning.
"Qí sī" is pronounced as xī sì fǎn.
Bùxié: pronounced similarly to "jiē" with a reverse tone.
《Hǎoshì》: pronounced "hūbào" with a reverse tone.
Zǐ Xuán's annotations,
when discussing their overall essence,
truly capture the essence of Zhuāngzǐ's philosophy.
Guō Shēng earlier lamented the superficial talk of the privileged,
and I too have lately witnessed the baseless discussions of the noble wanderers.
This is what is called different eras sharing the same trends,
how can it be spoken of again!
Some say:
Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ established their bond at the Háoliáng bridge,
setting a model like the Yǐng craftsman,
yet it is said his writings filled five carts,
but his words missed the mark—
why is that?
Could it be that their bond, like the Yǐng craftsman,
was praised as sharing the same axe,
yet they criticized each other so severely?
The reply is:
To fully express the breadth of teachings without losing intent,
and to spiritualize their words,
how could one not refine their language and exhaust their metaphors!
Zhuāngzǐ propagated profound teachings in his seven chapters,
presenting this literature to later [two] generations,
using weighty words to traverse the path of mystery,
engaging in affairs to unfold [three] the sequence of eloquent discourse.
Though his discussions did not prize argumentation,
his teachings were never empty proclamations.
However, his text is easy to read,
but its essence is hard to grasp;
those who ponder it without understanding
risk missing its principles.
To eliminate this flaw,
he extensively cited Huìzǐ's debates.
◎Lú Wénchāo said:
Regarding the two characters "bùshī,"
they are suspected to be redundant.
"Shén,"
in the Sòng edition, is written as "shēn."
Also, "presenting this literature to later generations" below,
the character "later" was missing in the old version,
now added.
Also, "engaging in affairs to unfold the sequence of eloquent discourse,"
in the current text, "unfold" is written as "zhǎn."
【Collation Notes】(1) The character is supplemented based on the following sentence.
(2) The Shidetang edition does not have the character "hòu" at the end.
(3) In the Shidetang edition, "fā" is written as "zhǎn".
